# The Wheel of Nemesis

Felix walked me to the shrine the morning before the games, as he always did, his iron-shod sandals striking the paving stones a half-step behind mine. He was a freedman, a former retiarius with three fingers on his left hand, and the lanista trusted him to bring me back. I suppose I trusted him too. Neither of us said so.

The city was already awake when we left the Ludus Magnus. Rome is never entirely asleep. The carts are forbidden by day, so they rumble through the dark, and by dawn the streets stink of what the oxen leave behind, mixed with woodsmoke and the sour breath of the fulleries where men stand knee-deep in vats of piss, treading wool. That morning there was something else on the air, sweet and greasy. Somewhere toward the Esquiline they were roasting a whole ox, for the Emperor had declared another hundred days of games to celebrate his conquest of Dacia, and the city meant to eat.

My country. His conquest. I had been taken eleven years before, in the first war, when I was sixteen and stupid enough to think the mountains would protect us. The second war had finished what the first began. King Decebalus had opened his own throat rather than walk in Trajan's triumph, and his head had been carried down the Via Sacra on a platter. I had not seen it. I had heard the crowd, though, from inside the ludus walls, a sound like the sea breaking against cliffs, and I had sat on my cot with my hands between my knees until it passed.

"You're quiet, Corax," Felix said.

"I'm always quiet."

"Quieter, then."

We passed the grain line at the Porticus Minucia. Hundreds of citizens stood there with their bronze tesserae clutched in their fists, waiting for the monthly dole. Old men with gray stubble, mothers with infants slung against their hips, a boy no older than eight holding his father's place. They were Roman citizens, every one, and many of them were thinner than I was. The lanista fed us barley and beans until we were thick as bullocks, because a fat gladiator bleeds dramatically without dying quickly. These people got their grain and their games, and in return they did not burn the city down. I had heard a senator's son say as much at a dinner where I had been displayed like a carved table. He had laughed when he said it. I did not think he was wrong.

A woman in the line looked at me. She saw the scars on my arms, the way I walked, the guard at my shoulder. Then her eyes slid away, as if I were a dog that might bite. Tomorrow she would scream my name, if I lived long enough for her to learn it.

We cut through the edge of the Subura, where the insulae lean so close above the alleys that the sky is only a ribbon. Laundry hung between the balconies, and water dripped onto my neck. A man was selling sausages from a brazier, and the fat spat and hissed on the coals. Two children chased a lame chicken through the mud. From an upper window came the sound of a woman singing a Syrian song I did not understand, and beneath it, steady as a heartbeat, a cobbler's hammer. I let it all wash through me. On the morning before the games, I always tried to drink the city in, in case it was the last time.

The shrine of Nemesis stood near the amphitheater, in a niche where the gladiators and the beast-hunters came to make their offerings. The goddess was carved in pale marble, her wings folded, a measuring rod in one hand and her wheel turning at her feet. A griffin crouched beside her. Someone had left a garland of violets there, already browning, and a small clay lamp still burning. The stone around her base was carved with the scratched names of men who had come before me. Some I knew were dead.

The Romans pray to Mars, to Hercules, to Victory with her palm branch. I have never trusted any of them. Victory belongs to the man who wins, and Hercules was a son of Jupiter, born with every advantage. But Nemesis does not care who your father was. She weighs. She measures. She is the goddess of the reckoning that comes for the proud man when he has climbed too high, and the wheel at her feet reminds you that it never stops turning. I had seen it turn. I had been the son of a chieftain who kept horses and drank from silver cups, and now I was property. Somewhere in this city lived a man who had once been a slave and now owned a villa at Baiae. The wheel turns.

I knelt and set down my offering, a pinch of salt and a copper coin. Felix stood back. He was a follower of Mithras now, and pretended he did not watch me.

Lady, I said silently, I do not ask you to let me win. I ask you to remember.

I did not tell her what I meant. I think she knew. Two days before, the lanista had told me that the editor of the games wanted a special pairing for the third day: a Dacian of the arena against a Dacian of the war, one of the new captives still sick from the long march over the Alps. The crowd would like it, he said. A little history lesson. I had said nothing. A gladiator who refuses to fight is beaten, then burned with irons, then sent into the arena anyway.

I wondered whether the boy, whoever he was, spoke the dialect of my valley. I wondered whether he had known my sisters.

When I rose, my knees cracked. The lamp flame trembled in a breeze I couldn't feel. Above us, the great curve of the amphitheater blotted out half the sky, its travertine arches gleaming like teeth in the morning sun. Workmen were already hauling sand through the gates in baskets, and sand brought from the coast to soak up what would spill tomorrow.

"Ready?" Felix asked.

I looked once more at the goddess and her wheel.

"No," I said. And we walked back together through the waking city, toward the walls, toward the barley and beans, toward whatever she had already measured out for me.

# The Sica

The doctor came before dawn to look at my teeth.

He did this every ninth day, prying my jaw open with fingers that smelled of vinegar and fennel, as though I were a horse at the Campus Martius market. Galen's people, the Greeks, believed a man's health could be read in his gums. I believed the doctor was paid by the lanista to tell him which of us was worth feeding barley and which could be spent cheaply. He grunted, wrote something on a wax tablet, and moved down the row of cells.

My cell was six paces by four. I had counted it many times. Through the slit high in the wall came the first gray light and the sounds of the city waking: shutters banging, a baker's boy calling his loaves, the last heavy carts grinding their wheels toward the city gates before the daylight ban, and somewhere a dog barking at nothing. The Ludus Magnus sat in the shadow of the Flavian amphitheater, and even before sunrise I could feel the great stone bowl looming beyond our walls the way you feel a mountain at your back.

That morning was different. Titus Calvus, our lanista, had sold an hour of my time to a senator's son who wished to be seen walking the Forum with a famous fighter. In two days I was to fight in the games Trajan had ordered for his Dacian triumph, and men who would never hold a blade wanted to stand near those of us who would.

They called me Ferox in the arena. My mother had called me Duras.

---

Before I was let out, the armorer brought my sica so that the senator's son could admire it. He would not let me carry it into the streets, of course. A slave with a blade in the Forum would cause a riot, or a crucifixion. But the boy had paid to hold it, and so I unwrapped it from its oiled leather for him in the courtyard.

It is a short sword, a Thracian blade, curved like a crescent moon caught in the act of rising. The Romans gave it to me because I fight in the style they call *thraex*, and the Romans like their categories. They do not know, or do not care, that in the mountains where I was born, my father carried a falx, a longer blade bent the same way, forward like a farmer's billhook. With such blades our warriors had split Roman helmets at Tapae. With such blades my people had made the legions bolt iron bars across the crowns of their helmets.

When the lanista first placed the sica in my hand, three years ago, I nearly wept. It was the only thing in Rome shaped like home.

The senator's son, Lucius, turned it in the light and tested the edge with his thumb. "It looks cruel," he said, pleased.

"It is only bent," I told him. "Cruelty is in the arm."

He laughed as if I had made a joke.

---

We walked out through the Subura. The smell of it struck me as it always did, a wall of things: urine from the fullers' vats, where men stamped togas clean in great tubs; fish sauce fermenting in clay jars; woodsmoke and boiling chickpeas; sweat and incense and the green rot of the open drains. Insulae rose five and six stories on either side, leaning toward one another until the sky was a ribbon. Laundry hung between them. A woman on a third-floor balcony emptied a pot into the street, and Lucius's slaves pulled him aside with practiced speed.

People stared at me. I am tall, and the brand on my arm is fresh enough to read. A child pointed and shouted my arena name, and an old man spat, and a young woman with painted eyes looked at me in a way that made Lucius walk closer to my side, as if to share in it.

Near the Argiletum a queue had formed outside a grain office, hundreds of men holding wooden tokens. The free bread of Rome. They stood quietly, in their patched tunics, citizens all, men who had never been chained and had never been fed better than I was. One of them caught my eye and looked away quickly, ashamed of something. Perhaps that a slave was better fed than he. Perhaps that he would cheer my death.

"The emperor is generous," Lucius said, following my gaze. "Bread now, games after. Dacian gold pays for both."

I said nothing. I had learned that silence in Latin sounds like agreement.

---

And then we came to it.

Beyond the old Forum, where the hill had been cut away, an entire mountainside of earth had been carted off to make room. Thousands of men swarmed over the site, hauling marble on rollers, chanting as they pulled. Cranes powered by treadwheels lifted blocks the size of houses. Dust hung white in the air and coated my tongue with the taste of chalk. The din of chisels was like a rain of hail that never stopped.

"Trajan's new forum," Lucius said proudly. "And there, you see the base? There will be a column. A hundred feet high. My father says it will show the whole war carved around it in a spiral, from the crossing of the Danube to the death of your king."

I looked at the base of the column, where workmen were setting the first drums of marble.

Decebalus had cut his own throat rather than be led through these streets in chains. I had not been so brave. I had been seventeen and bleeding from the scalp, and I had let them take me.

"Every stone of it," Lucius went on, "bought with gold from your mountains. Isn't that something? You will be part of history, Ferox."

There were Dacians among the workers. I could tell by their hair and their faces, and once, as we passed, by a word shouted in my own tongue, a curse at a slipping rope. No one turned. No one but me.

---

When the hour was done, Lucius pressed a coin into my palm, a silver denarius stamped with Trajan's calm face. On the reverse, a mourning woman sat beneath a trophy of weapons. Beneath her, the word: *DACIA CAPTA*.

That night, in my cell, I held the coin in one hand and the memory of the sica's weight in the other. In two days the crowd would roar for me, and I would bend toward my opponent like the blade itself, curved and forward, the shape of my father's mountains.

I would fight well. I had decided that, walking back through the stink and splendor of the city.

Not for Rome.

For the only thing in it shaped like home.

# The Free Supper

They walked us to the supper through the Subura, because the lanista said the people should smell us before they saw us bleed.

It was the hundred-and-somethingth day of Trajan's games for the conquest of Dacia, and the city had stopped counting. The streets stank of it: garum slopped from amphorae cracked in the heat, urine from the fullers' pots on every corner, pine smoke, wet straw, the sweetish rot of offerings left too long on the street-shrines. Laundry hung across the alleys like the sails of a fleet that had run aground. Above us, women leaned out of the fourth and fifth floors of the insulae and shouted our names. Not our names. The names Rome had given us.

Mine was Felix. Lucky. The lanista thought it was funny. I had been lucky for nine fights, which is eight more than most men get, and the crowd liked a joke that kept going.

We were twelve, chained loosely at the wrist. It was more for show than safety, because where would we run? Ahead of me walked Hilarus, the Syrian retiarius, humming a song from his village in a voice like a cracked bell. Behind me came the boy they called Ursus, who was not a bear but a Gaulish farmer's son who had sold himself to the ludus to pay his father's debts. He kept looking up at the women and blushing. I did not tell him what I had learned: that the women who cheered loudest were the ones who came to watch you die, and that they would weep at it, and that the weeping would be real.

The tables were set in the forecourt near the Ludus Magnus, under torches that spat and hissed in their iron cages. It was the cena libera, the free supper, the last meal before the games. It was a feast. Roast pork glistening with honey and pepper. Bread so white it looked carved from marble. Figs split open like wounds. Wine, real Falernian, not the vinegar they rationed us. A magistrate named Calpurnius was paying for all of it, and for tomorrow too, because he wanted the aedileship next year, and in Rome there is no road to the Senate that does not run through the arena sand.

And around the tables, held back by a rope and a few bored guards, stood the people of Rome, staring at us while we ate.

I have never grown used to it. They pressed close enough that I could smell them: the onion breath of the plebs who lined up each month at the Porticus Minucia for their free grain, the rosewater of a senator's son who had come slumming with his friends. They pointed. They debated our odds. A man with a wax tablet took wagers. A girl of perhaps six sat on her father's shoulders and asked him, very clearly, which one was going to die.

"Probably that one," he said, and pointed at Ursus.

Ursus put down his bread.

"Eat," I told him. "Eat everything. It is the only thing tomorrow cannot take from you."

That was when I saw the Dacians.

They had been brought in at the far end of the tables, perhaps forty of them, still in the rags they had been captured in. Some still had their long hair, though most had been shorn. They did not look like fighters. They looked like what they were, which was shepherds and smiths and the sons of minor chieftains, taken in the fall of Sarmizegetusa and marched across half the world to be killed for the anniversary of their own defeat. They would not be given real swords tomorrow. They would be given the noon slot, when the better people went home to eat, and they would be killed in groups by men like me while the crowd bought sausages.

I had not heard my own language in nineteen years. I did not expect to hear it then. But one of them, a youth with a scar through his eyebrow, said something to the man beside him. It was only an ordinary curse about the wine. And something in my chest came loose like a rotten beam.

I was taken in the first war, under Domitian, when I was younger than Ursus. My mother's name was Zia. I had not said it aloud since the slave ship.

The boy looked up and saw me watching. He saw the scars, the thick neck, the oiled skin, the Roman haircut. He saw a Roman gladiator, and his face closed against me like a door.

I wanted to tell him: *I know the river below your village. I know the songs.* I wanted to tell him that the Emperor had stripped his country's gold mines bare and built a forum and a column with the money, and that on that column, carved in marble, Roman soldiers were cutting off Dacian heads, and that Romans would walk past it for a thousand years and call it glory. I wanted to tell him to die quickly.

Instead I raised my cup to him, a little. He spat on the ground.

Fair enough.

After the supper, the guards marched us back to the ludus, and I asked for my usual small kindness. Old Pudens, the doctor, who had sewn me up seven times, walked me to the eastern edge of the yard, where you could see the Porta Libitinensis of the great amphitheatre. It was the Gate of Death, where they drag the bodies out on hooks.

I did what I have done the night before every fight since my first. I pressed my left palm flat against the cold stone of the archway, and I said my mother's name.

Hilarus thinks it is a prayer. Pudens thinks I am mad. It is neither. It is courtesy. I am introducing myself to the goddess Libitina, who keeps the gate, so that if she comes for me tomorrow she will know my true name and not the one the lanista gave me. I will not be dragged out as Felix. I will go out as the son of Zia, from the river country, who was a boy once, and free.

Nine times the goddess has looked at my face and let me go.

Walking back, I thought of the scarred youth. He would not know to do this. No one would tell him.

Calpurnius had promised that if I won tomorrow, he would give me the rudis, the wooden sword, my freedom. I would have it for the crowd's roar, and he would have the crowd's votes for it.

That night I lay on my straw and listened to the city grinding on through the dark: cartwheels on stone, a dog, a drunk singing about a girl from Ostia. Somewhere in the cells below, forty men were whispering in the language of my childhood. I tried to remember whether I had ever known the words to wish a man a good death.

I could not remember. I lay awake a long time, trying.

response:
# The Light at Muckle Flugga

---

**Muckle Flugga Lighthouse, Shetland**
**4th March 1957**

Dear Mam,

Arrived safe. The boat from Burrafirth took two goes at the landing because of the swell, and I was sick over the side in front of the Principal Keeper, Mr Laurenson, who said nothing, which was worse.

The rock is smaller than it looks in the photograph. You can walk round it in four minutes. I timed it. North of us there's only Out Stack, and then nothing till the ice. Mr Laurenson says that's the last bit of Britain. It looks like a broken tooth.

The work is fine. Brass, paraffin, the log. I'm on the middle watch.

Tell Agnes I've not forgotten her birthday. I'll send something when the boat goes.

Your son,
Davie

---

**14 Langlands Road, Govan**
**19th March 1957**

Dear David,

Your letter came Thursday and I read it out to Mrs Kerr on the landing. She says you were always a peely-wally sort of boy on boats and I told her to mind her own. Two goes at the landing is nothing. Your father took three goes at everything.

Agnes says she doesn't want anything, which means she wants scent. Not the cheap stuff from Woolworths.

The rent man has been and I paid him the full amount out of your first postal order, and I put a shilling aside for the gas. It's a good job, son. Folk round here would give their right arm for a government job with a pension. Remember that when you're polishing your brass.

Eat what they give you. You'll be wanting a vest.

Mam

---

**Muckle Flugga**
**2nd June 1957**

Dear Mam,

Sorry I've not written. The relief was cancelled twice for weather.

The days are very long now. It barely gets dark at all, so the light's hardly needed, and I've not much to do on watch except listen to the gannets. They never stop. I thought I'd get used to it.

Mr Laurenson plays draughts. He's beat me forty-one times. I'm keeping count. The other assistant, Bertie, writes letters to a lassie in Lerwick and won't tell us her name.

Did Agnes like the scent?

Davie

---

**14 Langlands Road**
**20th June 1957**

David,

Agnes liked it fine and wore it to the dancing at the Plaza and came home at half one, so you can take some of the blame for that.

You sound low, son. Is it the food? You were never a big eater. Get Mr Laurenson to teach you to fish.

I'm doing a bit of cleaning at the doctor's in the mornings now. Don't fret, it's light work.

Mam

---

**Muckle Flugga**
**28th October 1957**

Mam,

I've been thinking I might put in for a transfer. Or come home. Willie McGuire said his brother could get me on at Fairfield's.

I don't sleep right. It's dark at four now and the wind gets into the walls. You lie there and it sounds like someone trying to say a word over and over and never getting it out.

Bertie's lassie wrote to say she's marrying a fisherman from Whalsay. He's not spoken since.

I'm all right. Don't tell Agnes.

D.

---

**14 Langlands Road**
**9th November 1957**

David,

Fairfield's laid off two hundred men in September. Willie McGuire's brother is one of them, though Willie doesn't know that yet because his brother hasn't told him.

I'm not going to tell you to stay. You're a man. But I'll tell you what I know, which is that the first winter of anything is the worst one. The first winter after your father went, I sat in the dark so as not to put money in the meter, and I thought it would never end, and it did.

Try to stick it till the spring. Then decide.

Mam

---

**Muckle Flugga**
**6th January 1958**

Mam,

Happy New Year. We had a dram. Mr Laurenson sang. It was terrible.

Davie

---

**14 Langlands Road**
**4th February 1958**

David,

That's twelve words. I counted them. You used to write me two pages about nothing.

Mam

---

**TELEGRAM — LERWICK — 21 FEB 1958**

MRS J. ROSS 14 LANGLANDS RD GOVAN. DAVID UNWELL NOT SERIOUS. OFF ROCK RESTING AT SHORE STATION BURRAFIRTH. LAURENSON.

---

**TELEGRAM — GLASGOW — 22 FEB 1958**

LAURENSON SHORE STATION BURRAFIRTH UNST. COMING. ROSS.

---

**Shore Station, Burrafirth**
**3rd March 1958**

Mam,

You'll be back in Govan by the time this gets to you. I'm writing it anyway, because there are things I couldn't say with you sitting there knitting at me.

I'm sorry you had to come all that way. Two boats and the overnight sleeper, and you've never been further than Rothesay. Mr Laurenson says you gave the skipper at Lerwick a piece of your mind about the state of his tea.

I want to tell you what it was. It wasn't the gannets or the dark, not really. It was that I stopped being able to tell what I was for. I'd polish the lens and wind the clockwork and log the weather, and the light went round, and nobody ever said thank you, because nobody's out there. Just water. I started thinking that's what I was. A thing that goes round.

Then on Thursday you made Mr Laurenson walk you up Hermaness in the rain. I didn't know you'd done it. I was back on the rock that night, my first watch since, and at half eleven I saw a wee light on the cliffs where nobody ever is. It went on and off, on and off. Not any code. Just somebody with a torch who didn't know what she was doing.

I stood at the gallery rail and watched it for twenty minutes. Then I worked the shutter on the hand lamp, three long, which is the only thing I could think of, and the torch went mad, flashing all over the place, and I had to sit down on the iron floor because I was greeting like a wean.

Mr Laurenson told me after that you stood up there an hour. You were soaked through. He said you told him, "He needs to know there's somebody looking."

I've decided to stay. Not forever. Till the spring at least, like you said. Then I'll see. Bertie's taken up the fiddle, God help us. Mr Laurenson has lost at draughts twice, so things are looking up.

I owe you a pair of shoes. You ruined your good ones on the peat.

I'll write properly. Two pages about nothing.

Your son,
David

P.S. Agnes says you never told her where you were going. You told Mrs Kerr, but not Agnes. She's raging.

---

**14 Langlands Road**
**15th March 1958**

David,

Shoes are fine. Mrs Kerr has a cousin.

I've put the torch in the kitchen drawer with the candles and the good scissors. I didn't know what else to do with it.

Every night at half eleven I go out to the back green and look north. I know fine I can't see you. It's two hundred and fifty miles and a wall of tenements. But I go anyway.

So now you know. There's somebody looking.

Mam

# The Lighthouse Keeper

---

**Sule Skerry Lighthouse**
**2nd October 1958**

Dear Mam,

Arrived Tuesday. The relief boat couldnae get in close so they swung us across on a rope, me and the messages both. The tatties went in the sea. I didnae.

There are three of us. Mr Inkster is the Principal, an Orkneyman, and has said maybe forty words since I came, twelve of them about the brasses. The other is Fergus from Lewis, who plays the mouth organ. One tune. Not well.

The rock's about the size of the pond in Elder Park. No trees. Birds everywhere, and the racket of them all night. Fergus says you get used to it. He's been here two years and he doesnae look used to it.

Tell Mrs Kerr thanks for the socks.

Your son,
David

---

**Shaw Street, Govan**
**20th October 1958**

Dear Davie,

Your letter came on the Thursday, which the postie says is fast for a rock in the Atlantic. I have read it four times and I still don't know if you are eating. Are you eating.

Mrs Kerr says you're welcome for the socks, and mind the heel on the left one is lumpy, she was watching *Double Your Money* at the time. Senga McCall's lassie is expecting again and nobody is saying who to.

I was giving your father's good jacket to the Vincent de Paul and found something in the lining. His tally from Fairfield's. Eleven years I thought it was in the ground with him. I've put it in with this. You'll mind he opened his screwtops with it, that's the nick in the edge. The number side is near rubbed smooth from his thumb. He did that at Mass and I'd have to elbow him.

Keep it in your pocket. He always said it kept him off a few bad scaffolds.

Your loving mother

---

**Sule Skerry Lighthouse**
**11th December 1958**

Dear Mam,

Got the tally. 4471. The first 4 you can still read if you tilt it to the lamp, the rest you have to take on trust. It's warm from the pocket all day, which is more than I am. I've put it on a bootlace round my neck. Fergus asked was I in the army.

Weather's turned. No boat in five weeks. When it's thick the fog signal goes every ninety seconds and it's been thick nine days. You'd think you'd stop hearing it. You don't. You count it. I'm counting it in my sleep.

Mr Inkster said a whole sentence to me yesterday. He said, "You're no sleeping, lad." Then he went back to the brasses.

Your writing's gone awful big. Is it your specs? Get them seen to.

Merry Christmas, if this gets to you in time, which it won't.

David

---

**Shaw Street, Govan**
**3rd January 1959**

Davie,

Specs are fine. I'm writing big so you can read it in your bad light.

Shortbread in the parcel. If it's broken it was the Post Office not me.

Count something else. Count the times you've been a pain to me, that'll see you to Easter.

Mam

---

**Sule Skerry Lighthouse**
**9th February 1959**

Dear Mam,

I said when I took this job I'd not lie to you in letters, so here it is.

Sunday night I went down to the landing when I wasnae on watch. I don't rightly know why. I stood there a long while. The sea was flat, the flattest I've seen it, and that's what frightened me, Mam. How calm it was, and how calm I was looking at it.

Mr Inkster came down after a bit. He didnae say anything. He just stood next to me with his hands in his pockets, and after a while we went back up the steps together. Next morning he gave me his tobacco tin to keep. He doesnae smoke anymore, he says. He's never smoked, Fergus says.

I'm putting in for a transfer. I know what Da would say about that. I'm sorry.

David

---

**Shaw Street, Govan**
**26th February 1959**

Dear Davie,

This is Mrs Kerr's hand. Your mother is saying it and I am putting it down, so don't blame me for the spelling.

*Son, you'll not know what your father would say, because you never let him finish a sentence. I'll tell you what he'd say. He'd say climbing back up those steps was the hardest shift ever worked on that rock, and he'd be right.*

*Now I've a thing to tell you and I'll not dress it.*

*It's not the specs. I've been up the Southern General since the summer. It's the glaucoma. They left it too late, or I did. I've light and shapes and that's me. No more reading. That big writing was the last of it, and Agnes Kerr reads me your letters now, so watch what you put in them.*

*I didnae tell you because you'd have been off that rock in a week, and I wanted one of us to have a life that wasnae this close. That was wrong. You told me true and I owed you the same.*

*So that's us both told.*

*Put in for your transfer. And eat something.*

*Your loving mother*

P.S. from Agnes Kerr. She's fine, Davie. She's been fine. She made me take out a bit where she was greeting so I'm putting it back in.

---

**TELEGRAM — 17 APRIL 1959**
TRANSFER APPROVED STOP CLOCH POINT GOUROCK FROM JUNE STOP SAME FIRTH AS YOU MAM STOP DAVIE

---

**Cloch Lighthouse, Gourock**
**2nd June 1959**

Dear Mam,

Mrs Kerr, read this slow.

I'm here. There's a road to the door. There's a bus. There's a chip shop in Gourock where the woman already knows I'm "the new lighthouse boy," which I'm thirty-one and not a boy, but I let it go.

Aunt Bella wrote to say you're to stay with her in Dunoon over the summer. Dunoon is straight across the water from me, Mam. Ask her to take you down the front after dark.

I'm sending the tally back. Not for keeps. Just you have it a while. You can read the 4 with your thumb, the way Da did. I've been doing it every night for months and I reckon I've worn it down another hair, so between the two of us we'll have it smooth by Christmas.

Mr Inkster wrote. Two lines. *Glad you're ashore. Mind the brasses.*

Your son,
Davie

---

**Hunter's Quay, Dunoon**
**14th August 1959**

DAVIE

THIS IS ME WRITING. BELLA IS HOLDING THE PAPER STRAIGHT.

SHE TAKES ME TO THE FRONT AT NIGHT. I CANNOT SEE THE WATER OR THE HILLS OR THE BOATS.

BUT I SEE YOUR LIGHT.

EVERY TIME IT COMES ROUND I SAY THERE'S DAVIE. BELLA SAYS I'M DAFT. I SAY IT ANYWAY.

I HAVE THE TALLY IN MY HAND WRITING THIS.

COME FOR YOUR TEA SUNDAY.

MAM

response:
# The Lighthouse Keeper

**Dubh Sgeir Lighthouse, by Tiree**
**14th October 1962**

Dear Mam,

Landed Tuesday. They put you off the boat onto a ladder bolted to the rock and you climb while the swell decides whether to let you. I didnae drop my bag, which Mr Laing the Principal says puts me ahead of the last lad.

It's three of us. Laing is Free Church and says grace over corned beef like it was a roast. Wullie Shearer from Wick whistles the same four bars of something all day. He doesnae know the rest.

My room is round. You cannae hang a picture straight on a round wall. I've tried.

Tell Da I'm here. If he asks.

Your son,
Davie

---

**42 Langlands Road, Govan**
**22nd Oct**

Dear Davie,

Your letter came Thursday. Mrs Rennie downstairs says a lighthouse is a good steady job and her cousin's boy did it and only went a bit funny. So that's encouraging.

Mince is up again. The Fairfield men are saying there's to be more laid off before Christmas, your father is not saying anything which is how I know he's worried.

He did not ask. But he read your letter after I went to my bed, because it was folded the wrong way in the morning.

Wear your vest.
Mam

---

**Dubh Sgeir**
**3rd December 1962**

Dear Mam,

Relief was due the 18th. It's now the 29th and the boat's still sat in Scarinish waiting on the weather. We're on tinned peas and oatmeal and Laing has started rationing the tea. A man can thole a lot but not that.

I'll tell you the truth since there's nobody else to tell it to. It's no the wind or the food. It's that there's nothing to put your eyes on. On the Clyde there's always something, a crane, a tenement, a dug. Here it's sea and more sea, and after a fortnight your head starts making its own company. I caught myself counting the stairs. A hundred and fifty-one. I counted them again the next day in case they'd changed.

Wullie's still on his four bars.

Davie

---

**Govan**
**11th Dec**

Davie,

Your father had a wee turn at the yard on Monday. Dizzy, they sent him home. He's fine now, sitting in his chair complaining about the Rangers so you know he's himself. Don't fret.

I've put a cake in the post. If it's stale by the time it gets to you, dip it in your tea, if Mr Laing lets you have any.

Mam

---

**Dubh Sgeir**
**9th January 1963**

Dear Mam,

The cake came. It's a fine thing to eat a cake that tastes of your own kitchen when you're twelve mile out in the Atlantic.

Something happened at New Year I want to tell you. The lens turns on clockwork, a big weight that drops down the middle of the tower, and you wind it back up every forty minutes. Hogmanay night the governor sheared. No way to fix it till the engineers come. But the light has to keep its character, one flash every ten seconds, or a ship might take us for some other rock and steer wrong.

So we turned it by hand. All night. You push the brass rail round and keep your time by counting. Laing's method is to say the Lord's Prayer up to "trespasses," which he swears is exactly ten seconds. I said I didnae know it that well. He said, "You will by morning."

He was right. My arms were done by two o'clock. Then I minded Da telling me how the rivet squads kept their time, the heater and the holder-on and the man with the gun, all on the one beat without a word said. So I stopped praying and counted the way he showed me when I was wee, on the kitchen table with a spoon. It worked better. I didnae lose the time once till Wullie relieved me at four.

I don't know why I'm telling you this. I suppose I wanted him to know I remembered.

I've been thinking about putting in my notice, Mam. I'm no sure I'm made for it.

Is Da right? You only wrote the once about it.

Davie

---

**TELEGRAM — 19 JAN 1963**
**TO KEEPER MOIR DUBH SGEIR VIA TIREE**
FATHER IN SOUTHERN GENERAL STROKE COME IF YOU CAN = MAM

---

**TELEGRAM — 20 JAN 1963**
**TO MOIR 42 LANGLANDS RD GOVAN**
GALE NO BOAT CANNOT GET OFF WILL COME FIRST CHANCE TELL HIM = DAVIE

---

**Govan**
**2nd February**

Dear Davie,

He's home. He cannot use his right hand and his words come out in the wrong order but he knows me and he knows the cat.

I have to tell you something and I've started this letter four times. The wee turn in December was not wee. The doctor told us in November his pressure was bad and he was not to go back to the yard. He went back anyway because we needed the money, and he made me promise not to tell you, because he said you'd come home and give up the light, and he didnae want you to be a man who gives up a thing because it's hard. He said that was his job to be.

So I have been lying to you in my letters and I'm sorry. I have been sitting in this house with him and the wireless and nobody to say it to. I think I know a bit about your round room now.

I read him your letter about the lens. He made me read it twice. Then he took the spoon off his saucer with his good hand and tapped it on the arm of the chair. Ten. I counted.

He cannot say it so I will. Don't you dare give it up for us.

Mam

---

**Dubh Sgeir**
**30th March 1963**

Dear Mam,

Back on the rock a week now. It was good to be home, even with Da glaring at me for coming. I think he was pleased. Hard to tell with him, it always was.

I've not given it up. But I went to the Board office in Edinburgh on the way back and asked about the shore stations. There's a vacancy at the Cloch, by Gourock, in September. Laing wrote me a letter saying I'm steady and that I've learned my prayers, which is the nearest thing to a joke I've heard out of him.

The Cloch's a married keeper's station, with a cottage. There's room. There's a bus to Glasgow every hour. And from the lamp room you can see every ship coming down the Clyde from the yards. Da could sit at the window and tell me which squad riveted which hull, and get it wrong, and argue.

You'll have nobody to lie to then. You'll just have to talk to me.

The new governor works fine. I still count it sometimes, in his time, just to keep my hand in.

Wullie learned the fifth bar. It didnae help.

Your loving son,
Davie

# The Second-Hand Section

The bell above the door didn't ring so much as shriek. Julian Ashby shut the door behind him, flattened himself against the Local History shelf, and listened to the footsteps pound past the window and fade down the hill toward the harbour.

"We close at five," said a voice from behind the counter.

He turned on the smile. It had sold forty million dollars' worth of a film about a sad pirate. "Then I've got twenty minutes to make you fall in love with me. Plenty of time."

The woman behind the counter didn't look up from the book she was pricing. She was perhaps thirty, with dark hair held up by a pencil and a cardigan that had seen several winters. "You're dripping on the Ordnance Survey maps."

"Ah." He stepped away from the shelf. "Sorry. It's raining."

"It's Wales. It's always raining. That's why we have bookshops." She wrote *£2.50* in the flyleaf in neat pencil. "Are those photographers yours, then?"

"In a manner of speaking. I'm Julian." He waited the half-second for recognition. Nothing came. "Ashby."

"Ffion." She finally looked at him, briefly and evenly, the way someone checks a delivery against the invoice. "Pritchard. If you're hiding, the back room's warmer, but there's a cat in there who doesn't like men."

"Cats adore me."

"This one bit the vicar."

"The vicar probably deserved it." He leaned on the counter, which was how he did these things: get close, lower the voice, make it feel like a secret. "You genuinely don't know who I am, do you? It's all right. It's quite refreshing."

"I know exactly who you are. You were the pirate. And the one where you played the cello and died of something Victorian." She slid the book onto a pile. "My mam cried at that. I thought the cello was miming badly."

He laughed, and it came out higher than he meant it to. "The cello was not miming. I had six months of lessons."

"Well. The lessons were miming, then."

"That's—" He straightened up. "Most people tell me I'm very good in that."

"I'm sure they do." She turned a page. "Most people tell the doctor they only drink at weekends."

Julian opened his mouth and found nothing in it. That didn't usually happen to him. He wandered toward the Poetry shelf instead, mostly to have something to do with his hands.

*Oh, God,* Ffion thought, and wrote *£2.50* in a book she'd already priced. She rubbed it out with her thumb. *He's taller than on the telly. Why is he taller? They're supposed to be shorter.*

"You've got R.S. Thomas next to Dylan Thomas," he said. "Is that wise? I'd have thought they'd fight."

"Alphabetical. I don't make the rules."

"You own the shop. You literally make the rules."

"My taid made the rules. I just haven't had the heart to change them." She hesitated, which annoyed her. "He's been dead six years and I still can't move the Westerns out of the window."

Julian pulled out a thin, battered paperback. "*Song at the Year's Turning*. Do you know, I did a reading of this at a festival. Hay, I think. Everyone was very moved."

"Were you?"

"Was I what?"

"Moved."

He looked at the book for a long moment. When he spoke again the polish had gone out of his voice and it sounded flatter, and somewhere further north than RADA.

"I'll tell you something stupid. Second year of drama school, we did a showcase, all the agents in the front row. I had a big speech. Lear. Ridiculous at twenty, but there you are. I got four lines in and it just went. Everything. Like someone pulled a plug." He turned the book over in his hands. "I stood there for, oh, a minute. Felt like a year. And nobody laughed. That was the worst part. They were *kind*. Some agent in the front row actually started clapping, very gently, like you would for a child who's fallen off a bike. Encouraging."

Ffion had stopped pricing.

"I've never dried since," he said. "Not once. I learn everything three times over. But every single night, before I go on, I think, *what if they're kind again?*" He smiled, and it wasn't the pirate smile. "Which is mad, isn't it. Being terrified of people being nice to you."

"It's not mad," she said, too quickly. Then, more carefully: "You'd rather they loved you or hated you. Pity's the thing in the middle."

"Yes." He looked at her properly. "That's exactly it. How did you—"

"I run a bookshop in a town of nine hundred people. Everyone who comes in is very kind about how I'm *keeping it going*." She went back to the books and gave one of them far more attention than it needed. "They buy a postcard."

Outside, a car crawled past. Neither of them looked at it.

"I'll buy something," Julian said. "Not out of kindness. Out of genuine… literary appetite."

"Go on, then."

He put the R.S. Thomas on the counter. She turned it over. "That's four pounds."

"It says four-fifty."

"It's four pounds."

"Ffion Pritchard. Are you being *kind* to me?"

"I'm being efficient. I haven't got change for a fiver." She did. There was a full float in the till and she could feel it sitting there accusing her.

He handed her a ten-pound note. She gave him six pound coins one at a time, and he held his hand out flat for each of them, which was unnecessary and took far too long.

"I've been trying to charm you for a quarter of an hour," he said, "and I think you've charmed me instead. I don't know how I feel about that. I'll need to speak to my publicist."

"You weren't trying very hard."

"I was trying *enormously* hard. I did the lean. Nobody survives the lean."

"Is that what that was?" Her mouth twitched. She disciplined it. "I thought your back had gone."

He laughed properly then, from the stomach, surprised into it, and she found she had to look at the window for a minute. The Westerns sat there in the grey light, curling at the corners.

"It's five o'clock," she said.

"Is it?" He didn't move. "Do you know, I think the photographers have gone."

"They'll be in the Black Lion. It's the only place with Wi-Fi."

"Then I'd better stay away from the Black Lion." He tucked the book inside his coat. "Is there anywhere else that does a cup of tea at five o'clock on a Tuesday?"

Ffion picked up the pencil, put it in her hair, realised there was already one there, and took both of them out again.

"There's a kettle in the back," she said. "But I meant it about the cat."

# Chapter Seven: Second-Hand

The bell above the door didn't so much ring as shriek, and Ffion Pryce looked up from her stock ledger to find a man flattened against the inside of her shop window like a starfish on an aquarium.

"Don't mind me," he said, slightly breathless. "Carry on. Very important ledger, I'm sure."

Outside, the Morgan Arcade echoed with running feet and a flurry of shouting. Someone yelled *Theo! Theo, mate, just one!* and then the noise funnelled away towards St Mary Street.

The man peeled himself off the glass. He was wearing sunglasses, in November, in Cardiff, which was all she needed to know about him, really.

"We close at five," Ffion said.

"It's ten past four."

"So you've got fifty minutes to find something you want to buy."

He took off the sunglasses. She had been braced for this, the way you brace for a wave on Barry Island beach, and it still very nearly knocked her over. The eyes were exactly the colour they were on the side of every bus shelter in Britain. Possibly bluer. It seemed unfair of them.

"Theo Marlowe," he said, and held out a hand.

"I know."

His hand stayed where it was. A flicker crossed his face, delight, she thought, at being known, and then she watched him register that she hadn't moved from behind the counter and wasn't going to.

"Ah," he said. "You're a fan. You're playing it cool. That's adorable."

"I'm not a fan."

"Everyone's a fan of something I've done. Did you see *The Glass Admiral*? Bafta nomination. My mother cried. Strangers cried. A man in Leeds wrote to tell me he'd forgiven his father."

"I saw the trailer."

"And?"

"And I thought, there's a man who's very pleased with his own jawline."

Theo opened his mouth, closed it, and laughed. It was a proper laugh, startled out of him, not the one from the chat shows. Ffion looked down at her ledger very quickly and found she had written the same number in two columns.

"Right," he said. "Right. Okay. What's your name?"

"Why?"

"So I can put it in my memoirs. *Chapter Twelve: The Woman Who Hated My Jawline.*"

"I didn't say I hated it."

That had come out wrong. She felt the heat start at her collar and climb, and bent to straighten a pile of Penguin Classics that did not need straightening.

"Ffion," she said to Jane Austen.

"Ffion." He said it nearly right, which was more than most English people managed. The double-f soft, like a breath on a cold window. "That's beautiful. What does it mean?"

"Foxglove."

"Pretty."

"Poisonous," she said. "Stops your heart."

He leaned an elbow on the counter. "I'll risk it."

"Please don't lean on that. It's older than you are, and it's in better condition."

He removed the elbow with the wounded dignity of a cat knocked off a sofa. Then he began to wander. She watched him in the convex mirror by the door, the one she'd put up to catch shoplifters, and told herself that was why she was watching. He ran a finger along the spines in Poetry. Pulled out a battered R.S. Thomas, opened it, frowned, put it back upside down.

"Other way up, that is," she said.

"Do you do this to all your customers?"

"Only the ones who come in like a burglar."

"I was being *chased*, Ffion. Hunted. Those men out there would sell a photo of my bin bags." He turned the book the right way up, then glanced over. "You've no idea what it's like. Everywhere you go, people wanting something."

"Sounds awful. All that love."

"It isn't love." He said it lightly, but something underneath it wasn't light at all. "It's appetite. Not the same."

Ffion didn't answer. Outside, the rain had started again, ticking against the arcade's glass roof. Somewhere a busker was murdering "Calon Lân" on a saxophone.

Theo had stopped in front of the shelf by the window, the one with her handwritten cards tucked between the books. *If you liked this, try...* He picked one up.

"'Ignore the cover. The cover is lying. The inside is extraordinary.'" He looked at her. "Did you write this?"

"I write all of them."

"About a book?"

"What else would it be about?"

He held her gaze a moment too long, and the confidence went out of him a little, the way air goes out of a lilo. He looked, suddenly, a bit lost, and a good deal younger, like someone who'd been handed a script with the wrong pages in it.

"Can I ask you something," he said. "Honestly. No jawline."

"Go on."

"Why don't you like me?"

It should have been funny. It was, a little. But he actually wanted to know, and that was what undid her. Her mother would have said *duw, look at him, the poor dab*, and made him a cup of tea, and Ffion was not going to make him a cup of tea.

"I don't *know* you," she said. "I know a poster."

"Most people prefer the poster."

"Most people haven't seen you put Thomas back upside down."

He smiled then, not the famous one, the crooked one that went further up on the left than the right. She was going to be thinking about that asymmetry at two in the morning, and she resented it already.

"So what would you recommend," he said, "for a man whose cover is lying?"

Ffion came out from behind the counter, which was a mistake, because the shop was narrow and he was suddenly very close and smelled of rain and something expensive. She reached past him, careful not to touch, failing slightly, her sleeve brushing his, and took down a slim green paperback.

"Dannie Abse. Cardiff boy. Doctor and poet. He knew the difference between a performance and a person."

Theo took it. His fingers didn't quite touch hers.

"How much?"

"Four pounds."

"I'll give you forty if you sign the inside."

"It's not my book."

"I know," he said quietly. "I'd still like it signed."

The bell shrieked. They both jumped. A pensioner in a rain bonnet peered in, looked at Theo, looked at Ffion, said "Oh, sorry, love, didn't know you were busy," and left again.

"We're not busy," Ffion called after her, far too loudly.

Theo put four pounds on the counter, exactly four, and the sunglasses back on.

"Same time next week?" he said.

"We close at five."

"Then I'll come at ten past four."

The door shrieked shut behind him. Ffion stood very still for a long moment, then looked down at the ledger. In the margin, in her own handwriting, without any memory of doing it, she had drawn a small foxglove.

# Chapter Eleven: Ingrate

The bell above the door of Pritchard's Books gave a strangled little *ting*, as if it too had been taken by surprise. Nia didn't look up from the crossword.

"We're closed."

"Your sign says open."

"My sign is an optimist." She filled in a four-letter word. "I'm not."

The man pressed his back to the door and peered through the gap in the blinds at the rain-slick high street of Llanfair Caereinion, where three men with long lenses were jogging past the butcher's. He let out a breath, turned, and smiled at her. It was clearly a smile that had been insured.

"Right. Hello. Sorry. I'm—"

"I know who you are."

"Ah." He seemed pleased, and then, when she said nothing more, less pleased. "And?"

"And you're dripping on my Thomas Hardy."

He looked down. He was, in fact, dripping on a remaindered box of *Tess of the d'Urbervilles*. He stepped sideways with a dancer's neatness. "Theo Marlowe. Although you knew that. Which is lovely, actually, you've no idea how often people just say *you look like that bloke from the thing*."

"You do look like that bloke from the thing."

"I *am* that bloke from the thing."

"Well, there you are, then. Mystery solved." She tapped her pencil against the paper. "They'll go round the back by the Spar in a minute. They always think there's a car park. There isn't."

"You've done this before?"

"We had a minor royal in 2019. She wanted a Welsh-English dictionary and the toilet. Mostly the toilet."

Theo laughed, the real kind, startled out of him, and then caught himself and turned it into the professional kind, warmer and lower. He drifted toward the counter, trailing a hand along the spines of the poetry shelf like a man stroking a cat.

"This is a beautiful shop. Truly. It smells like a library had a baby with a church."

"It smells like damp. The roof's had it."

"Romantic damp, though."

"There's nothing romantic about a bucket on the stairs, Mr. Marlowe."

"Theo."

"Mr. Marlowe."

He leaned an elbow on the counter. Nia did not look at the elbow, or at the forearm attached to it, or at the way his wet hair had curled at the temple in a manner no continuity department would ever allow. She looked at seventeen across.

"You're not a fan," he said. It wasn't quite a question. There was something underneath it, thin as paper.

"I've seen one of your films."

"Which one?"

"The one with the boat."

"*Saltwater*. I was quite good in that, I thought. Did you think I was good in that?"

"I thought the boat was very convincing."

He put a hand over his heart. "You're wounding me. You're aware you're wounding me? I've had a very long week. Someone in Cardiff threw a scone at me."

"Was it a good scone?"

"It was a *magnificent* scone, that's what hurt." He tilted his head, trying a new angle, the way she imagined he'd been taught: find the light. "What's your name?"

"Nia."

"Nia." He said it carefully, properly, the vowel long. Something in her stomach turned over, stupidly, like a fish in a bucket. "That's gorgeous. Welsh?"

"No, it's Portuguese." She sighed. "Yes, it's Welsh. We're in Wales."

"Right. Yes. Fair." He laughed again, and this time didn't bother to fix it. He looked, for a moment, faintly lost, a man who had walked onto a stage and found no audience, just a woman with a biro and a cardigan with a hole in the elbow. He glanced down at the newspaper. "What are you stuck on?"

"I'm not stuck."

"You've been tapping that pencil like Morse code since I came in. That's a stuck tap. My nan used to do the stuck tap."

Nia hesitated. "Seventeen across. *Ungrateful one tearing about*. Seven letters."

"Oh, that's an anagram. *About*'s the indicator, isn't it? Tearing, rearranged." He didn't even pause. "Ingrate."

She stared at the grid. Counted. Wrote it in, slowly, in ink.

"Huh," she said.

"*Huh*?" He was grinning now, and it was a different grin altogether, lopsided, slightly gappy where a tooth sat crooked. It made him look about fourteen. "That's it? I solve your crossword and I get *huh*?"

"You do cryptics."

"Every day. Since I was nine." He rubbed the back of his neck. "Nan had a long stay at Whipps Cross. Nothing to do but the *Telegraph* puzzle and steal her custard. She'd make me explain my working or I didn't get the pudding."

"My dad did the *Guardian* one," Nia said, before she could stop herself. "Every Saturday, out loud, at breakfast. Drove my mother up the wall."

"Araucaria or Paul?"

She looked at him properly then, for the first time. "Araucaria. God rest him."

"God rest him," Theo agreed solemnly. "Absolute bastard of a setter. I loved him."

"*Everybody* loved him."

"Not everybody. I once wrote him a fan letter and he never answered."

"He was ninety."

"Still. Rude." He was leaning closer now, though she wasn't sure he'd noticed. Neither, she realised, had she. "Do you know, nobody ever asks me about this? They ask what I eat for breakfast. Whether I'm seeing someone. Whether I did my own stunts in the one with the boat."

"Did you?"

"I fell off the boat once. They kept it in." He paused. "Are you going to ask if I'm seeing someone?"

"No."

"Right." He nodded, and somehow seemed more delighted by that than anything else she'd said. "Right. Good. That's—good."

Outside, someone shouted. Running feet. A car door. Nia watched him flinch, just slightly, and pretend he hadn't.

She pulled the newspaper back toward her, and then, after a moment, turned it round so it faced him. She held out the pencil.

"Twenty-two down," she said. "Don't get cocky. I'll be checking your working."

Theo Marlowe, who had been on the cover of eleven magazines that year, took the pencil like it was something precious.

"Is there custard in it for me?"

"There's a kettle," said Nia, and went to put it on, so that he wouldn't see her face.

response:
# My Apocalypse Buddy

The world had not ended with a bang, nor with a whimper, but with a sort of prolonged, embarrassed cough, like a man who has realised halfway through a speech that his trousers are missing. One day the machines simply stopped. Nobody knew why. The few people who had understood how the machines worked had mostly been inside them at the time.

This left Midas.

Midas was a man to whom things happened. Not good things, or even interesting things, but the sort of things that happen to a dropped piece of toast. If there was a sinkhole within forty miles, Midas would find it. If there was a bear, it would be cross. His name, his mother had once explained, was meant to be aspirational. The universe had taken it as a dare.

He shared a converted bus shelter with Chewy.

Chewy was an animatronic koala, manufactured in the Before Time by a company that had believed what children truly wanted was a toy that blinked slowly and said affirming things in an Australian accent. Something had happened to Chewy since. Possibly a lightning strike, possibly sheer stubbornness. He now walked, opinionated, and ran on a solar panel strapped to his back like a tiny, furry, disappointed tortoise.

"Right," said Midas, on the morning in question. "Today's mission."

"Oh good," said Chewy, in a voice like a dying cassette. "I love the missions. Remind me how the last one went?"

"We found tinned peaches."

"We found a tin. Of something. Which you opened with a rock and which turned out to be paint."

"Peach-coloured paint," said Midas, with dignity.

They considered their predicament, which was the usual one. The food was low. The water tasted of the bucket. The bus shelter, though structurally sound, had a timetable on the wall promising the Number 14 at 9:42, and every morning at 9:42 Midas looked up hopefully anyway.¹

"There's the message," Midas said.

The message had appeared on the side of the old water tower two weeks earlier. It said, in large, lurching letters:

**SAFE HAVEN. FOOD. WARM. FOLLOW THE BLUE ARROWS. TRUST THE BEAR.**

"Trust the bear," said Chewy. "That's not a warning. That's a sales pitch."

"It could be a metaphor."

"Midas, the last metaphor you trusted was a dog."

But the blue arrows were real. They led out of town, past the dead car park where the vehicles sat in neat rows like a congregation waiting for a sermon that would never come, and into the wilds. And the wilds, Midas felt, owed him one.

---

The first thing that went wrong was the bridge.

It was a perfectly good bridge. It had survived the collapse, the floods, and a period when a local warlord named Gary had tried to charge a toll on it. It did not survive Midas, who stepped onto it, said, "See? Solid," and fell through the middle with the inevitability of a punchline.

He emerged from the river some time later, festooned with weed.

"That bridge," said Chewy, who had crossed the remaining planks with his usual finicky precision, "was fine until you were confident at it."

The second thing was the goats.

There is a common belief that goats are placid creatures. This belief is held exclusively by people who have never met a goat. The herd that occupied the hillside beyond the river had gone feral in the way only a creature with rectangular pupils can, and they took one look at Midas and recognised him, instinctively, as the sort of person a goat is put on earth to headbutt.

Midas ran. Chewy, who weighed about as much as a bag of sugar and had no smell of fear because he had no smell at all, simply sat on a rock and watched with the expression of a cinemagoer who has paid for popcorn.

"Help!"

"I'm a koala," said Chewy. "My skill set is leaves and judgement."

The third thing was the rain, which arrived in the manner of a guest who has heard there is a party and intends to be the life of it. Chewy's solar panel sulked. His voice dropped an octave and slowed, so that his commentary began to sound like a very tired bishop.

"Midaaaas. The arrooowws. They are going in a ciiiircle."

"Nonsense," said Midas, following one. "They're getting fresher. We must be close."

They were getting fresher. Midas didn't ask himself why. Midas rarely asked himself anything; his brain regarded questions as a sort of optional extra, like heated seats.

And then, as the light failed and the rain gave up out of sheer exhaustion, they came over a ridge and saw it. A low shape. A roof. A small, sheltered haven, half-hidden by brambles, with a painted sign above the entrance.

**NUMBER 14. 9:42.**

There was a long silence. It was the sort of silence that happens in an argument when one party has just been proved catastrophically right and is savouring it like a boiled sweet.

"That's our bus shelter," said Midas.

"Yes."

"We walked in a circle."

"Yes."

"Then who painted the—"

Chewy's eyes blinked, slowly, in the way his manufacturers had promised would soothe a child to sleep. On the end of one small, grubby paw, under the fur, was a smear of blue. Peach-coloured blue, if such a thing could exist. It was the paint from the tin, mixed with something from the river.

"You," said Midas.

"You needed a purpose," said Chewy. "You were staring at that timetable for three hours a day. A person needs a quest. Besides." He gestured, with enormous koala dignity, towards the shelter. "Safe. Warm. And there's food."

"There isn't any food."

"There is now." Chewy reached into the pouch that some long-dead designer had stitched into his tummy, presumably for the storage of affirming cards, and produced three wild apples he had pocketed from the goats' hillside while Midas was busy being headbutted.

"And the bear?"

"I," said Chewy, "am the bear."

"Koalas aren't bears."

"Then you'd better not trust me."

---

They sat in the shelter that night, Midas wet, bruised, and smelling powerfully of goat, Chewy charging dimly under the last of the light. They had been home all along, which was either a profound lesson about the nature of belonging or simply a very long walk. Midas decided not to work out which.

At 9:42 the next morning, he looked up anyway.

---

¹ *Hope, in the post-technological world, was a renewable resource. It was the only one.*

response:
# My Apocalypse Buddy

The world had ended on a Tuesday, which surprised nobody who had ever worked a Tuesday.

It ended gradually. First the phones stopped talking, then the cars stopped going, and finally the people who had promised everything would be back up and running by Thursday stopped promising. What remained was a great deal of quiet, a great many shopping trolleys, and Midas.

Midas lived in what had once been a laundromat. He had chosen it for its sturdy walls, its single defensible door, and its forty-two front-loading washing machines, which made excellent cupboards and, in emergencies, excellent places to hide. He shared it with Chewy.

Chewy was a koala. More precisely, Chewy was an *Interactive Cuddle Companion™ (Koala Edition, Batteries Not Included)*, built by a company whose marketing department had once believed that what children wanted most was a stuffed marsupial that could recognise faces, sing eleven songs, and report usage data to a server in a country nobody could point to. The server was gone. The children were grown or elsewhere. Chewy remained, slightly bald around the ears, with a voice box that had developed opinions somewhere around year three of the collapse.

"We are," said Chewy, "down to one battery."

His eyes glowed a weak, apologetic amber. Chewy's eyes had been designed to express Joy (green), Sleepy (blue), and Let's Play! (pink). Years of solitude, damp, and a lightning storm had expanded the range. Amber now meant *low power*. Red meant *danger*. A sort of bruised purple meant Chewy was lying, which was inconvenient for a creature who lied as often as Chewy did.

"And I," said Midas, "am down to one tin of peaches. Which may be beans. The label's gone."

"Schrödinger's dinner."

"Who?"

"Someone who had a cat. It doesn't matter." Chewy tilted his head with a faint whirr. "The Old Mall. Third floor. The electronics shop."

"The Old Mall has the Congregation in it."

"The Congregation has *batteries* in it."

This was the trouble with Chewy. He was always right about the batteries.

---

The Congregation of the Final Receipt had made their home in the Old Mall's food court, where they worshipped the last vending machine in the city that still lit up. Nobody knew what powered it. The Congregation believed it was faith. Midas suspected a solar panel on the roof, but he had learned that it is unwise to tell a man holding a sharpened mop handle that his god runs on sunshine and loose wiring.

They went in through the loading dock, which went fine. In Midas's experience the beginning of a plan always went fine. It was the plan softening you up.

The escalators had stopped years ago. An escalator that does not move is merely stairs that have given up on themselves, and Midas climbed them with the weary empathy of one failure for another. Chewy rode in his backpack, head poking out like a small, furry periscope.

The electronics shop had been looted, but looters are people, and people are lazy. Behind the counter, under a fallen display of headphones nobody could plug into anything, lay a sealed packet of AA batteries.

Chewy's eyes flared a brilliant, triumphant green. Lit up like that, he could be seen across the whole third floor.

And was.

"*BEHOLD*," boomed a voice from the balcony. "*THE GREEN LIGHT OF DISPENSATION.*"

Midas knew immediately that this was bad. He had never heard the phrase before, but it had capital letters in it, and in his experience nothing good had ever arrived in capitals.

Two minutes later, Midas was standing in the food court, surrounded by about thirty people in robes made from shower curtains. The Congregation's High Cashier, a gaunt woman wearing a crown of folded coupons, regarded Chewy with an expression usually reserved for prophets and surprisingly good sandwiches.

"The Machine glows green when it blesses us," she said. "Your beast glows green. It is a sign."

"He's a koala," said Midas.

"He is an *Envoy*."

Chewy's eyes, sensing an opportunity, shifted to a deep and saintly blue. "I am," he said, "an Envoy."

His eyes flickered purple.

Only for a second. Only around the edges. But the High Cashier had spent years watching the Machine's lights for omens, and a woman like that does not miss a flicker.

"*False prophet*," she whispered.

"Now hang on," said Midas, in the tone of a man about to make things worse. "Technically he never said what he was an envoy *of*—"

---

The Congregation chased them through Homewares, Ladies' Footwear, and the cosmetics counter, where Midas ran face-first into a cloud of something called *Midnight Orchid* that hadn't lost an ounce of potency in a decade. They were cornered on the second-floor balcony above the fountain, which no longer ran but still held six feet of green water and the accumulated wishes of a thousand dead pennies.

"Plan?" gasped Midas.

"Yes," said Chewy, and turned red.

Chewy's plan, it emerged, was that Midas should jump into the fountain while Chewy distracted the Congregation. Chewy did this by flashing every colour he possessed at once, singing "If You're Happy and You Know It" at maximum volume, and throwing himself off the opposite balcony.

He would have hit the floor, except that a large and ill-tempered seagull, which had been nesting in the skylight and had very strong feelings about singing, took him in its talons and departed through a broken pane.

Midas, meanwhile, discovered that the fountain was deeper than it looked and connected to a storm drain. The storm drain went to the river, and the river went, eventually and reluctantly, past the laundromat.

---

So they came home in several ways.

Midas came home by water at dusk, carrying the batteries and much of the river, and smelling of Midnight Orchid and things that should not be named.

Chewy came home by air shortly afterwards, released over the laundromat roof by a seagull that had finally worked out he wasn't edible, and was in no mood to be sung at further.

Midas's dignity came home last, by a long and winding route, and has not entirely unpacked.

That night, Chewy's eyes glowed a fresh, well-fed green. Midas opened the tin.

It was beans.

"Tomorrow," said Chewy, "we should go back for the vending machine."

His eyes, Midas noted, were not purple at all.
