response:
# My Apocalypse Buddy

The world had ended on a Tuesday, which surprised nobody who had ever worked through one.

It had not ended with a bang, or even a whimper, but with a sort of polite electronic cough, the noise a toaster makes when it decides it has given enough. All over the planet, machines simply stopped. The clever ones stopped first, having thought about it the longest.

This was why Midas found it so galling that the only machine still running was Chewy.

Chewy was a koala. More precisely, Chewy was an Animo-Tronic Cuddle Companion™ (Model K, Eucalyptus Edition), and he had been designed by a committee of people who had never met a child and believed them to be a kind of small, sticky customer. He had glass eyes, a voice box with the tone of a game-show host under heavy sedation, and fur that had once been grey and was now best described as *experienced*.

He also had two AA batteries, and they were dying.

"Right," said Midas, from the depths of the overturned bathtub that served as both bed and panic room in their home base, a former drive-through restaurant called, according to the surviving letters, URG. "Options."

Chewy's head turned with a sound like a reluctant drawer. "*Now available in family size,*" he said.

"Yes. Thank you. Very helpful."

Midas was a man with a gift. His namesake, according to the old stories, had turned everything he touched to gold. Midas turned everything he touched into an *incident*. He had once picked up a perfectly ordinary stick and, by a chain of events that took nine days and involved a goose, burned down a bridge that nobody had known was flammable. He had not set out to do it. He never set out to do anything. Trouble simply found him the way water finds the one cardboard box containing everything you care about.

"The Mall," Midas said. "Old Teg says there's a shop on the second level. Batteries. Hundreds of them. Little blister packs, all in a row, untouched because nobody can work out how to open them."

"*Some assembly required,*" said Chewy.

"Exactly. We go in, we get the batteries, we come home. No detours. No being clever. No goose."

There is a rule in the universe, little known but very strictly enforced, that any plan containing the words "we come home" will indeed bring you home, just not in the manner, order, or number of pieces you'd hoped for.¹

---

The Mall rose from the weeds like a beached concrete whale that had died of embarrassment. They went in through the food court, where the air still carried a faint ghost of cinnamon and despair.

The first thing to go wrong was the escalator.

It wasn't working, of course. Nothing worked. But a tribe of people had made their home around its foot, and somewhere in the long dark years they had decided that the frozen metal staircase was a god. They called it the Ascending One. They left offerings on its lowest step: shoes, mostly, and the occasional regretful cat.

The second thing to go wrong was Chewy.

As Midas edged past the shrine, smiling the smile of a man who would very much like everyone to stay calm, Chewy's voice box gave a crackle and announced, at full volume:

"*THE STAIRWAY TO SAVINGS IS NOW OPEN!*"

There was a silence of the very particular kind that comes just before a religion gets a new prophet.

"Ah," said Midas.

Within ten minutes Chewy had been placed on a throne made of shopping baskets, and Midas had been appointed his Holy Bearer, a position that apparently involved standing very still while people sang at him. The tribe's high priestess, a woman with a lanyard that said VISITOR, asked the Furred Oracle what the Ascending One demanded.

"*Limited time only,*" said Chewy.

This caused some alarm.

"*Act now!*"

This caused more.

The tribe concluded, after a theological debate that lasted almost forty seconds, that the god wanted to *move*. The god wanted to *ascend*. And since the god could not move itself, they would help. With ropes. And Midas. Mostly Midas.

He would later point out that he had not touched anything. This was true right up until the moment he grabbed the handrail to steady himself, and something deep in the escalator, some last spring wound tight since the before time, went *tunk*.

The Ascending One ascended. Briefly. Then it descended, a great deal faster, into the basement level, taking a good part of the floor with it.

---

What happened next is best told in the order things arrived home.

Chewy's body came first. It had been sitting in a shopping trolley at the top of the car park when the floor gave way, and the trolley, sensing its moment at last, set off down the long hill toward URG with the grim purpose of a thing that has waited forty years to finally be pushed. It hit the drive-through sign, flung its passenger through the order window, and came to rest in the ornamental pond, where it is still serving as a home to several grateful frogs.

Chewy's head came second, about an hour later, carried in the beak of an enormous and deeply confused crow, which had snatched it from the rubble in the belief that glass eyes were the most valuable thing in the world. The crow dropped it on the roof when the head said "*Your call is important to us*," and flew away to rethink its whole life.

Midas came last, at dusk, out of the storm drain, as most of his journeys tended to end. He was soaked, scraped, missing one boot, and wearing a lanyard that said VISITOR, because the tribe had decided he was now cursed and should be marked as such.

In his fist was a single blister pack of batteries.

He sat down heavily beside Chewy's reunited body and head, fished out a rusty knife, and spent twenty minutes opening the packet, which was harder than anything else he'd done all day.

They were nine-volt.

Midas looked at them for a long time. Then he looked at the koala.

Chewy's eyes rolled toward him with a whir that sounded almost sympathetic, and in a voice now so faint it was barely more than a breath, he said:

"*Batteries not included.*"

"Yeah," said Midas, lying back against the cold ground as the stars came out over the dead world. "I'd noticed."

---

¹ *This rule also applies to the phrases "it'll only take a minute," "what's the worst that could happen," and "hold my drink."*

prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge
Genre: Surreal Horror

JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered.

The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way.

Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it.

JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes.  JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move.

And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse.

JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head.

Writing Instructions:
Continue with the next chapter of the story, maintaining a style reminiscent of Stephen King—grounded realism blended seamlessly with unsettling surrealism. The atmosphere should convey subtle dread, isolation, and psychological ambiguity. JT's perspective is crucial, yet he is an unreliable narrator, caught in uncertainty about what he's perceiving. Include a mention of an abandoned hunting cabin, rumored to be inhabited by an unknown presence. Establish an undertone of creeping dread, establishing the isolation of JT's perspective, which he largely keeps to himself. Incorporate some dialogue. Build tension towards a payoff. 1000 words.
response:
**Chapter Two: The Tremblay Place**

Supper that night was venison chili from a Tupperware tub his mother had packed, reheated on the old Coleman range until the bottom scorched. Nobody complained. Nobody said much of anything. The propane lamp hissed on its hook above the table, throwing their shadows long against the knotty pine, and JT found himself watching those shadows more than the faces that cast them. Stupid. A grown man of nineteen, scared of shadows. But it seemed to him that his father's shadow moved a half-beat behind his father, the way the sound in a badly dubbed movie trails the lips.

*You're tired. You're tired and you're cold and you saw something weird in the clearing, which was probably nothing, and now your brain's making a meal of it.*

"Good chili," Mike said finally.

"Your mother's," their father said. He hadn't touched his. He was turning the spoon over and over in his fingers, the lamplight catching the bowl of it, flash, flash, flash.

JT cleared his throat. "That buck today. In the clearing. You had him, Dad. He was right there."

The spoon stopped.

For a moment the only sound was the lamp and the wind fingering the eaves. His father looked up, and JT would think about that look later, lying awake in the bunk, because it wasn't anger and it wasn't embarrassment. It was the polite, patient blankness of a man who's been asked for directions to a town he's never heard of.

"What buck?" his father said.

Mike laughed, a short bark with nothing behind it. "JT's seeing things. Tell him about the Tremblay place, Dad. That'll really get him going."

And just like that the moment slid away, smooth as a fish going back into dark water. JT let it go. He always let it go.

His father leaned back, and something like his old self came into his face, the storyteller who used to scare them half to death on this very porch when they were kids. "Lyle Tremblay," he said. "Trapped this whole country, back when you could still make a living at it. Had a cabin up past the beaver ponds, maybe two miles north. Fall of seventy-nine, he walks out his front door and doesn't come back. Left the coffee on the stove. Left his boots."

"Left his boots," Mike repeated, grinning, like this was the punchline.

"Game warden went up there that winter. Said the place was clean as a church. Said there were tracks in the snow all around it, circling and circling." His father's voice had gone softer. "Caribou tracks. Hundreds of them. And not a single one leading away."

"Somebody's living up there now," Mike said. "Rollie Dufresne at the Irving station said he saw smoke from the chimney last month. Said there's a light in the window some nights."

"Squatter," JT said.

"Sure," his father said. "Squatter." And he smiled, and JT saw that his teeth were very white in the lamplight, and very even, and he couldn't remember if they'd always been that way.

---

He didn't sleep. Around two the wind dropped off to nothing, and the silence that came after it was worse, a silence so complete JT could hear the blood ticking in his ears. He lay in the top bunk listening to his brother breathe below him. Slow. Deep. In, and out.

Like the buck in the clearing, chest rising and falling.

At some point he realized he couldn't hear his father's snoring from the other room. His father had snored every night of JT's life, a sound like a chainsaw idling, a sound their mother had threatened divorce over at least once a year. Now nothing.

JT climbed down. The floorboards were ice under his socks. His father's bunk was empty, the wool blanket folded square at the foot of it, military neat. His father had never folded a blanket in his life.

Through the window he could see the yard silvered by a fat moon, and the tree line beyond, black as a held breath. And there, just at the edge of the woods, his father's red-and-black Woolrich coat, moving away north. Toward the beaver ponds.

He should have woken Mike. He knew that later, and maybe he knew it then. But when he turned to the lower bunk, Mike's eyes were open. Open and fixed on the ceiling, catching the moonlight, unblinking. His chest went in and out, in and out.

"Mike?" JT whispered.

Nothing.

JT pulled on his boots without lacing them and went out the door.

---

The path to the ponds was the one they'd walked a hundred times, but in the moonlight it seemed longer, the spruce crowding closer, branches touching overhead like the fingers of clasped hands. He lost sight of the Woolrich coat almost immediately. He kept going anyway. He couldn't have said why. Some part of him had already decided, the way your foot decides the stair is there in the dark.

The tracks started at the second pond. Caribou, split-hoofed and broad, pressed into the frost-stiff mud. A few at first, then dozens, then so many they churned the ground to soup, all heading the same way he was.

The Tremblay cabin sat in a hollow among the birches, smaller than he'd imagined, roof swaybacked, one window glowing a dull, buttery yellow. Smoke rose straight up from the chimney into the windless air.

JT crept to the window. His heart was going so hard he could feel it in his teeth.

Inside, by the light of a single oil lamp, a man sat at a plank table with his back to the glass. Red-and-black Woolrich. Gray hair cut short, the same cowlick at the crown JT had seen every day of his life. Across from him, filling the far end of the room, its antlers scraping the rafters, stood the buck. Its dark, flat eyes were on the man. The man was nodding slowly, the way you nod when someone is telling you something you've been waiting years to hear.

*Dad,* JT thought. *Dad, get out of there.*

A hand settled on his shoulder.

It was a heavy hand, warm even through his jacket, and it smelled of gun oil and Old Spice and woodsmoke. It smelled like his father.

"You shouldn't have come up here alone, Jayce," his father said, behind him, gently. "Nobody comes up here alone."

JT didn't turn around. Through the window, the man at the table hadn't moved. The cowlick. The coat.

The hand on his shoulder squeezed, kind, patient.

"Turn around, son," his father said. "Let me look at you."

And slowly, because his body no longer seemed to be asking his permission, JT began to turn.

**Chapter Two: The Quiet**

Supper that night was Dinty Moore stew out of the can, heated on the woodstove in the same dented pot his mother had sent north with them every year since before JT was born. She hadn't come up in six years, not since the divorce, but the pot still made the trip. Some things you just kept doing because stopping felt like admitting something.

His father ate slowly, hunched over the bowl the way he always did, elbows planted like fence posts. Mike shoveled his food down and reached for the bread. The Coleman lantern hissed on the table between them, throwing their shadows up the log walls, huge and wavering, and outside the wind combed through the spruce with a sound like someone breathing through their teeth.

Nobody had said a word about the clearing. Not on the walk back, not while they'd cleaned the rifles, not now.

JT pushed a chunk of potato around his bowl. *Just let it go,* a voice in his head advised. It sounded a lot like his own voice, only older and more tired. *Let it go and in ten days you'll be home and none of this will matter.*

"Saw a big one today," he said instead. "Didn't I? Out past the ridge."

His father's spoon paused. Just for a second, maybe less. Then it went on to his mouth, and he chewed, and swallowed.

"Didn't see much of anything today," he said.

"In the clearing, though. The buck. You were right up on it." JT heard his own voice going thin and reedy, a kid's voice, and he hated it. "You could've touched it."

Mike laughed, a short bark that didn't have much in it. "You were back there tying your shoes like a first-grader, Jaybird. You didn't see squat."

"I saw it."

"Wasn't a clean angle," his father said. He set the spoon down very carefully, lining it up with the edge of the bowl. "Sometimes you don't get a clean angle. That's hunting."

"Dad, it was *right there.*"

His father looked at him then, and JT felt the rest of the sentence dry up in his throat. It wasn't anger in the old man's face. JT knew anger; anger he could have handled. This was something flatter. Something patient. The look of a man waiting for a noise to stop so he could go back to listening for something else.

"Eat your supper," his father said.

JT ate his supper.

---

He didn't sleep so much as drift, bobbing just under the surface of it like a fishing float. The bunkroom smelled of mothballs and old woodsmoke and Mike's feet. Somewhere around what his Timex told him was 2:40, he surfaced all the way and lay there listening, trying to figure out what had woken him.

The wind had died. That was part of it. The woods outside had gone so quiet that JT could hear the faint high whine of his own blood in his ears.

And under that, a creak. The porch.

He told himself it was the cabin settling. Old buildings talked to themselves in the cold; everybody knew that. He told himself that for maybe thirty seconds, and then he looked across the room at his father's bunk and saw the blankets thrown back and the mattress empty, and he stopped telling himself anything at all.

The floor was ice under his socks. He moved through the main room by feel, past the stove ticking as it cooled, past the gun rack where three rifles stood in their slots. Three. His father hadn't taken a gun.

The front door stood open about a foot. Moonlight lay across the floorboards in a long pale bar.

JT put his eye to the gap.

His father stood at the bottom of the porch steps in his long johns, barefoot in the frost. His back was to the cabin. His arms hung loose at his sides, and his head was tilted slightly, the way a dog tilts its head when it hears its name spoken in another room.

Beyond him, at the edge of the trees, the caribou were waiting.

JT couldn't count them. Twenty, maybe. Maybe more back in the shadows where the moonlight didn't reach. They stood in a loose line along the treeline, perfectly still, their breath rising in slow white plumes that hung in the air and didn't drift. Their eyes caught the moon and gave nothing back. Not the green shine of a deer in headlights. Nothing. Like holes cut in the night.

His father was talking. JT could see his jaw moving, could hear the low murmur of it but not the words. It had the rhythm of something rehearsed. A prayer, maybe, or the kind of half-singing his mother used to do over a sick child.

The big buck from the clearing stepped forward out of the line.

*Wake up,* JT thought. *This is a dream, you're in your bunk, wake UP—*

His father took a step toward it. Then another. The frost crunched under his bare heels.

"Dad." It came out a whisper. JT pushed the door wider, and the hinges let out a long rusty shriek that seemed to go on forever. "*Dad.*"

His father stopped.

Slowly—so slowly—he turned his head and looked back over his shoulder at the cabin. At the door. At JT.

His father's eyes were dark and flat and calm. They caught the moon and gave nothing back.

"Go to bed, Jason," he said, in a perfectly ordinary voice. "You're letting the cold in."

JT didn't remember shutting the door. He didn't remember getting back to his bunk. He remembered only lying there with the blanket pulled to his chin, shaking so hard his teeth clicked, listening for footsteps on the porch that never came.

---

In the morning his father was at the stove frying bacon, whistling something tuneless, the coffee percolator burbling beside him. Mike was lacing his boots. The day was bright and blue and utterly normal.

JT stood in the bunkroom doorway and looked at his father's feet. He was wearing his wool socks, the gray ones with the red heels.

"Sleep okay, bud?" his father asked, not turning around.

"Fine," JT said.

He didn't ask. He didn't say anything about the porch, or the treeline, or the eyes. He sat at the table and ate his bacon and kept his mouth shut, because that was always safer.

But when his father finally turned to set the pan on the table, JT saw the soles of those gray wool socks, and they were black with mud, and tangled in the wool, here and there, were coarse pale hairs—the long, hollow hairs of a caribou's winter coat.

**Chapter Two: What Dale Knew**

Dale Thibodeau had guided for the family since before JT was born. He was a big, loose-jointed man with a laugh like a dropped toolbox. He would talk your ear off about anything: the price of diesel, his ex-wife's new husband, the year the Habs should've won the Cup. Every season JT could count on Dale planting himself at the end of the long pine table after supper, beer in hand, telling the same stories with new lies stitched in.

This year Dale didn't come in for supper at all.

JT saw him through the kitchen window, sitting in the cab of his rust-eaten Silverado at the far edge of the gravel lot. The engine was running, and the dome light was off. The tip of a cigarette brightened and dimmed, brightened and dimmed, like something breathing in the dark.

"Dale not hungry?" JT asked.

His father didn't look up from his plate. He was cutting his venison steak, the last of the meat they'd brought up from home, into very small, very even squares. He'd been doing it for a while. The squares were nearly the size of dice.

"Dale's his own man," his father said.

Mike laughed at that, though it wasn't funny. Then he went quiet again and stared at the window over the sink, where there was nothing to see but his own reflection and the black wall of spruce behind it.

JT ate. He made himself. The refrigerator hummed and the woodstove ticked, and every so often the old lodge groaned the way old buildings do when the temperature drops, a settling sound, a shifting of weight. Normal sounds. He'd heard them every autumn of his life. Tonight they seemed to come from slightly too far away, as if the lodge were bigger on the inside than he remembered.

*You're tired,* he told himself. *You didn't sleep in the truck and you didn't sleep last night either. That's all this is.*

After supper his father sent him out for firewood. The cold hit him like a slap, and he stood on the porch a moment letting his eyes adjust. The moon hung above the tree line, swollen and lopsided, almost full but not quite, like a face with one cheek caved in.

The Silverado's door creaked open.

"Hey. Kid." Dale's voice was low and flat. "C'mere a sec."

JT crossed the gravel with his arms wrapped around himself. Up close, Dale looked bad. His face had a gray, sweated-through look, and his eyes kept sliding past JT toward the lodge, toward the lit kitchen window.

"You fellas get anything today?"

"No," JT said. "Not today."

"Huh." Dale dragged on the cigarette. His hand wasn't steady. "Your dad have a shot?"

JT thought about the clearing. The buck's flat, calm eyes. His father's trembling hand reaching out, the rifle hanging forgotten at his side.

"I don't know," he said. "I was behind. Bootlace."

Dale looked at him for a long moment, and JT had the uncomfortable feeling that the man could see straight through the lie and out the back of his skull.

"Listen to me," Dale said. "Moon's full Thursday. You get your people packed up and gone by Wednesday night. I don't care if you got your tags filled or not. I don't care what your dad says."

"Why?"

"Because I'm telling you."

"That's not a reason."

Dale's jaw worked. Somewhere out in the trees, a branch snapped. It was a heavy sound, something with weight behind it. Dale flinched so hard the cigarette jumped out of his fingers and landed sparking on the floor mat. He didn't reach for it.

"They used to run," he said, very quietly. "You know that? Whole time I been doing this, they run. You get maybe one look, then they're gone. That's how it's supposed to be." He swallowed. "This year they come right up. Stand there like they're waiting. Like they're the ones doing the hunting and they're just being polite about it."

"Dale—"

"Did he touch it?"

The question hung between them. JT's mouth went dry.

"Did your father touch it, kid?"

"No," JT said. "I told you, I didn't see."

Dale nodded slowly, like a man accepting a diagnosis. He reached over, pulled the door shut, and through the glass JT watched him finally stamp out the cigarette with one boot, grinding it down long after it was dead.

JT carried the wood inside. His father and Mike were sitting at the table exactly as he'd left them. He told himself they had moved while he was gone. Of course they had. People didn't just sit like that.

---

He woke sometime after two with his bladder aching and the room washed silver. The moon had come around to his window.

The bunk across from his was empty. Mike's sleeping bag lay flat and unzipped.

JT padded down the hall in his socks. The front door stood open, and a long wedge of frozen air reached into the lodge. His father and Mike were standing out on the porch in their long johns, barefoot on boards white with frost, facing the tree line.

Neither of them was shivering.

Beyond them, at the edge of the gravel lot where the moonlight gave out, JT saw shapes. Pale smudges. He counted six, then nine, then stopped counting. They were caribou, standing in a ragged line along the dark margin of the trees, perfectly still, their breath rising in slow plumes. Every head was turned toward the lodge. Toward the porch.

His father was humming. It was low and tuneless, almost a lullaby.

JT's mind did the thing it had done in the clearing. It shouted at him to turn around, go back to bed, pull the bag over his head like a little kid. And this time he listened. He backed down the hallway one careful step at a time, crawled into his bunk, and lay there with his heart slamming. He told himself it was a dream. He told himself that until the window went gray.

---

In the morning, Dale's truck was gone. There were no tire tracks in the frost, just a dark rectangle of bare gravel where it had been parked.

His father was at the stove frying eggs, whistling. Mike was setting the table. Both of them were cheerful, rested, pink-cheeked, like men coming back from a long vacation.

"Dale took off early," his father said. "Said he had family business. Doesn't matter. We know these woods."

He set a plate in front of JT and smiled. Up close, in the gray morning light, his father's eyes looked darker than JT remembered. They were flat and calm, and endlessly patient.

"They're not afraid of us anymore, Jayje," his father said softly, almost tenderly. "Isn't that something?"

Outside the window, at the edge of the trees, something pale stood watching.

Three days until the full moon.

# Carnival of Dangerous Intentions

The sodium lamps along the boardwalk could not decide whether to stay lit. They buzzed, guttered, and caught again, each flare washing the planks a sickly amber before dropping them back into blue dusk. Beyond the railing the Atlantic heaved itself onto the sand, and behind her the Wonder Wheel began its slow revolution, its cars swinging like censers in a church she had no business entering.

Margaret Hale held her pocketbook in both hands, as though someone might snatch it.

He was already there. Of course he was.

He leaned against the counter of the shooting gallery with a rifle cradled loosely in the crook of his arm. His jacket was off and his shirtsleeves were rolled to the elbow. Behind him the tin ducks clattered along their track, bright yellow and unbothered. He wasn't shooting. He was watching the mouth of the boardwalk, and when the lamp above him stuttered back to life, she saw that he was watching her.

*Turn around. Walk to the station. Be home before Arthur telephones.*

She did not turn around.

"You came," he said, when she was close enough that he needn't raise his voice over the calliope.

"I said I would."

"People say all sorts of things on Tuesdays." The light failed, and for a moment his face was nothing but the suggestion of a jaw and those dark eyes. Then it flickered back and split him into amber and shadow. "I didn't think a girl like you kept promises to men like me."

"And what sort of man are you?"

He smiled. It was not a reassuring smile. "The sort you came back to see."

The barker, a heavy man with a cigar gone cold in his teeth, looked between them and found something else to do at the far end of the counter.

*His locks.* There it was again, that ridiculous phrase from some novel her mother had hidden under the mattress. The sea wind had pulled one curl loose across his forehead, and she wanted very badly to push it back. She tightened her grip on the pocketbook instead.

"I don't know your name," she said.

"No."

"That doesn't strike you as strange?"

"It strikes me as careful." He turned the rifle over in his hands and studied the sight. "I know yours, Miss Hale. Margaret. Not yet Mrs. Arthur Whitcomb, though the announcement ran in the *Times* on the fourth of June. Page twenty-two. Lovely photograph."

The planks seemed to tilt under her heels. "How do you know that?"

"I read the papers."

"That isn't an answer."

"It's the only one that won't frighten you." He held the rifle out to her, stock first. "Have you ever fired one?"

"Of course not."

"Then tonight you have something to confess." He waited. The lamp buzzed overhead like a trapped wasp. "Go on. It's only ducks."

*It's only ducks.* She set the pocketbook on the counter and took the rifle. It was heavier than she'd expected, warm where his hands had been.

"Arthur is an assistant district attorney," she said, more to herself than to him.

"I know."

"He's prosecuting the Ferrante brothers this autumn."

"I know that too." He stepped behind her, not touching her, close enough that she felt the heat of him through the thin cotton of her dress. "Lift your elbow. No, higher. Now put your cheek against the stock."

She did. "Is that why you spoke to me? Last Tuesday, at the frozen custard stand. That wasn't an accident, was it?"

"Breathe out slowly. Squeeze, don't pull."

"Answer me."

His breath stirred the hair at her nape. "No. It wasn't an accident."

She fired. The crack was smaller than she'd imagined, and a yellow duck spun backward off its rail with a hollow *tonk*.

"There," he murmured. "You're a natural."

She lowered the rifle and turned. The lamp chose that moment to die completely, and in the sudden dark he was only a voice and a shape and the faint smell of tobacco and salt. "Are you one of them? The Ferrantes' people?"

"Would it matter?"

"Yes." She heard how unconvincing it sounded. "It ought to."

"*Ought* to." The light returned, jaundiced and wavering, and she saw he was no longer smiling. "That's a very different word, Margaret."

"Don't call me that."

"What should I call you?"

She had no answer. Down the boardwalk a girl shrieked with laughter on the Cyclone, and the sound unspooled into the dark like ribbon.

"Tell me your name," she said. "If you want anything from me at all, tell me that much."

He considered her for a long moment. "Nico."

"Is that your real name?"

"It's the one I'm giving you."

"That isn't the same thing."

"No," he agreed. "But it's more than I've given anyone else in a long while."

*He's lying.* She knew it with perfect certainty. *Or he isn't, and that's worse.*

He took the rifle gently from her hands and laid it on the counter beside her pocketbook. "Arthur will ask where you were tonight."

"I'll tell him I went to the pictures with Dorothy."

"Good. You lie well."

"I've never lied to him before tonight."

He tilted his head, and the flickering light caught the edge of something knowing in his face. "Yes, you have. You told him you loved him."

The words struck harder than the rifle's kick. She ought to slap him. She ought to gather her pocketbook and her dignity and take the BMT home to Brooklyn Heights, to the ring in its velvet box and the man who would one day be district attorney and the life laid out before her like a table setting.

"You don't know anything about me," she said.

"I know you came back." He held out his hand, palm up, an invitation and a dare. Above them the Wonder Wheel turned, patient and enormous. "Ride with me. One turn. Then you can go home and decide what I am."

*One turn.* The lamp sputtered. In the stuttering dark between flashes she could not tell whether his eyes held tenderness or calculation, and she understood with a sick, bright thrill that she did not want to know.

She left her pocketbook on the counter and took his hand.

# Carnival of Dangerous Intentions

The rifles at the shooting gallery were chained to the counter, and he leaned on one as though the chain were a formality meant for other men.

Clara stayed half-hidden beneath a striped awning and watched him take aim. Tin ducks lurched along their track, *clank, clank, clank*, beneath a painted sky flaking in the salt air. Behind her the Wonder Wheel groaned into another revolution, and somewhere a calliope wheezed out "The Way You Look Tonight," slightly flat. The boardwalk smelled of brine, frying dough, and the tar that went soft underfoot in July.

He fired five times. Five ducks went down.

*Go home.* The thought arrived clear and sensible, in her mother's voice. She had told Harold she was visiting her sister in Flatbush. On the BMT she had turned her engagement ring around so the diamond pressed into her palm, and she could feel it now through her glove, a small, hard secret.

"You came back," he said, without turning.

Her heart did something undignified. "I was passing."

"Through Coney Island. At dusk. In your good gloves." He set the rifle down and finally looked at her. The dark eyes were exactly as she remembered, which was a disappointment. She had hoped memory had exaggerated. "Nobody passes through here, miss. They come on purpose or they don't come."

"You don't know what I do."

"No," he agreed pleasantly. "That's what makes it interesting."

The barker, a heavy man working a toothpick, pushed a stuffed bear across the counter. The stranger didn't take it. He tilted his head toward Clara, and the barker, grinning, held it out to her.

"I don't want it."

"Then don't take it." He came toward her with his hands in his pockets, curls falling across his brow in a way that would have looked boyish on anyone else. On him it looked like a decision. "But you'll stand there and think about it. You think about everything."

"And I suppose you think about nothing."

"Very little. It saves time." He stopped close, closer than a stranger should, though not as close as she had feared. Not as close as she had hoped. She refused to examine which. "Walk with me."

"I don't even know your name."

"You didn't know it last Saturday either. It didn't stop you promising."

That was true, and unforgivable of him to say.

They walked. The crowd thinned past the gallery, where the boardwalk bent toward the darker end of the midway. Here stood a narrow booth draped in faded purple velvet, its sign hand-lettered in gold: **MADAME ILONA — THE PAST IS WRITTEN. THE FUTURE IS EXTRA.** A CLOSED placard hung crooked on the curtain. Tacked beside it, curling at the corners, were palmistry charts: great pale hands mapped like foreign countries, every crease labeled in a spidery script. *Line of Heart. Line of Fate. Girdle of Venus.* One hand bore a single red ink mark where the lifeline forked.

He stopped there as if he had meant to all along.

"Madame Ilona's gone to supper," he said. "Shame. She's very good. She told a cop last summer he'd die by water, and he drowned in a bathtub in September."

"That's a terrible story."

"It's a true one. Most of the true ones are terrible." He nodded at the charts. "Give me your hand."

"I'd rather not."

"You're wearing gloves. What could I possibly see?"

*Everything*, she thought, and wondered when she had become a woman who thought such things about a man on a boardwalk. Two weeks ago her greatest daring had been a second sherry at the Whitcombs' Easter dinner. She had sat beside Harold while his father talked about the Board of Estimate, and she had smiled until her face ached.

She held out her hand.

He didn't take it at once. He unbuttoned the little pearl at her wrist, slowly, as if he had all the time in the world, and peeled the glove down finger by finger. The air off the ocean was cool on her skin. Then he turned her hand palm up, and the diamond lay there, glittering foolishly in the carnival light.

Neither of them spoke. The calliope started the song over.

"Well," he said at last, softly. "Look at that. Your heart line runs right into a rock."

"It's not what you think."

"I think it's a carat and a quarter, Tiffany setting, and I think Harold Whitcomb paid too much for it." He traced the line of her palm with one fingertip, not quite touching the ring. "His father would have told him to."

The cold went all the way through her. "How do you know Harold?"

"I know a lot of names. It comes with the work."

"What work?"

"The kind that pays on Saturdays." His thumb rested at the center of her palm now, over the spot the chart called the Plain of Mars. Warm. Patient. "Don't look like that. I'm not going to tell him."

"Tell him what? I haven't *done* anything."

"No." He raised his eyes to hers. "Not yet."

She ought to have pulled away. She was aware of this the way one is aware of a train platform's edge, a firm and reasonable fact. Down the boardwalk, someone at the gallery hit three ducks and missed two, and the barker's laughter carried on the wind.

"Does Harold know you?" she asked.

"Harold knows *of* me. Most people prefer it that way."

"Then why me?"

For the first time something moved behind his expression, there and gone like a fish under dark water. "Because you were standing alone by the Steeplechase last week looking like you'd been let out of a box, and I wanted to see what you'd do with the lid off." He folded her fingers closed over the ring, gently, and handed back her glove. "Turns out you come back."

"Tell me your name."

He smiled. It was a lovely smile, and it frightened her more than anything else he'd done.

"Ask me again next Saturday."

He walked away into the lights. Clara stood before the palmistry charts with her bare hand clenched around the diamond, the red mark on the lifeline glaring at her, and knew, with a certainty Madame Ilona herself might have envied, that she would.

# Carnival of Dangerous Intentions

The gallery was a long counter of scarred mahogany. Beyond it, tin ducks paraded on a clanking chain, their painted eyes bright and stupid. Beside it, a vendor spun sugar into pink clouds, and the smell reached her before she could brace against it: burnt sweetness, a kitchen she had never stood in, a hand that wasn't her mother's closing around her small wrist. Then it was gone, the way it always went, like a door shut softly in another room.

"You came."

He was leaning against the gallery post as if he'd been planted there, a rifle cradled loosely in the crook of his arm. In the electric light the curls looked wet. His sleeves were rolled to the elbow, which no gentleman would do on a public boardwalk, and he seemed to know it.

"I said I would."

"People say all sorts of things on Thursdays." He smiled, but only at one corner. "Saturdays are when we find out what they meant."

Margaret tightened her grip on her pocketbook. Inside it, wrapped in a handkerchief, was the ring Charles had given her at Easter. She had taken it off on the subway at Atlantic Avenue and had not let herself think about why.

"I don't know your name," she said.

"No. You don't." He turned, sighted down the barrel, and fired. A duck went over with a tinny clank. "Does that trouble you?"

"It should."

"That isn't what I asked."

The barker, a heavy man with a toothpick, glanced between them and found something interesting in his cash box.

*Leave,* she thought. *Walk to Surf Avenue, take the train home, put the ring back on before Mother sees your bare hand.* The instructions arranged themselves neatly, the way her whole life arranged itself. She did not move.

"It troubles me a little," she admitted.

"Good. A little is honest." He fired again. Another duck fell. "Here. Try."

"I've never held a gun."

"Then you've never held a gun *yet*." He held it out, stock first. When she didn't take it, he stepped behind her, not touching, not quite, and set it in her hands himself. His breath smelled of peppermint and something sharper underneath. Rye, perhaps. "Shoulder there. No, closer. It kicks, and it doesn't care whose collarbone it finds."

"You speak as though it has opinions."

"Everything has opinions, Miss Whitlow. Most things just keep them to themselves."

The rifle dipped. She turned her head, and his face was very near. "I never told you my name."

"Didn't you?"

"You know I didn't."

He considered her with those dark, unhurried eyes, as though she were a sum he'd already solved and was only checking. "Your father's name is on the side of a building on Pearl Street. You have his chin. It wasn't difficult."

Cold slid down the back of her neck, and beneath it, shamefully, something warm.

"Were you looking for me that night on the pier?"

"I was looking at the water. Then I was looking at you." He reached around her and nudged the barrel up half an inch. His knuckles grazed her wrist. *The same wrist,* she thought absurdly, the one the hand in the cotton-candy memory had held. "Breathe out. Then squeeze. Don't pull. Pulling is for people who want to be seen trying."

She breathed out. She squeezed. The crack startled her more than the kick, and a duck at the end of the line spun on its hinge and went down.

"There," he said softly. "Now you know something about yourself you didn't know this morning."

"That I can shoot tin ducks?"

"That you like it."

She set the rifle on the counter with more care than it needed. "What do you want from me?"

"Who says I want anything?"

"Men who know my father's buildings always want something."

That earned her a real smile, quick and wolfish, gone as soon as it came. "You're sharper than they give you credit for at those dinner parties."

"You've never been to one of my dinner parties."

"No," he agreed. "But I've delivered to the back door of a few."

*Delivered what?* She didn't ask. Repeal was four years gone, but men with rolled sleeves and rye on their breath hadn't stopped delivering. They had only changed what was in the crates. She thought of her father's late telephone calls, the study door locked, the way Charles went quiet whenever certain names came up at the club.

"Is that a threat?" she asked.

"It's a fact. You collect those, don't you? I watched you on the pier. You looked at everything like you were memorizing it for an exam." He paid the barker without looking at him and lifted something from the prize shelf: a cheap glass locket on a chain, red as a cherry stone. He held it up so the lights ran through it. "Ride the Wonder Wheel with me."

"I'm engaged."

"I know." He didn't lower the locket. "I didn't ask you to marry me. I asked you to ride a wheel."

She should have said no. She heard herself say instead, "The swinging cars. Not the stationary ones."

His eyebrows rose a fraction. "Now who's dangerous?"

She took the locket. The chain was warm from his hand. Behind them the vendor spun another cloud, and the smell came again: the hand on her wrist, a man's low voice saying *don't tell your mother*. This time she nearly had it. She nearly saw the face, and she wasn't sure she wanted to.

"What's your name?" she asked.

He offered his arm, a gentleman's gesture from a man who had made no pretense of being one.

"Ask me at the top," he said, "if you still want to know."

Above the boardwalk, the Wonder Wheel turned slowly against the purpling sky, its cars swinging out over nothing. Margaret took his arm.

response:
# Lost & Found in Osaka

The guitar cut through Den Den Town like a blade through paper: through the electronic chirp of the arcade, the shouting hawkers outside the used-PC shops, and the bass leaking from a figure store. Kanade stopped walking. The bag holding the secondhand Korg volca she'd spent three months saving for swung against her knee.

She knew the song in four notes. *A Cruel Angel's Thesis.* But it was wrong in a way that made her chest tight. It was faster, and dirtier, and somehow it was *better*.

The girl playing it stood beside the arcade entrance in a denim jacket covered in patches. Her bleached hair was pinned up with what looked like a chopstick. She finished on a screaming bend, held it until a salaryman actually flinched, then let it ring out into the feedback.

A few people clapped. Somebody tossed a coin into the open guitar case. The crowd dissolved.

Kanade didn't.

"You've been standin' there for three songs," the girl said, wiping her palm on her jeans. Her Osaka accent was thick and bright. "You gonna request somethin', or are you just haunting me?"

"Oh! I— no. Sorry. I wasn't— sorry." Kanade bowed quickly. Her oversized headphones slid forward off her ears and clacked against her collarbone. She shoved them back up.

"Two sorries. That's a lot of sorry for a girl who didn't do anything."

"Sor—" Kanade caught herself. "Um. It was good. The playing."

"*Good,*" the girl repeated, grinning. "Wow. Stop, I'm blushin'."

"Really good," Kanade said, flustered. "I meant really good. The, um. The second chorus. You didn't do the key change."

The girl's eyebrows went up. "Huh."

"Not that it's bad! It's just that the original goes up, and you stayed down, and then you held the tension through the solo instead, so when you finally *did* go up at the end, it felt like—" She made a vague lifting gesture with both hands, then realized what she was doing and froze. "...like that."

"Like *that,*" the girl agreed, mimicking the gesture. "Okay. Nobody's ever noticed that. I've played that arrangement maybe two hundred times. You know how many people caught it?"

Kanade shook her head. The headphones slipped again.

"One. Just now. Some kid with headphones that don't fit." She leaned on her guitar. "I'm Aoi."

"Kanade."

"Kanade? Like, *to play music?* Your parents set you up for this, huh."

"My mom wanted me to do piano." Kanade looked at the pavement. "I do synths instead. She says that's cheating."

"Cheating how?"

"She says the machine does the work." Kanade's voice got steadier without her meaning it to. "But it doesn't. You build every sound from nothing. You start with an oscillator, just a raw wave, and you have to decide everything. How fast it fades in, how bright it is, what it does when you let go. A piano already knows what it is. A synth has to be *taught.*"

Aoi didn't say anything for a second.

Kanade's ears went hot. "That was a lot of words. Sorry."

"Nope. That was a *great* amount of words." Aoi pointed at the shopping bag. "Is that what's in there? A synth?"

"A volca keys. It's used. The guy at Hard-Off said one of the knobs is scratchy, but I can fix it, I think, with contact cleaner—"

"You're gonna open it up?"

"Probably tonight." She paused. "Maybe at the table, so my mom sees."

Aoi barked a laugh loud enough that a passing tourist turned to look. "Oh, I *like* you. Quiet ones are always secretly a little evil."

"I'm not evil."

"A little evil."

Kanade pressed her lips together, but the corner of her mouth twitched up anyway.

"So that song," Aoi said, kneeling to loosen her strap. "The original. What's the synth doin' under all that? I can never pick it out. I just hear strings and drums and a lady yellin' about angels."

"It's mostly a string pad, I think. Kind of a big, wide one. And there's a bass line that's way busier than people notice. If you took the vocals out, it'd almost sound like eighties city pop." Kanade hesitated. "You could do the bass line on your low strings during the verse. Under the melody. If you wanted."

Aoi stared up at her. "Both at once?"

"You're fast enough."

"Was that a compliment? From you? I should get that framed."

"It wasn't— it was just *true.*" Kanade nodded firmly. Her headphones dropped all the way down around her neck. She sighed and left them there.

Aoi snorted. "You ever think about gettin' a smaller pair?"

"They were my brother's. He's in Tokyo now." Kanade touched the worn padding. "They're good headphones."

"Yeah," Aoi said, more gently. "Sounds like it."

She snapped her guitar case shut. The coins inside rattled, and she weighed it in one hand. "Okay. Today's haul says I can afford maybe twelve plates of conveyor-belt sushi, if we're smart and stay away from the gold ones. There's a place round the corner with tablets at every seat, and you can order fried chicken on a sushi plate, which is wrong, and I love it."

Kanade blinked. "We?"

"Unless you got somewhere to be. Surgery on a synthesizer, maybe."

"No. I mean, yes, later. But not *now.*" She clutched the bag a little tighter. "Are you sure? You don't really know me."

"I know you heard a key change nobody else heard. I know you're gonna perform an operation at the dinner table out of spite." Aoi slung the case over her shoulder. "And I know you're gonna teach me that bass line, 'cause I'm *definitely* stealin' it."

"It's not mine to steal. It's from the—"

"Kanade."

"...Yes?"

"Say yes to the sushi."

Kanade looked down at the volca bag. She looked back toward the station, where she'd planned to go straight home. Then she looked at Aoi, who was bouncing on her heels and already halfway turned toward the crowd.

"Okay," Kanade said quietly. Then she said it again, louder, before she could lose her nerve. "Okay. Yes."

"Yes!" Aoi pumped her fist. "First rule of kaitenzushi: the tamago plate is a trap."

"I *like* tamago."

"Then you're wrong, and we'll fix that, too."

They stepped into the river of people together, and the arcade noise swelled behind them. Kanade's headphones still hung around her neck, and for once she didn't reach up to fix them.

response:
# Lost & Found in Osaka

The riff hit Mio before she knew where it came from. It cut through the electronic jingles, the shop barkers, and the clatter of Nipponbashi on a Saturday afternoon.

She stopped walking. The paper bag in her hand crinkled. Inside was a replacement voice chip for her Juno-106, eight hundred yen, which she'd been hunting for three weeks.

By the arcade entrance, under a flickering sign of a cartoon cat, a girl with bleached hair and a scuffed red Telecaster was tearing through "A Cruel Angel's Thesis." She played it fast and nasty, and a small crowd had gathered. A salaryman nodded along. Two kids filmed on their phones.

Mio drifted closer without deciding to.

The song ended with a squeal of feedback. The busker bowed theatrically, coins clinked into her open case, and the crowd dissolved back into the street. All except Mio.

"You're still here," the busker said, grinning. "Either you liked it or you're a cop."

"I— no. Not a cop." Mio clutched her bag. "Sorry. I was just. Um."

"Just um?"

"Listening."

"That's allowed. That's kinda the whole point." The girl twisted a tuning peg. "You got a request? I do Evangelion, Cowboy Bebop, Sailor Moon if I'm desperate. No Pokémon. I have standards."

"No, it's—" Mio stared at the pedalboard by the girl's sneakers. "You dropped it a half step. The key. The original's in C minor, but you played it in B."

The busker's hands went still on the strings. "...Okay. Who *are* you?"

"Sorry. Sorry, that's weird. I'm Mio. I don't— I just notice things."

"Nah, don't apologize. You're right. I tune down 'cause it makes the low end chunkier." She stuck out a hand. "Rin. Most people just say 'cool song' and leave. You're the first person to clock my tuning."

Mio shook it. Rin's grip was strong, with calluses on her fingertips.

"Your fuzz pedal," Mio said, then stopped.

"Go on."

"It's, um. It's cutting your highs. There's this frequency, around two kilohertz, where the melody should sit, and it's kind of— buried. If you had a mid boost—"

Rin threw her head back and laughed, loud enough that a passing tourist flinched. "Honma? You can hear that? On *this* street?"

"I make music. Kind of. With synthesizers." Mio lifted the paper bag like evidence. "I just bought a voice chip. For a Juno. They die, the chips. It's a known problem."

"A Juno, like the old Roland? The eighties one?"

"Yeah." Something in Mio's chest loosened. "The 106. My uncle gave it to me. Two of the six voices were dead, so it could only play four notes at once, which is actually fine for basslines, but for pads you need—"

"All six."

"All six," Mio agreed, and she was almost smiling.

"So you're telling me you hunted down a tiny computer chip to resurrect a forty-year-old keyboard."

"It's not a computer chip, exactly, it's an analog—" Mio caught herself. "Yes. That's what I'm telling you."

"That's the most metal thing I've heard all week." Rin crouched to loosen her strap. "What do you make? With the Juno."

"Mostly... I try to recreate old anime soundtracks. The synth parts. Like, the Bebop eyecatch music, or the opening of Akira, which is technically a gamelan thing, but there's—" She waved her free hand. "Layers. I like figuring out how they were made. Taking them apart."

"So you're a sound detective."

"I've never— that's a good way to put it."

"I'm full of good ways to put things." Rin snapped her case shut on the coins. "Okay, Detective Mio. Real question. You hungry?"

Mio blinked. "What?"

"Hungry. Food. It's almost six, I've been playing since two, and I'm about to eat my own guitar pick. There's a kaitenzushi round the corner, plates are a hundred and ten yen. My treat. You can tell me everything wrong with my mix."

"I don't— you don't have to—"

"I know I don't have to. I want to." Rin slung the guitar over her shoulder. "Look, I meet a hundred people a day out here. They throw coins, they film me, they forget me by the time they hit the next shop. You're the first one who actually *heard* me. That's worth some salmon."

Mio opened her mouth. Closed it.

Then the sky cracked open.

A boom rolled over the street, then another. Bursts of gold and green bloomed above the rooftops, reflecting off every window and LED screen in Den Den Town. Shoppers stopped. Someone cheered. The arcade's speakers, still pumping out tinny game music, vanished under the noise.

"WHAT IS THAT?" Mio shouted.

"SOME FESTIVAL?" Rin shouted back, squinting upward. "OR A STORE OPENING? WHO KNOWS! IT'S OSAKA!"

Another shell burst, crimson and crackling. Mio found herself watching how the sound arrived late, a heartbeat after the light, and how the echo bounced between buildings like a delay pedal set too long.

The barrage faded, leaving smoke drifting over the street like a soft pad slowly decaying.

"Okay," Rin said, a little breathless. "I'm choosing to believe that was for us."

"The reverb was amazing," Mio said. "Did you hear it? The way it bounced off the—"

"Yeah, I heard." Rin was looking at her, not the sky. "So? Sushi?"

Mio looked down at her paper bag, at the tiny chip that would give her synthesizer its missing voices back. Then she looked up at Rin, at the red guitar and the bleached hair, and the grin that wasn't going anywhere.

"Okay," she said. "But I'm paying for my own tamago."

"Deal. And you're explaining the two kilohertz thing again. Slowly. With hand gestures."

"I can draw you a frequency chart."

"On a napkin?"

"On a napkin," Mio said, and this time she actually smiled.

They walked off together toward the glowing sign of the sushi place, the smell of gunpowder still hanging sweet in the evening air.

# Lost & Found in Osaka

The guitar cut through Den Den Town like a blade through paper. Over the arcade jingles, the maid café barkers and the hum of Sakaisuji traffic, Aoi heard the opening bars of "A Cruel Angel's Thesis," played way too fast and way too loud. She stopped walking. The shopping bag with the broken Casio keyboard bumped against her knee.

The girl playing it couldn't have been more than nineteen. Bleached hair tied up with a pencil. A battered red Telecaster. A tiny amp balanced on a milk crate. Her guitar case lay open at her feet with a few coins and a single, slightly sad-looking 1000-yen note.

She finished with a squealing bend, and the small crowd clapped and drifted off. Aoi didn't move.

"Oi. You've been standing there for three songs." The busker grinned and pointed her pick at her. "You a fan or a spy?"

"I... no. Neither. Sorry." Aoi took half a step back. "I was just... listening."

"Listening's allowed! It's literally the whole point." She tilted her head. "But you had a face on. Like a judge. Like I failed a test."

"No! It's not... you didn't fail." Aoi clutched the bag handle. "It's just... your delay."

"My delay?"

"It's set to dotted eighths. Which is right. For that song. But you're... um. You're rushing it. Slightly. So the repeats land early and it gets kind of... muddy. In the chorus." She went red to her ears. "Sorry. That was rude."

The busker stared at her. Then she crouched, squinted at the pedal by her foot, and laughed.

"Nande ya nen. You're right. I bumped the tempo knob on the train." She tapped it back. "Nobody's ever noticed that. Not even my bandmates, and they're supposed to be listening to me."

"I notice timing stuff. It's... a problem."

"That's not a problem, that's a superpower. I'm Kaede." She stuck out a hand.

"Aoi." She shook it, briefly, like touching a hot pan.

Kaede pointed at the bag. "What's in there? Body parts?"

"A Casio SK-1. It's broken. I'm going to... circuit bend it."

"Circuit bend. Like, torture it?"

"Kind of?" A small smile slipped out before Aoi could stop it. "You short the connections on the board and it makes sounds it's not supposed to. Glitches. Some of them are really pretty."

"Ehh, so you're a synth girl." Kaede pointed at her with both hands. "I knew it. Quiet ones are always synth people. You've all got bedrooms full of blinking lights."

"It's not full. It's... maybe half."

Kaede laughed so loud a salaryman flinched. She started packing up, coiling her cable around her elbow. "Okay, Synth Girl. I've been playing two hours and I've earned..." She scooped up the coins. "Enough for, like, fifteen plates of cheap sushi. You hungry?"

"Me?"

"No, the guy in the Pikachu costume behind you. Yes, you!"

"I... I don't want to take your money."

"You fixed my delay. That's a consultation fee. Come on, there's a kaitenzushi round the corner. The tuna's sad but the salmon's decent."

---

The restaurant was bright and narrow. The conveyor belt clattered past their booth with a slow parade of colored plates. Kaede grabbed two salmon nigiri before she'd even sat down. Aoi carefully filled two cups with matcha powder from the little tin and pressed the hot water tap.

"Oh, you're a tea-maker. Thank you, Synth Girl."

"You can just call me Aoi."

"Synth Girl's more fun." Kaede popped a salmon in her mouth. "So what got you into it? Synths, I mean. Most kids your age want, like, a guitar. Something cool."

"Guitars are cool." Aoi turned her cup in her hands. "I just... I like that with a synth you build the sound from nothing. Oscillator, filter, envelope. It's like... every sound has a skeleton, and you get to see it."

"Every sound has a skeleton." Kaede pointed her chopsticks at her. "That's a lyric. I'm stealing that."

"You can't steal it, I'm giving it to you."

"Even better." Kaede grabbed a plate of tamago off the belt. "Okay. Who's your synth god? Everybody's got one."

Aoi hesitated. "You won't know him."

"Try me."

"...Susumu Hirasawa."

Kaede put her chopsticks down. Slowly.

"Are you serious right now."

"Is that... bad?"

"*Paranoia Agent.*" Kaede slapped the table. "The opening! With all the characters laughing at the sky like lunatics!"

Aoi's eyes went wide. "'Yume no Shima Shinen Kouen.'"

"YES! I watched that show when I was way too young and it messed me up forever. But that song, ah..." She clutched her chest. "And Hirasawa plays guitar too, you know! That weird one with the..."

"The Talbo! The aluminum body!"

"The aluminum body!" They were both almost shouting now. The old man at the next booth glanced over. Kaede lowered her voice to a dramatic whisper. "Most people I play for want *Evangelion*. Every day. 'Play Eva, play Eva.' I love it, but I'd kill for one person who asked for Hirasawa."

"The *Paprika* soundtrack too," Aoi said, the words tumbling out now. "The parade song. The way he layers the vocal samples, it sounds like a thousand people and also like one person going crazy. I tried to recreate the synth line on my Korg for three weeks."

"Did you get it?"

"Mostly. The filter sweep is still wrong."

"Show me sometime." Kaede said it like it was nothing, reaching for an inari plate. "Seriously. I could play the guitar part. You do the synth. We'd be the only two people in Osaka covering Hirasawa outside an arcade."

Aoi looked down at her tea. Steam curled up from it. "You'd... want to do that? With me?"

"Synth Girl." Kaede leaned across the table. "You heard my delay was off from across the street. You know what a Talbo is. You're circuit-bending a Casio for fun." She grinned. "You're the coolest person I've met all month."

Aoi didn't say anything for a moment. Then, very quietly, she reached out and took a plate of salmon off the belt.

"...The filter sweep might take another week."

"I'll wait," Kaede said. "I'm patient. Sort of." She tapped the delay knob on the table like it was a pedal. "Dotted eighths, right?"

Aoi laughed, actually laughed, and the sound surprised them both.

response:
# Stolen Moments in Roma

**9:14 a.m. — Piazza di Trevi**

Ben Ashworth was reading about Nicola Salvi's hydraulic engineering when a red motorcycle came round the corner and stopped about six inches from his kneecaps.

"*Ma sei scemo?* You stand in the street like a lamp! Like a *pigeon*! You want to die in a guidebook?"

The rider pulled off her helmet. Out came a mass of dark curls and a face that looked sharp and furious and very nearly amused.

"I'm terribly sorry," Ben said. Then, reaching for his Duolingo: "*Mi dispiace. Sono... un tavolo.*"

She stared at him. "You are a table."

"I meant *turista*."

"No. You were right the first time." The corner of her mouth twitched, and then she laughed loudly enough that a nun turned to look. "Alessandra." She held out a gloved hand. He shook it and dropped the guidebook. She picked it up and flipped through his pencilled notes, his underlining, the little asterisks beside every church.

"This is a terrible way to see Rome."

"It's an excellent edition, actually."

"Get on the bike, Professor."

"How did you know I'm a—"

"You apologize in footnotes."

He noticed the dent then. It was a deep, fist-sized crater in the fuel tank, and someone had painted it over in turquoise, gold and magenta, so that it bloomed like a tropical flower.

"What happened there?"

Alessandra pulled her helmet back on. "A disagreement."

"With whom?"

"*Sali.*"

He got on.

---

**10:02 a.m. — Campo de' Fiori**

She wove through the market as if the stalls had been set up for her benefit. She argued with a fishmonger about football and kissed a flower-seller on both cheeks. When they came out the other side, she held up a perfect peach.

"For you."

Ben bit into it. Juice ran down his wrist. "Thank you. How much do I owe—"

She was already walking. He looked back at the fruit stall and the oblivious old man behind it, and then at the peach in his hand, which had become evidence.

"Alessandra, did you *pay* for this?"

"Eat faster," she said.

He did. It was the best peach he had ever tasted, and he felt terrible about it for nearly four minutes.

---

**11:30 a.m. — Via Giulia, a lawyer's office, the sixth floor**

"I have a delivery," she said. "You hold this." She handed him a manila envelope. "Look important."

"I am important. I'm a senior lecturer."

"Look *Italian* important."

The receptionist signed for the envelope. On the way out, Alessandra did not press the button for the lift. She pushed through a fire door instead.

"That says *vietato*," Ben said. "I know that one. Forbidden."

"Your Italian is improving."

The stairwell went up past the top floor to a hatch, and the hatch opened onto a roof. Terracotta tiles fell away in every direction. Domes swelled out of the city like bread rising, and swallows dived around the chimneys.

Ben stayed pressed against the hatch frame. "I don't love heights."

"Then don't love them. Just look." She sat on the very edge with her boots hanging over Via Giulia and lit a cigarette with a silver lighter that was engraved, he would later realize, with someone else's initials.

He crawled out, unforgivably slowly, and sat beside her. His heart was going like a pneumatic drill.

"There," she said, not looking at him. "You see? Not in the book."

---

**1:45 p.m. — A trattoria in Trastevere with no name**

"*Vorrei*," Ben told the waiter carefully, "*il pollo con i... suoi amici.*"

*The chicken with its friends.* The waiter looked at Alessandra, who had her face in her hands and her shoulders shaking.

"He wants the chicken with peppers," she managed.

"That's what I said."

"You said the chicken should bring guests."

They ate carbonara and drank a carafe of cold white wine. She asked him why a man would cross a continent to read in a different library. He told her more than he meant to: the ex-fiancée, the flat in Cambridge with the dripping tap, and the forty-one years he had spent being reasonable.

"And now?"

"Now I'm accessory to peach theft."

She smiled into her glass, and for a moment she looked at him with something unguarded in her face. Then it was gone. When they left, he saw the gleam of a silver spoon going into her jacket pocket.

He said nothing. He found, to his alarm, that he admired it.

---

**5:20 p.m. — Lungotevere, traffic**

She drove like a thrown knife. Ben held on round her waist and kept his eyes shut through two red lights and one roundabout, which she took in the wrong direction while a bus honked a long, mournful note behind them.

"*Open your eyes!*" she shouted over her shoulder.

He did. The Tiber flashed gold beside them, the plane trees went by in a blur, and the wind tore at his shirt. He started laughing. He couldn't stop, and he didn't want to.

---

**9:40 p.m. — The Gianicolo**

The city spread out below them like spilled embers. She sat on the motorcycle's seat, and he stood beside the painted dent and traced its petals with one finger.

"Will you ever tell me?"

"Maybe. If you are still here."

He reached for his pen to write down her number and found his pocket empty. His reading glasses were gone too.

"Alessandra."

She held up her hand. Pinched between two fingers was his library card from the Biblioteca Hertziana, with his photo, his name and his temporary address.

"Collateral," she said.

"For what?"

She shrugged, grinning, and pulled on her helmet. She kicked the engine to life, then patted her jacket pockets, then patted them again. Her grin faltered.

Ben raised his hand. Dangling from his fingers was her little brass key fob in the shape of the she-wolf, with the twins suckling beneath her.

"I believe," he said, in his most careful Italian, "*che siamo pari.*" We're even.

She stared at him for a long moment through the open visor. Then she reached out, grabbed his collar, and kissed him hard and fast, tasting of wine and smoke. When she let go, the key fob was back in her hand.

"Not even," she said. "Not yet."

The motorcycle roared off down the hill with its magenta flower flashing under the streetlamps. Ben stood alone in the warm dark and checked his pockets. His wallet was gone too.

He was smiling anyway.

response:
# Stolen Moments in Roma

**I. Trevi, 9:14 a.m.**

The motorcycle came out of nowhere, which, Ben would later learn, was where Alessandra Ferri preferred to come from.

He was standing in the mouth of Via delle Muratte, nose buried in *Rome: A Scholar's Companion*, trying to work out whether Neptune's left foot was original. Then there was a shriek of brakes, a smell of hot rubber, and a front tyre stopped close enough to his shin that he felt its heat through his corduroys.

"*Ma sei scemo?* You stand in the street like a lamp post! Like a *statue*! Rome has enough statues!"

She wore a scuffed red helmet, and a courier's satchel was slung across her chest. When she flipped up the visor, he saw dark eyes, furious and amused at once.

"I'm so terribly sorry," Ben said. "*Mi dispiace.* I'm, um, *sono*..." He groped for the word. "*Sono un turista stupido.*"

There was a pause. Then she laughed, loud enough to scatter pigeons.

"At least you are honest." She cut the engine. "You were reading about the foot. Everybody reads about the foot. Nobody looks at the water."

"Is the foot original?"

"Who cares?" She took the guidebook from his hands, closed it, and handed it back with a pitying look. "Get on."

"I'm sorry?"

"I have three deliveries and you have a terrible face, very lost. Get on, *Professore*."

He hadn't told her he was a professor. He got on.

**II. Campo de' Fiori, 10:40 a.m.**

He held her waist the way one might hold a museum artefact. She took corners as though they had personally offended her. By the time she dropped an envelope at a lawyer's office on Via Giulia, Ben's knees had stopped working and his heart had started working far too hard.

At the market she walked between the stalls like she owned them. She chatted with a fishmonger and flirted with an old woman selling artichokes. As they passed a pyramid of Amalfi lemons, her hand moved once, quick as a sparrow, and a lemon vanished into her jacket.

Ben stopped dead. "Did you just..."

"Just what?" She looked at him with absolute innocence and walked on.

He looked back at the stall and then at her retreating figure. He found, to his alarm, that he was smiling.

**III. A Locked Gate, Trastevere, 1:15 p.m.**

"This is private property," Ben said.

"This is a *view*," Alessandra corrected. She was already halfway up the wrought-iron gate, boots finding footholds in the curlicues. "Views belong to whoever is brave enough."

"That isn't a legal principle."

"It is a Roman one." She swung over the top and landed in a shower of bougainvillea. "Come, *Professore*. Or go back and read about the foot."

He had written two monographs on Renaissance patronage. He had never received so much as a parking ticket. He climbed the gate and tore his trousers on the way down.

The rooftop terrace at the top of the crumbling stairwell belonged to someone with excellent taste in geraniums. From it, Rome spread out in shades of terracotta and gold, with domes catching the light like upturned bowls.

"Well?" she said.

"It's..." He had no word for it in any language. "Yes."

She looked at him then, properly and for a long moment. Something unreadable crossed her face. Then she turned away and plucked a single geranium from its pot.

**IV. Via del Governo Vecchio, 5:30 p.m.**

The rain arrived without warning, the way everything did today. One moment the sky was bruised violet. The next it was emptying itself onto the cobblestones in sheets.

They ran. Alessandra was laughing and dragging him by the wrist, and they came skidding under the striped awning of a gelato shop just as the gutters began to roar.

They stood there, dripping and breathless. Water ran down her neck into the collar of her jacket. Ben's glasses had fogged completely.

"Here." She took them off his face, dried them on her shirt, and set them back on his nose. Her fingers lingered at his temple for exactly one second too long.

"Thank you," he said, and his voice came out strange.

"Pistachio or *stracciatella*?"

"I've no idea."

"Pistachio. You are a pistachio man. Serious, a little bit sad, secretly very good." She bought two cones and paid properly this time. He noticed this, and noticed himself noticing.

They ate in silence and watched the rain hammer the street. A waiter across the way was hurriedly stacking chairs, and a nun hurried past with a newspaper over her head.

"Why are you doing this?" Ben asked at last. "Why me?"

Alessandra licked her spoon thoughtfully. "Because you said *sono un turista stupido*, and you meant it. Do you know how rare that is? A man who admits he is lost?"

"I'm usually not. Lost, I mean. I usually know exactly where I am."

"That," she said, "is the saddest thing I have heard all year."

She leaned closer. He could smell rain and petrol and lemon on her. For a breathless moment he thought she might kiss him. Instead she reached up and straightened his collar, smiling the way a cat smiles at a bird it hasn't yet decided about.

**V. Ponte Sisto, 8:50 p.m.**

The rain had washed the city clean, and the Tiber reflected streetlamps in long, trembling ribbons. She walked him to the middle of the bridge and stopped.

"My bike is that way," she said. "Your hotel is that way."

"Yes."

"So."

"So," Ben agreed. He did not want to move. "Will I see you again?"

She shrugged, maddening and magnificent. "Rome is small. Maybe I nearly kill you again."

"I'd like that."

"*Lo so.*" She stepped close, rose onto her toes, and kissed him once at the corner of his mouth. It was quick, a theft more than a gift. Then she was walking away backwards and grinning.

"*Ciao, Professore!*"

He watched her vanish into the dark, her red helmet swinging from one hand.

Only later, back in his hotel room, did he take stock. His pen was gone, and so was his library card. *Rome: A Scholar's Companion* was nowhere to be found.

In his jacket pocket, where the guidebook should have been, he found a lemon. Written across its waxy skin in his own stolen ink was a phone number, and beneath it: *Look at the water.*

Ben sat on the edge of the bed, holding the lemon in both hands like something precious. For the first time in years, he laughed until he couldn't breathe.
