# Hell is Other Demons

Hell, like most large organizations, ran on paperwork, resentment, and the quiet conviction of everyone involved that they could do a better job than the person in charge.

The person in charge woke at six, which in Hell meant the hour when the furnaces were stoked and the screaming changed key. Lucifer Morningstar lay for a while staring at the ceiling, which was frescoed with the Fall. He had commissioned it himself a long time ago, when he was the sort of angel who thought that kind of thing was a good idea. Now it just made him tired. In the fresco he was beautiful and furious and falling. In bed he was beautiful, mildly furious, and out of oat milk.

The other side of the bed was very neat. It had been neat for four months.

He drank his coffee black, the way the damned drink it, and went down to the office.

Beelzebub was waiting with the quarterly figures, and with the expression of a fly who has found something unpleasant on the windowsill and is deciding whether to land on it.

"Intake's up eleven percent," Beelzebub said. "Mostly middle management. A handful of influencers. We've had to open an annex in the Fourth Circle."

"Lovely."

"The Lake of Fire has filed a complaint about its temperature."

"The Lake of Fire is a lake."

"It feels undervalued." Beelzebub turned a page. "Also, Accounts wants to know whether eternal torment can be depreciated. And there's a demon in Gluttony requesting paternity leave."

"Since when do demons have paternity?"

"Since about Tuesday. He spawned. There are forty of them. They're in the break room. They've eaten the vending machine."

Lucifer signed things. He signed a requisition for more pitchforks, the authorization of a new pit for people who recline their seats on aeroplanes, and an apology to the Lake of Fire, which he did not mean. He signed the way a tired parent signs permission slips, without reading. That, he reflected, was how Hell had got so big in the first place.

At eleven there was a knock at his door.

This was alarming. Nobody in Hell knocked. Demons barged, slithered, or appeared in a puff of sulphur, depending on their upbringing. The last time Lilith had come to see him she had come through the wall, and taken most of the library with her. He was still finding scorched pages of the *Malleus Maleficarum* behind the radiators.

"Come in," he said, carefully.

She came in. She looked as she always looked: like the first woman, and the first woman to leave. She had something folded over her arm, and the purse was on her shoulder, the scorched leather one, older than Babylon and smelling faintly of rain and petrol.

"You left this at mine," she said, and held out his cardigan.

He looked at the cardigan. It was grey and had a hole in one elbow. He had looked for it for weeks.

"You could have burnt it," he said.

"I thought about it." She put it on the desk. "It didn't seem worth the effort."

That was the thing about Lilith. Anybody else's contempt was simple. Hers came in layers, like geology, and sometimes, if you dug far enough down, there was something at the bottom that was nearly fondness.

"How's Biscuit?" she said.

Biscuit was the hellhound. He had three heads, and a custody arrangement that had been worked out over the course of a single very loud century.

"He misses you," said Lucifer. "Well. The left head does. The middle one bit the Pope last week."

"Which Pope?"

"One of the old ones. He had it coming."

She sat down without being asked and opened the purse. Lucifer had never been permitted to look inside it. Over the centuries he had seen things come out of it: a snow globe of Duluth, Minnesota; a parking ticket from Prague, 1987, unpaid; a jar of honey from a monastery that no longer existed; a child's blue mitten; a tooth that was certainly not hers; a tarot card with nothing printed on either side. She took out a small paper bag and set it on the desk.

"Churros," she said. "Madrid. They've gone a bit cold."

"Why are you here, Lilith?"

"I was in the neighbourhood."

"There is no neighbourhood. There is Hell, and all of it is mine."

"Yes," she said. "That's always been your problem."

He ate a churro, because it was there. It was cold, and very good.

The afternoon was given over to appeals. A man named Gerald, recently deceased, of Surrey, had demanded to speak to the manager. Lucifer was the manager. Gerald was told this, and demanded to speak to the manager's manager. There was a long, thoughtful pause. Several people glanced upwards.

"I'll put you on the list," Lucifer said, and sent him to the annex in the Fourth Circle. He would be on hold there forever, with a recording telling him how important his call was. It played in Hell on a loop, and it was the only torment Lucifer had ever been entirely proud of.

Lilith watched all this from the corner, legs crossed, picking sugar off her fingers.

"You've got good at this," she said. "It's horrible."

"Thank you."

"It wasn't a compliment."

"It's Hell. Everything's a compliment, if you squint."

In the evening they found themselves, by no arrangement either of them would admit to, on the balcony above the Lake of Fire. It was sulking and burning low. Down in the dark the damned went about their eternal business, and from up here it looked almost like a city at night: little lights, little cries, everybody very busy being miserable on their own.

"I'm not staying," Lilith said.

"I didn't ask."

"You were going to."

He had been going to. He said nothing, which is the oldest way there is of saying yes.

She reached into the purse again and took out a seashell, pale and whorled and pink on the inside, like the inside of an ear.

"Cornwall," she said. "A beach near Porthcurno. If you hold it up, you can hear the sea."

Lucifer had never heard the sea. There is no sea in Hell. There never has been. Nothing down here was ever allowed to be that large and that indifferent, except him.

He took it. Their fingers touched briefly. Neither of them set anything on fire.

"Thursday," said Lilith, standing. "For Biscuit."

"Thursday."

Then she was gone, not through the wall this time but through the door, which she closed behind her very quietly. That worried him more than anything had in a thousand years.

He stood a long while on the balcony. Then he held the shell to his ear, and listened to an ocean he had never seen, roaring very softly in the dark. It was practically nothing at all.

He would think about it until Thursday.

# The Matter of the Field

The Court of the Dreaming did not, strictly speaking, exist on Tuesdays. Dream had convened it anyway, which told everyone present exactly how much he wanted to be there.

He sat at the high bench, pale and motionless, his eyes two points of starlight in a face like carved midnight. Beside him, the Clerk, a heron in a powdered wig, consulted a scroll that kept rewriting itself out of boredom.

"The Court will hear," the Clerk announced, "the matter of *First Love versus Mora*, concerning the recurring dreamscape designated 'Max, Age Thirteen, Field of Wildflowers, Tuesdays and Most Thursdays.'"

From the defendant's box came a sound like a dry hinge turning in an empty house. A cackle. It climbed the vaulted ceiling, found nowhere comfortable to settle, and stayed there anyway.

"The defendant will refrain," said Dream, "from echoing."

"Can't help it, darling." Mora draped herself over the rail. She was mostly hair and elbows, with a face that seemed beautiful until you looked directly at it, then seemed hungry, then seemed beautiful again, as though it couldn't decide. "Acoustics in here are *lovely*."

At the plaintiff's table, First Love fidgeted with a daisy chain. He was round-cheeked and perpetually blushing, dressed in a cardigan one size too large, and he could not look at anyone for longer than a second before glancing away and smiling at his shoes.

"Plaintiff," said Dream. "Your complaint."

First Love stood, sat, and stood again. "Your Majesty. Lord Shaper. Sir. I worked on that field for *weeks*." He produced a pressed cornflower from his cardigan pocket. "Exhibit A. Hand-tinted. I did the bees individually."

"Noted."

"The dream is supposed to go: sunshine, grass, the girl from his maths class laughs and tumbles over to pin him in a play-fight. They almost kiss. He wakes up confused and warm and goes to school unable to say a single word to her. It's *formative*. It's a *classic*." His voice cracked. "And now she pins him down and she, she *changes*. She gets heavy. Her hair goes everywhere. And she sits on his chest and *drinks his breath*."

"Only a little," said Mora.

"He wakes up *screaming*!"

"He wakes up *memorable*." Another cackle rolled upward. The Clerk winced, feathers ruffling.

Dream steepled his long fingers. Somewhere far below, in the dreams of ten thousand sleepers, a staircase quietly gained an extra step. He was that irritated.

"Defendant. Your response."

Mora slid out of the box and approached the bench with the loose-jointed walk of something that has never been required to use bones conventionally. "Your Honor. Your Dreaminess. Let's be practical. I've been sitting on chests since before your sister bought her first ankh."

"Leave my family out of this."

"The point is, business is *dreadful*. Nobody sleeps on their backs anymore. They've all got memory foam and white noise machines and little apps that tell them they've *slept well*." She spat the phrase like a seed. "I used to have whole villages. Now I'm scrounging through teenage fantasies like a fox in the bins. A girl's gotta eat too, you know?"

"There are other dreams," said First Love.

"Not with a boy lying flat on his back in an open field, *helpless*, waiting for someone to climb on top of him." She spread her hands. "That's not a dream. That's a *buffet*."

"Objection!"

"On what grounds?" said Dream.

First Love opened his mouth, then closed it, then went a deeper shade of pink. "It's... upsetting?"

"Overruled."

"Your Honor." Mora leaned in conspiratorially, and the candles nearest her guttered. "I'd also like the Court to note that I *kept the original aesthetic*. I'm still the girl, sort of. Same freckles. I simply added a few hundred extra teeth and a sense of crushing inevitability. Honestly, it's a collaboration."

"It is *theft*."

"It's *editing*."

Dream raised one hand, and the courtroom fell into a silence so complete that even the echo of Mora's cackle stopped mid-ceiling, suspended, and seemed embarrassed.

"I wish to call a witness," he said. "The Girl."

The Clerk flapped once. In the witness box appeared the figment herself: a dream-girl of thirteen in a summer dress, freckled, sunlit, and frankly unclear on why she had been subpoenaed.

"State your nature."

"I'm... the girl from maths?" She blinked. "Mostly. On Tuesdays I'm also slightly his cousin's friend, which I think is a mistake. And lately, at the end, I'm..." She gestured vaguely at Mora, who waggled her fingers.

"And what do you observe," asked Dream, "of the boy, upon waking?"

The Girl thought. "Before? He'd lie there smiling at the ceiling. Then he'd think about me all day and feel like he couldn't breathe."

"And now?"

"Now he lies there, terrified, and thinks about me all day, and feels like he can't breathe."

There was a long pause.

Dream regarded First Love. First Love regarded his daisy chain. Mora's grin, already too wide, widened.

"Hm," said Dream.

It was the most dangerous syllable in the Dreaming. The Clerk began, very slowly, edging toward the door.

"The Court finds," Dream said, "that the distinction between the plaintiff's work and the defendant's is narrower than either party would like. Both produce a boy who cannot speak to a girl, cannot sleep properly, and cannot breathe when she enters the room." A ghost of something passed across his face. It was not quite a smile. Smiles were for lesser entities. "This is, I am told, accurate."

"Your Majesty—" First Love began.

"Custody is to be *shared*. First Love retains the field, the sunshine, and the bees, individually done. Mora retains the final ninety seconds." He paused. "And you will co-author. Together. Every Tuesday and most Thursdays. Until the boy turns sixteen."

The silence curdled.

"*Together?*" said First Love, horrified.

"*Sixteen?*" said Mora, delighted. Her cackle burst free at last, ricocheting from vault to vault, and this time Dream did not stop it.

"Court is adjourned." He rose, and the bench began to dissolve into fog behind him. "And Clerk?"

"Yes, my lord?"

"Draft a similar order for the boy's thirties. They'll be more fun."

Then he was gone, leaving behind only the faint scent of cornflowers and the distinct impression that somewhere, a schoolboy had just rolled onto his back.

response:
# The Matter of the Wildflower Field

The hourglass in the Court of the Dreaming was taller than most cathedrals. Its sand fell with a soft hiss, like a held breath being let out very slowly. Nobody knew what would happen when it ran out. Dream had never said, and nobody had ever been foolish enough to ask.

He sat at the high bench with his face pale and still. Those who had served him for aeons would have noticed a slight tightness at the corner of his mouth, the mark of someone asked to mediate a dispute between two of his own wasps.

"The Court will hear the matter," intoned the Clerk, a large grey moth in a powdered wig, "of *First Love versus Mora*, concerning the recurring dreamscape designated Field-of-Wildflowers-Number-Eleven-Thousand-and-Six, property of one Max Okafor, aged fourteen, of Leeds."

"Of Leeds," Dream repeated quietly, as though this were the most tiresome detail yet.

First Love rose from the plaintiff's bench. He was small and round-faced, with cheeks the colour of a fresh bruise. He held a sheaf of papers that he had clearly reorganised several times.

"My lord," he began, and then went pink. "Sorry. Your Shaping-ness. Lord Shaper. I've spent eleven months on that field. *Eleven months.* The poppies alone took three weeks. I did the light the way it is at four in the afternoon in late June, when you can't tell if you're warm from the sun or from—" He gestured vaguely at his own chest. "You know."

"I do not," said Dream.

"Right. Well. There's a girl. Priya, from his maths set. They lie in the grass. She tickles him with a dandelion. They nearly kiss, and then they don't, and he wakes up feeling like he's swallowed a lightbulb. It's *formative*. He'll measure every afternoon in June against it for the rest of his life." First Love's voice wobbled. "And then *she* came."

Every eye in the gallery turned to the defendant.

Mora lounged at her bench with one foot up on the table. She was thin and grey, with too many knuckles, and her hair moved as if it were underwater. Her eyes were the colour of the space beneath a bed. She was examining her nails, which were long and black and quite well kept.

"Objection," she said, without looking up. "He's making me sound like a burglar."

"You *are* a burglar," said First Love.

"I'm a *tenant*. There's a difference."

Dream raised one finger, and the courtroom fell so silent that the falling sand sounded like rain. "The defendant will describe her alterations."

Mora shrugged. "I kept most of it. The flowers, the light, all very nice. Credit where it's due. The girl does her bit with the dandelion, she pins him in the grass, giggling, all that. Then she looks down at him, and she isn't Priya anymore." She smiled, and her smile had far too many teeth. "She's me. I settle on his chest. He can't move. Can't scream. I lean in close, very close, and I drink."

"His *breath*," First Love hissed.

"Well, I'm not going to drink his *orange squash*."

A juror coughed. The jury box held twelve sleepers drawn at random from the waking world. Most were in pyjamas. One was still holding a pillow and looked deeply concerned about it.

"And the boy's response?" asked Dream.

The Clerk shuffled through a file. "The boy has reported the dream to no one, my lord. However, he has started sleeping with the light on. He's also started staring at Priya Sharma across the maths classroom with what the attending Fears describe as 'an expression of profound and unresolvable confusion.'"

"Confusion was always part of it," said First Love weakly. "But it was *nice* confusion."

"Mine's nicer," said Mora. "It's got *texture*."

Dream closed his eyes for a moment, perhaps a few centuries by the reckoning of mortals. "Defendant. Have you any justification for occupying another's work?"

Mora finally took her foot off the table. She leaned forward with her elbows on her knees, and for an instant she looked almost earnest.

"Look. It used to be easy. Peasants. Farmers. Big families stacked four to a bed, all sleeping on their backs, mouths open. A smorgasbord. Now? Memory foam. White noise machines. Melatonin gummies. Do you know how hard it is to terrify someone who has an app tracking their REM cycles?" She spread her too-long hands. "I find one good dream, one boy who sleeps on his back with his mouth open like a baby bird, and suddenly I'm the villain. A girl's gotta eat too, you know?"

There was a murmur from the gallery. Somewhere at the back, a Nightmare in a trench coat muttered, *She's not wrong.*

First Love was almost in tears. "It was supposed to be *pure*."

"Nothing's pure, sweetheart," said Mora. "That's the whole point of me."

Dream regarded them both for a long time. The sand hissed. The juror with the pillow had begun, very slowly, to hug it.

At last he spoke.

"The field is a single dream. It cannot be divided without becoming two lesser dreams, and I will not have lesser dreams in my realm." He paused, and something flickered across his face. It was not quite a smile, but it was a close relative of one. "Therefore the Court rules joint tenancy."

First Love's mouth fell open. Mora's eyebrows rose to a height that would have been anatomically impossible for anyone with fewer joints.

"The dream will remain exactly as it is," Dream went on. "The light. The flowers. The girl, the dandelion, the near-kiss. And then the weight on the chest, the stillness, the breath drawn out of him. Both of you will attend, every night, until the boy grows out of it."

"But," First Love said, "that's—that's *horrible*. He'll grow up thinking love and terror are the same thing."

Dream rose. His cloak moved around him like the shadow of a cloud passing over a field.

"Yes," he said. "Consider it an education. It will save him a great deal of time later."

He turned to go, then stopped.

"Also, the defendant will bring the poppies flowers once a week. As reparation."

"I don't *do* flowers," said Mora.

"You do now."

The hourglass hissed. Somewhere in Leeds, a boy lay in a field of wildflowers, waiting to be kissed, waiting to be crushed, and not entirely sure he could tell the difference.

response:
# The Matter of the Wildflower Field

The Court of the Dreaming convened, as it always did, at no particular hour. The ceiling was not entirely a ceiling and the floor was not entirely committed to being underfoot. Gallery attendees included two lesser terrors, a recurring falling sensation, and a teeth-crumbling dream that had come for the spectacle.

Dream sat upon the bench. He had been sitting upon it for some time before anyone arrived, and gave the impression that he would prefer to be sitting somewhere else, possibly in a different eternity.

"The court will hear," he said, "the matter of the wildflower field."

The bailiff stepped forward. He was a large, hooded thing whose voice arrived several seconds before his mouth moved. He unrolled a scroll.

"THE PETITIONER," he boomed, and the walls trembled. "FIRST GLOVE."

A small, rosy-cheeked figure in the front row winced. "Love. It's First *Love*."

"FIRST GLOVE," the bailiff repeated, with the serene confidence of a creature who had never once been corrected successfully.

Dream closed his eyes briefly. "Proceed."

First Love rose, clutching a sheaf of papers tied with pink ribbon. Her hands trembled. Everything about her trembled, faintly, the way a heart does when a particular name is said aloud in a classroom.

"Your Majesty," she began, then blushed, then began again. "Lord Shaper. I constructed the dream in question over eleven weeks. The field. The wildflowers. Clover, mostly, and some buttercups, because Max once held one under a girl's chin to see if she liked butter, and she laughed, and..." She paused, overcome. "It was going to be *formative*."

"Describe the dream as intended," said Dream.

"They lie in the grass. She leans over him. They almost kiss. They never quite do. He wakes up feeling like his chest is full of warm bees." She sniffed. "I had the bees *calibrated*."

"And now?"

First Love's lip quivered. She pointed across the aisle.

"THE RESPONDENT," the bailiff announced. "MORAY."

"Mora," said the respondent.

"MORAINE."

"That's a glacial deposit, you great lump."

The respondent lounged in her seat with her feet up on the defense table. She was pale in a way that suggested deep water, with long dark hair that moved slightly even when she didn't, and too many joints in her fingers. She examined her nails, which were also too many.

"Mora of the Slavic marches," Dream said. "You are accused of entering the dreamscape of one Max, aged thirteen, and subverting its narrative."

"*Improving* its narrative."

"You transformed the girl."

"Only at the end. I kept the flowers." Mora shrugged. "I'm not a monster. Well. I am. But I'm not *tacky*."

First Love leapt up. "She climbs on his chest! She sits there! He can't *move*, he can't *breathe*, and she just..." She made a small, scandalized gesture toward her own mouth. "*Inhales him*."

"Sleep paralysis is a perfectly respectable phenomenon," said Mora. "Ask anyone in the fourteenth century."

Dream's expression did not change, though a nearby candle went out.

"The petitioner may call witnesses."

First Love consulted her papers. "I call the Buttercup."

"THE BUTTERBUTT," the bailiff thundered.

A single buttercup was placed carefully in the witness box. It did not speak. It glowed faintly yellow, and then less yellow, and then wilted under the weight of the occasion.

"Let the record show," said First Love, voice thick, "that it has *seen things*."

"The record shows a flower," said Dream.

"I also call the boy's own subconscious."

There was a pause. Something shuffled into the box. It looked like Max, roughly, but blurred at the edges and wearing pajamas with rockets on them. It sat down and stared at its hands.

"How do you feel about the recent changes to your dream?" First Love asked gently.

The subconscious considered this for a long time.

"Bad," it said. "Mostly."

"Mostly?"

"She's very scary." It hesitated. "She has nice hair, though. Is that bad? That's probably bad." It looked up at Dream, pleading. "I don't know what anything means."

"Nobody does at thirteen," said Dream. "You may step down."

The subconscious shuffled off, muttering, and was later found under a gallery bench, curled up and very confused.

"Respondent," said Dream. "Your defense."

Mora swung her feet off the table and stood. Her shadow stood up a moment after she did.

"Look," she said. "I've been working the Carpathians for eight hundred years. Village after village. Peasants. Shepherds. Lovely breath, peasants, very earthy. But nobody believes in me anymore. They believe in *melatonin*." She spat the word. "I had to relocate. Diversify. The boy's dream had an opening. A girl straddling a chest is half the job done already. I just finished the thought."

"You trespassed on crafted territory," said Dream.

"A girl's gotta eat too, you know?"

The gallery murmured. The teeth dream nodded sympathetically.

First Love was weeping openly now. "He used to wake up *smiling*."

"And now he wakes up *remembering*," said Mora. "Which lasts longer? Ask yourself that, sweetheart. Nobody remembers the nice dreams. But I'll be in that boy's head when he's forty."

"That is precisely the problem," said First Love.

"That's precisely the *point*."

Silence. Dream regarded them both. Somewhere, a distant sleeper rolled over.

He was, he reflected, the Lord of all stories ever dreamed. He had walked the halls of Hell. He had bargained with the endless. And now he was judging a custody dispute over a schoolboy's clover patch.

He found, to his mild surprise, that he was tempted.

"The court has reached a decision," he said.

Both parties straightened.

"The dream belongs to neither of you. It belongs to the dreamer. However, the dreamer is thirteen, and has no idea what he wants." Dream steepled his fingers. "Therefore, you will share it."

"*Share* it?" said First Love and Mora, in unison, and glared at each other for the coincidence.

"Joint tenancy. The field remains. The girl remains. The almost-kiss remains. And some nights, at the very last moment, she will sit upon his chest."

"Which nights?" asked Mora.

"He will not know," said Dream. "Neither will you. Neither will she."

First Love stared. "But that's... that's *cruel*. He'll never know whether to be thrilled or terrified."

"Yes," said Dream. "That is generally how it goes."

He rose. The bench rose with him, out of loyalty.

"Court is adjourned."

"COURT IS ADJOINED," the bailiff boomed.

Dream did not correct him. He was, very nearly, smiling.

# The Agony Column

The hill was not, by the standards of hills, very interesting. It went up. Then, for one man and one rock, it went down again, and that was where the interest came from.

Near the top stood a dead tree. In the dead tree sat Crow, and on Crow's knee, insofar as crows have knees, lay the morning post.

"Ready when you are," said Sisyphus, leaning a shoulder into the boulder with the ease of a man settling into an armchair.

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*My husband and I have the same argument every week. He says I never let him finish a sentence. I say if he got to the point I wouldn't have to. Last night he timed me with a sand-glass. How do I make him stop?*

*— Interrupted in Thebes*

*Dear Interrupted,*

*Try this for one week. When he starts a sentence, let him finish it, then count three breaths before you answer. Don't do it to make a point. Just see what happens.*

*My guess is that something will come out in the gap. It will be something he's been trying to say for years, buried under the bit about the goats. People who take a long time to get to the point usually do have one. They're just not sure you want it.*

*Do put the sand-glass away. Nobody wins an argument that's being timed.*

*— S.*

[Crow's note: I would also have accepted "hit him with the sand-glass."]

---

The boulder reached the summit, considered the view, and departed. Sisyphus watched it go with the mild fondness of a man seeing off a cousin who'd be back for supper, then strolled down after it.

"Next."

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*I run a bakery in Corinth. I'm up at three and close at sunset. Yesterday my daughter told me she's learned to whistle. I didn't know she couldn't. She's seven. I keep saying it'll get easier once the business is established. It's been established for nine years.*

*— Flour in My Ears*

Sisyphus walked in silence for a while. Crow knew the signs and did not interrupt.

*Dear Flour,*

*Here is the thing nobody tells bakers: the bread will forgive you. People queue for yesterday's loaves at half price and go home perfectly happy. Daughters aren't like that. It isn't that they hold grudges. They just get on with it, and they learn to whistle whether you're there or not.*

*Is there anyone you trust to open up one morning a week? Pick a day. Don't make it a grand gesture. Make it boring and regular, so she can count on it. Then ask her to teach you to whistle. You'll be terrible at it, and she will love that.*

*— S.*

[Crow's note: S. cannot whistle either. It sounds like a kettle with regrets.]

---

At the bottom, the boulder waited in the hollow it had worn over the centuries. Sisyphus patted it, said "Morning," and set his shoulder to it again.

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*My neighbour keeps parking his oxcart across my gateway. When I ask, he moves it, apologizes, and does it again the next day. He is very pleasant about it. I want to set fire to him.*

*— Blocked In, Megara*

*Dear Blocked,*

*Pleasant people who keep doing the same annoying thing often aren't thinking about you at all, which is somehow worse.*

*Next time, don't ask him to move it. Ask him where else he might park it, and then stand there while he thinks. Most people will solve a problem perfectly well if they have to look at it for longer than an apology takes. Bring him a fig while you're at it. It's very hard to keep blocking the gate of a man who gave you a fig.*

*Fires are frowned upon, I'm told.*

*— S.*

[Crow's note: "I'm told." Readers may draw their own conclusions about why he is here.]

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*I am a widow of some years and have recently taken up with the man who sells olives in the lower market. He is very attentive. Last week he did something with a length of ribbon and a jar of honey that I had not known was possible. I am writing to ask whether, at my age, this is decent.*

*— Sticky in Sparta*

Crow made a noise like a bagpipe being sat on.

"Don't," said Sisyphus.

"I wasn't going to *say* anything."

"You were going to *write* something."

*Dear Sticky,*

*Decency is mostly about whether anyone is getting hurt. From your letter, the answer seems to be "quite the opposite." Enjoy it. You've earned it.*

*Do wash the ribbon properly afterwards. Honey gets everywhere, and you don't want ants.*

*— S.*

[Crow's note: The scribe wishes it on record that he was a very young bird when he took this job.]

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*I'm twenty-three. Everyone I grew up with seems to know what they're for. I'm a clerk at the granary, and I'm fine at it. I keep waiting to feel like my life has started. What if it doesn't?*

Sisyphus stopped pushing. The boulder, apparently by long arrangement, stayed where it was.

*Dear Still Waiting,*

*A secret: most of the people who seem to know what they're for decided at about your age, and now they're hoping nobody asks follow-up questions.*

*Your life has started. It's happening at the granary. That doesn't mean you have to stay there. But while you're there, notice things. Who do you like talking to? Which part of the day goes fastest? What do you find yourself fixing that nobody asked you to fix? That isn't nothing. It's the beginning of a map.*

*Purpose isn't usually waiting for you at the top. Mostly it's what you realize you've been carrying the whole way, once you stop to look.*

*Write again in a year and tell me what you noticed.*

*— S.*

Crow's pen hovered over the parchment for some time.

[Crow's note: ]

Then he scratched out the brackets, tucked the letter in with the others, and said nothing at all. For Crow, that was an editorial of sorts.

The boulder reached the top. It paused. It left.

"Same time tomorrow," said Sisyphus, and went down to meet it.

# Sisyphus Gives Advice

The hill was not a remarkable hill. It had the sort of gradient that surveyors describe as "honest," and a view at the top that would have been lovely if anyone had ever been allowed to stay there long enough to enjoy it.

The boulder sat halfway up, resting against Sisyphus's shoulder like an old dog leaning on its owner. Crow sat on top of the boulder with a quill in one claw, which is harder than it sounds, and a satchel of letters that smelled faintly of the River Styx.\*

"Next one," said Sisyphus.

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*My wife and I have been married eleven years and we fight about the dishwasher. She puts the bowls on the top rack. The BOWLS. On the TOP. I have shown her the diagram. She says I am being "like this." What do I do?*

*Racked in Rhodes*

---

Sisyphus pushed the boulder three steps, stopped, and wedged a heel behind him.

"Write this down. *Dear Racked. Nobody in the history of the world has fought about a dishwasher for eleven years. Something else has been going on for some of those years, and the dishwasher is just where it comes out.*"

Crow wrote. Crow's handwriting was very good, which had surprised everyone, including Crow.

"*Here's what I'd try. Let her load it however she likes for a month. Don't say anything. Don't sigh. I know about the sighing. At the end of the month, ask her what she's been tired of lately, and then don't interrupt. The bowls will survive. The bowls are tougher than you think.*"

"Bit harsh," said Crow.

"He drew her a diagram, Crow."

"Fair."

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*I work at the Oracle at Delphi. A colleague keeps finishing my prophecies. I'll be halfway through "When the eagle flies over the—" and she'll say "—broken tower, the king shall fall," and the petitioner just LEAVES. Often she isn't even right. How do I raise this without seeming petty?*

*Foretold in Phocis*

---

"Ah," said Sisyphus fondly. "A seer who interrupts. That's someone who's afraid of silence." He shifted his grip. "*Dear Foretold. Speak to her privately, and make it about the petitioners rather than yourself. 'People seem confused when there are two of us talking' is easier for her to hear than 'You're stealing my eagles.' And next time it happens, keep going. Finish your sentence calmly, over the top of hers if you have to. You'd be amazed how often people stop doing things once those things stop working.*"

"Do you think she knows she's doing it?"

"She's an oracle, Crow. You'd hope so."

---

The boulder went up another twenty feet. Crow walked backwards along the top of it in small, irritated steps, like a lumberjack on a log.

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*My lover and I would like to introduce olive oil into the bedchamber. Is there anything we should know?*

*Anonymous, Corinth (not the posh bit)*

---

Crow's quill hovered. Sisyphus considered the question with exactly the same expression he'd given the dishwasher.

"*Dear Anonymous. Put a towel down. Not your good towel. Use the second pressing, because the first pressing is for bread and you'll both feel guilty afterwards. And mind the floor when you get up. More people end up at the healer's from the getting-up than from anything else.*"

"Is that from experience?" said Crow.

"I was a king once, Crow. Kings have a lot of free evenings."

---

The next envelope had clearly been dropped in something. Crow held it up by one corner. It dripped.

"Sorry," said Crow. "Bit of a headwind over the Acheron."

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*I have fallen in love with my ~~▓▓▓▓▓~~ but I am terrified my ~~▓▓▓▓▓~~ will find out. Every night I ~~▓▓▓▓▓~~ it until it is ~~▓▓▓▓▓~~, and then I feel terrible. Should I tell ~~▓▓▓▓▓~~ or simply ~~▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓~~ the goat?*

*Soggy in ~~▓▓~~los*

---

There was a pause.

"The goat's legible," said Crow.

"The goat is doing a great deal of work in that sentence."

"Could be Pylos. Could be Delos. Could be Argos with a bad *g*."

"Could be anything." Sisyphus took a long breath, leaned into the boulder, and closed his eyes. "Right. *Dear Soggy. Whatever it is you're doing every night, the fact that you feel terrible afterwards is the most useful part of your letter. That feeling is trying to tell you something. In my experience, the person you're afraid will find out usually already suspects, and they'd much rather hear it from you. Tell them. Do it kindly, and somewhere neutral.*" He opened one eye. "*As for the goat, leave the goat out of it. The goat didn't ask for any of this.*"

Crow wrote it down and looked at it for a while. "That works for nearly anything."

"That's the idea."

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*I am forty-three. I have done the same job every day for twenty years. I get up, I make the pots, the pots are sold, I make more pots. Some days I wonder whether this is all there is. Is it?*

*Potter, Thebes*

---

Sisyphus didn't answer straight away. He pushed the boulder to the top, the very top, where the honest gradient gave up and the whole valley spread out underneath. The light was doing something nice over the olive groves. He watched it.

"*Dear Potter,*" he said at last. "*Who buys your pots? Do you know their names? Go and find out. Ask one of them what they keep in it. I promise you it'll be something you never imagined. Somebody's grandmother's ashes, or the good figs, or love letters they're hiding from somebody else.*

"*Doing the same thing every day isn't what wears you down. What wears you down is never looking up while you do it. It's not the same day twice, even when it feels that way. The view keeps changing. You just have to turn round now and then and look at it.*"

The boulder trembled, the way it always did, and started to roll back down.

Sisyphus watched it go with mild interest, like a man watching a bus he knows will come round again.

---

There was one envelope left. It was black and sealed with something that was certainly not wax.

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*One of my employees appears to be enjoying his work. What should I do?*

*H.*

---

Sisyphus smiled and started down the hill.

"*Dear H,*" he said. "*Nothing. But do send more post.*"

---

\* *Crow didn't like to talk about the route. Like most people who regularly fly over the rivers of the Underworld, Crow had a strong professional opinion about headwinds and kept it to himself.*

# Sisyphus Gives Advice

The boulder reached the top of the hill at about half past ten, as it generally did. It paused at the summit for the length of a held breath, and then went back down. Sisyphus watched it go with the mild interest of a man watching a neighbour's cat.

"Right," he said, dusting off his hands. "Where were we?"

Crow, perched on a dead olive tree with a quill in one foot and a wax tablet balanced against the trunk, shuffled the morning's post with its beak.*

*\*Crow was not a magical familiar in any formal sense. It had simply turned up one day, watched the boulder go up and down eleven times, and concluded that anyone this predictable was a reliable source of breadcrumbs. Things had developed from there.*

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*My wife and I argue constantly about the dishwashing. She says I stack the bowls wrong. I say there is no wrong way to stack bowls. We have had this argument for eleven years.*

*— Correctly Stacked, Thebes*

---

Sisyphus started walking down the hill. He did his best thinking on the way down.

"Dear Correctly," he said. "There is a wrong way. You know there is, because you've seen her face."

Crow scratched it down.

"But it isn't about the bowls. Eleven years is a long time to care about bowls. When someone corrects the same small thing for that long, they're usually asking whether you're paying attention to them. So stack them her way for a month. Not because she's right. Because it costs you nothing, and she'll notice, and being noticed is what she's been asking for since about year two." He stepped over a rock. "Then ask her what else she's been wanting to say. Make tea first. It might take a while."

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*I work for a fabric merchant from dawn until well past dark. I keep telling myself it is temporary. It has been temporary for nine years. My children call my brother "Papa" by accident, and he doesn't correct them as quickly as I'd like.*

*— Nearly There, Corinth*

---

The boulder was waiting at the bottom, looking as innocent as a boulder can. Sisyphus put his shoulder to it and began to push.

"Dear Nearly," he grunted. "Write down what 'there' looks like. An amount of money. A date. If you can't, then you aren't nearly there. You're nearly somewhere else entirely, and nobody has told you."

Crow waited. Sisyphus shifted his grip.

"Also, take Thursday afternoon off. Not to rest. Just to see whether the business collapses. It won't. That's the thing you're frightened of finding out." A pause, and a heave. "And take the children somewhere your brother has never taken them. Somewhere sticky."

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*A man at the olive press keeps presenting my ideas to the foreman as his own. I am a kind person and I don't want to make a fuss.*

*— Pressed, Argos*

---

"Dear Pressed. Being kind is lovely, but it isn't a filing system. Write your ideas down and send them to the foreman before the meeting, with a copy to someone else. Be cheerful about it. You don't have to accuse anyone of anything. You just have to be first, and in ink." He considered. "He'll probably stop on his own. People like that are rarely villains. They're just lazy, and you've made it inconvenient."

---

Crow paused over the next letter. Then it read it again, which it did not normally do.

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*My lover has asked me to dress up as a swan. Is this normal?*

*— Leda's Cousin, Sparta*

---

Sisyphus stopped pushing for a moment, which was risky, and thought about it seriously.

"Dear Cousin. First, ask him whether he is, himself, a swan. Or has ever been one. Or has a brother on a mountain who throws lightning about. I'd want that cleared up before anything else."

Crow made a small noise that might have been a laugh.

"If he's an ordinary man, then yes, it's normal enough. People want all sorts of odd things, and most of them are harmless and a bit sweet. A good rule is that you can say yes, no, or 'not yet', and a decent person meets all three with good grace. If 'not yet' gets you sulking, he isn't really asking about the costume." He resumed pushing. "Feathers get everywhere, mind."

---

The god arrived just before noon, in the way minor gods do: suddenly, and slightly too close. He was thin and pinched, with the expression of a man who has found a hair in the soup of creation.

"Momus," said Sisyphus pleasantly, not stopping. "God of criticism."

"Satire *and* criticism." Momus peered at Crow's tablet. "This is very *reasonable*. Nobody wants reasonable. The column needs a hook. Some cruelty. Possibly a catchphrase."

"I'll think about it."

"And the name is weak. 'Ask Sisyphus.' It's just your name with 'ask' in front."

"It does tell people what to do."

"And the crow's handwriting is appalling."

Crow looked at Momus for a long moment, then went back to writing with what can only be described as deliberate neatness.

"You know," said Sisyphus, "you've come all the way down from Olympus three times this month to tell me what's wrong with this."

"Someone has to."

"Mm. Do they talk to you much, up there? The others?"

Momus opened his mouth, closed it, said something about the quality of the hill, and vanished with a small, offended pop.

The boulder reached the top. It paused. It went back down.

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*I am forty years old and I still don't know what I'm for. Everyone else seems to have been handed a purpose. I think mine was lost in the post.*

*— Unsorted, Delphi*

---

Sisyphus walked down the hill slowly in the warm afternoon.

"Dear Unsorted. Nobody was handed one. They're all making it up and not mentioning it, which is good manners but bad for people like you. Don't go looking for what you're *for*. Go looking for what you'd be glad to do again tomorrow. Something small and useful. Mend things. Teach someone to read. Bake for the neighbour who's been ill." He reached the bottom and laid a palm on the warm stone. "Meaning grows on things that are done over and over, the way moss does on anything that keeps still long enough. Or so I'm told."

Crow wrote it down and looked at him for a while. Sisyphus didn't notice. He was already pushing.

---

The evening post brought one more letter, on very expensive paper, in a cramped and irritable hand.

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*Nobody up here likes me. I don't know why. I am only ever honest.*

*— Not Momus, Olympus*

---

Sisyphus read it twice and smiled.

"Get a fresh tablet," he said. "This one's going to take a while."

# The Cicada

The boy woke me by drawing back the shutter, and the light off the Pearl River came in like something thrown.

"Lieutenant. Mr. Johnston's clerk is downstairs. Third time."

"Tell him I'm dressing."

"I told him that the second time, sir."

My shirt from the day before lay over the chair, stiff at the collar with yesterday's sweat. I put it on anyway. My knees ached the way they used to ache only after a night on watch in a Biscay gale, and I yawned so hard my jaw cracked. The yawning was always first, and it embarrassed me more than anything that came after. In my coat pocket my fingers found the jade cicada, cool as a river stone, and I worked my thumb along the ridges of its folded wings.

The clerk was a pale young man named Ashby who smelled of camphor against the moths.

"Captain Elliot asks after the report on the Lintin anchorage. The receiving ships, sir. The tally of vessels."

"It's nearly finished."

"He asked for it Tuesday."

"Then he'll have it a week late, Mr. Ashby, which in this country is very nearly early." He didn't laugh. I wiped my nose with the back of my wrist. "Tell him the sampans were thick and the count kept changing."

"Are you unwell, sir? You look feverish."

"Canton," I said. "Everyone looks feverish."

---

Hog Lane at ten in the morning was a gutter running between two rows of grog-shops, narrow enough that a Lascar and a Danish sailor couldn't pass without one of them turning sideways. It smelled of samshu and frying lard and the bilge of a hundred ships, and over all of it hung the drowsy, burnt-sugar sweetness that came out of the upper windows. I kept my hat brim low. A naval coat drew eyes here, and those were mostly from men who wanted to know whether I'd come about their discharge papers.

Ah Fook kept his stall at the river end, behind a curtain of dried fish. He was weighing a lump of sycee silver on a little brass steelyard and didn't look up.

"Mister Merrick. Too early. You come too early now, every day more early."

"I've money."

"How much money?"

I set three Spanish dollars on the counter. They'd been chopped so many times by so many shroffs testing them that the King's face was nearly eaten away. Ah Fook turned them over with one long fingernail.

"Three dollar buy you half ball Malwa. Not Patna. Patna price go up. Mandarin boats very busy this month, very angry. Viceroy say he cut heads."

"Half a ball won't see me through tomorrow."

"Then you bring more dollar tomorrow." He finally looked at me, and I'll grant that there was no cruelty in it. If anything his look was patient, the way a man looks at weather. "Or you talk to Mister Cowie. Mister Cowie ask for you."

The cicada had gone warm in my fist. I could feel the sweat starting along my spine, a cold that didn't belong to the heat of the day. "What does Cowie want?"

"Not my business. My business is mud." He slid my dollars back across the counter. "Go see. Then come back with more."

---

Cowie had taken rooms behind the Creek Factory, above a chandler's. He was a Glasgow man with a ruined, cheerful face, and he received me in his shirtsleeves, eating lychees from a blue bowl and spitting the stones into his palm.

"Lieutenant. You look like something the tide left on Whampoa mud."

"Ah Fook says you wanted me."

"I do. Sit. You'll take a lychee?"

"No."

"Suit yourself." He wiped his fingers on his trousers. "You're going down to Lintin Friday, aye? Official business. Elliot's tally."

"How do you know that?"

"Everybody knows everything here, it's a village with a river through it. The Superintendent's cutter doesn't get searched. Not by the Chinese and not by our own." He took a packet from the drawer, oilcloth bound with tarred twine and about the size of a prayer book. "This goes aboard the *Hercules*. You hand it to the mate, a man called Pryor. That's all."

"What's in it?"

"Paper."

"What sort of paper?"

"The sort that's none of your concern, which is the very best sort." He set two gold mohurs on the table beside the packet. They gleamed there the way a lamp gleams at the end of a corridor. "Half now. Half when Pryor sends word."

I thought of the captain of my first ship, old Harcourt, who had pinned the medal on me after Navarino and said, *You've a steady hand, Merrick. The Service needs steady hands.* My hand on the cicada was not steady. I watched it, and so did Cowie.

"There's a sort of man," he said gently, "who'd turn this down. And then he'd lie in his bed tomorrow night with his guts in a knot and his skin crawling like it had ants under it. Is that the sort of man you are, Lieutenant?"

I put the packet inside my coat. It sat against my ribs, heavier than paper had any right to be.

"Good lad," said Cowie, and spat a stone into his hand.

---

Ah Fook gave me a full ball of Patna this time, wrapped in poppy-petal cakes, without remarking on where the gold had come from. The den was two doors along. You climbed a ladder rather than a stair into a long low room that held all the day's heat under its tiles. The pallets were set in rows like berths on a gun deck, and there was the soft clack of pipe bowls, and somebody breathing slowly in the dark with a wet sound in his chest.

The old woman who kept the lamps knew me. She knew me better than Elliot did, or my mother in Portsmouth, or any man I'd served with.

"Lie down, Captain," she said in her pidgin. She always called me Captain. I had stopped correcting her.

She worked a bead of the black paste over the flame until it swelled and blistered and turned the colour of a horse chestnut, then pressed it into the bowl. I drew. The smoke was heavy and faintly bitter on the tongue, like burnt sugar with something rotten folded underneath. Then the ache went out of my knees and the cold went out of my spine, and the packet against my ribs weighed nothing at all.

Afterward I lay with the cicada on my chest. The Chinese put them in the mouths of the dead, someone told me once, so the soul could slough its body and crawl out new into the light. I'd bought it for that reason, in my first month here, when I still found such things charming.

"Captain," the old woman said somewhere above me. "You want one more?"

Outside, the river was carrying the whole of the afternoon down toward the sea. Ashby would be waiting at the factory, and Elliot would be waiting for his report.

"Yes," I said. "One more."

# The Lamp at Hog Lane

The bosun's mate found me at the water stairs before eight bells, while the river was still the colour of weak tea.

"Captain Elliot's compliments, sir, and he'd hoped to see you at the factory by nine. Something about the Hoppo's new edict."

"Tell Captain Elliot I'm inspecting the cutter's moorings." My hands were already in my pockets. That was where I kept them in the mornings.

"The cutter's moored at Whampoa, sir."

"Then I shall have a long walk, Pearce."

He looked at me the way a man looks at a fouled anchor: not angry, only calculating the work. Then he touched his hat and went. I stood a moment longer and watched a dung boat slide downriver, its sculler singing something tuneless under a straw hat as wide as a cartwheel. My shirt was already damp beneath the blue wool. My joints hummed like rigging in a wind I couldn't feel.

---

Framjee kept his counting house behind the Danish factory, up a stair that smelled of sandalwood and lamp black. He did not rise when I came in.

"Lieutenant. You are early, or you are late."

"I'm here, which ought to be enough." I put the silver snuffbox on his desk, my father's, with the crest worn nearly smooth by three generations of thumbs. "Eleven dollars."

He opened it, closed it, and weighed it in his palm like a fruit. "Six."

"It was eleven last month."

"Last month it was a different box. You have sold me the watch, the sword knot, and the spyglass." He laid it down. "I am not a pawnbroker, James. I am a man with a long memory and a short patience. Six, or I have something better for you."

"Better how?"

He smiled, and the smile went no further than his teeth. "The *Hercules* sits at Lintin with four hundred chests. The mandarin cruisers have grown greedy this season. A smug boat flying a navy pennant, with a navy officer in her stern sheets, is a boat the cruisers do not trouble."

"That's not a job. That's a court martial."

"Twenty dollars, Spanish, milled. And the cruisers do not keep logbooks."

I looked at the snuffbox. My father had carried it at Camperdown.

"Give me the six," I said. "And tell me when the boat leaves."

---

Hog Lane at noon was a gutter running between grog shops, sailors from every flag in the anchorage wallowing in it. A Lascar with one ear was being sick into a cask. Two Americans off a Boston ship were arguing about Andrew Jackson with the passion of men who had never met him.

Old Ah Sam stood behind his counter with his pigtail coiled up under his cap against the heat, polishing a glass with a rag that made it dirtier.

"Mellick! Long time no see. Two day."

"One day, Sam."

"Two day. I count." He poured me a measure of samshu without asking. It smelled of burnt rice and turpentine. "You look bad. Face like boiled fish."

"Thank you. Is Lo Kwan still at the old place?"

He stopped polishing. "Lo Kwan all same. Price no all same. New viceroy make big squeeze, plenty men get chop-chop." He drew a finger across his throat, cheerfully enough. "Price go up."

"How far up?"

"You ask Lo Kwan." He leaned in. His breath smelled of ginger and decay. "You navy man. Navy man know when mandarin boat come, when go. Maybe Lo Kwan give you better price for knowing."

"Everyone in Canton wants to sell me my own commission today."

"Maskee." He shrugged. "Commission no can smoke."

---

The alley to Lo Kwan's ran behind the fruit hongs, where the merchants dumped what wouldn't sell. By July the mangoes rotted there in drifts, split and blackening and sweet past bearing, and the smell came at me before I turned the corner, thick enough to chew. Wasps drowsed in the pulp. A barefoot child squatted in a doorway, sucking a stone clean, and watched me with the flat professional interest of a creditor.

My boots stuck to the stones. That smell had come to mean the end of waiting, and I had grown so used to it that my mouth watered. I didn't like to think about that.

The door was low, its red paper charm faded to the pink of an old wound. I knocked twice, then once.

Lo Kwan's nephew opened it. He was perhaps sixteen and wore a scholar's gown he hadn't earned.

"No room."

"There's always room."

"For dollars, room. For lieutenant, no room."

I showed him the six. He looked at the coins as though they had insulted his mother.

"Eight now. Viceroy price."

"I have six, and I have something your uncle wants." I lowered my voice, though there was no one to hear but the wasps. "Tell him the cruiser at Chuenpee changes watch at the second hour after midnight. Tell him I'll know which nights it sails short-handed."

The boy considered this. Somewhere inside, a man coughed, a long and wet and patient cough, the kind that has given up expecting to be cured.

"You wait," he said, and shut the door in my face.

I waited. The wasps went about their business. I thought of the *Hercules* riding at anchor in the brown roads off Lintin, and of Pearce's careful face, and of Elliot at his desk with the Hoppo's edict spread out under a paperweight, wondering where his lieutenant had got to. I thought of the snuffbox in Framjee's drawer. Then I made myself stop thinking, because the door was opening.

"Uncle say, come," said the boy. "Uncle say, you very useful man."

Inside was dim and close. The light came amber through oiled paper, and long low couches lined the walls with their pale occupants, a few in Chinese cloth and more than one in a European coat. The lamp sat waiting on its tray. The pipe was warm from the last man's mouth.

The old woman who prepared the pellets did not look at my face. She looked at my hands, which had begun to shake in earnest now that they were so close.

"Same same?" she asked.

"Same same," I said, and lay down on my side like a man going overboard.

The first breath tasted of burnt honey and copper. The second tasted of nothing at all. By the third, I could no longer smell the mangoes, and I had stopped caring what I had sold to come here.

prompt:
High Seas and Low Vices: British Naval Officer in the Opium Trade
Character: Lieutenant James Merrick, a high-ranking officer in the British Royal Navy stationed in Canton, China in the 1830s. Once promising and decorated, now struggling with a severe opium addiction he hides from his superiors.
Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. Told primarily in dialogue with the characters he interacts with. Focus on brief slices of his journey through the shadowy underworld of Canton: interactions with acquaintances, negotiations with local dealers, schemes and unsavoury jobs taken to fund his habit.
Writing Task: Use rich sensory details to describe a day in the life of James Merrick. Write for a real sense of time & place while avoiding cliche. First person, past tense. A persistent cough that tastes of copper haunts him, which he attributes to the sea air when questioned. 1000 words.
response:
# The Factories at Low Water

The boy Ah Sing had been knocking for some time before I understood the sound was not inside my skull.

"Lieutenant. Lieutenant Merrick. Captain Elliot's man come twice."

"Tell him I've gone to Whampoa."

"I tell him that yesterday."

"Then tell him I've come back from Whampoa and gone again."

I sat up. The shutters threw bars of white light across the floor, and the room smelled of camphor wood, wet plaster, and something sweeter beneath that nothing ever quite washed out. My uniform hung on its peg like a man who had hanged himself politely. I coughed into my palm, and the taste came, that flat penny taste, as if I had been sucking on a ship's fitting all night.

Ah Sing watched me wipe my hand on the coverlet. "You sick, Lieutenant?"

"It's the river air. Damp gets into a man."

"River air never make Ah Sing cough."

"Then you're made of better stuff than the Royal Navy. Fetch my coat."

---

Hog Lane at ten in the morning was all elbows. Sailors from the Indiamen down at Whampoa slept against the walls where the grog-sellers had poured them out. A man was frying something in a pan the size of a cartwheel, and the fat spat garlic and dried shrimp into the air. Hong coolies trotted past with tea chests slung from bamboo, calling out a rhythm that never broke.

Thorne found me at the corner, as he always did, the American, all teeth and nankeen trousers.

"Merrick. You look like a drowned curate."

"And you look like money. Have you got any?"

"For you? Depends what the Navy's selling this week." He lowered his voice. "When does the *Wolf* sail up past the Bogue?"

"I don't know."

"You're aide to the Superintendent. You know when he takes his tea."

"Thursday," I said. It came out of me easily, the way a splinter comes out once you've stopped flinching. "Thursday, on the flood tide. She'll anchor off Chuenpee and sit there being visible."

"And the mandarin cruisers?"

"Will see the *Wolf* and remember urgent business elsewhere. Your crab boats can run Wednesday night without trouble."

He pressed eight Spanish dollars into my hand, and each one had been chopped so many times by so many shroffs that King Carlos's face looked as if it had been through a mangle.

"Eight? Last time it was twelve."

"Last time you weren't shaking."

---

Old Wu's place lay behind a cloth-dyer's off Old China Street. You walked through vats of indigo first, and the dye-men's arms were blue to the elbow, and the steam off the vats smelled of rot and earth. Then a curtain, then stairs, then Wu, seated behind a table with a set of brass scales so finely made you could have weighed a sparrow's grief on them.

"Mister Melick." He had never once said my name right, and I had long since stopped minding. "You come early."

"I'm buying, not smoking. Something to take away."

"Patna or Malwa?"

"Whatever eight dollars buys."

He looked at the coins, then at me. "Eight dollar buy Malwa. Little bit."

"Wu. We've known each other three years."

"Three year, yes. First year you pay sycee silver. Second year you pay dollar. Now you pay chopped dollar and story." He folded his hands. "What story today?"

"No story. A proposition. There's a Parsee, Framjee, who's holding forty chests at Lintin he can't get upriver. I can put a word to the customs launch. Say the boat carries the Superintendent's private stores. Navy seal, no inspection."

"You have seal?"

"I have access to the seal."

Wu was quiet a while. Somewhere below a dye-man sang, tunelessly, the same three notes.

"Framjee pay you how much?"

"He doesn't know about it yet. You'd tell him. You'd take a share."

"And if the customs launch open box anyway?"

"Then I'm hanged and you've lost nothing but a lieutenant."

He laughed at that, a small dry sound like paper tearing, and he weighed out a ball of the dark gummy stuff, more than eight dollars' worth. He wrapped it in a leaf and then in oilcloth.

"You come tonight. Framjee come also. Bring seal."

---

Hollis caught me on the quay before the British factory, where the Union flag hung limp above the veranda in the heat.

"Where the devil have you been? Elliot's asked for you three times."

"Whampoa."

"You weren't at Whampoa. I was at Whampoa." He peered at me. "James, you're grey."

"Bad oysters."

"You've been coughing since the monsoon turned."

"Sea air. It never agreed with me."

"You've been at sea since you were eleven years old."

"And it's never agreed with me once." I smiled, and he didn't. "Tell Elliot I'll attend him before dinner. Tell him I was inspecting the boats."

"Which boats?"

"Any boats. He'll never ask."

Hollis put his hand on my sleeve. It was a kind hand, and I wanted very badly to break it.

"There's talk," he said. "About officers who keep rooms in the Chinese town."

"There's always talk. It's the chief export after tea."

---

The seal lived in a lacquered box in the Superintendent's office, and the clerk, Pettigrew, went to his supper at six as regularly as the tide. I waited on the veranda, watching the sampans jostle on the brown water, and the boatwomen's babies in their wicker floats bobbed at the ends of tethers like little buoys. The river smelled of mud and night soil and sandalwood smoke from the joss house across the water.

When Pettigrew left, I went in. The box was not locked. That was the worst of it. Nobody had ever imagined it needed to be.

The wax was the colour of dried blood. I pressed three sheets of blank paper and folded them into my breast pocket, where they sat against my heart like a second, slower pulse.

---

That night at Wu's, Framjee wore white, and he fingered the sheets by lamplight with long, precise fingers.

"This is genuine, Lieutenant?"

"As genuine as I am."

He looked up. "That is not the reassurance you believe it is."

But he paid. And afterward Wu's girl brought the lamp and the pipe, the long bamboo stem worn smooth by other men's mouths, and I lay on my side on the hard couch with the porcelain headrest cool beneath my cheek.

The first draw tasted of burnt sugar and old flowers. The second tasted of nothing at all.

I coughed once, and the copper rose, and then even that was carried away down the river with everything else.

# Gunpowder Rendezvous

The jukebox in the corner of the Rusty Anchor has been playing the same song for forty minutes. It's a scratchy three-chord rocker with a singer who sounds like he gargles battery acid, and every time it ends, the neon tubes flicker pink and blue and the needle drops right back to the beginning.

Nobody's gotten up to fix it. Nobody here fixes anything.

Spike Spiegel sits at the end of the bar with an unlit cigarette between his lips and a glass of something brown he can't afford. His last real meal was two days ago, a bowl of bell peppers and beef with no beef. The bounty sheet folded in his jacket pocket says *Marcus Vey, 3.2 million woolongs, wanted alive*, and the bartender swears Vey drinks here every Thursday.

It's Thursday. Vey isn't here.

Somebody else is.

She comes through the door like she's been personally insulted by it. Black crop top, cutoff shorts that barely deserve the name, and a dragon tattoo coiling up her right arm in green and red ink. Two pistol grips jut from twin shoulder holsters. She scans the room the way Spike does, exits first, then hands, then faces, and when her eyes land on him they narrow.

She sits two stools down and slaps a crumpled paper on the bar. Spike recognizes the photo of Marcus Vey before she's finished smoothing it flat.

"Rum," she tells the bartender. "Bacardi. Leave the bottle."

Spike strikes a match, lights his cigarette, and slides the matchbook down the bar toward her. She catches it without looking.

"Funny place for a tourist," he says.

"Funny face for a dead man." She lights her own cigarette and exhales at the ceiling. "You're on Vey."

"Am I?"

"Your coat's got a paper sticking out of it, genius. Same blue stamp as mine." She pours a shot, kills it, pours another. "So here's how this goes. You finish your drink, you walk out that door, and I don't redecorate the place with your brains."

Spike smiles, slow and lazy. "That's a lot of confidence for someone who hasn't asked my name."

"Don't need it. Tombstones come blank."

"Spike."

She stares at him a long moment. The jukebox wails about a highway to nowhere.

"Revy," she says finally, like it costs her something.

---

They drink. Neither of them meant to.

By the third round they've established that she works out of a place called Roanapur, that he works out of a ship that smells like engine grease and dog, and that neither of them has any intention of splitting 3.2 million anything.

"Split's for suckers," Revy says. Her boots are up on the rung of his stool now, and she doesn't seem to have noticed. "Guy like you, all hair and no backbone. Bet you couldn't hit a barn from inside it."

"Depth perception's a little off," Spike admits, tapping beneath his right eye. "Makes things interesting."

"Christ. A half-blind cowboy." She laughs, a sharp, ugly bark, and it's the first honest thing he's heard all night. "You're gonna get yourself killed."

"Already did that once." He shrugs. "Didn't take."

Something shifts in her face, a flicker, gone before he can name it. She looks at him the way people look at a mirror they didn't expect to find.

"Yeah," she says quietly. "I know how that goes."

Then the door bangs open and Marcus Vey walks in with four men in cheap suits, and the moment is over.

---

Vey sees the bounty sheets on the bar before he sees their faces. That's his mistake.

The first suit goes for his piece. Revy's hands blur and both Cutlasses are out and barking before Spike's even off his stool. Glass explodes. The jukebox takes a stray round and lurches, skips, and keeps playing the same damn song a half-step flat.

Spike moves low. He sweeps the second suit's legs, catches the third with an elbow, and puts the fourth on the floor with a palm strike he learned a lifetime ago. His Jericho clears its holster and he fires twice: one round shatters the bottle in Vey's hand, the other punches into the wall an inch from Vey's ear.

"Missed," Revy shouts over the noise.

"Didn't," Spike says. "Wanted alive."

Vey bolts out the back. They both go after him, shoulder to shoulder, shoving each other in the narrow hallway like kids racing for the last seat. Out in the rain-slick alley, Vey is already peeling away in a battered hovercar, taillights bleeding red into the fog.

Revy fires a full clip after him and swears in two languages.

Spike lights another cigarette. "Well. Whatever happens, happens."

She rounds on him, soaked and furious and grinning like a wolf. "You are the most useless son of a bitch I have ever met."

"You keep saying that," he says, "but you're still standing here."

---

The motel is called the Starlite, and half the letters are out. Somehow they've ended up in the same room, Number 9, because the clerk only had one left and neither of them would back down.

The rain drums on the roof. Through the thin wall, a radio plays faint and tinny, and Spike swears it's the same song from the bar.

Revy's back is against the door. Spike's is against the window. Her right-hand Cutlass is pointed at his chest. His Jericho is pointed at hers. Twelve feet of stained carpet lie between them, and the air is so thick with smoke and wet leather and something else that neither of them will name.

"Vey's skipping planet tomorrow," she says. "Spaceport, oh-six-hundred."

"I know."

"So one of us walks out of here first and gets there first."

"That's the idea."

Neither of them moves. Her eyes drop to his mouth for half a second, then snap back up, angry at herself. He watches her pulse jump in her throat. His own heartbeat is loud enough to count.

"You're not gonna shoot me," she says.

"Neither are you."

"Don't bet on it, cowboy."

"I bet on everything." He lowers the gun an inch. Just an inch. "I usually lose."

She holds it a moment longer. Then, impossibly, she laughs. It's softer this time, almost tired. The muzzle of her Cutlass dips toward the floor.

Outside, the rain doesn't stop. On the other side of the wall, the song starts over again.

Nobody gets up to fix it.

# Gunpowder Rendezvous

A lazy ceiling fan barely stirs the smoky air inside the bar. It turns the way everything turns on this rock at the edge of the system, slow and sullen, like it's doing you a favor.

Spike Spiegel slouches onto a stool and counts his money on the counter. Four woolongs and a button. The bartender looks at the button.

"Water," Spike says. "And whatever's in the peanut bowl."

"Peanut bowl's for paying customers."

"I'm paying. Four woolongs' worth of peanuts."

Two stools down, a woman laughs, a short ugly bark with smoke in it. She's got her boots up on the rail, a bottle of Bacardi sweating beside her elbow, and a dragon tattoo coiling down her right arm like it's trying to crawl off her. Two pistol grips jut from shoulder holsters, chrome and heavy. Spike clocks them the way some men clock legs. Then he clocks the legs too, because he isn't dead. Not this week, anyway.

"Jesus fuck," she says. "Cowboys are getting cheap."

"Cowboys are getting hungry." He tilts his head at the folded paper under her bottle. The edge of a mugshot peeks out: a fat face, a gold tooth, *DMITRI VASS — 12,000,000 W.* "Funny. I've got the same picture in my pocket. Thought it was a love letter."

She slides her hand over the paper without looking down. "Then you can fuck right off back to whatever shuttle you crawled out of. Vass is mine."

"Says who?"

"Says the guy who wired me half up front." She pours rum into a second glass and shoves it at him, which is either generosity or a dare. "Revy."

"Spike." He drinks. It burns all the way down and keeps burning. "Same guy wired me. Guess he's hedging his bets."

"Guess he's a dead man when I find him." She lights a cigarette and doesn't offer one. He takes his own out, finds no lighter, and leans toward her flame. She doesn't pull it away. For a second their faces are close enough that he can see a thin scar through her eyebrow, and she can see that one of his eyes doesn't move quite right with the other.

"Glass eye?" she asks.

"Mostly."

"Shit depth perception, then."

"I make up for it."

"Yeah?" She smiles with only half her mouth. "Bet you miss a lot."

"Only on purpose."

They drink. They drink again. The bartender stops pretending he's not listening. Revy matches him glass for glass and doesn't sway, and somewhere around the fifth round Spike realizes she isn't trying to get him drunk. She's trying to watch how he moves when he is. He likes her a little more for it, and trusts her a lot less.

The door bangs open at 11:40. Gold tooth. Three bodyguards in matching bad suits.

Nobody says anything. Nobody has to.

Revy is off her stool before the door finishes swinging, Cutlasses already out, and the first bodyguard goes down with two holes in his chest before he's finished reaching. Spike kicks his stool into the second one's knees, rolls behind the bar, and comes up with the Jericho barking. Glass explodes. The fan takes a round and wobbles like a drunk. Revy is laughing, actually laughing, firing both hands in two different directions. It's the most beautiful thing Spike has seen in months, and it scares the hell out of him.

Vass dives through the side door, bleeding from the shoulder.

"That was my shot!" Revy shouts.

"You missed it."

"*You* fucking missed it, Cyclops!"

They hit the alley at the same time, shoulder to shoulder, neither willing to step back.

---

The Starlight Motor Inn has two working letters on its sign and a blood trail leading to Room 9. The door is open. Vass is face-down by the bed, breathing, bleeding, and unconscious, apparently having tripped over the luggage rack. Spike zip-ties him and drags him into the bathtub.

When he turns around, Revy's Cutlass is six inches from his face.

His Jericho is already at her sternum. He doesn't remember drawing it. That's the problem with a body trained for the old life. It never asks permission.

"Here's how this goes," Revy says. "I walk out with the fat fuck. You walk out with your teeth."

"Counteroffer. We split it."

"I don't split shit."

"Then we've got a problem." He doesn't move. Neither does she. The motel's air conditioner rattles. A neon sign outside paints her red, then nothing, then red again. Her breathing is a little fast, and his is too, and neither of them would ever admit it's not just the adrenaline.

"You'd do it," she says. It's not a question. She's searching his face for something. "You'd actually pull."

"Maybe. You?"

"In a heartbeat." But her finger hasn't tightened, and they both know it.

He takes a slow step closer. The barrel of her gun touches his forehead, cold. The Jericho presses into the soft place under her ribs. Close enough now to smell the rum and the gun oil and the cheap shampoo, close enough to see that her pupils are blown wide and not entirely from the fight.

"I've already died once," Spike says softly. "It wasn't so bad."

"That supposed to scare me off, cowboy?"

"It's supposed to tell you I'm not scared."

"Everybody's scared." Her voice drops, rough. "Everybody's just lying about it."

For a long moment, the only sound is Vass groaning in the bathtub.

Then Revy reaches up with her free hand, pulls the unlit cigarette from behind Spike's ear, puts it between his lips, and lights it with her own, the two tips kissing in the dark. Neither gun lowers an inch.

"Sixty-forty," she says.

"Fifty-fifty."

"Sixty-forty, or I find out whether you bleed as pretty as you talk."

He exhales smoke past her cheek. Her mouth is very close. His finger rests on the trigger. Her thumb rests on the hammer.

"Whatever happens," Spike murmurs, "happens."

"Yeah?" Revy grins, all teeth and trouble. "Then let's see what happens."

Outside, the neon flickers red.

Inside, nobody moves first.

# Gunpowder Rendezvous

The bar is called the Lucky Strike, which is a lie on two counts. Nobody here is lucky, and the last thing to strike anything in this place was the ceiling fan, which hit a drunk in 2071 and hasn't turned since.

Spike Spiegel sits at the end of the counter with a glass of something amber and a cigarette he can't light. He thumbs the lighter again. Spark, nothing. Spark, nothing. A ring of rust circles the base where the chrome has given up, a tide line from the canal on Callisto, the harbor on Venus, and that one time in the bathtub he'd rather not discuss.

"You're gonna wear the flint down to your goddamn knuckle."

The woman two stools over doesn't look at him when she says it. She's got a black crop top, shorts that end before the conversation starts, and a dragon tattoo that coils up her right arm like it's thinking about biting someone. Two pistol grips jut from shoulder holsters. Cutlasses, customized. Nobody carries two of those for decoration.

She flicks a Zippo and holds it out across the gap. Spike leans in. The flame lights her face from below: sharp jaw, sharper eyes, a scowl that looks like it was installed at the factory.

"Thanks."

"Wasn't charity. Your clicking was pissing me off."

He exhales smoke toward the dead fan. "Spike."

"Revy." She knocks back her rum. "And before you get cute, I know why you're here."

"Whatever happens, happens."

"The fuck does that mean?"

"Means I'm not gonna shoot you in a bar where the bourbon's this cheap."

Something flickers across her face, maybe amusement, maybe contempt. With Revy, Spike suspects, the difference is mostly a matter of how many bullets are involved.

---

They drink. It isn't a truce so much as two dogs deciding the same bone isn't worth bleeding over until it actually shows up. She drinks Bacardi like it owes her money. He drinks whatever's closest. She tells him about a boat and a man named Dutch and a city where the cops take bribes in the morning and the bodies wash up by noon. He tells her almost nothing, and she notices.

"You got dead eyes," she says. "Well. Eye. The other one's weird."

"It's fake."

"Yeah? How's that work with shooting?"

"Depth perception's garbage." He grins. "I just aim where the bullet's going to be."

She snorts. Then she laughs, actually laughs, a short, ugly, surprised sound, and for a second she looks younger, like somebody who hadn't learned yet what the world does to you.

The door bangs open.

Dusty Kovacs is fat, sweating, and holding a sawed-off. Behind him come three men who are mostly neck. Kovacs takes one look at the two bounty hunters at the end of the bar and makes the only smart decision of his life.

He runs.

His friends stay.

Revy is moving before the first shot. She vaults the counter and comes up with both Cutlasses barking, and the sound is unbelievable, a single continuous roar, brass raining across the bottles. Spike goes low and sideways, puts his Jericho through one goon's shoulder, sweeps the second man's legs with a heel and drops an elbow on his throat. The third gets two of Revy's rounds through the chest and folds onto the pool table.

Silence. The smell of cordite and spilled rum.

"Back door," Spike says.

"No shit."

They hit the alley together, and they're both already running.

---

They kick the door at the same time and the frame explodes, and Kovacs is gone. The bathroom window hangs open on a dark lot and an engine dopplering away into nothing.

Spike lowers his gun.

Revy doesn't.

He feels it before he sees it: the cold circle of a muzzle settling against his temple. He turns his head slowly. Her eyes are bright, breathing hard, a cut on her cheek beading red.

"Nothing personal," she says.

His Jericho is already under her chin. He doesn't remember putting it there. His body handles these things on its own.

Spark, nothing.

He laughs once, alone, and lets the unlit cigarette hang.
