# Chapter Seven: The Gentleman from Antares

The transfer vessel's air filtration system hummed with a persistent mechanical drone, the kind of sound a man stops hearing after an hour and starts hearing again after three. Arthur Neegan had reached the third hour.

He sat strapped into an acceleration couch that had been designed for someone shorter, in a cabin that smelled faintly of ozone and machine oil. The single viewport showed Mars falling away beneath them, rust-red and pocked, the great scar of the Valles Marineris visible as a dark thread across its face. Somewhere down there, in a prefabricated dome on the edge of the Tharsis plateau, his supper was still on the table. They had not given him time to eat it.

There had been six of them. They had worn grey uniforms with silver piping, and on each shoulder was the eight-pointed star of the Antares Diplomatic Corps. Their leader, a thin young man with a voice like a hotel clerk's, had said, "Mr. Neegan, your presence is requested," and had kept one hand resting on the holster at his hip the whole time he said it.

"Requested by whom?" Arthur had asked.

"By someone who would very much like to make your acquaintance."

That had been the whole of the explanation. Arthur had considered refusing, but only briefly. A mining engineer learns early to recognize a load-bearing wall.

Now he turned to the young man, who sat across the cabin reading a bound report.

"I don't suppose you'll tell me where we're going."

The young man did not look up. "Phobos Station, Mr. Neegan. Docking in forty minutes."

"Phobos is a Terran Authority installation."

"Phobos," said the young man, turning a page, "is whatever the people standing on it say it is."

---

The meeting room had been carved directly into the moon's interior, and its walls still showed the bite marks of the boring machines, smoothed over with a lacquer that gleamed amber under the fluorescent strips. A long table of genuine wood, which must have cost more to ship from Earth than Arthur earned in a year, ran down the center. At its far end, a man was pouring two glasses of something dark.

He was older than Arthur had expected, perhaps seventy, with a neat white beard and the soft, unhurried movements of someone who had never once needed to run. He wore no insignia at all.

"Mr. Neegan. Please, sit. You'll forgive the theatrics of your escort. Young men with sidearms do tend to mistake firmness for courtesy." He slid a glass across the table. "Martian whiskey. Distilled from hydroponic barley. It's dreadful, but it's local, and I find that matters."

Arthur sat. He did not touch the glass. "You're not Antares."

The old man smiled. "What makes you say that?"

"Antares men wear the star the way a priest wears a collar. You're not wearing anything."

"Observant. Good. I was told you were." He settled into his chair. "Let us say I am a friend of Antares. Antares has many friends. Most of them are quite unaware of it. You may call me Mr. Halloran, which is not my name, but is a perfectly serviceable one."

"All right, Mr. Halloran. What do you want?"

"Directly to the matter. Excellent." Halloran folded his hands. "I want to talk about arithmetic, Mr. Neegan. Do you know how much Azra has been extracted from Mars in the eleven years since its discovery?"

"Something under four tonnes, last I read."

"Three point eight. Every gram of it accounted for, assayed, and fought over. Three point eight tonnes, and it has already redrawn the map of human space. The Jovian Combine has built two ships capable of reaching Alpha Centauri in under nine years. The Terran Authority has built something considerably less peaceful, which it keeps in orbit around Venus and does not discuss." He sipped his whiskey and grimaced. "Now. The geological survey of your parcel, the one you were foolish enough to file publicly, suggests a vein of perhaps six hundred tonnes."

Arthur said nothing. The air handlers hummed in the walls.

"You understand what that means," Halloran continued gently. "Whoever controls your plot controls more Azra than has existed in the whole of human history, by a factor of one hundred and fifty. It is not a mine, Mr. Neegan. It is a lever long enough to move the solar system."

"Then I suppose you want to buy it."

"Buy it?" Halloran laughed, a short, dry sound. "My dear fellow, if I simply bought it, I would be dead within the month, and so would you, and so would the clerk who notarized the deed. No. I want to offer you something rather more interesting."

He reached beneath the table and produced a thin folder, which he placed in front of Arthur.

"Inside you will find a charter. It establishes your parcel, and a radius of forty kilometers around it, as an independent extraction zone under neutral administration. No corporate leases. No indentured labour. Wages paid in Antares scrip, convertible anywhere in the system. You would be its director."

Arthur opened the folder. The paper was heavy, cream-colored, embossed. The language was precise in the way that only lawyers and liars bother to be.

"Neutral," he said. "Neutral under whom?"

"Under a council of three. Yourself, a representative of Antares, and a third party to be named later."

"And who guarantees it?"

Halloran's eyes, pale and steady, met his. "The guarantee, Mr. Neegan, is that everyone else wants it too badly to let anyone else have it. The Combine will not permit the Authority to seize your land. The Authority will not permit the Combine. And neither will permit the mining syndicates, who would sell to both. Antares proposes to stand in the middle and keep the scales level. That is what a diplomatic corps is for."

"I've seen what your diplomatic corps is for. It came to my house with guns."

"It came to your house first," Halloran said quietly. "Consider what that means. Consider who would have come second."

Arthur closed the folder. His hands, he noticed, were perfectly steady, which surprised him.

"There's something you aren't telling me."

Halloran was silent for a long moment. Then he set down his glass.

"Azra accelerates decay, Mr. Neegan. You know this. What is less widely known is that it does so in proportion to its own mass, and not linearly. Our physicists have a curve. It rises very gently for a long while, and then it does not rise gently at all." He paused. "Six hundred tonnes, sitting quietly in the Martian crust, is a geological curiosity. Six hundred tonnes concentrated, refined, stockpiled in a single vault by a single government that believes itself clever, is something else entirely."

"How much else?"

"Enough," said Halloran, "that the question of who owns Mars may soon become rather less important than the question of whether there will continue to be a Mars to own."

The fluorescent strips buzzed. Somewhere beyond the amber walls, the vast machinery of Phobos Station turned over in its sleep.

"You have forty-eight hours," Halloran said, rising. "My young friends will see you home. I would advise you to lock your door, Mr. Neegan. Not that it will help. But it is the sort of thing a man ought to do."

# Chapter Four: The Courtesy of Antares

The transfer vessel *Meridian Courtesy* had been built for comfort, and Arthur Neegan found that more unsettling than anything else about the day.

He sat in a padded acceleration couch upholstered in burgundy leather, beneath a ceiling of brushed chrome ribs that curved like the inside of a whale. A porthole the size of a dinner plate showed Mars dropping away, the rust-colored desert going violet and then black at the limb. Somewhere below, beneath that vast indifferent crust, was his eighty hectares of scrub and regolith, his prefab dome, and the vein.

He tugged at his collar again. The suit had arrived that morning in a flat gray box, delivered by the same six men who now stood at intervals along the cabin wall. They wore charcoal uniforms with a single emblem at the shoulder: a red star inside a broken ring. *The Antares Diplomatic Corps.* Arthur had seen that emblem twice before, once on a newsreel about the Ganymede Settlement and once on the hull of a cruiser parked above Phobos with its gun ports open.

"Is the fit unsatisfactory, Mr. Neegan?"

The steward was young and smiled too evenly. He carried a tray with a single bulb of coffee, still steaming through its valve.

"The fit is fine," Arthur said. "It's the occasion I'm not sure about."

"I'm afraid I can't speak to the occasion, sir."

"No," said Arthur. "I didn't imagine you could."

He took the coffee. It was real coffee, Earth-grown. On Mars, a bulb like that cost a week of a miner's wages. Someone wanted him to notice that.

---

The orbital station had no name painted on it, which was itself a kind of name. The *Courtesy* docked with a series of soft clanks, and Arthur was escorted through a pressure lock and down a corridor lit by amber globes. The air smelled of ozone and lemon oil. Teletype machines chattered behind frosted glass doors. A pneumatic tube overhead thumped as a canister shot past.

At the corridor's end was a round room with a single great window looking out on Mars, which hung there enormous and patient. Before the window stood a table of black glass, and behind the table sat a man of perhaps seventy. He had a narrow, lined face, wore a plain white tunic with no insignia at all, and was polishing a pair of spectacles with a handkerchief.

"Mr. Neegan. Please, sit. You may call me Lambert. It isn't my name, but it will do the work of one."

Arthur sat. The guards withdrew, and the door sighed shut.

"Your men wear Antares colors," Arthur said.

"They do. The Corps was kind enough to lend them to me, and a few other things besides." Lambert settled the spectacles on his nose. "Do you know, Mr. Neegan, how many interstellar vessels are presently under construction in the inhabited system?"

"No."

"Four hundred and twelve. Two years ago there were nine. The difference is Azra. A gram of it, properly cradled in a reaction chamber, persuades a slug of uranium to give up in an hour what it would otherwise surrender over geological ages. It is the most useful substance humanity has ever found, and quite possibly the last one we'll need to find." He folded his hands. "Your land holds what our survey estimates at eleven thousand metric tonnes."

Arthur kept his face still. His own estimate had been six thousand, and it had frightened him badly enough.

"That's more than every other known deposit put together," he said.

"Roughly three times more. You see the difficulty."

"I see that a lot of people want to buy my land."

"Seventeen parties, at last count. The Callisto Mining Combine. Helion Consolidated, who hold your neighbors' labor contracts and would happily hold yours. The Terran Defense Ministry, through four separate shell companies that do not appear to know about one another. And Antares itself, naturally." Lambert smiled faintly. "I am not Antares, whatever my escort suggests."

"Then who are you?"

"Someone who has done the arithmetic." Lambert rose and went to the window. Against the red glow of the planet he looked very thin. "Consider. At present, the great powers each hold a little Azra, so each fears the others roughly equally. That fear is the only peace we have. Now hand eleven thousand tonnes to any single one of them. What follows?"

Arthur said slowly, "The others can't let that happen."

"They cannot. They would go to war to prevent it, and it would be the first war fought with weapons that accelerate decay. Do you know what such a warhead does to a city, Mr. Neegan? It doesn't explode it. It *ages* it. The steel rusts away in an afternoon, and the concrete crumbles to sand. And the people—" He stopped. "We have tested one. Once. On an asteroid. I have seen the films."

The pneumatic tube thumped again, somewhere far away.

"What's your offer?" Arthur asked.

Lambert returned to the table. "We will pay you four million credits a year, Mr. Neegan, to do nothing whatever. You will keep your title. You will refuse every buyer. You will mine nothing, sell nothing, and remain precisely what you are now: a modest engineer on a modest plot. We will see to your protection, discreetly."

"You want me to sit on the vein."

"I want you to be the one thing in this system that no one owns."

Arthur turned his coffee bulb in his fingers. "That's a fragile arrangement. One man."

"Yes. It is the very fragility that makes it work. Nobody fears you, so nobody needs to destroy you. Not yet."

"*Not yet*," Arthur repeated.

Lambert was quiet for a moment. Then he slid a thin folder across the glass. Inside was a single sheet of spectrographic data, columns of figures and a jagged trace.

"Our assayers dated a sample from your property. Isotopic ratios, crystalline lattice, the usual methods." He tapped one line. "The Azra in your ground is roughly nine billion years old."

Arthur frowned. "The solar system is four and a half."

"Quite so."

"Then it's from somewhere else. A meteorite. A captured body."

"Perhaps." Lambert took the folder back and closed it. "Or perhaps it was put there. I suspect that is the real question, Mr. Neegan, and I would very much prefer that we be the ones to answer it, quietly, rather than seventeen frightened governments with drills."

Mars turned beneath them, enormous and silent.

"And if I refuse?"

"Then you will be returned home with every courtesy." Lambert removed his spectacles and began to polish them again. "And I shall hope, sincerely, that you continue to have one."

Arthur reached up and adjusted his collar. It still did not fit.

# Chapter Seven: The Embassy at Phobos

The transfer vessel *Courtesy* had been built for comfort, which Arthur Neegan found more alarming than if it had been built for war.

He sat in a padded acceleration couch upholstered in burgundy leather. Indirect lighting hummed behind panels of brushed aluminum, and a small display screen on the bulkhead cycled patiently through its diagnostics in green phosphor text:

```
REACTOR CORE.........NOMINAL
HULL INTEGRITY.......99.7%
LIFE SUPPORT.........NOMINAL
AZRA DAMPING FIELD...ENGAGED
```

He read the last line four times. He had never heard of an Azra damping field. As far as he knew, as far as anyone on Mars knew, there was no such thing.

That morning there had been six of them on his doorstep, standing in the thin red dust with their pressure visors politely raised. They wore charcoal uniforms with silver piping, and the eight-pointed star of the Antares Diplomatic Corps was stitched on each shoulder. They carried sidearms in a casual way that made the weapons seem more serious, not less.

"Mr. Neegan," their leader had said, a young man with a careful smile, "you are invited to a conversation."

"And if I decline the invitation?"

The young man had looked genuinely pained. "Then I'm afraid we would have to invite you again, sir. More insistently."

So Arthur had packed a bag.

---

The *Courtesy* docked at Phobos four hours later. The tiny moon had been hollowed out a century ago for the old Terran Survey, then abandoned when the survey money ran dry. Someone had brought it back to life since, quietly and at great expense.

The room they brought him to had been carved straight out of the moon's rock and polished to a black gloss. One wall was a single viewport, and Mars filled it: rust and ochre, the great scar of the Valles Marineris running across its face like a healed wound. Somewhere down there, too small to see, was his house. Somewhere down there was his plot, and beneath it the vein.

A man stood at the viewport with his hands clasped behind him. He was perhaps sixty, silver-haired, dressed in a grey suit cut in a fashion that had gone out on Earth twenty years ago. When he turned, Arthur saw that his eyes were very pale and very tired.

"Mr. Neegan. Thank you for coming."

"I wasn't aware I had much choice."

"Everyone has a choice. The difficulty is that most choices are bad ones." The man gestured to a pair of chairs beside a low table, where a silver coffee service steamed. "Please. My name is Sebastian Orlov."

"You're with Antares?"

Orlov smiled faintly as he poured. "I am *adjacent* to Antares. The Corps lends us its insignia and its ships, and in return we lend it a certain deniability. It's an old arrangement. Cream?"

"Black." Arthur sat. "What does 'us' mean, exactly?"

"In time." Orlov handed him the cup. "First, let me tell you what you are sitting on. I suspect you don't fully know."

"I know it's a large vein."

"It is the largest concentration of Azra yet discovered in the settled systems. Our surveys put it at roughly four times the combined known reserves of the Tharsis claims." Orlov sipped his coffee. "You understand what Azra does?"

"It accelerates radioactive decay. Brings half-lives of millennia down to seconds."

"Quite so. Put it in a drive and a ship crosses to Alpha Centauri in eleven months instead of eleven decades. Put it in a warhead and..." He set down his cup. "Well. Put it in a warhead, and the question of who governs the settled worlds is answered very quickly, and only once."

Arthur's mouth had gone dry. "The Directorate would never allow—"

"The Terran Directorate is a committee of nineteen men who cannot agree on lunch. Meanwhile the Helion Consortium holds labour leases on forty thousand indentured workers on Mars alone, and the Kepler Combine has been building hulls at Ganymede that their shipping manifests do not account for." Orlov leaned back. "Did you know your neighbour, Mr. Dacosta?"

"Ruiz Dacosta? A little. He sold his claim last year and went back to Earth."

"He sold his claim to a Helion shell company. He did not go back to Earth." Orlov let that settle. "His transport has no record of him boarding."

Outside the viewport, a dust storm was creeping across the Martian plains, slow and enormous, a brown stain spreading over the planet's face.

"Why are you telling me this?" Arthur asked quietly.

"Because I'd like to make you an offer, and I'd prefer you to understand why it's a good one." Orlov drew a thin folder from his jacket and placed it on the table. "We propose to register your homestead as sovereign diplomatic territory. An embassy, legally speaking. Under the Ceres Accords, no corporation may lease it, no Directorate assessor may condemn it, and no armed party may enter without inviting a war with the Antares Compact."

"And in exchange?"

"You remain the owner. You will be paid a generous royalty. And every gram of Azra extracted from your vein will be sold to us, and to no one else."

Arthur stared at the folder. "So I'd be trading one master for another."

"You'd be trading many masters for one, which is generally an improvement." Orlov's pale eyes didn't waver. "And we don't intend to build weapons, Mr. Neegan. We intend to make sure nobody else can."

"That sounds very noble. How would I know it's true?"

"You wouldn't. That's the honest answer, and I'd ask you to note that I gave it to you."

Arthur turned his cup slowly in his hands. Something had been nagging at him since the ship, and at last he said it.

"Your vessel has an Azra damping field."

For the first time, something passed across Orlov's face. Surprise, perhaps, or respect. "You read diagnostic screens. Good."

"There's no such thing as a damping field. Azra can't be shielded. Every paper I've read says so."

"Every paper you've read was written by people who were permitted to publish." Orlov rose and returned to the viewport. "Here is something else you won't find in the journals, Mr. Neegan. Azra has no natural formation pathway. None. Our geologists have tried for a decade to explain how it came to be deposited in Martian rock, and they cannot." He paused. "One begins to wonder whether it was *deposited* at all, or whether it was *placed*."

The silence stretched. The diagnostic screen ticked over in the corner of Arthur's mind: *ENGAGED. ENGAGED.*

"You have seventy-two hours," Orlov said gently. "After that, I'm afraid the others will make their offers, and they will be considerably less polite than mine."

# Chapter Four: The Pomegranate Gate

They had told me at Hain-Ekat that a good envoy learns a world through its protocols, and a better one learns it through what the protocols are designed to hide. I was twenty-six and had been on Orrery for nine days. I believed the second half of that sentence more than the first.

The reception at the Hall of Accord was in its third hour when I left. No one stopped me. A junior attaché in borrowed formal grey looks much like a servant, and on Orrery servants are not watched; they are simply not seen. I went down the long stair and out through the Pomegranate Gate into the evening.

The city of Tessaly is built of a pale basalt that holds the day's heat long after dark, so that walking its streets is like walking along the flank of a sleeping animal. Every lintel is carved. My briefings had called the glyphs "decorative survivals of the Founding culture." They were not decorative. Above the Gate a woman was eating six seeds from a split fruit while a man waited for her below the earth. On the fountain in the first square a boy fell from the sky on melting wings, and someone had worn his face smooth with touching. Further on I passed a tower carved round with workers who could not understand one another, their mouths open on different shapes. The first settlers had brought very little with them across the long dark, and they had chosen to bring these stories, and to put them where their children would have to walk beneath them every day.

The briefings said Orrery's three lineages lived apart. There were the Tallfolk, descended from the original ship's crew, long-boned and slow to age. There were the Kesh, who had gone down into the cave-valleys of the south four centuries ago and come back broad-chested, large-eyed, and able to see in a light that would leave me blind. And there were the Marrowborn, bred in the first lean years for endurance by a science no one now admits to. The briefings described each group's grievances in tidy numbered paragraphs, and predicted that within a generation they would go to war.

The night market in the Square of the Ark had not read the briefings.

A Kesh woman sold lamp-oil from clay jars. Her customers were mostly Tallfolk, and they bargained with her in a trade-cant full of words from all three tongues. A Marrowborn child, thick-wristed and solemn, minded a stall of dried river-fish while her mother, who was not Marrowborn, slept on a mat behind it. I watched an old Tallman and a young Kesh man play a game with black and white stones on a board scratched into the paving. They did not speak, but when the young man won, the old one laughed and touched his own eyelid twice. I learned later that the gesture means *you saw further.*

None of this was hidden. That was what troubled me. Hain had sent observers to Orrery for sixty years, and their reports had described a wall between the lineages. Standing in that square I could not tell whether the wall had never existed, or whether it existed somewhere I could not see, among people who did not shop at night markets.

I bought a cup of something hot and bitter from a Marrowborn vendor. He looked at my offworld face and charged me triple, with great courtesy. I paid. It seemed a fair price for the lesson.

---

Commander Aseth was waiting in my quarters, sitting very upright in my only chair.

"Do you know what you are, Envoy Mirren?"

I said I believed I was a junior attaché of the Ekumen.

"You are a hostage," she said, "who has not yet been taken. Every faction in this city would find you useful. You walked among all of them tonight without an escort, without a recorder, and without telling anyone." She did not raise her voice. Hainish officers rarely do; they think it a kind of nakedness. "Tomorrow you will call on Minister Varo Teshennin. He has asked for you by name, which means he already knows where you were tonight. Find out what he wants. Do not give it to him."

---

The Ministry of Science stood beside a laboratory that had been closed for eighty years. The Minister's office had been someone's library once, and the shelves were still full, though I doubted he read anything on them. Teshennin was Tallfolk and old even by their reckoning, with skin like soft paper and a smile that never quite reached his eyes.

"You liked our market," he said.

"I did, Minister."

"Do you know what it is?" He poured two cups of the same bitter drink. "It is a performance. The lamp-seller's son sits on the Kesh council. The game-player is my cousin. We stage it every night. Not for you, Envoy. For ourselves. A people has to rehearse the thing it wishes it were."

I considered this. It was quite possible that he was lying. It was just as possible that he was telling the truth, and was telling it because the truth would serve him better.

"Then your reports to the Ekumen," I said, "the ones about the wall between the lineages. Those were a performance too."

The smile changed, very slightly. "Everyone performs for the guests. You came out of the Gate under the girl with the pomegranate, I think. Do you know her story?"

"She ate in the underworld, so she had to return there."

"She ate six seeds," Teshennin said, "and so she belonged to two places, and was trusted by neither." He set down his cup. "Your Ekumen wants Orrery to be either at peace or at war. Either one, they know how to write down. What we are is harder to write down. Tell me, Envoy Mirren, which report will you send?"

I understood then that this was the real question, and that he had been asking it since the moment I walked out through the Gate.

"The true one, Minister," I said. "As soon as I can find out what it is."

He looked at me for a long moment. Then he refilled my cup, which on Orrery, I would later learn, is how one acknowledges an opponent and not a guest.

The envoy’s cloak draws curious stares from locals who dress more minimally. Length: 1000 words.
response:
# The Weight of Cloth

They told me on the ship that Hesk was a hot world, and I believed them the way one believes a number. I did not understand it until the lander door opened and the air came in like an animal that had been waiting.

My cloak was grey wool, the formal cloak of the Envoy Service, cut long and heavy to signify that the one who wears it carries something. On Hesk it signified only that I was a fool. By the end of the reception at the Hall of Accord I had sweated through my undershirt and memorized the briefing three times over in my head, because there was nothing else to do while the speeches went on. *Two lineages. The Tarn, broad-chested, salt-plains people, who hold the land and the water rights. The Ovi, narrow and long-handed, canyon people, night-sighted, who hold nothing. Separation enforced by custom. No intermarriage. Labor bondage of the Ovi, unofficial but universal. Tensions rising.*

When the Second Consul began a speech about the ancient friendship between Hesk and the worlds of the Compact, I went out through the kitchen.

I do not entirely know why. I have told myself since that it was curiosity, or professional diligence, or heat. Perhaps it was only that I was twenty-four and had been told what I would find.

The streets of Ammaret go downhill toward the river, and the market lies where they meet it. I followed the smell of frying oil. The people I passed wore very little: a wrap at the hips, a band across the chest, sometimes a sort of open vest strung with shells that clicked when they moved. They looked at my cloak. They did not look at it with hostility, but the way you might look at a man carrying a door through a crowd, wondering where he thought he was taking it.

I saw Tarn and Ovi at once. The difference is not subtle. The Tarn are built like water jars, deep through the ribs, short in the leg. The Ovi seem drawn out of thinner clay, and their eyes, in daylight, are mostly black. I had expected to see the Ovi carrying and the Tarn buying. I saw an Ovi woman selling peppers from a mat, and a Tarn child of perhaps four asleep against her side, its fist closed on the end of her chest band. I saw two old men, one of each kind, quarrelling over a board game with the comfortable venom of people who have quarrelled over it for forty years. I saw a stall where an Ovi man was weighing out salt, and the salt is a Tarn monopoly, according to the briefing, guarded since the Founding.

I bought a skewer of something from the pepper woman and asked her, in my careful trade-tongue, whose child it was.

She looked at me for a while with those black eyes. "Hearth's," she said, as if I had asked whose the river was.

I asked whether the child's mother was Tarn.

"Yes," she said. "And I am its mother. And so is the one who bore it. You have one mother where you come from?"

I said that we did, usually.

"That must be lonely," she said, and gave me my change.

---

Command was waiting in my quarters, in the person of Deputy Envoy Sarai Holm, who had been in the Service thirty years and had never once, I think, gone out through a kitchen.

"You were seen," she said. "By everyone. In a ceremonial cloak. In the salt market." She did not raise her voice. Holm never raised her voice; she lowered it, and you leaned in, and then you were trapped. "Do you know what the salt market is?"

"A market," I said.

"It is the market the Accord Council has been trying to close for two years. You walked into the middle of the dispute we are here to mediate, wearing the Compact on your back." She let that sit. "Minister Dourne has asked to see you. Tonight. Alone."

"The Minister of Science?"

"There is no science in it. Dourne holds the post because it oversees the lineage registry. The registry decides who is Tarn and who is Ovi, and therefore who may own water." She turned to go. "Dourne asked for you by name. That is not a compliment. Take off the cloak."

---

The Minister received me on a roof terrace above the river, in the blue hour when the Ovi come out and the Tarn go in. Dourne was Tarn, or looked it, heavy and unhurried, wearing only a white hip-wrap and a registry seal on a cord. There was a bowl of cut fruit between us, which I did not touch.

"You went walking," Dourne said. "What did you learn?"

It was a test, and I knew it was a test, and knowing did not help. "That the briefings were incomplete."

"Briefings always are. Incomplete in which direction?"

"I saw an Ovi woman nursing a Tarn child. I saw an Ovi man selling salt."

"And what will you report?"

"That the separation is less absolute than we were told."

Dourne smiled and took a piece of fruit. "Do you know how many Ovi sell salt in that market? Eleven. All licensed by my office. Do you know why? Because a market where the Ovi sell nothing would be a market the Ovi burned. I am not a cruel man, Envoy. I am a careful one. Every exception you saw tonight is an exception I permit, so that the rule may stand." Dourne chewed. "So. Is the separation less absolute than you were told?"

I understood then what I was being offered. I could go back to Holm and say: *the Minister is reasonable, the system is flexible, there is room to work.* And the Compact would work inside the room Dourne had built.

"The woman told me the child had two mothers," I said. "She said it as though it were obvious. Does your registry record that?"

For the first time Dourne paused.

"The registry records lineage."

"Then it doesn't record her," I said. "Your exceptions are the ones you can see from this roof. I think I saw some you can't."

Dourne looked at me a long while, the way the pepper woman had. Below us the river had gone dark, and the market lights were coming on, Ovi lights, low and amber, made for eyes that need very little.

"You're younger than they usually send," Dourne said at last. "Keep the cloak. It tells people you don't belong here. That may be the most honest thing about you."

I walked back alone. Nobody stopped me. I carried the cloak folded over my arm, and found that it was heavy anyway.

# Chapter Four: The Color of Orrin

The briefing had said that the Tessit and the Kaldry did not share streets. Sael Imbaro had read this sentence on the long sleep-fall from Hain-Orbit, and again in the shuttle, and a third time in her quarters at the Legation, where the walls were painted the pale institutional green that seems to follow Ekumenical offices from world to world like a weed. Then she put on the plain gray coat the porter had left for her and went out by the kitchen door.

Teshe has a red sun, old and patient, and in its light everything looks a little like late afternoon even at noon. The Legation stood on a rise above the lower city. Sael followed the steps down because they were there, and because no one had told her not to. Strictly, no one had needed to. Protocol had told her, in four separate clauses.

The market began without announcement. First there was a wall, then a woman sitting against the wall with a basket of something like bread, then an awning, then a hundred awnings. The noise was the noise of every market: bargaining, children, a man singing badly. Sael found it reassuring. Some things do not diverge.

The people did. She had seen images, but images do not have weight. The Kaldry were short and broad, built for the heavy lowlands, with wide dark eyes adapted over eleven centuries to the dim sun. The Tessit were tall, narrow-shouldered, pale as paper. They descended, so the briefing said, from the ship's officers, who had kept their lines apart. Sael had expected to find them on opposite sides of some invisible boundary.

Instead she found them at the same stall, arguing about cloth.

The stall belonged to a Kaldry weaver, an old man with hands like knotted rope. His bolts hung from a frame of pale wood, and they were dyed in colors Sael had no names for. One was something like blue, but it did not stay blue. When the cloth moved it went toward green, then toward a color her eye kept trying to call gray and failing to. A tall Tessit woman was fingering the edge of it and complaining about the price, and the old man was complaining about her complaining, and they had clearly been doing this for years.

"What is it dyed with?" Sael asked, in the trade-speech she had learned on the voyage.

Both of them looked at her. Her body was neither shape, too tall for Kaldry and too dark for Tessit, and she saw them fail to place her and decide not to mind.

"Orrin root," the weaver said. "Boiled three days. Fixed with my own urine, and the secret of that is the diet." The Tessit woman laughed. "My granddaughter grows the root. Her father's people have the fields up past Arrow." He nodded toward the tall woman, and Sael understood, slowly, that the granddaughter's father was Tessit, and that this was not remarkable to anyone but herself.

She walked for three hours. She saw a Kaldry child riding on a Tessit man's shoulders. She saw a guildhall door carved with looms rather than lineages. She saw a wall where someone had painted *The Registry lies* in large Kaldry letters, and someone else had painted over half of it, and someone else again had painted it back. She saw no soldiers, and she saw nothing that looked like the edge of a war. That was not the same thing as there being no war. She knew that. She was young, not a fool.

She bought a square of the orrin cloth, overpaid, and climbed back up the steps.

---

Commander Hesk did not raise his voice. He was a Terran of the old school, and his anger came out as careful syntax.

"You are here," he said, "as a courtesy extended to the Ekumen by a government which has asked us, specifically, not to be seen among the population. You understand that we exist on this world by permission."

"I understand, sir."

"I doubt it. But you will have the opportunity to learn." He slid a card across the desk. "The Minister of Science has asked to meet the envoy who went walking. Word travels quickly here. Go tonight. Be careful what you say, and more careful about what you agree to."

"Is she a scientist?"

Hesk looked at her for a long moment. "No," he said. "The Ministry of Science keeps the Registry of Lines. It decides who is Tessit and who is Kaldry. It has not performed an experiment in four hundred years."

---

Minister Oura Valenth received her in a room full of books no one had opened in a long time. She was very old and very tall, and she sat as though sitting were a concession she made to others.

"You went to the market," she said. "What did you buy?"

Sael took the folded cloth from her coat. The Minister did not touch it.

"Orrin. A peasant dye. It fades in five years." She looked at Sael with pale, unhurried eyes. "Tell me what you learned."

"That your briefings to my government were incomplete."

"Were they? Or did you see what an offworlder sees in one afternoon: smiling people, sold a smiling story by an old man who saw your coat and your purse?" She folded her long hands. "Perhaps the briefings were written for those who stay longer than an afternoon."

It was a fair blow, and Sael let it land. "Perhaps. Then tell me what I'd see if I stayed a year."

"You would see that the Registry is all that stands between this world and a great deal of blood. That the old man's granddaughter cannot inherit her father's fields, and knows it, and smiles anyway. You would see how much smiling costs." The Minister paused. "And you would be asked, eventually, to choose a side. Everyone is."

"The Ekumen doesn't choose sides."

"The Ekumen *is* a side. It is the side that arrives." Valenth leaned forward slightly, and the lamp caught the fine bones of her face. "So, envoy. You have stood in my streets. You have looked at my people. Tell me which I am."

Sael understood that the question was a door, and that there were many wrong ways through it. If she said *Tessit*, she accepted the Registry. If she said *it doesn't matter*, she became the kind of fool who could be safely ignored.

She looked at the Minister for a long time: the height, the pallor, the long hands. Then she looked at the eyes, which were wider and darker at the center than any Tessit eyes she had seen that day, made for a dimmer light.

"I think," Sael said, "that you are the person who keeps the Registry. And I think you've read your own entry."

The silence went on long enough for the lamp to hiss.

Then Minister Valenth laughed, a short dry sound like a stick breaking. She reached out at last and touched the orrin cloth, and under her fingers it went from blue to green to the color that had no name.

"Come back tomorrow," she said. "We will begin again, and this time neither of us will lie quite so much."

response:
# TICK TOCK, YOU'RE DEAD

### Chapter Seven

The first time I used the watch, I didn't even mean to.

It came in a padded envelope with no return address. No note. Just a black band and a blank silver face that lit up when I touched it: **HELLO, MARCUS.**

I figured Uncle Ray sent it. Uncle Ray sends weird stuff.

So there I was in Mr. Dobbs's science class, sweating through my T-shirt, because he'd just called on me. "Marcus. The powerhouse of the cell?"

"The nucleus," I said.

Everybody laughed. Even Priya Shah, who sits in front of me and smells like strawberry shampoo. *Especially* Priya Shah.

I grabbed my wrist like I wanted to strangle myself. My thumb hit the little crown on the side of the watch and twisted it backward.

The room *lurched*. My stomach dropped like I was on the Screamer at Six Flags. Then—

"Marcus. The powerhouse of the cell?"

Mr. Dobbs was staring at me. Nobody was laughing. Priya was doodling a horse.

"The... mitochondria?" I croaked.

"Correct."

I looked down. The watch face read: **-00:00:30.**

Thirty seconds. I had gone back thirty seconds.

That's when I noticed the cat.

It was sitting on the windowsill outside. A scraggly gray stray with one torn ear that hung around the dumpsters behind the cafeteria. It was staring at me through the glass. Not at the class. At *me*.

Like it knew exactly what I'd just done.

---

Here's the thing nobody tells you about having a time machine on your wrist: you use it for *everything*.

Tripped in the lunch line? Rewind. Said "you too" when the bus driver said "have a good birthday"? Rewind. Missed a free throw in gym? Rewind, rewind, rewind, until the ball swished and Coach Fenner actually said, "Nice, Pell."

And every single time, the gray cat was there. On a fence. Under a car. On the hood of the principal's Buick. Watching me with those yellow eyes.

On Wednesday my voice cracked in the middle of saying "pizza." On Thursday my mom stopped me at breakfast.

"Did you get taller?"

"No," I said. My voice came out deep. Way deep. Like a radio DJ deep.

We both stared at each other.

"Huh," Mom said. "Growth spurt, I guess."

By Friday I had a mustache. Not cool peach fuzz. An actual *mustache*. My jeans stopped at my shins. My face had broken out in a constellation of zits so big they had their own weather.

And people were acting... strange.

Theo Martinez, my best friend since kindergarten, walked right past me at my locker. Just walked past.

"Theo! Dude!"

He turned around, and his eyes went wide. "Uh. Sorry, mister. Do you work here?"

*Mister.*

I ran to the boys' bathroom and stared in the mirror. A guy stared back. Maybe sixteen. Maybe *older*. Broad shoulders. Stubble. My eyes—my same brown eyes—sunk in a stranger's face.

I looked at the watch. Tiny gray letters I'd never noticed scrolled along the bottom of the screen:

**TIME BORROWED: 4 YEARS, 2 MONTHS, 11 DAYS.**

*Borrowed.*

Every rewind wasn't free. Every thirty seconds I took back, the watch took something from *me*. And it charged interest.

Outside the bathroom window, the gray cat sat on the dumpster lid. It blinked at me. Slowly.

Like it was saying: *Now you get it.*

---

I should have taken the watch off. I know that. You know that.

But that afternoon, Theo got hurt.

He was crossing the parking lot, staring at his phone, and Mrs. Kowalski's minivan came around the corner too fast. I heard the thud from across the field. I saw Theo's sneaker spin through the air.

I didn't think. I just grabbed the crown and *twisted*. Hard. Again and again and again. The world screamed past me in reverse—cars sucking backward, clouds unrolling, the sun sliding *up*—

When it stopped, I was standing in my kitchen. It was morning. Breakfast smell. Pancakes.

The watch read: **-06:14:52.**

Six hours. I'd saved Theo. I could just keep him out of the parking lot. Easy.

Then my mom walked in, saw me, and *screamed*.

"Who are you? How did you get in my house?"

"Mom! It's me! It's Marcus!"

She grabbed a frying pan. Her hands were shaking. "Get out! Marcus, honey, go upstairs!"

That's when I saw him.

Sitting at the kitchen table. Twelve years old. Skinny. Bad haircut. Syrup on his chin.

*Me.*

The other Marcus looked up at me, and his face went white. He wasn't wearing a watch. Not yet. Because the envelope was still sitting on the counter next to the mail. Unopened.

I'd gone back too far. Past where I'd started. And now there were two of us—and the world didn't have room for both.

The kitchen started to *flicker*. The walls rippled like a heat mirage. Outside the window, the sky turned the color of a bruise. The pancakes on the griddle went from golden to black to *raw* to golden again. A crack split the air above the table—a thin black line, like someone had torn the morning in half.

Mom was dialing 911. The other Marcus was crying.

And through the crack in the air, I saw *nothing*. Just a cold, empty dark that went on forever.

The watch buzzed.

**TIMELINE UNSTABLE. CORRECTION AVAILABLE.**

**COST: ALL REMAINING TIME.**

All remaining time.

I looked at my hands. The knuckles were thicker. A gray hair curled on the back of my wrist. How much time did I even *have* left?

The crack widened. My mom's scream stretched into a long, warbling sound, like a tape being chewed up.

I put my thumb on the crown.

"Don't open the envelope," I told the other me. "Promise me. *Don't open it.*"

Then I twisted.

---

Everything went gray.

Then everything went *big*.

I was lying on cold concrete. The world smelled amazing and terrible at the same time—garbage, french fries, rain. I tried to stand up, but my legs wouldn't work right. There were four of them.

I looked down.

Gray fur. Tiny white paws.

I was behind the cafeteria. Next to the dumpsters.

And across the parking lot, walking toward the school with his backpack sagging off one shoulder, was a skinny kid with a bad haircut. He was fiddling with something shiny on his wrist.

A black band. A silver face.

*No. No no no.*

I tried to yell. *Take it off! Marcus, TAKE IT OFF!*

What came out was: "*Mrrrow.*"

The kid stopped. He looked right at me, and a shiver ran up his back.

"Weird," he muttered. "That cat looks at me like it *knows* me."

Then he turned and went inside.

And I sat down on the dumpster, curled my tail around my paws, and waited.

Because I knew exactly what came next.

I'd already lived it.

**TO BE CONTINUED...**

response:
# Chapter Seven: Time's Up

The watch came in a box with no return address.

That should have been my first clue. But when you're twelve and something shiny shows up on your doorstep with your name on it, *MARCUS PELL* in spidery silver letters, you don't ask questions. You rip it open.

It looked like a regular smartwatch. Black band. Round face. But instead of apps, it had only one button on the side, and only one word glowing on the screen:

**AGAIN?**

I found out what it did on Tuesday. That was the day I tripped in the cafeteria and dumped a whole tray of chili down Brianna Okafor's back. Brianna Okafor, the girl I'd been trying to say a full sentence to since September.

Everybody laughed. Brianna screamed. And I jammed my thumb on that button out of pure panic.

*Click.*

The cafeteria lurched sideways. My stomach flipped like I'd gone over the top of a roller coaster. And then I was standing at the lunch line again, holding a full, steaming tray of chili.

Brianna walked past me. Clean. Smiling.

I stepped carefully around the wet spot on the floor. I didn't trip. I didn't scream.

I *grinned*.

---

After that, I used it all the time.

Botched a math quiz? *Click.* Took it again and aced it.

Struck out in gym? *Click.* Home run.

Said something dumb to Brianna? *Click, click, click.* By Friday, she was laughing at my jokes. *Actually* laughing.

Every time I pressed the button, I felt that stomach-flip. And every time, I noticed a tiny number in the corner of the watch face tick upward. *14. 37. 52.*

I figured it was keeping score. Like a high score in a video game.

I was wrong.

---

The first weird thing was my voice.

I was answering a question in social studies when it cracked. Right in the middle of the word "Mesopotamia." It went from squeaky to deep, like a tuba falling down the stairs.

Everyone snickered. I didn't press the button. For once, I was too surprised.

The second weird thing was my jeans. On Monday they fit fine. By Thursday, I could see my socks.

"You're growing like a weed," Mom said at breakfast, frowning. She reached over and touched my chin. "Marcus... is that *stubble*?"

I laughed it off. Puberty, right? It was supposed to happen sometime.

But it wasn't supposed to happen in *a week*.

---

Then people started treating me differently.

Mr. Garza stopped calling me "Marcus" and started calling me "Mr. Pell." The eighth graders let me cut in the lunch line. A substitute teacher asked if I was a student teacher.

And Brianna? Brianna stopped laughing at my jokes. She started looking at me funny. Kind of nervous.

"You seem... older," she said. "Like, a *lot* older. It's kind of creepy, Marcus."

My little sister, Josie, wouldn't even sit next to me on the couch anymore.

"You don't look like you," she whispered. "You look like Grandpa."

---

That night, I went into the bathroom and stared into the mirror.

Same messy brown hair. Same freckles. A couple of new pimples on my forehead, and a shadow of fuzz on my lip. Okay. Weird, but okay.

Then the bathroom light buzzed.

And the mirror *flickered*.

For one second, a different face stared back at me. A man's face. Deep lines around the eyes. Gray creeping in at the temples. A tired, sagging mouth.

*My* mouth.

He blinked when I blinked.

I stumbled backward into the towel rack. When I looked again, it was just me. Twelve-year-old me.

Mostly.

I looked down at the watch. The number in the corner glowed red now.

**31.**

Not points.

*Years.*

My age. The age my body was racing toward. Every rewind had been stealing time from somewhere. And the somewhere was *me*.

---

I should have thrown the watch in the river. I know that now.

But the next morning, my best friend Theo was mad at me. Really mad. I'd blown off his birthday party to hang out with Brianna, and he wouldn't even look at me at the bus stop.

*Just one more,* I thought. *One more, to fix things with Theo. Then I'll stop.*

I held the button down longer this time. I wanted to go back a whole day. Back before the party.

*Cliiiiick.*

The world didn't just flip. It *tore*. Colors smeared like wet paint. A sound like a thousand clocks ticking at once filled my skull.

And then I was standing in front of my house.

But it wasn't my house anymore.

The shutters were green, not blue. Mom's rosebushes were gone. And through the front window, I could see my family eating dinner.

Mom. Dad. Josie.

And a boy. A twelve-year-old boy with messy brown hair and freckles.

*Me.*

He was laughing at something Josie said. Happy. Normal. Like he belonged there.

Because in *this* timeline, he did.

I pounded on the door. Mom opened it, and her eyes went wide with fear.

"Can I help you, sir?" she asked, pulling Josie behind her.

*Sir.*

"Mom, it's *me*! It's Marcus!"

The boy at the table looked up. Our eyes met. And he went pale, like he was seeing a ghost.

Or seeing his future.

"I'm calling the police," Mom said, and slammed the door.

---

I ran until my lungs burned. Until my knees ached, which was new. When I finally stopped, I caught my reflection in a dark store window.

No flicker this time.

The face was just *there*. Gray-haired. Lined. Old.

I looked down at the watch. My hands were spotted and wrinkled. The screen still glowed:

**AGAIN?**

The number in the corner read **58**.

If I pressed it, maybe I could undo everything. Maybe I could go back to the doorstep. Back to the box. Maybe I could leave it unopened.

Or maybe the watch would take everything I had left.

My thumb trembled over the button.

Somewhere far away, a clock was ticking.

I pressed down.

*Click.*

---

*To be continued...*

# Chapter Seven: Wristwatch of Doom

The watch came in a box with no return address.

It was sitting on our porch the Monday after my twelfth birthday, wrapped in brown paper so old it crackled like dead leaves. Inside was a smartwatch. Sleek. Black. The face was blank until I slipped it on, and then letters glowed across the screen:

**CHRONOS. HOLD CROWN TO REVERSE.**

I figured it was some kind of fitness tracker. Boy, was I wrong.

---

The first time I used it was an accident.

Third period, Mrs. Feeney's math quiz. I'd written down 42 for question six, turned it in, and then watched Priya Shah whisper to her friend, "It was 24, obviously."

I groaned and pressed my thumb against the side of the watch, just fidgeting.

The world *lurched*.

My stomach dropped like I was on the Thunder Mountain coaster. Colors smeared. And then I was sitting at my desk with my pencil in my hand and the quiz in front of me. Question six. Blank.

The clock on the wall read 10:14. Five minutes earlier.

I wrote **24**.

For just a second, the watch face flickered. Red numbers flashed and then vanished:

**71:03:22**

I didn't think anything of it.

---

By Wednesday I was using Chronos for *everything*.

Tripped in the cafeteria and dumped spaghetti on my shirt? Rewind. Kyle Brunner's dodgeball heading for my face? Rewind, and duck. Said something dumb to Priya at her locker? Rewind, rewind, *rewind*, until I finally got it right and she laughed. She actually laughed.

I was untouchable. I was a genius. I was Danny Pruitt, Master of Time.

Every time, the watch flickered.

**68:11:40**

**63:02:15**

**59:47:09**

The numbers kept going down. I figured it was the battery.

---

On Thursday morning, my jeans didn't fit.

They'd fit on Monday. Now they stopped two inches above my ankles, like I was waiting for a flood. My sneakers pinched my toes.

"Growth spurt," Mom said, but she was staring at me funny over her coffee mug. "Honey… is that a *mustache*?"

I ran to the bathroom mirror.

It was. A dark, scraggly shadow on my upper lip. And there were three big red zits on my chin that hadn't been there the night before. When I said, "Mom, what's happening to me?" my voice came out *deep*. Then it cracked so high that our dog started barking.

My little sister Lily, who's seven, peeked around the doorway and said, "Why does Danny look like Uncle Rick?"

Uncle Rick is thirty-four.

---

At school, it got worse.

Mrs. Feeney called me "young man" in a nervous voice, like she wasn't sure I belonged there. A substitute in the hallway stopped me and asked if I was somebody's older brother picking them up. Kids I'd known since kindergarten moved out of my way. Kyle Brunner, who'd shoved me into a locker every week since fourth grade, actually said "Sorry, dude" when he bumped my shoulder.

Priya wouldn't look at me at all.

In the bathroom, I stared at the watch. The red numbers flickered again. And this time they stayed long enough for me to read the tiny letters underneath.

**52:18:33 — YEARS REMAINING**

My mouth went dry.

Not battery. *Me.* Every rewind, the watch was taking time, and it was taking it from *me*.

---

I should have stopped. I know that now.

But on the walk home, I saw Lily chasing her red bouncy ball toward Maple Street. And a truck was coming. Fast.

I didn't think. I just squeezed the crown and held it.

*Lurch.* Colors smeared, longer this time, and so cold it felt like falling through ice. I held on and held on, trying to go back far enough to grab her before she ever ran out.

When the world snapped back, I was standing on the corner. No truck. No ball. No Lily.

Everything was quiet. *Too* quiet.

I ran home. The house looked wrong. The shutters were green instead of blue. The swing set in the backyard was gone. And when I burst through the front door, Mom screamed.

She *screamed*. Like I was a burglar.

"Who are you? Get out of my house! I'm calling the police!"

"Mom, it's me! It's Danny!"

And then a voice behind her said, "Mom? Who's that man?"

A kid stepped into the hallway. Twelve years old. Brown hair. Too-big Spider-Man T-shirt.

*Me.*

The *real* me. The one who belonged here. The one who'd never found a box on the porch.

I staggered back and caught my reflection in the hall mirror. A tired, grown-up face stared back. Stubble. Broad shoulders. Somewhere around nineteen, maybe twenty.

"Where's Lily?" I croaked. "Where's my sister?"

Mom's face went pale and confused. "I don't have a daughter."

My knees buckled.

I'd gone back too far. Changed too much. Somewhere in all that rewinding, I'd broken something, and now my sister had never been born, my family didn't know me, and there was another Danny eating *my* cereal and sleeping in *my* bed.

Sirens wailed in the distance.

---

I ran until my lungs burned, and I hid behind the dumpster at the Quik-Mart. I looked down at the watch with shaking hands.

The face was flickering wildly now, red and black and red again.

**00:00:03 — YEARS REMAINING**

Three years. That's all I had left.

And beneath it, new words glowed:

**ONE FULL REVERSAL AVAILABLE. RESTORE ORIGIN POINT?**

Origin point. Monday. The porch. The box.

If I went back, maybe I could leave the package unopened. Maybe Lily would exist again. Maybe I'd be twelve.

Or maybe a full reversal would cost more than three years.

Maybe it would cost *everything*.

The sirens got louder. Blue lights flashed across the parking lot.

I thought about Lily's gap-toothed grin. Her terrible knock-knock jokes. The way she always stole the last waffle.

I pressed my thumb against the crown.

"Please," I whispered. "Please work."

And I held it down.

---

*Lurch.*

I woke up gasping in my own bed. Small. Skinny. Twelve. No mustache. My voice squeaked when I yelled, "LILY?"

"WHAT?" she yelled back from the hallway.

I almost cried. I ran downstairs and hugged her so hard she squirmed.

"Ew, Danny, let *go*! Look what I found on the porch!"

She held up her wrist.

A sleek black watch glowed against her skin.

**CHRONOS. HOLD CROWN TO ADVANCE.**

Lily grinned. "It says it can make me a grown-up!"

Her thumb was already on the crown.

response:
# Polymerase Chain Reaction

The thermocycler was three cooking pots and a dead man's wristwatch.

Teodora Vance had built it during the second winter, after the last real machine in the Saltmarsh settlement died. The first pot held water at a rolling boil, ninety-five degrees, hot enough to unzip DNA into single strands. The second sat at fifty-five on a fish-tank heater, cool enough for primers to find their targets. The third held seventy-two, where the polymerase did its work. A windshield-wiper motor swung a wire basket of tubes from pot to pot, and the wristwatch, wired to a relay, told it when to move. Thirty cycles took four hours and most of the settlement's solar budget. Each cycle doubled the sequence she wanted, so thirty of them turned one fragile strand into a billion copies.

When it worked, it felt like a miracle. Tonight it wasn't working.

"Degraded," she muttered, holding the gel up to the UV lamp she'd taken from a tanning salon in the drowned district. The agarose, cooked from kelp, showed a faint smear where a sharp band should have been. Her template DNA was falling apart, the way everything Verdance made fell apart.

Her eyes watered under the UV. She wiped them and her knuckles came away glowing a soft, sick green.

That was the marker gene. Three years ago her kidneys had started failing, because the Verdance gene therapy her mother paid for was a product, and products expired. The Sunset Clause was the industry's polite name for it: every engineered sequence carried a timed self-destruct. Crops lasted one generation and their seeds came up sterile. Livestock edits stopped working in the offspring. Medical therapies held for eight to twelve years, then quietly unwound, so you would subscribe again. The business model had worked beautifully until the subscriptions outlived the companies.

So Teo had built her own vector from salvaged plasmids and the half-legible notes of a dead postdoc, and injected it into her own flank with a sharpened veterinary needle. Her kidneys recovered. Her hair came out in patches and never fully grew back. Her hands shook before noon. Her tears fluoresced, and so, embarrassingly, did her sweat.

The changes had their uses, too. She hadn't caught a fever since. Her nose had sharpened into something almost canine, so she could smell bacterial contamination in a culture before it clouded. And she could tell, in a way she couldn't explain to anyone, when someone in the room was afraid.

The woman who came through the greenhouse door was not afraid at all.

"Dr. Vance." The broker took off a respirator that probably cost more than the Saltmarsh's entire water filtration system. She was tall and dressed in waxed canvas, and she smelled of diesel and cloves. "I'm Sable. Hollow Market sends regards."

"I'm not a doctor."

"Nobody's anything anymore. Titles are free." Sable's eyes moved over the lab, taking it in: the bicycle-wheel centrifuge, the hot-tub vat where Teo cultured heat-loving bacteria to harvest her own polymerase, and the shelves of empty steel canisters. Each canister was stamped with the green double-helix leaf and the slogan *VERDANCE GENOMICS — GROWTH, GUARANTEED.* They had held reagents once, in the old days. Now they held reagents again, made by hand from kelp and bacteria and Teo's own stubbornness.

Sable smiled at the slogan. "Poetic."

"Practical. They seal well." Teo wiped her hands on her apron. "What do you want?"

Sable set a small case on the bench and opened it. Nested in foam, frosted with cold, sat a single canister, unopened and still in factory shrink-wrap. The label read **MASTER LINE — TRITICUM V-7 — UNSUNSETTED — INTERNAL USE ONLY.**

Teo's breath stopped.

Every Verdance product had been built from an original template, a clean master sequence kept in corporate vaults. The Sunset Clause had been added later, at the packaging stage. If this label was true, the canister held wheat as the engineers first wrote it: drought-hardy, blight-resistant, and able to breed true forever.

"Where did you get this?"

"A vault in the Denver ruins. Three people died retrieving it, which is three fewer than usual." Sable closed the case. "We need someone who can amplify it, splice it into a viable seed line, and produce a harvest. You're the only one in four hundred miles with a working cycler and a reputation."

"And the payment?"

"Two hundred liters of diesel. A crate of broad-spectrum antibiotics, real ones, unexpired. Medical-grade solar panels." Sable paused. "And a seed allotment for your settlement. Ten percent of the yield."

It was more than Saltmarsh could earn in a decade. Teo could smell the children in the dormitory two buildings over, the stale sweetness of malnutrition. Last season's blight had taken the potatoes and half the beans.

"What's the catch?"

Sable took a folded contract from her coat and laid it flat. Teo read it under the tanning lamp, her tears glowing faintly onto the paper.

Most of it was standard. The fourth clause was not.

*The Contractor shall incorporate a generational termination sequence into the final seed line, such that progeny remain viable for no more than one (1) reproductive cycle. The Contractor shall retain no copies, samples, or derivatives of the master template.*

Teo looked up. "You want me to put the Sunset Clause back in."

"I want a sustainable business," Sable said. "Seeds that breed true sell exactly once. Surely you understand."

Teo understood perfectly. She understood that the people who built the collapse had probably said the same thing, in better offices, in a calmer voice.

"Ten percent of a one-generation crop," she said. "My people eat for one year, and then they come crawling to the Hollow Market."

"Then they'll be customers. Customers are kept alive." Sable held out a pen. "You can say no. Someone in the Gulf co-ops will say yes eventually. They'll be worse at it, and more people will starve while they learn."

The wiper motor ticked. The watch counted. Somewhere in the basket, a degraded template failed to copy itself again.

Teo took the pen and signed.

Sable left at midnight, satisfied and smelling of nothing at all. Teo waited until the engine noise faded into the marsh. Then she cut the shrink-wrap, drew a single microliter from the master canister, and dropped it into a fresh tube.

The first cycle began at ninety-five degrees. The strands unzipped.

She took an empty canister from the shelf, scrubbed it, and set it beside the cycler to wait. The slogan caught the green glow of her hands. *Growth, guaranteed.*

"We'll see," she whispered, and let the watch count to thirty.

response:
# Polymerase Chain Reaction

The thermocycler was three pots and a kitchen timer, and Dele was the part that moved.

Ninety-four degrees to split the strands. She counted thirty seconds on the dryer dial she'd bolted to the bench, then lifted the wire rack of tubes out of the first pot and dropped it into the second. Fifty-five, so the primers could find their places. Thirty more seconds. Then into the third pot, seventy-two, where the polymerase did its slow, faithful work. Then back to the first.

Thirty-two cycles. She had done this so many times that her wrists clicked in rhythm with the dial.

The pots sat on a stove she had built from a forklift battery and the coils of a pre-Collapse space heater. An aquarium thermostat held each bath within a degree, most days. On the bad days she checked them with a meat thermometer and swore.

Around her feet, the old Halvorsen Agritech field lab glowed. Pale blue mushrooms had pushed up through the cracked floor tiles years ago, spores left over from some forgotten luciferase trial. They had outlived the company that made them. Dele found that funny when she was tired, and lately she was always tired.

"You're slower than last time," said Vell.

The broker had been leaning in the doorway for ten minutes. He wore a respirator with one filter missing and a coat that had once belonged to someone with epaulettes. Behind him, the Saltmarch evening was going orange over the dead wheat.

"The rack's heavy," Dele said. "Polymerase is old. I'm stretching the extension step." She moved the tubes back to ninety-four. "You said you had terms."

Vell stepped inside and avoided the mushrooms. "Client wants cassava. True-breeding. Seed that makes seed that makes seed. No Halvorsen kill-switch."

Dele kept her eyes on the dial.

Everyone knew how it had gone. Halvorsen's Generational Licensing model was elegant, in the way a guillotine is elegant. Every crop they sold carried a terminator cassette, a stretch of engineered DNA that came apart within one generation. Plant the seed and you got a beautiful harvest. Plant the harvest and you got nothing, or worse than nothing: sterile husks, tubers riddled with toxic glycosides, corn that rotted standing. The shareholders thought you would simply buy more next season. Then the supply chains failed, and there was no next season, and the farms of three continents turned to chalk in a single spring.

What was left was degraded. Seed banks full of DNA that sheared apart if you looked at it wrong. Dele spent most of her days rescuing fragments before they decayed, copying them out of dying cells, stitching them into anything that might survive.

"I'm close on the cassava," she said. "The settlement gets it first. That was always the deal."

"Not this deal." Vell set a cold case on the bench and popped the latches. Inside, packed in frost, sat a row of factory-sealed vials. Fresh Taq polymerase, enough for years. Primers with clean labels. And beneath them, wrapped in foam, a real thermocycler block, small and grey and perfect.

Dele's hands stopped. The dial ran past thirty seconds.

"Exclusive," Vell said. "The client gets the sequence and the only viable line. Saltmarch gets nothing for five years. After that, you're free."

She pulled the rack out late and dropped it into the fifty-five bath. Somewhere in those tubes, a few thousand copies of something had probably just ruined themselves.

"Five years," she said. "People here eat bark in February."

"People everywhere eat bark in February."

She peeled off her gloves to rub her eyes, and Vell saw her hands. He didn't flinch, which she gave him credit for. Her fingernails were gone. The nail beds had healed over in smooth grey plates, faintly ridged, like the underside of a mushroom cap. Two years ago she had injected herself with a splice she'd pulled from a radiotrophic fungus sample, half to see what it would do and half because the Geiger counter by the old reactor road had started singing. Her nails had come out over a month. She'd lost the hair on her forearms and most of the feeling in two fingers. Some mornings her joints ached so badly she had to hold the kettle with both hands.

But she had walked the reactor road six times since, collecting seed, and come back without burns. And her eyes had changed. In the dark she saw a faint violet halo around things, ultraviolet bleeding into her vision. She no longer needed a tanning bed tube to read her gels. She could see the DNA bands glowing on her own.

"Who's the client?" she asked.

"Doesn't matter."

"It matters if they're going to sit on a staple crop and sell it back to starving people by the kilo." She looked at the vials. "That's Halvorsen with a different logo."

Vell shrugged. "Then don't sign. Keep cooking your DNA in soup pots until the polymerase runs out. Then what?"

The dial clicked. She moved the rack to seventy-two and watched the bubbles crawl up the side of the pot.

She thought about the sequence in her notebook. The repaired cassava genome, terminator cassette cut out at last, the gap patched with a fragment from a wild strain she'd found growing in a ditch. And she thought about how easy it would be to put something back in.

"I'll do it," she said.

Vell smiled behind the respirator.

"One condition. I deliver the line in ninety days. You don't test it past the first harvest before payment. Client's word on that."

"First harvest is all anyone tests."

"Then we have a deal."

He left the case on the bench. When his footsteps faded, Dele sat down on the floor among the mushrooms and pressed her grey fingertips against her eyes until the violet halos blurred.

She would give the client their cassava, beautiful and fat and true for exactly one generation. She knew where the old cassette went. She knew how to make it fail.

Saltmarch would get the other line.

The mushrooms pulsed softly around her, blue against the broken tile, the last honest thing Halvorsen had ever made. Dele got up, checked the thermometer, and moved the rack back to ninety-four.

Twenty-one cycles to go.

response:
# Útiseta

Astrid had the hide rolled under her arm like a sleeping bag, and she smelled of it all evening: old fat, smoke, something sweeter underneath that I didn't want to name. It had been in her grandmother's attic, she said, wrapped in newspaper from 1961. She'd shown me the date as proof of something.

"You don't talk," she said, as we crossed the Lindqvists' back field. "Not once you're under. Not to me, not to yourself. If you have to sneeze, swallow it."

"What happens if I sneeze?"

She looked at me with real pity, the way she looked at the girls in our class who still wore their hair in scrunchies. "Then you've told it where your mouth is."

It was the third week of August. Up there the nights had only just started coming back, thin and blue. Even at half past eleven the sky over the birches looked bruised rather than dark. I had my Walkman in my jacket pocket, the Cardigans tape still in it from the bus that afternoon. Astrid made me take the batteries out at the edge of the field and bury them under a stone. Nothing that hums, she said. Nothing that ticks. She'd already checked that I wasn't wearing my watch.

I remember being annoyed more than frightened. That's the part I want to be honest about. I was fifteen and furious with my father for bringing us to a place where the nearest cinema was ninety kilometres away. Astrid was the only interesting thing that had happened to me since June. The games had been funny at first: names written on paper and frozen in ice cube trays, a strand of Malin Berg's hair braided into red thread. When Malin tripped on the stairs at school the next Monday, Astrid had only shrugged. I'd laughed so hard I cried.

The mound sat past the old fence line where the Lindqvists stopped bothering to mow. It didn't look like much. A long low swelling, a few rowans leaning in at the edges, and grass gone silver with seed. If nobody had told you, you'd have walked over it. People had, Astrid said. That was rather the point.

She knelt at the northern end and took things out of her rucksack one at a time, the way my mother unpacked groceries. A pair of scissors, open, which she pushed into the turf with the blades pointing outward. A heel of bread. A little jar of something dark. A rusted horseshoe nail for each of us, to hold in our left hands.

"Iron's so you come back," she said. "Bread's manners."

"And that?"

She didn't answer. She unscrewed the jar and poured it in a line along the top of the mound, and it soaked in without a sound.

Then she sat down cross-legged, facing north, and pulled the hide up over both of our heads.

I've tried, over the years, to describe what it was like under there. It wasn't dark, exactly. The hide let through a dim brownish glow, like light through a closed eyelid. It was heavy and stiff, and it held the warmth of our breath so that within a minute the air was thick and damp. I could feel Astrid's shoulder against mine. I could hear her breathing, slow and deliberate, as if she were counting it.

You're supposed to wait. That's all útiseta is. You sit on the dead and you wait, and if they want to, they tell you things.

For a long while nothing told me anything. My legs went numb. Something crawled across my wrist and I didn't brush it away. I thought about Malin Berg on the stairs, and about the stone with my batteries under it, and about whether my parents had noticed my bed. I thought, quite clearly, *this is stupid*, and felt better.

Then the bell rang.

One stroke. It came from the south, from the direction of the church in Norrby, four kilometres away across the bog. It was deep and round and it carried the way sound carries over water. Astrid's breathing stopped.

The church in Norrby had no midnight service. I knew that because my mother had looked for one, our first Sunday, hoping it would help her settle in. It held services every second week, at eleven in the morning, and the bell was rung by hand by a man called Göran who was seventy-four and lived in Lycksele.

I waited for a second stroke. A bell rings the hour; at midnight it should ring twelve. But there was only the one. It went on humming in the air for a long time, and then it was gone, and the silence afterward was a different kind of silence.

I could hear the grass.

I mean that precisely. I could hear it moving, the dry seed-heads brushing one another, and it was moving all around the mound in a slow circle, though I could feel no wind on the hide. The sound went round once, and then round again, closer.

Astrid's hand found mine in the dark and gripped it hard enough to hurt. Her fingers were cold, so cold. Colder, I thought later, than they should have been under that hide in August with both of us sweating. The nail in my left fist had gone slick.

Then, very close to my ear, on the side away from Astrid, someone breathed in.

Not out. In. The way you breathe in to say something.

I did the one thing she had told me never to do. I opened my mouth.

I don't remember what I meant to say. *Stop*, maybe, or *Astrid*, or nothing at all, just the sound a body makes. But her hand clamped over my lips before any of it got out, and she held it there, and we sat like that until the brown glow of the hide went grey, and then pale, and the birds started up in the rowans.

When we finally crawled out, stiff and stinking, the scissors were still in the turf. The bread was gone. That could have been a fox. Of course it could.

Astrid packed everything away without looking at me. At the edge of the field, as I dug up my batteries, I asked her whether she'd heard the bell.

She was quiet for so long I thought she wouldn't answer.

"Gran says it only rings once," she said finally, "so you know you've been counted."

She wouldn't tell me what for. I didn't ask her again until it was much too late.
