response:
# Útiseta

Astrid said the hide had to be from an animal that died on its own. That was the first rule, and she told it to me the way you'd tell someone to bring a sweater, while unrolling the thing across my bedroom floor at eleven o'clock on a Thursday in September. It was a reindeer skin, grey-brown and stiff along the edges, and it smelled like a cellar.

"Farmor's," she said. "Don't tell anyone I took it."

I was fifteen. I had been in Kallsjön for four months, long enough to learn that the bus came twice a day and nobody at school had heard of anything I liked. Astrid had been the only one who talked to me. She talked to me as if I'd been waiting my whole life to hear what she had to say, and maybe I had.

We went out through the laundry room. My parents slept on the far side of the house, and my father's snoring had become a kind of permission. Astrid carried the hide rolled under her arm. In her jacket pocket she had a kitchen knife, a heel of bread, and a twist of paper with salt in it. I had my Walkman, which she made me leave on the porch step.

"Nothing that makes its own sound," she said.

The mound was a kilometre north, past the last farm, in a field the Lundqvists never ploughed. Everyone called it Kungshögen, the king's mound, though Astrid said there was no king, just someone who had mattered enough to be buried where people would have to walk around them forever. It rose out of the grass like the back of something sleeping.

The mist had come up from the lake while we walked. It lay along the base of the mound in a thick white collar and didn't move. The moon was nearly full, and the mist held its light so the whole hill seemed to float on something faintly luminous, like milk in a dark glass. I remember thinking it was beautiful. I remember being embarrassed that I thought so.

"Don't look back once we're through," Astrid said.

"Through what?"

She didn't answer. She walked into the mist and I followed, and it was cold in a way the air above it hadn't been, wet against my wrists and the back of my neck. Then the slope was under my feet, and we climbed out of it onto the crown of the mound where the grass was short and dry, as if nothing grew tall there.

She put down the hide and cut a line in the turf around it with the knife, a ragged circle, muttering something I couldn't follow. It wasn't Swedish, or it was very old Swedish. When I asked later she said it was just counting, and I've never known whether to believe her.

The bread went at the north edge. The salt she sprinkled in her own palm and licked off, then held out the paper to me. I did the same. It stung a cut on my lip I hadn't known I had.

"Now we sit," she said. "Back to back. Hide over our heads. You don't speak. If someone says your name, you don't answer. You don't lift the hide until I do."

"What if you don't?"

"Then you wait for the birds."

She said it like a joke. We had done other things that summer. Mirrors and candles, names written backwards and burned, a hair from Johanna Berg's brush buried under the school flagpole. Johanna had broken her wrist two weeks later, falling off her moped, and Astrid had looked at me across the cafeteria with such quiet satisfaction that I'd felt sick and thrilled at once. It was a coincidence. I told myself that every night.

We sat. The hide came down over us, heavy and close, and the world shrank to the smell of old fur and the warmth of Astrid's spine against mine and my own breath coming back at me.

For a long time there was nothing. My legs went numb. I heard a car far off on the county road. I heard Astrid breathing, slow and even. I started composing what I'd say to her afterward, something dry and unimpressed.

Then the cold came up through the ground.

It wasn't the night getting colder. It came from beneath, through my jeans, into the bones of my hips, the way cold comes off a stone floor. And with it a sense of depth, of the mound going down much further than a mound should, of how much was packed beneath us, how long it had been packed there.

Something moved in the grass outside the circle. A soft, deliberate shifting, like weight being set down carefully. A deer, I thought. A fox. It stopped near the north edge, near the bread.

Astrid's breathing had changed. It was slower now, so slow that between breaths I couldn't feel her back move at all.

"Linnea."

It came from in front of me, from outside the hide. It was my mother's voice. It was very nearly my mother's voice. It said my name the way she did when she found me asleep on the sofa, with the second syllable lifted, and it was close enough that I could have reached out and touched whoever said it.

I didn't answer. I bit the cut on my lip until I tasted blood and salt.

It didn't say it again. That was the worst part. It didn't need to. I felt it waiting, patient as the mound itself, as though it had all the time that had ever been and I was a small, brief thing that would eventually have to lift the hide.

I don't know how long we sat. When the first bird called from the birches, Astrid moved, and the hide came off, and the sky was pale grey and the mist was gone.

The bread was gone too.

Astrid stood and stretched and looked at me with her bright, ordinary face. "Well?" she said. "What did you hear?"

I told her nothing. I've thought about it for thirty years, and I'm still not sure whether I was protecting myself, or her, or whatever had sat so patiently just outside the circle, waiting to see which of us would answer.

response:
# Útiseta

Astrid had the cowhide rolled under her arm like a sleeping bag, and that should have been the first thing to stop me.

"It's from Morfar's barn," she said when I asked. "A blanket doesn't count. It has to have been alive."

We left her house at half past eleven, the last week of October, 1995. Her parents slept like the dead, she said, which I thought was funny then. Mine thought I was sleeping over to study for a geography test. The snow hadn't come yet, but the ground was hard with frost and crunched under my Doc Martens loud enough that I kept glancing back at the dark houses, as if anyone in Brännliden would be awake to see two girls walking toward the forest at midnight.

Astrid smoked a Marlboro Light on the way, cupping it against the wind like the boys at the bus stop did. At the edge of the trees she pinched it out with her fingers and put the butt in her pocket.

"No fire on the mound," she said. "And no light. Turn off your torch once we're through."

"Then how do we see?"

"We don't. That's the point."

She'd been explaining it all week, in pieces, in the cafeteria and on the phone with the cord stretched into her pantry so her mother wouldn't hear. You didn't eat after breakfast. You sat on a hide, on a grave, under the open sky. You didn't speak once you'd sat down. If someone called your name from behind, you didn't turn your head. Not for anything. Her mormor had told her that part twice, Astrid said, holding her wrist hard enough to leave marks.

"What happens if you turn?"

Astrid had shrugged and stolen one of my fries. "Then you go home with something extra."

The path through the pines was one she knew without looking. The wind came in long pulls off the river, and the trees answered it with a sound I had no word for in Stockholm. Not rustling, exactly. Something with consonants in it. I told myself it was needles.

The mound sat in a clearing that shouldn't have been there. Everything else around it had grown thick and crowded, but nothing taller than heather grew on the hump of earth, which rose about as high as a car. Astrid said it was Iron Age. Someone from Umeå University had come to measure it in the seventies and left. Nobody had dug. Nobody would.

She took a knife out of her jacket, an old one with a wooden handle gone black, and pushed it into the frozen ground at the foot of the mound. It took her three tries.

"Steel," she said. "So we can find the way back. And so it knows we're not staying."

"So *what* knows?"

She grinned at me, all braces in the torchlight, and switched mine off.

We climbed up and spread the hide over the frost, hair side down. Astrid sat first, then pulled me down so we were back to back, and dragged the loose edge of the hide up over both our heads. It smelled of barn and mildew and something sweeter underneath. Her Casio beeped twice as she set the alarm for one o'clock.

"Think about your question," she whispered. "Over and over. Like praying, but rude." Then she went quiet, and the rules had started.

My question was about Johanna Lindqvist, who had told the whole class my father had been fired in Stockholm, not transferred. I wanted to know why she hated me. I wanted, if I'm honest, to hurt her. That was what Astrid had promised these games were for.

The first ten minutes I mostly felt stupid. My jeans were soaking through. Astrid's back was a warm, solid shape against mine, and I could feel her breathing, slow and even, and I tried to match it. The wind came and went. When it came, the pines said their long, soft sentences, and when it went, the silence was so total that I heard my own pulse in my ears.

Then I noticed the breathing against my back didn't match the breath I could hear.

I told myself it was the hide. It muffled things. I told myself I was hungry and cold and fifteen, and that Astrid had spent a week priming me like a pump. I kept thinking *Johanna, Johanna, why,* but the words kept sliding away, and other words kept arriving in the gaps where the wind had been, and I couldn't tell if I was thinking them or hearing them.

Somewhere behind me, down toward the knife, someone said *Linnea.*

Not loud. Conversational. In my mother's voice, except my mother never said my whole name, only Linn, and the vowels were wrong, flattened and old, like a recording played too slowly.

I didn't turn. I want that on the record. I stared into the dark inside the hide until colours swam, and the warm back against mine pressed closer, patiently, the way a dog leans on you when it wants you to stay.

The Casio went off like a fire alarm.

Astrid flung the hide back and laughed, loud and shaky, and the stars were there and the clearing was just a clearing. "Did you get anything?"

She was sitting a full metre to my left. Not behind me. Sideways on the hide, knees pulled up, unwrapping a piece of Stimorol.

"You moved," I said.

"Ages ago. Your shoulder blades were killing me." She frowned. "Why?"

I looked down. Behind where I'd been sitting, the hide had bunched up into a rough mound against the slope, the way it would if you leaned back against it for an hour. That was all. Folded leather and heather and frozen dirt.

At the foot of the mound, the knife was lying flat in the frost.

Astrid saw it too. She didn't say anything. She picked it up, wiped it on her jeans, and we walked home much faster than we'd come. She talked the whole way, about Johanna and what she'd "received," about doing it again at Christmas. I didn't hear much of it. The wind kept pulling through the pines, and I kept my eyes on her back.

I've lived in Stockholm again for twenty-six years. I have a husband who snores and a daughter who thinks I'm boring.

I still sleep with nothing behind me but a wall.

# Gone South

## Chapter Two: Royal Street

The saxophone guy on Royal Street is playing something slow and wrecked, which feels a little on the nose, honestly. Like the whole city got a memo: *sad kid incoming, cue the soundtrack.*

I'm standing on a corner with a backpack containing: two shirts, one pair of jeans, a toothbrush, a phone charger for a phone I turned off somewhere around Meridian, Mississippi, and one hundred and forty-three dollars I took from the coffee can above the fridge. I'm going to pay that back. I tell myself that every forty minutes or so, like a prayer.

The guy who drove me here was named Russ. He had a Bass Pro Shops hat and a Jesus fish on his dashboard. He was nice for three hundred miles. Then somewhere past Slidell he looked at me for too long, *really* looked, and I watched his face do the math. Not the math I was worried about. The other math.

"You a boy or a girl?" he said.

And I was so tired. I'd been lying for forty-eight hours straight, lying with my mouth shut, at dinner, in my room, through the door while Mom cried on the other side of it. So I just said, "Neither, really. Or both. It's complicated."

He let me out on Canal Street at 6:40 a.m. and didn't say goodbye.

So. That's how I got here.

---

By noon I've learned three things about New Orleans.

One: it smells like beer and bleach and something sweet frying, all at once, all the time.

Two: nobody looks at you. Which is the best thing that has ever happened to me. Back home I couldn't buy gum at the Kwik Stop without Mrs. Pruitt asking how my mother was holding up, like Mom had a diagnosis and I was it. Here, a man in a silver bodysuit is standing perfectly still on an upturned bucket, and a woman is walking a pig on a leash, and I'm just a kid with a backpack. I'm *wallpaper.* God, I love it.

Three: I have no idea what I'm doing.

That one hits around one o'clock, outside a praline shop, when my stomach starts eating itself and I realize a hotel costs more than I have and I don't know where kids like me sleep. The sax player has moved to Jackson Square. I can still hear him, though, threading through the crowd like he's following me.

I think about calling home. I don't. I think about it again. My thumb finds the power button on the phone and just *rests* there, and I hate myself a little, because part of me wants Mom to answer and say *come home, baby, we'll figure it out,* and part of me knows she'd say *come home, Taylor,* in that voice, with my old name tucked in behind it like a knife in a napkin.

I put the phone away.

---

"You're gonna get rolled, standing like that."

The girl sitting on the church steps behind me has a shaved head, a Saints jersey three sizes too big, and a sunburn peeling off her nose. She's eating a hot dog with the focus of a surgeon.

"Standing like what?"

"Like a tourist who lost their mom." She chews. "Backpack on one shoulder. Looking up at the balconies. You might as well wear a sign. *Please steal my stuff.*"

I shift the backpack to both shoulders. She snorts.

"Cass," she says. She doesn't offer a hand.

"Taylor."

"Where from, Taylor?"

"Nowhere."

"Ooh. Love Nowhere. Very scenic." She tears off half the hot dog and holds it out. I stare at it. I stare at her. *Who gives away half a hot dog for free?* says a voice in my head that sounds exactly like my father. *Nobody. That's who. There's always a price.*

I take it anyway. I'm sixteen and hungry and stupid.

---

We walk. Cass talks like someone who hasn't had anyone to talk to in a while. She points things out: the shelter on Rampart that'll call your parents if you look under eighteen. The church that does sandwiches Tuesdays. The guy in the linen suit by the gallery who'll offer you "work" and a place to crash.

"Don't," she says, flat. "Ever."

I don't ask how she knows. Her voice tells me not to.

Somewhere on Frenchmen Street, the sun going orange, she says, "So what'd you do?"

"What?"

"To end up here. Nobody ends up here for nothing."

I could lie. I'm good at it. Ask the counselor: *concerning behavioural patterns.* I set the chem lab sink on fire in ninth grade because I wanted to see what would happen. I told half the school my uncle was in the Mafia. Drama. Invented. Because boredom felt like drowning, and drama at least felt like *air.*

But this isn't that. And I'm tired of making things up so nobody looks at the true thing.

"I told my parents I'm trans."

I brace. For what, I don't know. For the Russ face.

Cass just nods. "Cool. What do you want me to call you?"

And I almost cry right there on Frenchmen Street. Almost. I hold it behind my teeth.

"Taylor's fine. *They* is fine."

"Cool," she says again, like it costs nothing. Like it's the easiest thing in the world. Which, apparently, it is, for some people. Which makes me furious, suddenly, at everyone who acted like it was impossible.

---

It's when she pushes her sleeve up to scratch her arm that I see it. A band of pale skin around her wrist, whiter than the rest of her sunburn. The exact shape of a hospital bracelet.

She catches me looking. Tugs the sleeve down.

"Don't," she says. Same voice as the linen-suit guy.

"I didn't say anything."

"You were *thinking* it loud."

Her phone buzzes in her pocket. She has a phone. She doesn't check it. It buzzes again. She keeps walking like it isn't there.

*Issues,* my brain supplies. *Secrets. She's got both, and you met her four hours ago, and she knows you've got cash.*

But she gave me half a hot dog. And she said *cool.*

---

"There's a place," Cass says, when the streetlights come on. "Under the wharf, by the old warehouse. Few of us crash there. It's not nothing, but it's not the street."

The sax player is somewhere behind us now, faint, playing something with a little more lift to it. Or maybe I'm just hearing it that way.

I think about Mom. About the coffee can. About Russ's face.

I think: *I don't know if I can trust you.*

Then I think: *I don't know if I can trust anybody. I don't know if I can trust me.*

"Okay," I say.

And I follow her into the dark.

# Gone South

## Chapter Two: Powdered Sugar

The guy in the Silverado, Randy, or Rodney, or some name with an R and a gun rack, lets me out on Decatur Street at 6:40 a.m. He says, "This is as far as I go, kid." It's a lie. He's going to Metairie. He told me so outside Jackson, Mississippi, back when he still thought I was a boy running off to see a girlfriend.

Then I said the thing about my name, and the air in the cab changed. It was like when a dog stops wagging.

So. Here I am.

New Orleans smells like someone hosed down a hangover. The sidewalks are wet but it hasn't rained. A man in rubber boots is spraying the gutter outside a bar called something French I can't pronounce, and the water runs pink and brown and carries a single green bead past my sneakers like a tiny drowned planet.

I check my phone. **12%.**

Fourteen missed calls from Mom. Three from Dad, which is three more than I expected. One text from my brother Caleb: *where r u. shes freaking out.*

Not *Mom's freaking out*. Just *she's*. Like even Caleb can't decide what to call anybody in our house anymore.

I put the phone face-down against my thigh like that'll make it stop existing. Then I immediately flip it back over, because what if.

What if what, Taylor? What if they call and say *come home, we're sorry, we bought you a binder and a cake*? Sure. And what if the Mississippi River flows backward.

(It did once, actually. 2012, Hurricane Isaac. I learned that in Earth Science. Thanks, Mr. Pruitt.)

---

By nine I have walked the whole French Quarter twice and learned three things:

1. Beignets cost money, and I have $31.
2. Everybody here is performing something. The guy painted silver, the lady with the cat on her head, the tap-dancing boys with bottle caps glued to their shoes. Back home that was called *making a scene*. Here they call it *Tuesday*.
3. Nobody looks at me twice.

Number three should feel good. It's what I wanted. It's why I'm here. Instead I keep catching my reflection in shop windows, hoodie up, hair chopped with kitchen scissors, and thinking *who is that*, and then *oh*, and then a hot mess of feelings I don't have room for in my chest.

I sit on a bench in Jackson Square and do math. Thirty-one dollars. Twelve percent, no, **eleven**. Zero plans.

"You're doing it wrong."

There's a girl perched on the back of the next bench, feet on the seat, eating a beignet out of a paper bag. She's got green fingernails, chipped, and box braids pulled up in a scrunchie, and a canvas tote that says *I SURVIVED JAZZ FEST 2019*. She'd have been, what, nine?

"Doing what wrong?"

"Looking lost." She licks sugar off her thumb. "You look like a tourist who lost their tour. That's how you get picked up."

"Picked up by who?"

She shrugs, which isn't an answer, which is the whole answer.

"I'm Juniper," she says. "June. You want half of this? I can't finish it, they're like eating a cloud made of diabetes."

Every after-school special I've ever been forced to watch screams *don't take food from strangers*. But I haven't eaten since a gas station Slim Jim in Hattiesburg, and the beignet is still warm.

"Taylor," I say, and I take it.

It's the first time I've said my name to someone who didn't already know the old one. It comes out sort of cracked. June doesn't notice, or pretends not to, and I'm not sure which I'd rather.

---

June knows things. She knows the public library on Loyola has outlets nobody guards and bathrooms with locks. She knows which church does lunch on weekdays ("the Methodists, not the other ones, the other ones make you pray *first*"). She walks fast, like she's always half a block ahead of something.

"How long have you been here?" I ask, on the streetcar she sweet-talked us onto for free.

"Couple months."

"From where?"

"Around." She looks out the window. "Baton Rouge. Kinda."

"How old are you?"

"Nineteen."

She's not nineteen. She's got a retainer case clipped to her tote, and when the streetcar jolts she grabs my arm the way my little cousin grabs my arm on escalators. On the inside of her left wrist there's a pale band of skin, the kind you get from a watch, or a bracelet you wore for a long time, or the plastic kind they snap on you at a hospital.

I don't ask. I know what it's like to have the question hanging in the air while you decide whether to lie.

"You?" she says.

"Sixteen." Apparently I'm the honest one. Great. Love that for me.

"From?"

"Tennessee."

"Why'd you leave?"

The streetcar dings. I think about Dad standing in the kitchen doorway, not yelling. That was the worst part, the not yelling. Him looking at me like I was a car he'd bought that turned out to be a lemon.

"Family stuff."

June nods slowly. "Yeah," she says. "Family stuff."

---

The library is cool and quiet and smells like carpet glue. I plug in my phone in the corner by the biography section and watch it climb: **14%. 17%. 22%.** It's the most hopeful thing I've seen all day.

There's a new text from Mom.

*Taylor please. Just tell me you're safe. You don't have to come home. Just tell me.*

She used my name. The real one, the one I gave them two days ago. Not the old one.

Did she do it on purpose? Did she type the other one first and delete it? I stare at the screen until the letters stop looking like letters.

I don't answer. I don't know why. Maybe because if I answer, this becomes a thing I did *to* her, instead of a thing I did *for* me.

June slides into the chair beside me. She's found a charger from somewhere too, though I didn't see her bring one.

"So, listen," she says, low. "Where are you sleeping tonight?"

"I don't know."

"There's this guy, Marcus. He's got a house in the Seventh Ward. Lets kids crash. He's cool, mostly." She's picking at her green nail polish. "He just likes you to, like, help out sometimes."

"Help out how?"

June doesn't look at me. The silence goes on a beat too long.

"It's better than the street," she says finally. "Trust me."

And that's the thing, isn't it? *Trust me.* I've known June for six hours. She gave me half a beignet and showed me where the outlets are. She is also, very obviously, lying about at least four things, and one of them has a name and an address.

My phone buzzes. **31%.** Mom again: *I love you.*

I look at June, at her chewed nails and her fake age and the pale stripe on her wrist. I look at my phone. Outside the window the sun's starting to slant gold over Loyola Avenue, and I can feel night coming like weather.

I don't know who to trust. I'm not sure I've ever known.

But I know I'm not going to Marcus's.

"June," I say, "do you know where the shelters are? The real ones?"

She doesn't answer for a long time. Then, very quietly, like it's costing her something:

"Yeah. I know where one is."

"Will you show me?"

Her jaw works. For a second I think she'll get up and walk away, half a block ahead of whatever's chasing her.

Instead she says, "Only if you don't make me go in."

"Deal," I lie.

And I think she knows. I think maybe she wants me to.

# Gone South

## Chapter Two: Nobody Here Knows My Name

The trucker's name was Ronnie, and Ronnie had opinions.

He kept them to himself for most of Mississippi. Then somewhere past Slidell he asked what a "nice young man" was doing hitching at two in the morning, and I made the mistake of correcting him. By sunrise I'm standing on Canal Street with my backpack, my dignity, and roughly forty-three dollars.

The strap slips off my shoulder. I hitch it back up.

New Orleans at six a.m. smells like beer that has given up. A guy in rubber boots is hosing down the sidewalk on Bourbon, and the water runs past my sneakers in a grey river of cups and beads and something I decide not to look at. Everything is wet and old and leaning a little, like the whole city stayed out too late.

I love it immediately. I also want to throw up.

*You did it. You actually did it.*

My phone is off and buried in the bottom of the bag, because Mom has the Find My thing, and because if I turn it on I will see forty-seven texts. I will read every one of them and get back in a truck. Or I won't, and that's worse somehow. I keep thinking about her face at the kitchen table. Not angry. Just... *closed*. Like a store with the lights still on and the sign flipped.

Dad didn't say anything. Dad *still* hasn't said anything, probably.

The strap slips. I hitch it up.

---

By noon I've learned three things:

1. Coffee costs four dollars and I cannot afford coffee.
2. If you stand still in Jackson Square, someone will try to read your palm.
3. I have no idea what I'm doing.

I'm sitting on the steps up by the river, watching a barge the size of my high school slide by, when a dog sticks its whole face in my lap.

"Biscuit. *Biscuit.* Manners."

The dog is a brindle pit mix on a length of yellow rope. The girl on the other end looks maybe seventeen. Buzzed head, Sharpie doodles crawling up both forearms, a hoodie in this heat like she's daring the weather to make something of it.

"Sorry. She likes new people." She squints at me. "You're new."

"Is it that obvious?"

"You're sitting on your bag like somebody's gonna steal it." She drops down a step below me. "Which, fair. Greyhound?"

"Peterbilt."

That gets a laugh, short and surprised. "Respect. I'm Ren."

There's this moment. It's tiny, and it's enormous. She's waiting, and nobody in this entire city knows the name my parents gave me. Nobody's going to say it with that careful little weight, like they're holding it out to remind me what I really am.

"Taylor," I say.

"Cool." She scratches Biscuit's ears. "He, she, they, other?"

My throat does something stupid. I look hard at the barge.

"They."

"Cool," Ren says again, exactly the same way, like I told her I take my coffee black. Like it's *nothing*. I could cry. I don't, because I have some self-respect, but I could.

---

Ren knows things. She knows which church does lunch on Thursdays and which one makes you pray first. She knows the cops on Decatur won't hassle you before dark. She knows that the guy with the gold tooth selling "mixtapes" is not selling mixtapes.

"How long have you been here?" I ask.

"Long enough." That's all I get.

I notice things too, though. I'm good at noticing; my counselor called it *hypervigilance*, like it's a disease instead of a survival skill. I notice that Ren's left sleeve never comes up past her wrist. I notice that there's a hospital band under it, white plastic, the kind they don't let you take home unless you leave in a hurry. I notice she checks over her shoulder every time a white sedan goes by.

I don't ask. She didn't ask about mine.

Around four, a man sits down on the bench next to us like he's been invited. Forties, nice shoes, a smile with too many teeth in it. He smells like cologne and air conditioning.

"Ren! Who's your friend?"

"Nobody, Kev."

"Doesn't look like nobody." He turns the smile on me, and it's warm. That's the scary part. It's *so* warm. "You eaten today, sweetheart? I got a place over in the Marigny. AC, hot shower, whole fridge full. Some of the kids crash there. No strings."

And God, I want a shower. I want it so bad my skin itches. Something in me leans toward him the way Biscuit leaned into my lap. *He's being nice. Maybe people here are just nice.*

"Not today, Kev," Ren says. Flat. Final.

He holds his hands up, still smiling, and drops a card on the bench. "Offer stands. For both of you."

When he's gone, Ren picks up the card and tears it into very small pieces.

"No strings," she says, "is the biggest string there is."

I want to ask how she knows. I want to ask whether she's protecting me or just protecting her territory, whether there's even a difference out here. I want to ask why her hands are shaking.

I don't.

---

When it gets dark, Ren takes me to a spot under the I-10 overpass where a few other kids have set up. Tarps, a camp stove, someone playing a guitar badly. A boy with a lip ring nods at me. Nobody asks where I'm from.

My strap slips again. I swear at it.

"Hold still." Ren pulls a zip tie out of her pocket like she's been carrying it all day for exactly this. She cinches the strap to the buckle, snaps off the tail with her teeth. "There. Won't go anywhere now."

"I don't know," I say. That's the truest thing I've said all day, and it's the thing that finally makes my eyes sting. "I don't know if I want them to."

# The Underhold

The door gave without complaint. That was the first wrong thing.

The second was the light. Aya had expected darkness below, the clammy black of the old rendering cellars where the guild's forebears had boiled blubber down to lamp oil a century past. Instead the underhold blazed. A dozen whale-oil lanterns hung from hooks in the vaulted brick, and their glow lay greasy and amber across the flagstones, across the ribcage of some ancient leviathan bolted to the far wall, across the iron reliquary beneath it where the Scythan artifact slept.

Across the woman sitting on the reliquary, swinging one boot.

"Close the door, love," said Mag Corvane. "You're letting the damp in."

Aya's breath stopped somewhere beneath her sternum. *No. No, they took her. Simeon saw the wagon. Half the Lantern Ward saw the wagon.*

"Evening, Mag," Katra said, and only someone who had known her for years would have heard the crack in it. "Thought you'd be enjoying the Crown's hospitality."

"Did you, now." Corvane smiled. She was a broad, weathered woman in a sealskin greatcoat, grey hair cropped like a deckhand's, and the smile did not reach anything. "Funny thing about the constabulary. Pay a sergeant enough and he'll arrest anyone you like. Even yourself. Drive you twice round Gallows Quay and let you out the back of the wagon before breakfast." She tilted her head. "Then you sit and wait to see which of your children comes creeping down to rob your grave."

Shapes stepped out of the alcoves. There were six of them, big men in oilskins and leather aprons, and each held a flensing hook or a brass-bound harpoon pistol, its chamber hissing faintly with compressed air. Behind the trio the door swung shut. Someone threw the bolt.

Aya reached inward. She did not decide to do it; the reflex was older than thought. Beneath the skin of the world lay the immateria, the cold black sea her mother had taught her to hear, and it was full of hungry things that came when called by name.

Nothing answered.

There was only a thick, sweetish fog, and she could taste it now on the air: waxy and animal, faintly fecal, faintly floral.

"Ambergris," Corvane said, watching her face. "Burnt in the lamp oil. The old harpooners swore it kept the drowned from climbing aboard. I never credited it, myself, till I heard how quick a certain masked girl rose through my ranks, and what the boys whispered about the cold that followed her." She leaned forward. "Go on. Call something. I'll wait."

Aya stood very still. The immateria pressed against the inside of her skull like a hand against frosted glass, and she could not reach it.

"Right," Simeon murmured. "So that's the plan gone, then."

"Hands where Dorran can see them, Mister Pell. And the little knife in your sleeve. And the one in your boot, Katra, don't be precious."

Blades rang on stone. Rough hands found Aya's wrists and hauled them behind her, and cord bit into the skin. A man with a burn-scarred jaw seized the crown of her mask.

*Don't*—

Lacquered porcelain scraped away from her face. Cold air touched her cheeks, and the lanternlight was suddenly very bright.

The silence that followed was the worst sound she had ever heard.

"Well," Corvane breathed. "Well, well. I know that face. I've seen it on a broadsheet. Older, mind, and with a rope round its neck." She slid off the reliquary and crossed the flagstones, boots ringing, until Aya could smell tar and tobacco on her. "You're Lady Ilse Ravensworth's girl. The witch they hanged at Saltgate."

Aya made herself meet the woman's eyes. Somewhere beneath the floor, in the old drainage tunnels, water dripped with the patience of a clock.

*Father will know by morning. The whole of Harrowgate Terrace will know. They'll say it's in the blood. They'll say they always wondered.* She saw the drawing rooms she so despised, the teacups halting halfway to painted mouths. She saw her father's face going grey, as it had at Saltgate. She saw the scaffold.

She found that her voice still worked.

"Then you know what I'm worth."

Corvane's eyebrows rose.

"My father is Lord Edmund Ravensworth," Aya went on, quickly, before her nerve could fail. "He sits on the Admiralty Board. He signs the whaling charters for half the fleet in this harbour. He has already buried a wife in disgrace, Mrs Corvane, and he would sell his own soul to keep from burying a daughter the same way. Cut my throat down here and you get a corpse and a constabulary that stops taking your bribes. Keep me breathing and you get the Admiralty."

"Aya," Katra hissed.

"Shut it, Kat." Aya kept her eyes on Corvane. "Charters. Harbour manifests. The patrol rotations along the Brine Steps. Name it. He'll pay, and he'll pay quietly, because the alternative is the *Gazette* printing that Ravensworth's girl summons devils for a thieves' guild."

Corvane studied her for a long moment. Then she laughed. It was a low, wet, genuinely delighted sound, and it was worse than any threat.

"Oh, you're your mother's daughter, right enough. Bargaining on the trapdoor." She reached out and took Aya's chin between a thumb and forefinger, rough as rope. "But you've the sums wrong, my lady. A ransom's paid once. A secret like yours pays every quarter-day till his lordship dies." Her grip tightened. "And it's not *you* I'd ransom. It's your silence."

Far out in the harbour, beyond the walls and the black water, a foghorn sounded. One long, mournful note. Then a second. Then a third, and it hung in the vaults like the lowing of something vast and drowned.

Corvane let go.

"Hear that? Three blasts. That's the *Covenant* coming in on the night tide. She's my ship." She turned away and gestured to her men. "Bring them. The pretty one and her friends ride in the hold with the casks till I've had time to think on what a witch is worth by the pound."

"And if her father won't pay?" asked the scarred man.

Corvane glanced back. The lanternlight caught her eyes and made them yellow, like old ivory.

"Then the Crown hangs witches for free, Dorran. I'm sure they'd be grateful for the tip."

They were marched toward the rear tunnel, where the sea-smell rose thick and cold. Aya stumbled once, and in that instant, beneath the cloying haze of ambergris, she felt something stir far down in the immateria. It was not answering her. It was only listening, as it had been listening all along, patient and attentive in the deep.

# The Underhold

The door gave without protest, and that, more than anything, was what turned Aya's blood to slush.

Beyond it, the underhold breathed. Gas lamps guttered in their brass cages along the walls, each flame a sickly blue-yellow that came and went like a failing pulse. Their light did not so much illuminate the vault as negotiate with it, throwing long, crooked shadows that stretched across the flagstones and climbed the ribbed ceiling. The ribs were bone, Aya realised. The whole vault was framed in the jaw of some vast leviathan, hauled up from the black water a century past. The air stank of rendered oil and old salt, and beneath that, faintly, of something sweet and spoiled.

At the far end, on a plinth of tarnished copper, sat the Scythan reliquary. It was smaller than she had imagined, no larger than a hymnal, and it hummed at a pitch she felt in her back teeth rather than heard.

*Too quiet. Too easy. You knew it, you stupid girl, and you opened the door anyway.*

"Ain't nobody here," Simeon whispered, and the lamps flared as if in answer.

"Oh, there's somebody, love."

The voice came from the shadows to the left of the plinth, low and roughened by forty years of pipe smoke and river fog. A figure unfolded from a high-backed chair Aya had taken for part of the dark. Mother Grisel Thorne wore her irons as other women wore pearls. The manacles still hung from her wrists, but the chain between them had been cut clean. Her greatcoat was black oilskin. In her right hand rested a long-barrelled pistol of blued steel, its hammer already drawn.

Then the shadows moved, and they kept moving. Six men stepped out from behind the leviathan ribs. They were Thorne's Gaffers, her old dockside hands, broad as coal barges, carrying harpoon-guns and blunderbusses with flared brass mouths. One of them held a contraption of copper coils and glass. Inside the glass, a pale spark crawled back and forth like a trapped wasp.

Aya knew what it was the moment she saw it. A Corrigan cage. The Inquisitorial Office used them to dampen immateria workings in the condemned. She had last seen one the morning they led her mother up the scaffold steps.

Katra's hand went to her knife. A dozen hammers clicked back in answer.

"Don't, Kat," Aya breathed.

"Sensible," Thorne said. "That's the first sensible thing any of you've done tonight." She tilted her head. "Arrested, was I? Dragged off by the Peelers in the small hours? It's a marvel what a body will believe when they *want* to believe it. Three days I've sat in this chair waiting to see which of my children would come creeping down for Mother's treasure." Her eyes settled on Aya. "I'll own I didn't think it'd be the Moth."

Aya reached anyway. It was instinct, the way a drowning woman claws for the surface. She stretched her mind toward the thin place behind the world, toward the cold and the whispering and the things with too many joints that waited there for an invitation. For half a heartbeat she felt them turn toward her, hungry and eager.

The Corrigan cage shrieked. The spark inside it flared white, and the immateria slammed shut on her like a coffin lid. Pain lanced behind her eyes. She dropped to her knees, tasting copper.

"Oh, I know what you are, girl." Thorne crossed the floor in no particular hurry, her boots ringing on the stone. "Half my crew's whispered about it for a twelvemonth. The Moth who makes the shadows bite. I paid a defrocked Inquisitor a king's ransom for that little toy." She crouched and hooked one gnarled finger beneath the edge of Aya's mask. "Now. Let's have a look at you."

*No. No, no, no.*

The mask came away. Cold air touched her face, and with it came a terrible, naked lightness.

For a long moment Thorne said nothing. Then she began to laugh. It was a low, wet, delighted sound that echoed off the bone ceiling.

"Well, now. Well, *now*." She turned to her Gaffers. "Do you lads know who this is? This here is the Honourable Aya Ashcombe. Lord Ashcombe's girl, of the Admiralty Board." Her grin showed a single gold tooth. "And her mother was the witch they hanged at Gallows Quay. I was there, girlie. Bought a pasty and watched her dance."

Behind her, Aya heard Simeon's sharp intake of breath. Katra said nothing at all, and that was worse.

*They didn't know. You never told them. You let them follow you down here and you never told them what you were.*

Thick hands hauled all three of them upright. Coarse hemp bit into Aya's wrists. Someone shoved Katra against a rib of the leviathan, and Simeon was forced to his knees with a blunderbuss pressed to his skull.

Thorne levelled the pistol at Aya's breastbone. "I'd meant to make an example of whoever came through that door. Hang 'em in the rookery for the gulls. But a lord's daughter, and a witch besides..." She clicked her tongue. "Decisions, decisions."

Aya forced her voice steady. It came out in the clipped drawing-room diction she had spent years learning to bury.

"Then decide wisely, madam. Dead, I'm worth nothing to you but a fortnight's gossip. Alive, I'm worth a great deal more."

"Go on."

"My father sits on the Admiralty Board. He has the ear of the Harbourmaster and the Lord Inquisitor both. He would pay..." She faltered, and hated herself for it. "He would pay a fortune to have me returned quietly, with no scandal and no questions asked."

"And would he pay to keep quiet that his darling daughter's been raising devils in the gutters with the likes of us?"

*He'd pay to see me buried*, Aya thought. *He'd pay to see me hanged before he'd see the name of Ashcombe dragged through the broadsheets a second time.* She saw the cellar of her childhood, her mother's chalk circles scrubbed away by servants, and her father's face like a shuttered window.

"He would pay," she said, "because the alternative is ruin. Mine, and his."

"And theirs?" Thorne jerked her chin toward Katra and Simeon.

"They're part of the price. All three of us walk out, or you get nothing."

Thorne studied her for a long time. The lamps sputtered. In the copper cage, the pale spark crawled faster, as though something on the other side of the world was pressing its face against the glass to listen.

"Bold," the old woman said at last. "Your mother was bold, too." She leaned in close, her breath sour with gin and tobacco. "But here's the trouble, my lady. A ransom gets paid once. A witch with a lordship's name, kept on a short chain, now *she* pays for years."

The reliquary hummed louder. Somewhere in the dark between the bones, something laughed with her.

# The Underhold

The door gave without protest. That was the first wrong thing.

Aya had expected resistance: the bite of a ward, the grind of tumblers, some last cantankerous lock forged by a paranoid smith. Instead the iron swung inward on hinges oiled so recently she could smell the rendered spermaceti, sweet and rancid, like a butcher's shop at the edge of the docks.

Beyond lay the underhold, a long vault ribbed with the bones of some ancient leviathan. Each arch was a curving rib bleached the colour of old teeth, and between them hung whale-oil lamps turned low, their flames guttering blue. At the far end, on a plinth of black basalt, rested the Scythan artifact. It was a disc of dull green metal no larger than a dinner plate, etched with spirals that seemed to turn if one looked at them too long.

And before it, seated in a high-backed chair as though she were taking tea in a Belgravia parlour, sat Mother Varn.

*Tick.* Simeon's watch sounded loud as a dropped coin in a chapel.

"Do come in, my darlings," said Mother Varn. "Mind the step. It's slick with old blood. Ours, mostly."

She was not in chains. She was not in Newgate. She wore a coat of oxblood leather with a fox stole about her throat, and across her knees lay a harpoon pistol of polished brass, its barbed bolt already seated. Behind her, stepping from the shadows between the ribs, came four men in oilskins with long guns. The fifth was the Dutchman, Haas, who carried nothing at all and needed nothing.

*Tick.*

Katra swore under her breath, a filthy word from the Shadwell tanneries. Simeon said nothing. Aya heard him swallow.

"The raid," Aya said. Her voice, filtered through the lacquered mask, came out hollow. "We watched the constables drag you out."

"You watched the constables drag *someone* out. Poor Bess. Same height, near enough, and she owed me eleven guineas." Mother Varn smiled. "It's an old trick, girl. Shake the tree and see what falls. I confess I didn't expect it to be *you*, little Moth."

*Tick.*

Aya felt the immateria stir at the base of her skull, the cold, crawling hunger of things that waited beyond the thin skin of the world. She could call them. She had done it before, in the alley off Pell Street, and the man who had drawn his knife on her had died screaming at something only he could see.

She reached.

Something reached back, and it was not hers. A thin, high whine filled the vault. Atop a brass tripod near the plinth, a device of copper coils and glass valves began to hum, and the blue lamps flared white. The immateria snapped shut like a door in a gale. Aya staggered. Blood ran warm from her nose beneath the mask.

"Faraday cage, of a sort," said Mother Varn. "Cost me a fortune from a lapsed Royal Society man in Clerkenwell. He swore it would choke the Devil's own breath. I never believed him." She tilted her head. "Until now. Haas."

The Dutchman crossed the floor in four unhurried strides. Katra moved, and the long guns moved with her. Six barrels found her chest, and she froze with her blade half-drawn. Simeon raised his empty hands. Haas took Aya by the throat, not hard, almost courteously, and with his other hand he peeled the mask from her face.

The cold air of the vault touched her cheeks. She felt more naked than if he had stripped her to the skin.

*Tick.*

There was a long silence. Then Mother Varn laughed, a low, delighted rasp, like coal sliding down a chute.

"Well, I'll be buggered. Lady Aya Ashcombe. Lord Ashcombe's girl." She rose and came close, close enough that Aya could smell the gin and clove on her breath. "I knew your mother's face. Saw it at Tyburn, swinging. Same jaw. Same eyes. The crowd threw cabbages at her. Did you know that? Rotten ones. I thought it a waste of good cabbage."

Aya's stomach turned. *Don't. Don't let her see it.*

"Bind them," said Mother Varn.

They did. The cord bit into Aya's wrists. Katra spat at one of the oilskins and caught a rifle butt to the stomach for her trouble. She folded, wheezing. Simeon knelt without being asked, and his watch ticked on against his ribs, steady as a hangman's drum.

*Tick.*

*Think,* Aya told herself. *You are an Ashcombe. You were raised at tables where men lie with every forkful. Think.*

"You'll kill us," she said.

"Eventually. I'm not a cruel woman. I'm a tidy one."

"Then you're a fool." Aya lifted her chin, though Haas's hand was still a collar about her neck. "Dead, I'm worth nothing to you. A body in the Thames. Alive, I'm the daughter of a peer of the realm, a man who sits on the Admiralty Board and holds shares in half the whaling fleets that dock at Wapping."

"A man," said Mother Varn softly, "whose wife was hanged for witchcraft. Whose daughter, I now discover, keeps the same company in the dark." She leaned close. "Shall I tell you what your value is, my lady? To the right buyer, a magistrate or a newspaperman or the Witchfinder's Office on Fleet Street, you are worth a great deal. A great deal more than ransom."

*Tick.*

There it was. Aya had known it from the moment the mask came away, and now she let herself look at it. Every gaslit ballroom, every drawing room where she had smiled behind a fan, every cousin and suitor and her father's tired, grieving face, all of it would curdle. Father would not survive a second scandal. He would be ruined, or worse, he would stand on the gallows' edge and watch his daughter drop as he had watched his wife.

*You knew,* said a voice inside her that sounded like her mother. *You always knew how this ended. You simply hoped to choose the hour.*

"Then sell me," Aya said, and was astonished at how steady she sounded. "But sell me *once*. Hang me, and you get a reward and a broadsheet. Keep me, and you own an Ashcombe. You own my father's ledgers, his votes, his fleet manifests. Every guinea that moves through the Admiralty. You'll have the ear of the House of Lords, Mother Varn. Is that not worth more than eleven guineas and a cabbage?"

Behind her, Simeon let out a breath that might have been a laugh or a prayer.

*Tick.*

Mother Varn regarded her a long while. Behind her, on its plinth, the Scythan disc gleamed, and its spirals were turning now, slowly, unmistakably, though no hand touched them. Aya felt it *watching*.

"Lock them below," said Mother Varn at last. "The girl gets the dry cell. The other two get the bilge." She turned away, then paused. "And Simeon, dear, do stop that damned watch. It's counting something, and I'd rather not know what."

response:
# The Last Outpost

## Chapter Four: Neat

The Vega whisky lives on the top shelf, behind a jar of Plinthian moonshine nobody orders twice. I reach for it without looking. Six years behind this bar and I could find any bottle blind, which is handy, because I'm watching the stranger instead.

Tentacled dreads, a Vashti, maybe, or half. Normally the tendrils drift on their own like kelp in a slow current. His are clenched tight against his skull, coiling and uncoiling. His jacket is courier-grade, scuffed at the elbows. He sits with his back to the wall, close enough to the end of the bar to reach the service hatch.

I know that seat. I used to pick it myself.

"Double Vega, neat." I set it down. "First one's on the Outpost if you tell me who's chasing you."

He freezes with the glass halfway to his mouth. "Nobody's chasing me."

"Sure. You're just sitting near the exit and staring at the airlock like it owes you money."

"Maybe it does." He drinks half the double in one swallow and winces. "That's real Vega."

"I don't water the good stuff. Only the bad stuff, and only for Dorrin." I nod down the bar at the old ore-hauler, who raises his mug without opening his eyes. "He knows. It's a whole arrangement."

That nearly gets a smile out of him. "You're the bartender they told me about."

"Depends who *they* are."

"A Kessine merchant at Tollgate Station. She said if I made it this far, I should find the woman at the Outpost who asks too many questions."

"Ah, Mira. She still owes me for a bottle of Ceti gin and an apology." I lean on the bar. "So you've found me. Now what?"

Behind me, Teodor and his wife Bel are arguing again over a Spinewheel board. Something about whether a fusion token can jump a dead sector. Teodor says something under his breath. Bel says something louder.

"I need to stay somewhere quiet for two days," the stranger says. "Maybe three. Then a freighter called the *Patient Lark* docks here, and I'm on it, and you never see me again."

"The *Lark* docks Thursdays. Today's Monday." I tap the bar. "Rooms upstairs are forty a night. Fifty if you want the one where the heater works."

"I can pay." He puts a credit chip on the bar and slides it over. It's thick with credits, far more than forty.

I don't touch it. "That's a lot of money for a heater."

"It's for quiet."

"Quiet costs extra here. Everybody talks. It's an asteroid. There's nothing else to do."

His tendrils tighten. "Then I'll pay for less talking."

"What's your name?"

"Does it matter?"

"I need to write something on the room ledger. I could put 'Nervous Tentacle Man,' but Haskel does the books and he'll ask questions."

He takes a breath. "Ilo."

"Hi, Ilo. I'm Nets."

"I know." He looks right at me then. His eyes are pale gold and completely steady. "That's what I wanted to talk to you about."

Something in my chest goes very still.

At the Spinewheel table, a glass hits the floor and shatters. The whole bar turns to look. Bel is standing with her hand over her mouth and a puddle of blue ale spreading around her boots. Teodor is laughing so hard he has to grip the table.

"Sorry, Nets!" Bel calls. "It slipped! Mostly!"

"Mop's by the kitchen," I call back, and my voice comes out normal. That's one of my talents. "Put it on Teodor's tab. It's his fault on principle."

"Hey!"

When I turn back, Ilo hasn't moved. He's the only person in the bar who didn't look at the broken glass. He was watching me the whole time.

"Okay," I say quietly. "Talk."

"I'm carrying something. Not on me. It's in my ship's memory core, and the core's locked to my biometrics." He turns his glass in slow circles. "It's a manifest. Seven years old. Dravik Syndicate shipping records from the Hollow Reach run."

I don't let my face do anything. My hands, though, my hands want to shake, so I give them a rag and a glass to polish.

"Never heard of it."

"You're a terrible liar."

"That's one of my flaws. Everybody here knows about it. It's part of my charm."

"Your name's in that manifest," Ilo says. "Not *Nettle*. The other one. Listed as the pilot on fourteen runs, including the last one. The one where the cargo hold opened at Hollow Reach and—"

"Stop."

He stops.

I polish the glass. It's already clean. I keep polishing it anyway.

"Who wants it?" I finally ask.

"A lot of people. The Concord prosecutors, for one. They'd give me amnesty for it." His tendrils curl. "And Dravik's people want it back, and they want everyone named in it to stay quiet. Permanently."

"So why come to me? Why not take your amnesty and leave me out of it?"

"Because Dravik's people have been following me since Tollgate. Two ships, maybe three. I lost them in the Cassen drift, but they're not stupid. They'll check every dock on the outer rim." He finishes the whisky. "And when they get here, they'll find me. And then they'll look at the manifest, and they'll look at the bartender, and they'll recognize her."

"So you led them here."

"I didn't know you were here until Mira told me. I swear it."

"But you came anyway."

"I came because you know how Dravik works. You know how they search. You know how to hide a ship." His voice drops. "I need a pilot who's been on the inside. And you need that manifest in friendly hands instead of theirs."

"Friendly." I set the glass down hard. "You're going to hand it to the Concord. My name goes in front of a tribunal either way."

"Maybe. Or maybe a cooperating witness gets the same deal I do."

Across the room, Bel is mopping blue ale and singing badly. Dorrin snores. Haskel is in the back, cursing at the water recycler. This place took me in when I had nothing but a stolen ship and a fake name. They don't know what I was. They've never asked.

The door chime sounds.

Ilo's tendrils pull flat against his skull.

I look up. Two figures stand in the airlock, still frosted from the docking tunnel. Long coats. Neither one is in any hurry.

"Ilo," I murmur, reaching for the Plinthian moonshine like I'm just tidying up. "Your friends. Are they early, or are they new?"

His voice barely comes out. "I don't know."

# The Last Outpost

## Chapter Four: Vega, Neat

The gravity hiccups just as I'm topping off Dobbs's ale, and the foam climbs the side of the glass like it's trying to escape. I steady it with two fingers and wait. Half a second later, the station remembers which way is down.

"You'd think," Dobbs says, wiping his moustache, "with what we pay in docking fees, somebody'd fix that."

"You pay docking fees?" I slide the glass over. "Since when?"

"Since I started meaning to."

Down the bar, Pell and Oyelaran are on round three of their argument about whether a Kessic sand-hauler counts as a pet or a vehicle. The jukebox is playing something mournful with too much harmonica. The recyclers hum. It's a Tuesday, or what passes for one out here, and I'm three hours into a shift that's been comfortably, beautifully dull.

Then the stranger sits down.

She doesn't so much sit as fold, like her knees gave up halfway through the decision. Her dreads are the tentacled kind, Varrin, I'd guess, and they're twitching against her shoulders, a few curling in on themselves like they're cold. Her jacket's a pilot's cut, scorched at the cuff.

"Vega whisky, neat," she says. "Better make that a double."

"Rough flight?"

"Rough life. The flight was just the latest chapter."

I pour. The amber settles, then tilts as the gravity dips again, sloshing a lazy circle around the glass. She watches it like it's personally betrayed her.

"Does it always do that?"

"Only when it's awake." I set the bottle down. "You get used to it. Most folks start drinking from the middle of the glass."

She knocks back half the double, winces, and holds the glass against her forehead. Up close, her tendrils have gone a sickly grey-blue at the tips. On Varrin, I remember, that's the color of fear, not exhaustion.

"I'm Nets," I say. "First drink's on the house if you tell me a good story. Second one, you pay for either way."

"Corra." She lowers the glass. "And I don't think you want my story."

"Everybody says that. It's never true."

"It's true this time." Her eyes flick to the door, then to the window behind me, where the belt drifts past in slow, tumbling grey. "How many ships docked tonight?"

"Four. Dobbs's rig, a water-hauler, a Guild survey skiff, and yours, I'm guessing. The *Little Mercy*?"

She stiffens. "How'd you know my ship's name?"

"Dock board's right there." I nod at the flickering screen above the taps. "I'm a bartender, not a mind reader."

Some of the tension goes out of her, but not much. She finishes the whisky. I pour another without asking, and she doesn't stop me.

"Corra, honey," Oyelaran calls from down the bar, "settle something. Sand-hauler. Pet or vehicle?"

"Leave her be, Oye," I say.

"It's a *simple question*—"

"Vehicle," Corra says, without turning around. "You can't love something that tries to eat you."

Pell slaps the bar. "*Ha!* Pay up."

"People love things that try to eat them all the time," Oyelaran mutters, but he's sliding a chit across the counter.

Corra almost smiles. Almost. Then the gravity dips again, harder this time, and her hand shoots out to clamp the glass before it can walk off the edge.

"I need to ask you something," she says quietly. "And I need you not to make a scene."

"I don't make scenes. I clean up after them."

She leans in. Her tendrils have gone still, which is worse than the twitching.

"Before I left Hadrian's Reach, a man told me that if I got this far out, I should find the bartender at the Last Outpost. He said she'd know what to do." She swallows. "He said to ask for Nettle Marrow."

I keep wiping the glass in my hand. Round and round. It's very important that I keep wiping it.

Nobody's called me Marrow in six years.

"Don't know who that is," I say. "Just Nets here."

"He said you'd say that."

"Did he." I set the glass down. My hands aren't shaking, which I'm proud of. "This man have a name?"

"Teague."

The jukebox switches songs. Something brighter, with horns. It feels obscene.

"Teague's dead," I say.

"He wasn't three weeks ago." She reaches into her jacket, slowly, keeping her eyes on me, and pulls out a data spike, matte black, the size of my little finger, with a red thread wound around the base. My stomach drops straight through the deck plating, gravity fluctuations be damned. I know that thread. I *tied* that thread, a lifetime ago, on a ship I set on fire.

"He gave me this," Corra says. "He said it belongs to you. He said they'd figured out where you went, and he'd bought you as much time as he could." Her voice cracks. "He said to tell you he was sorry it wasn't more."

"Put that away."

"Nets—"

"*Put it away.*"

She does. Down the bar, Dobbs has gone quiet. Dobbs is never quiet. I paste on a smile and raise my voice.

"Somebody tell Pell he's cut off before he starts singing."

"I'm not *singing*," Pell protests, and the room exhales and goes back to its noise.

I lean on my elbows, close enough that only Corra can hear.

"Who's *they*?"

"You know who."

"I want you to say it."

Her tendrils curl tight against her neck. "The Halcyon Accord. They pulled me over at the Reach checkpoint and searched the *Mercy* down to the bolts. They didn't find it. I had it in my—" she gestures vaguely, embarrassed, at her dreads. "But they tagged my hull. I scraped off two trackers. I don't know if there was a third."

"You don't *know*."

"I flew dark for nine days, Nets. I haven't slept. I came here because a dying man asked me to, and I didn't even—" She stops, presses the heels of her hands into her eyes. "I'm sorry. I didn't know where else to go."

Behind me, the dock board chimes.

I don't want to turn around. I turn around anyway.

*INBOUND — 1 VESSEL — DOCKING BAY 3 — REGISTRY: WITHHELD.*

Corra sees it too. Her glass starts to tremble, and this time, the gravity is holding perfectly still.

"Nets," she whispers. "What do we do?"

I look at the door. I look at Dobbs, at Pell and Oye, at the scuffed bar I've polished every night for six years, the only place that's ever let me be nobody.

Then I reach under the counter, past the spare glasses and the first-aid kit, until my fingers find the cold, familiar weight I swore I'd never need again.

"First," I say, "you finish your drink."

response:
# The Last Outpost

## Chapter Seven: Neat

The rag has a hole in it. I keep meaning to replace it, the same way I keep meaning to fix the flicker in the sign above the door, the one that turns *THE LAST OUTPOST* into *THE LAST OUT* every forty seconds. Bracken says it's honest advertising.

Tonight the bar's half full. Two Hesk ore-haulers are arguing over a game of tiles in the corner booth. Old Dobbs is asleep on his usual stool with his helmet still clipped to his belt. Moth, the station cat, if you can call a six-legged thing with opinions a cat, is curled on the warm spot above the reactor vent.

Then the door hisses and she walks in.

Lirrin, I think. Her tentacled dreads are knotted on one side like she slept against a bulkhead, and the tips flush a nervous violet. Her flight jacket has a scorch mark on the shoulder. She sits two stools down from Dobbs without looking at anyone.

"Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double."

"Rough jump?" I pour. Vega whisky smells like burnt honey and bad decisions.

"Rough week." She drinks half of it. Her dreads curl tighter. "Rough life, probably, if I'm honest. Which I'm not, usually."

"Nobody is out here." I start wiping the counter in front of her. It's already clean. "That's sort of the appeal."

She laughs, short and surprised. "You the owner?"

"Bartender. Owner's Bracken. He's in the back pretending to do inventory, which means he's napping."

"Hey," a voice calls through the kitchen hatch. "I heard that."

"You were supposed to," I call back.

The stranger watches this like it's a play in a language she half-remembers. "Is it always like this?"

"Like what?"

"Like..." She waves a hand. Her fingers are long, ringed with old docking-clamp calluses. "Like people live here."

"People do live here. That's the problem with the place. Folks come for one drink and stay for nine years." I keep wiping. Same spot. "I'm Nets."

"Kessa." She doesn't offer a family name, and I don't ask. "Kessa Moor. Courier. Freelance."

"What're you couriering?"

Her hand moves to her jacket and stops there, flat against her chest. "That's the rough part."

I wait. Waiting is most of the job. People will tell you anything if you give them enough silence and a refill, so I give her both.

"I took a contract out of Calloway Station," she says finally. "Good money. Too good, which I should've noticed. Deliver one sealed packet to one person, somewhere past the Drift. No address, just a name and a gene-tag. Client said the tag would ping when I got close."

"And?"

"And it pinged an hour ago. On approach." She looks at me, then around the room: the Hesk, Dobbs, Moth on the vent. "Here."

My rag keeps moving. Little circles. "Huh."

"Yeah. *Huh*." She finishes the double. I pour another without asking. "Here's the thing, Nets. Two days out from Calloway, I find a tracker sewn into the packet lining. Not mine. Not standard. So I pull it, and I toss it out the airlock like any sensible person would, and six hours later there's a ship on my tail. Black hull, no transponder. Didn't hail. Just followed."

"You lose them?"

"I lost them in the Fennick cluster. Scraped my shoulder doing it." She touches the scorch mark. "But they know my heading. They know the job. They'll be here. A day, maybe less."

In the corner, one of the Hesk slams down a tile and the other one howls. Dobbs snorts in his sleep. I keep wiping.

"So why not just deliver the packet and get gone?"

"Because I don't know who it's for." Kessa leans in. Her dreads have gone from violet to a deep, anxious blue. "The tag pings in a radius. Somebody in this station. And I've done this long enough to know that when someone pays triple and sends a hull with no name after you, whatever's in here isn't a birthday card." She pulls the packet halfway out of her jacket. It's grey, palm-sized, sealed with a wax-and-wire stamp I haven't seen in eleven years.

A circle inside a circle. Three lines through it.

The rag stops. Just for a second. Then it starts again.

"You recognize that?" Kessa asks.

"Should I?"

"I don't know. You stopped."

"Hole in the rag. Caught on my finger." I hold it up to show her. It's true, there is a hole. "What's the name? On the contract."

She hesitates. "Contract says confidential."

"Contract also had a tracker in it."

That gets a tired half-smile. "Fair." She glances down the bar. Dobbs is still asleep. She lowers her voice anyway. "Ysolde Harrow. You know her?"

Somewhere behind me the sign flickers. *THE LAST OUT.*

"No," I say. "Never heard of her."

"Nets." Bracken's head appears in the kitchen hatch, beard full of flour, eyes on me and not on Kessa. He's been listening, of course. He always is. "We out of the green citrus?"

We're not out of the green citrus. We've never once stocked the green citrus.

"I'll check in a minute," I tell him.

He holds my eyes a beat too long, then disappears.

Kessa turns her glass in slow circles on the counter, watching the whisky climb the sides. "Look, I'm not trying to stir anything up. I'm a courier, not a bounty hunter. I just want to know whether I'm handing this to someone who wants it, or someone who's about to have a very bad day. Because whoever's on that black ship..." She swallows. "I don't think they're coming to make sure it got delivered."

"What do you think they're coming for?"

"Honestly?" She looks at the packet, then at me. "I think I'm the bloodhound. I think they let me lose them. I think they just needed me to find the door."

The Hesk have gone quiet. Moth lifts her head off the vent and stares at me with all four eyes.

I've wiped this spot so long I can see my reflection in it now. Short hair. Old scar along the jaw that I tell people came from a mining accident. Eleven years of being Nettle, of pouring drinks and settling arguments and learning everyone's name, of being someone who belongs somewhere.

"Get some sleep, Kessa," I say. "Bracken's got a bunk in the back. On the house."

"And the packet?"

"Hang onto it. We'll sort it out in the morning."

She studies me for a long moment, and I can see her deciding not to ask the question sitting right there behind her teeth.

"Okay," she says quietly. "Morning."

She takes her whisky and goes. The door to the back hisses shut behind her.

I look down. The rag has worn straight through.

prompt: Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. Include references to the gladiator's favorite Roman deity or mythological figure. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
response:
# The Free Supper

They called it the *cena libera*, the free supper, and like most things in Rome the name was a joke that nobody laughed at anymore.

They laid our tables in the courtyard of the Ludus Magnus as the sky over the Esquiline went the color of a week-old bruise. Torches hissed in their iron brackets. Beyond the eastern wall the great amphitheater rose like a cliff of honey-colored stone, and even at that hour I could hear the carpenters inside, hammering the scaffolds for the morning's hunts, and under the hammering the low, grieving roar of the lions in the vivarium. They had not been fed in three days. Neither, it felt, had I. For once the lanista had given us pork instead of barley mash. The fat dripped onto the coals and filled the yard with a smoke so rich it made my eyes water.

It was the forty-first day of the Emperor's games for the conquest of Dacia. Men in the taverns swore the games would run past a hundred days. Trajan had brought home so much gold from beyond the Danube that the whole city seemed drunk on it. There was a new forum being carved out of the Quirinal hill. There was free grain in the Subura and free wine at the crossroads shrines. There were Dacian prisoners, too, sold so cheap in the Saepta that a cobbler could buy one.

That was the trouble. A city with ten thousand captives to kill did not need to pay men like me very much.

The public had been let in to watch us eat, as they always were. They pressed against the rope at the courtyard's edge: bakers still dusted with flour, a pair of senators' sons in tunics so white they glowed, freedwomen fanning themselves with palm fronds, a gambler with ink-stained fingers who stared at my hands the whole meal to see if they shook. A girl with a wig of gilded German hair called out a name. It wasn't mine, but I smiled anyway. That was part of the work. We were meat they could look at before it was cooked.

I tore the bread and dipped it in the garum, and the fish-stink of it took me home at once. I was born a citizen in the Subura, above a fuller's shop. I can still smell the urine vats when I dream. My father died owing four thousand sesterces to a moneylender named Fabius Crispus, and Fabius made it very clear what would happen to my mother and my sister if the debt went unpaid. So I went to the lanista and swore the oath the free men swear when they sell themselves to the sand: *to be burned, to be bound, to be beaten, to be killed by the sword.* I said it in a clear voice. My father would have been ashamed of me. He would also have been alive to be ashamed, if he had borrowed less.

Across the table sat the boy the lanista had named Decebalus, after the dead Dacian king. It was a joke. Most things were. He could not have been more than sixteen. His hair was the color of wet straw and his wrists still bore the raw pink rings of the slave-chains from the triumph. He had not touched his food. He stared at the pork the way a man stares at a snake.

"Eat," I told him. He didn't understand the word, so I pushed the bread toward him and mimed it, like a fool in a mime show. Someone behind the rope laughed.

He looked at me then. In his eyes I saw the river towns burning, and the long march south in the dust behind the Emperor's horses, and the crowds on the Via Sacra throwing rotten figs. Tomorrow he would go out among the *gregarii*, the herd, a dozen captives with wooden shields against trained men. I knew how that went. Everyone in the city knew how that went. They would cheer.

I wanted to tell him I had not chosen this either. But that wasn't true, and he would have known it in any language.

"Marcus!"

My true name, the one I'd left at the gate. I turned. My sister Tertia stood at the rope, her shawl pulled over her hair, her face thinner than at the Saturnalia. A guard moved to block her. I raised my hand, and Pollio, who owed me for a mended shoulder, let her lean close enough to speak.

"Fabius came to the shop," she said quickly. "He says the purse from your last fight only covered the interest. He's sold the note to a freedman of Senator Licinius. They're betting on you tomorrow, Marcus. Heavily. He said to tell you that." She swallowed. "He said to tell you to win well."

So that was how it would be. My debt had become someone's wager, and my life a line in some freedman's ledger. I nodded as though she'd told me the price of oil had gone up.

She pressed something into Pollio's palm and he passed it to me without looking: a small bronze disk, crudely stamped with a wheel and a griffin. Nemesis. Tertia had always known which goddess was mine.

"Mother lit a lamp for you," she said. Then the crowd shifted and swallowed her, and she was gone into the torchlight.

When the supper ended and the rope came down, I went to the little shrine at the mouth of the tunnel. Every man in the ludus touched it before he walked out onto the sand. The goddess was carved in worn marble, her measuring rod in one hand and her wheel at her feet. The fingers of a thousand doomed men had polished her toes smooth. I set my honey cake on the ledge. I did not pray to live. The men who pray to live are the ones Nemesis notices.

Instead I asked her for what she has always promised: that the wheel turns. That no fortune stays high forever. Not Fabius in his counting house, nor Licinius and his freedmen, nor the Emperor in his gold-bought forum. Somewhere above us all, she holds the rod, and she is measuring.

Then I went back across the yard, and I took the boy's untouched bread, and I sat beside him in the dark until he ate it.
