response:
# The Free Supper

They set our tables in the courtyard of the Ludus Magnus the night before the games, and the city came to watch us eat.

This was the custom: the cena libera, the free supper. It was free for us, at least, the one meal of the year the lanista did not dock from our keep. For the people it cost a copper at the gate, and Vettius stood there with a strongbox under his arm, taking coins from fullers and senators' sons alike and smiling at both with the same yellow teeth.

Torches burned in iron collars along the colonnade. Their pitch smoke hung beneath the awning so that everything tasted of it: the roast kid glazed in honey, the split and blackened sausages, the eggs, the olives, the garum so sharp it watered my eyes. The wine was better than any I had drunk since I signed myself away. Beyond the wall the great amphitheatre rose against the dark, its arches lit from within where slaves were raking the sand. I could hear the animals in the pens beneath it. Something roared. Something screamed like a woman. Under it all came the patient lowing of the oxen that would drag the carts out through the Gate of Libitina.

Trajan had come home from Dacia with so much gold that men said the Danube ran yellow. Now he meant to spend it on us. One hundred and twenty-three days of games. Ten thousand gladiators. Eleven thousand beasts. The numbers were painted on the walls of every bathhouse from the Subura to the Aventine, and people read them aloud to one another like verses.

I sat at the end of the third table with my back to the wall. I was a retiarius, and a retiarius sits where he is put. Even among men sold to die for the pleasure of others there are ranks, and the net-man stands at the bottom of them. We fight nearly naked. We carry no shield and wear no helmet, so ours is the only face the crowd ever sees. The murmillones at the head table liked to laugh about that. *A pretty face for the women,* they said. *A face to watch go grey.*

I minded it less than they hoped. When I was a boy in Ostia I mended nets on the quay beside my father, and he used to say that a fisherman who hides his face from the sea is a fool, because the sea already knows him.

My trident leaned against the wall behind my bench. We were permitted to show our arms at the supper, the points capped in leather, so the crowd could see what they were wagering on. Most men's weapons belonged to the ludus. The shaft of mine did, nine palms of ash, but the head was my father's. Three tines of Noric iron, bought from a smith in Portus the year I was born, they had taken eels from the mudflats at dawn for twenty years, where the river runs into the salt. The middle tine bore a nick where he had struck a stone on the morning my mother went into labor. He had cursed so loudly, she said, that the gulls rose off the water. I knew that nick the way I knew my own teeth.

When he died, the creditors took the boat, then the nets, then the room above the chandler's. They did not want the spear. I carried it to Rome with my mother and two sisters, and when the clerk at the Porticus Minucia told me the grain rolls were closed, that the Emperor's bread was for men already enrolled and there were a hundred thousand ahead of me, I carried it to Vettius instead. I swore the oath: to be burned, to be bound, to be beaten, to be killed by steel. Two thousand sesterces went to my mother. In exchange I became infamis, a man with no standing before the law, no face in the forum. The only place left where anyone would look at my face was the sand.

I had asked one thing of Vettius, which was to keep the iron. He laughed, said that was cheap, and handed me a net.

The crowd pressed against the rope that kept them from our tables. A wool merchant shouted for me to show my hands so he could judge my grip. A woman with kohl-dark eyes asked Vettius's boy what my sweat scrapings would cost, for her complexion. Men called odds back and forth: three to one against the net, four to one if I drew Pugnax. Someone threw an olive pit at the Gaul beside me, and the Gaul ate on without looking up. We had all learned this. You do not perform for free.

Across from me sat a Dacian. He could not have been more than sixteen, his hair cropped to the scalp, his wrist chained to the bench. He had not touched his bowl. He would go out at noon tomorrow, in the hour when the better sort went home to lunch and the sand was given over to the condemned. No net, no trident, nothing to hold. Somewhere across the city his brothers were hauling marble for the Emperor's new forum, where they said a column would rise with the whole war carved around it in a spiral, so no one would ever forget how Dacia was won.

I tore my bread, dragged it through the honey on my plate, and pushed it across to him.

He looked at it, then at me. He said something in his own tongue.

"Eat," I said.

He ate. Behind the rope a man laughed and shouted, "The fish feeds the barbarian!" Two more men put down coins, though I never learned what they were wagering on.

When the bread was gone the boy pointed past my shoulder at the trident. I lifted it down and laid it across the table between the wine cups. He reached out slowly, as if it might bite, and touched the middle tine, running his thumb over the nick in the iron. Then he said a word I did not know, and made a motion with his hand, an arc and a sharp downward stroke, the way a man spears a fish in shallow water.

So they had rivers in Dacia, then. And fathers.

I looked out at the faces pressed against the rope, ruddy and greasy in the torchlight, and found myself searching them for my mother's, though I had made her swear not to come. She kept her word. She always did.

Outside, the oxen lowed. Vettius counted his coins. In the morning the sand would be raked smooth, and the city would come to see my face.

**The Free Supper**

They fed us like senators the night before the games. That was the joke among the old hands at the Ludus Magnus: you only ate well when someone was planning to kill you.

The cena libera was laid out in the courtyard under strings of tallow lamps that spat and smoked and made the air taste of mutton fat. There was pork roasted with honey, and bread white as a matron's arm, not the barley mash they shoveled into us most days. There were bowls of garum so pungent it cut through the stink of the latrines along the eastern wall. There was wine, unwatered. Every man at those tables knew what unwatered wine meant.

Beyond the iron gate, the people of Rome pressed in to watch us eat.

That was the custom. Citizens came to look at the meat before the butchering. They hung on the bars, shopkeepers and laundry women and boys with snot crusted under their noses, and they called out names. Mine was Felix. The lanista gave it to me eight years ago when I came off a slave ship at Ostia with my ankles bleeding into the irons. *Lucky*, he called me, because I had survived the crossing when eleven others had not. I was seventeen. I have never told anyone in Rome the name my mother gave me, and I never will. A name is a thing they cannot take if you do not hand it over.

"Felix! Felix the Gaul!" A fat man in a stained tunic waved a leather cup at me. "I've got forty sesterces on you, you hear? Don't make me sell my wife!"

I lifted my bread to him. The crowd laughed. That was the work too: you gave them a little of yourself at the gate so they would love you in the sand. Love was worth something. Love was the thumb turned one way instead of the other.

Down the table, the veterans ate without speaking. Across from me, Crescens was dictating his will to a scribe the ludus provided for a fee. His voice was steady. *To my woman Prima, my savings, two hundred and six sesterces. To my brother in Capua, my good boots.* The scribe's stylus scratched in the wax. Crescens had fought nineteen times. He did not like his match tomorrow.

The Dacians sat at the far end.

There were thirty of them, brought in chains last month from the north, from the war the Emperor had won beyond the Danube. All Rome had gone mad for it. Trajan had come home with the gold of King Decebalus heaped in wagons, so much gold, people said, that he would build a new forum with it, and a column taller than any temple, carved with every battle from bottom to top. To honor the victory he had declared games that would run for a hundred and twenty-three days. Ten thousand men would fight. Eleven thousand beasts would die. The grain ships kept coming from Egypt, the bread dole kept flowing, and the plebs had their circus. Nobody in the Subura was talking about the price of oil or the senators who had been quietly exiled for grumbling. They were talking about the games.

The Dacians did not touch the wine. One of them, a boy with yellow hair cut ragged and a burn scar on his neck, kept staring at the gate, at the faces staring back. He could not have been more than sixteen. His name was Bitus. He had told me so in the yard three days ago, pointing at his own chest, and I had told him *Felix*, and he had nodded as though it were a real name.

They had not been trained. They had been given a few weeks with wooden swords, enough to make them hold a blade so the crowd wouldn't feel cheated. Tomorrow they would be marched out in the morning, before the main bouts, while the stands were still filling and the vendors were selling roasted chickpeas and sausages. Most of the city would barely notice them die.

I knew what it was to be the thing a war brings home. I had been a war's leftovers too. Some legate had wanted a triumph, and my village had been in the way.

"Gladiator."

A woman was at the gate, close to my end of the table. She wore a dark palla pulled over her head, and her face was thin and lined. She was not calling my name or laughing. She was holding out a small clay vial.

"Please," she said. "My son. He has the falling sickness. He shakes and foams and bites his tongue. The physician says the blood of a gladiator, drunk warm..." Her voice broke. "I can pay. Not much."

I had heard of this. The sick sometimes waited at the edge of the arena to catch the blood of fallen men. I had seen them in the tunnels, bribing slaves with buckets.

She wanted mine before I fell, I suppose, in case I did not fall. Or in case I did.

I looked at the vial in her hand. Then I took the small knife I used for my bread and drew it across the heel of my palm. It stung less than I expected. I let the blood run into her vial until it was a quarter full, while the men at the gate went quiet and then started whispering, and I pressed it back into her fingers.

"No coin," I said.

She stared at me as if I had grown a second head. Then she was gone, swallowed by the crowd and the smoke.

Later, when the lamps had burned low and the guards herded the gawkers away, I did what I do the night before every fight. I went to the little shrine of Nemesis in the corner of the yard, where the plaster goddess has lost half her nose to some old idiot's spear. I pressed my thumb to the chip on her face. Then I spat three times into the fold of my tunic, over my heart, the way my mother did whenever a raven crossed our path. *Turn it away. Turn it away. Turn it away.* Lastly I wound a strand of red wool three times around my left wrist, where the manica would cover it. The wool had come from her loom. It was frayed nearly to nothing.

Eight years. Twenty-two fights. It had not failed me yet.

When I turned back, Bitus was standing in the dark behind me, watching. He had seen it all.

I should have walked past him. A man who wants to live in this place does not make friends with the morning dead.

Instead I held out my hand and pulled one thread loose from the red wool.

response:
# The Lighthouse Keeper

---

*Muckle Flugga Lighthouse, Unst*
*3rd March 1962*

Dear Mam,

Arrived safe. The boat couldnae get in Tuesday for the swell so we sat two days at Burrafirth eating the relief man's biscuits. Mr Robertson is the Principal. He is from Stromness and says about nine words a day, four of them about the weather.

The rock is smaller than the photograph. Past us there's another called Out Stack, and that's the end of Britain. Nothing after it but Norway if you squint and the Pole if you don't.

Tell Aunt Bella I am not living on tins.

Your son,
David

---

*14 Elder Street, Govan*
*19th March 1962*

My dear Davie,

Read your letter to Bella on the stair and she says she does not believe a word about the tins. Neither do I. There is a fruit loaf in with this, wrapped twice. If it arrives as crumbs eat it with a spoon.

Mrs Galbraith's boy has been taken on at Fairfield's, so the yards are not finished whatever anybody says. I am not saying anything. I am only telling you.

I have moved the wireless into the kitchen so it is nearer.

Are you warm. Answer that one properly.

Mam

---

*Muckle Flugga*
*2nd May 1962*

Dear Mam,

The loaf survived. Robertson had two slices and said "Aye," which from him is a sonnet.

The gannets are back on Hermaness, across the sound. The whole cliff goes white like somebody's limewashed it, and the racket comes over the water day and night. Robertson says you stop hearing it.

You can leave Fairfield's, Mam. You know fine it's not about Fairfield's.

D.

---

*14 Elder Street*
*20th June 1962*

Davie,

All right, son.

I took the long way to the Co-op on Saturday and went past the Linthouse gate. I did not look in. Mr Stephen's sent a card at the anniversary, which was decent of them, I suppose.

Bella's Jim has a television now and she has me round Fridays. I don't care for it much. Everyone on it talks too fast.

I leave the wireless on at night now. You'll say that's daft.

Write me something long.

Mam

---

*Muckle Flugga*
*9th September 1962*

Mam,

Sorry. Nothing to write. Every day is the same, and I mean that exactly. I polish the brass. I wind the machine. The light goes round. Robertson does the crossword with a pencil he sharpens with a knife, very slow, like he's carving it.

I have started counting things. Steps to the lantern: 87. Gannets on one ledge, best guess: 340.

D.

---

*14 Elder Street*
*2nd October 1962*

David Lennie, that is three letters of mine you have not answered and one postcard. A postcard with a puffin on it that cost me fourpence.

What are you counting for.

---

*Muckle Flugga*
*18th December 1962*

Dear Mam,

The boat's not landed in nineteen days. No post, no relief. Robertson's rationing the tea and I've never seen a man so grim.

I'll answer you properly now, since you asked twice.

Last night I stood out on the gallery a long while. The beam comes round and Out Stack's there, black and wet, and then it's gone, and then it's there. I kept thinking how fast it was with Da. Somebody shouted, and then it was done, and I was standing on the berth with his piece box in my hand because he'd given it me to hold.

I came up here because I couldnae stand on the Clyde. I thought if there was enough water between me and it. But there's no amount of water.

What I'm finding, Mam, is that out here there's nobody to be fine for. In Govan I had to be fine for you, and for Bella, and for the boys at the gate. Here there's just Robertson and he doesnae ask. So I've stopped being fine, and I don't know what comes after.

I'm not warm. That's the true answer.

Davie

---

**TELEGRAM — LERWICK — 7 JAN 1963**

LETTER CAME TODAY. WRITING TONIGHT. YOU ARE NOT TO DO ANYTHING DAFT. MAM

---

*14 Elder Street*
*7th January 1963*

My son,

Your Mr Robertson wrote to me in November. Four lines. I expect it is the longest letter the man has ever written. He said you were going quiet in a way he had seen before on the rocks, and that he thought your mother ought to know. So you see you were wrong. There is somebody up there you have been not-fine for, and he noticed.

Now I will tell you something, since we are telling things.

There are days in this house I do not say one word out loud. Not one, Davie, from waking to bed. I leave the wireless on so there is a voice in the room. I go to Bella's for the television and I can't follow it, because I am sitting there thinking that the last person who knew how I take my tea is in Craigton Cemetery and the other one is on a rock at the top of the map.

I let you go because I thought that's what a mother does. I was wrong about that too.

I have been to see the factor. I have been to the Board in George Street, in my good coat, and a Mr Baird gave me a cup of tea and said keepers' mothers have kept house at the shore stations before. The keys go back on the 28th of February.

Don't you dare write and tell me not to.

Mam

---

*Shore Station, Burrafirth, Unst*
*14th March 1963*

Davie,

I am at the kitchen table and I can see it from here.

Mrs Inkster next door, whose man is on the rock with you, walked me up to Hermaness this afternoon. I've never been so blown about in my life. The birds are not back yet, she says, but they'll come. She showed me Out Stack. There's a story here that Lady Franklin had herself rowed out to it, when her husband was lost in the Arctic, so she could stand on the last bit of the country and send her prayers on north from there. Mrs Inkster says it's maybe not true. I said it doesn't need to be.

The relief is due the 22nd, weather allowing. There will be a fire on and soup, and you won't have to say a word if you don't want to. Robertson has taught me what that's worth.

It's going round now. Twice, then the dark, then twice again.

I'm counting too.

Mam

response:
# The Lighthouse Keeper

---

*Skerryvore Lighthouse*
*14th October 1957*

Dear Mam,

Landed Tuesday. The boat couldn't come alongside, so they swung us up on a rope with the stores, me and a crate of tatties, and I'd say the tatties took it better.

Mr Gillies is Principal. He's a Lewis man, Free Church, and he whistles the psalms through his teeth while he polishes the brass. Lachie's from Mull and talks about nothing but his whippet. They're decent enough.

The stairs make your calves burn. My bunk's curved to fit the wall, so you sleep like a banana. There's nothing out the window but water in every direction. You'd think you'd get used to the sea. I havenae yet.

Are you keeping the fire on? Don't save the coal for my sake.

Your son,
Davie

---

*17 Elder Street, Govan*
*22nd October*

Dear David,

A banana. I read that out to Mrs Kerr and she near choked on her biscuit.

Nothing new here. The Fairfield horn still goes at half seven and I still get up for it, which is daft, because there's nobody to make a piece for. Mrs Kerr's Billy has got himself engaged to a girl from Partick, and you can imagine how that's gone down. I've taken in alterations for the Co-op, hems mostly. It passes the evenings.

Wear the vest I packed. I know you'll have stuck it in a drawer.

Your loving Mam

---

*Skerryvore*
*19th December*

Dear Mam,

The relief's three weeks late with the weather, so this'll reach you after Christmas. Sorry.

We're on the tinned mutton now. Lachie's stopped talking about the whippet, which tells you something. Gillies still whistles.

You get to know things out here. The tower hums in a westerly. I know which step creaks. I can tell who's on the stair from his breathing.

I'm wearing the vest.

Davie

---

*Elder Street*
*6th January 1958*

Dear David,

I was clearing your faither's good jacket for the jumble and found this in the inside pocket.

You'll mind it, his check from the yard. It's brass, the size of a half crown, with 4471 stamped in the middle and FAIRFIELD round the top. Every morning for thirty-one year he took it off the board at the gate, and every night he hung it back, so they'd know he came out the same as he went in. The yard let me keep it after. One side's worn near smooth where he rubbed it with his thumb waiting on the tram. He never told me he did that. I only knew from the shine.

I don't know what use it is on a rock. Keep it in your pocket. When it's bad, it helps to hold on to something that belonged to somebody.

Mam

---

*Skerryvore*
*3rd March*

Mam,

Got the check. Thanks.

Nothing much to report. Weather. Lamp. Weather.

D.

---

*Elder Street*
*11th March*

David Rennie,

That's twelve words. I counted. You wrote me longer letters from the Boys' Brigade camp at Largs, and you were only away four days.

I'm not daft, son. Since you'll not tell me anything, I'll tell you something. Since your faither went, I've set out two cups every morning. Every single morning. I pour the second one and let it go cold, and I tip it down the sink at dinner time. I've never said that to a living soul. There. Now it's your turn.

Mam

---

*Skerryvore*
*2nd April*

Dear Mam,

All right.

Two weeks back I was on the gallery at four in the morning. It was a clear night, flat calm. I was looking down at the water and how still it was, and I stood there longer than I should have. Nothing happened. I'm telling you nothing happened. But I stood there, and I knew what I was thinking. Gillies came up for his watch and found me. He didnae say a word. He put his hand on my shoulder, whistled the hundred and twenty-first psalm, all the verses, and walked me down.

I had Dad's check in my fist the whole time. It left a mark.

I've written out my resignation. It's in the drawer with the vest I wasnae really wearing.

Davie

---

**TELEGRAM — 5 APRIL 1958**
**D RENNIE SKERRYVORE LT HO VIA HYNISH TIREE**
**LEAVE THAT LETTER IN THE DRAWER STOP COMING TO TIREE STOP TELL GILLIES GOD BLESS HIM STOP MAM**

---

*c/o Mrs MacArthur, Hynish, Tiree*
*14th June*

Dear David,

Well, I'm here. It took two trains and a boat, and I was sick over the side of the *Claymore* in front of a minister.

Mrs MacArthur's let me her back room. There's more sky here than I knew there was. From the end of the pier you can see your tower, a wee white stalk twelve mile out. I'd not have believed a person could live in a thing that thin.

I brought your faither's bicycle lamp. Gillies wrote to say you're on the middle watch Saturday. I'll be at the pier at one o'clock. I'll not know if you can see it, but I'll do it anyway.

Mam

---

*Skerryvore*
*22nd June*

Dear Mam,

I saw it.

Three flashes, wee and yellow, right where Hynish should be. Gillies brought up the hand lamp and I sent three back, and he looked away out to sea so I could greet in peace.

I've torn up the letter in the drawer. Gillies says there's a vacancy at the Hynish shore station in the autumn, and I've put in for it. Mrs MacArthur told Lachie, who told me, that the cottage next to hers is coming empty. I'm only saying.

I've still got the check in my pocket, but I'm not holding it so tight now.

Bring two cups.

Davie

**The Lighthouse Keeper**

---

*Sgeir Mhòr Lighthouse, 4th November 1961*

Dear Mam,

Landed Tuesday. "Landed" is a big word for being swung onto a wet ledge in a canvas chair while the boatman shouted at me to keep my knees in. The rock is about the size of Pilrig Park, if you took away the grass and the trees and the swings. Nothing grows. Everything smells of paraffin, including the bread.

Mr Gunn is the Principal. He's from Wick and says grace over tinned peaches. Tosh is the other assistant. He keeps racing pigeons in Kirkwall and talks about them like they're weans.

It's six weeks on and a month home, if the sea allows. Tell Tam I've not forgotten he owes me four pound.

Your son,
David

---

*14 Couper Street, Leith, 17th November*

Dear Davie,

Your letter came Friday. I read it to Mrs Rennie on the stair. She says a man who notices smells will be fine, and it's the ones who notice nothing you worry about. I don't know what that means either.

Tam owes everybody four pound. Get in the queue.

I've put in socks and tablet, though God knows what state it'll be in when it reaches you. Don't let them give you all the dirty jobs because you're youngest. Your father let them do that at the docks for eleven years.

From the back window I can see Inchkeith. I know it's not yours. I look anyway.

Mam

---

*Sgeir Mhòr, 22nd January 1962*

Dear Mam,

We've had fog for nine days. When the fog comes the horn goes, two blasts every ninety seconds, and it doesn't stop till you can see the North Rock from the gallery again, which we haven't. The engines that drive it need watching through the night, so you sleep in pieces, and in the pieces you're still counting. Last night I counted it in a dream. When I woke it was still going, and for a minute I couldn't tell which one was real.

My knuckles have split from the salt and the Brasso. Gunn gave me lanolin. It's the most he's said all week.

I've run out of things to say to Tosh. I've heard about every pigeon. Yesterday I went out on the gallery and said my own name, just to hear somebody say it. Don't tell Mrs Rennie.

The tablet survived. It was the best thing that's happened since November.

David

---

*Couper Street, 3rd February*

Davie,

I told Mrs Rennie. She said it was the most sensible thing she'd heard all winter.

When I was sixteen I went to the herring at Lerwick. There were twelve of us in a hut, gutting from five in the morning, and every one of us was lonely as sin in that crowd. I sang in my head the whole time, the same three songs, till I hated them. You don't get used to a thing like that, son. You get round it. Find your three songs.

And let Tosh talk about his pigeons. A man doesn't go on that long about something unless it's all he's got.

I've been to the doctor with my chest. It's the winter. It's nothing. Don't you start.

Mam

---

TO KEEPER LAING SGEIR MHOR VIA STROMNESS 9 MARCH 1962
YOUR MOTHER ADMITTED EASTERN GENERAL PNEUMONIA STOP COMFORTABLE STOP SHE SAYS DONT FUSS STOP RENNIE

TO MRS RENNIE 14 COUPER ST LEITH 10 MARCH 1962
RELIEF DELAYED SWELL STOP CANNOT LAND STOP TELL HER STOP DAVID

---

*Sgeir Mhòr, 21st March*

Mam,

I don't know when this will go. The boat has come out twice and turned back twice. You can see it from the gallery, sitting off in the swell, and then you watch it go home. Tosh says the sea doesn't care who's sick. I told him I knew that. I didn't hit him.

I'm writing because there's nothing else I can do. I trim the wicks and wind the clockwork and polish brass that's already clean. Every night I light the lamp and stand there while it turns, and I think: this thing is meant to bring folk home, and it can't do a thing for me.

I need to tell you something. When Dad died, I didn't join the Board for the money. I joined because I couldn't stand the house with his coat still on the peg. I left you alone with that coat. I've known it the whole time, and I let you write to me about tablet as if I didn't.

I've got my three songs. One of them is you on the stair, telling Mrs Rennie my business.

Please be there when the boat comes.

David

---

*Couper Street, 9th April*

Davie,

Your letter came the day they let me out, which your father would have called a sign and I call the Post Office.

I'm thin and cross and home. Mrs Rennie is doing my messages and telling me how to set my own fire.

Now listen. I gave that coat to the Salvation Army in 1960. You'd have known if you'd ever looked at the peg. You didn't leave me with anything. You went to work, same as he did. I'm not having you carry that out there on top of the paraffin.

On the ward they put the lights out at nine, and from my bed I could see Inchkeith going all night. I know fine it's not yours. But it kept me company, and I thought: that's what he does. Somewhere some poor soul is lying awake watching his.

Come home at the relief, not before. And send me Tosh's address. I want to ask him about the pigeons.

Mam

---

*Sgeir Mhòr, 3rd November 1962*

Dear Mam,

A year today.

Tosh got your letter. He read it four times and hasn't stopped talking since, so thank you very much. His blue chequer cock came second from Thurso. You'll be hearing about it.

We had fog again last week, four days of it. Somewhere in the second night I slept straight through the horn. When I woke it was still going, and I wasn't counting. I just lay there and listened to it doing its job.

Tell Mrs Rennie I said my own name on the gallery yesterday. Not because I needed to. I wanted to see if anybody would answer, and Tosh shouted up from the engine room, "What?"

I'm home on the 18th. Leave the back curtain open, so I can see what you've been looking at all this time.

David

response:
**Ar Agor**

The bell over the door of Pryce's Books didn't ring so much as shriek.

"Sorry. Sorry. Is there a back way out? Please tell me there's a back way out."

Bethan didn't look up from the invoice. "There's a back. It's for staff."

"I could be staff. I'm very good at pretending to be things. It's literally my job."

She looked up then, and wished she hadn't. Her eyes landed on a very famous face. It was rain-damp and slightly out of breath, and it was already smiling at her as if they were old friends.

Outside, something flashed against the wet window. Then it flashed again.

"Philosophy," she said. "Back left. Nobody goes in Philosophy."

He folded himself down between Kierkegaard and a water-stained Bertrand Russell, then leaned out with his hand extended across the carpet. "Theo Lennox. You probably—"

"I know who you are."

"Ah. Brilliant." The smile widened. "Fan, then?"

"You're on the side of the 280 bus."

"Which side?"

"The side that goes past the chippy."

"Is that a good side?"

"Somebody's drawn a moustache on you."

He laughed a beat too late, and something flickered across his face before he tucked it away. "Suits me, I bet."

"It's quite a good moustache," Bethan admitted, and went back to the invoice. She had read the same line three times. *Gwasg Gomer, 12 copies, 12 copies, 12 copies.*

"This place is gorgeous." He craned around a shelf. "Proper bookshop. That smell. What is that, dust and old Methodists?"

"Damp."

"Romantic damp, though."

"Expensive damp. The man's coming Thursday."

"And you're..." He read the sign above the till upside-down from the floor. "*Pryce.* Bethan Pryce?"

"Bethan. Yes."

"Bethan." He said it as though he were tasting it. "That's lovely, that is."

"It's very common. There were four of us in my year."

"Not the way you say it."

"I say it the way everybody says it."

Her ears had gone hot, which was ridiculous. She was thirty-four and owned a VAT number. She turned to the shelf behind her and straightened a row of Ordnance Survey maps that were already straight.

"So which one did you see?" he asked.

"Which what?"

"Which of my films. Everyone's got one. Usually it's the pirate one."

"I haven't seen any of them."

There was a long silence from Philosophy.

"None?"

"No."

"Not even the pirate one? Everyone's seen the pirate one. My nan saw the pirate one, and she's *dead*."

"Did she like it?"

"She said my hat was too big." He ran a hand through his hair. "But she *saw* it, Bethan."

The flashes outside had thinned. A man in a puffer jacket pressed his nose to the glass, squinted at the display of Welsh cookery books, and wandered off toward the Co-op.

"You're working very hard," Bethan said, not unkindly. "It's like watching someone push a car uphill."

"I'm not working. This is just my face."

"Your face is doing a lot."

"Most people *like* what my face does."

"I'm sure they do."

He opened his mouth, and for once nothing came out. He shut it and looked down at the spine of *Fear and Trembling* by his knee, then gave a small, honest snort.

"Can I tell you something stupid?"

"It's a bookshop. People tell me stupid things all day."

"I was Puck. Year Nine, *Midsummer Night's Dream*, Cardiff comprehensive, very bad tights." He picked at the carpet. "Big laugh on my first line. I mean massive, the whole hall. So I looked for my mum, because that's what you do. And she was looking at her watch. She wasn't being cruel. She had a shift at half nine and she was just... somewhere else." He shrugged with one shoulder. "So I thought, right, I'll be better, and she'll look up. I did the whole second act at her. I was *incredible*. She left at the interval."

Bethan had stopped pretending to straighten the maps.

"And now it's every room," he said. "Premieres, chat shows, the bloke who does my coffee. I find the one face that isn't with me, and I can't stop till it is. It's mad. A thousand people clapping, and I'm doing my best work for a fella in row K checking the football." He glanced up. "Today that's you, by the way. You're row K."

The shop was very quiet. Rain ticked on the window.

"I'm not *not* with you," Bethan said finally. "I'm doing the invoices."

"Same thing."

"It isn't." She put the pen down. "Not looking at someone isn't the same as not paying attention."

He looked at her properly then, and he wasn't doing anything with his face at all. That was much worse. She picked the pen back up purely so her hands had something to hold.

"Huh," said Theo Lennox.

"They've gone, I think. Your photographers."

"Right." He didn't move. "Right. Yes."

He unfolded himself from Philosophy and stood by the counter with his hands in his pockets, looking abruptly younger and less sure of what to do with his elbows.

"I should buy something. Make it look legitimate. What would you give me?"

She thought about it longer than she meant to, then reached under the counter and slid across a slim grey volume. "R.S. Thomas. He was a vicar who didn't like people much. You'll hate him."

"Will I?"

"For about a week. Then you won't be able to stop."

He held her gaze a moment too long. "Sounds familiar."

"Nine pounds ninety-nine."

He paid in cash and left the change in the RNLI tin. At the door he paused, with one hand on the handle and the bell trembling above him.

"Can I come back?"

"We're open Tuesday to Saturday."

"That's not a yes."

"It's the opening hours."

He grinned. It wasn't the bus-shelter grin. It was smaller and lopsided, and it seemed to catch him by surprise. Then he was gone into the rain with his collar up.

Bethan stood very still behind the till. Then she looked down and found she'd written *Theo* in the margin of the Gwasg Gomer invoice, in pen, twice.

"*Duw*," she said to the empty shop.

She scribbled it out. Then she took out her phone and typed, with great dignity, *pirate film hat too big*.

# Chapter Seven: Half Five

The bell above the door didn't ring so much as convulse.

"Don't scream," said the man who'd come through it, flattening himself against Poetry. "I'm not dangerous. I'm *famous*. Slightly different thing."

Non Pritchard didn't look up from her invoice. "We close at half five."

"It's twenty past three."

"Then you've got ages, haven't you."

Outside, half a dozen men with long lenses thundered down Castle Arcade, shouting a name that bounced off the Victorian glass roof. The man dropped into a crouch behind the Welsh History table and stayed there until the footsteps faded toward St Mary Street.

Then he stood, shook rain from a coat that probably cost more than her rent, and smiled. It was a slow smile, the kind that had clearly been working for him since primary school.

"Dominic Thorne," he said, offering a hand.

"Lovely." She did not take it. "Mind the drips on the Dylan Thomas, he's a first edition."

"He's in a *bin*."

"Bargain bin's a state of mind, not a judgement."

He let the hand fall and slid it into his pocket like that had been the plan all along. "You don't recognise me."

"I do, actually." She turned the invoice over. "You were in that advert. Broadband. You fell off a paddleboard."

"I was nominated for a BAFTA."

"For the paddleboard?"

"For *Ashgrove*. Three series. I played a disgraced Edwardian surgeon with a morphine habit and a tragic jawline." He tilted his head into the light, presumably so she could judge the jawline for herself. "People wept."

"Can't have been the jawline. Looks fine to me."

She heard it as it came out of her mouth. *Fine.* As if she'd been assessing it. She wrote £4.99 on a sticker and pressed it onto a book that already had a price on it.

He wandered. People like him didn't walk, she decided; they *processed*, as if a camera crew was tracking backwards in front of them. He ran a finger along the spines in Fiction.

"This place is extraordinary. Honestly. It smells like a library had an affair with a church." He looked back at her. "Did you name it? Ffenest. That's 'window', isn't it?"

"It is."

"Because books are windows into other lives."

"Because the sign was cheap and the word's short."

"You're lying."

"I'm thrifty. Different thing."

He laughed, properly, a bark that didn't sound rehearsed at all, and it seemed to take him by surprise. He covered it fast. "I'm filming down the Bay. Six weeks. Some Netflix thing about a lighthouse keeper who may or may not be a ghost. I'm a ghost, actually, that's a spoiler, don't tell anyone." He leaned on the counter. "I've been dying to find somewhere real. Somewhere nobody wants anything from me."

"I want you off my counter, you're on the Mabinogion."

He lifted his elbow. A damp patch shaped like Anglesey bloomed on the cover.

"Sorry. God. I'll buy it."

"You will."

"See, this is nice." He grinned. "Most people, I walk in, they go all—" he widened his eyes and flapped his hands, "—and it's exhausting, frankly, being adored. You're very restful."

"Thanks, I'll put it on the website. *Ffenest: Restful.*"

"And funny. Has anyone told you you're funny?"

"Nobody who was hiding from photographers behind a table of Owain Glyndŵr biographies, no."

There was the smile again, but she could see him working now. He was taking readings, adjusting, looking for the angle. She knew the look. Her brother did it when he'd scratched her car.

"Recommend me something," he said. "Anything. Whatever you think I'd like."

She didn't hesitate. She reached under the counter and slapped a paperback down beside the ruined Mabinogion.

He read the title aloud. "*The Picture of Dorian Gray.*"

"Thought you'd relate."

"That's *savage*." He looked delighted, then something flickered. "Hang on. Have you actually seen anything I've done? Genuinely?"

"One film. On a plane, to Malaga."

"Which one?"

"The one with the submarine."

"*Pressure Point.*" He brightened. "Did you like it?"

She considered lying. She'd been raised to be kind to idiots and strays.

"I fell asleep before you came on."

Silence. Somewhere down the arcade, a busker started murdering "Calon Lân."

"Right," said Dominic Thorne. "Right. Okay." He picked up the Wilde and put it down again. "I'm in the first scene."

"Must've been a long run-up to sleep, then."

He wasn't smiling now. He was looking at her as if she were a word he'd been mispronouncing for years. When he spoke again, the polish had gone off his voice. It sounded younger, and more northern than she'd expected.

"My mam used to take me to a shop like this. Bradford. Proper cramped, wonky shelves, bloke behind the counter who hated everyone. I used to hide in the back and read the endings first so I'd know everyone was all right." He scratched his jaw, the BAFTA-nominated one. "Don't know why I told you that. I don't tell people that."

Non found she was holding a pencil very hard.

"Did they?" she asked. "Turn out all right?"

"Hardly ever, in the good ones." He finally looked at her properly. "You've got ink on your face."

"I have not."

"Just there." He didn't reach for it, which was somehow worse. He just pointed, near enough that she could feel where his finger would have landed.

She scrubbed at her cheekbone with the back of her wrist. "Gone?"

"No. You've made it bigger. It's very fetching."

"Don't."

"Don't what?"

"Do the—" she waved the pencil vaguely at all of him, "—*thing*."

"I wasn't doing the thing." He frowned, apparently checking. "I don't think I was doing the thing. That's new."

The arcade outside had gone quiet. The rain had softened to that Cardiff drizzle that never quite commits. He glanced at the window, and she watched him register that it was safe, that he could go.

He didn't go.

"Twenty-three pounds," she said briskly. "For the Mabinogion. And Dorian's a fiver."

He paid in cash and didn't wait for change. At the door, he paused with his hand on the frame and the bell trembling above him.

"What time did you say you close?"

"Half five."

"Every day?"

"Most days." She pretended to read the invoice. "Tuesdays I'm here till six, doing the stock."

"Tuesdays," he repeated, as though he were learning a line. Then the smile came back, but crooked this time, as if he wasn't sure it would land. "See you, Non."

The door shut. The bell settled.

She didn't remember telling him her name. Then she saw the little brass plaque by the till, *Prop. N. Pritchard*, and felt absurdly, unforgivably disappointed that he'd only read it.

It took her another ten minutes to notice she'd been holding the invoice upside down the entire time.

response:
**Chapter Eleven: The Rogue**

The bell above the door of Pritchard's Books didn't ring so much as shriek.

"Sorry. Sorry, don't mind me." He shut the door with his shoulder and flattened himself against the Welsh History shelf. Outside, five men with long lenses jogged past the window, the Llandeilo rain bouncing off their hoods. "Is there a back way out?"

Nia didn't look up from her crossword. "Fire exit. It's alarmed."

"So am I, frankly." He took off his sunglasses, which in November in Carmarthenshire said everything, and gave her the smile. *The* smile, the one that had sold three hundred million pounds of cinema tickets and one regrettable aftershave. "Hello."

"Hello."

He waited. She wrote something in pencil.

"You know who I am," he offered.

"I know you're dripping on the Dylan Thomas."

He stepped smartly away from the shelf. "God. Sorry. That's practically sacrilege round here, isn't it? I'll buy it. I'll buy all of them." He fished out his wallet. "Do you take— what do you take? I can do cards, cash, eternal gratitude, a signed—"

"Kettle's on, if you want one," Nia said. "They'll go up as far as the Co-op and then come back. They always do."

"Always? You get a lot of fugitives?"

"You're the second this year. The first was a sheep."

He laughed, a real one that surprised him on the way out, and then caught himself and turned it back into the other kind, the warm, rumbling one from interviews. "Well. I hope I'm better company than the sheep."

"Sheep didn't talk as much."

*There it is,* she thought. *Lovely. Very cool. Keep going.* Her pencil had stopped moving. She made it move again. It wrote a word that didn't fit.

"Sebastian," he said, holding out a hand across the counter. "Crane. Though you clearly knew that and are being heroically discreet about it, which I appreciate more than you can possibly—"

"Nia."

She shook it. Briefly. His hand was cold from the rain and much larger than it looked on a screen, which was a stupid thing to notice, and she un-noticed it immediately.

"Nia," he repeated, as though he were tasting it. "That's beautiful. Welsh?"

"No, it's Portuguese." She tipped her head toward the back. "Milk's in the little fridge. Don't touch the biscuits, they're for Mrs. Eynon."

He did not go to the kettle. He leaned on the counter instead, chin on his fist, an angle he'd been told was his best by a woman in Los Angeles who'd charged him four thousand dollars to say it.

"Can I tell you something, Nia?"

"Could I stop you?"

"I've been in this town for six days. Filming up at the castle. And every single person has been *lovely*. The woman in the bakery gave me a free Welsh cake. The man at the garage called me 'butt,' which I've been assured is affectionate."

"It is."

"And you," he said, "have looked at me for a total of perhaps four seconds."

"Is that a problem?"

"It's a *novelty*." He paused. "It's a bit of a problem."

She looked at him then, properly, for a fifth second and then a sixth. He had a small scar through his left eyebrow they must cover with make-up, and he looked tired, really tired, in a way the posters didn't. Something in her chest did a small, treacherous somersault. She looked back down at the grid.

"Six down," she said. "'Make-up rearranged for a rascal.' Five letters."

"Sorry?"

"You're leaning on my crossword."

He straightened up and peered at it, upside down. And the smile went: not slowly, not on purpose. It simply slid off his face, and what was left underneath was a man frowning at a puzzle.

"Rogue," he said.

Nia blinked. "What?"

"R-O-G-U-E. 'Make-up' is rouge, 'rearranged' is your anagram indicator, 'rascal' is the definition. Bit of a cheap one, honestly. Who sets this?"

"Hywel. In the *Western Mail*. On a Saturday." She was staring at him now and couldn't seem to stop. "You do cryptics."

"I do the *Times* one on set. Between takes. Every day for fifteen years." He shrugged, suddenly and strangely shy. "Don't tell anyone. It's very bad for the image. My publicist wants me to have a motorbike."

"Have you got a motorbike?"

"I've got a motorbike. I hate it. It's loud and I fall off it." He turned the paper round to face him without asking, which should have annoyed her. "What's this one? Fourteen across. You've left it blank."

"Because I haven't got it."

"'Fool returns with Welsh river, keeps quiet.'" He mouthed it. "Seven letters."

"Taff's no good, it's too short," Nia said, leaning in despite herself. "And 'fool' could be 'twit,' or 'nit,' or—"

"'Ass.' Reversed is 'S-S-A.'"

"No, but it's 'keeps quiet,' so it's 'P' inside some—" She stopped. Their heads were very close together. He smelled of rain and expensive soap, and she was suddenly, horribly aware that she was wearing her dad's old jumper with the hole in the elbow.

"Inside some what?" he said softly.

"I've forgotten."

"You haven't."

"I have, now." She pulled back and took a breath. "Kettle."

"Nia." He didn't move. "Can I come back tomorrow? Not to hide. To do the crossword."

"It's a Sunday. We're closed."

"Monday, then."

"You'll be on your motorbike. Falling off it."

"I'll walk." The posters came back for a second, just the corner of the smile, and then he seemed to think better of it and let it go. "Please."

Outside, the photographers were trudging back past the window, defeated and wet. Neither of them looked up.

"Half nine," Nia said, to the crossword. "Bring your own biscuits."

He grinned, a lopsided, unrehearsed grin that would never have made it onto a poster, and she wrote ROGUE into six down in very neat capitals so her hands would have something to do.

The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear.

[characters]

response:
# My Apocalypse Buddy

The end of the world had not come with a bang, nor with a whimper, but with a sort of apologetic *click*, like a fridge giving up in the night. One day everything had worked. The next day it had stopped, and nobody had kept the receipt.

Midas had been named by parents of tremendous optimism and limited foresight. It was true that everything he touched turned into something. It was simply never gold. Usually it turned into a problem, and occasionally into a fire.

"Right," he said, spreading a damp map across the floor of what had once been the Sunny Smiles Family Dental Practice and was now Home Base. "Options."

Chewy, perched on the reception desk, rotated his head forty-five degrees with a noise like a gravel driveway clearing its throat. He was an animatronic koala from the Before Time. His manufacturer's name had worn off, but its confidence lived on in the label: GUARANTEED FOR LIFE.* His fur had the texture of a much-loved doormat. One eye glowed a faint, dutiful amber. The other had been replaced with a button that said VOTE.

*\*It had not specified whose.*

"HUG ME," said Chewy. "I'M CHEWY."

"Yes, thank you, that's very helpful."

Chewy had forty-one pre-recorded phrases, thirty-seven of which concerned eucalyptus. Over two lonely winters, Midas had learned to interpret them the way a priest interprets the entrails of a goat: with great confidence and a total absence of evidence.

"Option one," Midas said, "we stay here, eat the last tin of peaches, and die of something with a Latin name. Option two, we go and find out what *this* means."

He tapped the drawing he'd made of yesterday's graffiti. It had been sprayed in letters three feet high across the side of a dead supermarket:

**SANCTUARY. PAST THE GRINNING MAN. WHERE THE CHAIRS LIE BACK. FOOD. SAFETY. NO GOATS.**

"No goats," Midas said reverently. "Chewy, think of it. Somewhere with no goats."

There was a gang of goats on the high street. They had organised. Midas was fairly sure they had a leader, and that it held a grudge.

"LET'S GO ON AN ADVENTURE!" said Chewy. This was phrase nineteen, and it was the reason Midas had never thrown him in the river.

---

The mission went sideways at roughly the moment it began, which was something of a record even for Midas.

The first problem was the door, which fell off. The second problem was the goats, who were waiting outside the door, as though someone had told them.

There are moments in life when a man must decide who he truly is. Midas decided he was a man who ran. He did so with Chewy under one arm, reciting the nutritional content of eucalyptus leaves at full volume. The goats followed with the unhurried certainty of creatures who knew the town better than he did and had eaten most of it.

They lost the goats in the old multi-storey car park, mainly because Midas fell down a ventilation shaft. Goats, whatever their faults, are not stupid.

"Grinning Man," Midas wheezed twenty minutes later, having climbed out through a drain. "We need to find the Grinning Man."

"I LOVE YOU," said Chewy. His amber eye was flickering in a manner Midas chose not to think about.

They walked north, past the ruins of a garden centre where the roses had won. They crossed a bridge that had been structurally optimistic for a decade and chose that afternoon to become a realist. Midas made it across. Chewy's left arm, snagged on a railing, did not.* It went into the river, still waving. Midas watched it bob away with the particular grief one reserves for limbs that are not, technically, one's own.

*\*It was later collected by a heron, who carried it for some miles before concluding it was not a fish and dropping it in a car park on the edge of town. This will become relevant.*

By late afternoon they had been chased by a dog and rained on by a cloud that seemed to have taken a personal interest. They had also been briefly captured by a man who wanted to know whether Chewy was edible. ("NOT SUITABLE FOR CHILDREN UNDER THREE," Chewy had said, which settled it.)

And then, at last, as the light turned the colour of weak tea, they saw it. Rising over the treeline was a vast, peeling billboard of a man with impossible teeth, grinning like a god who had just heard a joke about you.

"The Grinning Man," Midas breathed.

Beneath it, in faded letters: **SUNNY SMILES FAMILY DENTAL — 2 MILES. WHERE THE CHAIRS LIE BACK AND YOU RELAX!**

There was a long silence. The wind moved through the grass. Somewhere, a goat laughed.

"Chewy," Midas said slowly. "When I had that fever. Last spring. Did I go out at all?"

Chewy's head rotated. His remaining eye flickered.

"LET'S GO ON AN ADVENTURE," he said, very quietly. Then, with a final ratcheting click, his battery died.

---

Midas returned to Home Base in several ways.

He returned physically, at two in the morning, limping, with Chewy strapped to his back like a small, judgemental rucksack.

He returned emotionally. He sat in the big reclining dental chair, stared at the ceiling, and accepted the facts. The sanctuary he had walked eleven miles to find, by a route of great creativity, was the one he had left that morning. The person who had promised food and safety and no goats had been him: delirious, holding a can of paint, and possessed of an unearned faith in himself.

And he returned the following week in a third and final way. He went out looking for batteries and found none. Instead, in a car park on the edge of town, he found a small grey arm, slightly pecked, still waving.

He took it home and sewed it on. He took the batteries from a smoke alarm that had never in its life detected anything, and put them in Chewy.

Chewy's eye blinked amber. His head turned. He regarded the dental surgery, the last tin of peaches, and the tired man with the needle.

"HOME," said Chewy.

Midas stared. That wasn't one of the forty-one.

Outside, the goats were gathering. Midas reached for the peaches.

"Yes," he said. "Apparently it's lovely. No goats."

[characters]
- the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time
- midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. Chewy’s eyes flicker colors in response to strong emotions—sometimes giving them away.

1000 words.
response:
# My Apocalypse Buddy

The world had not ended with a bang, nor with a whimper, but with a sort of apologetic click, like a kettle switching itself off. One morning the lights went out. Over the following decade everything else went out too, in an orderly fashion, as though it had been waiting for permission.

Midas lived in the deep end of what had once been the Arlesford Municipal Leisure Centre. The pool had no water, which was a disadvantage for swimming and an advantage for most other things. A sign above his bed read NO HEAVY PETTING, which Midas had always found faintly accusatory.

"Eleven percent," said Chewy.

Chewy was a koala. More precisely, Chewy was eighteen inches of grey acrylic fur stretched over servos, sensors, and the ambitious marketing that had once promised he would be Your Forever Friend™. Somebody in a boardroom had decided that children wanted a toy whose eyes changed colour with its mood. Nobody in the boardroom had considered that a toy might one day have moods worth hiding.

His eyes were currently a bruised amber. Amber meant Concern.

"Eleven's fine," said Midas. "Eleven's practically twelve."

"Eleven is practically ten, and ten is when I start losing nouns. Last time I called you 'the tall thing' for a week."

"I didn't mind."

"I called the *rain* 'the tall thing.'"

Midas pulled on his boots, which had been a matched pair once, in the way that cousins are related. "Batteries, then."

"Double-A. Four. And not from the Scrapper market, because last time that man sold you four painted pebbles."

"They were very convincing pebbles."

"They were convincing because you wanted them to be. That's the entire basis of commerce."

The plan, insofar as it had the shape of a plan, was the MegaSave on the ring road. Everyone knew the MegaSave had been picked clean years ago. Everyone also knew it was now occupied by the Congregation of the Final Transaction, who let nobody in, which suggested to Midas that there must be something inside worth not letting people in for.

This was the kind of reasoning that had got Midas into, at last count, three cellars, one well, and a brief, confusing marriage.

They set out under a sky the colour of old dishwater, Chewy riding in Midas's coat pocket like a periscope operated by a disapproving submarine.

They got in through the loading bay, which was easy, which should have been the first warning. In Midas's experience the universe only left a door open when it was curious to see what you'd do next.

Inside, empty shelves ran into the gloom like the ribs of a beached whale. At the far end, lit by candles arranged in the shape of a barcode, stood the altar: six self-checkout machines, dead and gleaming. On the central one, enthroned on a velvet cushion, lay a sealed pack of batteries.

Chewy's eyes went gold.

Not a discreet gold. They went the gold of a lighthouse that has just been told it's won the lottery, and they illuminated the entire nave.

"Chewy," hissed Midas.

"I can't help it!"

"Think sad thoughts."

"I'm *thinking about dial-up!*" The eyes flickered: gold, gold, an apologetic mauve, gold.

Forty heads in hi-vis tabards turned.

There is a particular silence that occurs when forty people realise there's an intruder, and the intruder realises that they've realised. It lasted long enough for Midas to note that some of the Congregation were quite small, others were quite large, and the large ones were holding the long hooked poles once used for fetching stock from high shelves.

The High Cashier stepped forward. She was elderly, with a magnificent badge reading SANDRA — HAPPY TO HELP, and she looked at Chewy the way a starving woman looks at a pie.

"Unexpected item," she breathed, "in the bagging area."

"Amen," said the Congregation.

Chewy's eyes went a hectic, pulsing red, bathing everyone in the light of a photographic darkroom. "Oh no," he whispered. "They've got a prophecy."

They had. It was written on the back of a laminated customer satisfaction card, and it foretold that an Item would come, glowing and unscannable, whereupon the machines would awaken, an Attendant would be summoned, and all would be Approved.*

It said nothing about the Item's companion. Sandra improvised. Companions, it was decided, went in the compactor.

What followed was not, strictly speaking, an escape. Escapes imply intent. It was more a series of things happening very quickly in roughly the right direction.

Midas grabbed the batteries. Chewy shrieked "LET'S BE BEST FRIENDS!" (a factory phrase that surfaced under stress like a hiccup) at a volume he had never been designed for, and the nearest acolyte dropped his pole out of sheer theological confusion. Midas vaulted a checkout, landed in a trolley, and discovered, as generations before him had, that trolleys possess a will of their own, and that will is mostly sideways.

The trolley went through the automatic doors, which did not open automatically, or indeed at all. It went down the car park ramp, across the ring road, and down the long embankment toward the canal, collecting speed, glass, and a following of people in tabards.

Halfway down, it hit a rock.

Midas went into the canal. Chewy went in several directions.

---

They came home, in the end, by four separate routes.

Midas arrived at dusk, having drifted two miles downstream clinging to a mooring rope and walked the rest, dripping, with the batteries clutched to his chest like a newborn.

Chewy's body arrived an hour later, sitting upright in the trolley, which had extricated itself from the canal and trundled home with the eerie certainty that trolleys sometimes have. It parked neatly by the shallow end.

Chewy's left arm did not come home, and was presumably now a relic.

Chewy's head arrived at midnight, carried by a small acolyte with a serious face, who explained that it hadn't been paid for and therefore couldn't be kept. She had stapled a receipt to its ear. Midas thanked her, and she left looking spiritually troubled, which he felt was probably good for her.

He set the head on the table, sewed it roughly back to the body, and tore open the pack with trembling fingers.

There was a long pause.

"These are triple-A," said Chewy. His voice had slowed to a treacle drawl. Four percent.

"They're *nearly* double."

"Midas."

"Same letter. Just more of it."

Chewy's eyes cycled through amber, red, and a weary grey, and then, unexpectedly, settled into a soft, steady blue, the colour the manual, long since pulped, had listed as *Content*.

"Tomorrow," he murmured, "we try the hardware shop."

"The one with the dogs?"

"The one with the dogs, you magnificent tall thing."

And the blue held, gently, until morning, and gave him away completely.

---

response:
# My Apocalypse Buddy

The end of the world, Midas had come to understand, was not so much an event as a long, slow afternoon that nobody had thought to end.

He sat in the bathtub he used as an armchair, in the laundromat he used as a fortress, and regarded the last tin of food. It had no label. It had lost its label sometime in the second winter, and since then it had been, in a philosophical sense, every food at once. It might be peaches. It might be beans. As long as nobody opened it, it was a little tin-shaped heaven, and Midas had no intention of collapsing it into something disappointing like pilchards.

"We have to go to the Mall," he said.

Chewy sat on the folding counter, as he always did. He was a koala, or had been designed by someone who'd had a koala described to them over a bad telephone line. Two-thirds of his fur remained. One eye glowed a faint, unblinking amber. Nobody knew what powered him, and Midas had stopped asking, on the principle that you don't check a gift horse for a battery compartment in case it hasn't got one.

Chewy's head swivelled with the sound of a small gearbox having second thoughts.

"*Now with thirty percent more!*" he announced.

"More what, though," said Midas. "That's always been my question."

Chewy did not answer. Chewy never answered. He just said things, like a prophet who'd been given the words but not the context, which, Midas reflected, was most prophets.

The plan was simple, and Midas had learned to fear his simple plans. Complicated plans failed in complicated ways you could at least admire. Simple plans failed the way a ladder fails, all at once, with you on it.

The Mall stood at the top of Ringroad Hill, a vast concrete shrine to a religion whose god had died and left only the car park. It was held by the Shoppers. The Shoppers were a tribe who had kept the old rites alive without remembering what they meant. They pushed trolleys in slow, solemn circles. They queued, sometimes for days, for nothing in particular. Their priests wore lanyards.¹

¹ *The lanyards bore the sacred names of the First Priests: BRENDA, KEV, and HAPPY TO HELP.*

Midas put Chewy in his rucksack, head poking out like a periscope, and set off.

The journey up was uneventful in the way that only makes the rest of the day worse. They slipped in through a loading dock. Inside, the Mall was cathedral-dark, lit by shafts of sunlight falling through the broken skylights onto rows of empty shelving. Midas crept down an aisle marked SEASONAL, which these days covered most things.

And there, on a bottom shelf, glinting like a dragon's hoard, were tins. Dozens of them. With labels.

Midas reached out a trembling hand.

"*Clean-up on aisle four,*" said Chewy, at a volume that would have embarrassed a foghorn.

The effect on the Shoppers was immediate. Forty heads rose from forty trolleys. Somewhere a priest dropped his clipboard.

"The Tannoy," someone whispered. "The Tannoy has *spoken*."

Here is a thing about holy voices. People spend generations waiting to hear them, and when they finally do, their first instinct is to look round for whoever's standing nearest and decide it's his fault.

In fairness, Midas was standing in aisle four.

They were very polite about it. That was the worst part. A woman in a lanyard reading HAPPY TO HELP took Chewy from the rucksack, raised him reverently above her head, and placed him on a plinth made from a stack of nappy boxes. Midas, meanwhile, was escorted to the Customer Services desk, where it was explained to him with genuine regret that he was to be Returned.

"Returned where?" said Midas.

"Without a receipt," said the priest gravely, and everyone shuddered.

Midas gathered this involved the old lift shaft.

On the plinth, Chewy's eye glowed. The Shoppers knelt.

"*Your call is important to us,*" Chewy intoned.

The Shoppers wept.

"*Please hold.*"

They held. Every one of them stood perfectly still, faces upturned, because the Voice had told them to, and they would hold, Midas suspected, until the sun burned out.

He did not wait to find out. He grabbed an armful of tins, then Chewy, who came away from the plinth minus one ear, and ran.

He'd had in mind the loading dock. What he got was the trolley park, which tilted downhill, which joined the car park, which was also downhill, which in its turn ran straight into Ringroad Hill. And Ringroad Hill was, as the name suggests, essentially a long argument with gravity that gravity always won.

Midas went down it in a trolley. Then, briefly, beside a trolley. Then underneath one. At the bottom, the trolley found the canal, and so did Midas, and so did the tins, which sank with the dignity of things that had always known how this would end.

Chewy floated. Chewy, it turned out, was mostly stuffing.

"*Batteries not included,*" he remarked, bobbing.

They got home three ways, which was two more than anyone should need. Midas came back partly by canal, partly by hedge, and finally, after a short but educational experience with the drainpipe, through the laundromat's own skylight, landing in the bathtub, which was at least where he'd meant to be sitting anyway. Chewy came home in two parts. The main bit was in Midas's teeth. The ear arrived later, delivered by a crow who seemed to want a reward and left in a huff when none was forthcoming.

Midas lay in the tub, dripping, bruised, smelling powerfully of canal.

"Well," he said. "That's that, then."

On the counter stood the last tin, unlabelled and untouched, still every food in the world.

He looked at it for a long time. Then, because the day could hardly get worse and he had always been a man to test a thing like that, he opened it.

Peaches.

Golden, glistening peaches, in syrup.

Midas laughed until it hurt, which, given the hill, wasn't long.

Chewy's head turned with its small, grinding sigh. His one amber eye regarded the tin, then Midas, then the slowly darkening sky through the hole in the roof.

"*Some assembly required,*" he said.

And for once, Midas thought, he'd got it exactly right.

prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge
Genre: Surreal Horror

JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered.

The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way.

Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it.

JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes.  JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move.

And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse.

JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head.

# Chapter Two: The Dunphy Place

Supper that night was venison chili out of a Tupperware tub their mother had packed, heated on the old Glenwood stove until the bottom scorched. JT ate without tasting it. Across the table his father spooned chili mechanically, eyes fixed on the window, where the last light was draining out of the spruce like dishwater down a sink.

He was humming. That was the thing. Dale Tremblay did not hum. In seventeen years JT had never heard his father carry a tune, not in church, not at Christmas, not with the radio going on the long drives north. But he was humming now, low and tuneless, three notes rising and falling over and over, the way you'd hum to a baby. Or to an animal you didn't want to spook.

*Or to call one.*

JT put the thought away. He was good at that. He'd had practice.

"Saw sign up past the flowage," Mike said, tearing a slice of Wonder Bread in half. "Big tracks. Fresh. Heading up toward the Dunphy place."

The humming stopped.

"Nobody goes up there," their father said.

"I'm just saying, that's where they're bedding down. Makes sense, right? Nobody's hunted that ridge in, what, twenty years?"

"Twenty-two." Their father set down his spoon. "And nobody's going to."

JT looked between them. He knew the story, the way every kid who'd ever come up to the lodge knew it. Lucien Dunphy had built the cabin himself in the fifties, a one-room box of hand-peeled logs up on the ridge where the old logging road gave out. One November he'd gone up alone and hadn't come down. The warden found his Winchester propped neatly beside the door, still loaded, and his boots set side by side on the step like he'd taken them off to go inside a church. No Lucien. Just a cabin that smelled like a barn, and caribou hair on everything, drifted in the corners like snow.

That was the version the grown-ups told. The version the kids told was that you could still see a light up there some nights, and if you were stupid enough to walk up and look in the window, you'd see Lucien sitting at his table, waiting for company.

"Old Lucien still keeping the lamp lit?" Mike said, grinning.

"I said that's enough."

It came out flat and hard, and Mike's grin faltered. For a second nobody said anything. The stove ticked. Out in the dark, something moved through the brush below the porch, heavy and unhurried, and JT waited for one of them to say *you hear that?* Neither of them did.

---

He woke sometime after two with a full bladder and the certain, cold knowledge that he was alone in the room.

Mike's cot was empty, the sleeping bag thrown back. JT lay still, listening. The lodge creaked and settled. Then the porch door: the long rusty groan of the spring, the slap of the screen.

He went to the window.

His father was walking across the frost-white yard in his long johns. Barefoot. Mike was a few steps behind him, dressed in nothing but boxers and a Bruins T-shirt, arms hanging loose at his sides. They didn't hurry. They didn't look back. They walked to the edge of the treeline and stopped there, side by side, faces turned toward the dark between the spruce trunks, and they stood like that for what JT's Timex said was eleven minutes.

Then they turned and walked back.

JT was in his bag with his eyes shut before the screen door slapped again. He heard Mike lie down. He heard his brother's breathing go slow and even almost at once, the way a little kid's does, and JT lay awake until the window went gray, telling himself he'd dreamed it.

In the morning there were pine needles stuck to the soles of his father's feet, and a thin scratch across Mike's shin, beaded with dried blood. Nobody mentioned it.

JT didn't either.

---

"Thought we'd try the ridge," his father said, shouldering his rifle.

JT stopped lacing his boot. "You said nobody goes up there."

His father looked at him. It was a perfectly ordinary look, a little puzzled, a little impatient, the look of a man whose kid is being difficult before coffee. "When did I say that?"

"Last night. At supper."

"Jamie." Mike laughed, not unkindly. "Dad didn't say that. You were half asleep in your chili."

JT opened his mouth. Closed it. *Did* he say it? He could remember the words, the flat hardness of them. But he could also remember the clearing, and the barefoot walk across the frost, and he was starting to understand that remembering something and having it happen were not always the same thing. Not up here.

They went up the ridge.

The logging road was mostly alders now, whipping back at his face. Nobody talked. Twice JT heard his father humming those three notes under his breath, and once he was almost sure Mike was humming them too, in a different key, so the two sounds rubbed against each other like a wet finger on a glass rim.

The cabin sat in a little hollow at the top, smaller than JT had pictured. The roof had gone swaybacked and green with moss. The door hung open.

"Wait here," his father said. "Keep an eye out."

"Dad—"

But they were already going in. First his father, then Mike, ducking under the low lintel, and then the dark inside the doorway swallowed them both, and the woods went completely silent. No jays. No wind. Not even the tick of a branch.

JT counted to a hundred. Then to two hundred.

"Dad?"

Nothing.

He made himself walk to the window. The glass was filmed with grime, and he had to cup his hands against it, and for a second all he could see was his own face floating there, pale, mouth open.

Then his eyes adjusted.

The cabin was empty. No father. No Mike. Just a plank table with three chairs pulled up to it, and three tin bowls set out, clean and waiting. The two chairs on the far side had coats hung over their backs, his father's red-and-black wool and Mike's orange vest.

The third chair, the one facing the window, had nothing on it at all.

Behind him, close enough that he felt it stir the hair on his neck, something let out a long, slow breath.

JT didn't turn around. He watched in the glass instead, where his reflection had been. He watched the dark shape rise up behind his shoulder, the great spread of antlers blotting out the sky, and on either side of it two more shapes, smaller, standing patient as fence posts.

"There you are, Jamie," his father said softly. "We saved you a seat."

And a hand, trembling, warm, impossibly gentle, came up to touch the side of his face.
