# Caribou Season at the Lodge

## Chapter Two: What the Hand Remembers

Supper that night was venison chili out of a Mason jar Mom had packed back in Thunder Bay, heated on the old Coleman two-burner until it popped and spat. That was tradition, and his father was big on tradition. First night, Mom's chili. Second night, whatever they shot. Third night, cards and Labatt's and Dad telling the story about the black bear in '89 that got into the outhouse, a story JT could recite word for word and still laughed at every time, because you were supposed to.

There was no story tonight.

His father ate standing at the counter, which he never did, staring out the window over the sink where there was nothing to see but his own reflection and the dark beyond it. Every so often he set down his spoon and rubbed the fingers of his right hand together, slowly, the way you'd test the grain of fine sandpaper. Then he'd bring the hand up near his face. Not quite smelling it. Not quite not.

*It's nothing,* JT told himself. *Arthritis. He's fifty-six. His knuckles ache in the cold. You've heard him say so a hundred times.*

Except it was the same hand. The one he'd lifted toward the buck's muzzle.

Mike sat across from JT at the plank table, shoveling chili and humming. JT didn't recognize the tune. It went up and down in a slow, lilting way, like a hymn, or a lullaby, and it set his teeth on edge without his being able to say why.

"Good chili," JT said, because somebody had to say something.

"Mm," said Mike.

The radio on the shelf was tuned to the CBC out of Sioux Lookout, or meant to be. Mostly it gave them static, with a voice surfacing now and then like a swimmer coming up for air: *...clear skies through Thursday... overnight lows near minus...* then gone again under the hiss.

JT pushed a kidney bean around his bowl. He'd been working up to it all afternoon, all through the long silent walk back, and now the words felt like stones in his mouth.

"Dad. That big buck today."

His father's hand stopped halfway to his face.

"Down by the clearing," JT went on, and his voice sounded too loud, too young, a kid's voice. "I saw it from the trail. It was right there. You could've—"

"Didn't see any buck." His father didn't turn around. "Saw some sign. Scrapes. That's all."

"It was *right there*, though. You had your hand out. You were practically—"

"JT." Just his name. Not loud. His father had never needed to be loud. "We didn't see anything worth a shot today. Tomorrow we'll try the ridge."

The static on the radio swelled. Mike kept humming.

And here was the thing, the part that would come back to JT later in the long sleepless hours: his father *believed* it. JT knew that tone of voice. It wasn't the voice his father used when he was hiding something, the hearty, too-quick voice he used when Mom asked how much the new outboard had cost. This was flat and calm and certain. The voice of a man reporting the weather.

So either his father was lying in a way JT had never heard him lie before, or JT had seen something that hadn't happened.

He wasn't sure which was worse.

---

He woke sometime after two. He knew it was after two because the woodstove had burned down to a sullen orange eye, and his father always banked it at midnight. The cabin was cold and smelled of chili and gun oil and the sour-wool smell of drying socks.

What had woken him was the door.

Not a slam. A careful, deliberate *click*, the sound of someone easing the latch so it wouldn't wake anybody. JT lay still in the lower bunk and listened to boots on the porch boards, one step, two, then the creak of the bottom stair that always complained, and then nothing.

He waited for the outhouse door. It didn't come.

*Get up,* said a part of him. *Go look.*

*Stay put,* said a smarter part. *Pull the sleeping bag over your head like you did when you were eight and the wind sounded like somebody whispering under the eaves. Whatever's out there, you don't want to know it.*

He got up.

The floorboards were like ice under his socks. He crept to the front window and used the cuff of his thermal to wipe a porthole in the frost.

His father stood at the edge of the yard in his long johns and unlaced boots, bareheaded under a sky so thick with stars it looked spilled. His breath smoked. His right hand was held out in front of him, palm up, the way you'd offer an apple to a horse.

Beyond him, at the tree line, the dark was full of eyes.

JT counted six pairs before he made himself stop. They hung at different heights in the black spruce, catching what little light there was and throwing it back green-gold, steady, unblinking. Not moving. Not grazing. Just *attending*, the way a congregation attends.

His father was talking. JT couldn't hear the words through the glass, only the low murmur, but he knew the cadence. It was the same rhythm Mike had been humming at supper. Up and down. A lullaby. A hymn.

Then his father stopped. Tilted his head, as if listening to an answer.

And slowly, his father turned around and looked straight at the window.

Straight at JT.

His face in the starlight was perfectly calm. His eyes were dark and flat, and JT, who had looked into his father's eyes every day of his life, did not recognize them at all.

JT dropped below the sill so fast he cracked his knee on the floor. He stayed there, curled and shaking, his heart going like a partridge drumming, waiting for the click of the latch.

It didn't come. After a long time he crawled back to the bunk and lay there with the sleeping bag clutched to his chin.

In the darkness above him, the upper bunk creaked.

"You should've come out of the bushes, Jaybird," Mike said softly. His voice was gentle. Sleepy. Kind. "It doesn't hurt. Not even a little."

JT didn't answer. He lay rigid, listening to his brother begin to hum, and outside, very faintly, from the tree line, he could have sworn he heard something hum back.

# Chapter Two: What Réal Didn't Say

Réal Gagnon talked. That was the thing about him, the thing JT had known since he was seven years old and Réal had pulled a quarter out of his ear, then spent twenty minutes explaining how he'd won it off a priest in Sept-Îles. Réal talked about his Ski-Doo, his bad knee, his ex-wife Monique, who'd run off with a Hydro-Québec lineman. ("Good for her, eh? Man's got a pension.") He talked while he gutted, talked while he ran the outboard, talked with a Player's hanging off his lip until the ash curled down like a question mark and somehow never fell.

This year, Réal didn't talk.

He'd carried their gear down from the truck the first afternoon and said maybe a dozen words, most of them about the generator. He didn't come over for cribbage the first night, or the second. His cabin sat across the cove, two hundred yards of black water, and each evening JT watched that single lit window from the porch and waited for the door to open.

It never did.

"Flu," Mike said, slapping down a card. "Fifteen-two. Guy's sixty-something. He gets the flu."

"He's fine," their father said. He was looking at his hands while he said it, turning them over in the lamplight like he'd just discovered them at the ends of his arms. "Leave the man be."

JT moved his peg and said nothing. Always safer.

---

On the third night he went out for wood and kept walking.

He told himself it was just to stretch his legs. The shore path was frozen hard, roots like knuckles under his boots, and the moon hung over the spruce fat and lopsided, as if someone had pressed a thumb into one side of it. When he reached Réal's dock, the old man was sitting at the end of it in the dark, smoking. A rifle lay across his knees.

Not leaning against a post. Across his knees. Ready.

"Réal?"

"Go back inside, Jonathan."

Nobody called him Jonathan. Not since his mother.

"You sick or something? Mike thinks you got the flu."

Réal laughed, and it was a bad laugh, a laugh with nothing underneath it. "Sick. Yeah. Okay." The cigarette glowed and faded. "When you go home?"

"Sunday."

"Moon's full Friday." He pointed the cigarette at it, the way you'd point at a dog that had bitten you once. "You go Thursday. Tell your father the truck is making a noise. Tell him whatever you want."

"Why?"

Réal didn't answer for a long time. The water licked at the pilings. Somewhere out across the lake, something was walking in the shallows: slow, unhurried splashes, the sound of a thing with nowhere special to be.

"Forty-one years I guide here," Réal said finally. "Most years, they run. Good years, they run. But some years..." He shrugged. "Some years they come to you. Stand right there. Nice, eh? Easy." He spat into the water. "Last time was eighty-nine. Party from Hamilton. Four men. Three went home."

JT's mouth had gone dry. "What happened to the fourth guy?"

"Nothing happened to him." Réal turned, and in the moonlight JT saw his eyes were wet and red at the rims. Not drunk. Scared. "He just stayed."

JT waited for the punchline. With Réal there was always a punchline: the priest, the quarter, the lineman with the pension. It didn't come.

"Your father," Réal said quietly. "He touch one yet?"

The clearing came back to him all at once: the buck's slow bellows breath, his father's trembling hand, the look on his face like a man about to hear a secret he'd been waiting for his whole life.

"No," JT said.

Réal held his eyes for a long moment. "Okay," he said, gently, the way you'd say it to a kid who swore he hadn't broken the lamp. "Thursday."

---

Walking back, JT worked hard at convincing himself. Réal was a storyteller. Réal had been telling stories to city sports for forty-one years, and maybe this was a new one, a better one, and maybe the old bastard was sitting over there right now laughing into his Labatt 50. Maybe the rifle was for wolves. Maybe JT hadn't really seen what he'd seen in the clearing. He'd been tired. He'd been cold. People saw things.

He almost had himself believing it by the time he got into his sleeping bag.

He woke at 3:10, by the green glow of his Timex. Cold air was pouring across the floor. The door was open.

His father's bunk was empty, the bag flung back.

JT got up and went to the window, and later he would remember that he'd known what he was going to see before he saw it, the way you know which stair is going to creak.

His father stood in the yard in his long johns, barefoot on the frost. The moon lit him blue-white. Beyond him, at the treeline, stood the caribou: a dozen, twenty, more than JT could count, so still they might have been cut from plywood. Their eyes caught the moonlight and held it. His father's head was tilted. One hand was raised, palm out, like a man waiting to be asked to dance.

And they were all breathing together. JT could see it in the plumes of vapor, his father's and theirs, rising and falling in the same slow rhythm.

JT opened his mouth to shout.

"Don't."

He spun around. Mike was sitting up in his bunk, wide awake, his face calm in the dark.

"He's just listening, JT."

"Listening to *what*?"

Mike smiled, a slow, patient smile JT had never once seen on his brother's face. "You heard it in the clearing. I know you were there." He tilted his head, just slightly. "You'd hear it now too, if you'd quit holding your breath."

JT realized he *was* holding it. He'd been holding it since he woke up.

He turned back to the window.

The yard was empty. Just frost and moonlight and the black wall of spruce.

Behind him, the springs creaked as Mike lay back down. A minute later the porch door eased open, and his father's footsteps crossed the floor, slow and soft, and the bunk across from JT took his weight with a sigh. Nobody said a word.

JT lay awake until the window went gray.

---

In the morning his father was at the stove, whistling, cracking eggs one-handed the way he always did. His feet, in their wool socks, looked perfectly ordinary. Outside, the frost had already burned off the yard.

On his father's pillow, JT found three coarse gray hairs. He rolled one between his fingers and felt it give, light and strange. Hollow. Réal had told him once, years ago, that caribou hair was hollow. That was how they kept warm.

Across the cove, Réal's boat was gone.

"Over easy?" his father asked, smiling at him with flat, dark, peaceful eyes.

Thursday was tomorrow.

"Yeah," JT said, and folded the hairs into his pocket, and said nothing else at all.

response:
# Carnival of Dangerous Intentions

The rifles were chained to the counter like dogs. Vera noticed that first, because it was easier than noticing him.

He leaned where the gallery's striped awning met the boardwalk rail, sleeves rolled to the elbow, holding an untouched paper cone of peanuts. Above him the sodium lamps stuttered: amber, then nothing, then amber again. His face kept arriving and departing, never staying long enough to be memorized. Behind the counter, tin ducks clattered along their track in an endless, patient parade.

*His locks.* There it was again, that absurd phrase from some novel her mother would have confiscated. Black curls fell over his brow, damp at the temples from the July heat. She had thought about them on the subway. She had thought about them at luncheon while Arthur explained the terms of the Harmon account, his fork tapping the rim of his plate.

*You should not have come.*

"You're late," he said, without turning his head.

"I'm not anything. I never said I'd come."

"You said, 'Perhaps.'" Now he looked at her, and the lamp chose that moment to fail, leaving only the dark of his eyes and the red pulse of the Wonder Wheel behind him. "Women who say perhaps always come. Women who mean no say no."

"And how would you know what women mean?"

"I listen." He offered the peanuts. She didn't take one. He seemed pleased by that, as though she'd answered a question correctly.

The boardwalk smelled of frying dough and creosote and the salt rot of the incoming tide. Down toward Steeplechase, a barker promised the Eighth Wonder of the World for a nickel. Shopgirls on the arms of sailors drifted past, and a father carried a sleeping boy slung over his shoulder. None of them looked twice at a woman in a good blue dress standing too close to a man she couldn't name.

"You haven't told me your name," she said.

"You haven't asked."

"I'm asking."

"Then you'll have to win it." He dropped a coin on the counter. The attendant, a toothless old man chewing a cigar stub, slid a rifle across without a word, the chain rattling. "Three shots. Hit three ducks, and I'll tell you."

"And if I miss?"

"Then you'll tell me something instead." He smiled. It was not an unkind smile, which was somehow worse. "Something true. Something you haven't told your husband."

The word landed like a slap. Vera's hand went, traitorous, to the bare place on her finger. She had slipped the ring into her purse at the Stillwell Avenue station.

"I'm not married."

"Engaged, then. The stone left a mark." He nodded at her hand. "You've been turning it all evening. Wondering if you'll get it back on before he notices."

*How long has he been watching? Since the station? Since before?* The thought should have sent her away on her heel. Instead she felt it low in her stomach, a slow warm coil. She had felt the same at fourteen, standing at the edge of the quarry outside Scranton, knowing the water was too far down and knowing she would jump anyway.

She picked up the rifle.

It was heavier than she expected. He stepped in behind her, never quite touching, and she felt the heat of him along her spine like a hand held just above a stove.

"Your elbow," he murmured. "Lower. You're holding it like it might bite you."

"Perhaps it might."

"Everything bites, if you hold it wrong." His breath stirred the hair at her nape. "Breathe out. Shoot in the space after."

The lamp flickered. The ducks marched. She breathed out and squeezed, and the first duck went over with a flat tin clang.

"Good," he said. The single word did something to her that she resented.

The second shot went wide, and the pellet sang off the back plate.

"You flinched," he said.

"I didn't."

"You thought about him. Arthur." He let the name sit between them. She had never told him the name. "Fine man. Good family. Owns half the paper mills in Pennsylvania, and the other half owe him money."

She lowered the rifle and turned. In the stuttering amber his face was all angles, beautiful and wrong, like a picture hung slightly crooked.

"Who are you?"

"Someone who's been asked to keep an eye on you." He took the rifle gently from her hands and set it on the counter. "I was told you'd be dull. That you'd be easy."

"Asked by whom?"

"That's a second question. You've only earned the one, and you didn't hit three ducks." His gaze dropped to her mouth, then lifted, slow and deliberate. "So now you owe me something true."

The carnival roared on around them: screams from the Cyclone, the calliope wheezing, the tide hissing under the boards. Vera thought of Arthur's tapping fork and his careful hands. She thought of the Harmon account, and of the men who sometimes came to the house after midnight. She had learned not to hear their voices through the study door.

*I could walk away. I could put the ring back on.*

She stepped closer instead. She was close enough to see the faint scar that split his left eyebrow, close enough that when the lamp went dark again there was nothing in the world but the smell of salt on his skin.

"Something true," she said quietly. "I knew you were following me. Since Tuesday. I came anyway."

For the first time, he had no answer ready. The light returned, buzzing, and she watched it find him. Something shifted behind those dark eyes: the look of a man who has just discovered the ducks can shoot back.

"Then we're both in trouble," he said.

"Yes," said Vera, and at last she took a peanut from his hand. "I rather think we are."

response:
# Carnival of Dangerous Intentions

The rifle cracked before she saw him.

Three tin ducks fell in quick succession, *ping-ping-ping*, and the barker, a sunburned man chewing a cigar gone soft at the end, whistled through his teeth. "Mister, you're bad for business."

"So I've been told."

He hadn't turned around. Evelyn stood at the edge of the gallery's sallow light, her pocketbook pressed against her ribs, and knew he was aware of her the way one knows a draft from an open window.

The boardwalk breathed around them: fried clams and hot tar, salt rot from the pilings, sugar burning somewhere in a copper kettle. Behind her the Cyclone groaned on its wooden bones, and a girl shrieked with the particular delight of someone who believes she is in danger and is not. To her left stood Madame Zora's booth, a narrow lacquered thing with a curtain the color of dried blood. Its painted sign showed an enormous open palm, every crease labeled in gilt script: *Heart. Head. Life. Fate.* The sun had bleached the fingertips nearly white, as though the hand were slowly vanishing.

He set the rifle down. When he turned, the dusk caught in his hair, black curls loosened by the humidity and fallen across his brow.

*His locks.* There it was again, that absurd word out of the novels her mother had confiscated from beneath her mattress. She was twenty-four years old and engaged. She did not think in words like *locks*.

"You came back," he said.

"I said I would."

"People say all kinds of things on the Fourth of July. Fireworks make liars of everybody."

"Then why were you waiting?"

"Who says I was waiting?" He slid a nickel across the counter, and the barker reset the ducks. "I come here to shoot."

"At ducks."

"Ducks don't ask questions."

"Neither do you, apparently. You never asked my name."

He smiled then, slowly, the way a door opens in a house you've been warned about. "Didn't need to."

She should be in Flatbush. Harold believed she was at her sister's, playing canasta and listening to the Philco. On the BMT she had worked the ring off her finger and dropped it into her pocketbook, where it now sat like a small, hard accusation. She had told herself it was the heat. Fingers swell in July.

His gaze dropped to her left hand. "You took it off."

"I beg your pardon?"

"The ring. There's a pale band where it sits. Sun's honest even when people aren't." He tipped his head. "Nice stone, I'd guess. Whitcomb money."

The air seemed to thin. "You don't know anything about me."

"Evelyn Hale. Gramercy Park, the brownstone with the green shutters. Your father's dead, your mother plays bridge on Tuesdays, and you're marrying Harold Whitcomb of Whitcomb and Lyle in September." He paused. "Harold plays poker Thursday nights on Mulberry Street. He isn't good at it."

Her mouth had gone dry. "How do you know that?"

"I asked around."

"Who *are* you?"

"Somebody who notices things." He stepped away from the counter, leaving the rifle and the rows of unharmed ducks. "Walk with me."

"I don't think I will."

"Then stand still, and I'll walk around you. It'll look stranger, but suit yourself."

Despite herself, despite the cold bead of sweat tracing her spine, she laughed. It came out too loud, startled from her, and his eyes darkened with something like satisfaction.

He led her the dozen steps to Madame Zora's. A card hung on the curtain's brass ring: CLOSED. THE FATES ARE RESTING. Up close, the palmistry chart was a map of small cruelties, its margins crowded with cramped annotations: *A broken line foretells sudden reversal. A cross upon the Mount of Venus: an unwise love.*

"Give me your hand," he said.

"Why?"

"Zora's out. Somebody ought to tell your fortune."

*Don't.* The word was sensible and clear, spoken in her mother's voice. Evelyn held out her hand anyway.

His fingers were warm, roughened at the pads, and he turned her palm toward the light with unnerving care. "That's your head line. Long. Means you think too much." His thumb traced a curve below her fingers. "And this one, your heart. See where it splits? Right there." He tapped the fork lightly, and she felt it in her throat. "Zora would charge you a quarter to say you're at a crossroads."

"And what do you charge?"

"Depends what you want to know."

"Your name."

"Tonight? Call me Sal."

"Is that your name?"

"It's *a* name." His thumb hadn't left her palm. "Your fiancé owes money to some men. Not me. Men I work for."

There it was, the thing beneath the floorboards she had heard creaking all week. She tried to withdraw her hand. He didn't hold it, exactly, but neither did he let it go.

"Is that why you spoke to me last Sunday?" Her voice came out steadier than she felt. "By the carousel?"

He was quiet a moment. Somewhere down the boardwalk, a calliope wheezed into "The Daring Young Man on the Flying Trapeze."

"That's why I noticed you," he said finally. "It isn't why I'm still standing here."

"I don't believe you."

"Good. You shouldn't." He let her go at last, and the night air rushed cool into her empty palm. "Go home, Evelyn."

"Is that a threat?"

"It's advice. There's a difference. You'll learn it, if you stick around."

She ought to have turned then. The Stillwell Avenue station was a ten-minute walk; she could be in Flatbush before ten, the ring back on her finger, the evening folded away like a letter never mailed. She knew that girl. She had been that girl for twenty-four years.

"And if I don't go home?"

His eyes held hers, black and unreadable as the water under the pier. "Then I'll take you up on the Wonder Wheel. From the top you can see where the whole city runs out of lights." He leaned closer, near enough that she caught the smell of gunpowder on his cuffs. "And I'll tell you exactly what's coming for Harold."

"Why would you do that?"

"Maybe I want something from you."

"What?"

He only smiled.

Above them, the chart's great painted hand hung open, its every road forking into gilt. Evelyn thought how strange it was that no one ever painted a hand closing.

She took his arm.

response:
# Carnival of Dangerous Intentions

The barker's patter had gone hoarse by now, a ragged loop of *three shots a nickel, three shots a nickel*, and beneath it the tin ducks clattered along their track with the patience of the damned. Vera Lindqvist stood at the edge of the planks with her pocketbook clutched before her like a hymnal and told herself, for the third time, that she was only passing through.

The air was thick with brine and frying grease and something sweeter. A vendor two stalls down was spinning sugar into pink clouds, and the smell reached her and caught: a kitchen somewhere, a woman's hands, a voice saying *don't tell your father*. Then it was gone, slipping away like a coin through a grate.

*Whose kitchen? Whose hands?* She had never been permitted cotton candy. Mother called it sugared lint.

"You came."

She did not turn at once. That was the first rule she had made for herself on the long subway ride from Gramercy Park: do not turn at once.

"I was walking," she said.

"Eleven miles. That's quite a walk." He came around to stand beside her, close enough that she could smell gun oil and bay rum. *His locks.* Absurd, that phrase. But there they were, darker than she'd remembered, falling over his brow as though no one had ever told him to cut them. "Most girls who promise to come back don't."

"I'm not most girls."

"No," he agreed, and something in the way he said it made it sound less like a compliment than an appraisal. "You're Vera Lindqvist. Your father keeps half the bonds at Hollister & Crane, and you're marrying a man named Whitfield in September."

The boardwalk tilted, very slightly.

*I never told him my name. I'm certain of it.*

"You've been asking about me."

"I've been listening. People talk at Coney. That's what it's for." He laid a nickel on the counter, and the barker slid a rifle across without a word. He didn't take it. He turned it, stock first, toward her. "Ever fire one?"

"Of course not."

"Of course not," he echoed, smiling. "Go on. It's only ducks."

She ought to have said no. Instead she set down her pocketbook and took the rifle. It was heavier than she'd expected, warm along the barrel where other hands had held it. He stepped behind her. He did not touch her, not quite, but she felt the shape of him at her back, the way you feel a storm before the first drop.

"Elbow down," he murmured. "Don't close the other eye. Everybody closes the other eye. You want to see what's coming at you."

"Is that a lesson?"

"It's advice. Lessons cost more."

She fired. A duck spun backward with a flat little *tok*.

"Well," he said softly. "Look at that."

Her heart was going like a trapped bird. She fired again and missed entirely, and laughed, a short, startled sound she hardly recognized as her own.

"You haven't told me your name," she said.

"No."

"That hardly seems fair."

"Fair." He tasted the word. "You'd know about fair. Grew up with it served on silver trays." He took the rifle from her, his fingers brushing her knuckles for exactly as long as it took to be deliberate. "Call me Dominic, if you need something to call me."

"Is that your name?"

"It's a name."

*Turn around. Walk back to the station. Ride home and write Arthur a long, dull letter about centerpieces.* She thought it with perfect clarity and did not move an inch.

"Why did you ask me to come back?"

He leaned against the counter, watching the ducks make their circuit. The lights had come on fully now, red and gold bulbs strung along the Cyclone's spine, the Wonder Wheel turning its slow jeweled circle over the water. In that glare his eyes didn't reflect anything at all.

"Because you looked at me like you wanted something you'd been told you couldn't have," he said. "And because I need a favor."

There it was. Cold beneath the warmth, like a stone at the bottom of a summer lake.

"A favor."

"A small one. Your father keeps a ledger in his study. Green leather. Locked drawer, left side of the desk." He said it as casually as he might have mentioned the weather. "I'd like to know what's written on the page for the fourteenth of June."

"You're insane."

"Probably." He turned to her then, and his voice lost its edge and became something worse: gentle. "But you came eleven miles, Vera. In your good gloves. You didn't tell your fiancé, and you didn't tell your mother, and you've been thinking about me since Tuesday. So maybe we're both a little insane."

*He's right, and he knows he's right, and that should frighten me more than it does.*

The cotton candy smell drifted past again, and this time the memory came closer: a woman with dark hair, not Mother, pressing a paper cone into her small hands behind a striped tent. A calliope wheezing somewhere. *Don't tell your father we were here.*

She had never been to Coney Island. She had always believed that.

"What happened on the fourteenth of June?" she asked.

Dominic picked her pocketbook up from the counter and held it out to her, the way a gentleman would.

"Come back Saturday," he said, "and I'll tell you what happened on a lot of days."

She took it. Their fingers did not touch this time, and she was ashamed of how much she noticed.

Lost & Found in Osaka

Slice of Life / Coming-of-Age: First Connection. Write one scene within a larger story set in Osaka, Japan. A shy, introverted teenager & synthesizer nerd, is browsing the electronics district of Den Den Town. She is drawn to the sound of an electric guitar. A girl, slightly older and radiating confidence, is busking near the entrance to a crowded arcade, playing a blistering rendition of a classic anime theme. The scene takes us through their initial awkward interaction, transitioning into a surprisingly easy conversation. The busker, intrigued by the teenager's quiet intensity and knowledge of music, suggests they grab some sushi at a nearby kaitenzushi (conveyor belt sushi) restaurant. response:
# Lost & Found in Osaka

The guitar cut through everything: the claw-machine jingles, the shop barkers on Ota Road, the hiss of the pedestrian crossing. Kei had been on her way home, still thinking about the secondhand Roland SH-101 she visited every Saturday at the shop on the third floor and could never afford. She stopped walking.

*Cruel Angel's Thesis.* But wrong. Heavier. Someone had dragged it through a distortion pedal and left it bleeding.

The girl playing it stood beside the arcade entrance with one boot up on an amp the size of a lunchbox, bleached hair clipped back with a Pikachu barrette. A small crowd had gathered. Kei stood behind them, then a little to the side of them, and then, somehow, in front of them when they drifted off after the last chord.

The busker looked straight at her.

"You stayed for the whole thing. That makes you my biggest fan. Congratulations."

"Oh. I, um. Sorry."

"Sorry? Nande ya nen. You're supposed to say 'that was amazing, Saki-senpai.'"

"I don't... know your name."

"Saki. Now you do." She grinned and twisted a tuning peg. "And you are?"

"Kei."

"Kei-chan. You've got a face like you're grading me. Go on. What'd I mess up?"

"Nothing! You didn't..." Kei nodded too hard, and her headphones slid off her head and landed around her neck with a thunk. She pushed them back up. "You didn't mess up."

"Liar. Your eyebrow did a thing at the bridge."

"It's... You skipped the key change. Before the last chorus. The original goes up, and you just... stayed."

Saki stopped tuning. "Huh."

"Sorry."

"Stop apologizing! You're right. I skip it because the fingering's a nightmare and nobody notices." She pointed the headstock at Kei like an accusation. "Except you, apparently. Who are you?"

"Nobody. I just... I make music. Sort of. On synthesizers."

"Synths? Like, beep-boop?"

"Sometimes beep-boop." The corner of Kei's mouth twitched. "Mostly I layer pads. Slow attack, long release. The original Eva track has this string section underneath that's almost hidden, and if you take it out the whole song feels empty. That's why your version works, actually. The distortion fills that space. It's like a pad, but angry."

Saki stared at her.

Kei realized she had said four sentences in a row to a stranger and felt her ears go hot. She nodded at nothing. The headphones slid again.

"Okay, those headphones are trying to escape you."

"They're my dad's. They're too big."

"Then why wear them?"

"Because when they're on, people don't talk to me."

"Ha! And yet." Saki spread her arms. "Here I am. Talking. Defeating your force field."

"They're not even playing anything right now."

"Wait, seriously? So you're just walking around Den Den Town wearing silent earmuffs?"

"They're good earmuffs."

Saki laughed loud enough that a salaryman by the crane games looked over. "Okay, you're funny. You're quiet-funny. That's the dangerous kind." She crouched to unplug her cable. "So what are you doing here? Buying robot parts?"

"I visit a synth. Upstairs at the used place. An SH-101. It's ninety-eight thousand yen."

"You *visit* it."

"Every Saturday. I play it for ten minutes and the old man pretends not to notice."

"That's the saddest, most romantic thing I've ever heard." Saki snapped her guitar case shut. "I visit a Telecaster in Shinsaibashi. It's gray. I named it Kenji."

"You named it?"

"Of course I named it. Did you not name yours?"

Kei hesitated. "...Momo."

"MOMO." Saki slapped the case. "Okay. Decided. I made," and she tipped the coins out of an old Pocky tin and counted with a finger, "eight hundred and forty yen today, plus one button that someone thought was funny. That's sushi money."

"Sushi?"

"Kaitenzushi. There's a place two blocks down, hundred-yen plates. The conveyor squeaks at the corner. It's my favorite sound in Osaka."

"You want me to... with you?"

"No, I want you to come watch me eat alone. Yes, with me. You owe me."

"For what?"

"For noticing the key change. Now I have to learn it, which means hours of suffering. The least you can do is explain to me what 'slow attack' means while I eat salmon."

Kei looked down the street toward the station, the safe, ordinary way home. Then back at Saki, who was already slinging the case over her shoulder like the decision had been made for both of them.

"I don't really talk much," Kei said. "At meals. Or... in general."

"You talked plenty about angry pads."

"That's different. That's music."

"Then talk music. I'll talk everything else. Honma, I never shut up, so you'll barely have to try." Saki started walking, then turned around and walked backward. "Do you eat tamago? Please say you eat tamago. If you don't, this can't work."

"I eat tamago."

"Perfect. Also the corn mayo one. Don't judge me."

"I wasn't going to."

"Your eyebrow was going to."

Kei touched her eyebrow without meaning to. Saki cackled.

They waited at the crossing while the signal chirped. Kei slid her headphones off and let them hang around her neck. They had been slipping all afternoon anyway.

"Hey," Saki said, glancing at them. "No force field?"

"It wasn't working."

"Told you." Saki bumped her shoulder lightly. "Next Saturday, you visit Momo, I visit Kenji, and then we meet back here and I play the key change. Properly. And you have to tell me if I get it right."

"I'll tell you if you get it wrong."

"Brutal. I love it."

The light turned green. Kei realized, halfway across the street, that she was smiling, and that she hadn't nodded nervously even once since the word *sushi*.

At the restaurant, the conveyor squeaked at the corner, exactly like Saki had promised.

"See?" Saki said, sliding into the booth. "Best sound in Osaka."

Kei listened. "It's almost a B-flat."

Saki dropped her chopsticks. "I'm keeping you forever."

Slice of Life / Coming-of-Age: First Connection. Write one scene within a larger story set in Osaka, Japan. A shy, introverted teenager & synthesizer nerd, is browsing the electronics district of Den Den Town. She is drawn to the sound of an electric guitar. A girl, slightly older and radiating confidence, is busking near the entrance to a crowded arcade, playing a blistering rendition of a classic anime theme. The scene takes us through their initial awkward interaction, transitioning into a surprisingly easy conversation. The busker, intrigued by the teenager's quiet intensity and knowledge of music, suggests they grab some sushi at a nearby kaitenzushi (conveyor belt sushi) restaurant. A sudden burst of fireworks outside the arcade momentarily drowns out the guitar. Write primarily in dialogue, capturing the distinct voices of the two characters: the teenager's hesitant and -- initially -- awkward speech, and the busker's more outgoing and playful tone. 
1000 words.
response:
# Eight Cents

The Cruel Angel's Thesis was coming out of a battered amp, played twice as fast as it should have been.

Mio stopped walking. A shopping bag swung against her knee. Inside it, wrapped in anti-static foam, was a voice chip for a Juno-106 she'd spent four months saving for. She meant to keep walking. She did not keep walking.

The girl with the guitar stood beside the arcade entrance, under the glow of crane machines. She had a bleached streak in her hair and wore a denim jacket covered in pins. She finished the last chorus with a slide that made two salarymen flinch, then bowed to nobody in particular.

A few coins hit the open case. The small crowd drifted away. Mio stayed where she was.

"You've been standing there for three songs," the guitarist said. "That's either a compliment or you're lost."

"I—no. Sorry. I'm not lost. I was just—" Mio looked at the amp, the pedalboard, anything but the girl's face. "Listening."

"Yeah? What's the verdict?"

"It's good. Really good. It's just..."

"Just?"

"Your low E is flat." The words fell out before Mio could catch them. "Like... eight cents. Maybe nine."

There was a long pause. Mio wanted the pavement to swallow her.

Then the girl laughed, loud and delighted. "Eight cents? You can hear *eight cents*?"

"Sorry. I didn't mean... it's a habit."

The girl crouched, twisted the tuning peg, and plucked the string. She clipped on a tuner, stared at it, and her eyebrows shot up. "Honma ni? It says minus eight. Who *are* you?"

"Mio. Fujikawa Mio. I'm nobody. I just... tune oscillators a lot."

"Oscillators." The girl grinned. "So you're a synth kid."

"Um. Yes. Kind of. I have a Juno. Well. Half a Juno." Mio raised the bag slightly. "One of the voice chips died. Voice four. It sounds like a dying cat. I found a replacement at the shop behind the maid café."

"Behind the maid café! You know the deep cuts." She stuck out a hand. Her fingertips were calloused and her nails were painted chipped green. "Kaede. I play here Fridays and Saturdays, unless the cops get bored."

Mio shook the hand, briefly and awkwardly. "You speed it up. The Eva song. You speed it up a lot."

"Too much?"

"No. I like it. But you skip the key change before the last chorus. The original goes up, and you stay put."

Kaede put a hand on her chest as if she'd been shot. "Okay, *ouch*. You noticed that?"

"It's the best part," Mio said quietly. Then, louder, surprising herself: "It's the part where it feels like the song is lifting off."

Kaede studied her for a moment. "My fingers can't do the jump that fast. Not cleanly. I fudge it."

"You could capo up and drop the riff an octave. Then the change is just... one shape moving." Mio traced the motion in the air with two fingers, like sliding a fader. "That's how I'd do it on keys. You don't move your hand, you move the transpose."

"Wait, wait, show me that again."

She showed her again. Kaede fumbled through it twice, swore cheerfully, and on the third try the riff rose a step and kept going. It came out bright and clean.

"*Oh*," Kaede said. "Oh, that's *nasty*. That's so good."

Mio felt her face go hot. "It's just theory."

"It's not *just* anything. Nobody who listens to me ever has notes. They say 'sugoi' and throw me a hundred yen." Kaede set the guitar against the amp. "How old are you, Eight Cents?"

"Sixteen. And please don't call me that."

"Too late, it's stuck. I'm nineteen. So I'm basically your elder. You have to listen to me." She jerked her thumb down the street. "Are you hungry? There's a kaitenzushi two blocks down. Plates are a hundred and ten yen each, and the tuna's surprisingly okay."

Mio blinked. "Now?"

"No, next spring. Yes, now. I made..." Kaede glanced into the case. "Eleven hundred yen tonight. That's ten plates. I'll split them with you if you tell me what else I'm doing wrong."

"I don't... I mean, I don't really... I usually just go home and..."

"Solder things alone in your room?"

"...Yes."

"Then the solder can wait twenty minutes. Come on. I want to know what a Juno is, and why you'd buy half of one."

"I didn't buy half of one. It came broken. That's why it was cheap. That's how you get anything good—" Mio stopped. She was talking too fast. She always did when it was synths.

Kaede only leaned in. "Keep going."

"You buy the broken ones," Mio said, more slowly, "and you fix them. Then they're yours in a way new ones never are. You know every part that's been replaced."

"Okay, that's poetic. You're coming to sushi. That's an order from your elder."

Mio opened her mouth, perhaps to say she couldn't, or that her mother expected her home. What she actually started to say was—

The sky above the arcade cracked open.

*BOOM.* Then another, and another, gold and red chrysanthemums bursting somewhere over the Namba rooftops. The light washed across the crane machines and the wet pavement. The noise rolled down the street and swallowed the arcade jingles, the traffic, and Kaede's amp still humming its open E.

Kaede shouted something. Mio couldn't hear it. Mio shouted something back. Kaede cupped a hand to her ear and laughed. The fireworks kept going, crackling overhead, and for a few seconds the two of them stood there grinning at the sky like idiots.

When it faded, smoke drifted in the orange streetlight. Somewhere, a car alarm whined.

"Where did *that* come from?" Kaede said.

"There's a festival by the river. I think." Mio's ears were ringing. "What did you say? Before?"

"I said 'that's your cue.' What did *you* say?"

Mio held the shopping bag tighter. The voice chip sat inside, small and important, a missing part.

"I said yes," she said. "I said okay. Sushi."

Kaede's grin went wide. She snapped the case shut, slung the guitar over her shoulder, and hefted the little amp.

"Great. You're carrying the pedalboard, Eight Cents."

"*Mio.*"

"Sure, sure. Walk and talk. I want to hear about voice four."

# Delay Time

The guitar cut through everything: the pachinko clatter, the maid café girls waving laminated flyers, the jingles leaking from every shop doorway along Sakaisuji.

Hana stopped with one hand still on the door of the used-gear shop. Across the street, by the mouth of an arcade, a girl in a cropped bomber jacket was shredding "A Cruel Angel's Thesis" through a battery amp the size of a lunchbox. A small crowd had formed. A salaryman was filming. A kid in a school cap was air-drumming.

Hana didn't mean to cross the street. Her feet did it anyway.

Three songs later, the girl flicked her pick into the air, caught it, and pointed it straight at her.

"Okay, Headphones. You've been standin' there forever. That's either a compliment or you're a real slow pickpocket."

"I— no. Sorry. I don't— I'm not a pickpocket."

"Good, 'cause there's like four hundred yen in that case and two of 'em are buttons." She grinned. "So which is it? You a fan, or what?"

"It was good. Really good. Just..." Hana's mouth kept moving before her brain could stop it. "Your delay."

"My what?"

"Your, um. Delay pedal. It's set a little slow. For the song. So the repeats land behind the beat, and the fast parts get... muddy." Her face went hot. "Sorry. It still sounded good. I just hear it."

The girl stared at her. Then she crouched, squinted at a battered green pedal, and nudged a knob. She played the opening riff again, crisp now, each echo snapping into place like a gear catching.

"...Ah. Ahh, that's *so* annoying. You're right."

"Sorry."

"Stop sayin' sorry, you just fixed my whole sound for free! What are you, some kinda guitar ghost?"

"I don't play guitar. I do synths. Mostly sequencing." Hana tugged at the cord of her headphones. "On a synth, everything is... time. You notice when it's wrong."

"Huh." The girl slung the guitar behind her back and stuck out a hand. "Tsubasa. Born and raised right here, two stops down. You?"

"Hana. Okabe. From Sakai."

"Hana. Cute. Way too cute for somebody who just roasted my pedalboard." Tsubasa jerked her chin at the shop behind them. "You were goin' in there. Buyin' something?"

"Looking. There's a Juno-106 in the back. It's broken. The voice chips die on them, so only four of the six notes play. But you can replace the chips, if you're careful, and then it's..." Hana realized she was talking with her hands and stuffed them in her pockets. "It's a really good synth."

"You fix 'em? Like, with a soldering iron?"

"I try. I've burned myself a lot."

Tsubasa laughed, a big, loud, unembarrassed laugh. "Okay. Okay, I like you. I'm starvin', and there's a kaitenzushi round the corner. Hundred-and-ten-yen plates. You're comin'."

"Oh, I— I don't want to bother—"

"You'll bother me more if I gotta eat alone and think about my delay time. C'mon. You can tell me everything else wrong with me."

---

The restaurant was bright and loud, plates gliding past on the belt in an endless, hypnotic loop. Tsubasa had already grabbed three: seared salmon with mayo, tamago, and something deep-fried that might have been chicken.

"That's not even sushi," Hana said, then covered her mouth.

"Oh, she's got *jokes* now." Tsubasa pointed her chopsticks. "Karaage on rice is sushi if I'm eatin' it at a sushi place. That's the law in Osaka. Look it up."

Hana took a plate of tuna, carefully, like it might spill. She filled her cup with matcha powder and hot water from the tap at the counter. Tsubasa watched, chin on her fist.

"So what's in the headphones? You've had 'em on your neck this whole time. Gotta be something good."

"You won't know it."

"Try me."

Hana hesitated. "The opening from *Paranoia Agent*. Susumu Hirasawa."

Tsubasa slapped the table hard enough to rattle the soy sauce. "The *laughin'* one! Everybody grinnin' in the worst places, the guy standin' on the building, the old man floatin' in the puddle—"

"You know it?"

"Know it? I watched that whole show at like thirteen and couldn't sleep for a week! That song's been stuck in my head for five years!" She leaned in. "I tried to learn it on guitar once. Couldn't. It's like the chords don't *wanna* be chords."

"That's because he doesn't really write it like a guitar song," Hana said. The words were coming easier now, smooth, the way they did when she was alone with her gear. "He builds it on computers. Old Amigas, from the nineties. He layers vocal samples so the melody feels like it's floating over the harmony instead of sitting on it. So when you try to play it as chords, you lose the... the drift."

"The drift," Tsubasa repeated, nodding slowly. "Yeah. Yeah, that's exactly it. It drifts. That's why it's creepy and happy at the same time."

"Like a parade where something's wrong."

"Like a parade where something's wrong!" Tsubasa pointed at her again. "See, you get it. Nobody gets it. I play that at the arcade and people think I'm just tunin' up."

Hana laughed. It surprised her, how easily it came out.

They stacked plates. Seven for Tsubasa, three for Hana. A little sushi train on the screen announced *Prize Game!* and nobody won.

"Here's the deal," Tsubasa said, wiping her hands. "I'm out there every Saturday. Same spot. You bring a synth, somethin' with batteries. You do the drift, I'll do the shreddin'. We figure out that Hirasawa song for real."

"I— my synths aren't very portable. And I've never played in front of anyone. And—"

"That's a lotta 'ands.'"

Hana looked down at her empty tuna plate. Then back up.

"I have a Volca. It runs on batteries. And I can sequence the vocal parts, maybe. If I sample them."

Tsubasa's grin spread slowly across her whole face.

"Saturday, then, Headphones."

"Saturday," Hana said, and didn't apologize for it.

This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges.

Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior.

The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). response:
# Stolen Moments in Roma

**Morning — Fontana di Trevi**

Ben Ashworth stepped backward off the curb to fit Neptune entirely into his field of vision, and Rome tried to kill him.

It came as a shriek of brakes and a blur of red metal. Then a front tyre stopped a hand's width from his shins, and a woman in a scuffed leather jacket was shouting at him in Italian so fast it sounded like percussion.

"—*ma sei scemo?* You walk with your eyes in a book, in *Roma*? You want to die beautiful, at the fountain, like a postcard?"

"I'm so sorry. *Mi dispiace.* *Sono*—" He groped for the phrase book in his head. "*Sono molto caldo.*"

She stared at him. Then she laughed, a real laugh, head thrown back, helmet dangling from one hand.

"You just told me you are very hot. In the *other* way."

"Oh God."

"It's fine. It's flattering." She pulled off a glove and pushed back a tangle of dark hair. "Alessandra."

"Ben. Benedict. Ben."

"Three names. Very English."

She bent to retrieve his guidebook from the cobbles and dusted it off with exaggerated care. Only later would he realise his fountain pen had left his breast pocket in the same motion.

He looked at the motorcycle, an old Ducati, its tank streaked with a violent slash of turquoise paint, as if something bright and unfortunate had kissed it at speed.

"What happened there?"

Alessandra smiled. "Ask me something else."

---

**Late Morning — Prati**

"I have four deliveries," she said, "and you have no plans."

"I have extensive plans. The Pantheon at eleven, the Capitoline Museums—"

"Get on."

He got on.

He had never ridden pillion on anything. He held her waist with the delicacy of a man handling a museum artefact until she took a corner the wrong way down a one-way street and he grabbed on properly, face pressed into leather that smelled of exhaust and oranges.

"Better," she shouted over her shoulder.

At a law office near the Vatican, she signed for a parcel. She flirted outrageously with an elderly receptionist, who blushed to her collar. When they left, a heavy silver letter opener was gone from the desk. Ben saw it vanish into her sleeve. He opened his mouth. He closed it.

He did not know why.

---

**Midday — Campo de' Fiori**

She haggled with a fruit seller as if it were a blood sport, both of them gesturing at the heavens. While the man appealed to the Madonna, a peach rolled into her jacket pocket.

She caught Ben watching and raised one eyebrow, a dare.

He bought two lemons he didn't need, paid too much, and said nothing about the peach. Walking away, his heart was going as fast as it had at the fountain.

They sat on the base of Giordano Bruno's statue. She split the stolen peach with her thumbs and handed him half.

"You're a professor," she said. It wasn't a question.

"Lecturer. Medieval manuscripts. I'm on sabbatical, writing a book about marginalia, the little drawings monks left in the borders. Snails fighting knights. Rabbits with swords."

"So you study people misbehaving where nobody is supposed to look."

He considered this. "I suppose I do."

"*Bravo.*" She licked juice from her wrist. "Finally you are interesting."

---

**Afternoon — A rooftop in Trastevere**

The building's door was locked. Alessandra was not deterred by locks. A drainpipe, a balcony with someone's geraniums, a second balcony, and then they were on terracotta tiles. All of Rome spread out below them, domes and aerials and swallows wheeling in the gold.

Ben, who had once filed a complaint about an uneven staircase, sat with his back to a chimney. He was shaking, and he was elated.

"Are we allowed up here?"

"Nobody is *allowed* anywhere, Ben. That's the secret of the whole city."

She lay back on the warm tiles. He looked at her, at the scar through one eyebrow and the restlessness that never quite left her hands, and found he had forgotten every word in every language he knew.

She turned her head. Their faces were very close.

"You're thinking something," she said.

"I'm thinking I've never done anything like this."

"I know." For a moment her expression flickered into something unguarded, almost sad. Then it was gone, and she stood, brushing dust from her jeans. "Come. The light is better on the bridge, and you look like a man who needs a drink."

---

**Evening — A bar off Piazza di Santa Maria**

Wine in thick tumblers. A waiter who knew her name and sighed when he said it. She told him nothing true about herself, or perhaps everything. A father who drove taxis. A brother in Milan. Three jobs she'd been fired from, each story more improbable than the last.

When the bill came, Ben looked at the small silver teaspoon on his saucer. Engraved, old, worn thin by a century of espresso.

He slipped it into his pocket.

Alessandra went very still. Then she smiled, slowly, the way you'd smile at a cat that had just learned to open doors.

"Look at you," she murmured. "Who taught you that?"

"I believe," Ben said, his voice not entirely steady, "it was you."

---

**Night — Fontana di Trevi**

She brought him back to where it started. The fountain was lit pale blue, still crowded, coins glinting under the water.

"Your hotel is that way," she said. "Five minutes. Even you can't get lost."

"Alessandra—"

She stepped close, rose onto her toes, and kissed him once. It was quick and warm and tasted of wine and peaches. Before he could do anything as foolish as speak, she pressed his fountain pen back into his hand.

"You dropped this," she said, which was a lie, and they both knew it.

She swung onto the Ducati. The turquoise scar caught the light.

"Will I see you again?"

She kicked the engine into a roar and didn't answer. She just lifted two fingers from the handlebar and was gone, swallowed by the traffic.

Ben stood there a long while. Then he reached into his pocket for the teaspoon, the first thing he had ever stolen, wanting to hold the proof of it.

It was gone.

In its place was a crumpled delivery slip. On the back, in fast, slanting handwriting, was an address in Testaccio and a time: *Domani, 9:00. Bring the guidebook. I want to see what you have underlined.*

He reached for the guidebook.

That was gone too.

Ben Ashworth, lecturer in medieval manuscripts and filer of complaints about uneven staircases, began to laugh alone in the blue light of the fountain, and he could not stop.

# Stolen Moments in Roma

**10:14 a.m. — Fontana di Trevi**

The scooter came out of the Via delle Muratte like a hornet out of a bottle. Ben Hartley had been reading about the 1762 completion of Salvi's masterpiece when the guidebook flew from his hands, the world tilted, and a front tyre stopped a hand's width from his shins.

"*Ma sei scemo?* You stand in the street like a lamppost! You want to die? Die somewhere else, I have a schedule!"

She pulled off her helmet. Black hair, a scar through one eyebrow, eyes like burnt coffee.

"I'm so terribly sorry," Ben said. "*Mi dispiace.* I am... *sono un...*" His mind offered him nothing but the menu from last night. "*Sono un formaggio.*"

She stared at him. Then she laughed, a loud, unladylike bark that turned three tourists around.

"You are a cheese."

"I meant *straniero*. Foreigner. Possibly also a cheese."

"Possibly." She looked him over: the linen jacket, the sensible shoes, the pen still clutched in his hand. "Alessandra."

"Ben. Benjamin. Ben."

"Three names. Very English." She plucked the pen from his fingers, examined it, and tucked it behind her ear as though it had always been hers. "I have three deliveries, Ben-Benjamin-Ben. Then I show you Rome. Not this Rome." She waved at the fountain, the selfie sticks, the coins. "The real one. Get on."

"I really shouldn't."

"No," she agreed. "Get on."

---

**11:02 a.m. — Monti**

He held her waist as if it might be electrified. They went the wrong way down a one-way street, mounted a pavement, and scattered a congress of pigeons. Ben said "Sorry" to every one of them.

At a lawyer's office she handed over an envelope, flirted briefly with the receptionist, and came out tossing a small glass paperweight from hand to hand.

"Was that a gift?"

"Everything is a gift, if you are quick enough." She dropped it into her courier bag. "Hold tight, *professore*."

"I never said I was a professor."

"You didn't have to. You apologize to birds."

---

**12:40 p.m. — Campo de' Fiori**

The market was a riot of artichokes and shouting. Alessandra moved through it like a fish through reeds, chatting with a vendor about his mother's hip while her hand drifted across his crates. When they emerged she pressed a peach into Ben's palm, still warm from the sun.

"Did you pay for this?"

"Eat it before it gets sad."

He should have taken it back. He knew exactly what his mother, his department chair, and his late Anglican grandfather would have said. He bit into it instead. Juice ran down his wrist, and Alessandra watched with the frank interest of a scientist observing a successful experiment.

"Good?"

"Criminally."

"Now you are learning Italian."

---

**3:15 p.m. — A rooftop somewhere near the Pantheon**

"This is someone's property," Ben whispered, halfway up a rusted fire escape.

"This is *my* property. For one hour." She hauled him over the parapet onto a terrace of terracotta pots and drying laundry. Below them the city spread out in domes and bell towers, honey-coloured in the afternoon haze.

They sat with their backs against a chimney. She asked what he studied.

"Medieval marginalia. The notes monks scribbled in the margins of manuscripts. Doodles, complaints. One wrote, *'Now I've written the whole thing, for Christ's sake give me a drink.'*"

"So you study people who write in books that are not theirs." She smiled slowly. "Little thieves of the margins."

"I've never thought of it like that."

"You think too much like that." She tapped his temple with his own stolen pen. "Not enough like this." She pressed the pen to his chest, over his heart, and held it there a beat too long.

Ben forgot how to breathe, which seemed unwise on a roof.

She stood abruptly. "Come. A woman is hanging out a bedsheet, and she has seen us."

---

**5:48 p.m. — Trastevere**

The sky split open without warning. One moment, gold light on cobblestones. The next, a grey wall of rain that sent waiters sprinting and Vespas skidding.

They ran, Alessandra laughing, Ben clutching his ruined guidebook, and crammed themselves beneath the striped awning of a tiny gelato shop. The canvas sagged and drummed. Water sheeted off the edges like a beaded curtain, sealing them in.

They were very close. He could smell rain in her hair, engine oil, and the faint ghost of peach.

She bought two cones: pistachio for herself, *stracciatella* for him, without asking. "You look like a stracciatella man. Nice, but with little surprises inside."

"Is that a compliment?"

"I haven't decided."

A drop of gelato slid onto his thumb. Before he could reach for a napkin, she caught his wrist, considered his hand for a long, unreadable moment, then let go and passed him the napkin instead.

"Not yet," she said, to no one in particular.

Ben had no idea what that meant. He suspected he would think about it for years.

While she paid, his eyes fell on the counter, where a jar of tiny pastel tasting spoons sat unattended. His heart pounded absurdly. He took one, a little pink plastic spade, and slid it into his jacket pocket.

When he turned around, she was watching him. Her eyebrows rose. Then she grinned, wide and wicked and utterly delighted, as if he'd recited a poem in perfect Italian.

"*Bravo*, professore," she murmured. "Now we are in trouble together."

---

**8:30 p.m. — Fontana di Trevi, again**

The rain had washed the crowds away. The fountain glowed turquoise under the floodlights, and the air smelled of wet stone.

"Full circle," Ben said. "You almost killed me here this morning."

"I almost *met* you here this morning. You should be more grateful." She straddled the scooter and pulled on her helmet. "Throw a coin. So you come back."

"I'm not leaving. Not for six months."

Something flickered behind the visor. Surprise, or calculation, or something softer she didn't want him to see. "Then throw it anyway. For luck. You will need it."

He fished in his pocket for a coin and found his wallet intact, which, given the day, felt like a minor miracle. He tossed the coin over his shoulder. When he turned back, the scooter was already roaring off down the Via delle Muratte, a red taillight swallowed by the dark.

She hadn't said goodbye. She hadn't asked for his number.

He reached for his pen to write down the day before it evaporated, and remembered that she still had it.

Then he opened his sodden guidebook. Tucked into the chapter on the Trevi Fountain was a crumpled courier slip, filled out in blunt capital letters:

*DELIVERY: ONE ENGLISH CHEESE.*
*RECIPIENT: ALESSANDRA.*
*SIGNATURE REQUIRED.*

Beneath it was a phone number and, clipped to the paper, his pen.

In the margin, in the same hand: *I return only what I want back.*

Ben stood in the rain-washed piazza, a stolen spoon in his pocket and a stolen heart he hadn't noticed going missing, and laughed out loud.

response:
# Stolen Moments in Roma

The scooter came out of Via delle Muratte like a hornet. Ben Hartley saw it only because he looked up from page forty-seven of *Rome: A Scholar's Companion* at exactly the wrong moment, or the right one.

Brakes shrieked. A front tyre stopped a hand's width from his shins. The guidebook flew and landed face-down in a puddle of gelato.

"*Ma sei scemo?* You stand in the middle of the street like a statue! Are you a statue? Are you made of marble? *Rispondi!*"

The rider pulled off her helmet, and a mass of dark curls tumbled free. She had a scar through one eyebrow and an expression that could have stripped paint.

"I'm so sorry," Ben said. "*Mi dispiace.* Terribly. *Io sono... molto...*" He groped for the word. "*Burro?*"

She stared at him. "You are butter?"

"I meant *mortificato*."

"No. You said butter." Her mouth twitched, then gave way entirely. She laughed, a loud, unbothered laugh that made two Japanese tourists turn around. "Okay, Signor Burro. You are not dead. I am not late. Well, I am late, but not because of you."

She bent, plucked his guidebook from the gelato, and frowned at it. "This is a terrible book."

"It was written by my doctoral supervisor."

"Then he is a terrible man." She tucked it into her courier bag. "Get on."

"I'm sorry?"

"You see the Trevi from a book. Stupid. Get on, I have three deliveries, and then I show you Rome. The real one."

He did not know why he got on. Afterwards he would decide it was the eyebrow.

---

Ben learned three things in the first hour.

The first was that Alessandra Ricci drove through Roman traffic the way a needle goes through silk, and that the correct response to a bus filling his entire field of vision was apparently to lean left.

The second was that her deliveries were very odd: a sealed envelope for a lawyer in Prati, a box of cannoli for a monsignor who tipped her in euros and a blessing, and a cello bow for a woman in a dressing gown who cried when she saw it.

The third he noticed at a coffee bar near Piazza Navona, where they drank espresso standing up because, she said, sitting was for Germans. When they left, the little silver spoon from her saucer was no longer on the counter.

He told himself he'd imagined it.

---

"This is closed," Ben said.

They were standing at a rusted gate behind a church on the Aventine. A chain hung across it, with a sign that even his Italian could manage: *VIETATO L'INGRESSO.*

"Closed is a suggestion." She was already over, landing lightly in the overgrown grass on the other side. "Come, Professore."

"I'm not a professor. I'm a senior lecturer in medieval paleography."

"I don't know what that is, and it sounds sad. Climb."

He climbed. His trousers caught on a spike and tore with a noise like a small scream. She clapped.

Beyond the gate was a forgotten garden: bitter oranges gone wild, a cracked fountain choked with ivy, and a stone bench where she lay down full length and looked up at the sky.

"My nonno used to bring me here," she said. "Before they locked it. Before they lock everything." She turned her head. "In England, do you climb gates?"

"I once returned a library book two days late," Ben said. "I still think about it."

She laughed so hard she nearly fell off the bench, and he felt, absurdly, as though he had won something.

---

Campo de' Fiori, late afternoon, the market packing up. Alessandra moved between the stalls like she owned them. A peach vanished from one crate. A sprig of rosemary disappeared from another. She tossed the peach to Ben, and he caught it before he understood what he was holding.

"Alessandra. Did you pay for—"

"*Ale!*"

A heavy woman in a flowered apron was bearing down on them, wiping her hands on a cloth. Ben braced for a scene. Instead the woman kissed Alessandra on both cheeks, scolded her in a torrent of dialect, and kissed her again.

Then she turned to Ben, looked him slowly up and down, torn trousers and all, and switched to careful English.

"You are with her?"

"I... yes? Today. I think."

The woman leaned close. She smelled of basil and cigarettes. "I am Pina. I know this one since she is six years old, stealing my apricots." She tapped his chest with a thick finger. "Listen to me. When she shakes your hand, you count your fingers after. *Capito?*"

"Pina!" Alessandra protested, all wide eyes and innocence.

"Your fingers, *inglese*," Pina said, walking away. "And your heart. Count that too."

Ben looked down at the peach in his hand. Alessandra plucked it back and bit into it, juice running down her wrist.

"She exaggerates," she said. "I only took her apricots twice."

"And the spoon at the café?"

She went very still. Then she smiled slowly, the way a cat smiles at a closed window it has decided to open anyway.

"You see more than you pretend, Signor Burro."

---

They watched the sun go down from the Gianicolo, the whole city turning gold and rose below them. Domes, bell towers, a thousand terracotta roofs. She sat on the parapet with her boots dangling over the drop, and he had stopped telling her to be careful hours ago.

"Why me?" he asked. "You nearly ran me over, and then you kidnapped me."

"You came willingly. That is not kidnapping." She considered the question honestly, which surprised him. "You looked like a man reading about his own life instead of living it. It made me angry." A shrug. "Also, you said you were butter."

She drove him back to his hotel near the Pantheon. Under a streetlamp, she pulled his guidebook out of her bag and pressed it into his hands, still sticky with pistachio gelato.

"Tomorrow, maybe," she said. "Maybe not. Rome is big."

Then she was gone in a snarl of engine and exhaust.

In the lobby, Ben reached for his grandfather's fountain pen to sign for his key, and found his breast pocket empty. He laughed aloud, alone, and the night porter looked at him with concern.

Upstairs he opened the guidebook. On the map of Trastevere, in his own green ink, from his own stolen pen, she had circled a tiny piazza:

*Domani. Ore 9. Bring something worth stealing. — A.*

Ben sat on the edge of the bed. Slowly, he drew his hand from his jacket pocket and opened it.

In his palm lay a tortoiseshell hair clip. It had come loose from her curls on the Aventine bench, and he had picked it up and, for reasons he could not explain to any medieval paleographer living or dead, said nothing about it at all.

He turned it over in the lamplight and smiled.

Two could play.

prompt:
Darkroom Revelations

Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. A stack of photo paper is accidentally exposed, rendering it useless mid-session. 1000 words.
response:
# Darkroom Revelations

The safelight makes everyone look like a secret.

I've thought that since my first semester, but I've never thought it as hard as I do now, watching Elliot bend over the developer tray. The red catches the silver rings stacked on his fingers and pools in the hollow of his collarbone where his thrifted mesh shirt slips sideways. His nail polish is chipped black. Mine is always perfect. I've started wondering which of us is more honest.

"Twenty seconds," he murmurs, rocking the tray. The image surfaces slowly: a stairwell, all hard diagonals. My shot. He's printing it better than I would have.

I'm used to being the one who decides things. Where we eat, when we leave, who kisses whom and how hard. People seem relieved when I take the wheel. My exes were all clean silhouettes, square-jawed boys or sharp, certain women, people I could read from across a bar. I like a defined subject, I used to tell my critique group. I like contrast.

Elliot is not high contrast. Elliot is all midtones.

"Can I tell you something weird?" he asks the stop bath.

"Weird is my favourite genre."

He tongs the print into the fixer and doesn't look at me. The timer ticks. Somewhere down the hall, a film dryer hums.

"I've been thinking," he says, "that maybe 'boy' is a coat I picked up because it was on the rack. And it fits okay. But I don't know if it's mine." He laughs, a small embarrassed puff. "That sounded better in my head."

Everything in me leans forward at once. I want to hug him. I want to tell him about the queer collective that meets Thursdays, the binder-and-makeup swap, the professor who changed her name junior year. I want to take him thrifting for something he's never let himself try. I want to fix it, which is what I do. I'm already opening my mouth: *Okay, so what you should do is—*

I close it.

Because it isn't mine to fix. Not the way I'd want to. He didn't hand me a problem. He handed me something fragile, and the worst thing I could do is grab it.

"It sounded fine," I say instead. "It sounded true."

He finally looks at me. In the red light his eyeliner is just a dark smudge, his eyes almost black. "You're not going to tell me what it means?"

"Do you want me to?"

A long pause. "No," he says. "I think I want to figure it out. But I wanted someone to know I was figuring."

"Then I know."

He smiles, and something in my chest does a thing I don't have a name for. That's the part that scares me. I always have a name for it.

We work in silence for a while, easier silence. He shows me a strip of negatives from his bag, self-portraits he shot in his dorm mirror. In the inverted image it's hard to tell what he's wearing: something with straps, something soft. He doesn't explain and I don't ask.

"I want to print one," he says. "I just haven't been brave enough to see it positive."

"We can do it tonight. Or not. Your call."

"Will you stay while I do it?"

"I'll stay as long as you want."

He feeds the negative into the enlarger, and I feel something unfamiliar: the urge to step back. To be the person holding the door instead of the person walking through it. It's so foreign it almost feels like vertigo.

And because I can't stand vertigo, I do something stupid.

I want to see his face. Really see it, not in this soaked crimson, but in plain light, to check whether he's okay or whether I'm just projecting. My hand finds the switch by the door before my brain catches up.

The overhead fluorescents slam on.

"*Dani—*"

The box of fiber paper is sitting open on the counter. A full box. Fifty sheets of the good Ilford stuff we split the cost of, sitting there drinking in the light like it's dying of thirst.

I slap the switch off. Red again. Too late.

Elliot stares at the box. I stare at Elliot. "I'm so sorry," I say. "I'm so — that was *ninety dollars*, that was the whole final, I just wanted to see if you were—"

"If I was what?"

"Okay," I say helplessly. "I wanted to see if you were okay. In real light."

For a second he says nothing. Then he pulls a sheet from the ruined box and slides it into the developer. We watch it together. No image, just white going gray going black, the whole page surrendering at once.

"That's what happens," he says quietly, "when you expose something before it's ready."

I flinch. He bumps my shoulder with his.

"I'm teasing. Mostly." He's smiling again. "You know you can just ask if I'm okay, right? You don't have to turn the lights on."

"Are you okay?"

"Yeah." He considers. "Weirdly, yeah. Are *you*?"

Nobody asks me that. I'm the one who asks.

"I don't know," I admit. "I don't really know what I'm doing here. With you. I usually know."

"Is that bad?"

I think about the stairwell print, the soft gray that made it beautiful. I think about how I've spent the whole semester watching him and calling it curiosity.

"No," I say. "I think it's new."

He nods like that's an answer, which maybe it is. Then he reaches past me, close enough that I can smell vetiver and fixer on his sleeve, and takes the one sealed packet we have left: ten sheets, the emergency stash.

"Ten tries," he says. "Better make them count."

He slides his self-portrait back into the enlarger and sets the timer. His hand hovers over the button, then he glances at me.

"Together?"

I could press it for him. A month ago I would have.

Instead I put my hand over his and let him decide when.

He presses down. The light blooms. And in the red dark, side by side, we wait to see what develops.
