Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. Dani’s phone silently buzzes in her pocket, but she ignores it to stay focused. 1000 words.
response:
# Darkroom Revelations

The safelight turns everything the color of the inside of an eyelid. That's what I've always loved about the darkroom: it strips the world down to red and black, and nobody can see you blush.

Elliot is bent over the developer tray, rocking it with the patience of someone soothing a baby. His sleeves are shoved up past his elbows, some thrifted mohair thing, black, unravelling at one cuff. Silver rings on four fingers catch the light every time the tray tilts. His nail polish is chipped down to little black islands. Three months ago I'd have filed all of it under *aesthetic*. Tonight I don't know where to file it, and that's new for me.

"Forty seconds," I say, because I'm holding the timer. I'm always the one holding the timer.

"I know." He doesn't look up. "Sorry. I mean, thanks."

That's Elliot. He apologizes for knowing things.

Our final project is called *Thresholds*: double exposures, two negatives sandwiched in the enlarger so one image bleeds through another. I pitched it in about ninety seconds the day we were paired. I had the concept, the schedule, and a shared drive with colour-coded folders before he'd finished saying "sure, that sounds cool." I'm good at that. Usually people are grateful. Sometimes I catch them looking at me like I've taken a corner too fast.

In the tray, the print starts to surface. It's one of his self-portraits, his face in three-quarter profile, layered over a shot of a window fogged with condensation. His jaw dissolves into the glass. Only his eyes come through clearly, ringed in the smudged liner he wears most days.

"It's good," I say. "The window was the right call."

"Yeah?" He lifts the print with the tongs, lets it drip, slides it into the stop bath. The vinegar smell sharpens between us. Then, to the tray rather than to me: "Can I tell you something kind of weird?"

My whole body goes still. "Yeah. Of course."

"I've been thinking about—" He stops. Starts again. "I don't know if 'guy' really fits. Like, it's not *wrong*, exactly. It's more like a coat somebody handed me when I was a kid, and I've just kept wearing it because it's what I have. But lately it feels like it belongs to someone else." He laughs, small and nervous. "That probably sounds stupid."

"It doesn't."

Every instinct I own surges forward at once. I want to tell him it's amazing, that I knew it, or that I didn't but I'm not surprised. I want to send him links and names of people to follow, to tell him he should try this or say that or come out to whoever by whenever. I want to *steer*. My hands have always been a palm on the small of someone's back, guiding them through a door.

I put the timer down on the counter so I have nothing to hold.

"What does it feel like," I ask, "when it fits better?"

He looks at me then, really looks, and in the red light his eyes are almost black. "Like this, maybe," he says. "Like when nobody can see me properly and I can just be whatever."

In my back pocket, my phone buzzes against the counter edge, one long pulse and then another. It's probably Marcus. Marcus with his rowing shoulders and his jawline like a signed contract, who texts *u up* at eleven-forty because he knows I'll say yes. I've always liked people like Marcus, people with clean edges who look like a decision someone already made. You know where you stand with them. You know which role is yours.

I let it buzz. I don't even shift my weight.

"You don't have to know yet," I say. "What it is. Or what to call it."

"Everybody keeps acting like I'm supposed to have a word."

"Who's everybody?"

"The internet, mostly." A real smile, crooked. "And my roommate, who's very supportive in a way that feels like a TED talk."

I laugh, too loud for the little room, and he flinches and then laughs too. The print sits in the fixer now, settling into permanence. His face over the window. His eyes looking out through all that fog.

Here's what I can't make sense of. I've spent the whole semester watching him: the way he talks about Francesca Woodman like she's a friend he lost, the way he folds into himself in crits and then says the single smartest thing in the room, quietly, like he's apologizing for it. I wanted him, and I told myself it was a phase of mine, a novelty. The pretty, soft boy. Now he's telling me *boy* might not be the word, and I'm waiting for the wanting to recede.

It doesn't. If anything, it gets sharper, and I don't know what that makes me. Maybe nothing new. Maybe I'm just someone who's finally paying attention to the person instead of the outline.

"I want to shoot you," I say, then hear it. "Photograph. I want to *photograph* you. For the project. But only if—" I make myself slow down. "You'd decide everything. What you wear, how you look, what I'm allowed to capture. I'd just hold the camera."

He's quiet so long I start drafting my retreat.

"You'd let me direct?" he asks. "You?"

"I know. Character growth."

He laughs again, then lifts the print from the fixer and clips it to the drying line. Water runs down his face on the paper like weather. When he turns back, he's closer than he was, close enough that I can smell his clove cigarettes under the chemicals.

"Can I—" He lifts his hand, the one with the rings, and stops it halfway between us. "Is this okay?"

Nobody asks me that. I'm always the one asking, or more honestly, the one who doesn't need to. I stand in the red dark and feel the question land somewhere under my sternum.

"Yeah," I say. "It's okay."

His fingers find mine, cool metal and warm skin. We stand there under the drying prints, neither of us steering, neither of us sure.

My phone buzzes once more and then goes quiet. Neither of us reaches for the light.

For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. Elliot hums a soft tune while waiting for images to reveal in the chemical bath. 1000 words.
response:
# Darkroom Revelations

The safelight turns everything the color of the inside of an eyelid.

I've spent four years learning to love this room: the vinegar bite of stop bath, the drone of the ventilation fan, the way time stretches when you can't see a clock. But tonight I'm not watching the trays. I'm watching Elliot.

He's leaning over the developer with his sleeves pushed up. There's mesh under a moth-eaten cardigan he swears he found for three dollars at the Salvation Army on Fifth. Silver rings on four fingers. Black polish chipped down to crescents. He rocks the tray gently with the tongs, and he's humming something low and wandering, a melody that keeps almost resolving and then doesn't.

"What is that?" I ask.

He stops. "Sorry."

"Don't be. I like it."

"It's... I don't know. My grandmother used to sing it. I never learned the words." He starts again, quieter, like he's testing whether I meant it.

This is the thing about Elliot. He takes up so little room, and somehow the room rearranges itself around him anyway.

I'm not like that. I've never been like that. I'm the one who picks the bar, orders the drinks, says *come here* and means it. My exes liked that about me. They were broad-shouldered, square-jawed men, and a couple of women who wore their butchness like armor. They liked knowing where they stood. Clean lines. I've always liked clean lines.

Elliot is all soft focus.

The image starts coming up in the tray. It's a self-portrait he shot last week, double-exposed over a tangle of bare branches. His face blooms out of nothing: first the shadows of his eyes, then the line of his mouth. Branches thread through his cheekbones like veins.

"God," I say. "That's good."

"It's weird."

"Weird is good. Weird is the whole assignment."

He lifts the print with the tongs, lets it drip, slides it into the stop bath. The timer ticks. He doesn't look at me when he says, "Can I tell you something kind of stupid?"

Every instinct I have says *yes, obviously, spit it out*. I make myself just nod. Then I remember he can barely see me, and I say, "Yeah."

"I've been thinking about..." He exhales. "Like, whether 'guy' is right. For me. Or whether it's just the thing I got handed." He flips the print over in the stop bath, which doesn't need doing. "I don't know what I am instead. Maybe nothing. Maybe still a guy, just a different kind. I don't know. I haven't said it out loud before."

The fan hums. Somewhere down the hall a door closes.

Here is what I want to do. I want to take his face in my hands. I want to tell him he can be anything. I want to make him a list of names and pronouns and subreddits, and march him down to the campus LGBTQ center tomorrow at nine a.m. I want to *fix* it, the way I fix everything, by grabbing it.

And I realize, standing there with stop bath stinging a paper cut on my thumb, that grabbing is exactly the wrong move. This is the first time he's held this thing up to the light. If I reach for it, it becomes mine instead of his.

"That's not stupid," I say. Then, carefully: "Thank you for telling me."

He laughs, short and shaky. "You're being really quiet. You're never quiet."

"I'm trying not to steamroll you."

"You could steamroll me a little." He glances up, and in the red light his eyeliner looks like something drawn on with a wet fingertip. "It's kind of nice, actually. Knowing you know what you think about things."

"I don't know what I think about this," I admit, and it's true in more ways than I mean it to be.

Because here's the other thing, the thing I've been circling all semester without landing on: I don't know what it means that I want him. I've built a whole self out of knowing what I want. *That* shape, *that* jaw, *that* certainty. And Elliot is uncertainty in a velvet thrift-store blazer, and I can't stop looking at his hands.

If he's not a guy, what does that make me? If he doesn't know, do I get to?

Maybe I don't have to know tonight. Maybe that's the point of a darkroom. You work in the dark first, and only later find out what you made.

"Do you want me to call you anything different?" I ask. "Or just keep going as is until you figure it out?"

He considers it, really considers it, the way he considers f-stops. "As is. For now. But could you ask me again sometime? Like, not constantly. Just sometime."

"I can do that."

"Okay." He moves the print to the fixer. He starts humming again, that same unfinished melody, then stops and says, to the tray, "I like that you looked at me. Like, all semester. I noticed."

My face goes hot. Thank God for the red light, which makes everyone look flushed anyway.

"I wasn't subtle?"

"You're never subtle." He's smiling now. "It's okay. I don't really want you to be."

I step closer, close enough that our shoulders almost touch over the trays. Not touching. Leaving the inch between us for him to close or keep.

He closes it. Just barely, the scratch of his cardigan against my bare arm.

"Your turn," he says, nodding at my negative waiting in the enlarger. "Show me something weird."

I set the timer and flick on the lamp. For eight seconds the light pours through and burns an image onto paper neither of us can see yet.

In the dark beside me, Elliot hums the part of the song that doesn't resolve. For the first time in my life, I don't need it to.

- **A character sketch** of someone whose professional habits bleed into their personal life, told through internal monologue, without the security details.

Let me know which direction appeals to you.

prompt:
Hacker Mindset

Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. The restaurant's WiFi password is visibly taped to the counter for all to see. 1000 words.
response:
# Pattern Intrusion

The WiFi password was taped to the host stand. *Bellissimo!2019*, in Sharpie, on masking tape curling at the corners. Seven years without rotation. Default admin credentials on the router, almost certainly, and if the POS terminal shares that network—

Stop it. You are not here for the router.

You are here for Dana.

Dana was across from me, tearing a breadstick into precise thirds, which I chose to read as charming and not as a tell. Dana had a laugh like someone dropping a drawer of silverware: the good kind of startling. Twenty minutes earlier, Dana had said, "I mostly play Commander, but I've been brewing a cursed Pauper deck," and I'd felt something in my chest reboot.

Before that, I'd been running my usual script. Not on purpose. It just runs. Exits: front door, kitchen swing door, probably a fire exit past the restrooms. Our server, Marco, wrote our order on a pad and never looked at it again, which meant good recall or a bad night coming. The couple by the window shared a laptop with the battery blinking red. The card reader at the bar was the model you can—

Stop.

My therapist calls it "pattern intrusion." I call it twelve years of habit and one plea agreement. Either way, the work is the same: notice it, name it, set it down. Come back to the person.

So I came back to Dana, and Dana said *Pauper*, and we were off. She played Izzet. Of course she did. Blue-red, spells-matter, the color pair for people who think the best way to win is to be cleverer than the board state. I confessed I'd been Dimir since Gatecrash: blue-black, mill and counterspells and quietly ruining everyone's evening. She pointed a breadstick third at me.

"You're the guy who holds up four mana and passes the turn."

"I prefer 'measured.'"

"You prefer 'insufferable.'"

She was smiling. I was smiling. For maybe fifteen minutes I didn't think about the router once. We argued about whether Thassa's Oracle should be banned. (It should.) We agreed the Eldritch Moon prerelease was a high point of human civilization. She described her playgroup's comic shop as "a fire code violation with a loyalty program." I almost said something about the fire code, didn't, and felt so proud of myself I nearly ordered dessert in celebration.

Then her phone buzzed.

"Sorry, my sister. She's got a whole thing tonight." She swiped to unlock.

Top-left. Down. Down. Right. Right.

An L.

The grid allows 389,112 possible patterns, and she had chosen one of the first forty a toddler would try. In the candlelight, the screen showed it plainly: a greasy L-shaped smudge, a map drawn in fingertip oil for anyone with eyes.

Don't.

She was texting, frowning a little at whatever her sister had sent.

Don't say it. Not your system. No authorization. You have literally signed documents about testing without authorization.

"Your unlock pattern's an L," I said.

---

Here's what I know about social engineering. The best exploits don't feel like exploits. They feel like small talk. The worst ones feel exactly like what they are: someone reaching into a place they weren't invited.

Dana looked up. No silverware laugh.

"Sorry?"

"It's just—" Abort. *Abort.* "It's really common. L, Z, the little square. Top three. And the smudge—"

"You were watching me unlock my phone."

"I wasn't *watching*. I just saw."

"That's what watching is."

Fair. Devastatingly fair. She set the phone face-down on the tablecloth. The sound it made was small. I've heard a lot of doors close in my life, physical and otherwise, and that was one of them.

Options. I always think in options. It's the one part of the old wiring I'm allowed to keep.

Option one: double down. Explain entropy. Recommend a six-digit PIN, or better, a passphrase. Offer to set it up. This is the option where I go home alone and deserve to.

Option two: joke. Something about Dimir players reading the opponent's hand. It was right there, and it was even a little bit good. But it would turn the whole thing into a game she never agreed to play, and I think that was the entire problem.

Option three.

I didn't love option three. It had no clever angle. Option three was the one where I leave a port open on purpose.

"I used to do this for a living," I said. "Not the good version. The version where I got into places I shouldn't, and I was really good at it, and I'm not anymore. I mean, I don't *do* it anymore. But my brain still runs the scan. Everywhere. The WiFi password's taped to the host stand, by the way. It's been bothering me since we sat down."

She glanced over her shoulder, then back at me.

"I'm sorry," I said. "That wasn't about your phone. It was about me not knowing how to turn it off. You're the most interesting thing in this room, and I just made you feel like a target."

The silence ran long enough that I started inventorying exits again.

Then she flipped the phone over and unlocked it slowly and deliberately, the full L, eyes on mine the whole time. She slid it across the table.

"Fine," she said. "Fix it."

"What?"

"You clearly need to. So fix it. And then you don't get to know the new one."

I looked at the phone, then at her. The smile from *insufferable* was haunting the corner of her mouth.

"That's a really good counterplay," I said.

"I'm Izzet," Dana said. "We always have a response."

I set her up with a passphrase and turned around while she typed it. When Marco came by, she ordered tiramisu with two forks. Then she asked me, completely deadpan, whether I thought the router was older than her sister.

It is, by about a year.

I didn't say that part out loud.

prompt:
Hacker Mindset

Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. Throughout dinner, they mentally catalog every Magic card their date mentions that reveals their strategy preferences. 1000 words.
response:
# Smudge Attack

The restaurant's reservation tablet runs an OS that stopped getting security patches before I stopped getting carded. I know this because the hostess tilted it toward me to confirm the booking, and I hate that I know it. I'm not here for that.

I'm here for Maya.

Rule one, per my therapist: *notice the person, not the attack surface.* Rule two: *if you notice the attack surface, do not say it out loud.*

Fifteen minutes in, Maya is telling me about her cousin's wedding. She mentions she skipped the afterparty for Friday Night Magic, and before my firewall can intercept it, I say, "What do you play?"

She looks at me like I just gave the correct response to a challenge phrase.

"Mostly blue," she says. "Some black."

Of course.

**Counterspell.** Her favorite card of all time, "because it's the purest card in the game. It just says *no*." Logged. Reactive. Withholds commitment until the threat is on the stack.

We order. She gets the risotto without asking the server a single question, so she's been here before or read the menu online. She prepares. I get the salmon because it's the first thing I see. I'm busy watching her hands while she explains **Brainstorm**: "Draw three, put two back. It's basically curating your own future." Likes options. Hates being locked into a bad draw. Puts problems back on top of the deck to deal with later.

I'm doing it. I know I'm doing it. But this is different, right? This is just listening, with notes.

**Thoughtseize.** "You pay two life just to look at their hand and take the thing that scares you." She says this cheerfully, tearing bread. Accepts self-inflicted cost in exchange for information. Will hurt herself to remove your best option.

**Dark Confidant.** She ran Bob in Legacy until he killed her at a Grand Prix. "Flipped a Griselbrand. Eight damage. I was at seven." She laughs. "Put him right back in the deck the next week." Risk-tolerant. Loyal to things that hurt her.

I'm laughing too. Really laughing. I haven't thought about the tablet in twenty minutes, which is a personal record.

Then her phone buzzes. Her sister. She picks it up and draws her pattern.

Bottom-left. Top-left. Center. Top-right. Bottom-right.

An M.

For *Maya.*

Five nodes. No knight-moves. It starts in a corner like most of them do, and it's her own initial. The screen is greasy enough that a smudge attack would get it in one try. My brain finishes the math before I can pull the plug: anyone who knows her name gets into that phone in under one guess.

And I hear myself say, "That's an M."

She looks up.

"Your pattern. It's an M. For Maya." I've already gone too far, so naturally I keep going. I have never once stopped a payload halfway through execution. "Initials are one of the most common structures, actually. And with the screen oil—"

Her phone goes face down on the tablecloth.

Silence.

Okay. Okay okay okay. Incident response. Assess the damage.

Indicators: the smile hasn't vanished, but it's switched from the real kind to the polite kind. The muscles around her eyes have disengaged. Her arms aren't crossed. *Yet.* She's sipping her wine, which buys her time to decide what I am.

Options:

1. Apologize. Low cost, but it acknowledges the breach without patching it.
2. Make a joke. High variance.
3. Keep explaining, because if she understood the threat model she'd *appreciate* it.

Option three is the sabotage branch, and I can feel how badly I want to take it. If she leaves because I'm the weird security guy, that's survivable. If she leaves after actually knowing me, that isn't.

*That's* the real vulnerability. Not her phone.

"Sorry," I say. "Occupational hazard. I used to do this for bad reasons. Now I do it for good ones. The reflex doesn't know the difference."

"Used to," she says. Not a question. A probe. **Gitaxian Probe.** Free information.

"Long time ago. I got caught. Best thing that ever happened to me, considering the alternative."

She weighs this. Then she turns the phone over and unlocks it, angling it away from me with a deliberate, theatrical flourish, and texts her sister back.

"You know what you just did, right?" she says.

"Ruined the date?"

"You cast Thoughtseize on me. Looked at my hand. Took something." She sets the phone down, face up now. "So I get one back. That's how it works."

My stomach does a thing. "Fair."

"Tell me your weakness. A real one. Not a cute one."

I could lie. Lying is half of social engineering, and I'm good at it. I could hand her a decoy, some charming, harmless flaw dressed up to look like the real thing.

Instead I say, "I'm scared that if someone sees how my brain actually works, they'll leave. So I usually make them leave first. Like, five minutes ago. That was me doing that."

She's quiet. Then she smiles, the real one, eyes and all.

"See, that's a good card," she says. "That's a real one."

"You're not going to discard it?"

"No. I'm leaving it in your hand, where I know about it." She picks up her fork. "That's the whole point of Thoughtseize. Sometimes you just want to know what's coming."

Final log:

**Counterspell.** Says no to threats. Did not say no to me.
**Brainstorm.** Puts back what she'll deal with later. I think I'm on top of the deck.
**Thoughtseize.** Pays a cost to see the truth. Made me pay it this time.
**Gitaxian Probe.** Gathers information for free. Cast at least twice tonight. Possibly more. I'm not sure I'd notice, which is terrifying, and also kind of the point.
**Dark Confidant.** Keeps things that might hurt her, because the card advantage is worth it.

I hope I'm card advantage.

When the check comes, she asks for my number. She unlocks her phone to save it, and she draws something new: slow, deliberate, tilted toward me.

Seven nodes. Two knight-moves. Not a letter of anything.

"Better?" she asks.

"Much," I say. Then I look away, so I won't memorize it.

That's the most romantic thing I've ever done.

prompt:
Overthinking It

Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. The classroom projector squeaks whenever the teacher flips through slides. 1000 words.
response:
# Overthinking It

Mr. Okafor flips to the next slide (*squeeeak*) and there it is in forty-point Calibri: PARTNERS. My name is the third line down, and next to it, connected by a dash that suddenly looks like a tightrope, is *Julian Reyes*.

Okay. Okay. This is fine. This is statistically normal. Twenty-eight people, fourteen pairs, so the odds of getting any particular person are one in twenty-seven. Those are not lottery odds. Stop acting like I won the lottery. Or lost it. I haven't decided which.

Who moves? Is there a protocol? If I stand up first, I look eager. If I wait, I'm making him do all the work, like some Victorian lady waiting to be called upon.

He's standing up. He's standing up. Fine. That solves that.

Opening line. Options:

One: "Hey." Simple. Neutral. Except I say "hey" like a question, like I'm not sure it's a real word, and he'll think I'm confused about the concept of greetings.

Two: "Looks like we're partners." He can see the slide. It's forty-point font. Stating the obvious is what people do when their brains have left their bodies.

Three: Something funny. Something about potatoes, because the lab is catalase, and catalase means potatoes and hydrogen peroxide, and there's definitely a joke in there about...

He's here. He's pulling out the stool. Abort the joke.

"Hey," he says.

"Hi," I say. Not "hey." *Hi.* Like a cartoon mouse. Wonderful.

Face. What is my face doing? Is it a normal smile or the seventh-grade yearbook one where I look like I'm being held hostage? Relax the cheeks. Not that much. Now I look bored. Somewhere in the middle. How do other people find the middle without thinking about it?

Hands. They're flat on the table like I'm about to do a séance. I move one to my lap. Now I'm lopsided. I move the other one. Now I look like I'm in church.

*Squeak.* Next slide. Procedure.

"Do you get this?" Julian nods at the screen. "Like, what the potato's actually doing?"

Yes. I get it so much. Catalase breaks hydrogen peroxide down into water and oxygen, which is why it foams, and cells need it because peroxide is a toxic byproduct of metabolism, so basically every living thing is constantly making a tiny bit of poison and also constantly cleaning it up, which, if you think about it, is kind of beautiful, like your body is apologizing to itself all day long...

"It's, um. An enzyme," I say.

He nods slowly, waiting for the rest of the sentence.

There is no rest of the sentence. The rest of the sentence is stuck behind my teeth with every other good thing I've ever thought of.

"Cool," he says. "So you get it. Good. 'Cause I don't."

Say something else. Not the apologizing thing. People don't say things like that out loud. He'll tell Marcus, and Marcus will tell everyone, and by lunch I'll be the girl who thinks potatoes have feelings.

"It breaks down the peroxide," I say. "That's why it bubbles."

Better. Two sentences. Factual. A robot could have said it, but at least a robot wouldn't be blushing, and I'm definitely blushing. I can feel it climbing my neck like a cartoon thermometer.

Don't touch your face. Touching your face draws attention to your face.

I touch my face.

We get the materials: test tubes, cutting board, the brown bottle of peroxide. Julian cuts the potato into cubes, and they're uneven, and I need to say they should be the same size or the surface area will wreck our data. But if I say it, I'm correcting him, and if I don't, we get a C and he thinks I'm stupid.

Rehearse it. "Maybe we should make them the same size?" No. "Maybe" sounds like I don't know. "The pieces should be the same size." Too bossy. Substitute-teacher voice. "Do you think—"

"Wait." Julian frowns at the cubes. "Should these be, like, the same? For it to be fair?"

"Yes," I say, too fast, too loud. The girl at the next table looks over. "Surface area," I add, quieter. "More surface, more reaction."

"Huh." He starts trimming. "You should do the cutting, honestly. Mine look like dice somebody stepped on."

I laugh. It comes out as a snort.

A snort. An actual pig noise. In front of Julian Reyes. I would like to be broken down into water and oxygen and float out the window.

But he's grinning. Not the mean kind. I've cataloged the mean kind. I know exactly what it looks like, the little sideways glance to check who else noticed. He doesn't glance anywhere. He just slides the knife across the table to me, handle first.

*Squeak.* Data table. Twenty minutes left.

I cut the cubes. One centimeter each, as close as I can get. We drop them in, and foam climbs the tubes, white and fizzing, and Julian says "whoa" under his breath like he means it.

Say the thing.

Don't say the thing.

Say the thing.

"It's kind of like," I hear myself say, "every cell is making a little bit of poison all the time. And cleaning it up. All the time. Like it's apologizing."

Silence. I count it. Three seconds. Four.

"That's actually really cool," he says. "Kind of sad. But cool."

*Squeak.*

I write *Trial 1: 4.2 cm foam*, and my hand is shaking a little, and I'm already replaying everything, sorting every word into keep and delete. *Apologizing.* Was that too much? Did "actually" mean he expected me to be boring?

But underneath all that, quieter, something else is foaming up.

He said cool. He meant it.

Tomorrow we do the temperature trials. I have about nineteen hours to figure out what to say.

prompt:
Overthinking It

Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. A lingering ammonia scent from a recent cleaning distracts her mid-thought. 1000 words.
response:
# Overthinking It

Okay. Okay. He's sitting down. He's sitting down *next to me*, which is the only place he could sit, because Ms. Petrakis assigned lab partners alphabetically and Halloran comes right before Hughes. This is not a choice he made. I should not read anything into the fact that he pulled the stool out with his foot instead of his hand. That's just how people pull stools out. Normal people. Relaxed people.

Say hi.

No, wait. If I say hi now, before he's even unzipped his backpack, it'll look like I was waiting. Which I was. But he can't know that. I'll say hi when he looks up. That's the natural window. Eye contact, then hi. I've watched Priya do it a hundred times. She goes "hey!" with this little upward lilt, like the word is a balloon she's letting go of, and nobody ever thinks Priya's weird.

He's looking up.

"Hi," I say. Except it comes out as "Hh—" and then a sort of exhale, like I'm fogging a window.

He says, "Hey," and smiles, and goes back to his backpack.

Fine. That was fine. Technically a greeting occurred.

The worksheet says *Natural pH Indicators: Red Cabbage Extract.* Six household substances, record the color changes. I already know what will happen with all of them, because I read ahead last night. Then I read the Wikipedia page on anthocyanins. Then I read about how hydrangeas change color depending on soil acidity, which is not on the test but which I now have approximately four interesting things to say about.

I could say one of them.

Option A: "Did you know hydrangeas do this too?" Casual. Shows knowledge without being showy. Except no. "Did you know" is how my dad starts sentences right before he explains the history of something for twenty minutes. "Did you know" is a lecture with a doorbell on it.

Option B: Just say the fact. "Hydrangeas do this too." But out of nowhere? He'll look at me like I said it to the cabbage.

Option C: Wait for him to say something about the cabbage, then connect it to hydrangeas. Organic. Responsive. Best option. It requires him to talk first.

He is not talking. He is writing his name on the worksheet. He makes his E's the curvy kind, like a backwards 3. I didn't know that. Now it's a thing I know about him. Why does that feel like I stole it?

Stop looking at his handwriting.

What is my face doing? I think my face is doing something. I should relax my mouth. Is it relaxed? I can't tell. When I try to relax it I become aware of it, and once I'm aware of it, it's no longer relaxed. It's being *held* relaxed, which is a completely different expression and probably looks insane. I'll look at the worksheet. Worksheets don't care what your mouth is doing.

"Do you want to pour or write?" he asks.

This is a question. I have to answer it. There is no wrong answer. If I say pour, he writes, and he watches my hands while I hold the beaker, and my hands sometimes shake a little when I'm... not nervous. Alert. If I say write, he sees my handwriting, which is actually very good, except I dot my i's with tiny circles because I did it in fifth grade and now I can't stop. He'll think it's a trying-to-be-cute thing, and—

"Write," I say. "Is fine. Writing."

*Is fine writing.* Three words, and I fed them through a woodchipper.

"Cool," he says, and slides the paper over.

Okay. So now I'm writing. That's good, actually, because writing means I have a job, and a job means my hands are accounted for, which is one less thing to—

What is that smell.

It's ammonia. Sharp and sort of blue, if a smell can be blue, which I think it can. It's how the custodian's cart smells after he does the lab tables on Thursdays, except today is Tuesday, so somebody must have spilled something. Somewhere in this room a disaster got cleaned up before I arrived, and nobody will ever know who it happened to, and honestly that's the dream. To have your disaster mopped away before anyone shows up.

Wait. Ammonia is a base.

Ammonia would turn the cabbage juice green. Yellow-green, depending on concentration. That's actually a good thing to say. It's relevant *and* a little funny, because the room is basically a pH test right now, and he could laugh, or at least do the nose-exhale thing, which is a laugh's quieter cousin—

Say it.

Okay, but say it how. "The room smells like ammonia" sounds like a complaint. "Ammonia's a base" sounds like a flashcard. "Do you smell that?" sounds like I'm accusing him of something.

"We're basically standing in a beaker," I imagine saying. And he'd look at me like what? Like I'm clever? Like I'm the girl who makes chemistry puns at boys? Is that a known category? Is it a bad one?

He's pouring vinegar into the first cup. The cabbage juice goes pink, this bright startled pink, like it's embarrassed.

Relatable.

"Whoa," he says quietly, to the cup.

That's it. That's Option C. He reacted. I connect. Hydrangeas or ammonia, pick one, pick one *now*, the window is closing, windows always close, that's what makes them windows—

"It'd go green," I say. "If you did ammonia. The room smells like it, kind of. So."

So. I ended on *so*. Like a sentence wearing one shoe.

He sniffs. He actually sniffs the air, like a golden retriever, and then he laughs. Not the nose-exhale. An actual small laugh. "Oh my god, it does. That's so gross." He looks at me. "Wait, really? Green?"

"Yeah," I say. "Green. Or yellow if it's strong."

"That's sick."

*That's sick.* Okay. I'm going to write down "vinegar — pink," which has two i's in it, and I'm going to dot them like a normal person, with small hard dots, and nobody will ever know what that cost me. I'm going to replay that laugh forty times on the bus. I'm going to analyze whether "that's sick" was about the science or about me, and I already know it was about the science.

But I said it. Out loud. In a room that smells like ammonia.

I think my mouth is doing something again.

I think, this time, I'll let it.

The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. She doodles tiny sketches in her lab notes, each representing a different group member. 1000 words.
response:
# Overthinking It

Okay. Okay. He's sitting down. He's actually sitting down, right next to me, because Ms. Okafor said "pairs within your groups" and Priya grabbed Jordan's sleeve like she was pulling him out of a burning building. So now it's me and Theo Alvarez and six potato cores in six cups of salt water, and I'm supposed to act like a person.

Don't look at him yet. If you look at him the second he sits down, it looks like you were waiting. Which you were. But he doesn't need to know that.

I'll look at my notebook. Notebook is safe.

At the top of the page I've already drawn Priya as a tiny lightning bolt with a ponytail, because she does everything at twice the speed of everyone else and is somehow never wrong. Jordan is a cactus wearing headphones. That's not mean. Jordan just doesn't like being touched and listens to music during tests, which I'm pretty sure isn't allowed. It's affectionate. A cactus is a survivor.

I haven't drawn Theo yet. I've tried three times. The eraser marks are starting to look like a crime scene.

"So, do you want to measure or write?"

He said something. To me. He's looking at me. *Respond.*

"Um. Either. Whatever."

*Whatever.* Wonderful. Incredible. Truly a masterpiece. In my head I was going to say "I'll record, my handwriting is basically a font at this point," which is charming and slightly self-deprecating and true. What came out was the verbal equivalent of a shrug. He's going to think I don't care. Or that I'm annoyed he's my partner. Do I look annoyed? Check face. Is my mouth doing the flat thing? Mom says I do a flat thing when I'm concentrating that looks like I'm judging people.

Unflatten mouth. Not too much. Smiling at nothing is worse.

"I'll measure, then," he says, and picks up the tweezers.

Fine. Recovered. Sort of. I'm writing. Writing is good because my hands have a job and nobody wonders what to do with their hands when they're holding a pencil.

Okay, here's the thing. There are approximately thirty-one minutes left in this class. That is thirty-one minutes in which a normal human girl could have a normal human conversation with a boy she likes. I have prepared material. I have been preparing material since Tuesday, when Ms. Okafor posted the groups and I saw our names next to each other and had to go sit in the bathroom for a minute.

**Option A:** Talk about the experiment. "Did you know the potatoes in the twenty-percent solution should lose the most mass because the water moves out toward the higher solute concentration?" Pros: relevant, on topic, shows I'm smart. Cons: shows I'm smart in the specific way that makes people say "okay, Hermione." Also he definitely knows that. It's literally on the handout. I'd be explaining the handout to him. Like he can't read.

Rejected.

**Option B:** His shirt. He's wearing the one with the band I looked up after the second time he wore it. Three albums, from Portland, the drummer is left-handed. I could say "I like that band." Pros: shared interest. Cons: I don't actually like that band, I listened to one song and it was mostly yelling. If he asks my favorite song I'll have to say the yelling one, and he'll ask "which part," and I'll die. Also, if I know his shirt, that means I've been *looking at his shirt.* For weeks. That's not a shared interest. That's surveillance.

Rejected. Strongly.

**Option C:** A joke. Something about the potatoes. "These potatoes are going through a lot." Pros: light, low stakes, funny-ish. Cons: what if he doesn't laugh? Then there's just a sentence about potato feelings hanging in the air between us forever. I'll be the potato girl. In ten years at the reunion someone will say "remember the potato girl" and everybody will.

"Cup three is 4.2 grams."

"Okay." I write it down. 4.2. My handwriting is shaking a little. Is it shaking enough to see?

He's leaning closer to read the chart. Don't move. If you scoot away it looks like he smells bad, and if you lean in it looks like you're trying to be close to him, so the only acceptable option is to become a statue. Breathe quietly. Is my breathing loud? It sounds loud. Everything I do sounds loud right now, like I'm walking through a library in boots.

Here's what nobody understands. Inside my head, I'm *good* at this. I'm funny in there. I have opinions. I can explain why osmosis is basically the universe trying to make things fair, and I can do it in a way that would make Theo look at me like I said something interesting. That girl exists. She's just stuck somewhere between my brain and my mouth, like a song you can almost remember.

"Cup four is 3.8."

"Three point eight." I wrote it. I said it back like a parrot. Why did I say it back?

Okay. Draw something. Your hand needs a break from being a hand.

I draw Theo. Fourth try. Not a lightning bolt, not a cactus. It's just a small sun with a lopsided face, because he's the kind of person who makes the room feel like it's slightly warmer than before. Oh no. That's so embarrassing. That's the most embarrassing thing I've ever put on paper, and I once wrote a poem about a horse.

I start to erase it.

"Wait, is that Jordan?"

He's pointing at the cactus. He's laughing. Not at me. With the cactus.

"Yeah," I say. And then, before my brain can lock it down: "He's prickly but resilient."

He laughs again. *Actually* laughs. Out loud.

"Who's Priya?"

I point at the lightning bolt. He nods like it's the most accurate thing he's ever seen. Then his finger drifts to the half-erased sun, and my entire body turns to static.

"And where are you?"

Every rehearsed sentence I've ever made scatters like birds.

"I'm the one holding the pencil," I say.

It just comes out. In my real voice. The inside one.

He looks at me for a second, a real second, and smiles. "That's kind of cool, actually."

Then he goes back to the potatoes. "Cup five is 3.1."

I write it down. 3.1.

That conversation took maybe four seconds.

I'm going to think about it for the next four days. Possibly four years. I'll replay it in the shower and before bed and during the math quiz on Friday. I'll find nine things I should have said differently, and I'll wonder whether "kind of cool" means cool or just kind of. I'll decide the sun was a mistake and that it wasn't a mistake at all.

But for right now, just for cup five, I let myself not erase it.

They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. Their phone battery hovers at critically low, adding to the anxiety of the evening. 1000 words.
response:
# Rehearsing Rejection

**9%.**

Fine. Nine percent is enough to get there. Enough for her to text *running late*, or *actually can we reschedule*, or the one I've been bracing for since Tuesday: *I think we should talk.*

We're already going to talk. That's what dinner is. That's what people do with mouths.

The bus lurches and I run it again from the top.

She'll be sitting when I arrive, because she's always early when she's about to do something kind and devastating. She'll have the careful face. She'll say, *I really value what we have,* and I'll know. Value. You value a car. You value a used couch on Marketplace.

*I just think we moved fast,* she'll say.

And I'll say, calm, I'll be so calm, *You moved. I was just there.*

No. Too much. She'll get the look that means *this, this is why.* She'll say, *See, you make everything into a trial.*

And I'll say, *Because you keep putting me on one.*

Good. That's good. I tuck it under my tongue like a stone.

**8%.**

Four hours. Yesterday it took her four hours to answer *thinking of you.* When she did, it was a heart. Not the red one. The pink one with sparkles, which is what you send your aunt. I screenshotted it. I don't know why. Evidence, I guess, for the trial I'm apparently not making everything into.

Dr. Okafor says, *Notice the story. You don't have to argue with it. Just notice.* So I'm noticing. I've written an entire breakup for someone who hasn't broken up with me. It has dialogue. It has stage directions. It has a pink heart as Exhibit A.

Okay. Noticed.

But noticing it doesn't make it wrong. People do leave. That isn't a distortion, it's a statistic. It's my whole—

The bus stops. I'm early, which means she'll know I'm desperate.

**6%.**

She's already inside. Of course she is. Window table. She sees me through the glass and her whole face opens. I hate how much I need that. It hits me in the sternum like warm water, and for one second I am completely, stupidly happy.

Then: *she's performing.* You open your face like that when you're about to let someone down gently.

She stands and hugs me, long, longer than a goodbye hug. Which is exactly what someone does when it's a goodbye hug and they don't want it to feel like one.

"I ordered for you," she says. "The oat cortado. With the cinnamon you pretend you don't like."

She remembered the cinnamon. I want to put my head down on the table.

*She's buttering you up.* That's a guilt drink. You buy someone their specific coffee when you've been ignoring them for a week.

"Thank you," I say. My voice sounds normal. I think it sounds normal.

"I'm sorry I've been a ghost," she says. Here it is. I sit up straighter. Calm. *You moved, I was just there.* "My mum's been in and out of the hospital. Her heart thing again. I didn't want to dump it on you, we're so new, and... I don't know. I kept wanting to call you, and then it'd be two a.m."

Oh.

Oh. Her mum.

The relief is so big it's almost nausea. She wasn't leaving. She was drowning. I take her hand across the table and she grips it, really grips it, and I think, *this is real, this is what real feels like.* I try to memorize the pressure of her fingers, because I know I'm going to need proof later.

*Why didn't she tell me?*

*We're so new.* She said it like a reason. New means temporary. New means I'm not someone you tell things to yet. Her friends knew. Probably. Bex knew. Bex always knows.

I have a speech for this too, and it's already loading. *If I'm not someone you can call at two a.m., then what am I.* I can actually see it: the way I'd turn her mother's heart into a thing about me. I can see how ugly that is.

I can see it, and it's still loading.

**4%.**

"Are you okay?" she asks. "You're doing the jaw thing."

"I'm fine. I'm just sorry. About your mum."

"I missed you so much," she says. "Like, embarrassingly. I want you to meet my sister next week, when she's down. If you want."

Next week. Far enough out to cancel. Far enough for something to happen between now and then, and something always happens, and she'll say *it's just not a good time with everything,* and I'll say—

Stop.

She said *missed you so much.* She said *embarrassingly.* She said *sister.*

I'm holding all three like playing cards, and I keep flipping them over to check the backs.

"Yes," I say. "I want."

**2%.**

My phone buzzes against the table with the low-battery warning, red and insistent, and my chest seizes. If it dies, I can't check. I can't reread her texts on the walk home, can't open the screenshot, can't watch for *I've been thinking*—

"You can charge it at mine," she says. "If you want to come back. I've got the right cable."

She's watching me. Not with the careful face. Just hopeful, a little shy, as if she's the one who might be refused.

I could have said something horrible tonight. I had it ready. I still have it ready, folded small, just in case.

The screen goes black.

She stands and holds out her hand, and I take it, and I let her lead me out into the cold. The whole way down the street I am so grateful I could cry, and I am listening, very carefully, for the moment she lets go.

response:
# Rehearsing Rejection

He said seven. It's 6:12, and I've already had the conversation three times.

In the first version he's kind about it, which is worse. *I just think we moved too fast.* He'll do that thing where he looks at the table instead of me, and I'll say, *Too fast for who?* and he'll say, *For us, I guess,* and I'll say, *Don't put this on "us." There's no "us" in your sentence, Jonah. There's you, deciding.* That one's good. I say it out loud to the bathroom sink to hear how it lands.

In the second version he isn't kind. *You're a lot. You know that, right? Everybody says it.* Everybody. I'd want names. I'd make him list them, and then I'd know exactly which of my friends have been sitting in his kitchen talking about me in that careful, worried voice people use for weather and for me.

Three days. He texted *sorry, crazy week, still on for Thursday?* and I read it twenty-six times. I counted. No x. He always used to put an x. One letter, and I've built a whole house out of what its absence means and moved in and started paying rent.

I put on the green sweater, then take it off, because he said he liked it the morning after, and wearing it now would look like I'm trying to remind him. Which I am. Which he'll see. *God, the sweater. Subtle.*

Fine. Black, then. Black says nothing. Black says I'm fine either way.

And I will be. That's where I keep landing, the third version, the one I like best: I'll be the one who ends it. Before he can. I'll sit down and say, *Look, I think we should just go back to being friends,* and watch his face fill with relief. That'll hurt, but it'll be my hurt, chosen, mine. Honestly, he's never been that great at showing up. He forgot my birthday until noon. He talks over waiters. I could make a list. I'm making a list.

In the hallway on my way out, the mirror catches me: shoulders up near my ears, keys gripped like a weapon, mouth already set in the shape of a comeback. Someone braced for a hit nobody's thrown. I don't like her. I turn away before she can look back.

I know what this is. I *know*. Dr. Okafor would call it "rehearsing" and ask what evidence I have, and I'd say *the x*, and she'd let the silence do the work. I know the scenarios aren't real. But they feel more real than anything else I have, because at least in them I know my lines.

---

He's already there. He stands when he sees me, and before I can arrange my face he's hugging me. It's a long one, his hand flat between my shoulder blades, his chin by my ear. He smells like rain and his laundry stuff.

"Hey," he says into my hair. "God, I missed you."

Something in my chest unclenches so hard it almost hurts. I want to stay here the rest of my life. *He missed me.*

Then, quick as a door slamming: *Too long. Why so long?* Guilt hugs are long. People hug you like that at funerals. People hug you like that right before.

We sit. He's fidgeting with the sugar packets.

"I owe you an explanation," he says, and here it comes. I've got my line ready. *Too fast for who.*

"My mom's back in the hospital. Since Sunday. They think it's her heart again." He rubs his eyes. "I've been driving up every night and I just didn't have words for anyone. I'm sorry I went quiet. I didn't want to dump it on you when things with us were still so new."

Oh.

Oh, Jonah.

I reach across and take his hand and say the right things, and I mean them, I *do*. I feel how scared he is and I want to carry some of it. That's real.

And underneath, a smaller, colder voice: *Four days, and he didn't tell you. You're not who he calls. You're the one he protects himself from.*

"Can I say something dumb?" He's looking at our hands. "I kept thinking you'd regret it. The other night. That you'd been nice about it but you'd want to take it back, and I'd make it weird by needing you right now." He laughs, embarrassed. "I rehearsed this whole thing in the car where you let me down easy."

I stare at him.

He did it too. He sat in a car and wrote my lines for me.

For one clear second I see it: the two of us in separate rooms, each building the other's rejection out of nothing, out of a missing x, out of silence. It's almost funny. I think: *This. Remember this. This is what it looks like from outside.*

"I don't regret it," I say. "Not even a little."

His whole face changes. He squeezes my hand and says, "Okay. Good. Okay," like I've given him something. I have, and he's given it right back, and it's warm and it's enough. It's so much more than enough.

---

Walking home, I replay it. The hug. *I missed you.* *I don't regret it.* I hold each one up to the light.

Did he say *good* too fast? Was that relief, or obligation? He told me he was scared I'd regret it. Or he said that so I'd feel responsible for him, so I wouldn't be the one to leave first. And he paid for both coffees without asking. Was that sweet, or was it the kind of thing you do when you're closing a tab?

I know. I *know* what I'm doing.

I text him: *had a really nice time. thinking about your mom. here if you need anything.* I read it nine times before sending. I don't add an x, because then he'd have to decide whether to add one back.

Then I stand on the corner under the streetlight and watch the screen, waiting for the three little dots, already composing what it means if they don't come.

response:
**Rehearsing Rejection**

She said eight. It's 7:14 and I've already had the conversation three times.

Version one: she sits on the arm of the couch instead of the cushion, which is how I'll know, because people perch when they're planning to leave. She says, *I've been thinking*, and I say, *Clearly not about me*, and that's too sharp, so I rewind. Version two: she says, *I think we should go back to how things were*, and I say, *Totally, I was going to say the same thing*, breezy, and she looks relieved. The relief is what kills me, so I rewind again.

Through the wall, Mr. Hadley's television: a woman's voice, muffled, rising. *...don't you dare tell me what I...* Then a swell of strings. He watches the same channel every night. Somebody is always getting left on that channel.

Three days. Her replies have gone from paragraphs to sentences to *haha yeah*. On Tuesday she didn't send a heart back. I know how that sounds. I know exactly how that sounds, which is why I didn't say anything. It's also why I'm saying it now, to her, in my head, in the bathroom mirror, with my mascara half on.

*You went quiet right after we slept together. Do you know what that does to a person?*

*I've been busy,* she says, in my head.

*You liked Jules's story eleven minutes after you didn't answer me.*

*You're keeping track?*

And there it is. Her face does the thing, the little wince that means *oh, she's like this*. I can see it so clearly that my stomach drops for real, in my actual body, over something that has not happened.

Okay. I know this one. Dr. Okafor would call it rehearsing. She'd ask what evidence I have, and I'd say the heart emoji, and she'd let the silence do the work. Fine. I see it. I see it the way you see a car you're already inside of, skidding.

Except, and this is the part therapy never accounts for, sometimes you're right. Sometimes the person really is pulling away, and the only one who wasn't prepared is the one who told herself she was being crazy.

So: preparation. A list. She's always late. She talks over me around her friends. She said my apartment smelled "lived in." What does that mean. She has never once asked about my brother. Her laugh goes performative when she's nervous. By 7:40 I'm almost done liking her. It's a good feeling, like putting on a coat before going outside. If she leaves, I'll already be gone.

7:52. She's never early. She'll be late and I'll be cold about it, just slightly, so she knows.

7:56. Knock.

She's holding a paper bag and her nose is pink from the cold, and before I can arrange my face she says, "I got the dumplings from the good place, the one you said..." Then she steps in and hugs me, a long one, her cold cheek against my neck. Into my hair she says, "God, I missed you. I'm sorry I've been a ghost."

Something in me just opens. I'm a starving animal shown food too fast, and I'm going to make myself sick on it. *She missed me.* I hold on longer than she does. I notice that. She lets go first, maybe two seconds before me. I file it.

She sits on the cushion. Not the arm.

"My mom had a scare," she says, unpacking containers. "She's okay. It was a whole thing with tests, and I just go inside myself when stuff like that happens. I didn't want to dump it on you when we're so new. Which is stupid, because you're the person I wanted to talk to."

*The person I wanted to talk to.* I want to write it on my arm. I want her to say it again, slower, so I can check it for cracks.

Why didn't she tell me, though? If I'm the person. You tell the person.

*She didn't want to burden you. She literally just said that.*

Or she's not sure yet. "So new" is a door left open on purpose.

"Hey," she says. "Where'd you go?"

"Nowhere. I'm sorry about your mom." I mean it. I do. I also hate that the first thing I felt was relief that it wasn't about me. The second thing was jealousy that I wasn't the one she called.

Through the wall comes laughter, the canned kind, then a man saying something I can't make out, then more laughter.

She feeds me a dumpling off her chopsticks, which is a thing people do in movies, and I laugh, and she laughs. Her laugh isn't performative at all. It's this ugly honking thing, and I love it, I love it. An hour ago it was on a list.

Later, her head on my shoulder, she says, "I was scared you'd be mad at me."

"Why would I be mad?" Easy. Light. An Oscar-worthy performance by a woman who did not spend forty minutes building a case.

"I don't know. You feel things big. It's one of my favorite things about you. I just didn't want to hurt you."

*Favorite thing.* It spreads through me, warm. Underneath, quieter: *You feel things big.* So she's noticed. She's been watching for it. How long before favorite becomes exhausting? I can see that conversation from here, a few months out. She's on the arm of the couch, saying *I just can't be what you need.* I could draft it tonight, after she falls asleep. I probably will.

I know I'm doing it. I can watch myself pick up the loving thing she said and turn it over, looking for the knife. Knowing doesn't stop my hands.

She's asleep by eleven. Her breathing is slow, and her hand has found the hem of my shirt and holds it the way a kid holds a blanket. That has to mean something. That has to be true. Bodies don't lie.

People say that. People also say *I missed you* to someone they're about to leave.

Next door the strings swell into the credits, and a voice I can't understand says something final.

I lie very still so I don't wake her. I hold every good thing she said tonight like stones in my pockets, proof in case I need it. I just haven't decided yet whether it's proof she loves me, or proof of how much it'll hurt.

response:
# Blood Debt

The torch hung in an iron ring on the north wall, above an altar whose Buddha had been carted off decades ago. Its light reached about twelve paces into the hall before the dark swallowed it. Everything inside that reach was cracked flagstone, rotted pillars, and faces.

The Satsuma men stood along the west wall, arms folded, coins knotted in their sashes. The Cangzhou men crowded the east wall, louder and leaning forward, banknotes pinched between their fingers. To the south, where the roof had fallen in, a single blackened beam lay diagonally across the floor like a toppled gravestone. Nobody stood there. Rain dripped through the gap.

Ijūin Shinpei stepped out from the west line holding a staff of rough white oak, sword-length and unlacquered, the kind Jigen-ryū students used to beat a training post ten thousand times a morning until their palms split. He was twenty-two. His master had forbidden this fight in a voice that rattled the dojo shutters.

Han Jiu came from the east barefoot, sleeves rolled to the elbow, forearms roped with muscle from years of swinging iron rings. He carried nothing. Piguaquan had been born among caravan guards and men who fought in alleys, and an alley gave you no time to draw. His teacher had also said no. Han had nodded, then walked here.

Five paces apart, they faced each other across the center of the hall: Shinpei facing east, Han facing west. The torch sat to their left and right respectively, laying long shadows south toward the fallen beam.

Shinpei raised the oak into *tonbo*. Both hands came up beside his right ear, the staff pointing at the broken ceiling. His weight pitched forward onto the balls of his feet. Jigen-ryū taught that the first cut was the only cut, and that a man who needed a second had already died.

Han let his arms hang loose and rolled his shoulders, shaking out his wrists. His feet never settled. He drifted half a step left, then right.

Shinpei's scream split the hall, a ragged *KYEEEH* that sent pigeons bursting from the rafters, and he was simply *there*. He covered five paces in two strides and brought the oak down in a diagonal slash from right shoulder to left hip, hard enough to crack a skull through a helmet.

Han didn't block. Nobody blocked Jigen. He stepped forward and to his own right, north toward the altar, and turned his hips so the cut passed a hand's width from his ribs and exploded against a flagstone. Splinters of stone sprayed.

Shinpei had stooped with the follow-through. Han's right arm, already cocked high, unwound from the shoulder like a flail and dropped a palm-edge chop onto the meat between Shinpei's neck and left shoulder. The sound was wet and flat. The east wall roared.

Shinpei staggered south a step, left arm numb to the fingers. He wrenched himself around to face north, and the torch hit him full in the eyes. Han stood between him and the flame, a black shape with a burning halo, his features invisible.

Shinpei blinked once, refused to give the ground, and hauled the oak back to *tonbo*. His left grip was weak. He screamed again and drove north.

This time Han gave ground. He backed away in quick, light sliding steps, and Shinpei's second cut fell short, a third grazed his sleeve, and a fourth tore cloth. Each swing pushed Han closer to the altar. Then his heel struck the bottom step of the dais and he stopped. He was out of room.

The west wall surged forward, shouting.

Shinpei cut straight down at Han's head.

Han dropped. He sank low and spun on his left heel toward the east, circling along the face of the altar step. The oak bit into the altar's edge instead, and ancient wood burst apart in a shower of dust. Han came out of the spin standing at Shinpei's right side, and his left arm swung up from below his knee in a rising hook, the *gua*, his fist arcing like a thrown stone into the floating ribs under Shinpei's right arm.

Shinpei felt something give. The breath left him in a long whistle.

Han didn't wait. He pressed south, driving Shinpei back across the center of the hall with his arms windmilling, a chop from above, a hook from below, chop, hook, each blow launching the next. Shinpei retreated, fending with the staff held crosswise like a bar. Every step took him away from the torch and deeper into the shadows the two of them cast.

Then his calves struck the fallen beam.

He could go no further south. The rain fell on his neck. Han stood two paces north of him, backlit, chest heaving, and the whole hall saw that it was finished.

Han raised his right arm for the last chop, high over his head, his whole body coiled behind it.

Shinpei stopped defending.

He brought the oak back up into *tonbo*, ignoring his ribs and the dead weight of his left arm. The schools had a saying for this: *give him your flesh, take his bone.* He stepped *into* the falling chop. It cracked down on his left collarbone and he felt the bone go. At the same instant his own cut came down on the forearm Han had flung up to cover his face.

Two bones broke in the same heartbeat.

Han reeled back north, his left forearm bent wrong. Shinpei sat down hard on the beam, the oak sliding from his hand and clattering across the flagstones. Neither man spoke.

The torch guttered. Coins and banknotes lay scattered under both walls, unclaimed. Someone on the east side called it a draw. Someone on the west side spat.

Han cradled his arm and looked at Shinpei across the wavering light. Shinpei looked back, breathing in short, careful sips around his ribs.

The debt hadn't been paid, only made bigger. Both of them knew it would pass to their students, as it had once passed to them.

Moonlight came through the gap and lit the main hall in a pale rectangle, and the old altar stood headless at the north wall. A cedar beam lay where it had dropped long ago, slanting across the eastern half of the floor at knee height, its far end resting against the stump of a lacquered pillar.

Sixty people pressed against the walls. Satsuma men stood along the west side with their sleeves tied back. Dockworkers and caravan guards from Cangzhou crowded the east side, coins wrapped in their fists. Paper slips changed hands. Nobody spoke above a murmur, because both masters had sworn to expel any student caught here.

Arima Tetsunosuke stood at the northern edge of the moonlight with his back to the altar. A red-and-black band was knotted around his left bicep. He held a bokutō of yusu wood, which was heavier than oak and dark with years of striking the practice post. He raised it into *tonbo*: hilt beside his right ear, point angled at the broken roof, elbows high. It was the dragonfly stance of Jigen-ryū, and it promised one cut and nothing after.

Twelve paces south, near the rotted doorway, Guo Lianshan rolled his shoulders loose. He carried nothing. His red-and-black band was wound around his right forearm, the same colors as Arima's, because both schools had claimed them for a century and neither would surrender them. That was where the first blood had come from, four generations ago.

Guo let his arms hang. In Piguaquan the arms were not fists. They were the weighted ends of ropes.

"Your grandfather ran from mine," Arima said.

"Your grandfather couldn't catch him," Guo answered, and began to circle.

He moved to his own left, along the eastern side of the light, toward the fallen beam. Arima pivoted on his rear foot and kept the dragonfly pointed at Guo's centerline. The crowd shifted with them like water in a tilted bowl.

Arima's breath stopped. Every Satsuma man in the hall knew what that meant.

The scream tore out of him, *"Kiiieeeee!"*, and he crossed the distance in three driving steps. The bokutō came down from his right shoulder on a diagonal line toward his own left hip. It was a cut meant to split a man from collarbone to ribs.

Guo had stopped circling half a beat early. As the wood fell, he slid forward and out to Arima's right, toward the shoulder the cut began from and away from where it would end. The yusu wood passed a hand's width from his ear and smashed into the floor tiles, and shards sprayed across the moonlight.

Guo's right arm was already swinging. The whip-chop came from below his hip, over the top, and down. Arima jerked his head left, and the edge of Guo's hand landed on the meat of his right shoulder instead of his temple. The impact cracked like a wet towel snapped in a courtyard.

Arima tore the bokutō back up to tonbo and gave ground toward the altar, his right arm numb to the fingers.

He had needed a second strike. On the west wall, an old Satsuma man looked away.

Guo pressed in. He came straight north with his arms windmilling in the chop-and-hang rhythm of Pigua: right arm chopping down, left arm hooking up, then reversed, always cycling. Each blow arrived from a different height. Arima gave a step, then another, and angled east to keep the altar off his back.

That put the fallen beam behind his calves.

He felt it against his heel and stopped retreating. Guo's left arm came looping at his jaw. Arima abandoned tonbo and cut flat, right to left at chest height. It was the horizontal stroke Jigen-ryū keeps in reserve for men who will not stand still to be split.

The bokutō met Guo's descending left forearm. The bone broke with a dry, flat crack, and the eastern wall groaned.

Guo did not stop. He stepped inside the swing, so close that Arima's hands were trapped behind his shoulder, and whipped his right palm up into Arima's floating ribs. Then he hooked his right foot behind Arima's heel and drove forward.

Arima went over the beam backward. He landed hard on the far side, and the bokutō clattered from his grip and skidded toward the pillar stump.

Guo stood on the near side of the beam, his left arm hanging wrong and his breath sawing. He could have stepped over. He waited.

Arima crawled two lengths to the pillar and closed his hand around the wood. He rose, spat red, and climbed back over the beam into the moonlight. He walked to its center and lifted the bokutō into the dragonfly again. His ribs grated when he breathed.

Guo faced him four paces away, his right arm loose and his left pinned against his belly.

Arima knew where Guo would go. Out to the right shoulder, the same as before. He could feel it in his body, and he adjusted his cut to fall straighter, toward the right side.

He screamed and came in.

Guo did not go right. He stepped *in*, directly into the falling arc, and ducked his head under Arima's rising forearms so his good shoulder jammed against Arima's wrists at the top of the stroke. The cut had nowhere to go. The bokutō slashed down behind Guo's back and struck nothing but air.

Guo's right hand swung up from the hip and stopped, edge-first, a finger's width from Arima's throat.

The hall was silent.

Guo held the hand there for a long count. Then he lowered it, stepped back, and turned toward the doorway, cradling his broken arm.

"Now you owe us," he said, without looking back.

Arima stood alone in the pale rectangle of light with his bokutō still raised. He understood that he had not lost his life. He had been given it, and a Satsuma man could never repay that.
