# Blood Debt

The rain had found its way into the Kannon-ji long before the gamblers did. It came through the split in the roof above the altar, ran down the cracked dais, and slipped into a fissure that crossed the main hall from north to south. The water ran a hand wide and left a slick sheen half a pace on either side before it vanished under the rotted doors.

Lanterns hung from the surviving beams. Beneath them, two crowds pressed against opposite walls. Satsuma men in dark hakama lined the west side. Dockhands, cooks and porters from the Chinese quarter lined the east. Between the factions, money changed hands in fists.

Ijūin Kaito stood on the west side of the stream, four paces from the water. He held his oak bokutō in the *tonbo* stance: hilt beside his right ear, point to the rafters, left foot forward, weight sunk so low his thighs trembled. His palms were calloused from ten thousand strikes against the training post. Since boyhood he had been taught that the first cut was the only cut. A Jigen man did not think about a second.

Across the water, Han Yao had brought no weapon at all. He stood barefoot on the east side, toes at the edge of the slick, his arms hanging loose from his shoulders like rope from a mast. Forty years ago, Ijūin's great-uncle had beaten his grandfather senseless in a Nagasaki street. The debt had never been settled, only inherited. Han rolled his shoulders once, and his arms swung with them, slack and heavy.

Neither master knew they were here. It was the only thing the two schools agreed on.

A coin fell. Before it stopped spinning, Ijūin screamed.

It was the monkey cry, a shriek that tore through the hall and set the lanterns shivering, and he moved with it. He took three driving steps toward the stream, sword high, body pitched forward. On the last step he planted his left foot at the western edge of the slick and let the cut fall from his ear with everything his hips could give.

Han did not retreat. He stepped forward and to his left, north toward the altar, and pivoted on the ball of his right foot so his body turned sideways to the blow. The bokutō came down through the space his head had occupied and struck the wet stone beside the stream. Flagstone cracked. Water leapt.

Han's right arm was already rising. It swung up and over like a flail on a hinge and came down as a chopping palm at the side of Ijūin's neck. But Ijūin's momentum had carried him onto the slick. His front foot skated, and instead of the neck the palm smacked across the meat of his left shoulder. Ijūin slid past, splashed through the stream, and caught himself on dry stone on the eastern side.

The fighters had traded banks. Ijūin now stood east of the water with his back to the Chinese crowd, who jeered and shoved him. Han stood west, near the altar end, with the Satsuma men muttering behind him.

Ijūin rebuilt *tonbo*. His left shoulder throbbed, and the arm answered slowly.

This time he did not charge. He came forward to the eastern edge of the slick and stopped, rooted. Han had drifted to the western edge to meet him, and Ijūin snapped a shorter cut diagonally across the water. Han swayed back from the waist, arms flinging outward for balance. The tip of the oak passed close enough to open his left cheek from ear to lip. Blood sheeted down his jaw and spattered into the stream.

The Satsuma wall roared.

Han touched the wound, looked at his red fingers, and smiled.

Then he stepped into the stream.

He did not step over it. His lead foot landed in the wet center and slid on purpose, a long skating stride that carried him a full arm's length farther than Ijūin's eye had measured. His left arm whipped up from below in a rising arc, and his knuckles cracked against the back of Ijūin's right wrist. The bokutō jumped in Ijūin's grip. Han's right arm followed with a downward chop at the left collarbone. Ijūin saved himself only by stumbling two steps back onto dry stone.

Han withdrew to the western edge. Water dripped from his trouser hems. Between them, the stream ran pink.

Ijūin's wrist was swelling, and his breath came short. He knew he had one more full cut in him: the cut his master forbade outside of killing, the one meant to split a helmet. He raised the sword so high the tip brushed a lantern cord, and for the first time all night he stopped thinking about anything at all.

He screamed and ran.

He took two steps on dry stone. The third was long and low, his left foot reaching across the water to land on the western slick. The cut began as his weight arrived.

Han went in.

He lunged forward under the falling arc, inside the length of the sword, and drove his right shoulder into Ijūin's chest. The blade passed behind him, but Ijūin's forearms and the hilt slammed down across Han's back with the full weight of the strike. Something in Han's shoulder gave with a wet snap. His right knee buckled and struck the slick stone.

But his left arm was free. It swung up from his hip in a tight circle, and the edge of his fist caught Ijūin beneath the jaw.

Ijūin's head snapped back. His forward foot shot out from under him on the wet stone, and he went down backward across the stream. His shoulders hit the dry eastern bank and his spine lay in the water. The bokutō clattered from his hands, slid, and lodged in the crack, the current nudging against it.

There was silence. Then both walls erupted at once.

Han stayed on one knee at the western edge, right arm hanging useless. Blood dripped from his cheek into the water running beneath Ijūin's back. Ijūin stared up through the broken roof at the rain and did not try to rise.

Han got his feet under him, stood, and looked down.

"Tell your family," he said, in careful Japanese, "we are even now."

Ijūin turned his head toward the sword caught in the crack and the water pooling red behind it.

"No," he whispered. "We are not."

response:
# Breaking Formation

The clock above the mirror reads **00:41:07** in red digits the size of my hand, and it doesn't care about me.

Twelve of us stand on blue tape in three rows of four. I'm in the back row, second from the left wall: C2, the spike mark worn pale under my left sneaker. The corner speaker is close enough that the kick drum hits my ribs before my ears. In the mirror I can see the whole grid. Eleven Korean kids in identical black joggers, identical posture, identical nothing on their faces. And me, the scholarship kid from North Philly, with a sweat-dark hoodie knotted at my waist because nobody told me the dress code was *be invisible*.

Teacher Kang sits on a stool beside the speaker, one finger on the laptop trackpad. She's trained half the groups on the billboards I passed on the subway this morning. The trainees whisper that she once made a boy run one eight-count for three hours until he stopped blinking on the wrong beat.

"*Hana, dul, set, net.*" Music.

On one, my right arm shoots to ten o'clock, palm flat, elbow locked. On two, my left mirrors it to two o'clock and my chin drops. On three-four, both fists pull to my sternum on a double hit. It's a hit, not a pop: a stop with no echo. Back home, a pop is a contraction you let ring, muscle flexing and releasing so your body hums like a struck wire. Here the hit has to die where it lands. *Kal-gunmu*, they call it. Knife choreography. Twelve bodies cutting one line so clean the camera can't find the seams.

My fists hit my chest, and my shoulders bounce.

It's barely anything, just the groove I've carried since I was nine, toprocking on a square of linoleum outside the laundromat on Lehigh. That bounce keeps you in the pocket so you can go anywhere off it. In the mirror it looks like a tremor in a still photograph.

Kang's finger lifts. Silence.

"Twelve."

She doesn't use names. I'm the sticker on my shirt.

"Your shoulders are talking. Nobody asked them."

Eleven heads don't turn, which is worse than if they did.

"Again. From one."

**00:38:52.**

On five-six we pivot a quarter turn left, weight on the ball of the right foot, and the mirror shows twelve right profiles. On seven the right knee lifts to ninety degrees. On eight we stomp, and the floor answers like a single board. My stomp lands a hair behind. It isn't late, exactly. It's laid back, sitting where the snare actually breathes. In a cypher that's called having pocket. In here it's a mistake, and it echoes: one sharp crack after the clean one, a rimshot nobody wanted.

"Twelve."

My jaw is working. Back home, if somebody called you out, you answered in the circle. You stepped in and burned them. Here there's no circle, only a grid. A grid has no center, which means it has no me.

Then comes the formation change, the part that's been killing me all week.

For counts one through four of the next eight, the back row holds while the front row drops to one knee. On five-six-seven-eight, we travel. I walk forward on a right diagonal, three steps and a pivot, threading the gap between Jiwoo at B2 and Min-seo at B3, and land on the yellow X just ahead of their line. The block becomes a wedge with me near its point. Every step falls on the count, heel first, arms locked at my sides like I'm carrying buckets.

My body doesn't walk on counts. My body glides. On the third step my right foot slides instead of planting, an old habit of the sneaker skating the floor like I'm cutting into a cypher, and I hit the yellow X half a beat early, ahead of Jiwoo's shoulder. The mirror shows a wedge with a bent tip.

Kang stops the track and stands. She walks the length of the room, past the kneeling front row, and stops in front of me. I can smell the cold cream on her hands.

"You can do six-step," she says in careful English. "I watched your audition video. Windmill. Air freeze. Beautiful." She taps my sternum with two fingers, exactly where the double hit lands. "But here your freedom is noise. Twelve people moving as one person. You want to be one person moving as one person, go home."

*Go home.* Home is where my mom works doubles at the hospital, and where she called the whole block when the acceptance email came. It's where my crew threw me a send-off battle on the court, and I won it with a freeze I invented that afternoon. Go home with what?

**00:21:30.**

We run it, and we run it again. I kill the bounce by locking my core until my abs cramp. I kill the glide by pretending the floor is wet cement. Each correction is a door shutting somewhere inside me. The groove doesn't leave. It just retreats somewhere I can't reach, pacing.

**00:03:00.** Final run.

Near the end the track has a break: two counts of pure silence while all twelve of us hold the last pose, right arm vertical, left fist on the hip, chin up. In a cypher, silence is an invitation. You fill it. That's the whole point of being alive in there.

Seven. Eight. The music drops away.

Everything in me wants to fill it. A chest pop that rings. A shoulder roll. Anything that says somebody from Lehigh Avenue was here.

In the mirror the clock reads **00:00:41** above twelve frozen bodies. The space between my raised hand and the ceiling feels like a dare.

I could break it. It's only two counts. She'd see, and everyone would see.

I hold.

I hold so still I can hear the speaker's hum and Jiwoo breathing behind my left shoulder. My own heart keeps time off the beat inside a body that isn't allowed to follow it. The music slams back in on one, twelve right arms cut down together, and for the first time the mirror shows no seam at all.

Kang says nothing for a long moment. Then: "Good. Now I can teach you."

**00:00:00.** The clock blinks and resets to **03:00:00** for the next group.

I walk to my bag. Somewhere under my ribs the groove is still pacing, waiting to see if I'll come back for it.

# Breaking Formation

The speakers are bolted high in the four corners of Studio B, and every one is a hair too loud. The kick drum doesn't come from in front of me or behind me. It comes from inside my teeth.

"Hana, dul, set, net." Han Seonsaengnim doesn't shout counts. She says them flat, like she's reading prices.

Twelve of us stand in window formation: three rows of four, staggered so the mirror sees every face. My tape is a blue X, back row, far left. It's the spot closest to the corner speaker, the spot for the kid who showed up six weeks late on a scholarship with a suitcase that still smells like my aunt's apartment. In the mirror I can see where I'm supposed to land on the line change: Seo-yeon's red X, front row, far left, against the wall.

Music up. 128 BPM, a synth stab on every two and four.

Count one: right arm shoots to forty-five degrees, palm flat, fingers sealed. Twelve arms make one shadow. Two: chin snaps left. Three, four: step right, drag the left foot in, heels kiss, and a chest hit on four. Not a pop, she told me the first day. A *hit*. A pop has a little echo at the end, and here echoes are mistakes.

Back home, the echo was the whole point. My cousin Marcus taught me popping on flattened refrigerator boxes outside the laundromat on Lehigh Avenue. He said a hit should ripple: contract, release, and the release keeps traveling down your arm like a rumor. Here the release dies at the elbow. A dime stop, and nothing after it.

Five, six: quarter turn right, left profile to the mirror, both fists to the sternum. Seven: half squat, thighs parallel. Eight: hold.

Hold is where I lose.

The bass on this track sits a sixteenth behind the synth, and my body has lived its whole life in that pocket. Every cypher I ever won, I won by sitting back on the beat and making people lean in to find me. So on eight, while eleven bodies freeze like they've been unplugged, my hips sink half an inch late and my shoulders roll into it.

Han's remote clicks. The four corners go silent so fast my ears keep ringing.

"Thirteen."

That's me. The others are One through Eleven. Nobody will tell me what happened to Twelve.

She walks the center aisle, sneakers squeaking, arms folded. She's five-foot-one. Trainees say she once made a girl run the same sixteen counts for nine hours, until the girl cried and then nailed it and debuted eighteen months later. They say it like scripture.

She stops beside me. In the mirror she's tiny next to my reflection, and somehow I'm the one who looks small.

"You are late," she says, in careful English. "No. Not late. *Behind.* Your body waits. Why?"

*Because waiting is where the flavor lives. Because a beat isn't a wall, it's a door.* I don't say it. I bow, and the bow is wrong too. Too fast, too American, the bow of someone who wants it to be over.

"Again. From line change."

Second eight. This is the part that's eating me alive.

On one, all twelve square to the mirror and the front row drops to one knee. On two, Ji-ho, middle row left, slides right and opens a lane along the wall. On three and four I travel two steps downstage through that lane while Seo-yeon rises and travels back through the same lane to my blue X. Two bodies cross in a space the width of a yoga mat. They call it *kal-gunmu*, knife-sharp group dance. The audience should never see where one dancer ends and the next begins.

Count three, I step. Count four, the snare rolls, and my right foot does what it's done ten thousand times on concrete. It kicks out into the first step of a six-step, heel slicing low, straight into Seo-yeon's path. She twists her hip to clear me. I see the sweat at her hairline and the flash of fear in her eyes, because if I'm wrong the line is wrong, and if the line is wrong we all run it again. I yank the foot back and land on the red X with my weight on the wrong leg. On five, eleven bodies pivot a quarter turn left on the ball of the right foot. I pivot on my left and spin the other way. The mirror shows eleven right profiles and one left one: me, facing the wrong wall like a typo.

Click. Silence.

Somebody in the middle row exhales through their nose. Not a laugh. Worse. Tired.

Han sits on the riser under the front-left speaker, right above my mark. "Everyone out. Thirteen, stay."

They file to the bench by the door where our shoes wait in a perfect row: Balenciagas, Nike collabs with the tags tucked in, and my Air Forces with creases I've been trying to steam out. Seo-yeon's mother sends a driver. Mine works doubles folding sheets at Temple University Hospital. She cried when I got the email and said, *Don't come back the same.* I still don't know if she meant it as a blessing.

"You have something," Han says. "I watched your audition tape. The battle video. Very raw. Very free." The word *free* sounds like a diagnosis. "Here, free is a problem. Twelve people, one body. You understand?"

"Yeah."

"Then show me. Alone. Sixteen counts. Exactly."

Click. The four corners blast it, too loud, the sound colliding at the center of the floor where nobody stands.

In the eight counts of intro, I see it clearly. If I do it my way, I'm on a plane by Friday. If I do it her way forever, one day I'll reach for a groove and find a grid.

One: arm to forty-five, sealed. Two: chin left. Three, four: step, drag, hit, dead at the elbow. Five, six: quarter turn, fists. Seven: squat. Eight: hold. I hold on the synth, not the bass, so still it burns.

Second eight. Square up. Two steps downstage through the empty lane. No kick. The six-step screams in my ankle and dies there. Land on the red X, weight right. Pivot left on the ball of the right foot. Right profile to the mirror. Clean.

But in the gap after eight, the *and* she never counts out loud, I let my ribs drop. Just my ribs, half an inch behind the beat, inside my chest, where the mirror can't reach.

Click.

Han looks at me for a long time.

"Again," she says.

She doesn't say *wrong*.

# Breaking Formation

The fan cracks shut like a knuckle popping, and twelve bodies freeze.

Eleven bodies. I'm still finishing the roll. My chest is dropping through the last of a wave my spine started on count three. In the mirror I watch myself arrive half a beat after everyone else, like a car rolling through a stop sign.

"Again," says Han Seonsaengnim. She never raises her voice. She doesn't need to.

Studio 4, eleventh floor, Gangnam. The front wall is all mirror, floor to ceiling, and the floor is gridded with white tape: three rows of four, each spot marked by a small X. Mine is back row, far left. Ji-woo stands on the X to my right, close enough that I can hear her counting under her breath, *hana, dul, set, net*, while sweat drips from her chin onto her mark.

Back in East Oakland, nobody counted. You found the pocket and you lived in it. My uncle taught me to turf on the BART platform at Fruitvale: glides, tuts, bone breaks, my whole body riding the space between the kick and the snare like a hand riding wind out a car window. The music breathes back there, he said. Get behind it.

Here, behind is wrong.

The click track restarts at 128 BPM. Han opens the fan and waves it slowly beneath her chin.

The eight-count goes like this. On **1**, the right foot steps out to shoulder width and the arms shoot up into a hard L, elbows at ninety degrees, fists at the temples. On **2**, both fists slam to the sternum. On **3–4**, a body roll top to bottom ends in a knee bounce. On **5**, the head snaps left. On **6**, it snaps right. On **7**, we make a quarter turn right to face the window wall. On **and**, the left arm cuts horizontally across the chest like a blade. On **8**, we pivot back to face the mirror and settle square on the X.

They call it *kal-gunmu*, knife dance: twelve people moving like one blade.

On 1 I'm clean. On 2 I'm clean. On 3, my body hears the snare coming and reaches for it. My roll isn't a roll. It's a wave, sternum to belly to hips, and it pours into my knees late and heavy, landing where the music actually lands instead of where the click says it should. Eleven heads snap left on 5. Mine is a hair behind, dragging itself out of the groove.

On 7 my muscle memory betrays me completely. Instead of pivoting on the ball of my right foot, my left heel slides out in a glide, heel-toe-heel, smooth as oil, and when I turn back to the mirror on 8 I'm standing four inches to the right of my X.

The fan snaps.

Han walks the length of the studio. Her slippers make no sound on the sprung floor. The trainees in my row don't look at me. They keep their eyes on the mirror, chins level, like soldiers ignoring the guy getting chewed out. She crouches at my feet and taps the tape X with the closed fan. Then she taps the toe of my sneaker, four inches away.

"Here," she says, the X. "Not here." My shoe. "Your feet lie to the floor."

My sneakers are the only pair in the room that aren't agency-issued white. I bought them with two months of tips from the taquería on International Boulevard. The scholarship covers the dorm, the food, the Korean tutor, and this floor, which costs more per hour than my mother makes in a week. Everyone here knows exactly what I cost. I feel it every time I'm wrong. Every mistake is a receipt.

Han stands. She's shorter than me, but it doesn't feel that way.

"Formation change," Han announces in Korean, then repeats it in English for me. She points the fan at Minseo, front row, second from the left. "Back." Then at me. "Center."

Nobody moves, but I feel twelve sets of eyes shift in the mirror.

The second eight goes like this. On **1–2**, the two middle dancers in the front row step outward, opening a lane. On **1–4**, I cross the diagonal, forward and right, one step per count, from my back-left corner through the lane to a fresh X taped one meter in front of the front row's center. On **6–7–8** comes the killing part: a solo tut, the arms building a box frame around the face, one right angle per count.

A tut. The thing my uncle taught me under the Fruitvale fluorescents. The angles that came out of King Tut and Oakland and LA, cleaned up and sold back. She chose it on purpose. I know it the way you know when someone's watching you across a cypher.

The click starts.

I hit the first eight dead on. I roll on the kick, not the snare. It feels like singing a song without the melody. On 7 I pivot, I don't glide, and on 8 I'm centered on my X.

The second eight. On 1 the lane opens. I step diagonally, one, two, three, four, threading between the front pair, and Minseo's shoulder passes mine going the other way. My right foot lands on the new X on four, square, exact.

On 5 I face the mirror. On 6 my right forearm goes vertical beside my cheek. On 7 the left goes horizontal across my brow, a perfect corner.

"Again," she says.

It's the same word as before. It doesn't sound the same.

response:
# Therapeutic Boundaries

The diagram is the first thing I see every Tuesday and Thursday, because Marcus always starts me on my back.

Some intern colored it in by hand. The quadriceps are raw salmon, and the iliotibial band is a pale strap of gristle running down the outside of the thigh. Beside the teardrop of muscle just above the kneecap, someone has lettered *VASTUS MEDIALIS* in neat capitals. Eleven weeks ago a surgeon cut a strip from the middle of my patellar tendon, drilled tunnels through my tibia and femur, and threaded it through to replace the ligament I shredded on the eighth hurdle in Zurich. My left VMO has since withered into something soft and humiliating. On the wall, it's fat and proud.

"Quad's guarding," Marcus says. "Let it go."

"It's gone. That's the whole problem."

"Reyes."

He stands at my left hip. My leg lies straight on the table, heel resting on the vinyl. He boxes my kneecap between his hands, the webbing of his right thumb and index finger seated against its lower edge and his left against the upper. The contact registers twice. First as information: heat, pressure, the faint grind of a joint that has forgotten how to glide. Second as something I refuse to name.

Twelve years ago he was the decathlete in my training group. We did hurdle mobility side by side on the infield at dawn. He'd brace my trail leg while I drilled the hip opening over and over, his palm on the back of my knee, both of us laughing at nothing. When his hamstring tore at twenty-six, he quit, went back to school, and got the letters after his name. At a party I called him a coward for it. Now his name is on the door of this clinic, and I'm the one lying down.

He pushes the kneecap toward my foot.

The scar where they harvested the tendon runs vertically down the front of my knee, and it pulls tight as a hot wire drawn through wax. My toes curl. My breath stops halfway down my throat.

"That's the adhesion," he says, clinical. "Superior now."

He reverses, thumbs at the lower pole pressing the patella up toward my hip. It moves more easily that way, a few millimeters of slide. Then he shifts both thumbs to the outer edge of the kneecap and presses inward, toward the midline of my knee. This is the direction that's worst. My quad fires without my permission, the whole thigh clenching, the patella locking in its groove like a drawer slammed shut.

He doesn't fight it. He waits, thumbs resting there, and I can feel his patience in the stillness of his hands.

"Breathe out."

I do. The muscle unclenches in stages. The kneecap gives and slides, and gooseflesh rises across my thigh from knee to hip in a wave I can't hide on a bare leg under fluorescent light. He must see it. He keeps his eyes on the joint.

"Good," he says, half a register lower than before. He clears his throat. "Flip over."

I roll toward the wall, keeping the left leg straight, and settle face down with my forehead in the cradle. The diagram disappears. Now there's only the gray floor through the oval opening, the squeak of his shoes as he comes around, and my own breath, too loud.

His right palm lands flat across the back of my pelvis, the heel of his hand on my sacrum. I know why. Lying prone, my hip is extended, which puts the rectus femoris, the one quad muscle that crosses both hip and knee, on full stretch. When the knee bends far enough, that muscle yanks the pelvis forward and my hips try to rise off the table to steal slack. His hand is there to pin them. It's a mechanical necessity. It's also the weight of a man's hand pressing my hips into a table, and my body doesn't care about the distinction.

His left hand wraps the front of my ankle. He bends my knee, and my heel arcs up toward my glute. Sixty degrees, easy. Eighty. At ninety, the front of my knee starts to burn, a deep stretching ache across the top of the joint, the scar tightening like a zipper pulled from both ends. At ninety-five, my hips push up against his palm.

He presses down. They stay.

"Ninety-eight," he says. "Same as Thursday."

"Then stop measuring."

"Hold-relax. When I say, push your shin back into my hand. Twenty percent. Don't move the leg, just push."

"I know what hold-relax is, Marcus."

"Then do it right this time. Push."

I drive my shin back against his grip, trying to straighten the knee. The quad contracts against resistance and goes nowhere. His forearm takes it without a tremor. I can feel his pulse in his fingers against the tendons of my ankle, or I imagine I can. Five seconds. My thigh shakes.

"That's not twenty."

"It's twenty of what I used to have."

A pause, too long. His hand on my sacrum doesn't move, but his thumb shifts a half-inch along the top of my waistband, an adjustment of grip. Neither of us acknowledges it.

"Relax," he says quietly.

I exhale, and the contracted muscle goes briefly slack. He uses the window, folding my heel closer to my glute. The burn sharpens to a bright point at the top of the kneecap. I press my mouth shut and make a sound anyway, low and ugly, from the back of my throat.

"One-oh-three," he says. His voice is not quite steady. "Stay with me. Breathe."

"I'm breathing."

"You're holding it. You always held it. Every rep on the infield, you'd go purple."

I hate that he remembers. I hate the way it lands under my ribs like a hand.

He holds me at end range for thirty seconds that last a year. His palm is warm through my shirt, his grip on my ankle unyielding, my hips pinned, my knee screaming in one clean note. Somewhere above me he is breathing slowly and deliberately, a man counting his own breaths so he has something to think about.

Then he lowers my leg in a slow, controlled arc until my foot rests flat on the table again.

His hand leaves my back a beat late. Or a beat early. I can't tell which would be worse.

I roll over. The diagram returns, every muscle labeled, every fiber accounted for. It has no name for whatever just happened in the space between his hands and my skin.

"Thursday," he says, already writing, not looking at me.

"Thursday," I say, and stare at the wall until he leaves.

response:
# Therapeutic Boundaries

The lavender is new. It comes from a little ceramic diffuser on the windowsill, a thin white plume that does nothing against the bleach-and-neoprene smell underneath. Someone decided this room needed softening. I resent the diffuser almost as much as I resent my knee.

"On your back," Theo says. "Leg straight. Let it go dead."

I lie down on the crinkling paper and stare at the ceiling tiles. I know them well by now: forty-two, one water-stained. My right leg lies extended, the scar running pink and puckered down the front of the knee, eleven centimetres from the bottom of the kneecap to the top of the shin, where they harvested the tendon twice.

He pulls the stool close. His hands settle on my kneecap, thumbs on its upper edge, index fingers curved along the bottom. I've seen those hands chalk a pole. Taped them before he threw the javelin. Watched them shake on a start line in Doha, when we were twenty-two and certain.

He presses the patella downward, toward my foot.

My quad fires. It's involuntary, a hard twitch that yanks the kneecap back up under his thumbs like a startled animal.

"Guarding," he says quietly.

"I know what it's called."

"Then stop doing it."

I breathe out through my teeth and try to unclench a muscle I spent fifteen years teaching never to unclench. He waits. The second time, the quad stays soft, and he glides the kneecap down, then up, then nudges it toward the inside of the knee with the pads of his thumbs. Something deep in the joint scrapes. It isn't pain exactly. It feels like sand where there should be oil.

Then lateral. His fingertips hook the inner edge and draw it outward, and there's a sharp hot line along the scar where the tissue has knit itself to everything nearby. My breath catches. His fingers stop at once, holding but not pushing.

"Scale of ten."

"Four."

He looks at me, eyebrows lifted. He knows I'm lying, and he knows I lied to the team doctor about my hamstring in 2019.

"Six," I amend.

He holds it for ten seconds. I count the stained tile.

"Flexion," he says, and stands.

He slides one hand under my heel, cupping it, and lays the other across the front of my shin just below the knee. He lifts. My hip bends to ninety, thigh pointing at the ceiling, shin parallel to the table. Then he begins drawing my heel toward my backside, his lower hand guiding the foot while the upper hand keeps the knee tracking straight so it doesn't drop inward.

The first stretch of the arc is fine. Then comes the wall.

It always arrives at the same place, a dense, tightening pressure across the front of the joint, as though the scar were a strap cinched one hole too tight. My toes curl. My hands find the edge of the table.

"Breathe."

I breathe. He takes up another degree, then another. Heat spreads up the front of my thigh. The pressure turns bright and sharp at the bottom of the kneecap, right where the graft anchors, and I make a sound I'd rather not have made.

He holds me there. He doesn't push further, and he doesn't let go either.

Close up, he smells of the clinic's green soap and, faintly, of the coffee he still drinks black, the way he did on bus rides to meets. I'm aware of exactly where his forearm rests against the outside of my calf, and of the heat of his palm on my shin. My body notices these things with an attention I can't afford, and I hate it for noticing.

He reaches for the goniometer and lines its axis up with the outside of my knee, one arm along my femur and the other along my fibula.

"One-oh-four."

"Last week was one-oh-one."

"Yes." He doesn't say *good*. He learned not to.

"Roll over."

I turn onto my stomach, face in the cradle, and the lavender is suddenly closer, cloying. He stands at my right side. One hand lands flat on my lower back, across the sacrum, firm and broad.

"Your hip's going to try to lift to cheat the stretch," he says. "I'm holding your pelvis down."

"I know."

"I'm telling you anyway."

His other hand wraps the front of my ankle. He bends the knee, bringing my heel toward my glute. It's the same movement as before, but gravity has turned it over and it's worse. With my thigh pinned flat to the table, the quad has nowhere to borrow length from. The front of the knee burns, and the pressure builds until my pelvis tries to tip upward exactly as he said it would. His palm stops it cold.

The pressure of that hand goes through me, and I clench my jaw.

"Contract-relax," he says. His voice has gone lower, the even, measured tone he used to use for counting my hurdle strides. "Push your heel back into my hand. Twenty percent. Six seconds."

I press my shin back against his grip. My quad engages, and his hand absorbs the force without yielding.

"—five, six. Relax."

I let go. In the brief, stunned slackness that follows the contraction, he eases my heel closer. The burn flares, then levels off. I gained a degree, maybe two, before my nervous system could object.

"Again."

We do it three times. By the third, sweat is cooling at my hairline, and I'm breathing like it's the final hundred metres. His hand on my back has not moved at all, and I've stopped pretending I don't feel each finger.

He lowers my leg slowly, supporting the shin all the way down until it lies flat, the way you'd put down something you didn't want to break. Then he takes his hand off my spine, and the place where it was goes cool.

I sit up too fast. The knee throbs in time with my pulse.

"One-oh-nine," he says, writing. He keeps his eyes on the chart.

"You're going to tell me I'm doing well."

"I'm going to tell you you'll walk downstairs without thinking about it by spring."

"I used to run 54 seconds over ten barriers, Theo."

He finally looks up. There's nothing triumphant in his face, which makes it worse. He knows what spring means and what it doesn't.

"I know," he says. "I was there."

The diffuser hisses. I pull my leg off the table and stand on it, and it holds my weight.

response:
# Therapeutic Boundaries

Theo calls it "the knee," never "your knee," as if it's clinic property I'm only borrowing.

"On your back. Leg long."

I lie down on the treatment table and straighten my right leg as far as it will go, which isn't all the way. The back of the knee hovers a finger's width above the vinyl, two degrees short of straight. It's been eleven weeks since a surgeon rebuilt my ACL from a strip of my own hamstring tendon and sutured the torn meniscus back to its rim. Eleven weeks since I came off the long jump board in the fifth event of a heptathlon and heard the sound a career makes when it ends.

Theo slides a rolled towel under my heel so that gravity can work on the extension. Then he cups the kneecap: thumbs along its upper edge, index fingers bracketing the lower. His forearms are wrapped in the same compression sleeves he wore in Doha, teal and orange chevrons faded to the colors of an old swimming pool. I bought a matching pair that week. Mine are in a drawer I don't open.

"Quads off," he says.

I try. The muscle above my knee flickers anyway, guarding, and the kneecap locks under his fingers.

"Maren."

"I heard you."

I exhale and let the thigh go slack. He pushes the patella down toward my foot. It glides maybe a centimeter, then catches on scar tissue, and a tight, bright ache spreads under the bone like a bruise being pressed from the inside.

"Number?"

"Five."

He holds it there. Ten seconds. His thumbs are warm. I fix my eyes on the ceiling tiles and count the holes in one of them, because the alternative is to watch his face, which is concentrating on the knee with the same frown he used to wear over a takeoff mark. I am not interested in his face. Then he shifts his grip and glides the kneecap sideways, toward the inside of my leg, and the ache sharpens along the outer edge where the tissue is tightest. My toes curl involuntarily.

"Six," I say before he can ask.

"Good. That's where we want to live."

*We.* As if he's living anywhere near here.

"Flip over."

I roll toward the wall with the knee kept straight, as he taught me in week two, and settle face-down, my forehead on my stacked hands. The table paper crackles beside my ear. He moves to my right side, near my hip. I feel his left palm settle flat on the back of my pelvis, the heel of his hand on my sacrum, and my shirt rides up two inches, so the contact is skin against skin. He's pinning me down for a reason. When the quad is tight, the hip lifts off the table to cheat the stretch, and his hand is there to stop me from cheating.

His right hand cups the front of my ankle, the lowest part of the shin, just above the foot.

"Bending now."

He draws my heel toward my glutes. For the first ninety degrees it's nothing, just the weight of my lower leg moving through an arc. Past ninety, the front of the knee begins to tighten, and the skin over the incision pulls like a seam about to give. At a hundred, the stretch reaches deep into the joint itself, a dense, grinding pressure wedged behind the kneecap. My hip tries to rise. His left hand presses it back down, firmly and unhurriedly, and the pressure sends heat up my spine that has nothing to do with the knee.

I hate that. I hate it more than the pain.

"Seven," I say into my hands.

"Stay with it."

He smells of eucalyptus liniment. Everyone at the national training center smelled of it, but he wore it the most, rubbing it into his Achilles before every session. I remember sitting on a cold track in Gateshead while he taped my ankle, his head bent over it, and thinking things I never said out loud. He decided to stop at twenty-nine. He retired on his own terms, finished his degree, and got hands that heal instead of a body that breaks. I didn't decide anything. My body did the deciding.

"Contract-relax," he says. "Push your foot back into my hand. Twenty percent. Don't kick me."

I push, trying to straighten the knee against his palm. The quad engages and the burning inside the joint eases, the muscle working instead of being worked. He counts to five aloud. His voice is level, a voice you'd use with a stranger.

"And let go."

I release, and as the quad goes slack he takes up the slack, folding my heel another few centimeters toward my body. The muscle has nowhere to hide. The pain rises steeply. Eight. My breath stops in my chest, and a hot prickle of sweat breaks out along my hairline. The muscles of my right hamstring jump in a small spasm.

"Breathe," he says quietly.

Then his thumb moves. Just once, across the base of my spine, a single short stroke. It isn't clinical, it isn't stabilization. It's what he used to do in a call room before a final, to tell me I was okay.

It stops at once. His hand goes flat and still again, as though it never happened.

I breathe out. The pain settles back to seven, a dull pressure I can live inside.

"Holding thirty seconds," he says, a little too evenly.

Neither of us speaks. The wall clock ticks. I can feel his pulse through my ankle, or maybe it's mine. I can't tell where the line falls, which is exactly the problem.

He lowers my leg slowly, the knee straightening in stages, and the relief arrives as a flood of warmth that feels almost worse than the stretch. Then the goniometer. He positions the pivot over the outside of the knee joint, on the lateral femoral condyle, lines one arm along my thigh toward the bony point of my hip and the other along the outside of my shin toward the ankle bone. Then he bends my knee once more, to the point where I tell him it's a seven.

"A hundred and eight," he says. "Up six from Tuesday."

"Wonderful. In another year I can sit cross-legged."

"In another year you can run."

"I could run before."

He doesn't answer. He writes the number on my chart and pulls my shirt back down over the small of my back, his knuckles barely grazing my skin, as careful as if the fabric might break.

"Thursday," he says.

I sit up and swing my legs over the side, and the knee throbs in time with my heartbeat. He is already rolling the sleeves down his forearms, teal and orange, folding them away. He doesn't look at me, and I can tell how hard he is working not to.

prompt:
Hell is Other Demons

Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Write a day in the life of this power couple, with elements of dark comedy & fantasy. Use understated irony & absurdity by merging the black immorality and everyday business of running hell, against relatable domestic relationship drama. Take cues from Neil Gaiman. Lucifer’s pet hellhound won’t stop chewing on the iron throne’s leg, adding to the tension. 1000 words.
response:
# Hell is Other Demons

There are no mornings in Hell, but Lucifer Morningstar keeps one anyway, the way some widowers go on setting out two cups for tea. At what he has decided is six o'clock, he opens his eyes, and the first thing he hears is chewing.

"Biscuit," he says.

The chewing pauses, considers, and resumes.

Biscuit is a hellhound the size of a small cathedral, with eyes like coals that have just been given bad news. His true name is eleven syllables long and sours milk in three counties when spoken aloud. Lilith named him Biscuit. She said it suited him. Lucifer said a great many things about this at the time, most of them in the old tongue and some of them while things were on fire. Biscuit he remained.

What Biscuit is chewing is the left rear leg of the Iron Throne.

The Throne was forged from the chains that bound the Fallen in the first days, hammered on an anvil of grief by a smith whose name has since been eaten. It has endured rebellions, three schisms, and a brief period in the fourteenth century when Beelzebub tried to introduce cushions. It now wobbles. When Lucifer sits upon it to pass judgement, it lists gently to the left, so that the damned, gazing up at the Adversary in all his terrible glory, get the faint impression that he is trying to hear something.

He sits. It lists. The day begins.

---

Beelzebub arrives with the clipboard. There are always flies around Beelzebub, and there is always a clipboard, and Lucifer has never been sure which came first.

"Intake's up eleven percent," says Beelzebub. "The Lake of Fire's at capacity. Facilities want to reclassify it as a pond, so we stop having to meet the regulations for lakes."

"Whose regulations?"

"Ours."

"Do it."

"Also, a fellow in the Seventh Circle has filed a complaint. He says his torment is disproportionate to his sins."

"What were his sins?"

Beelzebub consults the clipboard. "Mostly he reclined his seat on long-haul flights."

"And his torment?"

"Boiling."

Lucifer considers this. "Seat someone in front of him who reclines," he says. "Forever. Keep the boiling."

Beelzebub writes this down with profound satisfaction. It is good, Lucifer reflects, to be good at one's job. It is something to hold on to when you are alone in a very large room at the bottom of everything, with a dog eating your furniture.

---

A carpenter is summoned, a small horned imp named Pell with a pencil behind each horn. He looks at the leg for a long time and sucks his teeth, of which he has many.

"That's original chain-iron, that is," says Pell. "Can't get it anymore. They don't bind the Fallen like they used to."

"How long to fix it?"

"Eternity." He thinks. "Give or take. Depends on parts."

In the meantime, he folds a contract of damnation into a neat square and wedges it under the leg. The Throne steadies. Somewhere, a soul will now spend eternity propping up furniture, which Lucifer supposes is a kind of justice. Pell's invoice comes to a soul and a half.

Biscuit removes the contract and eats it.

---

Lilith arrives at noon, which is to say the moment Lucifer has decided is noon. She once called this habit charming, a long time ago, before the business with the library.

She does not knock. She has never knocked. The doors of Hell, which withstood the Harrowing, open for her the way cats go to people who are allergic to them.

"I left my good knife," she says.

"You took your good knife. You took it in October. You put it in my shoulder."

"Then I left my other good knife."

Biscuit abandons the leg and goes to her, his whole enormous body wagging, which collapses a minor colonnade. She scratches him behind the ears, where the flames are softest.

"You're feeding him souls again," she says. "I can tell. His coat goes dull."

"He likes souls."

"He likes being given things. That isn't the same." She looks at Lucifer, and Lucifer looks at the ceiling, which is a long way up and has nothing on it.

Last month she came to burn the archives. The month before that, she came to curse his name in a language older than the moon. These were, in their way, honest visits. Lately, though, she has been coming for knives she doesn't own, cardigans she has never worn, and a jar of something. "The jar," she called it, as if there had only ever been one. On Tuesday she came to return a book. It was not his book, and they both pretended it was.

"You look thin," she says.

"I am a being of pure light and malice. I don't have a weight."

"You look thin," Lilith repeats. She sits on the arm of the Throne, and the Throne lists toward her, as things in Hell always have.

---

They do not talk about the library, or the four thousand years before the library, or the morning she left with nothing but Biscuit's lead, then came back an hour later to return it because he had cried. Neither of them has ever specified who "he" was.

Instead they talk shop. She thinks the reclining man's torment is sentimental. He thinks her new demon-princes are mostly hair. She asks after Beelzebub's flies by name. In the afternoon they stand on the balcony above the Pond of Fire, as it is now officially known, and listen to the screaming the way other couples listen to the sea.

"It's nice," she says. "This time of day."

"There isn't a time of day."

"I know," she says. "It's still nice."

Biscuit lies between them with his chin on her foot, chewing nothing, for once.

---

She leaves at what he will later decide was six. At the door she turns, as if she has forgotten something, and he waits to hear what it will be this time. A scarf, perhaps, or a spoon, or the other jar.

"Thursday," says Lilith. "I'll come for the knife."

"There is no knife."

"Then I'll have to look for it, won't I," she says, and is gone. The doors of Hell close behind her rather slowly, the way doors do when they would prefer to stay open.

Lucifer returns to his Throne. Biscuit has returned to the leg. There is a groove in it now, deep and patient, and the whole great iron seat of Hell's dominion leans a degree or two toward the door.

He could have it fixed. Pell says it would take eternity, give or take.

He sits down, slightly crooked, and lets the dog chew.

# Hell is Other Demons

The ash began falling a little before dawn, which in Hell is more of a formality than an event. It came down soft and grey and patient, as it had for eleven thousand years, settling on the battlements and the brimstone and the small ceramic gnome that someone had placed beside the Gates.

Lucifer Morningstar woke on the left side of the bed. He had slept on the left side for four hundred and six days, which was exactly how long the right side had been empty. Every one of those mornings he had told himself that this was simply where he preferred to sleep.

He made coffee. In Hell, all coffee is slightly burnt. This is not a punishment; it is merely the climate. He drank it at the window and watched the ash collect on the sill. He did not look at the cupboard where her mug still sat, the black one with the chip on the handle. He had not thrown it away, because throwing it away would have meant something, and he was not ready for things to mean anything yet.

---

The morning meeting ran long. They always did.

"Sinner intake is up nine percent," said Beelzebub, buzzing faintly. "Mostly the usual. Avarice. Wrath. One man who replied-all to a company-wide email." He paused. "He's asked to file a complaint."

"About?"

"His punishment. He says it isn't bad enough. He says he deserves worse, and that our failure to provide it is causing him distress."

Lucifer rubbed his temples. "Then isn't it working?"

Beelzebub opened his mouth, closed it, and made a note.

There followed forty minutes on the blood shortage, since the damned had grown stingy about signing in it, and a proposal from Accounting to move the Lake of Fire to a four-day week. Lucifer approved it without reading it. He had been approving things without reading them for about four hundred and six days.

---

She arrived just before lunch, which was new.

For the first few months, Lilith had come only at night, and only to kill him. It was never permanent; it was more of a statement. Once she had put a spear through his chest during a budget review and left it there, quivering, while she explained that his new haircut was a cry for help. He had kept the spear. It was in the umbrella stand.

Today she walked in through the door like a normal person, shaking ash from her hair.

"I'm here for my knives," she said.

"Your knives."

"The good ones. With the bone handles."

"They're in the kitchen drawer. Where you left them." He said it lightly, the way one carries a very full cup.

She went to get them. She took a long time. When she came back she had the knives in one hand and a biscuit in the other, and she was frowning at him.

"You're eating at your desk."

"I'm the Lord of Hell. I eat where I like."

"You're eating cereal. At your desk. At noon." She looked at the bowl the way she had once looked at the armies of Heaven. "Lucifer, are you all right?"

Nobody had asked him that in a very long time. Nobody asks the Devil that. It is one of the less advertised drawbacks of the job.

"I'm fine," he said. "Coaster, please. That's mahogany."

She set her biscuit directly on the wood and held his eyes while she did it. For a moment it was almost like before.

---

The afternoon was a contract dispute. A man in Ohio had sold his soul for a winning lottery ticket. This was unremarkable, except that he had already sold it to a lesser imp in 1998 for a convertible, and the imp had sold it on, and now three separate departments were claiming him. The man himself was still alive and, by every account, rather smug about it.

"Can a soul be divided?" asked the Assistant Under-Secretary for Acquisitions.

"Everyone's is, eventually," said Lucifer, who was not listening. He was looking at his phone, where a message had appeared at 2:14.

*left my scarf. don't touch it.*

He found the scarf on the back of his chair, where it had not been that morning. It was red, and it smelled of smoke and night-blooming jasmine and the deep dark earth of the first garden. He did not touch it. He looked at it for about twenty minutes, which is a different thing entirely.

---

She came back at dusk. The ash was still falling. It softened everything, the distant screaming included, so that the whole Inferno sounded like a city heard through a closed window.

"My scarf," she said.

"On the chair."

She picked it up and did not leave. She went out onto the balcony instead, and after a while he followed. They stood side by side looking out over the burning plains, as they had on ten thousand other evenings before.

"Moloch's retiring," she said eventually. "He wants to spend more time with his worshippers."

"I signed the papers."

"You didn't read them."

"No."

She was quiet. Ash settled on her shoulders and she let it. "You never asked how I've been."

"How have you been?"

"Awful," said Lilith, with some satisfaction. "Absolutely awful. I drowned a ship. I started a cult in Belgium. I've been sleeping on the wrong side of the bed."

He looked at her. She did not look at him.

"I kept the spear," he said.

"I know. It's in the umbrella stand. It's a terrible place for a spear."

"It's a terrible place for an umbrella. It never rains here."

"It's raining now," she said. She held out her hand and caught the ash in her palm, grey and soft and endless, and that was the closest either of them would come to saying it.

She did not stay the night. But when she left, she took the knives and forgot the scarf, and in eleven thousand years she had never forgotten anything.

Lucifer went inside. He took her mug down from the cupboard, the black one with the chip, and washed it and dried it and set it beside his own.

Outside, the ash kept falling. It would fall tomorrow, too. It always had.

He found, for the first time in a long while, that he didn't mind.

# Hell is Other Demons

The thing nobody tells you about Hell is that someone has to run it.

Lucifer Morningstar woke, as he did every morning, at six, to the sound of a tax attorney screaming somewhere beneath the bedroom floor. He had not set it as an alarm. It had simply happened, the way a great many things in Hell simply happened, and after the first few centuries he had stopped trying to do anything about it.

He lay there for a while, looking at the ceiling, which was black, and at the other side of the bed, which was empty. It had been empty for eleven years. This was not long, as these things went. Once it had been empty for the entirety of the Byzantine Empire.

He got up. He made coffee. The coffee in Hell is always slightly burnt, always cold by the time you remember it, and there is never quite enough milk. This is not a punishment. It is simply what coffee is like everywhere, and Hell had merely been honest about it.

At nine he met with Beelzebub about the flies.

"They're unionizing," said Beelzebub.

"They're flies," said Lucifer.

"With respect, sir, so am I. Partially." Beelzebub produced a petition. It was covered in very small footprints, all of them sticky. Lucifer signed something. He was not sure what. He had signed the Treaty of Westphalia under similar conditions, and it had worked out about as well as anything did.

At ten there was the matter of the Seventh Circle's thermostat. It had been set to *Unbearable* since the Fall and was now, through some engineering oversight, merely *Uncomfortable*, which had drawn complaints from both the damned and the staff. At ten-thirty, a newly arrived televangelist insisted there had been a clerical error. There had not. There never was. Lucifer had stopped pointing this out, because it took the fun out of it for everybody.

At eleven-fifteen, the door to his office came off its hinges.

It did not fall. It was placed, quite neatly, against the wall, by a woman with hair like a midnight that had been left out in the rain, and eyes like the moment before you realize you've missed the last stair. She was carrying a leather purse that had been on fire at some point, possibly recently. It smelled of smoke, and of something floral underneath.

"Lilith," said Lucifer.

"I've come for my cardigan," said Lilith.

"You haven't got a cardigan."

"The grey one. With the moths."

"Those aren't moths. Those are the souls of—" He stopped. "It's in the wardrobe."

She did not go to the wardrobe. She sat down in the chair across from his desk, the one reserved for popes and particularly ambitious stockbrokers, put her purse in her lap, and looked at him.

The last time she had visited, in March, she had put a dagger through his left lung and set the drapes on fire. The time before that, she had turned all his fountain pens into small, disappointed snakes. He did not mention either of these things. Neither did she. It was, he supposed, a kind of progress.

"You look tired," she said.

"I run Hell."

"You've always run Hell. You didn't used to look tired."

She opened the purse. Lilith's purse was famous in certain circles, the way black holes are famous: things went in and did not, generally, come out, and if you looked too long you began to feel unwell. She took out a key card from a Holiday Inn in Duluth, a single child's mitten, a tin of Altoids, a rosary missing one bead, and a snow globe of the Eiffel Tower in which, if you looked closely, it was always snowing on a man who had just been told something terrible.

"I was in Minnesota," she said, by way of explanation.

"Doing what?"

"Tempting." She unwrapped an Altoid. "A dentist. He had a wife and a boat and a lovely laugh."

"Did he fall?"

"Oh, immediately." She sighed. "It was very boring. Nobody resists anymore. You used to have to *work* for it." She looked at him sideways. "Do you remember the desert? Those monks?"

"I remember you were magnificent with those monks."

The words came out before he could stop them. They hung in the air between them, like the smell of the purse.

Lilith turned the snow globe over in her hands. The man inside it went on being told terrible things.

"I brought you this," she said, and set it on his desk.

"Why?"

"I don't know. It reminded me of you." She shrugged. "Everything else in the gift shop was keychains."

Lucifer looked at the snow globe. Then he unlocked the bottom drawer of his desk, which no demon in Hell had ever seen open. It contained, in no particular order: a seashell from a beach that had sunk beneath the waves around the time of Atlantis, a Roman coin with a thumbprint pressed into the bronze, a ticket stub from the premiere of *The Rite of Spring*, a matchbook from a Las Vegas wedding chapel, and nine thousand years of other small, odd things she had left behind, on purpose or not, which he had never thrown away.

Lilith looked into the drawer for a long time.

"You kept the matchbook," she said.

"You set the chapel on fire with it."

"It was a very ugly chapel."

"It was," he agreed.

Somewhere far below, the tax attorney had started up again. The flies were humming something that sounded, horribly, like a union song. The Seventh Circle was still only Uncomfortable.

Lilith closed the purse.

"I'm not staying," she said.

"I know."

"I'm only saying. In case you thought."

"I didn't think."

She stood, went to the wardrobe, and took out the grey cardigan, which was not hers, had never been hers, and put it on. It fitted her perfectly. The souls in the wool fluttered, and settled.

"Thursday," she said, at the door, or at the place where the door had been. "There's a man in Lisbon. Very devout. Could take weeks."

"I'll see if I'm free," said Lucifer, who was always free on Thursdays, and had been for eleven years.

When she had gone, he put the snow globe in the drawer with the others. Then, after a moment, he took it out again and set it on the corner of his desk, where he could see it.

Then he found a screwdriver and began, quite cheerfully, to put the door back on.

# The Matter of the Meadow

Dream had presided over the trial of a god who ate his own children. He had judged a war between two halves of a dreaming whale. He had never, until this evening, been made to look at a storyboard.

"Exhibit C," said First Love, holding it up with both trembling hands. "The approach."

The drawing showed two small figures in a field, lying very close and not touching. Someone had drawn little hearts in the margins and then, perhaps in a fit of professional restraint, rubbed most of them out.

"Note the wildflowers," First Love went on, cheeks deepening from rose to something nearer plum. "Cornflowers, mostly. Some clover. I wanted his fingers to brush hers by accident. Then *not* by accident. Then nobody knows whose fault it was. That's—" a small, mortified swallow "—that's the important part."

"The court has noted the clover," said Dream.

From the defendant's bench came a sound like dry leaves dragged across a grave. The cackle went up into the vaulted dark and stayed there longer than it had any right to, circling the ceiling before dropping back down.

The Clerk, a large grey moth in a powdered wig, rapped its gavel. Nothing happened, because the gavel was also a moth.

"Order," it said, without hope.

Mora did not stand. She lay draped across the bench, elbows propped and chin in her hands, like a cat on a warm car bonnet. Her hair moved slightly when no air was moving. When she smiled, there were more teeth in it than there had been a moment before.

"Your Honour," said First Love, "I spent *three years* on this dream. I built it from the leftovers of a school trip and one look she gave him across the art room. I tuned it. Every Thursday it ends at the exact moment before the kiss, and he wakes up feeling like his ribs are full of birds." First Love's voice wobbled. "Now he wakes up feeling like his ribs are full of *her*."

"Objection," said Mora lazily. "Leading."

"I'm not leading anyone. I'm the plaintiff."

"Sustained," said Dream, mostly to see what would happen.

First Love stared at him. Mora gave a delighted little cackle.

Dream regretted it at once. Somewhere in the Dreaming a library was misfiling itself. Somewhere a nightmare had escaped into a bishop's sleep. And here he sat, an Endless, older than the stars' first doubts, ruling on an objection that had no grounds.

"Continue," he said.

"She comes in at the *climax*," First Love said, waving the storyboard at the bench. "The girl rolls over, laughing. She climbs on top of him, which is meant to be playful, a tickle-fight sort of thing, very wholesome, I had it vetted. And then—"

"And then *me*." Mora arched her back and her spine clicked like a rosary. "She leans down, sweet as a peach, and her face goes long and grey and lovely, and she sits on his little chest and drinks." She sighed happily. "He can't move. He can't scream. He just stares up at me with those big wet eyes."

"Is he frightened?" asked Dream.

"*Terrified*."

"Is he—" First Love's voice cracked. "Does he still think she's pretty?"

Mora paused. Then a slow, filthy grin spread across her face.

"That's the funny part," she said. "He can't work out *what* he thinks."

First Love made a noise like a kettle in grief.

Dream closed his eyes. When he opened them, the stars in his pupils had dimmed by perhaps one magnitude, which the Clerk, who had worked there six centuries, recognised as the equivalent of a man pinching the bridge of his nose.

"The defendant will state her case."

Mora rose at last. It took longer than standing should. Some parts of her seemed to arrive late.

"Your Honour. Members of the court." She nodded at the empty jury box, where three sleepwalkers sat with their eyes open, seeing nothing. "Let's be grown-ups. Children don't dream about wildflowers forever. Sooner or later every first love grows teeth. I'm just *early*." She spread her long fingers. "And frankly, a girl's gotta eat too, you know? You try living on retired farmers. It's all sciatica and regret. The young ones hold their breath so *sweetly*."

Her cackle went round the ceiling again. One of the sleepwalkers wept quietly in the jury box without waking.

"Precedent," squeaked First Love, scrabbling at a folio. "*Tooth Fairy versus the Grandmother's Attic*. *Krampus versus Christmas Morning*, which was settled—"

"Krampus versus Christmas Morning was settled by me," said Dream, "and I have regretted it every December since."

He was silent for a while. The court waited. In the Dreaming, a silence from its lord has weather in it.

The trouble, Dream reflected, was that both of them were right. He had watched a great many first loves. They were never only cornflowers. There was always a moment when the other person leaned close, and a boy's chest locked, and he could not breathe, and he did not know if he was dying or something better.

He found, unexpectedly, that he wished to be amused.

"The court rules as follows," he said. "The dreamscape remains the property of the plaintiff. The field, the flowers, the almost. All of it."

First Love sagged with relief.

"However." Mora's ears pricked up, quite literally. "The defendant is granted feeding rights. Not in the dream. In the waking world. To be exercised only when the boy sees the girl across a room and forgets how to breathe. Every breath he holds for her, Mora may have."

Mora considered this. Then she licked her lips with a tongue that went on too long.

"That's *loads* of breath," she said.

"He is fourteen," said Dream. "It will be a banquet."

First Love opened a mouth to protest and found nothing in it.

"Furthermore," Dream went on, and here a faint, terrible lightness entered his voice, "since the plaintiff and defendant have demonstrated such close interest in each other's work, the court orders that from tonight they share an office."

The silence that followed was the finest Dream had heard in a century.

First Love turned the colour of a fire alarm. Mora turned her head very slowly to look at her new colleague, and her smile kept widening long after a face should have stopped it.

Then she cackled, and it went up into the dark and did not come down at all.

"Court is adjourned," said Dream.

The moth struck the gavel. The gavel, for once, flew away.

# The Matter of the Meadow

The hourglass stood behind the bench, taller than the courtroom had any right to contain, and it dripped. Not poured. Dripped, one shimmering grain at a time, each landing with the soft finality of a closing eyelid.

Dream regarded it for a long moment before regarding anything else. It was, the clerk reflected, a bad sign.

"Case four thousand and eleven," announced the clerk, a raven in a powdered wig that sat askew. "The matter of a recurring dreamscape, registered to one Max Abernathy, aged fourteen. Wildflower meadow, afternoon light, one almost-kiss. Petitioner: First Love. Respondent: Mora."

"I have read the brief," said Dream.

"All of it, my lord?"

"Unfortunately."

First Love rose from the petitioner's bench. He was small and round-cheeked and seemed perpetually on the verge of apologising for something. He held a sheaf of papers tied with pink ribbon, and his hands trembled.

"My lord. Your Honour. Sir." He cleared his throat. "I spent eleven months on that meadow. *Eleven.* The clover alone. Do you know how difficult it is to make clover smell like the first day of summer holidays? And her hair. I got the hair exactly right. It moves when there's no wind. That's the whole point. Nothing makes sense and it's wonderful."

"Noted," said Dream.

"And the almost-kiss. It never lands, you see. That's the craft. He wakes up confused and warm and slightly embarrassed and spends the entire maths lesson staring at the back of her head. That's formative, my lord. That's foundational. That's what poetry is built on."

"Bad poetry," murmured someone in the gallery. Dream did not look, and the someone ceased to be in the gallery.

"And then," First Love's voice cracked, "*she* came."

At the respondent's table, Mora uncrossed her legs. She was long and pale and gave the impression of having more joints than strictly necessary. Her hair hung over her face like wet laundry. She was also, unfortunately, lovely, in the way a cliff edge is lovely. When she smiled, the candles leaned away.

"Objection," she said. "Characterisation."

"He has said nothing yet," said Dream.

"I could feel it coming."

"Overruled. Continue."

First Love placed a small glass orb on the evidence table. Inside, the meadow played in miniature: the boy on his back among the flowers, the girl laughing, the girl clambering onto him the way children do when one is winning a wrestling match—

—and then the girl was not the girl. Her laugh dropped an octave and kept dropping. Her weight settled on the boy's chest like a sack of wet earth. The boy's eyes went wide. He could not move. He could not breathe. Mora, in the orb, leaned down and inhaled, slow and luxurious, as if sampling a fine wine.

Around them, the flowers kept nodding pleasantly. First Love had made them well.

"He wakes up screaming now," said First Love. "Every night. He sleeps with the light on. Yesterday he saw her in the corridor and went grey. My lord, she's turned his first crush into a sleep paralysis episode."

"With respect," said Mora, "I've kept most of the original features. The meadow's still there. She's still technically there, at the start. I'm practically a co-author."

"You ate his *breath*!"

"I nibbled."

Dream closed his eyes. The hourglass dripped. Somewhere, a galaxy aged a little.

"Respondent," he said. "Your defence."

Mora stood. It took a while.

"Look," she said. "I'm a traditional spirit. I've got overhead. Eight hundred years ago I had my pick: every peasant from Kraków to Kyiv, sleeping on their backs after a heavy supper. Now? Weighted blankets. Melatonin. White noise machines. Someone invented a meditation app with a voice like warm honey and my intake dropped forty percent." She spread her long fingers. "I found an unattended dream with a perfectly good chest in it. What was I supposed to do, starve? A girl's gotta eat too, you know?"

"It was *not* unattended," said First Love. "I attend it every Tuesday and Thursday."

"Then where were you on Wednesday, Cupid?"

"Don't call me that. He's a different department."

"Order," said Dream. He did not raise his voice. The courtroom simply became quieter, the way a room does when someone opens a door onto a very long drop.

He considered the orb. He considered the boy within it, frozen mid-scream, his fear and his longing so thoroughly knotted together that no one, least of all the boy, would ever quite untangle them.

The clerk shuffled. "Precedent, my lord, would suggest restoration of the dream to its original architect, and a formal censure—"

"I am aware of precedent."

"Of course, my lord."

Dream was silent for a long time. When he spoke, there was something in his voice the clerk had not heard in several centuries, something that made him check his feathers for loose pins. It might have been amusement.

"Neither of you," said Dream, "is entitled to the whole of it."

First Love blinked. Mora's smile widened by a tooth.

"The dreamscape will be held jointly. First Love retains the meadow, the light, the hair that moves without wind. Mora retains the weight upon the chest, and the breath. You will share the dream each night until the dreamer outgrows it."

"*Share* it?" First Love's cheeks drained from rose to something closer to dishwater. "My lord, how will he ever tell which part is which?"

"He will not," said Dream. "That is the sentence."

"That's monstrous," whispered First Love.

"That's adorable," said Mora.

"That," said Dream, rising, "is what the mortals call adolescence. They seem to survive it. Mostly." He glanced at the hourglass, which had not dripped faster in eleven thousand years and did not intend to start now. "Next case."

The clerk consulted his list, and his feathers wilted. "The Tooth Fairy, my lord, versus the Dream of One's Teeth Falling Out. She's alleging trademark infringement."

Dream sat back down. He did not sigh. He was far too old and far too dignified to sigh.

The hourglass did it for him.

# The Matter of the Wildflower Field

"ALL RISE," the bailiff boomed, "FOR THE LORD OF THE DREAMING, PRINCE OF STORIES, KING OF... SLUMBERING... THINGS."

The bailiff was a moth the size of a wardrobe. He had held the post for nine centuries and had never once read a name correctly.

Dream took his seat. The Court rose, then sat, then rose again because the moth had not said they could sit. Dream let this happen twice before raising one pale finger.

"Sit."

They sat.

"The matter," Dream said, in the tone of a man reading his own obituary and finding errors, "of the recurring dream designated Field, Wildflowers, Almost-Kiss. Petitioner?"

First Love stood. Her cheeks were the colour of a slapped peach. She held a folder covered in small hand-drawn hearts, and she clutched it like a shield.

"Um," she said. "Me. Hello. Sorry."

"And the respondent."

Mora did not stand. She lounged across the defence bench like spilt ink, wearing a black shift and a face that suggested something had died in her vicinity recently and she had been glad about it. She waved.

"Hiya, Lord D."

Dream's eyes, two distant stars at the bottom of a well, did not blink. Somewhere in the gallery a lesser nightmare whispered *oh, she's done for*.

"Petitioner. State your grievance."

First Love opened her folder. Several pressed daisies fell out. She picked them up, apologised to them, and began.

"I built that dream from scratch. Fourteen months. Max lies in the field. Priya lies next to him. They talk about nothing, sort of, and then she rolls over, and they nearly kiss, and he wakes up feeling..." She made a vague, fluttering gesture. "You know."

"I do not," said Dream.

"Well. Good. It's very good. I won an award." She held up a small ribbon. Nobody had ever seen this ribbon before. "Then *she* turned up."

"Objection," said Mora. "Turned up implies I wasn't invited."

"You weren't."

"His window was open. That's practically a welcome mat in my culture."

"Overruled," said Dream. "Continue."

"Now Priya rolls over, and she sort of playfully pins him, like a game, and then she..." First Love lowered her voice. "Changes."

"Into what?"

"Me," said Mora cheerfully. "But with Priya's hair clip. I kept the clip. Continuity matters."

"And then she sits on his chest," First Love said, her voice cracking, "and *drinks his breath*."

There was a murmur in the gallery. A small Fear of Falling fainted and was carried out.

"The worst part," First Love went on, "is that he still... he still sort of likes her. When she's like that. He wakes up screaming and *also* blushing. He doesn't know which one to do first. It's ruining my arc."

Dream closed his eyes briefly, the way a mountain might close its eyes when someone begins yodelling.

"Respondent. Your defence."

Mora sat up, which took a while, as she seemed to have more joints than strictly necessary.

"Look. I've been doing this since before your lot had a word for *Tuesday*. I sit on chests. I eat breath. It's very traditional. Slavic grandmothers will vouch for me. And frankly, the pickings are slim. Nobody sleeps on their backs anymore. They sleep with phones on their faces. Have you tried feeding through a phone? It tastes like blue light and regret."

"That is not a defence."

"It's context." She shrugged. "A girl's gotta eat too, you know?"

"The prosecution would like to call a witness," First Love said quickly. "To establish prior zoning."

"CALLING," the moth bellowed, unfurling itself to its full and terrible height, "SPUTT... KWAZZ."

A small, sweating figure in a cardigan shuffled to the stand. It carried a pencil that was always slightly blunt.

"Spot Quiz," it muttered. "It's *Spot Quiz*."

"You may speak," said Dream.

"I've had the boy since Year Seven," Spot Quiz said. "Tuesdays and Thursdays. Unprepared for an algebra test, wearing no shoes. Very standard. Last spring I applied for the field on weekends and was told it was zoned *Romantic, Formative*. Strictly no anxiety." It glared at Mora. "So how come *she* gets in?"

"Because I don't fill out forms, darling."

"CALLING," roared the moth, apparently unprompted, "MAKZ, THE SLEEPER."

There was a pause.

"He is asleep," said Dream. "That is rather the premise of the jurisdiction."

The moth folded slowly, mortified, and sat on its own antennae.

Dream steepled his fingers. He regarded the bashful thing with her ribbon, and the hungry thing with her borrowed hair clip, and the boy who was neither present nor absent but simply lying in a field somewhere, waiting to be told what love was.

For a moment, very briefly, something passed over Dream's face. In a lesser being it might have been called a smile. The gallery leaned back in alarm.

"I have considered," he said, "awarding the field to the Spot Quiz."

Spot Quiz brightened. First Love whimpered. Mora groaned.

"I have also considered ruling that the boy wakes precisely before either of you completes your work. No kiss. No meal. In perpetuity."

"That's *cruel*," said First Love.

"That's *Tuesday*," said Spot Quiz.

"I have instead decided," Dream said, rising, "on joint custody."

Both claimants stared at him.

"The field remains. The almost-kiss remains. The girl rolls over." He looked at Mora. "You may have the chest. A modest portion of breath. No more than a sigh."

"A *sigh*? I'm not a hummingbird—"

"And you," he said to First Love, "will stop pretending your work and hers are different crafts."

First Love opened her mouth. She closed it again. She looked at Mora, who looked back at her. Something unspoken and deeply professional passed between them.

"He'll be confused," First Love said finally.

"Yes."

"For years."

"Yes."

"He'll grow up to have a *type*."

"He will," said Dream, and swept from the bench. "Court is adjourned."

"ALL RISE," boomed the moth, a full minute late, to an empty room.

Mora stretched and fished Priya's hair clip from somewhere unpleasant. "Drinks?" she asked.

First Love hesitated. Then she tucked her ribbon away.

"Just one," she said. "And you're paying."

"I don't have money, sweetheart. I have *breath*."

"Then breathe on the bartender."

Spot Quiz watched them go, sharpening its pencil, and quietly scheduled the boy for Wednesdays as well.
