# Sisyphus Gives Advice

The hill had been designed by someone who understood hills. It was not steep enough to be dramatic, nor gentle enough to be pleasant. It was precisely steep enough to be *work*, which is the cruellest gradient there is.

Halfway up, a man in a sweat-darkened tunic was leaning companionably into a boulder. On top of the boulder sat a crow with a pencil clamped in one foot.

"Next," said Sisyphus.

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*
*My husband and I have been married twenty-two years. Lately everything he does annoys me. The way he breathes. The way he says "righto." He has started humming while he eats soup. I don't want to leave him. I just want to stop wanting to throw the soup.*
*— Simmering, Thebes*

*Dear Simmering,*
*Twenty-two years is long enough that you are no longer married to one man but to several, one after another, and some of them hum. This is normal, and nobody warns you.*
*When everything about a person annoys us, it usually isn't about them. It's about something we haven't said, which sits in the room and makes the air close. Is there something? It needn't be big. Often it's small and old, and you've carried it so long it feels like posture.*
*If there isn't, try this: for one week, each time he annoys you, also notice one thing he does that doesn't. You're not trying to be a saint. You're just making the ledger honest.*
*Also, a man who hums over soup is a man enjoying his soup. There are worse sounds to be married to.*
*— S.*

*[Crow's note: I would throw the soup. — C.]*

---

The boulder reached the top at the moment it always did, which was the exact instant a reasonable man might allow himself a small breath of satisfaction. Sisyphus allowed himself one. Then the rock tipped and went bounding back down the slope with the cheerful stupidity of large objects.

He watched it go the way a man watches a dog chase a stick.

"Lovely morning for it," he said, and started down. Crow followed on foot, complaining.

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*
*I manage the counting-house for a grain merchant in Corinth. I arrive before dawn and leave after dark. My daughter recently drew a family portrait, and I was a small grey smudge in the corner labelled "Papa (working)." My employer says the busy season will end soon. He has said this for four years.*
*— Smudge, Corinth*

*Dear Smudge,*
*A busy season that lasts four years isn't a season. It's the climate, and you'll need to dress for it.*
*Choose one evening a week. Not three. You won't hold three, and failing at three will feel like permission to give up. One. Tell your employer the day and the hour you'll be leaving. Tell him, don't ask him. Asking invites a conversation, and you will lose the conversation, because he's had more practice.*
*Then go home and actually be there, not thinking about ledgers. If you're thinking about ledgers, she'll know. Children can smell an absent parent at forty paces.*
*Corinth will be counting grain long after both of us. Your daughter will only be seven for about a year.*
*— S.*

*[Crow's note: He used to be king of Corinth. He knows what he's talking about. He doesn't like to talk about it. — C.]*

*[Second note: Ask her to redraw it in six months. If you're still grey, write again. — C.]*

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*
*My new gentleman friend has asked whether, during intimate moments, I might wear a costume involving feathers. Specifically swan feathers. He was very particular about the swan. Is this normal?*
*— Ruffled, Sparta*

Sisyphus paused mid-push, which the boulder took personally.

"Sparta," he said thoughtfully.

"Don't," said Crow.

"I wasn't going to."

"You were going to say something about Zeus."

"I was going to say something *near* Zeus."

*Dear Ruffled,*
*In your part of the world it's very nearly traditional.*
*"Normal" is less useful a question than this: does the idea delight you, amuse you, or make you want to leave by the back window? All three are respectable answers. If it's delight or amusement, enjoy yourself and buy good feathers, because cheap ones moult. If it's the window, say so plainly. A man worth keeping can hear "no" about swans and still be pleasant at breakfast.*
*If he ever offers to be the swan himself, have a quiet look round for thunderbolts.*
*— S.*

*[Crow's note: He said he wasn't going to. — C.]*

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*
*My neighbour's goat eats my washing. When I complain, he says goats will be goats. I have lost four tunics and most of my temper.*
*— Threadbare, Argos*

*Dear Threadbare,*
*Ask your neighbour for a favour. Something small, like borrowing a sieve or asking his opinion on your figs. It sounds backwards, but people find it oddly hard to stay at war with someone they've helped. They start telling themselves a story in which you're the sort of person worth helping.*
*Once there's a sieve between you, raise the goat again. Don't make it a complaint. Make it a shared problem: "What do you think we could do about her?" Note the "we." Note also the "her." Learn the goat's name. A goat with a name is a neighbour's animal. A goat without one is an act of war.*
*Meanwhile, move the washing line.*
*— S.*

*[Crow's note: Or eat the goat. I'm not saying. I'm only noting it's an option. — C.]*

---

The light, or the polite smear that passed for it down here, had shifted. From somewhere across the valley came the sound of Tantalus swearing at a grape.

Crow drew out the last letter. It was on good paper and had been folded many times, as though the writer kept opening it to check it still said what they meant.

Sisyphus took it and read it himself. Twice.

*Dear Sisyphus,*
*I am forty-three. I have not done anything important. I keep a small shop. I mend sandals. I go home. I sometimes think that when I'm gone, nobody will know I was here.*
*— Nobody, Megara*

*Dear Nobody,*
*Everyone walking about Megara with dry feet knows you were here. They just don't know they know, which is how most important things work.*
*It took me a long while to learn that the work that matters mostly doesn't stay done. Sandals wear through. Soup gets eaten. Children need feeding again by teatime. It's tempting to think that makes it pointless. It means the opposite: people needed you yesterday and will need you tomorrow, and you'll be there. That isn't a small life. That's the whole thing, really. Everything else is statues.*
*Go home tonight and notice who is glad to see you. Count them. Write back with the number.*
*— S.*

*[Crow's note: — ]*

---

The boulder reached the top. It paused. It went.

"Any more?" asked Sisyphus.

Crow shook out the satchel. "Empty."

"Pity." He set off down the hill at an easy, unhurried pace. Somewhere around the halfway mark he began, very quietly, to hum.

Crow looked around for something to throw.

# Sisyphus Gives Advice

The hill had no name, because nobody who could name it ever wanted to go there twice. Sisyphus had been up it several million times and thought of it privately as Gerald.

Crow landed at the usual spot, a third of the way up, where the path kinked and the boulder liked to lean on you like a drunk uncle at a wedding. He dropped a satchel onto the rock.

"Post," said Crow.

"Lovely," said Sisyphus, shouldering in. "Who've we got?"

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*My husband of eleven years says "I'm fine" when he is clearly not fine. Last week he said it while sitting in the dark holding a single sandal. How do I get him to talk?*

*— Worried in Corinth*

---

"Oh, I know this one. Take this down.

*Dear Worried,*

*Stop asking him across a table. Men like your husband will tell you anything so long as you're both looking at something else. Ask him to help mend the fence. Walk with him to market. Sit beside him, not opposite. Then say nothing for slightly longer than is comfortable. He'll fill it.*

*Also, find out about the sandal. A man does not hold one sandal in the dark over nothing.*"

Crow scratched it out with a claw dipped in squid ink.¹

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*I run a bakery in Thebes. I'm up before the sun and abed after the moon. My children say they never see me. But the bread doesn't make itself.*

*— Floury*

---

Sisyphus set his heels. The boulder grumbled forward a foot.

"*Dear Floury,*

*You bake two hundred loaves a day and I'd wager forty go stale. Bake a hundred and sixty. Close the day after the festival, when everyone's still eating leftover honey cake anyway. Teach your eldest to knead. She'll complain, and in ten years she'll be the only person in Thebes who can make your rye.*

*The bread doesn't make itself, true. But you'd be amazed how little of it needs to be made by you.*"

---

They reached the top an hour later. The boulder paused, considered its options with the air of a cat on a mantelpiece, and went back down.

"Bye," said Sisyphus fondly, and they strolled after it.

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*My husband has seen something on a vase and now he wishes to try it. I have examined the vase. I do not believe it is anatomically possible, and I think one of them is a goat.*

*— Concerned in Athens*

---

Crow's beak twitched. Sisyphus didn't break stride.

"*Dear Concerned,*

*Most of what's painted on vases was painted by men who have never done it, for men who never will. That doesn't make your husband silly. It means he's curious and doesn't know how to say so. Ask him what he liked about it. Usually it isn't the thing. It's being wanted that much. You can give him that without involving livestock.*

*If the goat is a firm requirement, write again and we'll talk.*"

"You're going to get a reply," said Crow.

"Oh, I hope so."

---

The next letter had come by sea, and the sea had had opinions.

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*I have recently ▓▓▓▓▓ my ▓▓▓▓ ▓▓▓▓▓▓ and now it won't stop ▓▓▓▓ing. My wife says I should ▓▓▓▓ it, but my mother says that's how we lost Uncle ▓▓▓▓. It is now in the ▓▓▓▓▓▓ and the neighbours have started ▓▓▓▓▓▓▓.*

*Please help. It is ▓▓▓▓ing right now.*

*— ▓▓▓▓▓▓ of Ithaca*

---

Crow held it up to the light. Sisyphus squinted.

"'Married my sister's brother'?" Crow offered.

"That's just his brother."

"'Inherited my late father's goat.'"

"There's a lot of goats this week." Sisyphus scratched his beard. "Could be 'repaired my old roof' and it won't stop *leaking*."

"Then why's it in the—" Crow peered. "That's either 'larder' or 'temple.'"

"And the neighbours have started *praying*. Or *charging*. Or *leaving*."

"How did they lose the uncle?"

They looked at each other.

"Right," said Sisyphus. "Cover everything.

*Dear friend in Ithaca,*

*If it is an animal, it is frightened and wants food and quiet. If it is a roof, there's a man called Dion near the harbour who is good with roofs. If it is a relative, listen to your wife, who is closer to the problem than your mother. If it is any kind of god, do not, whatever you do, try to ▓▓▓▓ it. Trust me on this.*"

"Should I smudge that bit on purpose?"

"Seems only polite."

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*I am twenty-four. I have no idea what my life is for. Everyone else seems to have a plan.*

*— Lost in Megara*

---

Sisyphus said nothing for a long while. Long enough to get the boulder past the kink.

"*Dear Lost,*

*Nobody else has a plan. They have a guess they've said out loud long enough that it sounds like one. You're allowed to do that too.*

*Purpose is rarely found. Mostly it's what's left behind after you've been kind to the same people for long enough. Learn something you can do with your hands. Feed someone on a Tuesday for no reason. Find something heavy enough to matter and small enough to get your hands on, and lean into it, and see what happens.*

*Write and tell me how you get on. I mean that. I'll be here.*"

Crow wrote it down without comment, which from Crow was practically a standing ovation.

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*Every time my mother-in-law visits, she rearranges my kitchen cupboards. I have asked her to stop. She says she's "only helping." I am going to throw a ladle at her.*

*— Rearranged in Sparta*

---

"Ah," said Sisyphus, with real warmth. "

*Dear Rearranged,*

*Put down the ladle. People who reorganise other people's cupboards are almost always trying to be useful in a house where they're no longer sure they're needed.*

*So give her a job that's genuinely hers. The spice shelf, say. Tell her nobody does it like she does, and mean it a little. Watch how quickly she leaves the rest alone.*

*After she goes, put everything back, except one thing. Leave that where she put it. Next visit, thank her for it.*

*You'll never get your kitchen back entirely. But you might get a mother-in-law, which is rarer.*"

Crow sealed it. "Is that the lot?"

"For today." Sisyphus set his shoulder to the stone, which was warm now from the afternoon sun, and smelled faintly of thyme from the hillside. "Ask around about that fellow in Ithaca, would you? I'd like to know how the uncle went."

The boulder, which had heard all of this before, began once more to climb.

---

¹ *Crow had tried quills, but felt that writing with a feather was, in his words, "a bit much."*

# From the Hill
*Advice for the Living, from Someone Who Has Had Time to Think About It*

The boulder reached the summit at a quarter past the post, which was ideal. Sisyphus watched it pause on the lip, considering its options, and then go back down the way it always did, with the air of something remembering an appointment.

He sat on a rock that had worn itself into the precise shape of him. Crow landed on his knee, shook out a satchel, and produced a pencil from somewhere it was better not to ask about.

"Bit of a pile today," said Crow.

"Festival season," said Sisyphus. "People see their families."

---

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
> *My husband has started baking bread. Every Sunday. He has a starter in a jar and he has named it Hector. He talks to Hector. Last week he got up in the night to feed Hector, and I lay there and realised I was jealous of a jar of flour. Am I mad?*
> *Second Fiddle, Thebes*

"Hm," said Sisyphus.

> *Dear Second Fiddle,*
> *You aren't mad. He is giving something his patient, unhurried attention, it isn't you, and that stings. Fair enough.*
> *But a man doesn't usually start getting up at night to feed a jar unless he has been wanting, for a while, to look after something and watch it come good. Next Sunday, ask him to show you how. You needn't care about bread. I suspect he has been hoping someone would ask, and had stopped expecting it to be you. Then one night, be the one who gets up. See what he says in the morning.*

Crow wrote this down, then added, "Hector's a stupid name for a starter."

"Everyone's starter has a stupid name. That's how you know they love it."

---

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
> *I'm an attendant at the Oracle at Delphi. Everyone assumes it's glamorous. The hours are appalling, the fumes give me headaches, and pilgrims want their prophecies by the end of the week. I haven't seen my sister in three months.*
> *Steam-Addled, Delphi*

> *Dear Steam-Addled,*
> *Pick a time to go home. Leave at that time, even if something is unfinished, because something always will be. The first time is the hardest. Visit your sister. Have your headache somewhere with a view.*
> *The future will still be there in the morning. That's rather the whole point of it.*

---

The boulder had settled at the bottom with a contented sort of crunch. Sisyphus strolled down, set his shoulder against the familiar flat bit, and started up again. Crow flew alongside at ear height and read.

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
> *There's a man at the weaving collective who repeats my ideas in meetings, louder, about ten minutes after I've said them. Everyone nods at him. I want to push him into the dye vat.*
> *Indigo with Rage, Corinth*

"Corinth," said Sisyphus fondly, through his teeth.\*

> *Dear Indigo,*
> *Don't push him into the vat. It's a waste of good dye, and they'll know it was you, because you'll be the one smiling.*
> *Next time, say warmly: "Thanks, Dorian, that's what I was getting at earlier. Shall I take it forward, since I did the groundwork?" The warmth is the important part. You aren't fighting him. You're just tidying up.*
> *Men like this are rarely villains. Usually they're terrified of being the one in the room with nothing to say. That doesn't mean you have to let them. It means you can stop him without hating him, and hating people is tiring and doesn't pay.*

"You don't know his name's Dorian," said Crow.

"It's always a Dorian."

\* *He had been king there, once. It hadn't been nearly this interesting.*

---

Crow read the next one, stopped, read it again silently, and looked up with the expression of a bird who has seen things.

"Go on," said Sisyphus.

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
> *My wife and I have been married twelve years and things are good, but lately a rather magnificent swan has been visiting our pond, and my wife has suggested that the three of us—*

"I'll stop there," said Crow.

Sisyphus heaved. The boulder crept another yard. "Does it say how the swan introduced himself?"

Crow scanned the page. "Says he seemed to already know her name."

"Ah." Sisyphus took a dozen more steps before he answered.

> *Dear Adventurous, Sparta,*
> *What two adults and a pond get up to is their own business. However, any swan who arrives already knowing your wife's name is not a swan. Ask him politely to show you his feet. If he hesitates, or there is a smell of ozone, take your wife indoors and lock the shutters. Possibly move.*

"That's not advice," said Crow.

"It's the most useful advice anyone in Sparta has had in a generation."

---

Near the top, a small cloud arrived uninvited, and out of it stepped a god about the size of a disappointed accountant.

"Momus," said Sisyphus pleasantly.\*\*

"I read your column," said Momus.

"That's kind of you."

"It wasn't. You've never been a woman in Thebes. You've never worked at an oracle. You aren't qualified."

"No," Sisyphus agreed.

"And you dictate it, so it's practically ghostwritten. The title is twee. 'Possibly move' is abrupt." He glared at the boulder. "And you can't even get *that* to stay put."

"Also true," said Sisyphus, and gave the boulder its last shove. It wobbled at the crest, thought about it, and went back down, passing close enough to Momus to ruffle his robe.

Momus opened his mouth and found nothing left to object to. This seemed to upset him more than anything else had. He left in a sulk of vapour.

"Pointless," said Crow.

"He drops in every few centuries. I think he's lonely."

\*\* *God of criticism. He was expelled from Olympus for pointing out that Athena had built a house with no wheels, so nobody could move away from bad neighbours. He had been right, which never helps.*

---

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
> *I'm forty-three and I make sandals. My brother founded a city. I've done nothing that matters.*
> *Sole Trader, Argos*

Sisyphus sat on his rock for a long moment before he spoke.

> *Dear Sole Trader,*
> *By a rough count, you've made four thousand pairs of sandals. That's four thousand people who walked to markets, funerals and their daughters' weddings without stepping on anything unpleasant. Not one of them thought about you, which is how you know you did it well.*
> *Your brother's city will fall down one day. They do. I've watched. Someone will walk out of the rubble, and with any luck they'll be wearing good shoes.*
> *The things that matter are rarely done just the once. Make the next pair.*

Crow wrote it out without comment, which was its version of applause.

---

The next week's post brought a letter on expensive cloud-paper, unsigned, in a cramped and peevish hand.

> *Dear Sisyphus, nobody invites me to anything. Why?*

Sisyphus read it twice, smiled, and walked down the hill toward the boulder.

"Take a letter," he said, and leaned in.

response:
# The Cicada

The tide had turned at Whampoa before the sun was properly up, and the river smelled of it: mud, night soil, the sweet rot of something floating. I had been awake since the middle watch, listening to my own joints.

"Dispatches for the Superintendent, sir." Midshipman Pell held out the oilskin packet as though it were the Host. He was fifteen and had freckles that the sun kept adding to. "Captain says you're to wait for a reply."

"Then I shall wait for one."

"You look done in, sir. Shall I fetch the surgeon's..."

"It's the damp, Mr Pell. Get in the boat."

The cutter took us up past the pagoda and the hulks, past tanka boats where women scaled fish with infants strapped to their backs and stared at my coat. I sat in the stern sheets with my hand in my pocket, thumbing the jade cicada until its wings were warm. A man in Old China Street had sold it to me my first week ashore, three years since. *Put in the mouths of the dead*, he'd said, *so they come out of the ground again.* I had thought it a pretty superstition. My nose was running. I yawned so hard my jaw cracked, and Pell pretended not to see.

At the factory stairs I gave him a dollar. "Buy yourself a lacquer box in New China Street. Be back here at four."

"And the dispatches, sir?"

"Are in my care."

Hog Lane was eight feet wide and lined with grog shops whose doors stood open like mouths. Bartolomeu had his stool out already, his Macanese face shiny as varnish.

"Tenente. You owe me eleven dollars."

"I know what I owe you."

"Then you know I don't pour for you." He leaned back against the doorpost. "But Uncle Loh asked after you. He says the price is up. The Governor's men took two crab boats at the Second Bar on Tuesday, and on Wednesday they strangled a man at the execution ground. Very bad for business."

"Very bad for the man."

He laughed at that, which I resented.

Loh's room was behind a cooper's, up a ladder. The walls had been papered with old account sheets, so the whole place was written over in columns of figures nobody would ever settle. The lamp was already lit. That small blue-hearted flame nearly made me weep. My shirt was stuck to my back and I was cold.

"Lieutenant." Loh did not rise. He was cleaning a pipe bowl with a hairpin. "You come with silver?"

"I come with three dollars and a promise."

"Promise." He turned the word over the way a money-changer turns a coin, hunting for the chop marks. "Promise very cheap this month. Malwa very dear."

"Patna, then."

"Patna dearer."

I put the three dollars on the mat. They had been chopped so many times they looked chewed. Loh didn't touch them.

"My hands are shaking, Loh."

"I see." He set down the hairpin. "Mr Framjee has small trouble. You talk with him. Maybe you smoke today. Maybe tomorrow also."

The jade was slick under my thumb. "What sort of trouble?"

"Talk with him."

Framjee received me in a counting room above the Chow-chow hong. He wore white, smelled of sandalwood, and poured the tea himself as if we were equals, which by then I suppose we were.

"A small boat comes up from Whampoa tonight," he said. "Nothing aboard but rice and some chests of... let us say, books. The mandarin cruisers have grown enthusiastic. However, they do not stop a boat carrying an officer of His Britannic Majesty. Since Lord Napier they are very anxious to avoid incidents."

"You want me to sit in the stern in my coat."

"I want you to sit in the stern in your coat and look bored. You are very good at looking bored, Lieutenant. I have seen you at the Company dinners." He slid a paper across the table. "Twenty dollars. And Loh will be generous this afternoon, on my account."

I thought of my father, who had left an arm at Camperdown and wept when my commission came through. I thought of it the way you watch a ship founder on the horizon: very sad, and very far off.

"The Superintendent's dispatches," I said. "I'm meant to wait for a reply."

"Then leave them with my clerk. He waits beautifully."

Afterward Loh was generous. The first pull went down like warm water through a cracked hull, filling every place that had ached. The columns of figures on the wall went soft and lost their meaning, and I loved him, and Framjee, and the man strangled on Wednesday, and Pell's freckles, and every soul on the river.

A sampan took me down at dusk to meet her below Whampoa. She was a crab boat of forty oars, long as a church, smelling of tung oil, and we came up on the flood with the rowers chanting low and the chests lashed under rice sacks. Near the Second Bar a mandarin junk swung a lantern our way. I stood so they could see the gold on my shoulders, and I yawned at them. The lantern went away.

Pell was waiting at the factory stairs when I got back, near ten. He held the dispatches and a reply sealed in red wax.

"A Parsee gentleman's man brought them, sir. He said you'd been called away." He looked at me with that terrible freckled trust. "Was it naval business, sir?"

"Of a kind."

In the cutter going back I found the cicada in my pocket and held it. I wasn't rubbing it now, only holding it. I thought how strange it was to put such a thing in a dead man's mouth, when surely all the dead want is to be left in the ground.

# The Gallantry Glass

Pollard caught me on the stairs of the Danish Hong before I had my coat buttoned.

"The Superintendent wants your report on the Bogue forts. He asked twice yesterday."

"Then he'll have it on the third asking. That's the custom of the service."

"It isn't, actually." Pollard adjusted his spectacles. The damp had fogged them already. It was June, and the river breathed on everything. "Merrick, you look like a boiled pudding. Are you ill?"

"Fever. Touch of it. Lend me five dollars, would you?"

"I lent you five dollars on Tuesday."

"And you'll have it back, with Tuesday's, when the Admiralty remembers I'm owed four months' pay."

He looked at my hands. I put them behind my back, the way one does on the quarterdeck, and the trembling became a private matter between me and my spine.

"I'll tell him Thursday," Pollard said, and went up without giving me anything.

---

The square before the factories was already loud. Coolies jogged past under bales of tea. The bamboo poles creaked like a ship's knees in a swell. A Parsee merchant was arguing with a fruit seller in a language neither of them spoke. I crossed to Dunmore's office through the smell of tar and river mud and other men's tobacco. My shirt had soaked through under my blue coat before I reached his door.

Dunmore was a Glaswegian with a face like a well-hammered nail. He did not stand.

"Lieutenant. You've thought on it."

"I have. Explain it again."

"Nothing to explain. My cutter goes down to Lintin at dusk. You sit on the deck, in that coat, with that hat. Smoke a cigar. Look bored. The mandarin boats see a King's officer and they think twice. They'll think thrice if you look at them."

"And if they don't think at all?"

"Then you're a British officer being fired upon by Chinese revenue men, and Captain Elliot writes a very angry letter, and I'm compensated. Either way I'm content." He opened a drawer. Spanish dollars, the old Carolus coins with the king's face rubbed smooth by a hundred thumbs. "Half now."

"All now."

"Half now, Merrick. I know where the other half would go before dusk, and I need you upright on that deck."

I took the half. The silver was cool, and for a moment that was enough.

---

Hog Lane was barely wider than my shoulders. It ran down to the river between grog shops where the sailors from Whampoa drank samshu until they forgot their names. A sailor was being sick into a gutter, very neatly, holding his own hat. I stepped round him.

Chow's shop sold lacquered boxes, chopsticks and porcelain dogs to Americans. Behind the bead curtain it sold the other thing. Chow was fanning himself with a ledger.

"Lieutenant Mee-lick. Long time."

"Two days, Chow."

"Long time for you." He smiled. He had very good teeth, which I had always resented. "Patna, today, very fine. Twelve dollar the ball."

"Twelve? It was eight in May."

"In May no Hoppo man walk up and down my street. Now Hoppo man walk up and down. I pay him, you pay me. All same chain."

"I have seven."

He stopped fanning and looked at me with real sympathy, which was worse than contempt.

"Seven buy Malwa. Malwa no good for you. Make your belly sick. You know this."

I did know it. I unbuttoned my coat and took out the telescope. It was brass and mahogany, with an inscription that I had once read every morning: *Lt. J. Merrick, H.M.S. Genoa, for Gallantry at Navarino, 1827.*

Chow turned it over in his fingers. He read the English slowly, moving his lips.

"Gallantly," he said.

"Gallantry."

"What is?"

"It means I stood on a deck while Turks tried to kill me, and I didn't run."

He nodded, as though this were a reasonable thing to have done once. "Okay. Patna, one ball. And I keep glass one month. You bring twelve dollar, you take back."

"I'll bring it."

"Sure, sure." He was already wrapping the black cake in a leaf. "Everybody bring."

---

The alley behind Thirteen Factory Street had no name I ever learned. You reached it through a fruit-seller's yard, past baskets of mangoes too far gone to sell. Wasps worked over them. The sweetness had turned to something like wine and something like a dead dog. That smell lay over the whole passage, thick enough that I breathed through my mouth and tasted it anyway. To this day I cannot eat a mango.

The boy who kept the door was perhaps twelve. He wore a sailor's cast-off waistcoat with nothing underneath.

"You have?" he said.

I showed him the leaf. He sniffed it, like a purser sniffing beef.

"Is Patna. Okay. Two hundred cash for lamp, for pipe."

"I've given you more than two hundred cash this month alone."

"So you know price." He held out his palm.

Inside it was dark and low, and cooler than the street. That surprised me every time. Men lay on wooden platforms with their heads on porcelain pillows, curled toward their lamps the way a sleeping dog curls toward a fire. A Lascar seaman. Two Cantonese clerks still in their good blue gowns. A white man I half recognised from the American hong. We did not acknowledge one another. There was a rule about that, and nobody had ever needed to say it aloud.

The boy rolled the paste over the flame on his needle. It swelled and browned and smelled of burnt sugar and wet straw. He pressed it into the bowl and handed me the pipe.

"Lieutenant go on boat tonight?" he asked.

I looked at him. "How do you know that?"

"Mister Dunmore man come yesterday. Ask me, which day you come, which time. I tell him." He shrugged. "He pay me also."

So Dunmore had known I would say yes before I knew it. Of course he had. Everyone in Canton knew the price of everything, and it seemed mine was public.

"You come back tomorrow?" the boy said.

"I'll be at sea tomorrow. Lintin."

"Okay." He trimmed the wick. "Then you come back day after."

I drew on the pipe. The world softened and went slack, like a sheet when the wind fails, and the shaking left my hands for whoever wanted it next. Somewhere behind the mango stink and the lamp smoke, a cutter was waiting for a man in a blue coat. He would sit very still on her deck, and look bored, and be brave for wages.

I had six hours. I meant to use every one.

# The Hollow Hour

Ah Sum found me on the veranda before the gun at Whampoa had sounded, my coat buttoned wrong and my hands trembling around a cup of tea I could not taste.

"Captain Elliot send chit, Mister Merrick. Ten o'clock. He want report on Lintin ships."

"Tell him I'm indisposed."

"Yesterday you indispose." He set a dish of rice congee beside me that I would not touch. "Day before also. Captain Elliot say, very sorry for indisposition, ten o'clock."

The cough took me then. It came up from somewhere low and private, and I bent over the rail until it passed. When I wiped my mouth, the handkerchief came away with a faint rust stain, and the taste behind my teeth was of old pennies.

Ah Sum watched without expression. "Doctor Colledge can see."

"It's the river damp. Twelve years at sea and the air still gets into a man." I folded the handkerchief inward. "Tell the Captain half past eleven."

---

The Factory Square stank of low tide, joss smoke and the dung of the sedan-bearers. Hog Lane was narrower than a frigate's gangway and fouler than her bilge. Kendrick of Russell & Company was already drinking at the back of a grog shop whose proprietor called himself Old Jemmy, though he was plainly neither.

"Lieutenant." Kendrick pushed a glass toward me. It held samshu, which smelled like burnt sugar and lamp oil. "You look like a drowned man somebody forgot to bury."

"I'm told it's a fashion here."

"Not among the living." He lowered his voice, though nobody nearby would have cared. "The *Corinna* came up from Lintin Tuesday. Rice and cotton piece goods, according to her papers."

"How fortunate for her papers."

"Your Captain Elliot has decided that Her Majesty's officers must show the Viceroy they're clean of the trade. He wants a naval inspection of every country ship that's moved upriver this month." Kendrick turned his glass. "I'd like you to have inspected the *Corinna*. Thoroughly. And found her wholesome."

"I haven't been aboard her."

"No. That would be the part I'm paying for." He slid a folded paper across the table, and I could feel the weight of the coins inside it. "Forty dollars. Spanish, not chopped to ribbons."

I thought about my commission and the gilt on its seal. I thought about the morning I had stood on the quarterdeck of the *Wellesley* while an admiral pinned a medal on my coat, and the gulls had screamed as though they meant it.

"Sixty," I said.

"Fifty, and you sign it in your own hand today."

I signed it in my own hand.

---

Widow Ho kept her rooms above a coffin-maker's on Old China Street. The camphorwood smell from his shop rose through the floorboards and mixed with the sweet, scorched-treacle smell of chandu that clung to every curtain she owned. She spoke better English than the Superintendent's secretary, and she rarely bothered to hide it.

"You are early, Lieutenant. That means you are either rich or desperate."

"I'm both, today." I put the dollars on the lacquer table, and she counted them without touching any. She simply moved her eyes across the stacks.

"Patna," I said. "Not that Malwa muck you sold me last week. It tasted of horse."

"Malwa is honest opium from honest Bombay thieves." She opened a drawer and took out a ball wrapped in dried poppy petals, as round and dark as a cannonball. "Patna is dearer now. The Emperor has stopped being patient. They strangled a dealer outside the factories in December. Did you see it?"

"I was indisposed."

"Of course." She shaved a portion from the ball with a small knife, as delicately as a woman paring fruit. "They say a new commissioner comes from Peking in the spring. A man called Lin. An honest man." She said *honest* the way a sailor says *lee shore*.

"Honest men don't last long in Canton."

"No," she agreed. "But they can make a great deal of trouble on their way out." She weighed the shavings on a brass scale no bigger than my palm. "This is less than last time, for the same money. I am not cheating you. It is the weather."

"What weather?"

"The kind that comes from Peking." She studied me. "You coughed on my stairs. I heard it through the floor."

"Sea air."

"You have not been to sea in a year, Lieutenant." She pushed the packet toward me. "My husband had sea air too. He took it to his grave very slowly."

---

She kept a room for customers at the back, behind a curtain of glass beads that clicked like rigging in a breeze. The boy who prepared the pipes was perhaps twelve. He worked the bead of opium over the lamp with a long needle, turning it until it swelled amber and soft, and then pressed it into the bowl. The pipe's stem was old bamboo, polished dark by the grip of a hundred hands.

"Captain have letter," he said, nodding at my coat, where Elliot's chit was folded against my chest.

"I'm a lieutenant."

"Everybody English say *captain*." He held the bowl over the flame. "Then nobody get angry."

I lay on my side on the hard couch and drew. The smoke went into me like warm water into a cracked hull, filling every hollow place I had. The ache in my chest folded itself away. The copper taste softened into something almost sweet. Through the beads I could hear the coffin-maker's mallet below, steady as a ship's bell, counting someone's measure in planks.

Half past eleven came and went somewhere beyond the river.

"Again," I said.

The boy was already turning the needle in the flame.

Later, when the light through the shutters had gone the colour of weak tea, I found Elliot's chit in my hand. I could not remember taking it out. The ink had blurred where my thumb had sweated on it. *Ten o'clock*, it said, and below that, in the Captain's own small, worried hand: *James, I would rather hear it from you.*

I coughed. I folded the paper inward over the stain, and I asked the boy for one more.

# Gunpowder Rendezvous

The jukebox at the Tin Halo has been playing the same song for three hours. Somebody jammed a coin in sideways back when all the neon letters still worked, and now there's only this: a fuzzed-out guitar riff, a singer who sounds like he gargles gravel, a chorus about a highway that goes nowhere. Then the needle skips back to the start like a dog chasing its own tail.

Revy has decided she's going to shoot it before the night's over.

She's on her fourth rum, boots up on the rail. The dragon on her right arm is slick with sweat under a ceiling fan that wobbles more than it turns. The bounty sheet sits folded under her glass: *Lazlo "Teeth" Moreau. Gunrunner. Wanted alive or otherwise.*

The door bangs open. A lanky guy in a blue suit that's seen better decades wanders in. His green hair looks like a storm hit a bird's nest, and he already has a cigarette going. He drops onto the stool next to hers and smooths a crumpled flyer flat on the bar.

Same mugshot. Same gold teeth.

"Whiskey," he tells the bartender. "Put it on her tab."

Revy doesn't look at him. "Touch my tab and I'll put you on a slab."

"That rhymed." He takes a long drag. "You rehearse that one?"

"I rehearse shooting assholes."

"Must get a lot of practice."

Now she looks. Lean, loose, sleepy-eyed, the kind of guy who'd nap through an earthquake. But his right eye is wrong somehow. The color is a shade off and it catches the neon like glass. And he's sitting with his weight forward on the stool, ready to move.

"Your eye's fucked," she says.

"It's fake. Can't judge distance worth a damn."

"So how the hell do you shoot?"

He smiles, slow and crooked. "I get close."

Something low in her stomach does a stupid little flip. She kills it with rum.

"Spike," he says.

"Didn't ask."

"Didn't have to." He nods at her shoulder holsters, the twin Berettas with their custom grips. "Two guns. You're the one they call Two Hands. Heard about you."

"Then you heard I don't split bounties."

"I'm broke and I haven't eaten since Tuesday. I'm not proud." He slides the bartender's whiskey toward himself. "Sixty-forty."

"Hundred-zero, and I let you keep your teeth."

"Teeth's the one with the teeth."

She almost laughs. It comes out as a snort, and she hates it.

The song loops. *Highway to nowhere, baby—*

They drink. It turns into a contest without either of them saying so, shot for shot. He tells her nothing true and she tells him less. He watches her hands when she lights a cigarette. She watches his mouth when he talks. Neither of them says anything about it. The air between their stools grows thick and close, like before a storm.

On the eighth round, the bartender's eyes flick to the door, then to the floor.

Spike sees it a half-second before Revy does. That bothers her more than anything else tonight.

Five men come in fast with sawed-off shotguns. Somebody tipped Teeth that hunters were waiting.

Revy is moving before the first one clears the threshold. Both Cutlasses come up together and the bar fills with thunder. Two men drop. A third ducks behind a pillar, and she sends plaster flying off it in chunks, laughing high and wild. Glass rains down. Rum soaks the floor.

Spike rolls behind the bar, comes up beside a shotgunner, and slaps the barrel aside with an open palm. He drives an elbow into the man's throat and follows with a spinning kick that sends him crashing into the jukebox. A stray round punches through its glass. The needle jumps.

*—to nowhere, baby, highway to—*

It keeps playing.

Spike's Jericho barks twice. The last man folds. Silence follows, apart from that song.

Through the shattered front window they both see Teeth's gold grin under the motel sign across the street. Then he bolts into the Starlite.

They look at each other for one beat, then run.

Room nine. The door hangs open. Spike goes in low and Revy goes in high, and the room is empty. Cheap paneling, a sagging bed, a bathroom window still swinging. Out back, tires screech as a car fishtails into the dark.

"Son of a *bitch*," Revy snarls.

She turns and finds the Jericho's muzzle resting lightly against her sternum.

Her left Cutlass is already pressed under his jaw. Her right is on his belly.

Neither of them breathes. Across the road, the jukebox loops again, faint through the thin walls.

"Funny," Spike murmurs. His breath smells like whiskey and smoke. "Figured you'd go for the head."

"I'm going for both. Two Hands, dipshit." Her pulse is hammering, and not from the run. "You were gonna cut me loose the second we caught him."

"Weren't you?"

"Fuck yes."

"So we're even."

He's close enough now that she can see the seam where the fake eye meets real skin. He can't judge distance, he said. He doesn't need to. There's none left between them.

"You trust me?" he asks.

"I don't trust *anybody*."

"Good." He tilts his head, slow, so her barrel drags along his jaw. "Me neither."

She could pull the trigger. She has done it for less. Her finger rests on it, then eases off by a hair.

"Why aren't you scared?" she asks, and her voice comes out rougher than she means.

He shrugs, gun still steady. "Already died once. Whatever happens, happens."

"That's the stupidest fucking thing I've ever heard."

"Probably."

Neither of them moves.

Then Spike does something she doesn't expect. He reaches up with his free hand, slow enough that she can track it, and plucks the half-burnt cigarette from the corner of her mouth. He takes a drag and puts it back between her lips.

His thumb brushes her bottom lip, and her whole body goes tight as a drawn wire.

"Teeth'll go to ground," he says. "Somewhere close. He'll have to sleep sometime."

"So will you, cowboy."

"Yeah." He backs up one step and sits on the edge of the bed, the Jericho resting loosely on his knee, still pointed at her. "Guess we take shifts."

Revy stays standing. Her guns stay up. The dragon on her arm twists in the bad light as she exhales smoke toward the ceiling, never taking her eyes off him.

"You fall asleep," she says, "and I might kill you."

"You might." He leans back against the wall and grins. "Or you might not."

Across the street, the needle skips, and the song starts over.

# Gunpowder Rendezvous

A lazy ceiling fan barely stirs the smoky air inside the bar. It turns the way everything in this port town turns: slow, grudging, ready to quit.

Spike Spiegel sits at the far end of the counter with his elbows planted beside a bowl of peanuts he's been quietly emptying for an hour. His glass holds two fingers of the cheapest whiskey the place pours, and he's making it last. The bounty sheet lies folded under his palm: *Dario Vance. Chemist. Fifty million woolongs, alive.* Fifty million is a lot of beef with actual beef in it.

The door bangs open hard enough to rattle the bottles.

The woman who walks in is wearing black and very little of it: cut-off shorts, a crop top, holsters under both arms. A dragon tattoo coils from her right wrist to her shoulder. She drops onto the stool two down from Spike, slaps a crumpled bill on the bar, and says, "Bacardi. Leave the bottle."

Then she unfolds her own copy of the bounty sheet and smooths it flat with the heel of her hand.

Spike glances at it, then at her. "Small world."

She doesn't look up. "Fuck off."

response:
# Gunpowder Rendezvous

The bar has no name, just a buzzing neon sign that says BEER in a font nobody has used in decades. The ceiling fan turns slowly enough that the flies ride it. Spike Spiegel sits at the far end of the counter with his back to the wall. He works through a bowl of complimentary peanuts with the patience of a man whose last real meal was two days ago.

The bounty sheet lies folded beside his elbow. *Hector Varga. Fence, arms broker, sentimental about his mother. 3.2 million woolongs.* Spike has already spent it a dozen times in his head, mostly on beef.

He flicks his lighter. It sparks twice before it catches. A ring of rust circles its base like a tide line, the mark of a thing that has gone into the drink more than once and climbed back out every time. He lights up and lets the smoke curl toward the fan.

The door bangs open.

She walks in like the room owes her money. She wears black cut-offs that barely qualify as clothing and a crop top, and a dragon tattoo coils down her right arm from shoulder to wrist. Two pistol grips jut from shoulder holsters. Long Beretta frames, custom work. She takes the stool beside him, slaps a folded paper on the counter, and Spike sees Varga's face staring up from it.

"Rum," she tells the bartender. "Bacardi. Leave the bottle."

Spike slides his own sheet next to hers, face up. Two Hector Vargas regard each other.

She looks at the papers, then at him. Her eyes are dark, flat and amused, like a shark that has spotted something bleeding.

"Oh, you gotta be *shitting* me."

"Small galaxy," Spike says.

"Who the fuck hired you?"

"Same guy who hired you, probably. He likes to hedge his bets." He pops another peanut. "Spike."

"Revy." She pours three fingers and puts them away like water. "Here's how it goes, cowboy. You finish your little nuts, walk out that door, and I don't put a hole in that stupid hair."

"I like my hair."

"Then go like it somewhere else."

He doesn't move. Neither does she. She pours another. He reaches over and takes the bottle, fills his own glass, and drinks it without breaking eye contact. One corner of her mouth twitches. It isn't quite a smile, but it might be related to one.

"You're broke," she says. "I can smell it on you."

"And you're hungry. For something." He tips his glass at her. "Just not peanuts."

"Keep talking and you'll find out what."

They drink. The bottle drains by inches. She tells him about a boat and a city called Roanapur where the cops are a pension plan for the mob. He tells her nothing, and she seems to like that better. When she reaches across him for a cigarette, her arm brushes his chest. She takes her time pulling it back.

"Light," she says.

He flicks the rusted lighter. She leans in, close enough that he can count the scars at her hairline. Close enough that the flame makes the moment feel like a dare.

The door opens again. Hector Varga walks in with two bodyguards and a bad suit.

Everything happens at once. Revy's hands blur and both Cutlasses come out together, roaring in stereo. Spike rolls off his stool, his Jericho already up. The bodyguards hit the floor, one with a hole in his shoulder from her and one with a hole in his knee from Spike. The bartender vanishes. Glass rains from the shelves in glittering sheets.

Varga runs out the back.

"*Mine!*" Revy vaults the counter.

"Debatable." Spike goes over it right behind her.

The alley is wet and black. Taillights flare at the end of it and peel away. Revy empties a magazine after them, swearing in two languages. Spike lowers his gun and lights another cigarette.

"He's sentimental about his mother," he says. "There's a motel on Route 9. She runs it."

Revy turns slowly. "You were gonna keep that to yourself."

"I just told you."

"Because you're drunk."

"Because you're interesting."

---

The Starlite Motor Inn has eleven rooms and one working light. Varga's car sits outside room seven. Room eight is empty, and Spike has picked its lock in four seconds. Revy is inside before he finishes, and she kicks the door shut behind them.

They don't turn on the lamp. Neon bleeds pink through the blinds and lies across the bedspread in stripes.

"We wait till he sleeps," Spike murmurs. "Then we go through the wall."

"*I* go through the wall."

"Revy."

The click is very soft. When he turns, a Cutlass is three inches from his face.

His own gun is already at her ribs. He doesn't remember drawing it. His body remembers things his mind would rather not.

They stand there. The air conditioner rattles. On the other side of the thin wall, a television murmurs a game show.

"Split it," he says.

"I don't split."

"You don't trust."

"And you do?" Her laugh is low and ugly. "Guys like you don't trust anything. You just stopped giving a shit whether you get burned."

He tilts his head. His right eye catches the neon wrong, and for a second it looks like glass, because it is. "I died once already. The second time's just paperwork."

Something shifts in her face. It's recognition, and it's worse than anger.

"Fuck you," she says. Her voice has gone quiet.

She steps closer, gun still raised, until the barrel rests against his cheekbone and his presses under her heart. Her breath smells of rum and smoke. His smells the same. Neither of them blinks.

"You gonna shoot me, Spike?"

"Haven't decided." He smiles the lazy smile that has gotten him killed in a dozen ways. "You?"

"Thinking about it." Her eyes drop to his mouth, then come back up, hard. "Thinking about a lot of shit."

The silence goes on too long and lands too heavily.

Outside, an engine turns over.

They both hear it. Varga's car is pulling away, its taillights sweeping across the blinds. The television next door is still talking to an empty room.

Revy doesn't lower her gun. Neither does Spike.

"There goes three million," he says.

"Yeah." She doesn't look at the window. "There it goes."

He reaches into his pocket with his free hand and pulls out the rusted lighter. He offers it to her between two fingers. After a long beat she takes it, thumbs the wheel, and watches the flame stutter and catch.

"You drop this in water a lot?"

"It keeps coming back."

She lights her cigarette, then his, then pockets the lighter.

"Whatever happens," Spike says, "happens."

Neither of them moves toward the door.

A crimson harvest moon casts ominous shadows on the deserted village streets. Length: 1000 words.
response:
# Blood Moon

The moon over Dravenholt hangs low and swollen, the color of a wound that will not close. It paints the thatch, the mud, and the empty doorways the same rust, so the whole village looks as though it has been dipped in something and left to dry.

Yennefer of Vengerberg walks the main street with her skirts held clear of the muck and her left hand loose at her side. Her fingers are already shaped for a spell she has not yet decided to cast. A burgrave who would not come himself paid her handsomely to learn why forty souls stopped answering the church bell. She has her answer by the time she reaches the square. The smell gets there first: old blood, new blood, and beneath it something sweetly rotten, like fruit left too long in a cellar.

The katakan hangs pinned to the church door by a black iron shape. She takes it at first for a crossbow bolt. Stepping closer, she realizes it is no weapon she has ever seen. The creature's chest is gone. It has not been torn. It is simply gone, as if something decided it should not be there.

"It begged," says a voice behind her. "They always beg."

He sits on the lip of the village well with one long leg drawn up, as if the well were a throne and the night his court. He wears a red coat and a hat with a brim wide enough to shelter a family. His spectacles are tinted the orange of a forge, which is absurd at midnight, and behind them she can see nothing at all. A pistol the length of her forearm rests across his knee, and he handles it with the careless affection a man might show a hound.

Yennefer does not turn quickly. Turning quickly is what prey does.

"You've ruined my contract," she says.

"I've completed it." His grin opens too wide. He has too many teeth, and they are too white, and the moonlight does something unpleasant to them. "Such a long way to come alone, sweet thing. You should thank me."

"I'm not sweet, and I'm not some maiden in need of saving." She tilts her head. After a century of practice the Sight comes to her as easily as breath, and she lets it slide over him. She nearly staggers. Where a man should be, there is a hole in the world, a depth with no bottom. Faces press against the inside of him like drowned things against ice, thousands of them, mouths open. He is not a vampire as she understands vampires. He is no higher vampire, no alp, nothing from any bestiary in Aretuza. He smells of a sphere that should never have touched this one.

"You don't belong here," she says.

"Neither does your face." He says it mildly, the way one remarks on the weather.

Cold goes through her, sharp and specific. He leans forward with his nostrils flaring, and she understands that he is not looking at her. He is smelling her. He reaches past the lilac and the gooseberry, down to the old blood. He finds the bones that were broken and reset in a tower in Aretuza, the spine that was straightened, the womb that was paid away.

"Ah," he breathes. "Lovely. You carved yourself out of something crooked. What did it cost, I wonder?"

She lets the spell go.

It is not subtle. Lightning leaves her palm white and screaming. It takes him in the chest, lifts him off the well, and throws him across the square into the side of a granary hard enough to splinter the boards. The smell of scorched wool and meat fills the air. Yennefer lowers her hand. Her fingers tingle. She hates that they are shaking, very slightly.

The thing in the wreckage laughs.

He stands up in pieces. That is the only way to describe it. Parts of him are shadow and parts are eyes, dozens of them blinking open along the line of his arm. The hole she burned in him fills not with flesh but with darkness, and as she watches the darkness becomes flesh, like ink spreading through water in reverse. His hat is still on. Somehow that offends her most.

"Again," he says, delighted. "Do that again."

"No."

"Why not? You enjoyed it."

"I don't perform on request." She makes herself walk toward him. Every instinct she has, and every lesson Tissaia beat into her, tells her to open a portal and be gone. She does not. "And you didn't feel it."

"I felt it." He tilts his head, mirroring her. "I feel everything. That is rather the point of me."

They are close now. She can see her reflection doubled in his glasses: violet eyes, black hair, a face she built. He is very tall. She refuses to look up at him, so she looks at his throat instead. There, under the collar, faint as old embroidery, she sees a sigil. Then she sees another on his glove. They are bindings, layers of them, worked into him like stitches in a wound.

Now it is Yennefer who smiles.

"Someone holds your leash," she says softly.

For the first time, he goes still. It is not the stillness of a predator. It is the stillness of a thing caught.

"Whoever made those knew what they were doing," she goes on. She traces the air an inch from his collar, close enough to feel the spellwork hum. "Elegant. Cruel. You could break this village in half, and you came here because someone told you to. Didn't you? For all your teeth, you're a dog."

His grin returns, slower now, and there is something in it that is almost fond. "A dog chooses its master, sorceress. Tell me. Who chose yours?"

The question lands somewhere she has not let anyone touch in a long time. She thinks of the Brotherhood, and of every king who smiled at her across a council table believing he owned her. She does not answer. She does not step back either.

Above them the moon slides behind a scrap of cloud. For one breath, then two, the red drains from the square. Then it floods back.

"You came looking for something to kill you," she says. It is a guess, and it is not a guess.

"And you came looking for something to fix you." He bends until his mouth is beside her ear, and his breath is as cold as a crypt. "We should both be so lucky."

When she turns to answer him, the well is empty. The only sounds in Dravenholt are a bat's wingbeat and laughter that seems to come from the moon itself.

Yennefer stands alone in the crimson light for a long moment. Then she opens a portal. Before she steps through it, she looks back over her shoulder.

She does not know whether she hopes to see him there.

A broken cart wheel lies abandoned near the village gates, hinting at a hurried departure. Length: 1000 words.
response:
# Blood Moon

The wheel lies in the mud beside the village gate, three spokes snapped like finger bones, its iron rim bent where it struck the post. Whoever owned the cart did not stop to mend it. They unhitched the horse, Yennefer guesses, and rode bareback into the dark. They left behind a sack of turnips, one child's shoe, and the gate swinging on a single hinge.

She steps over the wheel without lifting her skirts. The mud parts for her of its own accord.

Above, the moon hangs swollen and copper-red. It is not her moon. The portal that spat her here smelled wrong, of rust and old incense, and the stars arrange themselves in constellations no astrologer in Aretuza ever charted. She followed rumors of a relic, a chalice said to restore what magic has taken. She is beginning to suspect someone lied to her. She is beginning to plan what she will do to them.

The tavern door stands open. Candlelight spills out, which is odd, because the rest of the village is dead.

He sits at the far table with his boots propped on a chair, a goblet of something dark in his gloved hand. He wears a red coat and a wide hat, and spectacles tinted the color of forge-fire, though there is no sun to shield against. He does not look up.

"They ran," he says, "the moment they saw me. Not even a pitchfork. I'm almost offended."

"Perhaps they had good instincts."

Now he looks. The spectacles slide down his nose. The eyes beneath are red, not bloodshot but red all the way through, like the moon outside. He smiles, and his teeth are too many and too long.

"And you didn't run," he says. "So either your instincts are poor or your opinion of yourself is very high."

"I'm told those are the same thing." Yennefer takes the chair opposite without being asked. "What are you?"

"Rude." He sets down the goblet. "You first, witch. You smell of lilac. And gooseberries. And under that," he inhales slowly, theatrically, "lightning. You came through a door that shouldn't exist."

So he felt the portal. She files that away.

"Yennefer of Vengerberg."

"Alucard." He tips his hat. "Of nowhere in particular, tonight."

She reads him the way she would read a stranger at a royal banquet: posture, hands, pauses. Except there is nothing to read. Beneath the coat she senses not a man but a crowd, thousands of voices pressed together in the dark like grain in a sack, all of them screaming without sound. Her stomach turns. She does not let it reach her face.

"You're hollow," she says. "Stuffed with other people."

Something flickers behind his smile. It is interest, not offense. "Very good. Most take far longer to notice."

"I'm not most."

"No." He leans forward. "Show me."

The pistol is in his hand before she sees him move. It is an enormous thing, black and silver, wrong for this century and for any century she knows. The barrel points at her heart. The hammer clicks back.

Yennefer does not flinch. She lifts two fingers, and the air between them thickens to amber. When he fires, the roar shakes dust from the rafters. The bullet hangs a hand's breadth from her breast, spinning, smoking, silver.

Her arm trembles. Only slightly. He sees it anyway.

"Heavy, isn't it?" he murmurs.

"Blessed silver. Crude." She twists her wrist, and the bullet reverses lazily and buries itself in the table between his hands. "I've seen finer work from drunken dwarves."

He laughs, delighted and awful, like a wolf discovering the lamb has teeth. "Oh, I *like* you."

"How unfortunate for you."

She speaks a word, and chains of blue light erupt from the floorboards. They coil around his arms, his chest, his throat, and pin him to the chair. The spell costs her. She feels it in her spine, in the old ache she paid so dearly to erase. She keeps her face smooth as glass.

Alucard looks down at the chains, then up at her. Then he simply comes apart. His body unravels into shadow, into a swarm of black wings and lidless eyes, and the chains close on nothing. A heartbeat later he stands behind her chair, his breath cold on her neck.

"Your glamour is exquisite," he whispers. "But I see what's under it. The curve of the spine. The girl they hid away."

The tavern goes very silent.

Yennefer rises slowly and turns to face him. The candles gutter. Violet light kindles in her eyes, and the shadows draw back from her as if burned.

"Look all you like," she says. "I chose this face. I paid for it, and I'd pay again. What did *you* choose? Or did you simply lack the courage to die?"

His smile holds, but it sharpens into something cold and genuine. "I chose to be a monster. Most never get the dignity of that choice. They stumble into it, whining."

"And you despise them for it."

"I despise anyone who lies about what they are."

"Then we have one thing in common." She steps closer, close enough to see that his spectacles hold no reflection of her. "Though you haven't asked why I came."

"For a cup." He sounds bored again, but his eyes never leave her. "There's a chalice in the chapel crypt. The monks claimed it could make the barren fruitful. They were wrong. I drank from it four hundred years ago." He spreads his gloved hands. "Nothing grows in me."

She keeps her voice level. It costs more than the chains did. "Then there's nothing here for me."

"Nothing for either of us," he agrees, almost kindly. Then the kindness drains away. "Unless you'd like to try killing me. I'd let you try."

"You'd enjoy it too much."

"I would." He tilts his head. "Would you?"

She considers him: the hollow king, the crowded dark, the thing that longs to be ended and will not lie down. She thinks of a white-haired man in another world who would already have drawn his sword. She finds she does not want to be here when the sun rises, or whatever passes for a sun in this place.

"Another night," Yennefer says. "When I'm bored."

She opens a portal with a flick of her wrist, and violet sparks scatter across the floor. She does not look back, which is how he knows she wanted to.

Alucard sits, retrieves his goblet, and plucks the silver bullet from the table. Outside, the red moon watches over the empty road, the swinging gate, and the broken wheel.

"Another night," he agrees, to no one.

She stands, brushes frost from her skirts, and does not shiver. Shivering is for people who have not yet decided what they are.

"About forty years of study and a great deal of pain." She lifts one hand, and violet light coils around her fingers like a serpent waking. "Shall I demonstrate?"

His grin splits wider. "Please."

She does not hesitate. Hesitation is the luxury of people who will live to regret it. The spell leaves her in a white-hot lance and takes him through the chest. The force lifts him off his feet and pins him to the chapel wall, and the old stones crack behind him.

For one heartbeat, she has won.

Then he laughs.

The hole in his chest is wet and smoking, and he laughs at it with real delight. His body comes apart. It does not fall. It *unravels* into a churning mass of shadow, red eyes opening along it by the dozen, all of them looking at her. Something with too many teeth drips onto the snow. The darkness pools, rises, and knits itself back into a man in a red coat, adjusting his hat.

"Again," he says, breathless as a lover. "Do that again."

Yennefer's stomach turns. Not from fear, she tells herself. From disgust. The thing is an abomination, a wound in the shape of a man.

And yet she cannot look away.

"What are you?" she asks.

"A dog," he says. "A king. A corpse that forgot to lie down." He steps closer, and she does not step back. "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame. And you? What are you, beneath all that?"

He reaches toward her face. Not quite touching. His gloved fingers hover near her cheek, and she feels the cold coming off them.

"You wear yourself like a mask," he murmurs. "Very good work. Masterful, even. But I can smell the bones under it, sorceress. They are crooked. They remember."

The wolves howl again, much nearer, a single broken cry.

Yennefer goes very still.

The girl with the twisted spine and the father who could not bear to look at her has been buried under decades of perfect posture. And this creature has dug her up with one breath.

He sees it land. Of course he does. His smile turns almost tender, and that is worse than anything.

"There," he whispers. "There you are."

She could flinch. She could teleport away and leave him laughing in the ruins. Instead she catches his wrist.

Her magic does not seek his flesh, which is useless and will only regrow. It reaches past it, into him, and what she touches is ancient and vast and *tired*. Five hundred years of hunger. She looks up at him, and now she is the one smiling.

He smiles.

response:
# Prison Strings

The light above Cell Block D buzzes, dies, and comes back half a second too late, as if it had to think about it.

Jolyne Cujoh counts the gaps. Three seconds dark. One lit. Five dark. There's no pattern, and that's the point. Whoever built the Hollow Ward wanted its inmates to stop trusting their own eyes. Stand users, devil-touched, things that came back wrong: all of them are down here below the waterline, where the walls sweat salt.

When the light returns, a woman is standing outside her bars.

She wasn't there in the dark. Jolyne would have felt her footsteps through the string she keeps threaded along the floor seams like a spider's tripwire.

"Hello," the woman says. She has an auburn braid, a sharply pressed white shirt, and a black tie. Her eyes are yellow and ringed like targets, and her smile looks practiced in a mirror until the mirror gave up. "You're Jolyne. I've wanted to meet you."

"Yeah? Get in line." Jolyne doesn't get up from the cot. "Who the hell are you, the new chaplain?"

"Makima. I'm here to observe." She tilts her head. "They tell me you can unmake yourself. Turn your body into thread."

"They tell you a lot of shit."

Dark. Light. Makima is closer now, one hand resting on the bars. Two guards stand behind her with rifles slung, staring at nothing.

Jolyne's skin prickles. She knows these guards. Mendez cracks jokes about her buns. Okafor sneaks her cigarettes. Neither of them blinks.

Under the cot, a single strand of Stone Free slips loose from her ankle. It snakes across the concrete, through the bars, and up the inside of Mendez's sleeve until it rests against the vein in his wrist.

His pulse is slow and calm, and it matches Okafor's beat for beat.

Like a pack walking at heel.

"You're not here to observe," Jolyne says. "What'd you do to them?"

"Nothing they didn't want." Makima's voice is soft as warm milk. "Mendez was so tired of being afraid. Okafor wanted someone to tell him he was good. So I told him." Her gaze drops to the floor, to the thread Jolyne thought was invisible in the gloom. "That's very pretty. May I touch it?"

Jolyne yanks it back. Makima watches it go, delighted, the way a child watches a goldfish.

"I'll be honest with you, because I think you'd prefer it," Makima says. "I collect useful things. Your father can stop time. I find that very interesting. I'd like to meet him."

The temperature in Jolyne's chest drops ten degrees.

"How do you know about my dad?"

"He's in a coma, isn't he? Somewhere far from here, without his memories." Makima's smile never changes. "I could arrange for you to see him. I could arrange a lot of things: your appeal, your record. All you'd need to do is make a small promise."

Dark.

In the dark, Jolyne moves. String pours off her forearm as the butterfly tattoo unspools wing by wing. She lashes it across the gap and around Makima's wrist, cinching tight enough to cut.

Light.

Makima looks at the thread on her wrist, then at Jolyne. Behind her, Mendez has raised his rifle and pressed the barrel to his own temple.

"Let go, please," Makima says.

"Tell him to put it down."

"I didn't tell him to pick it up." She sounds almost apologetic. "He just knows what upsets me. Good dogs do."

Jolyne's jaw tightens. While Makima was talking, she slipped a fresh strand back onto Mendez's wrist, and his pulse thrums through it, steady as a metronome. He would do it. He'd pull the trigger with that same slow heartbeat, and it wouldn't even be fear.

"You're sick," Jolyne says.

"I'm honest. Isn't that what you wanted?" Makima leans in until the thread bites her skin and draws a bright red bead. She doesn't seem to notice. "You think I'm threatening you. I'm not. I'm showing you how simple it is. Everyone here is on a leash, Jolyne: the wardens, the guards, the other inmates. You've just been holding the wrong end of it."

That's the part that lands, because suddenly Jolyne understands the last three days. The brawl in the yard that broke out just before she could reach the infirmary. The transfer request that vanished. Okafor's cigarettes, always Okafor, always on the days she was about to try something. Little nudges. Little doors closing. She wasn't escaping. She was being herded.

This whole conversation is a test. Makima didn't come to recruit her. She came to see what Stone Free does when it's cornered.

Jolyne laughs, ragged and loud, and it echoes off the wet walls.

"Something funny?" Makima asks.

"Yeah. You. You show up in your little tie with your little smile, and you think you can sell me a happy ending." Jolyne rises from the cot, slowly. "Lady, if there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney. I don't take deals from things that only smile with their mouths."

She lets go of Makima's wrist.

In the same motion, the strand on Mendez snaps taut. It doesn't go for his throat. It threads through the trigger guard and behind the trigger itself, knotting tight as wire so the trigger can't move.

Makima glances back. Mendez squeezes. Nothing happens.

For the first time, something stirs behind those ringed eyes. It isn't anger. It's interest, almost hunger.

"Oh," Makima says quietly. "You're going to be fun."

Dark.

When the light comes back, the corridor is empty except for the two guards. They're blinking and confused, and Mendez is staring at the rifle in his hands as if he's never seen one before.

Jolyne sits back down on the cot. Her hands are shaking. She makes them stop.

On the bars, right where Makima's hand had rested, someone has tied a small red ribbon into a perfect bow.

Like a tag on a collar.

Like a gift that hasn't been opened yet.

# Prison Strings

The chain-link fences in Ward D's yard rattle whenever an inmate passes by. Jolyne Cujoh has stopped hearing it, the way people who live by train tracks stop hearing the trains. A rattle for a con shuffling toward the weights. A rattle for two guards with batons. A double rattle for Ermes cutting across the dirt to bum a cigarette.

So she notices the moment it stops.

The woman crossing the yard wears a pressed white shirt and a black tie, with auburn hair braided over one shoulder. She walks within a hand's width of the chain-link, and the fence doesn't even tremble. Three inmates follow her in single file. They aren't cuffed. They don't need to be. Each of them watches the back of her head the way a dog watches the hand holding the treat.

"Who the hell is that?" Jolyne mutters.

Ermes squints. "Transfer from some Japanese facility. Public Safety. Supposedly she's here to *consult*." She shrugs. "Warden's been grinning like an idiot since breakfast."

The woman stops at Jolyne's bench. Her eyes are yellow and ringed like a target. Her smile is soft as warm milk.

"Jolyne Cujoh," she says. "I'm Makima. I've been hoping to meet you."

"Yeah? Get in line."

"You've had such a hard time." Makima sits without being invited and folds her hands in her lap. "Framed. Abandoned. And your father..." She lets it hang exactly long enough. "I'm sorry. Truly."

Everything about it is right: the tilt of the head, the lowered voice, the little crease of sympathy between the brows. It's right the way a department-store mannequin is right. Jolyne's skin crawls.

"Lady, I've been lied to by lawyers, cops, and my own boyfriend. You're not even top five. What do you want?"

Makima's smile doesn't move, but something behind it does. "Show me."

"Show you what?"

"The thread."

Jolyne goes still. Under the bench, a single strand has already unspooled from her fingertip, slipped through the dirt, and coiled lightly around the leg of Makima's chair. She did it without thinking, the way she always does with someone she doesn't trust.

"Most people can't see it," Makima says. "I can. It's beautiful. Your body comes apart, and you still control every piece. Do you know how rare that is? Most people are only ever one thing."

"And you collect rare things."

"I take care of them."

The three inmates behind Makima haven't blinked. One of them is Sal, loud and mean, who broke a guard's nose last month. A thin red mark circles her throat, like a collar worn too long.

Jolyne pulls the thread tighter and feels through it. Wood. A metal bolt. Then, where Makima's ankle rests against the chair, nothing. No pulse. No warmth. It's like touching a photograph.

"You're not human," Jolyne says.

"Does it matter?" Makima leans closer. "I could have you out of here in a week. Your conviction overturned. The priest who did this to you found and dealt with. Your father awake." Her voice drops, kind as a lullaby. "All you have to do is make a contract with me."

There it is. Jolyne's gut, which has never once been wrong about a bad deal, clenches like a fist.

"And I'd be what, number four?" She jerks her chin at the inmates. "Sit. Stay. Roll over."

"You'd be safe."

"I'd be on a leash."

Makima considers her the way someone considers a puzzle box. Then she lifts one hand, almost lazily. "Sal."

Sal steps forward. Her eyes are wet and her mouth trembles, but her hands rise toward Ermes's throat.

"Hey!" Ermes stumbles back into the fence. It rattles, loud.

"I don't want to hurt anyone," Makima says, and she sounds like she means it. "I want you to understand that everyone here already belongs to someone. The guards belong to the warden. The warden belongs to me. You belong to a priest who's using you as bait. I'm only asking you to choose a better owner."

Jolyne's stomach turns as the shape of it comes into focus. The warden's grin. The transfer nobody announced. The tower guards who haven't moved since Makima entered the yard, every one of them facing inward and perfectly still. This was never a meeting. It's a demonstration. Makima arranged the whole yard before she sat down, like a hostess setting a table.

"You set this up," Jolyne says.

"I set everything up." Makima's smile warms another degree. "That's what love is."

Sal's fingers close on Ermes's collar.

Jolyne moves.

Stone Free bursts out of her in a spray of thread. It doesn't go for Makima, which is what Makima expects. It goes into the chain-link. A hundred strands lace through the diamonds of the fence, and Jolyne yanks. The whole length of it screams, a rattle so loud it rings off the towers. Sal flinches out of her trance for one heartbeat, and that's long enough for a loop of string to snare her wrists and haul her back onto her heels.

"Ermes, move!"

Ermes moves.

Jolyne's other hand has already done the real work. While the fence howled, a single strand slid up the chair leg, across Makima's lap, and settled around her throat, light as a hair.

Makima looks down at it, then up at Jolyne. For the first time, her smile becomes something genuine, and that is so much worse.

"You'd kill me?"

"I'd try." Jolyne's voice is steady. It's her father's voice. "Call off your dogs."

"They're not dogs. They're people who love me." Makima turns her palm up. "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners. But you aren't a dog, are you, Jolyne? Not yet."

Up in a tower, a guard silently raises his rifle and aims it at Jolyne's head.

She doesn't look up. She keeps the string taut and her eyes on those ringed yellow ones, and finally she understands the whole terrible shape of it. Makima isn't afraid of the thread at her throat. She's *delighted* by it. Every move Jolyne makes is one more thing for Makima to learn how to hold.

Jolyne grins with all her teeth. "Not yet, and not ever, you creepy bitch."

Across the yard, every fence begins to rattle at once.
