response:
# Prison Strings

The camera above Cell Block D blinks red, steady as a heartbeat, until the woman in the white shirt walks beneath it. Then it goes dark.

Jolyne Cujoh notices because she's been counting. Six weeks in the Annex, a federal facility for inmates nobody can explain, have taught her to count everything: guards, doors, the seconds between patrols. The camera stays dead for exactly as long as the woman is in its line of sight. Once she passes, the little red eye flickers back on as if nothing happened.

"Who the hell is that?" Jolyne mutters.

Her bunkmate, a wiry arsonist named Dee, doesn't look up from her cards. "Government. Some special division from overseas. Warden's been sweating through his shirt all morning."

The woman stops at the mess hall entrance. Auburn hair in a loose braid, a dark tie, and a smile like warm milk. Behind her, two guards Jolyne has watched crack an inmate's ribs for talking back stand with their hands folded and their eyes soft, waiting like retrievers for a thrown ball.

Then the woman looks straight at Jolyne. Her eyes are yellow, ringed like targets, and something old and patient is sitting at the bottom of them.

She walks over and sits down across the table without asking.

"Jolyne Cujoh," she says, as if tasting it. "I'm Makima. I've been looking forward to meeting you."

"Yeah? I haven't." Jolyne leans back and folds her arms, the butterfly tattoo flexing on her bicep. "Visiting hours are Sundays. Take a number."

Makima laughs, light and pleasant. It's a perfect laugh, and it sounds the way laughs do in commercials. "You're exactly as described. Your file says you can turn your body into string."

Jolyne's jaw tightens. Nobody outside this building should know that.

"My file says a lot of stuff. Most of it's bullshit."

"Most of it," Makima agrees. "But not that part."

Under the table, Jolyne lets a single thread unspool from her fingertip. It's thinner than hair and invisible in the fluorescent glare. She threads it across the floor and up the leg of Makima's chair, then loops it once around her ankle, featherlight. Stone Free can feel a pulse through string. Jolyne has caught liars this way before, because hearts jump when people lie.

Makima's heart doesn't jump. Jolyne isn't sure it beats at all, or if it does, it beats like a metronome someone forgot to turn off.

"Something wrong?" Makima tilts her head.

"Your face," Jolyne says. "It's doing a thing faces do, but you're not behind it."

For half a second, the smile holds a little too still. Then it warms again, and that's worse.

"You're perceptive. I like that." Makima folds her hands on the table. "I'll be honest with you, Jolyne. I know you didn't kill that man. I know who arranged your conviction. I could have you released by Friday, record expunged, no questions asked." She pauses, gentle and precise. "And your father. I understand he's in poor condition. I have resources that could help him."

The mess hall goes quiet in Jolyne's ears.

She hasn't told anyone here about her dad. Not Dee, not the guards, nobody.

"How do you know about him?"

"I make it my business to know what people want most." Makima's voice drops, intimate, like a secret shared between friends. "All you'd have to do is work for me. A simple arrangement. A contract."

There it is. Jolyne has heard men sweet-talk her before, pretty boys with pretty promises, and one of them is the reason she's wearing an orange jumpsuit. She recognizes a hook when she sees one, and this one has bait on it shaped exactly like her father's face.

"Pass," she says.

Makima doesn't blink. "Dee."

Across the hall, Dee sets down her cards, stands up, and walks over, slow and dreamy. She kneels beside Makima's chair and rests her cheek against Makima's knee like a tired dog. Her eyes are open, but she isn't in them.

"Dee?" Jolyne half rises. "Dee, what the fuck—"

Makima strokes Dee's hair absently. "She's always wanted someone to tell her what to do. Most people do. It's a kindness, really." From somewhere in her sleeve, Dee produces a sharpened toothbrush and lifts it to her own throat. Her hand is perfectly steady. "I'd prefer you said yes, Jolyne. I don't enjoy waste."

The guards don't move. No one in the mess hall moves. Above them, the camera's red light has gone dark again.

That's the moment Jolyne understands the real game. Makima isn't trying to recruit her. She's teaching her what it costs to refuse, and the lesson is being written on somebody Jolyne cares about.

Jolyne's heart is hammering, but her voice comes out cold and flat, her father's voice.

"Look down."

Makima glances down. A web of string, hundreds of strands, has been weaving silently across the floor this whole conversation. It's wrapped around the shiv in Dee's hand, around Dee's wrist, around every leg of Makima's chair, and in a tight, patient coil around Makima's own throat.

"You can make people your puppets," Jolyne says, "but string doesn't take orders from anybody except me. I tighten this, and your head ends up three tables over. Let her go."

For a long moment, Makima studies the threads at her neck with open delight, like a child finding a rare beetle.

"You'd do it, too," she murmurs. "How wonderful."

Dee blinks, gasps, and drops the shiv. She scrambles backward, shaking, with no memory in her face of how she got there.

Makima rises, unbothered by the string, and smooths her skirt. Somehow the coil has gone slack around her throat. Jolyne never loosened it.

"You're not a dog, Jolyne," Makima says softly. "Not yet. But I'm very good at training."

She walks away, and the guards trail after her. One by one, the cameras die above her head and wake again behind her.

Only after the doors close does Jolyne realize her hands are trembling. When Makima mentioned her father, for one terrible heartbeat, she almost said yes.

"If she comes back," Jolyne whispers to the empty doorway, "I'm cutting the strings first."

prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception.

First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense.

Notes are always written on standard Foundation memo paper, even when the researcher keeps it locked away. Length: 1000 words.
response:
**SCP-7183: "Don't Watch the Door"**

**Item #:** SCP-7183

**Object Class:** Euclid (provisional)

**Special Containment Procedures:** Dr. Elise Halloran is to remain at Site-77 under Level 2 observation. All Form FM-2 memorandum stock has been removed from her quarters. Recovered notes are to be photographed and stored in Locker 7183-A. Dr. Halloran is not to be told whether new notes have been found.

**Description:** The following account was written by Dr. Halloran at the Site Director's request. It is unedited.

---

I found the first note on a Tuesday, folded once and tucked under my keyboard. I recognized the paper before the handwriting. It was Form FM-2, Standard Interdepartmental Memorandum, pale green stock with the Foundation seal faded into the corner. I had used it for nine years.

The handwriting was mine.

> *14th, 0310. Wing C. It goes out through the ventilation maintenance hatch, not the door. Don't watch the door. — E.*

It was the 3rd. Wing C housed SCP-4471, a mimetic entity I had studied for eighteen months. It couldn't reproduce voices or faces, only gestures and handwriting. I knew that better than anyone. I had written its containment procedures.

I reported the note within the hour. That was the last uncomplicated thing I did.

---

Dr. Okafor ran the analysis. Graphology matched my pen pressure, my slant, the way I crossed my sevens because of a teacher I'd had in Lyon. The ink matched site-issued ballpoints. The lot number matched the ream in my desk.

"So either you wrote it," Okafor said, "or something that's watched you write for a year and a half wrote it."

"Or I *will* write it."

He didn't answer.

At his suggestion I counted my remaining memo sheets, three hundred and eleven, and locked them in the safe in my quarters. Only I knew the combination. Security trained a camera on it.

Two days later:

> *They moved the camera. Doesn't matter. Count again. Okafor is dead, Okafor was dead on the 14th, why are you talking to him*

There were three hundred and ten sheets. The footage showed the safe closed for all forty-eight hours. Okafor was in the next room eating an apple, very much alive.

---

The Foundation proposed two hypotheses and, to its credit, didn't tell me which it favoured.

**Hypothesis A:** a genuine retrocausal event. A future version of me, in the aftermath of a breach, was sending warnings backward, and they were degrading, either in transit or because *she* was.

**Hypothesis B:** SCP-4471 had found a way to influence me remotely, and I was writing the notes myself in fugue states to provoke containment changes that would free it.

Under B, following the notes was how the breach would happen. Under A, ignoring them was.

---

We designed a test. I wrote a phrase on a slip of paper, sealed it in an envelope, and handed it to Security unseen. If a future self existed, she would remember what I'd written.

The phrase was *the orchard behind the chapel*. I remembered choosing it. I remembered the pen dragging on the second *h*.

The next note appeared on my pillow.

> *the orchard behind the chapel. there. now do you believe me. tell Mara I tried*

Security opened the envelope in front of me. The slip read *blue kettle, eleven spoons*.

It was in my handwriting. I had no memory of writing it. I didn't know anyone named Mara.

After that, I stopped being sure which of my memories I could submit as evidence.

---

The notes came faster, and most were no longer coherent.

> *the lake at site 77 froze the night it got out. you could see it under the ice wearing your face*

Site-77 had no lake.

> *DON'T COUNT THE SHEETS IT LEARNS FROM THE COUNTING*

> *it isn't 4471. it was never 4471. 4471 is the only thing that tried to stop it*

> *Elise I'm so tired. I've written this 200 times. you always do the envelope. you always pick the orchard*

I read that one four times. I had never told anyone about the orchard. The phrase existed only in my head and, apparently, in the head of someone who was or would be me.

Or in the head of something that had been in my head long enough to know what I would choose.

---

On the 11th, Procurement confirmed something I hadn't thought to ask about. Every note had been written on FM-2 Revision 7, the version we stocked. The pillow note was on Revision 9.

Revision 8 was still in draft. Revision 9 did not exist.

Okafor studied the sheet for a long time. "Elise," he said quietly, "I need you not to take this badly. Are you sure it says what you read to me?"

I looked down. It said exactly what I'd read. I was certain.

I asked him what he saw. He wouldn't tell me. He put it in his report, and I was never cleared to read it.

---

I wrote this final section on the 13th, at 2340.

Containment on SCP-4471 had been doubled. The ventilation hatch in Wing C had been welded shut. That was my recommendation, the Director accepted it, and I couldn't stop thinking about it.

If the notes were true, I had saved lives.

If the notes were the entity, I had done exactly what it wanted, and I couldn't see what that was.

I had been told the safe was emptied and that there was no memo paper anywhere in my quarters.

But there was a sheet on the desk in front of me. It was pale green, with the seal in the corner, blank and waiting. I was holding a pen I didn't remember picking up.

I had counted the sheets before they took them. Three hundred and eleven. I was almost sure it was three hundred and eleven.

I decided I would write one thing, then put the pen down and hand this account to Security.

What I wrote was: *Don't watch the door.*

---

**Addendum 7183-1:** Dr. Halloran's account was recovered from her quarters at 0310 on the 14th. Wing C containment held. No memo paper of any revision was found in the room.

Dr. Halloran has asked repeatedly whether Dr. Okafor is all right. Per procedure, she has not been told.

prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception.

First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense.

Ink analysis reveals trace elements not matching any office pen. Length: 1000 words.
response:
**Item #:** SCP-6142

**Object Class:** Euclid (Provisional; see Addendum 6142-4)

**Special Containment Procedures:** All handwritten material recovered from the quarters, office, or person of Dr. Anneliese Corr is to be photographed, sealed, and forwarded to the Temporal Anomalies Desk. Dr. Corr is not to be shown note contents before recovery by Security. Monitoring of Cell 9 (SCP-3388) has been doubled.

**Description:** SCP-6142 designates a series of 31 handwritten notes recovered between 4 March and 11 April. Dr. Corr's statement follows, appended at her own request.

---

The first note was in my coat pocket on the 4th of March. I found it while reaching for my badge.

> *Cell 9. April 11. 0340. They will tell you the seals are fine. Check them yourself.*

It was my handwriting. It wasn't similar to mine. It was mine: the slanted capital C my grandmother taught me, the habit of crossing my sevens. Nobody at Site-43 had seen enough of my writing to forge it that well. I knew of only one thing on site that could.

SCP-3388 had been in Cell 9 for eleven years. We called it the Correspondent. It had no shape anyone remembered afterward, but it wrote letters to staff in the handwriting of people they had loved. There were three suicides before we learned to keep paper away from it. It had no paper now. That was the first thing I told myself.

I reported the note, of course. I am not a stupid woman, whatever the later notes suggested.

> *You reported it. Good. It won't matter. Dr. Asante will say it's 3388 and he'll be half right.*

That one was taped inside my locker the following week. Dr. Asante, the Site psychologist, had not yet been assigned to me. He was assigned two days later.

---

Asante was kind. He ran me through standard cognitohazard screening, and I came back clean. He asked whether I'd ever written something and forgotten it.

"Everyone has," I said. He wrote that down, and I wished I hadn't said it.

The Foundation opened two lines of inquiry. The Temporal Anomalies Desk wanted to know whether the notes came from the future. Containment wanted to know whether they came from Cell 9, or from me, written in fugue under 3388's influence and hidden from myself. I wanted to know which answer I was hoping for. I still don't.

They put a camera in my quarters. The next note appeared under my pillow on a night when the footage showed me sleeping, unmoving, for six hours.

> *the camera is fine its not about the camera. April 11. I keep writing April 11 but I dont remember if its still April 11 on your side. Is Daniel ok*

I do not know a Daniel.

---

The ink report came back on the 22nd. The pigment base matched nothing in Site supply and no commercial pen in the database. Suspended in it were trace particulates of a lead-bismuth-tin alloy whose ratio exactly matched the composite shielding in Cell 9's inner walls. Okonkwo, the lab tech, walked me through the isotope work. The alloy had been exposed to temperatures above 1,100 degrees Celsius.

"The walls of Cell 9 have never been heated," I said.

"No," he said. "Not yet."

He meant it as a joke. Neither of us laughed.

Containment pointed out, reasonably, that 3388 had spent eleven years inside those walls and knew their composition better than we did. Producing a convincing particulate fit its documented capabilities. Temporal pointed out, equally reasonably, that 3388 had never once demonstrated the ability to produce matter. Both were right. I began to understand what the note meant by *half*.

---

As March turned to April, the notes changed.

> *the sky was green that morning remember that, you said it looked like bile*

> *DONT LET THEM MOVE YOU TO SECTOR C you have never been to sector c but you will*

> *I think Mum would have liked this, or I think Id have liked to tell her. Did she die? Here she died. Here a lot of things*

My mother is alive. She lives in Norwich and phones on Sundays. I rang her after that one, and she asked why I was crying. I couldn't tell her, which is its own kind of cell.

The handwriting deteriorated. The C survived, but the lines drifted and the letters doubled over, as though written by shaking hands, or by someone who had forgotten how to be me and was working from memory. Some notes were written over older ones. One was only my name, forty times, pressed harder each time until the pen tore the page.

I started checking my hands for ink. I kept a log of things I knew were true (Mother alive, no Daniel, sky blue) and read it every morning. Asante said this was healthy. Then, at the bottom of my own log, I found a line in my own hand that I did not remember writing:

> *the sky is blue for now*

That night I stopped trusting the camera, and the next morning I stopped trusting the log. I could not stop trusting my eyes, because I had nothing else left to see with.

---

On 9 April, at my request, Containment ran a full seal audit on Cell 9. Everything was nominal. On the 10th, at my request, they ran it again and let me watch. I checked every seal myself. I touched the walls. They were cool.

I did not sleep that night. I sat in the observation corridor with Asante and two security officers, and we watched the clock pass 0340 and keep going. Nothing happened. 3388 did not move. Or if it did, nobody remembered it moving, which with 3388 amounts to the same thing.

At 0412, Asante put his hand on my shoulder. "It's over."

When I returned to my quarters, there was a note on the desk.

> *It didnt happen. Im so glad. I cant tell if it didnt happen because you believed me or because you didnt, and I cant remember which one of us I am anymore. Tell Daniel Im sorry. Burn this. Dont*

That was the last one. It ends there. The page is not torn.

---

The Foundation never closed the file. Temporal maintains the notes formed a causal loop, resolved by intervention. Containment maintains that 3388 finally learned to write in the one medium we couldn't take away from it, which was me, and that the notes themselves were the breach. Asante's report describes me as "lucid, cooperative, and grieving something she cannot name."

They asked me to write this statement by hand, and I have been careful. I have reread every line. It is my handwriting, and I remember writing all of it.

I have checked that twice. I am checking it again now.

Last week in the commissary, a new junior researcher introduced himself: Dr. Daniel Pryce, transferred from Sector C.

I have not decided what to tell him.

response:
# SCP-7714: "Correspondence From Tuesday"

**Item #:** SCP-7714

**Object Class:** Pending (provisionally Euclid)

**Special Containment Procedures:** All documents recovered from the desk of Dr. Teodor Halloran, Office 4-117, Site-19, are to be collected, photographed, and stored in Locker 7714-A. Dr. Halloran is to remain under continuous observation. His testimony is preserved below at the request of the Ethics Committee.

---

**Account of Dr. T. Halloran**

The first note was waiting under my coffee mug on a Monday. It was a torn half-sheet of Site letterhead, and the handwriting was mine. I knew it the way you know your own face in a shop window before you have consciously recognized it.

> *Don't let them move 4471 to Wing C on the 14th. Check the seal on door C-9. Please trust me. —T*

I assumed it was a prank. SCP-4471 was a minor assignment of mine, a dormant cognitive entity with no recorded activity in six years. Nobody had scheduled any transfer, so I threw the note away.

Two days later, a transfer order for SCP-4471 arrived. The destination was Wing C, and the date was the 14th.

> *They filed it. You didn't stop them. The light on C-9 will show green when it should be red. You have to SAY something.*

That was when I went to Security. I asked them to pull the footage of my office from the hour before the second note appeared, and we watched it together. The recording showed my empty desk, then 0.4 seconds of static, then the desk again with a folded sheet on it. The timestamp of the glitch matched the time I had left for lunch. It was exact to the second.

---

The Foundation took my report seriously, which frightened me more than ridicule would have.

They set out two hypotheses. Under Hypothesis A, SCP-7714 was a genuine temporal anomaly, and the notes were being sent back by a version of me who had survived a breach. Under Hypothesis B, SCP-4471 was not dormant at all. It was influencing me, and I was writing the notes myself during fugue states while the entity scrubbed both the cameras and my memory.

The evidence did not favor either one. Graphological analysis matched my handwriting completely, including a slight tremor in the descending strokes that I did not yet have. The ink came from a supply batch scheduled for delivery to Site-19 the following month. The letterhead carried a revised Foundation logo that was still under committee review.

Dr. Asante, who led the investigation, explained the difficulty plainly. "A temporal source would produce all of this," she said. "So would an entity that can read the inventory forecasts in your head."

They assigned an agent to watch me around the clock. He sat in my office, ate with me, and stood outside the lavatory door. On Thursday I was reviewing a file when the overhead monitor flickered. When I looked down, there was a note on the desk beside my elbow. The agent swore he had not looked away, and he was badly shaken when he said it.

> *Tell Hannah I'm sorry. She's the one who opens it. She doesn't know what she's looking at. None of us did.*

I didn't know anyone named Hannah. A search of personnel records found no Hannah connected to Wing C, to SCP-4471, or to me.

---

The notes grew worse after that.

> *the moon was the wrong colour last night, did you notice, you will notice*

> *Stop taking the stairs to the fourth floor. Site-19 doesn't have a fourth floor. It never did.*

My office was on the fourth floor. I was sitting in it when I read that.

> *it was never 4471 it was never 4471 it was the DOOR the door is the thing the door was always the thing*

I began to check things obsessively. I counted the stairs every morning and photographed the moon. I asked colleagues to describe the color of my office walls, then compared their answers against my own. I could not tell anymore whether I was examining the anomaly or whether the anomaly was examining me through my own eyes.

Every psychological evaluation came back clean. Dr. Asante pointed out that this proved nothing either way. If 4471 were responsible, a clean result was exactly what it would want us to see.

---

I designed one test of my own. I wrote a passphrase on an index card, a private memory that I had never spoken aloud or written down anywhere else. I sealed the card in an evidence bag, locked it in Dr. Asante's safe, and addressed my future self out loud: *If you're real, tell me what's on the card.*

The next note arrived nine hours later, after another 0.4 seconds of static.

> *"The blue kite on the Ardmore cliffs, and Dad letting go of the string on purpose." You're testing the wrong thing, Teo. Anyone in your head would know that.*

The answer was correct. It was also useless, because the note was right. The test could only show that the author had access to my mind. A future self would have that access, and so would a parasite living inside my thoughts.

---

On the 13th, I formally recommended that the transfer be cancelled. I cited the notes and stated in writing that I could not distinguish between a genuine warning and a manipulation intended to make me act. The Director approved the cancellation anyway, on the grounds that keeping a dormant entity where it already was carried little risk.

The 14th passed without incident. Door C-9 stayed sealed, and its indicator light showed red all day. I slept that night for the first time in weeks.

The final note was waiting when I woke up.

> *Thank you. It worked. Everything is fine now. You'll start writing these on the 20th. Don't stop, even when it frightens you. Hannah says hello.*

---

**Addendum 7714-1:** Dr. Halloran does not recall writing the sections of this account that state Researcher Hannah Halloran does not exist. Researcher H. Halloran is his younger sister. She has been employed at Site-19 since 2019 and was originally assigned to the Wing C transfer team.

When this account was shown to him, Dr. Halloran said he had always known his sister, and that he could not explain why the document said otherwise. After a pause, he added that he could not prove he had always known her, either.

Site-19 has three floors. Office 4-117 is not listed on any schematic.

**Addendum 7714-2:** On the 20th, Dr. Halloran was observed sitting at his desk and writing by hand on Site letterhead. The observing agent reported that Dr. Halloran was weeping and did not respond when spoken to. Camera footage of the incident is limited to 0.4 seconds of static.

All unmarked doors share identical scratches around the doorknob area. Length: 1000 words.
response:
# SCP-6614: "The Reading Room"

**Item #:** SCP-6614

**Object Class:** Keter (Provisional)

**Special Containment Procedures:** All known instances of SCP-6614-A are to be sealed with welded steel plating and kept under remote observation. Seals are to be inspected weekly. Any seal found removed *from the interior side* is to be reported directly to Site Command and **not** to the O5 Liaison Office.

*(Revision 4. See Addendum 6614-4.)*

**Description:** SCP-6614-A designates 41 confirmed doors in abandoned structures across 19 countries, including a collapsed textile mill in Łódź, a flooded hospital outside Pripyat, and a shuttered elementary school in Ohio. Each instance is a gray-painted wooden door measuring 2.03 m by 0.81 m. Each has a brass knob, no keyhole, and no visible hinges. Prior architectural surveys confirm that every instance appeared in a wall that previously had no opening.

All instances bear an identical pattern of seventeen fine scratches radiating from the knob. The patterns match to micrometer tolerance, including a distinctive hooked gouge at the four o'clock position.

Every instance opens onto the same antechamber of SCP-6614-B, a library-archive of indeterminate size. Stairwells within SCP-6614-B descend and arrive above their starting point. Shelving recedes beyond the range of all lighting equipment. The material is overwhelmingly paper, cataloged in a script that Foundation linguists have partially deciphered as an ancestor of no known language.

---

**Exploration Log 6614-03**

**Team:** MTF Theta-9 ("Card Catalogue"). Sgt. Adaeze Okafor (lead), Specialists Brandt and Ilyinova, and Dr. Hale Morrow (archivist).

The team entered through the Łódź instance at 0912. The antechamber matched prior reports. It contained a long oak desk, a brass lamp that was already lit, and a sign-in register bound in gray cloth. Okafor photographed the register's open page without touching it.

They proceeded into Stack 4. Morrow worked as they walked, reading spines by flashlight and muttering translations into his recorder. Most of the material was administrative: inventories, requisitions, and incident summaries. By the forty-minute mark he had stopped muttering.

> **Recovered Document 6614-B-112** *(translated excerpt)*
>
> *Bulletin of the Wardenry of the Kept. Circulated to all Holdings.*
>
> *Following the breach at Holding Ninety, the Wardenry regrets to confirm that the condition is no longer local. The sky is no longer contained. Personnel are reminded that the Archive must be preserved at all costs, so that whoever comes after may learn what we were for.*

"Wardenry," Brandt said. "Holdings. Kept." He looked at the others. "That's us. That's just *us* with different words."

Morrow didn't answer. He had found a drawer labeled with a glyph his team had already decoded: PERSONNEL.

The files were arranged alphabetically under a transliteration scheme the Foundation had developed only eight months earlier. Morrow found Okafor's file first. It contained her photograph, which was clearly her, rendered in a silver-emulsion process with no modern equivalent. Ilyinova took a fiber sample from the folder. Carbon dating would later place it at roughly 1640 CE.

> **Recovered Document 6614-B-340** *(translated excerpt)*
>
> *Ledger of the Wardenry, Year of Holding 1,114.*
>
> *MORROW, HALE. Function: Archivist. Clearance: Fourth Ring.*
>
> *Remarks: Has been to the Archive. Will go again. Do not allow him to read his own file.*

Morrow read it twice. Then he closed the folder and asked to move on.

---

At 1047, Ilyinova reported movement in Stack 6.

Four figures stood forty meters ahead, between the shelves. They wore fully encapsulated suits in a faded industrial yellow, and their visors were mirrored and opaque. They were removing material wholesale. They swept entire shelves into wheeled bins, unbolted the uprights, and rolled them away. Behind them stretched a long corridor of bare wall, still marked with pale rectangles where the shelving had stood.

Okafor called out in English, then Polish, then in the Wardenry script Morrow had coached her on.

The figures turned in unison and ran. They abandoned one bin and left the cart rolling on its own. They moved with the stiff, heavy gait of people in Level A protection, but faster than anyone in such suits should be able to move. They rounded a shelf end and were gone. Pursuit found only more bare wall.

The abandoned bin held about three hundred documents. All were titled some variant of *Holding Ninety: Causes of Failure*, and every page had been blacked out by hand in fresh, still-tacky ink.

Brandt found the glove on the floor beside the bin.

It was a standard heavy chemical gauntlet with a ring of raised reinforcement studs around the palm and a hooked steel clasp at the wrist. Okafor held it up to the photograph of the Łódź door's scratches, then fitted the glove over the brass knob of a nearby reading-room door and turned it.

The studs traced seventeen lines. The clasp left a hooked gouge at four o'clock.

Stenciled inside the cuff was a Foundation inventory number. Logistics has confirmed that the number belongs to a production batch scheduled for issue in **2031**.

---

**Addendum 6614-4: Antechamber Register**

Analysis of the register photographed on Exploration 6614-03 identified 2,212 entries in multiple hands. Among them:

> *O5-7. Purpose of visit: Reference. Item withdrawn: Minutes of the Wardenry Council, Final Session.* — dated **14 March 2024**
>
> *O5-11. Purpose of visit: Reference.* — dated **2 September 2025**

The Foundation did not discover SCP-6614 until February 2026. Handwriting analysis matched both signatures to their respective Council members with high confidence.

O5-7 and O5-11 were queried through formal channels. Both denied any knowledge of SCP-6614. The Council issued a single directive in response:

> *Continue exploration. Do not enter Stack 9.*

No exploration team had previously identified a Stack 9.

---

**Addendum 6614-5**

During a follow-up expedition, Dr. Morrow located a duplicate copy of the withdrawn minutes in a misfiled box in Stack 2. One passage was legible:

> **Recovered Document 6614-B-901** *(translated excerpt)*
>
> *Motion carried, eleven to two: the Archive shall be emptied before the next Wardenry finds it. They must not learn that they have done this before. They must not learn how it ends. The Council will see to the clearing personally, as it always has.*

---

**Note appended by Site Command, 9 November 2026:**

Remote observation of the antechamber shows the register open to a new page. The most recent entry is dated three days after Exploration 6614-03:

> *O5-1. Purpose of visit: Retrieval.*

Dr. Morrow's personnel file is no longer in Stack 4.

Dr. Morrow has not reported for duty since.

The weld seal on the Łódź door was found intact. A fresh set of scratches has appeared beneath it, on the inside of the plate.

response:
# SCP-7741: "The Stacks"

**Item #:** SCP-7741

**Object Class:** Keter

**Special Containment Procedures:** Known instances of SCP-7741 are to be secured behind locked partitions and monitored remotely. Buildings hosting instances are to be acquired through Foundation front companies and listed as structurally condemned. Entry into SCP-7741-1 requires Level 4 approval. As of Addendum 7741-C, entry requires approval from the Ethics Committee rather than the O5 Council.

**Description:** SCP-7741 consists of 214 identical doors found in abandoned structures across 41 countries. Each door measures 2.1 by 0.9 meters. Each is made of grey-green painted hardwood with a plain brass knob, and none bears a number, plaque, or manufacturer's mark. Instances appear only in buildings unoccupied for at least six years. No instance has been observed in the act of manifesting.

Many instances are older than the structures that contain them. A door in a shuttered 1974 shopping arcade in Leeds shows paint worn through to bare grain at hand height, as if from centuries of use. Dendrochronological analysis dated its timber to approximately 1340 CE. A door in a Detroit auto plant, built in 1952, has hinges oxidized to a degree consistent with four hundred years of exposure. The doorframes, however, are always contemporary with the building, and they fit their doors exactly.

Every instance opens onto the same space, designated SCP-7741-1: an archive of unknown extent. Its shelving corridors exceed the dimensions of any containing structure. Its staircases ascend to floors located beneath their points of origin. Measured distances change on return trips. The archive is lit by a sourceless amber glow.

---

**Exploration Log 7741-02**

Team Lead Dr. Ana Ferreira and Agents Okonkwo and Leclerc entered through the Leeds instance. Their tethers paid out 300 meters before Leclerc noted that the corridor behind them had become noticeably shorter than the line.

The shelves held bound volumes, document boxes, and card catalogs filed under a numbering system that Ferreira tentatively identified as a containment registry. The stamped headers repeated a single phrase in an unknown script. Translation software later rendered it, with low confidence, as *THE CURATORIUM — SECURE. RETAIN. PRESERVE.*

Okonkwo pointed out that the phrase had three clauses, as did the Foundation's own motto. Ferreira instructed him to keep collecting samples.

---

**Recovered Document 7741-D-14** *(partial translation)*

> *...the breach at Holding Nine cannot be reversed. All Wardens are to begin final archival procedures. Whatever comes after us must be able to find this. The Concordance believed that no anomaly could outlast the hand that kept it. The Concordance was wrong. It was never the objects that we failed to hold.*
>
> *Seal the stacks. Leave the doors where the next Keepers will find them, in the empty places, where they always go.*

---

**Exploration Log 7741-04**

Ferreira's team reached a section that the card catalog designated "Personnel — Active." The team spent four hours there. At hour three, Leclerc stopped speaking and handed Ferreira a folder.

The file was dated *Year 311 of the Second Keeping*. Carbon analysis of its vellum later returned an age of 600 to 650 years. Inside was an engraved portrait of Dr. Elias Halvorsen, current Site Director of Site-43. The engraving reproduced the scar above his left eyebrow, which Halvorsen received in 2009.

The team recovered 37 further files corresponding to living Foundation personnel. Each was complete with accurate biographical details, clearance levels rendered in Curatorium notation, and handwritten evaluator comments.

Ferreira did not locate a file for herself. Okonkwo found one for himself and declined to read it. It was retrieved for analysis over his objection.

---

**Recovered Document 7741-D-88** *(excerpt from the file of Agent D. Okonkwo)*

> *Reliable. Asks the right question one step too late. Recommend retention through the final Keeping. Recommend he not be told.*

---

**Exploration Log 7741-05**

Two kilometers in, by tether measurement, the team heard rolling wheels.

In a cross-corridor, six figures in pale yellow full-body containment suits were emptying a shelving bay. The suits had no visible seams, zippers, or respirator housings, and their faceplates were opaque. The figures worked in silence. They lifted entire shelving units, contents included, onto flatbed carts. The bay behind them was bare floor, with no bolt holes or dust outlines where the shelves had stood.

Each suit bore an emblem on the left shoulder: three concentric rings and three arrows. It matched the Foundation insignia except that the arrows pointed outward.

Ferreira called out a standard non-hostile greeting. All six figures froze. Then they ran. The movement was described as clumsy and frightened, "like interns caught somewhere they shouldn't be," in Leclerc's words. They abandoned one cart and fled around a corner. When the team followed seconds later, they found a dead end and no figures.

The abandoned cart held fourteen document boxes labeled, in translation, *CAUSE OF FAILURE — HOLDING NINE*. Every box was empty. The cart's handle had been wrapped in black electrical tape of a type the Foundation commonly stocks.

Upon returning to the Leeds door, the team found that the corridor they had taken in was now 40 meters shorter. Two shelving bays they had photographed on the way in were gone.

---

**Addendum 7741-C**

During Exploration 7741-07, a visitor's ledger was found on a lectern in a vestibule about 90 meters inside the Detroit instance. Most of its entries were in Curatorium script. The final eleven were in English.

Handwriting analysis matched four signatures to O5-3, O5-6, O5-9, and O5-11, based on comparison with authenticated Council correspondence. The entries span 2011 to the present. None correspond to any authorized exploration, and the Council's records contain no reference to SCP-7741 before its formal discovery in 2023.

Representative entries:

# SCP-7340: "The Antecedent Stacks"

**Object Class:** Keter

**Special Containment Procedures:** All known SCP-7340 instances are to be sealed behind reinforced concrete and monitored remotely. Field agents in regions with high concentrations of abandoned structures are to sweep unlit interior spaces quarterly for instance emergence.

Per O5 directive, further exploration is suspended indefinitely. Personnel who participated in Explorations 7340-1 through 7340-4 are to be reassigned and are not to be amnestized. Requests for clarification of this directive will not be answered.

**Description:** SCP-7340 is a recurring phenomenon. Identical doors manifest in abandoned buildings worldwide. Each door is 2.1 meters tall and made of an unidentified grey hardwood. None bears a handle plate, hinge marking, or manufacturer's stamp. Instances appear only in rooms that have gone without light for at least seventy-two hours. In complete darkness, a faint glow escapes through the door's edges. Spectrographic analysis matches the glow to sodium-vapor lamps of a type that has never been manufactured.

All instances open onto the same space, designated SCP-7340-A. It is an archive of indeterminate size. Its corridors of shelving intersect at angles that sum to more than 360 degrees. Documents within SCP-7340-A are written in modern languages. They describe a global civilization that predates recorded history and ended in what the texts call "the Unbinding."

---

**EXPLORATION LOG 7340-2**

**Team:** MTF Lambda-12 ("Bookworms"). Team Lead: Dr. Imani Okafor. Agents Castellanos, Reyes-Whitlock, and Huang.

**Point of Entry:** Instance 7340-19, a disused textile mill in Łódź, Poland.

The team passed through the door at 0912. Agent Huang reported that the air inside was cool and dry and smelled of paper and ozone. The sodium lamps hung on chains that disappeared into darkness overhead. Castellanos released a tethered drone, which reached its maximum cable length of 400 meters without finding a ceiling.

Dr. Okafor directed the team to the nearest shelf. The spines were labelled in a filing system that used English with unfamiliar abbreviations. She pulled a folder marked **CUSTODIATE — INCIDENT SUMMARY — TERMINAL**.

> **RECOVERED DOCUMENT 7340-2-A (excerpt):**
>
> *...by the forty-first hour, containment had failed at all nine Primary Sites at once. The Directorate believes this was no cascade. Something was opened deliberately, from inside. The Council of Thirteen has authorized Protocol Ember. Archive personnel are to remain at their posts and preserve the record. Someone must know what we were, so they can recognize what they are becoming.*

Agent Reyes-Whitlock noted the phrase "Council of Thirteen." Dr. Okafor told the team to keep moving.

At 0958, the team reached a section labelled **PERSONNEL — ACTIVE ROSTER**. The folders were arranged alphabetically. Agent Huang found one under his own name.

> **RECOVERED DOCUMENT 7340-2-B:**
>
> **CUSTODIATE PERSONNEL FILE**
> **Name:** Huang, Wei-Lin
> **Designation:** Field Archivist, Second Class
> **Date of Commission:** Third Month, Year 1184 of the Concord
> **Notes:** *Steady under pressure. Do not assign to deep stacks. He goes quiet before he panics, and we lose him in the quiet.*
> **Status:** *Deceased — the Unbinding.*

The photograph clipped to the folder showed Agent Huang. A healed fracture scar was visible above his left eyebrow, matching an injury he received in 2019.

Dr. Okafor ordered the team to collect samples and withdraw. During the withdrawal, Agent Castellanos reported movement two aisles east.

> **AUDIO TRANSCRIPT (excerpt):**
>
> **Castellanos:** Contact. Four, maybe five figures. They're wearing suits, full hazmat, yellow. They're carrying boxes.
>
> **Okafor:** Ours?
>
> **Castellanos:** No insignia I recognize. They're clearing a shelf. Just sweeping everything into crates.
>
> **Okafor:** Announce yourself.
>
> **Castellanos:** Foundation personnel! Stop where you are!
>
> **[Sound of footsteps, running, receding.]**
>
> **Castellanos:** They dropped everything. They're gone. They ran like *we* were the containment breach.

The shelf the figures were clearing was labelled **FOUNDING — PRECURSOR TRANSITION**. All of its folders had been taken except one, which had fallen behind the shelving.

> **RECOVERED DOCUMENT 7340-2-C (excerpt):**
>
> *...the survivors will rebuild. They always do. They will build the same institutions with the same people, because the pattern runs deeper than memory. We have seen it in the cycles before ours. The Archive must not be found too early. If they learn the shape of the ending before they reach it, they will hurry toward it, thinking they are running away.*

---

**EXPLORATION LOG 7340-4**

**Team:** Lambda-12. Agent Huang was declined for this exploration at Dr. Okafor's request.

**Point of Entry:** Instance 7340-31, a decommissioned hospital in Detroit, Michigan.

The team returned to map the extent of the removals. Dr. Okafor estimated that roughly a third of the shelving visited during Exploration 7340-2 was now empty. Bare metal brackets ran in long, clean rows.

At 1340, the team found a reading alcove. It held a writing desk and a leather-bound ledger titled **REGISTER OF VISITORS**. Most entries were in Custodiate script and dated within the precursor calendar. The final eleven entries were recent, and they were written in English.

> **RECOVERED DOCUMENT 7340-4-A (transcription, final entries):**
>
> | Date | Name | Section Consulted |
> |---|---|---|
> | 2024-03-11 | O5-4 | Council Records, Terminal |
> | 2024-03-11 | O5-9 | Council Records, Terminal |
> | 2025-07-02 | O5-4 | Protocol Ember |
> | 2025-12-19 | O5-1 | Founding — Precursor Transition |
> | 2026-01-04 | O5-1 | Founding — Precursor Transition |
> | 2026-01-04 | O5-11 | Personnel — Active Roster |
> | ... | ... | ... |
> | 2026-08-30 | O5-4 | *[Field left blank]* |

No Foundation record documents any O5 Council member entering SCP-7340-A. The earliest entry is dated two years before the first instance was discovered.

Agent Reyes-Whitlock photographed the ledger. Dr. Okafor told the team to replace it exactly where they found it.

At 1412, the team encountered the hazmat figures again. This time they did not retreat right away. One figure stood at the end of the aisle, holding a crate. The narrow window of its visor reflected the lamplight. Dr. Okafor stepped forward alone and spoke to it.

> **AUDIO TRANSCRIPT (excerpt):**
>
> **Okafor:** We're not here to stop you. We need to understand what happened.
>
> **[Eleven seconds of silence.]**
>
> **Okafor:** Who sent you?
>
> **[The figure sets the crate on the floor and slides it toward Dr. Okafor. It turns and leaves at a walk.]**

The crate contained a single folder.

> **RECOVERED DOCUMENT 7340-4-B:**
>
> **CUSTODIATE PERSONNEL FILE**
> **Name:** Okafor, Imani
> **Designation:** Senior Archivist
> **Notes:** *Went into the stacks against Council orders. Found the ledger. Told no one, as instructed.*
> *She was right to tell no one. It made no difference.*
> **Status:** *Reassigned to Removal Detail at her own request.*
> *She said someone had to make sure the next ones arrived late enough.*

Dr. Okafor closed the folder and placed it back in the crate. The team withdrew at 1430.

---

**ADDENDUM 7340-1:** Dr. Okafor's after-action report on Exploration 7340-4 consisted of one sentence: *"Recommend immediate suspension of all exploration."* The O5 Council approved her recommendation within nine minutes. No Council session was convened.

**ADDENDUM 7340-2:** During routine sweeps, field agents report that sealed SCP-7340 instances still show a faint glow through the concrete. The glow is growing dimmer. Analysts believe the archive is nearly empty.

# Chapter Seven: The Courtesy of Antares

The transfer vessel's air filtration system hummed with a persistent mechanical drone, and Arthur Neegan found that he could not stop listening to it. The sound was a low B-flat, he decided, slightly wavering, as though some bearing deep in the ductwork were wearing itself toward failure. An engineer noticed such things. A frightened engineer noticed little else.

He sat strapped into a padded acceleration couch of a design he had not seen since his training days on Luna: chrome tubing, cracked green leatherette, a small brass plate reading *Hollister-Kaine Orbital Works, 2241*. Across from him sat the two men who had come to his door that morning. Their uniforms were charcoal gray, cut with the severe elegance of men who never had to dig. On each collar gleamed the insignia of the Antares Diplomatic Corps: a red star within a broken ring.

They had been very polite. They had knocked. They had wiped their boots on the mat his late wife had woven from reclaimed hydroponic fiber. They had also carried sidearms, and the larger of them had stood in such a way that the door could not quite be closed.

"Ambassador Halvane requests the pleasure of your company," the smaller one had said, as though a request were a thing that came with an escort of four.

Now, through the porthole, Mars fell away, rust-red and pocked, the scars of the Tharsis open pits visible even from altitude like claw marks on old leather. Somewhere down there was his forty hectares, his prefab dome, his half-finished greenhouse, and three hundred meters beneath it, a vein of Azra that the assay computer at Ares Station had at first refused to believe. It had printed the result on punched tape three times before the technician called him in person, whispering.

That had been nineteen days ago. Since then, Arthur had received eleven letters from corporate solicitors, two visits from the Colonial Land Office, one anonymous transmission consisting entirely of a photograph of his own front door, and, last night, a dead man's coyote-dog left on his doorstep, its throat neatly cut.

He had told no one about the dog.

---

The ship docked with a clang that rattled his teeth. Arthur was led through a pressure lock and down a corridor paneled in genuine wood, an extravagance so absurd at this distance from Earth that he stopped to touch it. Walnut. Real walnut, carried up a gravity well at a cost of perhaps a thousand credits a kilogram.

"The Ambassador," murmured his escort, "appreciates the old ways."

The stateroom beyond was round and dim. One wall was entirely glass, and through it hung Mars, enormous, filling the view like a held breath. Before the window stood a man of perhaps seventy, slender, with white hair combed straight back and the kind of face that seemed to have been designed for listening. He held two glasses.

"Mr. Neegan. Thank you for coming."

"I wasn't aware I had a choice."

"You always have a choice." Halvane offered him a glass. "It is merely that some choices are more comfortable than others. Brandy. From the Rhône. I'm told the vines are now three hundred years old, which is older than anything on that planet, including its oldest grievance."

Arthur took the glass but did not drink. "Your men wear Antares insignia."

"They do."

"Antares doesn't have a diplomatic corps. Not one that does diplomacy."

Halvane smiled with evident pleasure, like a teacher whose pupil had surprised him. "You've read the Tamsin Accords."

"I've read the newspapers. Antares Combine signs a trade treaty with a colony, and six months later the colony's governing council has been replaced by men who prefer Antares."

"That is a cynical reading of history."

"It's the only reading I've seen confirmed."

The Ambassador set down his own glass on a low table of black lacquer and settled into a chair. He gestured, and after a moment Arthur sat too.

"Let me tell you what you have, Mr. Neegan. Not what you think you have. What you actually have." He folded his hands. "Azra was isolated eleven years ago. In those eleven years, the speed of interstellar transit has tripled. A journey to Alpha Centauri that once required a generation now takes four years. Do you know what that means?"

"Faster trade."

"It means the end of distance. For three centuries, distance has been humanity's great peacekeeper. Earth could not hold the colonies, and the colonies could not threaten Earth, because the space between them was simply too vast. Every empire in history has been limited by how quickly it could move its soldiers. Azra removes that limit." He paused. "And then there are the weapons."

"I've heard rumors."

"Then let me give you a fact. Eight months ago, a test was conducted in the outer Kuiper Belt. A device using four grams of refined Azra. *Four grams*. The object it was aimed at was a comet nucleus twelve kilometers across." Halvane's voice did not rise. "It is no longer there. Nor is the observation vessel, which was positioned at what the physicists assured everyone was a safe distance."

The air system hummed. Arthur found his throat dry, and drank.

"Your vein," Halvane went on, "by the estimate of my own surveyors, who visited your property two weeks before the Ares assay, contains perhaps forty tonnes."

"Two weeks before—" Arthur stopped. "You knew before I did."

"We knew before *anyone* did. That should concern you less than the fact that we are not the only ones who did."

Arthur thought of the dog. "What's your offer?"

"Two hundred million credits. Citizenship in the Antares Combine, a residence of your choosing on any of our eleven worlds, and passage departing in nine hours."

The number was so large it had no meaning. It was like being told the distance to Andromeda.

"And Antares gets forty tonnes of Azra."

"No." Halvane leaned forward, and for the first time something hard showed beneath his courtesy. "Antares gets forty tonnes of Azra that *stays in the ground*. We will purchase the land, seal the shaft, and garrison it. No one will mine it. Not us, not Earth, not the Ceres Syndicate, not the Martian Independence League that is, I promise you, funded by all three."

Arthur stared at him. "Why would you buy something you don't intend to use?"

"Because the balance of power in human space currently rests on the fact that no one possesses enough Azra to be certain of victory. Your vein would change that for whoever holds it. And a man who is certain of victory, Mr. Neegan, is the most dangerous creature in the universe."

"And I'm supposed to believe Antares is the exception?"

"No. You are supposed to believe that I am." Halvane picked up his glass again. "Whether the Combine's directors share my view is a separate question, and one I would prefer to settle after the shaft is sealed."

Arthur looked out at the red world below. Somewhere down there, men were already moving toward his home.

"And if I refuse?"

The Ambassador was quiet for a long moment.

"Then you'll go home," he said gently, "and I will pray for you. I find that I am not very good at it."

# Chapter Seven: The Antarean Courtesy

The transfer vessel *Perihelion Grace* had been built in an age when space travel was still meant to be beautiful. Its passenger lounge was panelled in imitation walnut and its chairs were upholstered in a deep oxblood leather that sighed when Arthur Neegan shifted his weight. Brass fittings gleamed along the bulkheads. A chronometer above the hatch ticked with an audible, deliberate clack, which Arthur suspected was entirely for show.

He ran a finger beneath his collar for the eleventh time since departure. The shirt had been delivered to his door in a flat grey box, pressed and starched, along with a jacket of charcoal wool and a card that read, in elegant engraving: *Formal attire is requested.* Requested. Arthur had never owned anything that required cufflinks. He had spent twenty minutes that morning working out how they fastened, and the effort had felt like the last private act of his former life.

The escort had arrived at dawn. There were four of them, in slate-blue uniforms cut so cleanly they might have been poured. They had wiped their boots on his mat. One had complimented his hydroponic tomatoes. And on every shoulder, embroidered in silver thread, sat an eight-pointed star over a crimson disc: the sigil of the Antares Diplomatic Corps.

Everyone on Mars knew what that sigil meant. The Corps negotiated in the way a glacier negotiates with a valley.

"You understand, Mr. Neegan," the lead officer had said, "this is an invitation."

"And if I decline?"

The officer had smiled with genuine warmth, which Arthur found more frightening than any threat. "Then we would be obliged to invite you again."

Now Mars hung in the viewport, a vast rust-coloured curve scarred by the long white gashes of the Valles Marineris. Somewhere down there, beneath forty metres of regolith and an unremarkable prefab house, lay the largest Azra deposit ever surveyed. Arthur had found it with a borrowed seismograph and a slide rule. Within a week, every power in the inhabited systems seemed to know about it.

*That* was what troubled him most. He had told no one.

---

The *Perihelion Grace* docked with a soft magnetic shudder against something that did not appear on any registry Arthur knew. Through the porthole he glimpsed a long, dark hull, matte and windowless, of a class he couldn't name. A steward in white gloves led him down a corridor lit by amber globes and opened a door onto what looked, impossibly, like a library.

There were real books, bound in cloth and leather. A fire burned in a grate. Arthur knew it had to be a projection, but he could feel its heat on his face. In a wingback chair beside it sat a slight, silver-haired man in a suit of midnight blue, pouring tea from a porcelain pot.

"Mr. Neegan. Thank you for coming. Please sit. Milk?"

"I wasn't aware I had a choice in the matter."

"About the milk? Certainly you do." The man's eyes crinkled. "About the rest, I'll concede the point. I am Envoy Idris Malvane. I apologise for the theatre. The young men who fetched you are very earnest, and earnestness is so difficult to restrain."

Arthur sat and tugged at his collar. Malvane noticed and said nothing, which Arthur somehow found worse.

"You're Antarean," Arthur said.

"I wear the star. That is not quite the same thing." Malvane handed him a cup. "Tell me, Mr. Neegan, what do you know about Azra?"

"It's a transuranic lattice that accelerates nuclear decay by a factor of roughly ten to the ninth. Put it next to a fissile core and you get a century of output in an afternoon. Build a drive around that and you could reach Centauri inside a decade. Build a bomb around it and..." He shrugged. "You don't need me to finish."

"Precisely and admirably put. Now tell me what you *don't* know."

Arthur hesitated. "I don't know why it works."

"Neither does anyone else. That is the first thing to understand." Malvane set down his cup. "Eighteen months ago, a research station orbiting Ganymede attempted to find out. They placed a refined Azra sample, nine grams, about the weight of a wedding ring, inside a shielded test chamber. The station is no longer orbiting Ganymede, Mr. Neegan. A good deal of Ganymede's surface is no longer where it used to be, either. The official report blames a reactor fault."

The fire crackled. Arthur realised he was holding his breath.

"Since then," Malvane continued mildly, "the Terran Concord has quietly tripled its naval appropriations. The Centauri Combine has stopped answering certain diplomatic letters. Three mining consortia on your own planet have bought controlling interests in labour-lease brokerages, which means they now effectively own some forty thousand indentured workers. Can you guess why a mining company would want to own the people rather than simply rent them?"

"Because owned people don't leave," Arthur said slowly. "And they don't talk."

"You see? You are not nearly as simple as your file suggests." Malvane smiled. "Your vein, by our estimates, holds more Azra than all other known deposits combined. Whoever controls it will not merely win the race. They will end it."

"So you want to buy it."

"Heavens, no." The envoy looked almost wounded. "If Antares bought your land, the Concord would regard it as an act of war within the month, and they would not be wrong. No. I want you to *keep* it."

Arthur stared at him.

"You'll remain the sole, legal, entirely independent owner," Malvane said. "A private citizen, a first-generation settler, an engineer of no political consequence. Nobody can claim you as theirs, and so nobody can seize you without provoking everybody else. In exchange, we would provide certain protections, discreetly. We would ask only that you sell to no one, and that you consult us before you dig."

"Protections," Arthur repeated. "From whom?"

Malvane turned his gaze to the false fire and was quiet for a long moment.

"Your predecessor on the Tharsis claim, a Mrs. Okonjo, filed an assay report much like yours, eleven years ago. It was lost in transit. So, shortly afterwards, was she." He looked back at Arthur, and for the first time there was no humour in his face. "You asked how everyone learned of your discovery so quickly, Mr. Neegan. I can tell you that it was not us. I would very much like to know who it was."

Arthur's hand drifted to his collar again. This time, he left it there.

"And if I refuse?"

"Then I shall have the young men take you home, with my compliments." Malvane lifted the teapot. "And I shall light a candle for you. More tea?"

# Chapter Seven: Cargo

The transfer vessel *Hesperus* had been built for ore, not men, and it showed.

Arthur Neegan sat strapped into a fold-down seat that someone had bolted to the bulkhead as an afterthought. Above him, a small display screen cycled through its diagnostics in patient green letters:

```
HULL INTEGRITY ........ 99.7%
REACTANT MASS ......... NOMINAL
CABIN O2 .............. 20.9%
PASSENGER MANIFEST .... 1
CLASSIFICATION ........ CARGO
```

He had read it eleven times now, and the last line had not improved with repetition.

It had been six hours since the knock. Arthur had opened his pressure door expecting the water assessor and found four men in charcoal greatcoats, the silver eight-pointed star of the Antares Diplomatic Corps on every collar. The man in front had removed his cap, which Arthur thought was a nice touch.

"Mr. Neegan. You're invited to a meeting."

"With whom?"

"With the person who invited you, sir."

Arthur had looked at the sidearms, holstered and unmentioned, and said he would fetch his coat.

Now he watched Mars fall away through the porthole, the rust-and-ochre curve of Tharsis dwindling until the great volcanoes were pimples on an old man's face. Down there, in the company towns along the Valles, forty thousand leased labourers were working the Azra seams under contracts that ran longer than most of their lives. Up here, it seemed, the people who signed those contracts were finally taking an interest in him.

*Six weeks ago,* he thought, *I was a man with a bad water pump and a plot of land nobody wanted.*

---

The *Hesperus* docked with a shudder that rattled his teeth, and Arthur was escorted through a series of corridors that grew progressively better carpeted. The station was small and orbited close to Deimos. Through one viewport he caught the moon's lumpy grey flank sliding past, so near he could see the old survey beacons blinking.

The room they brought him to had a desk made of real wood.

Arthur stopped in the doorway and stared at it. He calculated, without meaning to, the cost of lifting that much oak out of Earth's gravity well and hauling it a hundred million kilometres. It was more than his homestead had cost, and the desk had plainly been chosen so that visitors would do exactly that sum.

Behind it sat a small, round man with thinning hair and the mild eyes of a provincial schoolmaster. He was eating dates from a paper bag.

"Mr. Neegan. Do sit down. Date?"

"No. Thank you."

"They're from Earth. Grown in actual soil. I find they help me think." He folded the bag closed with great care. "My name is Sorrel. I apologise for the theatrics. The uniforms, I mean."

"You're not Antares."

"I'm not *not* Antares." Sorrel smiled. "Let us say the Corps lent me some coats and some men, and will be very surprised to learn it did. You're an engineer. I'll be plain with you. Do you know what lies under your land?"

"Azra. A vein."

"A vein." Sorrel seemed amused by the word. "Mr. Neegan, the independent survey, the one you didn't commission and won't be shown, puts your deposit at roughly four hundred thousand tonnes. Do you know how much Azra has been extracted from the whole of Mars since its discovery?"

Arthur didn't.

"Nineteen thousand tonnes. You are sitting on twenty times the known supply of the most strategically important substance in human history."

The room seemed to tilt a little. Arthur gripped the arms of his chair.

"Let me explain what that means," Sorrel went on gently, as though teaching a slow but promising pupil. "Azra shortens a half-life from millennia to seconds. Packed around a fissile core, it gives you a drive that can reach Antares in eleven years instead of four hundred. Packed around the same core and pointed at a city, it gives you something else. Today three powers hold Azra in roughly equal measure: the Terran Directorate, the Antares Concord, and the Belt Syndics. None can strike the others without being struck back. It's an ugly balance, but it holds."

"And my land tips it."

"Your land *ends* it. Whoever controls your claim can build fleets the others can't match, and they'll know it within a decade. Wars, Mr. Neegan, are not started by the strong. They're started by the frightened, who see the strong coming and decide it's better to move first."

Arthur thought of Halvorsen, his nearest neighbour, who had sold his plot a month ago to a company nobody had heard of. He had shaken Arthur's hand and boasted that he would retire to Luna. He had not written since.

As if he had read the thought, Sorrel said, "Your neighbour made an unfortunate choice of buyer. I'm sorry."

"What's your offer?"

"Ah." Sorrel took a sheet of paper from his drawer. It was real paper too. "Eighty million Directorate credits, held in trust on Ceres, beyond the reach of any one government. In return you sign the extraction rights to a consortium I represent, and you stay on as chief engineer."

"A consortium of whom?"

"Of people who'd like the balance to hold."

"That's not an answer."

"No," Sorrel agreed. "It isn't."

Arthur looked at the paper, then at the little man and his bag of dates. "And if I refuse?"

Sorrel's mild eyes did not change, which was somehow worse than if they had.

"Then you go home. Nobody here will stop you. But you'll find, Mr. Neegan, that this is the first invitation of several. The Syndics are already moving. The Directorate's people landed at Olympus Port yesterday. The *real* Antares Corps will be furious about the coats and will want to make up for lost time." He spread his hands. "I'm the politest man who'll ever sit across a desk from you. I thought you ought to meet me first."

"How long do I have?"

"Forty-eight hours. After that, I suspect, the decision will be made by someone else."

---

They returned him to the *Hesperus* with the same impeccable courtesy. He was strapped into the same fold-down seat, and Mars swelled again in the porthole, red and patient and indifferent.

Above him, the little screen flickered through its cycle.

```
HULL INTEGRITY ........ 99.7%
REACTANT MASS ......... NOMINAL
CABIN O2 .............. 20.9%
PASSENGER MANIFEST .... 1
CLASSIFICATION ........ ASSET
```

Arthur Neegan read it twice. Then he closed his eyes and began, very carefully, to think.

response:
# Offworlder

## Chapter Four: The Hour Between

*From the Ekumenical briefing file on Arhet, section 2: "The two lineages do not mix. The Tesh hold the surface and the daylight; the Ahn keep below. Envoys should expect hostility from both."*

---

I left the reception at the second bell, when the Tesh dignitaries had begun the long formal toasts that I had been told would last until dark. Nobody stopped me. I think nobody imagined that an envoy would walk out of her own welcome, and what people cannot imagine they rarely prevent.

The city of Ennu Tor is built of a grey stone that holds the day's heat and gives it back at evening, so that walking its streets at dusk is like walking past a sleeping animal. Every lintel and pillar is carved. I had read about the glyphs in transit and had expected decoration. They are not decoration. Over one doorway a man climbed a tower toward a sky that had been chiseled away to nothing. On a fountain wall a girl ate six seeds from a split fruit. At the corner where the street dropped toward the river, a man walked upward out of the stone with his head turned back over his shoulder, and behind him there was only a smooth hollow where someone had been.

The settlers brought these stories from Earth, eleven hundred years ago, in two ships that landed forty years apart. The stories have outlasted the ships. They have also outlasted the settlers' sense of what they mean, or so I had assumed.

The market was in the lower town, under awnings of oiled cloth. The briefing had said the Ahn come up only at night, that they cannot bear the sun, that they and the Tesh keep separate hours as they keep separate everything. It was the hour between when I arrived, the sun down but the sky still white, and both peoples were there.

The Tesh are tall, dark, long in the limb. The Ahn are smaller and pale, with eyes so large and dark that at first they seem to have no whites at all. I watched an Ahn man sell lamp oil to a Tesh woman. They haggled without heat and without looking at each other's faces, the way old neighbors do. A Tesh child was asleep on the shoulder of an Ahn grandmother who was weighing out dried fish. Nobody remarked on it. I asked a spice-seller, a Tesh, whose child it was.

"The hearth's," she said, as if I had asked whose the river was.

"Which hearth?"

She looked at me then, at my offworld face, which belongs to neither of their kinds. "Hers," she said, and nodded at the grandmother. "And mine. You count by blood where you come from?"

I said that we did, mostly.

"That's the Ministry's way too," she said, and went back to her scales, and would say nothing more.

---

Commander Esk was waiting in my quarters when I returned. He did not raise his voice. He has a gift for disappointment that makes shouting unnecessary.

"You were seen by at least four hundred people," he said, "none of whom were cleared to see you. The Tesh Council considers your absence an insult. I have spent two hours explaining that offworlders tire easily."

"The briefing is wrong," I said. "They share the market. They share children."

"The briefing was prepared by the Ministry of Science, which is the only office here that will talk to us at all. You'll go to the Minister tomorrow and repair this. Apologize if necessary. Learn something if possible."

"The Minister is a scientist?"

Esk almost smiled. "The Minister keeps the lineage books. Who descends from which ship. Who may marry whom, and inherit what. Here that is called science. Be careful. Oruen Hal has outlasted four Councils."

---

The Minister received me in a room with one window and no glyphs. That struck me before anything else: in a city where every surface tells a story, this room had been left blank.

Oruen Hal was Tesh, very old, and sat so still that the stillness itself felt like a kind of speech. Tea was not offered. I gave the apology I had prepared. The Minister let it fall into silence and lie there.

"You walked down Weir Street," Oruen said at last. "Past the fountain. To the corner above the river. Which carving did you stop at?"

There was no point lying. Everyone in Ennu Tor seemed to know where I had been. "The man looking back."

"Your kind always stop there." The Minister did not say it unkindly. "Do you know the story?"

"He went down to the dead to bring his wife back. He was told not to look behind him on the way up. He looked, and lost her."

"That is the story the first ship brought. The second ship told it differently. In their telling, the man doesn't look back from doubt. He looks back because he hears her stumble, and he cannot bear to leave her alone in the dark, even if turning means losing her. Which is the true story, Envoy?"

I understood then that this was the conversation, and the apology had only been the door.

"I think," I said slowly, "that you keep the books that decide which telling is official."

The Minister's eyes, which were very dark, did not change. "Go on."

"The market doesn't count by blood. The hearths don't. Your office does. So when the Ekumen asks where the tension on Arhet lies, your office tells us it lies between the Tesh and the Ahn. Because if it lies anywhere else, it lies between the city and the books."

"That is a dangerous thing for a guest to say in a host's house."

"You asked me which story was true. I could have told you the one I was raised on."

For a long moment Oruen Hal said nothing. Outside, a bell rang the hour between.

"Your Commander sent you to apologize," the Minister said. "Mine would have sent me to lie to you. We have both disobeyed." A hand rose, and a servant came in with two cups. "This room has no carvings because I had them cut away. I didn't want anyone to have to choose. Drink, Envoy. Then we'll talk about the dark, and who stumbles in it, and who looks back."

The tea was bitter, and I drank all of it.

response:
# Offworlder

I was told, before I came down to Iyoh, that the people of the dry belt went nearly naked, and that I should therefore dress with care, so as not to seem to mock them. So I wore the grey cloak of the Service, which covers a person from throat to ankle, and walked out into the noon of Iyoh looking, I suppose, like a pillar of ash that had learned to move.

I was not supposed to walk out at all. There was a reception at the Hall of Lineages, and I was expected to stand in it and be looked at by those whose looking mattered. But the reception would not begin until the second shade, and the door of the guesthouse was not locked. On Iyoh doors are not locked; it is considered an accusation.

The briefings had been very clear. There were two peoples on Iyoh, descended from two ships that had come four thousand years apart in the old dispersal. The Tall, the first-comers, had kept their lines pure by law and by marriage-ledger. They were long-boned and pale-eyed, made for the cold nights of the plateau. The Dust, who came after, had been shaped by the lowland furnace into something compact and dark and enduring, with an inner eyelid against the sand. The Tall ruled. The Dust served. The tension, the briefings said, was the ordinary tension of the ruled against their rulers, made sharper because the two could no longer bear children together.

I went down the street of steps toward the market at Cheyu, and within a hundred paces the briefings began to come apart in my hands.

The market lay under awnings of woven reed, and it was full of both peoples, and I could not tell which of them was in charge of anything. A Dust woman, broad as a doorway, sat at a scale weighing salt for a Tall man who bent nearly double to hear her prices. He argued, and lost. Two Tall children ran past holding the hands of a Dust grandmother. She was no servant. She scolded them in the voice that belongs to grandmothers on every world. At the water-stall the queue was sorted neither by height nor by color but by some order the people in it knew as they knew the shapes of their own mouths.

And they looked at me. There was no hostility in it. A boy of perhaps six, of neither people that I could name, came up to me. He had the long bones of the Tall and the hooded eyes of the Dust, which the briefings said was impossible. He took a fold of my cloak between his fingers and rubbed it, the way one tests cloth at a stall.

"Are you sick?" he asked.

I said I was not. He considered this.

"Then are you ashamed?"

His mother called him back, laughing behind an oiled hand. I stood there in my modesty, sweating like a cheese.

I asked the salt-woman, in my careful Iyoth, what people the boy belonged to. She looked at me a while.

"His mother's," she said, as if I had asked the color of the sky, and went back to her scale.

When I returned, the second shade had fallen and the reception had begun without me. The screen in my room was lit. Command does not raise its voice; it does not need to. I was reminded that I was not a tourist, that the mission had been eleven years in preparation, that my absence had been noticed by the Hall and interpreted. I was told that I would now go to the Minister of Science, Hosk Avarrenen, who had particularly asked to see me, and that I would repair what I had broken.

"What is the Minister's field?" I asked.

There was a pause the length of the light-delay and somewhat longer. "It is a political appointment," Command said. "He keeps the marriage-ledgers."

He received me in a room with no furniture but cushions and a long window full of evening. He was Tall and very old, his pale eyes gone milky at the rims. He wore undyed linen and a great deal of silence. He did not rise. He let me stand in my cloak until I understood I was meant to feel it.

"You went to Cheyu," he said.

"Yes."

"Alone. Unguided." He seemed pleased. "And what did the Envoy learn about Iyoh in an afternoon?"

There is a kind of question that is a door with a pit behind it. If I claimed to have learned much, I was a fool. If I claimed nothing, I was a coward.

"That my briefings were written by someone who had never bought salt," I said.

His laugh was dry, like reeds. "Your briefings were written by us. Your people asked what we were, sixty years ago, and we told you."

"You told us the Tall and the Dust cannot have children together."

"They cannot."

"I met a child this afternoon."

"Did you?" He turned his clouded gaze to the window. "And how did you know what he was?"

I opened my mouth and found nothing in it. I had known by his bones and his eyes. I had known by the categories I brought down in my luggage.

"You see," the Minister said gently, "you are already doing science. You looked at a boy and sorted him. That is my ministry. It has nothing to do with lenses or the counting of stars. On Iyoh, science is the deciding of what people are, and someone must decide it. The ledger says that boy does not exist. So the ledger is a lie, and so the ledger is a very great power. Do you see now why it is not given to a scientist?"

"Because a scientist might correct it."

"Because a scientist would think correcting it was the end of the matter." He gestured, at last, for me to sit. The cushion was still warm from the day. "Your people sent you because of the tension. It is not between the Tall and the Dust. It is between the ledger and the market. Every year the market wins a little more, and every year the Hall is more afraid. Then you walked into Cheyu in your cloak, the Hall's own nightmare: an offworlder come to look, who will go home and write it down. Which will you write, Envoy? The boy, or the ledger?"

"What would you have me write?"

"Ah." For the first time he seemed disappointed. "No. Don't ask me that. That is a servant's question, and your Command will want a servant. I asked for you because you left the reception. I hoped you were something else."

The window had gone dark. Below us the market was closing. I could hear the awnings coming down, a sound like many people breathing out.

"I'll write the boy," I said.

"Then you will make enemies in the Hall."

"You told me I already have."

"I told you they interpreted you." Hosk Avarrenen closed his eyes. "Take off the cloak next time you go down. They will still know you for what you are. But they will know you came to be seen, and not to hide."
