response:
# Offworlder

## Chapter Four: The Dyers' Street

I was told before I came down that the two peoples of Ahrend do not mingle. The briefing was thorough and confident, as briefings are. It said the Sefar, who descend from the sealed habitat-ships, govern from the high terraces. It said the Kethi, whose ancestors walked out onto the open plains nine hundred years ago and let the long red seasons change them, labor below and resent it. It called the tension *structural* and *acute*. It recommended that the envoy keep to the Legation and the Assembly Hall, and travel only by covered car.

On my third evening, after a reception where everyone spoke to me and no one said anything, I took off the grey coat that marked me as an offworlder and went down the stairs into the city.

Ahrend's sun is old and large, and it sets slowly, so that dusk lasts most of an hour. The streets of the lower town were full of that light. I found the market by its smell before I saw it: wet wool, smoke, and something sharp and resinous that I learned later was the mordant the dyers use.

The stalls ran the length of a long crooked street. Most of them sold cloth. It hung from poles in heavy folds, handwoven, coarse at the selvage and fine at the center. Its colors made me stop walking. There was a blue that was not quite blue, that turned toward violet when the wind moved it. There was a deep wet green the color of nothing I had a name for. And there was a pale shade, almost white, that seemed to gather the red dusk into itself and give it back as gold. The woman at the stall told me this last was called *ash-of-morning*. It came from a lichen that grows only on the north faces of the plains rocks, where it is scraped off by hand in the cold season.

She was Kethi. I knew it from the broad chest and the heavy lids that close halfway against the glare. The man buying from her was Sefar, slight and pale, his fingers long. She named a price. He laughed and named a smaller one, and she laughed back, and they went on that way for some time with every sign of enjoying it. When he paid, he paid in the square bronze tokens the briefing had said were used only among the Kethi. He also bowed to her, a short dip of the head. The briefing had said that bow is given only by an inferior to a superior.

I watched for perhaps an hour. I saw Sefar children running among the stalls with Kethi children, all of them shouting in the plains dialect. I saw an old Sefar woman sitting on a Kethi doorstep, shelling beans into a bowl held in the lap of a Kethi man. Neither of them spoke. They had the ease of people who had shelled beans together many times. I saw that the dyers were all Kethi and all women, that the buyers were of both peoples, and that the money seemed to flow downhill, toward the plains-folk and away from the terraces.

None of this was in the briefing. I do not say the briefing was a lie. I say it described a different city, perhaps the one seen from the covered car.

---

Legate Morrow was waiting in my quarters when I returned. He did not raise his voice. He has served the Concord for thirty years and has learned that a quiet voice frightens people more.

"You were seen," he said. "By the Sefar household guard, by at least two Assembly delegates, and by our own security, who spent ninety minutes believing you'd been taken. Do you understand what you are here, Envoy? You are not a person. You're a signal. Everything you do is read."

I said I understood.

"Then you will make yourself useful. The Minister of Science has asked to see you. Tonight." He let that sit a moment. "Tuvar Esk has held that office for twenty-two years. He's never published a paper or run an experiment. He holds the post because whoever controls the Ministry controls the census, and whoever controls the census decides who is Sefar and who is Kethi. Go carefully."

---

The Minister received me in a small room high on the terraces. The windows looked down on the lower town, where the market lamps were coming on one by one. He was old for a Sefar, and very thin, and he poured me a cup of something hot before he said a word.

"You went walking," he said.

"Yes, Minister."

"What did you see?"

I told him. I tried to tell it plainly, without drawing conclusions, as I had been trained. He listened with his eyes half closed, almost the way the Kethi close theirs.

"And so you think," he said when I had finished, "that your briefing is wrong. That we are friends down there, and the trouble is only up here, among the old men."

"I don't think anything yet, Minister. I only saw."

"Ah. Only saw." He turned his cup in his long fingers. "Tell me, Envoy, what did the woman charge for the ash-of-morning?"

I told him.

"And what did the man pay?"

"Less. About two-thirds."

"And he bowed." He smiled a little. "Did you ask yourself why a Sefar would bow to a dyer and pay her in plains bronze? Did you ask who holds the lichen-rights on the north rocks? Or whose name is on the deed to the street you walked down?"

I had not. I said so.

"No. You saw people laughing and you were glad, because you are young and kind and you've come a very long way hoping to be glad." He set the cup down. "I do not say you were wrong. I say you were one evening in a city nine hundred years old. The bow means something, Envoy. It may not mean what your briefing says. It may not mean what you hoped, either."

"Then what does it mean?"

He looked at me for a long moment, and I had the feeling of being weighed, not unkindly, the way a dyer weighs wool.

"Go back tomorrow," he said. "Not as an envoy, and not as a tourist. Go and ask the dyer what she owes, and to whom. If she tells you, come and tell me. Then perhaps we will both have learned something."

"And if she doesn't tell me?"

"Then you'll have learned a great deal more," said the Minister of Science, and he rang for someone to show me out.

They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more.

A stray cat near the school looks at the student with uncanny recognition after each rewind. Length: 1000 words.
response:
# Chapter Seven: Rewind

The first time I used the watch, it was to un-spill a carton of chocolate milk.

That's it. That's how it started. Not with saving the world or stopping a bank robbery. Just me, Owen Pratt, age twelve, sitting in the Westbrook Middle cafeteria, watching brown milk soak into my only clean jeans while Tyler Briggs laughed so hard he snorted.

I jabbed the little silver button on the side of my new watch. I wasn't trying to do anything. I was just mad.

The world *hiccupped*.

Milk flowed backward up the table and into the carton. Tyler's laugh sucked back down his throat. The carton stood itself upright with a soft *tock*.

Then everything was normal again. Ten seconds earlier. Tyler was reaching across the table, the way he'd done before he knocked it over.

This time, I moved the milk.

---

My aunt had sent the watch for my birthday. No note. Just a plain black band and a face with no numbers, only a thin red hand that ticked *counterclockwise*. I'd thought it was broken.

It wasn't broken.

Over the next week, I used it maybe forty times. Okay, maybe sixty. I rewound pop quizzes after I saw the questions. I rewound the moment I tripped in front of Jenna Ruiz. I rewound dodgeball so many times that Coach Hendricks started calling me "The Ghost."

And every single time, the cat was watching.

It was a scrawny orange thing with a torn left ear. It lived by the bike rack behind the gym. Nobody fed it. Nobody petted it. It just sat there.

But after every rewind, it would turn its head and look straight at me. Not the way cats usually look at you, like you're furniture. It looked at me like it *knew*. Like it had seen the milk spill too.

Like it remembered.

---

The first weird thing was my voice.

I was answering a question in social studies, and halfway through the word "Mesopotamia," my voice dropped about an octave. The whole class cracked up. My face went hot.

I reached for the button. I stopped myself.

*It's just puberty*, I thought. *It happens to everybody.*

Then my jeans got short. Really short. Like, ankles-out, flood-pants short, in the span of four days. Mom squinted at me over breakfast and said, "Did you get *taller*?"

Then the zits. Then the shadow on my upper lip that didn't wash off. Then I woke up one morning and my feet hung off the end of my bed.

At school, things got stranger. Mrs. Okafor, the front office lady, stopped me in the hallway.

"Can I help you find someone, sir? Are you here to pick up a student?"

*Sir.*

Jenna Ruiz walked right past me. Tyler Briggs stopped picking on me. He looked kind of scared of me, actually.

That night, I stood in front of the bathroom mirror for a long time. The kid staring back looked sixteen. Maybe seventeen. He had my eyes. Everything else belonged to a stranger.

I looked down at the watch. For the first time, I noticed the tiny numbers etched around the rim of the band, so small I'd thought they were a pattern.

They weren't a pattern. They were a counter.

**4 YRS 11 MOS.**

That was how much I'd spent.

Every second I'd taken back, the watch had taken something from me.

---

I should have thrown it in the river. I know that now.

But the next morning, something terrible happened. My little sister, Bea, was crossing Maple Street to the bus stop, and a delivery truck came around the corner way too fast, and I saw it, I *saw* it about to happen...

I jammed the button down and I held it.

I didn't let go. Not after ten seconds. Not after a minute. The world screamed backward around me. The sun dragged itself down the sky. Cars zipped in reverse. Birds flew tail-first.

When I finally let go, I was standing on my own front porch. It was early. The street was quiet. Bea was safe.

I nearly cried with relief. I opened the front door.

My mom was in the kitchen, making pancakes. She turned around. Her smile vanished.

"Who are you?" she said. "How did you get in here?"

"Mom, it's me. It's *Owen*."

Then I heard footsteps on the stairs. Someone small. Someone yawning.

A twelve-year-old boy shuffled into the kitchen in my dinosaur pajamas. My hair. My face. My chipped front tooth.

He looked up at me and frowned. "Mom? Who's the weird guy?"

Mom grabbed the phone. "I'm calling the police."

I ran.

---

I didn't stop running until I reached the bike rack behind the gym.

The watch hadn't rewound me. It never had. It rewound *everything except me*. And this time I'd gone back so far that the world had simply made a new Owen. A fresh one. The right age.

I was the leftover. I was the mistake.

The orange cat was sitting in its usual spot. It stood up, stretched, and padded over to me. For the first time, it let me touch it.

That was when I felt the collar, buried deep in its fur. A worn leather strap with a tag so old it had turned green.

I squinted at the letters.

**KEVIN PRATT. 1994.**

My skin went cold. Uncle Kevin. Mom's big brother. The one who vanished when he was thirteen. The one nobody ever talked about.

Behind the tag, wrapped around the collar, was a tiny black band. A watch face with no numbers. Its little red hand had stopped dead.

The cat looked at me with yellow, tired, *human* eyes.

I looked at my own watch. The counter now read **5 YRS 8 MOS.** And beneath it, a word I'd never noticed before, blinking softly.

**ONE MORE?**

Maybe if I went back far enough, past the morning, past the pancakes, past the moment I opened that birthday box, there'd only be one Owen again.

Or maybe I'd end up like Uncle Kevin.

The cat pressed its head against my hand. Like it was saying *don't*.

Or maybe like it was saying *good luck*.

I took a deep breath. I put my thumb on the button.

And I pressed it.

*To be continued...*

response:
# Chapter 7: Time's Up

The watch cost me two dollars at Mr. Grimsby's yard sale, and it was the best two dollars I ever spent.

At least, that's what I thought on Monday.

It didn't look like much. Black strap. Cracked silver face. One red button on the side, sticking out like a pimple. The hands didn't even move. But when I pressed that button during Ms. Ferraro's pop quiz, after I'd written *Abraham Lincoln* as the answer to "What is the powerhouse of the cell?", the room *shuddered*.

Like a TV channel changing.

And suddenly I was sitting there with a blank paper again. Thirty seconds earlier. Ms. Ferraro was still saying, "Pencils *up*, people."

I wrote *mitochondria*. I got an A.

I'm Jake Morrow. I'm twelve years old. And by Wednesday, I was basically a god.

Dodgeball to the face? *Click.* I ducked.

Spilled chocolate milk down my shirt in front of the whole cafeteria? *Click.* Never happened.

Said "Love you, Mom" to Mr. Pruitt, the gym teacher? *Click, click, click.* I pressed that one three times just to make sure.

I didn't notice the other stuff at first. Or maybe I didn't *want* to notice.

Like how my jeans suddenly stopped two inches above my sneakers.

Like how my voice cracked so hard in English class that Tyler Benson fell out of his chair laughing. (*Click.* He didn't.)

Like how, on Thursday morning, Mom stared at me across the breakfast table with her coffee halfway to her mouth.

"Jake," she said slowly. "Is that a *mustache*?"

I touched my lip. Fuzz. Real, actual fuzz.

"Puberty, I guess," I mumbled. My little sister Lily made gagging noises into her cereal.

Mom kept staring. Not the way moms look at you when you're growing up. The way you look at a stranger who's wandered into your kitchen.

---

By Friday, things got weird.

The substitute in homeroom asked if I was there to pick up my kid.

The lunch lady called me "hon" instead of "sweetie." Then she called me "sir."

And Emma Castillo, who has never said one word to me in my entire life, smiled at me in the hallway. *Smiled.* Then her friend whispered something, and they both looked at me like I was a creepy high schooler hanging around the middle school.

I didn't feel older. That's the thing. Inside, I was still me. I still liked cartoons. I still slept with the hall light on.

But my body hadn't gotten the memo.

---

Here's where I messed up. Here's where I *really* messed up.

At the end of the day, I finally worked up the nerve to ask Emma to the Fall Fling.

She said no.

Actually, she said, "Um, aren't you, like, *nineteen*?"

So I pressed the button. And I held it.

I'd never held it before. I'd only tapped it. But I wanted to go back further, back to before I'd ever opened my mouth, back to lunch, back to the morning, back to—

The world didn't shudder this time.

It *screamed.*

A sound like tearing metal. The hallway stretched like taffy. The lockers melted into colors I don't have names for. My teeth ached. My *bones* ached.

And then I was standing in the hallway again. Same spot. Same time on the clock.

But everything was wrong.

The lockers were green, not blue. The trophy case said *Westbrook Wolverines* instead of *Westbrook Wildcats*. My best friend Theo walked right past me.

"Theo!" I grabbed his arm.

He yanked it away. "Dude. Do I know you?"

---

I ran home. All the way home, with my too-long legs and my too-deep breath.

The house was the same. Yellow shutters. Crooked mailbox.

I pounded on the door. Mom opened it.

She didn't hug me. She didn't yell at me for being late. She just held the door half-closed, the way she does with salesmen.

"Can I help you?"

"Mom, it's me! It's *Jake*!"

Her face went pale. "I don't have a son," she whispered. "Please leave, or I'm calling the police."

Over her shoulder, I could see down the hall. The door to Lily's room was open.

It was full of boxes. Just boxes. No unicorn posters. No glow-in-the-dark stars.

No Lily.

The door slammed in my face.

---

I locked myself in the bathroom at the gas station on Elm Street. My hands were shaking so hard I could barely turn on the faucet.

I splashed water on my face. Looked up into the mirror.

A kid looked back at me. Tall. Gangly. Pimples on the chin. Fuzz on the lip. Fifteen, maybe sixteen.

Okay, I thought. Okay. I can work with this.

Then the fluorescent light buzzed.

And the reflection *flickered.*

For one second, just one, the face in the mirror wasn't a teenager. It was a man. Gray hair at the temples. Deep lines around the eyes. Tired. *So* tired.

He was staring at me. And his lips were moving.

*Don't.*

The light steadied. The teenager was back. I stumbled backward into the paper towel dispenser.

---

I looked down at the watch.

The hands were moving now. For the first time ever. But not forward.

Under the cracked glass, where the number twelve should have been, tiny red letters glowed:

**YEARS REMAINING: 61**

My stomach dropped through the floor.

Every click. Every do-over. Every dodged dodgeball and un-spilled milk.

It wasn't free. It had *never* been free.

The watch had been *eating* me.

And now there was only one way to fix it. One way to bring back Lily. One way to make Mom know me again. I had to go back further than I'd ever gone. Back to Monday morning.

Back to before I bought the watch.

How many years would that cost? Ten? Thirty?

*All* of them?

I thought about Lily's glow-in-the-dark stars. I thought about the way she gagged into her cereal.

I put my thumb on the red button.

And I pushed.

---

The world screamed. My bones burned. I felt myself stretching, *thinning*, like a rubber band pulled too tight—

—and then there was sunshine. Birds. The smell of cut grass.

Mr. Grimsby's yard sale. Monday morning.

I made it! I was back!

I looked down at my hands.

They were wrinkled. Spotted. *Old.*

And sitting on the card table in front of me, behind a sign that read *$2*, was the watch.

A boy wandered up. Twelve years old. Jeans that fit. Messy brown hair. *My* hair.

He picked up the watch and turned it over in his hands.

"Hey, mister," he said. "Does this thing work?"

I opened my mouth to scream *NO*.

But what came out, in a cracked, dusty old voice, was:

"Oh, it works, kid. It works *great*."

prompt:
Teen Horror (Goosebumps style)

Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more.

The watch face occasionally flickers to show a countdown. Length: 1000 words.
response:
# Time's Up

The first time I rewound time, it was because of chocolate milk.

I was carrying my lunch tray past Kelsey Fontaine's table, trying to look cool, which for me means not tripping. Then I tripped. The carton flew. Brown milk splattered across Kelsey's white sweater like a Rorschach test of my entire social life.

The whole cafeteria went *OOOOOH.*

My face burned. I squeezed my wrist without thinking, right where the watch sat, and my thumb pressed the little silver knob on the side.

The room *shuddered*. The sound went backward, a sucking *HOOOOO* as everyone's laughter got pulled back down their throats. The milk un-splattered. It flew back into the carton, and the carton landed back on my tray.

I was standing at the lunch line again. Ten seconds earlier.

Kelsey's sweater was perfectly white.

I stared down at the watch. I'd bought it that Saturday at a yard sale on Hollow Lane for three dollars. The old man selling it had liquid gray eyes and hands that trembled so badly he could barely make change.

"It's only got so much left in it," he'd said. "Use it wisely."

I thought he meant the battery.

For half a second, the black screen flickered. Glowing red numbers appeared.

**61:211:04**

Then it went back to showing the time. 12:14.

Weird, I thought. And then I forgot about it, because I had just discovered I was basically a superhero.

---

Over the next week, I rewound *everything.*

I rewound the pop quiz in science after seeing which answers I'd gotten wrong. I rewound dodgeball every time Brock Hammond pegged me in the face, until I could dodge like I was in a movie. I rewound the moment I said "Love you too, Mom" to Ms. Okafor in front of the whole class.

I got a hundred on the quiz. I was the last kid standing in dodgeball. Nobody would ever know about the Mom thing.

Life was *perfect.*

Except for my pants.

By Wednesday, my jeans stopped two inches above my ankles. My sneakers pinched my toes. My mom frowned at me over breakfast and said, "Owen, honey, did you have a growth spurt?"

"I guess," I said.

Except it came out as "I *GUH*-ess," because my voice cracked in the middle like a dropped plate.

By Thursday, I had pimples. Not one pimple. A *constellation*. My best friend Theo stared at my face at the bus stop and said, "Dude. What happened to you?"

"Nothing," I said. My voice was deep now. Really deep. I sounded like a radio announcer.

Theo took a step back.

That afternoon, a substitute teacher walked into our classroom, looked straight at me, and said, "Oh, good, you must be the student teacher. Can you take attendance?"

Everybody laughed. I didn't.

At lunch, the lunch lady gave me an adult-sized portion and charged me four dollars extra. Kelsey Fontaine asked me if I'd gotten held back. Twice.

And in the bathroom mirror, I saw it.

A mustache.

A thin, fuzzy, *real* mustache on my upper lip.

I'm twelve.

I looked down at the watch with my heart hammering. The screen flickered.

**54:089:17**

The numbers had gone *down*. Way down. Like, *seven-of-something* down.

I did the math in my head, and my stomach dropped through the floor.

Fifty-four. That wasn't hours.

That was *years*.

Every time I rewound time, the world went backward.

But I didn't.

---

I should have stopped. I know that now.

But that night at dinner, my mom put down her fork and stared at me. Not the way moms stare when you forget to clear your plate. The way you stare at a stranger who's wandered into your house.

"Owen," she whispered. "You look... you look *seventeen*."

My little sister Maddie started crying. She wouldn't come near me.

Mom picked up her phone. "I'm calling Dr. Patel. No — I'm calling someone. Something is *wrong* with you."

And I panicked.

I didn't think. I just grabbed the knob and *twisted*, harder than I ever had. I wanted to go back to before any of it. Before the milk. Before the mustache. Before Hollow Lane.

*Don't buy the watch,* I told myself. *Just go back and don't buy the watch.*

The kitchen screamed. Colors smeared. The walls peeled away like wet paper, and the numbers on my wrist spun so fast they blurred into a red stripe.

**31:000:00**

**12:000:00**

**02:000:00**

I tried to let go. I couldn't. My thumb was frozen to the crown.

---

Sunlight.

Warm, ordinary Saturday sunlight.

I was sitting in a folding chair on Hollow Lane. In front of me was a card table covered in junk: chipped teacups, a broken lamp, a box of old records.

And a watch.

*It worked,* I thought. *I made it. I'm back. Now I just walk away and —*

I tried to stand up. My knees creaked like rusty hinges.

I looked down at my hands.

They were spotted. Wrinkled. *Trembling.*

A little hand mirror lay on the table. I picked it up, shaking so badly I almost dropped it.

An old man stared back at me. Liquid gray eyes. White hair.

It was him. The man from the yard sale.

It was *me.*

"Excuse me?"

I lowered the mirror. A kid stood at the table. Skinny. Brown hair sticking up in the back. Too-big T-shirt.

Twelve years old.

He picked up the watch and turned it over in his hands. "How much is this?"

*No,* I tried to say. *Put it down. Run.*

But what came out of my mouth, in a dry, crackling voice I didn't recognize, was:

"Three dollars."

He grinned. Dug in his pocket. Handed me three crumpled bills.

And the strangest thing happened. I heard myself say, "It's only got so much left in it."

The boy laughed and walked away down Hollow Lane, strapping the watch to his wrist.

That's when I noticed my *other* wrist.

There was a watch on it, too. The same watch. Scratched and dull with age.

The screen flickered.

**00:000:41**

Forty-one seconds.

Down the street, the boy turned the corner. In a week, he'd be spilling chocolate milk on Kelsey Fontaine. In two weeks, he'd be sitting right here.

Unless.

I pressed my shaking thumb against the crown.

**00:000:22**

One more turn. Maybe it would fix everything.

Maybe it would make everything worse.

**00:000:09**

I closed my eyes.

And I turned it.

response:
# Polymerase Chain Reaction

The solar rig dropped again at 2:14 in the afternoon, and Teague watched the thermocycler's readout slump from 94 degrees to 91 before the forklift batteries caught the load.

"Come on," she whispered. "Hold."

The batteries were three generations of scavenged lead-acid wired in a configuration no electrician would have signed off on. They groaned under the strain. Out on the roof, six mismatched panels drank weak October light through a haze of ash from the burning to the west, and every time a cloud crossed the sun, the whole lab went through a small death.

The thermocycler was her proudest ugly thing. It was an aluminum block milled out of a Ford engine housing, sandwiched between Peltier tiles pulled from a dozen dead minifridges, with a cracked Arduino clone deciding when to heat and when to cool. Thirty cycles: denature at ninety-four, anneal at fifty-five, extend at seventy-two. Each cycle doubled whatever sequence she'd primed for. Or it would, if the voltage held. If it didn't, she got nothing. A tube of salty water and wasted enzyme.

The enzyme was the expensive part. She'd cultured her polymerase from heat-loving bacteria scraped out of the core of the settlement's compost heap. It took four months to grow enough for a dozen runs.

"You're nervous," said Pell Orrin from the doorway.

"I'm working."

"You talk to it when you're nervous."

The broker had arrived that morning on a horse with Verdance AgriSciences branding still faintly legible on its flank. That made the horse at least nine years old, one of the last licensed stock. It was sterile, like everything the corporations had ever sold. That was the business model: Generational Fidelity Limits, written into the genome as a methylation timer. Your wheat grew beautifully, your cattle grew fat, your daughter's gene-edited pancreas made insulin, and the next generation got nothing. The seed came up sterile, the calves were stillborn, and the therapy wore off in a decade. Every living thing was a lease, and you renewed it by subscription.

Then the subscriptions stopped shipping. The companies' own engineered staff had sunset clauses too, which nobody had found funny at the time.

Now there were people like Teague, who took the decaying sequences apart before they finished dying.

---

The contract had come in a lead-lined thermos. Pell had set it on her bench like a man setting down a live grenade.

"Verdance renewal key," he'd said. "Master sequence. It was pulled off a regional distribution server in Tulsa before the building flooded. My client paid for the extraction team. Two of them didn't come back."

Teague had unscrewed the thermos with her bad hand. The tremor in her left fingers was worse in the mornings. That was the price of the myostatin hack she'd tried two winters ago, when she needed to haul water and couldn't afford to be weak. The muscle had come, dense and fast. So had the shaking, and it never left.

Inside the thermos was a single cryovial, frost-furred, with a handwritten label: *GFL-R7 / MASTER*.

"It's degrading," Pell said. "They always are. My client wants it amplified, verified, and sequenced onto stable carrier before it's gone. You're the only one within three hundred miles with a working cycler."

"And the payment?"

He'd smiled. "A new inverter. Pure sine wave, German-made, sealed in factory foam. Plus four fresh lithium cells."

Her lights flickered as he said it. The universe had a cheap sense of humor.

"One condition," Pell added. "Exclusive. You run it once. Every copy goes back in the thermos. My client owns the key."

She knew what that meant. Whoever held the renewal key could make crops breed true. They could feed a settlement, or starve one into obedience.

---

The cycler beeped. Thirty cycles were done, the voltage had held, and somewhere a god of scrap metal had been merciful.

Teague pulled the tube and loaded the gel. The gel box was a Tupperware tray. The electrodes were platinum filaments she'd pried out of spark-plug tips, and a car battery supplied the current. She killed the overhead light.

Normally she'd use the transilluminator, a box of bug-zapper tubes behind smoked glass, to make the DNA bands fluoresce. She didn't need it anymore. The tapetum graft had been a gamble. She'd spliced the reflective eye-layer from a feral cat into her own retinal cells, half out of curiosity and half because the lamp oil had run out that winter. She'd been blind for six days and screaming for two of them. Now her irises threw back torchlight like coins, she couldn't stand noon sun without welding goggles, and she could read a gel in near darkness.

She saw a single crisp band at the right size. It was the renewal key, amplified a billion times over.

"Well?" Pell asked from the dark.

"It's clean."

She heard him exhale. "Then we're done."

---

She packed the amplified product into the thermos while he watched, every microliter of it. She let him check the tubes and let him count.

She did not tell him about the pipette tip.

It was a single glass capillary she'd drawn the sample through, then dropped into her coat pocket with the same casual motion she used for everything. A few nanoliters were stuck to its walls. That was enough DNA to start again.

After Pell left with his thermos and his old sterile horse, Teague sat in the dark lab and listened to the batteries hum. She knew what happened to people who held things that warlords had paid for in blood. She'd seen what the Tulsa crews did to defectors. A copy in a freezer was a copy that could be found.

So she drew a sterile buffer into a syringe, flushed the capillary, and added a carrier plasmid she'd been building for her gut flora. It was supposed to help her digest the blighted rye. It would hold anything she asked it to.

Her body had been a laboratory for six years. It had cost her the steadiness of her hand and two molars, and it had given her a liver that could break down ergot and eyes that could see in the dark. It could carry one more risk.

She swallowed the solution with a mouthful of well water and felt it go down cold.

Out on the roof, a cloud passed over the sun. The lab flickered, held, and kept running.

response:
# Polymerase Chain Reaction

The rice cooker clicked from WARM to COOK, and Teodora Vass started counting.

Ninety-four degrees for thirty seconds to pull the strands apart. Fifty-eight to let the primers find their places. Seventy-two for the polymerase to rebuild what heat had split. The cooker couldn't hold a temperature to save its life, so she'd wired its element to an aquarium thermostat and a microcontroller pulled from a dead traffic signal on Route 9. The display still said WALK when the cycle finished.

Thirty cycles. She'd done this so many times she counted in her sleep, on the nights she slept. Since the retinal therapy she slept about two hours, and woke with copper on her tongue.

The reagents sat on the shelf above the bench in brushed aluminum canisters, each stamped with a stylized wheat sheaf and the words CERELIS BIOSCIENCES · HARVEST FOREVER™. Under that, smaller: *Return for deposit.* Cerelis had died with the rest of the world, but its containers were everywhere: stacked in culverts, rusting in co-op silos, used as drums at funerals. They were well-machined and sealed tight. Teo had labeled hers in grease pencil: TRIS. EDTA. SALT. DNTP (LAST OF IT). Her handwriting got worse every month. The tremor had started with the therapy, along with everything else.

Footsteps crunched on the gravel outside the greenhouse. She knew the gait. She pulled the cloth down over her eyes before she opened the door.

"Teo." Dace stood with the dusk behind him. He traded between the river settlements and dressed in layers, so you couldn't see what he was carrying or what had been done to him. "You look worse."

"I look the same. You're seeing better." She stepped back to let him in. "Is this business?"

He set a canister on her bench. It was a Cerelis can like the ones on her shelf, except the seal was intact and a cold pack hissed faintly in the collar.

"Sealed stock," he said. "My client needs a fragment amplified and verified. Primer sequences are in the lid. One run and a confirmed product."

"And they pay?"

He laid the second item beside the first: a glass vial with a factory crimp and a typed label. *Thermostable DNA Polymerase. 500 units/μL.*

Teo kept her face still and her hands steady, which was the harder of the two.

The polymerase she had was her own, cultured from hot-spring bacteria and purified through coffee filters and patience. It made mistakes and died young. Every batch of maize she rescued from Cerelis's legacy came out a little mangled. The drought gene she'd been chasing for two years was degrading on the shelf faster than she could copy it. Cerelis had built its crops to last one generation. Every engineered sequence carried a decay cassette, a molecular fuse that shredded its own construct after a single harvest so farmers had to buy again next season. When the company fell there was nobody left to sell to and nothing left to buy, and every field in the country burned its last generation of seed.

Teo had spent five years cutting those fuses out with tools held together by wire.

"Plus coordinates," Dace said, "to a cold vault in Ashland. My client says there's unspliced heritage stock there. Old corn. Real corn."

"Your client is generous."

"My client is in a hurry."

---

She ran it that night. The thermocycler ticked. Dace slept on the potting bench with his boots on.

Afterward she poured the gel into a cut-down plastic lunchbox and wired it to a tractor battery through a resistor bank she'd built from Christmas lights. The samples sank into their wells as blue smears and began crawling toward the positive pole.

There was no transilluminator. The last UV box in the county had shattered during the Grain Riots. What Teo had instead was the therapy: an expired Cerelis gene-delivery kit for macular degeneration, meant to replace dying photoreceptors. She'd injected it into her own vitreous humor four winters ago, when cataracts and the arsenic in the well water were taking her sight. The kit had overshot. Her cones had rewired into something the manufacturer had never tested, and probably never imagined.

She could see fluorescence now, at levels no normal eye could catch. A bug zapper's weak violet glow was enough to make the stained DNA burn orange for her. It had cost her daylight, a retinal bleed every few months, and the migraines. In return she could read a gel in the dark.

She pulled off the cloth and looked.

One clean band, about twenty-four hundred base pairs.

She knew that number. She'd seen it a thousand times, flanking every engineered sequence she'd ever pulled from a dead field. It was the Sunset Cassette, Cerelis's fuse.

Teo sat back on her stool. The tremor ran up into her shoulders.

Someone wanted the decay cassette amplified, verified, and ready to splice. Somewhere a person with a sealed Cerelis canister and factory polymerase was planning to put the clock back into the seed trade. They'd sell crops that grew beautifully for one season and then crashed, and then they'd own whoever had planted them.

She looked at the requisition slip tucked in the canister lid. The printed header showed a wheat sheaf with a new slogan beneath it. *Harvest Again.*

---

Dace woke at dawn to the smell of burnt coffee. Teo handed him a sealed tube and a gel photograph she'd drawn by hand, since no camera could see what she saw.

"Clean product," she said. "Twenty-four hundred base pairs, one band. Your client can sequence it if they don't trust me."

"They don't trust anybody." He pocketed the tube. "But they trust you more than most."

He left the vial of polymerase and the coordinates on a scrap of seed catalog, and then he was gone down the river road.

Teo turned back to the bench. In the trash lay the spent battery she'd opened the night before. She had leached its manganese salts into the reaction, unbalanced the nucleotides, and pushed her failing homemade polymerase as hard as it would go. It was error-prone PCR, the oldest trick in directed evolution. The tube in Dace's pocket held the right size, the right band, and the right sequence on a quick read. Inside it, though, the cassette was riddled with point mutations, hundreds of small typos spread through the fuse.

If anyone planted it, it wouldn't detonate. If anyone sequenced it carefully, they'd know.

She figured she had a month, maybe two.

She cracked the factory crimp on the vial, loaded her drought-gene samples, and set the rice cooker to COOK. The display blinked WALK.

Teo started counting.

response:
# Polymerase Chain Reaction

The thermocycler was a rice cooker with ambitions.

Ines had gutted it in the second winter, wired its heating plate to a thermostat salvaged from a hospital incubator, and bolted a computer fan to the lid so it could drop from ninety-five degrees to fifty-five in under a minute. It clicked through its cycles on the bench now, *melt, anneal, extend*, thirty times over, while she watched the readout and chewed the inside of her cheek. The cheek was bleeding again. That was the vitamin C cassette. Her liver made its own ascorbic acid now, courtesy of a goat gene and a retrovirus she'd cooked in this same room, but it had never been sure how much to make.

Around her feet, the mushrooms were glowing.

They'd come up through the cracked floor tiles three years ago, after she'd spilled a luciferase test culture and failed to bleach it properly. Now they grew in every seam of the old Halvorsen-Agri field station, pale blue caps no bigger than thumbnails, pulsing faintly as they breathed. The settlement kids called the lab the Chapel. Ines called it lighting she didn't have to pay for.

The door rattled. Nobody knocked in Coldwater, so it wasn't anyone from Coldwater.

"It's open," she said, "but if you touch anything I'll know."

The man who came in wore a waxed coat and a respirator with the filters painted red, the way the river traders did to show they weren't carrying rot spores. He pulled the mask down. Fifties, clean-shaven, which meant he had razors, which meant he had money.

"Ines Vasko," he said. "They told me you'd be younger."

"I was, last year." She didn't turn from the readout. "Your filters are expired. I can smell your breath from here."

He laughed, surprised. Most people didn't know about the nose. It had come from a dog-olfactory splice that was supposed to let her sniff out blight in grain stores, and it did. She could also smell fear, menstruation, lies told with a dry mouth, and every meal the man had eaten in the past day. Smoked eel. Real coffee.

"Teodor Lann," he said. "I broker for the Ascension compound, upriver."

She knew Ascension. Six hundred people behind concrete, running the only intact hydroelectric dam within two hundred miles. They had power. They did not have food that bred true. Nobody did.

That was the joke at the heart of the end of the world. Halvorsen, Corteva-Myriad, the Sino-Brazilian combines: every one of them had built their crops to last exactly one generation. The engineered sequences carried a molecular clock, a methylation cascade that silenced the yield genes in the second filial generation and then, for good measure, fragmented the inserted DNA entirely. *Generational Licensing*, they'd called it. You bought your seed every spring. When the companies went under in the Collapse, there was no seed to buy, and the heirloom strains had been bought up and burned a decade before. What the world had left were fields of plants that grew beautifully once and then forgot how.

Ines spent her days catching that forgetting in the act. She harvested first-generation tissue, extracted the engineered sequences before they could degrade, amplified them in the rice cooker, and spliced them into the hardy, bitter, ungrateful wild stock that still grew in the ditches. Most attempts died. Some worked for a season. Coldwater was alive because of the some.

"Sit," she said. "Not there. That's a centrifuge."

It was a bicycle wheel with test tubes zip-tied to the spokes. Lann sat on a crate instead.

"Ascension has a cryo-vault," he said. "Pre-Collapse. Halvorsen's regional master library, still at minus eighty because of the dam. Clean source sequences, no clock, from before they added the kill cascade. Original drought-tolerance. Nitrogen fixation for cereals. The lot."

Ines finally looked at him. Her eyes adjusted the way they always did now, pupils flaring wide, the mushroom-light sharpening his face into high contrast. The rhodopsin tweak. She'd paid for it with two months of migraines and a permanent sensitivity to sunlight that kept her indoors from ten to four. It had been worth it.

"And Ascension wants?"

"A crop." He set a steel cylinder on the bench, frosted and sweating. "This is a sample from the vault. Proof. You keep it either way."

She didn't touch it. "What kind of crop?"

"Wheat. High yield, fast maturing. Good enough that the Delta settlements will want it." He paused. "And sterile after one generation."

The rice cooker clicked into its extension phase. Somewhere under the floor, a mushroom pulsed.

"You want me to rebuild the clock," Ines said.

"We want reliable trade partners. If the Delta depends on us for seed every spring, they don't come up the river with guns." He spread his hands. "It's not cruelty. It's architecture."

"That's what Halvorsen said."

"Halvorsen was selling to people who had alternatives." Lann's voice stayed level, and she could smell that he believed it, which was worse than if he'd been lying. "In return, Coldwater gets full access to the vault. Every sequence. You'd never splice a dying gene again."

She thought about the bleeding cheek. About the white streaks in her hair from a melanin regulator that had misfired. About the tremor in her left hand that came and went, the price of a neural-repair splice that had also, inexplicably, made her immune to the rot fungus that had killed her brother. Every gift in her body had a cost attached, and she had chosen every one of them herself.

The Delta wouldn't be choosing.

"I'll need time," she said.

# Útiseta

Astrid said the hide had to be from an animal that had died badly, or it wouldn't work.

"Badly how?" I asked. We were in her grandmother's woodshed, and the flashlight kept catching our breath and turning it into smoke.

"Hit by a car. Shot and not finished." She pulled a reindeer skin down from a hook and shook it out, and something small and dry fell from the fur onto the floor. "This one walked around for two days with a bullet in its lung. Mormor said that's the best kind. It's already halfway."

"Halfway where?"

She looked at me the way she did when I said something especially Stockholm, and handed me the skin.

It was the last week of October 1995. I know the date because I had a Walkman in my jacket pocket with a Kent tape in it that my friend Sara had mailed from home, and the postmark said the twentieth. I was fifteen. I had been in Norrbotten for four months, long enough to learn that the dark comes fast up there, and that nobody in the village locked their doors, and that Astrid Nilsson was the only person under forty who would talk to me.

We left through her bedroom window at a quarter past eleven. That part was ordinary. Every teenager in Sweden has climbed out a window. The rest was not.

Astrid had a list, and she went through it on the walk out past the last farm, across the stubble field where the frost crunched like sugar. Her voice was flat and practical, as if she were reminding me what to bring on a school trip.

"You sit facing north. You keep the knife under you, blade down, so you're touching the iron the whole time. You put the hide over your head and you don't take it off. If you hear your name, you don't answer. Not even if it's me."

"Why would you call my name?"

"I won't." She kicked a clod of frozen earth. "That's the point."

The mound was beyond the field, at the edge of the spruce, a low hump you'd mistake for a hill if nobody told you. There was a sign about it near the road, put up by the county, faded green, saying it was Iron Age and protected. Kids from the village came out here in summer to drink. There were beer caps in the grass. I remember finding that comforting.

Astrid made me give her a hair. She wound it around a heel of rye bread and pushed the bread into a crack in the earth at the mound's foot. "So it knows who's asking," she said. Then she took her own place on the south slope, and I took mine on the north, and we couldn't see each other anymore.

I want to be clear about what we came for, because it matters. We wanted to know whether Johanna Lindgren had really slept with Astrid's cousin at the midsummer party. We wanted to know who had written *STOCKHOLMSHORA* on my locker. That was all. That was what we thought this was for.

I pulled the hide over my head. It smelled of old fat and something sweeter underneath. I sat on the cold knife and faced north, into the trees, and waited.

At first it was only boring and cold. I counted my breaths. I thought about Sara, and about the subway, and the smell of Hötorget in the rain. My legs went numb. Somewhere a dog was barking, very far off, and then it stopped all at once, the way a radio stops when you pull the plug.

The bell rang at midnight.

One stroke. It came from the south, from Övre Byn, where the church was. The old wooden church held services once a month, and the bell had to be pulled by hand. I knew that because Astrid had told me about her grandfather pulling it when he was a boy. There was no reason for anyone to be in that tower on a Tuesday night in October.

It rang once, and the sound hung over the field much longer than it should have, and then the silence that followed it felt *thicker*. It didn't feel empty. It felt full.

I heard something walking.

I'll say now what I've told myself many times since: it was a fox. It was a moose at the edge of the trees. It was Astrid, getting up to stretch her legs and scare me. Sound behaves strangely in cold air. The ground was frozen and the forest was close.

But it was walking around the mound. Slowly. All the way around. It passed behind me, and I felt the hide on my shoulders grow heavier, as if it had been soaked, and I smelled the sweet smell more strongly. I put both hands flat on the frozen grass and pressed down on the knife until it hurt.

Then someone said my name.

It used my mother's voice. It didn't sound like her calling me in for dinner. It sounded the way she said my name when she was very tired, the way she'd said it in the car on the drive up, staring at the road, when I'd asked if we could please just go home. *Linnea.* Low and close. Right beside my ear, on the side where Astrid couldn't have been.

I didn't answer. I want credit for that, at least. I bit the inside of my cheek until it bled, and I didn't answer.

And then I knew a thing. I don't know how else to say it. I didn't hear it so much as discover it, the way you discover in the morning that you've been dreaming. It was nothing about Johanna, or my locker. I knew that Astrid's grandmother had not taught her any of this. I knew Astrid had found it all in a library book in Luleå, and that she was more frightened than I was, and that she was out here because she was lonely too.

I knew one more thing, which I won't write down.

We left when the first bird sang, an hour before light. Astrid's face was grey. Neither of us spoke until the stubble field.

"Did you hear anything?" she said finally.

"No," I said. "Did you?"

"No."

Behind us, in the frost around the mound, there was a single ring of tracks, unbroken, which neither of us had made.

"Fox," Astrid said.

"Fox," I agreed, and we didn't look back, because she'd told me not to. Even now, I haven't.

# Útiseta

Astrid said we had to go on a night with no wind, and that it should be a Thursday, because that was the old day. I asked her old to whom, and she just looked at me the way she always did when I said something Stockholm.

It was October 1995. I had been in Granberg for four months, long enough to learn that the village had one shop, two churches, and a mound behind Lundqvist's pasture that nobody's grandfather had ever let them play on. Astrid's grandmother was the exception. Astrid's grandmother, she said, had sat out on it herself, in 1941, and learned which of the Persson boys would come home from the border and which wouldn't.

"And she was right?"

"She's always right," Astrid said. "That's the problem with it."

We left my house at half past eleven. I climbed out over the porch roof. Astrid was waiting at the road with a rucksack and her bike, and she made me take my Walkman out of my jacket and leave it in the ditch.

"Nothing that talks," she said. "Nothing that ticks. Give me your watch."

I gave her my Swatch. She put it in the ditch too, face down, as if it could see.

The pasture was white with frost, and the mound rose out of it like the back of something sleeping. It wasn't big, maybe the height of a man, but up close it was very round and very deliberate, and the mist had gathered at its base in a thick ring, glowing under the moon so that the mound seemed to float. I remember thinking it looked like a photograph of itself. I remember thinking we should go home.

Astrid unpacked the rucksack on the grass. A reindeer hide, stiff and grey, that she said was her grandmother's. A bread knife with a black handle. Half a loaf of rye. A can of her father's Norrlands Guld.

"Iron goes in the ground," she said, and pushed the knife into the turf at the foot of the slope, blade down. "So we can find the way back. Bread for the one who lives here. Beer because Mormor says they like it better than milk, and we're out of milk."

She laughed when she said it. That was the thing about Astrid: she said half of it like a girl stealing her dad's beer and half of it like she was reading from a list, and you could never tell where the line was.

"Who are we asking about?" she said.

"I don't know. Jenny Holmgren?"

"What about Jenny Holmgren?"

"Whether she's the one who wrote that about me. On the bus seat."

Astrid nodded like it was a serious question. Maybe to her it was. "Then think about it the whole time. Only that. Don't let your thoughts wander, or something else answers."

The rules, as she gave them to me while we climbed:

We sit back to back, me facing north, her facing south.

The hide goes under us, fur side down.

Once we sit, we don't speak. Not to each other. Not to anything.

If someone calls your name, you don't answer. Not even if it's me. *Especially* if it's me.

We don't come down until the first bird.

"What if there's no bird?"

"There's always a bird," she said, and spread the hide.

Her back was warm against mine. Then it wasn't, or I stopped noticing. The cold came up through the hide and into my spine, and the mist, which had been lying at the bottom of the mound, began to climb. Not quickly. Like water filling a bath. I watched it come up the slope toward my boots and told myself it was just the temperature dropping, which it was, which is exactly what mist does.

I thought about Jenny Holmgren. I tried to.

The first sound was the beer can. I heard it tip over at the foot of the mound, that hollow aluminium knock, and then the glug of it emptying into the grass. Astrid's shoulders went rigid against mine. A fox, I thought. An elk. The wind, except there was no wind.

Then something walked around the mound.

I want to be precise about this, because I have told it badly before. It didn't sound like feet. It sounded like weight, settling and shifting, settling and shifting, the frost cracking under it in a slow circle. It started on Astrid's side and came round to mine. I stared straight ahead into the mist, which was glowing now, all of it, white and full of moonlight, and I could not see anything in it. I could not see anything, and I could hear it breathing.

I thought about Jenny Holmgren so hard my teeth hurt.

The circling stopped somewhere in front of me. And then, from inside the mist, from maybe three metres away, Astrid said my name.

"Linnea."

Her back was still against mine. I could feel her breathing. I could feel her *shaking*.

"Linnea. Come down. I want to show you something."

It was her voice exactly. It had her Norrland vowels, the little catch she had on the double *n*. It was patient. It sounded like it would wait as long as it took.

I don't know how long I sat. I know my eyes were watering from not blinking. I know that at some point I was thinking not about Jenny Holmgren but about my mother, and about a lump in her breast that nobody had told me about yet. They told me two years later, and when they did, I already knew.

A bird called from the birches. Astrid was up before it finished, dragging me by the sleeve, and we ran, and she yanked the knife out of the ground without stopping, and neither of us looked back.

At the road, she bent over with her hands on her knees, and when she looked up at me her face was grey.

"Why did you answer it?" she said.

"I didn't."

"I heard you. You said *yes*. You said *yes, I'm coming*."

I didn't say anything. I hadn't said anything. I know I hadn't.

We found my Walkman in the ditch. The Swatch we never found, though we looked until it was light.

I have had thirty years to decide what happened on that mound: cold, fear, two girls with too much imagination and a can of stolen beer. Most days I believe that. But I have never gone back to Granberg, and I have never been able to say for certain, not once in all that time, that I didn't answer.

# Útiseta

Astrid said you had to bring something you'd owned since you were small, so I brought the plastic hairclip shaped like a strawberry that had lived at the bottom of my pencil case since first grade. She examined it under her torch like a doctor reading an X-ray, then nodded.

"Good. It has to cost something."

It was the last week of August 1995, and it had only been properly dark at night for about two weeks. Up there, summer doesn't end so much as get switched off. I climbed out my bedroom window at quarter past eleven, crossed the woodshed roof my father still hadn't realised worked as a staircase, and met Astrid behind the Konsum. She was sitting on a stack of bread crates, smoking one of her brother's menthols.

Her rucksack held her dead grandfather's wool coat, a bread knife, half a loaf of limpa in a plastic bag, and a Walkman with a Roxette tape in it.

"What's that for?"

"In case we need to drown something out." She laughed, and so did I, because we were fifteen and that was what you did with a sentence like that.

The mound sat on Kråkberget, above the village, past the last summer cottages and up a logging track that had grown soft with moss. The county had put up a sign: *Gravröse, bronsålder*, with a little drawing of a man in a horned helmet that Astrid said was wrong in every possible way. Someone had shot at the sign with an air rifle. The pellet dents made a constellation over the man's face.

She gave me the rules on the way up, flatly, as if reading a bus timetable.

"You don't say your name. Not once, not until we're back on asphalt. If something calls you, you don't answer. We sit facing north. Coat goes over our heads, so we can't see. The knife goes in the ground between us." She flicked ash into the dark. "Farmor says they don't like iron. That's the point. You want them to talk, not come close."

"Who's *they*?"

"Whoever's in there." She shrugged. "Or nobody. Then we've sat on a pile of rocks and frozen our arses off, and you can tell your Stockholm friends we're all mad up here."

I didn't have Stockholm friends anymore. I'd stopped writing back in June. She knew that.

We'd agreed on our questions in her room the week before, lying on her bed under a Kent poster. Astrid wanted to know who had told Lindqvist about the vodka at the end-of-term disco. I wanted to know what Malin and the others said about me when I left the canteen. It had seemed so small and funny in daylight. *Ask it simply,* Astrid said. *Farmor says they're very literal.*

The röse was bigger than I'd pictured, a low dome of grey stones furred with lichen, with a hollow at the top where someone had dug, centuries ago, looking for silver. We climbed into the hollow. Astrid pushed the knife into a seam of moss between two stones until only the handle showed. She set the bread on a flat rock and pointed at it, and I laid my strawberry clip beside it, feeling suddenly, stupidly, like I was going to cry.

Then the coat came down over both our heads.

It smelled of mothballs and pipe tobacco and, underneath, of something like a cellar. The world went black, then grey-black, and then all that was left was sound.

At first it was Astrid breathing, and my own heart, and an owl somewhere down toward the river. Then the wind came up through the pines.

I have spent thirty years telling myself what wind in pine trees sounds like. I could give a lecture on it. It's a long, layered hiss, needles brushing needles, rising and falling like breath. Your brain is built to find voices in noise. I know all of that.

But I sat there under that coat and listened to the wind come up the hill, and it came in *syllables*. Soft, unvoiced, many at once, like a classroom where everyone has been told to read silently and not all of them can. It rose and fell, and every time it fell I strained after it, the way you lean toward a conversation in the next room.

Astrid had stopped breathing loudly. I couldn't hear her breathing at all.

The cold came up out of the stones and into my tailbone. It wasn't night-cold. It was steady and patient, like water rising in a basement.

Then, from down the hill, in the direction of the village, I heard my mother call my name.

Not shouted. Just said, at normal volume, the way she said it from the kitchen when dinner was ready. *Linnea.* As if she were standing at the foot of the mound with a dishcloth over her shoulder.

My mouth opened. I felt the shape of *Mamma?* in it. Astrid's hand closed on my wrist so hard I had bruises for a week.

The wind dropped. Behind us, on the slope of the mound we weren't facing, a stone shifted. One stone, settling, a small dry knock. Then something lighter, like moss being pressed by a weight.

Very close to the hem of the coat, close enough that I felt it on my ankle more than heard it, something whispered. I didn't know the words. I'm not sure there were words. But I knew, in the way you know things in dreams, that it wasn't answering my question. It was asking one of its own.

"Now," Astrid breathed. "We go. Don't look back."

We went down the logging track with the coat still around our shoulders, holding hands like children, and I didn't look back. I wanted to so badly my neck hurt. Neither of us spoke until our shoes hit the asphalt by the first streetlight, and then Astrid said "Astrid" out loud, and I said "Linnea," and my own name sounded borrowed.

"Did you hear it?" she asked. She was grinning, but her lips were grey.

"Hear what?" I said. I still don't know why.

She looked at me for a long moment. Then she lit a cigarette with shaking hands and walked home without saying goodbye.

In the morning, my strawberry hairclip was on my windowsill, beaded with dew.

Astrid knew about the woodshed roof. Astrid could have picked it up when I wasn't watching and walked it over before dawn as a joke. I've told myself that for thirty years, too.

But the bread knife was never in her rucksack again. When I asked about it, weeks later, she said she'd left it up there on purpose.

"So they know where we are," she said, "and stay there."

# Gone South

## Chapter Two: Somewhere a Saxophone

The guy in the Silverado didn't even say goodbye. Just "This is you," like New Orleans was a bus stop, and then his taillights were swallowed by a street that smelled like fried dough and last night's beer and something sweet and rotten underneath, like a fruit bowl somebody forgot.

So. Here I am.

Somewhere a saxophone is playing. Not a song I know, just one long, bending note that climbs and climbs and then falls apart. Honestly? Same.

Decatur Street at nine a.m. Tourists in matching T-shirts. A man hosing vomit off the sidewalk with the bored dignity of a priest. And me, with a backpack holding two hoodies, a phone I switched off outside Jackson, Mississippi because I've seen enough *Dateline*, sixty-three dollars, and my sister's eyeliner. I stole it on the way out, and out of everything, *that's* what I feel guilty about.

The sax player is an old man on an upturned bucket, eyes closed. Three dollars and a button in his case. I stop without meaning to. That note sounds the way my chest has felt since Tuesday, when I said the words at dinner and Dad set his fork down so carefully, like it might go off.

Mom cried. That was the worst part. I'd rehearsed comebacks for yelling in the shower, but she cried like somebody had died. And I kept thinking: *I'm right here. I'm sitting right here.*

I drop a dollar in the case. Sixty-two.

He opens one eye. "Don't spend it all in one place." I laugh, which surprises us both.

---

By noon I've learned three things. Everything in the French Quarter costs eleven dollars. If you stand still too long, a cop looks at you. And I'm not the only one.

She's on the steps of a shuttered shop on Chartres, eating a praline out of a paper bag, watching me watch her. Seventeen, maybe. Box-dye red hair with two inches of black roots. A Saints jersey four sizes too big. Around her wrist is a thin pale band of skin where a hospital bracelet used to be. I know because I had one once.

"You've walked past me four times," she says.

"It's a free country."

"It's really not." She holds out the bag. "You look about to pass out, Tennessee."

I freeze. "How do you—"

"Your hoodie says *Maury County Wrestling*." She grins. "Also you said 'y'all' to the cashier at Rouses. I was behind you."

Every after-school special ever made is screaming at me to keep walking. But I haven't eaten since a gas station Slim Jim at two a.m., so I sit. One step away from her. Like that matters.

"I'm Dez."

"Taylor."

"That your real name?"

It's a weird question. A good one. "Yeah," I say finally. "It's the one thing they got right."

She nods like she gets it, which she can't. Which maybe she does. "What do you want me to call you? He, she...?"

Nobody has ever asked me that. Not once in my whole life. And this stranger with sugar on her fingers just *asks*, like she's ordering coffee.

My throat does something embarrassing. "They. They's good."

"Cool." She brushes off her hands. "They want to see the river?"

---

Dez knows everything. Which restaurants dump decent food at three. Which bathrooms don't need a code. Which corners to avoid after dark, and which guys you never, ever take a cigarette from. She talks fast and laughs loud and never says where she's from. When I ask, she says "Around." When I ask about her wrist, she tugs her sleeve down and says, "Look, a pelican." There's no pelican.

Fine. I've got secrets too. I'm practically made of them.

On the levee, watching a barge crawl past, I tell her about Tuesday. Not all of it. Not what Dad said, the thing I'm not going to think about right now. Maybe ever.

"They'll come around," Dez says. "Or they won't. Either way, you're here now."

"Is that supposed to make me feel better?"

"It's supposed to be true." She picks at the jersey. "Where you sleeping tonight?"

That's the question I've been not-asking myself since the Silverado pulled away.

"I don't know."

"I stay with a guy. Marcus. Place in the Seventh Ward. He lets people crash. You just help out sometimes."

Something cold slides down my spine. *Help out.* She isn't looking at me. She's looking at the barge, jaw tight, like she's chewing something that tastes bad.

"Help out how?"

The saxophone drifts up from Jackson Square, maybe the same one, maybe a different one, slow and stupidly beautiful.

"He asked me to bring people," Dez says, very quietly. "New ones. Young ones."

My heart's going so hard I feel it in my teeth. I'm already calculating. Which way is the street? How many people are around? How fast can I run?

"I'm not gonna," she says. "Okay? I'm telling you so you *don't*. Not with me, not with anybody who offers. There's a place on Rampart, for kids. They don't make you call anyone. They've got beds." She swallows. "I used to stay there."

"Why'd you leave?"

She finally looks at me, eyes wet and furious. "Because Marcus said he loved me, Tennessee. And I'm an idiot."

---

She walks me to the door on Rampart but won't come in. I ask her to. I actually beg a little, which is humiliating. She just shoves her hands in her jersey pockets.

"Maybe tomorrow."

I don't know if I believe her. I don't know if I believe anything anymore. Not my parents, not my town, not this girl with a ghost bracelet and a man waiting for her across the city. Everything I thought was solid turned out to be water.

But she asked what to call me.

That has to count for something.

"Tomorrow," I say. "Chartres Street. I'll bring the pralines."

She laughs that loud laugh, and then she's gone into the dark. I'm left on the steps with sixty-two dollars, my sister's eyeliner, and a heart so full and so scared I can't tell which is which.

Somewhere, a sax holds one long note.

I push open the door.

The trucker's name was Dale, and the last thing Dale said to me was, "This is as far as Jesus wants you to go, kid." Then he reached across and popped my door like I was a raccoon he'd found in the cab.

So now I'm standing on Canal Street at 7:40 a.m. with a backpack, eleven dollars, and a phone that says **12%** in a red so aggressive it feels personal.

New Orleans smells like fried dough, old beer, and river. The air is so thick I could chew it. Somewhere a guy is already playing trumpet, which seems like a lot of commitment for a Tuesday.

I don't check my messages. I *know* there are messages. Mom's texts arrive in clusters, like hail. I can feel them in my pocket like a hot coal.

*You did this. You picked the worst possible way to do this.*

Also: *You're two states away and nobody here knows your deadname. Nobody.*

Both are true. My brain has been running two radio stations at full volume since Sunday.

---

By noon I've learned three things.

One: a beignet costs more than I want to admit, and I bought one anyway, and it was worth it, and I hate myself a little.

Two: if you stand still in the French Quarter, someone will try to sell you something. A poem, a tarot reading, a hand-drawn caricature of yourself as a pirate.

Three: everyone looks at you. Not mean, mostly. Just *reading* you. I can't tell what they see. Boy? Girl? Lost? Easy?

That last one is the one that makes my spine go tight.

**9%.**

I'm sitting on the edge of a planter in Jackson Square, doing math about bus fares I can't afford to places I don't want to go, when a girl drops down next to me like we've known each other since kindergarten.

"You're doing it wrong," she says.

She's maybe my age, maybe older. Bleached hair with an inch of dark roots, a men's flannel tied around her waist in this heat, and a deck of tarot cards held together with a hair tie.

"Doing what wrong?"

"Being new." She nods at my backpack, which I'm hugging like a life raft. "You're holding that like there's a kidney in it. Every creep from here to Bourbon can smell it on you."

"Cool. Thanks. Very comforting."

"I'm not comforting. I'm *accurate*." She sticks out her hand. "Lux."

"Is that your real name?"

"Is anybody's?" She grins. She's missing a molar on one side. "What do I call you?"

And there it is. It's the simplest question in the world, and nobody has asked it of me before. Not once. Not my mom, not my brother, not the stupid smug counselor with her stupid smug lanyard.

My throat does something embarrassing.

"Taylor," I say. Then, because she seems like the kind of person who'll ask anyway: "They/them. Mostly. I'm still... figuring it out."

Lux shrugs like I told her my favorite color. "Cool. Taylor. You hungry, Taylor?"

---

She knows things. She knows which café throws out day-old muffins at two o'clock. She knows which bathrooms don't need a code. She does a ten-minute tarot reading for a sunburned couple from Ohio and tells the wife she's "standing at the crossroads of a great transformation." The wife cries a little and gives her twenty bucks.

"Is any of that real?" I ask when they're gone.

"She *is* at a crossroads. Everybody is. You just say it confident." Lux tucks the twenty into her sock. "Tourists don't want the future. They want permission."

I think about that longer than I want to.

Around four, a man in a nice linen shirt stops by us. Fifties, soft voice, smells like expensive cologne.

"You kids look worn out," he says. "I run a little shelter-type situation over on Esplanade. Hot shower. Charge your phones." He looks right at me. "No questions."

I swear my phone *hears* him. **6%.**

A hot shower. My skin practically begs.

Then Lux's hand closes on my wrist, hard.

"We're good, Mr. Vernon," she says, sweet as syrup. "Tell Benny I said hey."

The man's smile doesn't move, but something behind it does. He tips an invisible hat and walks off.

"What the hell was that?"

"That," Lux says, still watching him, "is the most dangerous man in a three-block radius, and he's gonna be real nice to you for about four days." She lets go. There are white marks on my wrist where her fingers were. "Rule one. Nothing here is free. If it looks free, *you're* the price."

I don't ask how she knows his name. I don't ask who Benny is. I want to. I don't.

*You don't know her either*, says Radio Station One. *She found you in about forty seconds. Same as him.*

*She asked your name*, says Radio Station Two.

---

When the sun goes down, the Quarter gets louder and meaner. Lux takes me to a church on Rampart with a deep side doorway, out of the wind, where the cops don't bother you before two.

We sit with our backs against the cool stone. Somebody's brass band is playing three streets over, all wrong notes and joy.

That's when her phone buzzes.

She has a phone. A good one, too, with a full battery. She angles it away from me, but not fast enough. I see the screen.

**Mama — 38 missed calls.**

Earlier, at the muffin place, she'd told me her mom died when she was nine.

She sees me see it. For a second her whole face goes bare, and she looks about twelve.

"Don't," she says quietly.

So I don't.

I pull out my own phone. **2%.** Thirty-something unread messages. The top one from Mom, preview cut off mid-sentence:

*Please just tell me you're safe, I don't care about any of the*

Any of the what? Any of the *trans stuff*? Any of the *drama*? Any of the *you*?

I could open it. I could find out. I could find out she doesn't mean it, or that she does.

The band hits a high note and holds it way too long.

I hold down the power button until the screen goes black, and I tuck the phone deep in my backpack. I'm saving it for an emergency, whatever an emergency even looks like here.

Lux bumps her shoulder against mine. She doesn't say anything. Neither do I.

Two liars in a doorway, I guess. Or two people who haven't figured out which version of the truth gets them killed.

Either way, it's the first night in a long time anyone has called me by my name.

response:
# Gone South

## Chapter Two: Anything Helps

The first thing New Orleans does is smell at me.

Not *smell*. Smell *at*. Like it has opinions. Fried dough, river rot, last night's beer hosed into the gutter and not hosed hard enough.

Earl the trucker had said "I don't judge" at the state line. He judged pretty hard somewhere around Jackson, once the sun came up and he got a good look at my chipped black nail polish. At 6:40 a.m. he pulled over on Canal Street and said, "This is you."

It wasn't me. Nothing is me. That's kind of the whole point.

The strap slips off my shoulder. I hitch it back.

Here's what's in the bag. Three shirts. A binder I bought with birthday gift-card money and hid in a tampon box, because nobody in my house would ever touch a tampon box. A charger with no phone, because Mom has the phone "until you come to your senses." $212. One granola bar. That's it. That's the life I packed in thirty minutes.

Great job, Taylor. Real visionary stuff.

---

I walk, because standing still feels like waiting for someone to pick me up. I don't know who does the picking up around here. Cops. Social services. Worse.

The French Quarter at seven a.m. is a hangover with balconies. A man power-washes the sidewalk outside a bar. A woman in a sequin dress, heels in hand, cries into a payphone I'm pretty sure doesn't work. Nobody looks at me twice.

Back home, everybody looked at me twice. You couldn't buy a Slurpee without Mrs. Dawkins asking after your mama.

I thought being invisible would feel like relief. It feels like falling.

Strap. Shoulder. Hitch.

Nobody tells you that the adrenaline runs out around hour nine. After that you're just a kid in a strange city with sore feet and nowhere to pee.

---

By noon I've ended up in Jackson Square, which is basically a theme park for people who think they're interesting. Tarot readers. A guy painted silver pretending to be a statue. A brass band playing for nobody.

A girl sits on the cathedral steps with a scruffy brown dog and a cardboard sign: ANYTHING HELPS (EXCEPT JESUS).

"You're gonna lose that bag," she says.

"What?"

"Strap. It's been falling off since you walked up. Somebody'll lift it right off you." She holds out a hand. I don't give her the bag. She rolls her eyes. "I'm not gonna *steal* it, Tennessee."

"How'd you—"

"You say 'what' like it's got two syllables." She grins. "Wha-ut."

I hand it over. She ties a knot in the strap, quick and tight, and gives it back. It sits right on my shoulder for the first time in a hundred miles.

"Remy," she says. "That's Biscuit. He bites cops."

"Taylor."

"Cool. He, she, they?"

My throat does something weird. Forty-eight hours of my dad saying *son* like a threat. My mom crying *I didn't raise a—* and never finishing the sentence. And this girl with dirty fingernails just *asks*. Like it's normal. Like it's the weather.

"They," I say. "For now. I'm figuring it out."

"Mostly she," Remy says, pointing at herself. "Sometimes 'hey you.' Hungry?"

---

She buys me beignets, which is either kindness or a strategy. I can't tell yet.

She talks fast. Which churches do lunch on Tuesdays. Which cops will just move you along and which ones will run your name. Stay off Bourbon after dark. Never get in a car with a man whose name ends in *-y*.

"Where are you from?" I ask.

"Baton Rouge."

Twenty minutes later she mentions "back in Houston" without blinking. Her phone keeps buzzing, a phone way too nice for someone with a cardboard sign. She flips it face down every time. Her sneakers are white. Actually white. Nobody sleeping outside has white sneakers.

I file all of it away. Sixteen years in a house where you learn to read the weather before anyone opens their mouth, and you get good at filing.

"You got somewhere tonight?" she asks.

"Working on it."

"My friend Marcus has a place in the Marigny. Couch is free. He helps kids out."

The powdered sugar turns to sand in my mouth.

Here's the problem. My gut says *nobody is this nice for free*. Then some other part of me, softer and stupider and starving for something that isn't food, says *she asked your pronouns before your last name*.

Who do you trust: the alarm, or the ache?

"Maybe," I say.

---

We kill the afternoon. Biscuit chases pigeons. A tarot lady with silver rings tries to read my palm. "You already left, baby," she tells me. "Now you gotta arrive." I don't pay her. Remy laughs so hard she snorts.

For a couple of hours it feels almost like having a friend.

At dusk we walk toward Esplanade. The streetlights buzz on. Remy's phone buzzes too. This time she reads it, and her face closes up like a door.

At the corner, she stops.

"Okay," she says. "I'm gonna tell you something and you're gonna be mad."

I wait. My hand finds the knot on my strap.

"Marcus gives me fifty bucks for every kid I bring." She won't look at me. "It starts with the couch. Then it's 'you owe rent.' Then it's other stuff."

The street goes very quiet, even though it isn't.

"Then why—"

"Because if I bring somebody," she says, flat, "I don't have to do the other stuff that week."

I want to scream at her. I want to hug her. I'm doing neither, just standing there with my mouth open like a fish while every alarm I ignored all afternoon goes off at once, way too late to be useful.

She pulls a crumpled card from her pocket. A youth shelter, an address on Rampart Street.

"They do beds. Food. They won't call your mom unless it's, like, serious. Go there. Not with me."

"Come with me."

"He's got my ID." She shrugs, like it's nothing, like it's the weather. "Maybe tomorrow."

She doesn't believe it. Neither do I.

"Remy—"

"Don't make it weird, Tennessee." She whistles for Biscuit and walks off toward the Marigny, white sneakers glowing under the streetlights until she turns a corner and they're gone.

---

The knot holds all the way to Rampart Street. I check it maybe forty times.

At the front desk, a tired woman with reading glasses on a beaded chain looks up and asks the question I've been dreading since Canal Street.

"Okay, hon. What name do you want me to put down?"

Not *what's your name*. *What name do you want.*

I open my mouth.

I'm still deciding what comes out of it, but for the first time in two days, it feels like the choice is mine.
