**The Underhold**

The door swung inward on hinges that had been freshly oiled. That was the first wrong thing.

Aya noticed it the way a tongue notices a missing tooth. Every other door in the guildhouse had shrieked tonight, swollen with harbour damp and a century of neglect. This one opened like a held breath.

The underhold exhaled cold air that smelled of tallow, brine and the cloying sweetness of rendered blubber. Whale-oil lamps hung in iron cages along the vaulted ceiling, each turned low, so that the long chamber swam in a jaundiced half-light. At its far end, upon a plinth carved from a single leviathan vertebra, sat the reliquary that held the Scythan artifact.

Before it, in a high-backed chair as though in her own parlour, sat Madam Orsolya Vask.

"Close the door, love," she said. "There's a draught."

Katra swore under her breath. Simeon said nothing at all, which was worse.

Men stepped from the alcoves on either side, six of them, then eight. They carried none of the guild's usual knives and cudgels. Each held a brass-barrelled harpoon-pistol, and the barbed heads gleamed a dull, unlovely grey. At every throat hung a little phial of salt on a chain.

*They knew. They knew what I would bring.*

The immateria stirred behind Aya's eyes, that old familiar pressure, like a palm laid flat against the far side of a windowpane. Something in the dark between worlds turned toward her, curious and patient and hungry. She had only to open the latch.

"I wouldn't," Vask said mildly. "Them barbs are dipped in quicksilver and church-iron. Whatever you call up, girl, it'll come through to find you bleeding out on my flagstones. Then it's just a hungry thing in a cellar with nobody to tell it *heel*. Bad for all of us."

Aya let the pressure ebb. It withdrew reluctantly and left a taste in her mouth like old pennies.

"You were taken," Katra said hoarsely. "I watched the bluecoats drag you down Tanner's Row in irons."

"You watched what I paid them to show you." Vask rose, unhurried. She was a broad woman with grey hair scraped into a sailor's knot, and a scar ran from her ear to the corner of her mouth like a seam in old leather. "A guild's like a hull, Katra. Every so often you haul her up on the slip and see what's been gnawing at the timbers." Her pale eyes found Aya's mask, the lacquered black raven's beak. "Didn't reckon on it being the Raven, mind. Thought you was content."

Hands seized Aya from behind before she could answer. A ninth man had come in by the door they had so obligingly left open. Katra twisted and spat until a pistol butt cracked against her temple and she sagged, groaning. Simeon simply raised his hands, his spectacles flashing in the lamplight.

"For the record," he said, "I did mention it was too quiet."

"You did, Simeon," Aya said through her teeth. "Thank you."

Vask crossed the chamber, took the beak of the mask between finger and thumb, and lifted it away.

The cold air touched Aya's bare face and she felt it like a blade. For two years that thin shell of lacquer had been a wall between two lives. On one side were the drawing rooms, the quadrilles and her father's silences at supper. On the other were the rooftops, the ledgers and the whispering dark. Now the wall was gone, and the two lives came crashing together.

Vask unhooked a lamp from its cage and held it close. The flame guttered. For a long moment she said nothing. Then she began, softly, to laugh.

"Blood and brine. I know that face. It's in the broadsheets every Season, simpering beside the Commissioner." She leaned in, and her breath smelled of rum and cloves. "Lady Aya Dravenska. And you've your mother's gift, haven't you? I was at Gallows Quay the morning they hanged Mirela Dravenska. Sold oranges to the crowd. Tidy profit."

The shadows at the chamber's edges leaned inward, as if listening. Aya made herself breathe.

*Father will know. Whatever happens now, he will know.* She saw him reading the report in his study, the lamplight on his spectacles, and her mother's portrait turned to the wall these eleven years. She saw the rope.

"You have a choice to make, Madam Vask," she said. Her voice came out steadier than she had any right to expect. "I suggest you make it with your purse rather than your temper."

One of the bodyguards snorted. Vask raised a hand, and he went quiet.

"Go on, then."

"Kill me, and by Thursday you have a corpse the Admiralty will tear this city apart to account for. Marines, not bluecoats. They don't take bribes, and they don't stop." Aya held the woman's gaze. "Sell me to the Brass Synod, and the Inquisitors will want to know how a Harbour Commissioner's daughter came to be in your cellar. They are thorough men. They will ask you a great many questions."

"And alive?"

"Alive, I am leverage. My father signs every whaling licence in Morska. Every barrel of oil that lights every lamp in this room passes across his desk. Dead, I'm one afternoon's wages. Alive, I'm ten years of them."

Vask turned the raven mask over in her hands, considering it.

"And these two?"

"Are part of the price." Aya did not look at Katra, swaying in the guard's grip, or at Simeon. If she looked at them, her voice would break. "Unharmed. All of us, or none of us."

"Bold, for a girl on her knees."

"I was raised among the Admiralty, madam. Boldness on one's knees is practically a family tradition."

Somewhere beyond the thick stone walls, out across the black water of the harbour, a foghorn sounded. Its long, mournful bellow shivered through the floor. It came again, and then a third time.

The guards shifted. One of them touched the salt at his throat.

"Three for a drowning," Vask murmured. "So my old mum used to say." She tossed the mask to the nearest man. "Put 'em in the brine cells. Separate. Iron on the girl's wrists, and salt in a ring round her door. I'll want paper and ink by morning." She paused at the plinth and laid a proprietary hand on the reliquary. "You'll write to your father, my lady. Very prettily, I should think."

They hauled Aya to her feet. Across the chamber she heard Katra, muzzy with pain, still managing to curse their mothers in three dockside dialects.

As the dark of the corridor swallowed them, Aya felt the thing beyond the windowpane again, close and patient.

*Not yet,* she told it.

It did not leave.

response:
# The Underhold

The door gave inward on oiled hinges, without so much as a whisper, and Aya knew at once that something was wrong. Doors in the Morska hold did not open quietly. They shrieked, they groaned, they announced you to every cutpurse and fence for three floors. This one had been greased, and recently.

Beyond it the underhold stretched long and low, its vaulted ceiling ribbed with the bleached bones of some leviathan the guild's founders had dragged up from the harbour a century past. Gas lamps guttered in iron sconces along the walls. Their light did not so much illuminate the chamber as argue with it, and the shadows of the great ribs fell across the flagstones in long black bars, like the slats of a cage.

At the far end, upon the plinth where the Scythan reliquary ought to have sat, a woman was seated with her boots crossed at the ankle.

"Shut the door, there's a draught," said Ilsabet Crane.

*Hanged. Shackled. Rotting in the Brinewater gaol.* Aya had heard it from three separate mouths before dawn. She had believed it, because she had wanted to.

Shapes peeled away from the shadows between the ribs. Six men, perhaps seven, in oilskin coats that stank of rendering fat. Two carried Halloway repeaters, all brass and walnut, their pressure-bulbs hissing softly. The largest held a flensing hook as long as Aya's arm. His face was a ruin of old burns, and he smiled at Katra as though he knew her.

"Ilsabet," Simeon said, very carefully, in the tone of a man addressing a dog of uncertain temper. "You're looking remarkably un-arrested."

"Am I? How kind of you to notice, Simeon." Crane rose. She was smaller than her legend, grey at the temples, with a seaman's rolling gait and a pistol thrust through her sash as casually as a gentleman's handkerchief. "I bought the constables a fortnight's drink to put on that little pantomime. Cheaper by half than rooting out the rot myself. I said to Garrick, I said, leave the door open and see which rats come scurrying for the cheese." She spread her hands. "And here you are. My clever little rats."

Aya reached inward, past thought and breath, toward the cold place behind her eyes where the immateria pressed against the thin skin of the world. She felt the things that waited there stir and turn their blind attention towards her—

—and then a sound like a dentist's drill set into her skull, and the cold place slammed shut.

She staggered. Against the wall, half hidden behind a leviathan rib, squatted a contraption of brass coils and glass baffles, its innards sloshing with luminous whale oil. It thrummed. Aya tasted copper.

"Hartley damper," Crane said. "Cost me a king's ransom from a defrocked Admiralty engineer. I'd heard whispers we had a *practitioner* among us." She spat the word, and two of her men made the sign of the anchor across their chests. "Seize them."

There was no struggle worth the name. Katra got a knife half free before the burned man's hook was at her throat. Simeon raised his hands at once, which Aya would have thought cowardly an hour ago and now thought merely wise. Rough hands forced her to her knees on the freezing stone.

Crane crouched before her. Her breath smelled of clove and gin.

"Now then. Let's see the face of the thing that's been calling devils up through my floorboards."

*No.* The word rang through Aya like a bell. *Not this. Anything but—*

The mask came away. Cold air struck her cheeks.

For a long moment Crane only stared. Then she laughed. It began low and rose until it bounced among the ribs overhead, and her men shifted uneasily.

"Well, God's teeth. The Halvorsen girl. Lord Halvorsen's own precious daughter." Crane tilted Aya's chin up with one callused finger. "I saw your mother swing, you know. Ashgate Square, nine years back. Pissed herself at the end, poor cow. They all do."

Aya's vision swam red. Behind her eyes the immateria clawed at the damper's iron silence and could not get through.

*Father will learn of it. The broadsheets. The Lords' Inquiry. They will dig up her bones to see if she taught me, and they'll find that she did.*

"Garrick," Crane said, standing. "The canal. Weight them proper this time."

"Wait." The word left Aya's throat like a cough. "Wait. You're a merchant, Ilsabet, whatever else you are. Do the sums."

Crane paused. "Go on, then. Entertain me."

"My father sits on the Board of Leviathan Concessions. He holds four shares in the Kessgard Rendering Company and the Admiralty's ear besides." Aya forced her voice level, forced it into the drawing-room cadence she had despised her whole life. "Drown me and you get nothing but a corpse and a city full of constables. Ransom me and he'll pay. He'll pay quietly. He's spent nine years paying to keep my mother's name out of polite company."

"Aya," Katra hissed. "Don't you dare beg her."

"I'm not begging. I'm *bargaining*."

Crane circled her slowly, boot-heels clicking on the flags. "And the other buyer? You've forgot the other buyer, love. The Witchfinder's Office pays forty sovereigns a head for a proven practitioner. A lord's daughter?" She whistled. "They'd have you on the gallows before Michaelmas, and they'd pay me a hundred for the privilege of the sermon."

*She's right.* The thought was a stone dropped down a well. *There is no version of tonight where I go home and wear the green silk to the Ashcombes' supper. That girl is dead already. She died the moment the mask came off.*

"Then sell me to whoever pays best," Aya said, and was surprised at how steady she sounded. "But not tonight. Hold me. Let them bid against one another. My father will pay to keep me hidden; the Witchfinders will pay to drag me out. Set them against each other and you'll bleed both dry." She held Crane's gaze. "And let these two go. They're worth nothing to anyone."

"Speak for yourself," Simeon muttered.

The gas lamps flickered. For an instant the shadows of the ribs seemed to lengthen and lean inward, as though something on the far side of the damper's silence were pressing its face against the glass of the world, waiting.

Crane looked at Aya for a long while.

"Lock them in the brine cellar," she said at last. "All three. I'll think on it."

As they dragged her away, Aya felt that cold presence follow, patient and hungry, just beyond the brass.

# The Underhold

The door gave without protest. That, more than anything, turned Aya's blood to slush.

Beyond lay the underhold, a vaulted cistern of old Scythan stone, its ribs slick with centuries of seep. Whale-oil lamps hung from flensing hooks along the walls, throwing a jaundiced, greasy light that made every shadow look like something crouching. The air stank of tallow, brine, and the sweet, rotten musk of ambergris. At the far end, upon a plinth of leviathan bone, sat the reliquary: a black iron casket bound in chain, humming at a pitch Aya felt in her molars more than heard.

*Tick. Tick. Tick.* Simeon's pocket watch counted out the silence from his waistcoat.

"Bit quiet," Katra muttered, thumb on the hilt of her gutting knife. "Don't like quiet. Quiet's what you get before the constable's whistle."

"Quiet," said Simeon, "is what you get when someone has arranged for it."

Then the lamps flared, all at once, as if the oil itself had drawn breath.

They stepped from the alcoves as neatly as dancers: six of them, harpooners from the guild's dockside crews, each shouldering a brass-banded pneumatic carbine with valves still hissing. And between them, unhurried, came a woman in widow's black, her silver hair pinned beneath a veil of jet beads. Her cane clicked against the flagstones. Its head was a carved sperm whale's skull, the eyes set with ground glass.

Madame Ilsabet Grayne. The Widow of Morska. Who had, by every account Aya had bribed, cajoled, and stolen that morning, been dragged from her bed in irons at four o'clock and carted off to Blackwater Gaol.

"Good evening, children," the Widow said. "Do mind the step. Damp gets into everything down here."

*Tick. Tick.*

Aya's hand twitched. Beneath her ribs, the immateria stirred, that cold, bottomless place her mother had called *the other tide*, where things with too many joints waited to be invited. She reached for it.

It recoiled from her like a slug touched with salt.

"Ah," said the Widow, watching Aya's face with interest. "You feel it. Hallowed oil, pressed by the Sisters of St. Cael and cut with quicksilver. Dreadfully expensive. I've been burning it in every lamp on this level since dawn." She smiled with yellowed teeth. "I'd heard tell one of my lieutenants could call up devils. Thought it prudent."

"Your arrest," Simeon said evenly. "A fiction."

"A *lure*, Mister Hale. The constabulary owed me a favour, and I wished to learn which of my dear ones would come sniffing at my strongbox before my bed was cold." She tilted her head toward the casket. "Three, it seems. I confess I'd hoped for none."

Katra spat on the stones. "You'd have done the same, you dried-up old—"

A carbine barrel pressed under her jaw. Its valve breathed a soft, wet hiss. Katra fell silent.

"Lay down your steel," the Widow said. "I'll not ask twice. There are plenty of hooks on these walls."

*Tick.*

Aya did the arithmetic of it. Six guns. Hallowed oil choking her gift. A drowned stone room with one door. She dropped her stiletto. A heartbeat later, Simeon's revolver followed. Katra's knife was last, and it clattered loudest.

The harpooners bound their wrists with tarred rope that stank of the slaughterdecks and forced them to their knees on the wet flagstones. Then the Widow crossed to Aya and, with the crook of her cane, lifted the lacquered mask from her face.

Lamplight fell on her skin. Aya watched recognition arrive in the old woman's eyes the way frost spreads across a pane.

"Well," the Widow breathed. "Well, well. Lady Aya Vantreil."

The name rang off the vaulted stone like a bell for the dead.

*There it is,* Aya thought. Her throat had gone tight as a garrotte. *Not the guns. Not the rope. That.* Her name, spoken aloud in this pit, chained to everything she'd done in the dark. She saw it all unspool: her father's face as the magistrate's letter arrived, the scandal sheets crying *WITCH'S GET UNMASKED*, the salons of Saltcourt Row going silent when she entered. And at the end of it, the gallows on Morska Square. The same crossbeam. The same knot. She remembered her mother's bare feet, turning slowly in the wind.

"The witch's daughter," the Widow murmured, almost fondly. "Hanged, wasn't she? I watched. Half the city did. She didn't scream, I'll give her that."

"No," Aya said. Her voice came out steadier than she had any right to. "She didn't. And neither shall I, Madame, so if you mean to have me weep, you'll be disappointed."

*Tick. Tick.*

"I mean to have you dead, girl. All three of you. In the harbour, with ballast in your coats."

"Then you're a poor merchant," Aya said, "and I'd heard better of you."

The Widow's brow arched. The beads of her veil clicked.

"Go on, then," the Widow said, with frank amusement. "Sing for your supper."

Aya drew breath. *Speak as Father speaks to the Admiralty. As though the outcome were already settled.*

"Dead, I'm a corpse in the harbour, and corpses talk. My father has the ear of the Harbourmaster, the Lord Lieutenant, and three directors of the Leviathan Company. When I fail to come down to breakfast, he will tear this city apart plank by plank, and he'll begin with the docks. Your docks." She held the old woman's gaze. "Alive, I'm leverage. A ransom paid quietly. A key to every house on Saltcourt Row. A Vantreil in your pocket, Madame, rather than a Vantreil at your throat."

"Or," said the Widow softly, "I deliver you to the Witchfinders bound and gagged, collect the Crown's bounty, and let your father's name drown in your mother's shame. Who'd hear a word he said then?"

Aya felt the floor tilt. Beside her, Simeon's watch counted on, maddeningly calm.

*Tick. Tick. Tick.*

"You could," Aya said, and her voice did not break, though something inside her did. "Once. A bounty pays once. I'd pay for the rest of my life."

For a long moment, the only sound in the underhold was the drip of seep water and the patient ticking of the watch.

Then the Widow of Morska began, very quietly, to laugh.

response:
# The Last Outpost

## Chapter Three: Vega, Neat

The Vega is the good stuff, so I reach past the bottle I water down for Brannoc and pull the real one from the top shelf.

"Rough shift?" I ask, pouring a generous two fingers.

"Rough month." The stranger's tendrils are curled tight against their skull, the way a Kesh's go when they've been holding their breath too long. "Rough year, honestly. Is it always this quiet?"

I glance around. Brannoc is asleep in his booth with his boots on the table. The Halloway sisters are cheating each other at dice. Two drill-jockeys by the viewport are pretending they aren't in love, which has been going on for four months and is the best entertainment we've got.

"This is a busy night."

"Good." They knock back half the double. "Quiet's good."

"You'd be the first person to say so. Most folks who wash up here are bored inside a week."

"I could do with a week of bored." They turn the glass slowly, watching the amber catch the light. "I could do with a year of it."

Behind me, a glass shatters.

The stranger nearly comes off the stool. Their tendrils flare out like a startled anemone, and their right hand disappears inside their coat. Across the room, Teo stares at the shards around his feet with the look of a boy watching his wages evaporate.

"Easy," I say. "That's just Teo. He breaks one a night. We've started a pool."

Slowly, the hand comes back out. Empty. "Sorry. I'm... sorry."

"Don't be sorry. Just know that whatever's in that coat stays in that coat. House rule." I lean on the bar so my hip rests against the stun baton clipped beneath it. Old habits. "Anything else I should know?"

"Probably." They wrap both hands around the glass. "You're Nettle."

It isn't a question, and I don't like that it isn't. "Most people call me Nets."

"Not the people who sent me."

I keep my face pleasant. Pleasant is a muscle, and I've had six years to build it. "And who sent you?"

"My name's Pell." They pause, as if the name might mean something. It doesn't. "Iridia Vance sent me."

The room doesn't change. Brannoc still snores. The Halloways still squabble. But the floor under me seems to tilt half a degree, the way it does when the grav-plates hiccup.

"Iridia's dead," I say.

"She is now." Pell's tendrils droop. "She wasn't three weeks ago."

I pour myself a drink. I don't usually drink on shift. I drink it anyway.

"Three weeks ago," I repeat.

"She'd been hiding on Dresh Station. Running a little repair shop, if you can believe it. Fixing nav-units for freighters."

"I can't believe it, actually. Iridia couldn't fix a sandwich."

The smallest smile crosses Pell's face. "She said you'd say that. She said a lot of things about you."

"I'm sure she did. Most of them true and none of them flattering." I set the glass down harder than I mean to. "What happened?"

"Some people found her. The same people she was hiding from. The same people you're hiding from, she said." Pell glances at the door, then back at me. "She gave me something before they got to her. Told me if anything happened, I should find the Wren. Said the Wren would be pouring drinks at the edge of the universe, pretending to be someone else."

Nobody has called me that in six years. Hearing it from a stranger's mouth feels like finding a stranger wearing my coat.

"The Wren is retired," I say.

"She said you'd say that too."

"Did she tell you what I'd do next?"

"She said you'd threaten to throw me out an airlock."

"Clever woman." I don't smile. "What did she give you?"

Pell reaches into the coat, slowly this time, eyes on mine, and sets a small object on the bar. It's a nav-core, palm-sized, the casing scorched along one edge. A tiny blue light pulses inside it, steady as a heartbeat.

I know that pulse. I helped steal the thing that makes it.

"Put that away," I say quietly.

Pell does. "You know what it is."

"I know exactly what it is, and I know exactly who wants it back. Which means I know exactly what's coming through that door." My voice stays low, conversational, the voice I use for drunks who are about to throw a punch. "How far behind you are they?"

"I don't know. A day. Maybe two. I took the long way, through the Corvan drift—"

"A day." I close my eyes. "You led them here."

"I didn't have anywhere else to—"

"There are forty people living on this rock, Pell. Miners. Families. A boy who can't hold a glass. That man in the booth has been sleeping in that exact spot for eleven years. They took me in when I had nothing but a fake name and a bad cough. They didn't ask questions." I open my eyes. "And you've just painted a target on every one of them."

Pell flinches, and somehow that's worse than if they'd argued. "I know. I know. I'm sorry. But she said you were the only one who could get it to the Archive. She said you knew the route through the Hollow."

"Nobody knows the route through the Hollow. That's the point of the Hollow."

"She said you'd done it twice."

"Then she also told you what it cost the second time."

A long silence. Pell finishes the Vega. Their tendrils curl and uncurl, curl and uncurl.

"She told me to tell you something," Pell says at last. "If you said no."

"I haven't said no."

"You haven't said yes."

I wait.

"She said the *Cassiopeia* wasn't your fault." Pell holds my gaze. "She said she should have told you that a long time ago."

The bar is very quiet now, or maybe it just feels quiet. I find myself studying the scratches in the countertop, the ones I've wiped over a thousand times, the ones I know by heart.

"Nets?" Teo appears at my elbow, holding the broken pieces in a rag. "Sorry about the glass. Put it on my tab?"

"Sure, Teo." My voice sounds normal. I'm almost proud of that. "Who had Tuesday in the pool?"

"Brannoc, I think."

"Course he did."

Teo wanders off. Pell is still watching me, waiting.

I take the Vega down from the top shelf and pour two more.

"Drink," I say. "Then start from the beginning. All of it."

Outside the viewport, the asteroids drift past in the dark, slow and patient, the way they always have. For the first time in six years, I find myself counting the hours.

response:
# Chapter Seven: Wobble

The gravity hiccups at twenty-two hundred, right as I'm topping off Grandma Tull's ale, and the foam lifts off the glass like it's considering a career change.

"Easy," I tell it, and press my thumb to the rim until the field settles. The foam sinks back down, chastened.

"You talk to the beer now?" Tull asks.

"Beer listens. You don't."

She cackles, a sound like a rock drill with a head cold, and carries her glass back to the corner where the Okonkwo brothers are losing at holo-dice to a Brask merchant with four very honest-looking hands. Somebody's put old Earth jazz on the speakers again. The recyclers hum. Ice clinks. The Last Outpost is doing what it does best, which is being the warmest place within forty light-minutes.

That's when the stranger sits down.

They're Vahrani, I think: tall, grey-green, with a crown of tentacled dreads that are supposed to drape loose and lazy. These are knotted and twitching, half of them pointing the wrong way, like they've been slept on in a cargo crate. Maybe they have.

"Vega whisky, neat." A pause. "Better make that a double."

"Rough shift?"

"Rough year."

I pull the bottle from the top shelf, the real stuff, not the stills-in-the-airlock stuff, and pour. Halfway through, the gravity dips again. The whisky sloshes sideways in the glass, climbs one wall, and slides back. The stranger grabs the bar with both hands.

"First time on the Outpost," I say.

"That obvious?"

"Nobody grabs the bar after the first week. The station's got a heartbeat. You get used to it." I slide the glass over. "I'm Nets."

Their dreads go still. Every one of them. That's not a good sign in a Vahrani. That's a held breath.

"Nets," they repeat. "Short for something?"

"Short for 'I don't tell strangers my full name.'"

"Fair." They drink half the double in one swallow and wince. "I'm Ilo."

"Welcome, Ilo. Mining or merchanting?"

"Neither." Ilo turns the glass slowly on the bar, watching the amber tilt with each tiny pulse of the field. "I'm looking for someone."

"Plenty of someones out here. Most of them are looking to not be found."

"This one used to be a cartographer. Jump routes. Very good. The kind of good where people say your name in the same breath as a curse." Ilo's eyes come up. They're black, with a ring of silver, and steady in a way the rest of them isn't. "Nettle Ashvane."

I keep wiping the glass in my hand. I've been wiping it for a while. It's very clean.

"Never heard of her."

"You're lying."

"I'm a bartender. It's half the job." I set the glass down. "The other half is knowing when to cut someone off."

"I'm not drunk."

"Not yet."

Ilo reaches into their jacket. Across the room, Tull's laugh stops mid-cackle; she's got a sixth sense for a hand going into a coat. I shake my head at her, small. She settles back, but she doesn't stop watching.

Ilo lays a data-shard on the bar and taps it. A hologram blooms between us: a woman in a Corvane Syndicate uniform, hair cropped regulation-short, standing in front of a star map that glows like a wound. She's younger. Leaner. She doesn't look like she's ever laughed at anything.

I haven't seen her in nine years. I was hoping to keep it that way.

"Put that away," I say quietly.

"So you do know her."

"Put it away, Ilo."

They do. The light dies. The jazz keeps playing, and somewhere behind me the dishwasher drone bumps into the same corner it always bumps into, and none of it feels like home anymore.

"Who sent you?" I ask.

"You know who."

"Corvane doesn't exist anymore. The Accord broke it up."

"The Accord broke up the *name*." Ilo finishes the whisky. "The people are still there. They just wear nicer clothes now."

"And they want me back."

"They want the Thessaly route."

The gravity drops, hard this time, a real stomach-lurcher, and every glass in the bar lifts a millimetre off its coaster. A dozen patrons say *whoa* in a dozen languages. Then it catches, and everything thunks back down.

I don't move. I'm not sure I could.

"There is no Thessaly route," I say.

"There's a rumour you mapped a way through the Thessaly Drift. Uncharted. Unpatrolled. Six weeks shaved off the run to the core worlds. And there's a rumour that the night before you vanished, you burned every copy except the one in your head."

"Rumours are cheap out here."

"Not this one." Ilo's dreads start to move again, slowly curling inward. "They've got my sister, Nets."

Oh.

Oh, no.

"Her name's Kesa," Ilo says, and their voice cracks right down the middle. "She's nineteen. She owed money to the wrong people, and the wrong people sold the debt to the worse people. They told me: find Ashvane, bring her in, and Kesa walks. I've been looking for eleven months. I followed a rumour about a bartender who could fix a nav-computer by listening to it. I didn't think..." They laugh, and there's nothing funny in it. "I didn't think you'd be *nice*."

"I'm not that nice."

"You gave me the good whisky."

I look at the bottle. I did. Damn it.

"Have you told them?" I ask. "That you found me?"

Ilo is quiet for too long.

"My ship has a tracking beacon. Theirs, not mine. It pings every thirty-six hours with my location." They swallow. "It pinged when I docked."

"So they know you're here."

"They know I'm *here*. They don't know you are. Not yet." Ilo slides the empty glass toward me. "I've got until the next ping to decide what I tell them."

"And what happens when you decide?"

"That depends on you."

Behind me, the station creaks, a long settling groan. The whisky bottle trembles on the shelf. Across the room, Grandma Tull rises from her chair and starts walking toward the bar, slow and deliberate, the way she walks when she's about to get involved in something.

I pick up the bottle.

"Thirty-six hours?"

"Thirty-four, now."

I pour us both a double. The liquid shivers in the glass, and this time I don't steady it.

# The Last Outpost

## Chapter Three: The Ring

The ring on the counter has been there longer than I have. Somebody set a mug of Ganymede stout down hot on the synthwood maybe a decade ago, and no solvent in the belt has shifted it since. I wipe it anyway. It gives my hands something to do while my ears do the real work.

Tonight my ears are on Pell and Ysolde at the end of the bar, who are pretending not to be in love over a shared plate of fried krill-chips. They're also on Old Marrow, who is losing at cards to a hauler bot and blaming the ventilation.

Then the airlock cycles, and a stranger stumbles in looking like she's been dragged backward through a debris field.

She's Thessan, by the dreads: a dozen thick, tentacled ropes that ought to hang in a neat fall down her back. Instead they're askew and twitching, coiling and uncoiling like they can't agree on which direction to flee. Their tips have gone a bruised violet. She plops onto the stool in front of me without looking at anyone.

"Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double."

"Rough shift?" I pour. Vega's the good stuff, amber with a faint blue shimmer. I slide it over and go back to my ring.

She drinks half in one swallow. "Rough month."

"Those happen out here. Belt's hard on everyone." Wipe, wipe. "I'm Nets."

"I know who you are."

My rag stops for a second. Then it starts again, the same slow circle.

"Most folks do, eventually," I say. "Only bar for six hundred thousand klicks. I'm practically a landmark."

"No." She sets down the glass. One of her dreads uncurls toward me, then thinks better of it. "I mean I *know* who you are. Nettle Ashkaar. Formerly of the Concord Auditory Corps."

Down the bar, Ysolde laughs at something Pell said. Old Marrow swears at the bot. The air scrubbers hum. The whole little world of the Outpost carries on, and nobody notices that mine has just tipped fifteen degrees off its axis.

"Don't know the name," I say.

"Sure." She reaches into her jacket. My free hand drifts toward the shelf under the counter where I keep a few things that aren't glasses. But she only pulls out a data slate and lays it face-up between us.

It's me. Younger. Hair regulation-short, uniform collar sharp enough to cut glass. My eyes in that picture are colder than I remember them being.

I wipe the ring. "Handsome girl. Shame about the haircut."

"There's a bounty on her, issued six days ago. Two hundred thousand credits, alive." She taps the slate. "Concord wants her back for something called the Halvery inquiry."

I know what Halvery is. I know the smell of it. I keep wiping.

"And you came all this way to collect."

"I came all this way because I took the job." Her dreads curl tight against her skull. "I'm a tracer. I find people. I followed fuel receipts, a freight manifest, and one very drunk ore broker on Kessik Station, and they all pointed here."

"So why are you drinking instead of cuffing?"

She finishes the whisky. I pour her another without being asked. My hands are steady. I'm proud of that.

"Because I read the file," she says quietly. "The real one, not the summary they gave the tracers. I had a cousin on Halvery when it happened. The file says you're the one who blew the whistle. Then it says the whistle got buried, and the Corps put your name on the charge sheet instead of theirs."

Wipe. Wipe. The ring doesn't budge. It never does.

"That's a nice story," I say. "Lots of nice stories in the belt."

"Stop that."

"Stop what?"

"The rag." The violet at the tips of her dreads is bleeding toward red. "You've cleaned that exact spot forty times since I sat down. It's not getting any cleaner."

I look down. She's right. I fold the rag and set it on the counter, and suddenly I don't know what to do with my hands at all.

"What's your name?" I ask.

"Quill."

"Okay, Quill. Say I'm this Nettle person. What happens now?"

"Now's the part I don't like." She turns the glass slowly. "I'm not the only tracer on the contract. Concord put it out wide. I'm just the fastest. There's a crew behind me: Bastian Rook and his people. Two days, maybe three. They won't buy you a drink first."

The name lands like a cold hand on the back of my neck. Everyone on the outer rim has heard of Rook.

"And you're telling me this why? Two hundred thousand is a lot of reasons to keep your mouth shut."

"I know." She laughs, but there's nothing in it. "My ship's loan comes due in thirty days. If I don't bring you in, someone else will, and I lose the ship anyway. So I'm sitting here trying to figure out whether I'm warning you or apologizing in advance."

At the end of the bar, Pell has finally worked up the nerve to take Ysolde's hand. Old Marrow has won a round and is crowing about it. These people took me in with no questions when I came off a cargo hauler three years ago with one bag and a name I'd made up on the trip.

If Rook comes here, he won't care who's in the way.

"Which is it?" I ask. "Warning or apology?"

Quill looks at me for a long time. Her dreads hang still and colorless, waiting.

"Ask me again tomorrow," she says.

She drops a credit chip on the bar, more than the whisky's worth, and doesn't get up.

I pick up the rag. I find the ring. And I start to wipe.

Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. Include references to the gladiator's favorite Roman deity or mythological figure. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
response:
# The Free Meal

They set out the tables at dusk on the night before the games, so that Rome could come and watch us eat.

The lanista called it the *cena libera*, the free meal, as if the freedom were ours. It was not. It belonged to the fullers and clerks and bakers' wives who had paid a doorman two coppers to crowd the benches of the practice ring and count our teeth. I had sat on those benches once. I remembered the smell from up there: roast pork, cheap wine, and something sour underneath, like fear sweating through wool. From the floor of the Ludus Magnus I learned that the sour smell is your own.

There was meat that night, real meat. There were sausages split and blistered over charcoal, a boar with its tusks gilded for show, and figs drowned in honey. Most days they fed us barley and beans until we were thick as wine jars. *Hordearii*, the crowd called us. Barley men. Fat bleeds slow and shallow, and a slow bleed makes a long fight. Tonight there was Falernian, watered, poured by a boy with a burn scar up one arm. Thrax, beside me, ate as though it were his last meal, which was a joke nobody at those tables ever made out loud.

And the noise. Rome was another animal after dark. Wheeled carts were banned from the streets by day, so at sundown the city filled with iron rims grinding over basalt, drivers cursing their mules, and oxen groaning under marble bound for the new forum the Emperor was building with Dacian gold. Over that came the crowd: wagers shouted bench to bench, a hawker crying hot chickpeas, a woman's laugh like a dropped pot. And my arena name, thrown down at me like a coin.

"Pistor! Hey, Baker!"

I was a baker's son from the Subura. My father's ovens stood four streets from the men shouting at me. When the tenement above the shop burned, the year I turned nineteen, he borrowed to rebuild, then borrowed again to pay the first loan. The man who held the debt was patient the way a river is patient. My father died owing. In Rome a debt does not die with the man. It moves into the house and sits at the table.

So I walked to the ludus and swore the oath. *Uri, vinciri, verberari, ferroque necari.* To be burned, to be bound, to be beaten, to be killed by the sword. The lanista put two thousand sesterces into my mother's hands for those words. She wept, and then she counted it, because she was not a fool.

The crowd loves a free man who sells himself. A slave on the sand is just meat; there's no story in him. A citizen who walks in through the gate on his own feet gives them something to chew on. They called to me the way you'd call to a horse you'd known as a foal.

At the far tables sat the Dacians.

There were forty of them that night, out of the thousands Trajan had dragged back across the Danube in chains. Ten thousand gladiators, one hundred and twenty-three days of games: the heralds cried the numbers in every forum, as though the size of it were the point. Perhaps it was. King Decebalus's treasure had come home in carts, and those carts were rumbling past us in the dark, and Rome would eat and watch and never ask who paid.

The Dacians didn't touch the food. They sat with their long hair unbound and their palms flat on the boards, looking up at the crowd exactly the way the crowd looked down at them. One was a boy with a first beard, no older than my sister. Someone on the benches threw a fig. It struck his cheek and dropped into his lap. He did not move.

When I took the oath I told myself I was different from them. I chose. I tell myself that still. But my choice was made by a fire and a debt and a moneylender with soft hands, and the boy's was made by an Emperor who needed a triumph. When I tried to find the place where those two things stopped being the same, I couldn't.

Before the meal I had gone down to the shrine of Nemesis at the mouth of the tunnel that runs to the great amphitheater. Every man in the ludus has his god. Thrax swears by Hercules, who was a slave once and labored his way onto Olympus. Thrax likes the arithmetic of that. I never cared for Hercules. Hercules won. I keep to Nemesis, she of the wheel and the measuring rod with the griffin crouched at her heel, who sees what is owed and sees that it is paid. I was a baker's son. I understood measures. Short a man his loaf by an ounce and the aediles will fine you. Short the gods, and she comes.

I had pressed my thumb to the cold stone of her wheel and asked her for nothing so small as victory. I asked her to keep the account honest. Whatever I was owed, and whatever Rome was owed, let it come round.

Near the end of the meal I saw my sister at the rail.

Tertulla was fifteen, with our mother's chin, and she was clutching a cloth bundle to her chest. A guard waved her off. I stood, and the lanista, who knew the value of a good story, let me go to her.

She had brought bread. Of course she had. It was a small round loaf, scored into eight wedges the way our father scored them, still faintly warm from an oven that was no longer ours.

"Mother says eat it in the morning," she said. "Not tonight. Tonight you'll be full of their food."

I couldn't speak, so I nodded. Her eyes went past me to the Dacians. "Will they make you fight one of them?"

"I don't know," I said, which was true. The order of bouts wasn't posted until dawn.

She went back into the crowd, and the crowd closed over her like water.

On the way to my bench I passed the far tables. I broke a wedge from the loaf and set it before the boy, beside the fig. He looked at the bread, then at me, and did not take it.

Later, when the torches had guttered and the guards were herding us down to the cells, I looked back. The fig was still on the table. The bread was gone.

All night the carts went on above us, grinding gold into marble. I lay with the loaf against my chest and tried to work out what I owed, and to whom, and I could not make the sums come right.

# The Shape of September

The armorer let me hold the sica for the length of one honey cake, which was how Pudens measured all time. He sat on his stool by the armory door and ate slowly. The guard behind me rested his spear point a hand's width from my kidneys, and I drew the whetstone down the inside of the curve the way my grandfather had taught me to sharpen a vine knife.

The blade was as long as my forearm and bent near the middle, like a finger beckoning. The Romans call it a Thracian weapon. To them there is no difference between a Thracian and a Getan and a Dacian. We are all one creature from beyond the Danube, trousered and long-haired and good for an afternoon. But I knew that curve before I ever saw a sword. In my father's valley every boy carried a little sickle-bladed knife at harvest to cut the clusters from the vine. When the lanista's man first pushed the sica into my hand four years ago, my palm closed around it and I nearly wept. It was the shape of September. It was my mother's hands, stained purple to the wrist.

They do not know that. They gave it to me because it suited the costume.

"Done," said Pudens, licking honey from his thumb. I laid the sica back on its rack, the spear point went away, and I was a man with nothing in his hands again.

---

The cena libera began at dusk. Before every great day of games, the city is invited to watch the men who may die tomorrow eat their last free meal. So the long tables were set out in the courtyard of the Ludus Magnus, the gates were thrown open, and Rome came in to look at us.

I remember the smell first. There was roast pork crackling in its fat, and fish sauce, and the sour reek of cheap wine. Under that came torch pitch and the sweat of three hundred spectators pressed against the rope. Beneath everything lay the smell that never left the city in late summer: the Tiber, sluggish and green, carrying the tanneries and latrines down to the sea. Beyond the walls, the cranes of the Emperor's new forum still creaked on their treadwheels. Trajan was building with Dacian gold. Everyone said so. They said the river Sargetia had been turned from its bed to uncover Decebalus's treasure, and that there was so much of it the price of gold had fallen in the Subura. They said our king's head had been thrown down the Gemonian Stairs, and the crowd had cheered until it rolled into the street.

I had not seen it. I had been here, oiling my skin, learning to die beautifully.

Licinus sat beside me, tearing a loaf into pieces he did not eat. He had been a citizen once. When his father's debts came due, he sold himself to the lanista for two thousand sesterces and swore the oath: to be burned, bound, beaten, and killed by the sword. He still wore his grain token on a cord around his neck, a bronze tessera that had once entitled him to the monthly dole. A man who swears the gladiator's oath is infamis. He cannot vote, cannot plead in court, cannot be buried among decent people. Licinus could not use the token anymore, but he could not bring himself to throw it away.

"Look at them," he said. "My old neighbors. Half of them collected free grain at the Porticus Minucia this morning. Now they get us."

"You are bitter."

"I am Roman," Licinus said. "By the end of the month, it is the same thing."

A girl leaned over the rope and held a ribbon out toward me, laughing, until her friend pulled her back by the arm. A fat man in a good tunic took wagers on a wax tablet. Farther down, a senator's son with the broad purple stripe stared at a Gaul named Arvernus as if he were pricing a horse. Arvernus stared back and slowly put a whole fig into his mouth. The boy looked away first, and I liked the Gaul for that.

I ate, which disappointed the crowd. They prefer a man who cannot. I ate the pork and an egg and the bread and drank my wine watered. I thought about how strange it is to be fed by people because they want to watch you bleed. The Emperor feeds them grain so they will not riot. He feeds them us so they will love him. He had promised months of games for his victory over my people, ten thousand fighters, the criers said. The city had cheered the number as if it were a harvest.

Near the end, when the torches had burned low and the crowd had thinned, the lanista came down the line. Aulus Ninnius was a soft man with ringed fingers and a voice like a physician's. He stopped behind me and rested his hand on my shoulder.

"You've heard the new shipment came in," he said. "From Sarmizegetusa."

I had heard. All afternoon, through the wall of the holding pens, men had been speaking my language. It was not the clipped thing I spoke now, worn smooth by four years of Latin, but the old mountain tongue with all its edges still on. One of them had been singing a threshing song. Every valley sings it with its own last line.

"The procurator wants something special for the opening," Ninnius said. "Dacian against Dacian. The raw thing against the polished thing. He thinks the crowd will appreciate the comparison."

He squeezed my shoulder kindly, the way a man pats a dog he means to sell.

"They're giving him a falx, the long one. You'll have your little sica. I thought you'd want to know."

When he had gone, Licinus said nothing. He only pushed the rest of his bread toward me. Across the courtyard, the cranes had finally stopped. In the quiet I could hear, very faintly, the man in the pens still singing. I found my lips moving with him. When he reached the end, he sang it with my grandmother's last line.

# The Free Supper

They fed us in the open the night before the games, the way a farmer shows a horse at market.

The tables stood along the colonnade of the Ludus Magnus, so close to the amphitheatre that its great travertine flank blotted out half the sky. Torches spat in their brackets. The cooks had been at it since noon, and the air hung thick with pork crackling in its own fat, with garum and pepper, with bread still steaming from the ovens on the Caelian. Every other night we ate barley: barley and beans, barley and broth, barley until a layer of soft fat lay over our ribs like a second hide, so that a blade would bleed us loud and slow and give the crowd its money's worth. *Hordearii*, they called us. Barley men. Tonight there was meat, and wine that had not been cut with vinegar, and the Romans had come to watch us eat it.

They pressed against the rope the lanista's men had strung between the columns. There were shopkeepers from the Subura with fish scales on their sleeves, freedmen sweating in borrowed linen, and a knot of young equestrians whose slaves had shoved them a path. They pointed. They made wagers. They studied the way we held our cups, as if a man's death could be read in his knuckles.

"That's the Dacian," someone said, and I did not have to turn to know who they meant.

Five years I had been in Rome. Five years since the first war, when the legions led me out of the burning hills above the Marisus with a rope at my throat and my brother's blood drying in the creases of my hands. My Latin was good now. It was good enough to understand everything they said about me.

Tomorrow the Emperor would open his games. A hundred and twenty-three days, the criers had shouted from every crossroads shrine: ten thousand fighting men, eleven thousand beasts. All of it was paid for with Dacian gold, and all of it celebrated the fact that there was no more Dacia. King Decebalus's head had been thrown down the Gemonian Stairs months ago. I had not gone to see it. Brennus had, and when he described it to me afterward he chose his words so carefully that I knew it had been worse.

He sat across from me now, gnawing a chicken thigh, his red Gaulish beard shining with grease. "Eat," he said. "They don't feed the dead pork."

I ate. The meat was good. That was the shameful part, how good it was.

A woman in a saffron stola leaned over the rope and asked whether she might touch my arm. The man beside her laughed and held her elbow while she did. Her fingers were cool and dry. "For luck," she said. Her eyes were very bright, and I understood that she would watch me tomorrow with those same bright eyes. The jurists named us *infames* and ranked us with actors and pimps. We could not give testimony or be buried among decent people. Yet their wives bought the oil scraped from our skin as face cream, and their brides had their hair parted with a spearpoint dipped in a gladiator's blood. Behind the woman, a man with a clay jar on a strap was asking the guards which of us fought first. Epileptics paid in silver for blood drunk warm from the sand. I watched him write my name on his wax tablet and blow on it gently, as if it were already wet.

Then the carts came.

Wheels were forbidden in the city by day, so at night Rome groaned with them as wine and marble, lime and timber ground over the paving stones until dawn. These carts were drawn by oxen and fitted with cages, and the torchlight slid across the bars and caught on faces. These were not fighters. We were fighters; we had been trained and oiled and fattened. These were the condemned, meant for the beasts at midday, when the better sort went home for lunch. They were men with wild hair and bare feet. There were a few women, and there were boys.

They were speaking my tongue.

I had not heard it in five years except in my own mouth, alone, whispering to keep it from rusting. Now it poured out of the cages, ragged and frightened. A man was calling for water. Someone was praying to Zalmoxis in the old cadence my grandmother used. The crowd jeered and threw bread crusts. The oxen lowed. The first cart turned toward the tunnel that ran beneath the street into the belly of the amphitheatre.

From the third cart, a voice said my name.

It was not the name the lanista gave me. It was my name, the one my mother chose, spoken in an old man's voice, cracked as a dry riverbed. I stood so fast the bench went over. Two guards were at my shoulders before I took a step. Gratus, the lanista, watched from the doorway with his face perfectly still. It was the face of a man who remembered Spartacus every night of his life.

Brennus's hand closed on my wrist. "Sit," he said quietly. "Whoever it is, you can't help him from a cross."

The cart rolled into the dark. The voice did not come again.

Later I lay in my cell. The stink of the latrine trench seeped under the door, and somewhere above me the amphitheatre breathed like a sleeping animal. I did what I had done before every fight since my first. I unwound the red thread from my left wrist. My mother had tied the first one, against the evil eye, and I had knotted on a new length for every man I'd killed. As I retied it, I said their names aloud, in order. Tertius. The Syrian who would not tell me his name, so I said the one the crowd had chanted, Ferox. Aulus. Crixus. There were eleven names. A man who is remembered does not come back to drag down the one who forgot him. That was not a Dacian belief. I had learned it here, from a Thracian who did not survive his third summer. I said his name too, though I had not killed him.

Tonight, when I reached the end, I said a twelfth name. It belonged to the old priest who had blessed my father's spear when I was a boy, and I was nearly certain now that his voice had come from that cart. I said it twice, so he would know someone in Rome still spoke it.

Outside, the carts rolled on until dawn, and every one of them was full.

response:
# The Lighthouse Keeper

**Muckle Flugga Lighthouse, Shetland. 14th March 1961**

Dear Mam,

Landed Tuesday. They couldnae get the boat in on Monday for the swell, so I spent the night at the shore station at Burrafirth eating a stranger's soup.

The rock is smaller than it looked in the photograph. You can walk round the whole thing in the time it takes to boil a kettle. North of us there's one more lump of stone, Out Stack, and then nothing at all till the ice. The Principal, Mr Laurenson, told me that like he was handing me a present.

There's three of us. The work is fine. I sleep fine.

Dinnae send the Courier. It'll be a fortnight old.

Your son,
Robert

---

**Hilltown, Dundee. 23rd March**

Dear Robert,

Your letter came Thursday and I read it out to Mrs Docherty on the stair. She says she's never heard the like, a rock you can walk round while the kettle boils. She wanted to know where you go to the toilet and I said I'd not be asking. I'm sending socks, two pair, and tablet, and the Courier anyway because a fortnight old is still news to you. The coalman's put his price up again. I've moved your father's chair to the window so it gets the sun and I'm not looking at it all night.

Eat your dinners.

Your loving Mam

---

**Muckle Flugga. 30th May 1961**

Dear Mam,

The birds are back. Gannets on every ledge of the stacks, thousands of them, and the racket never stops. There's no night now anyway. You can read on the gallery at midnight.

Mr Laurenson and Geordie have not spoken in nine days over a game of draughts. I carry the messages. "Tell him the tea's mashed." "Tell him I heard."

Geordie ate most of the tablet. Tell Mrs Docherty there is a toilet, it's indoors, and that's all I'll say.

Robert

---

**Hilltown. 17th June**

Dear Robert,

That made me laugh, the draughts. Your father was the same with dominoes. He once didn't speak to Archie Bell from Hogmanay till the Dundee holidays. I've not been to the kirk since Easter. It's my knees, and the stair. Mrs Docherty gets my messages in. I'm fine, don't you be worrying. Write me something longer.

Mam

---

**Muckle Flugga. 9th November 1961**

Mam,

Relief was three weeks late. Wind from the north-west the whole of October and the boat couldnae come near. We were down to tinned peas.

I don't want the Courier. I know I said that before. I'm saying it again. I cannae read about the Overgate and Lochee and folk just getting on with it.

Something daft. I count the stair every night going up to the lamp. I've never got the same number twice.

Robert

---

**Hilltown. 20th November**

Dear Robert,

I'll not send the paper. I'll tell you something instead, since you've told me something. There are days I don't say a word out loud until the wireless comes on at six, and then I say good evening to it, like a daftie. Mrs Docherty has gone to her daughter's in Kirkcaldy. The chair's still at the window. I sit in it now, which I never thought I would.

So we're a pair, you and me. The both of us counting.

Mam

---

**Muckle Flugga. 4th January 1962**

Mam,

At New Year I went down to the landing at two in the morning. I don't know what for. There was a big sea running and I stood at the edge of it a long while. Geordie came and got me. He never said a word to Mr Laurenson, and he gave me what was left of his bottle, and I'm all right now.

I never told you why I took this job. It wasn't the money. It was coming in the door to that chair. So I went and left you sitting with it.

I've written this last bit four times and burnt three.

Rab

---

**Hilltown. 19th January 1962**

Robert, you listen to me.

I have been to Edinburgh. I have never been to Edinburgh in my life, and on Tuesday I went on the train to the Lighthouse Board in George Street in my good coat. A Mr Spence told me nobody but keepers goes on the rock. Not mothers, not anybody. So I asked him where was the nearest I could stand. He got a map out. He was very kind in the end, once he saw I wasn't leaving.

It's a cliff called Hermaness. He's looked at your turns. The 4th of August, the afternoon. You watch for me. I'll be sick in the boat and I don't care.

And that chair is a chair. You didn't leave me with your father. He was gone already. You left me with a chair.

Mam

---

**TELEGRAM. LERWICK. 2 AUG 1962**

LANDED SEASICK DONT LAUGH = MAM

---

**Muckle Flugga. 5th August 1962**

Dear Mam,

I was on the gallery from dinnertime with the glass. Geordie took my watch and wouldnae hear otherwise. Near three o'clock two wee figures came over the top of Hermaness, and one of them was swinging her handbag at the bonxies, and I knew.

Then you held up the tablecloth. The good one, Gran's, the one that only comes out at New Year. I don't know how you got it open in that wind, you and Mrs Laurenson, but it was white against all that green and I could see it plain from here.

Mr Laurenson stripped the sheet off his own bunk. He said, "That's my wife up there with your mother, so." We hung it off the rail. I hope you saw it. I hope it didn't look like we were surrendering.

I've done my sums. Nine days till relief, then the boat to Lerwick and the train. Put his chair back at the table. I'll sit in it.

Your son,
Rab

P.S. Counted the stair last night. Same number as the night before.

response:
# The Lighthouse Keeper

**Sule Skerry Lighthouse, 11th March 1975**

Mam,

Got here Tuesday. Boat couldnae land for two days so we sat off the rock being sick. Two others on: Mr Macaulay the Principal, a Lewis man, and Davie Ross from Wick, who is nineteen and talks enough for all three of us.

The cake came but the sea got in the tin. Dinnae send another. I'm eating fine.

Rab

---

**14 Craigneuk Street, Motherwell, 2nd April 1975**

Dear Robert,

Two days being sick and you tell me in one line. I read it to Agnes Docherty twice before she believed that was the whole letter.

I've given the birds to Jimmy Rae. I couldnae stand them circling the loft at teatime looking for your father.

I'm sending you something. When the Blue Lady died your father cut the ring off her leg with my good scissors and kept it in his waistcoat pocket till the day he went. You'll mind the story: Nantes, 1956, every other bird home by the Sunday and her walking in through the trap on the Wednesday with half a wing, like she'd been to the shops. The ring's that thin now you could bend it with a fingernail, and the numbers are near rubbed off from his thumb. Mind and not lose it.

Are you sleeping?

Your loving Mam

---

**Sule Skerry, 19th June 1975**

Mam,

It doesnae get dark. You light up at eleven and by two the sky's going white over Orkney and the gulls start. I lie with my eyes shut pretending.

The ring's on a bootlace round my neck. Macaulay saw it and asked was I a Catholic.

A pigeon came down on the gallery Thursday in a westerly. Red chequer cock, half dead. Ring says SU 75 W 0442. I've got him in a box in the oil store eating porridge oats. Will you give the number to Jimmy.

Davie's ashore on leave. It's quieter. I thought I'd like that.

Rab

---

**Craigneuk Street, 10th July 1975**

Dear Robert,

Jimmy had him traced in one evening. The bird belongs to a Mr Tom Haldane in Wishaw, who lost him off a Rennes race in May and had given him up. Mr Haldane came round himself to say thank you, in a good jacket, and stayed for his tea. He lost his wife in '72. He says keep the bird dry and quiet and it'll go when it's ready, and don't push it.

He knew your father from the club. Everybody did.

Mam

---

**Sule Skerry, 30th September 1975**

Mam,

Bird's fit. Does two circuits of the tower and comes back in to the oil store. Macaulay caught me talking to it.

That's four letters with Haldane in them.

Rab

---

**Craigneuk Street, 18th November 1975**

Dear Robert,

Yes it is. I'll not pretend to you. Tom has taken me to the pictures twice. I'm sixty-one and I don't need anybody's permission, but I would like yours.

There's a room made up for Christmas.

Your loving Mam

---

**Sule Skerry, 9th December 1975**

Mam,

Da's no two year in Airbles cemetery. You gave his birds away and now you're at the pictures with a man who's only at your door because I lifted his pigeon off a rock. I'm staying on over Christmas. Macaulay's family needs him more than you need me.

Rab

---

**TELEGRAM, 3rd February 1976**

ROBERT KERR SULE SKERRY LIGHTHOUSE = NOTHING SINCE DECEMBER = ONE LINE WILL DO SON = MAM

---

**Sule Skerry, 21st February 1976**

Mam,

The bird went on the eighth of January. Clear morning, wind behind him. He went up and round and off south-east, and I watched till I couldnae tell him from my eyes watering.

Then I stood at the gallery rail most of an hour. I'll not dress it up. I was thinking how far down it was, and how quick, and that you'd have Haldane. Macaulay came up and stood beside me and never said a word. After a while he took my elbow like I was an old woman, and we went down, and he made tea and put sugar in it without asking.

I'm sorry for what I wrote. I don't know what's wrong with me. I hear the engines when they're off.

Rab

---

**Craigneuk Street, 4th March 1976**

My son,

I've read your letter more times than I could tell you. It's in the drawer with your father's things, where it belongs.

There's something you were never told. The winter you were nine, when your father "did his back", it wasnae his back. He didnae rise out his bed for seven weeks and he couldnae say why. The doctor gave him tablets and he put them in the fire. What got him up in the end was Jimmy chapping the door to say the Blue Lady was off her feed. Your father went down to the loft in his semmit, and he came back up for his dinner. That was the spring before Nantes. He was ashamed of it all his days. I should have told you before you went out to that rock, and I'm sorrier for that than you'll ever be for one letter.

You'll put in for a shore station, Robert. Today.

And this. The red chequer walked into Tom's loft on the twelfth of February. Five weeks from your rock to Wishaw, feathers out, thin as a rake, ate like a horse. Tom phoned me at seven in the morning greeting like a wean.

He'd like to show you him. He'll wait. He's good at that.

Mam

---

**Corsewall Point Lighthouse, Stranraer, 12th June 1976**

Mam,

Shore station. There's a house with the job, a garden with nothing in it, and a bus to Stranraer twice a day. The light still turns, but I can see sheep from the kitchen. A man came by on a bicycle last night and said it was a fine evening, and I nearly asked him in.

I've two days off from the 26th. I'll come to Craigneuk Street.

Tell Mr Haldane I'd like to see the bird. And tell him I've a ring he should look at, off a hen that came home from Nantes in '56 with half a wing. He'll have heard of her. Everybody did.

Rab

# The Lighthouse Keeper

**Govan, 3rd October 1961**

Dear David,

I hope this gets to you. I've never posted to a rock before and the man at the counter wasn't sure either. Your father asked was it high enough above the sea, the rock, so I said I'd ask. There's socks in the parcel and a slab of tablet. Don't let the other men at it. Mrs Docherty's Brian got took on at Fairfield's, she's never done telling me on the stair. Your father says nothing about that, which you'll know means plenty.

Write when you can.

Mam

---

**Dubh Sgeir, 19th October**

Dear Mam,

Tell him it's high enough, but the spray comes over the gallery in a westerly, so he's something to look pleased about.

There's three of us on at a time. Mr Muir's the Principal, a Lewis man, says grace over a kipper. Tam Reid's the other, and he whistles. I've the middle watch, two till six, winding the clockwork that turns the lens and pumping the paraffin up to pressure. You'd like the brass. Everything's polished till you can see your face in it.

Tam's had most of the tablet.

Davie

---

**Govan, 2nd December**

Dear David,

Your father says to tell you about Dundee putting five past the Rangers at Ibrox, but I'll not, he's still not right about it.

His chest's bad with the fogs we're having, and the yard's on short time anyway. Coal's up again. Will they let you home for the New Year or is that daft to ask.

Mam

---

**Dubh Sgeir, 30th January 1962**

Mam,

It's daft to ask. It's my turn on.

We'd fog from the Tuesday to the Saturday. When it comes down the horn goes, two blasts every ninety seconds, day and night, and the engines that drive it need minding, so there's no sleeping anyway. You count without meaning to. You lie in the bunk with your whole body waiting on the next one, and when it comes you feel it in your teeth. Muir says after twenty year you stop hearing it. I said I hoped I'd not be here twenty year to find out. He didn't laugh. Nobody laughs much.

Dad'll say I left the din of the yards for this and it serves me right.

I've started having conversations with Mrs Docherty in my head. That's how bad.

Davie

---

**Govan, 14th February**

Dear David,

Don't tell her, she'd be thrilled.

I'll not fuss. Your father's been off his work three weeks. The doctor says stop the Woodbines and he says they're the only thing holding him up. He's deafer than ever, forty year of the riveting. I've to write things on the back of the rent book.

You'll be home in March for your leave. Be civil with him, son. He's not got the words. He never had.

Mam

---

**Dubh Sgeir, 20th April**

Mam,

I'm sorry about the Saturday. I shouldn't have said what I said about the yard, and not in front of you. I've written him separate. Don't read it to him, just give it him.

We'd a bad night Tuesday. The birds go back north this time of year and the light pulls them in. Redwings, Muir says. You hear them hit the glass like somebody chapping a door. In the morning there were forty-odd on the gallery and Tam and me put them over the side with a shovel. Muir said a wee prayer. I didn't mind it.

Davie

---

**Govan, 5th June**

Dear David,

He got it. He read it twice, which for your father is near enough a novel, and put it in the pocket of his good jacket. He's said nothing. I know that doesn't look like much from where you are.

Mam

---

*TELEGRAM — 9 NOV 1962 — NORTHERN LIGHTHOUSE BOARD FOR RELAY TO KEEPER D KERR DUBH SGEIR = FATHER VERY ILL COME IF YOU CAN = MAM*

---

**Dubh Sgeir, 21st November**

Mam,

I don't know when you'll get this. They told me on the radio Tuesday.

The boat came out the Friday after your telegram. I watched from the gallery. It stood off the landing an hour in the swell. Muir and Tam had the rope ready and they couldn't get near. Then it turned and went back. It came again on the Sunday and didn't get past the point. I had my bag packed nine days. I've unpacked it now.

I wanted to tell him I'd stopped minding the horn. I'd started thinking of it like his riveting, a noise you put up with because there's a ship on the other end of it. I never wrote that because I thought there'd be time to say it right.

I'm sorry you were on your own with it.

And Mam, I know he never said any of it. The rock being high enough, the Rangers. That was you. I didn't mind. I'd have taken it from anybody.

Davie

---

**Govan, 4th December 1962**

Dear David,

Your letter came Monday.

We buried him Thursday. Brian Docherty took your cord. Half the yard came, in the rain.

The Rangers was me, aye. The rock wasn't. He asked that himself.

And here's a thing he made me promise not to tell you. Every night since you went he had the wireless on for the shipping forecast, with the ears he had left, his head right against the cloth. He couldn't make out the half of it, so I'd write it down for him on the rent book. Hebrides. Malin. Westerly seven. He'd look at it and say, he'll no get off the morn. Or, they'll get the boat out to him. Every night, David. Fourteen months.

I've kept it on. I don't understand it any better than he did. But last night it said Hebrides, northwest three or four, good, and I thought, that's the boat getting out to him, and I went to my bed.

Stay if you want to stay. You're good at it. He knew that too.

Your loving Mam

# Gareth Is At Lunch

The bell over the door didn't ring so much as scream, and the man who came through it brought half of Cardigan Bay in with him.

He shut the door and pressed his back to it. Through the rain-streaked glass, camera flashes stuttered like lightning that couldn't commit.

"Back door," he said. "Please tell me you've got a back door."

Ffion didn't look up from the till. "I've got a back door. It opens onto the bins and a very territorial gull."

"I'll risk the gull."

"He's called Gareth. He once had a pasty off a vicar."

That got a laugh out of him, low and surprised. Then he did something she would later resent: he looked at her. Properly. The way they must teach at drama school.

"Hi." He peeled off his sunglasses. "Sorry. I'm—"

"Dripping on the Penguin Classics."

He glanced down and stepped sideways, and then the smile arrived. It was slow and expensive, the same one that had been on the side of every bus in Cardiff last summer. "Callum Rees."

"Ffion."

He waited for the rest of it. She let him wait.

"You don't—" He gestured at the whole wet six-foot business of himself. "No?"

"Should I?"

"No! God, no. That's refreshing. That's lovely, actually." He leaned on the counter. "Most people do this thing with their face. Like they've seen a dog do a backflip."

"I'll try not to do it, then."

"You're very good at not doing it."

She moved a stack of Ordnance Survey maps from one end of the counter to the other, for no reason she could have defended in court.

He picked up a book from the shelf by the till. "Staff picks. Who's staff?"

"Me."

"So these are all you. Plath. R.S. Thomas. A book about... peat bogs?"

"It's a very good book about peat bogs."

"I believe you. I'd believe anything in that voice." He tilted his head. "Has anyone ever told you you'd be brilliant on the radio?"

"Has that ever worked on anyone?"

"Constantly. It's a very reliable line." A beat. "It's not working, is it."

"Not as such."

He drummed his fingers on the counter. "Have you seen any of my... no. Appalling question. Forget it."

"I saw the one with the submarine."

His whole face lit up. "*Pressure Point!* And?"

"On a plane. To Malaga."

"And?"

"I woke up over Bordeaux."

He put a hand flat to his chest as if she'd shot him. "You slept through me."

"I'd had a gin."

"I was nominated for a BAFTA for that."

"It was a very restful performance."

Someone rapped on the window. Callum flinched, a small and real flinch, and turned his face toward the Travel section.

"They'll get bored," Ffion said. "It's Aberaeron. Nothing holds anyone's attention here except the honey ice cream."

"You'd be amazed what holds their attention." He rubbed his jaw. "Tomorrow there'll be a photo of me legging it into a bookshop, and some genius will write that I'm having a breakdown. Or I've found God. Or I'm shagging the owner."

The word landed between them and sat there.

"Sorry," he said.

"For the language?"

"For the headline. Not that it'd... I mean, not that you'd..." He stopped. "I'm normally much better at this."

"At what?"

"Talking." It came out thin. "It's sort of my job."

She realised she was turning a bookmark over and over in her fingers, and put it down.

"You've gone a bit Valleys," she said.

"I have not."

"'Shagging the owner.' Pure Pontypridd, that was."

He stared at her. When he answered, his voice had slid seventy miles south-east and twenty years back. "Tonypandy. Don't tell anyone. My agent spent a fortune sanding it off."

"Why?"

"Nobody casts a boy from Tonypandy as a Russian submarine captain." He picked up the peat bog book again, not reading it. "D'you want to know something stupid? I was ten. Urdd Eisteddfod, recitation. Some poem about a fox. I'd practised for months, in the bath, in the car. Mam knew it better than I did. And I walked out on that stage and every word just went. Three hundred people looking at me, and nothing. Forty seconds. Mam timed it afterwards, off the video. Forty seconds of a boy in a school jumper with his mouth open."

Ffion said nothing.

"And that's..." He shrugged and put the poster smile back on, though it didn't fit anymore. "Every premiere, every chat show, I'm still waiting for the bit where they find out there's nothing in here. Just the jumper."

The rain had softened. Outside, the flashes had stopped.

"The fox," Ffion said. "R. Williams Parry?"

He blinked. "...Yeah."

"I did that one. Year after you, probably. Came third."

"Third's good."

"There were three of us."

This time she was the one who laughed, before she could stop it. He looked at her as though she'd handed him something. Which, she supposed, she had.

"They've gone," she said, nodding at the window.

"Have they." He didn't move.

"Back door's still there. Gareth's probably at lunch."

"I'll risk the front." He slid a twenty across the counter. "I'll take the peat bogs."

"It's eight ninety-nine."

"Keep the change. Buy Gareth a pasty." He put his sunglasses on, then took them off again. "Are you open tomorrow?"

"Tuesday to Saturday. It's on the sign."

"I didn't read the sign."

"Nobody reads the sign."

"I'll read it tomorrow." He opened the door, and the bell screamed. "For the record, I'm much better in the lighthouse one."

"I'll look out for it."

"You'll fall asleep."

"Depends on the gin," she said.

He grinned, and was gone.

Ffion stood very still. Then she rang up the peat bogs at £89.90, voided it, and rang it up again. She slid the *Western Mail* out from under the counter, where it had been since nine o'clock that morning, open at page seven. His face smiled up at her.

"Don't," she told it.
