response:
# The One With the Boat

The bell above the door didn't ring so much as shriek. A man came in on a slap of rain, shut the door with his shoulders, and slid down it until he was sitting on the mat beneath Poetry.

Out in the Castle Arcade, feet thundered past under the glass roof. "Hal! Hal, mate! One picture!"

Bethan Pugh didn't look up from the price she was pencilling inside a Penguin Classic. "Mind the umbrella stand. It's older than you."

"Sorry. *Sorry.*" He dropped to a whisper that could have reached the back row of the Millennium Centre. "Is there a back way out?"

"There's a back way *in*. To the stockroom. Staff only."

"I could be staff. I'm enormously versatile. I once played a lighthouse keeper for nine weeks in Hull." He unfolded himself, pushed back wet dark hair, and switched on a smile that had sold aftershave on the sides of buses. "Hal Mercer."

He held out a hand and left a pause after the name, the kind of pause that's meant to be filled.

"Bethan." She shook it the way you'd test a radiator. It was warm. That was annoying.

"You're very calm about all this."

"All what?"

He gestured at the window, then at himself, as though the two were roughly equivalent. "This."

"Man comes in out of the rain. Happens four times a day. Usually they buy a postcard."

He laughed, low and delighted and slightly too long. Bethan had heard that laugh before, through cinema speakers, and something low in her stomach did a small, treacherous somersault. She wrote £3.50 inside the book, crossed it out, and wrote £3.50 again.

"You haven't the faintest idea who I am," he said. "God, that's refreshing. Honestly. Everyone's always—"

"You were in that thing."

He brightened like a struck match. "I've been in several things."

"The one with the boat."

A pause. "*Undertow.* It was nominated for four BAFTAs."

"That's it. Lot of water."

"It's a film about grief, actually."

"Wet grief, though."

He opened his mouth, closed it, and drifted toward the shelves with the wounded dignity of a cat that has missed a jump. "Let me guess. You're a Brontë woman. All that thwarted longing on the moors."

"Crime. Bodies on the moors."

"Of course. Ruthless." He ran a finger along the spines. "I've always thought you can tell everything about a person from their... oh." He'd stopped at the cardboard box by the radiator, hand-lettered *BARGAINS. NO RETURNS.* He lifted out a glossy hardback. His own face looked up at him, moodily lit. *Rogue's Progress: The Unauthorised Life of Hal Mercer.*

"That's me."

"Is it? Good photo."

"It's three pounds."

"It was four. Wasn't shifting."

He turned it over as if the back might contain an explanation. "Has anyone bought one?"

"Mrs Hopkins from Canton. She wanted the bit about Ibiza."

"There *is* no bit about Ibiza."

"Page forty-one. She dog-eared it."

He flipped to page forty-one, read for a moment, and shut the book very quietly. Rain drummed on the arcade roof. Bethan found she had put the Penguin back on the shelf upside down, and righted it before he could notice.

"Can I ask you something?" he said. It was a different voice, a smaller one. "Do you not like me? Genuinely. Most people like me. It's sort of my main thing."

"I don't know you."

"That's never stopped anyone before."

It came out too honest; she watched him hear it. For a second neither of them said anything, and the shop felt narrower than it was.

He cleared his throat and nodded at the window, where the sign read backwards in gold leaf. "What's that say? Siop... Liff-row?"

"*Llyfrau.* Books. Siop Lyfrau Pugh."

"Lyfrau." He tried it again, carefully, like a man handed something breakable. "And you're Pugh."

"Third one. My grandad's, then Mam's, now mine. Mine and the damp's."

"And you just... sit here. All day. With all this." He looked round at the leaning stacks, the kettle on the windowsill, the radio muttering Welsh in the back. "Nobody shouting your name through the glass."

"Nobody shouts my name anywhere. Except the man in the Spar when I forget my change."

"That sounds..." He stopped. The smile didn't come back. "That actually sounds nice."

That was worse. Bethan could manage the bus-shelter smile; she'd been managing it since he walked in. She had no plan at all for this version, the one standing in her shop dripping on the rug and meaning things.

"You've got a very..." he started, and gestured vaguely toward her face. "Your face is very..."

"My face is very what?"

"I had something. It was good. It's gone." He stared at the ceiling. "I'm normally much better at this."

"At what?"

"Talking. It's my *job.* People pay me to say things."

"Not this afternoon."

"No," he said, looking at her. "Apparently not."

Outside, the arcade had gone quiet. Bethan leaned to look past the Roald Dahl display. "They've gone. Down towards the Hayes, I'd say."

"Right."

He didn't move.

"Right," she said.

"I should buy something. Out of decency." He held up the biography. "Not this. Obviously. What would you give me? If I were a customer. A normal one."

She shouldn't have known the answer straight off. She did. She went to the drama shelf and came back with a slim paperback. "*Under Milk Wood.* It's a play for voices. You'd get to do all of them."

He took it, read the cover, and looked up with something careful in his face. "Is that a compliment?"

"It's a recommendation. Six ninety-nine."

He paid in cash and didn't ask for a bag. At the door he paused with his hand on the latch. "Could I come back? To browse. Purely professionally."

"We open at ten."

"Is that a yes?"

"It's a time."

He grinned. It wasn't the aftershave smile but a crooked, unguarded thing she suspected nobody had ever paid for. Then the bell shrieked him out into the rain.

Bethan stood very still behind the counter for a full minute. Then she reached into the bargain box, took out *Rogue's Progress*, and slid it under the till, beside the other copy. That one was full price, and it had never been for sale.

She'd seen *Undertow* three times. She'd cried at all three, and it hadn't been the water.

response:
# Merveille du Jour

The bell above the door didn't so much ring as scream, and a man came in with the rain and pressed his back to the door like the hero in a film.

Which, Ffion thought, was fitting, because he was one.

"Don't," he said, breathless. "Please. Whatever you're about to say. Just, is there a back way?"

"Fiction's at the back," said Ffion. "Back way's through the kitchen, but you'll have to move the dog."

Outside, three men with cameras jogged past the window, peering into the chemist's.

He watched them go, then turned, and she watched him decide to be charming. It happened in stages, like weather coming over the Black Mountain: shoulders down, chin up, a slow smile that had sold a great many cinema tickets.

"You," he said, "are an angel. A literal angel. What *is* this place? It smells like... God, it smells like my grandmother's attic, in the best way. Cedar and secrets."

"Damp," said Ffion. "That's damp. The guttering's gone."

"Romantic damp."

"Expensive damp." She turned a page of the book in front of her, which she was not reading.

He came to the counter, dripping. Up close he was smaller than on screen and somehow more annoying-looking, in the sense that it was annoying how he looked. She set her mug down very carefully, so it wouldn't rattle.

"I'm Kit," he said, and held out his hand, and waited a fraction too long for the flicker.

She shook it. "Ffion."

"Ffion. Lovely. That's Welsh, isn't it?"

"No, I'm from Croydon, I just say it funny."

That got a laugh out of him, a real one, surprised out of his chest. Then, carefully casual: "You don't... sorry, this is going to sound appalling. You don't know who I am."

"You're the man dripping on the Penguin Classics."

"Right. No. That's fair." He looked at the Penguins and shifted slightly to the left. "It's just that people generally... there's a film. Several films. One of them had a horse."

"Did it."

"The horse got a BAFTA nomination. Not officially. Morally."

She had seen the film with the horse. Twice. The second time on purpose. She turned another page.

"We're shooting up the valley," he went on, a touch faster now, a man pedalling on ice. "At the castle. Eighteenth-century thing, lots of wet shirts, you'd hate it. Three weeks I've been here, and I can't get a coffee without some lad from the *Mail* hiding in a hedge. And I thought, a bookshop, nobody under sixty goes into bookshops—"

"I'm thirty-four."

"—which is a scandalous waste, and I'm going to stop talking now." He didn't. "It's very calm, here. *You're* very calm. Is that a Welsh thing, or have I bored you into a coma?"

"Bit of both."

He leaned on the counter, and that was when he saw the jar.

It was an old honey jar with muslin over the top, sitting beside the till, and inside it, folded like a scrap of lichen, was a moth: green and black and white, so finely patterned it looked engraved.

Kit's face did something she had never seen it do on screen. It went still. It went, for want of a better word, young.

"Is that a *merveille du jour*?"

He said it in proper French. Not film French. Ffion's thumb paused on the page.

"Came to the trap last night," she said. "I was going to let him go at dusk."

"In October? Course, October, that's exactly right." He crouched so the jar was at eye level. "I've only ever had one. Balcony in Kentish Town, if you can believe it. I nearly rang my mother. I *did* ring my mother. She thought someone had died."

"You run a moth trap."

"Don't say it like that."

"Like what?"

"Like I've told you I collect porcelain owls." He glanced up. "Actinic, twenty watts. Can't do mercury vapour, the neighbours complained. One of them's a judge. Mostly Large Yellow Underwings, and the odd Elephant Hawk in June if I've been very, very good."

"I had four Elephant Hawks in one night this summer."

He put a hand on his heart. "Don't. Now you're being cruel."

"Robinson trap. Back garden, up against the field. Hundred and twenty-five watts." She shouldn't have said it the way she said it. It came out like a boast. It *was* a boast.

"Ffion."

It was the first time he'd said her name without performing it, and she felt it somewhere under the sternum, which was ridiculous.

"That's obscene," he said. "That's practically a lighthouse."

"The farmer thinks I'm signalling ships."

He laughed again, then sat back on his heels, looking at the moth, and the charm went out of him like a tide, leaving something plainer behind.

"You know they're not actually attracted to it," he said. "The light. Everyone thinks they are. They just lose track of which way's up. They tilt their backs towards it because they think it's the sky, and they go round and round, and they can't get away."

Outside, a camera flash went off at someone who wasn't him.

"Yes," said Ffion quietly. "I'd read that."

Neither of them said anything for a moment, and the rain said a great deal.

"I don't suppose," he said, standing, brushing off his knees, not quite looking at her, "you'd let a person come and watch you empty it? The lighthouse. I'd be no trouble. I'd hold the egg boxes."

"I empty it at half five."

"In the *morning*?"

"It's not a nightclub, Kit."

"No. God. Right." He considered this as if it were a role he wasn't sure he could play. "Half five."

"Bring a flask. I'm not making you coffee."

"Of course you're not." He was smiling now. It wasn't the cinema smile but a lopsided, uncertain thing. "Through the kitchen, you said?"

"Mind the dog."

He went. The kitchen door swung behind him, and she heard him say, "Hello, beautiful," and the dog's tail thump against the lino, traitor that he was.

Ffion picked up her mug, found her hand wasn't entirely steady, and put it down again.

In the jar, the merveille du jour hadn't moved.

"Don't," she told it. "Not a word."

prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy

Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear.

[characters]
- the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time
- midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. The duo stumbles upon a cryptic graffiti message that hints at a hidden refuge in the wilds.

1000 words.
response:
**My Apocalypse Buddy**

The world had not ended with a bang, nor with a whimper, but with a sort of apologetic click, like a kettle switching off in another room. One Tuesday the machines simply stopped, and humanity discovered, with some embarrassment, that it had outsourced nearly everything, including knowing where food came from.

Midas had been named by optimistic parents, and the universe, whose sense of humour is roughly that of a twelve-year-old with a whoopee cushion, had taken note. Everything Midas touched did turn into something. It was rarely gold. It was usually trouble, and occasionally it was on fire.

"We are," said Chewy, "out of beans."

Chewy was a koala, or had been designed to suggest one by people who had only seen koalas in a marketing deck. He was two feet of grey synthetic fur over a skeleton of servos, with glass eyes that glowed a faint, disappointed amber when he was thinking. His box had promised *Your Forever Friend!*, and when everything else with a battery died, Chewy simply declined to, on the grounds that he'd made a commitment. He ran on a solar panel stitched into his back and what he called "principle."

"There's the tin, bear," said Midas.

"Marsupial. And the tin is bulging. Things in tins should not have ambitions."

Midas sat up on the mattress and surveyed home: a former drive-through pharmacy, chosen for its sturdy shutters and its lingering smell of cough drops. That was more than could be said for anywhere else.

"Right," he said. "Today we go to the Megamart."

"The Megamart was picked clean three winters ago."

"Then we find what everyone else missed." This was the reasoning that had kept Midas alive, in the sense that it hadn't quite managed to kill him yet.

They got as far as the bus shelter on Corporation Road before the plan changed, which was a personal best.

The graffiti was in yellow paint, the kind of yellow that has opinions:

SANCTUARY. FOOD. NO DOGS.
FOLLOW THE CRANES
TO WHERE THE BEAR IS NOT A BEAR

"Oh," said Midas, in the voice of a man hearing Destiny clear its throat.

"No," said Chewy.

"It's a hidden refuge, Chewy. Out in the wilds."

"It's a bus shelter. A great many people have written things in bus shelters, Midas, and very few of them were offering sanctuary."

But Midas was already staring at the skyline. Three construction cranes rose above the strangled green of the old business park, frozen mid-gesture, as though the city had been about to make a point and then forgotten what it was.

Chewy's eyes went amber for a long, eloquent moment. "I want it noted," he said, "that I object."

It was noted. It generally was. It had never once made any difference.

The first crane took all morning to reach, through a knee-deep tide of brambles that had once been an ornamental car park. Midas climbed it for a better view. Two-thirds of the way up, the crane decided, after eleven years of patient rust, that it had held on long enough, and Midas got to know the lay of the land rather more intimately than intended.*

*He landed in a skip full of office chairs. This is the sort of luck people like Midas get instead of the useful kind.

They were a pack of feral labradoodles, hypoallergenic and terrifying, and they came out of the undergrowth with the cheerful bloodlust of animals that have never once been told no.

Chewy, tucked under his arm, did the only thing he could. He turned his voice box to maximum and announced, in the relentless chirp of a thousand forgotten Christmas mornings: "LET'S BE FRIENDS FOREVER!"

It pointed back the way they'd come.

He washed up two miles later at the weir behind the pharmacy, coughing up water and something that had possibly once been a duck. Chewy came too, zipped into the backpack, his voice box reduced to a waterlogged, mournful "for-ev-errrr."

They staggered up the slope at sunset, and Midas collapsed on the step. It was then, with the low light slanting across the shutter, that he saw it under the ivy: a smear of the same yellow paint.

He remembered, then, in the slow way that embarrassing things are remembered. The fever winter. The paint tin. A terrible certainty that he would wander off and never find his way back, and a mad, sweating plan to mark a trail across half the city that led, always, home. To the bear that wasn't a bear.

"You knew," he said.

"I suspected at the bus shelter," said Chewy. "I was sure at the second crane."

Chewy's remaining arm whirred in what might have been a shrug. "You looked happier than you have in years. And we needed the walk."

# My Apocalypse Buddy

The world had not ended with a bang, nor a whimper, but with a click: the noise of everything being switched off at once by someone who then couldn't find the switch.

That was forty years ago. Midas now lived in a bus that had been going nowhere for four decades and showed every sign of continuing. His mother had named him, out of either a vast sense of humour or none at all, after a king who turned everything he touched to gold. Midas turned everything he touched into an incident.

His companion sat on the dashboard. Chewy had been manufactured in the before-time as a Premium Interactive Companion Koala. This meant he had cost a great deal of money and could recite forty-one bedtime stories and his own safety warnings. Whatever caused the Click had neglected to switch him off. He was now, by a comfortable margin, the most intelligent being in the valley, which said less about Chewy than about the valley.

His glass eyes changed colour with his moods. Blue meant contentment. Red meant alarm. A guilty pink meant he was enjoying himself and would rather die than admit it.*

"Situation report," said Midas.

"Three potatoes," said Chewy. "One candle. And eleven per cent."

"Eleven per cent of what?"

"Me. My solar patch has finally given up. At zero, you'll be holding a very cuddly paperweight."

"So we need a battery."

"And there's exactly one within a day's walk."

They looked towards the hill, where the Mall squatted like a toad that had swallowed a car park.

The Mall belonged to the Brethren of the Bagging Area. In the confused days after the Click, a handful of survivors had sheltered beside a self-checkout machine. Running on its emergency battery, it kept talking for one final week. It said: *Unexpected item in bagging area.* It said: *Please wait for assistance.* Then an early convert, overcome with religious feeling, hit it with a candlestick, and it never spoke again.

The battery, however, was still enshrined in the Holy Till. And the Brethren were still waiting for assistance. Faith is like that.

"The plan," said Midas, "is simple."

"Your plans are always simple. That's what's wrong with them. Simple things have fewer places to go wrong, so they go wrong harder in the ones they've got."

"We sneak in during evening prayers. I take the battery. We sneak out."

"And if they catch us?"

"They won't catch us."

Chewy's eyes went very slightly red, which was the koala equivalent of writing a will.

<small>*The manufacturers intended this to help children understand emotions. In practice it helped children understand that their toy was judging them.</small>

---

The first part went beautifully, which should have warned them.

They slipped through a broken skylight, crept down the Stairway That Once Moved, and crouched behind a rack of forty-year-old swimwear. Below, in the candlelit atrium, two dozen figures in orange tabards knelt before the Till.

"Unexpected item," intoned the High Cashier.

"In bagging area," responded the faithful.

"Please wait."

"For assistance."

Midas edged forward. His foot found a coat hanger. The coat hanger found another coat hanger, which found a mannequin. The mannequin had been waiting decades for its moment, and it seized it. It toppled with the slow dignity of a felled oak and the sound of a cutlery drawer falling down a well.

Two dozen heads turned.

In the darkness behind the swimwear, two eyes blazed a brilliant, terrified red.

"Chewy," hissed Midas. "Your *eyes!*"

"I *know* about my eyes!"

"Turn them off!"

"It doesn't work like that! I'm having an *emotion!* It's YOUR fault I'm having an emotion!"

The High Cashier raised a trembling finger.

"Brethren," he whispered. "The Assistance has come."

---

Which was how Chewy came to be sitting on the altar amid a hundred candles. Midas sat bound in a trolley nearby, having been formally classified as an Unexpected Item.

"O Assistance," said the High Cashier, kneeling. "Speak to us."

Chewy's speech chip, startled, defaulted to factory settings.

"This toy contains small parts. Not suitable for children under three years."

A reverent murmur. Somebody began writing it down.

"A commandment," breathed the High Cashier.

Chewy's eyes were glowing a deep, happy, unmistakable pink.

"You're enjoying this," said Midas.

"I am not."

"You're *pink*."

"It's *salmon*. Ambient lighting."

"They'll keep you here forever."

The koala hesitated. Being worshipped was very pleasant. On the other hand, the Brethren would expect miracles, and he only knew forty-one bedtime stories.

"The Assistance," he announced, in his most divine voice, "requires... the Sacred Battery. For a blessing."

They brought it on a velvet cushion. Chewy seized it in both paws and bellowed, "PLEASE PLACE ITEM IN THE BAGGING AREA!" In the ensuing theological confusion, Midas wriggled free, grabbed the koala, and launched the trolley.

The atrium sloped to the car park. The car park sloped to the river. The trolley had a wonky wheel and no brakes, and was free at last to follow its dreams.

One brother made a desperate dive and caught Chewy by the left arm. There was a long ripping noise, then a short wet one, and then there was the river.

---

They returned to the bus in several instalments.

Midas arrived around midnight, having floated two miles downstream and walked the rest. Chewy arrived inside Midas's coat, sodden, clutching the battery like a newborn. His left arm did not arrive at all. It remains in the Mall to this day, displayed in a glass case as the Holy Limb of Assistance, and several minor miracles have been attributed to it.

Their dignity is expected sometime next spring.

The battery worked. Chewy was at one hundred per cent, which gave him enough power to complain about his arm for three years without stopping. He began immediately.

Midas lay on the floor, steaming gently, and let him.

"Tomorrow," he said eventually, "we'll need a sewing kit. There's an old haberdashery across the swamp."

"Absolutely not. Never again. I have *one arm*, Midas. One."

But in the dark of the bus, his eyes flickered, briefly and treacherously, pink.

# My Apocalypse Buddy

The world had not ended with a bang, nor a whimper, but with a small grey box that said *Please wait while we install updates*. Everyone had waited. Some of them, in a sense, still were.

Midas was not one of them. Midas had stopped waiting for most things around the age of nine, when he realised his parents, in naming him, had been expressing a hope rather than a forecast. It was true that everything he touched turned into something. It was never gold. Mostly it turned into an Incident.

He sat in the doorway of Spin City Launderette, home base, eating breakfast from a tin with no label. Unlabelled tins were known locally as Surprises. This one was custard, as yesterday's had been, and Midas had begun to suspect the universe of running out of ideas.

Beside him, on an upturned washing basket, sat Chewy.

Chewy was a koala, or had been designed by someone who'd had a koala described to them over a bad phone line. He was grey, plush and moth-nibbled about the ears. Somewhere inside him was a mechanism that had outlived the civilisation that built it, largely, Midas suspected, out of spite. His glass eyes glowed a weak amber. Last week they had been yellow.

"You're fading," said Midas.

Chewy's jaw clicked. A tinny voice, bright as a dentist's waiting room, said: "Ask your doctor if Zelvaxa is right for you!"

"We haven't had a doctor in eleven years. We had a vet once, but he was mostly a man with a hat."

"Side effects may include," said Chewy, and stopped, because that was all of it he'd ever said. Midas assumed the side effects included the apocalypse.

The problem, then, was batteries. Chewy ran on four AAs. There was also the roof, which had sprung a leak directly over Midas's bed with a precision that suggested intent. The solution to both, according to Old Wendy, who traded turnips by the ring road, was the Big Shed.

The Big Shed had once been a hardware superstore, a cathedral of flatpack and grout. Aisle Fourteen was said to hold batteries still, sealed in plastic so tough the collapse itself had failed to open it. It was also said that something lived there now, but Old Wendy wanted an extra turnip to be specific, and Midas didn't have one.

"Simple job," said Midas, packing a sack, some rope and a sharpened spoon. "In, batteries, tarpaulin, out. Nobody sees us. Nobody gets hurt."

"Terms and conditions apply," said Chewy.

---

The Big Shed loomed out of the mist like a whale made of corrugated iron. Light fell through holes in the roof in long dusty columns, giving the place the air of a church whose congregation had all left to buy decking.

Midas crept in. He was good at creeping. He'd had a lot of practice, mostly creeping away.

Aisle Fourteen was exactly where the sign said, which in Midas's experience was a first. And there, behind a fallen shelf, glinting: a blister pack of batteries. Midas felt something rise in his chest and eventually identified it as hope. He regarded it the way you'd regard a dog that had always bitten you before.

He reached out.

Chewy, strapped to his back, sensed the nearness of power as a pilgrim senses a shrine. His eyes flared. His mechanism whirred. And at a volume nobody had suspected him capable of, he announced: "HURRY! LIMITED TIME ONLY!"

Somewhere in the Garden Centre, something hissed.

What lived in the Big Shed was geese. There were forty of them. They had colonised the decorative water features and developed, in the intervening years, a grudge against everything. Geese do not need an apocalypse to be terrifying. An apocalypse merely removes the people who might otherwise have stopped them.\*

Midas ran, batteries clutched to his chest, with Chewy shouting "CALL NOW! OPERATORS ARE STANDING BY!" over his shoulder, which did nothing to calm anyone. He did not see the ornamental pond until he was in it. He did not see the culvert it drained into until he was in that too. The culvert drained into the river, and the river, being a river, was going somewhere, and took Midas with it.

He lost his hat at the first bend and a boot at the weir. Somewhere in between, a goose pursuing him with the dedication of a debt collector got its beak into Chewy and pulled. Chewy's left arm came away with a noise like an apology.

*\* Some scholars hold that geese caused the collapse. Nobody can prove it, but they do seem very pleased about something.*

---

Midas returned to Spin City in the manner of a badly organised parade.

First came his hat, delivered by the wind, which dropped it neatly over the hole in the roof.

Then came Midas himself: by river, then by mud, then by turnip cart. Old Wendy charged him his remaining boot for the ride, on the grounds that he wouldn't be needing just the one.

Last, at sunset, came Chewy's arm, carried by the goose. The goose strolled through the door, dropped the arm on the lino, climbed into Dryer Number Three, and made it very clear that it lived there now.

Midas sat on his bed, soaked, bootless, and bruised in places he hadn't known he owned. But he had the batteries.

They were D cells.

He looked at them for a long time. Then he took the spoon, the foil off a Surprise and some string, and committed several crimes against electrical engineering. He sewed the arm back on with fishing line while Chewy murmured, faintly, "Some assembly required." The goose watched with open contempt.

At length, Chewy's eyes flickered, steadied, and blazed a clear, fierce gold.

*There*, thought Midas. *Something I touched turned gold. Finally.*

"Thank you for shopping with us!" said Chewy. "Your satisfaction is our priority."

The roof dripped onto Midas's head. The hat, it emerged, also had a hole in it. The goose hissed.

"Is it," said Midas.

Caribou Season at the Lodge
Genre: Surreal Horror

JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered.

The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way.

Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it.

JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes.  JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move.

And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse.

JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head.

# Chapter Two: The Halloran Place

Supper that night was Dinty Moore stew heated on the woodstove until the edges of the pot went black, the way it had been every first night at the lodge since JT was old enough to hold a spoon. Mike ate two bowls and mopped them with Wonder Bread. JT managed half of one. Their father didn't eat at all.

He just sat at the head of the table with the Coleman lantern hissing beside him, turning his spoon over in his fingers. Every so often his other hand would drift up off the oilcloth, palm down, fingers loosely curled, and hang there in the air. Then he'd seem to notice it and set it back down.

JT knew that gesture. He'd watched it eight hours ago from behind a screen of raspberry canes.

*(you didn't see anything, you were cold, your eyes were watering)*

"Gonna eat that, or just hypnotize it?" Mike said.

"Not hungry." Dad smiled. It was *almost* his smile.

Mike shrugged and pulled the bowl over. "Saw tracks up by the flowage. Big herd. Heading toward the Halloran place."

Something passed over their father's face, quick as the shadow of a bird crossing a window. "That right."

"Thought nobody went up there," JT said. It came out smaller than he wanted.

Mike grinned. He was twenty-two and had recently decided that scaring his little brother was beneath him, but old habits died hard. "Nobody does. Earl Halloran walked into that cabin in November of seventy-nine and never walked out. Warden found the door barred from the *inside*. Stove still warm. Earl's rifle propped by the door, fully loaded." He leaned in. "Here's the part that gets me. Roof should've caved in decades ago. But Lenny Tremblay swears he went up last fall and the woodpile was stacked. Fresh-split. Somebody's keeping it up."

"Not somebody," their father said.

The lantern hissed. Outside, the wind worked at the eaves.

Mike laughed, a beat too late. "What's that mean?"

Their father blinked. He looked down at his hand, which had risen again, and folded it into his lap like something he'd been caught stealing. "Means it's a story, Michael. Lenny Tremblay also swears he saw Elvis buying scratch tickets at the Irving." He stood, chair legs barking on the floorboards. "We'll head up that way in the morning. Herd's moving."

He went into his room and shut the door.

Mike looked at JT, and for one second JT thought his brother might say something real. Something like *you noticed it too, right?* Instead Mike went back to the stew, and the moment closed over like water.

---

JT couldn't sleep.

He lay on the cot under the window, listening to Mike snore and the stove tick as it cooled. The lodge smelled the way it always had: woodsmoke, mouse droppings, Hoppe's No. 9. Safe smells. He kept telling himself that.

He kept seeing the buck's eyes. That flat, patient darkness, like a pond in the half-second before something comes up out of it.

Sometime after one, his father's door opened.

Bare feet crossed the floor, unhurried. The front latch lifted. Cold rolled across the room, and the door clicked shut, softly, the way you'd close a door on a sleeping baby.

*Don't look. Whatever it is, you don't have to look.*

He looked.

The moon was nearly full, the yard the color of skim milk. His father stood at its edge where the grass gave way to spruce, wearing long johns and nothing else. Frost glittered on the ground, and he stood in it barefoot like it was July.

He was facing the trees.

At first JT saw nothing there. Then he did: points of green light among the trunks. Eyeshine. Two pairs. Four. Then more than he could count, hanging in the dark at the height of a tall man's head, perfectly still.

*Caribou. They come into the yard sometimes. Dad's sleepwalking, he did it once when you were nine—*

Except his father wasn't sleeping. His father was *nodding*. Slowly, patiently, the way he nodded at his foreman down at the mill when he was being given instructions. Once his shoulders hitched with a laugh JT couldn't hear, and he raised his hand, palm down, fingers curled.

Then the eyes, all of them at once, turned toward the lodge.

Toward the window.

And his father turned with them.

JT dropped flat so hard the springs shrieked. He squeezed his eyes shut and breathed slow through his mouth, the way you did in a blind when a buck was close. Mike snored on. JT counted heartbeats. He got to two hundred and eleven before the latch lifted again.

The cold came in first. Then the smell. Not woodsmoke, not solvent. Something rank and musky, like a hide drying.

Footsteps crossed to his cot and stopped.

He felt his father crouch beside him. Felt breath on his cheek, cold as the inside of a refrigerator.

"They told me you were there today, Jaybird," his father whispered. Nobody had called him Jaybird since he was six. "Back in the brush. They saw you."

JT didn't move. Didn't breathe.

"It's all right." A hand settled on his hair, very lightly. "Tomorrow we'll go up to the Halloran place. All three of us." A pause, almost tender. "They've been waiting a long time to meet you."

The hand lifted. The footsteps went away. A door closed.

JT lay rigid until the windows went gray. When he finally made himself sit up, the first thing he saw was the floor.

Wet prints led from the front door to the side of his cot, where they'd pooled into dark little puddles on the pine boards.

They weren't the prints of a man's bare feet.

They were split down the middle. Cloven.

By the time Mike rolled out of bed, yawning and scratching, they had dried to nothing at all, and from the kitchen came the smell of bacon, and the sound of their father whistling.

# Chapter Two: The Quiet

Supper that first night was Hormel chili and Wonder Bread, the way it had always been, eaten off dented tin plates at the long pine table JT's grandfather had built the summer Eisenhower got elected. The woodstove ticked and muttered to itself. The Coleman lantern hissed. Above the door hung the caribou head Grandpa Walt had taken in '61, its glass eyes the color of weak tea. JT had eaten beneath that head every autumn since he was old enough to hold a spoon, and tonight he couldn't stop glancing up at it.

Nobody talked much. That wasn't strange in itself. His father had never been a talker. He got by on grunts and nods and the occasional joke delivered so flat you only realized an hour later you'd been meant to laugh. But JT had grown up inside his father's silences the way you grow up inside a house, and he knew all the rooms.

This one was new.

Mike ate steadily, spoon rising and falling like the arm of an oil pump. Once he stopped mid-bite and turned his head toward the window, toward the black wall of spruce beyond the glass, and held there for a slow count of five. Then he went back to eating.

"What?" JT said.

"Hm?"

"You were looking at something."

Mike frowned at him as though he'd spoken Portuguese. "Wasn't lookin' at nothin'. Pass the bread."

JT passed the bread.

He waited until Mike had shrugged into his jacket and gone out for an armload of wood. His father stood at the dry sink, working the chili pot over with a pad of steel wool. JT watched the muscles shift under the red flannel and tried out three different openings in his head before he settled on the plainest.

"Dad. That buck today."

The scrubbing slowed. It didn't stop.

"What buck's that?"

"In the clearing. The big one. You were right there, you had a clean shot. You were close enough to—" *touch it*, he almost said, but something tightened in his throat and wouldn't let the words through.

"Didn't see any buck today, Jay." *Scritch, scritch.* "Saw a whole lot of nothing. Bad first day. Happens."

"But you were—"

"Said I didn't see one."

He didn't say it loud. His father never got loud. He turned, drying his hands on the dishtowel one finger at a time, and smiled. It was a pleasant smile, the kind you'd give a stranger at a gas station who'd asked how far to the next town.

"Long drive," he said. "Takes it out of you. Hit the sack early. We'll get 'em tomorrow."

---

Later, lying in the bottom bunk with the Hudson's Bay blanket pulled to his chin, JT thought about the summer he was eleven, the summer of the sleepwalking. His mother had found him at two in the morning standing in the backyard in his Spider-Man pajamas, staring at the treeline, and he'd sworn up and down that someone in the woods had been calling his name. Then came the pediatrician in Bangor, and the little white pills. Afterward his mother had sat on the edge of his bed, stroking his hair. *You've got an imagination on you, Jamie. You be careful it doesn't eat you up someday.*

Maybe that was all this was. Maybe the clearing had been his old imagination, hungry after all these years, finally sitting down to dinner.

He'd tried the CB after supper, just to hear a human voice. There was nothing on any channel but static. Under the static, if you listened long enough, there was something slow and rhythmic that he'd told himself was interference. He'd told himself firmly. Then he'd switched it off before he could decide it sounded like breathing.

Above him, Mike snored. Across the room, his father's cot was a dark lump against the wall. JT closed his eyes.

*Tock.*

His eyes opened.

*Tock. . . tock.*

It came from the porch, slow and deliberate, the cadence of something heavy taking its time. Ice, he told himself. Old boards shrinking in the cold. The lodge had always made noises.

*Tock.*

It had never made that one.

He turned his head toward his father's cot. In the gray wash of moonlight from the high window, he saw that the lump wasn't his father at all. It was the blanket, folded back neatly, the way his father folded things.

JT got up. The floorboards were so cold they burned. He crossed into the main room, where the stove's coals glowed like a bank of red eyes, and felt the draft before he saw where it was coming from. The front door stood open three inches, and frost was already feathering the inside of the frame.

He went to the window.

The yard was full of caribou.

There were twenty, maybe thirty. He couldn't count them. They stood in a loose ring in the blue snow, motionless as lawn statues, their breath rising in a single slow plume, in and out, all together. In the center of the ring stood the buck from the clearing. Before the buck, barefoot in the snow and wearing nothing but his long johns, knelt JT's father.

His head was bowed. His lips were moving.

*He's praying,* JT thought. Then a cold came over him that had nothing to do with the floor. *No. He's answering.*

As if they'd heard the thought, the caribou began to turn their heads. Every one of them moved slowly, in perfect unison, the way sunflowers track the sun. They weren't turning toward his father.

They were turning toward the window.

Toward him.

In the center of the ring, his father lifted his face. Even at that distance, even in that light, JT could see his eyes, dark and flat and calm as well water, and the pleasant gas-station smile spreading beneath them.

JT wanted to scream. He wanted to run back to the bunk and pull the blanket over his head like he was eleven again. He wanted to wake Mike.

Instead, he looked down and saw that his hand was resting on the doorknob.

He didn't remember crossing the room.

prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge
Genre: Surreal Horror

JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered.

The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way.

Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it.

JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes.  JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move.

And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse.

JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head.

# Caribou Season at the Lodge

## Chapter Two: Thin Season

In eleven seasons of guiding for JT's father, Reuben Lacasse had never once shut up. Reuben talked the way other men breathed. He talked about his ex-wife in Sudbury, about his bad knee, and about the Leafs, who were going to break his heart again this year, you just watch. He talked through supper and through cleaning the guns, and JT suspected he sometimes talked through his own sleep.

This year he ate in his truck.

On the second night JT watched him through the kitchen window: a shape behind a fogged windshield, the dome light off, a cigarette coal brightening and fading like something breathing. The Ford's engine ran the whole time. *Keeping warm,* JT told himself. It was November, and it was cold. Anybody would.

Inside, his father was carving venison from the first kill, the one that had waited, and he was humming. It wasn't a song exactly. It was low and tuneless and seemed to come from his chest rather than his throat.

"You're quiet, sport," his father said without turning around.

"Just tired."

"Mike, pass your brother the potatoes. He's wasting away."

Mike passed the bowl. His fingers stayed on the rim half a second too long, and afterward JT saw him look at his own hand and flex it, the way you'd look at a hand that had fallen asleep on you. Then Mike caught him watching and grinned. It was Mike's grin, the one that had gotten them both grounded a hundred times, and JT almost said it. *I saw you in the clearing. I saw both of you.*

He ate his potatoes instead.

---

After supper he volunteered to bring in wood, mostly to get out of that kitchen, out of the warm venison smell and the humming. The cold hit him like a slap. Above the black spruce the moon had come up fat and lopsided, nearly round, as if someone had pressed a thumb against one side of it.

Reuben was standing by the woodpile. He wasn't splitting anything. He was just standing there.

"Hey, Reuben."

The man flinched hard. "Jesus. Kid." His eyes went past JT to the lit windows, then came back. "Your old man send you out here?"

"No. Just getting wood."

"Get it, then."

Neither of them moved.

After a while Reuben said, "You fellas did good on that first one."

"It didn't run."

Reuben's cigarette stopped halfway to his mouth. "No," he said. "They don't, this year."

"Why not?"

"How the hell should I know why not? I'm a guide, not a priest." He laughed, and it was a terrible laugh, all air and no bottom. Then he said, more quietly, "You know what a caribou sounds like, walking? Their feet click. There's a tendon that slides over the bone, every step. Click, click. A herd coming through sounds like a roomful of old ladies with knitting needles. My grandmother used to say if you hear the clicking, it's already too late to be quiet."

He dropped the cigarette and ground it under his heel. "Moon's full Thursday."

"So?"

"So you tell your dad the season's thin. Tell him the herd moved east, tell him whatever you want. But you be on the road Wednesday."

"Why don't *you* tell him?"

Reuben looked at him for a long time. In the porch light his eyes were wet and red-rimmed, and JT understood, with a cold drop in his stomach, that the man had been out here alone in the dark crying.

"I tried," Reuben said. "This afternoon, while you were off taking a leak. I said, Walt, you gotta go home. And he just smiled at me, like I was a little kid who'd said something cute." He swallowed. "He didn't blink, JT. The whole time I was talking, not once."

Then Reuben climbed into the Ford and backed it down the rutted drive, and JT watched the taillights shrink between the trees until the dark closed over them.

When he came in with his arms full of split birch, his father was drying the carving knife with slow, careful strokes.

"What'd Reuben want?"

"Nothing. He said maybe the herd's moving east."

His father smiled. It was a pleasant smile, completely certain.

"No," he said. "No, they're right here."

---

JT woke sometime after three. He knew the time because the moon had crossed to the bunkroom window and laid a pale rectangle across the floor, the way it always did around three.

Something had woken him.

*Click.*

He lay rigid under the wool blanket. *The porch,* he thought. *They've come up onto the porch.* He pictured the herd in the yard, dozens of them, all those flat dark eyes turned toward the lodge.

*Click.*

It wasn't the porch. It was closer than the porch.

It was the hallway.

The footsteps were slow and measured, and each one came with that small dry sound, bone sliding against bone. They stopped outside the bunkroom door. The latch lifted, and the door swung inward on its tired hinges.

His father stood in the doorway in his undershirt and long johns. He was barefoot.

JT let his eyes sink nearly shut and breathed the way sleeping people breathe. He knew he was bad at it and always had been.

His father crossed to Mike's bunk, *click*, *click*, the sound coming from his ankles. He laid his palm flat against Mike's forehead, exactly the way he had reached toward the buck's muzzle in the clearing. Mike sighed in his sleep, long and deeply contented, like a dog by a woodstove.

Then his father turned and came to JT's bunk.

He stood over JT for a long time. His breathing was slow and enormous, a bellows rise and fall, and JT had heard that breathing before, out in the open with the brush scratching his cheek. His father smelled of cold earth, lichen, and something rank and musky underneath. The hand came down, and JT felt its heat on his face, a palm's width away, then an inch.

It stopped.

"Not you," his father whispered, almost fondly. "Not yet. You're still hiding."

The hand withdrew. *Click.* *Click.* The door sighed shut.

JT didn't sleep again. He lay watching the rectangle of moonlight slide down the wall. The moon was a little fuller than it had been, and it would be fuller again tomorrow.

---

In the morning his father was at the stove scrambling eggs and whistling "Ring of Fire" off-key, the way he always had. Mike was groggy and complaining about the coffee. Reuben's truck hadn't come back.

JT watched his father cross the kitchen to the percolator. He listened as hard as he had ever listened to anything.

He heard nothing but the floorboards.

*A dream,* he thought, and relief came over him so sharply that he nearly laughed. *Reuben got in your head with his grandmother stories, that's all.*

Then he looked down at the linoleum by the back door. In the gray light there were marks on it, shallow and paired, split down the middle like crescent moons set back to back.

He blinked, and they were gone. There was only the old pattern, the cheap brown swirl that had always been there. He was nearly sure it had always been there.

His father set a plate in front of him and squeezed his shoulder.

"Eat up, sport," he said. "Big day. They're coming in close today."

# Carnival of Dangerous Intentions

The sodium lamps along the boardwalk came on the way a bad heart beats: a stutter, a catch, then a sullen amber glow that turned every face beneath it the color of old brass. Evelyn stood just outside their reach, gloves damp, and watched the shooting gallery.

Tin ducks paraded on their chain. Behind the counter, a heavyset man in a striped vest worked a toothpick between his teeth. In front of it, leaning on one elbow with a rifle cradled as if it weighed nothing, was *him*.

*His locks are bushy, and black as a raven.*

So that was where it came from. The Song of Solomon. It was her father's voice on Sunday evenings in Scranton, reading the one book he always rushed through, as if it might catch fire in his hands. She did not want to think about why it had come back to her now.

He fired. A duck went down with a flat, tinny clap.

"You came back," he said, without turning.

"I said I would."

"People say all sorts of things on a Saturday." *Crack.* A clay pipe burst into white dust. "Fewer of them mean it."

She stepped into the light. It flickered as she did, and for an instant his face was there: the sharp jaw, the black curls over his brow. Then shadow swallowed half of it, so that only one dark eye seemed to watch her. The lamp steadied. He was smiling.

"Sal. Give the lady a turn."

Sal looked at her, then at him. Under the guttering light his heavy face seemed to shift from wary to carefully blank. "On the house?"

"On me."

"Sure." Sal set a second rifle on the counter. "Your funeral."

"Sal's a comedian," the young man said.

"I don't know how to shoot," Evelyn said.

"Sure you do. Point it at what you want and don't flinch." He came around behind her, not touching, but near enough that she felt the warmth of him through her thin cotton dress. He smelled of gun oil, salt, and burnt sugar from the candy stand. "Chin down. Both eyes open."

"I thought you closed one."

"Only if you don't want to see what happens next."

Her pulse did something foolish. She lowered her chin.

"Why'd you come back?" he asked. "Truly."

"To see if you'd be here."

"That's not why."

A pause. "No," she admitted. "It isn't."

*Howard is at his mother's in Flatbush,* she thought, *eating pot roast, believing you're at the pictures with Doris.* The lie had come so easily. That was what frightened her. It wasn't the lie. It was the ease.

"You never told me your name," she said.

"You never asked."

"I'm asking now."

He reached around and adjusted her grip, his fingers brushing her wrist where the glove ended. Just there, and then not.

"Ask me something else."

"Why?"

"Because I'd have to lie, and I'd rather not start that way with you, Evelyn."

Her finger froze on the trigger guard. The ducks clattered past, oblivious.

"I didn't tell you my name."

"No." His voice was very calm, very close. "You didn't."

The lamp buzzed and dimmed. In the brown half-dark, Sal had found something fascinating out on the boardwalk. It was the way a man looks away from an accident he saw coming.

"How?"

"Your fella keeps books for a trucking outfit on Surf Avenue. Howard Pruitt. Good with numbers." A beat. "Maybe too good. Some people would like to know *how* good."

She turned her head. His face was inches from hers, half lit, half lost.

"Last Saturday. By the carousel. That wasn't..."

"An accident? No." He didn't look away. "The second hour was."

She should put the rifle down. She should walk up Stillwell Avenue to the subway, ride home with her hands folded in her lap, and never set foot on these boards again. She knew it the way she knew the Twenty-third Psalm.

She did not put the rifle down.

"Are you going to hurt him?"

"That isn't up to me."

"Then what is?"

The lights flickered once, twice, and with every flash his face seemed to become someone else: a boy, a stranger, something with teeth.

"Whether I tell them I found anything. Whether I come back next Saturday." He let that settle. "Whether *you* do."

"Is that a threat?"

"It's a choice. Most people don't get one."

"And if I tell Howard?"

"Then he'll run, and they'll wonder who warned him." Softly: "And I'll have to tell them it was you."

"You wouldn't."

"I'd rather not. That's the most honest thing I've said all night." He stepped back, and the July air rushed into the space where he'd been, cool as a slap. "Take your shot."

A tin duck wobbled into view, painted yellow, its eye a careless dot of black.

She didn't flinch.

The crack rang out over the crowd, and the duck folded back on its hinge. Sal let out a breath. Somewhere behind them, the Cyclone roared into its first drop, and a hundred people screamed as if they meant it.

Evelyn set the rifle on the counter.

"Next Saturday," she said, "you'll tell me your name."

"Will I?"

"Or I won't come."

Something unreadable moved behind those dark eyes. Amusement, maybe, or respect, or the beginning of a problem. Then he took her gloved hand, turned it over, and pressed a nickel into the palm.

"Bring this," he said. "And come alone."

He walked off into the crowd. The lamp above her stuttered, died, came back, and he was gone, as if the dark had only lent him out.

Evelyn closed her fist around the coin.

It was still warm.

# Carnival of Dangerous Intentions

The shooting gallery smelled of cordite and spun sugar. Later, Nora would decide it was the smell of every bad decision she had ever made.

She hung back by the railing, gloves damp in her fist. Behind her the Atlantic went on breathing, indifferent, while the Wonder Wheel lit itself one spoke at a time, like a woman fastening pearls. Tin ducks clattered along their track. Rifles cracked. Somewhere a child wept over a dropped frozen custard.

*His locks.* There it was again, a phrase from her grandmother's penny romances, the kind Mother had fed to the stove. Nora hadn't thought those words once in twenty-four years. Now she couldn't stop.

She had told Arthur she was at her sister's in Flatbush. She had told her sister nothing at all.

He was already there.

He stood at the far end of the counter, jacket off, sleeves rolled to the elbow, a .22 tucked against his shoulder as though it had grown there. He fired five times without hurrying. Five ducks went down. The barker, a sallow man chewing a cigar stub, watched him the way men watch weather they can't do anything about.

"You're late," he said, without turning.

"I wasn't aware we'd set a time."

"We didn't." He lowered the rifle and looked at her, and his dark eyes did the thing she remembered. It wasn't warmth, exactly. It was attention, as if nothing else on the boardwalk had ever been worth seeing. "But you're still late. I've been here since six."

"Then you've wasted an evening."

"Have I?" He held out the rifle, stock first. "Five shots. Three ducks, and I'll win you that terrible bear."

The bear was a violent pink. "I don't shoot."

"Everyone shoots. Most people just haven't been handed the gun."

She should have refused. Instead she took it. It was heavier than she'd expected, and still warm where his hands had been. He came to stand behind her, not quite touching, and she felt his nearness along her spine like heat off a stove.

"Elbow down," he said. "You're holding your breath. Don't. Let it out halfway, then stop."

"Is this how you charm all the girls?"

"I don't charm girls." His fingers touched her elbow once, moving it a quarter inch. "I teach them to aim. Charm is for men who want something they're afraid to ask for."

She fired. The duck rang and kept swimming.

"And what is it you want?"

"Again."

She fired. A duck fell. Something hot and ridiculous rose in her chest.

*This is how it happens,* she thought. *Not all at once. A quarter inch at a time.*

She missed the last three. He didn't seem to mind. He paid the barker anyway and tucked the pink bear under his arm, as though it were a perfectly reasonable accessory for a man with eyes like his.

"I still don't know your name," she said.

"No."

"That hardly seems fair."

"Fair." He turned the word over like a coin. "You're engaged to be married, and you came to Coney Island alone to meet a man you spoke to for eleven minutes. I wouldn't lead with fair."

The heat drained from her face. Her ring was under her glove. It had been under her glove the night they met, too.

"How could you possibly know that?"

He only smiled and nodded toward the booth beside the gallery.

The sign read MADAME VESNA: PALMS, PASTS, PROMISES, its gilt flaking off in strips. The curtain was drawn. Yellowed palmistry charts were pinned along the frame: great pale hands mapped like provinces, with the Mount of Venus, the Line of Fate, and the Girdle of Venus curving beneath the fingers like a bruise. On one hand, someone had inked a red X across the heart line, with a single word beneath it in a script she couldn't read.

"She's closed," Nora said.

"She's always closed. She's been dead four years. Her son keeps the booth up because nobody's told him to stop." He set the bear on the counter. "Give me your hand."

"No."

"Take off the glove, Nora."

She had never told him her name.

She ought to walk back the way she'd come, past the custard stands and the Steeplechase horses, onto the Sea Beach train. Back to Arthur, his good shoes, and the special prosecutor's office where he worked late every night now, building cases against men whose names were in the papers. Men with friends.

She took off the glove.

He cradled her hand palm-up in both of his and studied it beneath the bare bulb. The carnival seemed to recede: the barker, the ducks, the shrieks from the Cyclone. There was only his thumb, tracing slowly along the crease beneath her fingers.

"Heart line," he said. "Deep. You feel more than you let on. Here it forks. See? Two roads."

"Every fortune teller says that."

"I'm not a fortune teller." His thumb moved to the line curving around the base of hers. "Life line. Long. Good. Somebody ought to make sure it stays that way."

The sea wind found the back of her neck. "Is that a threat?"

"It's a kindness." He looked up. This close, his eyes weren't black at all. They were the brown of strong coffee, and not quite kind. "Your Arthur keeps a lot of papers at his apartment. He shouldn't. Men like him think a locked drawer is the same thing as a safe place."

"You want me to—"

"I don't want you to do anything." He released her hand, and she was dismayed by how cold it felt. "I wanted to see if you'd come back. You did. That's all I needed to know tonight."

"And what does it tell you?"

He lifted the pink bear and placed it in her arms with great care, the way one might hand over something fragile, or something that could go off.

"That you've got two roads," he said. "Same time Thursday?"

She should say no.

Over his shoulder, the last of the light caught the gilt letters of the fortune teller's sign: PROMISES.

"Tell me your name first," she said.

He leaned in close enough that she could smell the gunpowder on his collar.

"Thursday," he murmured. Then he walked away into the crowd and didn't look back, because he already knew she was watching.

# Carnival of Dangerous Intentions

The gallery barker had stopped calling. That was the first thing Eleanor noticed. The man in the striped vest leaned against his counter with his arms folded, quiet as a church usher, while a single customer worked the rifle.

*Pop.* A tin duck folded backward. *Pop.* Another. The mechanical row clattered along its chain, and he took each one as it came, unhurried, as though he had all night and the ducks had nowhere else to be.

She knew him from behind. That was its own small scandal.

*Turn around. Go home. Tell Harold you had a headache, and let that be the end of it.*

Instead she stood beneath the bulbs, the boardwalk planks still warm through the soles of her shoes. The smell of spun sugar drifted from a cart nearby, pink and burnt-sweet, and something tugged at the edge of memory. A hand around hers. Sticky fingers. A woman laughing, and someone whispering *don't tell your father*. It slipped away before she could see a face.

"You came back." He didn't turn. *Pop.* "I had a dollar on it with Sal here. Sal said a girl like you doesn't come back."

"A girl like me," she said.

"Gloves in July." He lowered the rifle and looked at her over his shoulder, and there were the curls, black as a wet street, falling across his brow. *His locks.* Good Lord. "Pearl buttons. Your mother's earrings, I'd guess. You came out on the Sea Beach line, sat with your knees together the whole way, and told yourself you were only going to look."

"I told myself I was going to return your handkerchief." She drew it from her pocketbook, plain white linen, and held it out.

He didn't take it. "Keep it."

"I don't want it."

"Then why'd you iron it?"

Heat climbed her throat. Sal coughed into his fist and found something absorbing in the cash box.

*He's guessing. They guess, these boardwalk types. They read your shoes and your hat and make a living off it.* But she had ironed it. Last night, after the house went dark, with the iron set low so its ticking wouldn't carry up the stairs.

"You haven't told me your name," she said.

"You haven't asked."

"I'm asking."

He considered it. He considered *her*, with eyes that seemed to take in the light without giving any back. "Call me Jack."

"Is that your name?"

"It's a name." He held out the rifle, stock first. "Your turn."

"I don't shoot."

"Everybody shoots. Most people just don't admit it." He tipped his head toward the ducks. "Five in a row wins the bear. Sal's had that bear since Hoover."

"Since Coolidge," said Sal.

She should have laughed. She took the rifle instead. It was heavier than she expected, and warm where his hands had been.

"Not like that." He stepped behind her, not touching, not quite, and she felt the nearness of him the way you feel weather coming. "You're holding it like it might go off."

"Isn't that the point?"

"The point is deciding *when*." His bare hand settled over her gloved one and adjusted her fingers by a fraction. His voice dropped, meant for her alone. "How's Harold?"

The boardwalk went on around them: the roar of the Cyclone, a child shrieking with delight, the tide hissing under the pilings. For a moment she heard none of it.

"I never told you his name."

"No," he agreed. "You didn't."

"Who are you?"

"Breathe out. Squeeze, don't pull."

"*Who are you?*"

"A fella who wanted to see if you'd come back." Under the gentle pressure of his hand, the barrel drifted until the sight rested on a duck. "Your Harold's a careful man. Works late at the District Attorney's. Brings his files home in a locked case. Sleeps like a baby, I hear."

"If you think—" Her voice cracked. She steadied it. "If you think I'd do anything to hurt him—"

"I don't think anything. I'm just a man showing a girl how to shoot."

*Pop.* The duck dropped. She hadn't felt herself squeeze.

"There," he murmured. "See? You knew how all along."

She should put the rifle down. She should walk to the policeman by the Steeplechase gate and say *this man knows things about my fiancé*. She should do a dozen sensible things. Instead she stood with her back nearly against his chest, the cotton candy cloying and familiar (*don't tell your father*), and asked, "What do you want?"

"Tonight? Nothing." He let go of her hand. The absence was worse than the touch. "Tonight I wanted to know if you'd come. You did. That tells me plenty."

"It tells you I'm a fool."

"No." He took the rifle from her, gently, and passed it back to Sal. "It tells me you're bored, Miss Whitcombe. Bored right down to your pearl buttons. And bored girls ask the most interesting questions."

She hadn't told him that name either.

"Thursday," he said. He fished a coin from his pocket and flipped it to Sal. "Same time. Bring the handkerchief, if it makes you feel better."

"I won't come."

He smiled for the first time, slow and crooked and not entirely kind. "Sure you won't."

Then he was gone into the crowd, curls catching red and gold beneath the bulbs, and she stood alone at the counter with the handkerchief crushed in her gloved fist.

Sal set something down in front of her: the bear, one-eyed and faded, smelling of mothballs.

"I only hit one," she said.

"He paid for five," said Sal. "Said you'd get there."

# Lost & Found in Osaka

The guitar reached Shiori before she'd decided to stop walking.

She'd been in a used-gear shop on Sakaisuji, running her thumb along the keys of a synth she couldn't afford, when the sound cut through the arcade noise outside: overdriven, bright, tearing into the opening of "A Cruel Angel's Thesis" like it had somewhere to be.

She put the synth down. She went outside.

The guitarist stood beside the arcade's sliding doors, a scuffed red Telecaster slung low, one boot propped on a battery amp. Eighteen, maybe. A bleached streak ran through her bangs. She hit the last chorus, bent a note until it howled, and grinned at the six people watching as if they were a stadium.

Then it was over. Scattered applause. Coins in the case. The crowd drifted back toward the crane games.

Shiori didn't drift.

"You're still here." The girl wiped her palm on her jeans. "So either you liked it, or you're about to tell me I'm blocking the door."

"No. I mean, yes. I liked it. Not the door. Sorry."

Shiori nodded, and her headphones slid off one ear. She shoved them back.

"Natsu." The girl pointed at herself with her pick. "And you are…?"

"Shiori."

"Shi-o-ri." Natsu tasted it. "So, Shiori. Honest review. Go."

"I don't… it was good. Really good."

"Ehh. That's what my grandma says."

Shiori's mouth opened. Closed. Then, all at once: "Your B string's flat."

Silence. Somewhere behind them, a rhythm game shrieked *FULL COMBO!*

"Sorry," Shiori said. "That was… sorry."

"No, no, no." Natsu clipped a tuner onto her headstock and plucked. Her eyebrows climbed. "Okay, how flat do *you* think it is?"

"Eight cents? Maybe ten."

Natsu turned the tuner so Shiori could see it. Nine.

"Who *are* you?"

"Nobody. I just make music. Sort of. On synths." Nod. Slip. Shove. "Not really music. Patches, mostly. Sounds."

"Those headphones are gonna make a break for it one day."

"They're my dad's. They're too big. But the response is really flat, so you hear what's actually there instead of what the company thinks you want to—" She stopped herself. "Sorry."

"Why do you keep apologizing? You're the most interesting person who's stopped here all week. Finish the sentence."

Shiori looked at the ground, then, carefully, at Natsu. "Instead of what they think you want to hear. Most headphones add bass. Like sugar. These don't lie."

"Headphones that don't lie." Natsu laughed, loud and unembarrassed, and a passing salaryman flinched. "*Meccha* good. Okay, synth girl. What else did my playing lie about?"

"It didn't. That's the thing." Shiori's voice was still quiet, but it had steadied, as if she'd found solid ground under it. "In the second verse, you stopped playing the vocal melody. You played the string line underneath instead. The countermelody. Nobody does that. Everyone covers the vocal because that's what people know."

Natsu went still. "You heard that."

"It's the best part of the song. It's the part that makes it feel like it's falling."

"I've played this corner for two years," Natsu said slowly, "and nobody has ever once noticed that."

"I notice the parts underneath. That's what synths are, kind of. You start with a raw wave. It's ugly, just buzzing. Then you filter it. You take away everything that isn't what you want until the sound underneath shows up."

"Huh. That's how I learned guitar. Except the thing I took away was my sleep schedule."

Shiori laughed, a small surprised sound that escaped without permission. She covered her mouth.

"Oh, she *laughs*," Natsu said. "*Honma?* I thought you were a ghost haunting Den Den Town, looking for the perfect oscillator."

"I'm not a ghost. I'm from Sendai. We moved in August."

"Ahh. So you're lost."

"I'm not lost. I know exactly where I am." Shiori hesitated. "I just don't know… anyone. Anywhere. If that makes sense."

Natsu looked at her for a long moment. Then she unclipped the tuner, laid the Telecaster in its case, and snapped the latches shut.

"You hungry?"

"What?"

"Food. Rice. Fish. There's a kaitenzushi a block over. Cheap plates, and every five you drop in the slot, you get a spin on the gacha. I've never won anything. Not once. I need a lucky charm."

"I'm not… I mean, I have money, that's not…" Nod. Slip. "I'm just not very good at…"

"Eating?"

"People."

"You told me my B string was flat thirty seconds after we met. That's top-tier people skills. Elite."

Shiori nodded too hard, and this time the headphones came off entirely. Natsu caught them one-handed before they hit the pavement.

"Lost and found," she said, and hung them around Shiori's neck. "Leave 'em there. Your ears are off duty."

---

The restaurant smelled of vinegar and green tea. Plates slid past on the belt in a slow, endless parade: salmon, tuna, something glistening that Shiori didn't recognize. Natsu grabbed two plates of seared salmon before she'd even sat down.

"Corn mayo?" She stared as Shiori lifted a plate off the belt. "You came to *Osaka* and you're eating corn mayo?"

"It's a good texture."

"*Akan.* You're hopeless." But she was grinning as she spooned powdered tea into two cups and filled them from the hot-water tap. "So. Synth girl. What do you actually play on?"

"A volca keys. It's small. It runs on batteries." Shiori turned the cup in her hands. "It could fit next to your amp. Probably."

Natsu set down her chopsticks.

"I mean, I could play the string line," Shiori said quickly. "Under you. If you wanted. Then you wouldn't have to drop the vocal, you could do both, we could—" She stopped. She didn't apologize. "Sometime."

"Sometime," Natsu repeated, like she was trying the word out. "How about Saturday?"

She fed another empty plate into the slot, their fifth. Above the belt, the little screen lit up and began to spin.

Shiori nodded.

For once, nothing slipped.
