response:
# Lost & Found in Osaka

The guitar found Mitsuki before she found it.

She'd just stepped out of a junk shop on Sakaisuji, a plastic bag hugged to her chest. Inside was a Casio SK-1, eighteen hundred yen, battery cover missing. Then the riff cut through the crowd. "A Cruel Angel's Thesis." Overdriven. Twice as fast as it had any right to be.

The girl playing it stood at the mouth of an arcade, boots planted, bleached hair escaping a backwards cap, a battery amp at her feet. Crane-game jingles spilled out behind her like a rhythm section that had never rehearsed. She was maybe nineteen. She played like the song owed her money.

Mitsuki didn't decide to stop walking. She just did.

Three songs later, the last chord rang out, coins clattered into the open case, and the crowd melted back into Den Den Town. Mitsuki was left standing exactly where she'd been, alone, in full view.

"You've been rooted there since the first song," the busker said. "Fan or undercover cop?"

"Oh, no. Sorry. Sorry, neither. I mean... sorry."

"That's three sorries. You're gonna run out."

"I wasn't staring. I was listening. Which is... I know that's what people do. With music." A pause. "Sorry."

"Four." The busker grinned and swung the guitar onto her back. "Relax, I'm teasin'. Listenin's allowed. Payin's better, but listenin's allowed."

Mitsuki fumbled for her wallet, nearly dropped the bag, and caught it against her knee.

"Whoa, careful. What's in there? You're holdin' it like a baby bird."

"It's a sampler. Well, a keyboard. That samples. A Casio SK-1, from nineteen-eighty..." She stopped. "It's old."

"Honma? So it records stuff?"

"About eight seconds. It sounds kind of crunchy. That's sort of the point."

"Crunchy." The busker tilted her head, studying her. "Okay, Professor. You sat through my whole set. Gimme the verdict."

"I... it's not my place..."

"I'm askin'. That makes it your place."

Mitsuki looked at the pavement. When she spoke, the words came out faster and flatter, as if she were reading them off a screen only she could see.

"The build before the last chorus. The original piles everything on: strings, brass, all of it. You can't do that on one guitar, so you rolled the volume knob in on each note and let the delay carry it. Dotted eighths, I think. So it doesn't hit, it... blooms." She swallowed. "It was better than the strings. Not that the strings are bad. It was good."

For a second the busker didn't say anything at all.

"Two years," she said finally. "Two years I been doin' those swells, and nobody's ever clocked 'em. Not once." She stuck out a hand. "Rei."

Mitsuki shook it. "...Like..."

"Don't."

"I wasn't going to."

"Everybody's gonna. Mum's a massive Eva fan. So I learned the theme song outta spite, and now it's my biggest earner. Life's weird."

"I'm Mitsuki. I'm not named after anyone. I don't think."

"Mitsuki." Rei tried it out. "So, Mitsuki. You play out? Gigs, open mics?"

"No. Just my room. Headphones. My mum thinks I'm doing homework, which... sometimes I am. Sort of." She hesitated. "I made a track out of our rice cooker once. The beeps. When it's done."

Rei barked a laugh so loud a passing salaryman flinched. "No way. Play it for me."

"It's on my laptop. And it's four minutes of a rice cooker."

"That's the most punk thing I've heard all week, and I hang out in Amerika-mura." Rei perched on her amp. "Why synths, though? Like, why not this?" She patted the guitar.

Mitsuki considered it. "With a guitar, it's your hands. Everyone can tell it's you. With a synth, I can build a sound nobody's ever heard before. From nothing. So for a little while, it's only mine."

"Sounds kinda lonely."

"...Yeah. Maybe." Mitsuki shrugged one shoulder. "It's quiet, though."

"Quiet's overrated." Rei nodded at the bag. "Could you sample me? Eight seconds of Rei. Make it crunchy."

"I'd need batteries. And to figure out where the cover went. But yes. I could do that." Something almost like a smile. "I could pitch you down until you sound like a whale."

"Meccha rude. I love it." Rei's stomach growled, loud enough to compete with the arcade. "Right, that's it, I'm starvin'. There's a kaiten place round the corner. Hundred-yen plates, tuna's honestly great, tamago's a bit suspicious. Come with. You can tell me everything my amp's doin' wrong."

"Oh. I... I don't usually... with people I've only just..."

"You've known me four sorries. That's practically family."

"I mostly just get cucumber rolls."

"Okay, now you've gotta come, 'cause that's a cry for help."

Mitsuki laughed, a small, surprised sound, like she hadn't known it was in there.

"One more song first," Rei said, swinging the guitar back around. "Request?"

"The swells. Could you... do the swells again?"

"For you, Professor? Anything."

She hit the opening riff. People slowed and turned. Rei tore into the last chorus, rolled the volume knob in, and the first note began to bloom.

And the sky over Shinsekai cracked open.

Red. Gold. A white starburst right above Tsutenkaku Tower. The boom swallowed the guitar whole. Mitsuki could see Rei's fingers flying but couldn't hear a single note. All around them, phones shot up into the air.

Rei kept playing anyway, laughing, shouting something Mitsuki couldn't catch.

"WHAT?"

"I SAID..." Another volley. Rei cupped a hand round her mouth. "SUSHI? YES OR NO?"

Mitsuki took a breath.

"YES!"

The fireworks stopped at that exact instant. Her voice rang down the street, clear as a bell. A dozen strangers turned to look at her.

Mitsuki went scarlet. "...Sorry."

"Five." Rei unplugged, snapped the case shut, and threw an arm around her shoulders. "C'mon, Cucumber. Tuna's waitin'."

response:
# Lost & Found in Osaka

The used-gear shop on the third floor smelled like dust and solder. Mio had been staring at the same Roland for twenty minutes when the guitar cut through the window.

She knew the melody before her brain caught up. *Cruel Angel's Thesis.* But wrong, gloriously wrong, every note bent sharp and dragged back, the distortion fuzzy at the edges.

She left the Roland.

Downstairs, Sakaisuji Street was its usual Saturday noise: maid café girls with flyers, the electronic shriek of crane games. At the mouth of the arcade, a girl with a bleached streak in her hair and a battered Telecaster was tearing the song apart for nine people and one pigeon.

She finished with a squeal of feedback. The nine people clapped. The pigeon left.

"Ookini, ookini! Coins are good, bills are better, compliments are free!"

The crowd thinned. Mio didn't. She realized this too late, when the girl looked straight at her.

"You've been standing there the whole song. You lost?"

"N-no. Um. Sorry. I'm... no."

"No you're not lost, or no you're not sorry?"

"...Both? Neither. Um." Mio pointed at the little amp by the girl's sneakers, then pulled her finger back like it had done something rude. "Your batteries. They're dying."

"My what?"

"The amp. When the voltage drops, the clipping gets... softer. Saggy. Your last chorus was mushier than your first one. Not *bad.* Just... mushy."

The girl crouched, popped the battery compartment, and squinted.

"Honma? You *heard* that?" She shook a battery next to her ear like it might confess. "I swapped these Thursday."

"It's a cheap amp. Sorry. I mean, it's a good amp for, um. For how cheap it is."

The girl laughed, head back, loud enough to turn heads at the crane games. "Oh, you're *mean.* I love it. I'm Natsu."

"Mio."

"Mio. You play?"

"Not guitar." Mio hugged her tote bag. Something boxy bulged inside. "Synths. Mostly. I just bought..." She stopped.

"Bought what? Show me. Come on, I showed you my dead batteries. That's very personal."

Mio tilted the bag open. "It's a Volca. Secondhand. The filter knob's a little scratchy, but I can clean it with contact spray, and the sequencer's only sixteen steps, but if you chain two together you can..." She heard herself and shut her mouth.

"Keep going."

"You don't actually want to know about the sequencer."

"Mio. I just played anime songs to a pigeon for three hours. I *desperately* want to know about the sequencer."

So Mio told her. About step sequencing and swing settings, and how the Volca's little speaker made everything sound like it was coming through a wall, which she actually liked. Natsu packed her guitar while she listened, asked questions, and actually waited for the answers.

When the case clicked shut, Natsu slung it over her shoulder. "Okay. You've officially talked longer than I played, and I'm starving. There's a kaitenzushi around the corner. Hundred-yen plates. Come on."

"Oh. I... I should probably..."

"Probably what? Go home and clean your scratchy knob?"

"...That was the plan. Yes."

"Knob can wait. Fatty tuna can't. Also, Osaka *invented* conveyor-belt sushi, so it's basically your civic duty."

"Is that true?"

"Totally true. Some guy over in Higashiosaka watched beer bottles going around a factory and thought, *what if fish.* Absolute hero."

---

The restaurant was bright and loud, with plates circling the counter like slow little planets. Natsu grabbed salmon before she'd even sat down. Mio watched three plates go past before taking a tamago.

"Egg? First pick, and you go *egg?*"

"It's... safe."

"It's *boring.*" Natsu slid a plate of seared scallop in front of her. "Try. If you hate it, I'll eat it and pretend I didn't see your face."

Mio tried it. Her eyebrows went up.

"Ha! Look at that. Okay, my turn to be nosy. Why synths? Most kids your age want a guitar so they can look cool in front of arcades."

"Most kids your age don't busk in front of arcades."

"Ooh, she bites back now. Answer the question."

Mio turned her teacup around on the counter. "My dad had all these CDs. Susumu Hirasawa, mostly. When I was eight, I heard the opening to *Paranoia Agent*..."

Natsu set down her chopsticks very slowly.

"Shut up."

"S-sorry?"

"No, *shut up*, as in *no way.* 'Dream Island Obsessional Park'? With everyone laughing in the weird places? The old man in the... and the girl on the..."

"Standing on the cliff edge. Yes."

"I tried to learn that on guitar for a *month!*" Natsu pressed her palms flat on the counter. "I can't get the vocal right. Hirasawa does this thing where he..." She hummed a phrase, stumbling over its middle.

"He sings across the beat," Mio said. "Not on it. He stretches the phrase so it lands late, and the synths underneath stay perfectly in time, so it feels like... like the song is slipping. Like everything is fine except for one thing, and you can't tell what the one thing is."

Natsu stared at her.

Mio's ears went hot. "Sorry. That was a lot."

"No. That's *it.* That's exactly it. You say stuff like that like it's nothing." Natsu grabbed a plate of tuna without looking. "Did you know he plays a laser harp live?"

"I've watched every video of it." It was the quickest thing Mio had said all day. "It's just beams of light, and he plays them. Like they're strings."

"That's the coolest sentence anyone's ever said to me in a sushi place, and I've had some *meccha* weird sushi conversations."

Plates kept circling. Natsu's stack grew. Mio's reached four, then six, and somewhere between them she'd stopped turning her teacup.

"Okay. Deal," Natsu said, pointing a chopstick at her. "Next Saturday, you bring your little Volca. Program me the backing for 'Dream Island.' I play the melody badly. We scare the pigeon together."

"I... in front of people?"

"In front of nine people. Ten if the pigeon comes back."

Mio looked at the bag by her feet. At the scallop plate, empty now.

"...You'll need new batteries."

Natsu grinned. "I'll buy new batteries."

"Rechargeable. They hold voltage better under load."

"Oh my *god.* Yes, ma'am."

Mio reached for the next plate as it came around. It wasn't egg.

response:
# Stolen Moments in Roma

**I. Trevi, 9:40 a.m.**

Ben Ashworth was checking exactly how many euros the Trevi Fountain swallowed each day when the motorcycle found him.

It came out of Via delle Muratte like a thrown knife. Brakes shrieked, hot rubber gusted, and the tyre stopped so close he felt its heat through his chinos. The guidebook leapt from his hands. A gloved fist caught it mid-air.

"Ma sei scemo? Dove guardi? È una strada, non una biblioteca, Madonna santa—"

The rider wrenched off her helmet. A great deal of black hair came out with it, framing a face that seemed assembled entirely from objections.

"Mi dispiace," Ben said. "Molto. Io sono... I'm terribly... sono un turisto."

"*Turista*. And no. You are a lamppost. Lampposts also stand in the road, reading."

"Lampposts don't read, technically."

"This one does." She weighed his book, unimpressed. "*Rome in Three Days*. Romulus took longer to kill his brother."

He laughed, a startled bark that surprised them both, and she looked at him as though he'd pulled a coin from her ear. Then she reached out and straightened his collar, which did not need straightening. He wouldn't discover until noon that his fountain pen had left with her hand.

"Alessandra," she said. "You have plans?"

"The Pantheon at eleven, and then—"

"No. Get on."

**II. The Ducati, 10:15 a.m.**

The motorcycle was an elderly Ducati the colour of dried blood. Along its tank ran a long, furious gouge packed with somebody else's paint, a vivid streak of pistachio green, like a scar that had healed wrong and was proud of it.

"What happened there?"

"A disagreement."

"With whom?"

She kicked the engine awake. "He lost."

Ben had never ridden pillion on anything. He held her waist the way one handles a museum exhibit, until she took Largo Argentina at a speed that made him abandon all scruple and cling. He felt her laughing through her jacket.

She had deliveries: a lawyer's envelope in Prati, and a clinking crate for a convent in Monti, where an elderly nun gave Alessandra a look of long acquaintance and counted the bottles twice.

**III. Campo de' Fiori, 12:30 p.m.**

At a fruit stall she held two apricots up to the light. She argued with the vendor about his mother, his football club and the scandalous price of courgettes, then walked away with no money changing hands that Ben could see. She gave him one. It was warm from the sun and tasted faintly of accusation.

"Did you pay for this?"

"Did you enjoy it?"

"That isn't the—"

"Eat, Professore."

He reached for his pen to note the stall's name, an old habit, and found his pocket empty. He looked at her. She was examining a pyramid of artichokes with saintly absorption.

**IV. Trastevere, 3:00 p.m.**

"So," she said over espresso, "what do you profess?"

"Medieval history. *Furta sacra*, mostly. Holy thefts. Ninth-century monks who stole saints' bones from rival monasteries. Afterwards they'd write these marvellous accounts claiming the saint had *wanted* to be taken. That the relic practically climbed into the sack."

Her cup paused halfway to her mouth. Something crossed her face, quick and private, and was gone.

"And you believe them? These monks?"

"I believe they believed it." He shrugged. "Things want to belong somewhere."

She studied him for a long moment, the way one might study a lock.

When they left, the café's little silver spoon was no longer on her saucer. Ben noticed. Ben said nothing. He was astonished to discover he didn't want to.

**V. A Roof in Monti, 7:45 p.m.**

"This," Ben whispered, halfway up a rusting fire escape, "is breaking and entering."

"Is not breaking. I have a key." She dangled it above him.

"Where did you get a key?"

"I found it."

"Where?"

"In a pocket."

The roof belonged, she explained, to a count who lived in Lausanne and did not deserve a view like this. There were lemon trees in terracotta pots and a wrought-iron table. Beyond the parapet the whole city was turning gold, a hundred domes catching the last light like upturned bowls.

She produced a bottle of wine he was fairly sure was also the count's.

"Why did you come to Rome, *lampione*?"

He considered lying. "Fifteen years in the same library. Same carrel. Same sandwich. I realised I'd written four hundred pages about people who took things, and I'd never taken anything in my life."

"Not even a risk?"

"Especially not that."

She was very close now. The light did unfair things to her eyes. He thought, with academic precision, *this is the moment*. Then a door banged open below, and a man's voice bellowed up the stairwell in an accent that suggested he was very much not in Lausanne.

They ran. Ben missed the last rung of the fire escape, landed in a heap of geraniums, and came up laughing so hard he couldn't breathe. Alessandra hauled him onto the Ducati, and they were gone before the shouting reached the street.

**VI. Trevi, 11:20 p.m.**

She brought him back to where it started. The fountain was lit like a stage set, and the crowds had thinned to lovers and pickpockets.

"I don't do tomorrow," she said, before he could ask.

"Of course. No. Quite right." He was nodding too much. "It's been... I don't have a word. In either language."

"Good. Words are your problem."

She took his face in both hands and kissed him. It was unhurried and thorough, the kind of kiss one could write a monograph on. Her hands drifted down his chest, across his jacket, and away.

Then came the helmet, the engine, the pistachio scar flashing under the streetlamps, and she was gone.

Ben stood there for some time. Eventually, out of habit, he patted his jacket for his guidebook.

It wasn't there.

In its place, in his breast pocket, was the café's silver spoon, wrapped in a paper napkin. On the napkin, in the green ink of his own stolen pen, she had written:

*Domani. Ore 10. Stesso posto. Guarda dove cammini.*

He read it three times. Tomorrow. Ten o'clock. Same place. Watch where you walk.

She had taken his plans, he realised. Every one of them, all three days.

Ben Ashworth, who had spent fifteen years doubting the monks, stood by the fountain and finally understood them. Some things don't resist. Some things practically climb into the sack.

response:
# Stolen Moments in Roma

**9:40 a.m. Piazza di Trevi**

The front tyre stopped so close to Ben Hartley's shin that he felt its heat through his chinos.

"*Madonna santa!* *Ma sei cieco?* *Guarda dove cammini, tu e quel libro*..."

Ben clutched his guidebook to his chest like a shield. The rider flipped up her visor to reveal dark eyes, a smudge of yesterday's eyeliner, and a face built entirely out of opinions.

"*Mi dispiace*," he managed. "*Enormemente.* *Io sono*... I was reading about *la fontana*. *Sono molto stupido.*"

"You are," she agreed in English, tugging off her helmet. A rope of black hair tumbled loose. "Very stupid. Also, you say 'I am very stupid' like you are ordering a cappuccino."

"It's the only way I know how to say anything."

She laughed, sudden and loud and completely unrepentant, and a coach party turned to stare. Then she plucked the guidebook from his hands and leafed through it. "*Rome in Seventy-Two Hours*. Seventy-two? Rome takes a lifetime, and you want to do it like laundry."

"I'm on sabbatical, actually. I'm writing about the aqueducts..."

"Boring." The book vanished inside her leather jacket. "Get on."

"I'm sorry?"

"You nearly killed my bike. Now you owe me a morning." She handed him a second helmet. A sticker on the back read *PROPRIETÀ DI MARCO*.

"Who's Marco?"

"Nobody, now."

---

**10:15 a.m. Somewhere between lanes on Via del Corso**

Ben had never prayed in earnest, but it turned out he knew how. The motorcycle slid between a bus and a delivery van with the clearance of a sheet of paper. His arms were locked around her waist, and she smelled of petrol and oranges.

"You hold too tight!" she shouted.

"I'm holding exactly as tight as I'd like to live!"

She dropped a parcel at a notary's office near the Pantheon and was inside for ninety seconds. When she came out, she was twirling a silver fountain pen she had not gone in with.

"Was that..."

"A tip," said Alessandra.

---

**11:30 a.m. Mercato di Testaccio**

She knew every stallholder by name and kissed half of them. While she argued football with a fishmonger called Enzo, her hand drifted across a fruit stall and came back holding two apricots. She pressed one into Ben's palm without breaking eye contact with Enzo.

Ben looked at the apricot. He looked at the stall's owner, an old woman shelling peas. He thought of his mother, who returned shopping trolleys in the rain.

He ate it. It was the best thing he had ever tasted.

Over Enzo's shoulder, one corner of Alessandra's mouth lifted, as though he'd passed a test he hadn't known he was sitting.

---

**1:00 p.m. A rooftop in Trastevere**

"We're not supposed to be up here," Ben said. This was obvious from the padlock she had just opened with a hairpin.

"Nobody is supposed to be anywhere." She sat on the parapet with her boots dangling over six storeys of air. Below, terracotta roofs tumbled toward the river like a spilled deck of cards. "Sit."

"I'd honestly rather..."

"Ben."

It was the first time she had used his name. He sat, and his knees trembled. Domes and bell towers spread before them, along with laundry strung like bunting and a seagull regarding them with open contempt.

"Why aqueducts?" she asked.

He considered the lecture he usually gave, then didn't give it. "Because someone built a thing that carried water for a thousand years, and nobody remembers their name. I find that comforting."

She studied him. "That is the saddest thing I ever heard."

"Is it?"

"You want to be forgotten." She produced a packet of cigarettes. He was fairly certain it had been sitting on a café table in the piazza below. She didn't light one. "Me, I want everyone to remember me and nobody to catch me."

---

**4:20 p.m. Via dei Coronari**

The sky split without warning. One moment the cobbles were gold. The next, rain came down in ropes, and Alessandra seized his wrist and hauled him under the striped awning of a gelateria. They stood pressed shoulder to shoulder while the water drummed inches from their noses.

Her hair was plastered to her cheek, and his glasses were useless. She took them off his face, dried them on her shirt, and settled them back on his nose with a gentleness that undid something in his chest.

"*Pistacchio*," she told the girl at the counter. "And for him..." She looked him up and down. "Something brave."

"I usually have vanilla."

"Of course you do. *Fico e ricotta.*"

She paid for both, counting out exact change with great care. Absurdly, this surprised him more than anything else she'd done all day.

They ate while the street turned into a river. Their arms touched, and neither of them moved.

"Why did you bring me along today?" he asked eventually.

"You walked into my wheel."

"People must walk into your wheel all the time."

She licked her spoon, thinking. "Not like you. You said sorry to my bike."

"Did I?"

"Twice." She looked at him then, without any mischief, and for a moment he saw something tired and lonely flicker at the back of her eyes. It was gone before he could name it. "Nobody says sorry to anything anymore."

The rain had not quite stopped when she stepped out into it, arms wide, face tipped to the sky. Ben, who owned three umbrellas, followed her. For the first time in his life, he did not care that he was getting wet.

---

**9:50 p.m. Piazza di Trevi**

She brought him back to where she'd found him. The fountain glowed gold and blue, and the crowds had thinned to lovers and pickpockets.

"Tradition," she said, pressing a coin into his hand. "Over the left shoulder. Then you come back to Rome."

He threw it. When he turned around, she was very close.

"Ben."

"Yes?"

She kissed him, quick and fierce, tasting of fig and rain. She was back on the bike before his brain had finished the sentence it was composing. The engine snarled, and she was gone in a red smear of taillight.

He stood there a long while. Then, out of habit, he patted his pockets.

His wallet was there, and so was his phone. The guidebook was gone, but he'd known that. His own pen was also gone, the battered one with his initials on it.

In its place, in his breast pocket, he found the notary's silver fountain pen, wrapped in a crumpled delivery slip. An address in Monti was scrawled across it in eyeliner, with tomorrow's date and *8:00*.

Underneath, underlined twice, she had written: *I have something of yours. Come and steal it back.*

Ben Hartley laughed out loud in the emptying piazza. He had never stolen anything in his life, and now he began to plan a robbery.

response:
# Stolen Moments in Roma

**Morning: Fontana di Trevi**

The motorcycle came out of nowhere. Ben would later learn that nowhere was where Alessandra Ferri preferred to come from.

He had been standing in the narrow mouth of Via delle Muratte, nose in his guidebook, reading about Agrippa's aqueduct, when a dented red Moto Guzzi shrieked to a stop close enough that he felt the engine's heat through his trousers.

"*Ma sei scemo?* Standing in the street like a statue! *Guarda dove cammini, Madonna santa—*"

"Sorry, terribly sorry, *mi scusi*," Ben said, clutching the book to his chest like a shield. "*Io sono… molto eccitato di essere a Roma.*"

The torrent stopped. She pushed up her visor. Dark eyes, a scar through one eyebrow, a mouth trying very hard not to laugh.

"You are very *aroused* to be in Rome," she said in English. "At nine in the morning. *Complimenti.*"

Ben turned the colour of Campari. "Excited. I meant excited."

"No, no. You said it." She looked him over: the linen jacket, the sensible shoes, the euro coin pinched between his fingers, ready for the fountain. "You were going to throw that?"

"It's tradition. One coin, and you return to Rome."

She plucked it from his hand and dropped it into her jacket. "You don't pay the fountain to come back, *professore*. You need a reason." She slapped the seat behind her. "Get on."

"I'm sorry?"

"You will be. Get on."

He got on.

**Late Morning: Via del Corso**

Rome in a guidebook was marble and footnotes. Rome from the back of Alessandra's bike was a scream. She threaded between buses with inches to spare, cut across a pedestrian zone with a cheerful wave to a furious policeman, and talked to Ben over her shoulder the entire time, which seemed the most dangerous part.

"You are what? Tourist?"

"Academic. Classics. I'm on sabbatical, writing a book on Latin funerary inscriptions."

"Dead people writing to dead people."

"Well, to the living, actually. That's rather the point—"

She stopped outside a law firm to deliver an envelope and came back out eating a fig. There was no fig tree on the street. Ben decided not to ask.

**Midday: Largo di Torre Argentina**

"This is where Caesar was killed," Ben said, leaning over the railing above the sunken ruins with something like reverence. "The Curia of Pompey. Twenty-three stab wounds, according to Suetonius—"

"Now it's for cats." A one-eyed tabby wound around a broken column below. "Better use."

She was wearing sunglasses. Ben was fairly sure she had not been wearing sunglasses five minutes ago. He was absolutely sure they had been perched on the head of the German woman beside them.

"Alessandra—"

"Hm?"

He opened his mouth. Closed it. Something hot and unfamiliar was climbing his spine. It wasn't quite disapproval. It was closer to delight.

**Afternoon: A Roof Above Piazza Navona**

The door said *VIETATO L'ACCESSO*. Ben could translate that perfectly well.

"So your Latin is useful," Alessandra said, working the lock with a hairpin, "for reading what you are not allowed to do."

Six flights of service stairs and a hatch later, the city lay open beneath them: domes like overturned bowls, Bernini's river gods foaming in the piazza, swifts carving the gold air. She sat on the warm terracotta with her boots dangling over a gutter four storeys up. Ben lay flat on his back and did not look down.

"Why are you doing this?" he asked the sky.

"Doing what?"

"Me. This. You don't know me."

She tilted her head. For a second the mischief dropped out of her face, and something more careful looked out.

"You walk in front of motorcycles reading about aqueducts," she said. "Somebody has to keep you alive."

**Evening: A Bar in Trastevere**

The barman was enormous, with forearms like hams and a laugh that rattled the bottles. "Ale!" he roared. Then he saw Ben, and the laugh turned into something pitying.

"Rocco, he's a professor. Be nice."

"I'm always nice." Rocco set down two Negronis and waited until Alessandra had slipped off toward the back. Then he leaned in. "Listen, *amico*. I know her since she was fourteen. She took my Vespa. Twice. She took my cousin's wedding ring, and he was *wearing* it. Whatever she says, whatever you feel—" He tapped Ben's breast pocket. "Count your things."

Ben patted himself down. Wallet. Phone. His passport was safe at the hotel. Everything present.

"Thank you," he said, and was surprised to hear his own voice come out steady and slightly reckless. "But I think I'll take my chances."

Rocco gave the shrug of a man who had seen this film before. "Everybody does."

**Night: Fontana di Trevi**

She brought him back where she'd found him. The fountain was lit gold and seething with tourists. Alessandra killed the engine but didn't get off.

"So. Your sabbatical. How long?"

"Six months."

"Long time to read dead people."

"I might," Ben said carefully, "be persuaded to read fewer of them."

She laughed, low, and caught his tie, pulling him down until he could smell exhaust and oranges in her hair. The kiss was brief and entirely unhurried, as if she had stolen a hundred like it and knew exactly what this one was worth.

Then the engine snarled, and she was gone into the dark mouth of the street.

Ben stood there grinning like an idiot for some time before he noticed his wrist was bare. His father's watch was gone.

In his jacket pocket, where it had certainly not been that morning, was his euro coin. It was wrapped in a page torn from his own guidebook, the page about Agrippa's aqueduct. Across the text, in a slanting hand: *Domani. Stessa ora. Se rivuoi l'orologio.*

Tomorrow. Same time. If you want the watch back.

Around him, a hundred strangers turned their backs to the fountain and tossed coins over their shoulders, paying it for a reason to return.

Ben put his coin in his pocket. He already had a reason.

Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. A stack of photo paper is accidentally exposed, rendering it useless mid-session. 1000 words.
response:
# Darkroom Revelations

The safelight turns everything the color of the inside of an eyelid. That's what I've always liked about the darkroom: it strips the world down to red and black, to the things that matter.

Elliot is at the enlarger with his mesh sleeves shoved to the elbow. A cheap silver cross knocks against his sternum every time he leans over the easel. Three hours in, his eyeliner has gone soft at the edges, smudged into something that looks less like a choice and more like a bruise he's proud of. I've been watching him all semester. I'm not proud of that, but I'm not ashamed of it either. I'm twenty-five, and I know what I look at.

"Grade two," he says, sliding the filter in. "Your last one was too harsh."

"I like harsh."

"I know." He doesn't look up. "Everything you print is grade five. All blacks and whites, nothing in between."

He doesn't say it like a criticism. He says it in that low, careful voice, like he's reading the label on something that might be poison. He's right, though. I like edges. I like jawlines you could cut paper with, and girls in red lipstick who know exactly what they are. I have said, out loud, at parties, *I know my type.* I like knowing where to put my hands.

He exposes the sheet, counts under his breath, and slides it into the developer. We stand shoulder to shoulder over the tray, watching his photograph surface: a laundromat at two a.m., a woman folding a wedding dress.

"Can I tell you something weird?" he says.

"Weird is my whole brand."

He rocks the tray, and the dress blooms out of nothing. "I've been thinking maybe 'guy' isn't the right word. For me. Or it is, but not the way everyone means it. I don't know." A breath. "I still want 'he.' I think. It's just that sometimes I feel like I'm wearing someone else's coat and everyone keeps complimenting the fit."

Here is what I want to do. I want to take his face in both hands and tell him he can be anything, that I'll fight anyone who says otherwise. I want to tell him I know a whole group chat of people who've been exactly here, and that we can figure it out tonight, right now, together. I want to make a plan. I always want to make a plan.

I bite the inside of my cheek until I taste copper.

"That doesn't sound weird," I say instead. "It sounds like you've been thinking about it for a while."

"Since I was, like, twelve." He laughs, short and embarrassed. "You're the first person I've said it to out loud."

The weight of that lands somewhere under my ribs. I take the tongs from him, a reflex I've acted on a hundred times, and move the print to the stop bath. Then I realize what I've done. I hand them back. He looks at me, puzzled, and I feel absurd.

"Sorry," I say. "Your print."

"It's okay."

"It's not. I do that." I make myself look at him. "I take over. You just told me something huge, and I'm scared I'll do it with this too. Like I'll start telling you who you are."

He's quiet. The vent fan hums, and acetic acid stings the back of my throat.

"What would you tell me?" he asks. "If you did."

That's the trap. I could tell him. I've built whole versions of him in my head this semester, but they were mine, not his.

"Nothing," I say. "I want to watch you find out."

That's when it happens. I lean back against the counter so I can see his whole face, and my shoulder finds the light switch.

White floods the room like a slap. Elliot yelps. I spin around, and there's the paper box with its lid off. He pulled a fresh stack ten minutes ago, and now twenty-odd sheets of fiber-based Ilford are sitting naked under the fluorescents.

I kill the light. Too late. The room goes red again, and both of us are blinking away spots.

"Oh my god," I say. "That's like sixty dollars of paper."

"Seventy-two." His voice is shaking, and it takes me a second to realize he's laughing. "You flashbanged us."

"I'm so sorry."

"Dani." He's bent over with one hand on the counter, shoulders doing all the work of a silent laugh. "You were trying so hard not to take charge you took out the lights."

I start laughing too. I can't help it. We're both wheezing in the red dark, and when it fades he takes a sheet off the ruined stack and slides it into the developer. We watch it go black. It never passes through gray. It's just black, total and even, edge to edge.

"There," he says softly. "Your grade five."

"It's empty."

"It's not empty. It's everything at once. It just got too much light." He looks at me sideways, eyeliner wrecked, a little half-smile on his face. "That's kind of what being looked at by you feels like. Too much. In a good way, I think."

I don't know what to do with that, and I always know what to do. My whole life, I've walked up to people and told them what's happening. But I don't know what I want from him, exactly, and I don't have a name for it. I don't know what it makes me, wanting someone who doesn't have edges yet. I only know I want to stand here while he finds them.

So I don't move. I put my hand flat on the counter between us, palm up, and leave it there.

Elliot looks at it for a long time. Then he sets the tongs down and laces his chipped black fingernails through mine.

"Grade two," he says. "Next time."

"Next time," I agree, and for once I let someone else set the exposure.

Dani’s phone silently buzzes in her pocket, but she ignores it to stay focused. 1000 words.
response:
# Darkroom Revelations

The first rule of the darkroom is that you can't rush anything. I've broken it every week this semester.

I'm a tray-rocker. I slosh developer like I'm trying to shake it awake. I pull prints at forty seconds when they need ninety, because I want to *see*. Elliot watches me do it with the patience of someone watching a dog chase its tail.

"You're going to muddy the shadows," he says, not unkindly.

"The shadows can handle it."

"Can they, though."

Under the safelight he's all red and black: mesh sleeves under a moth-eaten cardigan he swears cost three dollars, silver rings stacked to the knuckle, black polish he chews off when he's thinking. Everything on him looks found and then chosen on purpose. I clocked that the first week of September, when he walked into Experimental Processes in a velvet blazer over a Siouxsie shirt and sat as far from everyone as the room allowed. I'm not someone who notices quietly. I'm someone who walks up and says something. With Elliot, for some reason, I just kept noticing.

Then we got paired for the final. Twelve prints. Elliot named the series *Latent*, after the image that's already in the paper before the developer touches it. It's there the whole time, just invisible.

Two hours ago he handed me a contact sheet of self-portraits and said, "I should probably tell you something before you print these."

Then he didn't say anything for twenty minutes.

I waited. That isn't nothing, for me. I've ended relationships in fewer words than I've spent waiting for Elliot to finish a sentence. But something about the safelight makes people talk eventually. It's a confessional booth that smells like vinegar.

Now the print he's been circling all night is in the tray between us, and I'm trying very hard not to touch it.

The paper is blank, then not. A grey bloom of jaw. A mouth. Something glossy on the mouth, lipstick, dark. Then the rest arrives: Elliot in a slip dress, one strap fallen, looking straight down the lens like he's daring it.

"So," he says. "That's. Yeah."

My hand drifts toward the tongs. He sees it.

"Let it go the full time," he says quietly, and I don't think he's only talking about the print.

I pull my hand back.

"I don't know if I'm a guy," he tells the tray. "Or only a guy. Or what. I've been trying words on like clothes and nothing fits yet, and I keep thinking maybe I'm just doing it for attention, except nobody's paying attention, because I haven't told anyone." A small, cracked laugh. "Except you. Now. So. Hi."

"Hi," I say.

Every instinct I have is shouting. I want to tell him it's okay. No, better than okay, *incredible*. I want to hand him pronouns, vocabulary, the name of the girl at the queer center who runs the clothing swap. I want to fix it. I'm good at fixing. I'm good at deciding. People like me because I walk into a room and take the wheel, and they let me, and I'm used to being thanked for it.

But this isn't mine to steer. If I start naming things for him, I'm doing what everyone's done to him his whole life, just with a better haircut.

"Do you want me to call you anything different?" I ask instead. "Or not yet."

He looks up. In the red, his eyes are nearly black. "Not yet. Elliot's fine. He's fine." A pause. "For now. Can it be for now?"

"It can be for as long as you want."

The timer goes. I lift the print into the stop bath, my hands steadier than I feel, and the acid smell rises sharp between us.

Here's what I'm not saying. I have a type. I've had it since I was fifteen: clean lines, high contrast. Men who were unmistakably men, women who were unmistakably women, people I could read at a glance. I liked knowing what I was walking into. I told myself it was an aesthetic preference, like liking hard shadows.

And here's Elliot, who is all midtones. Who I've wanted since September without ever deciding *what* I wanted. And it turns out the not-knowing was the point. I've been looking at an image before it's fixed and loving it for being unfinished.

I don't know what that makes me. I'm twenty-five and I thought I had the answer key.

My phone buzzes against my hip. Probably Jonah, asking whether I'm coming tonight. I leave it. The screen would fog everything anyway, and I don't want to look away.

"You're quiet," Elliot says. "You're never quiet. It's kind of freaking me out."

"I'm trying not to make this about me."

"Make it a little about you." He swallows. "I want to know what you think. I don't need you to be careful with me. I've had a lot of careful."

So I tell him. Badly. That I've noticed him since the first week. That I don't usually go for... and I stop, because every way to end that sentence is wrong.

"For whatever this is," he finishes, very lightly.

"For whatever you are," I say. "Which I don't need to know. Which I think I *like* not knowing. Which is extremely new for me, and I have no idea what I'm doing."

He moves the print into the fixer with his bare fingers, which you're not supposed to do, and holds it under a second longer than he needs to. "That makes two of us."

The image is permanent now. He's looking at it. I'm looking at him. The safelight hums.

I want to kiss him. The old me would already have done it: hand on the jaw, decision made, apologize later if necessary. Instead I say, "Can I—" and don't finish, because I want him to be the one who decides how that sentence ends.

He decides. He steps in, rings cold against my wrist, chemistry wet on his fingertips, and kisses me like a question he's stopped being afraid to ask.

When we come apart, he's smiling. I've seen that maybe four times all semester.

"We should wash that," he says, nodding at the print.

"In a minute," I say, and for once, I don't rush.
