Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. Elliot hums a soft tune while waiting for images to reveal in the chemical bath. 1000 words.
response:
# Darkroom Revelations

The safelight turns everything the colour of the inside of an eyelid. I've always loved that about the darkroom: it strips the world down to one shade and makes you find everything else by feel.

Elliot is humming again.

He does it every time a sheet goes into the developer. It's low and wordless, and he rocks the tray with two fingers like he's soothing something. Tonight it's that Cocteau Twins song where nobody knows the lyrics because there aren't really any, just Elizabeth Fraser making shapes with her mouth that *feel* like words. I asked him once what she was saying. He said, "Whatever you need it to."

I'm leaning on the counter beside him, closer than the space requires. That's the thing about me: I don't hover. If I want something, I step toward it. Six weeks ago I'd have already said something filthy and charming, watched him go pink, and decided by Friday whether he was worth the trouble. That's my method. It works.

It is not working.

"Thirty seconds," he murmurs, and keeps humming.

In the tray, the paper is still blank. Then the shadows come up first, the way they always do: a dark curve that becomes the line of a jaw, the hollow of a throat. It's one of mine. I shot him three days ago against the brick wall behind the ceramics building. He wore that mohair cardigan with more holes than wool, silver rings stacked on every finger, black polish chipped down to islands. I told him to look at the lens. He looked just past it.

"You print too soft," I say, because I have to say something. "Grade one. Everything's grey. Go grade five and let the blacks be black."

"I like the middle." He lifts the print with tongs, lets it drip, and slides it into the stop bath. Vinegar sharpens the air. "Everything interesting happens in the middle."

He doesn't move it to the fixer. He just stands there looking down at himself, and the humming stops.

"Dani. Can I tell you something kind of weird?"

"Weird is my whole brand."

He almost laughs. "I've been..." He stops and starts again. "When you took that, I kept thinking, *I don't know if that's a boy.* In the picture. I've been thinking about it a lot. For a while, actually. Whether 'he' is right, or just the thing I got handed. Whether I wear this stuff because it's cool or because it's..." His ringed hand makes a shape in the red air. "Closer."

My body does what it always does. It gets ready to fix things. I already have a list: my friend Ash, who runs the queer zine. The one campus therapist who doesn't suck. My oxblood lipstick, which would look *unreal* on him, and I could do his eyes, I'm good at eyes, I could...

I close my mouth on all of it.

Because this isn't mine. I can feel how easily I could take it from him, and how grateful he might even be to have someone finally tell him what he is. It would just be one more thing handed to him.

"Thank you for telling me," I say, and it comes out smaller than my voice usually is. "Do you want me to... I mean, should I call you anything different, or..."

"No. I don't know yet." He glances at me, quick, then away. "Is it okay that I don't know?"

"Yeah." I swallow. "It's more than okay."

Here's what I don't say. I've always known what I like: men who look like they could carry a couch alone, and women who wear red lipstick like a weapon. Clean lines. High contrast. I've built a whole self around the certainty of my wanting. It's the one thing about me nobody has ever needed explained.

And for an entire semester I've watched Elliot pick at his nail polish during critique. I've listened to him take Sontag apart in a voice so quiet the professor has to lean in. I've wanted him in a way I didn't have a box for, and I told myself it was the clothes, the novelty, a phase of *mine*.

Standing here, I realise it's the middle. All of it. I can't tell where the soft ends and the sharp begins, and I don't need to.

That's terrifying. I'm twenty-five. I thought I was finished being surprised by myself.

But underneath the fear there's something brighter, something almost giddy. I'm watching someone come up out of the blank. I'm watching it happen in real time, and he *chose* to let me see it.

"Is it strange," I ask carefully, "that I feel kind of lucky? That you told me?"

He finally moves the print into the fixer, then the wash. Cold water runs over his face in the tray. "No," he says. "I picked you on purpose. You don't flinch."

"I flinch constantly. I just do it loudly, so nobody notices."

That gets a real laugh, quiet and surprised, and it does something unfair to my chest.

We both reach to straighten the print at the same time, and our fingers meet under the running water. His rings are cold. My first instinct, my *only* instinct, is to take his hand and pull him toward me, to make it simple and make it mine.

I don't. I leave my hand there, open, under the water, and I wait.

It's the longest four seconds of my life.

Then he hooks one finger through mine. Just one. Tentative, like he's testing the temperature.

"Dani?"

"Mm."

"Your lipstick. The dark one." He's looking at the print, not at me. "Not tonight. But sometime. Would you show me how?"

All the things I wanted to offer, and he's asking for one of them, in his own time, on his own terms. It's so much better that way. I didn't know it could be better that way.

"Whenever you want," I say. "You say when."

His finger tightens around mine. In the wash, his photographed face keeps looking just past the lens, at something I can't see yet.

The timer goes off. Neither of us moves.

After a while, he starts humming again. I still don't know the words.

I'm starting to think that's the point.

prompt:
Hacker Mindset

Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. The date drops breadcrumbs of personal information that could easily answer security questions. 1000 words.
response:
**Threat Model**

Her name is Priya and she reorders her cutlery when she's nervous. Fork, then knife, then fork again, a little nervous tell I clocked before the appetizers, and the old reflex lit up like a dashboard: *she's anxious, anxiety is a trust accelerant, people disclose to fill silence.* Stop. Stop it. I am not casing her. I am on a date. These are two different verbs and I have spent eighteen months and roughly four thousand dollars of copay learning to keep them apart.

Focus on her face. Nice face. Open face. She's talking about her commute and I'm nodding, but underneath the nodding my brain is a packet sniffer I never got to uninstall, pulling metadata out of everything. *Lives near the Orange Line. Mentioned a dog named after a planet. Birthday was "last Tuesday," which means late October.* Each fact drops into a little mental form field labeled SECURITY QUESTION ANSWER and I hate myself, genuinely, because she is lovely and I'm indexing her like a breach dump.

Then she says it. She says, "Wait, is that a—are you wearing a Jace pin?"

And everything recompiles.

Because yes. Yes, I am wearing a tiny enamel Jace, the Mind Sculptor, because I am exactly that much of a coward, I wore a conversational honeypot on my lapel in case I ran out of words. And her whole body changes. The nervous cutlery stops. She leans in, and the next ninety minutes are the best ninety minutes I have had in a calendar year.

She plays Commander. Of course she plays Commander. She's running a Meren reanimator deck that is, by her own gleeful admission, "a little mean," and I tell her about my Niv-Mizzet spellslinger pile and she *gasps*, actually gasps, and says "oh you're one of *those*," and for once in my life my pattern-recognition is being used for good, for joy, for the sacred nerd work of establishing which of us would win a game we are not currently playing. We argue about whether Dockside is too strong. We agree that it is. We are aligned on the deep questions. My hands aren't doing the thing where they map exits. I am *here.* I am a person at a table with a person.

This is the part of the night I would, later, give anything to extend. Remember that.

Because then her phone buzzes face-up on the table, and she picks it up to silence it, and she draws the unlock pattern, and I see it.

I don't *try* to see it. That's the thing I'll want her to understand and won't be able to say. Seeing it isn't a choice any more than hearing a smoke alarm is a choice. Her thumb traces a big lazy capital **L** down the left column and across the bottom, three nodes, maybe four, the most-drawn pattern on earth, the one that lives on the top of every list of patterns that are not patterns so much as surrenders. The oils on her screen probably trace it even when the phone's asleep. I could draw it from across the table. I could draw it in my sleep. I could—

"You should change that," I say.

Out loud. Like an idiot. Like a man actively dismantling his own evening with a tiny screwdriver.

She blinks. "Change what?"

And here is the fork in the road, and I take the stupid branch, I take it at full speed, because the compulsion has the wheel: "Your unlock pattern. It's an L. It's—everybody uses the corner-anchored ones, the thumb wants the corners, and you can read the smudge, and honestly with a four-node pattern there's only—" I watch her face close like a laptop lid and I keep going anyway, that's the horror of it, "—I just, I'd feel bad if I didn't say something."

Silence. The cutlery does not move. That's worse than if it moved.

*Damage assessment.* I have just told a woman I have known for two hours that I was watching her hands, that I deconstructed her private gesture, that some part of me was running an attack I'll never run. I have revealed the sniffer. I let her see the thing under the nodding. On a scale of charming to restraining-order I have landed somewhere around *you should probably not know where I live.*

Options. I always have options, that's the sickness and the gift. Option one: double down, make it a bit, become the quirky hacker guy, lean into the party trick—no. That's social engineering. That's using the charm as a pick. I promised myself the charm stays in its holster. Option two: over-apologize, flood the channel, make her manage my guilt. Also a manipulation, just a wetter one. Option three—

Just tell the truth. Raw. Unoptimized.

"I'm sorry," I say, and I put my hands flat on the table where she can see them, an olive branch in body language she won't consciously read but might feel. "That was a really weird thing to say and I want to tell you why instead of pretending I didn't. I used to break into things. Legally, now—it's my job now, companies pay me to find the holes. But my brain never clocked out. I notice vulnerabilities in everything, all the time, buildings, networks, people, and tonight I have been fighting it the whole time because I actually, really did not want to do it to *you.* And I lost one round. With the phone. I'm sorry."

She looks at me for a long four seconds. I don't fill them. For once I let the silence sit instead of exploiting it.

Then she picks up her phone, holds my eyes, and deliberately draws a new pattern. Long, ugly, nonsensical, a pattern with no dignity and no corners, a pattern an attacker would weep at.

"Like that?" she says, and there's the ghost of a smile fighting onto her mouth.

"That's a terrible pattern," I breathe, meaning *that's perfect,* meaning *thank you,* meaning *please let there be a second date.*

"Good," she says. "Your turn. Tell me everything wrong with my password."

Reader, I did not. That's growth.

prompt:
Hacker Mindset

Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. The restaurant's WiFi password is visibly taped to the counter for all to see. 1000 words.
response:
# Responsible Disclosure

The WiFi password is taped to the counter by the host stand. *BellaNotte2019!*, in Sharpie on a strip of blue painter's tape, one corner curling up like it's trying to escape the humiliation.

I catalogue it the way other people notice a nice light fixture. Capitalized proper noun, opening year, an exclamation point to satisfy a complexity rule some IT contractor waved at them six years ago. Probably the same network as the card reader. Router probably still on default admin creds.

*Probably.* I don't check. I want that on the record.

Dr. Okafor says I have to stop treating rooms like engagements. *Not everything is a scope document, Theo.* She's right. I'm here to eat pasta and be a person with a stranger. I am not here to notice that the hostess leaves the reservation tablet unlocked and facing the door, or that the server's badge has a barcode legible from four feet.

Okay. Stop.

Maren is already seated. She's in green, she's early, and she stands to hug me, which is a risk I didn't prepare for. I hug back. Nobody dies.

The first twenty minutes are standard handshake protocol. Job: she's a vet tech; I say "security consultant" and watch her eyes do the polite glaze I'm counting on. Hometowns. The weather, God help us. I'm performing fine, but part of my brain is still on table six, where a guy just read his card number into his phone like he's dictating a will.

Then she reaches into her bag for lip balm, and a deck box tumbles onto the tablecloth. Dragon Shield, matte forest green, battered at the corners.

Something in my chest reboots.

"You play," I say. Not a question. A greeting, in a language.

She goes pink, then defiant, chin up, braced for the joke. "Commander. Mostly Gruul."

"Of *course* you're Gruul," I say. She laughs, and that's it. We're gone.

She plays enormous, stupid creatures and attacks with all of them every turn. I play Dimir control, which she declares "the most annoying archetype in the history of cardboard" and "deeply on brand for a guy in security." I tell her about the night I countered three of a friend's spells in a row and he didn't speak to me until Thursday. She tells me about swinging for lethal with a 40/40 Hydra while the whole table applauded. We argue about whether Sol Ring should be banned. We agree that anyone who brings a cEDH deck to a casual pod deserves whatever happens to him in the parking lot.

Somewhere in there I realize I've stopped inventorying the room. I don't know where the exits are. I haven't looked at table six in fifteen minutes. For the first time since I was fourteen, there's no background process running.

It's terrifying. It's wonderful. I want to text Dr. Okafor immediately.

"Wait, I have to show you," Maren says. "I pulled the alt-art Hydra last week. You're going to cry."

She picks up her phone.

And here's the thing about a long-running process: you can't kill it. You can only suspend it, and the instant it gets an interrupt, it resumes exactly where it left off.

Her thumb lands bottom-left. Up. Diagonal to center. Diagonal up. Down.

An M. Seven nodes. Her initial.

My mouth opens before my judgment finishes loading.

"Oh no, your *initial*? That's, like, the first thing anyone would try. Letters are a huge chunk of all patterns, and the owner's initial is—"

I hear it the way you hear a glass leaving the edge of a table: after it's too late, before the sound.

She looks up. The screen glows with the Hydra, all teeth and foil, and nobody is looking at it.

"Did you just," Maren says slowly, "shoulder-surf me. On a date."

Incident response. Right. Contain, assess, remediate.

Contain: the breach is the sentence I just said. There's no rollback.

Assess. Options, ranked:

One: laugh it off. *Occupational hazard!* Classic minimization. She smiles, and over tiramisu she quietly decides never to text me back.

Two: double down. Explain why it matters: smudge attacks, the research, the whole TED talk. Technically correct. Socially a fork bomb.

Three, and I feel this one rise like an old friend: make it worse on purpose. Be weird enough that she ends it now, so I don't have to wait three weeks for her to find the bug on her own. Cleaner. I've done it before. I'm very good at it. If you're always the one who breaks things first, nobody else ever gets the chance.

Dr. Okafor has a name for option three. It's my own unpatched exploit, and I've been running it for a decade.

Four: tell the truth.

Nobody picks four. Four has no failsafe.

"Yeah," I say. "I did. I didn't mean to. I see everything. The WiFi password's taped to the counter. The hostess's tablet is unlocked. Table six just read his credit card out loud. It doesn't turn off. Except it did, actually, for the last half hour. With you. So I wasn't ready when it came back on." I breathe. "I'm sorry. That was a lousy thing to say."

The silence lasts exactly long enough for me to calculate the check split.

Then Maren turns her phone around and slides it across the table.

"Fine," she says. "Fix it."

I stare at it. Unlocked. Her entire life, sitting on the tablecloth between the bread and the olive oil. It's the most frightening thing anyone has handed me in years.

I push it back.

"No. You do it. I'm not supposed to know."

Something shifts in her face, a small recalculation, a threat model updating in real time. She tilts the screen away, cups it with her palm, and taps through settings with her tongue between her teeth.

I don't watch. I watch *her* instead: the green dress, the corner of a smile she's losing the fight to hide.

"There," she says, and nudges her deck box toward me like a dare. "Nine nodes. You'll never get it."

She's right. For the rest of dinner she's the one thing in the room I can't read, and I've never been so happy to be locked out.

prompt:
Hacker Mindset

Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. Throughout dinner, they mentally catalog every Magic card their date mentions that reveals their strategy preferences. 1000 words.
response:
# Threat Model

The guest Wi-Fi password is chalked on the specials board, right between the branzino and the burrata. *Bellamy2023!* Capital letter, a year, an exclamation point to satisfy a complexity rule written by someone who's never met an attacker. Three years stale. I clock it the way normal people clock the exits.

Stop. You are here for her.

Her name is Wren. She's apologizing about the parking garage, and I'm nodding. Then she says, "So my Rhystic Study gets Naturalized and the whole table *applauds*," and every background process in my brain shuts down at once.

*Card log, entry one: Rhystic Study. Taxes every spell an opponent casts. Pay up or feed her cards. Patient. A little petty.*

"You play Commander?" My voice cracks like I'm fourteen.

What follows is the best forty minutes I've spent with a human being since I traded my old handle for a W-2. She runs Grand Arbiter Augustin. Of course she does.

*Entry two: Grand Arbiter Augustin IV. Her spells cheaper, everyone else's more expensive. She doesn't want to win the race. She wants the race to be unaffordable.*

"Propaganda," she says, counting on her fingers. "Ghostly Prison. Nobody gets to swing at me for free."

*Entries three and four. Attack tax, twice. Redundancy. She builds perimeters.*

"And Cyclonic Rift. Overloaded. Only at the end of someone else's turn. I'm not a monster."

*Entry five. Instant-speed reset. Holds the hammer and makes you watch her not drop it.*

I'm compiling her like a scope document. Hardened perimeter. Layered defenses. Punishes unauthorized access. I find this unbelievably attractive, and I'm aware that says something bad about me.

The waiter keys our table into his handheld: 1-1-1-1. He's done it all night. The guy at the bar has his work badge flipped face-out, and I could tell you his employer, his building, and probably his manager's name in about ten minutes. I don't look at any of it. I've *seen* it, which isn't the same thing. Try explaining that to a jury.

Then Wren says, "Oh, you *have* to see my playmat." She pulls out her phone, tilts it toward the candle, and draws her unlock pattern.

Top-left. Straight down. Straight across.

An L.

Five of nine nodes, the second most common shape after the Z, traced under a candle that throws the smudge trail into perfect relief. I didn't have to shoulder-surf. She basically handed me a printout.

The Propaganda player. The Ghostly Prison player. Two mana per attacker, and her front door is an L.

I have a lot of vulnerabilities. My mouth is the one with a public CVE.

"You know an L is basically the second thing anyone tries, right?"

The screen goes dark in her hand.

"Were you watching me unlock my phone?"

"No. I mean, not *watching*. It's more like hearing your name across a crowded room..."

That's worse. I can tell it's worse because her face does what a good firewall does: nothing visible, everything dropped.

*Entry six:* nothing. She's stopped naming cards. That's the scariest data point all night.

Here's the problem. I know the playbook. Mirror her posture. Make a self-deprecating joke, offer a sincere compliment, ask about the cat on the playmat, and let her tell a story where she's the hero. The rapport rebuilds itself. I could recover this in four minutes. I've recovered worse with strangers on the phone while pretending to be IT.

Which is exactly why I can't. If I run that play on her, I'm not on a date. I'm on an engagement.

Part of me wants to sabotage it properly instead. It's the part that used to stay up until four a.m. inside other people's networks. Lean in. Explain entropy. Explain smudge attacks. Recommend a six-digit PIN and biometrics with a lockdown fallback. Be so technically correct that she leaves, and I get to tell myself it was her loss.

I actually open my mouth to say "entropy." I can feel it there, loaded.

What I say instead is: "I'm sorry. I used to do this for worse reasons. Now I do it for a paycheck, and apparently also on first dates, which nobody pays me for. It's the least interesting thing about me, and I just made it the only thing."

Responsible disclosure. Report the flaw, don't exploit it, and accept that the vendor might hate you.

She looks at me a long time. The candle gutters. Somewhere in the kitchen, a POS terminal beeps its factory-default tone.

"What do you play?" she says.

"...Yawgmoth."

"Combo." She nods slowly, like she's confirming something she already logged. "You see a line and you can't not take it. And you'll pay any amount of life to get there."

"That's... yeah. That's fair."

"You've been looking at that specials board like it owes you money since I sat down. And the waiter's machine. And the guy at the bar with the badge." She picks up her fork. "I play control. I watch what people do on their turn."

Oh.

Oh no. She's been running recon the whole time. I was so busy cataloging her cards that I never checked whether she was cataloging mine.

She turns the phone away, below the table edge, and changes something. I hear six taps. I genuinely do not look.

"Better?"

"I honestly couldn't see it."

"Good." She flips the screen around to show me the playmat: a fat orange cat drawn as a planeswalker, loyalty counter in the corner. Then she sets the phone face down between us, like a card held in reserve.

"That's the Ghostly Prison," she says. "You want to swing at me again, it costs two."

"Two what?"

"Two hours. Next Saturday. Game store on Fourth. You're buying the booster box."

*Card log, final entry:* she didn't name a card this time.

She just cast one.

I pay the two.

prompt:
Overthinking It

Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. The classroom projector squeaks whenever the teacher flips through slides. 1000 words.
response:
# Overthinking It

The projector squeaks. Mr. Halvorsen flips to a slide that says PARTNERS in a font suggesting he believes partners are fun, and I scan for my name the way you'd read a diagnosis.

Emma K. and Priya. Jaden and Luis. Me and—

Okay.

Okay okay okay.

Me and Theo Marsh.

Don't look at him. Looking at him the instant the slide goes up is what a girl does if she's been waiting for the slide to go up. Look at the slide. Read it like it's interesting. It's Comic Sans. Read it anyway. Nod slightly, like someone absorbing logistics. Not that much. Bobblehead.

*Squeak.* "Go ahead and find your partners," Mr. Halvorsen says, and the room becomes a chair-scraping migration, and I am a gazelle who has forgotten how legs work.

Here is the problem: whoever moves is the one who wanted it more. Stay seated, I'm cold. Get up too fast, I'm eager. The correct speed is a person going to throw away a tissue.

He's still sitting. Is he waiting for me? Or does he just not care, because he has a normal nervous system that doesn't treat chairs as a referendum?

I get up. Backpack on one shoulder, because both looks like a hike. Walk. Don't walk in that careful way where you're thinking about walking. Too late. My knees feel like someone else installed them.

What do I say when I get there.

Option one: "Hi." Clean. Also what you say to a cashier. And if I say it wrong it comes out at that pitch that goes up at the end, *Hi?*, like I'm checking whether I'm allowed.

Option two: "Looks like we're partners." Which is what a character says right before a montage. He knows we're partners. I'd just be narrating.

Option three: "I think the projector is trying to communicate with us." In my head this lands with the timing of a late-night host. Out loud it'll come out mumbled, he'll say "What?", I'll have to repeat it, and a repeated joke is a joke executed in the public square.

Option four: nothing. Sit. Let him start.

I sit. I choose option four, which I always choose, which is less an option than a weather pattern.

"Hey," he says.

See, he just did it. One syllable. No evidence of a committee meeting beforehand.

"Yeah," I say.

*Yeah.*

He said *hey* and I said *yeah*, like *hey* was a yes-or-no question. Somewhere in my brain there's an entire library. I know what a catalyst is, I know why salt melts ice, I read all of *Rebecca* last summer and have opinions about the second Mrs. de Winter's posture. And the librarian handed him *yeah.*

*Squeak.* New slide: *Design an experiment testing a factor that affects reaction rate.*

Theo pulls the worksheet toward him, then, considerately, slides it to the middle, which means our elbows will be four inches apart for forty minutes and I need a plan for mine. Lap looks like a funeral. Table, but no leaning. Leaning is a commitment.

"What do you think?" he says. "Temperature? That's kind of the obvious one."

And I have an idea. It's fully formed and gorgeous: Alka-Seltzer tablets, same volume of water, but vary the surface area (whole, halved, quartered, crushed) and time the fizzing. It's better than temperature because we won't need the hot plate everyone's going to fight over, and the data will make a clean curve, and I've already pictured the graph.

What comes out is: "Maybe, like... crushing it? The tablet."

He looks at me. My face is doing something. Fix it. Neutral. What *is* neutral? What do my eyebrows do when I'm not thinking about them? I've never not been thinking about them.

"Oh, like surface area?" he says. "That's actually smart."

*Actually.*

That could mean *genuinely*, like legitimately smart. Or it could mean *contrary to expectations*, like he came over braced for nothing and got a small something. I'll be thinking about this word until roughly Thursday.

"Thanks," I say. Fine. Thanks is fine. Smile. Not with teeth, because teeth is a toothpaste ad. Closed mouth. No, closed reads smug. A little teeth. Is this a little teeth? I can't see my own face. I'm piloting it blind from somewhere behind the eyes, a mech suit with a broken monitor.

He's writing our hypothesis in all capitals, which I didn't know, and now I'll know it forever. There's a doodle on his knuckle in blue pen. A small lopsided planet.

Say something about the planet.

No. That says I'm looking at his hands. Which I am. But he can't know that.

*Squeak.* Mr. Halvorsen goes back a slide, then forward, and the projector protests both ways, a long mechanical whine like a horror-movie door. Theo winces and mutters, "That thing needs an exorcism."

And before the committee can convene, before anything runs through the filters (*too weird, too eager, too much*), my mouth says, "Or WD-40."

It's not a good joke. It's barely a joke. It's a lubricant.

But he laughs. Short, through his nose. Real, I think.

I stare at the worksheet very hard. My ears are burning. Tonight I'll replay this eleven times, adjusting my tone, and on most replays decide it was fine, and on one, around 11:40, decide it was the worst thing I've ever said.

*Squeak.*

But for four seconds, just now, I didn't think first.

I'll think about it later. A lot.

prompt:
Overthinking It

Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. A lingering ammonia scent from a recent cleaning distracts her mid-thought. 1000 words.
response:
# Overthinking It

Okay. Okay. The thing to say is *hi*.

Not "hey," because "hey" is for people who wear their hoods half up on purpose. Not "hello," because "hello" is what you say answering a landline in 1987. *Hi.* One syllable, one vowel. Humans have been saying it for centuries without incident.

Samir Haddad is pulling out the stool next to mine, and I have not said hi.

Now it's too late for hi. Hi has a window, and the window is roughly the time it takes someone to sit down, and he is sitting down. He has sat. If I say it now, it will sound like I've been working up to it, which I have, which is the problem.

Ms. Okafor is explaining the lab. Red cabbage indicator, six household solutions, record the color changes, write a conclusion that "demonstrates understanding of the pH scale." I could write that conclusion right now, in pen, without the cabbage. Anthocyanins shift from red in acids to purple at neutral to green and yellow in bases, because the molecule changes shape when it gains or loses hydrogen ions. I know it the way I know my own locker combination.

What I don't know is what to do with my hands.

They're on the table. Is that normal? Folded looks like I'm praying. Under the table looks like I'm hiding something. I put one on the worksheet and one on my knee, which is the posture of a woman in a catalog for chairs.

Here are the options I prepared last night between 10:40 and 11:55 p.m.:

**Option A:** Ask if he wants to measure or record. Practical. Lab partners say this. Risk: if he says "whatever," I have to choose, and the choice reveals something. Recording means I'm controlling. Measuring means I don't trust his hands. This did not seem like a real risk at eleven p.m. It feels extremely real now.

**Option B:** Mention Friday's basketball game, since he plays. Risk: I know nothing about basketball. If he asks a follow-up, I'll have to admit I only know from the athletics email, and nobody reads the athletics email, and he'll wonder why I did, and the answer is him, and he'll see the answer on my face, because my face is a window with no curtains.

**Option C:** Say nothing and let him talk first. This is the option I always end up with. It's less an option than a natural disaster I live inside.

"You want to pour or write?" he says.

He took Option A. He took *my* Option A and did it in six words without thinking, the way you'd ask someone to pass the salt.

"Um," I say. "Either. Whatever. Yeah."

Three answers. None of them answers.

In my head, I said: *I'll write, if that's okay. My handwriting's small and the data boxes are tiny, so it just makes sense.* It was a perfectly good sentence. It had a clause. It had a reason. It got stuck somewhere between my brain and my mouth, a distance of maybe four inches, and what came out was the verbal equivalent of dropping a lunch tray.

"Cool, I'll pour," he says.

Am I smiling? I feel like I'm smiling. I adjust to neutral. Neutral might look annoyed. I try for something small and pleasant, like a substitute teacher. Now I've been watching him pour cabbage juice for a long time, which is weird. Nobody looks at cabbage juice this much.

I look down at the table instead and start planning what to say when we get to the vinegar. I'll mention that acetic acid is weak, so it should go pinkish rather than full red, and that's a good thing to say because it's—

What is that *smell*?

It's coming off the table. Sharp, almost cold, the kind of smell that skips your nose and pokes the backs of your eyes. Mr. Delgado must have wiped everything down this morning. The surface has that faint streaky shine. Ammonia. Window cleaner. My grandmother's kitchen on Sunday mornings, the radio on, the glass so clean the birds hit it.

Ammonia is a base. NH₃. It grabs hydrogen ions. If cabbage juice dripped right here by my elbow, it would go green.

Oh.

That's actually interesting. A real, true, relevant-to-this-exact-second interesting thing, and it's sitting in my mouth like a cough drop.

*Don't.* It's showing off. He'll think I'm the kind of girl who corrects teachers. (I have corrected one teacher. Once. In sixth grade. About Pluto. I still think about it at night.) He'll think it's weird that I'm smelling the table. *Is* it weird? Everyone can smell the table. It's not a choice. It's chemistry. Literally.

"The table's a base," I say.

That is not the sentence. The sentence had context. The sentence had a *beginning*.

Samir looks up. "What?"

My whole body becomes a heat lamp. Okay. Recovery. One chance to turn this into something a human would say.

"They cleaned it. With ammonia. You can smell it? So if we spilled the cabbage stuff, it'd turn green. Probably."

*Probably.* As if I don't know. I know.

He leans down and sniffs the table. Samir Haddad, sniffing a lab table, because I basically told him to.

"Oh, gross, yeah," he says. "Wait. Should we test it?"

"It's not on the list."

Why did I say that? Why is my first instinct always to be a hall monitor?

"So?" He's grinning a little. He tears off a corner of paper towel, dips it in the juice, and drags it across the tabletop. It leaves a blue-green streak between us, like a tiny highlighter mark.

"Huh," he says. "You were right."

I know I was right. I've been right about the pH of household substances since I was nine. But nobody has ever said it to me like that, like it was a nice surprise instead of an annoying fact.

"Yeah," I say.

Yeah. Again. One syllable.

But I think (I'm not sure, I'll have to check, I'll replay it on the bus and at dinner and definitely at 11:40 tonight) I might have been smiling when I said it. A real one. Not the substitute-teacher one.

I write *table (ammonia residue): green* in tiny letters in the margin of the data sheet, where it doesn't belong.

I don't erase it.

prompt:
Overthinking It

Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. She doodles tiny sketches in her lab notes, each representing a different group member. 1000 words.
response:
# Overthinking It

Okay. Okay okay okay.

Mr. Haddad said "pairs of four," which isn't a thing, which is what I would have said out loud if I were a different person, and everyone would have laughed. The good kind, the *with you* kind. Instead I wrote *groups of 4?* in my notebook and underlined it twice, like I was going to follow up.

Then he read the names.

Priya Shah. Dominic Leblanc. Me. Owen Reyes.

So now Owen Reyes is sitting eleven inches from my left elbow. I know it's eleven inches because the lab tables are thirty-six inches wide and divided roughly into thirds by stains, and he's on the far side of the middle stain. This is a normal thing to know.

The lab is reaction rates. Alka-Seltzer in water at three temperatures, time the dissolving, graph it, draw conclusions. I could do the whole thing alone in eight minutes. What I can't do is figure out what to do with my hands.

Folded looks like a principal. Flat on the table looks like I'm waiting to be handcuffed. I'll hold my pencil. A pencil is a reason to have a hand.

Priya is talking. Priya is always talking, in a way I envy so much it hurts somewhere behind my sternum. She's telling Dominic about her cousin's wedding. Dominic is nodding with his eyes mostly closed.

In the corner of my data table I draw Priya as a sparkler, little lines shooting off it. Dominic is a turtle, very small, fully retracted.

Then me. A snail. The shell is very large. That's on purpose.

"Should we, like, split up jobs?" Owen says.

He says it to the table. Not to me. But I'm part of the table, so technically to me, which means I'm allowed to answer, which means I should answer, which means I've now been silent for one second, two seconds...

Option one: "I can do the timer." Safe. Except the timer is the easiest job and he'll think I'm lazy.

Option two: "I'll do data." Which I'm already doing. Which he can see. Which makes me sound like a tiny dictator of graph paper.

Option three: "Whatever you guys want." No. That's what people say after they've given up on having a personality.

Option four, which I won't say but compose anyway, in full: "I can record, since I already set up the table, but if anyone wants to switch halfway, that's fine, I don't want to hog the clipboard." A perfectly normal sentence. It even has a little joke in it. *Hog the clipboard.* It's good.

What comes out is: "I have the... paper."

I hold up the paper. Like evidence.

"Cool," says Owen. "I'll do timer, then."

*Cool.* Cool can mean *cool*, or it can mean *I'm being nice to the girl who just held up a worksheet like a hostage proving what day it is.*

Priya takes the thermometer. Dominic is assigned tablets, which he accepts like a man receiving a life sentence.

Now I have to draw Owen, because I drew everybody else, and if I don't it'll be conspicuous. People notice absences. That's basically all of astronomy.

I start a circle. Lines coming out of it. Halfway through the third line I realize I've drawn the sun.

I drew him as the *sun*.

In pencil. On a document I have to turn in. A little diagram that says *you are the center of the solar system and I orbit you*. Mr. Haddad will see it. Owen will see it, because he is eleven inches away and has eyes.

I add two hands in the middle. Now it's a clock.

It's a clock because he's the timer. That's the logic. It's airtight. Nobody in human history has ever had feelings about a clock.

"Hot one," Priya says. Dominic drops a tablet in, Owen hits the stopwatch on his phone, and the bubbles go up, and it's sort of beautiful how fast it goes. Heat is just molecules moving faster. More collisions. Everything bumping into everything, more and more often, until something changes.

That's probably a metaphor. I decline to think about it.

"Twenty-two seconds."

I write *22*. I make the twos less round so they don't look babyish. Now they look angry. I don't fix it.

Should I have smiled just then? Not a teeth one. A small, scientific, appreciating-the-reaction smile. Too late. If I smile now it's at nothing. I'd just be a girl smiling at a beaker.

The cold one takes forever. Owen leans back and says, to nobody, "This is lowkey satisfying."

And I have something. I have the whole explanation ready: less kinetic energy, fewer collisions, slower reaction. He might think it's interesting, or he might think I'm a know-it-all, or he might think I'm trying to impress him, which I would be, which is the entire problem.

My mouth opens anyway.

"It's like the molecules just... bump into each other less. They're, um. Shy."

Silence. Half a second. An eternity. Several eternities, laid end to end, reaching the moon.

Owen laughs. Not a mean laugh. A real one, short, like it surprised him out of his body. "Shy molecules," he says. "That's actually kind of funny."

Then the timer beeps and he's reading out *fifty-eight seconds* and Priya is arguing about whether the thermometer was all the way in, and it's over. The whole moment lasted maybe four seconds.

I write *58*.

I'll replay it tonight. I already know. I'll hear that half-second of silence four hundred times. I'll decide the laugh was pity, then that it wasn't, then that it was.

But mostly I'll think about *actually*.

*That's actually kind of funny.*

As in: he didn't expect me to be funny. As in: he had a baseline expectation of me. As in: at some point, for at least one second, he thought about me long enough to form a hypothesis...

I look down at the clock in the margin.

I give it a very small smile.

I erase it.

I draw it back, smaller.

prompt:
Rehearsing Rejection

Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of someone with borderline personality disorder who frequently plays out worst-case scenarios of how friends and loved ones might judge them. They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. Their phone battery hovers at critically low, adding to the anxiety of the evening. 1000 words.
response:
# Rehearsing Rejection

Four percent.

I put the phone face-down on the dresser, as if that will slow it down. The charger is at the office. Of course it is. Everything I need is always somewhere I'm not.

Her text from this afternoon: *see you at 8*. Lowercase. No x. Two weeks ago it was *can't WAIT to see you xx* and a picture of a dog in a raincoat, because she said it looked like me when I sulk. I laughed, and I saved it, and I have looked at it maybe thirty times since Tuesday, which is when the x's stopped.

Okay. So. She'll be sitting down already. She'll have ordered for herself and not for me, which is fine, which is a small thing, which is exactly the kind of small thing that is never small.

*I think we need to talk about what happened.*

And I'll say, What happened? Nothing happened. We slept together and then you got busy.

*That's not fair. You know it's more complicated.*

Is it? Explain it to me. Slowly. Since I'm apparently too much to have it explained the regular way.

*See, this is what I mean. You make everything into a trial.*

I button the green shirt. Unbutton it. She said she liked the green shirt, but that was before. If I wear it she'll think I'm trying, and trying is the most pathetic thing a person can be caught doing.

Black shirt. Armor.

And honestly, she's not that good at friendship herself. She was late to my birthday dinner in March and spent twenty minutes on the phone with her sister. I said it was fine. Apparently I've been keeping it in a drawer since then, because here it is, folded and ready.

She always does that. Arrives late, leaves early. Keeps one foot out the door so she never has to be fully anywhere.

I hear myself. I do. Dr. Amari calls this *building the case*: I prosecute someone for a crime they haven't committed so the verdict is ready when they do. I know the name of it. I could draw you a diagram.

But a pattern having a name doesn't make it wrong this time.

Three percent.

If she cancels while I'm on the bus and I don't see it, I'll walk in and she won't be there, and I'll stand by the bar like a coat nobody came back for.

\*

She's there. She's already in the booth by the window, and when she sees me she stands up, actually stands, and pulls me into her so hard my face is crushed against her collarbone. She smells like the cedar soap from her bathroom, and for four full seconds I am not thinking anything at all.

"God, I missed you," she says into my hair.

It goes into me like water into a cracked pot. I can feel every drop of it land. I want to stay right here in the aisle, in everyone's way, forever.

*Missed.* You miss things that are gone. You miss things you chose to leave.

She ordered for both of us. The fries with the garlic thing I like.

She's known me nine years. Of course she knows what I order. That's not a gift, it's a fact. Anyone could—

"I owe you an apology," she says, and my whole body becomes a held breath. Here. Here it is. "I've been awful at texting. Mum had another fall, and I've been driving out there every night, and I didn't want to..." She rubs her eyes. "I didn't want the first week after us to be about my mum's hip. That felt like a shitty thing to dump on you. Which was stupid. I should've just told you."

Relief so huge it's almost nausea.

Then, right behind it, quick as a pickpocket: *convenient.* A sick mother. Unanswerable. Who argues with a hip?

I hate that voice. I hate that I listen to it. I hate even more that I'm a little grateful for it, because it got here first, because at least it's on my side.

"You're not saying anything," she says.

*You're doing the silent thing again. It's exhausting, honestly.*

She didn't say that. She didn't say that. I look at her actual face, and it's worried. Not irritated. Worried. I think.

"I'm sorry about your mum," I manage. "I thought you were..."

What? Done with me. Embarrassed. Running the numbers on how fast she could get out.

"...busy," I finish.

My phone buzzes against my thigh. The two percent warning. I flinch like it's a smoke alarm.

She laughs, not at me, the soft laugh, and reaches into her bag and sets a charger on the table between the ketchup and the candle. "I know you," she says. "I brought it for you."

*I know you.* She has a file. She's been tracking all my forgetting, every dead battery, every lost key, adding them up...

Or she put a charger in her bag this afternoon because she was thinking about me.

Both of those play in my head at the same volume, and I can't find the knob.

She plugs it into the wall herself, takes the phone out of my hand, and connects it. Her fingers stay on mine afterward.

"I want you to stay over tonight," she says. "If you want. No pressure. I just liked waking up with you. I've been thinking about it all week."

All week. All week she was thinking about me, and all week I was in my room drafting her breakup speech for her, revising it, giving her better lines than she'd ever actually say.

I might cry. I want to say yes so badly my teeth hurt.

She'll get tired of this. Not tonight. In a month, or six, the first time I go quiet in the car and she has to ask what's wrong four times. That's when. I should remember that. I should keep it close.

"Yes," I say. "Yeah. I'd like that."

She squeezes my hand. I squeeze back too hard, then loosen my grip, then worry the loosening looked like pulling away.

The screen lights up. The little lightning bolt.

Four percent. Five.

It's climbing. I watch it climb. And somewhere behind my eyes, without asking me, I've already started rehearsing what she'll say in the morning.

They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. A hallway mirror offers a glimpse of their anxious posture before they turn away. 1000 words.
response:
# Rehearsing Rejection

*Still on for 7? x*

I've read it eleven times. The x is lowercase. She always uses lowercase, but last week there were two of them, *xx*, and before that a heart. I'm not crazy. That's a trajectory. That's data.

It's been three days of *haha* and *sorry, mad week* and one voice note I've replayed so often I can hear her fridge humming behind her. She sounded tired. Or she sounded like someone working out a kind way to say something unkind.

Here's how it goes. She'll be at the corner table by the window, because she wants to see me coming. No, because she wants an exit. She'll say, *I think we moved too fast*, gently, the way you'd coax a cat out of a tree, and I'll say:

*Honestly? I was thinking the same thing.* Light. Shrug. I've practised the shrug.

She'll look relieved, and the relief will be the worst part. Then she'll say, *You're just a lot sometimes. It's exhausting.*

And I'll say, *Says the person who vanishes for three days and expects me to be fine.*

And she'll say, *This. This is what I mean.*

My hand shakes doing my eyeliner. I'm furious at her for something she hasn't said. I know that. I *know* that. Dr. Okafor calls it rehearsing. She says I'm trying to get the pain over with in advance, like paying a bill before it arrives, and that the bill usually never comes.

Usually.

Knowing doesn't stop it. Knowing just means I get to watch myself do it from a slightly better seat.

And there's evidence anyway. She left the party in September at eleven. She said *we'll see* about Lisbon. If you line them up, they make a shape.

(Don't line them up.)

They make a shape.

Coat. Keys. The hallway mirror catches me on the way out. There's a woman in it with her shoulders hiked up to her ears and her arms wrapped across her ribs, like she's holding something in or keeping something out. Her jaw is set for an argument with nobody. She looks braced for a car crash. She looks like someone you'd want to leave.

I turn away before I can decide which.

It's a fifteen-minute walk. Enough for one more round.

She'd say, *I care about you so much, and that's why—* and I'd stop her. I'd stand up first. I'd leave exact change for my drink and walk out, and she'd be the one left sitting there. Later I'd text her something cold and perfect. I'm drafting it now: *I hope you find someone easier.*

It's devastating. I feel almost better. There's a cleanness to hating someone before they can hurt you.

Somewhere far back, a small voice says, *She hasn't done anything.* I hear it. I put it away.

She's not at the corner table. She's outside the door, and she sees me first. She's already walking toward me with her arms open, and then she's holding me. Not a quick hug. A long one, her face pressed into my neck. She smells like her hair oil and something sharper underneath, clinical. *Whose soap is that?*

"God, I missed you," she says into my collar.

Something in my chest unclenches so fast it hurts, like I've been gripping a stone all week and someone just took it from me. I almost cry. *She missed me.* I want to live inside that sentence and wrap it around me like a blanket.

*Whose soap is that?*

Inside, she takes my hand across the table and doesn't let go, even when the waiter comes.

"I'm sorry I've been crap this week," she says. "Dad had another fall. I've been at the hospital every night, and I didn't want to text you half-asleep and miserable. I wanted to actually be *with* you when I saw you. Properly."

Her dad. Of course. The relief floods in and I'm gulping it down, I'm so thirsty—

Then the other voice, quick as a slap: *Convenient.* Guilty people over-explain. And *properly*, as opposed to what? She's holding my hand the way you hold a patient's hand, gently, like I might break. Like this is a kindness she's doing me.

"You okay?" she asks. "You've gone somewhere."

"I'm fine. I'm so sorry about your dad."

I mean it. I'm also searching her face for the tell.

She tells me about the ward, the nurse who sings, her dad calling her by her aunt's name. She laughs, and her eyes fill, and she squeezes my hand. "Honestly, thinking about tonight is what got me through Thursday."

That one gets in, right under the ribs. For a second I'm just a person on a date with someone who loves me.

Then: *Only Thursday?*

I hear myself think it. I hear how unhinged it is. This is the part where I'm supposed to notice, breathe, and come back. I notice. I breathe. The voice keeps talking anyway, patient and reasonable, so much more convincing than she is.

She walks me home. At the door she kisses me slowly, her hand on my face. "Tomorrow? I'll bring breakfast."

"Yes," I say. "Yes. Please."

I don't look at the mirror. I sit on the stairs in my coat and replay it all: the hug, the hand, *I missed you*, *got me through Thursday*. I line them up. They make a shape. It's a good shape. It's love, probably. It's almost definitely love.

But the kiss was shorter than the one two weeks ago. Four seconds, maybe.

Tomorrow I'll know. If she's late. If she isn't.

response:
# Rehearsing Rejection

Seven o'clock, he said. *See you at 7.* No x. He used to put an x. Not always, I'm not insane, but often enough that its absence is a sentence.

Through the wall, Mr. Ferreira's television is doing its usual murmuring: a studio audience laughing at something whose setup I can't hear. That's how tonight will go. Everyone will understand the joke but me.

Okay. Practice.

He won't sit. People who are leaving don't sit. He stands by the door with his jacket still on and says, *I think I need some space.* And I say, very calm, *That's fine.* No. Too calm. He'll think I don't care, and then he'll feel justified. I say, *You could've told me nine days ago, when you started answering my texts in four hours instead of four minutes.* Good. Specific. He can't argue with timestamps.

Then he says, *See, this is what I mean. You keep score.*

And I say, *Somebody has to, since you clearly stopped playing.*

God, that's good. I should write that down.

He'll say I'm too much. They always arrive there eventually. It's a train station everyone gets off at. *You're a lot, Lena.* And I'll say *You knew that when you kissed me,* which is true. He kissed me in his kitchen with flour on his hands and said *you're so much* and meant it as a good thing, or said he meant it, and maybe that was the first lie and I just didn't catch it.

Honestly, his laugh is kind of performative. He laughs at waiters' jokes. Who does that. And he never asks follow-up questions. I tell him about my sister and he says *that's rough* and then talks about his commute. I've been generous, really. I've overlooked so much.

The audience next door laughs again.

I notice what I'm doing. I do. Dr. Okafor would call it *rehearsing*. She'd ask what evidence I have, and I'd say the x, and she'd make that small neutral face. I know this is the thing where I build the house just so I can burn it down before anyone else gets the matches.

But knowing it's a pattern doesn't make it false. Sometimes the alarm goes off because there's actually a fire.

The buzzer.

---

He's holding a paper bag with grease spots. Cardamom buns from the Swedish place across town. I mentioned them once, weeks ago, offhand, in the dark. He remembered. He drove forty minutes for a thing I said in the dark.

*Hi,* he says, and hugs me. Long. Longer than usual. His chin on the top of my head.

Oh. Oh, I could live here. I could stay exactly here. I'd give up anything.

Why is it so long, though? That's an airport hug. That's the kind where you're memorizing someone because you won't have them anymore. And the buns. Guilt buys pastries. Guilt drives forty minutes.

He sits. People who are leaving don't sit. Does that count? It should count. Write it down.

*I'm sorry I've been weird,* he says. *My dad's scans came back bad again. I didn't want to unload all that on you. Things have been so good with us, and I didn't want to make it heavy.*

His dad. His dad is sick, and I was cataloguing his laugh.

A hot, sick wave goes through me. That's the shame. Then, right behind it and faster: *things have been so good.* Have been. As in, up until now.

No. Stop. He's telling you something real.

I take his hand. I say the right things, I think. I say *you can unload on me*, and I mean it so hard my throat hurts. He looks at me like I've given him something. Like I'm the one who brought the pastries.

*I missed you,* he says. *Like, a stupid amount.*

I want him to say it again. I want to record it and play it in the car, in the shower, at three a.m. I want to tattoo it somewhere I can read it without a mirror.

*Are we okay?* I hear myself ask.

*We're really okay.*

*Really?*

He laughs. It's not the waiter laugh. It's softer, maybe tired. *Really, Lena.*

That's twice I asked. He'll remember that. He'll tell some future person, *She always needed to be told.* He was patient tonight, but patience runs out, and I just spent some of his.

He kisses my forehead. We eat the buns out of the bag on the couch, and he gets cardamom sugar on his jeans and tells me about the oncologist, who has a ponytail and calls everyone *my friend*. I laugh at the right part. I think I laugh at the right part.

---

He's asleep now, on his side, one arm flung toward where I was before I got up for water and didn't go back.

I'm standing in the dark kitchen, replaying. *A stupid amount.* That's good. That's evidence. I'm filing it. *Things have been so good.* I've decided that one's fine. Mostly.

But he didn't say *I love you*. He's said it twice before, both times a little drunk. Tonight he was sober and he didn't. Which means sober Theo maybe doesn't…

I know. I know. I can watch myself do it, like watching my own hand reach for a hot pan. Seeing it isn't the same as stopping.

Through the wall, Mr. Ferreira has fallen asleep with the TV on again. Someone muffled is saying *…just tell me what you want from me…* and the audience, who isn't really there, laughs and laughs.

I go back to bed. I lie down carefully so I don't wake him, and I put my hand flat on his back to feel it rise. I'm so full I could cry, and I'm already practicing what I'll say when he leaves.

# Blood Debt

The torch had been jammed into a crack in the west wall, above the toppled altar, and it was the only light in the hall. Everything it touched trembled: the stumps of lacquered pillars, the bare ribs of the roof against the stars, the faces of forty men packed along the walls. Mexican silver changed hands in the dark. Someone was calling odds in two languages.

Neither master knew. Both had forbidden this in nearly the same words.

Ijūin Kaname stood at the east end of the cracked flagstones, his back to the doorway where the Nagasaki night breathed in. He held a wooden sword of unpolished oak, its grain darkened by ten thousand blows against the striking post at home in Satsuma. His feet were bare. His face was already flushed.

Eight paces away, the torch behind him, Ma Jun shook out his arms like a man drying his hands. He had brought nothing. His shadow lay long across the floor, its head nearly touching Kaname's toes.

"My uncle died in this city," Kaname said, "with a Ma fist in his throat."

"Your uncle drew steel on an empty-handed man." Ma rolled his neck. "Try wood. See if it goes better."

To Ma's right, along the south wall, a fallen roof beam lay knee-high across a pillar stump. Nobody stood near it. The crowd hugged the north wall and the doorway.

Kaname lifted the oak into *tonbo*: hands high beside his right ear, the tip angled back toward the broken roof, left elbow thrust forward. Then he went still. That was the doctrine. The first strike is the only strike. Meet it with a block and the block goes into the ground with you.

So Ma did not mean to meet it. He drifted, weight sliding heel to toe, half a step in, half a step out, working closer, and with every shift his shadow lurched across the flagstones, stretching and shrinking, lying about the distance.

Kaname screamed.

It was not a shout but a shriek, high and tearing, the monkey cry of his school, and he was moving before it ended. In three strides the oak fell from beside his ear on a diagonal toward Ma's left collarbone.

Ma slid back and to his right. The oak struck the flagstone where his lead foot had been and sprayed chips of stone across the front row. As Kaname's weight finished forward, Ma's right arm came around from the hip in a flat, whipping arc. The power came from his waist, not his shoulder, and his cupped palm burst against Kaname's left ear.

Kaname stumbled half a step north. The Chinese side roared.

He turned, already rising back into *tonbo*, and now he faced the south wall, with Ma between him and the fallen beam. Kaname saw it before Ma did. He advanced in short, flat steps, the oak high, and Ma gave ground until his calves touched timber.

The shriek again. The cut.

Ma went up and back, onto the beam. The oak fell where he had stood and bit into the rotten edge of the timber where his shins had been pressed a moment before. It sank deep and stuck for half a heartbeat. Standing above his enemy, Ma swung both arms over in a windmill, one after the other, and the second came down like a flail across Kaname's left collarbone.

Everyone heard it crack.

Kaname's left hand jerked off the grip. With his right alone he wrenched the oak free and whipped it backhand along the top of the beam into Ma's ankles. Ma's feet flew out. He fell sideways off the timber, hit the flagstones on his shoulder, and kept rolling west, away from the oak, until he came up beneath the torch. His left ankle was already refusing his weight.

Kaname turned to face him. Now the light was in Kaname's eyes. Ma was a silhouette with fire behind him and the altar a step at his back.

Kaname raised the oak. His left hand found the grip again and shook there, barely closing. The Satsuma men had gone quiet. They knew what that arm was worth now.

Ma could not retreat. He could not circle on that ankle. He set his feet and let his arms hang.

Kaname did not wait. His school never waited. He shrieked and charged, and the oak fell from his right side toward Ma's left shoulder. It came down weaker than before, because the broken left side could not pull it through.

Ma stepped in on the ruined ankle, because there was no other way. He went forward and to his own right, toward Kaname's injured side, inside the arc. The tip of the oak never reached him. The last third near the grip came down across the top of his left shoulder, and something there gave with a wet sound.

His right arm was already rising. It came up from beside his knee in a hooking arc, palm open, the full turn of his hips behind it, and struck Kaname under the jaw. Kaname's head snapped back. At the top of its swing the same arm reversed and fell like a cleaver against the side of his neck.

Kaname dropped to his knees. The oak clattered away toward the beam. Then he toppled onto his right side, away from Ma, and lay still.

No one cheered.

Ma stood over him with his left arm hanging wrong, breathing through his teeth. Blood ran from Kaname's ear in a thin line and found the cracks in the floor.

Two Satsuma men pushed through and lifted Kaname by the armpits. He was breathing. One of them looked at Ma. He did not look angry, only careful, the way a man looks at a name he intends to remember.

"Now," he said in Japanese, "you owe."

They carried Kaname out through the east door. The crowd followed in pieces, money still changing hands, quieter than before. Ma's own people came to take his good arm.

He looked back once. The torch had burned down to a stub in its crack. The pillar shadows no longer danced. They leaned, long and patient, across the place where the debt had been paid and written again.

# Blood Debt

The roof of Seigan-ji had come down in a typhoon twenty years ago, and no one had ever paid to raise it. Moonlight fell through the bare rafters in a pale square on the stone floor of the main hall. Around that square, beneath lanterns hung from the surviving pillars, two hundred people shoved for a view.

The Satsuma men held the north side, below the empty altar dais. The porters and dockhands of the Chinese quarter held the south, packed into the broken doorway. Money crossed between them in fists: coins, a week's wages, the pawn ticket for somebody's grandfather's sword.

Ijūin Kaname stood at the north edge of the moonlight. Lin Qiao stood at the south. Ten paces of stone lay between them. Along the west edge of the square, the great roof beam lay where it had fallen, thick as a man's waist. On the east, one cracked pillar still stood, a lantern nailed to it.

Both wore armbands. His was black banded with red, hers red banded with black. From the back of the crowd you could not tell them apart, and both schools found that unbearable.

Fourteen years ago, Lin's teacher's son had died on this floor with his skull opened by a Jigen stick. Both masters had forbidden any return. Kaname's master forbade it because there was nothing to gain by proving the obvious. Lin's master forbade it because she was the best he had left.

Kaname lifted his weapon. It was a rough length of isu wood with no guard, the same kind he had driven into the striking post ten thousand times each dawn until the bark smoked. He raised it to *tonbo*: hands high beside his right ear, stick angled skyward, left foot forward. His school taught one truth. *Doubt nothing in the first cut. The second cut is defeat.*

Lin's sleeves were bound at the elbow. Her arms hung loose from her shoulders like ropes with stones tied to the ends.

She moved first, circling to her right, toward his left side and away from the raised stick. Kaname did not step. He turned in place with small grinding shifts of his feet, keeping her square before him, until he faced east and she stood two paces from the cracked pillar. Only then did he understand. The lantern hung directly behind her head. She was a silhouette, and he was squinting into the flame.

The Chinese side laughed. A Satsuma man spat.

Lin stepped in. One long sliding step put her head inside his reach, bare, offered.

Kaname screamed. It was the shriek his school was known for, high and animal, a sound meant to stop an enemy's heart before the wood arrived. He came with it in three driving steps, and the stick fell from beside his ear like a dropped blade.

Lin was already turning. She pivoted on her right heel and swept her left foot back in a wide arc, rotating edge-on to the cut and carrying herself half a step to his left. The isu wood passed close enough to stir her collar and struck the floor where she had stood. Stone chips sprayed across the moonlight. The shock went up Kaname's arms into his teeth.

Now she was at his left shoulder, and he was bent over a stick buried in its own follow-through.

The turn that had saved her became her windup. Her right arm rose behind her and came over in a full vertical circle, shoulder loose, hand edge-first, and crashed down onto his left collarbone. The same arm rebounded off the impact, reversing up the circle it had come down, and the back of her fist cracked across his left ear. Chop and hook, one wheel, half a second.

Kaname staggered away from her. Blood ran from his ear down his neck. The Chinese side roared.

He did not strike again. He backpedaled five steps, then six, dragging the stick up to *tonbo* with his left arm shaking, until his heels met the fallen beam on the west edge and he could go no farther.

Lin followed, unhurried. She saw what everyone saw. His left side was failing and his grip was crooked. With the beam at his heels, he had no room for the charge, and a Jigen cut without its charge was only a man swinging a stick.

She came in at long range, outside his reach, and threw her right arm in a high overhand whip at the crown of his head. It was a strike meant to land with nothing but fingertips and wrist, snapping like the end of a rope.

Kaname did not scream this time. He stepped forward half a foot and cut again.

It was short, silent, and ugly. The second cut slanted down from beside his right ear and met her right forearm at the top of its arc. It broke the bone between wrist and elbow. The sound carried to the doorway.

On the north side, the Satsuma men went quiet. Not one cheered.

Lin's broken arm folded, but her body did not stop. Pigua never stops, because every circle feeds the next. The falling weight of the ruined arm dragged her shoulders through their turn. Her left arm, already rising behind her, came over the top in the next revolution of the wheel, and the hammer of her fist dropped onto his right temple.

Kaname went backward over the beam. His legs stayed draped across it. His head and shoulders struck the stone beyond, and the stick rolled away into the dark.

Lin stood over him, right arm hanging at an angle no arm should hang. The moonlight had shifted onto his face. His eyes were open.

"That was the second cut," she said.

"I know." He was staring up through the rafters. "I wanted to win more than I wanted to be Jigen."

Behind them the crowd broke apart. The Chinese side shouted victory. The Satsuma side shouted that it didn't count, that a man who cut twice was no Jigen man at all. Hands grabbed for money everywhere. Someone at the doorway yelled that the masters were coming up the hill.

Lin looked down at the two armbands, his and hers. Soaked through with sweat and blood, in the lantern light they had gone the same dark color.

Fourteen years of debt, she thought. Tonight they had only added to it.
