# Blood Debt

The temple on the hill above Nagasaki had lost its roof to a typhoon and its monks to cholera. In the thirty years since, it had found a new congregation.

They lined the walls tonight by lantern light. On the east side, the Satsuma men stood along a fallen pillar with their sleeves tied back, placing bets in clipped Kagoshima dialect. On the west, Cangzhou dockhands and caravan guards crouched over heaps of copper and laughed too loudly. Between them lay the main hall's open floor, thirty paces of cracked flagstone, and down its middle ran the water.

It seeped from a split in the altar base at the north end and crept south toward the broken doors. The trickle was a hand's width wide and never deeper than a fingernail, but it had run for years, and the stones along its path wore a skin of black moss.

Ijūin Hayato stood east of the water. Gao Lin stood west.

Neither master knew they were here. Both had forbidden exactly this, as their own masters had, all the way back to the night a Satsuma retainer cut down a Chinese bodyguard below the Tōjin quarter and the bodyguard's brother answered with a cleaver. Every generation since had added a name to the ledger.

Ijūin raised his sword. It was not steel, because since the sword ban oak was all a Satsuma man could carry. But it was the heavy yusu wood of his school, thick as a wrist, and he had struck the training post with it ten thousand times before breakfast. He lifted it into *tonbo*, hilt beside his right ear, tip angled at the sky, left foot forward. Jigen-ryū taught that a man needed one cut. A second meant the first had been unworthy.

Gao let his arms hang. He turned his left side toward the Japanese and sank his weight onto his back leg, his hands loose as wet rope. His school had never owned swords. It had owned long arms and shoulders loose enough to throw them.

"Your grandfather ran," Ijūin said.

"Mine walked," said Gao. "Yours limped after him."

Ijūin screamed.

It was the Jigen cry, a shriek like tearing sheet metal, and it carried him across the floor. He took three strides, and on the third he leapt the water entirely and landed west of it with the oak already falling. It came diagonally from his right shoulder toward Gao's collarbone.

Gao did not block. Nobody blocked that. He drew his front foot back behind his rear one and swung his whole body a half-turn away, like a door on a hinge. The oak passed a finger's breadth from his chest and broke a chip from the flagstone. As the door swung, so did his arm. His right hand came over the top in a long whipping chop, *pi*, and its ridge snapped across Ijūin's cheekbone.

The skin split. Ijūin did not flinch.

A Jigen man whose first cut misses does not retreat. He cuts again. Ijūin ripped the oak back up to his shoulder and drove forward, alternating left and right diagonals like the morning drill at the post. Gao gave ground west and then north, each step a sliding half-circle, and the Cangzhou men scrambled back from the wall.

The last standing pillar rose at the northwest corner of the floor. Gao slipped behind it.

Ijūin's next cut bit into the pillar's edge. Old cedar splintered, and the oak shuddered in his hands. In that half-beat Gao swung out from the pillar's east side, now between Ijūin and the stream, at the Japanese man's right flank. His arm rose from his hip in a full vertical circle, a hanging backfist, *gua*, that cracked into Ijūin's floating ribs.

Ijūin grunted and pivoted to face him, now looking east. He drove the oak's butt into Gao's breastbone with his whole weight behind it.

Gao stumbled backward three steps. The third found the water.

His heel shot out on the moss, and he went down hard on his left hip in the stream. The east wall roared.

Ijūin rose into *tonbo*. Two strides was all the distance left. He screamed and came on, and the oak fell toward Gao's skull.

Gao could not stand in time, so he did not try. He shoved off the dry stone with his right palm and let the moss take him. He slid south along the wet channel on his hip, a full body's length, the stream carrying him like a sled. The oak struck where his head had been, and the whole force of the cut went into stone. Something cracked. It was the yusu wood, split along its grain.

Ijūin's left foot came down in the stream.

Jigen-ryū never holds anything back. The cut is all of you. His lead foot skated forward, and his hips followed the broken sword past the point of balance. He crashed down onto his left knee in the channel, facing the east wall, his right side open to the south.

Gao rolled out of the water onto the dry east bank and came up on his feet at Ijūin's right shoulder. He planted, turned his waist, and threw his right arm down from the shoulder in an overhead arc, loose as a flail. The ridge of his forearm struck the side of Ijūin's neck below the ear. His left arm followed on the rebound in a rising *gua*, and his backfist caught the hinge of Ijūin's jaw.

Ijūin's head snapped sideways. He folded forward, face-down in the stream.

The hall went silent except for the water.

Gao stood over him, chest heaving, his cotton jacket soaked black down one side. The trickle parted around Ijūin's face. Blood from the split cheek threaded into it, a thin red ribbon running south toward the broken doors.

Gao bent, took Ijūin by the collar, and turned his face out of the water. It was not mercy. A drowned man was a debt neither school could pay in copper.

On the east side, the Satsuma men stepped down off the fallen pillar. On the west, the Cangzhou men rose from their crouch. Coins slid off a sleeve and rang on the stone.

Gao watched the red ribbon thin and lengthen, sliding past the doors toward the hill path and the city below. By morning, both masters would know. By evening, someone would be opening the ledger again.

response:
# Breaking Formation

The clock above the mirror is red, six digits, and it only counts one direction.

00:38:12.

Seven of us stand in a wedge of spike tape, its point aimed at the glass. Ji-woo holds mark one, front and center. I'm on mark six, the back-left corner, close enough to the door to smell the hallway's lemon disinfectant. Yoon-seonsaengnim sits on a stool beside the speaker in the front-right corner, a clicker in her fist. Last month she broke a boy from Busan in four days. He left his shoes on mark three.

"Hana, dul, set, net." Click, click, click, click.

The track drops and the wedge moves like one animal.

One: right arm cuts to the high diagonal, forty-five degrees, palm flat, fingers sealed. Two: fists slam to hips, knees bend into a half-squat. Three-and: chest hit forward, chest hit back. Four: quarter-turn right on the balls of the feet, facing the barre. Five-six: drop to the right knee, left arm sweeping overhead like a blade. Seven: rise, snap back to the mirror. Eight: freeze, right hand framing the jaw, chin cut thirty degrees left.

In the glass, six girls do exactly that. The seventh is me, doing something adjacent.

My arm reaches forty-five degrees, but it travels there on a wave, shoulder to elbow to wrist, because that's how an arm moves where I'm from. My squat has bounce in it. My chest hits land a hair behind the click, because the snare lands a hair behind the click. I spent nine years in Bronx cyphers learning to ride the pocket, not the metronome.

Click. Music dies.

"Yuk-beon." Number six. She doesn't use my name. "You are dancing to the song."

"It's a song," I say.

Ji-woo's shoulders go rigid in the mirror.

"You dance to my count. The song is decoration." Yoon stands. "*Kal-gak.* Knife angle. Your arm does not tell a story. It arrives. It stops. *Dasi.*"

00:34:40.

These girls have trained since they were eleven. They bow when they enter. They drink from glass bottles etched with the academy logo. I drink from the bathroom tap, because those bottles cost four thousand won and my stipend has to cover the phone card I use to call Mami after her second shift at the laundromat. My sneakers are taped at the toe. The block threw me a party when the scholarship email came. A kid I taught to toprock asked if I'd be famous. I said yeah.

Hana. Arm cuts. I kill the wave. Dul. I lock the bounce out of my knees, and it feels like breathing through a straw. Set-and. Hit, hit, on the click, and the snare slides past me like a train I'm not allowed to catch. Net. Quarter-turn.

Daseot. Drop.

And my body goes home.

My right hand plants before my knee does. Weight tips over the wrist, left leg already sweeping, threading under, and the first three steps of a six-step roll out before my brain can object. Every time music has told me to go down, I've gone down and *spun*.

By ilgop the wedge has risen. By yeodeol six girls are frozen, chins cut left, and I'm scrambling upright with my back to the mirror.

The clock eats four seconds.

Yoon walks the center line, past Ji-woo, between marks two and three, then four and five. She veers into my corner and stands over me.

"Your way. Eight counts. Show me."

No click. I listen for the snare and take it.

Toprock first: Indian step, right crossing over left, arms open, bouncing in the pocket. Drop on four. Six-step, full circle, palm hot on the wood. Shoulder down, I whip my legs into a windmill, one rotation, two, legs in a wide V. On eight I snap into a chair freeze, elbow jammed into my hip, tilted on one palm, breathing.

In the mirror, I'm the only thing in the room that looks alive.

Yoon crouches until her face is level with mine.

"That," she says quietly, "is why I chose you." She taps my locked elbow. "And that is why you will go home. *Kal-gunmu*: seven blades, one cut. If one blade is beautiful, the cut is crooked." She stands. "Find out if you can be one-seventh."

We drill for thirty-four minutes. My wrist learns to stay off the floor. My knees learn to stop listening. Somewhere inside me, a cypher goes quiet.

00:00:19.

"Last run," Yoon says. "Clean, or everyone stays."

Six girls look at me in the glass without turning their heads.

Hana: the arm arrives and stops. Dul: fists, squat, no bounce. Set-and: I let the snare go by. Net: quarter-turn. Daseot, yeoseot: right knee down. *Knee*, not hand, and every nerve in my wrist screams. Ilgop: rise. Yeodeol: freeze.

Second eight: the inversion. On five, Ji-woo travels straight back down the center line while I travel three steps diagonally forward from my corner. She passes my right shoulder close enough that her ponytail brushes my sleeve. On six I hit my new mark, front row, just left of center. Exactly.

Yeodeol. Final freeze: hand at the jaw, chin cut thirty degrees left.

And in the mirror, for the first time, I can't find myself. Seven hands. Seven jaws. I search the glass the way you search a crowd for your mother, and every face is turned away at the same angle.

00:00:03.

In the Bronx, a freeze is the period at the end of a sentence you wrote yourself. Here, it's a period someone else typed.

00:00:02.

I bring my chin back to center and look straight into the glass, at the girl I almost lost a second ago. Everything else holds the line. Thirty degrees. That's how much of me breaks formation.

00:00:01.

Yoon sees it. I see her see it.

00:00:00.

The clock goes dark. She clicks once.

"Chin, yuk-beon. Fix it tomorrow."

She's at the door before she adds, without turning, "Desiree."

It's the first time she's said my name. I still don't know if it was a warning.

**Breaking Formation**

The tape on the floor tells me where I'm allowed to exist.

Blue X, back row, left window. That's the gap behind Seo-yeon and Ji-woo, placed so cameras that aren't here yet can see me between them. Five trainees, five colors. Back in Oakland, turf meant *Taking Up Room on the Floor*. Here the room comes pre-measured, and Director Kang calls me by my tape.

"Blue. Again."

She stands at the center of the back wall, watching us through the mirror. I see her over my own reflected shoulder: black tracksuit, arms folded. She built three groups by breaking trainees down to the studs. When she walked in this morning we bowed ninety degrees, and I was the first one up. I'm always the first one up.

Two speakers hang above the mirror's corners, two above her. All four hit the downbeat together, a hair too loud, so the kick doesn't come from anywhere. It just arrives in my molars.

"*Daseot, yeoseot, ilgop, yeodeol*—"

One: right foot out to second, arms snap to a high V. Two: arms slice down to a T, palms flat. In the mirror my left hand vanishes behind Seo-yeon's right forearm at exactly the wrist, like the last forty times. Three: left fist to sternum, elbow level with the shoulder.

And-four: chest pops.

Two hits. Pop, pop, head locked like it's bolted to a shelf. But I learned popping on the Fruitvale BART platform from my cousin Dre, and in the Town a pop is a door, not a wall. You hit it, then you walk through it. So on the second pop my sternum fires and the wave just goes, through my ribs, down my stomach, out my hips. An eighth of a beat of liquid nobody ordered.

In the mirror, four statues and one ripple.

Five: quarter turn left. Hips square to the soundproof foam on the side wall. The mirror swings to my right, and now it shows five profiles stacked like a flipbook. Six: right arm shoots forward, finger aimed at the foam. Seven: drop to a deep squat, heels flat, spine vertical.

Eight: hold.

This is where it gets me. The producer swung the hi-hats just slightly, and my knees hear it. They want to settle behind the beat, in the pocket, where the funk lives. So I land a hair after the others. In a cypher, that's flavor. Here it's a crack in the wall everyone can see light through.

Next eight. One-two: rise, snap back to face the mirror. Three through six: the line change. I take four steps forward into the gap between Seo-yeon and Ji-woo while Seo-yeon slides left to widen it. Hae-won mirrors me on the right while Min slides out. One step per count. Toe, ball, heel.

I don't walk. Twelve years of laundromat linoleum on International Boulevard take over, and I glide, heel-toe-heel. I reach my second mark, a blue dash, on five. A full count early. My left shoulder nearly clips Seo-yeon's while she's still clearing.

The music dies in all four corners at once. Silence presses in from the same places the sound did.

Kang switches to English. That's its own punishment, because now everyone knows who it's for.

"I asked for two hits. You gave me two hits and a sentence. In the squat, late. In the walk, early. You are never where we are."

"It's on the beat," I say. "Just in the pocket."

Min's eyes find mine in the mirror, then drop.

"There is no pocket." Kang walks up the empty floor where the back row used to be. She stops a meter behind me, so we're stacked in the glass, her face over my shoulder. "This is *kalgunmu*. Knife dance. Five blades, one cut. What does a knife do when one blade is curved?"

I don't answer.

"It tears." She taps the blue dash with her toe. "Your body is the best instrument in this room. I mean that. And you play it like you're the only one in the band."

She walks back to the wall.

I think about my mother on the overnight shift at the Walgreens on High Street, crying at SFO over a scholarship letter she'd already read twenty times. I think about the other four, whose parents pay more a month for this floor than she makes. I think about Dre: *Don't let them sand you down.*

And here's what nobody tells you: I can do it. That's what scares me. If I couldn't, I could go home a martyr. But my body is already learning. Every run, the wave gets a little shorter, cauterized a little more. One more month and it might not come at all, and I won't know if I killed it or it left.

"Reset. From the top. Full out."

I walk backward to the blue X. *Daseot, yeoseot, ilgop, yeodeol.*

V. T. My wrist disappears behind Seo-yeon's. The pops land like dime stops and die there, the wave caged in my ribs, beating at the bars. Quarter turn, point, squat. I land on the front edge of the beat, with them, and it feels like swallowing a word I've already said. Rise. Toe, ball, heel, four counts, arriving on six exactly as Seo-yeon finishes clearing. Seven: arms cross in an X over my face. Eight: hit.

In the mirror, five identical bodies. For a second I genuinely can't find myself. I have to look down at the tape.

The final chord rings out of the corners and starts to decay.

And in that tail, after the count, inside the hold, where technically there's nothing left to get wrong, I fold my right index finger. One knuckle, ninety degrees. The smallest tut there is. My name, in the only alphabet I brought.

Kang's eyes go to it in the mirror. Stay there. The reverb thins to nothing.

"Again," she says.

She doesn't say what to fix.

# Breaking Formation

The fan cracks shut like a knuckle, and the music dies mid-bar.

Seven of us freeze where we land. The mirror covers the whole front wall, so I get to watch exactly how wrong I am: six bodies in a clean line, blue tape Xs hidden under their sneakers, and me half a step closer to the glass than anyone, sticking out of the line like a chipped tooth. My blue X is somewhere behind my heels. I glided right over it.

"Four," says Han Seo-yeon.

That's me. Nobody here has said my name in three weeks.

She doesn't rise from her stool by the speaker. She just aims the closed fan at the floor behind me, and we all walk back to our yellow Xs. Mine is back row, second from the right, with Jiwoo on my left and Minseo on my right. The front row stands ahead of us like a fence with gaps in it: Yuna dead center, Hyunwoo on her right. The gap between them is mine. On five through eight I travel straight forward through it. Four steps, sixty centimeters each. Someone taped a meter stick to the wall the first day. I thought it was a joke.

"*Hana, dul, set, net*—"

One: right arm punches out to the side, shoulder height, palm down, fingers welded together. Mine want to ripple. Back home on International Boulevard a hand never just stops. It keeps talking, a wave rolling out through the knuckles, a finger tut folding the air into boxes. I clamp it, and it costs me.

Two: head snaps left, chin level. I'm good at this one. A hit is a hit anywhere.

Three: chest pops forward, then back on the *and*. My sternum goes out and my spine tries to follow it down. It's the start of a body wave, hips answering chest the way water answers a dropped stone, and I have to kill it at the ribs. It leaves me jerking like a car that won't turn over.

Four: wrists cross in front of the breastbone.

Five through eight, I lift my feet. I make myself, heel-toe, heel-toe, like stepping over puddles. Where I learned, on the BART platform at Fruitvale and a mattress somebody dragged behind the liquor store, you don't lift. You glide: toes driving, heels floating, the floor turned to ice. My feet don't know how to *walk* to music. They hit the blue X on the *and* after eight.

*Crack.*

"Late."

Everyone holds the end pose, fists at hips, breathing through their noses. Their sneakers are the kind that come in limited drops. Mine have duct tape over the left toe from toe-stands. Yuna's been training since she was eleven. Jiwoo's father came to monthly evaluation in a coat that cost more than my mom's car. I'm the scholarship, and everyone knows it. They bow to Han and murmur *seonsaengnim*, bow to the seniors and murmur *sunbae*, and I bow a half second behind, the way I do everything here.

That's what nobody warned me about. The track is 128 BPM, kick on every downbeat, and they live on the kick. I live in the hi-hat between kicks. Turfing is all *and*. Where I'm from, the song doesn't tell you where to land. You tell the song.

Han stands and walks the line until she's at my shoulder. With the tip of the fan she lifts my right wrist into the count-one line, then nudges the elbow up two centimeters.

"Your hit on two is the cleanest in the room," she says. She switches to English for me and talks slow, the way you talk to a dog you haven't decided to keep. "Who taught you?"

"Nobody."

"Nobody also taught you to dance alone." The fan rests on my sternum. "Here, seven bodies is one body. One breathes different, the camera sees a mistake. Raw is nice. Raw is meat. I don't sell meat." She walks back to the corner. "Again."

We reset to the yellow Xs.

I give her the machine. One: arm out, fingers dead. Two: snap. Three: pop and back, spine locked like rebar. Four: cross. Then sixty, sixty, sixty, sixty, and on eight I plant on the blue X, square between Yuna's shoulder and Hyunwoo's, landing with Jiwoo and Minseo to the millisecond. *Kal-gunmu*, they call it. Knife-sharp group dance. Seven blades cutting one line.

No crack. Han nods once.

It's the first nod I've gotten. It feels like nothing. It feels like wearing someone else's skin that fits a little too well. In the mirror there are seven people, and I can't find myself.

And I think: two years of this, and I go home and step into the cypher at Fruitvale and my arm stops dead on one. My fingers forget how to talk. Somebody says, *damn, what happened to you*, and I don't have an answer.

"Full section," Han says. "From the top."

Yellow X. Jiwoo left, Minseo right, the gap ahead exactly one body wide.

*Hana.* Arm out, fingers dead. I give her that. *Dul.* Snap. *Set.* Pop, back, locked. *Net.* Cross.

Five.

I don't lift my feet.

My toes drive and my heels float and I glide straight down the center of my gap, not wide, not flashy. I go slow on five and six while Jiwoo and Minseo step and cover ground beside me, and I fall a few centimeters behind. Then I let it run on seven, the slide carrying me level with them, and on eight my heels drop flat onto the blue X, square with Yuna and Hyunwoo. In the mirror, six people walked to the line. One got poured there.

*Crack.*

Nobody breathes. Han stares at my feet for a long time.

"Slow on five, six. Fast on seven." Her voice is flat. "You averaged to eight."

"I hit my mark."

"You hit it." She opens the fan and folds it shut again, one rib at a time, quiet this time. "Tomorrow you do my way one hundred times. Clean. Then maybe you show me yours once." She turns to the room. "Again."

I walk back to the yellow X. *Hana*, she counts, and I lift my feet.

One.

Somewhere under my ribs I fold the glide up small, the way she folds that fan, and I pray it's still there at a hundred.

# Therapeutic Boundaries

The man on the wall has no skin. Someone peeled him for educational purposes and pinned him above the treatment table, arms out, palms forward, every muscle labelled in tidy serif. *Vastus medialis. Rectus femoris. Sartorius*, angling across his thigh like a sash. He stares straight ahead at nothing, and his left knee works perfectly.

Mine rests on a pillow, almost straight, forty-nine days out of surgery.

"Quads soft," Owen says. "Let it go."

I let it go, as much as anything goes these days.

He takes my kneecap between his thumbs and index fingers, the way you'd lift a coaster off a wet table, and pushes it down toward my foot. It resists. Scar tissue has glued it in place, and the glide is a gristly reluctance I can *hear* inside my leg. He pushes it up toward my hip, then braces his thumbs against its outer rim and drives it inward. The stiff tissue along the inner joint pulls taut as a wet sheet.

"Number."

"Three."

"Liar."

Owen and I trained in the same group for six years. Same coach, same 7 a.m. hurdle drills in rain that came sideways off the reservoir. He ran the 110s, I ran the 100s, and I was better at mine than he ever was at his. He retired at twenty-six and got a degree, then this clinic and these hands. I got to twenty-nine, a European silver, and a clipped fourth barrier in Rome that folded my left knee sideways at nine metres a second.

The federation's disability policy pays out only after twelve weeks of documented rehabilitation. So here I am, being recovered. Nobody says what I'm recovering toward. The surgeon's word was *recreationally*. I'd rather he'd taken the leg.

Owen slides a rolled towel under my heel so my calf hangs over nothing. He sets the heel of his hand on my thigh just above the kneecap and leans. My knee is five degrees short of straight, and those last five degrees live in the capsule at the back of the joint. The pressure arrives there as a hot wire drawn tight across the crease. My hamstrings fire, trying to fold the knee back up. He waits them out, weight steady, until they quit.

"Breathe out."

I breathe out. The knee sinks a millimetre. The wire glows.

"Thirty seconds." I count aloud with him, because counting is something to do with my mouth that isn't swearing.

He pulls the towel away. "Quad set. Press the back of your knee into the table."

He lays two fingers on my inner thigh, just above and inside the kneecap, where the vastus medialis should bulge like a teardrop. Mine used to. Now when I tighten it, it flickers under his fingertips like a bulb that won't catch.

"Again. Hold ten."

I hold ten. His fingers stay, warm and dry and very still. The skin of my inner thigh rises in goosebumps all the way to my hip. He sees it. I see him see it. His gaze goes across me to the wall, to the flayed man, and stays there, as if he's checking my anatomy against the poster.

"Good," he tells the poster.

"Roll over."

I roll prone and turn my head right, cheek on the paper sheet, facing the wall and away from him. Owen moves to my left side. His left hand settles flat on the back of my thigh, just below the crease of my buttock. It's there to pin the pelvis. Rectus femoris is the only quad that crosses the hip, and when the knee bends far enough, it drags the pelvis off the table to cheat. I know all this. Knowing doesn't help.

His right hand wraps the front of my ankle, and he begins folding my heel toward my backside.

Ninety degrees is nothing. A hundred is a dull, stretched ache across the graft scar. Past a hundred and ten, the whole front of my thigh catches fire, the quads hauled long over a joint that has forgotten how to bend. My hip tries to lift. His palm presses it down. It is the only part of me that doesn't hurt.

"Number."

"Six."

"Kit."

"Seven."

He used to stretch me on the infield after sessions. I'd lie on the wet grass with my straight leg propped on his shoulder while he leaned in, my hamstring opening, both of us laughing at something stupid. Sometimes I hooked my heel behind his neck and pulled him down, just to annoy him. Same hands. They didn't mean anything then. Or they did, and we were too busy to notice.

"Push into me," he says. "Twenty percent. Five seconds."

I drive my shin back against his hand, trying to straighten the knee, and he holds without giving. *Five. Four.* My breath rasps against the paper. *Two. One.*

"Relax."

I relax, and in the instant the muscle lets go, he takes up the slack: two degrees, three. The burn goes white. A sound escapes me that I haven't permitted. My fingers clamp the table's edge. Water leaks from my upper eye, across the bridge of my nose, into the sheet. My toes curl against nothing.

He doesn't push further, and he doesn't let go. He holds me exactly at the edge. Above me I can hear his breathing, and it isn't quite as steady as his voice.

"Eight?" he asks quietly.

"Eight."

"Ten seconds. You're nearly there."

*Nearly where?* I want to ask. *Stairs? Recreationally?*

I count to ten. He lowers my heel in stages, the knee unfolding slowly, and blood floods the front of my thigh like warm water. His hand leaves the back of my leg a beat later than it should. Then it leaves all at once, as if burned.

He steps back and writes on his clipboard. "One-sixteen. Up four."

I stay facedown. My cheek is wet, and I won't wipe it while he's watching.

"You could've handed my file to Priya," I say into the sheet. "Day one. You didn't have to take me."

The pen stops.

"I could have," he says.

He doesn't say why. He goes to fetch the ice.

Above me, the flayed man holds out his open palms, every muscle named, nothing left beneath the skin to hide.

# Therapeutic Boundaries

The lavender is his idea: a white diffuser on the windowsill breathing out a cold ribbon of vapour that never quite beats the disinfectant on the plinth. I hate it. Lavender is for people who are supposed to relax. I'm here because a surgeon and an insurance clause say I have to be.

"Patella first," Callum says, and I lie back.

The paper sheet crackles under my shoulder blades. My right knee looks borrowed: a vertical scar running down over the patellar tendon, two portal marks either side like cigarette burns, the quad above gone slack. There's a hollow where my vastus medialis used to bulge when I settled into the blocks. Second reconstruction, then scar tissue knitting the joint shut from the inside.

He sets the pad of his thumb against the top edge of my kneecap and pushes it toward my foot, a few millimetres. Then he reverses, hooking the bottom edge and drawing it up toward my hip. Then he stacks both thumbs along its outer border and nudges it inward, toward my other leg. A healthy patella slides like a coin under a sheet. Mine moves like a coin glued to the table.

"Tight on the superior glide," he says, to nobody.

"It's tight everywhere."

"I know."

Four years ago he'd have said something cruder. We trained under the same coach for six seasons, him in the 400 flat, me over the barriers. We cooled down together on the infield, his palm on my heel shoving my leg toward my face while I swore at him. Then his hamstring tore three times in eighteen months, and he went to university. Now there's a framed degree behind his head and his name stitched on a navy polo. He landed on his feet. I don't have feet worth landing on.

"Roll over."

I turn prone. The vinyl is cool where my shirt rides up, and I tug it down too fast. He doesn't look. He's very good at not looking. That's the worst thing about him.

He stands at my right side. One hand wraps the front of my shin just above the ankle. The other settles flat across my sacrum, the heel of his palm on the bony plate at the base of my spine, fingers spread toward my left hip.

"That's so your pelvis doesn't cheat," he says. "Rectus femoris crosses the hip. When the knee bends, it'll try to lift your hip off the table."

"I know what rectus femoris does."

"Then don't let it."

He bends my knee. My heel lifts and arcs upward. Ninety is easy, my shin vertical, foot pointing at the ceiling. Then he keeps going, drawing my heel down toward my glute. Somewhere past a hundred, the front of my knee goes tight as a drumskin. The scar pulls first, a dry, papery sting along the incision. Then something deeper takes over, a pressure behind the kneecap, as if the joint has been packed with wet sand.

My hip tries to rise. His palm on my sacrum presses down, not hard, just immovable, and the pull through my quad doubles. My left hand finds the edge of the plinth and grips.

"Number," he says.

"Six."

"Liar."

"Seven."

He holds. The longer he stays, the more the pain changes texture, sharp edges going dull, a burn spreading into the lower third of my thigh. Sweat beads in the crease where calf meets hamstring. His fingertips rest against the outside of my Achilles. I hate that I can feel them. Out of every screaming signal in my leg, my brain has flagged that one warm point as worth attention.

"Hold-relax," he says. "Push your shin into my hand, like you're straightening it. Twenty percent. No more."

I push. My quad wakes up in a weak, stuttering contraction, fibres twitching visibly under the skin. He meets the force with exactly equal force, so nothing moves. He counts six under his breath. His voice is low and even and close, because he's leaning his weight over my pelvis.

"Let go. Breathe out."

I exhale. As the quad releases, he takes up the slack, and my heel sinks another few centimetres toward my glute. A hot white line flares along the inside of the knee. My toes curl. A noise comes out of me that I didn't authorise.

"Okay?"

"Fine."

His hand on my sacrum shifts, a fraction, a reflex. It's almost a soothe, and then it stops itself. I feel him decide not to. His fingers go still, and that restraint lands on my skin louder than any touch.

Again: push, six seconds, release, another centimetre. Again. On the third round goosebumps ripple down my calf and across the backs of my arms. I press my face into the face-hole so he can't see whatever it's doing.

He lowers my leg slowly. The knee unfolds through the arc and the quad sings with relief until my foot rests flat on the table.

"Turn over. I'll measure."

Supine again. He lines up the goniometer. The pivot goes over the bony knob on the outside of my knee, one arm reaching up my thigh toward the hip, the other down my shin to the ankle bone. He bends my knee as far as I'll allow, my heel sliding up the paper toward my backside.

"One-eighteen." A pause. "Up from one-ten."

As if that's something. You need about one-thirty to tuck a trail leg flat over a barrier. I used to have one-fifty-five. I could kneel, sit back on my heels, and lay my chest on my thighs.

"You'll get stairs back properly," he says. "Cycling. Squatting."

"Squatting," I say. "Great."

He types on the tablet. A white scar crosses the knuckle of his first finger, one I don't remember. I look at the ceiling tiles instead.

"Mara." He doesn't look up. "It's allowed to be shit."

The diffuser hisses. Lavender, disinfectant, my own sweat. My knee throbs in time with my pulse, and the base of my spine still holds the exact shape of his palm.

"Same time Thursday," I say, and sit up before he can offer me his hand.

# Therapeutic Boundaries

The sleeves are the first thing I see every Tuesday and Thursday, and I hate them more than the knee.

Cobalt, with orange lightning bolts zigzagging from wrist to elbow. He bought them outside the stadium in Doha the year I made the triple jump final and he didn't get out of long jump qualifying. He wore them for every sled pull after that, until the morning he told our coach he was done and enrolled in physiotherapy school like it was nothing. Like you could just set a life down.

Now he's Dr. Jonah Adeyemi, DPT. His framed degrees hang above the plinth where I lie on my back in shorts, right leg straight, a fresh pink seam down the front of my right knee where they went in for the third time.

"Quad off," he says.

"It is off."

He rests two fingers on the muscle just above my kneecap. It's twitching, a flicker under the skin like a trapped moth. I hadn't noticed. He waits. I make myself go slack, and he sets both thumbs against the top edge of my patella and pushes it down, toward my foot.

It barely moves. Scar tissue has glued the kneecap high in its groove, and the glide feels like dragging a coin through wet sand. A thin, bright line of pain draws itself up the inside of the joint.

"Number."

"Three."

"Liar." He shifts his thumbs to the outer edge and presses the patella inward, toward my other leg. Then the inner edge, pushing it outward. Each direction gives a millimeter, then a wall. His forearms are inches from my thigh, and I can see the weave of the fabric over his tendons, the lightning flexing when his grip tightens. I watch the ceiling tiles. There are forty-two. I counted them in week two.

"Extension."

He slides a rolled towel under my right heel so the back of my knee hangs over nothing. Then he stacks his palms on the lower end of my thigh, just above the kneecap, locks his elbows, and leans.

The back of my knee answers like a guitar string tuned too high. I'm still four degrees short of straight, and every one of those degrees lives behind the joint, in the capsule and the hamstring tendons, and he is pressing them flat with the steady weight of his body. Heat floods up the back of my thigh. My toes curl. My hands find the edges of the plinth.

"Breathe," he says, and I know that voice. It's the one he used crouched beside the runway when I couldn't stop shaking before my last attempt in Doha. *Breathe, Mara. It's just sand.*

He holds for thirty seconds, lips moving silently as he counts, and I make the mistake of watching his mouth. When he eases off, blood rushes back into the hollow behind my knee in a warm, prickling wave, and gooseflesh rises along my arms that has nothing to do with the air conditioning.

He sees it. I watch him decide not to see it.

"Flip over."

I roll onto my stomach and press my face into the cutout. The vinyl sticks to my cheek. I hear him move to my right side. His left hand settles flat across my sacrum, the bony plate at the base of my spine, the heel of his palm just above my waistband. Its job is to pin my pelvis so my hip can't lift off the table and cheat the stretch. I know that. I still feel each of his fingers separately.

His right hand cups the front of my ankle. Slowly, he folds my knee, drawing my heel toward my glute.

At ninety degrees, nothing. At a hundred, the front of my thigh starts to burn, the long quad muscle stretched across both the hip he's pinning and the knee he's bending. At a hundred and five comes something deeper: a crushing ache at the back of the joint, right where they stitched the meniscus, as if my calf and thigh were closing on it like a jaw.

My hip tries to rise. His hand presses, gently, and keeps it down.

"Number."

"Six." It's an eight. My eyes are wet against the cutout. I'm glad he can't see.

"Three more degrees and I'll hold."

He eases the heel closer. My quad seizes, an involuntary guard that drives my shin back into his palm, and he doesn't fight it. He waits, hand steady, thumb resting on the knob of my ankle bone, until the spasm lets go. Then he takes the three degrees.

I make a sound I'm not proud of.

"There," he says quietly, and holds.

It's not the pain I hate. I used to pay for pain; I chased it up runways and bounding hills. I hate what it's *for*. Every degree he wins brings me closer to a knee that climbs stairs and kneels in gardens, and further from the one that jumped fourteen meters. Recovery is just a slower way of letting go.

He lowers my foot to the table, and the ache drains out of the joint like a tide going out.

He sets the goniometer's pivot against the outside of my knee and lines one plastic arm along my thigh, the other along my shin. "One-oh-eight. Up four since Tuesday."

"Congratulations."

"They're yours." He wraps the ice pack around my knee. His fingertips skim the scar as he smooths the Velcro, and he pulls back fast, the way you lift a hand from a stove.

I lift my face out of the cutout. "Do you miss it?"

He's quiet so long I think he won't answer. The lightning bolts catch the fluorescent light as he folds his arms.

"Every day," he says. "Thursday, ten o'clock."

He leaves the door open behind him. I lie there with my cheek against the vinyl, the ice burning, the shape of his hand still warm at the base of my spine.

response:
# Hell Is Other Demons

Lucifer Morningstar woke at six. This was a lie, because he did not sleep and Hell does not have a six. But he had found, over the long ages since the Fall, that a day goes better if you pretend it has a shape.

The first thing he heard was the chewing.

It came from the throne room, three halls and a minor abyss away. It was a patient, contented sound, the sound of something with too many teeth doing exactly what it wanted.

The hellhound was the size of a hearse and roughly the same colour. It lay at the foot of the Iron Throne with one leg of it in its jaws, working away as calmly as a cow at its cud.

"Darling," said Lucifer. "No."

Lilith had named the dog. She had named him Darling specifically so that the Adversary, the Morning Star, the Prince of This World, would have to stand in the great hall of Pandemonium saying *Darling, no* and *Darling, drop it* and *who's a good boy* in front of the staff. She had always understood the precise cost of things.

Darling wagged. Somewhere in the Third Circle, a glutton was crushed slightly flatter by the draught.

The throne had been forged from the first iron ever to fall out of Heaven, not counting Lucifer himself. It had stood for eleven thousand years. It had not been built to be delicious. The front left leg was now distinctly shorter than the others. When he sat in judgement the whole thing listed, and he had to lean the other way to stay upright. Leaning, he had been told, made him look sympathetic.

This was bad for business.

---

Business, at nine, was Beelzebub with the quarterly figures and a quantity of flies.

"Intake's up eleven percent," said Beelzebub. "But efficacy's down."

"Efficacy."

"The torments, sir. They're not landing." He consulted a ledger bound in something that had once complained. "There's a man in the Fourth Circle who's been rolling a boulder uphill for four hundred years. Says he finds it meditative now. He's written a book. There's a waiting list for the boulder."

Lucifer rubbed his temples. Down the hall, faintly, Darling chewed.

"Also, the Lake of Fire says it's lukewarm."

"Says who?"

"The Lake of Fire, sir. It's very sensitive."

Mammon suggested a new throne, which Lucifer pretended not to hear. You did not replace a throne. Replacing a throne was an admission. It was like replacing a door after someone had walked out of it.

At eleven he condemned a property developer, a minor dictator, and a man who had given every restaurant in Leeds one star. He did all three leaning slightly to the right, and he thought the dictator found it comforting.

---

Lilith arrived at three. There is no three o'clock in Hell, but Lucifer kept one anyway, out of nostalgia for afternoons.

For most of the last nine centuries, when Lilith came to Pandemonium she came to set it on fire. It was understood. She would arrive like weather, and there would be shrieking and structural damage. Once, memorably, she had left a knife in his back, between the wings, and he had kept it there for a fortnight on principle.

This was her third visit this month, and she had burned nothing at all.

Last week she had come to return a cardigan. The week before, she had come to tell him about a dream she'd had, and then left without explaining it. That was worse than fire. He had thought about it for days.

Today she stood in the doorway in her long grey coat. Darling saw her, and his entire back half began to wag so hard that two minor demons were thrown into a wall.

"He's still doing that," she said, nodding at the throne.

"He misses you."

"He's a dog."

"He's *your* dog."

"*Our* dog," she said, and then neither of them said anything for a while.

She crossed the hall and scratched Darling behind one of his ears. He had several, in no particular order. Then she looked up at Lucifer on his tilted throne.

"You're leaning."

"I'm handling it."

"You look like you're about to ask someone how they're feeling."

"Are you seeing anyone?" he said, which was not at all what he had meant to say.

She considered this. "Apparently I'm seeing you," she said. "Most Tuesdays."

"It's Thursday."

"I know what day it is."

The chewing filled the silence, steady and wet.

"How are you?" she asked. It was not quite a question. It was more like pressing on a bruise to see whether it was still there.

"Fine."

"That's very poor workmanship," said Lilith, "from the Father of Lies."

"It's beneath me."

"Everything's beneath you. That was rather the point of the arrangement."

He laughed despite himself, and the sound went out through the halls of Pandemonium. Here and there the damned looked up from their torments, puzzled, the way people look up at a noise they remember from childhood and cannot quite place.

Lilith reached into her coat and took out a sheet of paper, folded many times and gone soft as cloth at the creases. He knew what it was. He had signed it nine hundred years ago, in a hand that had shaken only very slightly. It declared, in the formal language of the Infernal Courts, that they were finished forever. Hell was large enough for both of them, it said, provided neither was ever in the same part of it.

She had been carrying it all this time.

She knelt, nudged Darling's head aside, and wedged it under the short leg.

The throne settled. Lucifer sat level for the first time in months, and found he did not know what to do with his hands.

"Thursday, then," said Lilith from the doorway. She did not say which one.

When she had gone, Darling considered the situation. Then he rose and padded round to the back of the throne. With the air of a creature who has all of eternity and intends to use it, he began, very happily, on another leg.

response:
# Hell is Other Demons

The ash fell on Hell the way rain falls on certain northern towns: without drama, without malice, but with the patient conviction of something that had been doing this since before the towns were built and intended to carry on long after.

Lucifer Morningstar woke at six, as he had every morning for eleven thousand years, and lay for a while listening to it settle on the roof. Then he put on his dressing gown and made coffee.

There were two mugs in the cupboard. One said WORLD'S OKAYEST ADVERSARY, which had been a joke once. The other was black, and chipped along the rim where Lilith had thrown it at his head in 1347. He took down the first. He looked at the second for a moment longer than was strictly necessary, and then he closed the cupboard.

⁂

His nine o'clock was Abrasax from Operations, a demon with the face of a rooster and the soul of a spreadsheet.

"The Lake of Fire," said Abrasax, "is running four degrees cool."

"Is it."

"Complaints are down eleven percent." Abrasax said this the way a doctor might say *the lump has grown*. "Some of the damned have started describing it as *pleasant*. One of them has brought a towel."

"Where did he get a towel?"

"We're looking into it."

Lucifer signed something. He signed a great many things in the course of a day: the damnation of the man who had invented the reply-all button; a requisition for new pitchforks, the old ones having gone blunt on a particularly stubborn Pope; a memo about the queue at the Gate, which now stretched back past the Styx and had developed its own small economy, including a man selling umbrellas against the ash at three souls apiece.

"Also," said Abrasax, "she's here."

Lucifer did not look up. "Who?"

Abrasax's comb trembled in a silence that was, in its way, an answer.

⁂

Lilith was in his kitchen. She had let herself in, because she had never given back her key, and he had never changed the locks, and neither of them had ever said anything about either of these facts.

"I came for my knives," she said.

"You took your knives in March. You put one of them in me."

"The *other* knives."

He leaned in the doorway. She was wearing the green coat, the one she knew he liked, and there was ash in her hair like grey confetti at a wedding nobody had wanted to attend.

Last Tuesday she had come to return a book she had never borrowed. The week before, it had been to tell him in person that she hated him, which she had previously managed by letter, many times, over many centuries, in a beautiful copperplate hand. The week before *that*, she had actually tried to kill him, which had at least had the virtue of honesty.

"There are no other knives," said Lucifer.

"Then I'll have a coffee," said Lilith. She opened the cupboard and took down the black mug without looking, as though her hand still knew where it lived.

⁂

There was always work in the afternoons. A new arrival needed sentencing: a landlord from Leeds who, in forty years, had never once returned a deposit.

"Boiling," said Lucifer. "Standard. Seventh Circle."

"Boiling," said Lilith, "is lazy."

"Boiling is *traditional*."

"You always do this. You go for the first thing. You did the same with the Borgias."

"The Borgias were boiled *beautifully*."

The landlord looked from one to the other with the expression of a man who has come home early to find the furniture rearranged and his parents arguing about it in the hall.

"Make him fix things," said Lilith. "Forever. A boiler that never works. A tenant who rings at three in the morning. A tap that drips, and drips, and every time he fixes it there's another one, and the tenant says *sorry to bother you* in a voice that makes it very clear she isn't."

Lucifer considered this. It was very good. It was the sort of thing he had loved her for, back when loving her was something he did on purpose. It was also the sort of thing that had made him throw her into the abyss, twice, though she had climbed out both times and been extremely unpleasant about it.

"Fine," he said. "The tap."

"Thank you."

"I was going to say the tap."

"You were going to say *boiling*."

From the corridor, the landlord could be heard explaining to somebody that it wasn't his fault, it was wear and tear.

⁂

At six o'clock the light did whatever it did in Hell instead of fading. Lilith stood at the door with her coat buttoned and her hands in her pockets, and did not leave.

"The Lake's running cool," Lucifer said, because he had to say something.

"I heard. Someone brought a towel."

"Was that you?"

She smiled, which she did not do often, and which was worse, in its way, than the knives.

There was ash on her shoulder. He reached out without thinking and brushed it away, and she let him. Then she said, "Don't," but she said it softly, the way you say it to someone who has already stopped.

"Thursday?" he said.

"I might need to return something."

"You haven't borrowed anything."

"Then I'll have to borrow something first," said Lilith, and took the black mug with her when she went.

⁂

Lucifer washed the remaining mug and stood at the window. A Frenchman who had arrived in 1980, and complained about it ever since, had once told him that Hell was other people. Lucifer had thought about this a good deal. He had decided the Frenchman was right but had missed the important part, which was that Hell was also the absence of them.

The ash kept falling. It settled on the rooftops and the queues and the Lake of Fire, which was running cool. It settled on the long road out, where a woman in a green coat was walking home with a stolen mug, and not hurrying.

response:
# Hell is Other Demons

Hell does not have mornings, strictly speaking. It has the same sullen red light at all hours, the colour of a brake lamp seen through fog. But Lucifer Morningstar kept mornings anyway, the way some widowers keep setting two places at the table. He didn't expect anything. Stopping would simply have meant admitting something.

He woke at what he had decided was seven and made coffee from beans grown on the slopes of a volcano, which made them, technically, local. He drank it from his own mug. The other mug, which said WORLD'S OKAYEST MOTHER OF DEMONS, stayed on its hook. It had hung there for eleven months. He dusted it on Thursdays.

At eight, Belphegor brought the morning briefing.

"The violent against nature are complaining about the burning sand," he said.

"They're meant to complain. That's the point of the sand."

"They say it's gone lukewarm. More of a beach, now. Some of them have started building things." He produced a photograph of a sandcastle of considerable ambition, with turrets.

Lucifer looked at it for a long time. "Fix the boilers," he said. "Then knock that over. Make sure he watches."

This was what nobody understood about running Hell. People imagined thrones and screaming and the delicious crunch of souls. There was some of that, but mostly it was boilers. Sartre, who had been down here since 1980, liked to say that hell was other people. In Lucifer's experience it was mostly other demons, and boilers, and memos asking whether the lustful could be blown about by the infernal whirlwind on a rotating schedule, to save on wind. Eternity, it turns out, is chiefly an exercise in maintenance.

---

She arrived just after lunch, which is to say just after Lucifer had eaten a cold sandwich over the sink, the way men eat when no one is watching.

He knew it was her before he turned. The temperature of a room changes when Lilith enters it, though never in the direction you expect.

"I'm not here to stab you," she said, the way other people say *I'm only staying for one drink*.

Over her shoulder hung the purse. It was old leather, scorched along one side as if it had been rescued from a house fire, which, on at least three occasions, it had.

"I came for my records."

"You took your records."

"I took *some* of my records."

She went and stood before the shelves and did not take any records, and they both pretended this was not happening.

"You moved the sofa."

"It was blocking the view of the Lake."

"You hate the view of the Lake. You said it was like living above a car park."

"Things change," said Lucifer.

She sat on the sofa in its new position and opened the purse. This was what she did when she wanted to talk and didn't want to be seen wanting to. Lilith walked the mortal world more than he did. She had always walked it, in the places between streetlights, and she came back with her pockets full.

She set the things on the coffee table one at a time.

A snow globe from Duluth, Minnesota, in which a tiny moose was perpetually snowed upon and did not seem to mind.

A parking ticket, issued in Lisbon to a car she had certainly not been driving.

Half a roll of peppermints.

A baby tooth in a matchbox.

"Where did you get a baby tooth?"

"Someone left it under a pillow. It seemed rude not to." She shook the snow globe, and they watched the moose vanish into plastic weather. "I thought you'd like the moose."

"I do like the moose," he admitted.

There followed the long, careful sort of silence that happens between two people who have had every possible argument and are now only deciding which one to have next.

"Belphegor says you've been eating over the sink."

"I always eat over the sink."

"You never ate over the sink when I lived here."

"You never let me," he said, and it came out softer than he meant.

Lilith looked at the moose. "You only ever talked about work. Twelve thousand years of quarterly torments. I'd say, *Lucifer, I've just watched the sun come up over the Ganges*, and you'd say, *That's nice, the gluttons are over capacity.*"

"They *were* over capacity."

"That," said Lilith, "is exactly what I mean."

He was the Father of Lies, and he could have said any number of clever things. Instead he took the other mug down from its hook and made her coffee the way she liked it, black and slightly too hot to drink. He set it beside the baby tooth.

She looked at it for a while. "You kept it."

"I dust it on Thursdays."

"That's pathetic."

"Yes," he agreed.

She drank. It burned, and she didn't mind, because nothing burns Lilith that she hasn't agreed to first.

---

She left at what Lucifer had decided was six. She did not kiss him. Neither did she stab him, which, in their particular relationship, was something close to a sonnet.

At the door she rummaged in the purse and pressed something into his hand. Then she was gone, into the red light and the distant screaming and the ordinary noise of everybody else's eternity.

It was a hotel key card from a Holiday Inn in Leeds. On the back, in lipstick, she had written: *Thursday?*

Lucifer stood in the doorway for some time. Then he went back inside, where the moose was still waiting patiently in its little blizzard. He moved the sofa back to where it had been, and he did not look at the Lake at all.

response:
# Squatter's Rights

"All rise," said the bailiff, and the gallery drifted gently upward, because in the Dreaming one did not so much stand as become briefly unmoored.

Dream took the bench the way frost takes a window. The jury, twelve sheep and freshly counted, regarded him with the vacant reverence of animals who have been doing this for centuries and have never once been asked for a verdict.

"The matter of *First Love versus Mora*," intoned the clerk, a heron in a powdered wig. "Concerning title to the recurring dreamscape of one Max Pilecki, aged thirteen, of Leicester."

Dream closed his eyes for a moment longer than a blink. Somewhere, a star was collapsing. Somewhere, a god was being forgotten. And here he was.

"Proceed."

First Love rose. She was small and round-cheeked and appeared to be blushing at the furniture. She clutched a folder to her chest like a hymnal.

"My lord. Thank you. Sorry. Um." She opened the folder, and dried petals fell out. "The dream in question is a field. Wildflowers. Max, lying on his back. Beside him, Hannah Okafor from Year Nine."

"I'm aware of the dream."

"Fourteen months, my lord. Fourteen months of work. The light comes in sideways, like the end of a summer that hasn't happened yet. She leans over him. Their noses nearly touch. And then…" First Love's hands fluttered. "Nothing. A muddle. He wakes up feeling like he's swallowed a lightbulb. He'll remember it when he's forty and not know why. It's my best work."

From the defence table came a sound like a gate swinging in an empty farmyard. It was a cackle, faint and dry, and it climbed the vaulted ceiling and lingered there in the dark like something that had found a good place to nest.

Dream did not look up. "Exhibit A."

The heron unstoppered a jar. The courtroom filled with afternoon. There was the field, there the boy, there the girl, laughing, pinning his shoulders the way children do when a game has run out of rules.

And then she grew heavy.

Not larger. Heavier. Her hair lengthened into something wet and roped. Her skin went the grey of cellar stone. She folded herself onto his chest with the patience of a cat on a warm engine, leaned close, and drank his breath in long, contented sips. The boy lay rigid, eyes wide, unable to move a finger.

The heron re-corked the jar. Someone in the gallery coughed.

"He wrote her a poem," said First Love, very quietly. "Afterwards. He rhymed 'suffocate' with 'second date.' He doesn't know if he's frightened or if he wants to buy her flowers. *He's thirteen.*"

"Let the record reflect the poem," said Dream, with the air of a man who wished it wouldn't.

The court stenographer, a large moth, ate the relevant page.

"Counsel for the defence."

Mora did not rise. Mora *unfolded*, joint by joint, from a chair that had not been large enough for her a moment ago. She smelled of damp linen and old wells. Her smile had too many teeth and seemed aware of it.

"Your Worship." Another cackle, soft, trickled down the walls. "I'll be brief. A girl's gotta eat too, you know?"

"That is not a legal argument."

"It's the *only* legal argument." She spread her long grey hands. "Do you know what I'm up against? Melatonin gummies. White noise machines. Weighted blankets. I've been replaced by a *blanket*, my lord. From a *catalogue*. Fourteen pounds, machine washable. A thousand years I've been sitting on chests across the Carpathians, and now people *pay* for the feeling."

"Objection," squeaked First Love. "Relevance."

"Overruled," said Dream. "I find I am curious."

"So I go looking," Mora continued, "and there's this field. Sun. Flowers. Nobody guarding it. Same dream every night, like a pie left cooling on a windowsill. Three weeks I've been in there. Unopposed." She inclined her head. "I believe the term is *squatter's rights*."

The sheep shifted uneasily. One of them, near the end, had begun to cry.

"I *built* that field," said First Love.

"And I *improved* it. He'll never forget it now. Can you say that?"

"I literally just said that."

"Order." Dream's voice did not rise. The room simply arranged itself to be quiet. He regarded the two of them for a long moment: the crush and the crushing weight. Something moved behind his eyes, ancient and dark and, very faintly, entertained.

"I have heard the arguments," he said. "I have ruled this realm since before your kind had names. I have arbitrated wars between gods. I did not anticipate a custody hearing over a thirteen-year-old's afternoon."

"Sorry," said First Love.

"Not sorry," said Mora, and cackled.

"The court finds as follows." Dream folded his pale hands. "The field belongs to First Love. The weight belongs to Mora. Neither of you may hold the dream alone. You will share it. Every night. In full."

First Love blinked. "Share?"

"You will remain for the ending," Dream told her. "Every time. You will watch what becomes of your almost-kiss, and you will learn that wanting has teeth." He turned. "And you, Mora, will arrive at the beginning. You will lie in the wildflowers beside him for the entire afternoon, with nothing to eat, and wait, while a boy looks at you as though you are wonderful."

Mora's smile faltered by a single tooth. "That's cruel."

"It is instructive. The arrangement holds until he is old enough to be disappointed while awake." Dream rose, and the gallery floated up after him. "It will make a poet of him, I expect. I apologise to no one."

The heron struck the gavel, which was a bell, which was a heartbeat.

In Leicester, Max Pilecki woke gasping, unable to move, and smiling, and could not have told you why.

High above the empty courtroom, a faint cackle went on echoing. If one listened closely, though, it had begun to sound rather like a giggle.

response:
# First Love v. Mora

*Heard before the Court of the Dreaming*

The hourglass stood behind the bench, taller than the room should have held. It did not pour. It dripped. Each glowing grain fell through the dark and landed with the faint sound of someone, somewhere, turning over in bed.

Dream watched it. That was better than watching the litigants.

"The court will hear the matter of First Love against Mora," intoned the Bailiff, a tall, indistinct figure who was in fact the Sensation of Falling. Everyone in the gallery gripped their seats a little whenever he spoke. "Concerning the dreamscape designated *Field, Wildflowers, Recurring*, property of one Max Adeyemi, aged fourteen."

"Property of no one," said Dream. "The boy merely sleeps there. Proceed."

First Love rose. He was small and pink-cheeked, and he carried a binder thick enough to stop a door. He had tabbed it. The tabs were colour-coded. He had, Dream suspected, cried while making them.

"Your Majesty. Lord Shaper. Sir." He swallowed. "I built that field over eleven months. Two hundred and six varieties of wildflower, none of which bloom together in nature, all of which bloom at once for him. The breeze is calibrated to lift her hair at the precise moment he notices her eyes. And then there's the..." He coloured fiercely. "The almost."

"The almost," Dream repeated.

"Where they nearly kiss, but somebody's elbow gets in the way, and they both laugh, and he wakes up feeling like he swallowed a lightbulb." First Love clutched the binder. "It was perfect. It was meant to run until he was sixteen. Then *she* came."

All eyes turned to the defendant.

Mora sat with her feet on the defence table. She was a heavy, pale woman with long black hair that moved slightly whenever nobody looked at it directly. She was eating sunflower seeds and spitting the shells into a small pile that had begun, unsettlingly, to resemble a sleeping man.

"Objection," she said.

"No one has asked you anything," said Dream.

"I'm getting ahead of it."

"Exhibit A," said First Love, his voice wobbling. The sand in the hourglass paused mid-fall, gathered, and shaped itself into a scene above the courtroom. The field. The flowers. The boy lying among them, the girl beside him. She laughed, rolled over, and clambered onto him the way children do when they wrestle.

Then she was heavier. Then she was *wrong*. Her face lengthened into something beautiful in the way a drop from a great height is beautiful. She settled, almost companionably, on the boy's chest, leaned down, and inhaled.

The boy in the sand could not move. His eyes were very wide. A single daisy in the corner of the vision wilted out of sympathy.

The image collapsed. In the gallery, a minor deity of picnics fainted.

"The defence may respond," said Dream.

Mora brushed shells from her lap. "Look. I'm not saying it's *nice*. I'm saying a girl's gotta eat too, you know?"

"There are other sleepers."

"Are there?" She leaned forward. "You know who my clientele used to be? Carpathian farmers. Chests like rain barrels. Slept like the dead after fourteen hours ploughing. You could sit on one of those for a week. Now?" She flicked a seed. "Melatonin. White-noise machines. Everybody's on their phone till three, then sleeps like a cat on a radiator. And Anxiety's undercutting me everywhere. Does it for free. Doesn't even show up in person."

"That is not this court's concern."

"Then take the kid. He's got a good chest, Your Honour. Healthy lungs. Swimmer, I think. And he was already lying flat on his back with his eyes shut, waiting for somebody to lean over him." She spread her hands. "I didn't break in. The door was open. There was practically a welcome mat."

"That was *my* welcome mat," First Love whispered.

"And it was a lovely mat, sweetheart. Very tasteful."

Dream closed his eyes. In his time he had settled wars between rival pantheons. He had walked into Hell and argued with its management. He had once spent four centuries ruling on jurisdiction over the recurring dream in which one's teeth fall out.

And now this.

"Counsel for the plaintiff," he said. "What harm has been done? Specifically."

"He wakes up gasping! He can't look at her in maths anymore! He thinks something's *wrong* with him!" First Love's voice cracked. "He's started reading *poetry*."

A murmur went through the gallery. Somebody at the back said, "Oh, no."

Dream opened his eyes. The stars in them had dimmed slightly, the way a lamp dims when someone in another room switches on something greedy.

He looked at the hourglass. The sand dripped on, unhurried. Beyond it the docket stretched away for miles. He could already see the next case: *Tooth Fairy v. Orthodontics*, with a cross-claim from Teething.

Very faintly, the corner of his mouth moved.

"The court has reached a decision," he said. "The field remains the work of First Love. The flowers, the breeze, the elbow. All of it."

First Love sagged with relief.

"However," said Dream, "the almost belongs to Mora."

Silence.

"She may sit precisely where she sits now. She may take one breath, and only one, in the moment before the kiss. Each time the boy wakes, he will not know whether what he felt was terror or love." Dream folded his long pale hands. "For the rest of his life, he will never be entirely sure they are different. He will write very bad poems about it. Eventually, some good ones."

"That's not justice," First Love said. "That's just..."

"Adolescence," said Dream. "Yes. I did not invent it. I merely enforce it."

Mora was grinning. "One breath?"

"A small one. You are a guest."

"I can work with small." She swept the shells off the table, and the little husk-man sighed as he scattered. "Pleasure doing business, Your Honour."

First Love gathered his binder in silence. At the rail, he paused. "Will it hurt him?"

Dream gave the question more attention than he had given anything all day.

"Yes," he said. "That is how you will know it worked."

The Bailiff stepped forward, and the whole room lurched, briefly, as if it had missed a stair.

"Next," said Dream, and the sand kept falling.

# Alternate Thursdays

"ALL RISE," boomed the bailiff, a thing of granite and grievance, "FOR THE LORD OF THE DREAMING, PRINCE OF STORIES, KING OF—"

"Sit," said Dream.

The court sat. Several members of the gallery did so without having bodies, which took some doing.

Dream regarded the docket. It was long. It was always long. Somewhere in the waking world a man was dreaming of his teeth falling out for the four-hundredth time, and the Lord of the Dreaming would rather have been attending to that.

"THE MATTER OF THE WILDFLOWER FIELD," the bailiff intoned. "RECURRING. PROPERTY OF ONE MAX, SCHOOLBOY. THE PLAINTIFF: FIRST LOAF."

A small, pink entity half-rose from the plaintiff's bench. "It's... Love. First Love."

"THAT IS WHAT I SAID."

"Proceed," said Dream.

First Love shuffled her index cards. She had written them in her best handwriting, crossed things out, then drawn a small heart in the corner of one and visibly regretted it.

"My lord. I built that field over six weeks. Every petal. The light is four in the afternoon in June, which is the *correct* light. There's a bee that never stings. She laughs, and she pushes him over in the grass, and she leans down, and—" Colour climbed her cheeks like a rash. "And then nothing happens. Beautifully. He wakes up not knowing what he feels. That's the whole point. He's supposed to carry that for forty years."

"And now?"

"And now she sits on his chest and *eats* him."

"Objection," said the defendant. "Sips."

"THE DEFENDANT," the bailiff announced, a little late, "MORAY."

"Like the eel," said Mora pleasantly. "It's Mora."

"THAT IS WHAT I SAID."

She lounged across the defendant's bench as though it were a fainting couch, picking her teeth with what appeared to be a child's milk tooth.

"Does the defendant dispute the facts?" said Dream.

"Dispute them? I'm proud of them." Mora sat up. "Look. Lovely field. Very nice. Bee, whatever. But she's built a recurring dream where a girl tumbles onto a sleeping boy and then just *stops*? That's a nightmare waiting to happen, your worship. That's an open door. I didn't break in. I walked in."

"'My lord,'" First Love corrected faintly.

"My lord," said Mora, "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?"

Dream's face did not change. It never did. But the candles along the walls shrank a quarter-inch, and in the gallery a minor Anxiety quietly left.

"Call your witness," he said.

First Love consulted her cards. "I call the Smell of Cut Grass."

"THE COURT CALLS," the bailiff thundered, "THE SMELL OF CUT GLASS."

Something entered the witness box. It smelled, unmistakably, of summer lawns. Everyone regarded it with deep suspicion anyway.

"You were present on the night in question?" asked First Love.

"I'm present every night," said the Smell, a little wounded. "I'm load-bearing."

"And what did you observe?"

"It was going normally. Light, bee, laughing. She pushes him over. Then her face goes..." The Smell searched for a word. "Long. The eyes get very far apart. She sits on his chest and he can't move, and he breathes out, and it all goes into her. Like a straw."

"Was the boy frightened?"

The Smell shifted. "Yes. Mostly."

"*Mostly?*"

"She kept the hair clip," the Smell said unhappily. "The little yellow one shaped like a daisy. He... looked at the hair clip a lot."

First Love made a noise like a kettle. "No further questions."

"Cross?" said Dream, who wanted very badly for there not to be a cross.

"Oh, absolutely." Mora strolled to the witness box. "Smell. Pal. Before I arrived, how many times had the boy had this dream?"

"Thirty-one."

"And how many times did he remember it on waking?"

A hesitation. "Twice."

"And since I got involved?"

"...Every time."

"Every time," Mora repeated to the gallery. "He's started a notebook. He's *sketched* me. Badly, the boy cannot do hands, but with feeling. So tell me who's crafting the formative experience now."

"Objection!" First Love was on her feet, scarlet to the ears. "She's leading the Smell!"

"Overruled," said Dream. "It is a smell. It goes where it is led."

"THE COURT CALLS," the bailiff began, squinting at the next card, "THE HIPPO NICK JERK—"

"No," said Dream. "It does not."

Somewhere out in the Dreaming, a large and ungainly falling sensation sighed and went back to its paperback.

Dream steepled his fingers. He considered the field. He considered the girl who was not a girl, the bee that did not sting, the breath going up the straw. He considered how much simpler things had been when nightmares simply ate people and nobody filed motions about it.

He considered awarding the dream to Mora outright and watching First Love weep into her index cards. He considered returning it to First Love and remanding Mora to the dreams of a tax assessor in Swindon. He considered the bailiff, and whether one could be sentenced to a recurring dream about pronunciation.

Then something happened at the corner of his mouth for which the court had no precedent.

"Judgement," said Dream. "The field is held jointly."

Both parties turned.

"First Love will build the dream. Every petal. The light at four o'clock. She will bring him to the edge of the kiss, as before." His gaze moved to Mora. "And then you will have him. Every time. In perpetuity."

"Joint custody?" said Mora slowly. "Of one dream?"

"He'll never know which it was," First Love whispered. "Love, or—"

"No," Dream agreed. "He will be confused about it for the rest of his life. He will fall for people who frighten him. He will be frightened of people who love him. He will lie awake at night unable to move, and not entirely mind."

"That's monstrous," said First Love.

"It is first love," said Dream. "You of all entities should know."

He rose. The court rose with him, including the parts that had no knees.

At the door, he paused. "Also, he will become a poet."

Mora laughed out loud. First Love put her face in her hands.

"COURT IS ADJOURNED," boomed the bailiff. "NEXT CASE: TEETH, FALLING OUT OF, IN RE—"

But the Lord of the Dreaming was already gone, and very nearly smiling.
