# Sisyphus Gives Advice

The hill in Tartarus was not especially tall. It didn't need to be. Height is really a matter of how many times you have to climb a thing, and by that measure it was the tallest mountain in creation.

Halfway up it, a man was pushing a boulder. On top of the boulder, like a disgruntled figurehead, sat a crow with a satchel of letters. Tartarus does not issue familiars. Crow had simply turned up one century and stayed, on the grounds that the boulder was the only thing in the Underworld that went anywhere.

"Next," said Sisyphus.

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*My husband leaves his sandals in the doorway. Every single day. I have asked him forty-one times. I have counted. Last week I fell over them carrying a pot of lentils. How do I make him stop?*

*— Tripping in Thebes*

Dear Tripping,

You have asked him forty-one times, which means that somewhere around the ninth, the two of you stopped talking about sandals. Now you're arguing about whether he listens to you, and he's arguing about whether you think he's a child. Neither argument can be won in a doorway.

Put a basket by the door. Make it the easiest thing in the world for him to get it right, and say nothing when he does. Then, some evening when neither of you is holding lentils, ask him what small thing *you* do that drives him mad. Listen without defending yourself. You'll be surprised how quickly the sandals move after that.

*[CROW: He leaves his own sandals at the bottom of the hill. They've been there since the Bronze Age. I'm just saying.]*

---

The slope steepened, and for a while the only dictation was breathing. Over the centuries the boulder had worn a smooth groove into Sisyphus's left shoulder, and he had worn a smooth groove into the boulder, and they had arrived at the sort of understanding usually found only in long marriages and certain kinds of furniture.

"Right," he said, when the ground levelled. "The scribe."

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*I copy records for the Archon from first light until the lamps burn out. My wife says I married the Archon. My son calls me "the man who sleeps here." I keep promising it's only until the harvest accounts are done. That was four harvests ago. How do I find balance?*

*— Ink-Stained in Athens*

Dear Ink-Stained,

"Balance" is what people ask for when they're hoping to keep everything. You can't. So choose one thing, say one evening a week, and guard it as if the Archon were trying to pick your pocket. Go home that evening even if the ledgers are on fire. *Especially* if the ledgers are on fire. It'll be good practice.

The harvest accounts will never be done. There is always another harvest. That's rather the point of harvests.

In my present situation I meet a great many of the recently departed. They talk about all sorts of things. Not one of them has mentioned the Archon.

*[CROW: Plenty mention their wives, though. Some of them fondly.]*

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*My wife has asked whether, in the bedroom, I might pretend to be a swan. She says she read about it somewhere. I don't know how to feel. Is this normal?*

*— Feathered in Sparta*

Dear Feathered,

Normal is a number, not a virtue. The useful question isn't whether it's normal. It's whether you're curious or just frightened of saying no. Either answer is fine, but tell her which one it is. A marriage survives an honest "no" far better than a reluctant "yes," and a great deal better than a reluctant swan.

Should you proceed: swans are, by temperament, enormous bastards. Method acting is not required.

*[CROW: Let the record show I took this one down under protest, on behalf of birds everywhere.]*

---

They reached a place Sisyphus thought of as the Shelf, where the boulder could be held for about the length of a short letter if you wedged it with your hip and didn't sneeze. He had never sneezed.

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*There's a man at the Corinth market who corrects everything I say. If I say it's hot, he says, "Actually, it's warm." If I say good morning, he informs me it's nearly noon. I am starting to have thoughts. What do I do?*

*— Seething in Corinth*

Dear Seething,

A man who corrects everything usually has very little else that makes him feel useful. That doesn't make him less tiresome, but it does make him easier to manage. Next time, before he can start, ask him a real question about something he actually knows: olives, roof tiles, the proper way to haggle for a goat. Then let him talk.

You will either make an unexpected friend or bore him into avoiding you. Both are a vast improvement on the thoughts.

Give my regards to Corinth.

*[CROW: For the record, it was warm. I was there. Also, he used to be king of the place. He'd rather you didn't bring it up.]*

---

The last letter had been written very carefully, by someone who had crossed most of it out first. Sisyphus read it twice, which he did not usually need to do, and said nothing for most of a switchback.

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*I make pots. Decent ones. I'm thirty-four. Lately I lie awake wondering whether any of it matters. Everything I make, somebody eventually breaks, and then I make another. I don't know what I'm for.*

*— Pointless in Piraeus*

Dear Pointless,

Somewhere tonight, someone is pouring wine from one of your pots for a friend they haven't seen in years. Somebody's grandmother keeps her olives in one, and her grandchildren will quarrel over it when she's gone, and not because of the olives. Somebody dropped one this morning and laughed, because it was only a pot and the day was nice.

None of those people know your name. That isn't the same as you not mattering to them. Your pots aren't meant to outlast anything. They're meant for Tuesdays, and Tuesdays are most of life.

As for making another, and another: doing a thing again is not the same as doing it for nothing.

Write back. I mean it.

*[CROW: He does mean it. Last month he had me fly to Piraeus three times for a cobbler. I'm not even a pigeon.]*

---

At the top, the boulder paused, as it always did, as though considering its options. Then it went the way it always went.

Sisyphus watched it all the way down, bouncing companionably off rocks he knew by name. He dusted off his hands and started walking.

"Anything else in the bag?"

Crow rummaged. "One from a Mr. Tantalus. Three pages. Mostly about fruit."

"Ah," said Sisyphus, and his step quickened a little. "Read it to me on the way down."

response:
# Sisyphus Gives Advice

The gods had thought very carefully about the uphill part. They had considered the gradient, the weight of the stone, and the precise moment it should slip from his fingers.¹

What they had not considered, because gods rarely consider the bits in between, was the walk back down. It took about forty minutes, and Sisyphus had been using it for correspondence.

¹ *Just before the top. Always just before the top. The gods are many things, but subtle is not one of them.*

---

"Next one," he said, stepping around a rock he had named Doris some centuries ago.

Crow shook a letter out of the satchel. Crow was no longer, technically, a crow. It had been one until it flew too close to the mouth of Tartarus and was, in the bureaucratic phrase, *retained*. Now it carried the post for a column that ran in four city-states and one very confused oracle.

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
> *My wife says I never listen. Last night I told her this wasn't true, and she said, "Then what did I just say?" And I didn't know, because I hadn't been listening.*
> *— Deaf in Corinth*

Sisyphus smiled. He had been king of Corinth once. Some things didn't change.

*Dear Deaf,*
*When she starts talking, put down whatever you're holding. I don't mean that metaphorically. Put down the actual object: the cup, the chisel, the lamb. Your hands are terrible liars, and she's been watching them for years.*
*When she's finished, ask her one question about what she said. Not a clever one. Just one that proves you were there. Within a fortnight you'll find you've stopped pretending. She's interesting. That's why you married her.*

Crow took it down in a hand composed mainly of scratches and puncture wounds.

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
> *I work fourteen hours a day at the counting-house. I haven't seen my children awake since the spring festival. My master says the ledgers will never be finished, so I must try harder.*
> *— Weary, Athens*

*Dear Weary,*
*Your master is quite right. The ledgers will never be finished. I'd take that as the reason to go home on time. Work that can't be completed doesn't mind when you stop. It'll be there in the morning, exactly where you left it. Possibly a little further down.*
*Your children won't be. Not these ones. These ones are leaving at a rate of one day per day. Go home and catch a few.*

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
> *My brother-in-law corrects everything I say. At dinner I said the fish was nice and he explained to me what a fish actually is. How do I stop myself hitting him with the fish?*
> *— Simmering, Thebes*

*Dear Simmering,*
*Ask him about something he genuinely knows, and then listen to the whole answer. Men who correct everybody are very often men nobody asks. Give him somewhere useful to put it and he'll stop leaving it all over your dinner.*
*If that fails, the fish remains an option. Serve his first.*

The path flattened. Sisyphus set the satchel on top of the boulder, put his shoulder to the stone, and went up. Crow rode on top and read ahead, making the occasional small noise. Near the summit the boulder did what it always did. "Mind yourself," said Sisyphus. Crow lifted off as the stone went back past them with the gathering enthusiasm of something let off its lead.

They started down again.

Crow pulled out the next letter, read it, and tried to put it back.

"Crow."

With enormous reluctance, Crow produced it.

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
> *My new gentleman friend is a satyr. Last night he asked if I'd like to try something he called "the Arcadian Wheelbarrow." I said I'd think about it. I've thought about it all day and I'm none the wiser.*
> *— Curious, Delphi*

Sisyphus walked some distance in thoughtful silence.

*Dear Curious,*
*Thinking about it all day is perfectly normal. Where people go wrong is thinking about it all day and never asking him. Ask him to describe it. A good partner will be glad to explain, and may even draw you a diagram. If he goes vague, or the diagram needs a second sheet, you have your answer.*
*Either way, stretch first.*

Crow wrote this one very small.

The next letter had clearly been through the Styx. Crow did not wish to discuss it.

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
> *Three weeks ago I ▒▒▒▒ a ▒▒▒▒ at the market and now it won't stop ▒▒▒▒ing me. My husband says I should ▒▒▒▒ it, but I think that's cruel, especially now it's started ▒▒▒▒ing in the bed.*
> *— ▒▒▒▒, Argos*

"Bought a goose," said Sisyphus.

Crow tilted its head. "Met a man," it said. Crow spoke rarely, and never to agree.

"Possible. Then it's 'won't stop following me.'"

"Biting."

"Or haunting. Argos has a lot of haunting."

"Bed," said Crow.

"Yes. I'd assumed the bed was where it got complicated."

They walked on. Eventually Sisyphus cleared his throat.

*Dear Argos,*
*Whatever it is, it has decided you're its person, which is more than most of us manage at the market. Your husband is right that something must be done, and you're right that it shouldn't be cruel. Agree together on where it sleeps. A basket by the hearth suits most things. For the rest, there are priests.*
*If it's a man, he should have written in himself. If it's a goose, keep it off the bed. They're nowhere near as affectionate as they think.*

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
> *I'm forty-four and I sell turnips. Everyone I grew up with is a magistrate or a hero or gloriously dead. What is the point of me?*
> *— Root Vegetable, Megara*

Sisyphus stopped walking for this one.

*Dear Root,*
*I've known a great many heroes. Most were exhausting, several are down here with me, and not one of them, I promise you, ever fed anybody.*
*Last night a good many kitchens in Megara had soup because you got up early. That isn't the consolation prize. That's the prize. Everyone else is just louder about theirs.*
*If you're still restless, grow a better turnip. There's always a better turnip. That's the fun part.*

The path flattened again. The boulder was waiting where it always waited, with the faintly expectant air of something that has never once been stood up.

Crow was buckling the satchel when one last envelope slid out. It was black and sealed with black wax, and Crow regarded it the way small birds regard large cats.

> *Sisyphus,*
> *I have an employee who appears to be enjoying himself. This was not the intention. Advise.*
> *— H.*

Sisyphus read it twice. Then he dictated:

*Dear H.,*
*Have you tried asking him why? He's usually free on the way down.*
*Warmly, S.*

Crow looked at him for a long moment, then left for the upper air at a speed suggesting it didn't want to hold that particular letter any longer than necessary.

Sisyphus set his shoulder to the stone, said good morning to it, and started up. He was humming.

# Sisyphus Gives Advice

The hill was about the height of a decent temple, if the temple had been designed by someone with a grudge against knees.

Sisyphus reached the top a little before what would have been eleven, had Tartarus bothered with hours, and the boulder did what it always did. He watched it go with the mild interest of a man watching his neighbour's cat, then sat down and held out his hand.

Crow put a letter in it.\*

*\* Crow was not, strictly, a name. It was a job description that had stopped looking for anything better.*

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
>
> *My husband has started a sourdough mother. He has named it Doris. He feeds it twice a day, keeps it by the stove so it won't catch a chill, and last night I heard him tell it that it was doing ever so well.*
>
> *He has not told me I'm doing ever so well since the olive harvest before last. Am I mad to be jealous of a jar?*
>
> *Second Fiddle to Flour, Thebes*

Sisyphus read it twice. The second time he went more slowly, the way you walk back over ground where you think you've dropped something.

"Dear Second Fiddle," he said, and Crow's quill began to scratch. "You're not mad. But I don't think the jar is the problem. I think the jar is the only place in the house where your husband feels safe practising.

"Some people can only say tender things to something that can't answer back. It usually means the tenderness is there and has nowhere to go.

"Tomorrow, when he feeds Doris, stand in the kitchen and ask how she's getting on. He will tell you about bubbles, at length. Let him. Somewhere around the second rise he'll look up, and you'll see a man who has been waiting for someone to ask."

"Second rise?" said Crow.

"It's a bread thing."

"You've never made bread."

"I've had a lot of letters about bread."

---

He walked down to where the boulder waited in the hollow it had worn over the centuries, like a dog in its basket, and put his shoulder to it. Crow rode on top, reading aloud. They had found this saved time.

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
>
> *A man at the press keeps explaining things to me. Olives, mostly. I've worked the press twenty-two years. I trained him. Last week he explained where olives come from. How do I stop myself putting him in the press?*
>
> *Explained At, Megara*

"Dear Explained," said Sisyphus, between heaves. "Next time, let him finish. Then say, 'Yes, I know.' Don't say it crossly. Say it the way you'd mention it's raining, and then carry on. Do it every time. You're not trying to win. You're trying to become very boring to explain things to.

"Also, leave him out of the press. They can always tell."

"Can they?" said Crow.

"The oil goes cloudy," said Sisyphus, who had once had a letter about that too, and had replied by return.

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
>
> *I work every day. The customers never stop and nobody asks how I am. They hand me a coin and stare at the water. I have not sat down since the reign of Kronos. How do I find balance?*
>
> *Name Withheld, Riverside*

Sisyphus looked at the handwriting, which was spiky and smelled faintly of damp. Then he looked down the slope to the river, where a hooded figure stood in a boat, very carefully not looking up the hill.

"Dear Name Withheld. Take Thursdays off. Nothing will fall apart. The people waiting for you are, forgive me, extremely patient by nature; it's the one thing they're all good at. Bring a sandwich. Sit on the bank and look at the water from the side that hasn't got work in it.

"And for what it's worth: how are you?"

Down by the river, the boat rocked slightly, as though someone in it had sat down.

---

The god arrived halfway up the fourth ascent, with more sparkle than the occasion required.

"Momus," he announced. "God of Criticism."

"I know," said Sisyphus, not stopping. "You told Athena her house should have wheels."

"I was right." Momus fell into step. "This is beneath you. *Advice.* You're an eternal punishment; you ought to be brooding. People would come miles to watch you brood. There's a whole tradition." He sniffed. "And your crow's handwriting slopes."

"Upwards," said Crow. "It's optimistic."

"And that rock," said Momus, "ought to have a handle."

Sisyphus considered this for the next forty yards.

"Yes," he said. "It ought."

Momus waited for an argument. None came, and he left with noticeably less sparkle than he'd arrived with.

"He'll write in," said Sisyphus.

"Bet you a beetle," said Crow.

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
>
> *A swan has taken to visiting my wife while I'm at market. She says it's just a very friendly swan. Is it nothing?*
>
> *Probably Nothing, Sparta*

Sisyphus was quiet for a while.

"Dear Probably. No.

"Be kind to her, whatever she tells you and whatever she doesn't. She didn't pick the swan. Nobody ever picks the swan. And don't report it to anyone. I did once, about that family, and look where it got me."

"That'll get us in trouble," said Crow.

"Very likely. Send it anyway."

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
>
> *I'm forty-three. I make sandals. I lie awake thinking I was meant for something, and I'm afraid this is it. What's it all for?*
>
> *Just Sandals, Argos*

At the top, the boulder went. Sisyphus watched it all the way down, then sat a while with the letter on his knee.

"Dear Just Sandals. At a guess, there are a few thousand people in Argos who would otherwise be limping. They don't know your name. Every one of them got where they were going today a bit more comfortably because of you.

"I don't think purpose is something you find. It's mostly something you notice you've been doing all along, once you stop staring at it. I find the walk back down is where most of the thinking gets done.

"Make a really good pair this week, for yourself for once. Then go for a long walk in them."

---

The next morning's post included an envelope of very expensive paper, which shed glitter when opened.

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
>
> *People keep walking away from me at parties, usually in the middle of a perfectly reasonable observation. Why?*
>
> *Not Anyone You Know, Olympus*

Crow produced a beetle from somewhere, with bad grace.

"Dear Not Anyone," said Sisyphus warmly, and settled in.

response:
# The Evening Gun

Dawlish found me at the bottom of the stairs, where I had apparently elected to sleep.

"Superintendent's asked for you twice, sir. Wants the Macao dispatches copied fair before the cutter goes down on the ebb."

I sat up. Hog Lane was already at its business: a barber twanging his steel tongs for custom, a peanut seller calling, wet laundry slapping stone. Through the doorway came the lane's morning breath of last night's samshu, frying dough and the river.

"Tell him I've a fever."

"Told him that Tuesday, sir."

"Then tell him it's returned. Fevers do."

My hand had already found the cicada in my waistcoat pocket. It was green jade, no longer than the top joint of my thumb, the kind they once laid on the tongues of the dead so they might rise again. I had worried its left wing so long that the carving had gone smooth as a river stone.

Dawlish's eyes went to my pocket, then to the wall. He had been my coxswain at Navarino and had watched me take a Turkish ball through the shoulder without a word. He had the decency not to compare the two men.

"Aye, sir. Evening gun, then?"

"Evening gun."

---

Grisewood's counting-house smelled of tea dust and camphorwood, and the punkah overhead stirred the heat without lessening it. Fairlie, the junior partner, did not ask me to sit.

"You look like a drowned curate, Merrick."

"I've something on the Hoppo."

"Everyone has something on the Hoppo."

"Not this. A letter came to the Superintendent from the Co-hong yesterday. The mandarin boats go down to Lintin on the twentieth, and this time they don't mean to make a show of it. They mean to burn something."

The abacus in the corner stopped clicking. Fairlie waved the clerk out and opened a drawer. "Prices will want to rise before then. Twenty dollars."

"Fifty. I'm selling my honour."

"Then I'm overpaying. That was sold years ago." He counted thirty onto the blotter. They were Carolus dollars, each one hacked and stamped by so many shroffs that the old Spanish king's face had become a ruin of chisel-marks. "If you're wrong, don't come back."

"And if I'm right?"

"Don't come back either. I've a reputation."

---

By noon the ache had settled in my knees, and I could not stop yawning. They were great jaw-cracking yawns that brought water to my eyes. Under the factory flags, the Union, the Stars and Stripes and the Dutch tricolour bleached to the colour of weak tea, I sweated and shivered at once. The cicada went round and round in my pocket.

The Pearl River is not pearl anything. It is khaki and slow, and that afternoon it carried cabbage leaves, a split melon and the low hulls of night-soil boats making for the paddies upstream. A Tanka girl of twelve or so took me out in her sampan. She worked a single long oar at the stern with a motion like a fish's tail and never once looked at me. She knew where I was going. They all knew.

Mrs. Lo was shelling lotus seeds under the matting roof of her boat. She did not look up either.

"Lieutenant. You owe nine dollar."

"I have thirty."

"Then you have twenty-one." She held out her palm and I filled it. She rang each coin against the gunwale, head tilted like a woman tuning a lute, and set two aside. "Lead inside. Somebody cheat you."

"Somebody always does."

"Englishman cheat Englishman, Englishman cheat China, China cheat everybody." She smiled at the lotus seeds. "Very good river for business."

"I want the Patna. Not the Malwa. It gives me a head like a gun deck."

"Patna cost more."

"I've nineteen dollars."

"Nineteen dollar buy Malwa and a bad head." She split another pod with her thumbnail. "Nineteen dollar and one small favour buy Patna."

I knew the shape of her favours. A cramp went down through my bowels like a fist closing. "Say it."

"Tomorrow night, one boat come up from Whampoa. Hoppo's men maybe stop it. You stand on deck in your coat. You say, this boat belong King of England, you want a war, go ahead." She brushed the husks into the river. "Mandarin does not want a war tomorrow."

"If the Superintendent hears I lent the King's coat to a smug-boat..."

"Superintendent drinks your tea and eats your lies. He hears nothing." Now she looked at me, and there was no malice in it, which was worse. "You are shaking, Lieutenant."

"It's the river damp."

"Yes. Very damp." She called something over her shoulder, and the matting at the back of the boat was drawn aside.

---

The girl who prepared the pipe had a face like a shut door. She dipped the needle into the pot and turned the dark bead over the lamp until it blistered and swelled and browned like a chestnut on a hearth. Then she pressed it into the bowl's small crater. The smell came first: burnt treacle, and beneath it something green and secret, like hay gone damp in a loft.

I drew. The smoke was thick as broth. It went down into me and found the knot in my belly and untied it with patient fingers. Then it found the ache in my knees, and then the low, buzzing dread I had carried since I saw Dawlish's face at the bottom of the stairs.

Downriver the evening gun went at Whampoa, a soft thud through the hull, like a door closing in another house. The dispatches lay uncopied on the Superintendent's desk. I did not count the hours I owed, or the dollars, or the men.

I lay with the cicada in my open palm, and for the first time since morning I did not need to hold it.

Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. response:
# Chapter Six: Mango Wood

Haskett found me before I had managed my boots.

"Captain Elliot's compliments, sir, and he'd be obliged for the Whampoa returns by noon."

"Noon." A yawn took me so hard my jaw clicked. "The returns are with the purser."

"I asked Mr. Dowd, sir. He says they're with you."

"Then Mr. Dowd is a liar, and you may tell the Captain I said so." My nose was running. Every joint ached as though I'd been folded wrong and left overnight in a drawer. "No. Tell him I have the flux. Everyone in Canton has the flux. He'll believe it."

The boy's eyes went to the washbasin, then to my hands. I put them in my pockets.

"Aye, sir."

---

At that hour Hog Lane stank of last night's samshu and of the river at low water, a grey, fat smell like the inside of a wet boot. Lim's shop was a slot between two grog-sellers. His shelves held things sailors had no business selling: quadrants, Bibles, a ship's bell with the name filed off.

He turned my watch over and read the inscription, his lips moving.

"Navarino," he said. "What thing Navarino?"

"A battle. Turks. Long time before."

"You win?"

"We won."

He set it on his scale opposite a chopped dollar, as though gallantry had a weight. "Six dollar."

"It's gold, Lim. Look at the hallmark."

"Gold, yes. Name also." He tapped the engraving with a long yellow nail: *J. Merrick, Midshipman, from the gunroom of HMS Genoa.* "Name very hard sell. Six dollar. Maskee, you no like, you take go."

I took the six.

---

Rennie kept his rooms in the Creek Factory, where the punkah never stopped and the claret was always open. He poured me a glass and watched me not drink it.

"It's a small thing, James. Thursday night a boat goes down to Whampoa with forty chests. You sit in the stern-sheets in your coat and hat."

"And the mandarin cruisers?"

"They see a King's officer and remember urgent business upriver. They always do." He smiled. "That's what the coat is for out here. It's the only thing it's for."

"Elliot's given orders to clear the river of..."

"Elliot gives a great many orders. Thirty dollars."

"Fifty. And ten now."

"Thirty, and nothing now. If I give you anything now you'll be no use to me Thursday." He leaned back. "I'm not a fool. I've seen the colour of you."

"Five, then. Five, or find another coat."

He looked at me a long moment. Then he counted five onto the table one at a time, the way you'd feed a dog you didn't much like.

---

The way to Leung's ran behind Thirteen Factory Street, through a gut of alleys where the fruit-sellers threw whatever wouldn't sell. In June that meant mangoes, hundreds of them, gone black and burst in the gutters. Their sweetness had turned sharp and vinegary, and it caught at the back of the throat. Wasps crawled drunk over the split skins. The cobbles were slick with pulp, and I walked the way I'd once walked a heeling deck, knees loose, never trusting the next step.

They say the Patna chests are made of mango wood. I have never been certain whether the smell in that alley came from the fruit or from what waited at the end of it.

Leung sat behind his abacus as if he'd been carved there.

"Eleven dollars," I said, and laid them down.

He rang each one on a flat stone by his elbow and listened, the way the shroffs do. On the eighth he stopped and slid it back across to me.

"This one bad. Lead inside."

"It came from a Navy..." I stopped. It had come from Rennie. "Ten, then."

"You owe nine from before." His beads clicked. "Ten dollar. Nine for old. One for new. One dollar, one pipe."

"One pipe? For God's sake, Leung, I've been coming here two years."

"Two year you owe me. Every time Thursday. Thursday, Thursday." He shrugged. "Patna finish. Got Malwa."

"Malwa is mud."

"Mud, one dollar. You want, you smoke. You no want..." He opened his hand toward the door and the mangoes.

I wanted.

---

The back room was low and hot, and its walls sweated brown. On the next pallet someone lifted his head. It was Pruett, the American clerk, his cheeks fallen in since spring.

"Merrick. Heard you'd given it up."

"I did. Tuesday."

"Which Tuesday?"

"A good one."

He laughed without sound and lay back down.

Leung's boy knelt by the lamp, twirling a bead of the stuff on a needle until it swelled and browned and smelled like milk scalding in a pan. He pressed it into the bowl and turned the pipe toward me. I drew, and held, and let it go.

The ache went out of my knees first, then my back, then my hands. It didn't go all at once. It went the way water leaves a tide-pool: you look down and it has simply gone. The yawning stopped. The returns, Haskett, Elliot's mild and disappointed face all drifted to a comfortable distance, like a coastline seen from a ship making good way.

Outside, the night watchman's clapper went by. *Tok. Tok-tok.* Second watch.

"Lieutenant." The boy was holding out the needle. "Next pipe?"

"I paid for one."

"Leung say Thursday."

I thought of the stern-sheets and my good coat. I thought of forty chests of mango wood riding low in the black water, and a King's officer sitting on them with his hat on straight.

"Yes," I said. "Thursday."

response:
# The Sea Air

The tide had gone out in the night and left the mud beneath the factories to speak for itself. I woke to the smell of it, and to Hollis at the door.

"Lieutenant Merrick, sir. Captain Elliot's compliments, and the Whampoa returns want your signature before the ten o'clock boat."

"Leave them on the chair."

"He'd like you to read them, sir."

"Then I shall read them on the chair."

The cough came before I could stand. It was the deep one, rising from somewhere beneath the ribs like a bucket hauled up a well. I bent over the basin until it was done. It left the taste it always left, bright and metallic, as though I'd been sucking a brass button.

"Dr. Colledge sees Company men every morning, sir. He'd see you."

"Sea air, Hollis. Six years of it. A man's lungs take on barnacles."

"We're forty miles up a river, sir."

"Then it followed me."

He went. My hands were no use until near nine. They steady by degrees in the mornings, as if the body were deciding, reluctantly, to extend one more day's credit. I signed the returns without reading a line.

---

Hog Lane at midday was eight feet wide and roofed with laundry. Sailors from the Whampoa ships drank samshoo from teacups in the doorways, and every grog-shop wore an English name painted by someone who had heard English once, from a distance. Ah Kew's was called the Jolly Admiral. I had stopped finding that funny.

He was weighing something on his little ivory steelyard when I came in, and he did not look up.

"No can."

"I haven't asked."

"You come, you ask. Always same." He slid the weight along the beam with one long fingernail. "Mandarin catch two boat last week, Lintin side. Burn all chest. Now price go up."

"I paid you on Tuesday."

"Tuesday pidgin finish. Today new pidgin."

I put the watch on the counter. He knew the watch. He had bought its gold case from me in the spring. What remained was the movement, in a pinchbeck replacement, and on the inner lid the engraving nobody had thought worth scratching off: *Presented by the Officers of HMS Glasgow, Navarino, 1827.*

Ah Kew read it, or pretended to.

"This one, nobody want. Inside part only." He pushed it back. "But Parsee want see you. He say bring the coat."

---

Cursetjee kept his counting-room on the second floor of the Chow-Chow Hong. On the landing a boy pulled the punkah rope with his toe while doing sums on a slate. The room smelled of sandalwood, lamp oil, and the vinegar the shroffs used to clean their coin.

"Lieutenant. Sit, sit. You will take tea."

"I'd sooner take whatever you're offering."

"Ah." He smiled with great courtesy, which in Cursetjee was the same as a frown. "Tonight a boat goes down to the Second Bar. Forty oars. Nothing aboard that concerns you. At the customs station there is a junk with a gong and a very anxious officer. I should like that officer to see a gentleman of the Royal Navy standing in our stern, looking bored."

"And if he hails?"

"He will not hail. He will see your coat and think of frigates, and of the Viceroy's letters, and of what happens to minor officials who start wars. He will look at the moon." He counted twenty dollars into a stack. They had been chopped by so many shroffs' stamps they looked chewed. "Ten now. Ten when you are home."

"If Elliot hears of it..."

"Captain Elliot retires at half past nine and reads Paley until he sleeps. I know his habits better than you know your own."

The cough took me there, in his chair, and I could not stop it. He offered a handkerchief of clean linen. When I gave it back he studied the mark on it with a merchant's appraising calm, then folded it away.

"The sea air," I said.

"Of course." He nudged the coins toward me. "My father had the sea air. In Bombay. It took him two years, and he was a careful man."

---

The boat was thin as a paper-knife and sat so low the river slapped her gunwales. The rowers chanted under their breath, a sound like men walking through dry leaves. Their oars came up glittering with the phosphor that lives in that water in summer. I stood aft with my hat squared, and the buttons I had not yet sold caught the lantern.

The customs junk lay where Cursetjee said it would. Its gong sounded once. A figure on the deck raised a lantern toward us, and I looked back at him and thought of nothing at all, which is a skill.

The lantern lowered.

The headman beside me spat a red thread of betel into the river.

"Good face," he said. "Very English face. You do again Friday?"

"Ask the Parsee."

"Parsee say ask you."

"Then yes."

---

Ah Kew's upper room had a window onto the river and a mat on which better men than me had lain, and worse. He took my ten dollars and gave back nothing. He rolled the bead himself over the lamp, turning the needle until the paste swelled, blistered, and went the colour of dark honey. It doesn't smell sweet, whatever they say in London. It smells of burnt sugar with something animal underneath, like a stable on fire.

"Tomorrow you come?"

"Tomorrow I'll come."

The first draw went down my throat like warm water poured into a cold jug. I waited for the cough, the climb from under the ribs, the button on my tongue.

It did not come. It never does, here.

Hollis would call that the drug. Colledge would call it something in Latin. But I lay on my side and breathed all the way down to the bottom of myself, for the first time since morning, and I should like to see either of them tell me it is not a cure.

response:
# Gunpowder Rendezvous

The jukebox in the corner of the Blue Saint is playing "Sundown Mile" for the fourth time since Spike walked in. The needle catches on the same scratch every pass, *I'm burnin' down the—burnin' down the—*, before it lurches on to the chorus.

Nobody gets up to fix it. Nobody in this port town gets up for anything that isn't money or a fight.

Spike shakes the rain off his jacket and drifts to the bar like he has nowhere better to be, which is true. Two stools down, a woman sits with her boots crossed on the counter, a dragon coiling down her right arm from shoulder to wrist. She wears a black crop top and cutoffs that barely qualify as clothing. A pair of stainless Berettas ride in shoulder holsters, worn the way other people wear jewelry.

She doesn't look at him. That's how he knows she's already looked.

"Whatever she's drinking," he tells the bartender. "On her."

"The fuck it is," the woman says.

"Worth a shot."

"Yeah? So's this." She slides her glass of rum an inch to the left so her right hand is free. Spike notes it and smiles at his own reflection in the bar mirror.

He pays with the last crumpled bills in his pocket and eats three handfuls of complimentary peanuts before the glass arrives. She watches that too, contemptuous and a little fascinated, like he's a stray dog doing tricks.

"Rough week, cowboy?"

"Rough decade." He lays a creased bounty sheet on the bar and smooths it flat. It shows a soft-faced man with nervous eyes: *Elias Corva, bookkeeper, wanted for embezzlement*, plus an unfortunate habit of remembering numbers. "Seen him?"

She stares at the sheet a long moment. Then she reaches into her back pocket and slaps an identical photo down beside it.

The jukebox stutters. *Burnin' down the—burnin' down the—*

"Well," Spike says. "That's awkward."

"Fifteen grand," she says. "I been sitting in this shithole two days."

"Fifteen million woolongs."

"The fuck's a woolong?"

"Lately? Nothing I've got." He tries to light a cigarette, but the lighter only sparks dry. She sighs like it physically pains her, leans over, and presses the cherry of her own cigarette to the tip of his. For a second they're close enough that he can smell gun oil and Bacardi and rain in her hair. Her eyes are dark and flat and very steady.

"Name's Revy," she says around the filter. "Remember it, so you know who to haunt."

"Spike. I already tried the haunting thing. Didn't take."

She pulls back and studies him. Something flickers across her face, maybe one bad animal recognizing another.

They drink. They drink again. She matches him shot for shot and then pulls ahead out of spite. Somewhere around the fifth glass, the back door opens and Elias Corva walks in with three men in rain-slick suits behind him.

Corva sees the photos on the bar. He sees the two people sitting over them.

His face does something tragic.

Then everything happens at once.

Revy is off the stool before the first suit clears leather, both Cutlasses up and barking, a muzzle flash in each hand like she's conducting an orchestra. The first goon goes down. The second dives behind a booth. Spike moves the other direction, low and fluid, a flicker of a man. He catches the third suit's wrist as the gun comes up, turns it, and drives an elbow into his throat. The pistol clatters away, and Spike drops him with a kick that ends somewhere near the ceiling.

A bottle explodes beside Spike's head. He ducks half a second late because the bad eye has misjudged the distance again, and glass rains down his collar.

"Can't see for shit, huh?" Revy shouts over the gunfire, delighted.

"Half of me can." He puts two rounds from his Jericho through the booth, and the second goon stops shooting.

A stray bullet punches through the jukebox glass. Neon sputters. The song keeps playing anyway, slower now, warped and drunk. *Burrrnin' dowwwn the—*

The back door bangs. Corva is gone.

They hit the alley together, shoulders slamming as they both try to go first. Rain sheets down. Across the gravel lot the Starlite Motel flickers pink and green, and a door marked 6 is swinging shut.

"He's mine," Revy says.

"He's fifteen million woolongs."

"He's fifteen grand and my goddamn reputation."

They kick the door at the same time. It flies open on an empty room with a sagging bed and a flickering lamp. The bathroom window hangs open on the night, its curtain sucking in and out with the wind.

Spike stands there. Revy stands there.

"Son of a *bitch*," she breathes.

# Gunpowder Rendezvous

A lazy ceiling fan barely stirs the smoky air inside the bar. It turns like it's thinking about quitting, and nobody in the Last Chance would blame it.

Spike Spiegel has been nursing the same glass of something amber for an hour, about forty minutes longer than his woolongs should allow. He's working through a bowl of complimentary peanuts with the devotion of a man who hasn't eaten since Tuesday. By the door, a wanted poster curls in the heat: TOMAS "THE CLERK" VARGA, forger and launderer. Twelve million. Last seen here.

The door bangs open.

She comes in like weather. Black crop top, cutoffs that barely qualify, a dragon coiling down her right arm from shoulder to wrist. Two big nickel-finished pistols ride under her arms. Every man in the room suddenly finds his drink fascinating.

Spike doesn't. He watches her read the poster. Her mouth tightens, and her eyes sweep the room and land on him like a laser sight.

She takes the stool beside him, though six others sit empty.

"Bacardi. Bottle." The bartender doesn't argue. She pours, knocks it back, pours again. "You're in my seat, cowboy."

"Funny. I was here first."

"Yeah, and I'm still here second, so what's that tell you?" She lights a cigarette and doesn't offer him one.

He pats his jacket, finds an empty pack, crumples it. "Mind if I—"

"Yeah, I mind."

He lifts one from her pack anyway, quick as a pickpocket. Her muzzle is in his ribs before the cigarette reaches his lips. He doesn't flinch. He leans in and lights it off the end of hers, close enough to smell rum and cordite on her breath.

"Thanks."

"Do that again and I'll ventilate your liver."

"Go ahead. Saves me drinking."

Something flickers across her face. Annoyance, maybe interest. She holsters. "You're here for Varga."

"Am I?"

"Don't fuck with me. You got the look. Broke dog sniffin' for scraps." She grins, all teeth. "Name's Revy. I'm takin' that son of a bitch's head, and you're stayin' outta my way."

"Spike. And I've never been any good at staying out of the way."

The back door swings. Four men in cheap suits fan out, and behind them, sweating through a linen shirt and clutching a briefcase like a life raft, is the Clerk himself. He sees the two of them at the bar and goes white.

"Ah," Spike says.

"Shit," Revy says, delighted.

The first shot takes out the fan. Then the room explodes.

Revy is off her stool before the first table hits the floor, both guns out and talking in stereo, and two suits drop before they clear leather. Spike flows the other way. He ducks a wild haymaker and slides inside it: palm to the jaw, snap kick to the knee, the wet crack of cartilage. The Jericho appears in his hand and puts a round through a fist reaching for a shotgun.

"That one was *mine!*" Revy shouts over the din.

"Didn't see your name on him."

"I'll carve it on your ass!"

The last suit falls between them. They both pivot toward the back door. It's swinging, empty. Tires scream in the lot.

Revy kicks a chair across the room. "*Fuck!*"

Spike crouches and palms something off the floor. Her Cutlass is on him instantly.

He holds up a plastic key fob. "Starlight Motel. Room seven."

She stares. "You were gonna keep that to yourself."

"Still might."

---

The Starlight has eleven rooms and one working light. Room seven's door hangs open, the bed stripped, the bathroom window busted out. Varga is a ghost, and so is the briefcase.

That should be the end of it. Instead Spike hears the soft click of a hammer drawing back, and when he turns, Revy's pistol is level with his heart.

The Jericho is already on her. He doesn't remember drawing it. That's usually how it goes.

"You tipped him," she says. Her voice has gone low and flat, the sneer gone. "Somebody did."

"Guys like you always got an angle."

"Guys like me are *mostly* angles. Doesn't make me the one who sold you out." He tilts his head. "Who taught you that everybody's selling?"

"Everybody."

It comes out too fast and too honest, and she hates it. He watches her hate it. The muzzle doesn't waver.

"Don't do that," she says.

"Do what?"

"Look at me like you're gonna figure somethin' out."

He steps forward, then again. Her barrel meets his sternum, and his rests against her collarbone. Rain has started outside, ticking through the broken window. The room smells of mildew and gunpowder and her.

"Close enough to blow your heart out your back."

"Yeah. Figured it was something like that."

"You'd really pull it," he says. It isn't a question.

"Maybe. Maybe not." She shrugs, and the gun shrugs with her. "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here."

"Me too." One corner of his mouth lifts. "Died once already. Didn't take."

The engine revs. Rain hammers the glass.

Spike Spiegel takes the stool two down from her anyway. Two is polite. Two is also exactly within reach.

"Whatever's cheapest," he tells the bartender, and fishes a bent cigarette out of a crushed pack. The lighter takes four tries. It's a scuffed steel thing with a ring of rust crusted around the hinge, the kind of corrosion that only comes from going under and coming back up. More than once.

"The hell'd you do to that?" She doesn't look at him. A dragon coils from her shoulder to her wrist, and the pistol keeps ticking off fan blades.

"Dropped it."

"In what, a toilet?"

"Ocean. Couple times." He gets the flame, cups it, inhales. "Once in a river, but I was falling out a window, so that one doesn't count."

That earns him a look. Dark eyes, sharp grin, nothing friendly in it. "And you kept it."

"It still works."

"Barely."

"So do I."

She snorts and sets the pistol on the bar. It isn't holstered, he notes, just resting, her hand an inch away. She nods at the folded paper sticking out of his jacket. "Lemme guess. Fat guy, gold tooth, name like a skin condition."

"Teodor Varga."

"Fuck." She slaps an identical photo down next to his drink. "How much they promise you?"

"Forty thousand."

Her jaw works. "Sixty."

The fan turns. In the back, a jukebox skips the same three notes of a song nobody chose. Two hunters, one bounty, two prices. Somebody's being used as bait, and neither of them has decided yet whether it's the other one.

"Revy," she says eventually, like it costs her something.

"Spike."

"Stupid name."

"I've heard."

She signals for a bottle of Bacardi and pours two glasses without asking. "Drink. You look like you haven't eaten since Tuesday."

"Thursday."

"It's Wednesday."

"I know."

That almost gets a laugh out of her. They drink. She pours again. Her knee finds his under the bar and stays there, and he can't tell if it's an invitation or if she's positioning herself to kick the stool out from under him. He suspects she can't tell either.

"Your eyes don't match," she says on the fourth round.

"One of them's a liar."

"Which one?"

"Haven't decided."

The front door bangs open. Three men in cheap suits come through, then two more, then a gold tooth glinting behind them all. Varga takes one look at the two of them sitting together and does the math faster than they did.

"Kill them," he says, and runs.

Revy is moving before the word finishes. Both pistols come up. The second one was on her hip the whole time, Spike realizes, and he never even saw her reach. She fires them in a rhythm that sounds like applause. Spike goes over the bar, comes up with his Jericho, and puts a man down through a cloud of exploding liquor bottles. Another gets close enough to swing, and Spike slips the punch like water around a stone and answers with a heel to the jaw.

"That's two!" Revy yells, laughing, actually laughing. "I got three!"

"You're counting?"

"Somebody's gotta!"

The last suit drops. The back door is swinging. Out in the alley, taillights fishtail through a puddle and vanish.

Revy spits. "Starlite Motel. Room twelve. Everybody in this shithole knows where Varga sleeps."

"Then why hasn't anybody collected?"

She grins at him, all teeth. "Nobody's been this motivated."

---

Room twelve smells like bleach and cigarettes and somebody else's bad decisions. The bathroom window is open, rain blowing through it. Varga is gone.

Spike turns around, and Revy's Cutlass is six inches from his heart.

His Jericho is already under her ribs. He doesn't remember deciding to draw it. From the look on her face, neither does she.

"Sixty grand," she says softly. "Split's a lot smaller than whole."

"Forty," he corrects. "For me."

"Maybe I take yours too."

"Maybe."

Neither of them moves. Rain ticks against the glass. Her breath smells like rum and gunsmoke, and this close he can see a pulse jumping in her throat that has nothing to do with fear. Her finger is on the trigger. So is his. It would be the easiest thing in the world.

"You're not gonna shoot me," she says.

"You don't know that."

"No," she admits. "I don't." She presses in harder, the barrel digging into his sternum, and somehow closes the distance between them in the process. "That's the fun part."

"So what now?"

"You're still here."

Something flickers across her face. Anger, maybe, or recognition. "Yeah," she says. "I'm just here."

response:
# Blood Moon

The harvest moon hangs over Vâlcele like a wound that refuses to close.

Its light runs red down the thatch, pools in the ruts of the road, and slicks the well-rope where a bucket still sways, though there is no wind. Every shutter in the village is barred. Every door stands open. Yennefer of Vengerberg has seen enough massacres to know which detail matters.

She steps over a dropped distaff, black skirts whispering against the mud, and follows the smell of iron to the square.

The thing she has hunted for eleven days lies in pieces at the foot of the chapel steps. It was a boyar once, judging by the rings. Now it is a ruin of grey flesh and silver-scorched bone, its chest blown open as if by cannon. The heart she came for is a smear on the cobbles.

"Disappointed?"

The voice comes from above. A man sits on the chapel roof with one knee drawn up, a red coat spilling around him like something poured. He wears a wide-brimmed hat and small round lenses the colour of embers, absurd at midnight. In one gloved hand, resting lazily against his thigh, is a weapon of black metal longer than her forearm. It is still smoking.

He looks like nothing this century has made.

"Annoyed," Yennefer says. "I had a use for that."

"For *him*?" He laughs, low and delighted. "He wept at the end. He begged God. A creature that drinks children, begging God." He drops from the roof and lands without a sound, closer than she would like. "He was not worth your trouble, witch. Or mine."

"Sorceress."

"Is there a difference?"

"Several decades of study and an excellent tailor."

His grin widens, and keeps widening, past the point where a human face would stop. Too many teeth. Yennefer does not step back. Over a long life she has learned that the first step back is the one that gets you killed.

Instead she lifts two fingers and speaks a single word in the Elder Speech.

The air around him clenches. Chains of violet light erupt from the cobbles and lash his arms, his throat, his chest, cinching tight enough to crack ribs. The weapon clatters to the ground. She feels his weight against the spell like a bull against a fence. Then she feels nothing at all. He has stopped struggling.

"Oh," he breathes. Behind the lenses his eyes burn red. "Oh, that is *lovely*. Do it again."

"I'm holding you."

"You are." He tilts his head, and the bindings creak. "And now I am curious how long you can."

His body comes apart.

It does not tear. It comes *unmade*. The red coat collapses into a sheet of black, and the black becomes eyes, dozens blinking open in the dark, and the eyes become bats, a shrieking hurricane that shreds her chains to sparks. Yennefer throws up a shield an instant before the swarm hits. It breaks on the dome of force like hail on glass, circles once, and reassembles behind her.

She feels breath at her ear. It is cold, with no heartbeat to drive it.

"Lilac," he murmurs. "And gooseberries. You perfume yourself like a bride."

"Touch me and I'll boil you from the inside."

"You could try." He does not touch her. Somehow that is worse. "But I *see* you, sorceress. These eyes were made for the dark. Under the pretty face there is a crooked girl with a curved spine, and she is still so very angry."

The words slide into her like a blade between plates of armour. For half a breath the old shame rises: the pigsty, the stick, her father's face. Yennefer lets none of it reach her eyes.

She turns slowly. Violet meets red.

"And under yours," she says, "there's a man who has been dying for centuries and can't manage to finish."

Silence. The bucket sways on its rope.

She brushed his mind as she spoke, the lightest fingertip on the surface of black water, and what she glimpsed nearly made her retch. A forest of stakes. A field of the impaled, writhing at sunset. A prince kneeling in blood, cursing heaven, drinking. And beneath it all, vast and patient, a hunger that has nothing to do with blood. He hungers for an ending, and for someone strong enough to give it to him.

He knows she saw. She watches him decide whether to kill her for it.

Then Alucard laughs, genuinely, head thrown back, the sound rolling off the empty houses.

"Splendid," he says. "Truly. You are the first thing in this miserable age that has not bored me."

"I'm thrilled."

"Why did you want his heart?"

She considers lying, and considers it carefully. "Old blood is said to undo certain workings. Ones that shouldn't be undoable."

His gaze drops, unhurried, to her belly, then rises again. He knows. Of course he knows. He can probably smell the emptiness in her the way a wolf smells a lame deer.

"His blood was thin," he says. "Weak. It would have done nothing for you." He lets a pause fall, deliberately placed. "Mine, on the other hand…"

There it is: the hook, glinting. Yennefer looks at it for a long time.

"And what would that cost me?"

"Oh, nothing much." He retrieves his weapon from the cobbles and slides it into his coat. "Only a dance. Some night, when you have grown strong enough to truly hurt me. I would very much like to see you try."

"You want me to kill you."

"I want you to *want* to." The grin returns, all teeth. "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame. I have been tame a long while, sorceress. It does not suit me."

"I'm not your saviour," Yennefer says. "And I'm not your executioner. I'm not anything you get to collect."

"Not yet."

He bows. It is an old bow, a court bow, from a court that crumbled to dust long before she drew breath. The shadows take him by the edges and fold him away.

Yennefer stands alone in the square with the dead boyar and the swaying bucket and the red moon watching. Her hands, she notices, are perfectly steady.

She waits until she is certain he is gone before she lets them shake.

# Blood Moon

The wheel lies on its side in the ditch beside the village gate, three spokes snapped clean, its iron rim sprung loose like a broken bracelet. Yennefer of Vengerberg crouches beside it, careful of her skirts, and lays two fingers on the split hub.

Fear leaves a residue. It clings to wood the way smoke clings to wool, and this wheel is soaked in it. She sees, though not with her eyes, a cart heaped with bedding and children, a man whipping a mule past exhaustion, and a woman looking back at the chapel. The wheel struck the gatepost. Nobody stopped to mend it.

Above the thatched roofs, the moon rises the color of a fresh wound.

"They left three days ago," says a voice behind her. "You're late."

She doesn't startle. She spent years teaching her body not to startle. She stands, brushes off her palms, and turns.

He leans against the gatepost as though he grew out of it. A long red coat pools around his boots, and a wide hat brim tilts low over his face. Before his eyes sit two small lenses of amber glass that catch the moonlight and give back nothing. He is smiling. *Too many teeth*, she thinks, and then: *no, exactly the right number*, which is worse.

"I'm precisely when I intended to be," Yennefer says. "The question is what *you* are doing here."

"Waiting." He tips his head. "For something interesting."

The air around him has the flat, pressed quality of a sickroom whose windows have never been opened. She has met higher vampires, the sort who discuss philosophy over wine while watching your throat. This one sits in the world like a stone in a shoe.

She doesn't bother asking politely. She speaks four syllables and closes her fist, and threads of violet light snap tight around his wrists, ankles and throat, pinning him to the post.

He laughs. It's a delighted sound, almost boyish.

"Oh, that's *lovely*. Again. Tighter."

Then he isn't there. The binding closes on darkness that spills through it like water through fingers, and the darkness has eyes in it, dozens of them, blinking and sliding over one another. Yennefer's stomach turns. She holds her ground.

Cold breath touches the nape of her neck.

"Lilac," he murmurs, very close. "And gooseberries. You've dressed your scent the way you've dressed your face, Witch."

Fire blooms in her palm before she decides to summon it. She turns into him and holds it an inch from the amber lenses. He doesn't flinch either. The flames throw red across red.

"Sorceress," she says.

"Is there a difference?"

"Decades of study and an enormous amount of pain."

His face sharpens with interest. "Pain," he repeats, tasting it. "Yes. I can see where they cut you." His gaze travels down her body. It isn't lewd. It is worse than lewd, clinical as a surgeon's. "Your spine was crooked once. They straightened it. Fine work. And here…" His eyes settle low on her belly. "They took something out and left the room empty. Nothing grows in you."

The fire in her hand gutters for one heartbeat. She wills it back to a roar, but he has seen it, and his smile widens.

"There," he says softly. "There you are."

Yennefer lets the flame die. She doesn't need it. Instead she steps closer, close enough that the dead-room smell of him fills her throat, and she *looks*, with the second sight they beat into her at Aretuza, the kind that burns behind the eyes.

What she sees nearly drops her to her knees. There is no man. There is a hole in the shape of a man, and crammed into it, layer on layer, are thousands of others: soldiers, children, priests, a woman still screaming. He has eaten them all and is still hungry. Beneath the hunger, at the very bottom, something small and tired is waiting for it all to end.

She is revolted. She cannot stop looking.

"You talk about what they took from me," she says, her voice steady, "as though you've kept everything. But you're starving. You've swallowed a thousand lives and you're still searching for someone strong enough to finish you." She tilts her head, mirroring him. "That's why you waited at the gate. You weren't waiting for something interesting. You were waiting for something that might *win*."

For the first time, he goes still. It isn't a predator's stillness. It is the stillness of a struck bell after the sound fades.

Then his hand moves faster than her eye can follow, and something presses beneath her chin. It is long, made of black iron and engraved silver, heavier than any crossbow, and it smells of sulfur and oil. She doesn't know what it is. She knows exactly what it's for.

She doesn't look away from the lenses.

"Go on, then," Yennefer says. "Though I'd hate for you to waste me. I'm told I'm difficult to replace."

The moon climbs. Somewhere in the empty village, a shutter bangs in the wind.

Slowly, the iron leaves her skin.

"Not tonight," he says. He sounds almost grateful, or almost disappointed. With him, she suspects, they're the same thing. "In the chapel you'll find what drove these people out. A newborn thing. A pack of distant wolves howls at irregular intervals, creating an eerie backdrop. Length: 1000 words.
response:
# Blood Moon

The moon comes up the color of an opened vein, and somewhere beyond the tree line, the wolves begin.

Not in chorus. One voice, then a silence long enough to forget it, then three at once, ragged and overlapping, then nothing. Yennefer of Vengerberg has heard wolves in a hundred forests. These are wrong. They sound like something is making them sing.

The abbey crowns the pass like a broken jaw, half its roof open to the sky. The villagers below told her, between prayers, that the bells stopped a fortnight ago, and that those who climbed up to ask why did not come down. She expected a bruxa. A katakan, perhaps, if the bishop's purse justified the portal.

She did not expect the man on the altar.

He's long and loose-limbed beneath a coat the red of a cardinal's silk. A wide-brimmed hat is tipped low, and over his eyes sit orange-tinted lenses that make no sense at all at midnight. A pewter chalice hangs from his gloved fingers. It isn't wine.

"A witch," he says, as though she's a dish he ordered. "I smelled you from the valley. Lilac. And something tart beneath it. Gooseberries?"

"Sorceress." She halts at the end of the nave, among the pews where the monks are. She doesn't look at them. Looking would be a concession. "And I won't return the compliment. You smell like a butcher's drain."

He laughs, and the laugh goes on a beat too long.

A single howl. Cut off mid-breath.

Yennefer doesn't waste words. She lifts her hand and the air folds. A lance of white fire crosses the nave and takes him through the chest, through the altar, through the wall behind. Stone bursts. The chalice rings on the flagstones.

What remains of him is a hole with arms.

Then the hole fills. It fills not with flesh but with darkness, wet and churning, studded with eyes that open one by one and fix on her. Ribs knit. Red cloth weaves itself back across them like a tapestry unpicked in reverse. He stands and brushes ash from his lapel.

"Again," he says.

Her stomach turns, and some cold, scholarly part of her leans closer, hungry to understand. She lets neither reach her face. She has watched a higher vampire gather itself from a bloodstain, and this is not that. That was healing. This is something that has never been wounded, only briefly interrupted.

"No incantation," he muses, stepping down. His boots make no sound. "No gesture worth the name. Do you know how long it has been since anyone made me *bleed*? In my day, they burned women for far less."

"In mine, they tried." She turns as he circles, keeping the pews between them. "Most of them are compost now."

"Mm." His smile is too wide for his face, and growing. "Show me what else you can do."

So she does. She drops her gaze to the moonlight pooled on the floor, to the long shadow he casts across it, and speaks one word in the Elder Speech. Violet light lances down like a nail. His shadow pins to the stone.

He stops mid-stride. Looks down. For the first time, the smile falters.

Yennefer allows herself to breathe. "Your kind are always so proud of being untouchable. You forget you're still standing in the world."

The wolves erupt, four, five, a frenzy, then go silent all at once, as if a hand has closed around their throats.

"Oh," he says softly. "Oh, you are *good*."

His hand moves faster than she can follow. Something black and enormous appears in it, a slab of iron as long as her forearm, and the abbey explodes with thunder. A pew beside her disintegrates into splinters. Her hair stirs in the wind of it. She does not flinch. She will be damned before she flinches.

"I could put the next one through your pretty skull before you finish your next word," he says. "But I won't. Not yet. You're the most interesting thing to climb this mountain in a century." He tilts his head, nostrils flaring. "And you smell of more than lilac. Your blood tells stories, sorceress. Bone that was broken and set straight. A spine that remembers being crooked."

The cold starts at her collarbone and spreads.

"And beneath that," he murmurs, almost tender, "a room locked from the inside. Empty. Waiting." He breathes it in like a connoisseur. "What did you trade it for? Was it worth it?"

For a heartbeat, the binding wavers.

He feels it. His grin returns in full.

But Yennefer has been cut by better knives in finer courts, and she has learned that the only answer to a blade is another blade. This time she reaches with her mind instead of fire, and brushes against his.

It's like plunging her hand into a well with no bottom. Centuries. Battlefields. A forest of stakes, and a man on a hill counting them. And under everything, older than hunger, lies a single wish he has never once spoken aloud.

She withdraws, pale, but her voice is steady. "You want someone to win."

The wolves howl once, long and lonely.

He says nothing. It's the first thing he hasn't had an answer for.

"All this," she gestures at the dead, the ruin, the moon, "is an audition. You're waiting for someone strong enough to end you. And you're terrified no one ever will be."

Silence stretches between them, taut as a garrote.

Then he laughs again, quieter this time, and something has changed in it. "*The bird of Hermes is my name,*" he says, "*eating my wings to make me tame.*"

The violet nail shatters. His shadow peels free of the floor and rears up behind him, vast, writhing, full of teeth.

Yennefer doesn't step back. A portal blooms behind her instead, crackling at the edges, smelling of ozone and lilac.

"Don't mistake me for something sweet," she says, "or for a maiden who needs saving. Least of all from you."

"I would never." He sweeps off the hat and bows, deep and mocking and, perhaps, a little sincere. "Come back when you're ready to kill me, sorceress. I'll wait."

"You'll wait a long time."

"I'm very good at that."

She steps backward into the light, and is gone.

Alucard stands alone among the dead and listens. For the first time all night, the wolves sing together.

A dim overhead light flickers in the prison corridor at irregular intervals. Length: 1000 words.
response:
# Prison Strings

The light above the Annex corridor stutters: on, off, on. Jolyne has tried to count the rhythm and can't. Three seconds, then one, then a long seven that makes the hallway feel like the inside of a closed mouth.

"Keep walking, Cujoh."

She keeps walking. The guard at her elbow is new, young, and smells like burnt coffee. Behind the bars on both sides, the other inmates are quiet. That's the first wrong thing. The Annex is never quiet. People end up here because they bend spoons with their minds, or chew through steel, or hear voices that turn out to be real, and none of them ever shut up.

The second wrong thing is sitting on the bench outside the warden's office.

It's a woman in a white button-down and black tie, hands folded on one knee, auburn hair braided over her shoulder. She looks up when the light returns, and she smiles like Jolyne is the person she's been waiting for all day.

Her eyes have rings in them, gold and concentric, like a target.

"Jolyne Cujoh," the woman says. Her voice is soft, a library voice. "I'm Makima. Thank you for coming."

"Didn't come. Got dragged." Jolyne stops. The guard stops with her, at exactly the same half-second, like a shadow. "You the new shrink? 'Cause I already told the last one all about my daddy issues."

"I'm with Public Safety. A different branch than you're used to." Makima tilts her head. "I read your file. Framed for murder, fifteen years, and then something strange. Witnesses say you came apart. *Unwound.*" Her gaze slides down to the butterfly tattoo on Jolyne's forearm. "I'd very much like to see it."

There it is. It isn't interest. It's appetite. Jolyne has seen men look at her like that through bars, but never so politely.

"Peep show's closed, lady."

Makima laughs a little behind her hand. It's a perfect laugh, and that's the problem. It's the laugh of someone who studied laughing.

The light dies. In the dark, Jolyne lets a single thread spool from her fingertip, thin as a hair. She feeds it across the floor to the guard's boot, up his trouser leg, and against the inside of his wrist.

His pulse is slow, sleeper slow. And he hasn't blinked since they stopped.

The light comes back. Makima hasn't moved, but now she's watching Jolyne's hand.

"I can have your conviction overturned by morning," Makima says. "Your father has been trying for months, hasn't he? Lawyers. Appeals. It must be wearing on him." Then, gently: "I could make it easy. All I'd ask in return is that you work for me."

The words slide in sideways and find the soft spot: Dad, exhausted, alone on the wrong side of the glass. Jolyne feels them land and hates that they land.

"What'd you do to him?" She jerks her chin at the guard.

"Nothing. He's being good." Makima turns to him. "Officer, would you kneel?"

He kneels without hesitation. His knees hit the concrete so hard that Jolyne winces.

"Would you draw your sidearm and put it under your chin?"

"Hey—"

The gun is already moving. Jolyne doesn't think. Stone Free unravels her right hand into a lash of thread that snaps across the corridor. It coils around the pistol and the trigger guard and rips the gun out of his grip so hard it clatters off the far wall.

The guard stays on his knees, staring at nothing.

Makima's smile widens by a millimeter. "Faster than my voice," she murmurs. "How wonderful."

Jolyne gets it all at once, and it goes through her cold. The guard was never the point. Makima didn't need to hurt anyone. She needed Jolyne to *show* her the speed, the range, how the thread moves, and what Jolyne does when someone's about to die. The whole thing was a demonstration, and Jolyne performed on cue like a dog doing a trick for a biscuit.

"You set me up, you sick—"

"I asked nicely first."

"You'd have killed him."

Makima considers this the way someone considers the weather. "He belongs to me. It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners."

The light goes out.

This time Jolyne doesn't send one thread. She sends twenty. When the bulb sputters back, they're wrapped around Makima's throat and wrists, pinning her to the bench, pulled tight enough to dimple her skin.

Makima doesn't struggle. She doesn't even look down.

"Go on," she says. "Pull. But you should know that if you open my throat, someone else's opens instead. Somewhere far away. A schoolteacher, maybe, or a grandmother. Someone who has never heard your name." Her ringed eyes hold Jolyne's. "You'll never know who. You'll only know you did it."

Jolyne's threads tremble. She can feel Makima's pulse through them, and it's the calmest thing in the building.

"Liar."

"Maybe." Makima's voice drops, almost fond. "But you're kind, Jolyne. Kindness is the easiest part of a person to hold. You'd have to be *very* sure."

Jolyne isn't sure, and that's the whole trick. Makima doesn't need to control her if she can make her doubt. Jolyne hates it so much her teeth ache.

So she does the only thing that feels like winning. She loosens the threads.

All but one.

"Here's the deal," she says. "You wanted to see Stone Free. Now you've seen it. And there's a thread tied somewhere on you that you'll never find, and it's staying there. You go anywhere near my dad, I'll know. You come back here, I'll know. You so much as *think* about putting a leash on me—" She leans in. "I'll be closer than you think."

For a moment, Makima's face does something unrehearsed. It isn't fear. It looks more like delight.

"Then I'll know you're thinking of me," she says. She stands and smooths her tie.

The light dies.

When it comes back, the bench is empty. The guard blinks and gasps. He looks at his empty holster, then at Jolyne, with wild, wet eyes. In the cells, someone starts swearing, then someone else, and the Annex is loud again, the way it's supposed to be.

Jolyne flexes her fingers. The last thread runs down the corridor and out under the steel door, taut as a fishing line.

Then, gently, something tugs on it from the other end.

Twice.

Like a hand testing a leash.

response:
# Prison Strings

The fences at Blackwater Annex are wired with something older than electricity. Whenever an inmate walks past, the chain-link shivers on its posts, a dry metallic rattle that runs the length of the yard. The guards say it's how the place keeps count. Jolyne Cujoh says it's how the place keeps you crazy.

She's leaning against the north fence, rattling it on purpose with her shoulder, when the new girl walks in.

Auburn hair in a loose braid. An orange jumpsuit that somehow looks pressed. Hands folded in front of her like she's waiting for a train. The yard goes quiet, but not scared-quiet. It's the hush of a church just before somebody important stands up.

The new girl walks the whole length of the east fence.

It doesn't make a sound.

Jolyne straightens. The butterfly tattoo on her arm prickles the way it does before a fight.

"Hello." The woman stops a polite distance away. Her eyes are yellow and ringed like targets, or like something looking up from the bottom of a well. "I'm Makima. You're Jolyne, aren't you? Everyone talks about you."

"Everyone needs a hobby." Jolyne looks her up and down. "Fence didn't rattle for you."

Makima glances at the chain-link as if noticing it for the first time. "Maybe it likes me."

"Nothing in this dump likes anybody."

Makima smiles. It's a good smile, warm and a little shy, the kind that gets a guard to bring you an extra blanket. Jolyne has seen a hundred fake smiles in prison, and this is the best one yet. That's exactly what makes her skin crawl. Real people don't get it this right.

"I heard you can come apart," Makima says.

Jolyne doesn't answer. Beneath the cuff of her jumpsuit, a single thread of Stone Free has already slipped loose from her ankle. It winds through the bottom links of the fence, twenty feet of string thin as hair, feeling for vibration. If anyone moves toward her, she'll know.

"Your whole body, unspooled," Makima continues, as though Jolyne had said yes. "Can you feel through the strings? Can you pull?" She tilts her head. "It must be lonely, being able to hold so many things at once and having nothing worth holding."

"You a shrink or a cellmate?"

"A friend, if you'd like one." Makima steps closer. The fence stays silent. "I'm only here for a little while. I have work outside, and I could take someone with me."

There it is. Jolyne almost laughs. "Let me guess. All I gotta do is sign something."

"Nothing so formal. Just say yes." Makima's voice drops, soft and intimate. "Your father is very sick, isn't he? Lying somewhere cold. You could be there when he wakes up."

The string at Jolyne's ankle goes taut.

She hasn't told anyone here about her father. Not one person.

"A free ride outta here, my dad, a big hug at the end?" Her voice comes out flat and steady, her father's voice. "Lady, if there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney. Who the hell told you about him?"

"You did. Just now." Makima's smile doesn't move. "Your hand went to your chest. People always touch the place where they keep things."

Jolyne looks down. Her palm is pressed flat over her sternum. She drops it.

Then the string feels them: footsteps. Not one set. Dozens.

All across the yard, the fences start to rattle. It's not the usual scattered clatter. It's a rising roar, chain-link shuddering on every side as inmates drift away from the weight benches and the card tables and the shade of the guard tower. Their faces are slack, their eyes unfocused. They move toward Makima the way water moves toward a drain.

Up in the tower, the guard turns his back.

"You were right," Makima says. "Nothing in here likes anybody. But they do listen."

One face in the crowd stops Jolyne cold. Ermes. Ermes, who split a smuggled candy bar with her on her first night, who would spit in the warden's coffee on a dare. She walks to Makima's side and kneels on the asphalt without being asked.

"Ermes." Jolyne's voice cracks. "Hey. *Ermes.*"

Nothing.

"She'd die for me if I asked." Makima rests a hand on Ermes's head, gentle as a pet owner. "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners."

Jolyne moves.

Stone Free erupts from her arm in a blur of blue thread and lashes around Makima's wrists, cinching tight enough to cut. Jolyne lunges forward, fist cocked, ready to knock that perfect smile into the next zip code.

Makima doesn't flinch. She looks down at the strings binding her and seems pleased.

"You see?" she murmurs. "You do want to hold something."

That's when Jolyne notices.

She just took three hard steps toward the fence, close enough that her sleeve brushed the links.

And it didn't rattle.

Her stomach drops. She thinks back: the last minute of walking, of leaning, of shifting her weight. Silence every time. The fence counts inmates. Makima isn't one. Ermes, kneeling against the chain-link, hasn't made it ring once.

And neither has Jolyne. Not since she answered that first question.

"You've been agreeing with me for a while now," Makima says softly. "Little things. You answered when I asked. You accepted that I knew. Every yes makes a leash a little shorter." Her ringed eyes catch the light. "I've never held someone made of string before. I think you'd look lovely on a lead."

Jolyne feels it then, an invisible pressure at the back of her neck. It's the pull a collar makes when someone tugs.

*Fine,* she thinks. *Then I'll get rid of the neck.*

She unravels.

Her throat goes first, then her shoulders and chest, her whole body unspooling into a storm of thread that pours through the diamond gaps of the chain-link like wind through a screen. For one dizzy second there's no Jolyne at all, nothing for a collar to close around, only a thousand loose ends with nobody holding them.

She reweaves on the other side of the fence, gasping, and slams her fist into the links.

The fence *screams.* Metal shrieks on its posts, a glorious, ugly racket that rings across the whole yard.

Jolyne grins through her clenched teeth. "Still counted."

Makima studies her through the chain-link, and for the first time the smile slips. It doesn't slip into fear. It slips into something hungrier: open, naked interest, the way a collector looks at a rare piece she didn't know existed.

"Remarkable," she says. Then, almost absently, she takes her hand off Ermes's head.

Ermes collapses, coughing, blinking at the sky like she just woke from a nap she doesn't remember taking.

"Keep her," Makima says. "For now."

She turns and walks back across the yard. The fences stay silent around her, and the blank-faced inmates part to let her through.

Jolyne watches her go. She doesn't mention the single blue thread still knotted around Makima's wrist, too fine to see, trailing back across the asphalt to Jolyne's fingertip.

Two people can hold a leash.

Behind her, the fence keeps rattling.
