# Prison Strings

The rumor reaches Jolyne before the woman does.

"Cameras go dead when she walks," Ermes mutters over breakfast, chin tipped toward the observation deck. "Every one of 'em. Ward C lost forty minutes of footage yesterday and nobody even filed a report."

The facility has no official name. The guards call it the Annex: a concrete basin beneath the Florida swamp where the Speedwagon Foundation and some Japanese agency with too many acronyms bury people who do impossible things. Jolyne has been here eleven days. She has learned which guards take bribes, which inmates bite, and that the fluorescent lights hum a half-step flat.

At 2:14 p.m., she learns something new.

She's in the visitation hall, summoned for an "interview" she never requested, when the red light above the door blinks out. Then the one in the corner. Then the one behind the plexiglass, like someone walking down a hallway pinching out candle wicks.

The woman who sits across from her is pretty in a way that feels deliberate. Auburn braid, white shirt, black tie, posture of a schoolteacher. Her eyes are yellow and ringed like targets.

"Jolyne Cujoh," she says, warm as bathwater. "I'm Makima. Thank you for seeing me."

"Didn't have a choice." Jolyne leans back and crosses her arms so the butterfly tattoo faces out. "And you can cut the sweet act. Nobody smiles like that in here unless they want something."

Makima's smile doesn't flicker. "That's very perceptive."

"That's very not a denial."

Under the table, a single thread peels from Jolyne's fingertip, thin as spider silk. It slides across the floor, climbs a chair leg, and loops once, feather-light, around Makima's ankle. A cellmate once swore you could feel a lie in someone's pulse.

Makima's pulse is a metronome. Sixty beats. No more, no less.

"I'm with Public Safety," Makima says. "We're interested in people with your gift. The way you come apart." She tilts her head. "Most things, when you take hold of them, stay held. But you could slip out of anything, couldn't you? Handcuffs. Walls. Hands." She pauses. "I find that very interesting."

The thread around her ankle doesn't so much as twitch.

"Yeah, well, I find you creepy as hell," Jolyne says. "So we both learned something."

Makima laughs, a soft, perfect sound, the kind a person might practice in a mirror. "Your father is Jotaro Kujo. Marine biologist. Rarely home. When you were little, you had a fever so high your mother thought you'd die, and he didn't come." She says it gently, the way a nurse peels off a bandage. "You were framed, Jolyne. You're angry and alone, and the people who should have come for you didn't. I can get you out today. All you have to do is work for me."

There it is. Not a threat. A warm hand reaching for the sorest place.

Jolyne's jaw tightens. "How do you know that?"

"I know a great many things about people I'm interested in."

"Pass."

"You haven't heard the terms."

"Don't need to. Anybody who opens with my daddy issues is selling timeshares in hell."

For the first time, something moves behind those ringed eyes. Not anger. Appetite.

"Officer," Makima says, without looking away.

The guard by the door steps forward. It's Hendricks, a decent one, the one who slips Ermes extra pudding. His face is calm, pleasant even. He draws his sidearm, presses the barrel beneath his own chin, and waits.

"He's a good man," Makima says. "He has a daughter about your age. Would you like to reconsider?"

Jolyne moves before she can think. Stone Free erupts from her forearm in a blur of blue, a strand whipping through the trigger guard and wrenching. The pistol flies across the hall and cracks against the plexiglass. A second strand cinches Hendricks's wrists together, and he blinks like a man waking up in the wrong bed.

Jolyne is breathing hard. Makima hasn't moved.

"Four-tenths of a second," Makima says, almost to herself. "From decision to intervention. And you split your attention between two targets without losing tension on the one around my ankle." She finally glances down at the near-invisible thread. "That's very good."

Ice slides down Jolyne's spine.

She knew. The whole time, she knew.

"You weren't gonna let him die," Jolyne says slowly. "You just wanted to see how fast I'd move."

"I wanted to see *if* you would move," Makima corrects. "Some people don't. You did. You care about people who mean nothing to you." She folds her hands. "Do you know how rare that is? How useful? A dog that loves everyone will die for anyone. And that's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners."

Jolyne looks at Hendricks, who is trembling now and staring at his empty hands, and she understands. The summons she never requested. The one guard she trusts posted at the door. The cameras dying so no one would see what came next. This wasn't an interview. It was a lab, and she's been the rat since she walked in.

"You set up the whole damn board," she whispers.

"I set up a room," Makima says. "You did the rest. I only watched where you put your feet."

Jolyne stands. The threads in her arm wind back with a hiss. When she speaks, her voice is low and level. It's her father's voice, she realizes, the one she hates hearing in herself.

"Listen up, Public Safety. You can know every sad story I've got. You can make every guard in this place eat his own gun. But I'm not your dog. I'm not anybody's dog." She leans across the table, close enough to see her reflection trapped in those rings. "You can smile all you want. Call it an interview, call it a job offer, call it charity. But if there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney. And I don't see any Mickey here, lady. Just you, and a girl who's gonna figure out what you really are."

Makima rises, straightens her tie, and smiles as if Jolyne has just done something adorable.

"I look forward to it."

She walks out. Above the door, the red light blinks back to life.

Only later, back in her cell, does Jolyne feel it. The thread she looped around Makima's ankle is still attached. It's still stretching outward through the walls, farther than any thread of hers should be able to go.

Makima never cut it.

She wants to be followed.

Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception.

First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense.

Notes are always written on standard Foundation memo paper, even when the researcher keeps it locked away. Length: 1000 words.
response:
**Item #:** SCP-7140

**Object Class:** Pending

**Author:** Dr. Ines Varga, Researcher (Level 2), Site-117

**Special Containment Procedures:** None could be agreed upon. I was instructed to log each note within one hour of discovery and surrender it to Dr. Achterberg for analysis. I complied every time. I want that on record.

**Description:**

I found the first note on 3 March, tucked beneath my keyboard. It was written on standard Foundation memo paper, the 4x6 tear-off pads with the faint three-arrow watermark and form code F-11 in the lower corner. It was in my handwriting. My slant. My crossed sevens.

> *Ines. Cell 4 opens on the 19th. Not a fault. Someone lets it out. Don't trust the day.*

Cell 4 held SCP-6814, a gaunt humanoid entity I had interviewed eleven times. It never said anything beyond a single question at the start of every session: *What day is it?* Protocol forbade answering. I never had.

I reported the note. Cell 4 was audited and found secure. Graphology returned a match "with high confidence," which was what they said when they'd rather not commit.

The second note arrived on the 6th, on my pillow.

> *They will say you wrote these. You didn't. I didn't. Check the ink.*

We checked. The pigment matched a supplier batch not scheduled for delivery until late April.

That was when the Foundation stopped treating me as a curiosity and started treating me as a location. Two hypotheses were opened. Hypothesis A held that the notes were genuine retrocausal communications from a future version of me. Hypothesis B held that SCP-6814 had established some influence during our interviews, and that I was writing the notes myself in a dissociative state. Under B, the "future ink" was either a lab error or my perception of one.

I was asked which I believed. I said A. Then I lay awake and believed B.

On the 8th I gathered every memo pad in my quarters, all four of them. I counted the sheets and locked the pads in my safe. The next morning a note lay on my desk.

> *Paper doesn't matter. Paper was never the door.*

Its torn edge matched the top stub of the third pad in my safe. The pad was one sheet short. The safe's log showed no access.

Security removed every F-11 pad from my wing and sealed them in an evidence locker across the Site. Two days later:

> *Halvorsen is dead. You liked him. Stay out of Wing D.*

Site-117 had no Wing D. There was no Halvorsen in the personnel database, at this Site or any other I could query. The note's torn edge matched a pad inside the sealed locker.

A camera was installed in my quarters. On the night of the 12th, the footage showed me asleep from 23:04. At 03:11 there was a single frame in which I was sitting at my desk with a pen in my hand. In the next frame I was asleep again. The timestamps were continuous. Technical Services called it a compression artifact. Dr. Achterberg showed me the frame without comment and watched my face while I looked at it.

I didn't remember sitting up. But I didn't remember *not* sitting up either. I discovered that this was a distinction I had never needed to make before.

> *Teo keeps asking where you are. I said work. Is it a lie if you*

I had no one named Teo.

> *The sky over the Site was green for three days and nobody wrote it down except us. You remember. Please say you remember.*

I began keeping my own log of everything I could verify. The number of stairs between my quarters and the commissary was forty-one. I wrote down my sister's birthday. I recorded the colour of the sky each morning and then photographed it, because I no longer trusted the recording. The worst part was not that I didn't remember a green sky. It was that, when I tried, I almost could.

Dr. Achterberg proposed Class-B amnestics. Ethics vetoed it under Hypothesis A: if the notes were real, erasing my memory of them might be the very thing that caused the breach. Under Hypothesis B, erasure might simply hand 6814 a cleaner page. Nobody could tell me which was worse.

On the 14th, Dr. Achterberg interviewed SCP-6814 in my place. It asked him what day it was. He didn't answer. Then, for the first time in its file, it said something else.

"Tell her she already did."

> *it asked me the day and I TOLD it, I'm sorry, it had been so quiet for so long and I only wanted someone to know what day it was*

> *there were never two of us there were never two of us there were never*

> *F-11 F-11 they took the paper and it is still the paper*

The last note came on the 16th. The handwriting was mine, but younger. It was the rounded hand I'd had at fourteen, before I learned to slant.

> *Don't go in on the 19th. Or go in. I can't remember which one fixes it. I've tried both.*

Then nothing.

I was relieved of Cell 4 access and confined to quarters through the 20th. Chronometric surveys found no temporal signature anywhere on Site. My influence screening for 6814 came back clean. Both hypotheses remained open. I suspected they always would.

I wrote this account on the night of the 18th, at Dr. Achterberg's request, so there would be a record in my own words before the date passed.

He had come by an hour earlier for a routine orientation check: name, location, date. I gave him my name. I gave him the Site. Then he asked me what day it was, and I opened my mouth and found I could not make myself say it. It wasn't that I didn't know.

It was that something might have been listening for the answer.

He wrote down *Subject declined to answer.* I let him.

When I finished typing, I checked the room again. The pads were gone. The safe was empty. My pen was the only one in my quarters.

There was a sheet of memo paper under my left hand. It was blank.

I had not yet decided what to write on it.

Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception.

First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense.

Ink analysis reveals trace elements not matching any office pen. Length: 1000 words.
response:
**Item #:** SCP-7140
**Object Class:** Euclid (pending review)

**Special Containment Procedures:** All documents in handwriting attributable to Dr. Ilse Varga that Dr. Varga does not recall producing are to be photographed and sealed in Locker 7140-A. Dr. Varga is barred from Containment Wing C, which houses SCP-3318. Her quarters are under continuous video surveillance.

**Description:** SCP-7140 is a series of handwritten notes recovered from 2 March onward. Dr. Varga wrote the following account at the Site Director's request.

---

The first note was in my coat pocket on the morning of the 2nd, folded into quarters. I assumed it was a reminder I'd written and forgotten. It was certainly my handwriting: the hooked *t*, the dot over the *i* drifting right.

> *Ilse. Cell 9 fails on the 14th, 03:12. Eastern drain seal. Make Okafor check it. You keep Mama's ring in the toe of your left boot, so you know this is me. Please. You know I don't say please.*

I did keep my mother's ring there. I had never told anyone.

I brought the note to the Site Director within the hour. I want that on the record. Graphology confirmed the hand as mine, down to pen pressure. Dr. Okafor inspected Cell 9's eastern drain and found a hairline fracture in the seal housing. Maintenance logs suggested it predated 2019. It was repaired. Everyone was very calm.

Dr. Halloran's ink analysis was not calm. The base was iron gall, which no pen on Site uses, and it carried two trace signatures that matched nothing in any office supply on file. The first was human hemoglobin, type B negative. Mine. The second was a tantalum-hafnium laminate made for the lining of Cell 9 and installed nowhere else on Earth.

Cell 9 holds SCP-3318. I have been its lead researcher for six years. It is humanoid, seated, and has not moved since 1994. Its one documented property is that personnel exposed to it long enough begin remembering conversations with it that never took place.

So there were two hypotheses. Either the notes came from me, some later me, or SCP-3318 had found a way to make me write them and forget. Temporal Anomalies favored the first. Psychology favored the second. I wanted, very badly, for someone to tell me which one I was.

The second note was under my pillow on the 5th.

> *they fixed the drain didnt they. it was never the drain. its YOU. you walk in at 3:10 and open it because it asks in mamas voice and you were so tired*

The cameras went in that night. On the 7th, the footage showed me rising at 02:40, sitting at my desk, and writing for nine minutes. I have no memory of it. Psychology considered the matter largely settled.

Then Halloran slowed the footage down. There was no pen in my hand. I was dragging my index finger across the paper, and the ink was appearing a fraction of a second *before* my fingertip reached each point. It was as if I wasn't writing at all, but tracing something being written from the other side.

That note said only: *dont let them watch. it sees through anything that watches.*

Temporal Anomalies proposed a test. Dr. Raines prepared two hundred sealed envelopes, one word in each, and logged the list. On the 12th I would draw one at random. If a future me existed, she would remember the word.

The note I found on the 10th, two days early, said LANTERN sixty-one times, front and back.

Raines swore no envelope held that word. On the 12th I drew envelope 117. It said LANTERN. Raines's list, in his own hand, said LANTERN at 117. He looked at it for a long time, then asked to be excused.

I need to explain what that did to me, because it matters more than the ink. Until then the problem had been my memory. After that, it was everyone's.

The notes that followed stopped making sense in any way I could forgive.

> *tell Daniel im sorry about the boat. it wasnt his fault*

I do not know a Daniel.

> *Okafors funeral was so small. why did they hold it in the gymnasium*

I had coffee with Okafor that morning. Afterward, in the corridor, I touched his arm to be sure he was real. He let me.

> *the sky over the yard went white and STAYED white. 43 was never underground. who put it underground*

Site-43 has always been underground. I have pulled the 1971 construction records twice. I am aware that a witness who needs to check twice is not a reliable one.

This is the part I was asked to describe honestly. There are three of me in this account: the one who finds the notes, the one who writes them in her sleep, and the one who may be writing them from a 14th that has already happened somewhere. I cannot prove which I am. The one holding this pen believes she is the first. That belief is exactly what SCP-3318 would want her to have. It is also exactly what a future me, trying to save her, would need her to keep.

Either my future has already broken or my present is being edited. I can't tell from in here. I'm no longer sure anyone can.

I have been moved to Site-19, four hundred kilometres from Cell 9. It is the 13th, 23:50. There are two guards outside my door, and I have asked them to cover the camera.

Twenty minutes ago I found the eleventh note tucked inside this report, between pages I had already written. The ink was still wet.

> *good. youre far away. but it was never about distance. read the first one again. the ring isnt in the boot anymore Ilse. where did you put it*

I have just checked. The ring is not in the boot.

I do not remember moving it.

---

**Addendum 7140-1:** At 03:12 on 14 March, Cell 9 was confirmed sealed and intact. For the first time since 1994, SCP-3318 was observed to have changed position. Its right hand was closed.

Dr. Varga was found asleep at her desk at Site-19. Beneath her hand was a twelfth note. It was blank.

Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception.

First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense.

Security cameras glitch exactly at the moment new notes appear on the desk. Length: 1000 words.
response:
# SCP-XXXX: "Green Ink"

**Item #:** SCP-XXXX

**Object Class:** Euclid (provisional)

**Special Containment Procedures:** Pending. At the Ethics Committee's direction, this file was written by the affected researcher. I was told this would be therapeutic. I was also told it would be evidence. I have tried to write it as both.

---

**Description:**

The first note appeared on 14 March at 02:13, in my office on Sublevel 3 of Site-41. I know the exact time because the ceiling camera lost its feed for eleven frames, just under half a second. When the image returned, a folded square of paper was resting on my keyboard.

I was in the chair. I was looking at the keyboard. I did not see it arrive.

> *Don't let them move the Lantern on Thursday. Cell 9's seal fails at 04:40. You'll know it's me because you hate green pens.*

It was my handwriting: the leftward slant, the crossed sevens I picked up in Zurich. It was written in green ink. I do hate green pens. I have never told anyone that, because it isn't the kind of thing a person tells anyone.

No transfer was scheduled for SCP-████, the Lantern. I checked, and I filed a report anyway. On Wednesday afternoon, Logistics scheduled the transfer for Thursday.

I flagged it. Director Amsel postponed it. Thursday passed, the Cell 9 seal held, and nothing happened. That is the trouble with prevention: from the inside, it looks exactly like being wrong.

The second note came nine days later. Eleven frames. Green ink.

> *Thank you. Not enough. It was never the Lantern, it's what listens when we decide. Ask Priya about the east stairwell.*

Site-41 has no east stairwell. I don't know anyone named Priya. Records eventually turned up a Dr. Priya Desai, who was offered a post here in 2021 and declined it. I think about her more than I'd like: a woman I've never met, known well to someone who is supposedly me.

---

**Investigation:**

The Foundation pursued two hypotheses. I'll set them down fairly, because I have spent months unable to choose between them.

*Hypothesis A: Temporal.* Forensics matched the handwriting to mine at 99.6% confidence. The paper was Foundation stock, but its watermark batch number, 4471-C, had not yet been issued. Procurement confirmed that it would be, in roughly three years.

*Hypothesis B: Manipulation.* The Lantern is documented to induce what its file calls "anticipatory compliance." It seeds dread, then lets staff act on it. Its cell is forty meters from my office. Dr. Okonkwo, who ran my psych evaluations, put it gently: "Mara, has it occurred to you that the cameras might glitch because *you* do?"

Eleven frames is enough time to reach into a drawer. In my experience, it isn't enough time to write a paragraph. But I no longer trust my experience to be the judge of anything.

They tested both hypotheses. They sealed me in a bare observation room with two guards and no pens. At 03:51 the camera dropped eleven frames, and the note was on the table. Under polygraph, both guards swore it had been there when we walked in. Their bodycams showed an empty table right up until the same eleven-frame dropout.

> *They're going to give you the amnestic on the 2nd. Please don't. You forgot last time and I had to start over and I'm running out of paper.*

I took the amnestic on the 2nd. I don't remember the week before it, but the notes did. They referenced conversations I had lost and promises I had apparently made. One of them was apologetic in a way that frightened me more than any of the warnings.

---

**Escalation:**

Over the following months the notes deteriorated. The handwriting tightened, then sprawled. Some were still coherent:

> *How many of us are there. I find notes too. Mine aren't in our handwriting.*

Some contradicted things I know to be true:

> *Tell Mom the house on Kell Street is safe now. Tell her I'm sorry about the dog.*

My mother died in 2009. We never lived on Kell Street. We never had a dog.

> *Lila asked where you went. I told her work. Was that right*

I don't have a daughter. I've never wanted one, or I don't think I have. I lay awake that night trying to remember whether I ever had.

> *stop LOOKING at the Lantern it uses your looking it uses MY looking we keep deciding and every time we decide the seal*

> *04:40 04:40 04:40 04:40 04:40*

That number filled five sheets, front and back. Another note held a hand-drawn floor plan of Sublevel 3 with a corridor that does not exist. It was labeled, in my writing, *the way out.*

---

**On Perception:**

In June I started a control journal. Each night I wrote a single word in blue ballpoint and initialed it, so I would have a baseline of my present self to compare against. On 19 August I opened it and found an entry for the 18th that I don't remember writing. Blue ink. My initials. The word was *sorry.*

That was when I stopped believing I could solve this from the inside. Every test assumed a stable observer, and I wasn't one. If the Lantern was writing these notes, it was using my hand. If I was writing them, some part of me knew things that Procurement didn't. And if they were coming back from a future, it wasn't one future. It was many: one where I had a daughter, one where the house on Kell Street existed, one where Priya Desai took the job. Each note I obeyed bent things a little further from wherever the last one came from.

I've come to think the notes aren't warning me about a breach. I think they *are* the breach, a seal between versions of me that cracks wider every time one of us reaches back. That is what "listens when we decide."

It is also exactly what the Lantern would want me to believe. I can no longer tell those two possibilities apart, and I'm told the procedures for this file depend on which one I choose.

---

**Conclusion:**

My recommendation is that no researcher should act on any note, regardless of its content or handwriting. That includes mine.

Last week I found a green pen in my coat pocket. I didn't buy it. This morning I put it in the evidence locker.

As I closed the drawer, the camera dropped eleven frames.

There is a folded square of paper on my desk. I have not opened it. I'm not going to.

It is 04:39.

Write an SCP entry about a series of identical unmarked doors appearing in abandoned buildings worldwide that lead to a massive, architecturally impossible archive. Documents within reference a previous global civilization destroyed by an unspecified containment failure. Foundation researchers discover references to their own organization under a different name, including personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago. Include exploration logs revealing sections of the archive actively being removed by entities resembling hazmat teams who flee when approached, and evidence that O5 Council members have visited the archive without authorization.

All unmarked doors share identical scratches around the doorknob area. Length: 1000 words.
response:
# SCP-7140: "The Lending Library"

**Item #:** SCP-7140

**Object Class:** Keter

**Special Containment Procedures:** Known instances of SCP-7140 (currently 41) are to be sealed with welded plate and kept under remote observation. New instances can be identified by the scratch pattern described below. Personnel named in Appendix 7140-C are barred from exploration.

This restriction was put in place after Exploration 7140-04.

**Description:** SCP-7140 is a recurring phenomenon of identical doors appearing in abandoned structures. Confirmed sites include a shuttered textile mill in Łódź, a flooded hospital wing in Manaus, and a parking structure in Osaka slated for demolition. Each door measures 203 × 81 cm, is painted steel-grey and is fitted with an unmarked brass knob. No hinges are visible from either side.

Every instance bears the same scratches around the knob escutcheon: seventeen fine, shallow arcs running clockwise, identical to the micrometer. Tool-mark analysis suggests a thin metal band on the left hand of someone turning the knob quickly and repeatedly, without looking.

All instances open onto a single space, designated SCP-7140-1. It is an archive of indeterminate size. Shelving rises beyond the reach of flashlight beams. Staircases that descend arrive at the floor above. A corridor measured at 40 meters takes nine minutes to walk. The archive has no visible light source, yet it is lit, and it smells of dust and cold paper.

---

**Exploration Log 7140-02**

*Team: Dr. Adaeze Okonkwo (lead), Agent R. Pell, Agent D. Marrow, Junior Researcher T. Lisk.*

The team entered through the Łódź instance. Lisk noted that the door was warm on the archive side, as though a hand had only just left it.

The shelf labels were written in an unknown script, later designated Archival Theta. Partial translation became possible after Okonkwo found a primer: a child's alphabet book illustrated with shelves, locks, and a recurring symbol of three concentric rings bisected by a vertical line.

Lisk said it looked "like ours, but someone took the arrows out." Okonkwo photographed it without comment.

> **Recovered Document 7140-D-11** *(bound ledger, translated)*
> *Charter of the Custodial Assembly. We HOLD what must not be loosed. We KEEP what must not be known. We SHELTER the many from the few things that would end them. The Assembly answers to the Thirteen and to no other.*

> **Recovered Document 7140-D-19** *(loose sheet, ink smeared)*
> *Item One is not in its cell. Every site reports the same. There is no procedure written for this because we did not believe we would need one. The Thirteen have gone to the archive. We do not know why the archive. Light is failing in the east.*

---

**Exploration Log 7140-04**

*Same team. Entry via the Manaus instance.*

In an alcove labeled "Personnel — Active," Marrow pulled a folder at random and stopped speaking mid-sentence. He handed it to Pell without a word.

It was Agent Rowan Pell's service record. The photograph matched him in every detail, down to a scar Pell received in 2014. By Theta reckoning, the file dated to roughly 1580 CE.

The team found thirty-one more files matching current Foundation staff. Okonkwo found her own last.

> **Recovered Document 7140-D-40** *(personnel file, translated)*
> *Custodian-Researcher A. OKONKWO. Entered service: Year 211 of the Assembly. Left-handed. Wears a plain ring; do not ask her to remove it. She will ask what Item One was. Do not tell her. She will ask how she knows the corridors. Do not tell her. Note: this is her seventeenth file.*

Okonkwo read it twice, closed it, and returned it to the shelf. Lisk asked whether she wanted it logged. She said, "It's already logged."

---

**Exploration Log 7140-05**

*Entry via the Osaka instance.*

Okonkwo insisted on leading despite the new restriction. The O5 Council approved her request within four minutes, which is unusual.

Forty minutes in, the team heard movement. Past the next shelf they found six figures in pale grey full-body suits with opaque visors, working in silence. They were emptying an entire stack, perhaps two thousand volumes, into unmarked crates. Three stacks beyond them already stood bare.

Pell called out. The figures froze, then fled together, leaving the crates behind. Marrow chased them to a door identical to the external instances and reached it just as it shut. He reported hearing the knob turn on the other side several times in quick succession, "like someone whose hands were shaking."

One of the figures had dropped an index card.

> **Recovered Document 7140-D-52**
> *Section 9 cleared. Section 10 by morning. Leave nothing they can use to start over the same way. Leave the charter. Leave the files. They need to know who they are.*

Lisk asked who "they" were. No one answered.

Beside the bare stacks stood a reading desk with a sign-in ledger. The most recent entries were in Latin script, signed "O5-3," "O5-7," and "O5-11," and dated between 1998 and last month. None matched any authorized entry. The final signature, O5-7, was undated. A Foundation-issue fountain pen lay uncapped across the page, and the ink was still wet.

Paging backward, Okonkwo found older entries in Theta script. Translated, the signatures read *Third of the Thirteen* and *Seventh of the Thirteen*. The handwriting matched the modern entries stroke for stroke.

On the way out, the team passed the alcove where Okonkwo's file had been shelved. The file was gone.

At the exit door, Okonkwo raised her left hand to the knob without being asked. Pell's helmet camera recorded her ring settling into the uppermost scratch as though the groove had been cut for it.

She turned the knob quickly, without looking, and stepped through.

---

**Addendum 7140-1:** Twenty minutes after the team returned, remote observation confirmed that all 41 known instances of SCP-7140 now bear eighteen arcs.

**Addendum 7140-2:** Dr. Okonkwo submitted a formal request asking the O5 Council to disclose the nature of "Item One." The Council's response, in full:

> *Denied. You asked last time as well. Keep the ring on.*

# SCP-6417: "The Shelving"

**Item #:** SCP-6417

**Object Class:** Keter

**Special Containment Procedures:** All known instances of SCP-6417-A are to be enclosed in secured structures disguised as demolition hoardings. Municipal records for affected properties are to be amended to stall redevelopment indefinitely.

Exploration of SCP-6417-B is suspended pending Ethics Committee review. The O5 Council has been recused from oversight of this file (see Addendum 6417.4).

**Description:** SCP-6417-A designates 214 identical doors found in abandoned structures across 41 countries. Each is a single panel of unidentified hardwood, 2.1 meters tall, with a brass lever handle. None has markings, numbering, or a keyhole. Instances occur only in buildings that have been unoccupied for six years or longer.

Many instances are older than the walls that hold them. The door in a Łódź textile mill, built in 1896, shows surface erosion consistent with nine centuries of exposure. Dendrochronology on three instances returned ring patterns that match no climatic record on file, from any era.

Every instance opens onto SCP-6417-B. In one test, teams entered at the same moment through the Tokyo and Montevideo instances. They met inside within forty minutes.

SCP-6417-B is an archive of indeterminate extent. Its shelving reaches forty meters high, and its aisles have been surveyed past forty kilometers without reaching a wall. Temperature holds at 16°C and humidity at 45%. These are ideal preservation conditions, and no system can be found that maintains them.

The archive's contents were produced by an organization that called itself "the Fold." Its emblem is three inward-facing arrows within a circle, with the circle broken at its lowest point. Its motto is embossed on most bindings: *Keep. Hold. Shelter.*

---

**EXPLORATION LOG 6417-B-02**

**Team:** Dr. Ilse Marchetti (lead), Agent Tomás Rehder, Researcher Abena Owusu-Hale
**Entry:** Detroit instance

The team followed the primary aisle, designated Aisle Zero, for 2.3 kilometers before reaching labeled shelving. Owusu-Hale observed that the documents were written in dozens of languages, most still spoken today. It was as if the archivists had expected not to know who would read them.

Marchetti recovered the following from a binder marked HOLDINGS 4400–4499:

> **HOLDING 4471**
> **Status:** Kept.
> **Disposition:** Hold in a sealed room with no reflective surfaces. Rotate wardens every ninth day.
> **Note:** Wardens are reminded not to address 4471 by name. It has begun to answer.

Rehder noted that the procedure was functionally identical to the one used for an object currently held at Site-77. Marchetti instructed him not to say which object.

>

>
> There was no breach. We have inspected every seal, every ward, every door. Each held. We have come to understand that the separation was never ours to maintain. We were only permitted to believe it was.
>

**EXPLORATION LOG 6417-B-04**

**Team:** As above
**Entry:** Łódź instance

The team located a personnel wing near Aisle 3,118. The files were bound in vellum and indexed by name.

Rehder found a file under his own name, spelled *Tomas Reder*. It was dated *Year 311 of the Keeping*, and radiocarbon analysis later placed the vellum at roughly 600 years old. Inside was a silverpoint likeness of Rehder. It even showed the scar along his left jaw from a 2019 training accident. The file listed his postings in the correct order through his current assignment, then continued for three more entries. Rehder read them silently and declined to share what they said. He has since requested a transfer.

Marchetti identified files for thirty-one current Foundation personnel, her own among them. Each file was cross-referenced to an equivalent post within the Fold. Hers ended with a single line: *Reassigned to Shelving.*

At 14:20, the team heard wheels on stone. Two aisles over, four figures in sealed ochre suits were lifting files from the shelves into crates and loading them onto carts. The broken-circle emblem was printed across their chests, and their visors were opaque.

The figures had left one crate behind. It held the personnel files of nine Foundation staff members. Seven of them were on the team's planning roster for Exploration 05.

---

**EXPLORATION LOG 6417-B-05**

**Team:** Dr. Ilse Marchetti, Researcher Abena Owusu-Hale
**Entry:** Detroit instance

Aisle 3,118 was empty. Only outlines in the dust showed where the files had stood. The cleared area now covered eleven aisles. Throughout the visit, the team could hear carts moving in the distance, never in sight.

Near the entrance to Aisle Zero, Owusu-Hale found a small reading room. It held a writing desk and an open visitor's ledger. Most of the ledger was written in Fold script, but the final forty pages were in modern ballpoint ink.

The column headed *Purpose of Visit* reads: *Reconciliation. Reconciliation. Confirming counts. Reconciliation.*

> *Removal on schedule. They have found the Personnel wing. Accelerate.*

---

Dr. Marchetti submitted a formal inquiry to the O5 Council about the ledger. A reply arrived forty minutes later:

> *Exploration is suspended. All recovered materials are to be surrendered to O5 couriers.*
>
> *The Council acknowledges the ledger. The Council does not regard its visits as unauthorized. The Council regards them as maintenance.*
>
> *Dr. Marchetti is thanked for her thoroughness. It was anticipated.*

On 2026-09-14, a new instance of SCP-6417-A was discovered in the East Wing of Site-19. The wing has been vacant since it was decommissioned in 2020.

Write an SCP entry about a series of identical unmarked doors appearing in abandoned buildings worldwide that lead to a massive, architecturally impossible archive. Documents within reference a previous global civilization destroyed by an unspecified containment failure. Foundation researchers discover references to their own organization under a different name, including personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago. Include exploration logs revealing sections of the archive actively being removed by entities resembling hazmat teams who flee when approached, and evidence that O5 Council members have visited the archive without authorization.

# SCP-7391: "The Successor Custody"

**Item #:** SCP-7391

**Object Class:** Keter

**Special Containment Procedures:** Mobile Task Force Lambda-12 ("Night Watchmen") conducts nightly sweeps of abandoned structures in monitored regions. Sweeps are performed with all lights extinguished, because SCP-7391 instances can only be identified by the faint glow escaping along their edges. Each located instance is sealed behind a poured concrete partition and logged.

Entry into SCP-7391-1 is suspended indefinitely. See Addendum 7391-C.

**Description:** SCP-7391 is a recurring set of identical doors that appear inside buildings left uninhabited for at least eleven years. Each instance is 2.1 meters tall, painted a flat institutional green, and fitted with an unmarked brass handle worn smooth at the grip. No two instances differ by more than 0.2 millimeters in any dimension. This includes the wear pattern. To date, 214 instances have been documented across 37 countries.

In complete darkness, a pale amber light is visible around each door's frame, similar to a reading lamp seen through paper. The light has no detectable source and does not register on photometric equipment.

All instances open onto the same space, SCP-7391-1: an archive of indeterminate size. Shelving rises beyond the reach of any available illumination, and corridors have been observed to intersect themselves. One staircase has been descended for nineteen hours without reaching a landing. It has been ascended in four minutes.

The holdings are written primarily in a script designated Ledger Hand. A bilingual index allowed partial translation. The documents describe an organization called the Office of Abeyance, which existed to hold anomalous objects and phenomena in custody. Its insignia appears on most files: a circle crossed by three arrows pointing *outward*.

---

**Recovered Document 7391-A** (inscription above the Reading Room, Ring Four; translated):

> The Office holds what must not be loose. The Office keeps what must not be known. The Office endures so that the world need not.

**Recovered Document 7391-B** (final entry in a bound register; translated):

> Ring Nine reports breach. Ring Eight reports breach. Ring Seven does not report. The cause is known to the Directorate and will not be written here, for writing it was how it began. All personnel are to bring their files to the Archive. What survives here will be found. What is found will be repeated.

---

**Exploration Log 7391-4**

*Team: Dr. Ilse Varga (lead), Agents Okonkwo, Brandt, Sato.*

The team entered through the instance in a defunct textile mill in Łódź. As Okonkwo touched the handle, the amber glow at the door's edges brightened briefly. Varga later described it as "like something had noticed."

Three hours in, Sato found a section indexed under a term the key rendered as *Successor Custody*. The files were arranged by surname. Brandt pulled one at random and read the heading aloud: *Agent Tomasz Brandt, Clearance Level 2.* The intake date, converted from the Office's calendar, corresponded to approximately 1640 CE.

The photograph was Brandt. It showed the scar along his jaw, which he received during a containment breach at Site-19 in 2017.

Varga ordered the section recorded but left undisturbed. Before the team withdrew, Sato found a file bearing Varga's name. Varga did not open it. Sato noted that it was thicker than the others.

---

**Recovered Document 7391-C** (excerpt from the file of Dr. Ilse Varga; translated, recovered during Exploration 6):

> Subject demonstrates persistence in excess of instruction. Recommend she be permitted to reach the Archive. She will reach it regardless. Note for the record: this is the fourth time she has been assigned to this file.

---

**Exploration Log 7391-6**

*Team: Varga, Okonkwo, Sato. (Brandt declined to return.)*

At hour two, the team heard movement in Ring Three, and Varga ordered all lights extinguished. Through the stacks, the team saw six figures in sealed protective suits. The suits were pale yellow and the faceplates were opaque. The figures were pulling files from the shelves and packing them into gray crates, working with practiced efficiency. Each suit bore the Office insignia on the left shoulder, arrows pointing outward.

Okonkwo called out to them. The figures stopped and turned toward the sound in unison. Then they fled. They did not run. They walked quickly and without apparent effort into a corridor that the team's later survey showed did not exist.

They left one crate behind. It held files from *Successor Custody*, each stamped with a Ledger Hand word the key translated as *Withdrawn*. Every file belonged to a current Foundation staff member.

When the team checked the shelf where Varga's file had been, they found it empty.

---

**Exploration Log 7391-9**

*Team: Varga, Okonkwo.*

The team reached the Reading Room in Ring Four. A sign-in ledger lay open on the attendant's desk. Its most recent pages were not in Ledger Hand. They were written in English, in ballpoint, using Foundation-standard format.

There were seven entries spanning fourteen months, signed with designations only: O5-2, O5-7, O5-11, O5-7, O5-4, O5-7, O5-7. No Foundation record authorizes any of these visits. The *Materials Requested* field was identical in every entry: *Ring Nine, Directorate, cause of breach.* The *Materials Returned* field was blank in every entry.

While Okonkwo photographed the ledger, Varga saw the Reading Room lamps begin to dim one section at a time, starting at the far end of the hall and moving toward the team. Six yellow figures stood in the doorway the team had come through.

This time they did not flee. One of them raised a gloved hand and pointed at the ledger, then at Varga, then at the door.

The team withdrew. The figures did not follow.

---

**Addendum 7391-C:** Analysts reviewing Okonkwo's photographs found one more entry on the ledger's facing page. Neither team member recalls seeing it. The handwriting matches Dr. Varga's:

> *Varga, I. Materials Requested: Ring Nine, Directorate, cause of breach. Materials Returned: None. Note: I'm sorry. It was the only way to know.*

The entry is dated eleven days after Exploration 9.

On the night of Exploration 9, Dr. Varga disappeared from her quarters. Eleven days later, on the date written in the ledger, she was found in the Łódź mill. She was sitting in front of the sealed concrete partition, through which the glow of the instance was faintly visible. She has no memory of the intervening period.

She has spoken only once since. She asked that the O5 Council be told she "understands now."

The Council has acknowledged receipt.

All exploration is suspended.

# The Azra Gambit

## Chapter Four: A Matter of Property

The transfer vessel's air filtration system hummed with a persistent mechanical drone. It was the sort of sound a man stops hearing after the first hour and then, for no reason at all, cannot stop hearing again.

Arthur Neegan had reached the second stage some time ago. Through the porthole beside his couch, Mars was becoming something one looked at rather than stood on. He could see rust plains and the pale gash of the Valles. Along the night side, like spilled embers, lay the lights of the mining camps. Somewhere among them sat a prefab dome with a coffee cup going cold beside a slide rule.

They had come at breakfast: four men in charcoal uniforms, each collar bearing a red star inside an open ring. That was the Antares Diplomatic Corps. In the camp bars it was said the Corps was diplomatic the way a crowbar is a key.

Their lieutenant had removed his cap. "Mr. Neegan. You are invited to a meeting."

"With whom?"

"With the person who invited you."

"And if I decline?"

The lieutenant had looked genuinely pained. "Then I should be very sorry, sir. And you would still be invited."

A mining engineer learned to calculate load, stress and fracture. Arthur had never before felt so much like the rock.

---

The vessel docked at Deimos with a clank he felt in his teeth. He was led down a corridor of ribbed aluminum and amber indicator lamps, past a teletype chattering behind glass. Then came a stateroom so out of place it might have been lifted whole from a gentlemen's club on Earth. It had oak paneling, a brass lamp and a long curved viewport filled entirely with Mars.

A small, elderly man rose from a leather chair. He had mild grey eyes and the air of someone who had outlived most of his opponents through patience alone.

"Mr. Neegan. Please, sit. Lieutenant Haskell has instructions to be courteous, and he interprets them as most men interpret scripture: respectfully, and loosely."

"Your men wear the Antares star."

"They do. It would be a poor insignia otherwise."

"Is that who you are?"

"It is who has agreed to be responsible for me. That's not quite the same thing." He poured two glasses of something amber. "You may call me Mr. Vell. It isn't my name, but it's pleasant to say."

Arthur left the glass untouched. "What do you want?"

"Straight to it. Good." Vell settled back. "In the eleven years since Halvorsen first isolated Azra, humanity has refined four hundred and twelve kilograms of it. That's every lab, every foundry, every warship. Your core samples suggest your hillside holds something like ninety tonnes."

"Those cores were sealed."

"Yes. A seal is a kind of promise, and promises change hands every day on Mars." He said it without malice, the way one remarks on weather. "At present, the Terran Hegemony holds a little over half the world's Azra, and the Outer Combine holds the rest. That balance is the only reason no one has yet tested a decay-warhead on a city. Ninety tonnes tips it, whichever way it falls."

"So you want to buy my claim."

"I want to buy it and then do absolutely nothing with it." Vell smiled at Arthur's expression. "Certain parties, whom I won't name, have concluded that the safest place for that much Azra is under three hundred metres of basalt, owned by a man who does not dig. You'd keep title. The Corps would extend diplomatic protection, and your plot would become Antarean soil. You would be paid, very generously, to be a lock."

"And when someone comes to pick the lock?"

"Then you'll find Haskell is better at his work than at his manners." Vell turned his glass slowly. "Consolidated Ores has leased four hundred labourers for a 'regional survey' along your boundary. Survey crews rarely need blasting licences. And your neighbour, Mr. Okafor, sold last week. Has he answered his visiphone since?"

Arthur said nothing. Beyond the viewport, a dust storm the size of a continent crawled across Hellas like a slow brown thought.

"If I refuse?"

"Then you go home. I'm not a kidnapper, Mr. Neegan. But within a month you'll receive a better offer from someone less patient than I am. After that, someone will stop offering."

"And if I accept, I'm a target for everyone you're keeping out."

"You're a target now. I'm offering you a wall to stand behind."

"A wall with a door," Arthur said, "and you holding the key."

"All walls have doors. It's what distinguishes them from tombs." Vell set down his glass. "One more thing. I mention it only because you're an engineer and would notice eventually. Halvorsen's last notes, written before his accident, observed that Azra deposits are too regular. Ore doesn't grow in lattices." He shrugged lightly. "The physicists say Azra hastens decay. None can say why. A substance that changes the rate at which the universe ends things makes one wonder what else it changes."

Arthur studied him for a long moment. "Why not simply take the claim? You obviously could."

"Because a claim seized by force is an act of war, Mr. Neegan, and a claim purchased from a free citizen is a property dispute." The mild eyes held his. "My employers and I are working very hard to keep this a property dispute."

---

On the return voyage, the filtration system resumed its drone. Arthur watched the camp lights rise to meet him. There were thousands of them, each one a leased man in a leased bunk. He wondered how many of those men had once sat in a comfortable chair and been made a reasonable offer.

# The Azra Gambit

## Chapter Seven: The Courtesy of Antares

The transfer vessel had been built for people more important than Arthur Neegan, and it took every opportunity to remind him.

The seats were upholstered in something very nearly leather. The bulkheads wore panels of pale synthetic walnut, from a tree no Martian had ever seen grow. Beyond the viewport, Mars dwindled into rust and shadow. The great gash of the Mariner Valley shrank to a crack in old pottery. Arthur had spent eleven years with his nose in that dust, and he found he could not watch it for long.

He tugged at his collar. It was high and stiff, and it fastened with a clasp evidently designed by someone who resented necks.

"It is customary," said the officer opposite, "to leave it alone."

She was the senior of the four who had appeared at his airlock that morning. They had been unfailingly courteous. They had wiped their boots. They had also worn sidearms, and on each grey shoulder gleamed the eight-pointed star of the Antares Diplomatic Corps. Every miner on Mars knew the Corps was diplomatic in roughly the sense that a crowbar is a key.

"I'd leave it alone if it returned the favour," Arthur said. "Who am I meeting?"

"Someone who wishes to speak with you."

"This month, that's everyone in the system."

It was true. The assay had come back six weeks ago. Since then his little pressure-dome had received three corporate surveyors and a Consortium attorney. A man from the Terran Mineral Office had asked a great many questions and answered none. And someone had slipped a single folded note beneath his door, unsigned: *Do not sell to the first buyer.*

The officer permitted herself a small smile and said nothing at all.

---

The ship that swallowed the shuttle was enormous and silent, and it showed no name. Arthur was led down a corridor lit by amber globes into a room that had no business existing in orbit. It was a study, book-lined, with a desk of genuine oak and a broad window full of stars. A brass orrery ticked on a side table, its little Mars dragging a speck of a moon.

The man behind the desk was old and lean. His clothes were so plain they must have cost a fortune, and he wore no insignia whatever.

"Mr. Neegan. Sit, please. You may call me Orr. It isn't my name, but it is short, and we have a good deal to discuss."

Arthur sat. "Are you Antares?"

"I am Antares the way a passenger is the ship. The Corps has many vessels and a flexible conscience, and it rents out both." Orr poured two glasses of something amber. "You may touch your collar, by the way. Formality is chiefly useful for learning who will obey it. I've learned."

Arthur loosened the clasp with undisguised relief. "Then you'll forgive me if I skip ahead. What do you want?"

"First, to ask what you know about Azra."

"I know what it does. Bring it near a fissile mass and the half-life collapses. Uranium that ought to take four billion years to decay does it in an afternoon. A kilo of Azra in a drive lattice gets you to Centauri. A kilo in a casing gets you a crater the size of a city."

"Admirably concise. And do you know what it *is*?"

Arthur hesitated. "No. Nobody does."

"Nobody does." Orr turned his glass, watching the starlight move in it. "It has been eleven years since the first sample came out of the Hellas pits. The finest physicists on Earth still cannot tell us *why* it works. We are building starships and bombs on a principle we do not understand. Historically, Mr. Neegan, that is the moment just before something goes badly wrong."

"You didn't bring me up here for a physics lecture."

"No. A history lecture. Shorter, I promise." He gestured at the orrery. "Bronze made the first empires. Coal made the next. Then oil, then uranium. Each time, a single substance arrived at a single moment and rearranged the map. But never before has the whole of it sat beneath one man's potato patch."

Arthur said nothing. Somewhere in the walls, a ventilator sighed.

"There are three fleets in this system capable of reaching another star," Orr went on. "Earth's. The Jovian Compact's. And one that does not officially exist. All three run on Azra, and none has enough. That shortage is the *only* reason there is peace. Your assay suggests your claim holds more Azra than humanity has mined in its entire history."

"I'd gathered it was large."

"It is not large. It is decisive. Whoever holds your deed holds the next century."

He slid a sheet of paper across the oak. Arthur read the figure, then read it again, counting zeros the way he would check a pressure seal.

"That is for the mineral rights," Orr said. "In perpetuity. And I give you my word I will never mine a single gram."

Arthur looked up. "Then why buy it?"

"So that no one else can."

"Who are you working for?"

"People who have done the arithmetic." Orr's voice softened. "Consider the alternative. If that vein is opened, indentured crews will work it. Ten, twenty thousand men on twelve-year leases, breathing Azra dust for wages they'll never see. You're an engineer. You've been down the Hellas shafts. You know what the leasing companies call an acceptable loss rate."

Arthur did know. It was why he had stopped going down.

"The Consortium has made you offers," Orr said.

"Two. I declined both."

"The Consortium rarely makes a third. Your neighbour, Hesketh, two claims north?"

"Habitat breach. Pump failure."

"Yes," said Orr gently. "That is what the report says."

The ventilator sighed again. Arthur found his hand had drifted back to his collar.

"I'll want time."

"You'll have until the shuttle returns you to the surface. After that, I'm afraid I can no longer guarantee you'll be asked politely. By anyone."

Arthur stood. At the door he paused.

"The note under my door. *Do not sell to the first buyer.* Was that yours?"

For the first time, Orr's composure faltered. It was only a flicker, quick as the brass moon catching the light on its little track. He set down his glass very carefully.

"No," he said. "No, Mr. Neegan. It was not."

Walking back down that amber corridor, Arthur understood that the board was larger than either of them had supposed.

response:
# Chapter Five: The Courtesy of Antares

The display screen on the bulkhead had been cycling its diagnostics for forty minutes, and Arthur Neegan had read every line of it a dozen times.

`HULL INTEGRITY: NOMINAL. REACTOR OUTPUT: 94.6%. COOLANT LOOP B: NOMINAL. ATTITUDE CORRECTION IN 00:03:12.`

The green characters crawled upward and vanished, replaced by others exactly like them. He found it oddly comforting. Whatever else was happening to him, Coolant Loop B was nominal.

They had come at breakfast. There were six of them, in pressure suits of a slate grey so clean it seemed almost insolent against the red dust of the Tharsis flats. Their leader had removed her helmet in his airlock, which was a courtesy. She had called him Mr. Neegan, which was another. Then she had waited quite still while he read the document she offered, which was the greatest courtesy of all, since the document said nothing whatsoever. Its one meaningful feature was the seal: an eight-pointed star in a ring. The Antares Diplomatic Corps.

"Am I under arrest?" he had asked.

"Certainly not. You're invited."

"And if I decline?"

She had considered it as though it were a genuinely interesting question. "I'm afraid I'm not authorized to imagine that."

So here he was. Three weeks ago he had been a mining engineer with a mortgaged homestead and a drill that broke down every second sol. Then had come the core samples, and then the assay, which he ran three times because he did not believe it. Then the visitors arrived: Consolidated, Hesperian Holdings, a man from the Colonial Office who smelled of cologne and anxiety. Each was more agreeable than the last, and each looked past him at the ground beneath his feet.

The ship shuddered. The screen announced `DOCKING SEQUENCE INITIATED` and then, with what Arthur chose to interpret as sympathy, `PLEASE REMAIN SEATED`.

---

The room they brought him to was panelled in real wood, grained and polished and faintly fragrant, a hundred million miles from the nearest forest. A broad viewport filled one wall. In it Mars turned slowly, rust and ochre, with a dust storm smeared across Hellas like a thumbprint on glass.

The man waiting for him was small and old, with thin white hair and a suit of no particular cut. He wore no insignia. He held an unlit cigar.

"Mr. Neegan. Thank you for coming."

"I wasn't aware I had a choice."

"You had several. They were simply all worse." The old man gestured to a chair. "Smoking is forbidden aboard this vessel. I drafted that regulation myself, many years ago, which is the only reason I obey it. Coffee? It's from Earth. I'm told the low pressure ruins the taste, but I'm sentimental."

Arthur sat. "Who are you?"

"You may call me Sabatier. It isn't my name, but it has the virtue of being easy to say."

"You're not Antares."

Sabatier's eyebrows lifted, pleased. "What makes you think so?"

"The men who brought me salute you. But they're careful about it, like soldiers saluting a borrowed officer."

"Very good. Yes, I've borrowed them, as one borrows an umbrella. The Antares Corps owes certain parties certain favours." He set the cigar down with great care. "Let us talk about your property."

"Everyone wants to talk about my property."

"Everyone wants to *buy* your property. I want to talk about it. Do you know how much Azra exists in the known galaxy, Mr. Neegan?"

"Not exactly."

"Neither does anyone. But the best estimate, which is mine, is that your claim holds rather more than all other known deposits combined." He let that settle. "A ship with an Azra-catalysed drive reaches Antares in eleven weeks rather than eleven years. A warhead with an Azra core reduces a city to glass in the time it takes to say so. They are the same object, you understand, merely pointed in different directions."

Outside, the terminator line crept across Tharsis. Somewhere down there was his kitchen table, with his breakfast still on it.

"If Consolidated acquires your claim," Sabatier went on, "they will hold an auction, which is a polite word for selling the future to the highest bidder. If Antares takes it outright, Earth will respond, and the war will be fought here. Wars between the stars are always fought on somebody's colony. And the forty thousand leased labourers on this planet will dig for whoever wins, as they have dug for everyone else."

"So what do you want?"

"I want you to keep it."

Arthur stared at him.

"Register the claim under Article Nine of the old Colonial Charter, the independent homestead provision. Nobody has invoked it in sixty years, and most people assume it was repealed. It was not. I made certain of that." Sabatier smiled faintly. "My associates will finance the extraction. You will hire free labour only, no leases. And when you reach the main seam, the deep assays will come to me first. To me and to no one else."

"Why?"

For the first time, the old man hesitated.

"Has anyone told you," he said slowly, "what the decay products around the Azra seams look like?"

"Wrong," said Arthur, before he could stop himself. "The isotope ratios are wrong. I assumed my equipment—"

"Your equipment is fine. The surrounding rock is billions of years old. The Azra is not. Either it formed in a way no physics we possess can explain, or something put it there." Sabatier picked up the cigar again and turned it in his fingers. "I should very much like to know which, before anyone builds a weapon from it."

The coffee had gone cold. Arthur hadn't touched it.

"And if I refuse?"

"Then you'll receive other offers. Do you remember Emil Hollis? He held the Noachis claim, two years ago."

"Decompression accident."

"His airlock seals were inspected and certified six days before he died. The inspector has since retired, quite comfortably, to Ganymede." Sabatier's voice was mild. "I'm not threatening you, Mr. Neegan. The threat already exists. I'm merely the first person honest enough to describe it."

"Why should I trust you?"

"You shouldn't. Trust is a luxury for people with options. You should *calculate*." He rose, signalling that the interview was over. "You have until your shuttle touches down. After that, others will make their offers, and some of them will not trouble to be offers."

---

On the transfer vessel, the green text resumed its patient crawl.

`HULL INTEGRITY: NOMINAL. ALL SYSTEMS: NOMINAL.`

Arthur watched it for a long time and found that he no longer believed a word of it.

response:
# Chapter Five: The Thief Who Was Forgiven

The briefings said the city of Ammar was divided. I played them on the long drop from orbit until I could recite them. The Tall Folk of the river terraces were descended from the first ship, long-boned and pale, their eyes widened by four centuries of dim winters. The Sert of the high mines came from the second ship, short and broad, their blood thickened against the thin air. Between them stood a wall of law, labor-bond and grievance. The Concord had sent me, at twenty-six, to help take that wall down without bloodshed.

On the ninth day, during the third reception in the Hall of Sessions, I went out through a kitchen door and did not come back for six hours.

I have since been asked to justify this, and I find I can't. I was tired of being looked at. I wanted to look.

Ammar is built of a grey-gold stone that holds the afternoon light the way a hand holds warmth after it has set down a cup. Every lintel is carved. The first ship carried, along with its seed-banks and genomes, an archive of stories its people no longer had the context to read, and they cut those stories into their walls as other peoples cut prayers. Over the gate to the lower market, a man walked with a coal cupped in his hands, and above him hung a great bird with its wings half-folded. I knew him. A woman selling dried fish told me his name was the Thief Who Was Forgiven.

"Forgiven by whom?"

She looked at me as if I had asked who dries the fish. "By the bird. See." The bird's beak was closed. "It doesn't eat him. That's the whole story."

The market was not divided. It took me an hour to believe it. Tall Folk and Sert stood at the same stalls, haggled in the same quick river-dialect, carried each other's children on their hips. The broad men I had been told were bonded labor were selling copper and tin. The pale women I had been told were their masters were buying it, counting out coin with care, and sometimes being refused.

There was a division, but it ran elsewhere. Some people wore a blue cord at the wrist. These were served first and spoken to in a slightly higher register, and some of them were tall and some were broad. I asked a boy what the cord meant.

"Counted," he said.

Counted as what? He shrugged, the shrug of a child for whom a thing has always been so, and went back to hawking roasted nuts.

---

Commander Velasque was waiting in my quarters. She did not raise her voice, which was worse.

"You have no standing on this world outside the Hall," she said. "If you had been hurt, the Council would have blamed the Sert, the Sert would have blamed the Council, and we would have had the riot we came here to prevent, with your body as its first exhibit."

"The briefings are wrong."

"The briefings are what the Council gave us."

"Then the Council is wrong, or lying."

She studied me a long moment. "Minister Ithe has asked to see you. Tonight. I suspect she knows where you went." At the door she paused. "She is the Minister of Science. She has never conducted an experiment in her life. She has also outlasted four governments. Remember both."

---

The Ministry stood at the top of the terraces. Over its door was carved a tower, very tall, raised by many small hands. At its summit the hands reached for one another and missed.

Minister Ithe was old and tall, and in the lamplight her wide eyes were almost all pupil. She poured me a cup of something bitter and did not drink her own.

"Did you enjoy the market?"

On the climb I had thought about lying. "Yes."

"Good. A man who lies about the first thing lies about everything, and then I waste the evening learning which." She sat back. "What did you see?"

"People who were told they were two peoples, behaving as one."

"And the cords?"

"I don't know what the cords are."

"Yes, you do. You are too polite to say it in my house." She turned her cup a quarter turn. "My Ministry keeps the Count. At seven every child is measured: bone length, blood density, the shape of the eye. We record lineage, and land rights follow lineage. The Counted receive land. The Uncounted receive what they can get."

"Then the division isn't Tall and Sert."

"It is Measured and Unmeasured. Envoy, which am I?"

I looked at her. She was tall, yes. But her hands were broad and short-fingered, her wrists thick. I could not tell, and she watched me fail to tell.

"Neither can the Ministry," she said, "without the paper. That is why the Minister of Science is not a scientist. Instruments give numbers. Someone must decide what the numbers mean. That person is me."

"Then you could end it."

"I could end the Count tomorrow. The next day every Counted family on the terraces would be asked to prove its land and could not, and the Sert would be blamed, because the Sert are easy to see." She smiled for the first time. "Your Concord sent a boy to end a war between two peoples. There is no war between two peoples. There is a ledger. Can you burn a ledger without burning the house it is kept in?"

"No," I said. "But I can read it aloud."

She was quiet. The wind came off the terraces and moved through the carved tower above her door with a sound like breath across the mouth of a jar.

"In your old story," she said, "why did the tower fall?"

"Because the builders stopped understanding one another."

"Here we teach that it fell because one builder counted the bricks, and the others began to ask whose they were." She stood, and so I stood. "Come back in three days and bring your own numbers. I want to see whether you count the way we do."

I was halfway down the terraces, under the Thief and his closed-beaked bird, before I understood that I had been offered something and had not yet been told the price.

response:
# Offworlder

## Chapter Three: The Minister of What Is So

The briefings had been thorough, and they had been written by people who had never been to Hesh. I understood this only afterward, which is how one understands most things worth understanding.

I was to remain in the Residence until the Council received me. I was to accept no gifts, offer no opinions, and go nowhere without my escort, two pleasant young ammari men with long hands and nothing whatever to do. On the third morning, while they were at breakfast, I put on my cloak and went out through the kitchen garden. Nobody stopped me. Nobody on Hesh had imagined that a guest would wish to leave.

The cloak was a mistake, and I knew it at once. On Tessaly it is a spring garment of grey wool, worn open at the throat. Here the air lay on the skin like a damp hand. The people in the street wore a cloth at the hips, a cord of beads, sometimes a band of shade-paper across the brow, and nothing else. They looked at me the way one looks at a man carrying a door. A small child walked beside me for a long way and finally asked whether I was ill, or ashamed, or very cold inside. I said I did not know yet. She found this a reasonable answer and went off.

The briefings said there were two peoples, sundered nine hundred years ago when the first ship came down in two places. The ammari of the coast were tall, salt-tolerant, and thin-boned. The keth of the uplands were short, deep-chested, and slow-breathing, with a fine dun down along the spine. The briefings said the two did not intermarry and could not interbreed, that the keth were a laboring people with no voice in the Council, and that tensions were high and rising.

The market at the foot of the hill was run by keth women. That was the first thing. They sat on raised mats under awnings, and the ammari came to them, bent nearly double to hear, and paid what was asked. I watched a tall coastman argue over a basket of blue fruit for some time, lose, and laugh. The price was spoken in ammari. The laugh, I think, was keth. Everyone seemed to have both.

The second thing was the children. A girl selling oil in little clay bottles stood a head taller than her keth mother. She had the down along her spine, pale as dust, and the narrow hands of the coast. There were others. Not many, but nobody stared at them. They stared at me.

I bought a blue fruit, which was against protocol, and ate it, which was against advice, and walked back up the hill with juice on my chin.

---

Command did not raise its voice. Oyelaran never does. Her face on the screen in my room was weary and exact.

"You were sent to listen to the Council," she said. "Not to conduct a census."

"The Council is wrong about some things."

"The Council is the government. Whether it is wrong is a question for later, and not yours to ask." She let that settle. "Since you have made yourself conspicuous, you may as well make yourself useful. The Minister of Science has asked to see you, privately. Go. Be courteous. Say as little as you can."

"What does the Minister of Science do?"

"Very little science," said Oyelaran, and closed the link.

---

Minister Varrath received me in a room open on one side to the sea. She was ammari, very old, and wore only a hip-cloth and a great many rings. She did not rise. The chair she offered me was low, so that I had to look up at her. I thought this was likely deliberate, and sat in it.

"You went to the market," she said. "In that." She considered the cloak. "Do you sweat much on your world, Envoy Teo?"

"Not as much."

"Then you dress for a place you are not in. It is a common failing of guests." She took a slice of blue fruit from a dish and did not offer me one. "What did you see?"

I had been told to say as little as I could. "Fruit," I said.

She smiled a little. "And who sold it to you?"

"A woman."

"Of what people?"

"Of Hesh."

The smile went away, and something more interested took its place. "You know what my office is."

"You are the Minister of Science."

"I am the Minister of what is so. The Council asks me what is so, I tell them, and then it is so." She ate the fruit. "Nine hundred years ago it was so that there were two peoples. Forty years ago my predecessor certified that there were two species. It was a useful finding. It kept the coast from owing the uplands what kin owe one another. Do you understand me?"

"I understand that you are telling me something your Council does not want told."

"I am telling you nothing. I am asking what you saw." She leaned forward, and her rings clicked on the arm of the chair. "If you go back to your Ship and say *children*, Envoy, the Council will say you were deceived by mummers. Then they will go looking for the children, to learn who deceived you. Do you understand that?"

I did. It was cold in me, despite the heat. I thought of the girl with the oil bottles.

"Then why bring me here," I said, "if not to frighten me?"

"To see whether you frighten." She sat back. "You do, a little. Good. A guest who is not frightened is a fool. A guest who is only frightened is useless." She looked at the sea for a while. "My grandson sells nets at the third stall from the east well. He is very short, for a coastman. He has a fine back."

I said nothing. I had learned, at last, the use of that.

"The Council will not be told," Varrath said. "But a Council can be outlived. I am old, and I have been patient, and when I stop being patient I would like someone from outside standing beside me. Someone the Council cannot send people looking for." She glanced at me. "You will need to dress better."

"What should I wear?"

"Less," said the Minister of Science. "It is the first thing we teach our children. You cannot carry your own weather."
