response:
# Offworlder

**Chapter Six: Voss**

The briefings told me that the Keth and the Amm of Ostra do not eat together, do not marry, and do not touch one another's hands in trade. The people who wrote them had read it in older briefings, and those writers had read the first Legation's dispatches, sixty years stale. I set this down so it is clear that I did not go into the city meaning to disobey. I went meaning to look.

The reception at the Prefecture was in its third hour. I pleaded a headache, which was true in the way that boredom is a fever of the young, and left by the kitchen stair.

Harth is a city built for the long dusk. Ostra's sun is a dim orange coin that takes a Terran month to cross the sky, and its people have had nine hundred years to answer it. The Keth descend from the first ship. They are tall and narrow, and their eyes are so large and dark that meeting a Keth gaze is like looking down a well. The Amm came two centuries later, on a second ship, and settled the high plateaus where the air is thin. They are short and deep-chested, heavy-lidded against the snow-glare. Two peoples, the briefing said. Two hostile peoples. It used the word *subspecies*, and I remember thinking it a cold word to put in a diplomat's mouth.

The dyers' market lay along the river under awnings of stretched hide, and every stall was hung with cloth. There were reds and ochres I knew, and then a color I did not know at all. It lay somewhere past violet, where my eye expected black, and it would not hold still. Seen straight on, it was deep and cool. At the edge of sight it went faintly green, like a held breath.

"Voss," said the woman at the stall. She was Amm, broad as a doorway, stained to the wrists. "From the snowline moss. Grows nowhere else."

I bought a small square. While she wrapped it, a Keth man bent nearly double under her awning to argue the price of a bolt. She counted coins into his long palm, and their fingers touched, and neither of them noticed. On the back bench a child sorted thread. I could not have said which people the child belonged to. I am not sure the child could have said.

"Is this your work?" I asked.

"My hearth's." She nodded at the Keth man, who was, it turned out, her husband's brother.

---

Commander Tey was waiting in my quarters, which is never a good sign.

"You were seen," she said.

"I wasn't hiding."

"That is precisely the problem. You are not here to see, Envoy. You are here to be seen, in the right rooms, beside the right people." She let that settle. "The Minister of Science has asked for you by name. You will go tomorrow, and you will be agreeable."

"I didn't know Ostra had a ministry of science."

"It hasn't any science," she said. "It has a Minister."

---

Minister Arrin Holt was Keth, very old, folded into his chair like a heron. His office was walled with ledgers. On the table between us lay a bolt of voss.

"You admired this," he said.

So I had been followed. I decided not to pretend otherwise. "I did. I still do."

"Tell me what else you admired."

I told him about the coins, the hands, the child, the hearth. He listened with his well-dark eyes half closed.

"And from this you conclude that your briefings lie."

"I conclude they're incomplete."

"Everything is incomplete. What matters is who is permitted to finish it." He laid a hand on a ledger. "The Register of Descent. Every birth on Ostra, assigned to a line. That is my science, Envoy. I decide who is Keth and who is Amm."

"And the child at the stall?"

"Amm, on paper, because the mother is." He leaned toward me. "Which are you?"

"On my world we stopped counting."

"Then you forgot how. That is not the same as being free of it." He said it gently, which was worse. "Suppose I burned the Register tonight. Who owns the snowline tomorrow? Who owns the moss?"

I had come prepared to defend the market against the Register. I had not come prepared to learn that the Register might be the only wall between the dyers and the money in Harth. He watched me discover this.

"Shall I write to your Commander," he said, "that her envoy recommends we burn it?"

"You may write that her envoy asked a question. She'll find that very easy to believe."

He laughed, one dry breath. I held his gaze, though it cost me something. "If the Register protects someone, I'd like to know who built it, and whom it was built against."

For a long while he said nothing. The orange light lay on the ledgers and did not move.

"I built half of it," he said at last. "My predecessor built the other half, against me." He gave something not quite a smile. "Come back when you have walked the snowline. Then we will talk about what your Legation wants, and what it ought to want."

He pushed the voss across the table. I did not refuse it. Refusing would have been an answer, and I did not yet know what I meant to say.

That night, under the lamp, I unrolled it. The weave was two threads, one dyed and one bare, and the color I had no word for was in neither. It was in the way they lay together, and it changed whenever I moved.

Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more.

A stray cat near the school looks at the student with uncanny recognition after each rewind. Length: 1000 words.
response:
# Rewind

The box was sitting on top of the bike rack Monday morning, with a sticky note that said FOR TOBY.

There was no last name and no address, just my name in shaky handwriting.

Inside was a smart watch with a black band, a black screen, and one silver button on the side. When I strapped it on, the screen glowed green and showed a single number in the corner.

**12.**

Battery, I figured. Or steps. Whatever.

That's when I noticed the cat.

It sat on the chain-link fence by the bike rack. It was a skinny gray stray with a white smudge over its left eye, like someone had pressed a thumb there. I have a birthmark in the exact same spot. Mom calls it my thumbprint.

The cat stared at me. I stared back. Then the bell rang, and I forgot all about it.

---

The first time was an accident.

On Tuesday I was carrying a tray of sloppy joes past Priya Shah's table when my sneaker caught a chair leg. I watched the whole tray sail toward her white sweater in slow motion. I grabbed my wrist in panic. My thumb mashed the silver button.

The cafeteria went *backward*.

Priya's scream un-screamed itself. The sloppy joe peeled off her sweater and flew back onto my tray. My feet skidded in reverse. Everything smeared like wet paint, and then, *click*, I was standing at the end of the lunch line again, tray perfectly clean.

I walked around the chair this time.

Through the window, I could see the gray cat on the fence, watching me.

It wasn't the way cats watch birds. It was the way people watch someone they *know*.

---

After that, I couldn't stop.

Flunked a pop quiz? Rewind. Missed a free throw in gym? Rewind. Called Mr. Grady "Mom" in front of the whole class? Rewind, rewind, REWIND.

And every single time, the cat was there afterward. It sat on the fence, or the dumpster, or the hood of Ms. Okafor's car, staring at me with flat green eyes that said, *I saw that.*

I told myself it was a coincidence. Lots of cats hang around schools.

Right?

---

By Thursday, my sneakers pinched.

By Friday, my jeans stopped two inches above my ankles, and my voice cracked like a dropped plate halfway through every sentence.

"Toby," Mom said at breakfast, squinting. "Have you been using your father's razor?"

I ran to the bathroom mirror. There was fuzz on my upper lip. *Dark* fuzz. Three zits clustered on my chin like they were planning something.

School was worse. A substitute stopped me in the hall and told me the faculty lounge was the other way. Priya Shah wouldn't look at me. Jaylen, my best friend since kindergarten, stood at my locker and said, "Dude. No offense. You look like my uncle Ray."

Jaylen's uncle Ray is thirty-four and sells mattresses.

I looked down at the watch. The number in the corner wasn't 12 anymore.

It was **17**.

It wasn't the battery, and it wasn't steps.

It was *me*.

Every rewind sent the world backward and sent *me* forward.

---

I knew what I had to do. I had to go back all the way, to before I ever touched the stupid thing. Monday morning, before the box.

I stood behind the gym, jammed my thumb on the button, and held it down.

The world screamed backward. Days peeled off like old wallpaper: sun, moon, sun, moon. On the screen, the number climbed. 19. 22. 26.

*Let go,* something inside me whispered. *Let go NOW.*

But I wasn't back far enough. Not yet. Not yet...

I let go at **31**.

---

It was Monday morning. I could tell by the smell of cafeteria waffles.

I ran home. My knees ached. *My knees ached.* I pounded on our front door, and Mom opened it. Her face went tight and polite, the way it does with people selling things.

"Can I help you?"

"Mom, it's me! It's Toby!"

My little sister Bea peeked around her legs. "Who's Toby?"

Behind them I could see the school pictures in the hallway: Bea in first grade, Bea in second. There were none of me. My bedroom door hung open. It was a sewing room.

"We don't have a Toby," Mom said slowly, reaching for her phone.

I'd rewound so hard I'd torn myself right out of the world.

---

I heard the sirens before I reached the school.

The cat was waiting on the fence. Of course it was. It was the only living thing left that knew who I was.

It blinked at me, slowly, like it was saying, *Go on.*

The watch flashed **31**. Then the number vanished, and two words took its place:

**ONCE MORE?**

Red and blue lights swept across the parking lot.

I pressed the button.

---

Everything is very tall now.

The fence is cold under my paws. The sun is warm on my fur. Beside me, the old gray cat with the white smudge over its eye tucks in its tail and begins to purr.

I don't need a mirror to know I have a smudge too.

Below us, a boy walks up to the bike rack. He's twelve years old, in jeans that fit, with a birthmark over his left eye. His little sister Bea skips along behind him.

The world is fixed. Mostly.

He picks up a small black box with a sticky note on top.

*Don't,* I try to yell. *DON'T OPEN IT!*

It comes out as a meow.

The boy looks up at the two of us. Something flickers across his face, a funny feeling, like he knows us from somewhere.

Then the bell rings, and he straps the watch onto his wrist.

response:
# WATCH OUT!

The first time I rewound time, I was trying not to die of embarrassment.

The second time, I was trying not to fail a pop quiz.

By the sixth time, I'd stopped counting.

That was my first mistake.

---

Mom bought me the watch for my twelfth birthday at a store called Tempus Tech, squeezed between a nail salon and a vacuum repair shop. A sign in the window said EVERYTHING MUST GO.

The clerk was old. He had gray hair, tired eyes, and a chipped front tooth exactly like mine. He stared at me the whole time we were there. When Mom paid, he slid the box across the counter and said, "No returns. No exchanges. No do-overs."

Then he winked.

I should've thrown that watch in the trash right there.

It was sleek and black, with no brand name. It had a glowing face and, in the corner, a tiny number: **12**.

Battery percentage, I figured. Whatever.

---

On Monday, I found out what it really did.

I was carrying my tray past Priya Nair's table when my sneaker caught on nothing. Tater tots flew. Chocolate milk exploded. The whole cafeteria went "OHHHHH."

My thumb brushed the watch face in a little counterclockwise swipe.

The world smeared like wet paint.

And I was standing in the lunch line again, tray in hand, thirty seconds earlier. The tater tots were safe.

This time I walked past Priya's table very carefully. She smiled at me.

Priya Nair. Smiled. At me.

I almost passed out.

---

After that, I couldn't stop.

Pop quiz in science? Swipe. I peeked at Gus's answers, rewound, and filled them in before Mr. Grogan finished handing out papers.

Bombed a joke in front of Priya? Swipe. Better joke.

Missed a catch in gym? Swipe. I got Tyler Bruckner out for the first time in recorded history.

The number in the corner said **13**.

I didn't notice.

By sixth period, my sneakers pinched. My jeans had crept up to show my socks. During roll call, I said "here," and my voice cracked so hard I sounded like a stepped-on goose.

Everyone laughed. So I rewound.

I said "here" again. It came out deeper. *Way* deeper.

Nobody laughed. They stared.

"Dude," Gus whispered. "Did you get taller since lunch?"

"No," I said, looking down at him. Gus is the tallest kid in seventh grade.

My upper lip itched. I rubbed it and felt fuzz.

---

Things got weirder.

The lunch lady, who calls everyone "sweetie," called me "sir." Eighth graders nodded at me like I was one of them. Priya wouldn't look at me at all. And the seventh-period sub frowned and said, "High school's across the street, young man. Visitors sign in at the office."

I ran for the bathroom.

I splashed water on my face and looked in the mirror. Pimples on my chin. A shadow over my lip. A face stretching longer. Older.

Then the mirror flickered.

For one second, a different face stared back. Gray hair. Tired eyes. Deep lines around the mouth.

And a chipped front tooth.

I knew that face. I'd seen it somewhere.

Then it was gone, and it was just me again.

I yanked up my sleeve. The number glowed: **15**.

It wasn't the battery. It was *years*.

Every do-over had shoved me forward. I'd burned three years of my life on tater tots and pop quizzes.

I had to undo it. All of it.

So I swiped backward, and this time I didn't let go.

The bathroom blurred. Spun. *Screamed.* I held on until my thumb went numb.

---

When it stopped, I stumbled into the hall. Kids were rushing to homeroom. The clock said 7:58 a.m.

It worked!

I ran to Mr. Grogan's room and froze in the doorway.

Somebody was sitting at my desk. A skinny kid with a bad haircut and a chipped front tooth was laughing at something Gus said and fiddling with a black watch.

He looked up. Our eyes met. They were the same muddy brown.

It was me. Twelve-year-old me.

The short rewinds had always dropped me back into my own body. But I'd gone too far. Now there were two of us, and *he* was the one who belonged.

Mr. Grogan stood. "Can I help you?"

"Who's the creepy guy?" Gus said.

"Gus, it's me!" My voice came out deep and wrong. "It's *Owen*!"

Twelve-year-old me went white.

Grogan grabbed the wall phone. "Security to room 114. We have an intruder."

I looked at my watch. The screen had cracked straight through. Behind the crack, the number read **17**.

Beneath it, new words blinked:

**ONE REWIND REMAINING.**

Heavy footsteps pounded down the hall.

One more rewind could take me further back. Before Monday. Before Mom ever walked into that store.

Maybe I could stop all of it.

*Maybe.*

I swiped and held. The number climbed: 20, 30, 45. My knuckles swelled. Gray hair fell into my eyes. I did not let go.

---

I didn't land in school.

I landed behind a glass counter in a narrow store that smelled like dust and batteries. A sign in the window said EVERYTHING MUST GO.

My wrist was bare. My watch lay in the case below me, perfect and uncracked. In the corner, a tiny number glowed: **12**.

The bell over the door jingled.

Mom walked in. Behind her trailed a skinny kid with a chipped front tooth. He pressed his nose to the glass and pointed straight down at the watch.

"That one," he said.

I caught my reflection in the glass. Gray hair. Tired eyes.

I knew that face now.

"Hi," Mom said, smiling at me like I was a stranger. "I'm looking for a birthday present for my son."

I opened my mouth to say *Run.* To say *We're closed.* To say anything else at all.

But my hand was already reaching for the box.

prompt:
Teen Horror (Goosebumps style)

Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more.

The watch face occasionally flickers to show a countdown. Length: 1000 words.
response:
# Don't Turn Back the Clock

The smart watch cost four dollars at Cobb's Pawn & Curio. A brand-new smart watch, still in the plastic. That should have been my first clue.

"No returns," the old man behind the counter said, sliding it across the glass. It was sleek and black, with no brand name, just a glowing screen and a silver dial on the side. "And son? Don't spin that dial backward."

So of course, the first thing I did was spin it backward.

I didn't mean to. It was Monday, and I'd just dumped a whole tray of sloppy joes down the front of Brianna Castillo's white sweater. The cafeteria went silent. Then two hundred kids started howling.

I wanted to die. I grabbed my wrist in panic, and my thumb rolled the dial.

The world *zipped*.

Sloppy joe flew off Brianna's sweater and back onto my tray. Kids un-laughed. My feet walked backward to the lunch line on their own. My stomach dropped like I was on the Screamin' Eagle.

Then everything stopped. I was standing at the register holding a full tray. Brianna strolled past, sweater spotless.

I stared at the watch. For one second, the screen flickered red:

**61**

Then it went back to showing the time. 12:14.

---

After that, I couldn't stop.

Forgot to study for Mr. Haskell's science quiz? Spin. Peek at the answers. Spin again. A-plus.

Struck out in kickball? Spin. Home run.

Said something dumb to Brianna? Spin. Said something cool.

Every time, the red number flickered. **58. 53. 47.** I figured it was how many rewinds I had left, like lives in a video game. I'd just use them wisely.

I figured wrong.

---

The first thing I noticed was my voice.

I was answering a question in Language Arts when it cracked in the middle of "metaphor." It dropped from squeaky to deep, like a tuba falling down the stairs. Everybody laughed. I didn't rewind that one. I'd learned *some* things.

Then my jeans got short. Ankle-showing short. My sneakers pinched my toes. Mom squinted at me over breakfast. "Did you have a growth spurt, Tyler?"

"Maybe?"

By Thursday I had three zits on my chin and a dark shadow on my upper lip. It wasn't dirt. I scrubbed it with soap until it stung.

It didn't come off.

People started acting weird. Sixth graders scooted out of my way in the hall. Coach Ruiz asked if I'd thought about trying out for the *high school* team. A substitute stopped me at the classroom door. "Can I help you? Parent conferences are in the library."

*Parent.* She thought I was a parent.

Worst of all was Owen, my best friend since kindergarten. At lunch he picked at his tater tots and wouldn't look at me.

"What?" I said. It came out low and rumbly. A stranger's voice.

He shrugged. "You're just... different, man. You're like my brother's friends now. The ones who drive."

I looked down at the watch. **21**.

And I finally got it.

Every time I turned back the clock, the clock took something from me. My years. My *time.* The watch wasn't counting how many tries I had left.

It was counting how much of *me* was left.

---

I should have thrown it in the river. Instead, I made the biggest mistake of my life.

I decided to undo all of it. I'd go back to Saturday, before I ever walked into Cobb's Pawn & Curio.

I gripped the dial and spun. And spun. And *kept* spinning.

The world didn't zip this time. It *screamed*. Days tore past like pages ripped from a book. Sunrises became sunsets became sunrises. My bones ached. My skin stretched. Something hot and terrible poured through my chest.

Then there was silence.

I was standing on my front porch. Except the porch was painted blue. Ours is white.

I knocked. Mom opened the door.

She looked right through me, polite and wary, the way you look at a salesman. "Can I help you, sir?"

"Mom, it's me. It's Tyler."

Her face went pale. Behind her, someone came thundering down the stairs. A skinny kid with a cowlick and a gap in his front teeth. My teeth. My cowlick.

*Me.*

"Who's that, Mom?" the other Tyler asked.

Mom pulled him close and slammed the door. The deadbolt clicked. Her voice came through the wood, muffled and shaking: "I'm calling the police."

I stumbled down the steps. In the minivan window, I caught my reflection.

A man stared back. Stubble. Wrinkles around his eyes. Gray creeping into his hair.

I was older than my *dad.*

And this timeline already had a Tyler Pruitt. A twelve-year-old one. Which meant I wasn't Tyler anymore.

I was the leftover.

Sirens wailed in the distance. I raised the watch with shaking hands.

The screen flickered red.

**1**

One rewind left. Maybe it would fix everything and put the world back the way it was.

Or maybe it would use up the very last of me.

The sirens got louder.

I put my thumb on the dial.

And I spun.

---

"No returns," said the old man behind the counter.

I blinked. Cobb's Pawn & Curio. Dusty shelves. A moth-eaten moose head on the wall. My sneakers fit. When I gasped, it came out high and squeaky.

I was twelve. I was *me.*

The black smart watch sat on the glass between us.

"N-no thanks," I squeaked. "I don't want it."

The old man smiled. He had a cowlick. And a gap in his front teeth.

"That's what I said, too," he told me softly. "Every time."

I looked down.

The watch was already buckled around my wrist.

The screen flickered red.

**61**

Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction

Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a  biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract.

A rudimentary solar panel rig flickers with unstable voltage in the lab. Length: 1000 words.
response:
# Polymerase Chain Reaction

The solar rig died again at 2:14 in the afternoon, which meant the run was ruined.

Tamsin heard it before she saw it: the thermocycler's fan winding down from a whine to a sigh, then the click of the relay giving up. On the roof, six mismatched panels fed a bank of truck batteries that held a charge the way a cupped hand holds water. Two of the panels had come off a bus shelter and four off the dead Verdance kiosk in the old mall. Every time a cloud crossed, the voltage sagged. Every time it sagged, the machine forgot what temperature it was supposed to be.

She had built the thermocycler from a rice cooker and a thermostat pulled out of a Honda's cooling system. It cycled hot, cool, warm, hot, over and over, coaxing a few fragile strands of code into many. When it worked, it was the closest thing to prayer she had left. When it didn't, it was a rice cooker.

"Lost it?" Dov asked from the doorway.

"Third time today." She peeled back the lid. The little tubes sat in their drilled-out block like teeth in a jaw. "Doesn't matter. The sample was going anyway."

Nobody outside the lab understood that part. Verdance hadn't just built crops that died. It had built genes that *rotted*. Every Terminus Line seed carried a slow fuse in its own code, a clock that unspooled across a single season. Plant it and harvest it, and the second generation came up stunted and pale, if it came up at all. That gave the company twenty years of quarterly earnings, and then famine. The board had called it "renewable revenue." Most of them had died in the Denver riots, which Tamsin considered the only fair harvest of the whole era.

What was left was scraps of good code trapped in bad seed, degrading by the week. She had to copy what she could before it fell apart. She did it with a centrifuge made from a cordless drill and a salad spinner, a gel box cut from a child's lunch tin, and a UV lamp salvaged from a tanning salon called *Bronze Age*. She'd laughed about that name for days.

She flexed her hands. Her nails had gone the color of verdigris again, a deep sea-green creeping up from the cuticle. Dov noticed her looking and pretended not to.

Two winters ago her liver had been failing from too much bad water and too many years of eating whatever grew. She'd found a Verdance wellness patch in a pharmacy cold room, a thing designed to be sold monthly to rich people who wanted better skin. She'd tinkered with it and then injected herself. She hadn't told anyone about the tinkering.

It worked, mostly. Her liver came back. But her nails turned green, two molars loosened and fell out, and she ran a low fever that never broke.

There were other changes too. She could see in the dark now, not clearly, but in soft gray shapes. She no longer felt cold below freezing. And sometimes, crumbling soil between her fingers, she thought she could *taste* it: a metallic flicker on the back of her tongue when the ground was rich, a flatness when it was spent. She'd never been able to prove that one, so she told no one. Out here, a woman who tasted dirt was either a prophet or a problem.

"Someone's at the gate," Dov said. "From the Exchange. Says you're expecting him."

She wasn't. But she knew who it was.

---

Sallow sat on an upturned crate in the greenhouse, admiring her sorghum the way a man admires a horse he means to buy. He was thin and clean, which out here was its own kind of threat. Clean meant water, and water meant power.

"Third generation," he said, running a finger along a leaf. "Good seed set. No yellowing. You've done what Verdance swore couldn't be done."

"For one strain. In one valley."

"One strain is a dynasty." He smiled. "The Exchange wants it."

He laid out the offer like a meal. Forty deep-cycle batteries, still sealed. A chest freezer with a working compressor. Real antibiotics in blister packs. A regulated inverter that would stop her rig flickering forever.

Through the greenhouse plastic, Tamsin watched a cloud slide over the panels. Somewhere in her lab, the relay clicked.

"And what do you want?"

"Exclusivity. And one small change." He leaned forward. "Put the lock back in."

She stared at him.

"Just one season, same as before. We sell the seed, people plant it, they come back next year. It's not cruel. It's *sustainable*, for us. And the valley gets your power and your medicine. Everyone eats. They just eat on a schedule."

"That's what killed the world."

"No," Sallow said gently. "Greed killed the world. This is *management*. Would you rather people starve on free seed because your machines keep dying?"

The worst part was that he wasn't entirely wrong. She thought of Mrs. Abara's grandson, coughing all summer with nothing to give him. She thought of the batteries, and of runs that didn't fail at 2:14 in the afternoon.

"I need a week," she said.

"You have three days." He stood and brushed off his clean trousers. "I like you, Tamsin. Don't make me buy from someone worse at this."

---

That night she sat in the lab without a lamp, because she didn't need one anymore. Through the window, the sorghum heads nodded in the wind.

She pressed a pinch of greenhouse soil to her tongue. Iron, something sweet, something alive.

Seeds didn't care about contracts. Verdance had never really understood that. They blew on the wind, stuck in the fur of dogs, rode through the guts of birds. They wanted to go everywhere.

She could give Sallow his lock. She could also make sure it was the kind of lock that only held for a while.

Tamsin smiled in the dark, and her loose tooth ached, and she began to plan.

As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract.

Empty canisters from a defunct biotech giant serve as makeshift reagent containers. Length: 1000 words.
response:
# Polymerase Chain Reaction

The thermocycler had been a rice cooker once, and Oona could still see the ghost of a cartoon panda on its lid beneath the burn marks. Now it was one of three pots on the bench, held at ninety-five degrees, fifty-five and seventy-two. Above them hung the gantry of a dead 3D printer, its print head swapped for a clothes-peg rack of tubes. Every forty seconds the gantry whined, lifted, shuffled and dipped. Melt. Anneal. Extend. Her centrifuge was a ceiling-fan motor bolted into a paint bucket. Thirty cycles took two hours and most of Dunmore Locks' solar budget.

On the shelf above sat the reagents, in brushed-aluminum canisters stamped with the Halcyon Genomics helix and the slogan that had outlived the company by eleven years: SEASONS GUARANTEED. Halcyon had shipped everything in them: seed coatings, livestock boosters, the Clarity drops that kept her mother's eyes working, the gut flora that let a whole generation digest the company's patented starch. Every product was licensed for exactly one generation. Every engineered helix carried a nuclease cassette that waited a season and then chewed its host's DNA to ribbons.

It was a fine business model, right up until nobody was left to buy next year's.

Oona's sorghum had germinated at four percent this spring. She was trying to rescue the genes that mattered, drought tolerance and stalks that stood in wind, from cultivars dissolving under her hands. She meant to splice them into heirloom stock that hadn't been built to die. Most nights she lost the race.

"You keep it dark in here," said Pell Caddick from the doorway.

"I keep it dark so I can see." She pushed her welding goggles up and let him look. Most people flinched. Her irises had gone the flat silver of a fish's belly. Two years ago, as her mother's borrowed Clarity genes finally switched off in her own retinas, she'd spliced a cuttlefish opsin into a viral vector, cooked it up in this same rice cooker, and dripped it into her eyes. It cost her a month of fever and left her with migraines like nails. Daylight was a white scream now.

But she saw ultraviolet. She hadn't needed a UV lamp to read a gel since.

Pell set a cryo-tube on the bench like a chess piece, its frost long gone. Beside it he laid a contract, printed on the back of a Halcyon end-user license with the old terms struck through in red.

"Causeway wants forty copies. Purified. Three days."

Clause four set out the payment: forty units of nitrogen fertilizer, sixty liters of diesel, a cold box of insulin, and two hundred certified seed potatoes. It was enough to carry the Locks through this winter and the next.

Clause seven read: *Contractor shall retain no copies, samples, or records of the template. Premises subject to inspection on delivery.*

"How long's it been thawed?"

Pell shrugged, and a shiver ran down his sleeve. That was his own hack, a brown-fat gene that kept him warm on the Causeway barges. It burned so hot that he ate six meals a day and still hung like a coat on a hook. "Long enough they came to you instead of somebody careful."

She didn't waste time being offended. She drew an aliquot with a glass pipette she'd pulled over a candle. She mixed it with polymerase brewed from hot-spring bacteria, which she kept in a canister marked LIVESTOCK VITALITY, and racked the first tubes. Then she ran a test gel in agarose poured into a soap dish, with current from two tractor batteries.

The bands bloomed violet in her strange eyes. She sat down slowly on a crate.

"You know what this is."

"I know what I'm paid to know."

"It's the cassette. Halcyon's kill switch, but inverted." She'd stared at that sequence's ugly face for a decade and knew its flanking sites like her own handwriting. "It's the off key. Their breeders needed parent lines that didn't die. Put this in a seed and it stays a seed. It breeds true, Pell."

"Yeah," said Pell, tired. "And Causeway will sell it by the season."

The gantry whined, lifted, dipped.

She thought about refusing. Then she thought about four percent, and about the Morrow kids, whose patched gut bacteria let them eat grass but had ground their molars flat by age twelve. She thought about insulin.

She signed.

---

It took three days and ninety cycles. She purified the product through silica ground from window glass and eluted it into forty Causeway vials.

Pell came back with a Causeway inspector, a bleach sprayer, and a UV tube wired to a hand-crank generator. They emptied every canister into a barrel, took her notebook, and checked her arms for punctures. Then they doused the bench and swept the UV across it. The light burned like a small sun through her goggles, and she watched, very carefully, the shadows it threw. It never reached the underside of the gantry rail, the inside lip of the rice cooker, or the grooves of her pipette bulb.

When they'd finished, the inspector nodded, and Pell signed off.

At the door he hesitated. "No copies."

"None," Oona said. "I didn't keep any."

When the barge lights had faded down the canal, she wet a cotton swab and drew it along every shadow she'd memorized. She dropped it into an empty canister and screwed the cap down.

That was what nobody outside the work understood: you couldn't make just forty copies of anything. Thirty cycles turned one molecule into a billion. Every time a tube popped open, the product drifted out like pollen and settled on the bench, in her hair, on the cartoon panda on the lid. The old corporate labs had spent fortunes fighting it.

She'd been counting on it.

SEASONS GUARANTEED, said the canister. For the first time in eleven years, she thought it might be true.

Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a  biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract.

Glow-in-the-dark mushrooms sprout in cracked lab tiles, remnants of old splicing tests. Length: 1000 words.
response:
# Polymerase Chain Reaction

**I. Denature**

Noor dipped two fingers into the first crockpot and pulled them out at once. Ninety-four degrees, near enough. At ninety-five the template would cook. At ninety-three the strands wouldn't let go of each other. Since the fever winter, her fingertips had been more accurate than any thermocouple she could scavenge. It was the one kindness the splice had done her.

Her thermocycler was three crockpots on a plank, set to ninety-four, fifty-five, and seventy-two. A windshield-wiper motor from a dead Volvo swung a wire basket of tubes from bath to bath, timed by a gutted pacemaker programmer. Thirty-five cycles took most of a night and all of a car battery. She brewed the polymerase herself from bacteria cultured out of the settlement compost heap, and it still smelled faintly of turnips.

Around her feet, the mushrooms glowed.

They came up through the cracked floor tiles in clusters, pale green caps the size of fingernails. They were descendants of some Cerulean technician's reporter-gene test from before the collapse, and Noor read by their light at night to save the battery. As far as she knew, they were the only engineered organism in the valley still breeding true. Cerulean had built a sunset clause into every seed, every livestock line, and every gene therapy it sold: a nuclease cassette that waited one generation and then chewed its host's modified DNA to scraps. *One Season. Perfect.* Then you bought again. Nobody had bothered to sabotage a novelty mushroom. And nobody had planned for the company to stop selling the next season.

The door scraped. Kesh came in out of the rain carrying a foam cooler and smiling with too many teeth. His dental-regrowth splice had taken a little too well. A third row was coming in through black gums, and he had stopped hiding it.

"You're running hot," he said.

"Always." She had run at thirty-nine point four every day since the fever. The thermophile chaperone protein she'd spliced into her own liver had kept her alive while the fever killed forty people in the Cistern. It had also burned away her hair and left her skin flaking like the tiles. Now she ate twice what anyone else did. Nobody had ever said so to her face, and that was worse.

Kesh set the cooler on the bench. "Founder stock. Pre-clause sorghum, out of a Cerulean cryovault downriver. Germline clean."

Noor's mouth went dry. "That doesn't exist."

"It does for sixty hours. Then the vault's preservative cassette quits, and it starts eating itself like everything else."

**II. Anneal**

The client was the Dam. Everybody knew the Dam: four hundred guns, a working turbine, and grain silos it liked to point out to visitors.

"They want a drought strain that breeds true," Kesh said. "For their own fields. Half the founder sample is your fee."

Half was enough. Half meant the Cistern's children eating sorghum next year and the year after, grown from their own seed, forever.

"And the strain they sell to everyone else?"

Kesh's smile flattened. "That's clause two. The trade strain carries a sunset. One generation."

There it was. The Dam didn't want to feed the valley. It wanted to be Cerulean. Noor looked down at the mushrooms glowing blithely around her boots and thought about the forty graves on the hill, and the hundreds that had come before them, after the first sterile harvest.

"You'd be writing the clause," Kesh said gently. "Nobody else around here can."

She thought about her ribs showing through her shirt despite her double rations. She thought about saying no, and about the Cistern's seed stores, which smelled of mice and would last until March.

"Swab," she said.

He uncapped the tube, and she spat into it. Contracts were signed in genomes now. Kesh would sequence her markers and carry them to every runner between here and the coast. If she defaulted, nobody would trade with anyone who shared her blood.

"Fifty-nine hours," Kesh said, and left.

**III. Extend**

She didn't sleep. Sleep was for people whose bodies didn't run like boilers.

She thawed the founder stock and spun out the DNA in a salad-spinner centrifuge mounted on a ceiling-fan motor. Then she fed it through the crockpots while her hands judged the baths. Every hour she ran a gel in a sandwich box wired to nine-volt batteries and checked the bands under a blacklight. Every hour the bands were fainter. The founder DNA was already fraying.

By hour forty she had the drought genes amplified and stitched into the Cistern's hardy local sorghum, with no clause. By hour fifty she had finished the Dam's private strain, also clean.

Then came the trade strain.

Writing the sunset cassette took ninety minutes. Once she understood it, it was elegant. It waited, patient as a landmine, for the second generation. She hated how easily it came to her.

At hour fifty-four she sat on the floor among the mushrooms, burning through her last ration bar, and watched them glow.

*Nobody bothered to sabotage a novelty.*

The contract said one generation. It said nothing about secrecy.

She pulled the luminescence pathway from a mushroom cap: four genes, self-sufficient, needing nothing but a living cell. She tucked it in behind the sunset clause and wired it to the germination promoter. Dry seed would look like any other seed. But anyone who planted it, watered it, and waited for nightfall would see every sprouting root glow faint green in the dark soil.

It would mean nothing to the Dam's inspectors, or to the first buyer. But word traveled with the runners. Soon every farmer in the valley would know a simple rule: if your field lights up at night, the seed is lying to you. Go find someone who can fix it.

When Kesh came back, she handed him three labeled vials. He weighed them in his palm.

"All to spec?"

"To the letter."

He looked at the floor, where the mushrooms threw green light across her bare scalp. His third row of teeth showed in something like approval.

After he left, Noor pressed a single Cistern seed into a crack in the tiles beside the mushrooms and watered it from her canteen. Then she went home to eat more than her share.

Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words.

response:
# Útiseta

Astrid said the hide had to come from an animal that died without fear. When I asked how anyone could know that, she shrugged and said her mormor knew. The reindeer skin smelled of smoke and something sweeter underneath, like apples forgotten in a cellar. She'd carried it up in a Konsum bag.

It was the last Saturday of October, 1995. We'd left my house at half past eleven: my window, the drainpipe, the whole cliché. The ground was frozen hard enough to ring under our boots. The churchyard below the ridge was already full of grave lanterns, because Allhelgona was next weekend and the old women liked to start early. From the mound you could see them, dozens of small red flames trembling in the dark like something breathing.

The sign by the road said *Gravhög, järnålder*, and someone had scratched a penis into the enamel. Astrid called it Gubben. The old man. Everyone's grandparents called it that, she said, and nobody's parents did, and that was how you knew who still remembered.

"Rules," she said, unrolling the skin. She had an unlit Marlboro behind her ear, stolen from her brother. "We sit facing north. Backs together. Hide over both our heads, no gaps. Once we're under, nobody talks."

"For how long?"

"Until it's done."

"Astrid."

"Until you know something you didn't know before." She said it the way you'd explain kubb. Then she took her father's brännvin from her jacket and poured a long stripe of it across the frozen grass. "That's for him. Don't drink any."

I hadn't planned to. I'd tried schnapps once at a party on Söder and thrown up in a stairwell. But it bothered me, the way she said *him*. Like a neighbour.

She gave me the other rules while she buttoned her coat to the chin. If someone said my name, I wasn't to answer, even if it sounded like her. Especially if it sounded like her. If I felt a hand on my shoulder, I was to keep still. I wasn't to look toward the village. And I was to take off my silver chain, the one from my confirmation, and keep it in my pocket, away from my skin.

"Why?"

"Otherwise he won't come close enough."

I almost went home then. I want to be honest about that. I stood there with my Walkman cord looped around my neck and Kent on the tape and thought, quite clearly, *this is stupid, and I don't want to do it.* But Astrid had done this twice already. The second time, she said, she'd learned that Johanna Lindqvist's father hit her mother, and a week later Johanna came to school wearing sunglasses in October. Astrid told me this the way other girls told you who'd kissed whom. And I was fifteen and new. The alternative was another Saturday listening to my parents be careful with each other in a rented house that still smelled of the last family.

So I took off the chain.

We sat back to back. Astrid's spine was knobbly and warm through two coats. She drew the skin over us and the world went black and close and animal. I could hear her breathing, and mine, and the thin wire of my own blood.

For a long time nothing happened. Cold seeped up into my thighs. My nose ran. I counted breaths to three hundred and lost track. I thought about Stockholm, about the 4 bus, about how nobody here had heard of anything.

Then the bell.

One stroke from the church below, round and low. I felt it more than heard it, a pressure in my chest like a thumb. I knew without checking that it was midnight. I also knew, as everyone did, that the bell ran on a timer the kommun had installed in 1989. It rang at eight and at six and never at night.

Behind me, Astrid's breathing stopped.

Not slowed. Stopped. Her back was still there, still warm, but nothing moved in it. I wanted to say her name so badly my jaw ached.

Something walked across the top of the mound.

I'll tell you what I told myself then, what I still tell myself: frost cracks. Ground settles. A fox. But it was slow and heavy, and it stopped directly in front of me on the other side of the skin, and I smelled earth. Not frozen earth. Wet, turned, summer earth, rich as a fresh grave.

"Linnea."

My mother's voice, soft, the way she said it when I was small and feverish. My mother was asleep three kilometres away. I bit the inside of my cheek until I tasted metal.

It came again, closer, from my left, where the hide met the grass and there was no room for anyone to be.

Then a weight settled on my left shoulder. Not a hand, exactly. A heaviness, patient, the way a cat settles. And I knew something.

I don't know how else to put it. It was simply there, the way you know your own phone number. I knew Astrid's mormor had been dead for six years and had never taught her anything. I knew Astrid had found all of it in a library book in Härnösand and invented the rest. And I knew it didn't matter, because it had worked anyway.

The weight lifted. Astrid gasped behind me like someone surfacing.

When she pulled the hide back, the churchyard below was dark. Every lantern was out. Grave candles burn about twenty hours, and the old women had probably lit them all at once that afternoon. That's what I've decided.

Astrid stared down at the dark, then at me, her face white and thrilled.

"What did he tell you?"

I put the chain back on. The silver was so cold it burned.

"Nothing," I said.

It was the first time I lied to her. Two of us had walked up Gubben that night. Going down, I counted the tracks in the frost three times, and I have never told anyone what number I got.

response:
# Útiseta

Astrid said we couldn't eat after sundown, so by eleven I was lying on my bed with my stomach folding in on itself, listening to the house tick in the cold. Pappa had promised me the north would be quiet. He hadn't said the quiet would have texture, that it would press against the windows like something wanting in.

She threw a pebble at the glass at quarter past. I climbed out the way she'd taught me, over the woodshed roof, my jacket turned inside out because she'd said so, the seams scratching at my wrists.

"Did you bring it?"

I held up the coin, a five-krona piece, the shiniest I could find, because Astrid said *they* liked things that shone. She inspected it under her flashlight like a customs officer, nodded, and handed me a stick of Juicy Fruit.

"Are we allowed gum?"

"Mormor never said we weren't."

That was Astrid all over. She had rules handed down through four hundred years of women in her family, and then a shrug wherever the rules ran out. I had never met the grandmother. In three months of friendship, Astrid had never once invited me inside. *Mormor's resting*, she'd say, and steer us somewhere else.

The mound sat in a clearing past the last farm, a long low hump shaped like an upturned boat. Everyone in the village knew what it was, and nobody talked about it, the same way nobody talked about the Lindqvist boy who'd gone through the ice in '87. Astrid said archaeologists from Umeå had come to dig it in the seventies and the farmer had met them with a shotgun.

There was mist that night. It lay in a thick rim around the base of the mound, and the moon was nearly full, so the mist glowed. It didn't seem to reflect the light so much as soak it up and give it back slowly. The top of the mound rose clean out of it, dark and furred with frost-stiff grass. It looked like an island, the only dry place in a flood.

"*Útiseta*," Astrid said, rolling the word around her mouth. She'd found it in a library book in Skellefteå and liked it better than what her mormor called it, which was just *sitta ute*. Sitting out. "Okay. Rules."

She ticked them off on mittened fingers like a grocery list. We sit facing north. We sit back to back, so nothing can come at us from behind without one of us seeing. We don't speak, not one word, until the church clock strikes one. If someone calls your name, you don't answer. If someone calls your name in a voice you *know*, you especially don't answer.

"And if we see something?"

"You won't see anything." She pulled a folded reindeer hide from her backpack, grey and balding at the edges. "That's what this is for. You go under it, and you listen."

"For what?"

"Whatever wants to tell you." She grinned. "Tomorrow we'll know who Jenny Holm actually likes. Or whatever. Ask anything."

I was fifteen and from Söder, and I'd seen enough horror films at sleepovers to know exactly how this was supposed to go. I was counting on that, on it being a film whose shape I already knew.

We waded through the mist. It was colder than the air and wetter, and it clung to my jeans up to the knee. At the top Astrid pressed the coin into the frozen turf with her thumb and poured a capful of her father's Renat over it. Then we sat, spines together, and she pulled the hide over our heads.

Inside it smelled of old animal and woodsmoke and Astrid's apple shampoo. Her back was warm against mine. I could hear her breathing and the gum clicking in her teeth, and then that stopped too.

What I remember most is how long it took. You'd think these things happen fast. It was twenty minutes, maybe more, of my own heartbeat and the cold seeping up through the seat of my jeans, and I was already composing what I'd say to Astrid afterwards, something cutting and Stockholm about it.

Then the grass moved.

It wasn't wind. There had been no wind all night, and the mist hadn't stirred. Something was walking the base of the mound, slowly, the frozen stalks crackling under its weight as it circled. I felt Astrid go rigid against me, so she'd heard it too. Or she'd felt *me* go rigid and was only reacting to that. I've thought about that a lot since: two frightened girls back to back, each one the other's proof.

It went around once, then twice. On the third pass it stopped behind me, where Astrid was supposed to be watching. But we were under the hide and neither of us could see anything at all. The rule had been useless from the start, and Astrid must have known.

"Linnea."

It was my mother's voice. It was Mamma calling the way she called up the stairs when dinner was ready, a little tired, a little fond. Mamma was asleep two kilometres away with her earplugs in.

I bit the inside of my cheek until it bled, and I didn't answer.

"Linnea," the voice said again, closer. Then, in the same tired, fond tone: "Ask her where her mormor is buried."

Far away, the church clock began to strike. Astrid threw off the hide and the cold hit my face like water. The clearing was empty. The mist lay exactly where it had been, an unbroken white ring with no path through it except the one we'd made coming up.

"Did you hear that?" Astrid's eyes were huge. "The deer?"

"Deer," I said.

"Must've been." She was already laughing, the shaky laugh of someone badly relieved. "Did you get anything? I didn't get anything. That was so *boring*."

Then she crouched, dug the coin out of the turf with her house key, and pocketed it.

"What? It's five kronor."

I looked at her. I tasted blood. I thought about asking.

I didn't. I told her no, nothing, and we walked home, and I lay in bed with my jacket still inside out until the window went grey.

Years later I went back and walked the churchyard. There are a lot of Bergströms buried there. I didn't find the grandmother, but I didn't look very hard, and I left well before dark.

I still don't answer when someone calls my name from behind me. My husband thinks it's a hearing thing, and I let him.

response:
# Útiseta

Astrid knocked on my window at a quarter past eleven: three knocks, a pause, one more. I was already dressed. I'd been lying on top of the covers since ten in jeans and my father's old army jacket, listening to Kent on my Walkman with the volume low so I'd hear her.

It was the first week of October, 1995. The midnight sun was long gone, and the dark had come back the way it does up there, all at once, like a lid.

"Leave that," Astrid said when she saw the headphones around my neck. "They don't like noise that isn't yours."

She said things like that flatly, as if she were reading off a bus timetable.

We walked the gravel road past the Konsum and the last streetlight, then onto the logging track into the forest. Astrid carried a Myrheden IK sports bag under her arm. When I asked what was in it, she listed the contents, ticking them off on her mittened fingers: her grandfather's reindeer hide, two cans of folköl, a candle, matches, and the knife.

"What's the knife for?"

"Iron. You keep it in the ground beside you. Mormor says it's so they know you're not one of them." She shrugged. "Or so you can find your way back. She says it different ways."

The wind moved through the pines above us, and for a second it sounded like people talking low in the next room, voices coming through a wall without words. Then it stopped.

The mound sat in a clearing half a kilometre in. Everyone called it Kungshögen, though nobody knew which king. It was just a hump of earth under heather and lingonberry, about as tall as a man, with one crooked pine growing out of its side. In daylight, kids sledded on it. In the dark it looked larger than I remembered, and rounder, like something breathing very slowly.

Astrid stopped at the edge of the clearing and faced me. Her breath smoked.

"Rules," she said. "Once we step over the ditch, no talking unless I ask the question. Sit facing north. Hide over your head, all the way. Don't look out. If you hear your name, don't answer. If someone touches you, don't answer. If you hear footsteps, don't count them."

"Why not count them?"

"Because then you'll know how many there are." She almost smiled. "And when we leave, we don't look back. Not once. Okay?"

"Okay."

"We ask about Johanna Lindqvist. Whether she's the one who told Berg about the cigarettes."

That was the point, as far as I understood it. That was the game. The month before, we'd burned a strand of Patrik Nyström's hair over a candle, and the next day he'd fallen down the stairs at school, and we'd laughed until we couldn't breathe. It had felt like a dare. It still did, mostly.

We stepped over the ditch.

Astrid poured half a can of folköl into the heather at the foot of the mound, and the beer foamed pale in my flashlight beam. She pushed the knife into the earth up to the hilt. Then we climbed up, sat down side by side on the cold top, and she pulled the hide over both our heads.

It stank of mothballs and smoke, and underneath that, something I didn't have a word for. Something old, like the inside of a church.

Then there was nothing. My breathing. Astrid's. The cold soaking up through my jeans. A car somewhere far off on the E4, and then not even that.

The wind came through the pines again. I tried to hear it as wind.

Astrid spoke, quiet and very clear. "Did Johanna Lindqvist tell Berg about us?"

The wind stopped.

I mean it stopped completely. Up there you get used to a forest that always makes some sound: needles ticking, branches settling. All of it went out at once, and the silence that replaced it was so total I could hear my pulse in my ears, like someone walking on snow.

Then the hide got heavier.

Not by much. It was as if someone had leaned on it gently from behind. Astrid was on my left. I could feel her shoulder against mine and both her hands in her lap. The weight was on my right, and behind me, and it settled there the way a person settles when they've decided to stay a while.

I didn't move. I told myself it was the hide slipping, or the cold, or my own blood. I told myself very carefully.

"Linnea," someone said.

It came from below, from inside the mound, it seemed, though that wasn't possible. It was my mother's voice, exactly as it sounded when I was little and had a fever. Patient. A little tired.

I felt my mouth open. Astrid's hand found mine in the dark and squeezed until the bones ground together, and I closed it.

I don't know how long we sat there. Eventually the wind came back all at once, a long breath through the pines, and carried in it, so close to my ear that it stirred my hair, was something that was not quite a word. It had two syllables and an old burr to it, like the way Astrid's grandmother spoke when she forgot I was from Stockholm.

The weight lifted.

We walked out without looking back. I remember that the gravel behind us crunched just after our steps, every step, and stopped when we stopped. I did not count.

Under the streetlight, Astrid laughed too loudly. "Your face," she said. "God, your face." But her hands shook so badly she couldn't light her cigarette, and I had to do it for her.

"Did you hear it?" I asked. "At the end."

"Hear what?"

She was looking past me, at the dark between the trees.

"We left the knife," she said.

---

I'm in my forties now. My mother is dead. I never found out who told Berg about the cigarettes. Johanna Lindqvist moved to Umeå, and I think she's a dentist. I've decided that what I heard was the wind and the cold and two girls who badly wanted to be frightened.

But years later, I looked up the word in a dictionary of old Västerbotten dialect. I'd never been able to forget it.

As near as I can tell, it means *stay*.

response:
# Gone South

## Chapter Two

The saxophone guy on Royal Street is playing something slow and greasy, the kind of song that sounds like it's apologizing for something it would absolutely do again. I stop to listen because I don't know where else to stop.

Inventory: one backpack. Thirty-eight dollars. A phone I turned off somewhere around Jackson, Mississippi, because Mom has Find My iPhone and the instincts of a bloodhound. One granola bar. Zero plan.

Marlene, the trucker who picked me up outside a Pilot station, was nice for about three hundred miles. Then she asked how old I was, and I said nineteen, and she looked at me like I was a bad check. She dropped me on Canal Street at seven a.m. with a "Good luck, sugar" that meant *not my problem.*

Fair.

The street's already packed. Tourists carry drinks the size of fire extinguishers. A man painted silver stands perfectly still. Somebody's hosing puke off the sidewalk. The whole city smells like that and fried dough and the river, all at once. It's gross. It's also the most awake I've felt in sixteen years.

Then, because my brain is a jerk, I'm back at the kitchen table.

Dad didn't yell. That was the worst part. I had a whole speech ready for yelling. Instead he set down his fork and walked out to the garage, and Mom said, "We'll pray on it," like I'd told them I had a rash. My little brother Caleb asked if this meant I couldn't be on his kickball team anymore, and Mom said *Caleb, go to your room,* and that's when I knew.

I miss Caleb so much it's like swallowing a rock.

I don't miss the rest of them. I don't. I keep checking.

---

By noon I've walked the Quarter twice and eaten the granola bar. I'm on a bench in Jackson Square, watching a tarot lady read for a sunburned bachelorette, when a guy sits down next to me. Forties. Polo shirt. Nice teeth.

"Phone dead?" he says. "You keep looking at it."

I didn't know I was doing that.

"Got a charger in my car. And I'm about to grab lunch." He smiles. "You look like you could use lunch."

I could. God, I could. And he looks so *normal*. He's like every dad at every church potluck I ever got dragged to. That should probably be a warning, but instead it feels like a hand on my shoulder.

"I'm Ray," he says.

I open my mouth to say okay.

"*There* you are." Someone drops onto the bench on my other side and hooks an arm through mine. "Cuz, I been looking everywhere. Your mama's gonna kill us both."

Ray's smile doesn't move. Something behind it does.

"Family," the stranger tells him, bright as a knife. "Thanks, though."

Then I'm being walked, fast, past the cathedral and around a corner.

"What the hell—"

"Ray's not lunch," they say. "Ray's a car ride you don't come back from. Everybody out here knows Ray."

They let go. They're seventeen, maybe, with a bleached buzz cut grown out dark at the roots. There's a cast on their left wrist, covered in Sharpie. It's the same word written over and over, then scratched out until it's just black.

"Jules," they say. "You're new. You got that bus-station look."

"I didn't take a bus."

"Worse."

My heart's going like I ran a mile. Part of me wants to say thank you. Part of me wonders why a total stranger cares, and what it's going to cost.

"Why'd you do that?"

Jules shrugs. "Somebody did it for me once." Their phone buzzes. They don't look at it. "You eat?"

---

Jules buys us shrimp po'boys from a corner store on Dauphine, peeling a twenty off a roll of bills that definitely didn't come from a paper route. I don't ask. Jules sees me not asking and looks relieved.

We eat on a stoop. It's the best thing I've ever put in my mouth, and I'm halfway through before I realize I'm crying a little, which is humiliating. Jules just hands me a napkin.

"So," they say. "What're you running from?"

I could lie. I've been lying for years. That's the whole "concerning behavioral patterns" thing, really: me trying on different versions of myself to see which one people would let live.

"I told my family I'm trans," I say. "Went great. Ten out of ten."

Jules doesn't flinch. Doesn't say *are you sure.* Just: "What do I call you?"

"Taylor."

"That the real one?"

I think about Mom at the table, using my old name like a thumbtack, trying to pin me back down.

"It is now."

"Cool." Jules bumps my knee with theirs. "Taylor."

That's it. One person on one stoop says my name back to me like it's normal. I didn't know it would hit this hard.

The phone buzzes again. This time Jules looks, and something in their face shuts like a door.

"Gotta go do a thing."

"What thing?"

"A thing." They stand. "Covenant House is on Rampart. They got beds. They'll try to call your people eventually, so don't give 'em your real last name till you're ready." A pause. "Or meet me by the sax guy on Royal. Midnight. I know a spot."

"Why should I trust you?"

Jules grins, crooked. "You shouldn't. First smart question you asked all day."

And they're gone.

---

11:52 p.m. Royal Street.

I turned my phone on for nine seconds at sunset. Forty-one missed calls. One text from Mom: *Please just tell us you're safe.*

Not *come home.* Not *we love you.* Just that. I didn't know what to do with it, so I turned the phone off again.

The sax guy is still going, playing for almost nobody now. It's a song that keeps almost resolving and then doesn't. I drop a dollar in his case. Thirty-seven left.

Covenant House is six blocks away. Going there would be smart. Safe, probably.

Or I could wait for a kid with a cast full of scratched-out words and a phone they're scared of, who maybe saved my life today for reasons I don't understand.

The song ends. He wipes his face and starts another.

I stay.

response:
# Gone South

## Chapter Two: Make Groceries

The guy's name was Ray, or maybe Roy, and for six hours he was fine. Talk radio. Sunflower seeds. A Saint Christopher medal swinging off the mirror like a hypnotist's watch. Then somewhere past Hammond my phone lit up where it was charging off his dash. The screen said MOM, and underneath, in the preview, it said the name.

The old one.

Ray-or-Roy looked at it. Looked at me. You could actually watch him do the math.

So now it's 6:40 in the morning and I'm standing on Canal Street with a backpack, forty-three dollars, and a phone at 12%, because he yanked his cord out of the socket before I'd even shut the door. Like he was taking back a present.

New Orleans smells like somebody poured last night's beer in the gutter and then set the gutter on fire. It's already hot, a wet-mouth hot, like the air's been breathed before. A man in rubber boots is hosing down Bourbon Street, and the water runs past my sneakers, kind of brown.

I think: *You did it. You actually did it.*

I also think: *You are going to die in a city you know exclusively from a Disney movie about a frog.*

Both feel true. That's been happening a lot lately.

I walk, because walking is the plan. Walking is the *whole* plan. A guy's asleep in a doorway under a cardboard sign that says TOO UGLY TO PROSTITUTE, and I laugh. Then the laugh curdles into *how long till that's me*, and I walk faster.

11%. Three texts.

*Where are you.*
*Your father is driving to Kevin's.*
*Please just tell me your safe.*

No question marks. And *your*, wrong one, which means she was crying, because this is a woman who corrects my grammar at the dinner table. I hate how well I know her. I hate that I want to text back *it's you're*, just to make her laugh, like I'm still the kid she thinks I am.

I turn the screen off. Like that'll save the battery. Like the battery is what's draining.

---

The girl finds me, not the other way around.

I'm on the concrete steps by the river doing math on whether a four-dollar beignet is a reasonable use of ten percent of my net worth when somebody drops down two feet away and says, "Don't."

She's my age, maybe. Bleached buzzcut gone dark at the roots, cut-off Dickies, a gray pit bull leaning on her shin like a sack of flour.

"Don't what?"

"Whatever you're doing with your face. You look like a brochure." She does a voice. "*Runaways, Aisle Three.*"

"I'm not—"

"Backpack's too clean. Shoes are too clean. You keep checking a phone you're scared to turn on." She shrugs. "Tourists'll give you money. Other people'll give you attention. You don't want the attention."

"What other people?"

She shrugs again, at the whole city.

"I'm Wren. Like the bird. This is Gumbo." Gumbo thumps his tail. "What's yours?"

And here's the thing: nobody has ever asked me that. Not when I could actually answer.

"Taylor."

She just nods. Like it's a name. Like it's just *my* name. "Cool."

I almost cry over a dog named Gumbo, which is embarrassing for everyone involved.

---

Wren knows things. Which Walgreens bathroom doesn't have a code. Which café lets you fill a water bottle if you smile. Which cops are "fine" and which are "Lord, no." She buys me a beignet with a five she pulls out of her sock, and powdered sugar gets all down my black hoodie, and she laughs so hard Gumbo starts barking.

She says she's from Akron. Got here in March.

But later she says she needs to "make groceries." And earlier, when a lady in scrubs passed the cathedral, Wren pulled her hood up and faced the wall until the woman was gone. I'm from nowhere, but I'm not stupid. Nobody from Ohio says *make groceries*.

I don't call her on it. You don't get to ask about someone's lies on day one. That's, like, a day-three thing.

4%.

"You don't have a charger?" I ask.

"Nah."

Except when she bends to clip Gumbo's leash, her bag gapes open, and there's a white cord coiled at the bottom. Clean. New.

My stomach does a thing.

---

By the time the sky goes peach over the river, the brass band in Jackson Square is playing "When the Saints" for the four hundredth time and my feet feel like raw hamburger.

"So there's this guy," Wren says, not looking at me. "Dell. Got a place over on St. Claude. Fans. Shower. Doesn't care who crashes."

"What does he want?"

"Nothing."

Too fast. Way too fast. She picks at the frayed hem of her shorts.

And I don't know. That's the wall I keep walking into, all day, in the dark. I don't know if Wren is my friend or a really nice-looking door with something bad behind it. I don't know if Dell is a guy with a fan or a *guy*. I don't know if Mom is driving around Tennessee because she loves me or because she wants the old name back.

Probably both. Everything's both.

"Wren," I say. "There's a charger in your bag."

She goes still. Gumbo looks between us.

"It's my mama's," she says finally, real quiet, and the Ohio's gone right out of her voice. "She's in Gentilly. Fifteen minutes. I go when she's on shift."

"Then why are you out here?"

She watches the river for a long time. "Same as you, probably. Different, probably."

Then she unzips the bag and holds out the cord.

I don't take it yet. I pull out my phone instead. 3%. My thumb's shaking. *I'm okay.* I look at it. Then I add: *My name is Taylor.* I hit send before I can be a coward about it, and the screen goes black in my hand like it was waiting.

"Not Dell's," I say.

Something in Wren's shoulders comes down an inch. "Yeah," she says. "Okay. Not Dell's."

Gumbo stands, shakes himself off, and leads the way.

# Gone South

## Chapter Two: The Arriving Part

The strap slips off my shoulder for maybe the fortieth time since Earl kicked me out of his truck, and I hitch it back up like that's going to fix anything.

Earl was fine for three hundred miles. Jesus fish on the tailgate, Skoal in his lip, talk radio about the border. Then the sun came up past Slidell and he got a proper look at me: my hands, my jaw, the chipped polish I'd forgotten to pick off. The cab went quiet. I know that quiet. It's the same quiet that filled our kitchen two nights ago, right before Dad turned his back and faced the sink.

"This is you," Earl said on Canal Street. It was not me. Nothing here is me.

So. New Orleans.

Here's what nobody tells you: the running part is easy. It's the arriving that'll kill you.

I check my phone. Thirty-one missed calls. Mom: *Taylor please just tell me ur safe.* Nothing from Dad. Dad doesn't text. I power it off before I can do something stupid, like cry in front of a Walgreens.

Inventory: forty-three dollars. Four granola bars. One phone charger, no outlet. One extremely loud heartbeat.

The French Quarter at eight a.m. smells like bleach and last night's bad decisions. Men in rubber boots hose vomit off Bourbon Street while a sax player warms up on the corner like the world isn't ending. Iron balconies drip with ferns. Everything's beautiful and rotting at the same time. I'm thinking *I could love it here*, and also *I'm going to die here*, and both feel equally true.

I end up by the river because it's the only thing I recognize. Water's water, even when it's brown and the size of God.

"You're gonna want to quit that."

A girl sits on the steps of the Moonwalk, feeding pigeons a beignet I'd bet money she didn't pay for. Her shaved head is growing out patchy. Army jacket three sizes too big. Nails bitten down to raw pink.

"Quit what?"

"Looking up. Tourists look up. Cops look at kids who look up while carrying their whole life on one shoulder." She nods at my strap, which picks that exact moment to slide down to my elbow.

"I'm not—"

"Sure." She brushes sugar off her hands. "I'm Rook."

"That's not a name."

"Neither's whatever you're about to say."

"Taylor."

She squints, sizing me up, and I brace for it: the look, the quiet. Instead she says, "Okay, Taylor. He, she, something else?"

Sixteen years. Nobody has ever asked me that. Not once. My throat does something humiliating.

"They," I say. "I think. Yeah. They."

"Cool. You hungry, Taylor-they?"

And that's how fast it happens. One question, and I'd follow her into that river.

Which is exactly the problem.

---

Rook gives me the tour like she's a docent at the Museum of Being Fucked. St. Jude's does lunch Tuesdays and Thursdays. The library on Loyola lets you charge your phone if you pretend to read. Don't sleep in Armstrong Park. Don't take anything from anyone who calls you "baby."

"How long you been out here?" I ask.

"Year, about. Came over from Mobile."

An hour ago she said Baton Rouge. I don't mention it.

In Jackson Square, between the tarot readers and the guy painted silver, a man in a pressed polo smiles at us with every one of his teeth. "You kids look tired," he says. "Our mission's got hot showers. Real beds."

A real bed. My whole body leans toward the words.

Rook's fingers clamp around my wrist, and she steers me away so fast my backpack slides off completely.

"That's Gene," she says, two blocks later. "He's not a pastor, and it's not a mission."

"How do you know?"

She doesn't answer. Her thumb rubs the inside of her own wrist, back and forth over a pale raised line, and I decide that's an answer too.

Mom used to say nobody's nice for free. She said it about Jehovah's Witnesses and car salesmen and, once, about Mrs. Pruitt's casserole. I used to roll my eyes. Now I'm watching Rook buy me a Coke with change from a pocket that was empty an hour ago, and I'm running the math. What does she want? What's the catch? When does the bill come?

Around sunset she tells me to wait outside a laundromat on Rampart. Through the window I watch her cross the street and lean into the passenger side of a silver sedan. Thirty seconds. Something passes from his hand to hers. When she comes back she's got two shrimp po'boys and won't meet my eyes.

"Where'd you get money?"

"Found it."

I eat it anyway. That's something I'll have to think about later. It's the best thing I've ever tasted, and I hate myself a little for that.

---

Rook's place is a gutted shotgun house in the Marigny with a back door that only pretends to lock. Mattress, candle stub, a saint card of somebody I don't recognize taped to the wall.

"Your strap's been making me crazy all day," Rook says. She unlaces one of her boots, threads the lace through my busted buckle, and knots it twice. "There."

"Now your boot's gonna fall off."

"I got another lace." She doesn't. I can see both boots.

Later, in the dark, she says, "I got a brother. Eli. He's nine."

I wait.

"I wasn't from Mobile. Or Baton Rouge."

"I know."

"Yeah." A long breath. "If I go back, I'd have to tell somebody what happened. And then they'd take him somewhere, and it'd be my fault." The candle gutters. "Rook's not my name either."

"I figured."

"You can't tell anybody that."

"Who would I tell?"

She laughs, but not like anything's funny, and after a while her breathing goes slow.

I turn my phone on. Forty-four missed calls now. I type *I'm okay* and stare at it until the screen dims. Mom is in that phone. So is the kitchen, and the sink, and Dad's back. I think about Eli, nine years old, somewhere, and a girl who isn't named Rook, and a man in a silver car.

I delete it. Type it again. Delete it.

I don't know who to trust. Maybe not her. Maybe not me.

But I shoulder my bag to test it, and for the first time since Tennessee, the strap stays put.
