# The Morska Conspiracy

The door gave without a sound. Someone had oiled the hinges.

That was the first wrong thing, and Aya filed it away as she stepped into the underhold. Katra's breath was close behind her, and Simeon's heavier tread brought up the rear. The air was cold and thick with the stink of rendered blubber. The vault stretched long and low ahead of them, its ceiling ribbed with the bones of some leviathan the guild's founders had hauled up from the deep a century past. The great curved staves of yellowed bone sweated in the damp.

At the far end, on a plinth of black basalt, the Scythan relic waited under a bell of smoked glass. It was not quite metal. It caught the light and did not give it back.

So did Mother Harrow.

The lamps came up all at once, wicks hissing, whale-oil flame leaping behind brass cowls. Aya counted six men along the walls before she stopped counting. She saw lever-guns, a harpoon pistol with its barbed head gleaming, and a brute with knuckles of riveted iron.

The guild leader sat in a high-backed chair beside the plinth as though it were her own parlour. A lit pipe smouldered in one gloved hand, and a pepperbox revolver rested across her knee. She looked older than Aya remembered, or perhaps it was the lamplight, carving every line of her face down to the bone.

"Evenin', little Magpie," said Mother Harrow. "You're late. I'd the kettle on two hours past."

Behind Aya, Katra swore softly. "They said the Watch had you in irons. Said they dragged you out the Lantern Street door by your hair."

"They dragged out a woman in my coat. Cost me forty sovereigns and a second cousin." Harrow drew on the pipe. "Nothing flushes rats like a fire, Katra. And nothing flushes ambition like an empty chair."

*She staged it,* Aya thought. *The raid, the arrest, the whole of it. And we came running like hounds to the horn.*

Beneath her ribs, the immateria stirred.

It always came this way: a pressure behind the eyes, a cold like deep water, the sense of something vast turning over in the dark to look at her. She had only to open the door. The things on the other side were always hungry, and they were always near.

The shadows at the vault's edges began to thicken.

A click. The man beside Katra had a pistol at her temple.

"I'd not," said Mother Harrow mildly. "Whatever you're reaching for, girl, it'll want a moment to find its legs. Jory needs rather less."

Aya looked down. A pale line ran across the flagstones at her feet. It was coarse salt, poured thick as a finger and threaded with iron filings.

"Old wives' nonsense," Harrow said, following her gaze. "So I thought. Turns out the old wives knew a thing or two."

Aya let go. The dark withdrew, sullen, like a tide reluctant to leave the shore. She felt it lingering behind her eyes, waiting.

"Hands," said Harrow.

Rough hands came for her then, and cord bit into her wrists. Simeon made a low sound as they forced him to his knees. Katra spat at someone and earned a backhand for it. No one fought. There was no fight to be had.

Harrow rose and crossed the floor, unhurried, boot heels ringing on stone. She stopped before Aya and studied the mask, black lacquer with a magpie's beak, for a long moment.

Then she hooked one finger under its edge and lifted it away.

Cold air touched Aya's face. She held herself very still.

"Well, now." Harrow's voice changed. It softened, almost, and that was worse than any snarl. "Lord Veyle's girl. Gods' teeth. I'd wondered where the Magpie learnt to talk like she'd swallowed a dictionary."

Katra had gone silent. Aya didn't dare look at her.

"You've your mother's jaw," Harrow said. "I saw her hang, you know. Gallows Square, winter of 'sixty-one. Half the city turned out. She didn't scream, I'll give her that. Not even when the rope ran short and she danced."

*Don't,* Aya told herself. *Don't give her that.*

The memory came anyway. She saw her mother's bare feet, blue in the cold, and heard the creak of hemp. She felt her father's hand on her shoulder, gripping hard enough to bruise, as though he could hold her still enough that no one would ever look at her and see the same thing.

And now someone had. Whatever came of this night, there was no putting the mask back on.

"You'll want to think carefully," Aya said, and was distantly proud that her voice did not shake, "about what you do next."

Harrow's brows rose. "Will I?"

"I am the only daughter of Lord Edmund Veyle, Second Secretary to the Admiralty. My father sits on the Harbour Board. He signs the tariffs on every barrel of oil that passes through Morska." She held Harrow's eye. "Dead, I am a scandal that lasts a fortnight. Alive, I am a key to every customs house from here to the Northern Reach."

"Alive," Harrow said, "you're a witch."

The word dropped into the vault like a stone into a well.

One of the bodyguards shifted his weight. Another touched the brass charm at his throat. Aya saw the flinch, the old fear. These were men who trusted only steel and powder, and they looked at her now as though she might split open and something might crawl out.

*And they would not be wrong,* she thought.

"A witch," Harrow went on, "is worth a good deal to the Crown. The Inquisitors pay bounty by the head, and a bonus, I hear, when it's a lord's head that rolls with it. Your father'd swing beside you for harbouring. I'd be pardoned of a dozen sins by sunrise."

"Then you'd be a fool," Aya said. "A pardon is worth one night's sleep. My father is worth twenty years of them. Hand me to the Inquisitors and you trade the goose for a single egg."

Simeon, on his knees, let out a breath that might have been a laugh. "She's not wrong, Mother. Pains me to say it."

"Hold your tongue, Simeon. You'll have your turn."

Far beyond the walls, out across the black water of the harbour, a foghorn sounded.

Once. Twice. Three times.

The low notes shuddered through the stone, through the old bone of the ceiling, through Aya's ribs. Somewhere in the vault, a lamp guttered.

Simeon closed his eyes. "Three for a drowning," he murmured. "Always three."

Mother Harrow stood listening until the last echo faded into the dripping dark. Then she turned the magpie mask over in her hands, her thumb tracing the cracked lacquer of the beak.

"A goose, is it," she said softly. "Let's find out how loud you honk, my lady."

The door gave without a sound.

That was the first wrong thing. The underhold was older than the guild, older than Morska's harbour walls, and old things complained. This one only swung inward on a breath of cold air that smelled of wet stone, tallow, and the sickly sweetness of rendered blubber.

Gas lamps lined the passage beyond, their mantles sputtering in iron cages. Each one breathed light in ragged gasps, and with every gasp the shadows of the vaulted ceiling stretched across the flagstones and drew back again, like fingers testing the dark. The ceiling was whalebone, Aya realised: the ribs of some drowned leviathan, braced into the masonry.

"Smells like my nan's kitchen," Katra muttered.

"Your nan rendered whale?" Simeon whispered.

"My nan rendered whatever fell off the cart."

Aya raised a gloved hand. At the passage's end the vault opened into a round chamber, and upon a plinth of black basalt sat the reason for all of it: the Scythan Reliquary, a cage of yellowed bone no larger than a lantern, bound in tarnished silver chain. Even from here she felt it, a pressure behind the eyes, a tide drawing at something beneath her ribs. The immateria pooled thick about it, the way rainwater gathers at a drain.

*Too easy. Nothing in this city is ever this easy.*

She stepped into the chamber.

"Evening, petal."

The lamps along the far wall flared as someone opened the cocks, and the shadows peeled back to reveal Halina Brask seated on an upturned crate. A clay pipe was clamped in her teeth, and a harpoon pistol rested across her knees like a sleeping cat.

She did not look like a woman who had spent the night in the cells at Tidegate. Her greatcoat was dry. Her iron-grey braid was neat as a hangman's coil. Behind her stood four men in oilskins, each holding something brass and ugly: two scatterguns, a boathook, and a contraption of copper coils crowned with a glass bulb that buzzed faintly, like a fly against a windowpane.

Katra swore. Simeon said nothing at all, which was worse.

"Crushers came for me at four bells," Brask said. "Dragged me out in irons, very theatrical. Cost me a fortune to arrange, and you lot made it worth every farthing. Six hours, it took you, to start carving up my house."

Aya's heart hammered against her stays. Without quite meaning to, she reached for the place beneath the world, that cold seam where things waited, patient and hungry. On the flagstones, the shadows leaned toward her.

The man with the copper contraption threw a switch. The bulb flared violet, and something inside Aya's skull rang like a struck bell. The seam slammed shut. She staggered, and the shadows snapped back into their proper shapes.

"Ah-ah." Brask tutted. "Varnholt make. They call it a damper. Don't ask me how it works. Magnets, I'm told, and a dead man's teeth. Gentlemen, if you please."

There was no struggle worth the name. Katra's knives were stripped from her boots and sleeves, and Simeon's pepperbox was plucked from his coat. Rough hands forced all three to their knees on stone slick with seep-water, and cord bit into Aya's wrists.

Brask rose, knees cracking, and crouched before her. Her breath stank of tobacco and lamp oil.

"Now then. Let's have a look at my little ghost."

*This is the moment*, Aya thought, absurdly calm. *After this there is no going back to the drawing room.*

Fingers hooked beneath the edge of her mask. Cold air struck her damp face.

Brask stared. Then she laughed, a wet, phlegmy bark that echoed off the bone ribs overhead.

"Well, I'll be scragged. Lady Aya Ashcombe. I've seen that face in the *Courant*, love, simpering on your da's arm at the Regatta Ball." Her smile thinned. "Seen your mam's too. On the gallows bills."

Katra's head jerked round. "*Lady?*"

"You told us your father was a chandler," Simeon said quietly.

"I told you he dealt in oil." Aya did not look at them. "He owns the Ashcombe Rendering Company."

Katra made a sound that was not quite a laugh.

*Two lives*, Aya thought, *kept apart like oil and water.* Now they were running together, and she could see exactly where the mixture led. A cell at Tidegate. A priest of the Vigil with his iron and his questions. A short walk at dawn. And the sound she had never forgotten, of the trap dropping beneath her mother's feet.

"The Vigil pays fifty crowns for a live witch," Brask mused. "More for a titled one, I'd wager. They do love a lady on the scaffold. Draws a crowd."

Aya lifted her chin and found her drawing-room voice, the one that had made dukes' sons stammer.

"Fifty crowns. And you'd be a fool to take it."

"Go on, then, your ladyship."

"Sell me to the Vigil and they'll want to know how long a witch has been running jobs under your roof. Whose purses she lifted. Whose doors she opened." Aya held the old woman's gaze. "They'll have this place torn to the foundations by Sunday. But return me to my father quietly, and he'll pay. He spent two thousand guineas trying to keep my mother's name out of the papers. What do you suppose he'd spend on mine?"

"He failed, as I recall."

"Then he'll be all the more motivated not to fail twice."

Brask sucked her pipe. "And once you're home in your silks, what keeps you from sending the crushers down here for true?"

"The same thing that keeps you from selling me. You know what I am. I know where you sleep." Aya managed a small, cold smile. "Mutual ruin, madam. The most reliable contract in Morska."

"And them?" Brask nodded toward Katra and Simeon.

"They come with me. Unharmed. Or there's no bargain."

"You're haggling on your knees, petal."

"I've haggled in worse positions."

For a long moment, Brask said nothing. Behind her the damper buzzed, and the Reliquary sat silent on its plinth. Aya still felt its pull, faint through the violet haze. Beneath it, impossibly, came a whisper in a voice she had last heard through a nursery door. *Clever girl.*

She did not let herself believe the bargain would hold. Her father had stood stone-faced in the crowd at Tidegate and had not wept. Would he pay to recover a witch? Or would he pay the Vigil to make certain she never came home at all?

"Simeon, isn't it?" Brask said at last. "You write a fair hand, I hear. You'll pen the letter." She stood, and the shadows rose with her. "And if his lordship don't pay, your ladyship, I'll sell you to the Vigil by the pound."

The gas lamps guttered. The damper's whine faltered with a hitch and a stutter, then steadied.

No one else seemed to notice. But on the wall behind Aya, cast long across the stone by the failing light, her shadow had not knelt.

Whale-oil lamps hung dead in their brackets. The air tasted of brine and tallow, and beneath that of something older, a cellar-sweetness Aya knew from the family crypt at Hollesmere.

Behind her, Simeon's watch ticked. *Tick. Tick. Tick.* She had never noticed how loud it was.

"Lamps are cold," Katra breathed. "Grisham's crew should've had 'em lit."

"Grisham's crew," said Simeon, "should be a great many things."

Aya stepped past the threshold. At the far end of the vault, on its plinth of black basalt, the Scythan relic waited. It was a lattice of dark metal no bigger than a heart, threaded with veins that were not quite there. Even from forty paces she could feel it, the way one feels a held breath in a crowded room. The immateria pressed close here, thin as wet paper. Something on the other side turned to look at her.

Then the lamps came up all at once.

Light flared down the length of the hall, hissing, and with it came the clatter of brass. A dozen bolt-throwers levelled from the galleries, their harpoon heads glinting with salt-crusted iron. Six men in oilskin and riveted plate stood between the trio and the plinth. Before them, in a chair of carved whalebone she must have had carried down for the occasion, sat Agata Vey.

She was not in a cell. She wore a greatcoat the colour of a bruise and was peeling an orange with a gutting knife.

"Evening, little crows," she said. "Come to pay respects to the dear departed?"

Katra swore, low and filthy. Simeon said nothing at all. The watch ticked.

Aya reached without thinking, the way one reaches for a banister in the dark, for the cold place behind her eyes where the immateria lived. For a heartbeat she felt them answer, the long-fingered things, the patient things, crowding up toward the seam.

Then a bell rang somewhere above. Small. Brass. The sound went through her like a nail through a palm. The seam slammed shut, the things on the other side went silent, and Aya was on her knees on the wet brick with blood running hot from her nose.

"Hush-bell," Vey said pleasantly. "Ministry make. Lovely bit of engineering. They used one like it on a woman up Gallowgate way, oh, eight years past. Kept her quiet right up to the drop."

*She knows.* The thought arrived cold and complete. *She has always known.*

Hands seized her. Katra snarled and kicked until a cudgel butt found the back of her knee. Simeon raised his palms with the weary courtesy of a man declining a second sherry. All three were dragged forward and thrown down on the stones before the whalebone chair.

Vey leaned forward and hooked one finger under the edge of Aya's mask.

"Let's have a look at our clever bird."

The leather peeled away, and cold air touched her cheeks. Aya made herself lift her chin. *A Desmarais does not look at the floor.* Her father's voice, absurd and unbidden. She met Vey's eyes.

The guild leader's face did not change. Only the knife paused in its work.

"Well," Vey said softly. "Well, well. Lady Aya Desmarais. Lord Edmund's girl." She smiled, and it was not unkind, which was worse. "You've your mother's jaw. I saw her hang, you know. Stood near the front. She didn't beg. I respected that."

Katra's head jerked round. "*Lady?*"

"Later," Aya said.

"Oh, there'll be no later, pet," Vey said. "That's rather the point." She ate a segment of orange. "I let it be known I'd been lifted. Wanted to see which of my ravens would go for the eyes first. Didn't expect it'd be a peeress with a witch's blood in her." She gestured with the knife at the bodyguards. "These lads trust steel. Brass. A good harpoon. They don't trust *you*. Can't say I blame them."

*Better the knife,* some small, cowardly part of her whispered. She crushed it.

"You'd be a fool to kill me," she said. Her voice came out level, and she was distantly proud of that.

Vey's brows rose. "Go on."

"My father sits on the Admiralty Board. He holds the whaling charters for half the northern fleet. *Your* fleet, the ones you skim. If I vanish, he will turn this city inside out, every dock and every warehouse. You'll have constables in your bilges by Thursday."

"Or," Vey said, "he'll thank me. Quietly. A witch daughter's a dreadful embarrassment to a man in his position. One hanging in the family's misfortune. Two looks like breeding."

The words landed precisely where they were aimed. Aya let them. "Then sell me to him alive. A daughter returned is worth more than one fished out of the Morska with her throat open. He'll pay to keep it buried. He'll pay *forever*." She swallowed iron. "I'm not a corpse to you, Agata. I'm an annuity."

For a long moment the only sound was the watch.

Simeon cleared his throat. "If I might observe, it is a very good watch. Keeps excellent time. At present it tells me the Ministry's patrol passes the Cutwater Stair at a quarter past. If they heard that bell, madam, you'll want to decide what we're worth rather quickly."

Vey looked at him, then at Aya. Then, for the first time, she looked toward the plinth, where the Scythan relic sat dark and patient. Aya was certain of it now: it was listening.

The knife resumed its slow work on the orange.

"Bind them," Vey said. "All three. And somebody stop that bloody ticking."

response:
# The Last Outpost

## Chapter One: A Double, Neat

"Nets, the twins are cheating."

"The twins are always cheating, Brannock. You keep playing them anyway."

"Hope springs eternal." He slides his empty mug across the bar. "So should this."

I refill his ore-cutter's ale, and he shuffles back to the holo-tiles, where the Kessler twins grin at him in eerie unison. At the end of the bar, Dovi the spice merchant hunches over a napkin, drafting love letter number nine to the woman who runs the fuel depot.

"Nets. What rhymes with 'hydraulic'?"

"Nothing you want in a love letter."

The recyclers hum. The hydroponic mint on the sill is finally recovering from the night Kessler-the-younger tried to smoke it. It's a Tuesday at The Last Outpost, and I've spent four years building exactly this kind of boring.

Then the airlock cycles, and a stranger stumbles in with the cold still clinging to them. Thessaline, by the look of them: grey-blue skin, and tentacled dreads that should hang loose but are knotted up tight, twitching as if they're tasting the air for danger. They slide onto the stool in front of me the way you do when you're trying not to be noticed.

"Vega whisky, neat." A pause. "Better make that a double."

"Rough shift?" I reach for the real Vega, not the bathtub stuff I pour Brannock after his fifth.

"Rough year." Four-fingered hands wrap around the glass. "This is the Last Outpost?"

"Says so on the sign. Last stop before nothing."

"That's what they told me." One dread uncurls toward me, then snaps back as if it's been scolded. "Sorry. They do that."

"Mine do worse." I tug at my own copper tangle, uncut since I got here. "I'm Nettle. Nets, if you tip."

"Pell." They knock back half the double and shudder. "Is Nets short for something?"

There's a little hook in the question. I can always tell when someone's fishing.

"It's short for Nettle. Keep up."

Pell smiles, but the dreads don't. "I heard there's someone out here who used to fly for the Corvane Syndicate. Best ghost-runner on the rim. Could slip a hauler past a blockade and make the sensors apologize."

I polish a glass that's already clean. "You heard wrong. Out here we've got miners, merchants, and one very bad poet."

"I can hear you!" Dovi calls.

"You were meant to, sweetheart."

Pell doesn't laugh. "Thessaline can taste a lie. It's like copper on the tongue. You're very good," and a dread twitches my way, "but you're not *that* good."

Behind me, a glass hits the deck and bursts like a gunshot.

I'm crouched below the bar before I've decided to move, my hand reaching for a sidearm I sold two years ago. My heart's slamming. Across the room, Kessler-the-elder raises both hands.

"My bad, Nets! Put it on Brannock's tab!"

"The hell you will," Brannock growls.

I stand slowly. Brush off my apron. Pell watches me with eyes like dark water.

"Not a ghost-runner," they murmur. "Just jumpy."

"Everyone's jumpy out here. Asteroids." I pass a broom over the bar. "Kessler. You break it, you sweep it."

When I turn back, there's a data chip on the counter. Syndicate black, with a little silver crow pressed into the casing.

"Put that away."

"I need to disappear, Nets. Not change-my-name-and-pour-drinks disappear. Nobody-ever-finds-me disappear."

"Then you came to the wrong bar."

"I came to the *only* bar." Pell's voice cracks. "I kept ledgers for Corvane. I saw numbers I wasn't meant to see."

"What numbers?"

"Mining claims. Fuel depots. Little outposts with little red marks beside them." Pell holds my gaze. "Corvane wants the rim, and they don't plan to ask nicely. So I ran. They've got a cutter on my trail. Two days out. Maybe less."

Cold settles in my stomach. "And you led them here."

"I didn't have anywhere else to go."

"You had the entire galaxy."

"I had a rumor." Pell nudges the chip an inch closer. "And a ledger. Your name's in it. Not Nettle. The other one."

I don't touch the chip. I don't need to. I know which name it holds, and I know what the Syndicate does to people who leave without permission.

"I'm not going back."

"I'm not asking you to go back. I'm asking you to help me go *forward*." Pell finally lets the dreads fall loose, a curtain around their face. "Because whether you help me or not, they're coming. And they're not just looking for me anymore."

"What does that mean?"

"A bounty went up on the boards an hour ago. Both our faces. Fifty thousand credits each."

I make myself breathe. "How many people in here have seen it?"

Pell glances at the comm-bands glowing on half the wrists in the room. "Anyone who checks."

As if on cue, Brannock's band chimes. He glances at it, frowns, and looks up, straight at me. Then he looks back down at his tiles.

I look out at my people. Brannock owes twelve thousand on his claim. The Kesslers' rig has been held together with sealant and prayer since spring. Dovi wants to buy a ring he can't afford for a woman who hasn't answered letters one through eight. Mags is in the back singing off-key to the protein vats, and she's the one who gave me this job without asking a single question about where I'd come from.

Fifty thousand credits. They'd never. They'd *never*.

Probably.

"Nets?" Dovi waves his napkin. "Will you read this one? I need an honest opinion."

Honest. Right.

"In a minute, love," I call, and my voice comes out perfectly normal, which is the worst talent I've got.

Pell slides their empty glass across the bar. "So. Will you help me?"

I don't answer. I pour myself a Vega whisky instead. Neat.

Better make that a double.

response:
# The Last Outpost

## Chapter One: Within Tolerances

The gravity hiccups at a quarter past nineteen hundred, right on schedule, and every drink on the bar does a little shimmy in unison, like a chorus line that's had one too many.

Old Dobbs catches his ale before it climbs the rim. "Nets, you ever gonna get Tully to fix that?"

"Tully says it's within tolerances."

"Tully's within tolerances, and look at him."

In the corner booth, the Pyrrhic twins are bickering again, antennae crossed.

"Oi," I call. "If you're breaking up, do it quietly. If you're making up, do it in your quarters."

"We're not breaking up!" says one.

"We're *absolutely* breaking up," says the other, and steals his twin's fries.

Mother Spore, the lichen colony who runs hydroponics, pulses a contented green on the warm vent by the window. It's a soft night. A good one.

Then the stranger sits down.

She doesn't sit so much as fold. She's Thren. Thick tentacled dreads hang past her shoulders, every one askew and twitching like they've had a fright. Her flight jacket is scorched at the cuff.

"Vega whisky, neat." She presses her palms flat to stop them shaking. "Better make that a double."

I pour. The gravity dips as I set it down, and the whisky leans toward her like it wants to be drunk.

"Rough jump?"

"Rough week." She drinks half. "Rough life, if I'm honest, and I'm usually honest. Can't help it." One tendril lifts, tastes the air near my face, then curls back. "You're the bartender?"

"Nettle. Nets, if you tip."

"Sable." She almost smiles. "I'll tip, Nets. I've got nothing, but I'll tip."

"Nothing's a bit thin for Vega prices."

"Station master impounded my ship forty minutes ago. Docking arrears." She gives a small, frayed laugh. "So that's a fun development."

"Harlan loves his paperwork. Cry at him and he'll give you a week. He's soft about crying."

"I don't have a week." She slides the glass back, and I refill it without asking. "I'm here for work."

"Ore or cargo?"

"People." She lays a holo-chip on the bar. "Recovery. Bounty, if you want the ugly word."

The chip flickers. A woman blooms above the bar in blue light. She's younger, her hair cropped regulation short, her collar pinned with the caduceus-and-star of the Hegemony Medical Corps. She hasn't learned to smile with her eyes yet.

I know her. I used to see her in the mirror.

*DR. AUDRA VELL. THEFT OF CLASSIFIED BIOLOGICAL MATERIAL. DESERTION. 400,000 CREDITS. LIVE DELIVERY ONLY.*

I keep my hands moving. Wipe a rim. Set down a coaster.

"Pretty," I say. "What'd she steal?"

"They won't say. Which means it's embarrassing." Sable's tendrils drift toward me, slow as kelp. Thren don't read minds. They read sweat, pulse, the chemistry of fear. Everyone on the Rim knows you don't lie to a Thren. "Tip says she ran out this way and found work in service. Cooking, maybe. Bartending."

"Lot of rocks out here. Lot of bartenders."

"Mm." A tendril brushes the air an inch from my wrist. "Do you know her?"

There it is. Eleven years since anyone asked.

"I don't know anyone by that name," I say. True enough. Audra Vell died the night I walked off the *Benevolence* with a cold-case of plague vaccine under my coat.

Sable's tendrils hover. Their tips flush a faint, uncertain violet.

"That's a careful sentence."

"I'm a careful woman. You'd be amazed how many brawls I stop just by picking the right words."

"How long have you worked here, careful woman?"

"Long enough to know Harlan cries at weddings."

"That's not a number."

"It's a better story than a number."

Violet again, a shade deeper. "And before this?"

"Somewhere with worse whisky."

"Doing what?"

"Listening to people's problems. Same as now."

She laughs, a real one this time, and it surprises us both. "You're good at this."

"At what?"

"Not answering."

"Occupational hazard. You want answers, try the fortune machine by the airlock. It's broken, but it's *very* confident."

She studies me a long moment. Then she looks at the holo, and something in her face caves in.

"I don't want to do this, you know." She says it to the whisky. "I used to haul medicine. Clean work. Then my brother borrowed from the wrong people on Kesh, and now they own his contract. Four hundred thousand buys him back with change left over."

"And if you don't find her?"

"Then Teo works the Kesh refineries until his lungs give out." Her tendrils sag flat against her back. "So I find her."

"That's a hell of a thing to carry."

"Yeah." She taps the chip dark. "And I'm the nice option. The Hegemony posted it open-board this morning. Every skip-tracer between here and the Cinder Gate saw it. I just happened to be closest." She turns the empty glass in her fingers. "Give it four days and this place'll be full of people who don't say please."

"Four days," I repeat.

"Maybe three."

Dobbs slides down two stools, ale in hand. "You play Kesh stones, Sable? Nets here's hopeless. Owes me forty credits and a pie."

"Thirty," I say.

"Forty, with interest."

"Maybe later," Sable tells him, without taking her eyes off me.

Dobbs has known me nine years. He's never once asked where I learned to set a broken wrist. He doesn't move back to his stool.

The gravity drops, hard this time, a real lurch. Glasses rattle the length of the bar. Dobbs swears. The twins grab each other. Sable's whisky leaps clean out of its glass, hangs in a trembling amber bead for half a heartbeat, and splashes back down.

Everyone looks at the ceiling.

Sable looks at my hands.

They haven't moved. Eight years in operating theaters, eleven behind this bar. The Hegemony trained a lot of things into me, and I've scrubbed out most of them. Not the steady hands. Never the hands.

"Funny," she says softly. "Everybody flinched but you."

I pick up the bottle. "Lots of practice. Another?"

Her tendrils lift, all of them, and turn toward me like flowers finding the sun.

"Yeah," says Sable. "I think I'll stay a while."

response:
# The Last Outpost
## Chapter Three: The Same Spot

"Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double."

I reach for the bottle without looking: third shelf, behind the jar of pickled glimmerroot nobody orders. The stranger's dreads are curled tight against their scalp, tips tucked under like a sleeping lizard's tail. On a Quell, that means fear. Or a very bad hangover.

I pour two fingers, then a third, because I'm soft.

"Long haul?"

"Long enough." They knock half of it back and wince. "Is it always this loud?"

Behind them, Borrus is explaining to the entire crew of the *Dusty Patience* why it's not technically cheating if the other person is a hologram. Dee-Dee is pelting him with peanuts. The jukebox is playing Martian swing, because it only plays Martian swing.

"Tonight's quiet," I say.

The stranger almost smiles. Then their eyes flick to the door, and the dreads cinch tighter.

I pick up my rag and start wiping the counter by the tap. There's nothing on it. There hasn't been anything on it in three years.

"Expecting company?"

"Maybe." They turn the glass in slow circles. "Can I ask you something?"

"You can ask."

"How long have you worked here?"

Wipe. Wipe. "Long enough to know when somebody's asking the wrong question first."

That pulls the smile all the way out. It's tired and crooked, with two rows of small neat teeth. "Pell." They offer a hand with too many knuckles.

"Nets."

"Short for something?"

"Short for mind your own business."

"Fair." Pell finishes the whisky. I pour again without being asked. "I was told there'd be someone here who could help me. Someone who used to do... specialized work."

The rag's gone warm in my hand.

"We've got a mechanic in Bay Four," I say. "Kiro fixes anything with a fusion core and a few things without. Doctor comes through every other Tuesday. You need cargo hauled, Dee-Dee'll do it for a fair rate and a foot rub."

"I heard that!" Dee-Dee yells.

"You were meant to!"

Pell doesn't laugh. They reach into their coat, slow and careful, the way people move when they've been shot at recently, and set something between us. It's a data spike, matte black, with a seam of red light pulsing along one edge like a heartbeat.

I don't stop wiping. I do stop breathing for a second, which is worse.

"Concord encryption," Pell murmurs. "Ninth tier."

"Then put it back in your pocket before somebody sees it."

"I can't open it. Nobody I've found can. I was told the only person this side of the Spindle who ever cracked a Ninth was a slicer called Wren."

"Never heard of her."

"The man who sent me said you'd say that." Pell watches my hand. "He also said you'd be cleaning something that was already clean."

Wipe. Wipe. I make myself keep the rhythm.

"Who's the man?"

"Runs a noodle stall on Drift Nine. Missing an ear."

Hobb. Of course it's Hobb. "Hobb talks too much. And he owes me forty credits."

"He said you'd say that, too." Pell leans in. "Look. I'm not here to sell anyone out. There are forty-one names on this spike. Contract families from the Halcyon platforms who signed papers they couldn't read. The Concord's planning to relocate them somewhere there's no coming back from. This is the only copy of the proof."

"How'd a Quell end up holding the only copy of anything?"

"I was a clerk in the records office on Halcyon. I stamped those contracts." Pell's dreads twitch. "Forty-one times."

"So take it to the Miners' Union. The newsfeeds."

"The Union rep brokered the deal. And the feeds won't touch it sealed. Nobody believes a clerk."

"And somebody wants it back."

"A hired crew. They'll be here in six hours. Maybe less."

"What crew?"

Pell hesitates. "Their ship's called the *Lantern*."

The rag stops.

It's the first time in three years it's stopped on that spot without me deciding to stop it. My hand just quits. There's a pale patch worn into the varnish there, a thousand nights of me not thinking about anything.

"Nets?"

"Captain's tall," I say. "Silver tooth. Laughs like a busted airlock."

Pell's dreads loosen in surprise. "You know her."

I taught her to play cards. She taught me how to steal a ship. She held my hair back the night we got paid for the Corvain job, while I threw up everything I'd eaten that week. Then I walked off her ship with a jacket and a forged name, and never told her why.

"Hey, Nets!" Borrus bellows. "Another round for the table! And settle something: is a hologram a person or not?"

"Depends on the hologram, Borrus!"

"See? *See?*"

"She means *no!*" Dee-Dee shouts.

I pour his round on autopilot. When I come back, the spike is still pulsing on my counter.

"If she comes here," I say, low, "she won't just take that thing. She'll take this place apart looking for it." I tilt my head at the room: the miners, Dee-Dee, the ridiculous jukebox. "These people didn't sign up for that."

"Then help me open it, and I'm gone before she lands."

"And if I can't?"

"You can."

"You don't know that."

"No," Pell admits. "But Hobb did. He said Wren never met a lock she couldn't sweet-talk." A pause. "He also said she ran because of what was behind the last one."

I look at the spike. I don't touch it.

"Hobb," I say, "really does talk too much."

"Will you try?"

Across the room, Dee-Dee hits Borrus square in the forehead with a peanut, and the whole table cheers. Somebody's pilot boots are drying on the heater again. Everything I've built in three years is sitting in this room, warm and loud and completely unaware.

I pick up the rag. I start wiping again. Same spot.

"Drink your whisky," I tell Pell. "I'm thinking."

Behind me, the comm panel by the door chirps. Incoming docking request.

Nobody's scheduled until morning.

prompt: Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. Include references to the gladiator's favorite Roman deity or mythological figure. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
response:
# The Goddess Who Keeps Accounts

I woke before the trumpet, as I always did, to the last carts leaving the city. Rome forbade wheels in daylight, so the night belonged to them: ox-carts groaning down the Via Labicana under the dark, drivers cursing in six languages. By the time the sky over the Esquiline turned the color of watered wine, the wheels had stopped and the sparrows had started, and under the sparrows came the thing I listened for—the great hollow silence of the amphitheater next door, like a held breath.

My cell in the Ludus Magnus was four paces by three. I knew because I had paced it. The straw smelled of other men's sweat and the sulphur the slaves burned against lice, and over everything, every morning, drifted the stink of the fullers' vats on the hill behind us—urine and ash and wet wool—so that I had come to associate dawn with piss. Tetraites, the Gaul in the next cell, called it the smell of the city washing its face. Eleven years here, and a woman in the Subura who sold him beans cheap.

I had been here five.

I should be clear about something, because the plebs who scratched my name on the walls did not know it and would not have cared. I was not taken in war. I was no slave, no convict. I was born free in Puteoli, a citizen, son of a man who leased forty iugera from a senator's estate and lost them one bad harvest at a time, until the steward came with the tablets and my father could not read them and I could. The lanista paid two thousand sesterces for me. I stood in his office with the bronze lamp smoking and swore to be burned, bound, beaten, and killed by iron, and the words were ordinary, like any contract, until they were not.

That is what a free man is worth in Rome: a little less than a good mule, a little more than a cook.

The trumpet went. Doors scraped along the corridor. I went out into the courtyard, where the practice sand lay pale and raked and the palus posts stood in their row like men waiting for something. The smell of barley was already coming from the kitchens. We were *hordearii*, barley-men; the porridge came grey and thick with beans and a crust of fat, and after it the medicus made us drink the ash. Bone ash in vinegar, for the strength of the frame. It tasted like a grave. I drank it every morning and thought of my father, who had drunk vinegar and water in the fields because he could afford nothing else, and wondered what he would make of his son being fattened like a prize bull for the entertainment of the men who had taken his land.

I did not think it bitterly. I had stopped that in my second year. The thing simply sat in me, the way a stone sits in a field.

The Dacians were in the far pen. Forty of them, brought up the river the week before with their hair still long and their eyes still wild, men from beyond the Danube who had never seen a city with more than one road. Trajan had broken their king and taken his gold—so much gold, they said, that the emperor could feed every citizen on the dole for a year and still build his forum with the change—and now he was giving Rome one hundred and twenty-three days of games to celebrate, and ten thousand men to fill them. I watched a doctor try to teach a Dacian boy of perhaps sixteen to hold a wooden sword. He shouted, and shouted louder, as if Latin were a nail you could drive into a man. The boy stood with his arms at his sides and wept without any sound.

There was no time to train them. They would be handed real iron in a month and sent out in pairs, and the crowd would laugh, because a man who does not know how to die well is a comedy. I had watched the senators' boxes during such comedies. They did not laugh. They talked among themselves and looked at the women and sometimes glanced down, the way one glances at weather.

Tetraites came up beside me, chewing. "Don't look at them."

"Why not?"

"You'll catch it. Pity. It gets in the knees."

Before the first drill I went to the shrine, as I did every day: a small stone altar in a niche by the gate, black with lamp-smoke, and above it the goddess with her wheel and her measuring rod and her foot on the neck of Insolence. Nemesis. Most of the men prayed to Hercules or to Mars, gods of muscle, gods who liked a winner. I never understood it. Mars did not care who lived. But Nemesis kept the accounts. She watched the man who took too much—the emperor who took a kingdom, the senator who took forty iugera, the lanista who took a free man for two thousand sesterces—and wrote it down, and waited. She promised me nothing. I liked her for that. I put a worn *as* in the bowl, Domitian's face rubbed nearly smooth, and said what I always said, which was only: *You see this. You see all of it.*

Beyond the wall the city was rising. Bakers' smoke. A fish-seller crying mackerel in the Carinae. Somewhere a child being slapped; somewhere a schoolmaster beginning the verbs. From the far side of the Forum came the hammers where they were cutting a hill away to make room for the emperor's victory, and they said the Dacians would be carved there in marble so Rome could look at them forever. It seemed a strange thing, to make a people into a story while the people stood forty paces from me, learning to hold a stick.

Three fights. That was what remained on my tablet. Three, and then the wooden sword and the gate, and the road south to Puteoli, and whatever was left of my father.

I rubbed sand between my palms and took a practice blade from the rack. Its weight was more familiar than my own name. Across the yard the Dacian boy had stopped crying and was watching me, and I did not look away, though Tetraites had told me not to.

response:
**Barley Men**

Before the sun had cleared the Esquiline, the sailors were already up on the rim of the amphitheatre, calling to one another in the accent of Misenum, and I lay on my pallet and listened to them rig the awning the way other men listen to rain. They were fleet men, pulled from the harbour to haul canvas over fifty thousand heads. My father had sold fish to men like them. I knew that flat way of saying *rope* before I knew Latin properly.

Then the gong, and the smell of the ludus arrived all at once: barley thickening in the pots, the oil they rubbed into our shoulders, the piss-bucket the new boy had failed to empty, and under everything the sweetish rot that drifted from the amphitheatre whenever the wind came from the east. There was a room beneath the arena where they stripped the dead. We did not talk about the wind.

I took my trident down from the pegs before I ate. That was my habit.

It was a fuscina, the kind made for the sand: a haft of ash as long as I am tall, three iron tines, barbed at the tips so that what went in did not come easily out. My father's had been the same length and the same wood. His was for mullet and octopus in the shallows off Baiae, where the rich men's villas stood and the water ran warm from the springs. The barbs served the same purpose. That was the thing nobody in the ludus understood when they asked why I kept it so clean. The weapon had not changed when it came to Rome. Only the fish had.

I rubbed oil into the grain and checked the lashings where the iron met the wood. Sextus, our doctor, a secutor who had lived long enough to grow fat, said I handled it like a woman combing her hair. He meant it as an insult and I took it as one, but I did not stop. At fourteen I had stood in the bow of my father's boat and learned where the weight sat, learned to throw from the shoulder and not the elbow, learned that the sea gives nothing to a man who hesitates. The lanista had bought a retiarius without knowing it. He thought he was buying a tall boy with debts.

We ate in the yard. Barley and beans, and a cup of ash in water for the bones; in the streets they called us barley-men, *hordearii*, and it was not a compliment. Across from me the new Dacians sat in a row, eleven of them, wrists still raw from the march. They had come down from their mountains in chains behind the emperor's chariot, and now Trajan had decided the city required a hundred and twenty-three days of games to properly celebrate the gold he had taken from their king, and ten thousand men to fill them.

Ten thousand. Sextus said it the way a man says the price of grain.

The Dacians did not eat. The one they had named Felix, because the lanista found that sort of joke amusing, looked at his bowl and then at me, and I pushed mine toward him and mimed eating. He had a wound on his forearm closed with pitch. He had perhaps nineteen years. He would be on the sand within the month with a wooden sword's worth of training, and the crowd would call it a battle and go home satisfied that the Danube had been crossed.

I had cost the lanista nine thousand sesterces because I was trained and had survived six bouts and the crowd knew my face. A retiarius fights without a helmet; whatever else they take from you, they leave you your face. Felix had cost four hundred. I would be matched carefully, against a secutor of similar record, because I was an investment. Felix and his ten brothers would be marched out in groups against the men of some rival school, and the sand would be raked between them.

That was the empire, I thought, with the porridge going cold in Felix's hands. Not the eagles. This yard. A free man of the Campanian coast who had sold himself for his father's debts, beside a mountain man who had never been asked, both fed on the same barley, and only one of us worth keeping alive.

Over the wall the city came up like a tide. Hammers from the Quirinal, where the emperor's Syrian architect was cutting the hill away to make room for a forum the emperor would name for himself. Carts rattling to beat the daylight ban. A bread-seller crying loaves at the gate, because gladiators had coin sometimes and nowhere to spend it. Beneath it all the river, which I could smell even here, brown and sullen, nothing like the sea.

The coins call him the best of princes. He feeds the children of Italy from his own purse, and they say he means to raise a column carved with his war in pictures, so that men who cannot read will understand what was done in their name. I have no quarrel with him. I have never seen him closer than the imperial box. But I have noticed that the love of this city is bought in the same coin my trident was, and that the gold for the forum came out of the same hole as Felix.

Sextus barked, and we rose for drill. I took the trident with me, because the wooden ones felt wrong in the hand, too light, dishonest.

The sand was already warm. I set my feet the way my father had set his in the boat, and lifted, and the weight came back up through the shoulder exactly as it always did, and for the space of a breath I was not in Rome at all but in the grey light off Baiae with the mullet moving under the hull and my father saying, *Not yet. Wait. Now.*

Then Sextus called the pairings, and I heard my arena name, and the name of the secutor from the Ludus Dacicus who had killed Priscus in the spring, and I came back to the sand.

Felix was watching me from the wall with my empty bowl in his lap. I nodded to him. I did not know what else to do. In five days the awning would go up, and the Misenum men would be shouting *rope* above my head, and I would walk out under it with my face bare and my father's weapon on my shoulder, into a noise like the sea.

prompt: Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. Mention a superstition or ritual the gladiator performs before each fight. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
response:
**Barley Men**

They fed us in the open the night before we fought, so the city could look.

The lanista's people carried the long tables out of the refectory and set them under the colonnade, where the torchlight would reach our faces. Beyond the wall the amphitheater took up most of the sky. The sun went down behind it and for a while every arch was full of red, like the mouths of ovens.

I knew ovens. My father had kept one on the Vicus Patricius, and the smell that came over the wall at this hour—the Subura bakers setting the dough for morning—still found the boy in me before I could stop it. I had not been a baker's son for four years. I had stood before a tribune of the plebs with a notary at his elbow and sworn to be burned, bound, beaten, and killed by iron, and in return the lanista had paid the debt on the oven and my mother had kept her rooms. The notary had not looked up. Men like me were not worth the lift of a head. A gladiator cannot vote, cannot witness a will, cannot lie in the ground with decent people. The law has a word for what we are. The word is *infamis*, and the crowd shouted it at us with love.

The day had gone as the days went. Barley porridge at first light, with the ash-and-bone drink the doctor swore made a man's bones hard. Then the yard: the wooden sword against the wooden post until my shoulders burned, the doctor's voice behind me—*lower, lower, you lead with your face like a drunk*—and the slap of other men's practice all around. The city called us barley men. It was not a compliment. We were fat on purpose, so the iron would find fat before it found anything that mattered.

They came in at the second hour of dark: freedmen in togas too white, their wives in saffron, boys who had slipped out to count us and settle their bets. The smell of the city came in with them—perfume and garlic and the sour wool of the dole queue, river mud, the piss-vats of the fullers across the Tiber. A senator's wife stood at the end of our table with a scented cloth pressed to her nose. She looked at me the way I had once looked at loaves. She asked the lanista something, low, and he laughed and named a figure, and she did not flinch.

"Hilarus," one of the boys called. That was my name in the arena. Cheerful. The lanista had a sense of humor. "Hilarus, make us laugh tomorrow."

Old Marcus worked the crowd with his tray of little clay bottles: a sesterce for the sweat and oil scraped off us after training. The women rubbed it into their faces. I had stopped trying to understand it.

The Emperor's games had run ninety days and would run thirty more. Dacia had paid for them. The gold came down from the mountains under guard, and it came out again as grain at the Porticus Minucia, as silver pressed into the palm of every citizen who could prove a name on the rolls, as the new forum they were carving out of the Quirinal with a noise like the world being chewed. The Senate had voted him Best, and I did not argue. He had given the city bread and allowances for its children and a column going up to tell the story. He had also given it ten thousand of us. A city can love a man for both. It does not have to choose.

At the far table sat the men from the north. They had come in chains a month ago, and they still ate like men who did not expect the food to stay. They had been soldiers—you could see it in how they sat, backs to the wall—and in the morning they would be sent out dressed as themselves, with their own curved swords, to lose the war again before the midday executions. One of them was singing under his breath. The torchlight showed me his face and I looked away. I had learned not to keep faces.

Felix's place beside me was empty. He was in the surgeon's room with his shoulder packed in wine-soaked wool, one fight from his wooden sword and his freedom, and that afternoon he had asked me what I meant to do if the clerk who paired the bouts ever wrote his name on the same line as mine. I had not answered. It sat in my chest like a stone swallowed whole.

I ate nothing. Some men ate as though it were the last meal, which it might be, and some sat with the notary at the end of the colonnade telling him which woman should have their savings. I kept my own custom. Nothing the night before, nothing in the morning, and when I came through the tunnel from the Ludus into the dark under the arena, I would stop at the grating where the sand had sifted down and take a pinch of it between two fingers and set it under my tongue. I had done this ten times. I held it there through all of it—the gate, the light, the noise, the work—and I did not swallow until I had walked out on my own feet through the gate that was not Libitina's. The sand would have me in the end; everyone knew that. But this way I had it first, a little of it, and we were even before we started. The other men thought it was for Nemesis. I let them. It is easier to be a pious man than a frightened one.

Above us the sailors from Misenum were already in the rigging of the great awning, calling to one another in the dark like men far out at sea. The torches burned down. The senator's wife let her litter take her home. Old Marcus counted his coins. The crowd went back through the gate to sleep in a city that had never once, in all its years, run out of men.

I stayed where I was, with the bread smell coming over the wall and the Dacian still singing and Felix's question sitting where I had swallowed it, and I waited for the morning to come and ask me what I was.

response:
# The Lighthouse Keeper

**Dubh Artach Lighthouse, 14th March 1962**

Dear Ma,

Landed Tuesday. They swing you off the boat on a rope, and the Principal, Mr Buchan, took my hand at the top and said "You'll do" before I'd done anything. Three of us on the rock, and the rock you could walk round in five minutes if the sea let you, which it doesn't. North-east on a clear day there's the Torran Rocks, where the water goes white for miles like somebody's shaken out a sheet, and behind them Ben More on Mull with snow still in the gullies. On a dull day there's the brass and your own face in it.

I'm fine. The paraffin gets in your hair. Tell Mrs Docherty I asked after her.

Davie

---

**Florence Street, 2nd April**

Dear David,

Your letter came Thursday. On a rope. I'll not think about it.

A man that says you'll do before you've done anything is either daft or kind, and you'll ken which by now.

Nothing here. Mrs Docherty's knee. The Co-op's stopped the Friday van. Men from the Corporation were in the back court with a tape, measuring the middens like they were buying them. I gave them tea. You eat.

Mother

---

**Dubh Artach, 20th May**

Dear Ma,

Fog nine days. The horn goes every forty-five seconds and you stop hearing it the way you stop hearing a clock, then at three in the morning you hear it all at once and cannot stop. Hamish, the other assistant, whistles the same tune while he does the brass and doesn't know what it is. I've counted the stairs. A hundred and twelve, or a hundred and fourteen, depending on the night.

What did the Corporation want with the middens?

Davie

---

**Florence Street, 11th June**

Dear David,

The stair's coming down. The whole street from the pub to the chapel. They've offered me Castlemilk, a new house with a bath and a view of nothing I know. I told them I'd think about it. I've been in this house thirty-one years, so I'll think for thirty-one years and see how they like that.

Mrs Docherty's away to her daughter's in Paisley. Her window's boarded already. You'd think they'd wait till a body was cold.

It'll be "The Northern Lights of Old Aberdeen." It's always that.

Mother

---

**Dubh Artach, 23rd August**

Dear Ma,

I'll be honest, there being nobody here to be anything else in front of. I'm not managing. I've started saying goodnight to the lamp, out loud. Buchan heard and said nothing, which was decent, and I lay till the dawn watch with the sea coming up the tower like somebody climbing. Yesterday it cleared and there was Ben More so plain I could see the burns running down it, and I had to go below so Hamish wouldn't see my face.

Twenty-eight days to the relief. I'm thinking I'll not come back after. Tell me straight about the house.

Davie

---

**Florence Street, 15th September**

Dear David,

You'll not chuck it on my account. I've watched men chuck things.

Straight, then. I've signed for Castlemilk. The flitting's November. The house is fine. It's the stair I'll miss, and the Dochertys' wireless through the wall, which I cursed for twenty years.

I wasn't going to write this. Your father wrote regular the first year as well. Every fortnight from Halifax, then every month, then I was at the window for the postman telling myself it was the rent I was watching for. I'm no saying you're him. I'm saying I ken what a letter weighs.

Burn this.

Mother

---

**Dubh Artach, 19th November**

Dear Ma,

Didn't burn it.

Relief was due the 6th. Nothing can land. Wednesday night a sea came over the top of the tower, the whole tower, and the stone shook under the bunk like a tram going by. Buchan said in forty years it had done that twice. Then he made the tea.

I've read your letter more times than I've counted the stairs. You at the window and me out here staring at Mull as if it owed me something. The pair of us looking at land. You were never the one who stopped writing, and I'll not be either.

I've put in for a shore station. Buchan signed it. He says I'll do.

Davie

---

**14 Ardencraig Road, Castlemilk, 9th January 1963**

Dear David,

Your November letter came in December. I'd it read before my coat was off.

I'm in. Fourth floor, no lift. There's a bath and I've had two. From the kitchenette you see the Campsies with snow on them and not a soul I know for a mile. The buses are a disgrace. I brought the clock and the good chair and left the rest to the Corporation. Hogmanay I had the wireless on and the window open an inch so it would sound like it was coming through a wall.

Did they say about the shore station?

Mother

---

**Turnberry Lighthouse, Ayrshire, 4th March**

Dear Ma,

They said. Turnberry. Mainland, with a cottage on the end of it and a cooker that doesn't want paraffin. From the back step Ailsa Craig sits in the firth like a loaf left out, and the Girvan bus goes by the road end twice an hour.

There's a room at the back that gets the morning. I've measured it. The clock fits and the chair fits and I'm thinking you'd fit too. I'll be up on Thursday with a van and a lad from the station.

You'll not lift anything. Four flights. I ken.

Davie

---

**Castlemilk, 7th March**

Dear David,

Thursday then. I'll have the kettle on and the window shut.

Mother

response:
# The Lighthouse Keeper

**Sgeir Liath Light**
**14 October 1961**

Ma,

Landed Tuesday. They put me across from the boat in a breeches buoy like a sack of coal, and the Principal, Mr Guthrie, said that was the easy way. The tower is 130 feet and I've counted the stairs three times and got three answers, so either the stairs move or I do.

Three of us. Guthrie; a man Weir who cooks and talks about his greenhouse in Oban like it's a sick relative; me. The wireless gets the shipping forecast and the football if you hold the aerial out the window. Four weeks on, two off, if the boat can get in. Weir says it mostly can't.

I'm fine. Tell Mrs Rennie I'm fine. Don't send a cake, it'll arrive as crumbs.

Davie

---

**Kintra Street**
**2 November**

Davie,

Sent a cake anyway, in the tin, and you'll eat the crumbs.

The Thistle lost. Mrs Rennie's lassie is expecting again, God help her. A man came from the Corporation about the roof and went away again.

Your father's chair is where it was. I'm not moving it.

Write properly next time, not jokes. I can tell the difference, I had you for twenty-six years.

Ma

---

**Sgeir Liath**
**19 December**

Ma,

Relief missed. Nine days we've watched the boat come out and turn back. Weir has stopped mentioning the greenhouse. Guthrie plays patience and loses, and I've started knowing which card he'll turn before he turns it, which tells you how the days go.

You said write properly. So.

The quiet isn't quiet. The lens turns by clockwork and you wind it every half hour on watch, and the weight drops down the middle of the tower on a chain, and you hear it going all night like the building's a clock and you're the thing inside it. I go out on the gallery and there's nothing. Not dark. Nothing. Then the beam comes round and shows you the water and takes it away again.

I think about the kitchen. How the kettle sits on the ring. That's about all I think.

Davie

---

**Kintra Street**
**15 January 1962**

Davie,

Something's in with this, in the tissue paper. Your father's check from the yard. You'll know it—the brass one, size of a florin, stamped 1187, with the wee hole it hung by on the board at the gate. One edge is worn down flat where he thumbed it in his pocket. Thirty-one years through that gate. They stopped using the checks in '54 and he kept it, and when they let him go in '58 he still took it out mornings and set it by his plate, and I never said a word about it, not once in three years.

I don't know what you want with it. But it's a thing a man carried out the door every morning and carried back. Carry it.

The flat's fine. No need to ask about the flat.

Ma

---

**Sgeir Liath**
**6 March**

Ma,

The check's in my watch jacket. On the dark watch I set it on the sill beside the log, the way Da set it by his plate. Guthrie saw it and asked, and I told him, and he said his own father had one from Fairfield's and he'd not thought of it in twenty years. We talked till the light wanted winding. First proper talk I've had out here. So you've done something, sending it, whether you meant to or not.

Now. I never asked about the flat. You told me anyway.

The Herald came with the relief, three weeks old. Page five, Corporation clearance schedule, and Kintra Street in the list between a pub and a bakery. Tell me.

Davie

---

**Kintra Street**
**2 April**

Davie,

Aye.

The letter came in October, the week you left. Out by August. They're offering a house in Drumchapel with a bathroom and I'm told I should be grateful.

I didn't say because you'd have come back. You'd have thrown up the post and come to carry boxes, and then there'd be the two of us in Drumchapel with no work coming in, and I've done that already. I did it with your father. I watched a grown man set a brass check by his porridge for three years because it was the only thing left that had his number on it. I'll not watch his son do it.

So now you know. I'm not greetin' and you'll not either.

Ma

---

**Sgeir Liath**
**21 May**

Ma,

I'll tell you a thing I've not said. I didn't take this post for the rock money. I took it because after Da I couldn't sit in that kitchen with his chair in it and you not moving it. I thought a rock in the Atlantic would be easier. It's the same kitchen. I'm just the chair now.

There's a thing happens out here. Nobody looks at you, weeks at a stretch, and you stop being sure you're a person. The check helped. Not because of Da—because somebody at home had thought about what to put in an envelope.

I've written to the Board. There's a shore station on the Sound of Mull with a keeper's cottage and a second room. Less money. Guthrie says I'll get it; nobody wants shore stations now, they all want the rock money.

The chair would fit in the second room. I'm not asking. I'm telling you where it would fit.

Davie

---

**Kintra Street**
**9 June**

Davie,

I've told the Corporation they can keep Drumchapel.

The chair's going in the van. So's the kettle. Mrs Rennie can have the good carpet and welcome to it.

I read your letter twice and put it in the drawer with your father's pay slips and your school reports, which is where the things go that I keep.

Bring the check back with you. It's been through enough gates. I'll put it on the sill in the new place, by whichever window looks at your light, and you can set it by your plate or not as you please.

Ma

response:
# The Lighthouse Keeper

**Sgeir Dubh Lighthouse, 11th October 1962**

Dear Mam,

Landed Tuesday. They swing you off the boat on a rope and tell you not to look down, which is like telling a man not to think of a white horse. The tower is a hundred and twelve steps and there are three of us in it: Mr Gillies, the Principal, who has been on rocks twenty-two years and says about nine words a day; Macleod from Lewis, who says more, but in Gaelic and to himself; and me.

The light turns on a weight, like Granny's clock, only the weight drops down the middle of the whole tower. When it's down you wind it up again. Forty minutes, about. Gillies says you learn to sleep in forty minutes. So far I have learned to lie down in forty minutes.

Did the coal come?

Davie

---

**Greenock, 20th October**

Davie,

Coal came, two bags short, I told him. Mrs Drummond asks after you. Put newspaper in your boots at night, it draws the wet.

Mr Rennie from the Co-op has taken the back room. It's eight shillings and he's quiet.

Your Mother

---

**Sgeir Dubh, 6th November**

Dear Mam,

Thursday there was a fall of thrushes. That's Gillies' word for it, a fall. They come in the dark and go for the light, and the glass is thick enough but they are not. I swept forty-odd off the gallery at first light with the sea coming up white through the grating, and one of them still going in my hand. Then I went up and wound the weight.

I'm not sleeping, Mam. You get your forty minutes and your head starts to go under and the bell goes. I don't know that this job is for me.

Is Rennie feeding himself or is he eating my dinners?

Davie

---

**Greenock, 30th November**

Davie,

He pays for his dinners. He mended the mangle, which you never did.

Don't be daft about the job. It's a pension and a house at the end, and your father had neither. Everybody's tired.

Mr Rennie got us a wireless at a price. I have it on for the shipping.

Mother

---

**Sgeir Dubh, 29th January 1963**

Dear Mam,

The boat couldn't land for twenty-three days. The sea doesn't go down here, it only changes its mind about which side to come from. We were on tins, and Macleod's tobacco, which is like smoking a rope. Three of yours came together and I read them in order at the kitchen table and Rennie is in every one. Rennie and the mangle. Rennie and the wireless. Rennie and the blowlamp for the pipes.

Does he sit in Da's chair?

I've not had more than forty minutes at a go since October. I count it out now, lying there. Gillies says I'm doing fine. I don't know what fine is any more.

Davie

---

**Greenock, 8th February**

Davie,

The Clyde was froze at the edges, they say. Mrs Drummond's budgie died of it.

I'm glad you're fed.

Mother

---

**Sgeir Dubh, 14th March, four in the morning**

Mam,

You didn't answer about the chair, so I have my answer.

Eleven years. I was fourteen and I minded the fire and I minded you, and nobody asked was I tired. Now I'm stuck on a rock in the sea so you can have a pension at the end of it, and there's a man from the Co-op eating off Da's plates and you can't even write me his Christian name.

I'll not come home to that. You can tell him.

The bell's going.

D.

---

**Sgeir Dubh, 20th April**

Dear Mam,

The relief came Thursday and there was nothing in the bag for me. Macleod got four. His mother can't write, his sister does it for her.

I wrote you a letter I shouldn't have, in the middle of the night, which is the only time there is here. I know what I did. I'm not asking you to pretend I didn't.

Only write. Even if it's the coal.

Davie

---

**Greenock, 3rd May**

Davie,

I'll tell you what I know about tired.

I was on my own eleven years and you were on your own with me, and the two of us never once said it. That's not a thing to be proud of, it's just what we did. Now you've gone and found out on that rock what it is to lie awake and not be able to leave. Well. I knew that before you did, and I'd no bell to blame it on.

Mr Rennie's name is Thomas. He asks for nothing and he fixes what's broke and he doesn't sit in anybody's chair, he brought his own. Whether there's more to it than the rent is my business, and when it's yours I'll tell you.

You come home or you don't, Davie. The bed's made either way.

Mam

---

**Sgeir Dubh, 2nd June**

Dear Mam,

I slept forty minutes last night and woke before the bell. First time. Gillies says that's it now, I've got it, I'll be able to do it till I'm old. I don't know if that was a promise or a warning.

I'm at the shore station from the 15th of August. I'll get the train down. Tell Mr Rennie I'll bring a bottle, and he can show me the wireless, and if he wants to tell me what he paid for it I'll let him.

And tell him thank you for the mangle.

Davie

---

**Greenock, 11th June**

Davie,

Bring the bottle. Thomas says the 15th is a Thursday and the Glasgow train gets in at twenty past six and he'll be at the station, if you'll let him.

Put newspaper in your boots.

Mam
