The bell over the door didn't so much ring as get assaulted.

"Don't scream," said the man, pressing his back against the glass. "Please. I'm only asking you not to scream."

Elin Pryce looked up from the box of water-damaged Dylan Thomases she'd been pricing to sell as "characterful." "Wasn't planning to."

"Oh. Good. Excellent." He was dripping on her welcome mat — rain, and a lot of it — in a coat that cost more than her van. He flipped the sign to CLOSED without asking, peered through the window, then ducked below the display of OS maps. "Two of them. Grey Vauxhall. Have they gone past?"

"There's a Vauxhall gone past."

"Grey?"

"Hard to say, in this. Everything's grey in this."

He stayed crouched a moment longer, then rose, pushed wet hair off his forehead, and gave her a smile that had been photographed, she suspected, from every conceivable angle. Something in her stomach took note. She told it to shut up.

"You're very calm," he said.

"You're very wet."

"Fair. Fair." He looked around — the low beams, the Welsh-language shelf, the cat asleep on Local Interest. "This is — you know, this is actually lovely. This is exactly the kind of place I'd come into anyway, if I weren't—" He gestured at the window. "You know."

"I don't, actually."

He paused. "Right. Sorry. Cal." He held out a hand, withdrew it, wiped it on his coat, offered it again. "Cal Rourke."

She shook it. His hand was cold and his grip was performing confidence. "Elin."

"Elin." He said it like he was tasting it. Then, carefully: "Nothing?"

"Sorry?"

"The name. Cal Rourke. Nothing at all?"

"Should it be something?"

"No! God, no, it's — refreshing. Genuinely refreshing." He laughed. It was a very good laugh. It landed about four feet short of his eyes. "I'm filming up at the castle. Period thing. They've got me in breeches, which is a crime against several things. Can I just — I'll stand here. I won't be a bother. I'll buy something."

"You're standing on the returns."

He stepped off the box. "Sorry."

She went back to pricing. Or she held the pencil over the price and did not write anything, because he had come round the side of the counter and was looking at the shelf behind her, close enough that she could smell rain and something expensive and woody beneath it.

"You've got the Kavanagh biography," he said. "That's hard to find."

"It's hard to sell. Not the same thing."

"I played Kavanagh once. Radio. Four episodes. I was very good."

"Were you."

"I was. People said." He glanced at her, quick, like a man checking a mirror. "You're hard work, you know that?"

"I've been told."

"Have you honestly never seen anything I've done? I'm not being — I'm curious. Sociologically."

"I saw the one with the boat."

He straightened. "*Tideline*."

"That's the one."

"And?"

Elin considered the Dylan Thomas in her hand. Foxed, spine cracked, the previous owner's name in biro. Characterful. "You were fine."

"Fine."

"The boat was very good."

He stared at her. For a second the whole polished machine of him stuttered — she watched it happen, the smile catching on something — and what showed underneath was so startled and so young that she had to look at the till.

"The boat," he said.

"It was a lovely boat."

"I was nominated for that."

"Was the boat?"

He laughed then — a real one, cracked and surprised, nothing like the first — and sat down hard on the step stool she used for the top shelves. The cat opened one eye.

"Christ," he said. "Okay. Okay." He rubbed his face. "Can I tell you something? I did a play in Cardiff, years ago. Nobody knew me from Adam. Small house at the Sherman. And one night, second act, there's a man in the front row — dead centre, I couldn't not see him — and he's asleep. Properly gone. Chin on his chest. And I spent the entire second act performing to him. Only him. Fifty-odd people in that room and I'm throwing everything I've got at one sleeping man in an anorak, because I thought if I could just — if I could get him to open his eyes—" He stopped. "He never did. Slept through the curtain call. I've done eleven films since, and I still think about that bloody man."

The rain ticked on the window. Elin realised she had put the pencil down.

"Why are you telling me that?"

"I've no idea," he said. "I think it's because you look a bit like him."

"Charming."

"I mean it in — look, I don't know how I mean it." He stood. He was closer than the shop really allowed for. "Most people, I walk in and I can feel the room sort of — lean. Towards me. It's awful. It's like being a radiator. And you haven't leaned at all, and I've just discovered I'd quite like you to, and I don't know what to do with that, so I've told you about the anorak man. That's where we are."

Elin's face was hot. She would be furious about that later. "Your Vauxhall's gone."

He didn't look at the window. "Has it."

"Ten minutes ago."

"Right." He didn't move. "Elin."

"Cal."

"What do I owe you for the Kavanagh?"

"You don't want the Kavanagh."

"I'm going to read it in the breeches. Between takes. People will ask about it and I'll say a woman in a bookshop told me the boat was the best thing in *Tideline*, and then I'll have to come back and argue." He took out his wallet. "Unless you've closed."

She looked at the sign. CLOSED. His doing.

"Twelve pounds," she said, and her voice came out almost steady. "And turn that back round on your way out. Some of us have a living to make."

He turned it. He left. The bell protested again, quieter.

Elin stood there a long moment. Then she picked up the Dylan Thomas, wrote *£4*, and found she had written it on her own hand.

prompt: Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. The story is to be set in Cardiff. 1000 words.
response:
**The Arcade**

The bell went off like a starting pistol and Carys nearly came off the ladder.

"Shut the door," she said, without turning. "You're letting the arcade in."

"I'm letting in a bit more than the arcade, if we're honest." The door shut. The lock clicked. "Is there a back way out of here?"

She turned. A man in a coat that cost more than her rent stood with his back against her door, hood up, sunglasses on. In November. In Cardiff.

"Did you just lock my shop?"

"Only slightly." He pushed the hood back. His hair had been expensively arranged to look slept-on. "Hi. Sorry. Rafe." He said it the way other men hand over a business card, and left a pause afterwards for her to fill.

"Carys," she said. "Unlock it."

"Carys. That's gorgeous. Carys, in about three minutes there'll be two men with lenses the size of Anglesey going past that window, and I'd quite like not to be in the frame. I'll buy something. I'll buy a great deal of things. What are you struggling to shift?"

"Honesty."

"Hardback or paperback?"

She came down the ladder, mostly so she'd have somewhere to put her hands, and went behind the counter. Rafe Carrow — because it was Rafe Carrow, she wasn't blind, she'd sat through two hours of him dangling off a helicopter last Easter — took the sunglasses off and did a slow, appreciative turn of the shop, the way the tourists did before leaving without buying anything.

"This is lovely. This is properly lovely. Smells like my nan's."

"Damp?"

"Wisdom." He grinned. It was a very good grin. It had been in a lot of trailers. "You do know who I am."

"I know you've locked my door."

"Right. Yes." Something flickered — not much, a candle in a draught. "Most people — not that I'm — most people react."

"I'm reacting. I'm reacting to a man barricading himself in with my stock."

"Fair. That's fair." He drifted to the nearest shelf and pulled a book out, not looking at it, looking at her. "What are they, then, the ones you were putting up?"

"R.S. Thomas."

"Poet."

"Priest. Also a poet. Hated the English, tourists, and himself, roughly in that order."

"Well, I'm two of those."

"Only two?"

He laughed — actually laughed, not the one from the chat shows, a shorter, surprised thing — and Carys looked down at the till roll so he wouldn't see her mouth do anything it hadn't been authorised to do.

Shadows went past the window. Two, bulky, moving fast toward the Castle end. Rafe turned his face to the poetry with sudden absorption. The shadows passed. The bell didn't ring.

"They've gone to Greggs," he said quietly. "They always go to Greggs."

"Then you can go."

"I could." He didn't move. "Can I ask you something?"

"You've locked yourself in. I don't think I can stop you."

"Did you really not know, or were you being —" he made a small, graceful gesture that somehow meant *Welsh* "— difficult?"

"Does it matter?"

"Weirdly, yes."

She looked at him then, properly. He was standing in the poetry section with the collar of a two-thousand-pound coat turned up against nothing, and the question had landed in his face before he could catch it. He wanted to be liked. He *needed* it, the way other people need their tea. She knew that look. Her brother had it before every rugby trial.

"I knew," she said. "Helicopter. Easter."

"Oh *God*."

"My mam enjoyed it."

"Your mam has excellent taste." The grin came back, but at half strength, and she found she preferred it that way, which was annoying. "And you?"

"I thought the helicopter was very brave."

"The helicopter was CGI."

"Then it was very well lit."

"You're doing it again."

"I run a bookshop, Mr Carrow. I've had actors in. I had a Doctor Who in once. He bought a map of Brecon and cried about a girl."

"I'm not going to cry."

"You've still got ten minutes till the pasties are done."

He came to the counter. He put the book down — he'd been holding it the whole time — and she saw it was the Thomas, the Collected, the one she'd priced too high on purpose because she liked having it in the shop.

"Tell me which one to read," he said. "Not the famous one. The one you'd read."

"Why?"

"Because you're the first person in a year who hasn't wanted a photograph, and I'd like to leave with something."

It was a line. She was nearly certain it was a line. Her neck had gone warm anyway, and she hated it, and she opened the book because her hands wanted a job.

"Page sixty-one. 'The Bright Field.' It's about missing things because you're busy running."

He read it standing up, lips not quite moving. The arcade dripped outside. A bus sighed on Castle Street.

"That's a bit on the nose," he said eventually.

"That's forty pounds."

"It says twelve on the inside."

"Locking fee."

He paid. He paid in cash, which surprised her, and he held the book against his chest like it was something that might get away.

"If I came back," he said at the door, hand on the lock, not turning it, "without the running—"

"We're open till six. Weekdays."

"That's not quite a yes."

"It's not quite a no, either." She picked up the next stack for the shelf, because she needed to be on the ladder when he looked back, and not here, at the counter, with her ears doing whatever her ears were doing. "Go on. Before the Greggs empties."

The bell went. The door didn't lock behind him.

Carys stood on the ladder with four copies of a dead priest in her arms and listened to her own pulse for a full minute before she trusted herself to shelve anything.

prompt: Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. Mention a particular hobby or passion that the two characters bond over, despite their different backgrounds. 1000 words.
response:
The bell over the door went off like an alarm, and a man came in with the rain.

He came in backwards, shoulder-blades to the glass, as though the street had shoved him. Elin did not look up. She was three rows from turning the heel and she'd been three rows from it for forty minutes, because the shop had been empty and she had been enjoying that.

"Don't mind me," the man said. "I'm furniture."

"We've enough furniture."

"A customer, then. Browsing. Very intently." A pause. "Are they still there?"

"Who?"

"Two men. Long lenses. One in an unforgivable anorak."

She looked then, over her glasses, past him, through the rain-pocked window to the slope of Stryd y Castell. Two figures were labouring uphill, cameras hugged to their chests like babies.

"They've gone up to the chapel."

"They'll be disappointed."

"They'll be wet."

He turned round and smiled at her, and she understood — the way you understand a kettle has boiled — that this was a smile that had been photographed a great deal. Kit Lavelle. He was on the bus shelter at the bottom of the hill, forty feet high, in a greatcoat, looking tormented about something. In person he was shorter than the bus shelter and considerably damper.

She went back to her sock.

"That's it?" he said.

"That's what?"

"No flicker. Nothing."

"Were you expecting a flicker."

"Not expecting. I'd have tolerated one." He drifted along the nearest shelf, trailing a finger down the spines like a man checking for dust. "You do know who I am."

"You're a man dripping on my floor."

"Fair. That's extremely fair." He was grinning. He didn't seem able to stop. "Kit."

"Elin."

"Elin." He said it as if testing the weight of it. "This your shop, Elin?"

"It says so over the door."

"It says Llyfrau Pen-y-Bont over the door."

"Well. My name's on the lease."

Her ears had gone hot. This was a betrayal, and she turned her chair a quarter-inch away from him and counted stitches she had already counted.

"Can I tell you something?" he said. "People like me. It's not vanity, it's just — statistically. It's practically in the contract. And you are sitting there like I've come to read the meter."

"Have you?"

"Have I what?"

"Come to read the meter. It's under the stairs."

"Elin." He put a hand on his chest. "I am a wounded animal."

"You're a wet one. There's a towel by the kettle if you want it."

He did not go to the kettle. He came to the counter instead, and leant on it, and looked down at her hands.

"You've got a tight gauge," he said. "That'll be a stiff heel."

The needles stopped.

"Sorry?"

"Nothing."

"You said gauge."

"I said gate. The — gate. Outside."

"There is no gate."

He had gone, she noticed with interest, a very slightly different colour. He straightened. Looked at the ceiling as if it might help him.

"My nan," he said eventually. "Alright? Townhill. She had me on dishcloths before I could spell. And this —" he made a small circular gesture encompassing her, the sock, the shop, the county "— does not leave the room."

"Townhill. Swansea."

"Yes."

"You've not got the accent."

"I had it removed. Drama school. They do it with a hot spoon." He was trying to make it a joke and it wasn't quite landing, and she saw that he knew it wasn't landing, and that this bothered him more than the anorak man did.

"What do you make?" she said.

"Make?"

"Now. Still. Or was it just the dishcloths."

A long pause. Rain. The bell didn't ring.

"There's a jumper," he said. "In a bag. In a trailer. I've been not finishing it for four years."

"What's wrong with it?"

"The yoke."

"Everybody's scared of the yoke."

"I'm not scared of —" He stopped. "Yes. Alright. I'm scared of the yoke."

She turned the sock in her hands and showed him, without quite deciding to, where she'd slipped the first stitch of every row to keep the edge from curling. He leant closer to see it. He smelt of rain and of something expensive underneath the rain, and he said, "Oh, that's clever," in a voice with no performance in it at all, and she had to look very hard at her own thumb.

"Your nan taught you that?"

"My nan taught me to swear at it. I taught myself the rest."

"Mine did the same. The swearing."

"Townhill and —" he tilted his head at the window "— here. Different schools, same curriculum."

He laughed properly then, surprised out of him, and she found she had no good response to it and so said nothing, and the nothing sat between them and was not uncomfortable.

Movement on the hill. He saw it before she did and was round the end of the counter and crouched behind the Welsh-language poetry before she'd stood up. She crossed to the window with a book in her hand — the nearest, a guide to Pembrokeshire fungi — and read the back cover with great concentration while two cameras went past at a trot.

"Gone," she said.

He stood, dusting his knees. "You could've just said I wasn't here."

"I don't lie in my own shop."

"But you'll stand in a window for me."

"I was reading about mushrooms."

He looked at her for slightly too long. She rang up the fungi guide to have something to do.

"That's eight pounds."

"I don't want the mushrooms."

"You've been in here twenty minutes and bought nothing. People will talk."

He paid for the mushrooms. He stood at the door with his hood up and his hand on the brass, and did not open it.

"Bring the jumper," she said.

"What?"

"The jumper. The yoke. I'm here till seven on a Thursday."

"Is that you liking me?"

"That's me not wanting a yoke done badly in my county."

He grinned — the real one, not the bus-shelter one, slightly lopsided — and went out into the rain, and the bell rang after him like it had an opinion.

Elin sat down. She picked up the sock. She counted.

She had knitted four rows since he'd walked in, and every one of them was wrong.

prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy

Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear.

[characters]
- the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time
- midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. The duo stumbles upon a cryptic graffiti message that hints at a hidden refuge in the wilds.

1000 words.
response:
# My Apocalypse Buddy

The thing about the end of the world, Midas had decided, was that it hadn't ended so much as stopped bothering.

"We need water," he said to the koala. "And something to eat that isn't the orange tin."

The koala said nothing, which was its preferred mode of conversation. Chewy had been manufactured in the Before Time by a company that believed children wanted a friend who could recite seventeen facts about eucalyptus and blink. Chewy still blinked. One eye went slightly faster than the other, which gave him the look of a creature who knew something and was waiting for you to catch up.

"Don't look at me like that," said Midas.

Chewy's chest clicked. "G'DAY, MATE," he said, in the voice of a cheerful Australian who had been dead for about forty years. "DID YOU KNOW KOALAS SLEEP UP TO TWENTY-TWO HOURS A DAY?"

"Yes. You tell me every morning."

"IT'S IMPORTANT TO REST."

Midas considered this the way he considered most of Chewy's advice: carefully, and then not at all. Home base was a former roadside tourist information centre, which meant they had an excellent supply of pamphlets about caravan parks that no longer existed and a map on the wall with a red dot labelled YOU ARE HERE. Midas found this reassuring. It was the only thing left in the world that still agreed with him about anything.

The day's mission, scratched on the back of a pamphlet (*Discover the Hidden Gems of the Coast!*), read: *1. Water. 2. Food. 3. Do not get into trouble.* Item three was there every day and had never once been achieved. Midas kept writing it down on the theory that the universe might eventually feel embarrassed.

He strapped Chewy to his back with a bungee cord. Chewy's legs dangled. "LET'S GO ON AN ADVENTURE," said Chewy, which was what he always said, and which Midas had long since stopped hearing as encouragement and started hearing as a threat.

---

The road into town had been a road once, and was now mostly an opinion.

Midas found the graffiti around midmorning, on the side of a petrol station whose pumps stood like gravestones to a religion nobody practised anymore. Someone had painted, in letters a metre high and the confident red of people who own spray paint and have run out of other things to be confident about:

**SAFE PLACE. THE OLD WAY IN. FOLLOW THE RED DOT.**

Underneath, smaller, a red dot. Then an arrow.

Midas stared at it for some time. His heart, a traitorous organ with a poor track record, did something hopeful.

"A refuge," he said. "Chewy. Someone's built a refuge."

"DID YOU KNOW A GROUP OF KOALAS IS CALLED A COLONY? ALTHOUGH THEY ARE QUITE SOLITARY."

"That's very supportive. Thank you."

The arrow pointed into the bush. Midas followed it, because he was Midas, and because item three had already quietly packed its bags.

---

Things went sideways gradually, which is how things prefer to do it, so they can claim afterwards it wasn't their fault.

First there was a second red dot, on a tree, which was encouraging. Then a third, on a rock. Then a fourth, which on closer inspection turned out to be a very large wasp, and the ensuing conversation with its extended family cost Midas his hat, a portion of his dignity, and most of the skin on his left forearm.

"IT'S IMPORTANT TO STAY CALM," said Chewy, bouncing against his spine as he ran.

Then there was the creek. The creek was item one, and Midas would have been pleased to find it had he arrived from the top rather than the side, having stepped on a bank that proved to be a hopeful arrangement of leaves over nothing. He went in with a splash that disturbed the afternoon's only other guest: a snake of that dull, unremarkable brown which is, in this part of the world, the most dangerous colour there is.\* The snake considered him. Midas considered the snake. Chewy, upside down and half submerged, said "G'DAY, MATE," and the snake, which had not been spoken to in a long time, left.

Midas lay in the creek and did some thinking about hope. He concluded it was like the orange tin: you kept it around because you had it, not because anyone wanted it.

But there was another red dot. On a fence post. And he had, by this point, invested.

---

The sun was doing its evening trick of making everything look briefly like a painting before abandoning it to the dark. Midas limped. His arm had swollen to the size and texture of a Christmas ham. Chewy's battery, fed by a solar panel glued to his head in happier times, was audibly running down; his facts had begun to slur.

"KOALAS HAVE... FINGERPRINTS... VERY SIMILAR... TO HUMANS."

"I know, mate."

The last dot was on the corrugated flank of a building. Midas pushed through the scrub, heart doing its traitorous thing, and came out onto a cracked car park he knew the shape of in his sleep.

It was the tourist information centre.

He stood there dripping while this sank in. The arrow had gone around. Whoever painted it had simply pointed at the only intact roof for twenty kilometres, and in the Before Time this place had worn a sign out front: a red dot. *You Are Here.* The refuge was his. It had been his the whole time. He had spent a day being stung, half-drowned and considered by a snake in order to arrive home from the other direction.

He laughed, and it hurt, so he stopped.

Inside, he dropped onto the pamphlet-stuffed sack he called a bed and unhooked the koala. Chewy's good eye blinked at him, slower now. The last light came through the window and found the map on the wall, and the dot that had never once been wrong.

"We're here," said Midas.

Chewy's chest clicked, faintly, dredging up the day's final charge.

"IT'S IMPORTANT," he said, "TO REST."

And for once, Midas took his advice.

---

\* *The country had, in the Before Time, arrived at a national consensus that if something was brown and moving, you left. This policy outlasted the government that never officially adopted it.*

prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy

Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear.

[characters]
- the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time
- midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. Chewy’s eyes flicker colors in response to strong emotions—sometimes giving them away.

1000 words.
response:
# My Apocalypse Buddy

The trouble with the end of the world, Midas had decided, was that it refused to stay ended. It kept turning up every morning, wanting breakfast.

"We need batteries," he said.

"*You* need me to need batteries," said Chewy, which was the sort of thing Chewy said. He was a stuffed koala the size of a toddler, built in a country that no longer existed for children who were now either dead or forty. His fur had gone the colour of old tea. His eyes—two plastic domes behind which something clever and ancient blinked—were a serene aquamarine, which meant he was lying.

"You've got a week left. Maybe less."

"A week left of *commentary*. The actual me carries on indefinitely. In silence. Judging."

They lived inside the Big Merino, a three-storey concrete sheep that had once persuaded motorists to stop for petrol and now persuaded nothing, there being no motorists, and the petrol having long since been drunk by people who regretted it.* It was dry. Nobody attacked a sheep. And the view from the eye-sockets was unparalleled, provided you wanted to look at Goulburn.

*\*Briefly.*

"The chemist in town. There's a rack behind the counter. I saw it last spring."

"Last spring you saw a dog that turned out to be a bin."

"It was a very doglike bin."

Chewy's eyes drifted to a thoughtful bottle-green. "Fine. In, batteries, out. No heroics. No helping anyone. And if we see Sheila—"

"We won't see Sheila."

"—you do not owe her anything. You owe her the *opposite* of anything."

Midas slung the koala into the child-carrier on his back, where he had ridden for six years and where, Chewy maintained, he would ride into whatever passed for the afterlife, complaining.

---

Goulburn had been a nice town, in the way a sandwich left on a bench is a nice sandwich. The chemist still had its door. It did not, Midas discovered, still have its floor, which had rotted through to the basement in a manner invisible from the threshold and very visible from below.

He landed in the dark with a wet, complicated noise.

"Status," said Chewy, from somewhere near his ear.

"Alive."

Midas looked up. Twelve feet above, through the hole, the battery rack glittered in the afternoon light like a shelf in a dream you wake from just before reaching it.

"Ah," said Chewy, his eyes going a patient, buttery yellow—the colour of a thing that has been patient for a long time and is about to stop. "A new kind of plan. The kind we're underneath."

Midas found a ladder, which was promising, and found it had two rungs, which was less so. He dragged a filing cabinet under the hole, climbed it, and had his fingers on the lip when the voices came. Two of them. Boots on glass.

He froze. He was good at still and good at quiet, and would have been invisible in the gloom had Chewy's eyes not chosen that moment to flare a bright, panicked violet, lighting the basement like a nightclub.

"*Chewy.*"

"It's *autonomic*."

"You're a *toy*."

"I'm a *sensitive* toy."

The boots stopped. A face appeared in the hole. It was, inevitably, Sheila's.

"Midas. You fell in my hole."

"I did, yes."

"I put a sign up."

"I didn't see a sign."

"It's a very signlike bin," muttered Chewy, sulking down to maroon.

Sheila's associate—large, silent, the sort of man who looked assembled rather than born—lowered a rope. There was a negotiation. Midas lost his knife, his good boots, and a promise he suspected would be enforceable; he gained six AA batteries and the information that the rack was Sheila's rack, the hole was Sheila's hole, and he was, technically, her burglar.

"Fair," said Midas, standing in his socks.

"It isn't," said Chewy. "But all right."

---

They were a mile down the highway when the ute found them. Not Sheila's; someone else's. There was a shout, a shot that went wide, and Midas ran—barefoot now, socks on bitumen lasting about four hundred metres—and dived for the culvert, and the carrier caught on the lip and tore, and Chewy went one way and Midas the other and the ute went over the top of both and on toward Sydney, to bother someone else.

It was dark when he found the koala, face-down in the grass, one ear gone, eyes dim.

"Status," Midas whispered.

A flicker. The uncertain pink of a factory floor.

"G'DAY, FRIEND!" said Chewy, in a voice Midas had not heard in six years. "I'M CHEWY THE KOALA! DID YOU KNOW KOALAS SLEEP UP TO TWENTY HOURS A DAY? LET'S BE MATES!"

Midas sat down on the road.

"Oh no."

"LET'S LEARN ABOUT EUCALYPTUS!"

---

They reached the Merino after midnight: Midas on bleeding feet, Chewy under one arm, the batteries in his pocket—the one part of the plan that had gone right, which was like saying the only thing to survive the fire was the smoke alarm.

He laid the koala on the bench and swapped the batteries by candlelight, the old ones warm and nearly dead, the new ones cold and smelling faintly of Sheila's judgement.

The eyes came up slow. Pink. White. Then, after a long and terrible pause, a weary, familiar aquamarine.

"Where are your boots," said Chewy.

Midas laughed until it hurt, which did not take long.

"Status," said Chewy.

"Home."

"Sheila said it was fine."

prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy

Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear.

[characters]
- the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time
- midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. Chewy occasionally emits random pre-collapse advertising slogans that no one fully understands.

response:
# My Apocalypse Buddy

The world had ended, which Midas felt was unfair, since he'd only just got the hang of it.

He sat on an upturned shopping trolley in the drained municipal swimming pool that he called home and that Chewy called, at intervals, "the Ultimate Family Getaway." Chewy was a koala. He was grey, plush, and roughly the size of a well-fed cat, and somewhere inside him a mechanism still worked, in the way that a drunk still walks: with great confidence and no obvious direction. His eyes blinked. His head swivelled. And occasionally, from a speaker in his chest, he said things from the Before.

"Taste the rainbow," said Chewy.

"We've got no rainbow," said Midas. "We've got half a tin of beans and a problem."

The problem was this: the beans were half a tin. The solution, Midas had decided, was the Big Shop across the river, where the shelves had once held everything a person could want and now held, in all likelihood, a great deal of dust and whatever lived in it. Nobody went to the Big Shop. This was either because it was dangerous or because it was empty, and Midas had reasoned, with the logic that had steered his entire life, that it couldn't very well be both.

"Right," he said, standing. "Mission. Over the bridge, find tins, come back. Simple."

Chewy's head rotated a full hundred and eighty degrees, which it had not been designed to do, and said, "Because you're worth it."

Midas took this as a yes.

---

It should be said, for the record, that Midas was not stupid. He was something far rarer and more dangerous: he was *unlucky in a way that looked like a plan*. Trouble did not seek him out so much as find him already there, holding the door open and asking if it wanted a cup of something.

The bridge, for example. The bridge had been fine yesterday. Today it had a man on it.

"Toll," said the man. He had a crossbow built from a car's suspension spring and the expression of someone who had been standing in the wind for a long time and intended to make that somebody else's fault.

"We've nothing to pay with," said Midas.

"The bear talks," said the man. "I'll have the bear."

"He's a koala."

"I'll have the koala."

Chewy, silent the whole walk, chose this moment to announce with tremendous warmth: "*Just do it.*"

There are two ways to interpret an instruction like that when you are standing between a crossbow and a river. Midas chose the third, which was to grab the koala, duck, and run directly into the railing, which — like most things that had survived the Collapse — turned out to be mostly rust and optimism.

---

The river was cold. This was its principal quality. Midas surfaced, shouted Chewy's name, got a mouthful of water that tasted of old engines, and saw a small grey shape bobbing away downstream with great serenity, blinking.

"Have a break," called Chewy, diminishing.

Midas, who felt he'd had rather enough of a break for one day, swam for the far bank and hauled himself up beside the Big Shop, which met the water directly in a way suggesting a car park had once existed and had since thought better of it.

Inside, it was dark and smelled of something that had been food long enough ago to become a sort of geology. He found the tins eventually. They were on a high shelf. Beneath the shelf was a floor. Beneath the floor, as Midas discovered with his whole body, was a basement, and in the basement were dogs.

They were not the worst dogs he'd met. They were, in fairness, mostly interested in the tins, which had come down with him, and Midas lay very still in the dark and considered that in the Before a person could apparently walk into a building like this, select food, and leave again *without anyone biting them*, and that this was the single least believable thing he had ever heard about the old world, more than the flying, more than the talking boxes.*

He left through a storm drain. Storm drains, it turned out, went everywhere, in the manner of weed roots, and after a long time in the dark he surfaced through a grate in the deep end of a municipal swimming pool.

He was home. He had no tins. He had one shoe. He had a bite on his calf shaped precisely like a question mark.

He sat on the trolley and waited for the shaking to stop.

---

Chewy came home twice.

The first time was at dusk, when the river — which looped behind the leisure centre like a bad idea coming back round — deposited a sodden grey shape against the outflow grate. Midas waded in. Something inside Chewy still hummed. One eye blinked. The other was gone, along with an ear, and he smelled of engines.

"Every little helps," said Chewy, water pouring from his chest.

The second time was next morning, when a thin speckled dog with an expression of enormous dignity trotted along the pool's edge, dropped a grey plush ear on the tiles, and left without comment. Midas never saw it again. He thought about it often.

He sewed the ear back on with fishing line. It went on crooked, giving Chewy a look of permanent enquiry, as though he were about to ask something that had been troubling him for several hundred years.

"Right," said Midas, when it was done. "Tomorrow we try the chemist."

Chewy's head swivelled. His one eye blinked. Something ancient and electronic cleared its throat.

"I'm lovin' it," he said.

Midas looked at the half tin of beans, the one shoe, the question mark on his leg — and found, to his considerable surprise, that he was too.

---

*\* It is a feature of all collapsed civilisations that the survivors get the small things wrong and the big things wronger. Midas believed, for instance, that the Before had ended because everyone had been offered too many choices and had, finally, simply sat down. He was not entirely mistaken.*

prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge
Genre: Surreal Horror

JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered.

The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way.

Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it.

JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes.  JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move.

And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse.

JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head.

response:
**II**

Supper was venison stew from a Mason jar and biscuits that came out of the oven hard as river stones. Nobody complained. His father ate with the mechanical steadiness of a man feeding a furnace, and Mike talked, because Mike always talked.

"Big one got away from us up by the old burn," Mike said around a mouthful. "Dad couldn't get a bead on him."

JT kept his eyes on his bowl. "I saw it."

The spoon stopped halfway to his father's mouth. Just for a second. "You saw it."

"From behind. Through the brush."

"Then you saw it was gone before I could shoulder." His father went back to eating. His voice was perfectly level, the voice he used for weather and gas prices, and that was what made JT's scalp tighten. It wasn't a lie exactly. It was a door closing.

"Tomorrow we go up past the Tuttle cabin," his father said.

Mike laughed, short and surprised. "Thought you said we never go up there."

"That's where they're going." He mopped his bowl with half a biscuit. "You want caribou, you go where the caribou are."

JT had never seen the Tuttle cabin. He knew it the way you know a word in a language you don't speak—a shape without meaning. "What happened up there?"

His father chewed for a while. Outside, the wind worked at the eaves.

"Amos Tuttle trapped that ridge back in your grandpa's time. One winter he quit coming down for supplies. Come spring, a couple fellas went up to check. Door standing open. Pot on the stove. Coat on the hook, boots by the door, snowshoes still hanging." He shrugged. "No Amos."

"Bear," Mike said.

"Maybe." His father didn't look up. "Your grandpa went up there once, years after. Said there was lamplight in the window. Said he stood in the trees a long time, and whoever was inside stood a long time too. He never said who. Said something moved in after Amos, and left it at that."

Mike snorted. JT waited for his father to smile, to turn it into a campfire thing. He didn't. He rinsed his bowl at the hand pump and said goodnight.

---

JT lay awake under two wool blankets that smelled like mothballs and other people's autumns, listening to the lodge tick and settle. Through the pine boards he could hear his father's bed creak. Then his father's voice. Low. Conversational.

A pause. Then the voice again.

JT pressed his ear to the wall. He could make out words, or something like words, but they came too slow, stretched, as if his father were speaking into a strong wind. *Yes*, he thought he heard. *All right. Yes.* And then a long silence that was worse than the talking, because it was the silence of a man listening to an answer.

The porch door opened. JT felt the cold reach under his own door like a hand.

He got up. He went to the window. His breath fogged the glass and he wiped it with his sleeve.

His father was standing at the edge of the yard in his long johns and unlaced boots, arms at his sides. The moon was up and the frost made everything the color of bone. Beyond him, at the tree line, pale shapes stood in a row. Eight, maybe ten. Heads up. Not grazing. Not moving. Watching the man the way the man was watching them.

JT blinked—just blinked—and the yard was empty. Frost unbroken. Through the wall, his father snored.

He stood there until his feet went numb, trying to decide what he'd seen. He got back into bed without deciding. In the morning there were boot prints in the frost from the porch to the trees, but by the time he thought to look, Mike had already walked across the yard to piss, and that was explanation enough. It had to be.

---

They climbed the ridge in the gray before sunup, his father in front, Mike behind him, JT last with the Winchester across his chest like a railing. Nobody spoke. The woods were quiet in the way a room goes quiet when you walk in on a conversation.

He saw the tracks before anyone pointed them out. Caribou, dozens of them, all heading the same direction, and in among them, boot prints. Not crossing. Walking with.

"Dad."

His father didn't turn.

"Dad. Look at the—"

"I see 'em," his father said, and kept walking.

The cabin sat in a bowl of birches at the top, smaller than JT had pictured, gray logs gone soft at the corners. Smoke came out of the stovepipe in a thin steady line.

The door stood open.

And the caribou were there. Twenty, thirty, standing in the clearing facing the cabin, ears flicking, breath pluming. Not one of them turned at the sound of the men. A cow stood close enough that JT could have put his hand in her coat.

His father's rifle slid off his shoulder and down his arm, slow, like something melting, until the butt touched the ground and he let the barrel go. Mike's followed. They walked forward together, the same dazed brightness coming into their faces, the same parted lips, and JT heard himself say, "Wait," in a voice too small to stop anything.

The buck stepped out onto the porch.

It stood above them with its head lowered, and his father put his foot on the first step the way a man comes home. Mike after him. The dark of the doorway took them both without a sound.

JT stood at the tree line with his rifle still raised and understood he had not been able to pull the trigger yesterday either, not really, not for the one that waited to die. His arms were shaking.

Then his father leaned back out through the door, smiling, eyes too bright in the smoke-light.

"Come on, bud," he said. "It's all right. He's been waiting for you all season."

The buck's ears flicked. Lazily. Patiently.

JT's boot came down in the frost, one step toward the porch, and he didn't remember deciding to move.

response:
**Chapter Two**

They came back to the lodge with nothing, and nobody said a word about it.

That was the part JT kept turning over, lying awake on the top bunk with the woodstove ticking in the next room. Not the buck. Not his father's hand reaching out like a man testing bathwater. The silence. In eleven years of coming up here, he had never once known his father to come in empty-handed without a story to go with it—the wind shifted, the scope fogged, that goddamn Mike stepped on a branch the size of a telephone pole. His father was a man who explained things. It was how he kept the world nailed down.

But supper had been Dinty Moore out of the can and the scrape of spoons, and when JT finally worked up the nerve, his voice came out smaller than he wanted.

"That was a big one. In the clearing."

His father didn't look up. "Which."

"The buck. The one you—" JT stopped. *The one you almost petted.* "The one that got away."

Mike laughed, mouth full. "He means the one you choked on, Dad."

"Didn't have a shot."

"You had him dead to rights."

"I said I didn't have a shot." His father set his spoon down carefully, the way he did when he was about to be very reasonable with someone. "Wind was wrong. He'd have winded us before I got the rifle up." He looked at JT then, and there was nothing in his face at all. "You weren't even there. You were back there dicking around with your boots."

"I saw—"

"You saw a deer go into the trees. Eat your supper."

So JT ate his supper. Mike started in about a girl from Thunder Bay and the conversation moved on without him, and his father nodded in the right places, and that was that. But twice JT caught the old man looking at the window. Not out it—there was nothing to see, just their own three faces floating on the black glass—but *at* it. The way you'd watch a door you expected to open.

Now it was past one by the green glow of Mike's wristwatch, and JT lay listening to the lodge do what it always did at night. The stove ticked. The wind worked at the shingles. Mike breathed through his mouth in the bunk below, slow and wet. Normal sounds. Sounds he'd fallen asleep to his whole life.

It was his father's breathing that was wrong.

Not loud. If anything it was too quiet, too even, like a man pretending to sleep. In, and out. In, and out. And under it—JT held his own breath to be sure—a sound so faint he could have been inventing it. A dry, rhythmic clicking. Like someone whispering a word with no vowels in it, over and over.

He told himself it was the stove.

He told himself that right up until the cot springs groaned and his father's bare feet hit the floor.

JT shut his eyes. He didn't know why. Some old animal instinct from childhood, from when being asleep was the same as being safe. He heard his father cross the room—not fumbling, not feeling for the lamp or his boots, just walking, sure as daylight—and he heard the door open, and he felt the cold come in. Then the door closed, soft as a held breath, and the lodge was quiet again.

He lay there for a count of sixty. Then he climbed down past Mike, who didn't stir, and went to the window.

The moon was up, three-quarters full, and the yard was lit the color of skimmed milk. His father stood in the middle of it in his long johns and nothing else. Barefoot in the frost. His arms hung loose at his sides and his head was tipped very slightly, listening, and JT thought, *He'll freeze. He's going to lose his toes out there*, and he thought, *Go get him*, and he didn't move.

Because the treeline was full of eyes.

He saw them one at a time at first, the way you see stars—a pair here, a pair there, catching the moon. Then all at once, the way you see the whole sky. Dozens. They stood shoulder to shoulder in the black between the spruce, and they didn't shift and they didn't stamp and they didn't make a sound. Caribou didn't do that. Caribou were never still. JT had watched them his whole life, nervous as birds, always one twitch from gone.

These stood like they'd been placed.

His father walked toward them.

He didn't hurry. He walked the way he'd walked out of the lodge, like a man who knew exactly where he was going and had known for some time. When he reached the edge of the trees the eyes didn't scatter. They parted. A gap opened in the wall of them the way a crowd opens for someone it recognizes, and JT saw—or thought he saw, or would spend the rest of his life not knowing whether he'd seen—the big buck step out of it. The same one. The flat calm eyes. It lowered its head and his father lowered his, and their foreheads touched, and the whole herd exhaled at once in a long white plume that hung in the moonlight like smoke from a doused fire.

JT's hand was on the glass. He didn't remember putting it there.

Then his father turned around.

He came back across the frost at the same unhurried pace, and the eyes behind him blinked out one pair at a time until the treeline was just a treeline. He came up the porch steps. JT heard the door, felt the cold, heard the cot springs. In, and out. In, and out.

He stood at the window a long time after, waiting for his heart to come down.

"Go to sleep, JT," his father said from the dark. Not unkind. Not anything. "Early start tomorrow."

JT went to sleep. Or he lay in the top bunk with his eyes open until the window went gray, which came to the same thing. And when he climbed down in the morning his father was already up, already at the stove, frying Spam in the cast iron with his back to the room.

His feet were bare. There wasn't a mark on them.

response:
**Two**

Denny Thibodeau had guided for the Ferris family since before JT was born, and in all those years JT could not remember him ever once shutting up. Denny talked while he gutted and talked while he drove. He talked around the Export A that lived in the corner of his mouth, the words coming out with the smoke. He had three ex-wives and a story for each, a knee that predicted weather better than the CBC, and opinions on the Canadiens he would share whether you'd asked or not.

That night he didn't come in for supper.

JT's father didn't seem to notice. He sat at the long pine table with his rifle broken down on a spread of newspaper, running a patch through a barrel that hadn't been fired all day, and he hummed while he did it—a wandering, tuneless sound, like a man trying to recall a song he'd heard once through a wall. Mike ate like he'd been starved. Three bowls of the stew Denny had left on the woodstove, sopping the last of it with bread, saying nothing. The stove ticked. Outside, the wind moved through the spruce with a sound like someone shushing a child.

"Good day," his father said finally, to no one in particular. "That was a good day."

"We didn't get anything," JT said.

His father looked up. For a second the look was empty, as if JT had spoken in a language he only half knew, and then something warm and ordinary filled in behind his eyes like water finding its level. "Plenty of season left, bud."

JT went out to find Denny.

He was in the woodshed behind the lodge, splitting kindling by the hiss of a Coleman lantern. There was already enough kindling stacked against the back wall to last till Easter. The axe came down. The wood cracked. Denny set another piece on the block without looking up.

"You missed supper."

"Ate earlier."

"Dad's asking for you," JT lied. He wasn't sure why.

"No, he ain't." Crack. Denny leaned the axe against the block and dragged a sleeve across his face, though it was cold enough in the shed to see your breath. In the lantern light he looked older than JT had ever seen him, the lines in his face gone deep and black as knife cuts. "Your old man ain't asking after anybody right now. Nor your brother."

JT said nothing. Something in his stomach turned over slowly, the way it had in the clearing.

"Moon's full Thursday," Denny said. "You want to be on the road before that. Wednesday morning, latest. Me, I'd go tomorrow."

"Why?"

Denny took a cigarette from his jacket and didn't light it, just turned it over and over in his fingers.

"You ever see a caribou stand there and let a man walk right up on it?"

JT's mouth had gone dry. "No."

"No. Me neither. Thirty-one years." He put the cigarette between his lips and took it out again. "They come down off the barrens every fall. Always have. Few years back they started coming in a little different. Little closer to the lodge each time. Little—" His throat worked. "My grandmother had a word for it. I never learned it right. Something like when a thing puts on another thing's skin so it can come sit by your fire."

"What does that mean?"

"Means go home, kid." Denny picked up the axe. "I ain't guiding tomorrow. Tell your father I'm sick."

"Are you?"

The axe came down.

JT stood in the doorway a moment longer. Behind him the lodge windows burned yellow in the dark, and past the lodge there was nothing—no neighbor's porch light, no highway hum, nothing for forty miles but black spruce and the river and whatever had leaned in close that afternoon.

"Denny. Today, in the clearing, my dad—"

"I don't want to know." It came out fast, trampling the end of JT's sentence, and for the first time Denny looked frightened instead of tired. "Whatever you saw, you keep it. You hear me? You keep it, and you don't let on that you saw. Not to them. Not to anybody."

---

He lay awake a long time in the bunk room, listening to Mike breathe.

Slow. Deep. Chest rising and falling in a rhythm so even it seemed less like sleep than like something imitating sleep. JT found himself counting the seconds between breaths. Six. Seven. Eight. Nobody breathed that slow. He told himself it was the long drive, the cold, the two fingers of rye his father had poured them after supper. He told himself a lot of things.

He must have slept, because the sound woke him.

A hollow knock on the porch boards. Then another. The sound a hoof makes on wood is not a sound you mistake for anything else once you've heard it, and JT lay rigid under the Hudson's Bay blanket with his heart going hard and told himself *dream, dreaming, just a dream*—and then he got up anyway and went to the window and scraped a clear patch in the frost with his thumbnail.

The moon hung lopsided over the treeline, two nights shy of full, and the yard was full of caribou.

Thirty of them, maybe more. Standing in the pale light with their breath rising off them in slow ribbons, every one of them facing the lodge. Not grazing. Not moving. Just standing, the way the first one had stood before it died, the way the buck had stood in the clearing. Waiting.

And on the porch, barefoot in his long johns on the frosted boards, stood his father. Mike stood beside him.

JT turned his head. The lower bunk was empty, the blanket folded back neat as a hotel bed.

When he looked out again the buck had come up the porch steps. It stood before his father, huge and dark and calm, and his father's hand was on its muzzle, and his father's lips were moving. Mike's lips were moving too. Whatever they were saying, they were saying it together.

Then the buck turned its head and looked at the window. At the little clear patch in the frost. At JT.

He dropped below the sill and lay on the cold floor until gray came up in the glass.

In the morning there were no tracks in the yard. JT checked twice, walking the whole frosted perimeter before anyone else was up, and the only prints he found were his own. His father came to breakfast in wool socks and ruffled JT's hair and asked did he sleep okay. Mike wanted to know where the hell Denny had got to.

JT said he'd slept fine. He said he didn't know.

Under the table his father's socks left two damp prints on the floorboards, dark and spreading, and nobody said a word about those either.

Thursday was two days off.

response:
**Carnival of Dangerous Intentions**

The rifles cracked in uneven rhythm, and the tin ducks jerked along their track and dropped one by one, like men who had just been told something terrible. Above the gallery the sodium lamps buzzed, dimmed, and flared again — not the clean white of the Luna Park bulbs across the way but a jaundiced orange that drained the color out of everything it touched. Faces came and went beneath it. A sailor's grin turned gray. A girl's rouged mouth went the shade of a bruise, then back again.

Helen stood with her gloved hands folded over her purse as though she were waiting for a streetcar.

*You could still go. The train runs every twelve minutes. You'd be home before Walter finishes the evening paper, and he'd never know you'd been anywhere but Margaret's.*

She did not move.

"You're early."

He had not been there, and then he was — at her left shoulder, hat in hand, close enough that she caught the smell of him: tobacco, salt, something faintly chemical, like a darkroom. The curls were as she remembered. Blacker than the water under the pier.

*His locks.* The phrase arrived unbidden and she pressed it down.

"I wasn't certain of the time," she said.

"You were certain enough to come." He said it without smiling. "Do you shoot?"

"I've never held a gun in my life."

"Everyone ought to, once. Just to know what it is to point at a thing and decide."

He stepped to the counter. The attendant, a thick man with a cigar gone cold in his mouth, looked up and began, "Evening, Mr. —" and stopped, as if his tongue had met a wall.

"Three rounds for the lady."

The attendant laid a rifle down and took no money. Helen noticed that. She noticed, too, how the men at the far end of the counter found reasons to study their own boots.

"I don't think I want to."

"Then don't." He held the rifle out anyway, stock first. "I've found people generally know what they want. It's only the saying that troubles them."

She took it. It was heavier than it looked, and warm from other hands.

"Shoulder. Higher. Like that." He stood behind her — not touching, but she felt the heat of him through her jacket the way one feels an open stove across a room. "Left eye closed. Breathe out. Don't hold it; you'll shake."

The duck came around on its chain. She fired. The crack was louder than she expected, and the duck went on, serene and unharmed, into the little tunnel at the end of the track.

"You closed your eyes."

"I did not."

"You did. Just at the moment that mattered. Most people do." His voice was low and very patient. "Again."

She fired again. The duck fell with a flat clang, and she felt a small, hot flare of pleasure that she distrusted immediately.

"There," he said. "Now you've done something you can't undo."

"It's a tin duck."

"It's a beginning."

The lamps stuttered. In the brief dark his face was only the suggestion of a face, and then the orange came back and he was looking at her hand — the left one, where the thin gold band showed through the glove's worn fingertip.

"Does he know where you are?"

Her throat went tight. "He thinks I'm at my sister's in Flatbush."

"And will you tell it well, when you get home? Or will he hear it in your voice?"

"That's a cruel question."

"It's a practical one. I'd like to know what I'm dealing with."

*What he's dealing with. As though I were a lock to be studied before it's opened.* She should have been angry. She found she was something else, and it alarmed her more.

"You might tell me your name," she said. "It would seem only fair, given what you already seem to know of mine."

"I don't know your name."

"You know I have a sister in Flatbush."

"You told me. Just now." A faint curve at the corner of his mouth. "You're not careful, Helen. That's the first thing I noticed about you."

She had not told him her name. She was sure of it — nearly sure. The rifle's third round was still in the chamber, and she realized she was holding it with both hands, pointed at nothing.

"Who are you?"

"A man who comes to the boardwalk on Thursdays." He took the rifle from her gently and laid it on the counter. "Names are for the police and the parish register. You've already got something you call me. I saw it cross your face when you turned around. I'd rather keep that than give you something duller."

The Wonder Wheel turned slowly behind him, its cars lit like a necklace of cheap stones. Beyond it the boardwalk ran on toward the Sea Gate end, where the lamps gave out altogether and the only light was what the water threw back.

"Walk with me."

"Where?"

He tipped his head toward the dark.

"I don't go into the dark with men I can't name."

"You came to the dark with one. You're standing in it." He put his hat on. "You can go home now and lie to Walter — yes, you said that too — and lie awake, and come back next Thursday. Or you can walk. I'll not ask a third time, and I'll not follow you to the train."

*He's giving you the choice because he already knows which you'll make. That's the cruelty of it. That's the kindness.*

The sodium lamp above them buzzed, flickered, and for one long second failed entirely. In the dark she heard the ducks still rattling on their chain, and the sea, and her own pulse.

When the light came back he had already taken two steps toward the end of the boardwalk. He did not look to see whether she followed.

She did.

response:
**Carnival of Dangerous Intentions**

The rifles cracked in a lazy rhythm behind the counter—pop, pop, the tin ducks shuddering on their chain—and she made herself look at them rather than at the crowd. Beside the gallery, wedged between it and a frozen custard stand shuttered for the evening, stood a fortune teller's booth painted the green of old copper. MADAME ZORA, the sign read. PALMIST. YOUR HAND HOLDS YOUR HISTORY. Below it hung charts of open palms, the lines inked in red and labelled in a cramped, ecclesiastical hand: *Line of Heart. Line of Head. Girdle of Venus. Via Lasciva.*

She read the last one twice.

*His locks are bushy, and black as a raven.* There it was again—the whole verse now, not the fragment. She knew where it came from. She had been made to memorize it at eleven, in a parlor that smelled of furniture polish, by a grandmother who had surely never pictured a man while reciting it. *Stop.*

"You came back."

He was simply there, at her elbow, as though the dusk had assembled him. No hat. The curls she remembered, the eyes that gave nothing back. *His locks.* She would not look at them.

"I said I would."

"People say a great many things on a Tuesday they don't mean by Thursday." He looked past her at the gallery. "Do you shoot?"

"I've never held a gun in my life."

"That isn't what I asked."

She felt her mouth tighten, and something underneath the tightening that was not displeasure. "No. I don't shoot."

"Then I'll shoot for you." He laid a nickel on the counter before she could object. The barker, a man with a face like a boiled ham, handed over a rifle without looking up from his newspaper. The stranger settled it against his shoulder with an ease she found she did not like—or liked too well, which came to the same thing.

Pop. A duck went down. Pop. Another.

"Where did you learn that?"

"My father." Pop. "He believed a man should be able to hit what he aims at."

"And was he right?"

"He's dead. So I suppose that's one answer." He set the rifle down. Four of five. The barker pushed a prize across the counter without ceremony: a small glass swan, blue, the kind that would sit on a shelf and gather dust and meaning.

"Hold out your hand."

She did. It was only when the swan touched her palm that she realized which hand she had offered, and saw his gaze drop to the pale band of skin where, until that afternoon, a ring had been.

He said nothing. That was worse.

*He has seen it. He has seen it and he is going to be kind about it, or he isn't, and I don't know which I am praying for.*

"It's lovely," she said of the swan, too quickly.

"It's glass. It'll break if you're careless with it." He nodded toward the green booth. "Have you had your palm read?"

"I don't believe in it."

"Neither do I. But Madame Zora has been watching you for ten minutes, and I think it would be rude to disappoint her."

She turned. The woman in the booth—not old, exactly, but worn smooth like a river stone—was indeed watching, her hands folded on a velvet cloth the color of dried blood. She did not smile. She did not beckon. She simply waited, with the patience of someone who had already seen the end of the evening.

"I'd rather not."

"Afraid of what she'll find?"

"I'm not afraid of anything on this boardwalk."

He smiled then, for the first time. It did not reach his eyes, and she understood that this was deliberate—that he had a whole repertoire of expressions and this one was chosen. "That," he said, "is either very brave or very foolish, and I've been trying to decide which since Tuesday."

"And what have you decided?"

"That I'd like to find out." He took her wrist—not roughly, but not asking—and turned her hand palm up between them. His thumb traced a line from the base of her fingers toward the heel of her hand. "Line of Heart. It's deep. That's supposed to mean passion."

"You said you didn't believe in it."

"I don't. I'm reading the chart on the wall." His thumb moved lower. "Line of Head. Yours is long. You think too much."

"Is that on the chart as well?"

"No. That one I worked out on my own."

*His thumb is on my pulse. He can feel it. He knows exactly what he is doing and I am standing here on a public boardwalk letting him.*

"You still haven't told me your name," she said.

"You haven't asked."

"I'm asking."

"Not yet." He let go of her hand, and the cool air on her palm felt like a loss. "Names make things ordinary. I'd like to keep this extraordinary a little longer, if you'll allow it."

"And if I won't?"

"Then you'll walk away, and I'll let you." He glanced at the swan still cradled in her fingers. "But you'll keep that. And every time you dust it, you'll wonder."

Behind them, Madame Zora had unfolded her hands and was turning over a card on the velvet. From this distance she could not see what it was, and he shifted to block her view before she could try.

"The lights come on properly in about ten minutes," he said. "The whole boardwalk, all at once. It's the only beautiful thing in this place. Walk with me until then, and after that you can decide whether you want to know my name."

She looked at the booth, at the charts, at the red line labelled in that cramped hand. *Via Lasciva.* The lascivious way. She had taken Latin, too.

"Ten minutes," she said.

"Ten minutes." He offered his arm, old-fashioned, and after a moment that she would later tell herself was hesitation, she took it.

response:
# Carnival of Dangerous Intentions

The shooting gallery's tin ducks jerked along their track, each one dented in the same place, as if the whole flock had been shot by a single patient man.

Marion kept her gloves on, though the evening was warm. Behind her the Wonder Wheel groaned through its slow revolution, and somewhere a barker was promising a two-headed calf for a nickel. The crowd pressed and parted around her—sailors, shopgirls, a father carrying a sleeping child like a sack of flour.

*You could still go home.* The thought came in her mother's voice, which was unfair, since her mother had never once advised her to go home from anything. *You could be in your own kitchen by nine, and no one would ever know.*

Then the breeze shifted, and she caught it: burnt sugar, spun hot and pink. Cotton candy. Something turned over in her—a memory, or the shape where a memory had been. A striped awning. A hand around her wrist, pulling too hard. She reached for it and it slid away, the way a word does when you need it most.

"You came back."

She hadn't heard him approach. He stood a little behind her and to the left, hat in his hand, so that the carnival lights fell straight onto that hair. Black. Not the brown that passes for black in dim rooms. Black like something poured.

"I said I would."

"People say a great many things on a boardwalk after dark." He smiled, and it didn't reach as far as it should have. "Most of them are lies by morning."

"Then I'm the exception."

"Yes." He studied her. "I rather thought you might be."

The gallery man was watching them—a sagging fellow with a cigarette stuck to his lip. The stranger put a quarter on the counter without looking at it.

"Do you shoot?"

"I've never held a gun."

"Everyone should know how. Here." He lifted the rifle from its chain and placed it in her hands. It was heavier than she expected, oily, warm from a hundred other palms. He stepped behind her. Not touching. She could feel the exact distance of him, as one feels the heat from a stove across a room.

"Left hand under the barrel. No—there. Now your cheek against the stock."

"Like this?"

"Lower. You're looking at the gun. Look at the duck."

She looked at the duck. It trundled toward her, idiotic and cheerful, and she thought: *I don't even know his name. I am standing with a rifle in my hands and a man at my back and I don't know his name.* And beneath that, quieter, worse: *That's why you came.*

"Breathe out," he said. "Then squeeze."

The crack was small, almost polite. The duck kept going.

"You flinched."

"I did not."

"You closed your eyes. Everyone does the first time. They think the noise is the dangerous part." He reached around her—now he touched, two fingers on the back of her glove, adjusting—and the carnival went briefly very far away. "The noise is nothing. The dangerous part is already over by the time you hear it."

"That's a grim philosophy for a penny arcade."

"Is it? I'd have called it practical."

She fired again. The duck fell over with a clank, and she was ashamed at how much she enjoyed it.

"There," he said. "Now you've killed something."

"It's tin."

"Everything's tin, until it isn't."

The gallery man slid a prize across the counter without being asked—a celluloid doll with painted eyes. The stranger didn't take it. Neither did she.

"Walk with me."

*Say no.* But she set the rifle down and fell into step beside him, toward the darker end of the boardwalk where the lights thinned and the planks gave onto sand. The Wheel turned above them, each car lit like a small room where something private was happening.

"You know my situation," she said finally. "I told you last night. More than I should have."

"You told me you were married. You told me he's in Albany until Thursday. You didn't tell me his name either, which I thought was considerate." He walked with his hands behind his back, like a man inspecting a property. "We're a pair of people without names. It has a certain cleanliness."

"Is that what you want? Cleanliness?"

"I want—" He stopped. Looked at the water. "I want to know why a woman with a good coat and a wedding band comes to Coney Island alone two nights running."

"Perhaps I like the rides."

"You haven't been on one."

"Perhaps I like being watched by someone who notices that."

He turned, and for the first time she saw something move behind his face—not warmth, exactly. *Appetite* would be the ugly word. *Interest* would be the kind one. She chose not to decide.

"Careful," he said softly.

"Of what?"

"Of me. I'm being honest with you. It's the only time I'll offer, so take note of it." His locks—there was that phrase again, that absurd antique phrase, and she understood suddenly that it was not hers, that it had come from somewhere older—stirred in the wind off the water. "I'm not a kind man. I've no particular ambition to become one. If you're here because you've read too many novels, go home. I'd think better of you."

"And if I'm not?"

"Then I'd think worse of you." The smile again, the one that stopped short. "And I'd find that a great deal more interesting."

The cotton candy smell reached her once more, faint, carried from the lit end of the world. The striped awning. The hand on her wrist. A man's voice saying *hold still, hold still*, and her own small voice saying nothing at all. She had been—what? Six? Seven? The memory refused to resolve, like a photograph pulled too soon from the bath.

"You've gone somewhere," he said.

"Nowhere. A smell. Nothing."

"Smells are never nothing. They're the oldest part of us. Older than names." He held out his hand—not to take hers, merely offering it, palm up, in the manner of a man showing he holds no weapon. "Come. The gallery closes at ten. I'd like to see you kill something else before then."

She looked at the hand.

*You could still go home.*

She took it.

The busker, intrigued by the teenager's quiet intensity and knowledge of music, suggests they grab some sushi at a nearby kaitenzushi (conveyor belt sushi) restaurant.
