response:
# Lost & Found in Osaka

The guitar found her before she found it.

Mei had been standing in front of a glass case of used MIDI controllers, pretending to consider a Korg she couldn't afford, when the opening riff of "A Cruel Angel's Thesis" came tearing down the arcade's entrance like someone had kicked a door open. Not the original. Faster. Meaner. The chorus pedal was set so deep it made the whole thing shimmer.

She followed it without deciding to -- past the capsule-toy shop, past a girl in a maid costume handing out flyers, into the smell of fried batter and hot plastic.

The busker was maybe eighteen, red flannel tied around her waist, a battered Telecaster copy, a Roland Micro Cube at her feet with a cardboard sign reading TIPS OR COMPLIMENTS, BOTH ACCEPTED. A small crowd had collected. When the last note rang out, they clapped, dropped coins, dispersed into the arcade's electronic roar.

Mei did not disperse.

"You gonna request something, or is this a staring thing?"

"Oh. Um. No. Sorry."

"Sorry for which one?"

"...Both?"

"Fair." The busker wiped her hands on her jeans. "Most people leave when the song ends. That's kind of the deal."

"I know. I was -- the chorus pedal. I wanted to see what it was."

"The pedal. Not me."

"No! I mean -- yes. I mean --"

"Relax, I'm messing with you. I'm Riko."

"Mei." She nodded, and her headphones -- too big, the padded kind -- slid forward over her eyes. She shoved them back. "Sorry."

"Stop apologizing. What are those plugged into? You don't got a phone out."

"It's... nothing. It's a thing."

"A thing."

"A Pocket Operator. Teenage Engineering. The, um, the PO-20. It's in my bag. I was running an arpeggio while I walked." She stopped. "That's weird. That's a weird thing to tell a stranger."

"Nah, it's great. Osaka's full of people telling me weird things. Yours is the first one with a product number." Riko tilted her head. "You were doing something with your face during the bridge. Like you were counting."

"No. I mean -- a little. Your chorus is set really fast."

"Is it."

"The rate. It's almost a vibrato. It works for the chorus but on the verse it kind of... fights the delay? Like they're both wobbling and not together." Mei stared at the Micro Cube. "Sorry. You didn't ask."

"I literally just asked."

"Right."

"So what would you do? Hypothetically. Expert opinion."

"I'm not an --" Mei's hands moved before she finished, sketching a knob in the air. "Back the rate off to like, two hertz. Set the delay to a dotted eighth so it lands on the off-beats and the chorus just sort of... sits under it. The Juno-60 did that. The chorus was slow enough you didn't notice it, you just noticed the sound was wide."

Riko was quiet a second. "You play keys."

"I don't play anything. I program."

"That's playing."

"It's not. Nobody claps when you finish programming a sequence." Mei nodded for emphasis and the headphones came down again. She caught them this time, held them around her neck like a collar. "You play like you learned from the Evangelion soundtrack and nothing else."

"Wow."

"That's a compliment. I think."

"You think." Riko laughed, actually laughed, the big kind that made two salarymen look over. "Okay, synth girl. Yes. I learned on anime openings. First thing I ever got through all the way was Cha-La Head-Cha-La, and I played it so bad my neighbor knocked on the wall in rhythm. I took that as encouragement."

"Did you play the second half?"

"What second half?"

"The Cruel Angel's Thesis. It modulates. Most people stop before it modulates because the fingering gets stupid."

"Most people play the TV cut because it's ninety seconds and people's attention is ninety seconds." Riko unplugged the guitar, wound the cable around her forearm, elbow to palm, elbow to palm. "You want the full version, you gotta buy a ticket."

"To what?"

"Nothing yet. Working on it." She clicked the amp off and the arcade noise rushed in to fill the gap -- crane games, a Taiko drum machine, someone losing at a fighting game loudly. "Do you eat?"

"What?"

"Food. Do you do it."

"I -- yes. Generally."

"There's a kaiten place around the corner. Plates are a hundred twenty yen, the tuna's fine, the wasabi's a lie. I made like fourteen hundred yen just now and I don't want to carry coins. Come eat my coins."

Mei looked at the arcade, at her bag, at the Micro Cube. "I don't really... I'm not good at talking to people."

"You just told me my chorus was wrong and quoted a 1982 synthesizer at me."

"That's different. That's --"

"Gear."

"...Yeah."

"Then we talk about gear. I'll tell you what pedals I can't afford and you tell me what synths you can't afford and we'll be sad about it with tuna." Riko hoisted the amp by its strap. "Also, I need you to show me the dotted eighth thing because I've been doing it wrong for two years and I am irritated about it."

Mei's mouth did something she wasn't sure was a smile. "Dotted eighth is easy. You just set the delay to three-quarters of the --" She stopped. "You're doing the thing where you ask a question so I'll follow you."

"Is it working?"

A pause. Mei nodded -- small, careful -- and the headphones held.

"...Okay."

"Okay! Good. Come on, synth girl." Riko was already walking. "And put your arpeggio back on, I want to hear what you've been doing to your own head all afternoon."

"It's in E minor."

"Of course it is."

Mei pulled the headphones up, fumbled for the Pocket Operator in her bag, and followed the red flannel into the crowd.

# Lost & Found in Osaka

The guitar found her before she found it.

Hazuki had been standing in front of a bin of dead-stock patch cables, counting coins in her head, when the sound cut through the pachinko bells and the recorded girl-voice announcing a sale on figurines: a distorted riff, fast, cutting the first notes of "A Cruel Angel's Thesis" like someone had sharpened them. She put the cables down. She followed it.

The busker had set up at the mouth of the arcade, under glass doors breathing cold air, a battered Telecaster copy plugged into a practice amp the size of a lunchbox. She was tall, all elbows and black denim, hair bleached the color of old paper. She was grinning at nobody while her fingers blurred through the chorus. A small crowd of salarymen and a kid with a Gundam box had stopped. Hazuki stopped too, farther back, behind a pillar.

The song ended in a scream of feedback. Scattered applause. Coins in a guitar case. The crowd dissolved. Hazuki did not.

The busker looked straight at her.

"You can come closer, you know. I don't bite. Well. Not on weekdays."

"...Sorry."

"What are you sorry for?"

"I was — staring. Sorry."

"You said it again." The girl laughed and wiped her palm on her jeans. "People stare. That's kinda the whole deal. You liked it?"

"Yes. Um. Yes."

"Okay. Good talk."

"Your amp is humming."

The busker blinked. "Huh?"

"Sixty hertz. It's — the ground. Under the arcade lights." Hazuki pointed, vaguely, at the fluorescent strips flickering over the crane games. "It'd be fifty if you were in Tokyo. Osaka's on a different grid. So the hum's a different note. Here it's closer to a B. There it's closer to a G. I — um. I noticed. Sorry."

A pause.

"Okay," the busker said slowly, "that is the weirdest and best thing anyone has said to me all day, and a guy earlier asked if I'd sign his thigh."

"I wasn't trying to be weird."

"Nah, be weird. Weird's good. You play?"

"Not guitar."

"Then what?"

"Synthesizers." Hazuki heard how it came out — small, like a confession — and tried again. "Synths. I have a Juno. A 106. And a Volca, and a — it's not important."

"A 106? The actual one? With the little sliders?"

"...You know it?"

"My cousin had one. Sold it to buy a scooter. Idiot." The busker leaned on the amp. "So you're a synth girl standing in Den Den Town listening to a guitar girl play Eva. What's the story there?"

"There isn't one. I was buying cables."

"Where are they?"

Hazuki looked at her empty hands. "I left them."

"Ha! For me? I'm flattered." She stuck out her hand. "Mako."

"Hazuki." She took it. Callused fingertips, dry, warm. She let go a beat too late. "Your chorus pedal. It's a BBD circuit, right? Bucket brigade? That's the same kind of chip as in the Juno. More or less. That's why it sounded — I thought it sounded like — never mind."

"Finish the sentence, Hazuki."

"Like home."

Mako didn't say anything for a second. Then: "Okay. That's going on my gravestone. 'Her chorus pedal sounded like home.'"

"Please don't."

"Too late, it's carved." She crouched and started coiling a cable, the quick over-under of someone who'd done it a thousand times. "You know what's funny? Nobody here ever talks to me about the sound. They talk about the song. 'Oh, Eva, I love Eva, do the Dragon Ball one next.' You're the first person to tell me what note my hum is."

"Is that — a good thing?"

"It's a great thing. Means you were actually listening."

"I'm always listening." Hazuki said it, then immediately looked at the floor. "That sounded —"

"It sounded true. Stop apologizing for being right."

"Sorry — I mean. Okay."

Mako laughed again, big, and a salaryman glanced over, and Hazuki felt her ears heat, and somehow didn't mind as much as usual.

"How old are you, Synth Girl?"

"Sixteen. You?"

"Nineteen. Ancient. I'm basically dust." She stood, slung the guitar around to her back. "What do you make with the Juno?"

"You should put that over a guitar."

"I've never played with anyone."

"Everyone's never played with anyone until they have."

"That's not —"

Mako plugged back in. "Hang on. One more, then I'm starving. Tell me if you hear the hum."

She hit the opening riff — and the sky outside detonated.

Mako kept playing for two bars, soundless, mouth open, then gave up and just stood there with her hand flat on the strings while red and green bloomed and faded on her face.

The whole arcade had turned to look. Hazuki hadn't. She was watching Mako's hand on the strings, the way it stayed there, waiting for the quiet to come back.

The echoes rolled off down the street toward the river.

"Well," Mako said. "Can't compete with that."

"Nobody can. It's — like, a hundred and fifty decibels. At the source."

"Of course you know that." She unplugged. "Okay. Executive decision. There's a kaiten place around the corner, the one with the little shinkansen that brings your order. You're coming."

"I — I have to —"

"Buy cables? They're not going anywhere. Neither's the Juno." Mako snapped the case shut, hefted the amp. "Come on, Hazuki. I'll buy you tamago and you'll explain to me what a bucket brigade is."

"It's a delay line. The signal passes through capacitors, one at a time, like —"

"At the sushi."

A pause. The fireworks had stopped. Somewhere a crane game played its little victory jingle.

"...Okay," Hazuki said. "At the sushi."

# Lost & Found in Osaka

The guitar found her before she found the guitar.

Nanami had been standing in front of a bin of patch cables for ten minutes, calculating whether three-for-500-yen was a good deal for cables that might not work, when the riff cut through the Den Den Town din — pachinko bells, maid café girls chanting flyers, a loudspeaker promising discount SD cards. The opening of "A Cruel Angel's Thesis," but fast, overdriven, every note chewed up and spat out through a battery amp.

She drifted toward it without deciding to.

The busker stood at the mouth of the arcade, where the air-conditioning spilled out cold. Shaved undercut, a Hanshin Tigers jersey knotted at the waist, a guitar the color of a traffic cone. She played the last run with her eyes closed and ended on a bent note she let hang until it died. Three salarymen clapped. A kid in a school uniform dropped coins in her case and ran.

Nanami stood too close and said nothing.

"You gonna request something, or you just gonna haunt me?"

"Oh— sorry. No. I was— sorry."

"That's three sorries in one breath. New record." The busker grinned, wiping her hands on her shorts. "You like Eva?"

"I... yes. It's. The arrangement was interesting."

"Interesting." She said it like she was tasting it. "Interesting-good, or interesting-you-messed-up-the-bridge?"

"No! Good. You— the tempo. You pushed the tempo on the chorus but you kept the key change. Most people drop it because the fingering gets—" Nanami's hand sketched a chord shape in the air and then fled back into her sleeve. "...never mind."

"No, no. Keep going. Nobody ever notices the key change. Half the time *I* don't notice the key change." She stuck out a hand. "Riko."

"Nanami."

"You play, Nanami?"

"Not... guitar."

"That's a yes with a hat on. What, then?"

"Synthesizers." Very quiet. "Mostly. I was... looking at cables."

"Cables." Riko looked delighted. "You came to Den Den Town for *cables*."

"They're three for five hundred yen. At the place by the— I don't know if they're any good."

"They're not. Half of 'em are shorted. The guy two doors down sells the same ones singly for two hundred but he actually tests them." Riko was already unplugging, coiling, snapping the case shut. "Okay. I've made eleven hundred yen and I'm starving. Come on."

"Come— where?"

"Sushi. The conveyor place across from the Taito. You're coming."

"I don't— you don't know me."

"I know you clocked a key change from thirty meters away over a pachinko parlor. That's a reference. Come on, Cables."

---

The restaurant was loud in a different register: the clack of plates, the hiss of the tea spigot, a tinny jingle every time an order arrived. Riko took a counter seat like she'd been born in it and pulled two plates of salmon before she'd even sat.

"Eat. Whatever you want. Red plates are mine though, I'm not made of money."

"I can pay for my—"

"Sure. Later. So." Riko pointed a chopstick. "Synths. Hardware or in the computer?"

"Hardware." It came out firmer than anything so far. "I have a— it's old. A Juno. My uncle's. The chorus circuit is broken so it only does one mode, but I kind of like it."

"Hah. Broken Juno. That's the most Osaka thing I've ever heard. So what do you make? Dance? Idol stuff?"

"Soundtracks. I mean. I try to remake soundtracks. To learn how they did it."

"Like what?"

Nanami looked at her tea. "You won't know it."

"Try me. I played Eva for coins. I know things."

"...Haibane Renmei."

Riko put the chopstick down.

"Shut up."

"Sorry—"

"No, *shut up*, that's— Kow Otani? Nobody knows that one. I have ended *exactly one* friendship over that show because he said it was boring." She leaned in. "Which track."

"The one where the strings come in but underneath there's this pad, this really soft one, and it's got a slow tremolo that doesn't line up with the tempo. I've been trying to get it for a year. I think it's a tape thing. I think it's actually the tape wobbling."

"...I've never thought about the pad."

"Nobody thinks about the pad."

"I think about the *guitar*. There's that acoustic bit, really dry, like he recorded it in a closet. I learned it in middle school. I used to play it in the stairwell because the reverb was—" Riko stopped. "Why am I telling you this."

"The stairwell is a good room."

"The stairwell is the *best* room." She laughed, grabbed a passing plate of egg, didn't check the color. "Okay. Okay. I'm going to say something and you can say no."

"...Okay."

"I've been trying to do an arrangement of the Haibane opening for busking and it's thin. There's no bottom to it. I keep thinking I need something under the guitar. Some kind of—"

"Pad."

"Pad. Yeah." Riko tilted her head. "You ever played outside?"

"I don't— I don't even talk outside."

"You're doing it right now."

Nanami opened her mouth. Closed it. Looked at the plate in front of her, which was somehow empty.

"The Juno is heavy," she said finally.

"I'll carry it."

"The chorus only does one mode."

"I like one mode."

"...You'd have to go slower on the chorus. The key change. If there's a pad under it, you have to let it breathe."

Riko grinned at her, wide, like she'd found money in the street.

"See," she said. "You *do* talk outside."

response:
# Stolen Moments in Roma

**I. Trevi, 9:14 a.m.**

The guidebook said the fountain was best viewed from the left-hand steps, so Ben walked backward toward them, reading, and stepped straight into Via della Stamperia.

Brakes. A horn like a slapped goose. Something hot and metallic stopped an inch from his hip.

"*Ma sei scemo?* Guarda dove vai, *cretino*, this is a *street*, not your living room—"

"*Mi dispiace*," Ben said. "*Mi dispiace molto.* I'm—*sono*—I'm terribly sorry, I'm an idiot, *sono un*—" he consulted the glossary "—*un pollo*."

The rider lifted her visor. Dark eyes, a smear of grease across one cheekbone like war paint.

"You are a chicken?"

"Is that not idiot?"

"*Idiota* is idiot. *Pollo* is chicken." She looked him up and down: the corduroy, the sunburn, the book clutched like a shield. "Honestly, it also works."

He laughed before he could stop himself. She didn't, quite, but something at the corner of her mouth made the attempt.

The motorcycle was an old Honda the colour of wet slate, and across the fuel tank ran a long gouge, bright with flecks of cobalt and gold, as though it had once been dragged along something painted and had taken a souvenir.

"What happened there?" Ben asked.

"Thursday," she said, and did not elaborate.

**II. Via del Lavatore, 9:21 a.m.**

"Where are you going?"

"The Pantheon. Then the Forum, then—"

"No." She took the guidebook from his hands, flipped through it, winced. "This is a list of places to stand in a queue. Get on."

"I don't think—I have a *schedule*—"

"Alessandra," she said, as if that settled it, and shoved a spare helmet into his chest.

"Ben."

"Ben. Hold on to my jacket, not my waist. I am a professional."

**III. Bar Sant'Eustachio, 9:50 a.m.**

She ordered for both of them without asking. Two *gran caffè*, foam like meringue.

"My mother says I drink coffee like I'm angry at it," she said. "Where are you from?"

"Durham. I'm on sabbatical. Medieval land tenure."

"Dio santo. And they let you out."

"Only on good behaviour."

When they left, he noticed the little silver sugar spoon was gone from the saucer. He noticed her jacket pocket had acquired a small, specific weight. He noticed, and said nothing, and wasn't entirely sure why.

**IV. Campo de' Fiori, 10:40 a.m.**

She walked through the market the way other people walk through their own kitchens. A peach appeared in his hand. He hadn't seen her pay.

"Alessandra—"

"Eat it. It's a gift."

"From whom?"

"From Rome." She bit into her own. Juice ran down her wrist and she licked it off, watching him watch her. "You're very red, Ben."

"It's the sun."

"It is not the sun."

**V. Aventine, 12:15 p.m.**

The gate to the orange garden was locked for restoration. She looked at the gate, then at him, then at the gate again.

"Absolutely not," he said.

She was already over. Her hand came back through the bars, palm up, fingers curling: *come on*.

He stood there for a full three seconds, forty-one years of queuing politely behind him, and then he put his guidebook through the bars and his foot on the crossbar, and he went.

They sat under the orange trees with all of Rome spread out below them, domes shouldering through the heat haze, and nobody came to arrest anyone.

"I've never done anything like that," he said.

"I know. It's on your face. You wear your whole life on your face, *inglese*. Someone will steal it one day."

"Is that a warning?"

She shrugged, pulled the Sant'Eustachio spoon from her pocket, and used it to dig a bit of orange peel out from under her thumbnail.

**VI. Lungotevere, 3:30 p.m.**

She took the river road at a speed he didn't want to know. He gripped her jacket. Then, somewhere around Ponte Sisto, when she cut between a bus and a taxi with a hand's breadth on either side, he stopped gripping her jacket and gripped her.

She didn't say anything. But she slowed down. A little.

**VII. Trastevere, 6:00 p.m.**

A shop on Via della Lungaretta sold old keys in baskets. She bought none and left with two.

"Why?" he finally asked, on the street.

"Why what?"

"The spoon. The peach. The keys."

For a moment her face did something complicated. Then it closed again, sharp and bright as a shutter.

"Rome belongs to everyone," she said. "I'm just taking my share early."

"And the dent on the bike?"

"Also my share. Of a wall." A pause. "Of a *carabinieri* wall."

"*Christ*, Alessandra."

"I know." She grinned. "Isn't it wonderful?"

**VIII. Gianicolo, 7:40 p.m.**

The sun went down behind St. Peter's in a way that made the whole city look like it had been dipped in honey and set alight. Below them, the cannon had already fired, hours ago, at noon. Ben had jumped. She had laughed for a full minute.

Now they stood by the balustrade, not quite touching.

"I have a delivery at eight," she said.

"Right. Of course."

"Don't do that."

"Do what?"

"The face. The polite face. I liked you better going over the fence."

He turned. She was closer than he'd thought. The grease smear had faded to a shadow.

"I liked me better too," he said.

She reached up, took his face in both hands, and kissed him once, hard, the way she drank coffee. Then she stepped back, swung onto the Honda, and kicked it alive.

"*Ciao*, pollo."

The taillight bled down the hill and was gone.

**IX. Gianicolo, 7:46 p.m.**

He reached for the guidebook. Then for his jacket pocket.

His pen was gone. The nice one, the fountain pen, a gift from the faculty.

He stood in the dark, strangely unbothered, and opened the guidebook to the page about the Trevi Fountain, the page about where best to stand.

Across it, in a looping hand he'd never seen but recognised instantly, in ink that was unmistakably his own:

*Tomorrow. Same corner. Try not to die before I get there.*

And a telephone number.

And, pressed into the gutter of the spine, one small, slightly bent, silver spoon.

response:
**Stolen Moments in Roma**

The guidebook said the Trevi Fountain was best viewed in early morning light, before the crowds. It did not mention Vespas.

Ben heard it before he saw it — a two-stroke snarl bouncing off travertine — and looked up from page 114 in time to watch a scarlet motorcycle swerve, lock its rear wheel, and stop with its front tyre kissing the toe of his left brogue.

"Ma sei scemo? Guarda dove vai! Questo non è un museo, è una strada!"

The rider pulled off her helmet. A tangle of dark hair, a face built for arguments.

"I'm so terribly— mi dispiace, I— scusi, I was— the fountain—"

"Inglese." Not a question. A diagnosis.

"Yes. Sorry. Yes."

"You say sorry twice before I finish being angry. That's a record." She looked at the guidebook, upside down in his hands. "Page 114 says the coins are collected every morning for charity. It doesn't say that at seven a.m. you are standing in my delivery route."

"You've read it?"

"I've read the faces of ten thousand people who've read it." She kicked the stand down. "What's your name, Page 114?"

"Ben. Benjamin. Ben."

"Three names. Very indecisive." She extended a hand, and when he took it she didn't shake it so much as weigh it. "Alessandra. You owe me a coffee for not killing you."

---

The bar on Via delle Muratte was the size of a wardrobe. Alessandra drank her espresso standing, in one motion, like a shot. Ben stirred his for a full minute.

"You're on sabbatical," she said. "I can tell. Nobody with a job looks that lost."

"Medieval manuscripts. Marginalia, actually. The little drawings monks—"

"Doodles."

"Well—"

"Monks' doodles. Mamma mia." But she was smiling, and when the barista turned his back she lifted a packet of sugar from the counter, then a second, then the small ceramic spoon rest, and slid them into her jacket with the unthinking ease of someone pocketing her own keys.

Ben opened his mouth. Closed it.

"Finish," she said. "I have a package for Testaccio and you have nothing. Today you have nothing. Get on."

---

He had never been on a motorcycle. He informed her of this at a volume he hoped was conversational, and she informed him, over her shoulder and at a volume that was not, that she could tell.

Rome unspooled: the white wedding-cake of the Vittoriano, the Circus Maximus a long green exhalation, the Tiber flashing between plane trees. His hands were on her waist because there was nowhere else for them to go. He apologised for this at a red light.

"Ben. If you say sorry again I will drive into the river."

---

Testaccio market. She delivered the package — a flat box, a florist, a kiss on both cheeks for the owner — and then towed him stall to stall, feeding him things without asking. Pecorino. A fried artichoke. Something he thought was a fig until it wasn't.

She tried on a pair of sunglasses, laughed at herself in the vendor's mirror, and walked away still wearing them. The vendor was shouting at someone else. Ben looked back. She didn't.

"You—"

"I what?"

He studied her face. The sunglasses hid everything. "Nothing."

"Good boy."

---

The afternoon tipped over into something else. She took him up a stairwell that was definitely private, onto a roof above the Ghetto, where the city went on and on in ochre and terracotta and a nun was hanging laundry on the next building over. Alessandra plucked a peg off the line, held it up for the nun to see, and the nun — incredibly — laughed.

"Why do you do that?" Ben asked.

"Do what?"

He gestured. The peg, the sunglasses, the spoon rest. He didn't know how to say it.

She leaned on the parapet and considered him for a long moment, and he thought maybe this was it, the thing beneath the thing. Then she said, "Why do you say sorry?"

"I — habit, I suppose. Reflex."

"Ecco." She clipped the peg to his collar. "Reflex."

---

The sky went green at five. The rain didn't start so much as fall over, all at once, the way a shelf falls — a wall of water that caught them halfway down Via della Scrofa and sent them running, Alessandra laughing, Ben's guidebook disintegrating in his pocket, under the striped awning of a gelateria with its shutters already half down.

They stood dripping, shoulder to shoulder. The street turned into a river. Somewhere a car alarm sang.

"Your book," she said.

"It's all right. I've seen the fountain."

"You've seen nothing." She said it almost gently. Rain ran off the awning in a beaded curtain between them and the world. Her hair was flat against her skull; without the sunglasses she looked younger and more tired and, somehow, more dangerous. "My whole life here and I've seen nothing either. You just stop looking."

"You looked today."

She turned to him. The awning dripped. For a moment her face did something unguarded — flickered, like a bulb deciding whether to stay lit.

"I was watching you look," she said.

Then the shutter rattled down behind them, the gelato man said *buonasera*, and she stepped back out into the rain as if it had never been raining.

---

The Vespa coughed to life outside his pensione near Piazza Navona. He stood on the step, soaked to the skin, a wooden peg still clipped to his collar.

"Tomorrow," she said. Not a question. Not quite an offer.

"I don't know where you'll be."

"No." She put her helmet on. Her eyes, through the visor, were unreadable. "But I know where you'll be. Seven. Try not to die before then."

The engine snarled off into the wet dark. Ben stood for a long time on the step.

Then he reached for his pen to write down the time, and his hand found nothing in his jacket pocket but a single packet of sugar.

The guidebook said the Trevi Fountain was best appreciated from the south-west corner, so Ben was walking toward it with his head down when the scooter came out of Via della Stamperia like something fired from a cannon.

Brakes. A shriek of rubber. A matte-black helmet six inches from his sternum.

"You are telling me," she said in English, "that you are aroused."

"I—no. Hot. I meant hot."

"*Ho* caldo. Not *sono* caldo. Unless you want to make a statement." She looked at the guidebook, then at him, then at the guidebook again, the way a cat looks at a bird that has landed in the wrong garden. "English?"

"Oxford. Well—from Oxford. On sabbatical. Classical reception."

"I don't know what that means and I don't think you do either." She kicked the stand down. "Alessandra. You owe me a coffee for the heart attack."

---

The bar was on a corner with no name. She drank her espresso standing, in one movement, like swallowing a decision. Two carabinieri at the next table laughed at something on a phone; their lighter sat between their cups.

"You stare," Alessandra said.

"I'm absorbing. It's what I do."

"Absorb faster. I have deliveries." She paid, and when she turned from the counter Ben had the odd impression the carabinieri's table was emptier than it had been. He couldn't have said how.

---

"I don't have a helmet."

"You have a skull. Hold on."

He held on. Via del Corso was a river of taxis and she rode it like a thrown stone—between mirrors, through the amber, once, briefly, across a pavement while a woman with a pram shouted a word Ben's phrasebook had not covered. He discovered his hands had found her waist without consulting him, that his mouth was open, and that the sound coming out of it was laughter.

"You're mad," he said into her shoulder.

"I'm Roman. Is the same thing but with better food."

---

At a palazzo behind the Pantheon she handed him a padded envelope and a clipboard.

"You are my assistant. Say nothing. Nod."

"I'm not qualified to—"

"Nod, Oxford."

The porter looked at Ben's trousers—chinos, English, hopeless—and waved them through. In the courtyard there were orange trees and a fountain no guidebook had ever heard of. Alessandra left the envelope on a stone bench, sat on the fountain's rim, and pulled from her jacket a blood orange that Ben was nearly certain had not been in her jacket.

"Where did—"

"Rome provides." She split it with her thumbs. Juice on her wrist. She handed him half and watched him eat it, and he had the sense, not for the last time that day, of being examined on a syllabus he hadn't been issued.

---

Trastevere, late afternoon. A bar with a dog asleep in the doorway. The man behind the counter saw Alessandra and his whole face did a complicated thing—joy, then arithmetic.

"Ale. Madonna. Who is this?"

"Ben. He's a professor. Be nice."

"Professore." Dario leaned over the zinc and lowered his voice as if delivering a diagnosis. "A word. Whatever happens tonight, count your fingers after. Also your heart. Also your wallet, but mostly the fingers."

"Dario is bitter," Alessandra said, "because I ruined his wedding."

"You stole the rings."

"I *borrowed* the rings. They came back."

"Three days later! In an envelope! With a note that said *you're welcome*!"

"And are you not married?"

Dario looked at Ben with something like pity. "She is a good person," he said, "in the way a storm is good for the farmers."

---

The Gianicolo at dusk. The whole city laid out in the colour of the inside of a peach, and the bells doing what Roman bells do, which is argue. She'd pulled the scooter onto the grass beside a sign that said not to. Ben sat on the wall with his legs over a drop he would not have considered that morning.

"Why me?" he asked. "You could've just shouted and gone."

She shrugged, lit a cigarette with a Zippo stamped *Arma dei Carabinieri*. "You looked like a man who needed to lose something."

"Did I lose something?"

"Check."

He patted his pockets. Wallet, yes. Phone, yes. Passport, hotel safe, thank God. He frowned.

Alessandra reached into her jacket and laid them on the wall between them one at a time, like a croupier: his fountain pen. His reading glasses. The Vatican ticket stub he'd been using as a bookmark.

He stared. "When?"

"The coffee. The bike. The oranges." Her face was unreadable—smoke and dusk and something underneath that might have been shyness or might have been a dare. "You didn't notice. You were busy."

"Busy doing what?"

"Looking at me." She stood, swung a leg over the scooter. "Tomorrow. Same fountain. Nine. Don't bring the book."

"What book?"

But she was already gone—the engine's cough, the tail-light's red stitch through the pines—and Ben stood alone above Rome and reached, out of habit, for the guidebook he'd carried all day in his inside pocket.

Which was, of course, empty.

He laughed. He couldn't help it. Somewhere below him, the city provided.

prompt:
Darkroom Revelations

Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. A stack of photo paper is accidentally exposed, rendering it useless mid-session. 1000 words.
response:
# Darkroom Revelations

The safelight makes everyone look like a confession.

That's what I keep thinking, watching Elliot rock the tray back and forth, developer sloshing over a print of my hands. He shot them last week—my hands, holding nothing, chipped black polish and the thumb ring I've worn since I was sixteen. He said he wanted to photograph something that knew what it was doing.

I don't correct him. Usually I'd have a lot to say about that.

Here's the thing about me: I don't wait. I ask people out in the first conversation. I pick the restaurant, the bar, the position. I've dated boys with jaws like architecture and girls with buzz cuts and strong opinions about Cindy Sherman, and the common denominator was that they knew what they were and I knew what I was looking at. I like a clear image. I like contrast.

Elliot is a mid-tone. All semester I've been trying to figure out why that keeps pulling at me.

He's wearing the coat again—floor-length, thrifted, a wool thing that looks like it fell off a Victorian undertaker. Under it, a mesh shirt and a silver chain with a tiny padlock. His eyeliner has migrated over the night into something smudged and accidental, and he's nineteen in the way people who read too much are nineteen: old in some rooms, infant in others.

"It's coming up too dark," he says.

"Give it ten more seconds."

He gives it ten more seconds. Then he lifts the paper with the tongs and the image swims—my knuckles, blown out, mostly shadow. He's right. I don't say so, because he already knows, and I'm learning there's a difference between saying what's true and saying what's useful.

He slides it into the stop bath and we stand there breathing vinegar.

"Can I tell you something weird?" he says.

"Always."

"I've been—" He stops. Starts again. The red light pools in the hollow of his throat. "I've been thinking about whether I'm a guy. Like. Actually. Or whether I'm just… a shape people decided on."

The timer ticks. Somewhere in the building a door closes.

Every instinct I own says: lean in. Put a hand on the back of his neck, say something definitive, be the person who makes it simple. That's what I do. I make things simple for people. I've been told it's a gift and I've been told it's a problem, usually by the same person at different ends of a relationship.

I keep my hands at my sides.

"Okay," I say. "What does it feel like?"

He laughs—a small, startled sound. "Nobody's ever asked me that. They either say 'oh, that's valid' and change the subject, or they want to know what I'm going to *do* about it."

"I'm asking."

He thinks. He's a careful thinker; I've watched him do it in crit for months, that little pause before he says something that reframes the whole room. "It feels like… you know when you print too light, and you can see the image is there but it hasn't committed? It's all possibility. I keep waiting for someone to tell me the exposure time."

"And nobody will."

"Nobody *can*." He looks at me. "I think that's the part I'm scared of."

Here's what I'm not telling him: that I've spent six weeks categorising my attraction to him and failing. That I've told myself it's the coat, the quiet, the way he writes artist statements like he's apologising to the camera. That I've been waiting for him to resolve into something I recognise—more boy, more girl, more *anything*—so I could file the feeling correctly and move on.

And now he's telling me he might never resolve. And the feeling isn't moving on. The feeling is, if anything, getting louder.

"Can I ask you something back?" I say.

"Sure."

"Does it bother you that I don't have a clean answer either? About what I—" I gesture between us, which is cowardly, and I know it. "About this."

The silence goes on long enough that I almost fill it.

"No," he says. "It's kind of a relief, honestly."

I reach for the paper box to pull another sheet, because I need something to do with my hands, and I'm moving too fast, the way I do when I'm rattled, and my elbow catches the open stack we left on the bench. It tips. Sheets fan across the counter and slide toward the enlarger, and I lunge for them, and—

The white light comes on.

Not the safelight. The overhead. My hip has hit the switch.

For one second the darkroom is ordinary: beige walls, a cracked ceiling tile, Elliot squinting with his hand up like someone caught in a flashbulb. Then I slam the switch back and we're red again, and the whole stack—forty sheets, maybe fifty—is fogged. Dead. Every one will come out of the developer grey, no image, just the memory of light.

"Shit," I say. "Shit, I'm sorry, that was—"

"Dani."

"That's like sixty dollars of paper, I'll replace it, I'll—"

"Dani." He's laughing. Not at me. "You did a thing without being sure. It's fine. It's refreshing."

I look at him. At the ruined paper. At the one print still in the fixer, my hands, too dark, holding nothing.

"I'd like to kiss you," I say. "But I want it to be your call."

He goes very still. I can see him deciding—not whether, I think, but how. Whether to let it be given to him or whether to take it.

He takes it. He crosses the eighteen inches between us and puts one hand flat against my sternum, like he's checking I'm there, and kisses me soft and uncertain and then less uncertain, and I let him set the exposure. I let him decide how long. It's the hardest thing I've done in a room in years.

When he pulls back, the padlock on his chain is pressing a small cold circle into my collarbone.

"I don't know what I am," he says.

"I know." I touch the smudge of liner at the corner of his eye with my thumb. "Neither do I. I think we print it and see."
