**Blood Debt**

The roof of the Kannon hall had fallen in a century ago, and the moon came through the hole like a lantern lowered on a rope. It lit a square of broken flagstones at the center, a toppled Buddha head the size of a cartwheel against the east wall, a single cracked pillar still standing to the west, and the three steps of the altar dais at the north end where the Jigen-ryū men stood in dark hakama with their arms folded. The Piguaquan crowd filled the south doorway behind Lu Qing—dockers, carters, a rice merchant's bodyguard with his coin purse already open.

Both fighters wore red and black on the left arm. Ijūin Tatsuya's band was knotted at the shoulder, red over black, the way Satsuma men had knotted it for three hundred years. Lu's was black over red and tied at the bicep, and it had belonged to his uncle until a Jigen bokken had taken the use of that arm.

Ijūin raised his red-oak bokken into *tombo*—the dragonfly—blade vertical beside his right ear, hilt high, right foot forward, weight already leaning. Jigen-ryū did not believe in a second strike. The first cut was the whole art.

Lu stood eight paces south of him with his arms hanging loose as rope, left foot forward, hands open. He rolled his shoulders once. "Come on, then, lord's dog."

"CHESTO!"

The shout arrived before the man. Ijūin covered the eight paces in four strides, knees driving high, the bokken dropping in a straight line for the crown of Lu's head.

Lu did not step back. Stepping back from Jigen-ryū was how you died tired. He slid diagonally, forward and left—toward Ijūin's right, outside the sword arm—and the oak came down through the space where his skull had been and struck flagstone with a crack that made the crowd flinch.

Ijūin's hands were already turning. The cut had never meant to stop; it was becoming a rising horizontal, the tip whipping around toward Lu's ribs. Lu dropped under it—knees bent, spine folding like a hinge—and as the oak hissed over his back his right arm uncoiled from the hip in a long flat arc. The back of his fist cracked across Ijūin's jaw.

A glancing hit. But the lip split, and the first blood of the night fell on Ijūin's collar.

Ijūin spat and pivoted west to face him. Lu had come up out of the crouch already moving, circling, keeping that outside line, the pillar now behind his left shoulder and the edge of the moon-square between them.

Ijūin came again. Cut, cut, cut—short vertical strokes, each a full commitment, his feet eating ground. Lu gave it to him in curves, never straight back, arms swinging to keep the shoulders loose. Three paces from the pillar he did the thing the Pigua men had come to see: he swung around the stone like a child around a post, one hand slapping it to turn him, and Ijūin's fourth cut—thrown at the body he expected on the far side—caught the pillar's edge instead. Stone exploded. The shock went up the oak into Ijūin's wrists.

Lu was already coming around the pillar's far side, right arm whipping high and wide, a hooking palm meant for the ear—

Ijūin didn't retreat. He *shortened*, dropping his hands to his belly and driving forward under the arc. The palm whipped over his head and the bokken's pommel, both fists behind it, hammered into Lu's sternum.

The air left Lu in a grunt. He went backward across the moonlit square, feet scrabbling, lost them, rolled, and fetched up against the stone Buddha's cheek. The Jigen men on the dais roared.

Ijūin crossed the hall after him. *Tombo* again, sword high. Lu was on one knee, left hand on the Buddha's eyelid, breath coming ragged.

"CHESTO!"

The charge was perfect—shout, stride, drop. And Lu, who had been counting strides, moved on the fourth: not away this time but *into* it, rising off his knee straight up the line of the charge, so that the bokken had not yet begun to fall when he came up inside Ijūin's elbows.

Too close for oak. Lu's left forearm hooked up under Ijūin's wrists and hung there—*gua*—jamming the cut at its birth. His right hand rose over his own head and fell like a cleaver down the line of Ijūin's collarbone. It landed with a sound like a wet board breaking.

Ijūin's knees dipped. His face went grey.

Then his forehead smashed into Lu's nose.

They broke apart bleeding, Ijūin reeling north along the east wall until his heel found the lowest step of the dais, Lu three paces south of him wiping his eyes. The Jigen men had gone quiet. Ijūin's left arm hung wrong, but his right still held the sword, and in Jigen-ryū the sword was held by one hand or two or the teeth if that was what remained. Lu's face was a red mask, and he was grinning.

"Your uncle grinned too," Ijūin said.

Lu stopped grinning. He came forward.

It was the mistake his master would have struck him for. Pigua was circles. Pigua was patience. He came in straight, right arm already swinging, a whole-bodied whip from the ground to the palm aimed at Ijūin's temple—and Ijūin, who knew nothing in the world but straight lines, met him on one.

The bokken came down one-handed and broke Lu's left forearm, raised too late to guard. Lu's palm came through anyway and took Ijūin across the ear with the full weight of his turning spine behind it.

Ijūin went down backward onto the first step of his own altar, at the feet of his own school. The bokken rolled off the stone and lay in the moonlight. He did not move.

Lu stood over him with one arm hanging and blood dripping from his chin onto the red-and-black band on his arm, and nobody—not the dockers behind him, not the hakama on the dais—said anything at all.

The debt was paid. Both schools would be paying for it by morning.

# Blood Debt

The temple had lost its roof two winters ago, and moonlight came down through the beams in long gray blades. Water seeped from a crack that split the flagstones corner to corner—northeast to southwest—a dark, glistening stripe a hand's width wide, spreading a slick halo into the stones around it. The crowd had learned to keep clear of it. The fighters would not have that luxury.

Isaburō stood at the north end, beneath the headless Buddha on its collapsed dais. His people lined the east wall—Jigen-ryū students in pressed hakama, faces carved into contempt, coins already stacked. He raised the oak bokken into the dragonfly guard: hilt above his right shoulder, blade nearly vertical, left foot forward, elbows wide. He looked less like a man waiting than a man already falling forward.

Lu stood at the south end, by the door, among his own: dockworkers, bodyguards, two women who ran a noodle stall and a gambling table. He wore no stance anyone from the east wall would recognize. His arms hung loose from rolled shoulders; his weight slid from foot to foot like a man testing ice.

"Your grandfather broke my grandfather's hands," Isaburō said.

"Your grandfather needed a sword to do it."

The old man holding the bets dropped his arm.

Isaburō did not wait. The Jigen-ryū has one teaching: the first cut is the whole fight. He crossed the hall in four strides and a scream—the famous monkey cry that his school drilled into boys until it came out raw—and he hit the wet stripe at center without slowing, trusting speed to carry him across before the stone could take his footing. It did. The bokken came down vertical, a cut meant for the crown of Lu's skull.

Lu slipped right. Not far—a hand's width, east toward the Jigen wall—his torso folding sideways while his feet barely moved. The oak hissed past his left ear and cracked a flagstone where his head had been. Isaburō's momentum carried him a half-step past, and in that half-step Lu's left foot planted, his hips wrenched, and his right arm came around like a cart whip: loose, long, the fist landing hammer-first in Isaburō's left kidney with a sound like a wet sack dropped from height.

Isaburō grunted and turned into it—counterclockwise, left shoulder first—so that he now faced east, toward Lu, with the Pigua crowd at his own back and his own people behind his enemy. The water lay behind and to his left now, a dark line in the corner of his vision.

He reset to the dragonfly guard without pause. That was the arrogance of his school, and also its spine: no retreat, no doubt, only the next first strike.

He cut again, diagonal this time, descending from his right shoulder toward Lu's left collarbone. Lu bent at the waist like a reed and let the cut pass a finger's width from his chest. His left arm snapped upward and outward, palm striking Isaburō's forearm just behind the wrist—not stopping the blade but steering it, so the oak finished its arc low and wide of Isaburō's own left hip. Isaburō reversed it into a thrust, the tip driving at Lu's sternum.

Lu was already inside it. He stepped forward and to his right—north, past Isaburō's left side, toward the water—so the thrust slid harmlessly along his ribs, and both his palms came whipping around on the turn: the right slapping Isaburō's jaw, the left chopping down across his nose. Blood came instantly, black in the moonlight.

Isaburō staggered back and west. One step on dry stone. Two. On the third his heel found the slick halo around the crack and went out from under him.

He did not fall. He dropped to his right knee, the bokken braced flat against the stone, and the water ran around his shin.

The east wall groaned. The west wall roared. Lu heard the roar and let it move him—one step too eager, his right foot landing on the glistening stripe to finish the thing. Isaburō saw the foot touch wet stone and drove upward from the knee, the bokken rising in a single stroke from the floor. It caught Lu's left forearm on the bone. The crack was loud enough to silence both walls.

Lu's planted foot slid. He went down on his left hip with a bark of pain, cradling the arm, water soaking through his trousers. For a moment both men were on the ground three feet apart with the dark stripe between them: Isaburō kneeling, bleeding from the nose; Lu half-sitting, his forearm already swelling, skin split and running red down to the wrist.

They rose at the same time.

Lu backed west, onto dry stone, his hurt arm held across his belly. Isaburō stood on the east side of the water and lifted the bokken back into the dragonfly, and now his hands shook with something that was not fear. He looked at the stripe between them—the same ground that had nearly cost him, that had cost Lu—and Lu saw him look.

"Come on, then," Lu said. "Cross it."

The scream came. Isaburō charged.

Lu did not slip this time. He stepped forward instead—diagonally left, onto the water, meeting Isaburō at its center—so the vertical cut was still rising to full height when Lu's broken left arm swept up and jammed Isaburō's wrists against his own chest, killing the stroke before it began. His right arm, the whole good length of it, came around from the shoulder and chopped into the side of Isaburō's neck.

Both men's feet slid. The bokken came down anyway, strengthless, glancing off Lu's shoulder. They went over together into the water and the crowd surged forward from both walls and stopped, as if the stripe were a line no one else dared cross.

Isaburō lay on his back, the oak still in his right hand, its tip against Lu's ribs. Lu lay across him, right palm cocked over his throat, left arm useless between them.

Neither moved. Water carried their blood together down the crack and under the floor, and the old man holding the bets found he did not know whose debt had been paid.

response:
# Breaking Formation

The clock above the mirror reads 00:47:12 in a red so exact it's the red of a Hot Cheetos bag, and it is the only thing in this room that reminds me of home.

Twelve of us, three rows of four, each on a glow-tape X. Mine is back row, far left, nearest the door. I don't think that's an accident.

Yoon-ssaem paces the mirror. She demonstrated once, forty minutes ago; once is what you get. She wears a headset mic she doesn't need, because when she says "Five, six, seven, eight," the floor says it with her.

One: right foot out to shoulder width, stomp. Eleven feet hit the sprung wood like a single gunshot. Mine arrives a half-beat behind and makes no sound, because in Memphis you don't lift your foot to move it. You slide. My heel never left the floor. I'm on my mark. Late and silent.

Two: forearms snap up, crossed at the wrists in front of the face, fingers glued flat. Knife hands.

Three: right arm slices down and out to shoulder height, parallel to the floor, left hand to hip, head snaps right so the eyes land on the fingertips. Here my body lies to me. Eleven arms stop dead like they hit a wall. Mine rolls—shoulder, elbow, wrist, a wave—because I have never once stopped an arm mid-air without a reason.

Four is a hold. I can't hold. My fingers tut without permission, little right angles, the hand still talking after the sentence is over.

"Memphis." She doesn't look at me. She looks at me in the mirror, which is worse. "Your arm is a river. I asked for a blade."

Five: right foot pulls in to the left, feet together, rise onto the toes. Six: drop. Knees out, fists punch straight down between them. The others drop like the floor got yanked out from under them. I drop like water finding its level, hips rolling through, a bounce at the bottom.

Seven: left foot steps forward to the next X, right foot follows, and the whole formation breathes. Front row splits, two to each wing. Second row steps up to become the front. Back row steps up to become the middle. Now I'm middle row, far left, looking through the window between two front-row shoulders at Dahyun's shoulder blade an arm's length ahead and to my right. Eight: freeze. Chin down. Right arm pinned to the thigh. Left hand a pistol at the temple.

Freeze. The word doesn't mean what it meant in the lot behind the Kroger on Lamar. There, a freeze was punctuation. Here it's a photograph somebody already took, and you climb inside it.

00:31:00.

She cuts the music. The silence is wet with breathing. She walks straight through the front row, which parts for her, and Dahyun leans an inch away like I'm contagious. Yoon-ssaem takes my right wrist and lifts it. "Here." Places it. "Not here." Two inches. "Here." Her nails are short and perfect. I cut mine with clippers from the dollar store, and my tuition is a line item in somebody's marketing budget. Scholarship kid. Raw talent. Great story.

"Everyone else learned the killing part in two days. You've had six. Do you know why?"

The killing part: eight counts that'll be in every fancam. I know why. Everyone else has been in rooms like this since they were nine. They learned facing a mirror. I learned facing a circle. The cypher gives you one thing: a moment nobody can choreograph. The mirror gives you one thing too: evidence.

"Because you think the count is a suggestion."

00:14:08.

"Front. Center."

I walk between the rows to the lone X downstage of the front line—the main-dancer mark, empty all week—directly under the clock. From here the mirror shows me eleven faces behind me, and the numbers sit over my own head, and I understand this is the point.

"Alone. Full eight. Everyone else, watch what it looks like when someone decides."

Four counts before the drop. Four counts to think.

What I brought here fit in a carry-on. One pair of Air Forces gone soft at the toes. A slide nobody in this building can do and nobody in this building wants. I learned it at eleven from a man who's dead now, on asphalt that's a Dollar General now, and it lives in my heel, in the way my weight never fully commits to anything, because committing is how you get hit. I could put it in count one. Glide to the mark instead of stomping. Same mark. Same count. My road to it.

Or I could lift my foot.

Five, six, seven, eight.

I lift my foot. One: stomp. The floor makes the sound. Two: blades up, crossed. Three: the arm goes out and I make it stop—it's like slamming a door on my own fingers, the whole limb humming with a wave I'm strangling at the shoulder—and it stops. Four: hold. I lock my fingers until the knuckles blanch. The hand says nothing. Five: in, up. Six: I drop like a dropped thing. Seven: step. Eight: pistol, temple, chin down.

Nothing in the room is moving. Not the eleven behind me. Not her. Not me. Only the red numbers over my head, and I can't see them without breaking.

"Good," she says.

First time. It lands in my stomach like a coin in a dry well.

In the mirror, a dancer in a black academy sweatsuit holds a perfect shape under a clock. Every line clean. Every angle hers. I look at that dancer and search for the heel that never left the ground, the hand that kept talking, the river, and I can't find them, and I'm not sure if what I feel is grief or relief, and what scares me is that in a month I might not be able to tell the difference.

00:00:00.

"Tomorrow," Yoon-ssaem says. "Again."

response:
**Breaking Formation**

Four speakers, one in every corner, synced so tight the song comes from nowhere. That's the first thing that wrecked me. Back home sound has an address—the speaker's on the trunk of somebody's Impala and you dance toward it, you find the pocket by where the bass is standing. Here the bass stands everywhere. It's a flat wall, a hair too loud, 124 BPM, and nine of us stand inside it on blue tape X's while Baek-ssaem watches from the front-left corner beside her speaker.

Three rows of three. I'm back row, far left. Haeun's directly ahead of me, Minjun ahead of her in the front row, and when I look up my lane past their two heads, a little to the left, there's Baek. In the mirror I'm the smallest, the farthest, a face behind two faces.

"Hana."

Right arm shoots to the high diagonal—up and out at forty-five, palm flat, fingers glued, elbow locked. Left arm stays nailed to my seam.

"Dul." Hold.

Already I've failed. At the top of hana my wrist rolled. A tiny finish, a wave coming off the end of the line, because where I come from an arm doesn't stop, it arrives. Here it stops. A dime stop isn't a trick here; it's the whole language. Baek's eyes go to my wrist and come back off it. She doesn't say anything. She logs it.

"Set." Head snaps left, toward the wall. "Net." Right foot steps wide, weight splits fifty-fifty.

"Daseot."

Chest pop. Sternum fires forward one inch, the pure hit—and then my body does what it's done since I was eleven in a cypher on Van Dyke: the hit spreads. Shoulders roll behind it, ribs ride it, hips answer. It goes down me like a wave, because in my body a hit is the start of something.

"Yeoseot." Hold.

My knee's bouncing. Quarter notes. I can feel it.

Baek cuts the music. Silence hits from all four corners at once.

"Number nine."

I don't have a name here. I have a position.

"Why are you still moving?" She's crossing the floor toward me, and the eight trainees around me stand perfectly still, which is their version of staring. "There is nothing on six. Six is nothing. Six is you holding the hit so the audience can see it. You're erasing it with your knee."

"I'm keeping the groove."

"There is no groove. There is a count." Two fingers tap my sternum, exactly where the pop should have died. "This hits." She taps my shoulder. "This does not get an opinion."

Back home that's a diss worth a battle. Here I nod. I've learned to nod. My mother's working doubles at the Chrysler plant so I don't have to call and say I got sent home from the thing that was supposed to change us.

"Clean it. Second eight, formation." She walks back to her corner.

Music drops in. Seven-eight of the first phrase: arms slice down, cross at the wrists over my hips, head snaps front.

Second eight. The back row breaks—center holds, outside two travel. I walk forward up the outside of my column, left, right, left, on hana, dul, set, through maybe two feet of floor between Haeun's shoulder and the wall. On net I'm supposed to land on a new X one step left of Minjun. Front row. Three feet from Baek.

Except my walk is a walk. It's got bounce in it, a weight shift wide on every step, because that's how you move when the bass has a direction and you're leaning into it. On dul my right shoulder clips Haeun's left. She doesn't flinch—they're trained not to—but it knocks me off my line and I land on the *and* of net, a half count late, which to Baek is a lifetime. In the mirror I'm a frame behind eight other bodies, like lag.

Third eight: Seo-yeon's killing part. Center front, she drags splayed fingers down her face and her hip hits on dul—the move the fancams will loop—and the rest of us frame her. My job: body angled forty-five toward center, right arm back up on the diagonal, left hand flat on my hip. Freeze. Eight counts. Four seconds.

I have never been still for four seconds in my life.

Hana. Dul. Everyone's a statue. Set. My calf wants to pulse. Net. Eight people who learned this with parents paying by the month, holding so still their breathing is the loudest thing in the room—

Baek, three feet away, is watching me. Not Seo-yeon.

And on daseot, arm locked, sweat running down the inside of it, I understand: she's not watching for the mistake. She's watching for the fix. She wants to see if I'll kill it.

I could put the wave in. One roll of the wrist on yeodeol—a signature, one inch of me on a stage that isn't mine—and be on a plane Tuesday.

Or I could stop.

Yeoseot. I stop the calf. Ilgop. I stop the thing in my ribs that wants to answer the kick drum. Yeodeol. I stop my wrist before it even thinks.

For the first time in six weeks, Baek nods.

"Yes," she says. "That one. Again."

The music comes from everywhere. I stand on my new X, front row, closer to the mirror than I've ever been, and look for myself in it—and for a second I can't find me at all.

response:
Count one is a blade. Right arm up, ninety degrees from the shoulder, elbow locked, four fingers sealed together like a karate chop that forgot to swing. Nine of us do it in Studio B and eight of us land on the same photograph. My arm gets there too. It just gets there my way—shoulder firing first, a pop rolling down the humerus to the wrist, which flicks. A waack. A little hello. I don't decide it. My body says the sentence before I can read it.

In the mirror I'm the smudge in the back-left corner. Three rows of three, taped X's on the maple. Front row: Hana, Minseo, Dae. Middle row: Jiwoo directly ahead of me, then Tae and Bomi. Back row: me on the far left, then Soo-ah, then Yerin. Seo-ssaem paces the strip between the mirror and the front row, reading us left to right like a sentence she already knows has a typo.

Count two, heads snap left—mine too, chin level, I nail it. Three-four: right foot slides out to shoulder width, weight splits even, both arms chop down to the thighs. Five-six is what's killing me. "Hinge," she calls it. Fold at the hips, back flat as a table, then stand. No spine. On the West Side of Chicago, when a beat drops, my spine is where I live—chest rolls into belly, belly into hips, a wave going down to the floor and coming back up. So on five I fold with everyone else, but a ripple runs through my sternum on the way down, and on six my chest arrives half a count after my hips, like a kid late to the bus.

The fan snaps shut.

It's the sound of a folding chair closing in an empty church. Jun at the laptop kills the track mid-syllable. Eight bodies hold their freeze—*kalgunmu*, knife dance, that's the word here, nine bodies honed into one edge—and I'm the only one still finishing a motion.

She comes down the aisle between my column and the center one, stops at my right shoulder. Black folding fan, closed, in her right hand. She doesn't look at my face; she looks at me in the mirror. Nobody here looks at you directly. She puts the fan's tip against my sternum and pushes, light, like testing a melon.

"Here moves," she says. In English, for me. "Here should not." She drops the tip to my hip bone. "Here moves. Only here."

"Yes, ssaem."

"You are hitting. Nobody asked you to hit. Place."

Hitting—she knows the word. Hitting is a popper's muscles contracting and releasing on the beat, a punch thrown from inside the body. Placing is what a hand does when it's a hand on a clock.

She walks back to the mirror. The fan cracks open: resume.

Second eight. One through four is the re-blade—arms back up, head back center. Five through eight is the formation change, where I stop being a smudge and become a problem. Back row dissolves: Yerin cuts right to the wall, Soo-ah holds, and I take the long diagonal from back-left to front-center while Minseo takes it in reverse to my old X. We pass on each other's left. Four walking steps each. One per count. Heel-toe, upright, arms pinned to the seams.

My feet have other ideas. In footwork the floor is a hot skillet—160 beats a minute, nobody walks anywhere, you skitter, six steps where a civilian takes two. On five my feet start chopping before my brain signs off. I eat the diagonal in six quick steps on the balls of my feet, Minseo's sleeve grazing my left arm as I blow past her, and I'm planted on the front-center X on *seven*. A full count early. Dead still in the exact middle of the mirror while Minseo is still two steps from my old mark behind me and eight bodies are still moving around a ninth that's already done. A stopped clock in a room of ticking ones.

Snap.

Nobody laughs. Back home, when you eat it in the cypher, the circle lets you know—a groan, a *whoa*, somebody's palm on your back shoving you back in. Here the silence is the whole verdict. Here the shoes around me cost more than my mother clears in a week, and the word for me is *jang-hak-saeng*, scholarship kid, which everyone pronounces politely and which means: guest. Everyone else paid for this room. I'm the room's charity.

Seo-ssaem comes down the aisle again. Small woman, maybe fifty, hair pulled so tight it reads as a decision.

"Your feet are talented," she tells the mirror. "Your feet also do not listen. Who do you dance for?"

The circle. Three a.m. on Pulaski with a phone speaker as the sound system. "The team, ssaem."

"Then arrive with the team. Alone. From the top. Everyone else, sit."

Eight bodies melt to the walls. Just me on the center X, and a mirror full of one person.

Jun hits play.

Here's the thing I understand in the two silent beats before count one: she's not wrong. If I place instead of hit, if I hinge instead of wave, if I walk instead of skitter, I will be flawless. I can feel the flawless version waiting in me like a suit on a hanger. And I will not be in it. The girl in the suit will be from nowhere.

Count one: the arm. I place it. Ninety degrees, no pop, no flick. Two: head left. Three-four: step, split, chop. Five: hinge, back flat as a table, spine a dead plank. Six: stand. Seven: freeze.

Eight is a hold. Dead air. And in the dead air I let one ripple run through my chest—half an inch, the size of a breath. Not a hit. A ghost note. Something only a dancer would catch.

In the mirror she's watching. The fan is open, resting against her thigh.

It doesn't snap.

"Again," she says.

# Therapeutic Boundaries

The diagram on the wall has no face. Just a flayed man, red-roped and labelled, staring at the ceiling with a jaw that is only masseter. I know him better than I'd like. For eleven weeks he's been the thing I look at instead of Ilan.

"Prone," Ilan says. "You know the drill."

I know the drill. I get face-down on the table and turn my head toward the wall. *Biceps femoris, long head. Semitendinosus. Semimembranosus.* The three cords that used to fire me over ten hurdles in under thirteen seconds, and which, fourteen months ago, in the third stride off the blocks in Zürich, tore off my sitting bone like a tendon off a Christmas turkey.

His hand finds the back of my right knee. Warm, dry. Fingers in the crease, thumb along the outer tendon.

"Bend for me."

I flex the knee. He lets my heel come up toward my glute, then takes my ankle in his other hand and adds pressure, folding the leg until the stretch wakes in the front of my thigh—rectus femoris pulling long across the hip.

"Three," I say, before he asks.

"You said three last week with a different face." He doesn't let the ankle go. "I need the real number."

"Four."

He releases the leg slowly, the way you'd set down something you didn't want to wake, and I hate how much I feel the absence of his hands.

We shared a coach for six years. I remember him at nineteen, all shins and elbows, clipping hurdles with his trail leg and swearing in two languages. I remember him at twenty-six, hanging up his spikes after a national final where he came fifth and said *that's enough* like a man deciding he was full. He got letters after his name. He got shoulders—real ones, wider than when we used to hold each other's feet for sit-ups on the infield grass.

I got a surgical scar in the gluteal fold and a letter from my federation that used the word *regretfully*.

"Turn over."

Supine. The ceiling has a water stain shaped like Portugal. He stands at my right hip and lifts my leg straight, one hand cupping my heel, the other flat just above my kneecap, locking the knee out so the stretch goes where he wants it. Passive straight leg raise. He brings the leg up—thirty degrees, forty-five, sixty—and I feel the posterior chain tighten like a rope being paid out until it isn't.

At seventy the hamstring bites. Not the clean, musical ache of a healthy muscle at end range. This is uglier. It lives high up, under the sitting bone, where the surgeon anchored tendon back to pelvis with hardware I sometimes imagine I can feel. A hot wire. The muscle guards—I feel it clench against him without my say-so.

"There," he says. "Breathe."

"I am breathing."

"You're holding." His thumb shifts a half-inch on my knee. It doesn't mean anything. It's a therapist's thumb. "Contract-relax. Push your heel into my shoulder."

He tucks his shoulder under my heel and I drive down with everything the hamstring has—isometric, nothing moving, the muscle shortening against immovable him. Six seconds. His collarbone is hard under my heel; I can feel the seam of his polo through my sock. He counts under his breath and I watch the tendon in his neck stand out as he holds me.

"Relax."

I let go, and in the slack moment after, he takes the leg two degrees further. The hamstring, fooled, allows it. The wire goes hotter. My toes curl without permission. Gooseflesh breaks over my shin and travels upward, which has nothing to do with the stretch, and both of us know it.

"Number."

"Six."

"Good six or bad six?"

Good six means stretch. Bad six means I've torn it again and we're done forever this time. "Good," I say.

"Then stay."

He stays too. His forearm is along the inside of my calf now, bracing. The leg is heavy and he's taking all of it. I am lying on my back with my thigh pointed at the ceiling and his hand on my knee, thinking that I used to be a person whose legs were the fastest thing in a stadium, and now I'm a person who gets held up.

"Last one. Adductors."

He lowers the leg and guides it out to the side—abducting the hip, knee still straight, his hand on the inner thigh above the knee, the only place he can anatomically put it. The inner-thigh muscles pull taut. *Gracilis. Pectineus. Adductor magnus.* I read the names off the flayed man rather than look at the six inches between Ilan's wrist and the hem of my shorts.

"You're clenching your jaw," he says.

"You're measuring my jaw now?"

"I'm measuring everything." He says it to my knee. His voice is a therapist's voice. His hand on my inner thigh is a therapist's hand. The pulse jumping in his wrist—that I'm choosing not to assign a department.

Then the part I dread. He has me roll onto my left side, knees drawn up, and he finds the ischial tuberosity through my shorts—the sitting bone—and sinks his thumb into the scar tissue where the tendon re-rooted. Cross-friction. Short, hard strokes perpendicular to the fibre. This is not a stretch. This is a man pressing his thumb into the worst place in me, deliberately, in slow strokes, watching my face to see how much I'll let him.

The pain has edges. It runs down the back of my thigh along the sciatic nerve as a bright electrical hum, and up into my low back, and I bite the inside of my cheek and taste copper and do not make the sound that's in my throat.

"Eight," I say. He didn't ask.

"I know." His other hand steadies my hip. "Twenty seconds."

I count them watching the diagram. *Gluteus maximus.* The flayed man never got hurt. He never ran. He just hangs there, perfectly labelled, every muscle present and in the right place, and I envy him so much I could spit.

"Done," Ilan says. The thumb lifts. His palm stays a beat longer than it needs to, flat and warm over the place that ended me, and I feel it there—the thing neither of us will say, the weight of six years of handed-up feet and shared water bottles.

Then it's gone.

"Same time Thursday," he says, and turns to write it down, and I lie on my side with my scar still ringing and hate how much better it feels.

response:
# Therapeutic Boundaries

The diffuser is new. A white plastic egg on the windowsill, breathing lavender over the alcohol wipes and the warm rubber of the treatment table, as if a smell could make this a different kind of room. Cal's idea, I'm sure. He has a framed degree on the wall now that says he's allowed ideas.

"On your back."

I sit on the edge, lift my left leg onto the table with both hands cupped under the thigh the way I've learned to, and lie down. The paper crackles under my shoulders. Eleven weeks. I know this choreography better than I ever knew my hurdle rhythm, and I hate it more.

He stands at my left side and lays the goniometer against the knee without asking—hinge over the joint line, one arm running up the thigh, one down the shin. "Bend." I bend. It stops where it always stops, like a door hitting a chair. "Ninety-four," he says, neutral as a scoreboard. Thursday was ninety-two. The surgeon said a knee needs a hundred and twenty to come down stairs like a person. Nobody has told me what it needs to clear a hurdle, because nobody is going to say that sentence to me again.

"Quad off. Let me have it."

He means the kneecap. He already has it—thumbs along the outer edge, index fingers along the inner, the whole patella pinched between his hands like a stone he's about to skip. He pushes it toward himself. My thigh fires on its own, the muscle snatching the bone back, and he doesn't press harder, just waits, patient as weather, until the quad goes slack and the bone slides. Then away from him. Then down toward my foot, where the scar tissue has knit the tendon into something that refuses to move, and that one has a sound in it, a dry creak I feel in my teeth.

"Exhale when I push." His voice is pitched for a library. He never talked like that at camp; he yelled splits across the infield and laughed with his whole chest.

I count ceiling tiles. Eighteen and a half. His forearm is at the edge of my vision, the long flexors shifting under the skin, and there's the crescent scar on his knuckle from when he caught a hurdle wrong in Lisbon. I taped it. I was faster than him by then. He was already talking about anatomy classes.

"Heel slide. Slow."

I plant my left foot flat and drag it toward me. The knee folds through the easy range and then it isn't easy—the back of the joint fills with hot pressure, a balloon inflating behind the kneecap—and my foot stalls. He lays his palm over my shin just below the patella and leans, pushing the tibia down and back, driving the bend deeper.

"Number."

"Four."

"You've said four since September." He doesn't let up. "What is it."

"Seven."

"Thank you." He holds. Thirty seconds that have a different length than other seconds. Sweat starts at my hairline. Under the lavender I can smell his polo, clean cotton, and under that something I know from a hundred cool-downs and have no business recognizing.

"Turn over."

He steps back so I can roll without touching him. I notice that he steps back.

Face down, cheek on my folded hands. He takes my left ankle in his right hand and flattens his left across the back of my pelvis—heel of his palm on the sacrum, fingers spread over the glute—to pin the hip so I can't cheat by lifting it. He brings my heel toward me. Ninety. Ninety-four. Then he leans. The pressure at my pelvis is heavy and absolutely still; the pressure at my ankle is the slow steady weight of his whole body; together they mean I cannot go anywhere, and the knee is a cable tightening one click at a time. The quad stretches over the kneecap like skin on a drum. Inside the joint, something is being peeled. My toes curl. My hands make fists under my cheek. A sound leaves me that I didn't send.

"Eight," I say before he asks.

"I know." His thumb shifts a quarter inch on my glute. It's nothing—a man adjusting his grip. My whole body hears it anyway, because pain and the rest of it travel the same wires and all of mine are lit.

"You're guarding."

"I'm in pain."

"Those are different." A pause. "You never guarded. You went through things."

Because there was somewhere to get to. Because he quit while he could still choose it, both knees intact and a plan, and I got taken out mid-flight over hurdle seven by a plant foot and a sound like a branch, and the thing he's bending is just a knee now. Nothing I'm going back to.

"Then push."

He pushes. Something gives—not tears, *gives*, a small wet click deep in the joint—and my heel comes two fingers closer than it has ever been, and the pain spikes white and drops out the bottom into something I can only call relief. I'm breathing like the end of a four hundred. His hand on my pelvis stays exactly where it is for one second longer than it needs to.

Then lifts. "Supine. Hamstring."

I roll. He raises my straightened leg, sets my heel on his right shoulder, lays one hand flat over my knee to keep it from softening, and leans in. His face is above mine. Eighteen inches. We're both looking at the ceiling tiles. The pull runs from my heel to the bone I'm sitting on, bright and clean, almost a kindness after the other thing. His chest rises against my calf when he breathes. I can feel it. He knows I can.

"Count for me," he says, and I do, out loud, because it's something to do with my mouth.

Afterward, the goniometer again. "Ninety-nine."

Five degrees. For stairs.

"Good work," he says, already turning to write it down, and I hate how much I wanted to hear it. The diffuser sighs. Lavender settles over everything like it has somewhere to be.

response:
**Therapeutic Boundaries**

The table is vinyl, the colour of a hospital's idea of calm, and I hate it the way I hate everything in this room that was built to be gentle with me.

"Supine," Teo says. "You know the drill."

I do. I lie on my back and he takes my right heel in his palm—the left is fine, the left would still run if I let it—and lifts the leg toward the ceiling with the knee locked straight. His other hand presses flat across the front of my thigh just above the kneecap, keeping the joint from bending, keeping me honest. The stretch climbs the back of my leg and arrives, as it always does, at the place where my hamstrings tore off the bone.

Ischial tuberosity. Sit bone. A spot you'd never think about until three tendons let go of it at the eighth hurdle of a race I was winning.

"Number," he says.

"Four."

He pushes another two degrees. The scar tissue under my glute pulls like a knot in wet rope. "Number."

"Six. Christ. Six."

He holds. He doesn't apologise. That was the first thing I noticed when they assigned him—the apologies I'd braced for never came. Nine years ago we did block starts side by side at the national centre and he never apologised for beating me out of them either.

His compression sleeves are the same ones. I'd know them anywhere: a riot of teal and orange triangles, faded now, pulled over forearms that have grown denser since I last saw them bare. He wore them every session that winter. The whole group mocked him. He wore them anyway, and now he wears them to work, under the short sleeves of a clinic polo, like a man who never had to stop being who he was.

Thirty seconds. He lowers the leg slowly, taking its weight so the hamstring doesn't snap back to short. Relief runs up through me as a flush that reaches my face, and I turn my head so he won't see it.

"Prone."

I roll onto my stomach and fit my face into the padded cradle. Through the hole I see his trainers and a square of grey floor. This is the part I can't watch.

His hands start high, just below the fold where glute meets thigh—which is to say half an inch past where my shorts end. Heel of the palm first, warming the tissue in long strokes toward the knee and back. Then thumbs. He finds the scar, the transverse seam tucked under the crease where they went in to stitch tendon back to bone, and works across it rather than along it, dragging the healed ridges sideways against the grain.

It feels like a lit match held an inch from the skin. Not burning. Promising to.

My hip flexes before I can stop it—pelvis tipping up off the table, the whole leg trying to get out from under his thumbs.

"Stay." He lays his forearm across my sacrum. The sleeve is cool. His weight settles through it, pinning my pelvis flat so the tissue he's working can't escape by moving the bone it's anchored to. "Breathe out on the pressure."

I breathe out. He presses. My breath hits the vinyl beneath the cradle and comes back humid against my mouth.

"You're guarding."

"I'm lying still."

"Your adductors are guarding." Two fingers tap the inside of my thigh and, God help me, the muscle jumps. "Everything around the injury is trying to do its job for it. That's why you hurt in places that didn't tear."

He says it kindly. I'd rather he didn't. I was the one with the faster splits that winter, and he was the one who kept a notebook of everyone else's mechanics, and I remember thinking it was a strange hobby for a man who could run like that. Now he has a degree and a door with his name on it and I have a leg that doesn't belong to me.

"Knee flexion. Heel to your backside. Slow."

I bend the knee. At ninety degrees his hand closes around the back of my ankle and resists—not stopping me, just making the hamstring earn every further inch of its own contraction. The pain here is different: not the pull of a tendon being lengthened but the deep muscular ache of the repair being asked to work. My calf cramps in sympathy. I keep going. My heel comes within a hand's width of my glute before the muscle shudders and I feel his grip ease just enough to let it finish.

"Good," he says. "That's good."

I hate that I wanted him to say it.

"Up. Standing. We'll finish with the hinge."

He stands me facing the mirror, bare feet hip-width, and comes around behind. Both hands land on my pelvis—one on each iliac crest, thumbs on the bony points at the back, fingers wrapping forward toward my hip flexors.

"Hinge from here. Knees soft. Don't round."

I tip forward from the hips. He follows me down, hands riding the bones, close enough that I feel the heat off his chest along my spine before I feel the stretch. In the mirror his eyes are over my shoulder, fixed on my lumbar curve, not my face. Mine are on his. When the hamstring reaches the end of its length—four, five, six—his right thumb presses into the back of my pelvis and tilts it a fraction further forward, moving the stretch out of the muscle belly and up into the tendon. Into the scar. Into the bone.

I inhale sharply through my nose. His hands don't move.

"Number."

I could lie. He'd know.

"Seven."

"Hold it."

We hold it. Nine years, two careers, one scar, and the only thing in the room neither of us will touch is that he hasn't let go, and I haven't asked him to.

prompt:
Hell is Other Demons

Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Write a day in the life of this power couple, with elements of dark comedy & fantasy. Use understated irony & absurdity by merging the black immorality and everyday business of running hell, against relatable domestic relationship drama. Take cues from Neil Gaiman. Lucifer’s pet hellhound won’t stop chewing on the iron throne’s leg, adding to the tension. 1000 words.
response:
# Hell is Other Demons

Morning in Hell is a matter of consensus rather than astronomy. Somebody has to decide it is morning, and that somebody, for several thousand years, has been Lucifer.

He decided it at what he judged to be seven. The lake of fire adjusted itself from a night-time crimson to something more approaching breakfast. The screaming, which never stops, shifted key.

The hellhound was chewing the throne again.

"Beatrice," said Lucifer.

Beatrice did not stop. She had three heads, and the leftmost one was working at the back-left leg of the Iron Throne with the contented absorption of a creature that has found its purpose. The other two heads watched him with an expression he could only describe as supportive.

"That is wrought iron," he told her. "It was wrought. Someone wrought it. It is older than the concept of furniture."

The left head paused, considered this, and resumed.

---

The Undersecretary for Intake arrived at eight with the morning figures. He was a small demon called Pelz who wore a cardigan, because someone had once told him it put the damned at ease, and nobody had had the heart to tell him since that nothing did.

"Volume is up," said Pelz. "Mostly the usual. Lust, pride, people who stand on the left side of the escalator."

"We have a circle for that?"

"We've been meaning to. There's a sub-committee." Pelz turned a page. "There's also a proposal for a new wing for those who wrote 'per my last email.'"

"Approve it."

"The architect wants to know what the walls should be made of."

"Their last emails," said Lucifer, and Pelz wrote this down as though it were wisdom, which, in Hell, it was.

There was a splintering sound from the back of the room. The throne settled perhaps a quarter of an inch to the left.

"Sir," said Pelz carefully, "the dog—"

"I'm aware of the dog."

"Only there are firms. Specialists. I could have her—"

"No one is having anything," said Lucifer, and the lake of fire flared briefly, and Pelz remembered an urgent appointment elsewhere.

---

He ate alone, which he preferred, and which he had preferred for eleven months now, and which he would go on preferring until someone made him stop.

The trouble with being the Morning Star is that one is contractually disposed toward beginnings. He had read somewhere—on a scrap of paper that had fluttered down from above, as things sometimes did, torn from a magazine—that the key to a healthy relationship was to end things cleanly. He had kept the scrap. He was not sure why. Beatrice had eaten it anyway.

Lilith had come by last Tuesday.

She had not set fire to anything. That was the unsettling part. In the ordinary way of things, when Lilith visited Hell during an off period, it was to remind him of the ways in which the architecture was flammable. The library had gone up twice. The Hall of Minor Grudges, once, which he had secretly been grateful for.

But last Tuesday she had merely returned a book. His book. A book he had not lent her and which he suspected she had stolen in the fourth century, and which she returned with a note tucked inside reading *finished it, the ending was a bit much*, which was exactly what she had said about Revelation.

---

She arrived at three, by the door, which no one used.

"I was in the neighbourhood."

"There isn't a neighbourhood."

"There's a sort of a neighbourhood." She came in. She was wearing the coat he liked and had never told her he liked, which meant she knew. "What's wrong with your chair?"

"Nothing."

"It's listing."

"It has character."

"It had character. Now it has a dog in it." Lilith crossed the hall. Beatrice looked up with all three heads at once, which she did for no one, and thumped her tail, and went back to the leg. "Oh, she's lovely. Is she allowed to do that?"

"She's a hellhound. I've found it best to let her have a project."

"The throne of the Adversary is a project."

"The alternative was my shoes."

Lilith sat on the edge of the dais. Not on the throne—she had never once sat on it, in all their years, and he had never once asked her to, and they both knew what that was about and neither of them was going to be the one to say it.

"I came to say," she said, and then she said nothing for a while.

The screaming went on in the middle distance. Somewhere below them a sub-committee was voting on escalators.

"Pelz thinks I should have it looked at," said Lucifer. "The leg."

"Pelz is right."

"Pelz is a cardigan with ambitions."

"He's right anyway. It'll go, you know. Not now. But one day you'll be in the middle of damning someone and it'll go, and then where will you be."

"On the floor, I imagine."

"On the floor. In front of the sinners. In front of the demons. Satan, on the floor, because he wouldn't let anyone near his chair." She looked at him. "That's not about the chair."

"No," he agreed.

Beatrice chewed.

He thought about saying *stay*. It was a short word. He had invented worse. He had, in a sense, invented the circumstances under which the word needed saying at all, and there was a certain irony in that, which Lilith would have appreciated if he had pointed it out, and so he did not.

"Tuesday," said Lilith, standing. "I've got the other book of yours. The green one."

"I don't have a green one."

"You'll have it Tuesday." She stopped at the door. "Get a man in for the leg."

"I'll think about it."

"You'll sit on the floor."

"I'll think about it there."

The door closed. The lake of fire, which had been a warm late-afternoon sort of orange, deepened by a shade, which he had not told it to do.

He went and sat in the Iron Throne. It tilted him, very slightly, to the left, towards the door.

"Beatrice," he said.

The left head looked up. There was a question in it.

"Carry on," said Lucifer, and she did.

response:
# Hell is Other Demons

The ash started before dawn, which in Hell is a figure of speech. It came down fine and grey and patient, the way it always did, and Lucifer Morningstar stood at the window of his study and watched it settle on the balustrade and thought, not for the first time, that someone really ought to do something about it.

He had a department for that. He had a department for most things.

Breakfast was taken alone at a table built for forty. The damned who served it moved with the practised quiet of people who have learned that the Lord of the Pit does not like conversation before his coffee, and that his coffee is never right. Today it tasted of regret and burnt sugar. He drank it anyway. The chair at the far end of the table was empty, as it had been for seven weeks, and he did not look at it, in the deliberate way one does not look at a thing.

At nine there were audiences. A duke of the Fourth Circle wished to expand the Boiling Lakes into a neighbouring district, citing overcrowding. The neighbouring district objected. Lucifer listened to both, signed the expansion, and made a note to have the objecting duke boiled in it, which resolved the matter with what he felt was admirable economy.

At half past ten a soul was brought before him who had, in life, invented a particular kind of hold music. Lucifer studied the file for a long moment and then said, very gently, "I think we can do something quite special for you." The soul wept. Everyone had expected it to.

Ash gathered in the folds of his sleeves. He brushed it off. It came back.

---

She arrived at noon, which was unlike her. Lilith had always preferred inconvenient hours, trailing screaming, with something's head.

Today she had brought a plant.

"It's a fig," she said, setting it on his desk, where it dropped two leaves immediately and began, in a small and dignified way, to die. "I thought the place needed something green."

"Nothing green lives here."

"Then it'll fit in."

He looked at the fig. He looked at her. She had done something to her hair, and he knew better than to mention it, and he mentioned it.

"It's the same," she said.

"It's shorter."

"It was always this length. You never noticed."

He had noticed. He had noticed a great many things over eleven thousand years, and had learned that the noticing was never the problem; it was the saying. He offered her tea. She said she wasn't staying. She sat down.

They did not talk about the seven weeks. They talked about the Boiling Lakes, and she said he'd been too soft on the second duke, and he said she'd have gutted both and left the paperwork to him, and she said yes, obviously, that was the *system*, and for a moment it was almost the way it had been. Outside, the ash came down on the courtyard and the gargoyles and the small blackened orchard that had never produced anything, and she watched it with him, and he found he was not thinking about the empty chair.

"I'm not here to make up," she said, eventually.

"I know."

"I'm here because Asmodeus has been telling people I left."

"You did leave."

"I left *you*. I didn't leave. There's a difference, and I'd like it minuted."

He rang for a scribe.

---

The afternoon brought a riot in the Seventh, as the Seventh usually did. Lucifer attended personally, because he believed in being seen, and because the alternative was his study and the fig. He walked through the smoke with his hands behind his back and his wings folded like a closed umbrella, and the rioters fell silent in rings, the way water does when something very large passes underneath.

"What is it this time?"

"They've been told," said the overseer, a creature mostly made of teeth, "that there is a Heaven."

"There is a Heaven."

"Yes, my lord. They hadn't been told that bit before. It's caused some upset."

Lucifer looked out at the damned, thousands of them, ash settling on their shoulders, faces upturned and full of something that was not quite hope but was related to it by marriage.

"Tell them it's full," he said, and went home.

---

She was still there when he returned. This was unprecedented. She had moved the fig to the windowsill, where it would get the light that did not exist, and was reading his correspondence, which she had always done, and which he had always pretended not to notice, which was its own kind of intimacy.

"Beelzebub wants a title," she said.

"Beelzebub has four."

"He wants a fifth. He says the symmetry's off."

"Give him *Lord of Asymmetry* and see if he notices."

She laughed. It was not a kind laugh — none of hers were — but it was for him, and he had not had one in seven weeks, and he put it carefully somewhere inside himself for later.

Dinner was for two. The staff did not comment. The staff were damned, not stupid.

They argued over the fish, because they always argued over the fish, and the argument was old and comfortable and went nowhere, which was the point. At the end of it she stood and put on her coat, which was made of something that had once begged.

"I'm not staying."

"I know."

"I might come Thursday. There's a thing with the Lamia. You'll want a witness."

"I'll want a witness."

At the door she paused, the ash coming down behind her in the long grey evening that was also a figure of speech, and she said, "Water the fig."

"It's dead."

"Water it anyway."

He stood in the doorway a long time after she'd gone. Then he went back upstairs, and found a cup, and filled it from the one tap in the palace that ran something close to water, and stood at the windowsill and poured it, slowly, into the pot of the dead fig, while outside the ash fell on the whole of Hell, patient and grey and unremarkable, exactly as it had the day before, and would tomorrow, and had, if he was honest, for rather longer than either of them had been apart.

prompt:
Hell is Other Demons

Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Write a day in the life of this power couple, with elements of dark comedy & fantasy. Use understated irony & absurdity by merging the black immorality and everyday business of running hell, against relatable domestic relationship drama. Take cues from Neil Gaiman. Lilith carries a scorched leather purse containing odd trinkets from mortal realms. 1000 words.
response:
# Hell is Other Demons

There are no mornings in Hell. This is a matter of policy rather than physics; Lucifer had abolished them in the second century, after a Pit full of the damned began complaining that the dawn gave them hope. He kept a clock anyway. It said half past seven. It always said half past seven. He found this reassuring, the way one might find a dead houseplant reassuring: at least it was consistent.

He drank his coffee black, because the cream had been recalled. Someone in Procurement had sourced it from a cow that was technically still alive, and the paperwork had been a nightmare.

The first meeting of the day—he still called it a day—was with Asmodeus about the Eighth Circle. There had been a slowdown. The fraudsters were unionizing.

"They want representation," Asmodeus said. He had a face like a bad decision made by committee. "They say the pitch is too hot."

"It's Hell."

"I did mention that."

"And?"

"They've filed a grievance. In triplicate." Asmodeus set the papers on the desk. They were bound in something that had recently been a solicitor. "I also pointed out that they were only here because they'd spent their mortal lives being exactly this sort of person, and they said that was ad hominem."

Lucifer signed without reading. He had learned long ago that reading things only made them worse. "Lower the pitch for a week, then raise it by a degree every day for a century. Tell them it was a compromise."

Asmodeus bowed and left, and Lucifer looked at the empty chair across the desk, which was a thing he had been doing lately, and did not like that he had been doing.

---

She came at what the clock insisted was half past seven.

He heard her before he saw her, because Lilith had never in her existence entered a room quietly, and because the doors of Pandemonium, which were made of iron and spite, gave a specific whimper only for her. Then she was in the doorway in a coat that had belonged to a dead empress, and she had the purse.

The purse was leather, and it was scorched, and it had been scorched before he met her, which was before the invention of leather. Nobody knew what it was made of. Nobody had ever been brave enough to ask.

"You look terrible," she said.

"I'm the Prince of Lies."

"Then lie about it." She sat in the chair. His chair. The chair he had not been looking at. "I'm not staying."

"You said that last time."

"I didn't stay last time."

"You stayed three hundred years."

"Compared to eternity, Lucifer, that's a long weekend." She opened the purse. This was the ritual: she never announced why she'd come, she simply began taking things out, and somewhere in the taking-out the reason would surface like a body in a lake.

A snow globe of a city that had not yet been built. A tooth. A plastic lighter printed WORLD'S BEST DAD. A paperback whose title had been worn away entirely by thumbs. A key to nothing.

"They've invented a thing," she said, holding up a small flat rectangle of glass. "They look at it all day. It tells them what everyone else is angry about."

"We have that. It's called the Fourth Circle."

"Yes, but they *pay* for this one." She tossed it onto his desk, where it lay dark and smug. "I thought you'd want it. For the collection."

He did not have a collection. She had been bringing him things for six thousand years and he had been putting them in a drawer, and the drawer was now a wing, and he had never once said thank you, because the first time he'd said it she had hit him with a mountain.

"Is that why you came?"

"No."

A silence, of the sort Hell was supposedly made of, though he had never found any in the actual inventory.

---

Beelzebub interrupted to report that the Styx had developed an algae problem and the ferryman wanted hazard pay. Lucifer told him to pay it. Beelzebub looked at Lilith, then at Lucifer, then at the chair, and did a thing with his eyebrows that would have gotten anyone else eaten.

"They talk about us," Lilith said, when he'd gone.

"They're demons. They don't have anything else."

"They have a pool going. On when I'll come back."

"What are the odds?"

"I didn't ask." She picked up the tooth and turned it over. "It's a child's. I took it from under a pillow in Lisbon. I left a coin."

"That was kind."

"It was gold. The family will be investigated. The father will go to prison."

"Ah."

"But it *was* kind." She said it almost to herself. He had noticed, over the millennia, that she only argued with people who weren't in the room.

---

The last meeting was the Tally. Every evening, such as it was, the souls were counted, and the count was always wrong, and someone was always blamed. Tonight it was wrong by one. It was always wrong by one. Lucifer had long ago decided this was the only genuinely funny thing God had ever done.

Lilith stayed for it. She put the trinkets back one by one, except the glass rectangle, which she left on the desk, and the tooth, which she left beside it, and he understood that these were not gifts but hostages; that she would need, eventually, to return for them.

"I'll go," she said, at half past seven.

"You keep saying that."

"I keep meaning it." At the door she stopped, back to him, and said in the voice of someone reading an invoice, "You've changed the lighting."

"Asmodeus's idea. Softer. The screaming carries better."

"It's nice."

Then the doors whimpered and she was gone, and he sat with the little piece of glass that told you what everyone was angry about, and it stayed dark, and he found he did not want to know.

He put the tooth in his pocket. Not the drawer. His pocket.

The clock said half past seven. Somewhere, someone filed a grievance. The fraudsters sweated at a temperature precisely one degree higher than yesterday, and did not notice, and would not notice, which was the whole point.

It was, he thought, almost a good day. Which was the trouble with Hell: now and then it let you have one.

response:
**Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute**

The Court of the Dreaming did not keep hours, which was fortunate, because the case of *First Love v. Mora* had been going since before Max fell asleep and would likely outlast him.

Dream sat where he always sat. His face gave nothing, as his face gave nothing, but the raven on the arm of the throne had noticed that the Lord of the Dreaming had been pressing one pale finger to the bridge of his nose for some time, and the raven knew what that meant and had decided to say nothing about it.

"Continue," said Dream.

First Love rose. He was pink to the ears and had tied his brief with a ribbon, which he now could not untie.

"Thank you, my lord. As I was saying. The dream in question—the field, the wildflowers, the girl named Priya with the chipped tooth—represents fourteen months of work. I sourced the light from a September that never happened. The grass is calibrated to be exactly as itchy as the dreamer can tolerate before he'd want to get up. And the ending—" He faltered. "The ending is the important part. They lean in. There is a confusion. Nothing is concluded. He wakes up not knowing what he feels and spends the day not knowing. That's the *product*, my lord. That's the formative experience."

"Noted," said Dream. "And the defendant has altered this ending."

"She's *sitting on him*."

From the defense bench came a sound like a kettle that had learned to laugh. It rose into the vaults, met itself coming back, and hung there longer than acoustics should have allowed.

"The defendant will refrain," said the raven.

"Can't," said Mora. "It's a condition." She was difficult to look at directly—the eye slid off her like something was wrong, then slid back because something was also very right, then slid off again, embarrassed. She had come to court barefoot. "Look. I'll be straight with the court. I've been working the Kraków corridor for six hundred years and the Kraków corridor is dead. Everybody's on melatonin. Everybody's on a sleep podcast. You can't get a decent terror out of anyone past forty, they just lie there and think about their mortgage, and that's their own nightmare, it's not mine, I can't feed on that, it's got no *flavor*—"

"The question before the court," said Dream, "is ownership."

"I'm getting to it. So I'm travelling. And I find this field. Lovely field. And there's this boy lying in it, *waiting to be sat on*. Practically an invitation. The girl was already going to climb on top of him—"

"Playfully," said First Love. "She was going to climb on him *playfully*. There's a difference."

"Not from underneath there isn't."

The cackle again. The raven put its head under its wing.

"So I stepped into her. For the last bit. He gets his field, he gets his girl, he gets his confusion—believe me, he's confused—and I get ten minutes on a fifteen-year-old's chest, which, my lord, with respect, is the single best dining in Europe." She spread her hands. "A girl's gotta eat too, you know?"

"Does she," said Dream.

"It's not personal. I like the kid. I've left the wildflowers alone."

First Love had finally got his ribbon undone and was now holding a brief and a ribbon and had nowhere to put either. "She's left the wildflowers *alone*? My lord, Exhibit B." He gestured, and the dream came up in the air of the court like a lantern slide: a field, a boy, a girl with a chipped tooth swinging a leg over him, laughing—and then the laugh went on too long, and the face above Max's face was still Priya's face except it was also very much not, and it had *teeth*, and it leaned down and inhaled, and the boy's eyes rolled back in a way that could have been terror and could have been something else, and the court, collectively, found somewhere else to look.

"He's into it," said Mora.

"He's *paralysed*."

"Same difference at that age."

Dream closed the exhibit with a motion so small it might have been a thought. "Has the dreamer been deposed?"

"We did try, my lord," said the raven. "He was asleep."

"Bring him."

Max arrived the way sleepers arrive, which is to say he had already been standing there for some time and only now noticed. He was in his school uniform except the uniform had been replaced, around the waist, with a towel. He looked at the throne. He looked at Mora. He looked at Mora for considerably longer than he looked at First Love, who noticed and made a small wounded sound.

"Dreamer," said Dream. "This court will ask you one question. The dream of the field. Do you wish it returned to its former ending, or do you wish it to remain as it is?"

Max opened his mouth.

He closed it.

"I don't," he said. "I mean. It's—I don't *know*."

"Thank you," said Dream. "The court notes that the dreamer's testimony is in perfect accordance with the dream as originally designed."

First Love blushed so hard the lantern slide briefly flickered back on.

"Here is the ruling." Dream stood. He did not stand often, and the vaults seemed to lean down to hear him. "The dream belongs to the dreamer. It belonged to him before either of you touched it and it will belong to him when both of you are nothing but a smell in an old book. The defendant's trespass is recognised. The plaintiff's labor is recognised. The court finds both parties have, in their way, given the boy exactly what he came for."

Mora grinned. First Love did not.

"And therefore the court sees no reason to disturb the arrangement. The defendant may remain in the dream."

"My *lord*—"

"On the plaintiff's terms." Dream looked at Mora, and something moved at the corner of his mouth that the raven would later swear was not a smile. "The ending is an almost. The ending has always been an almost. The defendant may enter the dream, and mount the dreamer, and lean down to feed—and the dream will end there. Every night. The breath you want will be the breath you never quite get. You will know confusion, Mora. Fourteen months of it, calibrated. And you will not know what you feel, and you will wake, and spend the day not knowing."

The cackle started in Mora's throat and died somewhere around her teeth.

"That's not—" she said. "A girl's gotta—"

"Yes," said Dream. "Next case."

response:
# Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute

The hourglass was taller than the gallery and had been running since before the gallery was built. Sand fell through it one grain at a time, each grain catching the light as it dropped, each one somebody's hour of sleep. Nobody had ever seen the upper chamber empty. Nobody wished to be present when it did.

Beneath it, Dream sat and did not fidget, because he did not fidget. A certain tightness about the jaw suggested this was costing him.

"Case nine hundred and four," said the raven at the lectern. "In the matter of a recurring dreamscape: one field, wildflowers, afternoon light, perpetual. Claimant, First Love. Respondent, Mora of the Slavic nightmares, also styled the Chest-Sitter, also styled—"

"Just Mora is fine."

"Also styled 'Just Mora.' Property currently occupied by a sleeper, Max, aged fourteen, not present but asleep, and therefore summonable if required."

"Let us hope it is not required," said Dream.

First Love rose. He was pink to the ears and held his notes the way one holds a bird that might die. "My lord. Three years. Three years I built that field. Every grass stalk bent the correct way. The light at precisely the hour when faces look kinder than they are. The girl, Cass, laughing at something he said that wasn't funny, and him not knowing it wasn't funny. And at the end—" He pressed the notes to his chest. "The almost-kiss. The lean. The not-quite. He wakes and doesn't know if he's happy or sick. That's the craft, my lord. That's the entire craft."

"Noted," said Dream. "Respondent."

Mora did not rise so much as unfold. She was long-limbed and grey-lipped and had the look of someone who had slept on a great many people and not one mattress. "I found a boy on his back in a field with his lungs wide open. I sat down."

"On his chest."

"Where else would I sit?"

"You transformed the girl."

"I didn't transform anything. I came in through the girl. She climbs onto him, I'm already there, I let my face through." A shrug. "If it was unclear, I'd like it on record that nobody's told the boy it was unclear. He hasn't missed a night."

First Love made a small wounded sound.

"A girl's gotta eat too, you know?"

Dream regarded her. The sand dripped. A grain struck the pile with a sound like a fingernail on glass.

"That," he said, "is not a legal argument."

"It's a true one."

"The Dreaming is not short of true things. It is short of time." He turned his eyes, which held whatever anyone most feared to look upon, to First Love. "Your remedy?"

"Restoration, my lord. Eviction. An injunction. She's not to come within three dreams of anything of mine. She's done this before. There was a honeymoon in Kraków, nineteen-oh-six—"

"That was a different case and they both liked it," said Mora.

"They never spoke again."

"They never spoke again *fondly*."

The raven coughed. "The court reminds both parties that there is a sleeper. Who will wake. Who dreams this field roughly nightly and is, at present, in it."

"Then the court will view the premises," said Dream, and lifted one hand, and the floor was not a floor.

They stood ankle-deep in wildflowers. The light was honeyed and low. A boy lay on his back with his arms flung out, and a girl with a scraped knee straddled him, laughing, pinning his wrists—and then her laugh went on a fraction too long, and her face did something that was not quite a change. The eyes went deeper. The mouth stayed the same. She settled her weight onto his sternum like a cat finding the warm spot.

The boy's breath left him in a long, thin, astonished ribbon. He did not look afraid, exactly. He looked like someone who had been handed something and told not to drop it.

"You see," Mora said softly. "Where's the harm?"

"He can't move," said First Love.

"He couldn't move in yours either. You just called it a lean."

Dream watched the boy's chest fail to rise. Watched the girl-who-was-also-something-else bend until her grey mouth was nearly at his. Watched the almost. The not-quite.

He closed his hand, and it was a courtroom again.

Nobody spoke. The sand dripped.

"I am told," Dream said at last, "that the boy wakes confused. Elated and nauseated. Unable to say whether he wishes it to stop."

"Yes," said both parties.

"And this was the original intent."

"...Yes," said First Love, slower.

Dream was quiet for a long moment, and it was possible—just—to see something shift behind his face that was not irritation. Something older and worse. Something amused.

"The court finds," he said, "that neither party owns the dreamscape, since neither party is dreaming it. The court finds further that you have, by accident, produced a more honest rendering of the subject than either of you could alone, and it would be a waste to separate you."

Mora smiled. First Love did not.

"However." The next grain seemed, to the gallery, to fall faster. "A dream that has become a burden to its sleeper should be shared. Effective tonight, the field is relocated."

"Relocated where?" said the raven, pen raised.

"To the girl."

Silence.

"Cass will dream the field. She will dream the boy beneath her. She will feel her own face change and not know why, and feel the hunger, and feel the weight of him holding very still. She will wake not knowing whether she is happy or sick." He inclined his head to First Love. "That is your craft, as I understand it." And to Mora: "And you may eat. From her. She breathes a good deal more easily than he does. For now."

"My lord, that's—"

"That is my ruling." He stood, and behind him the hourglass went on falling, grain after grain, indifferent. "Next case."

Max woke the following morning rested for the first time in a month, and could not think why he felt he had lost something. In second period, Cass sat down across the room and did not look at him once, and looked at him for the entire hour.
