response:
**Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute**

The bailiff was nine feet tall and, as far as anyone could tell, made entirely of voice.

"ALL RISE," it said, and the gallery — a hundred half-things, dreams waiting their own turn — rose. "FOR THE LORD OF THE DREAMING. PRESIDING. IN THE MATTER OF FIRST LOVE VERSUS. MORAH. MOO-RAH. MORE."

"Mora," said the defendant, not getting up.

"MORE-AH."

Dream took his seat. He did not look at the bailiff. He did not look at anyone. He looked at the brief in front of him, which was a single sheet, and the look lasted long enough that the candles along the walls began, very slightly, to lean away.

"Proceed," he said.

First Love stood. He was pink to the ears and had been pink since arriving; he held his hat in both hands and had, at some point, bitten through the brim.

"Your Honour. My lord. The dreamscape in question is a field. Wildflowers, early summer, about four in the afternoon. The dreamer is Max Hollis, thirteen. The — other party — is Lucy from the bus. She is lying beside him. There is a bee. He is thinking about the bee so as not to think about her hand, which is near his hand. They sit up at the same time. Their heads nearly collide. There is a moment." He swallowed. "Then he wakes up and doesn't know what happened and lies there feeling like he's swallowed a lamp."

"The muddled almost-kiss," Dream said.

"Nineteen months of work, my lord. Four hundred and eleven nights. He'd started going to bed early."

"And the complaint."

First Love pointed with his ruined hat. "She's sitting on him."

Mora unfolded from her chair. She was tall and heavy in a way that had nothing to do with weight, her hair hung like wet rope, and there was something about her — the gallery had already noticed — that made you want to lie down. Not with her. Just down.

"Your Honour." Her voice was warm and bored. "I'd like to state for the record that I didn't build anything. I didn't touch the flowers. I didn't touch the bee. The boy was already on his back. The girl was already climbing on top of him — "

"Playfully," said First Love.

"— playfully, and all I did was take over at the point where the girl's face stops being Lucy's. Which is a small point. You'd barely see the join." She shrugged. "A girl's gotta eat, Your Honour."

"You take his breath," said First Love. "Every night."

"He gets it back."

"He wakes up screaming."

"He wakes up. That's the main thing. Has anyone asked what the boy thinks? Because I have, and — "

"Call the dreamer," said Dream.

"THE DREAMER KNOWN AS. MAAAX." The bailiff considered. "MACKS. MAXIMILLION HOLLIS. HOLLACE."

Max Hollis arrived in pyjamas with a cartoon on them he would have died before admitting he owned. He was thirteen in the way of a bridge mid-collapse. He sat in the witness box, looked at Mora, and then very quickly at his knees.

"Max." Dream did not raise his voice; the room simply arranged itself so that nothing else could be heard. "Describe the dream as you now experience it."

"It's the field. It's — Lucy. She sort of climbs on me. Laughing. And then." He stopped. "Her face goes. Not all at once. Her eyes stay Lucy's the longest. And she gets heavy. And I can't breathe, and I can't move, and she's sort of — leaning in — "

"And this is terrifying," prompted First Love.

"Yeah."

"And unpleasant."

Max said nothing. Mora examined her nails.

"Max," said First Love gently, "it's unpleasant."

"I don't — " The boy's ears had gone the colour of the plaintiff's. "I mean, I wake up really scared. I do. But I also." He looked at the ceiling, which obligingly became very interesting. "I don't want to answer that."

"Thank you, Max," said Mora.

"The witness is excused," said Dream, and Max was, mid-breath, somewhere else.

First Love turned to the bench with the expression of a man who has watched his case walk out of the room in cartoon pyjamas. "My lord. With respect. He is thirteen. He doesn't know what he wants."

"No," Dream agreed. "That was rather the point of your dream, wasn't it."

Silence. The hourglass on the bench ran, for a second or two, upward.

Dream sat back. He had settled the dreams of kings. He had drawn the borders of nightmares that nations were later named after. He had once spent a century arbitrating between two adjacent sleepers who each insisted the other's dream was keeping them awake. He had not expected, when he rose, to rule on whether a boy would rather be nearly kissed or nearly suffocated, and the fact that the boy himself could not say was not, Dream felt, a mitigating factor.

Something at the corner of his mouth moved. The gallery, which had seen that happen perhaps twice, went quiet in a different way.

"Judgment," he said.

"THE COURT WILL. BE SILENT. FOR JUDGMENT."

"It is silent."

"IT IS SILENT."

"The dreamscape is awarded jointly."

Both parties started to speak. Neither did.

"Mora. You may feed. But you will feed as the dream was built. You will lie in the grass. You will notice the bee. Your hand will be near his hand, and you will be unable to look at it, and when he sits up you will sit up, and you will miss. Every night. Only then may you climb onto his chest, and you will do it blushing."

Mora's expression did something it had not done in a thousand years.

"First Love. You will have your almost-kiss. You will have it sitting on his chest, with your full weight, while he cannot move, and you will take a little of his breath — not much — and you will find it is the only way he can be made to hold still for it. Neither of you will tell him which of you he is dreaming. He will work it out eventually." Dream picked up the next brief. "Everyone does."

First Love opened his mouth.

"The boy," Dream said, not looking up, "has already been told that love is a weight on the chest that steals your breath. He was told by you. He was told by every song on the bus. I have merely declined to contradict it. Bailiff."

"NEXT CASE. THE MATTER OF. THE DROWNING MAN VERSUS. HIS OWN. ANKLES."

**Sisyphus Gives Advice**

The hill had been there a very long time. So had the boulder. So had Sisyphus, which was rather the point of the arrangement, and over the centuries the three of them had settled into the kind of relationship that long-married couples achieve, where nobody says much because everything has already been said, several thousand times, mostly uphill.

The letters were new.

They arrived in the beak of Crow, who was not, strictly speaking, a crow. He was a raven who had decided early on that the extra syllable was more trouble than it was worth. He had come for the carrion and stayed for the conversation, and he now served as scribe, postal service and, uninvited, editor.

He opened the first one with a claw.

\*

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*Every time my wife is upset she reorganises the kitchen. Then she gets angry when I can't find the spoons. I have started keeping a spoon in my coat. Is this a marriage?*

*— Spoonless, Corinth*

Dear Spoonless,

Yes. It is one of the more common kinds.

The spoons are not about spoons. Your wife is upset and doesn't have the words yet, so she is making the room say it for her. Next time you come home to a cupboard full of surprises, don't look for anything. Sit down and ask her what happened today, and then — this is the important bit — help her move the cupboard.

Keep the coat spoon. A man should have a spoon.

[*He does not own a coat. He does not, in point of fact, own a spoon. — C.*]

\*

Sisyphus set his shoulder to the boulder and leaned. The boulder moved, in the way that it always moved, grudgingly and then all at once, like an argument. Crow rode on top, reading ahead.

\*

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*I run a bakery. I rise at three. Last week I fell asleep in the dough and woke up proving. My children have started calling me "the bread man," as if I were a tradesman who visits. How do people with ordinary jobs manage it?*

*— Half-Baked, Argos*

Dear Half-Baked,

They don't. They just complain about it at a more sociable hour.

You have an apprentice you haven't hired, because nobody does it right. Nobody does. Hire him anyway and let him do it wrong on Tuesdays. Be at the table on Tuesdays. Children don't remember who made the bread; they remember who was there when it was eaten. Burn a loaf a week on purpose if it helps you feel less necessary. You'd be surprised what a bakery survives.

[*He asked me whether dough was a real thing or a kind of weather. I have confirmed it is real. — C.*]

\*

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*My neighbour comments on everything. My washing. My goats. My face. Yesterday she told me my chimney "looked tired." I am considering moving to the sea.*

*— Watched, Megara*

Dear Watched,

Don't move. She'll write.

A person who has opinions about your chimney is a person with nothing of her own to look at. Give her something. Go round tomorrow and ask how she gets her onions so — whatever her onions are. Small. Not big. You're not making a friend; you're giving a dog a stick so it stops chewing the furniture. Within a month she'll be too busy being consulted to be critical.

Also, have the chimney swept. A chimney can look tired.

[*I flew over. It does. — C.*]

\*

The boulder reached the place, about two-thirds up, where it always developed opinions. Sisyphus waited it out, breathing through his nose, the way you wait for a kettle.

"Next," he said.

Crow coughed. "This one's from Thebes."

\*

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*My husband has asked if I would dress as a centaur. The back half, specifically. I love him. I am not sure I love him from that angle.*

*— Concerned, Thebes*

Dear Concerned,

Ask him who's the front.

If he says "me," you have learned something about your husband. If he says "you choose," you have learned something better, and I'd stop worrying. Either way, if the answer is no, say the word. People spend whole decades trying to say no with their eyebrows, and the eyebrows are never as clear as they think.

For what it's worth, the back half is where the kicking comes from. There's dignity in that.

[*Horses do not work like this. I have asked several. — C.*]

\*

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*I am thirty-four and I have done nothing. My brother built a bridge. People walk across it and say his name. I have built — a routine, I suppose. I feed the same cat. I fix the same step. Was I meant for anything?*

Dear Ordinary,

Your brother's bridge is finished. That's the thing nobody tells you about bridges. He built it, and now it just stands there, and he has to go and find something else to do with his hands.

You fix the step. Someone doesn't fall. The cat eats. Nobody says your name, because nobody says the name of the person who stopped the bad thing happening; they just have a day. You've given out, by my count, a few thousand days. That's a bridge too. It's only that people cross it without noticing, which is how you know it's working.

[*I was promised there would be none of that. He says it was the walking, not the stone, and so it doesn't count. I am recording here that it counts. — C.*]

\*

The boulder reached the top of the hill, considered the view with the air of something that had seen it before and been unimpressed then too, and rolled back down.

Sisyphus watched it go. Then he stretched, cracked his neck, and found a walnut in his pocket for Crow.

"Right," he said. "Anything else?"

"Thebes wrote back." Crow turned the letter over with his beak. "She wants to know what you think about tails."

Sisyphus started down the hill, unhurried, hands behind his back like a man taking the air.

"Tell her," he said, "it depends entirely on the tail."

# Sisyphus Gives Advice

The hill in Tartarus has no name, which is unusual for a hill, but then it has only ever had the one visitor and he was busy.*

Crow arrived at the summit around the time the boulder didn't. She carried the post in a satchel, because the alternative was her beak, and the one time she'd tried that an advice-seeker in Thebes had received a reply consisting mostly of "caw."

"Fourteen today," she said. "One's sticky."

Sisyphus stepped aside and let the boulder go. It went. He listened to it with the expression of a man hearing a favourite song he'd never chosen.

"Read me the first on the way down."

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*My husband and I have been married eleven years. He has started humming. Not songs — a note. He does it while he eats. I have begun fantasising about a quiet widowhood. Is this normal?*

*— Buzzing in Corinth*

*Dear Buzzing,*

*Entirely normal. The humming isn't the problem, which you know, or you'd have asked him to stop. Something else is happening in your house, and the humming is where it's decided to live.*

*Ask him what he's humming. Really ask. He may not know. Finding out together will get you further than widowhood, which I can tell you from this side is overrated. There is a great deal of quiet down here and almost nobody is improved by it.*

*And eat dinner facing the window for a week. It helps more than it should.*

---

Sisyphus set his shoulder against the stone. Crow perched on top of it, which she maintained was not cheating because she wasn't the one being punished.

"Next."

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*A man at my work finishes my sentences. Wrongly. Yesterday I said, "I think the shipment—" and he said, "—is cursed, yes, I've been saying so." It was not cursed. It was late. How do I kill him in a way that doesn't affect my prospects?*

*— Interrupted in Argos*

*Dear Interrupted,*

*Stop finishing your own sentences. Say "I think the shipment," and stop. Look at him pleasantly. Wait.*

*He'll fill the silence, because that is what he is for, and when he's done you say "No," and carry on. Do this four times. By the fifth he'll have learned that your pauses are not doorways. Men like this aren't malicious; they're frightened of a gap in the conversation, and you've been kindly papering over the gap for free.*

*Let him sit in it. It's the least cruel option, and I've reviewed them.*

---

The boulder reached the top, hovered — it always hovered; Sisyphus suspected someone was watching for a reaction — and departed.

"The sticky one."

Crow unfolded it with one foot. "Rained on. Or wept on. Or—" she sniffed. "Olive oil."

"Read what you can."

"'Dear Sisyphus. My—' smudge '—has been coming home late smelling of—' smudge '—and I found—' long smudge '—in the goat.'"

A pause.

"In the goat," said Sisyphus.

"Could be *on* the goat."

"Signature?"

"'Worried in'— gone. Sparta. Smyrna. Possibly a thumb."

Sisyphus looked downhill at the boulder, which sat in the ravine in the manner of something that knew it would be collected shortly.

"Right. Someone's husband, wife, or elderly parent is coming home late smelling of — let's say fish, it's usually fish — and something has been found in or on a goat. A ring. A letter. A second, smaller goat."

"We don't know it's fish."

"It's always fish. Write this."

---

*Dear Worried,*

*Your letter arrived weathered, so forgive me if I answer a question you didn't ask. Most questions are the same one underneath.*

*Ask them where they've been. Not with the goat in your hand — put the goat down — but at a table, with a drink poured for them.*

*If it's fish, they've bought a boat and were embarrassed to tell you. If it isn't fish, you already know, and you wrote to hear someone say "ask." So: ask.*

*Feed the goat. It's had a week.*

---

"You'll want to brace," said Crow.

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*My wife has asked me to do something in bed that I had, until recently, assumed was a wrestling hold. I love her and I'm willing, but I'm concerned about my back, and about what my mother would say.*

*— Flexible-ish in Thessaly*

*Dear Flexible-ish,*

*Your mother isn't invited, and I'm glad to hear it. Everything else is logistics.*

*Stretch first. Say "slower" when you mean slower. Laugh when it goes wrong, because it will, and the laughing is very nearly the point. You've a wife who still wants to surprise you after however many years. Men write to me weekly wishing they had your problem.*

*Mind the back. Pillows.*

The climb this time was steady. Sisyphus paused halfway to kick a loose stone out of the rut — it had been bothering him since Tuesday — and put his shoulder back where it went.

"Last one."

---

*Dear Sisyphus,*

*I'm thirty-four. I work eleven hours a day for a house I only see in the dark. My wife says I'm never present. I say I'm doing it for us. Every morning I think: is this it? I don't know what I'm for.*

*— Nobody in Particular*

*Dear Nobody,*

*"For us" is what people say when they've forgotten to check with the other half of "us." Ask her. I suspect she'd take a smaller house with a husband awake in it.*

*As for the morning question — "is this it?" is only ever asked by someone who's stopped looking at the thing in front of him. You list the house, the work, the wife like boxes. Go home at a reasonable hour tonight and look at her as if she'd just arrived. See if the question survives.*

*The days do repeat. That isn't the same as being the same. I'd know.*

*Also: eat lunch. Away from your desk. Outside, if there is one.*

---

Crow tucked the last reply into the satchel. Below, the boulder waited with the patience of something that had never once been in a hurry either.

"Same again tomorrow?"

"Same again tomorrow," said Sisyphus, and went down to get it.

---

# Sisyphus Gives Advice

The hill had, over the centuries, acquired a groove. The boulder had worn it into the hill, Sisyphus had worn one into the boulder, and Crow had worn a small personal one into a rock near the summit, from which it could see the whole business and not have to do any of it.

The letters came by Crow. There was no other post in Tartarus, Crow had decided there was, and nobody had thought to argue with a bird that could find you anywhere.

"Right," said Sisyphus, settling his shoulder into the stone. "First one."

Crow pinned the scroll flat with a foot and dipped its beak in the ink.

*Dear Sisyphus, My husband says he loves me but never says it first. I always have to say it, and then he says "you too." Is this a bad sign? — Waiting in Thebes*

Dear Waiting,

Does he bring you things? Not gifts. Things. A plum he thought you'd like. The good blanket when the nights turn. Does he walk on the road side of you?

Some people grew up in houses where words were expensive and got used sparingly, so they learned to say it with their hands. That's not nothing. That's a dialect.

But you shouldn't have to translate forever. Tell him: "I like hearing it. Say it first sometimes." Then let him be bad at it for a while. Most men are bad at new things in front of the people they love. That's why they practice on dogs.

S.

The boulder went up. The boulder came down. Crow waited with the patience of a creature paid in fish heads and not in a hurry.

*Dear Sisyphus, I run a tannery. I work dawn until the lamps go out. My wife says she's forgotten what I look like. I told her I look like money. She didn't laugh. — Hides of Corinth*

Dear Hides,

She didn't laugh because it wasn't a joke. You meant it a little, and she heard the bit you meant.

Pick one evening. Not every evening—one. Come home while it's light. Don't talk about the tannery. Don't talk about not talking about the tannery. Sit through the small things: the lamp, the bread, who said what at the well. You'll be bored for about an hour. On the far side of the boredom is your wife.

Also: wash first. Properly. You know why.

S.

*Dear Sisyphus, My neighbor Dion borrows my tools and returns them broken, late, or both. Last week he returned a ladder I don't own. When I say anything he acts wounded, as if I've insulted his mother. — Toolless*

Dear Toolless,

Dion isn't confused. Dion has learned that acting wounded works, because you're a decent person and decent people hate being the villain. He's not wicked. He's found a lever.

Say "No, sorry," and then stop talking. The stopping talking is the whole trick. He'll do the face. Let him. Faces aren't arguments. You can stand in a doorway watching a man be wounded for a surprisingly long time and nothing happens.

Keep the ladder. Call it interest.

S.

The god arrived around midday, insofar as Tartarus had one—there was a stretch when everything felt slightly more pointless than usual, and it was generally agreed that this was it.

He was a small god with the kind of carefully groomed beard that suggested nobody else had ever been asked to look at it. The plaque on his belt read LESSER APOLLONIUS, GOD OF UNSOLICITED FEEDBACK.*

"I've been reading your column," he said.

"Oh, good," said Sisyphus, not stopping.

"You're not meant to be *enjoying* this. There are rules. And honestly, the prose—" he flapped a scroll— "it's very *chatty*. You're the eternal emblem of futile labour. Where's the gravitas? You could be doing something with that."

"I thought about it." Sisyphus reached the top. The boulder paused with him, the way it did, like a dog deciding whether to bolt. "Then I thought: a man writes to me about his marriage and I tell him about *futility*? He knows about futility. He's got a tannery."

The boulder went down.

"I shall be mentioning this upward."

"Lovely," said Sisyphus, already walking after it. "Crow. Next."

*Dear Sisyphus, My wife wants to try something she saw on a vase. I've looked at the vase. I don't think it's possible, or not for a man my age with my knees. How do I say no without her thinking I don't want her? — Bent in Argos*

Dear Bent,

Vases are painted by young men with no knees to speak of and a great deal of imagination. Treat them like anyone else's cooking: nice to look at, not a contract.

Say this: "I want *you*. I don't want to be carried out of the bedroom." Then ask what it was about the vase that caught her. I promise it wasn't the geometry. It'll be something simpler—being looked at a certain way, being surprised, something she's afraid you've stopped wanting. You can give her that. It doesn't need knees.

Stretch first regardless.

S.

Crow made a noise that, in a bird, might have been a snort.

"Don't," said Sisyphus.

*Dear Sisyphus, I'm thirty-four. I make pots. I'm good at it. People buy them. Some nights I wake certain I've wasted my life. My brother is a general. — Clay*

Dear Clay,

Ask your brother, privately, what he thinks about at night. It won't be medals.

Pots break. Floors get swept and need sweeping. Battles get fought again over the same hill. Hardly anything stays done, and the people who look like they've finished something are usually just standing very still.

Waking up and wondering isn't a sign you chose wrong. Everyone gets it. The general gets it. I'd worry about a man who didn't.

Make the next pot. Someone will drink from it and never think of you, and that's exactly right. That's the whole job.

S.

The boulder reached the top and sat there for the length of a breath.

Sisyphus didn't watch it go. He'd seen it. He was watching Crow, who had already unrolled the next letter and was reading ahead with its head tilted, the way it did when the mail had got interesting.

"Well?"

"Someone's in love with their baker," said Crow.

"Oh, those are the *good* ones," said Sisyphus, and started back down.

---

\* There is a god of everything, if you go small enough. Most of them are not very busy, which is why so many turn up when they aren't wanted.

**High Seas and Low Vices**

The boy came at seven, while the river was still the colour of pewter and cocks were crowing in the hong yards behind Thirteen Factory Street.

"Mr. Merrick, sir. Captain Elliot's compliments, and he'll have the Whampoa returns before noon."

I kept my face to the wall. "Tell him I've the flux again."

"He said particular, sir—"

"What did he say, Hobbs?"

"That it was the third time this month."

"Then he can count. Go on."

When the door shut I found the toad already in my fist. Celadon jade, three-legged, no bigger than a thumb-joint, its back worn to the colour of weak tea by two years of my thumb. I'd bought it off a stall by the Consoo House the week I landed, when my hands were steady enough to count out the coppers myself.

The factory garden smelled of wet box and night soil. Beyond the gate, Hog Lane had opened its shutters: samshu in brown jars, a sailor from a Salem brig asleep in the gutter with his boots gone. Camphor dust drifted from the carpenters in New China Street, dried shrimp from the quay, and under all of it the river, warm and faintly sweet, like a pot left to boil dry.

Rennie kept a desk at the back of a tea-taster's in Old China Street. He did not stand up.

"You've the look of a man who's come to borrow."

"I've come to be useful."

"Same thing, in your case." He pushed a paper across. "Four chests, landed Tuesday off the *Red Rover*. The Hoppo's men want to know what's in them. I want it known they're medical stores consigned to His Majesty's ships at Lintin. Bark, calomel. A naval officer's signature would quiet things."

"They're not bark."

"They're whatever the paper says." He dipped a pen and held it out. "Twelve dollars and a ball of Patna. Or walk out and ask the Superintendent for an advance on your pay."

I signed. My name came out in my father's hand, the long loop on the M. It was the only thing about me that still looked like him.

"Patna's at Lao Chen's," Rennie said. "I don't keep it here. I'm not a fool."

Lao Chen sold birds. You went through the shop—thrushes, a mynah that said *chop-chop* in a Devon accent—and through a curtain that smelled of millet and cage-dung, and there was a second room with no birds in it at all.

"Rennie man say Patna," I said.

"Patna no have got." He did not look up from his scales. "Malwa have got."

"Malwa's half chalk and horse-dung."

"This Malwa number one. You no like, you go Lintin, buy ship-side."

He knew I could not go to Lintin. Half the Navy was at Lintin.

The first yawn took me then, the wide involuntary kind that wrenches the jaw, and after it the gooseflesh running up both arms under my coat though the room was warm as a mouth. Sweat started at my hairline. I took the toad out and worked it under my thumb: the chipped foot, the smooth back, the chipped foot again.

"You sick," Lao Chen said, and now he looked up.

"Rennie owes you for four chests. I'm the man who made them bark."

He weighed something. Put something back. Weighed again. "Patna have got. Little piece. Twelve dollar."

"Rennie said—"

"Rennie say, Rennie pay." He wrapped it in a square of red paper and held it just out of reach. "Twelve dollar, or you smoke Malwa, or you go sick-house with other foreign devil. All same me."

I counted out his twelve dollars with the hand that wasn't shaking.

The divan was above a cookshop by the Creek. Twenty couches, two lamps apiece, the lamp-glass green with soot. A boy no older than Hobbs cooked the pellet on the needle until it bubbled brown and spat, pressed it into the bowl, turned the pipe to the flame, and gave it into my hands like a wafer.

The man on the next couch was a Fukienese with a queue thin as string.

"Englishman," he said. "Navy."

"Flux," I said.

He laughed without opening his eyes. "All Englishman have flux."

The smoke tasted of burnt sugar and something beneath it, old and brown, like the inside of a church. The ache went out of my knees first. Then my shoulders put themselves down, as though somebody had been holding them up for me and had finally let go. The toad grew warm in my pocket. I did not need it. For three hours I did not need anything.

The sun was down behind the Dutch Folly when I came back along the quay, and the flower boats were lighting their lanterns, and Cathcart of the *Andromache* was standing by the factory stairs with his hat under his arm.

"Merrick. God. You look like something the river gave back."

"Flux."

"Elliot had me at the Whampoa returns all afternoon. Your figures. In your hand." He studied me. "They were good figures. Quite careful."

"I'm a careful man."

"You've a bit of red paper stuck to your cuff."

I looked at it. He looked at me looking at it.

"Merrick," he said quietly, "whatever it is, there are people who—"

"Goodnight, Cathcart."

In my room the boy had left a lamp burning and a plate of cold rice. I ate none of it. I lay down in my coat and took the toad out and set it on my chest, where it rose and fell, and I watched it, the chipped foot and the colour of weak tea, and waited for it to start being cold again.

The first thing I heard was my own teeth. They had been at each other in my sleep.

"Mr. Thornton's compliments, sir." Fane, the junior writer, stood in the doorway with the flat light off the river behind him. "He asks whether you mean to take the Lascars' depositions this forenoon. They are waiting in the godown."

"After the heat. Four o'clock."

"Then I shall have a short errand."

He looked at my eyes, which I knew were running, and at my nose, which was running too, and said nothing a writer of nineteen could say to a lieutenant.

In Old China Street the pawnshops stood taller than anything but the temple—whitewashed towers with slit windows, built to keep the goods above the floods and the thieves. Inside, the counter came to my chin. One did business looking up, like a child at an altar.

"Glass," said the clerk, when I passed up the telescope. He drew it out and snapped it shut, drew it out again. The lens caught the doorway and threw a coin of sun across his ledger. "Number one glass. Navy chop." He meant the broad arrow stamped on the barrel.

"Eight dollars."

"Four."

"To you." He wrote the ticket in brush-strokes too quick to follow. "Last month you bring silver box. Before, watch. I think you don't bring back anything. Five dollars."

Framjee's godown smelled of the Malwa he dealt in—a smell I had once taken for dried fruit and tobacco, and now took for breakfast. He had a punkah going and a boy to pull it, and he did not get up.

"Ah. Everyone has the flux in Canton. It is a very popular complaint." He turned the glass of water on his desk a quarter turn. "I have a chop boat coming up from Whampoa tomorrow on the tide. Tea chests. Perfectly legitimate tea chests."

"And beneath the tea."

"Beneath the tea is the boat, Lieutenant, and beneath the boat is the river. I am asking you to sit in the bow in your blue coat with the gold on the shoulder. The Hoppo's people are very respectful of that coat. They will not care to search under a British officer's feet and make an incident of it."

"You are asking me to run opium past the customs house."

"I am asking you to be rowed up a river. You have been rowed up a river before, surely." He waited. "Twenty dollars. Ten now."

The fan went back and forth. The sweat was starting again on my scalp, the gooseflesh coming up my forearms under the wool though the room was like the inside of a mouth.

"Fifteen now."

"Twelve." He counted them out without looking, which is how a man counts when he has done it a great many times. "Six o'clock. Do try to be sober, or whatever the word is."

---

Behind the Consoo House the lane narrowed until I had to turn my shoulders. The fruit sellers dumped their spoil here. Mangoes lay in the gutter in a yellow drift, skins gone the brown of old bruises, split and seeping, and the smell came up off them in the heat so thick it had a texture—sweet first, then sour, then under both a low brown drain-bottom smell that was neither. Wasps worked the pulp. The paving sucked at my boots. Cicadas sawed in the banyan over the wall.

Ah Sam's door was a curtain of blue cotton gone grey. Inside, the dark smelled of lamp-oil and that other thing—burnt sugar, roasted nut, cellar—that I had crossed the world for without knowing it.

"Lieutenant." She did not rise from her stool. "You come early. Sun not go down."

"I'm not well."

"No." She looked at me the way the pawnbroker had, pricing. "Today three mace, one dollar."

"Yesterday it was half."

"Yesterday no mandalin boat on river. Today mandalin boat. Today Ah Sam very brave woman." She held out her palm. It was small and dry and did not shake, which I noticed, because mine did.

I gave her two of Framjee's dollars and she gave me the bench by the wall, the porcelain pillow cool as a stone from a stream under my cheek, and the boy came with the tray.

"You want I cook?"

"Yes."

He took the brown pellet on the needle's end and held it over the lamp-glass, turning it, and it swelled and hissed and went gold at the edges, and the smell of it filled the little room and my mouth ran with water like a dog's. He rolled it, flattened it, pressed it into the pinhole of the bowl. Then he turned the pipe to me and tipped the bowl to the flame and I put my mouth to the dark bamboo and drew.

The knot that had been hauling my gut toward my spine since four in the morning let go. The ache went out of my shins. My skin stopped crawling and simply lay on me, the way skin is supposed to. The lamp made a small, steady sound.

"Better?" said the boy.

"Yes."

"Tomorrow you come back?"

I thought of the Lascars in the godown, and Fane's face in the doorway, and twelve dollars and a blue coat in the bow of a boat at six o'clock.

"Tomorrow I have an errand," I said. "After that."

Through the wall I could still hear the wasps at the mangoes—a faint, busy sound, like something sweet being slowly taken apart.

Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. response:
"You are wanted at the Superintendent's at nine, sir."

Hale stood in my doorway with the lamp still burning at seven in the morning, because the fog off the river had turned the window into wet paper.

"Tell Captain Elliot I've gone down to Whampoa to look at the water casks."

"The casks were looked at on Tuesday, sir."

"Then they shall be looked at again. Casks are not improved by neglect." I coughed into my fist and glanced at the palm afterward—a habit of some weeks—and wiped it on the lining of my coat. "This air. Lies in a man's chest like wet rope."

"Yes, sir." He was sixteen. He had not yet learned to make his face agree with his mouth.

---

By eight the fog had burned to a yellow haze, and the square before the factories smelt of night-soil boats going downriver and the first joss sticks going up. I kept my hat low past the Company flagstaff and turned into Hog Lane, where the samshu shops were already open and a sailor off the *Thistle* sat on a step being sick with great concentration.

Framjee kept his office above a shop selling paper umbrellas. He did not rise.

"Lieutenant. You have brought me my twenty dollars."

"I've brought you something worth more than twenty."

"Ah." He unfolded his hands. "Sit, then. You are grey, you know. Like the river."

"The *Andromache*'s boats go up to the Bogue Thursday and Saturday nights. Not Friday. They've been told Friday, but the pinnace wants caulking and there's no one to do it before Monday."

"And the cutter?"

"At Lintin. Waiting on the *Red Rover*."

He wrote nothing down. Men like Framjee never did. He pushed a stack across the lacquered table and I counted it without touching it—thirty-two Spanish dollars, some with the Mexican cap, some with old King Carlos's fat chin.

"Less the twenty," he said. "Less the interest. You see I am a fair man."

"You're a usurer."

"And you are an officer of His Majesty." He smiled with half his face. "We are both of us very far from home."

I took the dollars. The cough caught me on the stair, deep and wet, and I had to stop with a hand against the wall. The copper sat on my tongue all the way down to the water.

---

The boatwoman had a child bound to her back with a strip of blue cotton and sculled from the stern with one long oar, her whole body working it like a hinge.

"Honam side."

"Honam side, can do. One mace."

"Half."

She spat neatly over the gunwale. "Half mace, you swim."

I paid the mace. The river under us was the colour of weak tea and thick with things—cabbage leaves, a dead dog turning slowly, the white petals from some festival I had not been told of. Across the way the flower boats sat with their shutters closed, sleeping off the night. A gong went somewhere ashore, once, and did not go again.

---

Lao Yip's shop sold tea at the front. The back room sold the other thing, and smelt of both: dry leaves, and under them something darker, like a scorched pear.

"Lieutenant. Early."

"I've been earlier."

"True." He set the brass balance on the counter and did not hurry. "How much?"

"Two tael."

"Two tael, eight dollar."

"It was six last week."

"Last week was Malwa. This week Patna. Number one chop." He unwrapped the cake from its poppy-leaf and the smell came up and my mouth ran before I could stop it, which he saw, and which cost me the argument before I had made it. "You want Malwa, I have Malwa. Dusty. Full of ash."

"Patna. Seven."

"Eight."

"Seven and a half, and you let me use the room."

He weighed it out, scraping the knife on the pan, and said nothing, which was how Lao Yip said yes.

---

The room had one window papered over and a bench under it, and a boy who brought the lamp and went away again without looking at me. I did the pipe myself. I had learned to. The paste on the needle, turned and turned above the flame until it swelled and went gold at the edges, then pressed into the bowl, then the long bamboo stem laid across the lamp, warm as a living thing in my hands.

The first draw tasted of burnt sugar and something floral left too long in a vase. The second I did not taste at all.

The cough stopped. It always did. For an hour each day my chest was only a chest and not a bucket with a hole in it, and I lay on my side with my knees drawn up like a child and listened to the shop beyond the curtain weighing out tea, the scrape of the knife on the brass, the soft clack of an abacus, and I thought about nothing with great care.

---

It was dark when the boatwoman—a different one—put me back on the factory stairs. The lamps were lit along the hong fronts and the square had that end-of-day smell of cooking fat and river and the sweet rot of fruit skins.

Elliot was on the verandah with his pipe. The proper sort.

"Merrick. Where the devil have you been?"

"Whampoa, sir. The casks."

"The casks." He looked at me for longer than I liked. "You look like something fished out of a bilge. That cough's no better."

"Sea air, sir. It's always disagreed with me."

"Sea air." He knocked out his pipe against the rail. "We're seventy miles up a river, Lieutenant. There is no sea air in Canton."

I had no answer. I coughed instead, turned from him to do it, and tasted the pennies again, and when I had wiped my mouth he had already gone inside and left the door open behind him, which in that place was as much mercy as a man could ask.

response:
# Gunpowder Rendezvous

The neon jukebox has been playing the same song since Spike walked in. Scratchy guitar, a singer who sounds like he gargled gravel, the needle skipping on the chorus. Nobody in the bar seems to notice. Nobody in the bar seems to notice much of anything.

He takes the stool at the end, orders a beer he can't pay for, and clocks her in the mirror behind the bottles.

Black crop top. Shorts that are more suggestion than garment. A dragon coiling down her right arm, inked in colors gone muddy with sun. Two holsters, cross-draw, the grips worn pale. She is drinking something brown out of a glass that was never clean, and she is watching him right back.

"You're the other one," she says. She doesn't turn around.

"Other what?"

"Don't play cute, cowboy. Chang hired a Mars guy. Said he had hair like a mop and walked like he was already dead."

Spike touches his hair. "That's slander."

"Which part?"

He grins and doesn't answer. He slides two stools down, which puts them close enough that he can smell her — gun oil, cigarettes, the same cheap bourbon she's drinking. She has a lighter on the bar. He takes it without asking. She lets him, which is its own kind of answer.

"Rebecca," she says.

"Nobody calls you that."

"Nobody who's still breathing." She finally looks at him straight. Her eyes do a quick inventory: the Jericho under his jacket, the scar at the edge of his right eye, the way he holds the cigarette like he's afraid it will leave. "Revy."

"Spike."

"That's not a name. That's a thing you step on."

The jukebox hits the skip in the chorus. *Baby, baby — baby, baby —* and lurches on.

They drink. She orders him a bourbon and he lets her pay because he has nine hundred woolongs to his name and the woolong isn't legal tender here. The bounty is a Russian arms broker named Vasilenko who has been sleeping in the hotel upstairs for three nights and is worth eighty thousand to whoever drags him to the Triad warehouse at Pier Nine. The job came to both of them. Spike figures Chang did it on purpose. He figures Revy knows that too.

"So," he says. "We split it."

She laughs. It's a real laugh, surprised out of her, and it changes her face. "Fuck you. Split it. I don't split."

"Then one of us shoots the other."

"Yeah." She leans in. Her knee touches his and stays there. "That's how I was gonna do it."

"Before or after the drinks?"

"Haven't decided."

Her hand moves. His hand moves. Then the back door opens and three men come through it with Vasilenko's shaved-head bodyguard in front, and Spike realizes they were never the only ones who knew about this bar.

The first shot takes out the mirror. The bartender drops. Revy is already moving — she comes off the stool sideways, both Cutlasses clear before her boots hit the floor, and puts two rounds into the bodyguard's chest so close together they sound like one. Spike goes the other way, over the bar, Jericho out. He comes up and the depth is wrong — it's always wrong in bad light, the dead eye lies — so he fires where instinct says instead of where his eye says, and a man folds behind the jukebox.

The jukebox keeps playing.

"Two!" Revy shouts.

"Two!"

"Bullshit, that was mine —"

A shotgun blast takes the top off the bar and Spike drops, rolls, comes up kicking. His heel finds a knee. The knee goes the wrong direction. Revy shoots the man on the way down, almost absently, like she's correcting his form.

"Three," she says.

"I had him."

"You were *dancing* with him."

Then it's quiet, except for the gravel-voiced singer and the drip of something off the bar.

Vasilenko is not among the dead. Vasilenko is upstairs with the door locked, and when they kick it in he's half out the window with a suitcase. Revy grabs his belt. Spike grabs the suitcase. He is small and wet-eyed and says *please* in three languages before Revy knocks him cold with the flat of her gun.

---

The motel across the harbor is the kind where the sheets are optional. Vasilenko is zip-tied in the bathtub. The rain has started. Revy sits on the one chair with her boots on the bed and a bottle between her thighs, and Spike stands by the window smoking her cigarettes.

"Chang's gonna pay whoever walks him in," she says.

"I know."

"So one of us walks him in."

"I know."

The jukebox track is still in his head, the skip and the lurch, *baby, baby —* He thinks about Julia. He thinks about how every woman who ever pointed a gun at him had the same look this one has now, like she's deciding whether he's worth the bullet.

She stands. She crosses the room. She is close enough that he can see the pulse in her throat, and her left hand is on his chest, flat, warm, and her right Cutlass is under his chin.

His Jericho is in her stomach. Neither of them remembers drawing.

"Well," he says.

"Yeah."

"This is awkward."

"Shut up." She isn't smiling. She's close enough to kiss, close enough that he can taste the bourbon on her breath. "You're gonna try to talk me out of it."

"No."

"You're gonna say some shit about fate."

"Whatever happens," he says, "happens."

"Yeah, that's exactly the shit I meant." Her thumb moves on his chest. The gun under his chin doesn't. "I'm not a good person, cowboy."

"I know."

"I'm not a bad person either."

"I know that too."

"Then what the fuck are you looking at me like that for?"

He doesn't answer, because the answer is that he died once already and has never been sure whether he's supposed to be grateful. Because she smells like gunpowder and her knee is still touching his and he hasn't wanted anything in a long time.

Vasilenko groans in the bathtub.

Neither of them moves.

The rain picks up. Somewhere across the water, in a bar with no mirror and three bodies cooling on the floor, the jukebox hits the chorus again and skips.

A lazy ceiling fan barely stirs the smoky air inside the bar. It pushes the same gray cloud through the same slow circle, like it gave up on the job years ago and nobody filed the paperwork.

Spike Spiegel has been watching it for twenty minutes, because it's the only thing in the room moving slower than his tab. His glass is empty. His wallet is emptier. The bartender has stopped asking.

The door bangs open, and the woman who walks in doesn't so much enter the room as take it hostage. Cutoffs that barely qualify. Black crop top. A dragon inked down her right arm, coiled shoulder to wrist like it's trying to climb off. Two Berettas in a shoulder rig she isn't bothering to hide.

She looks at Spike. Spike looks at her. Then both of them look at the folded printout the other one is holding.

Same face. Same number.

"Fuck," she says.

"Yeah," Spike agrees.

She takes the stool two down from him—not next to, not far—and slaps the counter. "Bacardi. Leave the bottle." Then, without turning her head: "Who the hell are you supposed to be?"

"Nobody important."

"Good. I hate important people." She pours, drinks, pours. "Revy."

"Spike."

"That a name or a dog?"

"Depends who's asking." He shakes out his last cigarette, pats himself down for a lighter he already knows he lost. She watches him fail, sighs like it costs her something, and flicks a Zippo under his nose.

"Don't get used to it."

The rum goes down between them a glass at a time. She tells him nothing about herself and he tells her less, and somehow by the bottom third of the bottle each has a decent picture of the other. She clocks how he sits—loose, spine like wet rope—and knows it's a lie; nobody that relaxed has that many old scars on his knuckles. He clocks how her eyes flick to the door every time it opens, and knows it isn't paranoia if they really are coming.

"You've got a dead eye," she says.

"Just the one."

"Which?"

He smiles and doesn't tell her. She likes that more than she'd admit under torture.

"So here's how it goes," Revy says. "I take Delgado. You go home and cry into your noodles."

"Counter-offer. I take Delgado, you keep all your teeth."

"You couldn't take my teeth with both eyes."

"Probably not." He blows smoke at the fan. It doesn't help the fan. "Whatever happens—"

The door opens again, and this time it's four men who didn't come for the rum.

Revy's off the stool before the first one clears the frame, both Berettas out, and the sound is one sound—two shots so close they weld together. The lead man drops without finishing his thought. Spike doesn't stand so much as unspool; he's already behind the second guy, Jericho in one hand, the other catching a wrist and turning it until the gun points somewhere useful. It goes off into its owner's partner.

Glass sprays. The bartender vanishes like a magic act. Revy walks *forward* into the muzzle flashes, laughing—actually laughing—and empties both magazines in a sweep so even it looks mechanical. Spike kicks a man through a table he was going to have to pay for.

Twelve seconds. Then silence, except the fan.

A door bangs at the back. Through the shattered window, Spike watches Delgado's gut and bad suit fold into a taxi.

Revy's reloaded before he's done watching. "Motel on Ninth," she says. "His girl's there. Dumb bastard runs to the same hole every time."

"You knew where he was going."

"I did my homework, cowboy."

"Then why'd you come to the bar?"

She holsters one gun, keeps the other out, and looks at him like he's asked something rude. "Thirsty."

---

Room 14 smells like mildew and somebody else's perfume. Delgado is face down between the beds, wrists zip-tied, breathing wetly through a nose that's seen better minutes. The bathroom window is open; his girl had the sense to leave.

It took thirty seconds to put him there, and they did it the way they did the bar—without a word, like they'd rehearsed. That's the part that bothers Spike. That's the part that bothers her.

Now they stand over him with their guns on each other.

Her Beretta is under his jaw, pressing up, making him tilt his head like he's considering something. His Jericho is against her ribs, left side, under the hem of the crop top, where the skin is warm. Neither of them is breathing hard. Both of them are pretending not to notice that.

"He's mine," Revy says.

"You got here second."

"I got here with the address, dipshit."

"I got here with the body count." He glances down. "Our body count."

"Don't do that. Don't make it a *we.*"

The neon through the curtain cuts her face in half. He can smell the rum on her, the gun oil, the cigarettes—his brand or hers, they've been sharing for an hour and he's lost track. She's close enough that he can see where the dragon's tail ends, a flick of red just under her collarbone.

"You're thinking about it," she says.

"About what?"

"You know what."

"I'm thinking about the money."

"Liar." She doesn't move the gun. "You've got a face like a guy who already died once and didn't learn anything."

"Twice," Spike says. "Second time didn't take either."

Something crosses her eyes that isn't anger, and it's gone before he can name it. She shifts her weight, and the muzzle slides a quarter-inch along his jaw and stays. Almost a touch. If you were being generous.

"I don't do trust," she says.

"Who asked you to?"

"You're asking. Right now. You've got that look."

"I've got one working eye, Revy. I don't have *looks.*"

Delgado groans. Neither of them glances down.

"Say we split it," Spike says.

"Say you drop first."

"Say you do."

"Say I blow your head off and buy a boat."

"You'd miss me."

"I don't miss."

The fan in this room doesn't work at all. The air just sits. Her finger is on the trigger and his is on his, and the only thing moving in Room 14 is the sign outside, on, off, on, painting them red and un-painting them.

Spike exhales. It comes out close to a laugh.

"Whatever happens," he says, "happens."

"That's the stupidest fucking thing I've ever heard."

She doesn't lower the gun. Neither does he. Neither of them steps back.

response:
# Gunpowder Rendezvous

The bar doesn't have a name, just a neon fish with half its fins burned out. Spike ducks under the doorframe and the smell hits him first: fryer oil, spilled rum, something fermenting under the floorboards. He likes it immediately.

She's at the end of the counter with her boots on the next stool so nobody can sit there. Short shorts, black top, a dragon crawling up her right arm into the shadow of her shoulder. Two Berettas in a shoulder rig she isn't bothering to hide. On the bar in front of her, face up, is a photograph Spike has in his own jacket pocket—Benny Castellanos, forty thousand, wanted breathing.

Spike sits two stools over. Close enough to count.

"That seat's taken," she says, without looking.

"I'm not in it."

He puts a cigarette in his mouth and fishes out the lighter: cheap brass, dented, a ring of rust around the hinge the color of dried blood. It takes three strikes. She watches the third one catch.

"Piece-of-shit lighter."

"It's been in the water a few times."

"You go swimming with it?"

"Not on purpose."

That gets him a look, finally. Brown eyes, flat and hot at once, like a stovetop someone forgot to turn off. She exhales smoke at the pocket where his copy of the photograph is, which he hasn't produced. She just knows.

"You're the other one," Revy says. "Fuck. Figured you'd be taller."

"Figured you'd be subtler."

"Subtle doesn't pay." She knocks back her glass—Bacardi, from the bottle at her elbow—and pours another without offering. "Here's how this goes, string bean. Benny's got a girl who works here, and he's a creature of fucking habit, so he walks through that door before midnight. I shoot him somewhere non-fatal, drag him to the handoff, get paid. You sit here and drink and cry about it."

"That's one version."

"It's the only version."

"Whatever happens, happens."

She snorts. "The fuck does that mean?"

"Means I'm bad at planning." He reaches across her for the bottle. She lets him, watching his hand the whole way. "You're Two Hands. Roanapur."

"And you're the Bebop guy. Jet-whatever's pet."

"Jet's the pet. I'm the stray."

She laughs—a short ugly bark that makes the bartender flinch. Then she catches herself doing it and her mouth flattens out, and Spike watches her file the laugh away like something she hadn't meant to show. He knows the maneuver. He's got a drawer full of them.

"I don't do partners," she says.

"Me neither."

"Good."

"Good."

They drink. The neon fish buzzes. Her knee is maybe eight inches from his thigh, and neither of them does anything about the eight inches, which is its own kind of doing something.

At eleven-forty Benny Castellanos walks in with three men who are not creatures of habit, who are in fact professionals, and Revy says, "Oh, you asshole," with real warmth, and the table nearest the door goes over.

It isn't a plan. It's two people in a narrow room who both know exactly where the exits are. Spike comes off the stool sideways, Jericho already out, and puts two rounds through the first bodyguard's shoulder as the man clears leather. Revy stays seated. She draws both Cutlasses across her body, crosses them, uncrosses them, and the second and third men sit down hard with holes in their thighs, left and right, mirror images. She hasn't spilled her drink.

Benny runs. Of course Benny runs.

Spike gets to him first—long legs, stray's advantage—and takes him down at the door with a sweep that puts Benny's cheek into the floorboards. Then there's a gun barrel against the back of Spike's skull, warm from recent use.

"Mine," Revy says.

"I'm the one lying on him."

"I'm the one with the gun on you."

response:
# Blood Moon

The moon hangs over the village like a wound that has not decided whether to close.

Yennefer steps through a door that hangs by one hinge. Inside: bread furred green on the table, a child's shoe by the hearth, a chair on its side. No blood. She has walked from the well to the chapel and back and found the same thing in every house. No bodies. No blood. The village has not been slaughtered. It has been emptied, the way a cup is emptied.

She smells him before she sees him. Turned earth. Iron. Something sweet beneath, like fruit left too long in a cellar.

"You're late," says a voice from the chapel steps. "I've already finished."

He sits on the stone with his legs stretched out, a red coat pooled around him like something spilled. The hat shadows his face, but the moonlight finds his glasses—round, orange, ridiculous—and beneath them, the smile. Too many teeth, she thinks. Then: no. The right number. The wrong kind.

"Finished what?" She doesn't stop walking. Stopping would mean something.

"Cleaning up." He lifts a gloved hand toward the empty street. "This place had a vampire in its cellars. A fledgling. It ate the village and then didn't know what to do with itself. Sat among the ghouls weeping. It begged me, at the end." The smile widens. "Can you imagine? Begging. With eternity in its mouth."

"And the people?"

"Were already dead. I only made it true."

"The baron paid me three hundred crowns for this."

"Then you've been paid for nothing." He breathes in through his nose, slow and deliberate. "Lilac. Gooseberries. And underneath—" He tilts his head. "Seams. You've been taken apart and put back. I can smell the stitching."

Something in her goes very still. A lesser woman might touch her own shoulder, feel for the curve that was once there and isn't. Yennefer lifts her chin instead. "And under that coat?"

"Nothing you'd want to see."

"Try me."

For a moment the shadow beneath the hat deepens past what moonlight should allow. Eyes open in it—not two—and something with the suggestion of a hound's jaw breathes against the inside of the dark. Then it is a man again, if the word stretches so far.

Yennefer doesn't look away. She has seen worse in mirrors.

"Hm," he says, pleased.

She raises her hand and the air between them hardens. Not a wall—a question. She feels along the shape of him with the spell and finds no heartbeat to stop, no blood to boil, nothing a century of killing things has taught her how to grip. It's like reaching into a river for a stone and finding only more river.

"Rude," he says mildly, and the pistol is in his hand without having been drawn. The shot is enormous in the silence. Her shield takes it, and takes it badly—cracks spiderweb across the air, silver smoke curling where the bullet hangs an inch from her sternum.

She looks at it. Then she looks at him.

She closes her fist, and the bullet is gone from in front of her and reappears behind his left eye.

His head snaps back. The glasses skitter across the steps. For a heartbeat—hers, not his—the night is quiet.

Then he laughs. It starts low and climbs, and his head comes forward with the hole already closing, the eye already red and whole and delighted.

"There," he says. "There you are."

"You're insufferable."

"I'm honest. That thing in the cellar had all my gifts and spent them weeping. It wanted to be a man again. It wanted to be *forgiven*." He says the word like something he has stepped in. "I am what I am. I've never pretended otherwise."

"No. You just pretend it's a virtue."

He grins. "And what's yours, sorceress? You wear a face that isn't yours and stand on a spine you bought. What was the price?"

"None of your concern."

"Everything is my concern tonight." He leans forward, elbows on his knees, and his voice drops into something almost gentle, which is worse. "I could take the seams out. Make it permanent. You'd never age another day, never—"

"I know the shape of your kind of gift." Her voice is flat as a blade laid on a table. "I've already traded enough of myself for a face. I know exactly what it cost, and what I will never—"

She stops. Half a second late.

His nostrils flare. He has heard the shape of the sentence she didn't finish, the hollow where the end of it should be, and she watches him understand. Watches the glee rise in him like water in a dug hole.

"Ah," he says. "That's what's missing. Under the lilac. A—"

Her hand moves and the chapel wall comes down on him.

Stone, timber, three centuries of saints' faces, all of it folding inward with a sound like the earth clearing its throat. Dust rolls across the street and settles.

Yennefer stands in the middle of the road and breathes.

The rubble shifts. He walks out of it reassembling, a shoulder knitting as he comes, dust sliding off the red coat as though the coat has declined to be dirtied. He is still laughing, quieter now.

"You're not hard to read," she says. "Under all that. You're bored. You've been bored for centuries. You go looking for things that might kill you and you're disappointed every time."

"And will you disappoint me?"

"Tonight? Yes." She lets the last of the spell drain from her fingertips. "I don't do favors for monsters."

For a moment he only looks at her, head tilted, the moon pouring red over the brim of his hat. Then he sweeps the hat off and bows—a real bow, courtly, older than any court she has sat in.

"The bird of Hermes is my name," he says, straightening, "eating my wings to—"

"I've read it. It's not as clever as you think."

She turns her back on him, which is the most dangerous thing she has done all night, and opens a door in the air. Through it: her own rooms, her own fire, a decanter she intends to empty.

"Yennefer of Vengerberg," he says behind her. Not a question. He has pulled her name out of the dark somehow, and she decides she doesn't want to know how.

She looks back over her shoulder. "Don't wait up."

The portal closes on his grin.

He stands alone in a village of his own making and breathes in lilac and gooseberries until the wind takes the last of it. The smile stays. For the first time in longer than he cares to count, it isn't for anyone's benefit but his own.

A broken cart wheel lies abandoned near the village gates, hinting at a hurried departure. Length: 1000 words.
response:
The wheel lies on its side in the mud outside the gate, three spokes snapped, the iron rim still bright where it tore loose. Someone left in a hurry. Someone did not stop.

Yennefer steps over it without breaking stride. The village beyond is quiet in the way only recently emptied places are—doors standing open, a bucket turning slowly on its rope, bread going hard on a windowsill. No bodies. That is the part she doesn't like.

The smell reaches her before anything else. Not rot. Gunpowder, and beneath it something older, like a cellar that has been sealed for a century.

"They ran well," says a voice from the chapel steps. "Most of them. The ones who stopped to pack are in the well."

He sits with his legs stretched out, boot heels resting on the third step, a long red coat pooling around him like something spilled. The hat shadows everything but a mouth with too many teeth in it. Orange lenses catch the last of the dusk.

She does not stop walking. "You killed them."

"I killed *it*." He tilts his head toward the chapel door, which hangs from one hinge. Inside, something dark has been dragged across the flagstones in a long, deliberate arc. "A child of forty years who thought a flock of peasants made him a lord. He wept when I found him. Offered me the women, as though I'd want them." The mouth widens. "I despise that kind."

"And the villagers?"

"Were in the well before I arrived." He stands, and the movement is wrong—too much of him unfolding, as if the coat has been holding more than a man. "You're not frightened."

"I'm annoyed. I rode three days for that contract." Her hand drifts toward the pouch at her belt and stops there. "You've cost me two hundred crowns."

He laughs. It goes on too long.

Then he is simply *closer*, three steps gone in the space of a blink, and she speaks a single word.

The air locks around him. Not a wall—a fist. She has stopped charging knights with this, held a striga's jaws open while Geralt went in with a blade. Alucard hangs in it like a fly in amber, head cocked, and she feels the strain of him against the binding the way one feels a river against a bridge.

"Oh," he says, delighted. "*Oh.* Chaos. Raw and shaped by will alone. No gods in it, no blood. Where did you learn that?"

"Aretuza. You won't have heard of it."

"I've heard of everything. I've simply outlived most of it." And then he is not in the binding anymore. He is not anywhere. The spell closes on empty air, and the shadows along the chapel wall peel loose and run like ink, and something cold breathes against the back of her neck.

"Do that again," he says, inches from her ear.

She does not turn. Turning would be a concession. "Ask nicely."

"I never ask."

"Then you'll never see it." She steps forward, out of his shadow, and only then pivots to face him. Her violet eyes do not blink. "What are you? Not a vampire. I've met vampires. They had *manners*."

"I'm what they pray not to become." He sweeps the hat off and bows, mocking and perfect, a court gesture from a court that no longer exists. "Alucard."

"That's not a name. That's a riddle a child would solve."

"Everything about me is a riddle a child could solve. That's the joke." He straightens. The glasses slide down and his eyes are the red of something coughed up. "Lilac. Gooseberries. And underneath—" he inhales, slow, obscene, "—a crooked spine. A shoulder that sat higher than the other. Oh, you've *remade* yourself. Every inch of you is a monument to something you couldn't bear to be."

She does not flinch. She has had three centuries to learn not to flinch. But he sees the breath she doesn't take, and he smiles, and she hates that he sees it.

"Your gloves," she says.

The smile falters by a hair.

"The seals on the backs of them. I read them while you were posturing." She lets her gaze drop to his hands and back up, slow as a knife going in. "Someone owns you. A great devourer of worlds, and you come to heel when you're whistled for. You despise the weak ones who can't accept their nature? Yours is a dog's."

The silence stretches. Somewhere in the village the bucket's rope creaks.

"Careful," he says softly.

"No." She closes the distance herself now, close enough to see that he does not breathe except when he wants to. "You came here hoping. That's why you're still sitting on the steps of a church instead of gone into the night. You hoped that pathetic thing in there would be more than it was. You hoped it would *hurt*."

His hand comes up. She lets it. It stops at her jaw, not touching, a tremor in the fingers that she does not think is fear.

"Then end me," he says. "If you see so clearly. Try."

"I'm not your executioner." She turns her face a quarter-inch, so his knuckle grazes her cheek, so he understands she chose it. "I'm not anyone's anything. If you want to die, Alucard, find someone who cares enough to do it properly."

For a moment she thinks he will kill her. For a moment she thinks she will let herself be proven wrong about that.

Then he laughs again, quieter, and steps back, and sets the hat on his head.

"Your proof." He kicks something from the shadow of the steps. It rolls to her feet and stops, face-up, forty years of borrowed life ending in an expression of profound surprise. "For your two hundred crowns."

"Generous."

"Rarely." He is already walking, red coat swallowing itself into the dark between the houses. "When you tire of being small, Vengerberg, come and find me. Bring your chaos."

She watches until the night closes over him. Then she crouches, wraps the head in sacking without looking at it, and walks back toward the gate.

The wheel is still there in the mud. She does not step over it this time. She stops, and looks at it for a long while, and wonders who will be the first to come back.

response:
# Blood Moon

The moon rises the colour of a butcher's apron, and the wolves begin before it clears the treeline.

Yennefer steps out of the portal onto frozen mud and lets it collapse behind her with a sound like a snapped tendon. The village of Hollin—if it still deserves the name—is forty houses with the doors standing open. No lamps. No smoke. The ealdorman's letter spoke of a plague that leaves bodies dry, and offered a sum large enough to make her curious rather than insulted.

She draws her cloak tighter. Her boots are wrong for this; her mood is worse.

A howl, long and alone, somewhere east. Then nothing.

She finds the first body in the well-house. Then the second. The third is sitting upright against the church wall with his hands folded, placed, like a doll put away by a careful child. His throat is—she makes herself look—his throat is intact. The wound is lower, over the heart, neat as a tailor's work.

"You're not a higher vampire," she says to the dark. "They don't pose their meals."

"No," the dark agrees. "They don't."

He's standing in the church doorway, though she had looked there a heartbeat ago. Tall enough that the lintel shadows his face, and the rest of him is red—a long coat the exact shade of the moon, a hat broad as a cartwheel, round lenses of orange glass that take the moonlight and give nothing back. She has walked royal courts and sorceresses' conclaves and never seen anyone dressed so absurdly, nor anyone who wore absurdity like it was armour.

He breathes in. Theatrically. "Lilac," he says. "And something sour. Gooseberries." The grin that follows has too many teeth in it. "You smell like a garden somebody buried."

"You smell like nothing," Yennefer says, and it's true—where a man should be is a hole in the air, a place her senses slide off. "Which is worse."

Second howl, nearer, cut short. She notes the cutting. Something told it to stop.

Fire is the honest opener. She shapes it as she speaks—the kind that eats bone—and puts it through his chest from six paces.

He does not move. The coat burns, the shirt beneath burns, and the thing inside simply watches her through it with his head cocked while his ribs show white and then are not white and then are not visible, the flesh pouring back like wax running the wrong direction. The hat never catches. She'd bet gold it has never caught.

"Good," he says. His voice has a pleased, unhurried depth. "Most of them beg first."

"I don't beg." She has already reached for the next thing. "And I'm not finished."

She takes the ground from under him—not literally; literally would be cheap—but the ground of his standing: she drags the shadows he came out of into chains and locks them around his arms, his throat, pulls them taut against the church wall where the dead man sits grinning at nothing. It is old magic, Aretuza's deepest cellar. It holds dragons. It holds him for exactly as long as it takes him to decide it shouldn't, and then the chains are a coat and then they are *his* coat and he is wearing them, whole, straightening his cuffs.

"That," he says, "was interesting. Do it again."

"Make me."

He laughs then, head thrown back, and in the pause after, a wolf answers him from the treeline—three notes, falling. The sound goes through her like cold water. The wolves are his. The wolves have been his the whole time.

He produces the gun without seeming to reach for it: black, long as her forearm, ludicrous as the rest of him. She has seen hand cannons in Kovir—this is to those as she is to a hedge-witch. He lets her look at it. He doesn't point it.

"Silver," he says. "Blessed. Not for you. I keep it for things that disappoint me."

"And have I?"

"Not yet." The lenses tilt. Behind them something shifts that is not an eye, or is too many. "You've got a shape underneath the shape. I can see it. Spine like a drawn bow. You made yourself straight."

Her stomach drops, and she lets nothing reach her face, and knows he saw it anyway.

"Everyone does," he goes on, almost gentle, which is the cruellest register he has. "They just do it with bad wine and lies. You used your bones."

"You want to talk about what's underneath?" She steps forward—toward him, which no one does—until the burnt-blood smell of his coat is in her nose. "I've read you. Walls of shadow, a river under them, and the river is faces. Thousands. You eat them and keep them. You didn't want to be a monster, you wanted to be a *weapon*, and you got exactly what you wanted, and now nobody on this earth can give you the one thing you still need."

The grin stays. But the wolves stop. All of them, at once.

"Say it," he says.

"A death that counts."

The silence has weight. A roof-beam settles in one of the empty houses.

"Can you give it to me?" He asks it the way a man asks for the salt.

"Tonight?" She considers him—really considers, the way she considered Vilgefortz, and Emhyr, and the Lodge. "No. Tonight I'd lose, and I don't lose to men in hats." She lifts her chin. "But I'd like to learn how. Give me a decade."

"The bird of Hermes is my name," he says, soft, unaccountably, like a password. "Eating my wings to make me tame."

"Bad poetry. You should eat something else."

That earns a different laugh, shorter and almost human. The gun goes back into the coat. He touches two fingers to the hat's brim—courtly, mocking, both.

"Yennefer of Vengerberg," he says, though she hasn't given him the name. "I'll come find out."

"You'll find me armed."

"I'd be insulted otherwise."

And he's gone—not vanished, *unmade*, the dark in the doorway only dark now. The dead man against the wall goes on grinning. The moon has climbed clear of the trees and is losing its red, going to ordinary bone-white, as if ashamed of itself.

Yennefer stands in the ruined square until her hands stop wanting to shake, and then a little longer out of principle.

Somewhere east, one wolf howls. Then, after a long while, another, further off.

She opens a portal and does not look back, which is a kind of looking.

A dim overhead light flickers in the prison corridor at irregular intervals. Length: 1000 words.
response:
**Prison Strings**

The light above cell block D flickers—on, off, on, a long dark, on—like something breathing wrong. Jolyne Cujoh counts the gaps anyway. Habit. In Green Dolphin you learn to measure time by whatever breaks slowest.

Footsteps come down the corridor. Not guard boots. Heels, unhurried.

The woman who stops outside the bars wears a white shirt and a dark tie, and her hair is the color of dried blood where the light catches it, and her eyes—Jolyne's stomach drops before her brain finishes the thought—her eyes are yellow, ringed like a target.

"Hello," the woman says. "You must be Jolyne. I'm Makima."

Two guards flank her. They don't look at Jolyne. They don't look at anything. Their faces have the slack quality of men listening to a sermon in a language they almost understand.

"Great," Jolyne says. "Another suit. Let me guess—my sentence just got longer for breathing."

"No." Makima smiles. It's a lovely smile. It is exactly as lovely as a smile should be, and that is what makes Jolyne's skin crawl: there's no slippage in it. Real people's faces leak. "I'm here because of what you did in the laundry. The thing with the thread."

Jolyne's hand goes still against her thigh. "Don't know what you're talking about."

"You unraveled," Makima says gently. "Your arm came apart and went through the drain and came back. Three inmates saw it. They don't remember now." She tilts her head. "I made sure. As a favor."

The light goes out. In the dark, Jolyne hears the guards breathing—slow, synchronous, like one body.

The light comes back. Makima hasn't moved.

"Hell of a favor," Jolyne says. "What's it cost?"

"Nothing yet." Makima laces her fingers together, a schoolteacher's gesture. "I just want to see it. Please?"

*Please.* Something in Jolyne's neck prickles at the word—not fear exactly, more like being asked to step onto ice by someone standing safely on shore.

Fine. Let her look.

Stone Free unspools from Jolyne's wrist, a dozen threads of pale blue, and drifts between the bars like smoke that decided on a direction. One thread curls toward Makima's shoulder. Another, quieter, slips low along the floor, past the guards' boots, touches the concrete behind them, and listens.

Jolyne is good at listening with string. Vibration runs up her nerves like a phone line. Footsteps, heartbeats, a conversation two rooms over.

Three heartbeats. Makima's slow. The guards' slow—

Not just slow. Identical. Three chests, one rhythm, and the rhythm is Makima's.

"Oh," Makima breathes, watching the thread near her shoulder with naked delight. "It's a leash."

"It's a *Stand*."

"It's a leash," Makima repeats, kindly, correcting a child. "You pull, and things come to you. You wrap, and things stay." Her eyes slide to Jolyne's. "We're alike."

Jolyne snaps the string back so fast it stings. "Lady, I don't know what you are. But I know a bitch pretending to be nice when she's about to sell you something. So skip to the part where you sell it."

For a moment, Makima just looks at her, the way you'd look at a dog that did a trick you didn't teach it.

"Your father," she says.

The corridor gets very quiet.

"He's not well. You know that. There are people who could help him—people I know." Makima's voice doesn't rise or fall; it just arrives, warm and certain, in the center of Jolyne's chest. "I can have you out in an hour. Charges dropped. A car waiting. All I'd want is for you to work with me. Be my friend." A pause. "There's something I want very much, and I've never had a string long enough to reach it."

Jolyne's throat has gone thick. She hates that. She hates how the woman found the exact soft place on the first try, like she'd been handed a map.

And that's it, Jolyne thinks. That's the tell. Nobody finds it on the first try.

"You say that to all the dogs?"

Makima's smile doesn't flicker. The light does.

"Jolyne."

Her name in that mouth feels like a hand on the back of her neck. Her knees want to bend. *Come here*, something says, and it's not her voice, and it's not loud, and that's the terrifying part—it's reasonable. It sounds like good advice.

Jolyne bites the inside of her cheek until she tastes copper and drives her thumbnail into the butterfly on her arm, and the pressure lifts like a hand pulled away.

Makima's eyes widen—a fraction. Real surprise. The first real thing she's shown.

"Huh," Jolyne says, and her grin is all teeth. "Didn't take, did it."

"You're more than I thought." Makima says it like a compliment. Then she turns, slightly, to the guard on her left. "Hanson. Your sidearm."

He draws it with no expression at all and sets the muzzle under his own chin.

"Hey—*hey!*"

"He'll wait," Makima says. "As long as I ask. He's happy to." She looks back at Jolyne, serene. "You could wrap your string around my neck right now. Pull. I'd like to see what happens, actually. But you'd have to decide whether he's worth it." The light dies. Her voice goes on in the dark, unchanged: "Dogs are supposed to die for their owners. Are you going to make this one?"

Light.

Stone Free is already out, a hundred threads bristling between the bars like a held breath. Jolyne can feel the guard's heartbeat through the floor—Makima's heartbeat, borrowed, steady, unafraid.

She could take the gun. She's fast. She might not be fast enough.

Slowly, Jolyne pulls the threads back into her skin.

"Put it down," she says, and her voice shakes with rage, not fear. "Put it down, you piece of shit, and get the hell out of my hallway."

Makima regards her a long moment. Then she touches the guard's wrist, and he holsters the weapon and blinks like a man waking in the wrong room.

"That's the answer I hoped for," Makima says softly. "Good girls hesitate." She steps back. "I'll come again. I think, eventually, you'll ask me to."

Heels, receding. The guards follow at the exact same pace.

Jolyne stands at the bars until the sound is gone, hands aching, blood in her mouth.

The light flickers—on, off, on—and she realizes she stopped counting somewhere around the word *father*.

She starts again. From zero. Whatever's coming, she wants to know exactly how long it takes.
