response:
# Prison Strings

The chain-link rattles whenever an inmate passes. Most of the yard has stopped hearing it. Jolyne hasn't—she's run a single thread of Stone Free through the bottom row of diamonds along the east fence, and every rattle climbs the string into her wrist like a tap on the shoulder. Forty yards of fence, forty yards of nerve. She sits on the bleachers, elbows on knees, and lets the yard tell her where everyone is.

Then a woman walks the whole length of it and the fence says nothing.

No rattle. The thread shifts once, lightly, like something stepped over it instead of through it, and then the woman is standing in front of the bleachers in a coat too clean for this place, auburn braid, eyes the color of a stove left on.

"Jolyne Cujoh." She says it like she's confirming a reservation. "You're shorter than your file."

"The yard's for inmates."

"I'm with Public Safety. We're evaluating special cases." She sits on the bench below without being asked, knees together, half-turned. "May I?"

"You already did."

Jolyne notices the men. Not a crowd—a spacing. Six inmates have drifted into the gravel around the bleachers and stopped at even intervals, facing outward. Hector from B-block is one of them, Hector who trades her cigarettes for gum, and he doesn't look at her. Nobody does. In the tower, the guard has turned his back to the yard.

"Something touched my ankle at the gate," the woman says pleasantly. "A thread. I couldn't see it." She tilts her head. "Do you know how rare that is? For me not to see something?"

"Fishing line. Guys smuggle it in."

"No. It was warm. It had a pulse." The smile doesn't move while she talks, which Jolyne has never seen a face do. "What is it like, coming apart like that?"

The fence hums under Jolyne's thread: nothing within ten yards is moving. The whole east side is holding its breath for this woman.

"Who are you?"

"Makima." A small dip of the head. "I could have you walked out that gate by dinner. The conviction, the lawyer who sold you—gone. Your father, too. I know where he is."

Jolyne's string isn't only in the fence. She let a strand drift when Makima sat; it lies along the bench now, under the hem of that coat, against a stockinged ankle, and through it she feels a heartbeat. Sixty. Steady as a clock. It didn't change on *your father*. It doesn't change on the promise, either—and Jolyne has known a lot of liars, and every one of them had a heart that cared, at least, about getting caught. This one doesn't. Nothing in this yard is real enough to her to be worth a lie.

"What's the catch?"

"No catch. You just say yes."

"A contract."

"If you like."

"Lady, I got framed once already. I read fine print now."

Makima laughs. It is a perfect laugh—warm, correctly timed—out of a body whose pulse is still sixty, and Jolyne's skin tries to crawl somewhere else.

"I grew up in Florida," Jolyne says. "I know a costume when I see one. Big smile, bright gates, nobody home. If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney."

"Hector," Makima says, still looking at her. "Show her."

Hector walks to the fence. He puts his right hand on the razor wire along the top and closes it. The chain-link rattles—the whole run, a long metal shiver that climbs Jolyne's thread and into her teeth—and Hector doesn't make a sound. Blood threads down his forearm. He stands there holding on like a man waiting for a bus.

"Stop it."

"You stop it. You have the thread."

Stone Free is already unspooling from Jolyne's shoulder. It snaps around Hector's wrist and *yanks*; his hand comes free, he stumbles, catches himself. Then he straightens, walks back to his spot in the gravel, and faces outward again, bleeding, face empty. That's the part that turns her stomach. Not the blood. The nothing. Even a dog flinches.

Makima has watched the space between them with open delight, the way you'd watch a card trick. She saw him move. She didn't see what moved him.

"You moved him," she says softly. "I moved him. The difference is, he'll remember yours."

And there it is—Jolyne sees the whole shape of it, a knot pulling tight. Makima doesn't want her out. Makima doesn't want her at all. Makima wants to know how an invisible leash works, because everything else in this yard already has a collar on, and the one thing she can't see is the one thing she hasn't got.

"You don't give a shit about me."

"I care about everything that's mine." The smile hasn't moved. "You were never really his, you know. Your father. You've spent your whole life yanking on that line, waiting for him to feel it on the other end." Her voice goes gentle. "He never did. Doesn't that get heavy?"

The fence thread screams because Jolyne's fist has closed on it. Sixty beats a minute under the hem of that coat. She could wrap a strand around that throat. She could pull.

Instead she breathes. The way he would.

She draws the string back—fence, bench, ankle, all of it—forty yards of nerve winding home into her forearm, into the blue of the butterfly, until she is one solid thing again sitting on a bleacher with nothing in her hands.

"No."

Makima rises and straightens her coat. "It's okay. I'm patient. Dogs always find their way home."

She walks the length of the east fence and it doesn't rattle. The six men peel off after her one at a time, evenly spaced. Hector is last. He stops, looks at his bleeding hand like it belongs to somebody else, then at Jolyne.

"What—"

"Nothing," Jolyne says. "Somebody was walking you."

When the yard is empty she threads the fence again. Higher this time. Eye level. She's learned what to feel for, and it isn't the rattle.

It's the quiet.

response:
# Prison Strings

The cameras in D-Wing die one by one as the woman in the white shirt walks past them, little red eyes winking out like somebody blowing down a row of candles.

Jolyne watches from the mesh of the common area with her arms folded. She's heard the rumor—everybody at Green Dolphin Street has heard it. The inspector from some government outfit nobody can name comes through once a month, and the tape always comes back gray. Guards say it's the humidity. Guards say a lot of things.

"That's her," Emporio whispers from somewhere around her elbow. "Don't look at her eyes."

"I'll look wherever I damn well please."

The woman stops at the gate. Auburn hair in a loose braid, a tie knotted neat enough to pass inspection, a smile that sits on her face like it was placed there by a careful hand. Her eyes are yellow, ringed in concentric circles, and they find Jolyne across the room without searching.

"Jolyne Cujoh," she says. Soft. Pleasant. The kind of voice that reads bedtime stories. "I was hoping we'd get to meet. My name is Makima."

Something in Jolyne's gut turns over like a cold engine. She's known plenty of sweet-talkers—lawyers, prosecutors, the boy who put her in here—and every one of them had a tell. A twitch. A swallow. This woman has nothing. Her face is a locked door with a welcome mat in front of it.

"Hoping, huh," Jolyne says. "Who told you about me?"

"Your file. Your father's file. Both are very interesting reading." Makima tilts her head. "Would you walk with me? I've asked the guards to give us the corridor."

She has. Three of them stand along the far wall, and they're not standing like guards stand. They're standing like coat racks.

Jolyne goes, because turning your back on something like this is worse than facing it. But as her boots hit the painted line, she lets a thread spool out of her left hand—Stone Free unraveling from the ball of her thumb, thin as spider silk, blue in the fluorescent light—and lays it along the floor behind her like a tripwire for the truth. She's never had a conversation where she couldn't feel the floor.

"I'll be honest with you," Makima says as they walk. The next camera stutters, hums, goes dark. "I don't usually find humans interesting. But a girl who can turn herself into string, who can pull herself apart and stitch herself back together—" the smile deepens by a precise millimeter "—that's a kind of control I haven't seen before. You wrote it into yourself. Nobody gave it to you."

"Somebody did. Long story. Involves an arrowhead."

"Everyone's story involves something." Makima stops in front of a steel door Jolyne has never seen open. "I could take you out of here tonight, you know. Charges dismissed. Your father's memory recovered. I have—resources."

There it is. Jolyne's whole body wants to lean toward that sentence like a plant toward a window. Jotaro, somewhere in a hospital bed with his mind pulled out of him like a cassette tape. One sentence and she's back on the Florida highway, the gun in her hand, the car, the lie.

Which is exactly why she doesn't move.

"How do you know about my dad's memory?" she says. "That's not in any file."

Makima blinks for the first time since the gate. It's not surprise. It's recalibration.

"I know a great many things."

"Yeah. I bet you do." Jolyne steps closer, and she can smell it now—nothing. The woman doesn't smell like soap or sweat or prison or anything at all. "Let me guess how this goes. You get me out, I owe you. You hold a leash and I wear a collar, and when you need something ripped apart from the inside, you tug."

"That's an ugly way to describe loyalty."

"Loyalty goes both ways, bitch. What you're selling only goes one."

For a moment the corridor is very quiet. Down the hall, one of the coat-rack guards turns his head toward them—not because he wants to, Jolyne can see that, but because something pulled it—and Makima lifts two fingers without looking at him.

"Officer. Show her."

The guard raises his sidearm and presses the muzzle into his own temple. His eyes are wide and wet and completely awake.

"Hey—*HEY*—"

"He'll do it if I ask," Makima says, in the voice for bedtime stories. "He'd thank me first. That's what it means to belong to someone, Jolyne. It's a comfort. Most people are relieved when they stop choosing."

Stone Free moves before Jolyne tells it to. The thread on the floor snaps taut, whips up the corridor, and wraps the guard's wrist four times, yanking the barrel toward the ceiling. The shot goes off anyway. Concrete dust falls like snow.

Makima doesn't flinch. She looks at the thread, then at Jolyne, with something that is almost—almost—warmth.

"You see? That's why I wanted to meet you. You reached for him before you reached for yourself." She steps closer, and Jolyne realizes a second loop of her own string has been lying coiled around Makima's ankle this whole time, dragged there when she first laid the tripwire. Makima has known since the gate. She hasn't moved her foot once. "Keep it there if you like. I don't mind being tied to interesting things."

Jolyne reels the string back into her hand so fast it hums. Her palm bleeds a little where it re-knits.

"If there's no exit door on your deal," she says, "then it ain't a deal. It's a kennel."

"Everything is a kennel. Some are nicer than others."

The last camera in the corridor flickers back to life as Makima turns to go, as if the building is exhaling. The guard slides down the wall, sobbing, holding his wrist where the thread has left four red rings. Makima pauses at the gate and glances back over her shoulder, and for one second the smile is gone and there is nothing behind it—not cruelty, not hunger, just a vast, patient attention, like weather.

"I'll be back next month," she says. "Think about your father."

Jolyne watches her go. Then she looks down at her palm, at the thread already trying to re-spool itself, and makes a fist until it stops.

She'll think about her father. She'll think about him so hard the walls will come down. But she'll do it with her own goddamn hands.

Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception.

First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense.

Notes are always written on standard Foundation memo paper, even when the researcher keeps it locked away. Length: 1000 words.
response:
**Item #:** SCP-5983

**Object Class:** Euclid (provisional)

**Special Containment Procedures:** All SCP-5983 manifestations are to be photographed in situ and transferred to Secure Document Storage, Site-73. Dr. Ines Halloran is to remain on-site under continuous observation. Issuance of Form 7-C memo paper to Research Wing B is suspended. Containment of SCP-2106 (Cell 9) is not to be modified on the basis of information derived from SCP-5983.

**Description:** SCP-5983 is the recurring manifestation of handwritten notes addressed to Dr. Ines Halloran, apparently authored by Dr. Halloran at an unspecified future date. Notes appear on standard Foundation memo paper irrespective of storage conditions. Content concerns a containment breach at Site-73 that has not occurred. Hume readings during manifestation are nominal.

---

**Addendum 5983.1 — Account of Dr. I. Halloran** *(submitted at the request of the Ethics Committee)*

The first one was folded under my coffee cup.

> *Ines — Cell 9 seal fails 03:14, 14 March. Reinforce the secondary bulkhead. The handwriting is yours. The ink is yours. Check the pen in your left drawer.*

I checked. The pen was half-empty; it had been full the night before. The hand was mine down to the barred sevens I'd picked up in Vienna. I reported it within the hour, because that is what we are trained to do, and because I was frightened in a way I didn't want to examine alone.

Document Analysis confirmed the paper was Foundation stock, batch 7C-0419 — a batch issued to Site-73 but not yet distributed. Nobody could tell me what that meant.

SCP-2106 occupies Cell 9. It is a humanoid entity that induces false memories in sustained proximity. I had catalogued its effects for two years. Dr. Marsh, my supervisor, put the obvious to me kindly: an entity that manufactures memory, and a researcher who suddenly remembers writing a note she never wrote. Reinforcing anything in Cell 9 would mean opening it. He asked whether I'd ever felt the urge to open the door.

I said no. I had to think about it first, and he saw me think.

The second note was in my locked filing cabinet. I had emptied the office of memo paper the day before.

> *They didn't reinforce. Why didn't they reinforce? Sato is dead. Sato is dead and you were standing right there with the badge in your hand.*

There is no Sato at Site-73. There has never been a Sato at Site-73. Personnel pulled thirty years of records. I lay awake trying to picture Sato's face, and found I nearly could, which was worse.

Dr. Marsh moved me to observation quarters. Four cameras, no paper. I slept with my hands outside the blanket like a child. At 03:14 the footage shows me sitting up, taking a sheet of Form 7-C from beneath my pillow, where there had been nothing, and writing for ninety seconds before lying down. I do not remember this. I have watched it eleven times. The woman on the screen does not look at the page while she writes.

> *Stop testing the paper. The paper is not the point. You know what's in Cell 9 and you know it isn't what the file says. Ask Marsh why the file was rewritten in February. Ask him where you were.*

I asked. Dr. Marsh showed me the file's revision history. Untouched since 2019. He showed me patiently, the way you show a patient that the room is empty. Then he had my Hume baseline retaken, and my blood, and my sleep, and he asked whether I wanted a Class-A amnestic. I heard my own voice say "not yet" before I'd decided anything.

That night I began dating my own notes. Time and initials, every one. So I would know which were mine.

14 March came. I was in observation. Cell 9 held. Nothing failed at 03:14. I remember laughing, a little, alone.

The next note was in my sleeve.

> *It held because you reinforced. You don't remember reinforcing. That's what it costs. Every time you fix it you lose the fixing. There are three of me now and two of us are wrong and I can't tell you which from here.*

After that they came faster, and the handwriting began to lean.

> *don't take the amnestic the amnestic is the door it comes in through the door is*

> *TAKE IT. Take it. I'm sorry. Take it.*

> *ines the breach already happened it happened in february you held the door for it you held the door because it asked nicely and it had your face*

I stopped reading them on arrival. I logged them, bagged them, and read them later in a lit room with Dr. Marsh present, because I no longer trusted what the words did to me when I was alone.

By the time I wrote this, the Foundation knew the following: the notes were in my hand. The paper was ours. SCP-2106 denied involvement, which it would have done in either case. No Hume disturbance. No temporal signature. The breach had not occurred.

And I knew the following: I had not opened Cell 9. I had checked my hands for ink every morning. I composed this account at a terminal, in the observation suite, with Dr. Marsh at the glass, because I wanted one thing in this file that I was certain I had written.

I checked. I checked twice.

---

**Addendum 5983.2 — Note from Site Director Okafor:** Dr. Halloran's account was received by this office in handwritten form, on four sheets of Form 7-C memo paper. No terminal in the observation suite logged activity during the period in question. Dr. Halloran has been informed. She has asked that this addendum be included, and that we confirm, for her, the date.

Ink analysis reveals trace elements not matching any office pen. Length: 1000 words.
response:
**Item #:** SCP-7271
**Object Class:** Pending

**Special Containment Procedures:** All handwritten material recovered from Dr. Imani Aderele is to be sealed in shielded evidence bags and catalogued by Temporal Anomalies. Dr. Aderele has been relocated to Observation Suite 4, Site-81, and is to be provided no writing implements.

**Addendum 7271-A: Statement of Dr. I. Aderele**

The first note was under my coffee mug on the morning of March 3rd. I remember being annoyed because the mug left a ring on it.

> *Don't let them move 3341 to the east wing. The seal on the secondary door is wrong. Trust me. —I.*

It was my handwriting. Not similar — mine. The way I cross my sevens, the loop on the lowercase g my adviser hated. I assumed I'd written it half-asleep and forgotten. I threw it away.

The second was in my locker. The third was folded inside a textbook I hadn't opened since graduate school.

> *They moved it. I know because you didn't tell anyone. TELL SOMEONE. The breach starts in the storage cage, not the chamber. Eleven days.*

I told the Site Director. I expected him to laugh. Instead he bagged the notes, pulled my access to Wing C, and assigned two people to me — one from Temporal, one from Psych. That was when I understood nobody had laughed because this had happened before.

Dr. Weiss, from Temporal, treated it as an engineering problem. The paper was Foundation stock. The handwriting analysis came back a 97% match to my exemplars, with the caveat that pen pressure was heavier and the baseline drifted downward, "consistent with fatigue or impaired fine motor control."

The ink was the problem.

Site-81 issues one kind of pen. Everyone has a drawer full of them. The notes were not written with one. Spectroscopy showed an iron-gall base — a formulation nobody has manufactured commercially in a century — with trace iridium and a lead isotope ratio the materials lab flagged, re-ran, and flagged again. Weiss wouldn't tell me what the ratio implied. I found out later: lead that had spent a long time in a high-neutron environment.

Someone had made that ink by hand. Someone who didn't have pens anymore.

Dr. Hallam, from Psych, treated it as a different kind of problem.

SCP-3341 is contained in Wing C. I am not cleared to describe it here; it is sufficient to say its documented effects include confabulation, intrusive imagery, and in two prior cases, automatic writing. Both cases produced notes. Both researchers were certain they hadn't written them. Both were, eventually, filmed doing so.

Hallam was kind about it. He said the mind is very good at protecting itself from the knowledge that it has been compromised, and that I shouldn't take the videos personally when they came.

I agreed to cameras. I agreed to sleep in the observation suite. I agreed to have my hands bandaged in cotton mitts at night like an infant with eczema.

> *The mitts don't matter. I'm not writing these in your room, I'm writing them in mine. You keep thinking the problem is the hand. The problem is the door. Doors. There are more doors than there used to be.*

That one appeared inside a sealed evidence bag in a locked cabinet. Weiss stopped saying "if."

Hallam pointed out, correctly, that 3341's effects had never been tested against sealed bags, and that absence of a mechanism is not evidence of a different one.

Here is what I haven't said in any interview: I don't know which of them I wanted to be right.

If Weiss was right, there was a version of me somewhere ahead, in the dark, grinding oak galls and scraping lead off something I didn't want to think about, trying to reach back. If Hallam was right, there was a thing in Wing C that had learned my handwriting from the inside. I checked my hands for ink so often the skin cracked.

The notes got worse.

> *Tell Marcus I'm sorry about the lake. He'll know.*

I don't know anyone named Marcus.

> *there is a sub-level under C they tell you is a utility corridor it is not a utility corridor I have been down there I have been down there I have been down*

Weiss checked. There is no sub-level under Wing C. The plans were pulled, the floor was sounded, ground-penetrating radar found soil. Hallam wrote *confabulation, escalating* in his notes and didn't hide it from me.

> *Imani. Your daughter's name was Tendai. You named her for your grandmother. Please. I need you to remember her so that I can.*

I have never been pregnant. I have never wanted children. I sat with that note for an hour before I called anyone, and I cannot explain why I was crying.

It was Hallam who found the discrepancy. The two prior 3341 cases produced notes that were short, repetitive, and consistent with the researchers' existing anxieties. Mine contained something theirs did not: a verifiable prediction. Weiss had the secondary door seal on Chamber 3341-E inspected on day two, before the notes went strange. It was defective. It had been defective since installation.

So the notes were right about one thing, and wrong about a sub-level and a daughter and a man named Marcus, and I was left to decide whether I was reading a message degraded in transit or a liar who had told one truth to purchase the rest.

I asked Weiss whether that lead ratio could be faked by an entity with access to Foundation materials. He said he didn't know.

I asked Hallam whether a future version of me, irradiated and alone, might confabulate. He said he didn't know.

The last note was the shortest. I found it this morning under my mug. There was a ring on it.

> *Stop looking at your hands.*

I request that this statement be entered into the file, that I be kept away from Wing C, and that my mitts not be removed.

I would also like it on record that the ring on that note did not match my mug.

**Description:** The first note appeared on 14 March, between 03:11 and 03:13. I know the window because Camera 14-B lost eleven frames at 03:12:08, and the note was there when the feed returned. Folded once. Lined paper from the pad in my second drawer; the pad was down one sheet.

> *Don't go to Wing C on the 22nd. The seal on 4521's door fails at 14:40. You'll be standing right there. — You*

The handwriting was mine. I don't mean it resembled mine. I mean I recognized the way I cross a seven, a habit from a teacher I haven't thought about in twenty years.

I reported it, as protocol demands and as I would not have, given a night to think. Document analysis returned a 96% match on letterforms and 71% on pen pressure. Dr. Okafor said this was consistent with a forgery by someone who had studied me, or with a version of me writing under duress. She said it kindly.

On the 22nd I was not in Wing C. The seal held. Nothing happened, which was the problem, because nothing can be proven by nothing.

SCP-4521 is a humanoid that induces false memories in anyone who sustains eye contact for longer than four seconds. I have never sustained eye contact with it. I have reviewed every logged moment I've spent within thirty meters of its cell. The Foundation has reviewed them too, in more detail than I am comfortable with.

The second note came on the 25th. Camera 14-B, nine frames, 02:47:31.

> *It wasn't the 22nd. I got the date wrong — I'm working from memory and the clocks here aren't right. Second week of April. Please. Move the Tuesday briefing out of C.*

I moved the briefing. I also requested transfer to Site-43 for the duration of the investigation. It was approved within six hours, which told me someone above Ames wanted to know whether the notes would follow me.

They did. Site-43, Dormitory 2, a desk I had never seen before. Camera glitch at 04:02:15, a full second of grey. The paper was from my Site-19 pad, eleven hundred kilometers away in an evidence locker.

> *Tell Halloran the backup generators on sublevel three are wired wrong. He'll know what to do.*

There is no Halloran at Site-19 or Site-43. There is no sublevel three at Site-19; there are two, and the generators are on the surface. I spent a night confirming this, and another confirming that I had confirmed it, because by then I had stopped trusting the first pass of anything.

Dr. Okafor's working hypothesis, filed 2 April: SCP-7318 is not temporal. SCP-4521's influence produces confabulated memories with high internal consistency, and the notes may be a somatic expression of such a memory — meaning I write them. The lost footage would be the only genuinely anomalous component, and possibly not even that; the camera firmware has a documented stutter.

I asked why the stutter was so punctual. She had no answer. I asked how I was getting my own notepaper out of a locked evidence room. She said she didn't know, and that the honest version of her hypothesis was that she could neither rule me out nor rule me in.

I asked to be placed under continuous observation, including sleep. For nine nights I was watched by two people and four cameras. On the ninth night all four cameras dropped at 03:30:00 exactly, and both observers reported that for fourteen seconds the room had felt "too quiet," which is not an observation, and which they both knew was not an observation.

> *theyre saying its 4521 its not 4521 4521 is gone it got out in the breach thats the point thats what im telling you the breach is how it gets out and then it makes everyone think it never happened you have to stop them opening the door you have to you have to you*

The letters sloped down the page. The pen had torn through in two places.

I have read this note perhaps forty times. Here is what I cannot resolve: it describes the exact symptom I would expect if 4521 were manipulating me, and it describes it as something 4521 *will* do, after a breach I am supposed to prevent. It is a warning indistinguishable from its own cause. Every test I have proposed — opening 4521's cell under controlled conditions to see whether the notes change; refusing to open it to see whether they stop — is also something the note might want.

The Hume readings on my desk are flat. The paper is paper. The ink is from a pen in my own drawer. Dr. Okafor has begun looking at me the way I remember looking at D-class who had been near something too long.

I have started checking my own hands when the cameras come back.

The most recent note appeared four nights ago. The handwriting was steady again, lines straight, sevens crossed.

> *I was wrong. There is no breach. Nothing happens. The clocks here are fine. Stop reading these.*

I do not know which of us wrote that.

There has not been a note since. Camera 14-B has not glitched since. Dr. Okafor has recommended reclassification to Neutralized, pending thirty days of observation.

Last night I checked the pad in my second drawer. I counted the sheets twice, and then I counted them again, and then I put it back and did not write the number down.

response:
**Item #:** SCP-7718

**Object Class:** Keter

**Special Containment Procedures:** Structures containing instances of SCP-7718 are to be acquired through Foundation front companies and placed under passive surveillance. Instances are not to be destroyed; demolition of host structures has in every case left the instance standing as a freestanding frame. Entry is restricted to MTF Sigma-9 ("Late Returns") under Level 4 authorization. No printed material is to be removed from SCP-7718-1 without RAISA review.

All exploration footage is to be forwarded to the O5 Council prior to archival. (See Addendum 7718.3.)

**Description:** SCP-7718 designates a class of unmarked interior doors manifesting in abandoned structures worldwide. Forty-one instances have been confirmed, in locations including a shuttered textile mill in Łódź, a flooded metro station beneath Caracas, and a Hokkaido sanatorium unoccupied since 1961. Instances are indistinguishable: unpainted steel, 203 cm by 91 cm, brass knob, no visible hinges on either side. Each bears an identical pattern of 214 fine scratches within 6 cm of the knob—identical to the micron, as though every door were a copy of a single original. Forensic assessment describes the pattern as "consistent with prolonged attempts to fit a key that does not match the lock."

All instances open onto SCP-7718-1, a contiguous archival space of indeterminate extent. Shelving recedes beyond the range of laser rangefinding; a single stairwell returns explorers to the same landing at different elevations; reading rooms exceeding 400 m in length are roofed at 2.1 m. The interior is lit by a sourceless light and held at 18°C and 35% humidity—optimal conditions for paper.

SCP-7718-1 contains an estimated 10⁹ documents in roughly 300 languages, a third of them identified. Legible material describes a global industrial civilization closely resembling our own, terminated by an event rendered variously as "the Lapse," "the Opening," or "the Breach." No document describes the event. Several describe the days before it.

**Addendum 7718.1: Selected Recovered Documents**

> *Fragment 7718-R-0093 (translated, 68% confidence)*
>
> ...the Trust reminds all departments that discussion of the Thirteenth Site outside secured channels remains a dismissable offense. Overseer Four has requested the following phrase be struck from internal correspondence: "it was always going to." Compliance is mandatory.

> *Fragment 7718-R-0417 (English, undamaged)*
>
> TRUST FOR THE RETENTION OF ANOMALIES
> PERSONNEL RECORD — RESTRICTED
> Name: Okonkwo, Adaeze. Clearance: 3. Assignment: Site Lambda, Containment Review.
> Date of entry: 611.04.14 (Trust reckoning).
> Notes: Reliable. Overly curious regarding Site Thirteen. Recommend monitoring.

Radiocarbon dating places the paper's manufacture between 1640 and 1710 CE. Dr. Adaeze Okonkwo is a current Level 3 researcher at Site-19. The attached photograph is of her. The fingerprint card matches. Dr. Okonkwo has no recollection of the Trust, Site Lambda, or the seventeenth century. Fourteen further personnel records matching current Foundation staff have been recovered. Three match members of MTF Sigma-9.

**Addendum 7718.2: Exploration Log 7718-E-06 (abridged)**

MTF Sigma-9 (Cpt. Marsh, Sgt. Dulac, Dr. Okonkwo, Spc. Reyes) entered via the Łódź instance at 0900.

The team proceeded past Marker 11, the farthest point reached in prior explorations. At 0932, Dulac reported movement two aisles east. Marsh ordered weapons down and lights up.

Seven figures in white full-body suits and hooded respirators—gear resembling hazardous-materials response equipment, bearing no insignia—were dismantling a run of shelving approximately 40 meters long. They worked quickly and in silence, loading boxes onto wheeled carts. Reyes noted the carts made no sound on the floor.

Marsh called out. The figures stopped in unison. One turned its faceplate toward the team—Okonkwo later described the visor as "fogged from the inside, completely, like breath on cold glass"—and then all seven abandoned the carts and ran. They did not run toward any exit. At the end of the aisle they were simply no longer there.

The shelving they had been clearing was labeled, in a Trust hand, SITE THIRTEEN — INCIDENT — CAUSAL. The section was empty. A single folder lay on the floor, apparently dropped.

It contained a lending register. Each line was dated within the past fourteen months and signed. Reyes, a former document examiner, identified the signatures on sight: eleven of the thirteen members of the O5 Council, each appearing multiple times. The most frequent visitor had signed in twenty-six times. The most recent entry was dated the previous Tuesday.

No authorized Council visit to SCP-7718-1 is on record.

At 1004, the team located a reading room beyond Marker 11. A chair was pushed back from the table. A paper cup of coffee on the table was still warm. Beside it lay a Foundation-standard Level 5 access badge, face down. Marsh photographed it and did not turn it over.

Dr. Okonkwo requested permission to search for the remainder of the Site Thirteen material. Marsh denied the request pending review. The team withdrew at 1041.

**Addendum 7718.3:** RAISA notes that the "all footage to Council" clause in the containment procedures was inserted on 2024-03-02 by a Level 5 account with no corresponding vote in Council minutes. The clause has not been removed. The request to remove it is under review.

**Addendum 7718.4:** The final recovered fragment is reproduced without comment.

> *Fragment 7718-R-1120 (English, water-damaged)*
>
> ...fourth door this month, this one in the old grain exchange. Same as the others. Plain steel. Same scratches around the handle—we've checked, identical down to the scratch. It opens onto the library again. The Archivist's teams are still clearing shelves faster than we can read them. Overseer Seven says not to worry about who's doing the clearing. He says they're ours.
>
> He says they've always been ours.

Some doors appear more weathered than the building they’re in, as though older. Length: 1000 words.
response:
**Item #:** SCP-7604

**Object Class:** Keter

**Special Containment Procedures:** All reported instances of SCP-7604 are to be secured by the nearest Foundation site under cover of structural condemnation. Instances cannot be removed; attempts result in the door reappearing elsewhere within 72 hours. Entry into SCP-7604-A is restricted to Mobile Task Force Rho-41 ("Shelf Life"). All recovered material is classified Level 4/7604.

Per directive O5-9/7604-02, no personnel may enter SCP-7604-A for the purpose of locating or retrieving documents pertaining to Foundation staff. Rationale for this directive has not been provided to the research team.

**Description:** SCP-7604 is a series of identical doors (41 confirmed instances) appearing in abandoned structures worldwide. Each is a plain six-panel door of unidentified hardwood with a brass knob worn to dull pewter. Instances bear no markings, locks, or visible hinges.

All instances display weathering grossly inconsistent with their host structures. SCP-7604-17, located in a Lagos shopping arcade vacated in 2009, exhibits salt-pitting, dry rot, and tool-marks consistent with at least three centuries of exposure. The surrounding drywall is undamaged.

Each instance opens onto SCP-7604-A, a single contiguous archive with no measurable exterior. Its interior consists of reading rooms and stacks arranged in violation of Euclidean geometry: stairwells descend into the floors above them, a reading room measured at 4 km in length is visible in its entirety from an 11 m corridor, and several wings exhibit gravitational orientation rotated 90° from the point of entry. No staff have been encountered, with the exception of SCP-7604-B (see Exploration Log 7604-6).

Documents within SCP-7604-A are written in approximately 300 languages, roughly a third unidentified. Translated material describes a global civilization with no correlate in the historical record, whose collapse is consistently attributed to an event called "the Loosing."

---

**Addendum 7604.1 — Recovered Document Excerpts**

*Recovered from Stack 9, Reading Room "Perseverance." Translated from Linear K (provisional designation).*

> It was not the thing itself that ended us. It was the Keeping's certainty that it could be held. They built the vault deeper and the walls thicker, and the thing waited, as it had always waited, for the walls to be finished.

*Recovered from Stack 2,114. English, Foundation-standard formatting, dated by header to 1741.*

> **THE KEEPING — PERSONNEL FILE**
> **Name:** Adeyemi, Yusuf Olawale
> **Clearance:** Fourth Circle
> **Assignment:** Warden-Second, Holding Nineteen
> **Notes:** Subject has requested transfer from Holding Nineteen on three occasions, citing "the sound from the lower vaults." Requests denied. Subject is reminded that the Keeping does not retreat.

Dr. Yusuf Adeyemi is currently employed at Site-19. He was born in 1979. The photograph affixed to the file is his.

To date, personnel files have been recovered for 212 current Foundation employees, including all four members of MTF Rho-41. The files refer to "the Keeping" (*Hold. Keep. Endure.*). In no recovered document does the Keeping succeed.

---

**Addendum 7604.2 — Exploration Log 7604-6 (Excerpt)**

*MTF Rho-41 (Cpt. Marisol Ferreira, Agt. Teodor Nyquist, Agt. Chen Ruolan, Dr. Hal Senn) entered via SCP-7604-31, a condemned sanatorium in Hokkaido. Objective: locate stacks pertaining to the Loosing.*

Ferreira noticed the dust first. Every prior entry had found the archive uniformly coated, the kind of dust that took a long time to settle. Here, in a wing none of them had mapped, the floor was striped clean in long parallel lanes, as if something heavy had been dragged.

"Shelves," Nyquist said, pointing. Along the left wall the stacks simply stopped. Rectangular outlines marked where their bases had stood. Beyond that: bare stone, receding further than her light would reach.

Senn was already at the last remaining case, pulling volumes. "These are all Loosing-adjacent. Containment schematics. Casualty registers. Whoever's taking them is taking them in order."

Chen's light caught movement at the far end of the aisle. Four figures in white suits — full hazmat, hooded, faceplates mirrored — were lifting a shelving unit between them with the unhurried care of movers. Nothing on the suits. No insignia, no agency, no color-coding.

"Foundation!" Ferreira called. "Identify yourselves."

The figures set the shelf down. They did not run. They turned and walked away at a steady pace, and no matter how fast Rho-41 moved — Nyquist at a dead sprint — the distance did not close. At the end of the aisle the four figures and the shelf were simply absent. The dust lanes ended there.

Senn, breathing hard, held up the one volume he had managed to pull before the shelf went. A bound ledger. The cover read, in English: *Holding Nineteen — Final Access Log.*

Ferreira told him to bag it and not open it. He had already opened it.

---

**Addendum 7604.3 — Evidence of Unauthorized Access**

1. A visitor ledger at the entry to Reading Room "Perseverance." Fourteen signatures postdate Foundation discovery of SCP-7604. Graphological analysis matches three to O5-3, O5-9, and O5-11 at >97% confidence. No O5 entry into SCP-7604-A is on record.

2. A Foundation-issue tactical flashlight (serial traced to Site-01 Overwatch stores) recovered from Stack 3,002, beside an empty space where a shelving unit had been removed.

3. Security footage from SCP-7604-08's host structure (a disused Ostrava rail depot) showing an individual entering the door at 03:12 local time, eleven days before Rho-41's first survey. The badge reflects at Overseer luminance. The face is obscured.

4. The final page of *Holding Nineteen — Final Access Log*, listing the last entrants to the Keeping's deepest vault before the Loosing. The handwriting of the final entry matches the ledger signature attributed to O5-9. It is dated to the day of the Loosing. It reads: *Walls complete. Nothing to report.*

*Research Note (Dr. Senn):* We have asked the Council three times whether the Keeping is us, or was us, or will be. We have asked whether SCP-7604-B are theirs. Each request was formally withdrawn by order of O5-9 before a response could be issued. I note for the record that SCP-7604-B have not yet reached Stack 2,114. The personnel files are still there. Someone, it seems, wants them read.

**Object Class:** Euclid (Keter reclassification pending O5 review — see Addendum 6412-4)

**Special Containment Procedures:** Instances of SCP-6412-1 are to be sealed upon discovery and the host structure acquired or demolished. Abandoned buildings in urban centers are to be surveyed monthly under blackout conditions; a faint glow escapes through the door's edges in complete darkness, and this remains the only reliable means of detection. Exploration of SCP-6412-2 requires Level 4 authorization and a minimum team of three. No personnel are to remain inside longer than six hours. All recovered documents are to be catalogued by Site-19 Archival before any Foundation member named within them is informed.

**Description:** SCP-6412-1 is a series of identical, unmarked wooden doors (grey paint, brass knob, no visible hinges) manifesting in disused buildings worldwide. 214 instances confirmed to date. Doors appear on interior walls where no door existed and do not correspond to the structure's floor plan.

All instances open onto SCP-6412-2, a single contiguous archive. Internal geometry is non-Euclidean: corridors of shelving extend further than the host building allows, stairwells descend without reaching a lower floor, and teams entering from doors on separate continents have met inside within minutes. Shelving holds bound volumes, loose folios, and film canisters, lit by fixtures resembling gas lamps that burn no fuel.

Documents are written in a script that resolves into the reader's native language on second glance. They describe a global, industrialized civilization ending in what is consistently termed "the Breach." The nature of the Breach is never specified. Multiple documents refer to a containment organization called "the Vigil."

---

**Exploration Log 6412-E7**
Entry point: SCP-6412-1-131 (former textile mill, Łódź, Poland)
Team: Dr. Marguerite Sauer (lead), Agent Tomás Reyes, Researcher Devon Oyelaran

The team entered at 02:14. Sauer noted the air smelled of paper dust and ozone. Reyes marked the door with reflective tape; by the time Oyelaran had taken ten steps, the tape was no longer visible behind them, though the door remained where they had left it.

Shelving rose roughly twelve meters on either side. Reyes estimated the first corridor at four hundred meters before an intersection, where a brass plaque read ADMINISTRATIVE RECORDS — PERSONNEL. Sauer directed the team to proceed.

At the 00:40 mark on Reyes's camera, Oyelaran stopped. He had pulled a folio from the nearest shelf. He did not say anything at first. Then he handed it to Sauer.

*Recovered Document 6412-R-22 (excerpt)*

> **THE VIGIL — SERVANT RECORD**
> Name: Marguerite Anne Sauer
> Born: 14 Thermid, Year 1611 of the Settlement
> Posting: Reading Station Nine, Thaumic Materials
> Notes: Flagged for promotion. Objected formally to the Twelve regarding the Breach site's [illegible]. Objection struck. Servant reassigned.
> Disposition: Lost in the Breach.

Sauer confirmed the day and month of birth matched her own. The handwriting, in her assessment, was hers. Reyes located records for Oyelaran, two Site Directors, and himself; his was marked only PENDING. The team collected eleven files and continued.

At the 01:52 mark, Reyes reported movement at the far end of a cross-corridor. Six figures in white full-body suits with opaque faceplates were loading shelving contents into wheeled canvas carts. They worked quickly and without speech. Behind them, approximately forty meters of shelving stood empty. Brass plaques on the emptied sections had been pried off.

Sauer called out. The figures stopped. Reyes advanced with his sidearm lowered and free hand raised. The figures abandoned the carts and moved away at a walking pace that nonetheless outdistanced Reyes at a run. They turned a corner. When Reyes reached it, the corridor beyond was empty for its visible length, and the carts had gone with them.

Three folios remained on the floor where the carts had stood, all from a section plaqued THE BREACH — PRECEDING DECISIONS.

*Recovered Document 6412-R-24 (excerpt)*

> Minutes of the Twelve, closed session. The Eleventh asked whether the object could be moved before the Settlement's [illegible]. The First said the question had been asked before. The Fourth said: it has been asked before, and the answer has been the same, and we have been the same, and we do not learn from the archive because we do not permit ourselves to read it. The First moved to strike the Fourth's remark. Carried, eleven to one.

The team reached a reading room at the 03:30 mark — long oak tables, green-shaded lamps, and at the entrance a ledger on a lectern requiring signatures. Sauer photographed the last page.

*Recovered Document 6412-R-25 (ledger, final entries)*

> [Foundation cipher consistent with O5-3] — 19 days prior to exploration
> [Foundation cipher consistent with O5-7] — 19 days prior to exploration
> [Foundation cipher consistent with O5-11] — 6 days prior to exploration
> Purpose column, all three entries: *Review.*

On the nearest table lay a Site-01 access card, face-up. Beside it, a folio open to a page bearing a single stamped word: RETAINED.

At the 05:10 mark, Sauer ordered withdrawal. The team returned to the Łódź door without incident. Time inside: 5 hours 48 minutes. External elapsed time: 11 minutes.

---

**Addendum 6412-3:** Cross-referencing of recovered personnel files has identified records for 37 current Foundation staff. All predate the Foundation's founding by a minimum of four centuries. All list the same disposition.

**Addendum 6412-4:** Dr. Sauer's request for Council comment on Document 6412-R-25 was answered within the hour.

> *Exploration of SCP-6412-2 is suspended pending review. The ledger in question is anomalous and its entries are not to be taken as evidence of Council activity. Dr. Sauer is reassigned to Site-19 Archival, effective immediately. The matter is closed.*
> *— O5-1*

**Addendum 6412-5:** Blackout survey of the Łódź site three days later found the door removed. The wall behind it was bare brick. A faint glow was nonetheless observed through a seam in the mortar.

prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov)
The Azra Gambit
Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in.

The transfer vessel's air filtration system hums with a persistent mechanical drone. Length: 1000 words.
response:
The transfer vessel's air filtration system hums with a persistent mechanical drone. Arthur Neegan had spent eleven years listening to pumps and scrubbers in the Tharsis shafts, and he could tell from the pitch alone that this one was overbuilt—military grade, running at a third of capacity. Someone had money to waste on silence that wasn't quite silence.

He sat strapped into an acceleration couch that smelled of new polymer and watched Mars shrink in the port. Red, then rust, then a coin. Somewhere on that coin was a prefab dome with a kitchen table still set for one, and under the dome, under four hundred meters of basalt, a seam of Azra wide enough to drive a hauler through.

Three weeks ago he had been a man with a mortgage on a marginal claim. Now he was cargo.

The retinue had been courteous. That was the word that kept returning to him—*courteous*. Six of them at his airlock, grey uniforms with the blue starburst of the Antares Diplomatic Corps on the collar, sidearms holstered and never touched. The officer had removed her helmet, offered him a document on actual paper, and said, "Mr. Neegan, you are invited to a conference. Attendance is voluntary. Your transport departs in forty minutes." She had let the pause after *voluntary* do its own work.

He had gone. He was an engineer, not a fool. You did not argue with a pressure differential.

---

The vessel docked with something large enough that he never saw its edges. A steward in a white jacket led him through corridors of brushed aluminum and soft indirect light, past doors that bore no markings, into a room that would not have looked out of place in an Earthside bank of the last century. Wood paneling—real wood, or a convincing lie. A desk. Two chairs. A window showing the stars, which could not possibly be a window at this depth in a hull, and was therefore a very expensive screen.

The man behind the desk rose. He was perhaps sixty, with the compact build of someone born to full gravity and the unhurried manner of someone who had never once been kept waiting.

"Mr. Neegan. Thank you for coming. My name is Dr. Halvard Oyelaran. I hold a position with the Corps, though I'll spare you the title. Sit, please. Coffee? It's genuine Colombian. The Antares Protectorate has a standing arrangement."

Arthur sat. He did not take the coffee. "Diplomatic Corps," he said. "I didn't realize diplomacy required an armed escort."

"Diplomacy has *always* required an armed escort. The uniforms used to be more honest about it." Oyelaran poured himself a cup and settled back. "You're an engineer. Tell me what you know about Azra."

"Catalytic decay accelerant. Exposes fissile material and the half-life drops by six, seven orders of magnitude. Puts a grain of uranium in contact with it and you get a controlled release that used to need a reactor the size of a house. Makes a drive. Makes a bomb." He shrugged. "Everyone knows that."

"Everyone knows that. Yes." Oyelaran turned his cup slowly on its saucer. "Here is what fewer people know. The Belt consortiums have been mapping Martian Azra deposits for nine years by gravimetric survey. Every significant vein was accounted for, leased, and, where necessary, acquired. Your plot was surveyed four times. It showed nothing."

"Then the surveys were wrong."

"The surveys were *right*. That is the problem." He leaned forward. "Your vein does not sit in a gravimetric shadow, Mr. Neegan. It produces none. Which means either our understanding of Azra's density is wrong, or your Azra is not the same Azra. In either case, you are sitting on the only sample in the system that has defied prediction. Do you understand what that makes you?"

Arthur was quiet for a moment. The filtration hum filled the space. "A liability."

"An *asset*. Liabilities are what you become if you decline to be an asset." Oyelaran said it without menace, the way a man might remark on the weather. "Consider your position. The Martian Colonial Authority holds nominal title to the subsurface. The Tharsis Mining Compact holds your lease. The Ceres Group holds the Compact's debt. Terran Defense holds the Ceres Group's export licenses. Each of them has a legal claim to what lies under your floor, and each of them has, as of about sixty hours ago, a very keen interest in making that claim first."

"And Antares?"

"Antares has no claim at all." He smiled. "Which is precisely why we can afford to be generous."

He slid a folder across the desk. Paper again. Arthur was beginning to understand that paper, here, was a kind of theater—it could not be intercepted, and it could be burned.

"Full title to the plot, transferred to a trust in your name. A research position with the Protectorate's materials division, at a salary that will embarrass you. Relocation for yourself and any dependents to Antares Station, where the Compact's collection agents have no jurisdiction and the Ceres Group's accountants have no teeth. In exchange, exclusive extraction rights and your personal expertise regarding the seam's geology."

Arthur did not touch the folder. "And if I'd rather go home?"

"Then you'll go home. I told your escort to be clear on that point." Oyelaran's eyes did not leave him. "You will arrive at your dome approximately nineteen hours from now. I would estimate the Compact's legal representatives arrive in twenty-two. Terran Defense will not send lawyers. Terran Defense will send a survey team, and they will not ask permission, and the Colonial Authority will not stop them because the Colonial Authority imports its water on Terran hulls."

"You're saying I have no choice."

"I'm saying you have *one*. That's more than most men in your position get." He finished his coffee. "The history of resources, Mr. Neegan, is the history of men who discovered something valuable and were briefly, dangerously important. The clever ones understood that the window was short. The others became footnotes."

Arthur looked past him, at the false window and its false stars. Somewhere out there was Antares, a Protectorate that had built a diplomatic service with a navy's budget. Somewhere closer was a kitchen table set for one.

"Why does it matter?" he said finally. "If it doesn't register on gravimetrics. What does that actually mean?"

Oyelaran's expression did not change, but something behind it went very still.

"That," he said, "is the question that has three fleets quietly changing course. Take the folder, Mr. Neegan. Read it on the way home. You'll find the return address is one you can reach from any public relay."

He stood. The meeting was over.

"Nineteen hours," he said. "Spend them well."

**The Azra Gambit — Chapter Three**

The collar was wrong. Arthur Neegan had decided this somewhere past the orbit of Phobos, and nothing in the ninety minutes since had changed his mind. It was too stiff, too high, and fastened with a clasp that someone on Earth had evidently thought elegant. He tugged at it again and caught his reflection in the darkened viewport: a lean man of forty, reddened by Martian ultraviolet, dressed like a banker and sitting like a prisoner.

Beyond the glass, Mars had shrunk to a rust-coloured coin. Somewhere on it—on the Tharsis slope, in a plot of four hundred hectares he had worked for eleven years and that the Settlement Charter said was his—sat the richest body of Azra ever surveyed. He had found it by accident. A core sample had come up warm. Ordinary rock did not come up warm.

Six weeks later the men in grey had arrived at his dome. They had been very polite. The officer had removed his helmet in the airlock, which was a courtesy, and kept one hand on his sidearm, which was not. The insignia on his shoulder was a stylised red star, slightly off-centre: the Antares Diplomatic Corps. Everyone on Mars knew what the Corps was. No one could say with confidence what Antares itself was anymore—a syndicate, a flag, a set of ledgers in a vault on Ceres.

"Mr. Neegan." The officer—Lieutenant Oszkar, he had said, and nothing more—stood in the hatch. "The Envoy will see you now."

The transfer vessel docked with something that filled the viewport entirely. Arthur glimpsed a hull of dull brass alloy, a row of antennae like reeds, and a name in black: *Persephone*. Then the shutters closed.

The reception cabin was all walnut veneer and green baize, as if someone had moved a gentleman's club into orbit and forgotten to tell it. A chronometer ticked on the wall, set to Earth Standard. Behind the desk sat a slight woman with silver-white hair and the composed stillness of a person who had never once been hurried.

"Mr. Neegan. Please sit. You'll forgive the clothes; our tailors work from file photographs, and yours were taken for a mining licence." She nodded at his throat. "You may unfasten it. I won't tell anyone."

He did, and was annoyed at how grateful he felt. "You know my name. I don't know yours."

"No. And you won't, for the present, which I regret, because it makes me seem theatrical, and I am not." She opened a folder—paper, actual paper, with a broken wax seal. "Let me instead tell you what I know. Your claim runs to a depth of two kilometres. The Azra body beneath it masses between eleven and fourteen thousand tonnes. The total refined Azra in human hands as of last quarter was four hundred and six kilograms."

Arthur said nothing. He had worked the figure himself, with a slide rule and a bad conscience, and arrived at twelve thousand.

"You understand what a gram of it does. Set a gram beside a thorium pile and the pile burns through its fuel in days instead of decades. Put it in a drive bottle and a run to Jupiter takes three weeks. Put it in a warhead and—" She closed the folder. "Well. The Terran Directorate has done the arithmetic. So have the Consortium houses. So have we."

"And where does Antares stand in all this arithmetic?"

"Antares," she said, "is the only party that has not yet tried to kill you."

The chronometer ticked.

"That is not a threat, Mr. Neegan. It is a service. Three freeholders have struck Azra in two years. Dubrovnik on Hellas. The Amari brothers at Noctis. A woman named Gelsey, north of you, whose plot the Consortium now holds under a lease of indenture she signed, as I understand it, the day before she died of decompression." She let it settle. "The Charter is a fascinating document. It protects first-generation freeholds from corporate seizure absolutely. It is silent on freeholders who die, sell, or are found to have violated their licences. It is also silent on freeholders who enter into private partnership."

"That's your offer. Partnership."

"You keep your land, in your name, in perpetuity. The Charter is not merely a shield for you; it is a shield for us. A freehold cannot be nationalised by the Directorate nor leased by the Consortium without a hearing before the Earth Commission, and the Commission moves at a geological pace. Antares provides capital, equipment, and a security presence I am told is quite persuasive. In return we take seventy percent of refined output, and the right to say where it goes."

"Seventy."

"You're an engineer. Count what thirty percent of twelve thousand tonnes comes to, at any price you care to name." She leaned back. "There is also a scientific clause. We want to study the vein in place, not merely dig it out. Your core came up warm. Have you asked yourself why the rock a hundred metres away did not?"

He had. He had not liked the answer. "You think it's doing something else. Not just decay."

"I think a metal that makes radium behave like a candle may have other properties, and that the first party to understand them will not need to fire a single warhead. The others will simply find that theirs no longer work. That is the prize, Mr. Neegan. Not fuel. Not even weapons. The quiet end of everyone else's."

Arthur looked at the shuttered viewport. Somewhere behind it his dome sat on the Tharsis slope with an Antares seal on the sample vault and a lieutenant's men standing a guard he had not asked for.

"And if I say no?"

"Then this vessel returns you to Mars within the hour, with our thanks and a genuine apology for the clothes." The Envoy smiled, thinly. "I should add that a Consortium courier left Deimos four hours ago. They will be less polite, and they will not bring a tailor."

She slid the folder across the baize. The seal, he noticed, was not red but dull brass, and the star on it was slightly off-centre.

Arthur reached for it, and found his hand had gone to his collar instead.

response:
# The Azra Gambit

## Chapter Four: The Transfer

The transfer vessel had been built for cargo, not comfort, and apologised for neither. Arthur Neegan sat strapped into a fold-down seat bolted to a bulkhead that still bore the stencilled ghost of a manifest—ORE/REGOLITH/VOL.—and listened to the hull tick as it cooled. Across from him a small display screen cycled through diagnostics in patient green text. CABIN PRESS. NOMINAL. O2 PARTIAL 21.1. THRUST 0.00. The figures held steady, which was more than could be said for his thoughts.

Three hours ago he had been eating reconstituted eggs in his kitchen at Lowell Flats. Now he was in free fall between Mars and somewhere he hadn't been told, in the company of six men in grey who had called him "sir" and had never once let their hands stray far from their sidearms.

They had been very correct about it. That was what unsettled him. A knock, not a battering ram. A lieutenant with a courteous face and the eight-pointed star of the Antares Diplomatic Corps on his collar, inquiring whether Mr. Neegan might spare a few days. The word "might" had done a great deal of work.

He thought about the vein. Everyone did, now. Eighty metres beneath the frost-cracked plot he had bought with fourteen years of hazard pay, the survey drill had brought up a core the colour of tarnished silver that made a Geiger counter scream. Azra. A lump the size of a man's fist, set beside a kilogram of uranium, would walk that uranium through four billion years of half-lives in an afternoon. Load it into a reaction chamber and you had a drive that could reach Proxima in months. Wrap it in lead and you had something else.

ATTITUDE: HOLDING. The screen blinked.

The vessel docked with a jolt. The lieutenant unstrapped him personally.

---

The room beyond the airlock had been dressed to look like Earth—wood veneer, a carpet, an oil painting of a seacoast—but the curve of the floor gave the station away. Spin gravity, perhaps a third of a g. Behind a desk bolted to the deck sat a man of perhaps seventy, with the particular stillness of people who decide what to say long before they say it. His grey suit matched the retinue's. No star on his collar. He rose.

"Mr. Neegan. Director Osric Vane. Thank you for coming."

"I wasn't aware I had a choice."

"You had several. Most were worse." Vane gestured to a chair. "Please. The coffee is real."

Arthur sat. The coffee was real.

"You are," Vane said, "in a peculiar position. Do you know how peculiar?"

"I know I've had four lawyers, two Combine men, and a priest at my door this month."

"A priest?"

"Church of the Colonial Reformation. Wanted to know if I'd considered the moral dimension of mineral wealth."

"Had you?"

"I'd considered that my pump fittings are forty years old."

Vane smiled for the first time. "Good. Practical men live longer. Let me be practical, then. The Martian Mining Combine holds every productive Azra claim on the planet under corporate lease. Those leases are administered from Earth, which means the Terran Authority sets the price, the quota, and the destination of every gram. Your plot is different. You hold it in first-generation freehold under the Settlement Act of '71—a law written when nobody imagined there was anything under Mars worth owning. Freehold mineral rights vest in the holder. Not the Combine. Not Earth. You."

"I'm aware of the law."

"Then you are aware that you are the only independent source of Azra in the inner system. And you are aware of what that makes you."

"Rich?"

"Inconvenient."

The word sat between them. Beyond the viewport Mars hung rust-coloured and small, a coin someone had dropped.

"The Antares Confederacy," Vane went on, "is eleven colonies at four to nineteen light-years. We depend on Azra drives for everything—supply, governance, the simple fact of being one polity rather than eleven lonely ones. Earth sells us Azra at a price politely called 'strategic.' It is a leash, Mr. Neegan. A very long leash, but a leash."

"And you'd like to cut it."

"I would like to buy a second one, from a different hand. We offer this: Confederate citizenship for you and any dependents. Permanent appointment as Chief Engineer of the Neegan Extraction—we would keep the name; it has a ring—at a salary you may set yourself. Transport off Mars should you want it, and protection whether you want it or not. In exchange, the Confederacy takes an exclusive sixty-year supply contract on your vein at market price. Not Earth's price. The market's."

"And if I'd rather deal with the Combine?"

"The Combine does not deal. The Combine leases. Your indentured neighbours could tell you what that means, if they were permitted to speak with you." Vane leaned back. "Understand me. I am not threatening you. I am describing weather. There are men on Earth who have calculated what a freehold vein does to the balance of power in the Antares sector, and the arithmetic does not favour your independence. The Combine would prefer your claim tied up in court for thirty years. The Authority would prefer it nationalised. Certain other parties, whose insignia I will not insult you by naming, would prefer the problem simply removed."

"Removed."

"Seals fail. It is a hard world. You know that better than I do."

Arthur turned the cup in his hands. On the wall behind Vane, a screen he hadn't noticed cycled green text: HULL INTEGRITY 100%. SPIN 0.33 G. PROXIMITY: CLEAR. It was oddly comforting that someone was watching the numbers.

"Your lieutenant's collar said diplomatic corps."

"Diplomacy is the art of arranging matters so that force becomes unnecessary. Occasionally one must display the force, to make the point." Vane spread his hands. "I would rather make it with coffee."

"And if I say no?"

"Then you will be taken home, with my thanks and my card. And within a month someone will ask you again. They will not bring coffee."

PROXIMITY: CLEAR, said the screen. Arthur found he did not entirely believe it.

response:
# Offworlder

## Chapter Three: The Fire-Thief

The protocol said I was not to go out alone. It said so in three languages, one of them mine.

I went out anyway, at the hour when the household servants were sent down to the kitchens and the guard at the Residency gate was changing. I wore the gray that everyone wears on Hadh in the cold months and kept my hood up, which here is not suspicious but merely sensible. I am tall for an envoy of the Ekumen and short for a Lowlander; in the street I was neither, which is a kind of invisibility.

The city of Ammar is built of the pale yellow stone that comes out of the river cliffs, and on every lintel there is a carving. I had read about them. The briefings called them *decorative survivals of the Settlement period* and left it there. Walking under them I found a man bound to a rock with a bird at his liver, a woman turning to look back at a man who did not turn, a great boat with the animals going two by two up its ramp. Over a baker's door, the man with the stolen fire. Over the door of a house of the dead, the boat. The carvings were old; in places someone had painted them new colors, in others someone had chipped the faces off. I asked a child what the bound man was. She said he was the one who gives the bread its heat, and that you touched his foot going in so the oven would not sulk. She touched it. I touched it. It was worn to a soft hollow by ten thousand mornings.

So the briefings were wrong about that, in the way briefings are wrong: not by lying but by stopping too soon.

The market was in the old quarter, under arcades. There I saw what I had come to see, and what I had been told I would see, and the two were not the same. I had been told that Hadh has two kinds of human being: the Lowland lineage, tall, slow, long-boned, who hold the land and the offices; and the Gorrin of the hill country, short, broad, dense in the bone, dark-eyed, who were bred — the briefing's word was *adapted* — for thin air and the mines, and who serve. I had been told the castes did not mix, and that this was the root of the tensions I had been sent twenty-two years down the dark to help with.

In the market the money changers were all Gorrin. The woman who sold me a bowl of grain was Gorrin and her husband, who ladled it, was Lowland and bent to her; their son had her bones and his eyes. A Lowland boy with a lame foot begged at the fountain, and the Gorrin stallholders fed him without looking at him, as one feeds a cat. In a side court I found a shrine with the fire-thief carved above it and both kinds kneeling, and a third kind I had not been briefed on at all — very pale, with eyes that did not like the light, who kept to the arcade shadow and spoke a dialect I half-understood. Nobody looked at them either. That is what I wrote down afterward: on Hadh, who is not looked at tells you more than who is.

I was back before the guard changed again. I was not quick enough. The message from Command was already waiting on the set in my room, and it was short, as their messages are when they are angry and the relay delay is eleven minutes each way. The word *protocol* occurred four times. The word *alone* twice. At the end, as though it were a punishment rather than the work I had been sent to do, they told me the Minister of Science would receive me at the fourth hour.

I knew what the Minister of Science was. On Hadh the sciences are kept by the Gorrin guilds, and the title is a Lowland sinecure, given to whoever must be kept close and busy. It is a political post. It was also the only post that had agreed to see me.

The Minister's chamber was high up and cold and had one window. He stood in it, so that I had to look into the light to see him. He was very tall even for his kind, and old, and he did not sit or offer me a seat, and he did not speak for a long time. Lowlanders can hold a silence the way Gorrin hold a tune. I waited. That is most of what an envoy does.

"You went to the market," he said at last.

"I did."

"That was against your instructions."

"It was."

"Why?"

There were answers that would have flattered him and answers that would have flattered me. I said, "Because the briefings I was given were written by people who had stood at this window."

He turned then and looked at me properly, and I saw that his eyes were the dark Gorrin brown, not Lowland gray. His mother's, I thought. Not in any file.

"And what did you learn, in one morning, that we have missed in four hundred years?"

"Nothing you have missed, Minister. Only things you have agreed not to say."

"Name one."

"That the man over the baker's door is a thief who was punished for giving. Your people touch his foot for luck. Mine wrote him down as a hero. I think you understand him better."

He almost smiled. "You are young."

"Yes."

"My colleagues will tell you there are two kinds of human on Hadh. The guilds will tell you three. What will you tell your Ekumen?"

"That there is one," I said, "and it has been arguing with itself about which of its children to love. We do that everywhere. It is the oldest thing we brought with us. It is carved on your doors."

The silence after that was of a different kind. Then he sat, and after a moment so did I, and he began to tell me about the pale ones in the arcade shadow, and he did not stop for a long time.

response:
# Offworlder

It was the cloak they looked at.

Not the face, though Ansel Tir's face was wrong for Hesk too—too round, too unweathered, the face of someone raised under a sun that was never more than a cool coin in the sky. The market people wore thin kilts and went bare-armed, bare-shouldered, bare-headed under the glare. A wool cloak, hooded, thick as a blanket, in the middle of the day with the dry wind coming down off the plateau: that was a thing worth turning around for.

Ansel kept it on. It had been woven on Alaren by a woman who was now, by the arithmetic of the ships, eleven years dead. Taking it off would have felt like setting her down in the street.

The market ran along a dry canal under awnings of bleached cloth. The briefings had prepared Ansel for two peoples. There were the Long, who had gone up onto the plateau in the second century of the settlement and stayed—tall, dark as cured wood, chests deep as barrels to pull breath from the thin air, eyes narrowed by forty generations of glare. And there were the Hollow folk, who had kept to the sealed lowland warrens and come out only when the warrens failed: small, pale, quick, with the faint translucence of things grown in the dark. Two lineages. Two bloods, the briefings said, that had not mingled in eight hundred years and did not care to. The tensions the Envoy had been sent to ease lay, the briefings said, between these two.

Ansel stood by a stall of dried gourds and watched a Long woman lift a Hollow child onto her hip. The child had the woman's eyes and someone else's skin. Nobody looked at them twice. Everyone looked at the cloak.

What the briefings had not mentioned was the copper. Perhaps a third of the people in the market wore a band of it on the left wrist, Long and Hollow alike. Those who wore it walked down the center of the canal path. Those who did not kept to the edges, and when a banded man stopped to haggle, the unbanded behind him waited without complaint.

"Water-right," the gourd-seller said, when Ansel asked. He was Hollow, and old, and his wrist was bare. He said it the way one says the name of the weather. "You're from the ship."

"I am."

"Then you've water enough." He weighed a gourd in his palm, as if the gourd were the subject. "That's a heavy coat for a dry country."

"It's from a cold one."

The old man nodded as though this explained a great deal, and perhaps it did.

The Residence had noticed the Envoy's absence before the Envoy had noticed the time. Command's reply came through the relay two hours stale and did not waste words. *An Envoy who walks out of a state reception to buy gourds has told the host government its reception is not worth attending.* Ansel read it twice, standing at the window with the cloak still on. The second paragraph was longer. It named a man.

Minister of Science Oru Vashne received the Envoy in a room full of instruments that had not been used. A spectrometer under a cloth. A tank of something green that had died. Vashne was Long, grey, with a copper band so old it had gone brown, and he had the stillness of a man who has outlasted several governments by never being the one to speak first.

He spoke first anyway, which Ansel took for a courtesy, or a trap.

"They tell me you've seen our market."

"I've seen a market."

"And what did it tell you?"

"That the briefings I was given were written by people who never left this building."

Vashne's eyebrows did not move. "The briefings were written by your people."

"From what mine were told."

"Ah." He let the syllable sit. "So you've been here nine days and found us out."

"No, Minister. I've found out that I know nothing. That took nine days. I'm told it usually takes longer."

A sound that might have been a laugh. "You're very young."

"Yes."

"They sent us a child in a blanket."

"They sent you someone who would have to learn by looking," Ansel said, "rather than by remembering. Someone with no memory of Hesk at all. I'm told that was considered an advantage."

Vashne rose and went to the covered spectrometer and rested a hand on the cloth. "You know what this office is."

"A post."

"A reward. For a man who was useful in a bad year and has since become a man one does not wish to insult." He said it without bitterness. "I have not done science since I was your age. I keep the instruments because the title is on the door. You'll have been told to come to me because I am harmless."

"I was told to come to you because you are the only minister who has sat in government more than two years."

"Who told you that?"

"The man I bought the gourd from."

Now Vashne did laugh, briefly, and sat, and Ansel understood that the tone of the room had changed, though not in whose favor.

"Let me tell you what you saw," the Minister said. "Copper and no copper. And you thought: *there* is the real line, not Long and Hollow—there is the thing they hide from the ships. You will put that in a report, and someone eleven years from now will read it and feel clever."

"Is it wrong?"

"It's half. The water-right is old. It *was* Long and Hollow once; the plateau had the springs. Then the plateau dried. Then it was whoever had been standing there when it dried." He turned his wrist. "My grandmother was Hollow. Does your briefing say that?"

"No."

"Then your briefing is also half." He studied Ansel for a long moment. "I'll tell you something, Envoy, and you'll decide whether it is a confidence or a test. The Council wants to know if you can be managed. I was asked to find out. That is why you were sent to me, whatever your Command believes."

"And?"

"And you wore the cloak into my office in the heat of the day, when a wiser envoy would have shed it to seem less foreign. I think you cannot be managed. I think you can only be told things and left alone to be wrong about them." He stood. "Come back tomorrow. Leave the cloak. Not for their sake. It is forty degrees and you are sweating, and I've no interest in a dead envoy."

Ansel left the way one leaves a room in which one has been weighed and found neither light nor heavy, only strange. Outside, the dry wind came down off the plateau. The cloak was heavy. For the first time since the ship, the Envoy thought seriously about taking it off, and did not, and knew that the distance between those two things was the whole of the work ahead.
