**Offworlder**

I was told afterward that I had endangered the mission, and perhaps I had. But I had been on Thurn eleven days and had seen it only through glass: the reception hall, the compound, the car with its tinted windows. The briefings said the people of Thurn were divided into three stocks—the Broad, adapted to the gravity; the Pale, bred in the long dark of the northern settlements; the High, from the thin air of the ranges—and that these three stood in a fixed order, the Broad above. I had memorized the order. I wanted to see whether it was true.

So on the twelfth afternoon, while the delegation slept through the heat, I put on a plain coat and went out by the kitchen gate.

The market lay downhill, in the shade of the old landing-scaffold, which the city had never torn down and had grown around like a tree around a nail. The gravity pulled at me; I walked as the Broad walk, flat-footed and patient, and no one looked at me twice. That surprised me. I had expected to be marked.

The cloth stalls came first. Handloomed, heavy, dyed in colors I had no names for. There was a blue that went green at its edges, from a mineral they dig in the salt flats. There was a color between red and violet that would not resolve when I looked at it directly—the weaver, a Pale woman with eyes like a cat's, told me it came from a lichen that grows only on the north faces of stones, and that it would not fade, not in her lifetime, not in mine. She did not call herself Pale. She said she was of the Second Water. The Broad man at the next stall, who sold her thread, was also of the Second Water. They called each other sibling. When I asked, carefully, which of them stood higher, they laughed at me, and the man said, "Water doesn't stand. It goes down."

I bought a length of the unnameable color. It cost more than I had. The woman gave it to me anyway and told me to come back.

I walked for three hours. I saw a High man giving orders to a crew of Broad laborers, and saw them obey him, not grudgingly. I saw a Pale child nursed by a Broad woman. I saw, on the steps of a water-house, an argument between two women of what I would have called the same stock, in which the word that cut deepest was no name for a body but the name of a lineage—*Fourth Water*, *Seventh Water*—said like a slap. Whatever divided Thurn, it was not what my briefings said divided it. The bodies were the least of it. The bodies were what we offworlders could see, and so it was what we had been told.

When I came back through the kitchen gate the compound was lit and the link to Command was open and waiting for me.

They did not shout. Command does not shout; the lag of the relay forbids drama. The Commander said that I had broken protocol, that I had made myself unaccountable for three hours on a world whose hospitality was a matter of politics, and that if I had been taken the mission would have ended, and with it perhaps the contact. All this was true. I said so. I did not say I was sorry, and she noticed that I did not.

Then she said: "The Minister of Science has asked to see you. Tonight. Alone."

"Why me?"

"I imagine," said the Commander, after the lag, "because you were seen."

The Minister of Science was not a scientist. I had been told this and had understood it as one understands a fact; now, in the lamplit room where he received me, I understood it as one understands a person. His name was Idren Soa. He was Broad, and old, with hands that had never held an instrument, and he gave me tea before he said a word, and watched me drink it, and I knew he was counting the time I took.

"You bought cloth," he said.

"I did."

"From a Second Water loom. You paid too little."

"She wouldn't take more."

"No," he said. "She wouldn't. That is the trouble with them." He let that sit, to see what I would do with it—whether I would rush to defend her or rush to agree. I did neither. I drank my tea.

"Your people sent you with a map of us," he said. "Three kinds. One on top. Tell me honestly—it is a rare thing I ask—what did you think of the map, after today?"

"I think it was drawn by someone who looked at us through a window."

"At *us*?"

I had said *us*. I had meant *you*. I let it stand. "At Thurn."

He smiled then, not kindly. "Here is my difficulty, Envoy. The map is wrong, as you say. But it is the map the Council agreed to show you, because it is simple, and a simple Thurn is one your Terra can deal with as a unit, and not as forty Waters quarreling. If you go home and say the map is wrong, you make us complicated. Complicated worlds are left alone. Is that what you want for us?"

"I want to tell the truth."

"Everyone wants that, until they are asked to pay for it." He set down his cup. "What will you report?"

I thought of the weaver's face, and the color that would not fade. I thought of the Commander's silence across the lag. I thought that this man was offering me a door, and that on the other side of it was his trust, and that the price of it was a lie, and that he knew exactly what that lie would cost me, because he had paid it himself, many times, and was paying still.

"I will report what I saw," I said. "And I will report that the Minister of Science told me what it would cost. Both are true. Let them hold both."

He was quiet for a long time. Then he refilled my cup.

"Come back tomorrow," he said. "Wear the coat."

Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. response:
**Chapter 7: Twist**

The watch didn't come with instructions. It came with a cat.

Okay, not *with* a cat. But the gray one with the torn ear was sitting on top of the lost-and-found bin the day I dug the watch out from under a pile of mittens and single gloves. It watched me strap it on. It watched me walk out the door.

The watch was black and plain, no logo. The screen stayed dark no matter what I pressed. Then I found the little crown on the side and twisted it, and the screen lit up with a spiral — white on black, slowly turning.

I twisted it backward.

The world hiccuped. The hallway lights flickered, and everything slid — kids walking backward, lockers slamming open, the bell un-ringing. Then I was sitting at my desk in Mr. Okafor's room with my pencil in my hand, four minutes left on the quiz and every answer I'd gotten wrong still fresh in my head.

I got a 96.

Walking home, the cat was on the bike rack. It looked at me. Not the way cats look at you — bored, like you're furniture. It looked at me like it had *seen* me do something.

I told myself cats don't know things.

I used the watch again Tuesday, when I called Ms. Rivera "Mom" in front of the whole class. Twist. Un-said. I used it Wednesday, twice: a dropped lunch tray, a missed bus. Thursday I lost count.

Each time, the cat was there. Each time it looked a little less surprised.

Friday morning my voice cracked on "here" during roll call. The whole row laughed. Fine — that happens in seventh grade. But in the bathroom mirror there was a dark smudge on my upper lip that wasn't dirt. I scrubbed. It stayed.

My jeans stopped at my ankles. My sneakers pinched. Mom squinted at me over breakfast and said, "You shot up overnight!" and laughed, and I laughed, because what else do you do?

Then the weird part started. Not the growing. The way people changed.

The cashier at Walgreens called me "sir." A substitute asked what I was doing in a seventh-grade classroom and told me to get back to the high school. She wasn't joking. I had to show her my planner.

Mom started handing me things. The heavy groceries. The phone when the cable company called. "You deal with it," she said, like I was somebody who dealt with things.

Theo noticed last. Theo's been my best friend since we were four, and at lunch he looked at me across the table like he was trying to place where he'd seen me before.

"Dude," he said slowly. "Did you, like... start shaving?"

I laughed it off. I didn't look in a mirror for the rest of the day.

Saturday I didn't use the watch. Sunday I didn't either. I was going to stop.

Then Monday happened.

We were in the parking lot after school. Theo's basketball got away from him and bounced toward the pickup line, and he ran after it without looking. I saw the silver SUV before he did. I saw the driver looking down at her phone.

I yelled. He didn't hear.

I heard the brakes. Then I heard the sound after the brakes.

I didn't think. I grabbed the crown and twisted — hard, harder than I ever had. The spiral spun so fast it blurred into solid white.

And I was standing in the parking lot. Theo's ball was in his hands. The SUV was still three cars back. I grabbed his arm.

"Don't," I said.

He looked at me. Then he looked *through* me.

"Do I know you?" said Theo.

I thought he was messing around. I said his name. I said *my* name. His eyebrows went up — polite, the way you are with a stranger.

"Sorry, man. I think you've got the wrong guy."

He walked to his mom's car. He didn't look back.

I stood there until the lot emptied. My hands looked wrong. Bigger. Knuckles like my dad's. I checked my reflection in the gym doors, and a man looked back at me — my nose, my eyes, but with a jaw I hadn't had that morning and shadows under the cheekbones. Seventeen. Eighteen, maybe.

That's when I saw the cat.

It was on the bike rack, same as always. But it wasn't looking at me the way it had been. It was looking at me like it was *tired*. Like it had watched this happen too many times already. It stared at my face, then dropped its yellow eyes to my wrist.

Then back up.

I took out my phone. My lock screen used to be me and Theo at the water park, both of us making dumb faces. Now it was just me, alone on the slide, grinning at nobody.

I scrolled. Birthday parties. Halloween. The science fair. Theo wasn't in any of them. There weren't even gaps where he should've been.

I called Mom. She picked up on the second ring.

"Hello?"

"Mom. It's me."

A pause. "Who is this?"

My throat closed. "It's — it's Devin."

"I'm sorry," she said, careful now, the voice she uses with telemarketers. "I think you have the wrong number."

She hung up.

The cat jumped down from the bike rack and walked over, slow, and sat on my shoe. It looked up at me. Then it reached out one gray paw and touched the watch face. Once. A tap.

The spiral lit.

I understood it then. Or I thought I did. Every twist took something from me to pay for the change. Little twists, little costs — a few months here, a few there. But a life-sized twist cost more than years. It cost everything that tied me to anybody.

And the only thing I had left to pay with was whatever was left of me.

One more twist might bring Theo back. Might make Mom know my voice again.

One more twist might leave an old man standing alone in a school parking lot. Or nothing at all.

The cat waited. It had torn-ear patience. It had done this before — I was sure of it now — and it would do it again.

I put two fingers on the crown.

"Okay," I told it. "Okay."

And I twisted.

response:
# Chapter Six: Spring Forward

The watch came in a padded envelope with no return address. The label said DESMOND OKAFOR, AGE 12, like whoever sent it needed to remind me.

The box said KRONOS FIT. Steps, heart rate, sleep. Printed inside the lid was what I figured was a serial number: 78Y 0M. Dad thought Grandma sent it. Grandma thought Dad did. I thought it was free, so I strapped it on.

I found the extra setting on Tuesday, during Mr. Pell's pop quiz. I was scrolling the menu under my desk—STEPS, HEART, SLEEP—when a fourth option appeared that hadn't been there a second before.

REWIND.

I twisted the little crown on the side. One click.

The room hiccupped.

Mr. Pell was back at the whiteboard, uncapping a marker he'd just capped. The girl in front of me re-sneezed. And the quiz I'd handed in with the Mohs scale backwards was sitting blank on my desk, pencil still sharp.

I sat very still for a second. Then I fixed every answer.

The watch face glowed soft green, like it was pleased with me.

---

I told myself I'd only use it for important stuff.

I used it to catch my phone before it hit the gym floor. I used it to un-say "Love you too" to the lunch lady. I used it to put my hand down when Mrs. Garza asked for a volunteer, to redo a free throw, to take back the thing I said to my little sister Nia that made her cry. Click. Click. Click.

Ten seconds here. A minute there. Little things.

The band kept pinching. So did my shoes. I figured I was having a growth spurt.

---

Nobody said anything until Friday, when Mrs. Garza called on me and my voice came out of somebody else's throat.

"Yes, ma—" It dropped an octave mid-word, like a truck shifting gears. Half the class turned around. Tyler Wu laughed so hard he snorted.

"Easy, young man," Mrs. Garza said. She'd never called me *young man*. She called everyone *friends*.

At lunch I tugged my hoodie sleeves down and they stopped two inches above my wrists. My jeans had done the same thing. My shins itched under the denim, and when I scratched, I felt hair. Not fuzz. *Hair.*

The lunch lady slid my tray across. "You a new aide, hon?"

"I'm in seventh grade."

She looked at me for a long second. "Sure you are."

At dinner Dad kept glancing at me over his plate. "You doing okay, bud?" he finally said. "You look—" He didn't finish. Nia wouldn't sit next to me. She said I smelled like a grown-up.

---

That night I locked the bathroom door and looked.

The kid in the mirror was me. Mostly. Taller than the towel bar, which I'd never been. A shadow on my upper lip that wouldn't wash off, because it wasn't dirt. A pimple on my chin the size of a kidney bean.

"It's fine," I told the mirror. "It's just—"

The reflection flickered.

For half a second—less—the face looking back wasn't thirteen or fourteen or whatever I'd become. It was *old*. Gray at the temples. Deep lines bracketing the mouth. The eyes were mine, but tired in a way I didn't know eyes could get, and they looked at me like they were sorry.

Then it was gone. Just me. Just a kid with a mustache he hadn't asked for.

I looked down. The watch menu was open, and under REWIND, in letters so tiny I'd never noticed them, it said:

*Balance: 74Y 2M.*

I thought about the number inside the box lid. 78Y 0M.

That wasn't a serial number.

---

I should have taken it off right then. I know that.

But Saturday was Fall Fest, and Nia had talked about the Ferris wheel for a month, and when the operator held his hand flat against the height chart and said, "Sorry, bud, she's two inches short," and her whole face crumpled—

I didn't think. Click. Click. Click.

Three minutes back. I grabbed Nia's hand before we reached the line and steered her toward the funnel cakes. She never got measured. She never cried. Easy.

We were halfway through the powdered sugar when the screaming started.

The Ferris wheel was tilted. Not swaying—*tilted*, one support leg folded like a bent straw, the whole thing groaning over toward the midway in slow motion. Gondolas swung sideways. People scattered below it like pigeons. A woman in a pink jacket was at the very top, and I could see her mouth open.

Three minutes ago, in the version that didn't exist anymore, that wheel had sat empty while the operator argued with me about two inches. Now there'd been nobody to argue with. He'd loaded every car and pulled the lever on schedule, and something in that rusted old steel that had been waiting years to let go had finally let go.

Because of me. Because I'd skipped the line.

Nia's hand found mine. "Dez," she whispered. "Your nose."

She was staring at me the way she stares at strangers in parking lots.

I touched my face. Blood. And the hand that came away—the knuckles were thicker. Veins stood up under the skin like they belonged to my dad.

The watch buzzed.

*Balance: 63Y 7M.*

Three minutes had cost me almost eleven years. The price was going up. Of course it was.

Metal shrieked. The wheel dropped another ten degrees.

I did the math. Five minutes, maybe six, to get back before I ever grabbed her hand. Whatever that cost now, I'd pay it with the only thing I had left—and I didn't know how much of me would be standing here on the other side.

Maybe enough.

I put my thumb on the crown. It was warm. It was always warm now.

"Don't look," I told Nia.

Then I started to twist.

# TICK TOCK, TIME'S UP
### Chapter 9: Thirty Seconds Back

The first time I rewound time, I was trying to save a slice of pizza.

I'd tripped over Dylan Marsh's backpack in the cafeteria, and my whole tray — pizza, chocolate milk, the little cup of corn nobody eats — went airborne. Three hundred kids turned to look. Somebody started the slow clap.

I grabbed my wrist like it was a railing. My thumb mashed the crown of the watch.

The cafeteria sucked backward.

That's the only way to describe it. The clap unclapped. The milk leapt off the floor and poured itself back into the carton. My tray floated up into my hands, and I was standing three steps behind Dylan's backpack, which I stepped around like a normal person.

Nobody looked at me. Nobody had seen anything.

The watch had come in a box on our porch, no return address, my name printed on the label. Mom figured it was from Dad, who sends stuff from Phoenix when he forgets birthdays. It was black, heavier than it looked, with a face that stayed blank until you tapped it. Then it just showed the time.

Except now, for a second, it showed something else. Numbers. Flickering. Like a countdown.

Then it was 11:42 again.

---

I told myself I'd only use it for emergencies.

That lasted until Tuesday.

Math quiz, question six — rewind, erase, fix. Dodgeball, right in the face — rewind, duck, grin. I told Harper Linden I liked her hair and she said "okay?" in *that* voice. Rewind. I said nothing instead, which was better.

Every time, the little flicker. Numbers I couldn't quite read before they vanished.

By Thursday my jeans stopped at my ankles.

"Did you grow?" Mom asked, squinting over her coffee.

"I don't think so."

"You grew." She touched my chin. "Is that... hon, do you need to *shave*?"

I laughed. My laugh came out wrong. Lower. Like somebody had borrowed my throat and given it back stretched.

At school, Mrs. Okafor stopped me in the hallway. "Can I help you?" she said, in the voice she uses on parents. Then she blinked. "Noah? Oh — sorry. You look..."

She didn't finish.

Harper looked at me across the lunch table and didn't say anything at all. Just looked. Like I was a teacher who'd sat down in the wrong spot.

That night my little brother Theo didn't ask for a piggyback ride. He always asks. Instead he stood in my doorway, wrinkled his nose, and said, "You smell like Dad."

I went to the bathroom mirror.

A zit on my chin the size of a dime. A shadow on my upper lip. My shoulders filled out my T-shirt in a way they hadn't last week. I looked fifteen. Maybe sixteen.

I was twelve.

I counted on my fingers. Eleven rewinds. Maybe twelve.

I tapped the watch. The time came up, and then — flicker — the countdown. Clear this time.

**03 : 14 : 07**

I didn't know what it was counting. I was afraid I did.

---

I took the watch off. I buried it in my sock drawer.

I lasted until Saturday.

Theo was learning to ride without training wheels. I was supposed to be watching. I was texting. He wobbled down the driveway, picked up speed, and I looked up just as his front tire hit the curb and launched him into Maple Street —

and the Hendersons' SUV was right there.

I don't remember running inside. I remember the sock drawer, the watch, the crown under my thumb. I remember thinking *not thirty seconds. Further. Before he got on the bike. Before this morning.*

I held it down.

The world didn't suck backward this time. It *tore*. The sky strobed night-day-night-day. My knees buckled. Something in my face went tight, then loose. When it stopped I was on my bedroom floor and it was Saturday morning, and I crawled to the window.

The driveway was empty. No bike.

I stumbled downstairs. "Mom — where's Theo? Don't let him ride today, okay? Just —"

Mom was setting the table. Two plates.

"Who?" she said.

"Theo. *Theo*, Mom."

She put the forks down slowly. She was looking at me the way Mrs. Okafor had. The way you look at a man you don't know who has walked into your kitchen.

"I think you have the wrong house," she said, and her hand went behind her back for her phone.

I ran.

Theo's room was a sewing room. Theo's spot at the table was a stack of mail. The photo on the fridge was Mom and me, except the me in the photo was twelve, and the me in the hallway mirror —

Gray at my temples. Lines around my eyes. A stranger's face wearing my panic.

I'd rewound too far. I'd gone back past something — some tiny thing, a Tuesday, a sidewalk, a moment that had to happen for Theo to happen — and I'd unhappened it.

The watch was warm against my wrist. I tapped it.

**00 : 00 : 51**

Then **00 : 00 : 50**.

Seconds. It was counting seconds now.

Enough for one more. One big enough to undo the undoing — if a rewind that size didn't finish what the last one started. I'd seen what it cost. It was looking back at me from the mirror.

Downstairs, Mom's voice shook into the phone. "There's a man in my house —"

I thought about Theo in my doorway, wrinkling his nose. *You smell like Dad.*

**00 : 00 : 09**

I pressed the crown.

And held it.

# Polymerase Chain Reaction

The panels on the roof caught a cloud and the thermocycler sighed.

Dael watched the readout stutter—94, 91, 87—and swore at the ceiling. Denaturation needed ninety-four degrees and it needed it for thirty seconds, and the Peltier block she'd pried from a dead wine fridge couldn't hold temperature on brown-out voltage. Twelve cycles into forty. The reaction would still run, probably. It would give her smears, chimeras, garbage she'd have to read through squinting.

"Yusuf," she called. "Crank."

Outside, the boy started turning the bicycle generator, and the little green LED on the charge controller steadied like a held breath. The lab was a shipping container with its doors welded open and sheeted in greenhouse plastic. The centrifuge was a cordless drill clamped to a bench with a salad spinner's basket epoxied to the chuck. The gel box was a sandwich container, graphite electrodes shaved from carpenter's pencils. The incubator had hatched chickens once.

She was trying to amplify a four-hundred-base stretch upstream of a ripening gene in Verdance Line 7 maize. That stretch held the senescence cassette—the thing that made Verdance seed Verdance seed. Buy it, plant it, harvest it. Save the kernels and plant them again, and the cassette woke up: a methylation cascade that chewed a little more of the genome each generation. Second-year corn came up sixty percent. Third-year came up stunted, half-starch, kernels like baby teeth. The licensing agreement had called it *generational quality assurance*. The farmers had called it a leash. Then the trucks stopped coming and it had turned out to be a fuse.

The settlement's corn was fourth generation. She had maybe two seasons to cut the cassette out before there was nothing left to cut it from. The trouble was template. Degraded DNA came apart in short fragments, and her primers had nothing long enough to grab. It was like trying to photocopy a book someone had already put through a shredder—you could run the machine all day and only ever reproduce confetti.

The plastic curtain parted.

The man who came through was called Marrow, and he came from the Causeway, where the market was. He was clean in the way people with access to filtered water were clean. He carried a cold box, and the insulation was sweating, which meant something inside was actually cold, which meant he'd spent power to bring it.

"You look terrible," he said.

"Thank you."

It was true. Two winters back she'd run a fever that wouldn't break, and with the clinic shelf empty she'd cut a repair construct out of a livestock immune line—Verdance Bovine 3, the one that had kept feedlot cattle standing through anything—and dosed herself with it in a vector she'd built out of a cold virus. It had worked, in the sense that she was alive. Her hair came out in handfuls. Her gums bled when she chewed. She ran a permanent thirty-eight and a half, so she was always a little flushed and never quite hungry, and her joints felt packed with sand on cold mornings.

But the construct had done things she hadn't asked it to. A cut on her hand closed in two days, pink and clean. She slept four hours and woke sharp. And something had shifted in her corneas or her lens—she'd never had the equipment to find out—because now when she pulled a gel out of its box, she could see the bands without the blacklight. Faint violet ghosts, there under the fluorescent tubes. It saved her twenty minutes a run and a bulb she couldn't replace.

Marrow set the cold box on the bench. He opened it with the care of a man opening a reliquary.

Inside: a foil sachet, unbroken, stamped VERDANCE L7 FOUNDER STOCK—F0—LICENSED PROPAGATOR ONLY. Beside it, in a nest of frost, a rack of microtubes. She read the labels. Taq. dNTPs. Ligase. A restriction enzyme she'd been simulating with a kitchen-timer and prayer for a year.

Founder seed. Cassette dormant, genome whole. Everything she needed in one small bag.

"What do you want for it," she said. Not a question.

Marrow leaned on the bench. "There's a grower up at Hollins Reach. Woman named Pell. She's got a potato line, clean, open-pollinated, came out of some seed bank before all this. Good yields. And she gives it away. Walks into the Causeway with sacks of seed potatoes and just hands them out."

"Saint of her."

"Nobody comes to market for free potatoes, Dael. Nobody trades. The whole Causeway runs on people needing things." He tapped the sachet. "You've been trying to cut that cassette out for two years. I'm asking you to cut it out and put it somewhere else."

She understood then, and the understanding sat down heavy in her chest alongside the fever.

"You want me to put the leash on her potatoes."

"I want a potato that grows beautifully for exactly one year. Pell plants it, Pell shares it, and next season everybody who took one comes back to the Causeway because theirs came up rotten. And we have the real thing."

"You'd be building it again. The whole thing. The reason we're in a shipping container."

"I'd be building a market," Marrow said. "Somebody will. I'd rather it was me, and I'd rather you were paid in seed instead of promises."

Through the plastic she could hear Yusuf cranking, the chain ticking, and the thermocycler had climbed back to ninety-four and was holding, holding. Thirty-one cycles. Outside, the corn stood in rows along the old highway median, chest-high in August when it should have been over her head, the leaves already yellowing at the margins in a pattern she had come to know the way you know a relative's handwriting.

She thought about Pell, whom she had never met. She thought about two seasons.

"The cassette's a timer," she said slowly. "They built it to a schedule. One generation."

"Right."

"A timer can be set to anything."

Marrow looked at her for a long moment, and whatever he saw made him straighten up and lift his hands off her bench.

"I'll need the Taq now," she said. "And the ligase. I'll tell you yes or no when I've seen what's in the founder seed."

He nodded. He left the cold box.

The cloud passed. The panels drank. The voltage climbed and shivered and climbed, and Dael pulled on gloves with a hole in one finger and reached for the foil.

# Polymerase Chain Reaction

The thermocycler was a rice cooker.

More precisely, it was the heating coil from a rice cooker, a Peltier plate scavenged from a camp fridge, and a microcontroller that Dessa had reflashed eleven times before it stopped overshooting ninety-four degrees and cooking the enzyme. The whole assembly sat in a cut-down ammunition tin lined with wool. A bicycle computer taped to the lid counted cycles. Thirty-two down. Three to go.

She didn't watch it. Watching didn't help, and her eyes had been bad since spring, when she'd dosed herself with the retinal mod to work by candlelight. The upside was real: she could read a gel by the glow of a single LED. The downside was that daylight felt like thumbs pressing into her sockets, and the whites of her eyes had gone the faint yellow of old paper. Hollis said she looked like a goat. Hollis was eight and said what he thought.

Along the back wall, the Verdance canisters stood in rows—squat aluminum cylinders with the leaf logo half-scoured away, the ones that had once held Season-Lock pollen for licensed growers. Now they held her world. BUFFER, in grease pencil. PRIMERS—SORGHUM 7. TAQ (DON'T TOUCH). The Taq she'd bred herself, from a hot-spring bacterium somebody had carried down from the geothermal ruins in a thermos, and it was the only thing in the room that wasn't dying.

Everything else was. That was what Verdance had sold the world: a genome with a clock in it. Buy the seed, plant the seed, eat. Save the seed, plant it again, and watch the second generation come up stunted and sterile, telomeres shearing off like frayed rope. *Annual licensing*, they'd called it. A great quarter. Then the servers went dark and the licensing went with them, and the maize in every field on the continent had a year to live.

Four years on, Dessa was still trying to pull the clock out.

She pipetted from the PRIMERS canister with a glass dropper and a hand that was steadier than it had any right to be. The template came from a landrace sorghum an old woman in the Kettle settlement had kept in a coffee can since before the Collapse—unlicensed, unlocked, unengineered, and therefore worth more than anything anyone had owned in a decade. There was almost none of it left. Each failed cycle burned a grain's worth of DNA she couldn't get back.

Thirty-three.

The door scraped. She didn't turn. Nobody came in here without Marguerite waving them through, and Marguerite had a shotgun and opinions.

"You're the splicer." Not a question. A man's voice, dry from the road.

"I'm the person who's busy."

He came around into her light and she looked up anyway, because the smell of him had arrived first—gun oil, diesel, and underneath it the mineral tang of an unmodified body sweating in the heat. Another upside she hadn't asked for: the hepatic mod she'd taken to survive bad water had rewired her liver and her sense of smell together, and now she knew more about strangers than she cared to. He was healthy. He'd eaten meat recently. He was not from any settlement within sixty kilometers.

He set a case on her bench. Hard polymer, Verdance blue, seal intact. Cold rolled off it. Cold meant a chain of refrigeration from somewhere to here, and nobody had a chain of refrigeration.

"Open it."

She did. Inside, nested in foam: twenty vials of polymerase, factory-sealed. Primer libraries. Ligase. Restriction enzymes she'd only read about in salvaged manuals, their names like old gods. Enough to run a thousand reactions. Enough to pull the clock out of the Kettle sorghum ten times over and still have leftover to teach Hollis on.

"Who's asking?"

"Harbor Compact." He laid a folded paper beside the case. "They've got maize. Clean, true-breeding, pre-Verdance. Eight hundred hectares."

"Then they don't need me."

"They need Season-Lock."

Thirty-four. The bicycle computer ticked over.

She understood before he finished. The Compact held the only clean seed on the coast. If it stayed clean, it stayed free: anyone who traded for a sack could plant it, save it, plant it again, and the Compact's monopoly lasted exactly one season. But if their maize carried the lock—if every sack they sold grew once and died—then every settlement from here to the mountains would be back at their gate each spring, hat in hand. The thing that broke the world, rebuilt as a business plan.

"You want me to put it back in."

"We want you to put it in *theirs*. Yours stays clean. That's in the contract." He tapped the paper. "The case is half. The rest comes when the lock holds through a test generation."

Behind him the Verdance canisters stood emptied of what they'd been made for. Her hands had started to tremble, which they did now, a tic the retinal mod had left her like a receipt. In the ammo tin the block was climbing toward ninety-four degrees, the temperature at which the double helix lets go of itself and everything comes apart so it can be copied.

She looked at the vials. She thought about the coffee can and the last of the sorghum, and the nine settlements running out of time, and the fact that she could save all of them with what was in this case, and the only price was being the person who did it.

She did not tell him that Season-Lock had never been a single gene. That Verdance, being Verdance, had built a second sequence beneath the first—a corporate override, a master key, kept so the company could unlock its own crops if the licensing ever lapsed. That she had spent four years learning exactly where it lived, and that anyone who could write the lock could write the key.

Thirty-five. The cooker clicked off.

"Give me a week," Dessa said, and took the pen.

prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction

Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a  biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract.

Glow-in-the-dark mushrooms sprout in cracked lab tiles, remnants of old splicing tests. Length: 1000 words.
response:
# Polymerase Chain Reaction

The thermal cycler had been a windshield-wiper motor in its first life, and it still swept like one—left, center, right—carrying a rack of taped-together tubes through three mason jars of water. Ninety-four degrees to pull the strands apart. Fifty-five for the primers to find their seats. Seventy-two for the polymerase to run. Ines kept the hot jar on a hotplate pried out of a dentist's office and the cool one on a Peltier plate from a wine fridge, and she kept the time with a metronome, because a metronome didn't need a battery.

Thirty cycles. Ninety minutes. She had maybe five hours before the wheat stopped being wheat.

The seeds sat in their cold case on the bench—sixty of them, amber and perfect, each stamped at the molecular level with a Verdant Agrisciences sunset cassette. The cassette had been elegant once, the way a landmine is elegant. A methylase that silenced one gene per cell division, walking through the genome like someone switching off lights in a house, until it reached the germline and the plant set heavy, beautiful, sterile seed. *Buy again next year.* And the part that never made the brochure: a nuclease that woke up the moment tissue was damaged. Extracted DNA started eating itself. Six hours of sample life—long enough to confirm you'd bought the real thing, not long enough to steal it.

Verdant hadn't lasted. The cassette had.

"You keep telling me what you're doing," Pell said from the doorway. "I keep not needing to know." He hadn't taken off his respirator. River-market people never did indoors.

"You're paying for it."

He was paying a great deal. Two hundred units of lyophilized Taq—real *Thermus aquaticus*, not the sludge she fermented from the bacteria colonizing the cooling drains at the dead geothermal plant. Synthesized primers. Doxycycline. And a case of insulin that would carry the Oduya kid through winter.

The cost was in the second half of the contract, the part written small: *exclusive*. Every amplicon, every clean seed, every tube with a smear of the rebuilt line. He'd sell it back to the settlement at river prices. She'd be buying wheat from Pell the way her grandmother had bought it from Verdant.

She ground the seeds and swore at the clock.

Lysis buffer was dish soap, table salt, and the last of the meat tenderizer for its papain. The centrifuge was a Dremel bolted to the bench with a rotor somebody in Greybridge had printed before Greybridge went quiet. It screamed. She'd stopped hearing it years ago. Spin, pour, isopropanol from the medic tent, spin again. At the bottom of the tube: a white thread of DNA, already fraying at the ends.

Her gums bled when she bit down on a pipette cap. They'd bled for two years—since the winter she'd put a Verdant cattle-immunity splice into her own arm because the alternative was dying of a fever on a cot. The splice had been built for Holsteins and had opinions about being in a human. Her nails grew in ridged like bark. Her hair had come in white at twenty-nine. She ran a baseline of 38.1 and had learned to dress for it.

But she hadn't caught anything since. Not the river cough, not the fungal thing that took three people last spring. And she could smell contamination in a culture a day before the plate showed it—a sweet-rot note that made the back of her tongue ache. Useful, in a lab held together with electrical tape. The mod was fading too, of course. Everything Verdant made had a sunset in it. Some nights she could feel the fever ticking down toward normal like a clock running out.

She loaded the reaction. The primers she'd chosen flanked the cassette on either side—she couldn't cut it out, not with what she had, but she could decline to copy it. Amplify the clean loci, stitch them back together, leave the landmine in the original tube to chew itself to nothing. Sixty seeds' worth of genome, reduced to the parts that mattered.

The generator coughed. The overhead tube flickered and died.

She didn't stop. Didn't need to. Along the cracks in the floor tile, where the old luciferase tests had spilled years ago and found the grout to their liking, a hundred small mushrooms glowed cold green. Enough to pipette by. Barely.

"Christ," said Pell.

"Harmless." She set the wiper arm swinging. "They outlived the company that made them. Same as me."

The metronome ticked. The arm swept through its jars. Somewhere in the tubes, numbers were doing what numbers did: one became two, two became four, four became eight. By the twentieth cycle the nuclease was irrelevant—it could destroy the original all it liked. The original was a rounding error now.

She poured a gel from kelp agar in a Tupperware tub, ran it off a car battery with speaker-wire electrodes, and read it under a blacklight that had hung in a teenager's bedroom once. Bands. Clean, bright, the right size. The wheat her grandmother had grown, minus the part that killed it.

Pell took off his respirator for the first time, as if to see better. His face was younger than she'd thought. He had the river-market look—eyes that were always doing arithmetic.

"All of it," he said.

She packed it. The amplicons in sealed tubes, the overlap-extension products, the gel slab wrapped in plastic. She wrote the primer sequences on a card because a contract was a contract. He checked each item against his list and counted twice.

"And that's everything."

"Everything you paid for is in that box."

He nodded, re-masked, and was gone into the dark with the settlement's winter under his arm.

Ines stood in the green light a while. Then she gathered the used pipette tips, the paper towel she'd wiped the bench with, the rack the tubes had sat in, the gloves off her hands—and walked them out to the seed beds, where she turned them into the soil.

PCR had never understood the word *exclusive*. That was the entire point of it. You put in one copy and you got a billion, and some of them always ended up on your gloves.

Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment.

First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words.

A distant church bell chimes once at exactly midnight, though no service is scheduled. Length: 1000 words.
response:
Astrid said the mound had been there before the church, before the village, before anyone had bothered to give that bend of the river a name. That was the point, she said. You went to the oldest thing you could find, and you sat on it, and you waited.

I was fifteen that October, three months into my exile from Stockholm, and I had already learned that in Granträsk nothing was called what it was. The Iron Age grave out past Lindqvist's fallow field was just "the hill." What we were going to do on it was just "sitting out." Astrid said it the way she said everything, like it was weather.

She tapped on my window at half eleven. She'd put on her mother's lipstick, dark as lingonberry, and she carried a thermos that turned out to be Explorer vodka cut with Fanta, and her grandmother's grey wool blanket rolled under one arm.

"Check your coat," she said while I climbed out. "No zips. No iron on you anywhere. Keys?"

I'd left mine under the mat, as instructed. I asked why.

"Iron keeps them off." She started walking. "We want them to come."

The forest was bare pine and frost, the ground already hard. My Maglite made a white tunnel of the track and everything outside it ceased to exist. Astrid didn't use a torch. She talked instead, in that flat northern way, about Mikael Sundström, and whether he'd walked Pernilla Ek home on Friday, and how Pernilla had told half the ninth year that I'd been expelled from my old school for stealing, which was not true, and which Astrid said we could fix.

"Fix how?"

"You ask. Once, in your head. Then you wait." She said it like directions to a bus stop. "Three times round the mound before you sit. Against the sun. Motsols. Mormor was very particular. Then north, blanket over your head, and you don't speak."

"Why the blanket?"

"So you can't see what comes."

"That's reassuring."

"It's not supposed to be reassuring, it's supposed to work." She passed me the thermos. "They outlawed it in the old laws. Norway, Iceland, the Gulathing. Thirteenth century. You don't make something illegal unless people are doing it, and you don't keep doing it unless it works." Then, after a pause, in exactly the same tone: "If something says your name, don't answer the first time. The first time is never it."

"What's the first time?"

"Something that wants you to answer."

The mound was smaller than I'd imagined. A low swell in the field, treeless, the frost on it unbroken and faintly blue in the moonlight. The river moved somewhere behind us, black and talkative. We walked round it three times, widdershins, Astrid counting under her breath, and then we climbed up and sat side by side facing the dark wall of pines to the north, and she pulled the blanket over both our heads.

It smelled of her grandmother's house: woodsmoke, old wool, something medicinal. The dark inside it was total. Cold came up through my jeans like water. I could hear Astrid breathing to my left, slow and deliberate, and I tried to match it, and I asked, in my head, the question I'd actually come to ask, which was not about Pernilla at all.

Then the bell.

One stroke, from the east, from the church in Övre Granträsk four kilometres off. I knew that bell. It was electric, had been since '82, and it rang for services and funerals and for nothing else, and never once. I waited for the second stroke. I counted the way you count after lightning. It didn't come.

Astrid's breathing stopped, then started again, faster.

Under the blanket my own pulse was so loud I almost didn't hear the footsteps. Frost crunching, slow and even, somewhere down at the foot of the mound. Going round. I told myself it was Astrid, that she'd slipped out, that this was the trick, the part where the Stockholm girl screams. But her shoulder was against mine. I could feel her shaking through two coats. The steps went round once. Twice. Sunwise, I realised, the opposite way to us. Three times, and then they stopped on the north side, where we were facing, and the field was quiet except for the river.

Someone said my name.

Not loudly. Not strangely. That was the worst of it. It was said the way my mother said it from the kitchen doorway when she had something rehearsed, Linnea, gentle, a little tired. From perhaps three metres away, in a field in Norrbotten, at midnight.

I didn't answer. I bit the inside of my cheek until I tasted it.

The silence went on long enough that I began to think it was over. Then, again, from much nearer, from somewhere in the small warm dark under the wool: Linnea.

Astrid's hand found mine. Hers was ice.

And I heard a voice say, "Ja?"

I have spent a long time trying to decide whose voice that was. It was quiet, and it was close, and it came from under the blanket with us, and it was either hers or mine. I'd like to say I know. I don't.

Astrid tore the blanket away. She was standing, holding it bunched against her chest, staring north at the trees, and there was nothing there, no one, the frost at the foot of the mound unbroken all the way round except for our own three circles.

"Did you hear that," she said. It wasn't a question.

"You answered it."

"I didn't say anything." Her lipstick had come off on her teeth. "Linnea. I didn't say anything."

We left the thermos. We walked back fast and didn't run, because Astrid said you don't run, and at the edge of the forest she told me it was probably a hunter, or the Lindqvist boys, or the cold getting into our ears. She said it matter-of-factly, like weather.

I noticed she didn't say it was nothing. She never said anything was nothing again.

response:
# Útiseta

Astrid said the rules were simple. That was the first thing she got wrong.

We met at the bridge at half past eleven, the last week of August, the first week the sky over Gråträsk had gone properly dark again since spring. She had a canvas bag on her shoulder and a Blend going, and she looked me over the way she always did, like she was checking I hadn't been swapped.

"You didn't eat?"

I hadn't. She'd told me not to.

"Good. Mormor said hunger thins the skin."

Seven months I'd been in that village. Seven months of Pernilla Sjögren saying *Stockholm* like it was a diagnosis, of Jonas Lind looking through me in the corridor. Astrid was the only one who'd spoken to me the first week, and within a month she'd shown me the thing with the key and the Bible, the thing with the knife under the pillow, and we'd learned that Marcus Wiklund wet the bed until he was eleven, which may not have been true but which we used anyway. The games worked often enough. That was the trouble.

The mound lay past the Lindqvist pasture, where the fields gave out and the forest hadn't yet made up its mind to begin. Astrid called it Kungshögen, though every mound in Sweden is some king's. It wasn't tall—a flattened grass dome with one birch growing crooked from its north slope. The mist had got there before us. It lay thick around the base and nowhere else, so the mound stood in a moat of it, and the moon came down so hard the whole ring seemed to glow from inside.

"It does that," Astrid said, before I could ask.

She walked us round it three times against the sun. She made me unlace my Docs at the bottom—"You have to be touching it"—and the grass was so cold it hurt. At the top she pushed an old square-headed nail into the turf behind where we'd sit. Then salt, in a line, not a circle. "A circle keeps everything out. We don't want everything out."

"Did she do this? Your mormor?"

"Once. When she was fifteen, for a boy."

"And?"

"Married him." Astrid grinned. "She also told me never to do it. But she told me how. So."

We sat with our backs to the birch, facing west, hands open on our knees. The instructions came quick and flat, like a recipe.

Don't turn round. Whatever you hear. That's the main one.
Don't say your name or mine. If something asks, give nothing.
If your hands close, it's finished. You don't get another go.
You'll want to sleep. Don't. The ones who slept woke knowing nothing, or too much.
If you hear your name in your mother's voice, it isn't your mother.
One question. In your head. Not until you feel them come.

"Feel them how?"

"You'll know."

I had my question ready. I'm ashamed of it now—I was going to sit on a thousand-year-old grave and ask what Pernilla had told Jonas about me. But I was fifteen and a long way from home, and it was the only question I had.

The first hour was just cold. Astrid's breathing slowed beside me. A cow shifted somewhere in the pasture and I nearly laughed. I watched the birch's shadow swing a few degrees, and around one o'clock I decided this was all it would be, and felt the particular relief of a frightened person being let off.

Then the mist began to move.

Not toward us. Around. The wind was out of the north—I could feel it on my left cheek—and the mist turned against it, the whole ring, slowly, like water finding a drain. I've tried since to make that ordinary. Thermals off the mound, eddies. I don't know enough about weather to rule it out. I know what it looked like.

Something was walking at the base of the slope. Slow, heavy, patient. It went round once and the mist went with it. I told myself: cow. I told myself that for the whole of the second circuit.

"Don't," Astrid whispered, though I hadn't moved.

When I looked sideways her eyes were shut and her lips were going, and the sound coming out of her was low and not hers—one word, over and over, that I've never found in any dictionary. Her hands were closing. I watched them close, finger by finger, and thought: *she's out. I'm on my own.*

Then my mother said my name.

Clear, behind me, in her flat Södermalm vowels, tired and faintly annoyed: *Linnea. Come in now. It's late.*

Everything in me turned except my neck. I kept my eyes west and my hands open and I asked my question, because fear had scraped out everything else and it was all I had left to hold.

What came back wasn't a voice. A certainty, set in me like a stone in a pocket: *she said nothing. He simply doesn't like you.* Which I think I'd known. Which is exactly what a frightened girl might tell herself.

But under it, closer, almost at my ear: a name. Not Jonas's. Not anyone's I knew. Two syllables. I have never said it aloud.

Astrid stood so fast she kicked the salt. "Fuck," she said, too loud, laughing, "did you hear—" and we ran, shoes in our hands, straight through the mist without looking down. At the fence she bent double, and I saw she was shaking worse than I was.

"It worked," she said. "Didn't it. Say it worked."

That was when I understood she had never done this before either. That mormor's rules were things half-heard at a kitchen table and filled in, and she had no more idea than I did what we'd opened, or whether the salt had been the right shape.

We should have stopped there. I knew it then, standing barefoot in the wet grass, watching the mist settle back round the mound as if it had never moved.

But it had worked. That was the trouble.

response:
# Útiseta

I have told this story twice in thirty years, and both times I stopped before the end.

The mound lay north of the village, where the river bent and the pines closed in. In daylight it was nothing—a swelling under the trees, grown over with lingonberry, a county heritage sign someone had used for target practice. Astrid called it *högen*, the mound, as though there were only one in the world.

"After the sign, not a word," she said. It was the last week of September, 1995, and she walked ahead of me with a torch she refused to turn on. "Not if you trip. Not if you're cold. Not if I speak to you."

"Why would you speak to me?"

"I won't. That's the point."

I had known Astrid six weeks. She was the only person at the school who had never once called me *nollåtta*—the Stockholm area code, said like a diagnosis—and I had mistaken that for kindness. I understand now that she was simply the only one who had a use for me.

I had brought what she told me to. A grey wool blanket from my mother's airing cupboard. Nothing on me with metal—no earrings, no zip, my jeans buttoned, my Walkman left on the bed. And a pink hair elastic I had picked off the changing room floor after Malin Sjöberg dropped it, two days after she'd held a lighter under my braid in the lunch queue to see whether Stockholm hair burned differently.

"That goes under your tongue," Astrid said.

"I'm not putting Malin's hair tie in my mouth."

"Under your tongue. So you can't talk even if you want to." She stopped where the ski track met the trees. In the dark her face was mostly cheekbone. "Mormor said that's half of it. You sit, you shut up, and whatever's in the ground decides if you're worth telling anything."

Her grandmother had died in March. Astrid spoke about her the way other girls spoke about older sisters who had moved away—the clothes she'd borrowed, the things she'd been shown. The games before this one had been small. A key balanced on a Bible that swung toward *yes*. A candle, a mirror, a name said nine times. They had felt like something you'd do at a sleepover in Hägersten, and I think that's why I came. I thought this was the same thing in bigger boots.

"She never did this one for a person," Astrid said, almost to herself. "She said you don't bring the dead someone's name unless you want them to keep it." Then she shrugged. "But she's dead, and Malin isn't."

We passed the sign.

She put me on the east side of the mound and herself on the west, so that the whole of it lay between us. The blanket went over my head and shoulders and down to the ground, so I could see only the strip of moss between my knees. No looking up. No looking behind, however much it felt like I should. If I heard my name, it wasn't her—she would never say my name—and so whoever said it, I was not to answer.

"When do we stop?"

"When the birds start."

The elastic tasted of nothing and then of pennies. I sat.

The cold came up through my jeans in about ten minutes, and after that time went strange, the way it does when you're forbidden to check. The wind moved through the pines above us in long slow pushes, and each time it did, the sound broke apart into something sibilant—not words, but the shape of words, the rise and fall of someone speaking in another room. I knew what it was. I told myself what it was. The trees said *hush, hush*, and I listened for Astrid's breathing on the far side and could not find it.

Something walked around the mound.

I say *something*. I heard the lingonberry stalks give—a dry, soft snapping—at the pace of a person in no hurry. It started behind me, to the right, and went clockwise. Toward Astrid. Past where Astrid should have been, without pause, without her making any sound at all. Around, and back to me. It stopped where I had first heard it. My own breath was loud under the wool. I remember thinking, very clearly: a fox would have smelled us by now and gone.

Then the trees pushed again, and inside the sound of them, at the exact pitch of the wind, something said my name.

Not *Linnea*. The other one. The one my grandfather had used before he died, that nobody in the village could have known, and that I have not written down here because I still don't say it aloud.

I did not answer. I am almost certain I did not answer. The elastic was under my tongue. I bit down on it until my jaw ached and I stared at the moss between my knees until the moss was the only thing in the world, and the whispering in the trees went on and on, patient, as though it had all night and I was the one who would run out of something first.

It said one more thing. I have told two people that it was about Malin. One of them I married.

The birds began a little before five. I didn't move until Astrid pulled the blanket off me, and her face in the grey light was furious and white.

"You spoke," she said.

"I didn't."

"I heard you. You *answered* it." She was shaking. "What did you say to it? What did you say?"

I opened my mouth to show her the elastic, and there was nothing under my tongue.

She found it later, she told me, on the west side. Where she'd been sitting. I never saw it again, and I never asked her what she heard, and in two weeks Malin Sjöberg stopped coming to school, and that is where I have always stopped.

**Gone South**
*Chapter Two: Royal Street*

The truck driver's name was Earl, and Earl had Opinions, and somewhere around Hattiesburg Earl figured out which bathroom I'd been using at the gas stations. The rest of the drive was silence, then a door opening on Canal Street, then taillights. So now it's 6:40 a.m. and I'm standing on a sidewalk that smells like beer and powdered sugar and river, with a backpack containing two shirts, a phone at eleven percent, and forty-one dollars I lifted from the coffee can Mom thinks I don't know about.

Sorry, Mom. Consider it a refund.

New Orleans is not what I expected. I expected — I don't know. Mardi Gras. Instead it's garbage trucks and a man hosing vomit off a step and iron balconies dripping ferns like the whole city forgot to shave. It's beautiful. It's terrifying. Both of those are true and I can't make them stop being true at the same time, which is kind of my whole life right now.

Two days ago I sat at the kitchen table and said the sentence I'd been practicing in the shower for three years. Mom's fork didn't even make it to her mouth. Dad said "Well." Just that. *Well.* Like I'd told him the dishwasher was broken. Then forty-eight hours of doors, and my sister crying because everyone else was, and the counsellor's voice on speakerphone saying *concerning behavioural patterns* like I'd wandered in from a textbook.

Concerning. Lady, you have no idea.

I walk. Walking is the thing you do when standing still makes you a target. I learned that from TV, which is where I learned everything, which is a problem I'm choosing not to examine.

By noon the Quarter has filled up. Tourists in matching T-shirts. A guy painted silver pretending to be a statue. And on the corner of Royal, a man with a saxophone, eyes closed, playing something so slow and sad and golden that I actually stop. That's my mistake, because stopping is when the kid finds me.

"You're doing it wrong."

I turn. They're maybe seventeen. Bleached hair grown out two inches dark at the roots, army jacket in ninety-degree heat, a face that's all angles like someone drew it in a hurry. Sitting on a stoop eating a po'boy with the concentration of a surgeon.

"Doing what wrong."

"Standing there with your mouth open. Might as well wear a sign." They tear off half the sandwich and hold it out. "Eat this before you fall over. You look like you're about to fall over."

Every episode of every show I've ever seen says: *don't take food from strangers.* My stomach says: *shut up, TV.*

I take it.

"Cass," they say.

"Taylor."

Cass chews, looks at me for a long second — not up and down, more like *through* — and says, "That the name you came with, or the one you picked?"

My face goes hot. Nobody's ever — not one person, not even me out loud —

"Picked," I say. It comes out like a cough.

"Good name." And that's it. That's the whole conversation about it. Behind us the saxophone slides into something faster and Cass taps the rhythm on their knee, and I understand suddenly that I might cry on this stoop in front of this stranger, and I understand I'd rather die.

So I ask questions instead, because questions are armor.

Cass has been here "a while." Cass is from "up north." Cass sleeps "around." Every answer is a door closing softly. Their jacket sleeves stay down in the heat, and twice their phone buzzes and twice they flip it face-down without looking, and the second time their jaw does a thing — a clench, quick, like swallowing glass.

"Somebody looking for you?" I ask.

"Somebody's always looking for somebody." Cass smiles, and it's a good smile, a practiced one. "You got anywhere to be tonight, Tennessee?"

I didn't tell them I was from Tennessee.

Did I? The accent, probably. The accent I've been trying to sand off since I was twelve. Probably.

"I'm figuring it out."

"There's a place. Marigny side. Guy named Theo lets people crash, no questions, he's cool." A pause so small I almost miss it. "You'd like him."

Here's what I know: I know Cass gave me food when I was hungry and the right word when I didn't know I needed it. I know they haven't asked me for anything. I know that *no questions* is a phrase that sounds like safety and could mean its exact opposite. I know I am sixteen and two states from a bed that's probably been stripped already, and that the light is going orange and long down Royal, and that the sax man is packing up, and that night in a strange city is a door I've never had to walk through alone.

Mom used to say I'd trust anyone who was nice to me. She said it like a flaw.

"What's Theo get out of it?" I say.

Cass looks at me, and for one second the smile drops and there's something underneath — tired, maybe. Maybe scared. Maybe just seventeen.

"Smart," they say quietly. "Keep doing that."

Then the smile's back, and they're standing, brushing crumbs off the jacket, and they're not answering the question, and I notice they're not answering.

"Offer stands," Cass says. "Corner of Frenchmen. I'll be there till nine."

They walk off into the crowd and the crowd eats them.

I sit on the stoop a while longer. The sax player clicks his case shut and nods at me — just a nod, one tired person to another — and shuffles off toward the river. Forty-one dollars. Eleven percent. Nine o'clock.

I pick up my bag.

I don't know yet which way I'm walking.

**Gone South — Chapter Two**

The guy's name was Doyle and he drove a Silverado that smelled like Skoal and wet dog, and for seven hours he'd been fine—*fine*—right up until Canal Street, when he looked at me sideways in the gray pre-dawn and said, "What are you, anyway."

Not a question. I didn't answer. He pulled over anyhow.

So now it's 6:40 a.m. and I'm standing on a sidewalk that's wet even though it hasn't rained, the air thick enough to chew, and my phone says 12%.

Twelve percent. The charger is on my nightstand in Tennessee, plugged into a wall I'm never going to see again. Probably. Maybe. I don't know yet.

Here's what I know: I have $63, a backpack, a hoodie that was a mistake in this climate, and forty-one unread messages I haven't opened because opening them means watching the number tick down to 11, and because I already know what they say. Mom: *please just tell me you're safe.* Dad: nothing. Dad said everything he was going to say Tuesday night at the kitchen table, and it had the word *phase* in it and the word *sick* in it, and after that the house went so quiet I could hear the fridge.

I turn the phone face-down in my palm like a card I don't want to show.

Walk. Walking is a plan. Walking looks like you know where you're going.

---

By nine the Quarter has woken up and it's loud and ugly and gorgeous. Guys hosing vomit off the curb. A brass band tuning on a corner, three kids and a tuba. Everything smells like powdered sugar and piss and the river, somewhere to my left, big and brown and wrong-colored. I want to cry and I want to scream *I'm here, I did it, I'm actually here,* and I settle for buying a $2 Coke I can't afford and sitting on the steps of a church I don't believe in.

That's where Pike finds me. Or I find Pike. Hard to say.

"You're gonna get rolled sitting there like that."

I look up. Nineteen, maybe. Shaved head growing out fuzzy. A brindle mutt in a bandana, and a pack with a bedroll strapped to it like a real traveler—not like me with my school bag that still has gym clothes in it.

"Like what?"

"Like a kid who just got here. You've got the face. Fresh off the Greyhound."

"I hitched."

"Worse." Pike sits two steps below me, uninvited, and the dog puts her chin on my knee like we've met. "Where from?"

"Tennessee."

"Hm." Not a judgment. Just filing. "Pronouns?"

Nobody has ever asked me that in real life. Online, sure. Not out loud, not with a face attached. Something cracks open in my chest and I have to look at the dog.

"They," I say. It comes out hoarse. "Them."

"Cool. Pike, he/him, this is Biscuit, she don't care. You eat?"

---

Pike knows things. Pike knows the shelter on Rampart does intake at four but they'll call your parents if you're under eighteen—"so you're eighteen, got it?"—and that the library has outlets and won't hassle you till close, and that tourists on Bourbon tip a dollar if you say something funny and five if you cry.

"You don't have to actually cry," he says. "Just, you know. Access it."

He talks fast and doesn't look at me when he does it. There's a scar on his forearm, pink and straight and newish, and when I notice it he tugs his sleeve down without changing expression. He checks his own phone a lot. Not scrolling—checking. Like he's waiting on someone.

I want to trust him so bad it feels like a sickness. That's the thing nobody tells you about running: you get hungry for people the same way you get hungry for food, and you'll take it from anywhere.

Mom would say that's exactly the problem.

Mom cried Tuesday. Not *at* me, but it was somehow worse than Dad's silence, because I did that. I put that on her face.

*Please just tell me you're safe.*

I'm not. I don't know if I am. Eleven percent now. I checked.

---

Afternoon. We've made $14 and Biscuit's made more than that just by existing. Pike splits it with me, which I didn't expect. We eat red beans out of styrofoam on the levee and the river slides by, enormous and indifferent, and for about ten minutes I'm not scared of anything.

"My boy Dez has a place," Pike says. "Off Elysian Fields. Real roof. He lets people crash if they're cool."

"What's cool mean?"

"Means you don't steal from him and you pitch in."

"Pitch in how?"

Pike's quiet a second too long. "However you can."

And there it is. The thing under the thing. I feel it the way you feel a stair that isn't there in the dark—stomach first, then brain.

"Is that where you're going tonight?"

"That's where I always go." He stands, brushes off his jeans. Still won't look at me. "You don't have to. I'm just saying it's there."

The library closes at six. The shelter calls your parents. Pike's friend has a roof and a word for *pitch in* he can't say to my face.

My phone buzzes. Mom again. 10%.

I don't open it. But I don't delete it either.

"Let me think about it," I say, and Pike shrugs like it's nothing, like he hasn't been thinking about it since the church steps, and Biscuit licks my hand like she's sorry, and the sun goes orange and sideways over a city that doesn't know my name yet.

Either of them.

# Gone South — Chapter Two: Wet Towel

The strap slips again. Third time since the truck door slammed and Darryl-or-whatever drove off with my gratitude and the last of my beef jerky. I hitch it back up. It slides. I hitch it. It's a rhythm now, like breathing, like the thing I do with my thumbnail when Mom's voice gets tight.

It's 6:40 a.m. in New Orleans and the air is a wet towel somebody's holding over my face.

I didn't plan for the air. I planned for a lot in those thirty minutes — cash from the coffee can ($212), the hoodie that turns me into a shape instead of a gender, Dad's old Army pack with the busted buckle (hence: strap). I did not plan for a city that breathes on you.

Okay. Okay okay okay.

Rules. Rule one: don't look lost. Rule two: don't look at your phone, because the SIM card is in a ditch outside Jackson, Mississippi, and the phone is now a brick you keep for the camera and the illusion of being a person. Rule three —

I never got to rule three. There was a girl on the curb outside a shuttered bar on Decatur eating Takis like cereal, and she was looking at me like she'd read rules one and two straight off my forehead.

"You're doing it wrong," she said.

"Doing what wrong."

"Standing. You stand like somebody's about to call your name."

Something clenched under my ribs. My *name.* Fun fact: I never had to pick one. Taylor works. Taylor's always worked — the single gift my parents gave me without knowing. What doesn't work is how Mom said it two nights ago. *Tay-lor.* Two syllables stretched into a question, like she was checking it still fit. Like she was already measuring the box.

"Dez," the girl said, and held out the bag. I took one.

Rule four, apparently: accept chips from strangers.

---

Dez is nineteen, she says. Dez is *not* nineteen. Dez has a mouth that's older than the rest of her and a bracelet of yellow-green bruise around her left wrist that she keeps tugging her sleeve over, and I'm not going to ask because I know the exact face a person makes when they get asked. I've been making it for two days.

She knows things. Which Shell lets you use the bathroom without buying anything. The library on Loyola, opens at ten, outlets along the back wall. Which cops will roll their window down to talk and which ones just *look.*

"How long you been here?" I ask.

"Long enough."

"That's not a number."

"You're not eighteen either, so."

I didn't say I was eighteen. I was *going* to say I was eighteen. She'd just saved me the breath.

By noon we're in Jackson Square and the heat has gone from towel to actual hand on the back of my neck. A kid with a trumpet is playing something I half know. A woman with a tarot cloth catches my eye and I look away so fast I nearly walk into a horse.

Dez laughs. The first real one. "What, you scared she'll see something?"

Yes. Obviously yes. That's the entire problem with me — people see things. The counsellor saw *concerning behavioural patterns.* Mom saw a phase, saw the internet, saw a girl she could still fix if she talked slow enough. Dad —

Dad didn't see anything. That's the part I keep circling like a sore tooth. Dad set his fork down, said *well*, and went to the garage. No slam. No yelling. Just the garage door and then the TV out there, loud, like weather. Cody — he's eleven — asked, genuinely, *so do I say brother now,* and Mom said *we are not doing this,* and nobody did it. For forty-eight hours, nobody did anything at all.

I used to think the worst thing would be screaming. Turns out the worst thing is a house that keeps functioning around you like you've already left.

So I left. Call it efficiency.

---

Dez buys a muffuletta with a twenty.

Here's the thing: at 6:40 this morning Dez had Takis and a dead phone. Now she has a twenty. I saw her come out of the souvenir place on Chartres with her hands in her hoodie pocket, and I didn't ask then, and I'm not asking now, because half of this sandwich is the best thing I have eaten since I was a person with a kitchen, and I don't have the luxury of a conscience with a full stomach yet.

"There's a guy," she says, mouth full. "Cal. He's got a place, kind of Uptown. Couch, shower. He looks out for people like us."

*Like us.* She hasn't once asked what I am. She just slotted me into *us* like it was obvious. Like the hoodie wasn't fooling anybody and that was fine.

I should be relieved. Part of me is so relieved I could cry on this bench next to a horse.

The other part is listening to the way she said *Cal.* Flat. Rehearsed. The way you say a word you've been told to say.

"How's he look out for people."

She shrugs. Tugs the sleeve. "He just does."

---

Three-something. Her phone, which was dead, is suddenly alive and buzzing, and her face does a thing — shutters down, all at once, like a storefront at closing. "Gotta handle something. Six o'clock, right here. I'll walk you to Cal's. You cannot sleep outside your first night. Trust me."

Trust me. Everybody's favorite two words. The counsellor said them. Mom says them before every sentence that's going to hurt.

She leaves me the Takis. That's either kindness or bait, and I genuinely cannot tell, and *that's* the concerning behavioural pattern, right there, if anyone's taking notes: I can smell a trap from a mile off and I will still walk toward it, because the trap is at least warm. Because the trap, at least, said *us.*

The square empties and fills. The trumpet kid packs up. My brick phone says it's 5:52.

I think about Cody saying *brother.* I think about the garage door.

5:58. Dez comes around the corner by the cathedral, hood up, walking fast, and lifts her chin at me — *you coming?*

I don't know yet. I honestly don't. I only know my feet are moving and the strap is sliding off my shoulder again, and I catch it, the way you do, and hitch it back up.
