response:
The door gave without a sound, which was the first wrong thing.

Aya had expected the groan of iron, the stink of bilge. Instead the hinges had been oiled—recently, lovingly—and the underhold beyond was lit. Not by the sputtering tallow stubs of the upper halls but by proper spermaceti lamps, a dozen of them, burning clean and white in brass sconces the length of the vault. Their light fell on whale-rib buttresses, on casks sweating oil into the sweet rot-smell of rendered fat, on the far dais where the Scythan reliquary sat beneath its salt-ringed bell of leaded glass exactly as the rumors had placed it.

And on the woman seated before it.

"Shut the door, girl. You're letting the fog in."

Katra's knife was half out of its sheath. Simeon's hand went to the lamplighter's hook at his belt. Neither moved further, because the four men ranged along the walls had already leveled their harpoon-guns, and a harpoon-gun does not need to be aimed well at twenty paces.

Widow Tallow had not risen. She sat in a chair of black baleen with her boots up on a cask, a long clay pipe in one hand and a cup of something steaming in the other, and she looked—Aya thought, absurdly—like a grandmother who had waited up.

"You were arrested," Katra said. "The Harbourmen took you at the fourth bell. I *saw* the wagon."

"You saw a wagon." The Widow drew on her pipe. "Costs eleven shillings to hire a Harbourman's wagon for an hour, if you know which Harbourman. Cheaper than I'd have thought, for the trouble it's saved me." She exhaled. "Word goes out the chair's empty, and I sit down here with a cup of tea and count who comes running. Three, so far. I'd hoped for more. I'm an old woman and I like to be surprised."

Aya's mind was already reaching—past the lamps, past the brass, down into the cold place beneath thought where the immateria waited. She could feel it there like a tide against a sea wall. One word, half a breath, and something with too many joints would come unfolding out of the shadow behind the Widow's chair—

"Don't," the Widow said, without looking at her. "Lusk. Show her."

The nearest guard tilted his harpoon-gun so the lamplight caught the barrel. The iron head had been packed in salt; grey crystals crusted the barbs like frost. Aya's stomach turned over. Salt and cold iron. The old sailors' cure. It wouldn't stop a summoning, not truly—but it would stop *her*, if it went through her first, and the man's finger was already white on the trigger.

"Men who trust brass don't trust your sort," the Widow went on, mild as weather. "But they do learn. Simeon, put the hook down. Katra, the knife. There's a good girl. Now—" the pipe stem came up, pointed—"the mask."

No one moved.

"Lusk."

The guard crossed the floor in four strides. Aya did not step back; there was nowhere to step. His fingers found the knot at the nape of her neck, fumbled, caught, and the black silk came away in his hand. Cold air on her face. The lamps too bright.

Silence. Then the Widow set down her cup.

"Well," she said. "Well, well. Mercy on us."

*Don't say it,* Aya thought. *Don't say the name.*

"Ayantha Vell." The Widow rolled it around like a sweet. "Rysander Vell's girl. The shipping Vells, the *bonded-warehouse* Vells. I knew your mother, you know. Not to speak to. I stood at Gallows Point and watched them hang her, same as half the city. She was very composed. You've her chin."

Somewhere beyond the walls, out in the harbor, a foghorn sounded—long and low, like something grieving.

Aya felt the floor of her life tilt. Not the harpoon. Not the salt. The *name*. It would be in the Gazette by Monday. *Daughter of the hanged witch Vell found among thieves.* Her father's seat on the Harbour Board. The house on Candlewick Crescent with its shutters nailed. And then the inquest, and the doctors with their callipers, and the men from the Magistracy who had already measured her mother for a rope would find the measurements still on file—

"You've gone a very bad color," the Widow observed. "Lusk, if she faints, let her."

"She won't faint," Katra said tightly. "Aya—"

"I'm fine." Her voice came out steadier than she had any right to expect. Good. *Use it.* "Widow Tallow. Before you have us dropped in the oil-sump, I'd ask you to do a sum."

The second foghorn. The Widow raised an eyebrow. "Go on, then. I like sums."

"My father is worth eleven thousand a year and has one living child. If I vanish, he'll pay to know where. If I'm found in the harbor, he'll pay a great deal more to know *who*—and the Vells have bought Harbourmen for longer than you've been hiring their wagons." Aya made herself breathe. "But if I'm *returned*. Quietly. Then you hold a thing worth more than the reliquary under that glass. You hold the daughter of the Harbour Board. You hold a Vell who can be *hanged* on your word, any morning you choose, for the rest of her life."

"Aya, for God's—" Simeon started.

"I'm not finished. Kill my friends, and you've a hostage who hates you. Keep them, and you've one who'll do as she's told."

The Widow said nothing for a long moment. The spermaceti lamps hissed. Down in the cold beneath Aya's thoughts, the immateria pressed and pressed against its wall, and she held it there with everything she had, because she understood now that the Widow had been waiting for exactly that—for the witch to show her teeth and prove the salt was earned.

The third foghorn came and faded.

"Rysander Vell's girl," the Widow said at last, softly, "standing in my underhold offering me her own neck as surety." She reached for her tea. "Your mother was composed too, right up until the drop. I always wondered if it was courage or if she simply couldn't believe it was happening." She drank. "Sit down, Lady Vell. All three of you. Lusk, fetch chairs. Let's see what the Harbour Board's daughter thinks she's worth by daylight."

The door gave without protest, and that was the first wrong thing.

Beyond it the underhold opened like a throat. The whalers who had built Morska had sunk the vault into the carcass of a leviathan long before the guild took it: ribs of yellowed bone arched overhead, each thicker than a man, bolted to the stone with iron bands that wept rust down the walls. Gas lamps hissed in their brass cages. The flames guttered as the door swung wide, and the flickering gas lamps cast long, unsettling shadows across the stone floor — shadows that stretched toward the three of them and seemed reluctant to settle back.

The air tasted of tallow, old blood, and the sweet rot of ambergris.

At the far end, on a dais of scrimshawed bone, stood the reliquary. Behind it sat Mother Krask.

She occupied a wheeled chair of cane and brass, a blanket over her knees, a long-barrelled harpoon pistol resting across them like a sleeping cat. Six men stood in the gaps between the ribs with pneumatic bolt-guns raised. Steam sighed from the valves.

"Shut the door, Simeon," Krask said. "You'll let the damp in."

Simeon's hand went to the knife at his belt and stopped there, because one of the bolt-guns clicked. He shut the door.

*I watched them take her,* Aya thought. *I stood on the roof of the chandlery and watched the Watch drag her into the wagon.*

"They arrested you," Katra said. Her voice had gone flat, the way it did before violence. "I saw it."

"You saw a woman in my coat and my shawl with a sack over her head. Marta. Good girl. She's being paid handsome to sit in the Bastion a fortnight and say nothing." Krask's eyes, pale as boiled milk, moved to Aya. "Nothing flushes rats like an empty larder. I wanted to see who'd come down the stairs first. Thought it'd be Dunmore. Thought it might be the Felsom brothers." Her head tilted. "Didn't think it'd be our little masked miracle."

Aya reached — not with her hands. Beneath the stone, beneath the bone, beneath the world, there was a cold that was always listening, and she bent toward it the way one leans toward a lover in the dark. It stirred. It was *glad*.

"Don't," Krask said.

A bolt-gun had come to rest against the soft place under Katra's jaw. Katra did not flinch. Katra never flinched.

"I've seen what you call up, girl. Takes you a breath and a half to get it through the door. Pyotr there takes a good deal less." Krask drummed two fingers on the pistol. "Knives on the floor. Both of you. Slow."

Steel rang on stone. Simeon's, then Katra's.

"Now take the mask off her."

A hand, gloved and smelling of tar, closed on the lacquered whalebone. Aya felt the leather straps bite, then slacken, then the sudden awful coolness of the air on her cheeks. The lamplight found her face. She felt it find her face.

Krask leaned forward in her chair, and for a long moment said nothing at all.

"Well," she breathed. "Well, now. Valcourt."

The name fell on the stone and lay there.

*Tollgate. The scaffold draped in black bunting. Mother's hair coming loose beneath the hood. The Admiralty box with its brass rail polished for the occasion, and Father's face in it the colour of ash, and the word — immateria — passed mouth to mouth through the crowd like a bad coin.* Everything Aya had kept behind the mask was in her face now, and she could not put it back.

"I was in that crowd," Krask said, almost gently. "Picked eleven pockets while they hanged your mother. Good day's work." She sat back. "And here's the daughter. In my cellar. With her mother's hands."

"Mother Krask—" Simeon began.

"Not you."

Aya made herself swallow. Made herself find the voice they taught in drawing rooms — the one that did not shake. "You're owed the honour of this, I'll grant you. But I'd ask you to consider what I'm worth with my neck intact."

"Go on."

"My father sits on the Harbour Board. Magistrate Hollin, who signed the warrant for this morning's pantomime, dines at our table on Thursdays. The Valcourt name moves ships, Mother. It moves judges." Her mouth was dry. "A dead aristocrat under the guildhall is a hanging matter for every soul in this room. A living one is a letter you may send whenever you please."

Krask's fingers stopped drumming. "And what does your father write back, when he learns his daughter's a witch like her mother before her?"

*He'll hand you to the Constabulary himself,* said the cold beneath the world, in a voice that was very nearly her own. *He'll stand in the box again. He'll have the rail polished.*

"He'll pay," Aya said. "He paid once already to keep the second noose out of the broadsheets. He'll pay to keep it out a second time."

Silence, but for the hiss of the lamps. Somewhere behind the reliquary, water dripped into water.

"She has a point, Mother," Simeon said quietly. "Dreadful thing, a point. Hard to argue with."

Katra said nothing. Katra was looking at Aya, and Aya could not read what was in her face, and that was worse than the bolt-gun.

Krask studied the reliquary a while — the dull, impossible thing inside it, older than Morska, older than the sea — then turned her milk-pale eyes back on the girl without a mask.

"Pyotr. The brine room. Chain the men. Chain *her* to the iron — wrists and ankles, salt round the ring. Then fetch me pen and paper."

The gloved hands closed on Aya's arms. The lamps leaned sideways. Her shadow went long across the floor, and did not quite follow her.

"Let's see," said Mother Krask, "what a Valcourt fetches at market."

Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards.

Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. A pocket watch ticks loudly in Simeon's waistcoat pocket, marking each tense second. 1000 words.
response:
**The Morska Conspiracy**
*The Underhold*

The door gave without protest, which was the first wrong thing.

Aya had expected iron. A bar, a ward, a lock that wanted coaxing. Instead the oak swung inward on greased hinges, and the smell came up to meet them: whale-oil smoke, old brine, and beneath it the sweet rot of a lamp left burning too long on spent spermaceti.

Behind her, Simeon's watch ticked. A cheap thing, brass-cased, a dockside purchase he refused to be parted from, and in the stairwell's hush each second landed like a dropped coin.

"Too quiet," Katra breathed. Her knife was already out; Aya heard the leather creak as her grip tightened.

"I know."

The underhold opened before them, a vault hewn from the black sea-rock Morska was built upon, ribbed overhead with the jawbones of some leviathan dragged up a century past. Lamps burned in sconces of carved baleen. At the far end, upon a dais of fused coin and bone, stood the plinth.

Empty.

"Oh," said a voice, warm as tallow. "You were expecting it to be here."

Teodora Vask stepped out of the shadow of the ribs. She was not in irons. She was not in the Watch's cells on Gallows Row, where half the city had seen her dragged at dawn. She wore her grey hair pinned with whale-ivory and a harpooner's coat that fell to her boots, and the thing resting in the crook of her arm was a long gun, its stock inlaid with mother-of-pearl, its mechanism all brass and oiled intent.

Four men came with her. Aya counted without wanting to. Four, and the fifth she had not seen, who stepped out behind them and shut the door.

*Tick.*

"The raid," Aya said. Her voice came out level, which surprised her. "You staged it."

"I *let* it be staged. There's a difference, child, and you'll appreciate it presently." Vask came down the dais steps one at a time. "The Watch were paid to carry me out the front in chains. My own people were paid to believe it. Then I came down here, lit the lamps, and waited to see who would come for my heart while they thought it had stopped beating."

Simeon shifted. *Tick.* "Teodora, we—"

"You, I'm not surprised by. Nor the Hollen girl." Vask's eyes passed over Katra like a hand over a cold stove and settled on Aya. "It was the masked one I wondered about. Six months. Six months of my people coming back from jobs white as suet, telling me how the new one *opens doors*. How the dark does what she says. How you can hear the hinges of the world creak when she whispers."

Aya felt the immateria stir at the base of her skull, where it always lived: cold, patient, attentive. She could call it. She could have the chamber full of hungry shapes before Vask's finger found the trigger.

And then they would know. Not suspect. *Know*. And whatever came through would not go back quietly, not into a room full of frightened men with iron in their hands. Her mother had taught her that much before the end.

She kept her hands still.

"Take it off her," Vask said.

The man who did it was gentle, almost apologetic — a big fellow with harpoon scars laddering his forearms — and he lifted the mask over Aya's head the way one lifts the lid from a pot that may yet boil over. Her hair came loose. The lamplight found her face.

*Tick.*

Katra made a sound. Simeon did not; Simeon had known.

Vask looked for a long moment. Then she laughed, low and genuine, the laugh of a woman dealt a hand she had not expected and finds she rather likes it.

"Dravec," she said. "Oh, *Dravec*. Your mother hanged at Saltgate. I was there. Half the city was. They'd put a gag of pitch across her mouth so she couldn't speak the dark down on them from the drop, and still the gulls wouldn't settle on the yard for a week after." She stepped closer. "And here you are. In my house. With her look about the eyes."

*Here I am*, Aya thought, and the thought was very clear and very far away, the way thoughts are at the moment a thing cannot be taken back. Tomorrow, if there was a tomorrow, it would be in the broadsheets. *Lady Aya Dravec, Guild Witch.* Her father's face. The House stripped. And the Inquisitory would not bother with a trial, because why would they, when the mother had already shown them what the blood did.

*Tick.*

"Kneel them," Vask said.

They were knelt. Katra fought it enough to earn a split lip. Simeon folded like a man who had been expecting the floor for some time. Aya's knees met the black stone and the cold went straight up through her.

"My father," she said.

Vask raised an eyebrow.

"My father sits on the Admiralty Board. He signs the whaling charters for the eastern banks. Every ship that leaves this harbour with a harpoon aboard does so under his seal." Aya held the woman's gaze and did not look at the gun. "You want the Watch kept out of your cellars. You want your tonnage of grey oil moving without inspection. You want a hundred things a dead girl cannot give you and a living one can."

"Can she." Vask crouched, coat pooling about her. The gun did not waver. "Or does the Admiralty Lord look at a ransom note from the Morska Guild and send the Inquisitory to burn the whole quarter rather than admit what his daughter's been doing with her nights?"

Aya had no answer for that. It was, she thought, precisely what he would do.

*Tick.*

"Then don't tell him what I am," she said quietly. "Tell him what you *have*. A daughter. Unhurt. Discreetly returned. And a debt." She swallowed. "I am worth more to you unknown than dead on this floor. Hang me, and you have a corpse and a scandal. Keep me, and you have a hand in the Admiralty for as long as you hold your tongue."

Vask was silent. Behind her the lamps guttered, spermaceti burning low, throwing the whale-ribs into long reaching shadows that moved as if something in them had taken an interest.

Simeon's watch ticked.

"And your friends?"

"They're mine," Aya said. "They come with the bargain."

The old woman studied her the way she might have studied a whale sounding beneath the hull: measuring the shape under the surface, deciding whether it would pay to put the iron in.

"Bind her hands," Vask said at last. "In front. Where I can see them."

Cozy sci-fi
The Last Outpost
Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. A glass accidentally breaks somewhere in the background of the bar. 1000 words.
response:
# The Last Outpost

The Outpost is doing its midweek impression of a bar: half-full, half-awake, entirely my problem.

"Nets, he's cheating."

"He's not cheating, Dorrit. You're bad at tiles."

"I've been playing tiles since before his mother was spawned."

"Not the flex you think it is."

He slaps a chit down anyway and I slide him another ferment, because I'm soft and because he tips in actual ore. Behind him the Pellam twins are arguing over a hauling contract in the pitch they save for things they'll forget by morning. Old Hesk is asleep upright in the corner booth. The rock hums under the floor, that low grinding note I've stopped hearing except when I'm about to miss it.

I'm wiping the same stretch of counter for the third time when the door cycles and she comes in.

Frazzled doesn't cover it. She looks like she lost a fight with a dust storm and then apologized to it. Her dreads—thick, tentacled things that move a little on their own—hang tangled over one shoulder, and two of them keep lifting toward the door behind her, tasting the air. She takes the stool at the end nobody takes because the light's bad, and sits like her knees have given notice.

"Vega whisky, neat." A pause. "Better make that a double."

"Rough transit?"

"Rough everything."

I pour. The real Vega, not what I give the miners who can't tell. One of the dreads curls toward the glass before she does.

"That's the good bottle."

"You look like someone who'd know the difference. Also like someone who might die before paying, so I figure, why not."

She almost smiles. Takes half the double and holds it in her mouth like she's checking it's real.

"You're Nettle."

Not a question. The counter stops being interesting.

"Depends who's asking."

"Someone who was told you're the person on the rim to see if you need something to stop existing. Paperwork. Cargo. A name." Another swallow. "A ship."

"You were told wrong. I pour drinks."

"I know that's what you do now."

I keep my hands flat on the wood. Three years. Three years of pouring and listening and fixing other people's lives because mine was a thing I'd folded up and shoved in a vent. Nobody here has asked. That's the deal. The Outpost tolerates my mouth and my temper and the way I short the till the first week of every month, and in exchange I don't bring my old weather with me.

"Who told you?"

"Does it matter?"

"To me? Enormously."

She sets the glass down. "Kessam."

The name goes through me like a cold pin. Behind us a Pellam says something about tonnage. Hesk snores.

"Kessam's dead."

"Kessam's in a cell on Tarrow, which, same thing in a month. She gave me your name as a favor. Said you owed her one and this was her spending it."

"I don't owe her anything."

"Not how she tells it."

I pick up a glass that doesn't need polishing. "What are you carrying?"

"Didn't say I was carrying anything."

"Your dreads keep checking the door. You ordered a double without looking at the price, so either you're rich or you've stopped planning past tonight, and you don't look rich. What are you carrying, and who wants it back?"

Her dreads go still, all at once, which is somehow worse.

"That's the talent, then. Kessam said you read people like manifests."

"Kessam talks a lot for someone in a cell."

"Fair." She finishes the whisky. "It's a ledger. Hard copy, encrypted, about the size of your fist. Belongs to a consortium I'm not naming in a bar. They know roughly where I went. I'd put them two days out. Maybe less."

Two days.

I think about Dorrit's ore and the twins' bickering and Hesk's booth that nobody else sits in even when he's gone. The cot in the back with the blanket somebody's grandmother knitted. How long it took anyone here to stop watching their pockets around me.

"Then you need to not be here in two days."

"That's why I'm talking to you."

"No. You need to be *somewhere else*. The Outpost is a fuel stop with a bar attached. Fly on."

"My ship's holding atmosphere by sentiment. No clean transit code, no credit, and the only name I've got in this whole arm is yours."

"Then you've got nothing."

"Yeah." She turns the empty glass. "That was my read too."

Somewhere behind me a glass goes over—the bright, stupid sound of it shattering on the deck—and one twin yells *sorry, Nets* and the other laughs, and the room ripples and settles the way a room does when it doesn't know anything's wrong.

I don't turn around. I always turn around.

"What's your name?"

"Does it matter?"

"To me? Enormously."

That gets a real smile, tired and crooked. "Oriel."

"Oriel. I'm going to pour you another, on the house. Then you're going to sleep in your ship, and in the morning you're going to be gone, and I'm going to have never met you."

"And if I'm not?"

I pour. My hand is steady, which is the part I can't stand.

"Then I guess we find out what Kessam actually bought."

She lifts the glass. Doesn't drink. Watches me over the rim like someone who's sat across from a lot of people and waited to see which way they'd fall.

"She said you'd say no first."

"Did she say what I'd say second?"

"No." Oriel drinks. "She said that part was up to you."

Behind us the broom comes out, and the rock hums, and I'm still holding the good bottle. I haven't put it back.

The Last Outpost
Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. The station's artificial gravity fluctuates slightly, causing liquids in glasses to wobble. 1000 words.
response:
The gravity hiccups right as I'm topping off Pell's beer, and the foam leans left like it's trying to overhear something.

"You're doing it again," Pell says.

"Doing what."

"Waiting for the wobble. You could just pour."

"I could just pour, and you could have beer in your lap." I set the glass down. The head settles. "Eleven-minute cycle. You've lived here six years. You should have the rhythm by now."

"I have the rhythm. I just don't make a religion of it." She drinks. Lowers her voice. "Dunmore wants to put in for the Kessler claim."

"The Kessler claim is a rock full of nothing."

"I know."

"So tell him."

"I'm telling you. That's the system. I tell you, you tell him it was your idea, he listens because it's you."

"That's not a system. That's laundering."

"It works."

It does work. That's the problem with most of what I do here — it works, so nobody asks me to stop. I dry a glass. Behind Pell, old Gaskin is losing at cards to a kid half his age and pretending he isn't, and Dunmore's at the far end feeding the jukebox coins it stopped taking a year ago, because he likes the sound. The Last Outpost on a Tuesday. Eighteen people, two hundred stories, all of them mine to keep.

Then the airlock cycles and the stranger comes in.

I notice the dreads first — thick, dark, moving faintly on their own the way the Eshan-modified do — and that two of them are knotted around each other like they've been wrung out. The coat is good but slept in. The eyes find the bar and nothing else.

They sit three stools from Pell. Put both hands flat on the wood.

"Vega whisky. Neat." A breath. "Better make that a double."

"Vega's twelve a pour."

"Fine."

"Just so you know before you're attached to it."

"I'm attached. Pour."

I pour. The gravity's steady for another nine minutes, so it goes in clean — amber, the real stuff from the back shelf. They drink half in one go and hold the glass against their forehead afterward like a cold compress.

"Rough transit?" I ask.

"Rough year."

"That's a lot of year to put in one glass."

"It's a double."

Pell is openly watching. I give her the look, and she returns to her beer with enormous dignity.

"You came in on the *Cordial*," I say. "Ore hauler. Only thing docked since shift change."

"Does everyone here know what's docked?"

"Everyone here is waiting on something that's docked. Parts, mail, people." I shrug. "What are you waiting on?"

"Nothing." Too fast. They finish the glass. "Another."

"Twelve."

"I heard you."

I pour. They don't drink this one right away. They turn it in a slow circle on the bar, watching the surface.

"Does the gravity always do that?"

"Do what?"

"Lean."

"Every eleven minutes, give or take. Plating's older than the station. You stop noticing."

"I noticed."

"You've been here fifteen minutes."

"I notice things." They look at me for the first time, properly, and I don't love it. It's an inventory look. Height, hands, the scar on my jaw, the way I stand with my weight on my back foot. "You've worked here long?"

"Four years."

"Before that?"

"Before that I was somewhere else."

"That's a bartender answer."

"I'm a bartender."

They almost smile. It doesn't take. "I'm looking for someone. Was told she works the bar at the Last Outpost. Marisol."

My hands keep drying the glass. Good hands. Never let me down once.

"Nobody here by that name."

"Tall. Scar here." They touch their own jaw — left side, exactly where mine is. "Pours left-handed."

"There's a lot of scars on the rim."

"I'm sure."

"And I don't know a Marisol. Sorry."

Pell has gone very still three stools down. I love her, and she has never once in her life been able to act.

The stranger looks at the whisky. "That's a shame," they say, and for a second the frazzle drops and underneath it there's just tired. Bone tired. The dreads go slack. "That's a real shame. Because I was told she was the only person in this belt who'd know what to do about Aurelio Vance."

I set the glass down. Carefully, because the gravity's about to go and I don't trust myself with it.

"Who?"

"You heard me."

"Vance is dead."

"That's what I said. Loudly. On a recording. Which is why I've been on three freighters in six days and haven't slept on any of them." They pick up the double, finally, and drink it like medicine. "He's not dead, Marisol. He's about eleven hours out. And he knows I came here."

The lights flicker the way they always do right before. Every glass in the room leans.

"My name's Nettle," I say.

"Sure."

"It is. Nets. Ask anyone."

"Okay, Nets." They push the empty across. "Then I'll take a third, and you can decide who you want to be when this place finds out there's nothing it can do about any of this."

Down the bar, Dunmore's finally got the jukebox to swallow a coin. Something old plays. Gaskin folds a losing hand. Pell is staring at the side of my face like she's never seen it before, and I'm counting — nine, eight — until the gravity settles and I have an excuse to do something with my hands.

I pour the third one.

"Eleven hours," I say.

"Give or take."

"Then start from the beginning. Slowly. I've got a bar to run."

"Which beginning?"

"Your name's a good one."
