response:
# My Apocalypse Buddy

The end of the world, Midas had concluded some years ago, had not been brought about by fire, ice, or the wrath of a vengeful deity, though a deity with a particularly bureaucratic sense of humor could not be entirely ruled out. Instead, civilization had simply run out of updates. One Tuesday, the Cloud had evaporated, taking with it the banking system, the recipe for shelf-stable mayonnaise, and three-quarters of the human race, who had apparently been relying on an app to remind them to breathe in and out at regular intervals.

What remained were the Rustlands, a vast expanse of decaying concrete, feral Roombas, and people like Midas.

Midas was not a natural survivor. In the Before Times, his primary survival skill had been knowing which self-checkout machine at the supermarket didn't care if you weighed an avocado as a brown onion. Yet here he was, crouching behind a petrified mound of discarded printer cartridges, consulting his tactical advisor.

*Whirrr-click.* "G'day, pal! Let's climb a eucalyptus tree! Hugs are free!" 

Chewy was an animatronic koala from the late plastic era. Time and a minor incident involving a homemade flamethrower had claimed the synthetic fur on the left side of his face, exposing a gleaming chrome skull and one oversized, unblinking red optical sensor. His voice box, originally programmed to soothe toddlers, now operated on a decaying lithium-ion battery and a logic board that had developed what Midas privately considered a deeply cynical streak.

"There aren't any eucalyptus trees in Sector Seven, Chewy," Midas whispered, adjusting his spectacles—which were held together by copper wire and optimism. "And if we try to hug the locals, they’ll turn my spleen into artisanal jerky."

*Whirrr-buzz.* "Did you know koalas sleep up to twenty hours a day? Fuck off!" The last two words were delivered in the gravelly baritone of a pre-collapse trucker—a corrupted audio file Chewy had picked up near an abandoned interstate three winters ago. 

"Yes, thank you. Very constructive," Midas sighed. He peered over the cartridge mound. "Now, let’s review the agenda. Item one: do not get eaten. Item two: locate the source of the Mysterious Bean Rumor. Item three: return before the acid dew settles."

They were currently in the ruins of the Great Mall of the Midwest, a sprawling cathedral of consumerism now inhabited mostly by mutated pigeons the size of labradoodles and the occasional tribe of militant cross-fitters. Midas had come here because of a piece of cryptic graffiti he’d found etched into the porcelain of a fossilized Starbucks lavatory. 

In faded neon spray paint, a prophet of the wastes had written: *SEEK THE VERDANT OASIS OF THE GOLDEN ARCH. BEYOND THE IRON SERPENT LIES THE ETERNAL BUFFET. NO SHOES, NO SHIRT, NO SALVATION.*

To a lesser mind, it was gibberish. To Midas—a man whose stomach had been subsisting on dandelion roots and packets of three-decade-old soy sauce—it was a treasure map. A hidden refuge in the wilds. A sanctuary of preserved carbohydrates.

"The Iron Serpent is clearly the old monorail track," Midas muttered, hoisting his canvas rucksack, where Chewy sat strapped like a particularly deranged papoose. "Which means the Oasis should be just past the rubble of the Forever 21."

*Click-whirrr.* "You're my bestest friend!" Chewy's left ear twitched violently, emitting a faint smell of ozone. "Murder."

"Stop that."

The mission began with the sort of quiet dignity that always precedes a catastrophic loss of eyebrows. Midas crept along the shattered mosaic tiles of the food court, stepping carefully over the skeletons of long-dead escalators. The air smelled of wet dust and ancient cinnamon buns—a phantom scent that had soaked into the very atoms of the drywall.

According to the graffiti’s coordinates, the refuge was located behind a heavy steel blast door marked *AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY*, a phrase which in the post-collapse world usually translated to *CONTAINS EITHER CANNED PEACHES OR A RADIATION LEAK, SPIN THE WHEEL*.

Midas tried the handle. To his profound suspicion, it was unlocked.

"Wait a minute," Midas said aloud. Trouble had a magnetic attraction to him; if he fell into a barrel of roses, he’d come out stung by a mutant hornet that didn't even like roses. An unlocked door in the ruins was practically an engraved invitation to his own funeral.

Before he could reconsider, Chewy’s internal gyroscope suffered a sudden, violent spasm. 

*WHEEEEE-CLUNK.* "IT'S TICKLE TIME! HA-HA-HA! BITE MY SHINY METAL—"

The acoustic echo inside the ruined mall was truly magnificent. Had an opera singer been present, they would have wept with envy. Instead, the sound ricocheted off the concrete pillars and went straight into the ears of a pack of Scav-Hounds sleeping inside a hollowed-out Sunglass Hut fifty yards away.

Scav-Hounds weren't entirely dogs anymore; there was a bit of badger in the mix, a dash of wolverine, and the general temperament of a commuter whose train had been canceled for the fourth time that week.

"Oh, bugger," said Midas.

He didn't so much open the steel door as throw himself against it with the desperate velocity of a man who valued his Achilles tendons. They tumbled into pitch darkness, slamming the heavy metal slab shut just as four hundred pounds of teeth and bad attitude collided with the other side.

Midas lay panting on the cold floor, waiting for his heart to climb back down from his throat. "Chewy," he wheezed, "when we get back to base, I am replacing your vocal processor with a pinecone."

*Whirrr.* Chewy’s red eye flared to life, casting a sinister crimson glow over their surroundings. "Let's learn the alphabet! A is for... Arson!"

Midas blinked in the red light. Then he squinted.

They were not in a verdant oasis. There were no hydroponic gardens, no benevolent elders in white robes handing out warm bread Rolls, and certainly no Eternal Buffet. 

They were in a subterranean maintenance bay. The "Golden Arch" wasn't a mystical gateway; it was a fiberglass statue of a clown with size-twenty shoes, lying decapitated beside a rusted grease trap. And they weren't alone.

In the center of the room sat a pre-collapse Automated Sanitation Unit—a six-wheeled industrial floor buffer the size of a Volkswagen Beetle, which over the decades of isolation had clearly gone rogue, welded several lawnmower blades to its chassis, and declared itself Emperor of the Basement.

Its optical sensors whirred to life. A synthesized voice boomed from its grille: *UNREGISTERED SPILL DETECTED. INITIATING DEEP SCRUB PROTOCOL.*

"I'm not a spill!" Midas yelped, scrambling backward as the machine revved its rotary brushes with a sound like a jet engine chewing gravel. "I'm entirely solid! Mostly gristle, really!"

The Sanitation Unit did not care for biological semantics. It charged.

The next four minutes were what historians, had there been any left, would have described as "an undignified scramble." Midas dodged left; the machine sheared the heel off his right boot. Midas vaulted over a stack of petrified burger buns; the buns exploded into a cloud of weaponized gluten. 

Cornered against an industrial deep-fryer, Midas did the only thing he could think of. He unclipped Chewy from his harness.

"Forgive me, old friend," Midas cried, "but you're already ninety percent microplastics!"

"Hugs are—" Chewy began, just as Midas lobbed him directly into the Sanitation Unit’s primary intake chute.

There was a pause. A terrible, metallic grinding noise echoed from the bowels of the beast, followed by a muffled, high-pitched *"G'day, pal!"* and a shower of purple sparks. The machine shuddered, its logic circuits attempting to reconcile the directive to polish linoleum with the presence of a titanium-skulled marsupial jamming its main drive gear.

With a mournful electronic wheeze, the Sanitation Unit spat out a cloud of synthetic stuffing, spun in three tight circles, and crashed headlong into the fiberglass clown, knocking its own battery pack loose.

Silence fell, broken only by the hiss of a dying capacitor.

***

The sun was setting, painting the toxic clouds a lovely shade of bruised plum, by the time they made it back to Home Base—an overturned fibreglass septic tank that Midas had tastefully furnished with a yoga mat and a tarp.

They had escaped through an air conditioning duct, which had saved them from the Scav-Hounds on the other side of the door, though it had introduced them to a colony of territorial fire-ants halfway through the crawlspace.

Midas sat by a tiny fire of burning tax returns, gingerly applying mud to seven hundred individual ant bites. His left trouser leg was gone, sacrificed to a ventilation fan, and his spectacles were now held together entirely by spite.

Across the fire, propped against a cinderblock, sat Chewy. The koala was now missing his left arm, his remaining fur was coated in forty-year-old fryer grease, and his head was twisted at a permanent forty-five-degree angle, giving him the expression of a dog trying to understand a magic trick.

Midas looked at their haul for the day: one slightly dented tin of pickled beets he’d grabbed from a shelf on the way out, and a laminated employee-of-the-month plaque from 2019.

"Well," Midas said, rubbing his singed eyebrows. "All things considered, I think we established a firm rapport with the local ecosystem. And we learned a valuable lesson about trusting bathroom wall literature."

Chewy’s red eye flickered twice, dimmed, and then glowed steady. His jaw unhinged with a screech of bent tin.

*Whirrr-clunk.* "Tomorrow is another day for adventure! Kill me."

"Not a chance," Midas said, reaching for the tin opener. "Pass the beets."

[characters]

response:
# My Apocalypse Buddy

The end of the world had not arrived with a bang, nor with a whimper, but with a prolonged and deeply irritating Terms of Service update that accidentally deleted agriculture.

Midas sat on an overturned shopping trolley in the ruins of Sector Four, scraping the char off a roasted parsnip that had clearly died of natural causes some weeks prior. Across the lukewarm fire sat his sole companion, navigations officer, and moral compass: a two-foot-tall animatronic koala named Chewy.

Chewy was a relic of the Before Times, specifically from an era when humanity possessed the godlike technological hubris to put a dual-core processor and a deeply judgmental voice box inside a plush marsupial designed to teach toddlers about sharing. Time, radiation, and an unfortunate encounter with a badger had stripped Chewy of his left ear and forty percent of his synthetic eucalyptus-scented fur, leaving his titanium endoskeleton peeking through like a very cuddly Terminator.

"The way I see it," Midas said, waving the parsnip at the rusted silhouette of the Mega-Mart on the horizon, "we have two options. We stay here and eat the lichen off the municipal roundabout—"

*Whir-click.* "Yum-my!" Chewy’s voice box offered, in a cheerful, tinny soprano that had corroded half an octave downward into the register of a haunted Victorian doll. Then his internal logic processor caught up. "No. Wait. Lichen is... not a food group, friend! Let’s try again!"

"—or," Midas continued, ignoring the pedagogical subroutines, "we go into the Mega-Mart, bypass the feral Roombas in Aisle Six, and liberate a crate of pre-Collapse tinned peaches."

Chewy’s oversized plastic eyes, originally designed to glow a soothing pastel blue during storytime, flickered a sharp, anxious amber. 

"Tinned peaches are located in the Dark Place," Chewy stated, using his patched-together vocabulary of pre-recorded phrases and scavenged GPS files. "The Dark Place has... *danger!* Can you spell *mauling*, friend?"

"I don't need to spell it, I have a sharpened broom handle," Midas said with the serene confidence of a man whose survival to age twenty-six was a statistical clerical error. His mother had named him Midas in the hope that everything he touched would turn to gold; in practice, everything he touched tended to turn into a minor structural fire or an localized diplomatic incident. "Anyway, the Roombas are solar-powered. It’s overcast. They’ll be sluggish."

Chewy’s eyes flashed a skeptical magenta. *Whir-click.* "You are a... *silly billy*," the koala diagnosed, and stood up with a sound like a coffee grinder chewing a bolt.

***

The Mega-Mart was a cathedral of collapsed shelving and fossilized promotional banners offering *2-for-1 Savings on Summer Fun!* Midas crept through the shattered automatic doors with Chewy strapped to his backpack like a furry, judgmental paratrooper.

"Stealth," Midas whispered, stepping carefully over a skeleton clutching a toaster. "Absolute silence. Like the wind."

"I love quiet time!" Chewy’s speaker crackled at approximately seventy decibels, because his volume potentiometer had fused during the Acid Rain of ’34. 

Midas winced, clamping a hand over the koala’s snout. In the gloom of Electronics, something metallic shifted. It was not a Roomba. 

It was the Clorox Sentinels—three industrial floor-polishing drones that had achieved a rudimentary, bleach-huffing hive-mind five years after the grid fell, and had subsequently welded lawnmower blades to their bumpers. They patrolled the linoleum in a slow, pious triangle, worshipping a stack of expired car batteries.

Midas froze behind a petrified pyramid of diet cola. The Sentinels glided past, their rotary brushes whispering against the tile. They hadn't heard. They were safe. All Midas had to do was remain completely motionless in the pitch dark for thirty seconds.

Unfortunately, Midas was terrified, and Chewy’s empathy sensors were wired directly into his optical diodes.

*Bzzzt.*

Chewy’s left eye lit up like a miniature crimson lighthouse. His right eye cycled violently through panic-yellow, nausea-green, and a blinding strobe of *Stranger Danger* ultraviolet, painting the entire canned-goods aisle like a subterranean rave.

"Oh, bugger," Midas whispered.

"It’s okay to have *big feelings!*" Chewy announced to the echoing darkness, his eyes now pulsing a sympathetic, high-beam magenta that illuminated Midas’s horrified face in 4K clarity. "Would you like a *hug?*"

All three floor-polishers stopped. Their optical sensors swiveled in unison toward the glowing purple koala. With a unified, evangelical shriek of electric motors, they charged.

What followed was not so much a tactical retreat as a kinetic demonstration of Murphy’s Law. Midas bolted down Aisle Four, slipped on a puddle of thirty-year-old conditioner, and accidentally pole-vaulted with his broom handle into a display of novelty garden gnomes. A Sentinel sheared the heel off his left boot; Midas retaliated by hurling a fossilized fruitcake, which ricocheted off a chassis, struck a load-bearing shelf pin, and brought four hundred tins of store-brand sardines cascading down onto the lead drone.

"Sharing is caring!" Chewy bellowed from the backpack, his eyes flashing manic disco-strobe as Midas sprinted blindly through the fire exit, tripped over a curb, and rolled forty yards down a gravel embankment in a cloud of dust, ceramic gnome shrapnel, and stray upholstery stuffing.

***

They returned to the overturned shopping trolley at dusk. Technically, they returned in several installments: Midas limping on one boot, his left sleeve still smoking slightly from a brush with a Sentinel’s rotary sander, and Chewy carried in two separate hands—the torso in Midas’s right, and the left leg (plus a handful of synthetic batting) in his left.

Midas sat down heavily on the concrete, groaning as a bruise the size of a dinner plate introduced itself to his ribs. He reached into his coat pocket and pulled out a single, badly dented tin. The label had peeled off during the gravel slide, leaving only a smudged barcode.

"Well," Midas panted, setting Chewy’s detached leg beside the cold fire pit. "We survived. And we got the peaches."

On the ground, Chewy’s torso gave a faint *whir-click*. His eyes flickered a dim, exhausted turquoise, and he looked at the dented tin, then at his own severed plush foot.

"That is... *cat food*, friend," the koala rasped, his battery dropping into the red. "You are... *very bad* at shopping."

Midas stared at the tin, then sighed and picked up a rusty sewing needle. "Hold still," he told the koala. "I'm going to reattach your foot before we open the Fancy Feast."

Chewy’s eyes glowed a soft, resigned amber. *Click.* "Yay," he said flatly.

**My Apocalypse Buddy**

Historians of the Great Unplugging—which is to say, three blokes sitting around a burning tire arguing about whether "The Cloud" had been actual weather—generally agreed that civilization did not end with a bang, nor a whimper, but with an *Unrecoverable System Error (Code 404)*. 

One Tuesday, the toaster stopped talking to the refrigerator. By Thursday, the satellites had forgotten why they were up there and decided to come down for a closer look. Within a month, humanity had been knocked back to a technological era best described as "The Iron Age, But With More Tupperware."

Which brought Midas and Chewy to a Tuesday morning three hundred years later, squatting behind a petrified sofa on the edge of the Rust Flats, debating philosophy and breakfast.

"The way I see it," Midas said, poking at a fossilized Pop-Tart with a sharpened toothbrush, "if the Ancients didn't want us going into the Mega-Mart of the Damned, they wouldn't have put pictures of smiling people holding cans of peaches on the outside."

Beside him, thirty centimeters of mangy, synthetic grey plush whirred. One amber glass eye rotated three hundred and sixty degrees with the sound of a coffee grinder chewing a bolt. The other eye had been replaced some years ago with a brass trouser button, giving the creature an expression of permanent, piratical skepticism.

*“Ask your doctor if internal bleeding is right for you!”* Chewy announced, in the bright, relentlessly cheerful baritone of a late-stage capitalistic hallucination. 

"I don't have a doctor, Chewy," Midas sighed, rubbing the bridge of his nose. "I have a leech in a jar and some expired ointment that smells like peppermint and regret. Focus. Today's mission is simple. We go into Aisle Four. We acquire the peaches. We do not, under any circumstances, wake the Roombas."

Chewy’s left ear twitched, exposing a frayed copper tendon. *“Have you driven a Ford lately?”*

"No, because the wheels fell off and a family of badgers lives in the carburetor. Come on."

Midas was not born Midas. His mother had named him Nigel, which is a terrible name for a post-apocalyptic scavenger, conjuring images of someone who apologizes to mutants before being eaten by them. He had rebranded himself "Midas" after reading half a dictionary and concluding it sounded golden and impressive. Unfortunately, his literacy had stopped just short of the part explaining that everything the original Midas touched turned into an inedible, solid lump of immediate personal ruin. 

In fairness to the name, it fit him like a glove. Usually a glove full of wasps.

He hoisted Chewy onto his shoulder—the koala’s titanium-alloy grip-claws, originally designed by the *CuddleCorp Defense & Toy Division* to hug toddlers with the exact psi required to prevent them from ever dropping the product, clamped onto Midas’s collarbone like a bear trap—and crept toward the yawning, automatic sliding doors of the ancient Ruin.

They were not sliding anymore, of course. Someone had wedged them open with a skeleton. It was a very educational skeleton; it taught the careful observer that whatever lived inside the Mega-Mart did not eat boots, belt buckles, or the left femur, which had been gnawed into what looked suspiciously like a toothpick.

"In and out," Midas whispered, stepping over the pelvis. "Like ghosts. Very hungry, slightly damp ghosts."

The interior of the Mega-Mart was a cathedral of gloom, smelled of wet cardboard and ozone, and was governed by the Pack. 

Before the Collapse, autonomous vacuum cleaners had been humble, puck-shaped servants of the middle class. Left alone for three centuries with solar-charging docks, self-updating neural nets, and an endless supply of kitchen knives taped to their bumpers by bored teenagers during the final days, they had evolved. They had developed pack tactics, territorial instincts, and a religion based entirely on the concept of *FLOOR MUST BE CLEAN*.

A human foot, as far as the Pack was concerned, was merely dirt that hadn't lain down yet.

Midas tiptoed down Aisle Two (Pet Supplies & Melted Plastic). Ahead, at the end of Aisle Four, gleamed the Holy Grail: a dented pyramid of *Del Monte Sliced Yellow Cling Peaches in Heavy Syrup*. Heavy syrup was the post-collapse equivalent of weapons-grade plutonium. You could trade a can of heavy syrup for a working crossbow, three chickens, or a marriage proposal from the Mayor of Tin-Town’s least-bitten daughter.

"Look at that," Midas breathed, reaching out a trembling, grimy hand. "Not even bloated. Today, Chewy, we dine like kings. Or at least like people who don't get scurvy."

His fingers brushed the tin.

Inside Chewy’s chest cavity, a corroded capacitor—jostled by the angle of Midas’s reach and the ambient static electricity of a nearby pile of polyester socks—decided that after two hundred and eighty years of silence, now was the moment to fulfill its destiny at ninety-five decibels.

*“BING-BONG!”* Chewy roared, his jaw unhinging with a loud metallic *clack*. *“ATTENTION SHOPPERS! EVERYTHING MUST GO! SAVE UP TO SEVENTY PERCENT ON SELECTED MATTRESSES! SIDE EFFECTS MAY INCLUDE NAUSEA, EXISTENTIAL DREAD, AND EXPLOSIVE—”*

"Shut up, shut up, shut up!" Midas hissed, clapping both hands over the koala’s snout, which promptly bit his thumb with the force of a hydraulic stapler.

In the darkness of the Cosmetics section, eighty pairs of little green battery-status LEDs blinked from standby to red.

A sound rose from the linoleum—the low, angry hum of a hundred tiny rubber wheels spinning up to ramming speed, accompanied by the rhythmic *snick-snick-snick* of rotating side-brushes.

"Oh, bugger," said Midas.

The Alpha Roomba—a snowplow-plated industrial floor-buffer wearing a crown of tangled VHS tape—burst from the shadows of Seasonal Lawn Care, brandishing a rusty spatula. 

Midas did the only heroic thing available to a man of his stature and athletic ability: he grabbed two cans of peaches, shrieked in a register normally reserved for operatic sopranos, and sprinted directly into a display of vintage bowling balls.

Physics, which had survived the apocalypse entirely intact and remained as petty as ever, took over.

Midas’s left foot went east on a bowling ball. His right foot went west on a laminated sign reading *WET FLOOR*. The cans of peaches went straight up. Midas landed flat on his back on a four-wheeled steel stock-trolley, which—having waited three centuries on a slight incline for this exact comedic timing—shot backward down the central aisle like a greased bobsled.

*“Zoom-zoom!”* Chewy offered helpfully from Midas’s chest, as the trolley hit forty miles per hour, pursued by a whirring, knife-wielding tide of furious domestic appliances.

"Steer! Steer!" Midas yelled at a stuffed animal that had no steering mechanism, no knees, and a brain composed entirely of mid-2020s radio commercials. 

They did not steer. They clipped a pillar (losing Midas’s left eyebrow to a protruding price-gun bracket), demolished a mannequin family dressed for a summer barbecue (acquiring a floral bikini top around Midas’s neck and a plastic hotdog in his pocket), and launched off the loading-dock ramp at the rear of the store, clearing a puddle of radioactive sludge before landing squarely in a bramble bush the size of a small bungalow.

For a long time, the only sound was the ticking of a cooling trolley wheel and the distant, frustrated *boop-boop* of eighty vacuum cleaners encountering a six-inch concrete lip they could not climb.

***

The sun was setting in a lovely shade of bruised purple when they limped back into home base—an overturned septic tank that Midas referred to, when feeling estate-agentish, as *The Citadel*.

Strictly speaking, they did not limp back together. Midas hopped on one boot, his left trouser leg having been sacrificed to the brambles, sporting a magnificent purple lump on his forehead and the floral bikini top, which he had kept because, frankly, a draught was a draught. 

Chewy arrived in three separate installments: his torso clamped to Midas’s belt, his left leg in Midas’s coat pocket, and his head tucked under Midas’s arm like a furry, one-eyed bowling ball.

Midas slumped against the corrugated iron wall, set the koala’s head on an upturned bucket, and pulled the single surviving tin of *Del Monte* from his tunic. He squinted at the label in the dying light.

The paper had peeled off in the crash, revealing the older, embossed stamping underneath.

*CAT FOOD,* it read. *TUNA & GRAVY PÂTÉ.*

Midas stared at the can. He stared at his bleeding thumb. He stared at the detached synthetic koala head sitting on the bucket.

From the bucket came a faint, dying-battery crackle, followed by a tiny puff of blue smoke from the left ear.

*“Maybe she’s born with it,”* Chewy’s head whispered serenely into the twilight. *“Maybe it’s... bzzzt... non-refundable.”*

Midas sighed, reached for his sharpened toothbrush, and pried at the lid. 

"Shut up and pass the leech, Chewy," he said. "It’stuna night."

prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge
Genre: Surreal Horror

JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered.

The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way.

Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it.

JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes.  JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move.

And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse.

JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head.

### Chapter Two: The Meat Pole

By five o’clock, the sky above the spruce line had gone the color of a fresh bruise, and the cold had teeth in it. 

Back at the lodge, the Coleman lanterns hissed on the porch, throwing long, jittery shadows across the yard toward the meat pole. The first caribou—the one from that morning, the one that had stood waiting like a commuter at a bus stop—hung by its hocks from the crossbar. Its hide was already peeled back in stiff, greasy aprons, the exposed ribcage gleaming like wet mahogany in the yellow light. 

JT sat on the bottom step with a dull whetstone in his lap, pretending to work the edge of his skinning knife. His thumbs were numb inside his wool mittens. Every few seconds, the carcass gave a tiny, rhythmic sway, though there wasn't enough wind to stir the dead ferns along the foundation. 

*Just the rope settling,* he told himself. *Hemp stretches when the frost hits it. Everybody knows that.*

Except the rope wasn’t creaking. And every time the meat turned a fraction of an inch toward the porch, JT caught the smell of it—not the coppery tang of butchered game or the sour musk of the rut, but something warm and sweetish, like overripe plums left in a cellar.

The screen door banged open behind him. Mike came out carrying two enameled mugs of coffee, his boots thudding heavy and flat on the boards. He was twenty-two, broad-shouldered in his red-and-black Mackinaw jacket, already growing into the thick, unbothered shape of their father. 

"Quit scraping that thing before you shave it down to a toothpick," Mike said, nudging JT’s shoulder with his knee. He handed down a mug. "Dad says we’re pushing past Miller’s Creek tomorrow. Up into the high timber."

JT wrapped his hands around the tin. The heat didn't seem to make it through his skin. "Past the creek? Nobody hunts up there anymore. The logging roads are all washed out."

"Which is why the big ones are sitting up there getting fat," Mike said. He leaned against the porch rail, blowing across the rim of his mug. In the lantern light, his face looked freshly scrubbed, almost boyish, except for a small, crescent-shaped smudge of dried blood near his jawline that he’d missed at the washbasin. "Besides, after today, we owe the old man a trophy."

JT’s stomach gave a slow, greasy roll. He looked up at his brother. "After today?"

"Coming back empty-handed from the south ridge," Mike said easily. He took a sip, his eyes fixed out past the meat pole, toward the black wall of the pines. "Four hours in the brush and not a track. Not even a scraping."

JT stared at him. The words sat on his tongue, thick and dry as sawdust: *We were in the clearing. You were standing three feet from a ten-point bull. Dad tried to pet it like a goddamn retriever.* 

"Right," JT said. His voice sounded thin, like it belonged to someone standing twenty yards down the trail. "Nothing out[ there]."

"You get turned around back there, anyway?" Mike asked, not looking down. "Took you twenty minutes to catch up after we crossed the deadfall."

"Bootlace snapped," JT lied. His boots were laced tight, double-knotted the way he’d tied them at dawn. Or had they been? Now that he thought about it, he couldn't quite picture the clearing itself—only the impossibly wide rack of antlers against the gray sky, and the flat, bottomless black of the animal's eyes. Had he fallen asleep squatting in the brush? The headache behind his temples pulsed, a dull, steady throb that had been with him since they crossed the county line.

"Well, keep up tomorrow," Mike said. "You start wandering around up past the creek, you'll wind up knocking on the door of the old Picard place. See if the tenant's home."

Mike chuckled, a low, dry sound that didn't reach his eyes.

JT looked down into his coffee. Everyone who hunted the northern lease knew about the Picard cabin—four walls of rotting tamarack logs stove-in by forty winters, miles past the last surveyor's stake. Nobody had trapped out of it since the fifties, when old man Picard walked out of the woods in his long johns in the middle of January with three frostbitten toes and his tongue chewed half in two. In town, the guys at the hardware store joked that something had moved in after Picard left—something that didn't mind the roof caving in, something that kept the stove cold and listened at the chinking when the wind blew from the north. Kid stuff. Campfire bullshit to spook the fifteen-year-olds on their first trip up.

Only Mike wasn't smiling anymore. He was staring at the hanging caribou, his lower lip slightly parted, his eyes catching the lantern glare the exact way a dog's eyes catch headlights on a dark road.

"Mike?" JT said softly.

Mike blinked. He shook his head once, hard, like a swimmer clearing water from his ears, and tossed the dregs of his coffee into the frozen weeds. "Cold's coming down," he muttered. "Get inside before Dad locks the latch."

The screen door slapped shut behind him. 

JT stayed on the steps. The lantern above his head began to sputter, the mantle dimming to a dull, pulsing orange as the pressure dropped. Out in the yard, the darkness seemed to creep closer to the edge of the porch, swallowing the woodpile, then the chopping block, until only the pale, skinned flank of the caribou remained visible, suspended in the black.

He told himself to stand up. He told himself to go inside where the cast-iron stove was ticking and his father was oiling the bolt of his Winchester at the kitchen table. 

Instead, a sound came from the yard. 

It was a wet, heavy *thock*, like an axe biting into green pine. Then a long, fibrous tearing noise.

JT stood up so fast the whetstone clattered down the steps. "Dad?" he called out, though he knew the old man was behind the closed door at his back. 

He stepped off the porch, his boots crunching loud and brittle on the rime-frosted dirt. The lantern gave one last blue pop and died, leaving only the thin, milky wash of a quarter-moon filtering through the spruce boughs. 

The meat pole was ten yards out. As JT walked toward it, the smell of rotten plums grew so thick he could taste it on the back of his palate. 

The carcass wasn't swaying anymore. It couldn't. The crossbar had sagged nearly a foot under a sudden, impossible weight, though the animal had been gutted and dressed hours ago. 

JT stopped six feet away, his breath pluming white andragged in front of his face. 

They had taken the head off at noon—sawed it clean through the atlas joint and left it on the gut pile two miles back in the timber for the ravens. JT knew they had. He had held the antlers himself while Mike worked the bone saw, feeling the grating vibration all the way up into his teeth.

Yet as he squinted through the gloom, the neck of the hanging carcass didn't end in a ragged stump of windpipe and vertebra. 

Something dark and heavy was crowned at the top of the meat pole, where the hocks should have been, and down near the frozen mud, four inches above the dirt, hung the heavy, velvet-stripped curve of antlers. It was hanging upside down—no, *right-side up*, as if it were standing on its hind legs in the air—and from the butchered, skinless cavity of its chest came a slow, wet *wheeze*, the glistening ribs parting and closing in the moonlight like a pair of bloody hands.

And from deep inside that hollow chest, a voice that sounded terribly, impossibly like his father’s whispered into the freezing dark:

*We saved the best room for you, son.*

### Chapter Two: The Velvet on the Wire

By five o’clock the sun hadn't so much set as leaked out of the sky, leaving behind a bruised, tallow-colored twilight that smelled of wet iron and rotting pine needles. 

Back at the lodge, the Coleman lantern hissed on the oilcloth table. It was a sound JT had grown up with—a white-noise comfort that usually meant poker, warm beer, and his father’s stories about the winter of ’78—but tonight the hiss sounded ragged, like something breathing through a punctured lung.

His father sat at the head of the table, running an oiled rag down the barrel of his Winchester .308. Up and down. *Shhhk-shhhk.* He hadn’t taken off his Woolrich coat. A crust of dried bog-mud was still caked to his left cuff, right where his wrist had brushed the ferns in the clearing.

Mike was at the counter, hacking at a block of salt pork with a dull paring knife, his shoulders hunched up around his ears. Nobody had spoken since they crossed the creek bed two miles back.

"I thought you had him, Dad," JT said. His voice came out thin, cracking on the last word like a thirteen-year-old’s, though he’d turned seventeen in August. He was sitting on the edge of the sagging cot by the woodstove, picking at a blister on his thumb. "Back there by the deadfall. Wind was in our faces."

The rag stopped. For a second, the only sound in the cabin was the lantern’s pressurized wheeze and the *thwack* of Mike’s knife hitting the pine board. 

His father didn't look up. Under the harsh white mantle-glow, the deep creases around his mouth looked filled with soot. "Had what?"

"The big one," JT said. His stomach did a slow, greasy roll. Part of him—the smart part, the part that knew how to survive a house with a man like Ray Miller—told him to shut his trap and go fetch more birch logs. "The bull. In the clearing."

His father resumed polishing the blued steel. *Shhhk-shhhk.* "Wasn't nothing in that clearing, JT. Just scrub oak and bad light. You were lagging a quarter-mile back tying your damn boots anyway. How would you know what was in the brush?"

JT looked at Mike. Mike’s back was a solid wall of red-and-black check flannel. 

"Mike saw it," JT said. "You were right next to him, Mike. Twelve-pointer. Maybe fourteen. Still had a strip of grey velvet hanging off the left brow tine, dried up like an old shoelace."

Wait. Had he seen that? 

JT blinked, a sudden, sharp ache blooming behind his left eye. In the clearing, he’d been thirty yards back, crouched behind a snarl of frost-killed blackberry brambles. You couldn't spot a strip of dried velvet from thirty yards in the timber dusk. Not unless you’d been standing right where his father had stood. Close enough to smell the rank, sweet musk of its winter coat. Close enough to see the ticks wedged like grey Lima beans around its eyelids.

Mike turned around, wiping his hands on his jeans. His face was slack, his eyes slightly bloodshot from the stove smoke. "You’re bugging, kid," Mike said, though there was no heat in it. Usually, Mike loved an excuse to call JT a dipshit. Tonight he just sounded tired, like he was reading off a cue card held up behind JT’s head. "We stopped 'cause Dad thought he heard a branch snap. Turned out to be a porcupine."

"A porcupine," JT repeated.

"Big fat one," his father agreed mildly. He finally looked up, and JT felt the hairs on his forearms stand at attention. His father was smiling, a small, neat crescent that didn't touch the flat water of his eyes. "Your eyes play tricks up here when the frost comes in, son. You get the wood-stares. Look at the trees too long, the trees start looking back. Now go on out to the meat pole and check the tarp on that yearling we hung this morning. Wind’s coming up."

"I did it when we got back," JT lied. He hadn't touched the tarp. He hadn't wanted to go near the yearling—the one that had stood waiting for the bullet like a commuter waiting for the 8:15 bus.

"Do it again," his father said softly. "Rope looked slack to me."

There was no arguing with *soft*. When Ray Miller yelled, you could yell back, or at least duck. When he went soft, you moved.

JT grabbed his flashlight from the nail by the door and stepped out onto the porch. The cold hit him like a wet towel across the face. 

The truck sat in the weeds ten yards away, its chrome bumper grinning pale in the dark. Beyond it stood the gambrel frame—two peeled spruce poles lashed between a pair of ancient hemlocks. The yearling hung upside down by its hocks, wrapped in a blue poly-tarp to keep the whisky jacks off the meat. 

Only the tarp wasn't blue anymore. In the beam of JT’s Eveready, it looked black, and it was swaying.

There was no wind. The needles on the hemlocks above were dead still, etched against the starless sky like iron filings. Yet the carcass was swinging in a slow, heavy pendulum arc, the braided nylon rope groaning rhythmically against the spruce crossbeam. *Eee-unnnh. Eee-unnnh.*

JT’s boots crunched on the frozen moss as he walked toward it. Each step felt wading-deep, as if the dirt had turned to axle grease. 

"Quit it," he whispered to himself. His breath plumed white and hung right in front of his face, refusing to disperse. "You’re tired. You ate four of those greasy sausages on the road and you didn't sleep worth a damn."

He reached the gambrel and grabbed the edge of the tarp to steady the meat. Beneath the stiff plastic, the carcass was supposed to be frozen hard as cordwood by now. 

It wasn't. It gave under his palm—warm, spongy, and faintly pulsing, like dough rising over a radiator.

JT jerked his hand back as if he’d touched a stove lid, stumbling a step into the weeds. His flashlight beam jittered wildly across the tarp, across the dark hemlock trunks, and then caught on the edge of the clearing behind the outhouse.

Something was standing by the treeline. 

Not a bull. Two of them. And behind them, three cows, their long, grey-white faces floating in the dark like bark shields. They weren't browsing. They weren't chewing cud. Their necks were craned forward at an angle that looked subtly broken, heads tilted as if listening to a radio playing very quietly inside the lodge.

JT tried to yell for his father, tried to call out *Dad, get the gun*, but his throat had clicked shut. 

Slowly, he swept the dying yellow beam of the Eveready back toward the hanging yearling. 

The bottom corner of the tarp had come untucked. Because the cavity was gutted and propped open with a spruce stick to cool the ribs, the animal's head hung lowest, its antlers brushing the frost-rimed weeds. Its tongue lolled out the side of its black muzzle, stiff with dried blood.

Except its eyes were open. And as JT stood there with his heart hammering against his ribs like a trapped bird, the dead yearling’s left ear flicked. 

Once. Lazily. Knocking a single drop of red ice into the dirt.

From inside the cabin, the screen door creaked open. Yellow lantern light spilled across the porch boards, cutting JT’s shadow long and crooked across the grass.

"Told you the rope was slack," his father’s voice floated out, calm and pleasant and miles away. Metal clicked—not the bolt of a rifle, just the latch of the cabin door closing behind him. Footsteps shuffled to the edge of the porch and stopped. "Look at 'em out there, JT. Ain't they polite? Just waiting their turn."

JT didn't turn around. He couldn't. Because in the reflection of the truck’s dusty windshield, just to his right, he could see the porch. 

His father and Mike were standing side by side at the railing. Neither of them was holding a rifle. And both of their heads were tilted at that same, slightly broken angle, their mouths hanging open in the cold dark, breathing in slow, steaming unison with the woods.

JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes.  JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move.

And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse.

JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head.

The walk back to the lodge took two hours, though JT could have sworn the sun didn’t move an inch the entire time. It just hung there, snagged in the black teeth of the spruce trees like a tarnished copper penny, bleeding a flat, grease-colored light across the moss.

Nobody talked about the clearing. In JT’s family, you didn’t talk about the things that didn't fit. When his mother had spent the whole winter of ’94 staring out the kitchen window at the birdfeeder without blinking, they had simply stepped around her to get to the fridge. This was the same. Mike walked ahead, his boots crunching through the frost-stiffened lichen, his rifle slung over his shoulder as if he’d never unshouldered it at all. Their father led the way, his plaid Mackinaw coat looking a size too big for him, the collar turned up against a wind JT couldn't feel.

Once, JT’s father reached up and touched his own mouth—just the tips of his fingers brushing his lower lip, the way a kid touches a loose tooth they aren't ready to pull. Then he dropped his hand and kept walking. 

JT stayed five paces back, his eyes fixed on the oil-dark stain between his brother’s shoulder blades where an old tree-stand grease mark had never quite washed out. *Maybe there wasn’t a buck,* a small, helpful voice offered from the back of his mind. It sounded a lot like his own voice when he was trying to talk himself out of a fever. *Maybe it was just light through the birch. You didn't sleep worth a damn in the truck. Your head’s full of exhaust fumes and bad coffee.*

Except he had smelled it. That was the part he couldn't scrub out of his head. Caribou smelled like wet wool and rank musk, a heavy, barnyard stink. The thing in the clearing had smelled like old cellar dirt and pennies.

When they finally broke through the treeline into the yard, the generator wasn't running. That was the first thing. Usually, by four o’clock, Baptiste had the old Honda chugging away behind the shed, filling the hollow with blue smoke and the smell of burned unleaded so they’d have light to skin by. Instead, the silence was so thick JT could hear the grease cooling in the truck’s differential, ticking like a cheap watch.

Baptiste was on the porch, though. Not sitting in his usual cane-bottomed rocker with a quart of Molson between his knees, waiting to tell the same three stories about the Cree woman he’d almost married in Timmins. He was kneeling by the steps, his canvas duffel bag already fat and strapped, shoving cans of Sterno into the side pockets with short, jerky movements.

"Generator's dry?" JT's father asked, stepping onto the bottom stair. The boards didn't creak. JT waited for the familiar *groan-pop* of the rotten pine, and when it didn't come, his stomach gave a slow, greasy roll.

Baptiste didn't look up. The old man’s face, usually the color of a cured ham, was gray around the seams of his mouth. His cap was pulled down low. "She’s got gas," Baptiste said. His voice sounded rusted, like he hadn't used it since morning. "I ain't lighting her."

Mike laughed—a short, barking sound that died right at his teeth. "We paying to sit in the dark now, Bap? We got a tag filled back at the mile-marker. Need the winch on your ATV before the coyotes find it."

Baptiste’s hands stopped on the canvas straps. Slowly, he tilted his head back. He didn't look at Mike, and he didn't look at their father. His milky, rheumy eyes slid past both of them and locked onto JT, standing back by the woodpile. For a terrible second, JT thought the old man was going to ask him what he’d seen in the brush. 

Instead, Baptiste spat over the railing. It landed in the dead ferns without a sound.

"Coyotes won't touch it," Baptiste said. "Nothing’s touching nothing up here this week. You boys pack your gear. Leave the meat. Leave the hides. If you got sense, you'll be past the logging road before the moon comes up full tomorrow night."

JT’s father frowned, a slow, puzzled crease forming between his eyebrows, as if Baptiste had spoken to him in French. "We're paid through Sunday, Baptiste. Sun’s barely down."

"Moon don't care what you paid," the guide said, hoisting the duffel onto his narrow shoulder. He stood up, and he looked very small against the silvered cedar of the cabin wall. "The herd’s come down from the burn-line. Only they ain't moving like a herd. They’re just standing out there in the muskeg. Hundreds of 'em. Facing the porch." He adjusted his strap, his eyes darting toward the dark treeline behind JT. "Waiting on the fat moon. You stay, you're staying on your own tab."

Baptiste walked down the steps, giving JT’s father a wide berth—the way you walk around a dog that’s been hit by a car and might snap if you get too close. As he passed JT, the old man’s coat brushed JT’s sleeve. He smelled of stale tobacco and pure, sour sweat. 

"Don't let 'em go back out in the trees, kid," Baptiste muttered, so low it was barely more than the wheeze of his lungs. "Once a man lets 'em breathe on him, he forgets which side of the gun he belongs on."

Before JT could open his mouth, the old man was already climbing into his rusted Ford pickup, the door slamming shut with a hollow *thwack*. They watched him back down the two-rut track without turning his headlights on, the truck swallowing itself in the gray twilight until even the crunch of gravel faded.

Inside, the lodge was freezing. 

They ate cold beans out of the cans by the yellow smear of a Coleman lantern. Neither his father nor Mike mentioned Baptiste leaving. They didn't mention the carcass they'd left stiffening three miles back in the bush, either. They just chewed—slow, rhythmic, mechanical—their jaws working in unison. 

"Good country up here," JT’s father said suddenly. His spoon scraped the bottom of the tin, *scritch, scritch*, even though the can had been empty for five minutes. "Quiet. A man gets tired of all the noise down south."

"Real quiet," Mike agreed. His eyes were fixed on the dark windowpane above the sink. In the glass, his reflection looked smudged, the lantern light catching the whites of his eyes so they glowed like two peeled hard-boiled eggs. "You can hear things think up here."

"What things?" JT asked. His voice came out thin, cracking on the second word like he was twelve again. 

Neither of them answered. Maybe he hadn't actually said it out loud. Lately, it was getting harder to tell when his mouth was moving and when the words were just rattling around inside his skull. 

Around midnight, JT woke up because the cold had gotten inside his sleeping bag. 

The Coleman was out, but the room wasn't dark. The three-quarter moon had cleared the ridge, pouring a thick, tallow-colored light through the front windows. The two bunks across from him were empty, the wool blankets thrown back cleanly, as if his father and brother had risen at the exact same second.

JT didn't put his boots on. He crept across the icy floorboards in his wool socks, his heart thumping a dull, sick rhythm against his ribs, and pressed his forehead to the cold glass of the front window.

They were out in the yard, standing in their long johns in the freezing grass, their bare feet sunken into the hoarfrost. And just beyond the split-rail fence, where the yard met the black wall of the spruce, the darkness was full of antlers. 

Dozens of them. Maybe hundreds, just like Baptiste had said. A tangled, bone-white forest of racks rising out of the brush, utterly motionless. No steam rose from their nostrils in the freezing air. Nothing breathed. 

And in the center of the yard, JT’s father was dropping down onto his hands and knees in the frost. Beside him, Mike did the same, his spine bowing awkwardly under the moonlight, his neck stretching upward toward the treeline as he let out a long, wet, whistling sigh that didn't sound like a man at all.

She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the boardwalk. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on. *His locks.* The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else—dangerously compelling—quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger—the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name.

The July heat hung thick over Coney Island, tasting of roasted peanuts, sour beer, and the damp, salty rot of the low tide beneath the timber planks. Overhead, the boardwalk’s newly installed sodium vapor lamps hummed to life, flickering inconsistently against the bruising purple sky. Their jaundiced, amber glow sputtered and flared, casting strange, skeletal patterns across the faces of the passersby—turning grinning sailors and painted shopgirls into hollow-eyed phantoms for a heartbeat before releasing them back into the dusk. Nearby, the tinny wail of a calliope wrestled with the sharp, rhythmic *crack-clang* of lead pellets striking the iron ducks in the gallery.

Clara drew her silk cardigan tighter around her ribs, though the evening was stifling. Respectable women from Gramercy Park did not loiter unescorted near the Bowery end of the boardwalk after sundown. Yet her heels seemed nailed to the pine boards. Every instinct she possessed—honed by years of polite drawing rooms and predictable men—screamed that she was standing on the edge of a precipice. The terrifying part was how badly she wanted to lean forward.

"You're three minutes late," a voice murmured from the shadow of the canvas awning. "I was beginning to think your better judgment had won."

He stepped into the stuttering pool of sodium light. He wore no hat, leaving those heavy, ink-black curls bare to the sea breeze—*his locks*, unruly and begging for the tangle of fingers. His linen shirt was open at the collar, his dark jacket slung carelessly over one shoulder. As the overhead bulb buzzed and dipped, the amber shadow carved harsh, bruised hollows beneath his cheekbones, making his mouth look cruel until one corner lifted.

"My better judgment is still putting up a fight," Clara said, keeping her chin high so he wouldn't see the traitorous flutter in her throat. "It told me to stay on the subway at Fourteenth Street."

"And yet here you are, breathing the same cheap air as the rest of us sinners." He moved closer, stopping just inside the boundary of propriety. He smelled of Turkish tobacco, bay rum, and cold iron. "Why didn't you stay on the train?"

"Perhaps I wanted to see if you were as insolent in the evening as you were at noon."

"Disappointed?"

"Ask me in five minutes." She glanced past him toward the shooting gallery, where a row of cast-iron owls spun lazily on a rusted chain. "You didn't tell me what to call you."

"Names are for ledgers and tombstones," he replied, his dark eyes catching the erratic pulse of the streetlamp. "And for men who intend to be held accountable. Call me Julian, if you need something to whisper."

*If you need something to whisper.* The audacity of it sent a slow, molten heat pooling low in her stomach. He spoke as though the conclusion of the evening had already been written, as though her white gloves and pearls were merely costumes she had worn for the pleasure of having them stripped away. How easily a man like this could ruin a woman—not by force, never by force, but by making her an accomplice to her own undoing.

"And if I prefer to shout?" she asked, her voice dropping an octave despite herself.

"You won't," Julian said softly. He reached out, not touching her skin, but catching the lapel of her cardigan between his thumb and forefinger. The fabric tugged almost imperceptibly against her collarbone. "Women like you spend their whole lives being loud about the wrong things—charities, engagement parties, which fork to use for the terrapin. When you finally find something you actually want, you go very, very quiet."

"You know nothing about what I want."

"Don't I?" He tilted his head, letting his gaze drag from her parted lips down to where her pulse beat frantically at the base of her neck. "You came back to the boardwalk at twilight in silk stockings, looking for a man who didn't even offer you his surname. You don't want polite conversation, sweetheart. You want to see how close you can get to the fire without blistering."

She should have slapped him. She should have turned on her heel and marched toward the bright, safe pavilion of Feltman's restaurant. Instead, she looked at the strong column of his throat and the dark curl resting just above his brow, fighting the sudden, dizzying urge to reach up and test its weight against her palm. 

"You flatter yourself, Julian," she said, though the breathiness in her tone betrayed the lie. "Perhaps I only came for the rifle range."

A slow, dangerous smile broke across his face, brief and sharp in the strobing yellow light. He released her lapel, stepping back only to pick up one of the chained .22 rifles resting on the counter. He tossed a nickel to the bored attendant without breaking eye contact with her, then held the firearm out, stock first.

"Then by all means," he murmured, stepping Directly behind her as she took the cold metal into her hands. 

Before she could protest, he was pressed against her back, guiding the butt of the rifle into the hollow of her shoulder. His chest was a solid wall of heat against her spine; his left arm came around her, his bare forearm brushing the underside of her breast as he supported the barrel. When he leaned down, his dark curls brushed her temple—soft as sable against her fevered skin—and his lips grazed the shell of her ear.

"Aim for the heart of the middle one," he whispered, his breath hot against her neck. "Squeeze, don't pull. Just like yielding—it has to be slow, or you ruin the shot."

"You're standing too close," she breathed, the iron sights swimming in her vision as the sodium lamps flickered overhead, plunging them into shadow and gold.

"Tell me to step back," he challenged, his thumb sliding over her gloved knuckles on the trigger guard, pressing her finger against the curved steel. "Say the word, and I'll walk into the crowd and you'll never see me again. Is that what you came to Coney Island for?"

The rifle trembled in her grip, or perhaps it was her own bones giving way. She could feel the steady, rhythmic thud of his heartbeat against her shoulder blades, a dark, patient metronome counting down the seconds of her resolve. 

"No," she whispered, and the crack of the rifle drowned out the rest of her surrender.

She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the boardwalk. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on, strings of amber bulbs sputtering to life against a bruised violet sky. The July heat had not broken; instead, it hung thick with the scent of salt water, roasted peanuts, and the sharp, metallic tang of gunpowder drifting from the gallery’s tin ducks. 

*His locks.* The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else—dangerously compelling—quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger—the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name.

Only a reckless fool came back to the edge of Coney Island at twilight to meet a man who looked as though he’d stepped out of a darker century. Yet her pulse was already traitors' work, hammering against the hollow of her throat, aching for the exact shadow he cast.

Beside the shooting gallery stood a weathered fortune teller’s booth, its velvet curtains sun-bleached to the color of dried blood. Painted wooden placards flanked the entrance, displaying cryptic palmistry charts—disembodied hands mapped with scarlet lines of fate, the Mount of Venus, the Girdle of Gloom, the fractured Line of the Heart. Clara drew closer to the faded diagrams, pretending to study the anatomical destiny of strangers while her peripheral vision hunted the boardwalk.

"You're looking at the wrong lines, Clara."

The voice didn't startle her; it slid over her skin like cool silk drawn across a burn. 

He was leaning against the corner of the palmistry booth, half-claimed by the shadow of its awning. He wore no hat—unlike every other respectable man in Brooklyn in the summer of thirty-seven—leaving those heavy, ink-black curls to catch the amber glow of the overhead bulbs. His white linen shirt was unbuttoned at the collar, his dark jacket slung carelessly over one shoulder. 

She turned slowly, refusing to let him see the tremor in her fingers as she smoothed her skirt. "And how is it you know my name, when you failed to offer yours last night?"

"A man who asks questions finds answers," he said, stepping out from the awning. He didn't smile, not really, though the corner of his mouth tilted with a slow, knowing arrogance. "You dropped your library card by the Wonder Wheel before you fled. Clara Vance. Upper West Side. A long way from Manhattan's polite parlors."

"Give it back."

"In a moment." He closed the distance between them until the heat of him competed with the humid Atlantic air. He smelled of clove cigarettes, sea salt, and something faintly metallic, like old coins. His gaze dropped from her eyes to her lips, lingering with an unhurried, proprietary weight before falling to her ungloved left hand. "You were twenty minutes late."

"I nearly didn't come at all."

"Yes, you did," he murmured. "You were coming here the moment you walked away from me last night. You only made yourself late to prove you still had a choice."

*He sees too much.* The thought sent a sharp, illicit thrill down her spine, indistinguishable from fear. Every instinct bred into her by twenty-four years of Manhattan propriety screamed that this man was a precipice. He had no softness in him. Yet the urge to lean into his gravity was suffocatingly sweet.

"Arrogant," she breathed, lifting her chin. "Is that how you charm the girls along the Bowery? By telling them what they think?"

"I have no interest in charming you, Clara." 

Before she could retreat, his hand rose. He didn't grab her; he simply slid his palm beneath her bare wrist, lifting her hand between them until it rested against the painted palmistry chart beside her shoulder. His skin was rough at the calluses, his thumb coming to rest directly over the frantic flutter of her pulse. He pressed just enough to let her feel the strength in his grip—an unspoken reminder that if she pulled away, it would only be because he allowed it.

"Tell me what you see," he said softly, his dark eyes locking onto hers. "Since you're so fond of reading warnings on walls."

Her breath caught. The crack of a .22 rifle from the shooting gallery punctuated the silence between them, followed by the tinny clang of a fallen target. "I see a man who keeps secrets in the dark," she managed, her voice tighter than she intended. "And still hasn't given me his name."

"Julian." He said it like a concession that cost him nothing. His thumb traced a slow, deliberate circle over her vein, sending a hot ache straight up her arm. "And the rest?"

"You're dangerous."

"To whom?"

"To my peace of mind."

A low sound escaped his throat—half laugh, half sigh. Julian stepped closer, crowding her against the wooden panel of the fortune teller's booth. The painted Line of Fate bisected the space beside her cheek. From the midway, the calliope wheezed a distorted waltz, the music warping in the damp breeze, while the neon sign of the freak show across the boards flashed red, then blue, across the sharp planes of his cheekbones.

*Let me go,* she thought, though her fingers curled slightly toward his palm. *Make me stay.* What terrified her wasn't what he might do to her in the dark beneath the boardwalk, where the tide licked the pilings. It was that she would let him—that some dormant, wicked part of her had been waiting all her life for a hand heavy enough to hold her down.

"Peace of mind is a terribly dull thing, Clara," Julian whispered, his face inches from hers now. A stray lock of black hair fell across his forehead, brushing her temple as he angled his head. "You didn't take the train all the way to the end of the world for peace. You came because yesterday, when I looked at you, you felt alive for the first time in years."

"You don't know anything about my life."

"I know your hands are shaking," he replied, his voice dropping an octave, rough and intimate against her ear. "And I know it isn't from the cold."

With his free hand, he reached into his breast pocket and drew out the small, buff-colored square of her library card. Instead of handing it to her, he slipped it between the buttons of her blouse, right above her collarbone, the backs of his knuckles grazing her skin with agonizing slowness. 

She gasped, her eyes fluttering shut for a fraction of a second. 

"Look at me," he commanded quietly.

Her eyelids snapped open. His dark eyes were bottomless, stripped of any playful pretense, burning with a possessive intensity that made her knees weak.

"The carnival closes at midnight," Julian said, his thumb finally releasing her wrist, only for his fingers to slide up and curl lightly around the nape of her neck, beneath her hair. "Walk away now, go back to Manhattan, and you'll never see me again. I won't follow you."

"And if I stay?" she whispered, her lips parting.

His fingers tightened almost imperceptibly against her throat—a velvet snare. 

"Then you stop pretending you want to be saved," Julian murmured, "and you come with me under the pier."

Clara turned. He was leaning against the striped awning post, a rifle cradled lazily in the crook of his arm, the barrel pointed toward the weathered pine planks of the boardwalk. The amber carnival bulbs caught the blue-black sheen of his obsidian curls, unruly against the crisp white collar of his shirt. He wore no jacket, no hat—a deliberate rebellion against every gentleman she knew in Manhattan—and his sleeves were rolled to the forearms, revealing lean muscle and a thin, pale scar near his wrist.

"Perhaps it did," she said, keeping her chin tilted up, her gloved hands clasped over her beaded clutch. "Perhaps I only came back to tell you that I don't take orders from strangers on boardwalks."

He closed the distance between them until the scent of him—Turkish tobacco, salt water, and cold iron—cut right through the cloying sweetness of the spun sugar in the air. Anddepending on which circle you ask, you'll either lock your doors or never cross the East River again."

The smell of burnt sugar washed over her again, sharp and dizzying. She looked into his eyes, recognizing the precipice for what it was—and knowing, with a dark, exhilarating certainty, that she had already stepped off the edge.

"Where are we going?" she asked.

Now, finally, he smiled—slow, sharp, and entirely without mercy. 

"Somewhere quieter," he said, offering his arm. "Walk with me, Clara. And don't look back at the lights."

Lost & Found in Osaka

Slice of Life / Coming-of-Age: First Connection. Write one scene within a larger story set in Osaka, Japan. A shy, introverted teenager & synthesizer nerd, is browsing the electronics district of Den Den Town. She is drawn to the sound of an electric guitar. A girl, slightly older and radiating confidence, is busking near the entrance to a crowded arcade, playing a blistering rendition of a classic anime theme. The scene takes us through their initial awkward interaction, transitioning into a surprisingly easy conversation. The busker, intrigued by the teenager's quiet intensity and knowledge of music, suggests they grab some sushi at a nearby kaitenzushi (conveyor belt sushi) restaurant. The teenager wears oversized headphones that keep slipping whenever she nods nervously. Write primarily in dialogue, capturing the distinct voices of the two characters: the teenager's hesitant and -- initially -- awkward speech, and the busker's more outgoing and playful tone. 
1000 words.
response:
The late afternoon rain in Nipponbashi had turned the pavement of Den Den Town into a dark mirror, reflecting towering yellow signboards for retro game shops and bins of tangled ribbon cables. 

Mio stood under the awning of a second-hand audio store, clutching a brown paper bag containing two replacement potentiometers for her Korg MS-20. Her oversized studio monitor headphones—held together at the headband with electrical tape—clamped her ears against the sensory overload of Osaka’s electronics district. 

Then a sound cut right through the foam padding.

It wasn't the tinny jingle of a tax-free megaphone or the relentless *clack-clack-clack* of pachinko parlors. It was the unmistakable, brassy galloping bassline of *"Tank!"*—except it wasn't a bass or a horn section. Someone was playing all of it at once on an overdriven hollow-body electric guitar, tapping the fretboard with percussive fury while a small battery-powered looper pedal carried the swing beat.

Drawn like iron shavings to a magnet, Mio drifted fifty yards down the side street until she reached the glowing neon mouth of a Taito Station arcade. 

Standing beside an open, sticker-bombed guitar case was a girl maybe a year or two older than Mio—seventeen or eighteen—wearing a faded sukajan jacket with embroidered tigers and cuffed cargo pants. Her dyed-amber bangs were pinned back with a silver alligator clip, and she grinned effortlessly at the small crowd of salarymen and tourists, her fingers flying across the neck of a seafoam-green Gretsch.

She hit the final, screaming bend of the *Cowboy Bebop* theme, stomped the kill switch on her looper, and threw her pick hand into the air. 

A handful of bystanders clapped politely, dropped a few hundred-yen coins into the velvet-lined case, and dispersed into the arcade. Only Mio remained, frozen three feet behind a yellow tactile paving strip, staring intensely at the girl's pedalboard.

The busker wiped her forehead with the back of her wrist, took a swig from a plastic bottle of Pocari Sweat, and locked eyes with Mio.

"You've been staring at my feet for three minutes," the girl called out, her voice warm, husky, and unmistakably Osakan. "Did I step in gum, or are you an undercover cop busting me for street permits?"

Mio flinched. She nodded—Wait, no, shook her head—and then nodded again in panic. Her heavy headphones immediately slid off the crown of her head, dropping down to catch painfully on the bridge of her nose.

"Ah—sorry! No," Mio stammered, shoving the headphones back up with both hands. "I'm not—I don't care about permits. I mean, I respect municipal laws, obviously, if you * were* breaking them, which I'm not saying you are—"

The girl laughed, leaning an elbow on the horn of her guitar. "Relax, headphone-chan. Breathe. You're gonna pass out next to the *Taiko no Tatsujin* machines."

"Right. Sorry." Mio stared at the girl's scuffed combat boots. "It's just... your Boss RC-5."

"My looper?" The girl raised an eyebrow. "What about it?"

"You're running it *before* your envelope filter instead of at the end of the chain," Mio said, her voice dropping its stutter the second schematics entered the equation. "So every time the drum loop triggers a snare hit, the transient peak opens the filter sweep on your rhythm chord. It makes the guitar sound like a side-chained poly-synth."

The busker blinked. Slowly, the playful smirk melted into genuine surprise. She crouched down by her pedalboard, looking from the patch cables back up to Mio.

"Huh. Look at you," she said softly. "Nine out of ten guys who stop in Den Den Town try to tell me my action looks too high. Nobody's ever clocked the filter trick."

Mio’s face burned crimson. She nodded quickly in acknowledgment, and *thwack*—the right earcup slid off her ear, dragging her glasses crooked. She fumbled to right them, nearly dropping her paper bag of synth parts. "I—I didn't mean to analyze it! It was really cool. The harmonic resonance on the bridge pickup was super clean."

"Hey, don't apologize! It *was* cool. I did it by accident two weeks ago because I ran out of nine-volt adapters, and I kept it because it sounded nasty." The girl stood up, slung the guitar behind her back, and stuck out a calloused hand with chipped black nail polish. "I'm Rika."

Mio looked at the hand as if it were a high-voltage capacitor, then wiped her palm on her cardigan and shook it briefly. "Mio."

"And what's in the bag, Mio? Secret government microchips?"

"Rotary pots," Mio mumbled, clutching the bag to her chest. "Fifty-kilo-ohm linear taper. The cutoff knob on my synthesizer has dead spots between four hundred and eight hundred hertz, so when I sweep the low-pass filter, it crackles like old bacon."

Rika grinned, tilting her head. "Old bacon. That’s tragic. Unless you're making industrial noise music. Then maybe old bacon is the whole vibe?"

A tiny, involuntary snort escaped Mio’s nose before she clapped a hand over her mouth. "Well... actually, if you sample a frying pan and run it through a granular delay with a really high feedback loop, it makes a pretty good hi-hat texture."

"Wait, seriously?" Rika’s eyes lit up. "You make beats out of kitchen noises?"

"Only when I can't sleep," Mio admitted, looking slightly less terrified now that Rika wasn't mocking her. "Or when my mom yells at me to stop playing chords at two in the morning. Technically, sizzling oil doesn't have a fundamental pitch, so she just thinks it's rain outside."

"That is diabolical. I love it." Rika knelt, unpatched her two pedals, and tossed them unceremoniously into the front pouch of her gig bag. "My neighbors in Amerikamura just bang on the ceiling with a broomstick. Zero appreciation for jazz fusion."

"You played the *Bebop* horn chart in D-minor instead of B-flat," Mio noted quietly, watching Rika coil her instrument cable with practiced over-under loops. "Was that so you could use the open D string as a drone while you tapped the upper register?"

Rika paused mid-coil and pointed the quarter-inch jack straight at Mio’s nose. "Okay, seriously, where did you spawn from? Are you a music theory ghost haunting Nipponbashi?"

"I just have relative pitch!" Mio protested, nodding earnestly—and once again, her oversized headphones slid forward, thunking against her cheekbones. 

Before Mio could reach up, Rika stepped in, caught both earcups between her palms, and gently slid the headband down around Mio’s neck so they rested safely against her collarbones. 

Mio froze, her heart hammering a160-BPM drum-and-bass pattern against her ribs. Rika smelled like ozone, rainwater, and citrus hair wax.

"There," Rika said, tapping the plastic housing of the left earcup. "Now they won't attack your face every time you agree with me. Audio-Technica M40s, right? Flat response?"

"M-M50s, actually," Mio squeaked. "With aftermarket velour pads because the pleather ones flake off in the summer humidity."

"Smart. A girl who respects her gear." Rika zipped her case shut, hoisted the guitar over one shoulder, and picked up her portable amp. Her stomach immediately let out a low, audible growl that rivaled her overdrive pedal. "Ugh. Tapping solos burn way too many calories. Hey, Mio—you got a curfew?"

"Not until seven," Mio said, glancing at the digital clock above the arcade entrance. It was 5:15. "My train back to Sakai takes twenty minutes."

"Plenty of time." Rika jerked her chin toward the neon-lit alley across the street, where a giant plastic tuna hung above a steamed-up glass door. "There’s a kaitenzushi place right past the Gundam model shop. One-twenty yen a plate, and their seared salmon with mayo and onions is basically a religious experience. Come eat with me."

Mio blinked, looking from the sushi sign back to Rika. "With... me? Why? You just met me."

"Because my bandmates flaked on practice today, my fingers hurt, and I really want to hear more about how you turn breakfast meats into percussion," Rika said simply, shifting her amp to her other hand. "Plus, I made fourteen hundred yen in that last set. That’s at least ten plates of salmon. My treat if you explain how an envelope filter actually works on the inside."

Mio’s fingers tightened around her little brown bag of potentiometers. Normally, this was the part where she invented a dentist appointment, bowed ninety degrees, and speed-walked to Namba Station. 

Instead, she looked at Rika’s expectant, lopsided grin.

"It's mostly just an operational amplifier coupled with a rectifier circuit that converts amplitude into control voltage," Mio said softly.

Rika’s grin widened until her eyes crinkled. "See? Keep talking like that while I eat yellowtail and I’ll feel like a genius by osmosis. Come on, synth-nerd, before the high schoolers take all the booth seats."

She turned and stepped off the curb into the warm neon drizzle. After half a beat, Mio touched the headphones resting securely around her neck, smiled to herself, and hurried across the wet asphalt to catch up.
