Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. Elliot hums a soft tune while waiting for images to reveal in the chemical bath. 1000 words.
response:
**Darkroom Revelations**

The amber safelight in the basement darkroom had a way of stripping the world down to bone and shadow. At two in the morning, with the ventilation fan humming a low, steady B-flat and the sharp, metallic tang of stop bath hanging in the damp air, the rest of the campus felt a hundred miles away. 

I leaned my hip against the stainless-steel sink, watching Elliot’s hands as he slid a sheet of fiber-based paper into the developer tray. Even in the monochrome red glow, his style was killer—an oversized, frayed mesh sweater layered over a faded Bauhaus tee, chipped black polish on his fingernails, and silver rings that caught the dim light every time he rocked the plastic tray. All semester in Experimental Photo, I’d been quietly orbiting him from across the critique table. At twenty-five, having spent a few years working gallery jobs before coming back to finish my BFA, I was used to being the loudest voice in the room. My friends joked that I dated like I stretched canvas: taut, deliberate, and completely in control. I liked knowing what I wanted, and I liked going after it without hesitation.

Usually, what I wanted came in neat, unmistakable packages—broad-shouldered guys who wore their masculinity like a leather jacket, or high-femme women who knew their exact angles. And then there was Elliot. Nineteen, soft-spoken, with a mind that cut straight to the marrow of every reading we were assigned and a presence that refused to sit comfortably in any category I knew how to name.

As the chemicals washed over the blank paper, Elliot began to hum. It was a soft, wandering melody—something minor-key and half-remembered, vibrating quietly in his chest while we waited for the silver halides to react. 

"What is that?" I asked, my voice dropping automatically to match the hush of the room. "You’ve been humming it since midnight."

Elliot’s shoulders rose a fraction toward his ears. He glanced up at me through the dark fringe of his hair, his eyes wide and dark in the amber light. "Nothing, really. Just an old lullaby my grandmother used to sing. Sorry—is it annoying? I do it when I’m losing track of the timer."

"Don't apologize," I said, fighting the automatic edge of command in my voice and softening it instead. "I like it. It suits the room."

He looked back down at the tray, where the faint gray ghosts of our double-exposure portrait were just beginning to bloom from the white paper. It was a shot I’d taken of him three nights ago, superimposing the shadow of Venetian blinds across his collarbone and jaw. 

"Look at the contrast on the neck," I said, stepping closer so our sleeves brushed. My usual instinct was to put a hand on his waist, to tilt his chin up and make my interest plain. With anyone else, I would have closed the distance a week ago. But around Elliot, my trademark boldness felt too heavy, like boots on thin ice. He was six years younger, still unfolding into himself, and the last thing I wanted was to crowd him into a corner just because I was used to leading the dance.

"It looks like someone else," Elliot murmured, his tongs hovering over the print. He lifted the paper by its corner, letting the developer drip back into the tray before sliding it into the stop bath. He hesitated, his fingers tightening on the bamboo tongs. "Actually... that’s kind of why I like it."

I turned to face him fully, resting my elbow on the counter. "Because it doesn't look like you?"

"Because it doesn't look like *him*," Elliot said quietly. He set the tongs down and wiped his gloved hands on his apron, staring intently at the swirling liquid. "The guy everyone expects me to be when I walk into a room. Lately, when I look in the mirror, or when I get dressed in the morning, it feels like I’m putting on a costume that almost fits, but the seams are all in the wrong places."

The red light seemed to thicken around us, turning the narrow space between the enlarger and the sink into a confessional. My heart gave a strange, hard thump against my ribs.

"Have you been thinking about that for a while?" I asked gently, keeping my hands anchored to the edge of the sink so I wouldn't reach out and overwhelm him.

Elliot nodded, a shy, nervous smile tugging at the corner of his mouth. "All semester, honestly. Seeing how you work—how you just *own* the space you’re in—made me realize how much I’ve been hiding inside my clothes. I don't know if I want to be a boy the way other people mean it. Or if 'he' is just a habit I haven't figured out how to Question yet. Some days I want to wear lace and eyeliner and feel pretty, and some days I don't want to have a body with rules at all. Does that sound stupid?"

"Not even a little bit," I said, and the fierce, protective warmth that surged through me caught me off guard. "Elliot, look at me."

That was my old voice—the take-charge one—and for a split second I worried I’d pushed too hard. But Elliot looked up, and Instead of retreating, his posture steadied, as if my certainty gave him something solid to lean against.

"Watching you figure out who you are is the most honest thing in this whole pretentious department," I told him, my pulse racing as I realized how much I meant it. "You don't owe anyone a finished print before you're done developing."

A genuine laugh escaped him, bright and startled in the quiet room. "That was a terrible metaphor, Dani."

"Shut up, it’s two a.m.," I grinned, though my stomach was doing complicated flips. 

Looking at him—at the delicate curve of his jaw, the smudge of charcoal under his eye, the quiet bravery it took to hand me a piece of himself that didn't even have a name yet—I felt my own carefully curated labels slipping out of focus. I had always prided myself on knowing my type, on understanding the geometry of my own desire. Yet here I was, completely undone by someone standing in the threshold between definitions. Was I attracted to the boy I’d first noticed in September, or the person emerging beneath the red light right now? The answer, thrilling and disorienting, was both—or maybe that the boundary itself was what drew me in.

Elliot moved the print into the fixer, and as he leaned over the tray, he started humming that soft, minor-key tune again. This time, he didn't stop when he caught me watching. Instead, he stripped off his rubber gloves, his fingers brushing the back of my hand on the steel counter. 

He didn't pull away, and for once, I didn't grab hold. I just turned my palm up, leaving the space open between us, and waited breathless in the crimson dark as he laced his fingers through mine.

prompt:
Hacker Mindset

Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. The date drops breadcrumbs of personal information that could easily answer security questions. 1000 words.
response:
The host stand runs an unpatched build of Toast POS on a tablet held together by electrical tape and prayer. As the hostess led me to booth four, I clocked the default admin PIN taped to the underside of the cash drawer—*1234*, classic—and the exposed Ethernet jack behind the potted ficus, begging for a Raspberry Pi packet sniffer. 

*Stop it,* I told myself, sliding onto the cracked vinyl. *You’re off the clock. You have a W-2 now. You sign NDAs. Tonight, you are just a guy having a risotto with Maya.*

Except my brain doesn’t have an off-switch. Six years of black-hat social engineering and another four of corporate penetration testing will rewire your Threat Detection cortex permanently. You don’t see a cozy Italian bistro; you see an unsegmented guest Wi-Fi network named *Luigi_Free* and forty patrons broadcasting their Bluetooth MAC addresses into the ether. 

And then you see Maya, sitting across the table in a burgundy sweater, smiling around the rim of her Pinot Grigio, and you realize human connection is just a mutually agreed-upon vulnerability exchange. 

She was talking about her childhood, her hands animated, silver rings catching the candlelight. I tried to focus on the warmth in her voice, the crinkle at the corners of her dark eyes. I really did. 

"—so after we moved off Elm Street," she was saying, laughing, "my mom got us this ridiculous three-legged beagle named Barnaby to make up for switching schools."

* mental log: Childhood street: Elm. First pet: Barnaby. Mother’s maiden name is probably two glasses of wine away.* If she banked with Chase or Wells Fargo, I was already sixty percent of the way through her password recovery flow. Combine that with her public LinkedIn—where she proudly listed her high school Mascot, the Oakridge Fighting Badgers, Class of ’16—and her digital perimeter was basically Swiss cheese. 

*Delete the log,* I ordered myself. *Be a person. Smile. Ask a follow-up question that isn't a phishing attempt.*

"A three-legged beagle sounds like a logistical nightmare," I said, taking a sip of water to ground myself. "How fast could he run?"

"Faster than you'd think! He used to chase me all the way to my grandma’s house—she was a Miller, pure Midwest stubborn—until he’d get distracted by a squirrel."

*Mother’s maiden name: Miller.* Goddammit. People just hand out their root access keys for the price of an appetizer. Why do we even bother with 256-bit encryption when the meat-space firewall folds for a basket of garlic bread?

I needed to pivot the conversation away from her biographical attack surface before I accidentally audited her credit score in my head. My eyes dropped to her canvas tote bag resting on the seat beside her. Sticking out of the front pocket, nestled next to a tube of lip balm, was the unmistakable glossy corner of a Dragon Shield deck box. 

Wait. No way. 

"Is that—" I gestured with my fork, my heart doing a weird, unencrypted little flip. "Are you packing a Commander deck on a first date?"

Maya froze, her cheeks flushing a shade that rivaled her wine. "Oh god. I came straight from my local game store in Austin—well, my first job was at one back in Ohio, old habits—and I forgot to take it out. You know what it is?"

"Know what it is? Who’s your commander?"

The defensive posture vanished. Her eyes lit up with the pure, unadulterated zeal of a fellow nerd discovering friendly territory. "Atraxa, Praetors' Voice. Infect and proliferate."

I groaned, leaning back against the booth, genuinely grinning for the first time in months. "Infect? On a first date? That’s a war crime, Maya. I’m an Izzet spellslinger guy myself. Niv-Mizzet, Parun."

"Oh, so you’re the guy who takes twenty-minute turns drawing your entire library while the rest of the table dies of old age," she shot back, leaning across the table. 

For the next twenty minutes, the restaurant’s terrible network security ceased to exist. I didn't care about the busboy’s unattended unlocked iPhone or the unencrypted NFC terminal at the bar. We were deep in the weeds of mana curves, stack resolution, and why *Dockside Extortionist* deserved its ban. Listening to her passionately defend poison counters, I felt my own ports opening up. No spoofed credentials, no pretexting, no carefully crafted persona. Just me, talking about cardboard wizards with a woman who actually laughed at my terrible jokes about *Counterspell*. 

*See?* I thought, watching her reach for her phone to pull up her decklist on Moxfield. *You can do this. You can be normal.*

"Wait till you see the synergy I pulled off with *Vraska*," she said, tapping her screen to wake it. 

Because of the angle of the candle, the grease smudges on her tempered-glass screen protector caught the light like fingerprint powder, even before her thumb moved. 

Top-left. Straight down the left column. Straight across the bottom row. 

An *L*. 

A five-node, top-to-bottom *L* on a standard three-by-three Android pattern grid. No crossover points. Starting in the statistically most common node—44% of users start in the top-left corner. Combine the smudge vector with shoulder-surfing visibility from three booths away, and a toddler with a juice box could brute-force her device in one try. Once inside, her Moxfield app was the least of her worries; her Gmail was undoubtedly logged in, which meant two-factor authentication tokens, banking apps, saved passwords in Chrome—

"An *L*?" 

The words bypassed my internal outbound filter entirely. They just spilled out into the candlelit air, flat and horrified. 

Maya paused, her thumb hovering over her screen. She blinked up at me. "What?"

*Abort. Abort mission. Laugh it off. Say you meant 'Death Note.' Say literally anything else.*

"Your unlock pattern," I heard myself say, my voice tight with professional distress. "You just drew a capital *L* starting at node one. And you haven't wiped your screen since at least lunch, so the sebaceous oil trail practically highlights the path in neon."

Silence descended on booth four. The ambient clatter of forks and Billy Joel on the overhead speakers suddenly felt very loud. 

Maya slowly locked her phone and set it face-down next to her bread plate. The warm, nerdy camaraderie that had been humming between us seconds ago evaporated like a killed process. Her posture shifted—shoulders squaring, chin tilting up. The human firewall was slamming its ports shut, one by one. 

"Were you watching me put in my password?" she asked, her tone cooling by ten degrees. 

*Damage control. Think. You’re a social engineer; engineer your way out of being a creep.* 

Except every instinct I had was screaming two contradictory commands. Part of me—the lonely, reformed guy who really liked her laugh and wanted to build a janky two-headed giant deck with her—wanted to apologize profusely and explain my day job. The other part—the cynical, paranoid creature who knew that anyone who used an *L* pattern alongside four easily harvested security answers (*Elm, Barnaby, Miller, Badgers*) was a walking liability—wondered if I wasn't better off burning the bridge now before I ended up spending our relationship resetting her compromised Apple ID. 

Wait. No. That was a defense mechanism. I wasn't protecting her digital hygiene; I was sabotaging the connection because letting someone past my own perimeter terrified me. Finding flaws in the system is how you stay above the system. If you find the exploit first, you can’t be exploited. 

She was looking at me like I’d just played *Armageddon* on turn four and blown up all her lands. She was about to ask for the check. I had maybe three seconds before the connection timed out permanently. 

If I gave her a slick, rehearsed excuse, she’d smell the manipulation. Only one exploit left: radical transparency. Zero-day vulnerability, my side of the table.

I winced, rubbing the back of my neck, and reached into my pocket. I pulled out my own phone, unlocked it with a fourteen-character alphanumeric passphrase right in front of her, opened my work email ID badge, and slid it across the table. 

"I'm a penetration tester," I said, keeping my hands visible, palms up. "A white-hat hacker. Companies pay me to break into their systems and tell them why their security sucks. I can't turn it off, Maya. Since we sat down, I've cataloged the restaurant's Wi-Fi vulnerabilities, the POS admin code, and four of your bank security questions—Elm Street, Barnaby, Miller, and the Fighting Badgers."

Her eyes widened, shifting from my digital badge back to my face. "You memorized my—"

"Not on purpose! My brain just... parses data like an attacker. And when I’m nervous—like when I’m on a really great date with someone who plays *Atraxa* and is way out of my league—I default to looking for flaws so I feel like I’m in control." I let out a breath, feeling entirely unencrypted. "I’m sorry. That was invasive and weird. If you want to bail, the risotto's on me."

Maya stared at me for a long, agonizing five-second ping delay. Her eyes narrowed, scanning my face for deception, analyzing my packet header. 

Slowly, she picked up her phone, wiped the screen firmly against the sleeve of her burgundy sweater, and tapped into her settings menu. 

"Fourteen characters?" she asked, one eyebrow arching as a faint, wry smile tugged at the corner of her mouth. "On a tiny keyboard? Every time you check a text?"

My chest loosened. The connection hadn't dropped. 

"Password manager with biometric fallback," I admitted softly. "Look, if you let me stay for dessert, I'll show you how to draw a knight's-move pattern across the grid that leaves an unreadable smudge."

She studied me for another beat, then flipped her phone around to show me the *Change PIN* screen. "Only if you admit infect is a valid win condition."

*Vulnerability patched,* I thought, smiling back. "Deal."

prompt:
Hacker Mindset

Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. The restaurant's WiFi password is visibly taped to the counter for all to see. 1000 words.
response:
`TacoTuesday2019!`

It’s written in faded blue Sharpie on a strip of yellow masking tape, stuck directly to the faux-marble laminate of the hostess counter. Seven feet from the front door. Readable from the sidewalk. No guest VLAN segmentation—I already checked the ARP table from the bathroom out of sheer muscle memory before I remembered I promised my therapist I wouldn’t bring `nmap` on dates anymore. The point-of-sale terminal right next to that masking tape is running an unpatched build of Windows 10 IoT Enterprise, and the USB ports on the side of the square reader are completely exposed. Two seconds with a Rubber Ducky and I’d own the register, the kitchen printer, and probably the owner’s QuickBooks credentials.

Stop it. *Stop it.*

Look at Chloe. Chloe is a human being, not an attack surface. She has warm brown eyes, a slight chip in her left canine that makes her smile look conspiratorial, and she is currently gesturing with a garlic knot.

*Focus on the payload of the conversation, not the transport layer.*

Still, it’s hard to turn off twelve years of instinct just because the Department of Justice commuted my sentence into a lucrative consulting contract. Switching hats from black to white doesn’t change how your eyes work. You walk into a room and you don’t see architecture; you see missing patches. Look at the waiter—walking too fast, sweating through his collar, apologizing twice before he even sets the water down. Classic people-pleaser configuration. High empathy, low confrontation threshold. If I wore a hi-vis vest, carried a clipboard, and told him the fire marshal needed the back-office server key, he’d not only hand it over, he’d hold the door for me and offer me a breadstick. 

And Chloe? 

Early enumeration was promising, if a little guarded. Posture slightly angled toward the exit—good physical OpSec, honestly, I respect it for a Hinge date. Silver ring on her right thumb, which she spins whenever she’s auditing what she’s about to say before she deploys it. Low-level social anxiety, masked by rehearsed banter. An exploitable tell if you were trying to socially engineer her mother’s maiden name out of her, which I am *not*. I am trying to be a normal guy eating penne alla vodka.

Then she drops her guard. She reaches into her canvas tote to move her keys, and a corner of a matte-black Dragon Shield deck box pokes out.

My brain pings it before I can stop myself. Hundreds of hours in dimly lit game stores don’t leave your system any faster than bash scripting does.

"Wait," I say, actually smiling for the first time all night without calculating the facial muscles required. "Is that Commander, or are you grinding Modern?"

Her thumb freezes on the silver ring. The firewall drops completely. 

For the next twenty minutes, there are no threat vectors. No zero-days. Just two nerds arguing over whether *Dockside Extortionist* deserved the banhammer while our pasta gets lukewarm. She plays Golgari graveyard recursion—Aristocrats, sacrifice outlets, squeezing value out of things that are already dead. I tell her I’m an Izzet spellslinger main, all instant-speed interaction and fragile combo lines on the stack, and wait for her to judge me. Instead, she laughs—a real, unbuffered laugh that crinkles the corners of her eyes—and tells me I’m the exact kind of blue-red menace she builds her sideboard to ruin.

God, is this what normal people feel like? No packet inspection. Just an open, unencrypted handshake between two people who know what "paying the one for Rhystic Study" means. I’m actually doing it. I’m connecting.

"Hold on," she says, grinning as she pulls her phone from the table to show me a picture of her altered *Meren of Clan Nel Toth*. "My friend hand-painted the border, you have to see—"

She tilts the screen toward herself—not away from me, just a casual thirty-degree angle—and swipes her thumb across the glass.

Top-left node. Straight down the left column. Across the bottom row. 

An L.

A standard, five-node, top-to-bottom *L*.

My stomach drops like a mishandled SSH session. Not an L. Anything but the L. It’s the `123456` of Android lock screens. It’s the `admin/admin` of human touchpoints. Worse, the oleophobic coating on her screen protector is worn down along that exact path, and the garlic-butter sheen from the knots has left a gleaming, forensic-grade grease trail connecting nodes 1, 4, 7, 8, and 9. You could read that pattern from the International Space Station. If she leaves her phone on the table to go to the restroom, anyone within a three-booth radius has full read-write access to her digital life—email resets, 2FA authenticator apps, banking sessions, everything.

Keep your mouth shut. Look at the Magic card. Compliment the brushwork. Do not run an unsolicited pen-test on your date.

"You might as well tape your PIN to the counter next to `TacoTuesday2019`," I blurt out.

The words leave my mouth before my outbound filter can drop the packet. 

Chloe’s thumb hovers over her screen. The warm, conspiratorial crinkle around her eyes vanishes, replaced by the cold, flat latency of a connection timing out.

"What?" she asks.

*Abort. Roll back. Restore from backup.*

"Your unlock pattern," I say, because apparently when my brain panics, it doubles down on the exploit report. "The L-shape. Node one to seven to nine. Plus, the garlic butter from the breadsticks left a smudge trail right over the glass. Anybody sitting at the bar behind you could shoulder-surf that in half a second, and if your 2FA app isn't biometrically gated behind a secondary PIN—"

"Were you watching me put in my password?"

Her posture shifts. Forty-five degrees toward the exit again. The thumb is spinning the silver ring at high RPM. Firewall back up, all ports closed, IP blacklisted.

*Nice going, idiot. You found a critical vulnerability in the vibe and executed a denial-of-service on yourself.*

Now I’m at a fork in the logic tree. Option A: I lie. I laugh it off, pretend I saw a TikTok about phone smudges yesterday, and try to spoof a normal, well-adjusted accountant or whatever adjacent "cybersecurity analyst" sounds like to civilians. It’s the safe play. A clean social-engineering patch. 

Option B: I give her root access. 

She plays Golgari. She’s smart. If I feed her a sanitized corporate excuse, she’s going to smell the spoofed header from a mile away, and even if she buys it, I’ll spend the rest of the night maintaining a cover story instead of talking to her. Or maybe—if I’m being brutally honest with my own source code—part of me wants to sabotage this right now, while it’s still just a first date, before she finds out that my brain is permanently wired like a burglar alarm that never stops ringing.

I look at the yellow masking tape on the counter, then back at her.

"I wasn't trying to snoop," I say quietly, letting my hands rest flat on the tablecloth—open palms, non-threatening, though I’m not doing it as a technique this time. "I do penetration testing for a living. Ethical hacking. Well—ethical *now*. And my brain has this really annoying bug where it audits everything in the room whether I want it to or not. The unpatched register by the kitchen, the WiFi password on the counter, the grease smudge on your screen. I was trying really hard to turn it off tonight because I’m having a genuinely great time with you, and I completely failed."

Silence stretches across the table. The waiter hurries past, still sweating. Somewhere in the kitchen, the exposed POS printer rattles out an order over port 9100.

Chloe looks down at her phone. She tilts it against the overhead pendant light, catches the unmistakable garlic-oil streak of the *L*, and lets out a slow, reluctant breath through her nose.

"Ethical *now*?" she repeats, one eyebrow arching.

"It's a long patch history," I admit.

She wipes the screen across her napkin, destroying the forensic evidence, then locks the phone and sets it face-down next to her water glass. Her thumb stops spinning the ring.

"Okay, Izzet player," she says, leaning back in. "Tell me how you'd rob this restaurant, and then you can show me how to fix my settings."

prompt:
Hacker Mindset

Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. Throughout dinner, they mentally catalog every Magic card their date mentions that reveals their strategy preferences. 1000 words.
response:
The hostess stand runs on an unpatched build of Toast POS over an open guest SSID named *Trattoria_Guest*, and the maître d’ leaves his four-digit manager PIN—`1984`, judging by the shiny grease wear on the capacitive glass—exposed every time he pivots to grab menus. 

Stop it. Breathe. You are off the clock. You have a framed penetration-testing consultancy contract on your wall, a W-2, and a therapist who told you that viewing every room as an attack surface is a maladaptive defense mechanism. Tonight is about eye contact, active listening, and not enumerating the restaurant’s network topology before the breadbasket arrives.

Across the two-top, Maya is smiling. Her posture is open, shoulders unguarded, left hand resting near her water glass. Earlier, when she excused herself to wash her hands, she left her leather crossbody bag draped over the chair back—zipper open three inches, wallet RFID-unshielded, physical keys visible on the top layer. A thirty-second impressioning job with a blank and a file, or two seconds with a Flipper Zero if she uses a proximity fob for her apartment building. I had to physically sit on my hands to keep from zipping her purse shut for her.

Then she sat back down, noticed the wornmana-symbol keychain clipped to my messenger bag, and asked if I played Commander.

Just like that, the firewall dropped. For the last forty minutes, it hasn’t felt like social engineering; it’s felt like a clean, mutual handshake protocol. And because my brain refuses to stop indexing data even when I’m happy, I’ve been building a threat profile of her deck-building philosophy with every card she names.

*Item one: Counterspell.* Not *Mana Drain*, not *Force of Will*—she specifically professed an undying love for the classic two-blue-pip instant while we split the bruschetta. She values efficiency and clean resource trades. She doesn’t need flashy; she likes telling a problem *no* before it resolves onto the stack.

*Item two: Rhystic Study.* Dropped casually while the waiter poured the Chianti. "Do you pay the one?" she’d joked, raising an eyebrow. Classic tax-and-attrition mindset. She plays the long game, setting up passive telemetry that punishes her opponents for every action they take unless they pay a toll. She’s an analyst at heart—she wants card advantage, information superiority, and a full grip of answers.

*Item three: Cyclonic Rift.* Mentioned right as the entrées landed. An instant-speed asymmetric board wipe held in reserve until the exact moment an opponent overcommits. That tells me she’s patient. She’ll let you build your state, let you think you have lethal on board, and then bounce your entire infrastructure back to square one on your end step.

*Item four: Farewell.* She brought this one up mid-bite of her cacciatore, defending white-blue control with genuine fire in her eyes. Exile all artifacts, creatures, enchantments, *and* graveyards. Zero recursion. Total scorched-earth sanitization. Beneath the warm laugh and the careless purse zipper, Maya does not leave loose ends when she decides to lock a board down.

I’m halfway through falling for her—calculating how my reckless black-red *Rakdos, Lord of Riots* aggro deck would get systematically dismantled by her Azorius prison—when her phone buzzes against the white tablecloth.

She reaches over to check a text from her sister about dog-sitting. 

I shouldn't look. A normal date looks down at his pasta or takes a sip of wine. Instead, my peripheral vision locks onto the reflections in her wineglass and the angle of her thumb. Even without the glass, the smudge trail on her oleophobic screen coating is glowing under the pendant lamp like crime-scene luminol. 

Top-left node. Straight down the left column. Straight across the bottom row.

An *L*. A five-node, single-vector, top-to-bottom *L*.

My fork stops halfway to my mouth. The cognitive dissonance physically hurts. This is a woman who holds up two blue mana for *Counterspell* on turn two, who exiles graveyards with *Farewell* so nothing can ever be reanimated, and she’s guarding her entire digital life—banking apps, email password resets, two-factor authenticator tokens, private photos—behind the Android pattern equivalent of `admin/admin`. Forty-four percent of all pattern locks start in the top-left corner. An *L* is literally the first geometry a shoulder-surfer or a smudge-attack script tests.

Before my internal outbound filter can catch the packet, my mouth opens.

"An L-pattern starting top-left?" I say. "Really? With that much skin oil on the Gorilla Glass, I could’ve pulled that credential from across the dining room."

Silence hits the table harder than a *Rule of Law*.

Her thumb freezes on the screen. Slowly, she clicks the side button, locking the display, and sets the phone face-down beside her bread plate. Her posture shifts—shoulders squaring, chin tilting up, the casual warmth vanishing behind a sudden, crystalline air-gap.

"Excuse me?" she asks. Her voice isn't loud, just cool and clipped.

Panic floods my logs. *Abort. Roll back. Issue a patch.* You idiot. You absolute zero-day social disaster. You just ran an unsolicited vulnerability disclosure in the middle of a candlelit dinner. Why not pull out a notepad and write up a CVE on her purse zipper while you’re at it?

"I—sorry," I stammer, setting my fork down. Do I pivot? Laugh it off as a joke? Or do I intentionally torpedo the rest of the night right now so I can go home to my terminal where I can’t embarrass myself in front of someone I actually like? Self-sabotage is an easy exploit; it only takes one more arrogant sentence to trigger a connection reset.

Look at her, though. She isn’t flustered; she’s evaluating me, eyes narrowed, holding priority. Waiting to see how I resolve the stack.

I decide not to bluff. White hats don't hide the payload.

"I do security auditing for a living," I admit, rubbing the back of my neck. "And I have a terrible habit of reading rooms—and screens—like threat models when I’m nervous. Which I am. Because I’m having a really good time, and it broke my brain a little that someone who plays hardcore Azorius control with *Farewell* and *Rhystic Study* uses an unlock pattern that an aggro player could brute-force on turn one."

For three agonizing seconds, her expression doesn't budge. She looks from my face, down to her phone, and back up to my eyes. 

Then, the corner of her mouth twitches.

"That," she says slowly, leaning forward on her elbows, "was my decoy profile. It opens a sandboxed guest partition I use when I’m on public transit or out with strangers. My actual partition requires a twelve-character alphanumeric passphrase and a hardware YubiKey." She picks up her wineglass, her eyes glinting over the rim. "Kind of like leaving two mana untapped just to represent *Mana Tithe*. You bit on the bait."

My heart skips a clock cycle. *Item five: Mana Tithe.* One white mana to counter a spell unless the caster pays one—the ultimate psychological trap card for someone who thinks they’ve already calculated the board state.

I let out a breath I didn't realize I was holding, grinning like an amateur who just walked straight into a honeypot. "Okay," I say, raising my glass to hers. "You have priority. Pass turn."

prompt:
Overthinking It

Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. The classroom projector squeaks whenever the teacher flips through slides. 1000 words.
response:
*Squeak.*

Mr. Henderson clicks the remote, and the ceiling-mounted projector lets out that high, rusted-wheelbarrow whine it makes every single time the slide advances. Today’s slide is titled *Cellular Respiration: Partner Lab*, in forty-point Comic Sans, which is objectively a crime against typography, though I would never say that out loud because saying things like "crime against typography" is how you end up eating lunch in the stairwell between the library and the boiler room. Not that I do that. I eat at the end of the third table from the trash cans, four seats down from Maya Lin, pretending to annotate *To Kill a Mockingbird* while actually calculating the exact number of chews required to make a granola bar last twenty-two minutes.

And now Leo Vance is pulling his chair up to my lab station.

Okay. Posture check. Spine straight, but not *rigorously* straight like a Victorian governess or a person concealing a felony. Shoulders down. Where do hands go? On the black epoxy tabletop, folded? No, that looks like I’m conducting a performance review. Tucked into my hoodie pocket? Too defensive, signals *do not approach, feral mammal.* Resting casually near the colored pencils, left thumb lightly touching the edge of the worksheet? Better. Hold it there. Wait—is my thumb twitching? Why does my pulse live in my thumb now?

He sits down. His backpack hits the metal leg of the table with a soft *clink*. He smells faintly of laundry detergent and the cold November air outside, like cedar and wet pavement. Do not inhale noticeably. Breathing noticeably within three feet of another human being is how rumors start.

*Option A: Casual academic opener.* "So, do you want to handle the ATP diagram, or should we split the synthesis questions first?" 
Too brisk. Sounds like I’m trying to get this over with so I can go back to ignoring him, which I have been doing with Olympic-level dedication since September because the alternative is looking directly at his eyelashes and forgetting how verbs work.

*Option B: Light, relatable humor.* "I love how Mr. Henderson thinks two dried-out Crayola markers are enough to illustrate the Krebs cycle."
Wait. What if he likes Mr. Henderson? Mr. Henderson coaches track. Leo runs the four-hundred-meter dash. If I insult the markers, am I tangentially insulting the track program? Also, saying "the Krebs cycle" in a conversational tone might sound like I spent last night reading ahead in Chapter Seven. Which I did. Twice. Because I knew today was lab-partner day and the seating chart is alphabetical by last name—*Tarkowski, Vance*—a statistical inevitability I have been bracing for since the syllabus was handed out.

*Squeak.*

The slide changes to a blurry diagram of a mitochondrion that looks vaguely like a baked potato.

Leo unzips his pencil case. He has a 0.5-millimeter mechanical pencil with the little rubber grip missing. I have three extra mechanical pencils in my pouch—0.5, 0.7, and a drafted-weight 0.9 for shading—and for one terrifying half-second my brain suggests: *Offer him a pencil with a grip.* 
Absolutely not. "Here, I noticed your writing implement is structurally compromised" is the sentence of a Victorian ghost or a future serial killer. Besides, how would I know his grip is missing unless I’ve been staring at his hands? Have I been staring at his hands? Look at the worksheet. Look at the baked-potato mitochondrion.

"Hey," Leo says.

My nervous system immediately initiates a five-alarm fire. 

He said *hey*. Not *hi*, not *yo*, just a low, slightly raspy fourth-period *hey*. The gap between *hey* and my response is currently at 1.4 seconds. At 2.0 seconds, it becomes a pause. At 3.5 seconds, it becomes a clinical incident. Say *hey* back. Pitch it in the middle register—not the squeaky upper register that makes me sound like a stepped-on dog toy, and not the artificially low register I accidentally used during roll call last Tuesday when everyone turned around to see if I had bronchitis.

"Hi," I say.

It came out at forty decibels. Barely audible over the radiator. Did my mouth even move, or did I just ventriloquist-whisper *hi* into my own collarbone? And why did I immediately tuck my hair behind my ear afterward? That’s a movie gesture. People in movies tuck their hair behind their ears when they’re flirting. What if he saw the hair-tuck and connected the dots—*she whispered hi, she tucked her hair, she knows I got an 88 on the mitosis quiz because she passed the graded papers back three weeks ago, she is hopelessly, humiliatingly fixated on me*?

I untuck the hair. No, now I’m just touching my ear repeatedly like I have an inner-ear infection. Put the hand back by the colored pencils.

*Squeak.*

Mr. Henderson is explaining the rubric. Ten points for accuracy, five points for color-coding. 

Leo leans in slightly to look at the shared lab sheet between us. His elbow is four inches from my elbow. If I shift my weight to the left to give him room, the plastic shell of my chair might make that awful farting noise against the metal frame. If I don’t move, I am invading his personal perimeter. I hold my core muscles at a level of isometric tension usually reserved for planks in gym class, suspending ninety-eight pounds of eighth-grade anxiety half an inch above the seat plastic.

*Say something normal,* I tell myself. *You have a ninety-nine point four average in this class. You read three hundred pages a week. Form a declarative sentence.*

*Draft 1:* "I can do the labeling if you want to draw the membrane." (Safe, cooperative, egalitarian. Maybe a little bossy? What if he hates drawing? What if his art skills are a point of deep personal insecurity?)
*Draft 2:* "Which part do you want?" (Four words. Minimal vowel clusters to trip over. Let’s go with Draft 2.)

I inhale, parting my lips—and Leo taps the corner of the paper with his grip-less pencil, turns his head so he’s looking right at me, the little freckle under his left eye coming into high-definition focus, and says, "You’re really good at this stuff, right? How do we spell *adenosine triphosphate*?"

My brain stalls out completely. 

He knows I’m good at this stuff. Which means he knows who I am. Which means I am not an invisible, hoodie-shaped blur at the edge of his peripheral vision; I am a distinct entity with a known academic reputation. My face is getting warm. Can people see capillaries dilating under fluorescent lights? Please let the green tint of the bulbs cancel out the red.

*Spell it out loud?* No, spelling a twenty-two-letter word aloud in a noisy classroom is a trap; halfway through *triphosphate* my tongue will tie itself into a sailor’s knot and I’ll just pass away right here on the epoxy. 

Instead, I pick up my 0.7-millimeter pencil, slide the corner of the margin toward me—careful, don’t let the eraser brush his sleeve—and write *A-D-E-N-O-S-I-N-E* in my neatest, least-unhinged print. Not too neat. You don’t want it to look like a ransom note.

*Squeak.*

Mr. Henderson clicks to the timer slide. Forty minutes remaining.

"Thanks," Leo says, and he smiles—just a quick, crooked crease in his cheek—before leaning over to copy the letters onto the diagram.

Forty minutes. Two thousand, four hundred seconds. I let out a microscopic breath, un-clench my left thumb by three millimeters, and reach for the blue colored pencil, already drafting my next three syllables.

prompt:

Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. A lingering ammonia scent from a recent cleaning distracts her mid-thought. 1000 words.
response:
The statistical probability of Mr. Henderson pulling Leo Vance’s popsicle stick right after mine was roughly 3.7 percent, assuming all twenty-eight sticks were actually in the tin and he hadn’t lost any behind the radiator again. Yet here we are. Lab Station Four. Two black epoxy-resin stools, one scratched triple-beam balance, three beakers of varying volumetric capacity, and Leo, currently unzipping his backpack approximately fourteen inches from my left elbow.

Don’t look at the elbow. Adjust your posture. Not too straight—if you sit like a sentinel, he’ll think you’re either terrified of him or secretly a Victorian governess. Slouch slightly. No, not like that, now you look like an invertebrate. Split the difference. Keep your spine at a casual eighty-five-degree angle and rest your chin in your hand. Wait—is resting my chin in my hand squishing my cheek upward into that weird, doughy configuration that makes my left eye look smaller than my right? Abort. Hands flat on the table. Now I look like I’m awaiting sentencing at a tribunal. Fine, hold the pencil. Just hold the mechanical pencil like a normal human eighth-grader preparing to measure the density of irregular solids.

He’s pulling out his notebook. It’s the green spiral-bound one with the corner bent from when he dropped it in the puddle outside the gym on the second Tuesday of October. Don’t mention that you know when he bent his notebook. Obviously, do not mention that. If you reveal that you have cataloged the structural history of his school supplies, you might as well just hand him a laminated pamphlet titled *Reasons You Should File a Restraining Order Against Clara.*

Okay. Speak. Normal lab partners exchange introductory pleasantries before commencing data collection. I spent forty-five minutes last night staring at my ceiling fan, workshopping four distinct conversational gambits just in case the universe decided to align our popsicle sticks.

*Option A: Casual Academic Solidarity.* "So, how much do you actually remember about Archimedes’ principle, or are we just going to guess until the water stops spilling?"
Good. Self-deprecating, light, implies a shared struggle against the tyranny of eighth-grade physical science. Wait. No. Everyone knows I got a ninety-nine on the midterm—and only because Mr. Henderson docked me a point for not rounding to the nearest hundredth on question twelve, which was technically ambiguous anyway. If I pretend I don’t know displacement, Leo will know I’m lying. Why would I lie about fluid dynamics unless I was trying to seem relatable? It’s transparent. It’s patronizing. Scratch Option A.

*Option B: Observational Humor.* "I’m pretty sure this brass cylinder has been sitting in this exact tray since the Carter administration."
Wait. Does he know when the Carter administration was? Of course he does, he’s in honors history. Or does he? What if he doesn’t immediately place late-1970s executive timelines and then he feels awkward for not getting the joke, or worse, thinks I’m the kind of insufferable nerd who makes presidential references during fourth period? Which I am, apparently. Why can’t I just talk about TikTok or track tryouts or whatever normal fourteen-year-olds use as social currency?

*Option C: Direct Utility.* "Do you want to do the weighing, or should I fill the graduated cylinder?"
Safe. Functional. Completely devoid of personality, like an automated phone tree at a pharmacy, which means zero risk of sounding desperate. Except—what if "direct utility" comes across as cold? Last week when Maya asked to borrow my highlighter and I just handed it to her without speaking because my throat decided to constrict for no biological reason, she told Chloe she thought I hated her. If I just bark lab delegations at Leo, he’ll think I’m annoyed that we got paired up. He’ll think I wanted to be paired with Sarah, and then he’ll spend the next forty minutes silently resenting me while I silently hyperventilate—

Wait. What is that smell?

It’s sharp, right at the back of my nasal cavity, cutting straight through the usual classroom miasma of dry-erase markers and wet wool coats. Ammonia. Mr. Henderson—or the custodian—must have scrubbed the lab tables after third period’s baking soda disaster without diluting the floor cleaner properly. It’s aggressive. It smells like a hospital corridor, or my grandmother’s laundry room, and it’s making my eyes water slightly. Great. Now if I blink too much, Leo is going to think I’m crying over a triple-beam balance. Does he smell it? His nose just twitched. Maybe THAT’S the opener. *Option D: Sensory Commiseration.* "Does it smell like someone mopped the room with pure Windex to you?"

No, don’t say "pure Windex," Windex is a brand name, and saying "ammonia" sounds too clinical, and why am I analyzing cleaning solvents when he is literally turning his head toward me right now?

He’s looking at me. His hair is doing that thing where the front piece curls slightly over his eyebrow, and he has a tiny smudge of graphite on his thumb, and my brain has completely evacuated all grammatical structures of the English language. My vocal cords feel like two dry rubber bands stretched over a shoebox.

Say something. Smile. Not with teeth—you haven’t checked your teeth since lunch, what if there’s a microscopic fleck of spinach from that wrap my mom packed? Closed-mouth smile. Nod slightly. Keep your breathing silent; don't do that weird shallow inhale through your nose where you accidentally snort the ammonia fumes.

"Hey," Leo says. His voice cracks just a fraction on the vowel, warm and completely unbothered by the crushing weight of social existence. "Do you want to start with the rock, or the weird metal thing?"

Here it is. The moment for articulate, effortless wit. Tell him we should start with the brass cylinder because its uniform geometry makes calculating volume easier before we tackle water displacement. Say it casually, with a little laugh at the end so it sounds charming instead of encyclopedic.

I open my mouth. My tongue feels approximately the size of a dictionary.

"Metal," I say.

*Metal.* Just the noun. At a volume barely audible over the radiator’s hiss. I didn't even include a verb. I just grunted a periodic element category at him and tapped the brass cylinder with my eraser like a caveman discovering bronze.

He’s going to stare at me. He’s going to slowly pack his green notebook back into his bag and ask Mr. Henderson for a transfer.

Instead, Leo just grins, picks up the brass cylinder, and sets it on the pan of the scale with a soft metallic clink. "Cool. Metal it is. You write, I'll slide the little weight things?"

"Yeah," I manage, my pulse hammering against my collarbones as I pull the worksheet closer. Two syllables total so far. Truly, a triumph of human rhetoric. I press my pencil to the paper, praying my hand doesn’t shake, and breathe in the sharp, stinging ghost of ammonia and the impossible fact that he’s leaning in to read the scale right beside me.

prompt:
Overthinking It

Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. She doodles tiny sketches in her lab notes, each representing a different group member. 1000 words.
response:
The cursor of my 0.5mm mechanical pencil hovers over the top margin of my lab handout—*Investigation 4.2: Endothermic and Exothermic Reactions*—while my brain runs its fourteenth diagnostic check on the angle of my left elbow. If I rest it on the black epoxy surface of the lab table, I lookslouchy, uninvested, possibly feral. If I tuck it tightly against my ribs, I look like a Victorian orphan bracing for a gale. 

I settle for a forty-five-degreehover that is already giving my deltoid a slow, simmering cramp, and I draw a tiny, geometric cactus in the corner of my page. 

That’s Chloe. Sharp, self-contained, currently scrolling through her phone under the lip of the desk while chewing sour apple gum with the rhythmic, terrifying confidence of someone who has never once wondered what her face looks like from a three-quarter profile. 

Next to the cactus, I sketch a miniature tornado wearing a backwards baseball cap. That’s Liam, who is currently trying to balance a glass stirring rod on the bridge of his nose.

And then, three inches to the right, where the lined paper meets the Punched Hole of Doom, my pencil lead touches down with the delicacy of a bomb disposal robot. I draw a very small, slightly lopsided telescope pointed at a five-pointed star. 

Noah. 

He is sitting nineteen inches away from me. I know it is nineteen inches because the standard middle school lab table is sixty inches wide, divided roughly in half by the central gas tap, and he has angled his stool slightly toward the sink, leaving a nineteen-inch demilitarized zone of scratched black resin between his gray hoodie sleeve and my stiffly hovering forearm. 

*Say something,* the committee in my head demands. *You have been sitting in this group for four minutes and twelve seconds. At five minutes, silence calcifies into weirdness. Once you cross the five-minute threshold, you are officially The Girl Who Doesn't Talk, and there is no legislative path back to normalcy.*

Okay. Fine. Option A: *“Hey, Noah, did you get number four on the pre-lab? Because I wasn’t sure if Mr. Henderson wanted us to calculate the molarity or just describe the thermal transfer.”*

Wait. Abort. *Calculate the molarity?* What am I, a nineteenth-century apothecary? Eighth graders don’t say *thermal transfer* in casual conversation unless they want to be shoved into a locker, or worse, given that polite, tight-lipped nod people give you when they realize you read textbooks for fun. Besides, I already did number four. It’s written right there on my sheet in color-coded Muji pen. If he looks down and sees seven lines of neat cursive under question four after I just claimed I “wasn’t sure,” he will immediately deduce that I am a manipulative liar orchestrating a fraudulent academic crisis just to hear the sound of his voice. Which I am.

Option B: Casual observational humor. *“Pretty sure if Liam drops that glass rod, we’re all getting detention.”*

No. Too mean. What if he and Liam are secretly best friends from travel soccer? Then I’m the judgmental shrew disparaging his comrade. Also, what if my voice does the Thing? When I haven’t spoken aloud since second-period attendance—where my “here” came out sounding like a startled frog—my vocal cords have a statistical probability of 68% of either cracking on the first consonant or emerging at a volume only audible to neighborhood bats. Then he’ll lean in and say, *“What?”* and I’ll have to repeat a joke that wasn’t even funny the first time, louder, while my cheeks turn the exact shade of a fire hydrant.

I shade the little telescope’s tripod legs. My grip on the pencil is so tight my knuckles have gone white. *Loosen your fingers,* I tell myself. *You’re holding a writing implement, not dangling from a cliffside.* I consciously uncurl my pinky, which immediately twitches like a dying insect. Great. Now I have neurological damage.

Noah shifts his weight. The legs of his metal stool scrape against the linoleum. 

My entire nervous system interprets this two-inch movement as a five-alarm siren. Do I look up? If I look up the exact millisecond he moves, he’ll know I was tracking him in my peripheral vision like a velociraptor in tall grass. I have to count to three. *One-Mississippi, two-Mississippi—*

“So,” Noah says.

I look up on *two-and-a-half-Mississippi*, which causes my neck to jerk with the smooth, natural grace of a Haunted Mansion animatronic. 

He’s looking at the plastic bin of supplies in the center of the table—calcium chloride, baking soda, a digital thermometer, two zip-top bags. A lock of brown hair falls across his forehead, right over the faint scar near his left eyebrow that I definitely didn't notice three weeks ago during the mitosis unit and haven't thought about forty-seven times since. 

“Who wants to measure the calcium chloride?” he asks. He looks at Chloe, then Liam, and then his eyes land on me. Hazel. Mostly green around the center, with a ring of brown near the iris, not that I’m cataloging his ocular pigmentation like a creepy Victorian naturalist. 

*Speak,* the committee screams. *It is a direct inquiry. A simple declarative sentence. “I can do it.” Four syllables. Even a toddler could manage four syllables.*

Instead, my brain decides to audit my facial expression. Am I smiling? If I’m smiling too wide while volunteering to weigh industrial road salt, I look unhinged. If I’m not smiling at all, I look hostile. I attempt a genial, approachable half-smile, which feels, from the inside, like I am baring my teeth at him like an anxious chimpanzee. 

“I—” My throat clicks. Actually clicks. “I can.”

*I can.* Two words. Stripped of all syntax, warmth, and human charm. Why didn’t I say *Sure, I’ll do that*? Why did I deliver it with the solemnity of a knight accepting a suicide mission?

Noah’s mouth quirks up on one side. “Cool. Thanks, Maya.”

He knows my name. Obviously he knows my name, we’ve been in the same homeroom since sixth grade, stop acting like he just recited your Social Security number from memory. 

He reaches for the plastic weigh boat, and his fingers brush the edge of my handout—right next to the margin where the tiny pencil-drawn telescope is aimed directly at the little star. 

Panic, cold and electric, shoots straight down my spine. What if he looks at the doodles? What if he possesses an innate, Sherlockian ability to decode symbolic graphite marginalia and realizes that Chloe is the cactus, Liam is the tornado, and therefore, by process of elimination, he is the astronomical apparatus? Remember in fifth grade when he wore that NASA shirt every Tuesday? What if he connects the telescope to the NASA shirt, realizes I remember his elementary school wardrobe, and files for an immediate academic restraining order?

I casually slide my left hand over the margin, flattening my palm over the drawings. In doing so, my elbow knocks against my pencil case, which slides two inches and taps the base of the graduated cylinder. 

The cylinder wobbles. 

Time dilates. I watch the clear plastic tube tip at aifteen-degree angle, oscillate twice, and settle upright with a hollow *clack*. 

Nobody looks. Liam is now trying to balance the stirring rod on his chin. Chloe hasn’t blinked since 10:15. 

Noah is reading the procedure sheet, his brow furrowed slightly as he clicks a blue pen open and shut. *Click-clack. Click-clack.* 

I let out a breath I’ve been holding since the Carter administration, discreetly lifting my palm just enough to add a tiny, protective dome around the little pencil star. On the outside, I am a statue in a denim jacket, reaching calmly for the plastic spoon to measure out five grams of calcium chloride. On the inside, I am already drafting my apology for the way I’m inevitably going to hand him the thermometer three minutes from now.

prompt:
Rehearsing Rejection

Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of someone with borderline personality disorder who frequently plays out worst-case scenarios of how friends and loved ones might judge them. They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. Their phone battery hovers at critically low, adding to the anxiety of the evening. 1000 words.
response:
Four percent. The little battery icon in the top right corner of my screen is a sliver of angry crimson, a tiny guillotine blade waiting to drop. If it dies before seven, I won’t see the text. The text where Julian says, *Hey, something came up, let’s rain-check.* Which means: *I’ve had three days to think about Tuesday night, and I’ve realized you’re too much. You’re a black hole in a vintage sweater, and I’m getting out while I still have my skin.*

I plug the frayed lightning cable into the wall behind the bathroom sink, balancing the phone on the porcelain edge. Three percent. No—still four, with the little lightning bolt through it, though this cord only works if you bend it at a forty-five-degree angle and pray to a god that doesn't like you very much.

I lean toward the mirror, applying eyeliner with a hand that’s vibrating at the exact frequency of a dying refrigerator. 

*“I just think we moved too fast,”* Julian will say. He’ll do that thing where he rubs the back of his neck and looks at the table between us instead of my eyes, because people never look at what they’re about to throw away. *“You’re my best friend, Maya, and I don’t want to ruin what we have.”*

And I’ll laugh. Not a warm laugh—a sharp, glass-chewing laugh. *“Ruin what we have? You’re the one who kissed me in the rain outside the bodega, Julian. You’re the one who said you’d been waiting two years for the right moment. Don’t act like I’m some clingy lunatic who cornered you.”*

My reflection’s jaw is clenched so hard my molars ache. Look at him, already trying to rewrite history. Two years of late-night diner runs and shared playlists, and the second he actually gets me in bed, the novelty evaporates. Of course he’s been quiet since Wednesday. One four-word text on Thursday (*Swamped with deadlines, sorry*), and today just a thumbs-up emoji on my message confirming 7:00 PM at our bar. A thumbs-up. The universal punctuation mark of a coward. He’s probably spent the last forty-eight hours talking to his roommate about how suffocating I am. *She’s intense, man. You know how she gets.*

God, I hate him for that. I hate the way he lets me spill my guts out—telling him about my dad, about the semester I took off, about the way my skin feels inside-out when a room gets too loud—just to file it all away as ammunition. *Exhibit A: Why Maya Is Unlovable.*

Stop. Just—stop. 

I press the heels of my palms against my temples, careful not to smudge the liner. That’s the thing my therapist calls *fortune-telling*, or *splitting*, or whatever sterile clipboard word she uses when my brain starts building gallows out of toothpicks. Julian hasn’t said any of that. Julian isn’t even here yet. He’s an architectural drafter at the end of a fiscal quarter; he’s always buried under blueprints in November. 

Except he wasn’t too busy to post a photo of his dog on his story yesterday afternoon. Fifteen seconds to upload a golden retriever, zero seconds to tell me he still likes me. The prosecution rests.

The screen lights up on the sink ledge. My heart does a violent,sickening somersault into my throat, so hard I actually gasp.

**Julian:** *Almost there! Grabbed a booth in the back so we don’t freeze by the door. Wait til you see what I found for you today lol*

A booth in the back. An exclamation point. *Wait til you see what I found for you.*

The relief hits my bloodstream like warm morphine, so sudden and dizzying my knees go weak against the bathroom cabinets. He’s already there. Early. He got us the good booth away from the draft, because he remembers I’m always cold. He found something for me. He was thinking about me while we weren't together—while I was in here putting him on trial for treason, he was out in the world seeing something and thinking, *Maya.* 

I love him so much it feels like a bruise on my sternum. I want to crawl inside his ribcage and live there.

I unplug the phone—seven percent, pathetic, it’ll have to do—and shove it into my coat pocket, practically floating down the stairwell of my building and out onto the wet pavement. The bar is only three blocks away. The air smells like woodsmoke and exhaust, and for two whole blocks, the world is solid. 

Then I hit the corner of 4th Street, and the morphine wears off.

*Wait til you see what I found for you today lol.*

Why the *lol*? Since when does he use *lol* like a buffer? People use *lol* when they’re nervous. People bring gifts when they’re about to deliver bad news. It’s a consolation prize. *Here’s that used paperback you mentioned three months ago, and also, I think we should just be friends.* That’s why he got the booth in the back—so I won’t make a scene in front of the bartenders when he breaks it off. He thinks I’m going to cry in public. He thinks I’m fragile and pathetic and needs to be managed in a dark corner like a rescue dog that bites.

By the time I reach the heavy oak door of The Magpie, my chest is encased in ice. Fine. Let him try to soften the blow with a trinket. I won’t even take my coat off. I’ll sit on the very edge of the vinyl, keep my voice flat, let him see how little it touches me. *Actually, Julian, I’m glad you brought it up. Tuesday felt weird for me too.* Beat him to the blade before he can swing it.

I push the door open. The warmth of the bar washes over me, thick with the smell of fried garlic and spilled IPA. 

In the back corner, under the amber glow of a stained-glass sconce, Julian looks up from his phone. And before he has time to put on a mask—before he even knows I’m watching his face—his whole expression breaks open into this stupid, crooked, unmistakably soft grin. He stands up halfway, knocking his knee against the table, a small paper bag from my favorite bakery sitting beside two mugs of hot cider he already ordered.

“Hey,” he says, reaching for my freezing hands the second I’m within arm’s reach, tucking my fingers into the warmth of his palms. “God, I missed you. This week was hell.”

His thumbs brush across my knuckles, steady and real. My lungs expand, drinking it in like air at the surface of a deep, dark lake. He missed me. He bought cider. 

In my pocket, my phone vibrates once—the final, silent shudder as the battery hits zero and the screen goes black. And as I slide into the booth beside him, letting him pull my cold hands into his lap, a quiet, traitorous whisper at the back of my skull already starts counting the seconds until he lets go.

prompt:
Rehearsing Rejection

Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of someone with borderline personality disorder who frequently plays out worst-case scenarios of how friends and loved ones might judge them. They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. A hallway mirror offers a glimpse of their anxious posture before they turn away. 1000 words.
response:
**Rehearsing Rejection**

The grey sweater makes me look desperate, like I’m trying to look like I didn’t try, which is the worst kind of trying. I pull the black turtleneck over my head instead, the wool scratching my chin, already suffocating me. Six-fifteen. He said *around six-thirty*. "Around" is a coward’s word. "Around" is the buffer zone you build when you’re already dreading the obligation of someone’s company. 

Three days of two-word texts. *Busy today.* *Miss you.* A period at the end of *Miss you.* Who puts a period after *Miss you* unless it’s a eulogy? Last week, when we stayed in bed until two in the afternoon and he traced the knob of my spine with his thumb, there were no periods. Now there is grammar. Grammar is distance. 

I already know how he’s going to do it. We’ll sit at the corner booth at Miller’s—no, he’ll choose a table in the middle of the room so I can’t make a scene—and he’ll wrap both hands around his water glass without drinking. He’ll clear his throat in that soft, apologetic way I used to find gentle and now find spineless. 

*"I just think things moved really fast between us,"* he’ll say, looking at my collarbone instead of my eyes. *"You’re so important to me, and I don’t want to ruin what we had by forcing something neither of us is ready for."*

*Neither of us?* I’ll laugh, sharp and ugly. *Don’t put your cowardice on me, Julian. At least have the guts to say I’m too much for you. Say you got what you wanted last Tuesday and now that you’ve seen what it actually looks like to be close to me, you want the exit.*

*"That’s not fair,"* he’ll say, and his voice will get that tired edge—the one that means *Here she goes again. Just like everyone warned me.* *"You always twist things into an attack. It’s exhausting."*

My stomach drops as if he’s actually spoken the word out loud in my kitchen. *Exhausting.* My heart hammers against my ribs, hot and furious. How dare he call me exhausting when I have spent the last seventy-two hours swallowing every impulse to call him, paring myself down into a quiet, low-maintenance ghost so I wouldn't crowd his precious, fragile week? If he wants cold, I’ll give him Arctic. When he reaches across the table to touch my wrist, I’ll pull my arm back before his fingers even land. *Don’t,* I’ll say, my voice dead-flat. *You don’t get to comfort me to make yourself feel less guilty.*

Wait. Stop. 

I press the heels of my palms against my temples. He hasn't said any of this. He is currently on the northbound train, probably listening to a podcast about Roman aqueducts, completely unaware that we are on the third act of a bitter breakup in my hallway. Dr. Vance calls this *pre-grieving as armor*. I know what I’m doing. I’m building the pyre and climbing onto it so he can’t be the one to strike the match. 

I unlock my phone and stare at the message he sent twenty minutes ago: *Just got on the train! Starving. Can’t wait to see your face, I brought you that sourdough from the bakery by my office.*

For three seconds, the oxygen comes back into the room. *Can’t wait to see your face.* He remembered the bread—the one with the blistered crust I mentioned once, three weeks ago, in passing. A wave of relief so violent it makes my knees weak washes through me. He loves me. Or he’s close to it. Nobody carries a loaf of bread across town on a crowded commuter train for someone they’re about to discard. I want to curl up inside that sentence and sleep for a week.

Unless the bread is a parting gift. 

The thought slides in like a cold blade under a locked door. Of course it is. It’s a softener. *Look how thoughtful I am, look what a good friend I still am, even as I’m stepping backward.* It’s a bribe so I can’t call him a bastard when he tells me we should "go back to how we were." And that exclamation mark after *train!*—since when does Julian use exclamation marks? Overcompensation. Guilt has a punctuation style all its own.

I grab my coat and step into the narrow hallway, catching sight of myself in the oval mirror by the door. For a second, I don’t see the aloof, razor-tongued woman I’ve been scripting. I see a girl with her shoulders hunched up to her ears, her jaw clenched so hard a muscle is twitching by her ear, her knuckles white where she’s strangling the strap of her bag like a weapon. I look cornered. I look like a stray dog waiting for a kick. 

I jerk my gaze away from the glass, humiliated even by my own reflection. 

Downstairs, the autumn air hits my face, sharp with exhaust and wet leaves, and then I see him half a block away, walking toward my building instead of waiting at the restaurant. He has a brown paper bag tucked under one arm. When he spots me on the steps, his whole face breaks open—that crooked, unguarded smile that reaches the corners of his eyes before his mouth even finishes moving.

"Hey," he breathes, closing the distance in three long strides and pulling me against his chest. He smells like cold wool, cedar, and warm flour. He buries his nose in my hair and lets out a long, shuddering exhale. "God, I missed you. This audit nearly killed me. Just let me hold you for a second."

My arms go around his waist automatically, clutching the back of his coat as the warmth of his body sinks through my sweater. *He’s here. He came to the door. He’s holding me like he’s the one who’s been starving.* The desperate, aching hollow in my chest floods with light, so sweet it stings the back of my throat.

Then his grip loosens by a fraction of an inch as he shifts the paper bag.

*Just let me hold you for a second.* Why only a second? And why did he blame the audit right away—laying the groundwork for why he’ll be "too busy" next month, too? He’s hugging me this hard because he’s trying to convince himself he still feels it. 

As he pulls back to kiss my forehead, his eyes warm and unsuspecting, my spine goes rigid, the scripts already shuffling back into place behind my teeth, ready for the moment his smile drops.

The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears.
