Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. Muffled television dialogue seeps through the neighbor’s wall. 1000 words.
response:
The burgundy sweater makes me look desperate. If I wear the burgundy sweater, he’ll walk into the café, see the neckline—the one he kissed three weeks ago when we were tangled in his sheets and the radiator wouldn’t stop clanking—and he’ll think, *God, she’s trying to remind me. She’s setting a trap.* 

I pull it over my head and throw it onto the chair. Through the plaster behind my mirror, Mrs. Gable’s television hums, a muffled baritone bleeding through the studs: *“—the suspect was already at the station when the alibi fell apart—”*

*“Look,”* Julian will say, stirring his oat cortado without looking at me. I know the exact tilt of his chin when he’s trying to be gentle, which is just another word for cowardly. *“I think we blurred the lines too fast. You’re a lot, Maya. You require… a perimeter.”*

And I won’t cry. I’ll laugh, short and dry, and slide my mug across the table so the ceramic grates. *“A perimeter? Keep your perimeter, Julian. I didn’t ask you to stay over on Tuesday. You’re the one who brought your toothbrush in your jacket pocket. Don’t rewrite history just because you’re terrified of anyone actually seeing you.”*

My heart is already hammering against my ribs, sharp and triumphant and sick. I’m furious at him for the cortado he hasn’t ordered yet, for the way his knuckles will go white on the paper napkin when he tells me I’m suffocating him. Four days. Four days of one-line texts. *Swamped with the audit, sorry!* No exclamation point is ever innocent; an exclamation point is confetti thrown over a corpse. If you want to talk to someone, you talk to them while you walk to the subway. It takes eleven seconds to type *I miss your face.* He walks four blocks to the L train. That’s four minutes. Two hundred and forty seconds, and I wasn’t worth eleven of them.

My phone buzzes against the dresser. 

I don’t lunge for it. I count to five so the universe doesn’t think I’m starving, even though my stomach drops straight through the floorboards.

**Julian:** *Just got off the train! Stopped at that bakery on 4th because they had the cardamom buns you liked last month. Grabbed us a booth by the window :)*

A hot, dizzying rush floods my chest, so sudden my knees actually go weak. The cardamom buns. He remembered the bakery with the green awning—I only mentioned it once, in passing, while we were walking in the rain. He stood in a line for me. He put a smiley face. He’s sitting in a booth right now with a paper bag warming his lap, waiting for me, and he isn’t going to leave me. God, I love him so much it feels like a bruise. I pick the burgundy sweater back up and press it to my face, breathing in the cedar from my closet. He’s good. He’s safe. 

*“—always a paper trail when someone wants out—”* murmurs the television through the wall, followed by a tinny swell of violins.

Wait. 

*They had the cardamom buns you liked last month.* 

Why would he stop at a bakery ten minutes out of his way when he’s supposedly *swamped with the audit*? Unless he feels guilty. People buy pastries when they’re about to deliver bad news. It’s a bribe. A parting gift. *Here’s some sugar and butter so you don’t make a scene in a public restaurant when I tell you I’m sleeping with my project manager, or that I just realized how exhausting your moods are.* 

I can see the whole thing. He’ll hand me the brown paper bag across the laminate table with that soft, pitying crinkle around his eyes. *“I got you this,”* he’ll say, and what he’ll mean is, *See how nice I am? You can’t be mad at me when I tell you we should go back to being just friends.*

*“Keep your fucking bun,”* I whisper to the bathroom mirror, pulling on a black turtleneck instead—armor, high-necked, untouchable. *“I don’t want your guilt carbs, Julian. Just say it. Say you got what you wanted for three weeks and now that I actually have feelings, it’s inconvenient.”*

I pause with my mascara wand halfway to my eyelashes. My reflection stares back, pupils dilated, jaw clenched so hard my molars ache. 

*You’re doing the thing,* a quiet, clinical voice notes from somewhere behind my left ear—the voice that sounds suspiciously like Dr. Patel on Thursdays. *He bought you a pastry. Yesterday you were convinced he was ghosting you; today he’s at the café early with your favorite food, and you’ve turned a cinnamon roll into a breakup speech.*

I know. I *know* I’m doing it. I can see the gears of the machine grinding in my own head, chewing up every scrap of sweetness and spitting out razors. Stop it. Just put on the mascara, walk six blocks, eat the bun, let him hold your hand under the table. 

Except—what if I stop rehearsing, and I walk in there soft and open and believing in the cardamom bun, and he *does* do it? What if I let my guard down and he says, *“Maya, we need to talk,”* and I have nothing chambered? If I don’t hate him a little bit before I open that door, the drop will kill me. The rehearsal is the parachute. 

Through the wall, canned applause erupts, muffled and staticky, then a commercial jingle about car insurance. 

I grab my keys. My palms are sweating. Fifteen minutes from now, he’s going to reach across the booth and tuck that loose strand of hair behind my ear the way he always does, and his thumb will brush my cheekbone, warm and slightly rough. I’ll lean into it—God help me, I’ll close my eyes for a second because his skin smells like soap and cold air and everything I want to keep—and right before I let myself believe it, I’ll watch his eyes to see if he’s checking the clock. I’ll thank him for the pastry, and I’ll keep the knife right under my tongue, ready, just in case his hand pulls back half a second too soon.

Below it, the flagstones were slick with moss and cracked by ancient tree roots, forming an uneven twenty-foot square bordered by collapsed pillars. Around this makeshift pit, two dozen young men pressed shoulder-to-shoulder—half in the starched, indigo *hakama* of the Satsuma estate, the other half in the coarse hemp tunics and bound trousers of the dockside guilds. His right foot led, left heel slightly raised, the wooden blade held vertically above his right shoulder, his left hand gripping the pommel at the level of his ear. Weaponless, his forearms were wrapped in tightly wound layers of raw hemp soaked in rosin and dried to the hardness of cured leather. He stood in a low, coiled crouch, his left shoulder angled toward Kazuki, his torso loose and his arms hanging like heavy ropes. A crooked, mocking grin split his face. To Liang, the samurai’s rigid posture was a monument to aristocratic vanity—pretty in a courtyard, useless in the mud.

Liang’s downward forearm grazed the back of Kazuki’s shoulder, striking the linen of his *gi* with a sound like a beaten rug. Completing his spin with his back now facing the northern torch, Kazuki gripped the *bokken* with his right hand alone and lashed it horizontally at waist height, aiming to break Liang’s ribs.

Liang, whose weight had settled onto his front right leg after the chop, snapped his hips backward into a deep *xubu*—empty stance—sucking his abdomen back three inches. The tip of the oak blade sliced the air a hair’s breadth from his tunic. Before the wood cleared his line of sight, Liang stomped his left foot forward, closing the gap to mere inches—inside the effective arc of the long wooden sword.

 Shadows leaped wildly across the eastern pillars as the two bodies collided in the center of the pit. 

Liang’s shoulders rolled in alternating, violent waves. *Gua*—his left hand hooked downward over Kazuki’s extended right wrist, trapping the sword arm against Kazuki’s own hip. *Pi*—his right palm whipped over the top in a whistling overhand arc, slamming squarely into Kazuki’s sternum. 

Air burst from Kazuki’s lungs. His heels skidded backward across the slick moss toward the southern pillar, where his fellow Satsuma disciples shouted in alarm. Yet the Jigen-ryū training was forged in pain; even as his back hit the fluted stone of the southern column, Kazuki refused to yield the weapon. As Liang lunged in to finish him with a low, sweeping palm to the groin, Kazuki brought his left hand back to the hilt, raised both arms high despite his bruised chest, and drove the *bokken* straight down between his own knees like a man driving a stake.

Liang saw the vertical drop too late to retreat. Twisting his hips sharply to the right, he crossed his bound forearms into an X-block above his lead left thigh. The oak blade crashed onto the intersection of his hemp wraps. The shockwave traveled up Liang’s arms, numbing his fingers and forcing his left knee to buckle an inch toward the stone.

Kazuki’s teeth clacked together; the *bokken*’s downward arc went wide, smashing into the southern pillar and snapping four inches off its tip. Staggered, Kazuki stumbled two steps backward toward the eastern side of the pit.

Liang did not pause to wipe the blood streaming over his lips. Springing off his right foot like a uncoiling serpent, he covered the six feet between them in two diagonal bounds—*zoubian*, walking the circle—angling toward Kazuki’s right side to stay clear of the shortened blade. His arms windmillled in continuous, figure-eight loops, generating centrifugal force from his waist.

Kazuki, recovering his footing near the eastern wall, tried to pivot left to face him, thrusting the jagged end of the broken *bokken* straight at Liang’s throat. 

Liang ducked beneath the thrust, his chest nearly parallel to the flagstones, his left foot sliding past the outside of Kazuki’s right ankle. From that low crouch, Liang’s left palm slapped upward against the outside of Kazuki’s right elbow—pushing the sword arm across Kazuki’s chest—while Liang’s right arm whipped around from behind his own back in a full-circle horizontal backfist, *hengquan*.

# Blood Debt

Torchlight licked the fractured stone pillars of the sunken courtyard, casting long, jittering shadows across the moss-choked flagstones. Above, a jagged hole in the temple’s collapsed roof let in a cold drizzle that hissed against the braziers. Packed three-deep along the raised perimeter walkway and perched atop fallen lintels, forty men and women shouted curses and waved fistfuls of crumpled bills. On the eastern side stood the silk-jackets of the Shimazu dojo; on the west, the coarse-cotton dockworkers and bodyguards of the Black Crane hall.

In the twenty-foot square of cleared flagstone between them, two young men faced each other. 

Standing with his back to the eastern steps was Ren. At twenty-two, he wore the pristine dark indigo *keikogi* and pleated *hakama* of the Jigen-ryū, a bloodline style forged by Satsuma retainers who believed a fight should end on the first breath. Bound tight around his left bicep was a band of braided black-and-red silk. In his hands, he gripped a heavy, dense-grained *sunuke* wooden sword, forty inches of ironwood held not in front of his chest, but cocked high and vertical beside his right ear—the *tonbo-no-kamae*, the dragonfly stance. His chin was tilted up, his dark eyes Looking down the bridge of his nose with aristocratic disgust.

Twelve feet to the west, near a toppled stone incense burner, stood Zhao. He was bare-armed despite the autumn chill, his grey hemp trousers tied at the calves with leather thongs, a frayed strip of red-and-black linen knotted around his right forearm. Where Ren was a coiled iron spring, Zhao was loose, his shoulders rounded and his spine curved like a hunting cat’s. As a disciple of Piguaquan—the "hanging and chopping fist" born in the muddy alleys and caravan trails of Hebei—he carried no weapon save the callused edges of his palms and forearms.

"Both masters forbade the crossing of the river," Ren said, his voice cutting through the roar of the betting clerks. "Yet here you are, gutter-dog, tracking mud onto sacred stone."

Zhao spat onto the flagstones to his left, rolling his shoulders until the joints popped. "Sacred stone? It’s a rat-pit, rich boy. Put down the stick, or keep it—either way, I’m taking that silk rag off your arm."

Neither waited for a signal.

Ren exploded forward. In Jigen-ryū, there is no second thought (*ni-no-tachi irazu*). His left foot drove against the wet flagstone, propelling him across the twelve-foot gap in two blinding, low-skimming strides. As his right foot stamped down four feet in front of Zhao, he unleashed the *enpi*—the screaming, high-pitched ape-shriek designed to freeze an opponent’s nervous system—and brought the ironwood blade straight down in a vertical blur aimed at the crown of Zhao’s skull.

The air split with a sharp *whuff*. 

Zhao did not block; blocking a Jigen-ryū first strike meant shattered bones. At the instant Ren’s right heel touched stone, Zhao’s left foot slid forty-five degrees forward and outside to the north, his hips torquing violently clockwise. The wooden blade missed his left ear by an inch, smashing into the flagstone between his feet with a crack that sent stone chips stinging against his shins.

Before Ren could wrench the tip up from the stone, Zhao was already inside his right flank. Driven by the rotational snap of his waist, Zhao’s left arm whipped up from behind his hip in a wide, vertical arc—*pi*, the axe-chop—bringing the hardened bone of his left forearm crashing down onto the back of Ren’s extended right wrist.

Pain lanced up Ren’s arm, forcing his fingers to loosen for a fraction of a second. Simultaneously, Zhao’s right palm came whipping over his own left shoulder in a continuous windmill motion—*gua*, the hanging deflection—hooking behind Ren’s neck to yank his head downward toward the wet floor.

Ren’s training saved him. Rather than resisting the pull, the samurai’s heir dropped his weight and drove his left shoulder straight into Zhao’s sternum. The impact caught Zhao mid-pivot, lifting him off his heels and sending him skidding three feet backward toward the western pillars until his back heel clipped the base of the toppled incense burner.

Zhao barely regained his balance before Ren was on him again. The Jigen-ryū fighter didn't reset to a mid-guard; he used the rebound of the shoulder-check to yank the *bokken* back to his right ear and charged diagonally southwest, unleashing *nuki-uchi*—a rapid,連-fire barrage of vertical and steeply angled downward cuts. 

*Crack! Crack! Thud!*

The first strike grazed Zhao’s retreating left shoulder, tearing a red welt across his skin as he ducked under a cracked stone pillar to his right. The second shattered the corner of the stone incense burner where Zhao’s hip had been a heartbeat earlier. Forced into the tight corner between the western pillar and the burner, Zhao had no room to retreat. The Shimazu crowd roared, scenting blood.

Ren raised the wood high for the finishing blow, his right foot planted on the slick moss between the burner and the pillar, pinning Zhao against the cold granite column.

That closeness was Ren’s mistake. Piguaquan thrived at the extremes—either long-range whipping reach or chest-to-chest suffocation. As Ren’s arms rose to his ear, exposing his ribs, Zhao dropped into a deep, ground-skimming crouch (*pubu*), his left leg shooting out flat along the flagstones straight between Ren’s wide-planted feet. 

With his torso beneath the arc of the descending *bokken*, Zhao coiled his torso left and lashed upward with both arms in *shuang baishou*—the double lotus-leaf sweep. His right palm slammed into the underside of Ren’s right elbow, redirecting the descending blade into the granite pillar with a splintering crunch that snapped six inches off the wooden tip. An instant later, Zhao’s left palm whipped across in a horizontal backhand (*henglei*) that caught Ren flush across the right cheekbone.

Ren’s head snapped left, blood spraying from his split lip across the grey stone. The force of the strike spun him half-around toward the center of the courtyard. 

Zhao didn't let him breathe. Springing up from his low crouch, he chained his footwork into *taolubu*—stealing steps—closing the three feet of distance before Ren could pivot his hips. Zhao’s arms became two flails attached to a spinning axle. Left palm high to the temple, right palm low to the floating ribs, left forearm crashing across the collarbone. Every strike started from the ground, surged through his twisting waist, and snapped out through loose shoulders like wet rope cracking at the tip.

Driven backward toward the center of the arena, Ren absorbed a glancing blow off his forehead that left his vision swimming. Pride warred with panic. To be beaten barehanded while holding a sword was a disgrace that would haunt his family name for a century. 

As Zhao stepped in with his right foot to deliver a rising palm (*tiao*) toward Ren’s chin, Ren abandoned his sword’s reach altogether. Instead of stepping back toward the eastern steps, he threw his weight forward into the oncoming strike, tucking his chin so Zhao’s palm scraped harmlessly over his scalp. 

Now chest-to-chest in the dead center of the courtyard, Ren slid his left hand up to the middle of his broken *bokken* shaft, holding it like a short iron bar, and drove the heavy pommel upward in *tsuki-age* straight into the solar plexus beneath Zhao’s ribs.

The air left Zhao’s lungs in a wet gasp. His knees buckled, his whipping momentum severed at the root. 

With Zhao doubled over in front of him, Ren pivoted ninety degrees to his left—facing north—dropped the broken wood entirely, and seized the red-and-black linen band on Zhao’s right forearm with his left hand. Pulling Zhao’s arm tight across his own chest, Ren stepped his right leg behind Zhao’s planted right calf and drove his right forearm into the side of Zhao’s jaw in a brutal *osoto-gari* sweep.

Zhao’s feet whipped out from under him. His back slammed into the flooded flagstones with a splash that sprayed muddy water three feet high.

Yet even as his spine hit the stone, Zhao’s street-honed instincts fired. Refusing to release Ren’s wrist, he hooked his left heel behind the back of Ren’s right knee and scissored his right leg into Ren’s hip, dragging the off-balance samurai down into the mud beside him.

The crowd surged against the stone railings, shouting until their voices cracked.

They hit the flagstones entangled—Ren on his knees facing west, Zhao on his right side facing east. Ren wrenched his right arm free and raised a fist to hammer down into Zhao’s face, his black-and-red silk band soaked dark with mud and blood. Moving from the ground with his hips pinned, Zhao whipped his left arm in a tight, desperate circle from the floor, wrapping his forearm around the outside of Ren’s descending right arm, trapping it against his own chest, while his right hand shot up to clamp onto Ren’s throat.

Ren’s left handSimultaneously found the collar of Zhao’s trousers and his right thumb dug toward Zhao’s windpipe. Both froze, muscles trembling, blood from Ren’s lip dripping onto Zhao’s chest while Zhao’s fingernails drew four crimson beads along Ren’s carotid artery.

Before either could crush the other’s throat, the heavy bronze gong at the northern archway boomed three times.

"Watchmen on the hill!" a lookout screamed from the broken roof. "Lanterns at the south gate!"

Around them, the gamblers and disciples instantly scattered, vaulting over broken walls and vanishing into the dark drainage tunnels. On the wet flagstones, neither Ren nor Zhao moved for three ragged breaths. Slowly, Zhao uncurled his fingers from Ren’s throat. Ren released his grip, pushing himself up to one knee.

Reaching across, Zhao hooked a finger under the bloodied silk band on Ren’s bicep and tugged it loose as Ren tore the muddy linen strip from Zhao’s wrist. Without a word, each pocketed the other’s colors, turned toward opposite exits, and vanished into the rain.

The ruined nave of the Kannon-ji temple smelled of wet lime, lamp oil, and old grudges. Overhead, a split cedar beam let in a blade of moonlight and a steady ribbon of rainwater that splashed onto the flagstones, feeding a shallow, moss-slick stream that bisected the sunken courtyard from east to west. Around the perimeter, thirty men stood shoulder to shoulder behind crumbling stone balustrades—half in the starched indigo hakama of the Shimazu-backed Jigen-ryū dojo, half in the hemp tunics and bound calves of the dockside Piguaquan brotherhood. Strings of copper cash and silver ingots clinked on an overturnedoffering table at the north wall. Neither master knew their prize pupils were here. Neither pupil cared.

At the northern edge of the dry stones stood Kōjirō, nineteen and straight-spined, a heavy *isuhiki* oak bokken held vertical at his right shoulder in the high, skewed *tonbo-no-kamae*—the dragonfly posture. His left foot pointed dead south toward his opponent; his right heel was cocked, hips torqued forty-five degrees, every tendon in his forearms corded to turn a single descending cut into a skull-splitting verdict. To his school, there was no second thought, no defense—only *ichi-geki*, the first strike that ended all argument.

Twelve paces south, across the glinting fissure of running water, Liang Wei crouched low. His cloth-wrapped forearms hung loose as willow ropes from sloped shoulders, his weight settled seventy percent onto his rear left leg. Where Kōjirō was a cocked crossbow, Wei was a sling waiting for the spin. He spat onto the dry grit beside his right boot, eyes fixed not on Kōjirō’s glaring face, but on the space between the samurai’s collarbones.

"Dock-rat," one of the indigo-robed seconds muttered from the east pillar. "He didn't even bring steel—or wood."

"Wood snaps," Wei said, rolling his shoulders so his spine undulated like a shaken whip. "Tell the young lord to step over the puddle."

Kōjirō did not answer with words. He inhaled into his lower belly, his back foot bit into the dry flagstone, and he exploded forward in an *enzan* sprint—three rapid,stamping glides that closed nine paces in a heartbeat—before unleashing the shrill, lung-tearing *enpi* scream of Jigen-ryū.

At two paces out, just north of the wet fissure, Kōjirō’s hips snapped square and the heavy oak blade blurred down from his right ear toward Wei’s left collarbone. The wood hissed through the damp air with enough kinetic mass to shatter a horse’scannon bone.

Wei did not block; blocking Jigen-ryū head-on was suicide. As Kōjirō’s lead left foot planted on the northern lip of the cracked flagstone, Wei dropped his center of gravity four inches and stepped forty-five degrees to his own left—southeast—in a scissoring *toubu* steal-step. The oak bokken cleaved the empty air an inch past Wei’s vacating right ear and smashed into the stone floor where his boots had been a fraction of a second prior. The shock rattled up Kōjirō’s wrists, stinging his palms, the tip of the oak gouging wet limestone.

Before Kōjirō could wrench the heavy blade up for the rapid-fire *tate-gi* follow-up cuts, Wei’s waist coiled and uncoiled counterclockwise. His left arm whipped up from behind his hip in a wide, vertical *pi*—a chopping axe-hand powered not by shoulder muscle, but by the rotational snap of his spine. Simultaneously, his right palm swept upward underneath like an uppercut to clear Kōjirō’s extended left forearm.

Wei’s upward-sweeping right wrist struck the underside of Kōjirō’s lead elbow, deflecting the samurai’s arms two inches higher and jamming the bokken’s recovery. Half a beat later, the meaty heel of Wei’s whipping left palm slammed downward across the side of Kōjirō’s exposed right jaw.

The crack echoed off the broken rafters. Kōjirō’s head snapped left, momentum carrying his upper body westward while his planted feet stayed anchored by the fissure. Yet the Jigen-ryū prodigy had been beaten with hardwood poles since childhood; pain only triggered reflex. Instead of stumbling away, Kōjirō used the leftward torque of his own staggered body, pivoted hard on his left heel until his back faced the western crowd, and ripped the bokken horizontally from left to right—a savage, blind backhand sweep aimed at Wei’s ribs.

Wei, standing just southeast of Kōjirō, saw the oak blur coming at chest height. He tucked his chin,hollowed his chest in *tun* (swallowing the torso), and threw his weight backward onto his south-most foot while his arms scissored down in front of his floating ribs to absorb the grazing tip. Even at the end of its arc, the oak tip clipped Wei’s crossed forearms like an iron bar, bruising the ulna and shoving him two full paces back toward the southern balustrade.

The Jigen-ryū faction roared, fists pounding the stone rail. Kōjirō was already resetting, his eyes bright with bloodlust, blood leaking from a split inner lip. He raised the bokken straight back to the high dragonfly guard at his right ear and charged across the trickling fissure to finish it before the street fighter could uncross his numbed arms.

That single step across the crack was the hinge of the fight.

As Kōjirō’s lead left sandal came down on the southern edge of the fissure to launch his second overhead strike, the woven straw sole hit a patch of black silt and water. Instead of biting stone, his left foot skated four inches forward toward Wei, opening Kōjirō’s stance too wide and dropping his hips an inch below his strike plane.

Wei’s eyes narrowed. The downward vertical cut was already falling, aimed straight for the crown of his head, slightly slower and six inches shorter in reach because of Kōjirō’s splayed base.

Instead of retreating toward the southern wall behind him, Wei lunged *inside* the arc—straight north into Kōjirō’s chest—driving off dry stone while Kōjirō’s rear right foot was still crossing the wet crack. Wei’s body ducked under the whistling sweet-spot of the oak blade, taking the glancing, weaker shaft near the hilt against his sloped left shoulder. The impact drove Wei’s knees down an inch, a sharp grunt bursting from his teeth, but he was now chest-to-chest with the swordsman, inside the length of the weapon.

Here, in the phone-booth space over the wet stone, Piguaquan turned into Baji-flavored murder.

Wei’s right boot stomped down directly onto the instep of Kōjirō’s slipping left foot, pinning it to the slick limestone. With his left arm wrapping over Kōjirō’s dual-gripped wrists to trap the bokken hilt against his own ribs, Wei whipped his right arm in a full, windmill *gua* backfist—first upward to knock Kōjirō’s chin toward the rafters, then immediately snapping the same right elbow down and inward into the center of Kōjirō’s sternum.

Air left Kōjirō in a wet gasp. His rear right foot, resting directly in the trickling water of the fissure, shot out from under him as the downward elbow broke his posture.

Caught between the heel-hook behind his right leg and the downward-whipping collar pull, Kōjirō’s feet left the stone. Silence fell over the ruined nave, broken only by the trickle of rainwater pooling against Kōjirō’s indigo sleeve.

Back to scraping for rent.

**Breaking Formation**

In the floor-to-ceiling mirrors of Studio B, we are seven identical shadows in oversized black sweats, locked into a V-formation on the taped grid of the Gangnam basement. I am at Position 4—stage right, second row, two meters behind Min-jun’s right shoulder and three meters left of Ji-hoon. Back in East Oakland, a cypher breathes. Here at Haneul Entertainment, the air smells of expensive floor wax and terror, and the beat isn’t something you ride; it’s a guillotine you survive by fractions of a millimeter.

*Clack.*

The sound slices through the bassline. Director Baek stands dead center at the front glass, her black bamboo folding fan snapped shut against her palm. She doesn’t raise her voice. She doesn’t have to. Fifteen years ago, she choreographed the first billion-view idol group; today, she sculptures human bone into commercial gold.

“Again from the second pre-chorus,” Baek says in clipped Korean, switching to English just for the charity case in the back. “Count three. Our scholarship student is still swimming in the mud.”

My quads burn. My knockoff sneakers—scuffed Jordans that survived two winters on the BART platform—squeak as I reset my feet to the yellow tape marks at Position 4. All six of my line-mates wear pristine, agency-issued Balenciaga trainers. Their fathers are surgeons and corporate VPs who paid ten thousand dollars a month for private *hagwon* academies before they ever auditioned. I got here because a viral clip of me krumping in a parking lot caught a scout’s eye, and if I wash out, there’s no safety net waiting back home—just a shared mattress in my aunt’s living room.

“Five, six, seven, *tuck*,” Baek calls, tapping the closed fan against her wrist.

The track drops—a hyper-compressed, 130-BPM synth-trap beat. 

Count one: We execute a synchronized drop into a wide second-position plié, knees tracking directly over second toes, torsos upright like rods of iron, forearms crossed at a ninety-degree angle in front of our throats. 

Count two: A sharp *tutting* sequence. Wrists hinge ninety degrees outward, fingers blade-flat, creating a geometric frame around our chins, then snap down to lock parallel to our collarbones on the *and*-count. 

My body rebels before my brain can stop it. Where the choreography demands a sterile, lifeless isolation—*kalgunmu*, the "knife-group dance" where seven bodies must read as one blade—my chest instinctively hits a micro-pop on the snare, sending a liquid wave rolling down my solar plexus into my pelvis. In a battle, that texture is everything; it’s the *grooving* that proves the music is inside you. In the mirror, it looks like a glitch in a factory assembly line. While Min-jun at the apex and Ji-hoon to my right freeze like marble statues on the *and* of two, my right shoulder is still settling from the ripple.

Count three and four: The diagonal transition. I’m supposed to push off my left ball of the foot, execute a crisp *pirouette en dedans* turning inward to my right, and travel two meters forward and three meters left, threading the gap between Min-jun (who is sliding straight back to the upstage center mark) and Tae-yang (who is jeté-ing across from stage left). 

I push off, but ten years of house jacking and Turfing hijack my tendons. Instead of pulling my right ankle tight to my left knee in a clean classical *passé*, my heel drops into a low, sweeping *corkscrew* glide, my hips lagging a sixteenth-note behind the beat to drag the pocket. Because my center of gravity is two inches lower and my momentum arcs instead of slicing a straight Euclidean line, I arrive at the center-front apex a fraction of a second late—and six inches too far stage right.

My left elbow clips Min-jun’s ribs as he retreats. He gasps, stumbling off his axis, breaking the razor-sharp silhouette of the formation.

*CLACK.*

The bamboo fan snaps shut like a gunshot. The music dies. Six chests heave in silent, synchronized discipline; nobody dares wipe their sweat without permission. I stand frozen at the apex of the V, my sneakers straddling the neon pink tape mark I was supposed to hit dead center.

Director Baek’s heels click across the marley floor. She stops twelve inches from my face, smelling of white tea and cold iron. With the tip of her closed fan, she hooks my chin and lifts it half an inch, then uses the bamboo edge to whack the outside of my left knee, forcing it inward three centimeters to align with my hip bone.

“What is this?” she asks softly. “You are dragging your pelvis like you are carrying bags of wet cement. Why do you add a chest roll on the two-and?”

“The snare has a swing to it, Coach,” I rasp, my throat dry. “If you hit it straight on the grid, it feels dead. I was just filling the pocket—”

“The pocket does not belong to you,” Baek interrupts, her dark eyes boring into mine. “Out on the street, you dance so people look at *you*. Here, if the camera sees *you* instead of the line, you have failed. You have incredible fast-twitch power. Your isolations are stronger than anyone in this room. That is why I brought you to Seoul. But you are arrogant. You think your little habits are ‘soul.’ They are noise. Cut them out, or pack your bags.”

She steps back to the mirror, fanning herself once before snapping the pleated silk shut again. *Clack.* 

“Same transition. From the tutting frame on two. If the apex is off by an inch, everyone does fifty burpees—except him. He will watch you pay for his ‘soul.’”

My stomach knots. I glance in the mirror at Min-jun rubbing his bruised ribs, at Ji-hoon’s jaw clenched tight. If I mess up and make them pay, I’ll be a pariah in the dorms tonight. More than that, I see the trap laid out in front of me. If I give her what she wants—if I bleach the West Coast bounce out of my knees, lock my spine into her tin-soldier cage, and kill the instinct to answer the drum—I might actually debut. I’ll wear the silk shirts, pay off my aunt’s rent, and become a human metronome who can’t remember how to move without a tape mark on the floor.

Or I can blow the transition, prove I’m "untrainable," and take a coach flight back to nothing.

“Positions,” Baek commands.

I walk back to Position 4, two meters behind Min-jun, three meters left of Ji-hoon. I plant my scuffed Jordans on the yellow cross. I stare at my reflection under the fluorescent tubes—dark skin, braided hair damp with sweat, shoulders too loose. *Wait,* I tell my muscles. *Don't give away the game yet. Learn the cage so you know where the bars are.*

“Five, six, seven, *tuck*.”

Count one: I drop into the second-position plié. When the bass hits my sternum, my chest begs to pop. I clamp my lats down like a vise, strangling the impulse before it reaches my ribs. My knees track over my second toes. Exact.

Count two: The tutting frame. Wrists hinge ninety degrees, fingers welded together, snapping down to the collarbone on the *and*. No wave. No bounce. Just the cold, percussive geometry of a switchblade locking open.

His pupils are blown wide in the fluorescent light, his gaze dropping for one unguarded second to my parted lips, then down to where my fingers are whitening against his arm.

For three seconds, the clinical rhythm breaks; he doesn't oscillate the joint, just holds my leg cradled against his chest, his palms burning into the top of my thigh, his hip pressed flush against the edge of the mattress beside my waist. The tension between us is as taut and frayed as a tendon at its tear point.

He lowers my heel back to the paper-covered vinyl, though his hands linger for a beat around my ankle, his thumb brushing my medial malleolus before he steps back.

He turns toward the counter to reach for his clipboard, his shoulders rigid beneath the gray fabric of his shirt. Up on the wall, the flayed anatomical figure stares down at us—all exposed nerves and raw attachments, stripped of every defense.

**Therapeutic Boundaries**

The diffuser on the corner counter hissed every thirty seconds, releasing a thin plume of artificial lavender that couldn’t quite mask the underlying bite of chlorhexidine and cold vinyl. I lay supine on the treatment table, staring at the perforated acoustic tiles of the ceiling, my right leg—the hundred-thousand-dollar ruin of my livelihood—exposed from mid-thigh to ankle. The four-inch arthroscopic scar curving along the medial aspect of my patella was a raised, angry pink, a permanent seam where my ACL and medial meniscus had been stitched back together for a life I didn’t want to live. 

Rehab was an insult. Every degree of flexion gained was just preparing me to walk comfortably into a retirement I hadn’t chosen, while the league moved on without my name on a roster.

"You’re guarding again, Elena," Julian said. 

His voice was clinical, stripped of the ragged, breathless cadence I remembered from the Olympic training center in Colorado Springs. Back then, we had shared ice baths, tape jobs, and the brutal, singular obsession of the four-hundred-meter hurdles. Now, he wore fitted slate-gray scrubs that pulled across the broad, swimmers’ deltoids he’d kept even after hanging up his spikes. A gold wedding band wasn't on his finger, only the faint, pale indentation of calluses from weights and manual therapy. He had pivoted seamlessly—traded the track for a doctorate in physical therapy, whole and purposeful—while I was reduced to a broken hinge on his schedule.

"I’m not guarding," I lied, my voice flat. "My quadriceps just hate you."

Julian didn’t smile, though the corner of his jaw tightened. He stood at my right side, hip pressed flush against the edge of the padded table to anchor himself. The heat of his body radiated through my thin athletic shorts before his hands even made contact. 

"Scoot to the edge," he instructed quietly. "Right hip flush with the border. We need to clear the iliopsoas before I touch the knee, or your pelvis is going to tilt the second I load the joint."

I shifted rightward until the lateral aspect of my thigh hung slightly off the vinyl. Julian stepped between my left foot—which remained planted flat on the table for pelvic stability—and my dangling right leg. The proximity was suffocating. When he leaned over me to stabilize my left anterior superior iliac spine, the front of his scrub top brushed my bare knee, and that faint, maddening lavender scent mixed with the warm cedar and salt of his skin. 

His left palm settled flat and heavy over my left hip bone, pinning my pelvis to the table so my lumbar spine couldn't arch to cheat the stretch. His touch was scorching, professional, and entirely too familiar. My abdominal wall contracted involuntarily—not from pain, but from the sudden, electric weight of his hand so close to the waistband of my shorts.

"Breathe out," Julian murmured, his eyes fixed strictly on the alignment of my femur, refusing to meet mine. "Let the hip flexors lengthen."

With his right hand, he cupped the distal third of my right femur, just above the surgical site, avoiding direct pressure on the patellar tendon. Slowly, he leaned his torso forward, using his body weight to press my right thigh downward toward the floor into hyperextension, while simultaneously using his own shin against my calf to push my knee into ninety degrees of flexion. 

The pull started deep in the groin, a fierce, searing tautness along the psoas and rectus femoris that radiated down into the tight, fibrotic capsule of my reconstructed knee. A sharp gasp tore from my throat. Automatically, my right hamstring spasmed, trying to yank my leg back up to safety, and my right hand flew down to grip his forearm.

Beneath my fingers, the tendons of his forearm were corded like steel cable. His skin was warm, dusted with fine dark hair. When my nails dug into his flexor carpi radialis, Julian’s breath hitched—a microscopic sound, a crack in the clinical veneer. I looked up. His pupils were blown wide, dark and fixed on my mouth, his jaw clenched so hard a muscle feathered beneath his ear. 

"Don't fight the end-range," he said, and his voice dropped half an octave, rough around the edges. He didn't shake my hand off his arm. Instead, he shifted his stance wider, wedging his thigh firmer against my lower leg to trap the movement. "Push up into my hand. Twenty percent effort. Contract."

It was proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation—contract-relax. I knew the drill. Pushing my thigh upward against his downward resistance forced my hip flexors and quads into an isometric contraction while stretched to their absolute limit. The burn inside the joint capsule turned white-hot, a dull, throbbing ache blooming behind the kneecap where scar tissue refused to yield. Sweat broke out along my collarbone. I stared at the hollow of his throat, watching his pulse hammer frantically against his skin as he absorbed my strength with his own. For five seconds, we were locked in a trembling, static war—my body straining upward into his palm, his chest hovering inches above my ribs, our breathing ragged and synchronized.

"And release," he whispered.

I went limp. Before my nervous system could register the reprieve, Julian exhaled and sank another two inches into the stretch, driving my femur further toward the floor and nudging his shin forward to force another five degrees of knee flexion. 

A low, involuntary whimper escaped me as the scar tissue inside the medial joint line gave way with a microscopic, burning tear of adhesions. My back wanted to arch; his left hand pressed harder into my hip bone, pinning me down with bruising, steadying authority. His thumb grazed the bare skin just above my hip crease, a millimeter from the hem of my shorts, and a violent shiver rippled down my spine that had nothing to do with nociception.

"Right there," Julian breathed, his gaze finally colliding with mine. The clinical distance was gone, burned away by the heat trapped between our bodies. His fingers flexed against my hip, a fraction too tight, lingering on the bare skin as my leg trembled against his shin. "You're at one hundred and fifteen degrees, Elena. Stay with me."

I hated the knee. I hated the table. Most of all, I hated the way my pulse raced under his hands—traitorous, alive, and begging him not to let go.

I hate this room. I hate the resistance bands hanging on the wall like shed skins. Mostly, I hate the mandate from the federation’s insurance board requiring twelve weeks of documented rehab to release my medical retirement settlement, and the cosmic joke that put Julian Vance’s name on my intake form.

Julian steps between my hanging left leg and the edge of the table.

Seeing them on him while he holds a goniometer instead of a starting block makes my stomach twist with a bitter, claustrophobic heat. He survived the end of his career. He evolved. I just broke.

"Don't arch," he murmurs. 

Before I can snap that I’m not arching, his right hand lands flat over my left anterior superior iliac spine—the bony crest of my hip—pinning my pelvis to the table. His palm is broad, dry, and radiates a sudden, startling heat through the thin cotton of my shorts. The heel of his hand rests less than two inches from the crease of my groin.

My breath catches in my throat, an involuntary hitch that has nothing to do with my knee.

Julian’s eyes flick up from my hip to my face. From this angle, hovering over my side, the fluorescent light catches the sharp ridge of his cheekbone and the dark, stubbled line of his jaw. His pupils are wide, swallowing the hazel ring around them, and for half a second his thumb presses harder into my hipbone—not clinical stabilization, just grip. Then his jaw tightens, a muscle feathering beneath his ear, and he looks back down at my knee.

"Rectus femoris is still guarding," he says, his voice dropping half an octave, rougher than before. "I’m going to take you into passive knee flexion while maintaining hip extension. Tell me when the pull turns sharp."

He steps closer, wedging the outside of his right thigh against the lateral aspect of my hanging left thigh to prevent my hip from abducting. Through the fabric of his scrubs, his quadricep is rock-solid, a warm wall braced against my skin. His left hand wraps around my distal tibia, just above the ankle malleoli, his fingers spanning the bone.

Slowly, he uses his shin and hand to push my lower leg backward, bending my knee underneath the table edge.

At ninety degrees of flexion, the fascia across the front of my thigh pulls taut like winch cable. At one hundred degrees, a hot, iron band cinches around my patellar tendon. 

"Breathe through the nose, Clara," Julian says. He leans forward to leverage his weight against my shin, bringing his chest directly over my torso. The clean, cedar-and-salt smell of his skin cuts right through the lemon antiseptic. One of those neon compression sleeves brushes the bare skin of my inner knee as he adjusts his grip.

My left quadricep quivers, a rapid, involuntary fasciculation under the skin as the joint capsule resists the bend. My fingers dig harder into my right shin. A small, strangled sound slips from the back of my throat as he pushes past a hundred and ten degrees—that razor-wire threshold where the scar tissue inside the joint crease feels like it’s about to split open.

Julian freezes immediately, holding the exact angle with isometric precision. His breath hits my collarbone, warm and uneven. 

"Sharp?" he asks softly.

"Tight," I lie through my teeth, refusing to give the injury—or him—the satisfaction of calling it pain. "It’s fine. Push it."

He looks down at me, his face twelve inches from mine. A bead of sweat tracks down the hollow of his throat and disappears into the collar of his shirt. "You always were a terrible liar on the table," he whispers. 

Instead of backing off, he shifts his weight. He hooks my ankle against the front of his own hip, freeing his left hand. His fingers slide up my calf, over the back of my knee, and sink into the distal belly of my quadriceps, right where the vastus lateralis meets the iliotibial band. With the pad of his thumb, he applies a slow, brutal cross-friction pressure directly into the adhesions while keeping my knee locked against his pelvis.

The burn is exquisite, a bright white flare that makes my back arch half an inch off the vinyl before his right hand—still splayed over my hip crest—shoves me firmly back down. 

"Stay with me," he mutters, though his own fingers are trembling slightly against my thigh, his thumb stroking a slow, deep groove along the lateral channel of my muscle. Every pass of his hand drags my skin toward my hip, the heel of his other palm shifting against my pelvic bone with the rhythm of the leverage. My pulse hammers in my ears, confused by the signals: the surgical ache of the joint, the crushing weight of his hand pinning my pelvis, the intimate cradle of my ankle pressed tight against his groin as he rocks his hips half an inch forward to deepen the stretch by two more degrees.

My left hamstring spasms, pulling my heel harder against the front of his scrubs. Julian sucks in a sharp breath through his teeth, his fingers tightening on my bare thigh hard enough to leave white crescents in my skin. 

For three seconds, neither of us moves. I’m pinned under the triangle of his arms, my knee bent to its ragged limit against his hip, my chest rising and falling against the air he’s exhaling. If I lifted my chin three inches, my mouth would brush the pulse point jumping wildly at the base of his throat. 

Then Julian’s eyelids shutter closed. He steps back in one controlled, fluid motion, guiding my leg out of flexion until my foot hangs loosely again, the sudden absence of his heat leaving my skin prickling with goosebumps in the sixty-eight-degree air.

He strips his hands back up the magenta-and-cyan sleeves, his chest still heaving slightly as he turns toward the rolling metal cart.

response:
# Hell is Other Demons

The problem with absolute monarchy, Lucifer Morningstar reflected, was the paperwork. People above stairs—and below, for that matter—tended to imagine the Prince of Darkness spending his Tuesdays lounging in a lake of cinematic hellfire, cackling over the ruin of kings. In reality, he had spent the better part of the morning reviewing quarterly supply-chain requisitions for the Seventh Circle. There was a critical shortage of artisanal brimstone, the boiling pitch in Malebolge was three degrees below regulatory standards, and the Screaming Damned of Sector Four had formed a committee to complain about the acoustics.

*Crunch. Screeeeeeech. Crunch.*

Lucifer pinched the bridge of his nose and looked down. 

Barnaby, a three-headed hellhound the size of a respectable hatchback, had all three sets of jaws clamped firmly around the front-left leg of the Obsidian Throne—which, due to budget cuts during the Bronze Age, was actually cast iron painted matte black. Drool the temperature of molten lead pooled on the flagstones, hissing faintly.

"Barnaby," Lucifer said, his voice carrying the melodious, terrible resonance of a dying star, though right now it mostly sounded like a man who hadn’t had his second espresso. "Do stop that. You’re ruining the finish. Go chew on a bishop."

Barnaby’s middle head paused, offered a wet, sulfurous whine, and went right back to gnawing. Metal shrieked against tooth. The throne listed half an inch to the left.

Ever since Lilith had moved out in the autumn—taking the good silverware, half the legions of Dis, and the French press—Barnaby had developed separation anxiety. Frankly, Lucifer wasn’t doing much better. The Palace of Pandemonium had ten thousand rooms, and without Lilith stalking through them in a cloud of ozone and grievance, every single one of them felt entirely too large.

A polite knock echoed from the thirty-foot bronze doors. Azazel, Minor Duke of Accounting, poked his horned head in.

"Sire?" Azazel’s spectacles were askew. "She’s here again."

Lucifer’s heart, a cold and metaphorical organ, gave an inconvenient little flutter. He immediately smoothed the lapels of his bespoke charcoal suit. "Did she bring a siege engine?"

"No, my Lord. Just a tote bag."

"Ah," Lucifer said, striving for a tone of cosmic indifference. "Send her in, then. And tell the chorus of the wailing dead to keep it down to a dull roar. We’re trying to have a conversation."

Lilith entered the throne room the way she entered everywhere: as if she owned the freehold and was strongly considering knocking the walls down to put in an open-concept kitchen. She looked infuriatingly good. Her hair was the color of a winter midnight, and she wore a trench coat woven from the spun regrets of Victorian poets.

"Lou," she said, stopping just short of the puddle of magma-drool.

"Lilith," Lucifer replied, leaning casually against the right armrest so the throne wouldn't tip. "To what do I owe the pleasure? Have we forgotten to forward your mail again? I’ve spoken to the imps in the sorting office, though frankly, half of them are illiterate."

"It’s not the mail." She reached into her tote bag and pulled out a small, square plastic container. "You left your Tupperware at my citadel."

Lucifer stared at the container. "Lilith, we broke up four centuries ago. In the middle of the Thirty Years' War. You threw aleviathan at my conservatory."

"You were being passive-aggressive about my mother," she said reasonably. "And it’s a very good container. The lid actually snaps on all four sides. You know how hard it is to find airtight storage in the Pit? Everything warps from the humidity."

"You crossed the River Styx," Lucifer said slowly, "bypassed the Fields of Punishment, and braved the bureaucratic nightmare of the Visitor’s Desk, to return a piece of mid-grade plastic."

"I was in the neighborhood," she said, not quite meeting his eyes. "I had to curse a bloodline in the third district. Besides, I made soup."

"Soup."

"Lentil and damned-soul broth. Mostly lentil. You look thin, Lou. Have you been eating, or are you just brooding on the parapet and subsisting on the existential dread of mortals?"

"It’s very filling," Lucifer muttered, though he stood up—the throne gave a relieved *ping* as his weight left it—and walked down the dais to take the container. Their fingers brushed. A tiny arc of blue static snapped between them, smelling faintly of figs and the first night of creation.

*Crunch. Snap.*

The front-left leg of the Iron Throne finally gave way. With a sound like a dropped church bell, six tons of dark majesty listed sideways and crashed onto the flagstones.

Barnaby’s three heads froze, six ears pinned back in unison, before he abandoned the severed iron leg and trotted over to Lilith, all three tails wagging so hard his entire rear end oscillated.

"Hello, sweethearts," Lilith cooed, dropping to one knee to scratch behind six ears at once. The terrifying Mother of Abominations, Scourge of the Euphrates, dissolved into baby talk. "Who’s a good harbinger of the apocalypse? You are. Yes, you are. Is Daddy neglecting you? Is he making you listen to his harpsichord compositions?"

"He’s teething," Lucifer said defensively. "He’s only four thousand years old. And my harpsichord pieces are very nuanced."

Lilith stood, brushing ash from her knees. She looked at the fallen throne, then around the vast, shadowy hall. "You moved the tapestries."

"They were collecting soot."

"It looks bleak, Lou. Even for Hell." She sighed, a sound that had once toppled the walls of Jericho, though now it just sounded tired. "Are you still using the French press?"

"You took the French press, Lilith. In the settlement. Along with the Duchy of Carcassonne."

"Right." She tucked a strand of night-dark hair behind her ear. "Well. I suppose I don't really use it. The coffee at my place tastes like mud anyway. The water table is too close to the River Phlegethon." She paused, looking at his tie. "I could bring it back. Thursday, maybe. If you’re not busy torturing the wicked."

Lucifer looked at the plastic container of lentil soup in his hands, then at the woman who had been the thorn in his side since the Garden had wet paint. Outside the tall lancet windows, a rain of fire began to fall, pattering softly against the stained glass like an autumn drizzle in London.

"I have a four o'clock flaying," Lucifer said carefully, "and a brief meeting with the Horsemen—Pestilence wants to rebrand again—but I believe I could clear my evening. Provided you don't bring a leviathan."

A slow, wicked smile curved Lilith’s lips. "No promises, darling. Make sure you have wine. The good stuff from the 14th century, not that vineyard in Gaul you’re always trying to push."

She turned and walked out, her heels clicking a sharp, familiar rhythm against the stone until the bronze doors boomed shut behind her.

Lucifer stood alone in the quiet hall. After a moment, he looked down at Barnaby, whose left head was currently trying to eat the iron throne’s middle head's ear.

"Right," the Lord of Hell said to the empty room. "I suppose we'd better call a carpenter."
