response:
**Hell is Other Demons**

It was a Tuesday in Dis, which meant the ash was coming down sideways. 

It wasn’t the dramatic, apocalyptic ash of the brochures—the kind that buried Pompeii or choked the skies of Revelation. It was a fine, gray, bureaucratic drizzle that smelled faintly of burnt toast and old hair. It got into the window tracks. It ruined suede. 

Lucifer Morningstar stood on the balcony of the Obsidian Spire, holding a mug that said *World’s Okayest Demiurge* (a gag gift from Beelzebub three millennia ago, before Beelzebub got into mindfulness and stopped being fun) and watched the gray flakes settle onto the screaming fields of the Phlegethon. 

He was lonely. This was a difficult emotion for the Prince of Darkness to process, largely because his entire existence was predicated on being the ultimate individualist, and partly because there were currently nine billion souls within a five-mile radius, all of them clamoring for his attention. None of them, however, knew how he liked his tea, or would tell him when his brooding was crossing the line from Byronic to merely petulant.

"Sire," said a voice from the doorway. 

It was Azazel, his Chief of Staff, holding a clipboard bound in cured tax-auditor skin. Azazel wore spectacles on the end of his snout and had the perpetually harried look of a demon who had been trying to balance the torment budget since the Bronze Age.

"The pitchfork union is threatening a walkout in Circle Four," Azazel said, wiping a fleck of ash from his ledger. "They say the handles are splintering and the ergonomics are—I quote—'literally torture.'"

"It’s Hell, Azazel," Lucifer sighed, not turning around. "The clue is in the name."

"Yes, Sire. I told them that. They said the irony wasn't in their collective bargaining agreement. Also, we have a backlog in Fraud. Too many crypto-bros. We’re running out of boiling pitch, and the imps are complaining that the damned won't stop trying to pitch them decentralized Eternal Damnation tokens even while being flayed."

"Sublet them to the Ninth Circle. Let the ice deal with them."

"Very good, Sire. Oh, and... she’s in the lobby."

Lucifer’s wings, which he usually kept tucked neatly beneath his bespoke Savile Row pinstripe, gave an involuntary, feathery twitch. He did not turn around too quickly, because he had sixty-six hundred years of dignity to maintain, though he did spill a drop of Earl Grey onto his cuff.

"She?" Lucifer asked, aiming for a tone of glacial indifference and landing somewhere near a teenager trying to sound casual about a text message. "Do be specific, Azazel. Is she here to assassinate me? Because if it’s an assassination, she needs to fill out a Form 4B. After the 1920s unpleasantness with the garrote, we agreed on boundaries."

"She doesn't have a garrote, Sire. She has a Tupperware container."

Lucifer frowned. They were currently in the "Off" phase of a relationship that had been oscillating between "Passionate Co-Regency" and "Total Thermonuclear War" since before Mesopotamia had a zoning board. Their last breakup—triggered by a disagreement over who had left the Hellhound out in the sulfur rain, which had escalated into the sinking of Atlantis—had lasted four centuries. 

For the first three hundred years, Lilith had only visited to throw flaming spears through his stained-glass windows. Last month, she had thrown a brick with a note attached that read: *You’re out of coffee filters, you narcissistic bastard.* Last week, she hadn't thrown anything at all; she had simply materialized in his kitchen, eaten all the maraschino cherries out of his Manhattan jar, called his new haircut "very divorced," and vanished in a puff of brimstone.

Lucifer found himself smoothing his lapels. "Send her up. And tell the screaming choir in the courtyard to drop it by three decibels. I have a headache."

When Lilith entered the study, she brought the smell of ozone, night-blooming jasmine, and the ash drizzle with her. She was wearing a trench coat over a cocktail dress that looked like it had been woven from the concept of bad intentions. She brushed gray flakes from her dark hair, letting them fall onto Lucifer’s priceless Persian rug—a rug woven by a man who had been damned specifically for his terrible taste in patterns, though Lucifer had grown rather fond of it.

"You moved the credenza," she said, instead of hello.

"You threw the Duke of Normandy through the old one," Lucifer replied smoothly, leaning against his desk. "I had to redecorate."

"He was looking at me funny." She set a plastic container with a burping red lid onto a stack of Papal bulls. "I made pomegranate-blood reduction. Made too much. Figured I’d bring it over before it congealed, since I know you haven't eaten anything besides misery and Scotch since 1888."

"I eat," Lucifer said defensively. "I had a fig in the seventies."

"You look thin. In a desperate, 'I’m listening to Leonard Cohen on vinyl' sort of way." Lilith walked over to the balcony doors, peering out into the relentless, soft gray fall. "The ash is bad today. Is someone burning the heretics on the East Lawn again? I told you, when the wind blows from the Styx, the soot gets all over the upholstery."

"It’s Tuesday," Lucifer said, walking over to stand beside her—close enough to feel the static electricity that always hummed off her skin, far enough away to maintain plausible deniability if she had a dagger in her garter. "Tuesday is the gluttons. They’re very greasy."

"Mm." She leaned her hip against the balustrade. "Mammon called me."

"Mammon is a gossip and a sycophant."

"He said you went on a date with a Valkyrie."

Lucifer took a slow sip of his cold tea. "It was a networking dinner. We were discussing jurisdiction over warriors who die choking_on_pretzels. Hardly romantic. Besides, she spent the whole evening talking about her winged horse. Do you know how tedious horse girls are when the horse is immortal?"

The corner of Lilith’s mouth twitched. It was a microscopic movement, barely a millimeter, but to Lucifer, who had studied the cartography of her face since the dawn of time, it was practically a parade.

"I heard she tried to arm-wrestle you over the bill," Lilith said.

"She won," Lucifer admitted. "I let her."

"You didn't let her. You have weak wrists. You’ve always had weak wrists; it’s from all the harp playing in your youth." 

She turned to look at him then, her eyes dark and ancient and entirely too perceptive. Down below, in the courtyard, a three-headed dog was trying to catch falling ash on its three tongues while a minor demon in a high-vis vest attempted to sweep the steps with a broom that was on fire.

"I still have your sweater," Lilith said quietly. "The black cashmere one."

"All my sweaters are black cashmere."

"The one with the scorch mark on the left sleeve. From Prague."

"Ah," Lucifer said. Prague had been a very good century. "Keep it. It looks better on you anyway."

"It’s stretched out. And it smells like your cologne. Which is still too heavy on the sandalwood, by the way." She sighed, looking back out at the gray sky. "The furnace in my palace is making that clanking noise again. The one that sounds like a bishop being dropped down a well."

"Have you bled the radiators?"

"Of course I’ve bled the radiators, Samael, I’m the Mother of Abominations, not an idiot. The valve is stuck. It requires two pairs of hands. Or one pair of hands and someone to hold the flashlight while I swear at it."

Lucifer set his mug down on the balustrade. Already, a thin film of gray ash was forming on the surface of the tea. 

"I suppose," the Lord of the Pit said carefully, "that I could clear my afternoon. After I deal with the pitchfork union. Purely in an administrative capacity, of course. As your landlord."

"I don't pay rent," Lilith pointed out.

"And you're terrible at maintenance. It’s a miracle I haven't evicted you."

"You tried," she said, stepping toward the door, pausing just long enough to let her fingertips brush against the lapel of his suit, knocking a bit of soot from the silk. "In 1492. We ended up setting the kitchen on fire."

"We did," Lucifer murmured. 

"Bring the good wrench," she called over her shoulder as the heavy oak doors swung shut behind her. "And leave the Tupperware. If you lose the lid, I’ll flay your staff."

Lucifer stood alone in his office for a moment. Outside, the ash kept falling, soft and endless, blanketing the screaming pits and the brimstone spires in a quiet, domestic gray. He walked over to his desk, picked up the plastic container, and pressed the center of the lid until it made a small, satisfying *pop*. 

"Azazel!" he called out, his voice echoing down the halls of the damned. "Cancel my four o'clock flaying! And find me a flashlight!"

prompt:
Hell is Other Demons

Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Write a day in the life of this power couple, with elements of dark comedy & fantasy. Use understated irony & absurdity by merging the black immorality and everyday business of running hell, against relatable domestic relationship drama. Take cues from Neil Gaiman. Lilith carries a scorched leather purse containing odd trinkets from mortal realms. 1000 words.
response:
### Hell is Other Demons

The problem with absolute damnation, Lucifer Morningstar reflected, was the paperwork. 

People—mortals, poets, the occasional Renaissance painter with an overactive imagination—always assumed Hell was an improvisational jazz of torment. They pictured spontaneous flaying, artisanal lakes of fire, and demons with pitchforks acting on pure, joyful impulse. In reality, eternity required spreadsheets. If you boiled a corrupt seventeenth-century haberdasher in lead on a Tuesday when he was scheduled for the flesh-eating beetles, the union stewards from the Seventh Circle filed a grievance, and then nobody got tortured until Thursday.

Lucifer sighed, rubbing his temples. Outside his floor-to-ceiling obsidian windows, the sky of Dis was the color of a week-old bruise, and the River Styx was backed up again—mostly with middle-management consultants from Delaware who refused to board the ferry until Charon showed them his credentials.

He was lonely. That was the other thing the poets never mentioned. When you were the Lightbringer, the First of the Fallen, nobody ever asked if you wanted to split an appetizer. They just trembled, wept, or asked for the Wi-Fi password (there wasn't one; everyone had to use dial-up, which had been Azazel’s idea and had earned him a commendation).

The heavy bronze doors of the office swung open without a knock. Only one entity in all the Nine Circles ignored the receptionist—mostly because three centuries ago, she had turned the receptionist into a decorativesalt lick.

"You've changed the drapes," Lilith said. 

She was wearing a trench coat woven from the shadows of unkept promises and boots that clicked sharply against the bone-mosaic floor. Slung over her shoulder was her favorite purse, a battered, scorched leather satchel that looked as though it had survived a dragon’s sneeze and smelled faintly of peppermint and ozone. 

"They're woven from the despair of forgotten child actors," Lucifer said, trying and failing to sound indifferent as he set down his fountain pen. "They block the glare off the sulfur pits. To what do I owe the pleasure, darling? Have you come to stab me with a dagger of crystallized spite again, or is it a Tuesday?"

"That was one time, Luci, and you’d left your wet towels on the Altar of Unspeakable Agony," Lilith replied smoothly. She didn't draw a weapon. That was the third time this month she had arrived without attempting regicide. Lucifer tried not to let his hopes rise; hope was technically contraband on this floor.

Instead, she dropped into the leather armchair across from his desk, crossing her legs, and began rummaging through the scorched leather purse. The bag was smaller on the outside than the inside, and entirely governed by her whims.

"I was in Prague," she said, pulling out a half-eaten sourdough bagel, a rusted 1974 municipal parking meter from Des Moines, and a live, mildly confused pigeon, which she set on the edge of his desk. "And then Seattle. Anyway, you left this at my place in the Fourth Epoch."

She tossed a small object across the blotter. Lucifer caught it. It was a silver cufflink shaped like a weeping seraph. 

"You didn't have a 'place' in the Fourth Epoch," Lucifer pointed out, turning the cufflink over in his long fingers. "You were living in a haunted banyan tree outside Ur, and I distinctly remember taking both cufflinks with me after you set my chariot on fire."

"Details," Lilith said, waving a hand. She reached back into the scorched satchel, past the muffled sound of a brass band and what sounded suspiciously like the Lost Library of Alexandria. She pulled out a plastic snow globe of the Eiffel Tower—except instead of snow, it swirled with tiny, screaming French aristocrats—and a pair of novelty sunglasses with plastic Venetian blinds for lenses. "Here. I got you a souvenir."

She slid a ceramic mug across the desk. It read: *World’s Okayest Overlord.*

Lucifer stared at the mug, then up at the First Wife of Man, Queen of the Night, Mother of Monsters. "You went to a gift shop?"

"I went to an airport," Lilith corrected, examining her fingernails. "Airports are lovely now. Delayed flights, crying toddlers, eighteen-dollar egg salad sandwiches. Honestly, Luci, your boys in Malebolge are working way too hard. You should just outsource the whole operation to Newark Liberty International."

"It lacks theatricality," Lucifer murmured, though he pulled the mug closer. He hadn't been given a gift since Beelzebub had presented him with a plague of frogs for his birthday in 1347, and those hadn't even been housebroken. "Have you eaten?"

Lilith paused, looking up through her lashes. Since their most recent breakup—fourteen years ago, over a philosophical disagreement regarding whether to devour a hitchhiker in Albuquerque or simply give him bad directions—their interactions had consisted entirely of cursed telegrams and the occasional territorial skirmish in Purgatory. 

"I had a corrupt senator's self-esteem on the way down," she said. "Why?"

"The cafeteria is doing tacos," Lucifer said, standing up and smoothing his waistcoat. "Well, they're called tacos. In truth, they are the manifested regrets of gluttons wrapped in corn tortillas, and the salsa is mildly radioactive, but they have that little lime wedge you like."

Lilith looked at the pigeon on the desk, which was currently pecking at a requisition form for three thousand gallons of boiling pitch. She shoved the parking meter and the snow globe back into her scorched purse, snapped the brass clasp shut, and stood.

"Only if we can walk past the Lake of Ice on the way," she said, adjusting her coat. "I want to see if that pope is still frozen upside down."

"Which one?" Lucifer asked, offering his arm with acarefully neutral expression.

"The one with the funny hat."

"They all had funny hats, my sweet."

"You know the one I mean," she said, taking his arm. Her hand was warm, smelling of woodsmoke and stolen apples. "And afterwards, you can tell me why the Hell-hounds are wearing little knitted sweaters."

"It was drafty in the kennel," Lucifer said defensively, leading her out into the screaming, fire-lit hallway. "And Cerberus has three necks. Do you have any idea how hard it is to find a pattern for a three-necked turtleneck?"

"You're going soft, Morningstar."

"I am the Prince of Darkness," he replied mildly, stepping over a weeping tax auditor. "I just happen to appreciate a good cable knit."

prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions.
This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?"
Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement.
Mora emits faint cackles that echo uncomfortably through the vaulted ceilings. 1000 words.
response:
The bone gavel did not so much strike the block as sigh against it. 

High upon the obsidian bench, the Sovereign of the Dreaming rested his chin on one pale, spider-fingered hand. Usually, his face was a carving of timeless marble, an abyss into which mortals and immortals alike stared and despaired. Today, however, a muscle beneath his left eye was twitching. It was the third hour of the docket, and he had already adjudicated a boundary dispute between two tooth-loss anxieties and a zoning violation involving a labyrinthine high school hallway with no bathrooms.

"Case four-seven-B," droned the clerk, a tall pelican in a powdered wig. "In the matter of the Dreamer known as Max, aged fourteen, suburban Ohio. *First Love v. Mora of the Eastern Marshes*. A petition for an immediate cease-and-desist, plus damages for emotional muddling."

At the plaintiff’s table, First Love dabbed at his eyes with a lace handkerchief. He was a cherubic entity in a slightly rumpled pastel waistcoat, his cheeks perpetually flushed the color of a bruised peach. Whenever he sighed, three or four stray cherry blossoms drifted out of his collar and died on the flagstones.

At the defense table sat Mora. She was six feet of damp Slavic gloom, draped in tattered gray linen and smelling faintly of cellar mold and winter Pond water. She was currently filing a blackened fingernail against the edge of the mahogany table. Every few seconds, she emitted a faint, dry cackle that echoed uncomfortably through the vaulted ceilings.

Dream closed his eyes. The shadows in the corners of the courtroom deepened in sympathy with his headache.

"Proceed," Dream said. His voice was the rustle of dead leaves in an empty cathedral, edged with the unmistakable cadence of a magistrate who had skipped lunch. "And be brief. The Falling From A Tall Building Union has an injunction scheduled at four."

First Love stood, smoothing his waistcoat with trembling fingers. "My Lord. For six months, I have labored over the boy Max. He is at a delicate crossroads. Four weeks of careful subliminal priming! I procured a meadow of goldenrod—artisanally rendered, My Lord, not stock imagery—and introduced a vision of Chloe from his fifth-period algebra class."

"We have read the brief," Dream murmured. "The sunlight in her hair. The shared geometry textbook."

"It was art!" First Love’s voice cracked. "A slow build of yearning! Every Tuesday and Thursday between three and four in the morning, she laughs, trips over a dandelion, and tumbles playfully atop him. Their noses brush. His heart rate elevates to a healthy, formative flutter. Then he wakes up in a pleasant confusion of emotions, stares at the ceiling, and writes terrible poetry. It is the cornerstone of human romantic development."

First Love turned and pointed an accusing, trembling finger at the defense table. 

"Until *she* squatted in my meadow!"

Mora didn't look up from her nails. Another faint cackle escaped her throat, rattling off the high stone arches like dry peas in a tin cup.

"Tell the Court what happened on Thursday last," First Love demanded, his voice rising. "Go on!"

"Your Honor," Mora said, her voice like gravel being turned over with a rusted shovel. "I’m an old spirit. I have simple needs."

"You turned Chloe’s teeth into needles!" First Love shrieked.

"Only the canines," Mora corrected mildly. "And only after I was already straddling the boy. Honestly, you’d think I’d set the goldenrod on fire. I left the flowers alone, didn't I? Very nice flowers. Smelled like sneeze."

Dream’s fingers drummed once against the obsidian armrest. "Mora. You are chartered to the Third District of Nightmares. Sleep paralysis, suffocation terrors, the occasional hag-riding of superstitious woodsmen. What were you doing in a Class-One Adolescent Pastoral?"

Mora finally stood, her joints popping like green wood on a grate. "Have you tried haunting the Third District lately, My Lord? Everyone’s on melatonin and white-noise machines. Half the adults sleep with little plastic hoses strapped to their faces pumping air into their throats. Do you know what it’s like trying to sit on the chest of an accountant from Cleveland and suck his breath away when he’s hooked up to a CPAP machine? It’s like drinking from a leaf blower. Gives me terrible gas."

A murmur ran through the gallery, where several minor phobias were taking notes.

"So I took a stroll," Mora continued, shrugging her bony shoulders. "Found this nice, quiet little dreamscape. No machinery. Just a boy lying flat on his back—practically an invitation—already breathing heavy. Then the little blonde phantom climbs right on top of him. Well, the staging was already done for me! It would have been wasteful *not* to tag in."

"You weighed four hundred pounds!" First Love wept. "You pinned his sternum to his spine, turned your skin the color of a drowned turnip, and drank his exhalations while whispering in Old Church Slavonic!"

"A girl’s gotta eat too, you know?" Mora spread her clawed hands in a gesture of pure, practical reason. "Besides, I kept the blonde hair. And the algebra sweater. I thought it was a nice touch. Transitional."

She let out another low, rasping cackle. The pelican clerk shuddered and tucked his beak into his feathers.

"The boy is ruined!" First Love appealed to the bench, clutching his chest. "I checked his waking subconscious this morning. The pleasant confusion is gone! It has been replaced by... by a *deeply unpleasant* confusion! When the real Chloe asked to borrow a pencil in homeroom today, he broke into a cold sweat, couldn't move his legs, and found himself inexplicably aroused by the smell of damp peat! My work is contaminated!"

Dream stared down at the two of them. The eternal cosmic fabric of human longing, reduced to a landlord-tenant dispute. 

"Let me see the transcript of the waking residual," Dream said.

The pelican stepped forward and handed up a small, glowing glass orb. Dream peered into its depths. Inside, the fourteen-year-old boy was doodling in the margins of his notebook. It was a heart pierced by an arrow, except the heart had spider legs and the name *CHLOE* was written in jagged, terrified block letters.

Dream’s pale lips twitched. The irritation in his star-lit eyes receded by a fraction of an inch, replaced by a cold, ancient glint that those who knew him well had learned to fear far more than his wrath.

"Fascinating," the Lord of Dreams murmured.

"It is an abomination!" First Love insisted. "I demand an immediate purge of the memory, a restraining order keeping her three pastures away from my wildflowers, and full restitution of my Tuesday-Thursday slot!"

"And I move for dismissal," Mora countered, leaning an elbow on the table. "Possession is nine-tenths of the subconscious. The kid didn't kick me off. Granted, he *couldn't*, because I had his motor cortex locked down tighter than a root cellar in January, but still. His heart rate was through the roof. High engagement metrics."

Dream set the glass orb down. The courtroom fell into a hush so complete that only Mora’s soft, intermittent cackling broke the silence, bouncing off the high ribs of the ceiling.

"First Love," Dream said smoothly. "Your petition states that the purpose of this dreamscape is to initiate the boy into the realities of mortal romance."

"Yes, My Lord! The sweet ache! The dizzying precipice of affection!"

"Indeed," Dream said, steepling his pale fingers. "And yet, you present him only with goldenrod and nose-brushing. You leave him wholly unprepared for the... later stages of the human condition."

First Love blinked. "My Lord?"

"The paralysis," Dream mused, a faint, dark amusement curling the edges of his voice. "The crushing weight upon the chest. The sensation that one’s very life-breath is being slowly, methodically siphoned away by a creature wearing a familiar sweater, whom one nonetheless cannot stop looking at."

Mora tilted her head, a slow grin splitting her gray face.

"Surely," Dream continued, looking down his nose at the horrified cherub, "there is no purer preparation for his future romantic endeavors than learning to associate desire with existential dread."

"My Lord, he is fourteen!" First Love gasped. "He’s supposed to ask her to the spring semi-formal, not develop a lifelong penchant for goth girls who treat him like furniture!"

"The Tapestry of Fate is complex," Dream replied evenly. "Who are we to say whether Max of Ohio is meant to write sonnets, or to spend his thirties paying women named Raven to step on his throat? Both are valid avenues of human inspiration."

Mora barked a single, delighted laugh that echoed like a cracking tombstone.

"Therefore," Dream announced, lifting the bone gavel, "it is the judgment of this Court that the dreamscape shall be held in joint tenancy."

"Joint—?!" First Love choked on a cherry blossom.

"You shall retain Tuesdays, Thursdays, and the first five minutes of Saturday mornings," Dream decreed. "You may keep your meadow. However, at the precise moment the girl leans in for the muddled almost-kiss, Mora is granted a ninety-second easement to assume her form, crush the boy’s ribcage, and feed upon his terror."

"Wait," Mora frowned, suspicious now. "Just ninety seconds? And I have to wear the pastel cardigan every time?"

"And lip gloss," Dream added, his eyes glittering in the dark. "Strawberry. You wanted a steady meal without a machine, Mora. You shall have it—provided you giggle like a ninth-grader before unhinging your jaw."

Mora’s grin vanished. "That’s demeaning."

"That is the law," Dream said. "And you, First Love, will remain on the premises during the feeding to ensure the lighting remains soft and romantic while she suffocates him."

First Love looked as though he might faint. Mora looked as though she might spit on the floor. Neither dared to object.

"If either of you fails to cooperate," Dream concluded softly, "I shall reassign the boy’s nights to the Clown With Too Many Teeth, and put the two of you on wet-dream cleanup duty in the naval barracks."

The bone gavel fell with a sharp, final *crack*.

"Adjourned," Dream said, already rising in a swirl of night-dark robes. "Send in the Falling From A Tall Building Union."

response:
The Court of the Dreaming smelled faintly of ozone and wet ink. At its center stood a single, giant hourglass, its waist narrow as a wasp’s, dripping shimmering sand that chimed like tiny broken bells as it fell.

Behind the high bench of bone and polished night sat Dream. He rested his chin on one pale hand, his dark eyes fixed on the middle distance with the expression of an immortal sovereign who would very much prefer to be organizing his gravel.

"Docket item four-thousand-and-twelve," the bailiff—a raven in a slightly crooked powdered wig—rasped from his perch. "*First Love v. Mora of the Eastern Marshes*. A matter of territorial trespass, unauthorized transfiguration, and theft of nocturnal breath. Subject: Maxwell Sterling, age fourteen, of Surrey."

Dream’s fingers drummed once against the bench. "Proceed. Quickly. The sand does not wait, and my patience is already threadbare."

At the plaintiff’s table, First Love rose. He was a rosy-cheeked youth draped in a tunic the color of a bruised peach, smelling of crushed clover and nervous sweat. He clutched a sheaf of parchment to his chest like a love letter he was afraid to mail.

"My Lord," First Love began, his voice cracking slightly before settling into an earnest tenor. "For three months, I have tended the Sterling boy’s subconscious. It is delicate, loamy soil. Every Tuesday and Friday during his fourth-period Latin naps and REM cycles, I have curated Project Meadow."

"We have read the brief," Dream said. His voice was the rustle of dry leaves in an empty crypt. "A hill. Wildflowers. Clara Jenkins from the third row."

"Not merely wildflowers, Sire," First Love said, blushing up to his ears. "Buttercups. Specifically chosen to reflect the sunlight onto her chin. The wind is calibrated to sixty-two degrees—warm enough for comfort, brisk enough to justify shared body heat. The narrative arc is classic: a shared geometry textbook, an accidental brushing of knuckles, a playful tumble into the clover. She pins his wrists. She leans down. Her hair falls like a curtain of spun copper. Their lips part, separated by a single, trembling millimeter of agonizing, formative bliss—"

"And then," interrupted a voice like gravel grinding in a cold stove, "he stops breathing."

At the defense table sat Mora. She was slouched low in her chair, picking at her teeth with a splinter of dried ribs. Depending on how the courtroom light hit her, she looked either like a corpse pulled from a peat bog or a remarkably striking Eastern European woman who hadn’t slept since the fourteenth century. Her hair was damp, tangled with duckweed, and undeniably lustrous.

First Love pointed a trembling, manicured finger at her. "She hijacked the transition! Last Thursday, right at the moment of the Muddled Almost-Kiss, when the boy’s heart rate reached the optimal flutter of one-hundred-and-ten beats per minute—"

"One-fifteen," Mora corrected lazily, not looking up from her fingernails. "Kid’s a mouth-breather. High caloric yield."

"—she breached the perimeter!" First Love cried. "Clara Jenkins did not kiss him. Instead, her jaw unhinged by four inches, her eyes turned the color of stagnant pond water, and she gained four hundred pounds of dead, crushing weight directly upon his sternum!"

Dream’s gaze shifted, slow and heavy as tectonic plates, toward the defense table. "Mora. You are chartered to the Baltic pines and the damp bedrooms of consumptive cobblers. Why are you in a Surrey meadow?"

Mora sighed, a wet, rattling sound, and stood up. She smoothed down a dress made of woven shadow and moth wings. 

"Look around, Your Grace," she said, gesturing vaguely with the rib-splinter. "Have you tried haunting a cobbler lately? There aren't any. And the flats in Warsaw have double-glazed windows and central heating now. Nobody leaves a crack for the night air. Half my traditional clientele is on CPAP machines. Do you have any idea what pressurized plastic tubing does to the flavor of a panic-wheeze? Tastes like a bicycle tire."

"That does not explain the meadow," Dream said, though a muscle near his jaw twitched.

"I was passing through," Mora said. "Following a draft down a chimney. And there’s this kid, lying flat on his back—prime posture, noorthopedic pillow—just radiating surplus vitality. And this one," she jerked a thumb at First Love, "had already done the heavy lifting. The boy’s paralyzed with adolescent terror anyway. His chest is tight. His throat is dry. Frankly, transitioning from 'Clara Jenkins sitting on his ribs' to 'an ancient Slavic bog-hag sitting on his ribs' took almost zero structural renovation. A girl’s gotta eat too, you know?"

"You turned a formative romantic awakening into sleep paralysis!" First Love gasped, clutching his pearls—which were literal, and strung around his collar. "When she sits on him, she doesn't even bother to fully drop the Clara disguise! She keeps the pleated school skirt and the copper hair, just—rotting slightly at the edges while she siphons his lungs!"

"I left the skirt," Mora said defensively. "I’m not a Philistine. It’s called thematic continuity."

"It is a psychological catastrophe!" First Love appealed to the bench. "The boy woke up at three in the morning entirely unable to move his toes, terrified for his life, and deeply, irreconcilably aroused! The emotional metadata is completely corrupted! Yesterday in Latin class, Clara Jenkins dropped her pencil, and Max broke into a cold sweat and had to cover his lap with a dictionary because he thought she was going to unhinge her jaw and asphyxiate him!"

In the rafters, the raven bailiff let out a short, sharp *caw* that sounded suspiciously like a laugh, then coughed into his wing.

Dream stared down at the two of them. The giant hourglass chimed softly, a thousand grains of silver marking the passing of a mortal minute. For a long moment, the Lord of the Dreaming said nothing. The irritation in his eyes—that ancient, weary annoyance of a god forced to act as a municipal zoning board—slowly curdled into something sharper. Something colder, and infinitely more amused.

"Let me ensure I understand the evidence," Dream murmured. "The boy’s terror has increased?"

"Exponentially," First Love whimpered.

"And his... infatuation?"

First Love looked down at his sandals, his cheeks burning crimson. "Well. The adrenaline spike has technically reinforced the neural pathways associated with Miss Jenkins. By forty percent."

"Sixty," Mora said, grinning to reveal teeth like a row of tombstones. "He’s been googling gothic architecture and asthma inhalers all morning. The kid’s a natural."

Dream leaned back. The shadows of his robe pooled across the floor, brushing the base of the hourglass. A very small, very dangerous smile touched the corners of his pale mouth. Mortals were such fragile, ridiculous engines. Give them buttercups, and they grew bored by twenty. Give them a monster in a pleated skirt, and they wrote poetry for a century.

"The Court finds," Dream said smoothly, "that while Mora’s entry into the buttercup sector was unscheduled, the resulting dreamscape demonstrates... unexpected structural integrity."

"My Lord!" First Love protested.

"The boy is fourteen," Dream continued, his voice dropping an octave, rich with dark mischief. "Pure pastoral romance is wasted on the young; it lacks teeth. Literally, in this instance."

He raised a pale hand, gaveling the air itself. The sound echoed like a slamming cellar door.

"I hereby grant a joint easement. First Love, you shall retain custody of the first twelve minutes of the dream. You may keep the clover, the sixty-two-degree breeze, and the geometry textbook."

First Love blinked. "And the kiss?"

"At the moment of contact," Dream said, his eyes glinting like starlight on oil, "jurisdiction transfers to Mora for a period not to exceed four minutes of thoracic compression and mild soul-siphoning. Provided," he looked pointedly at the nightmare, "she keeps the copper hair and refrains from leaving pond scum on the boy’s duvet."

Mora spat her bone-toothpick onto the floor and offered a mock curtsy. "Fair enough. Pleasure doing business with you, Blondie." She winked a milky eye at First Love. "See you Friday. Bring the buttercups. I like a garnish."

First Love stood frozen, horrified, as Mora sauntered out of the courtroom, her shadow dragging three feet behind her. 

"My Lord," First Love whispered weakly. "What will become of the boy?"

Dream rested his chin back on his hand, watching the shimmering sand fall. "He will probably become an art critic," Dream said dryly. "Or move to Berlin. Bailiff. Call the next case."

prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions.
This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?"
Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement.
The bailiff mispronounces witnesses’ names with an ominous booming voice. 1000 words.
response:
The Magistrate’s Hall of the Dreaming smelled faintly of wet slate and forgotten appointments. Above the bench, the ceiling was a stretch of starless velvet; below it, Lord Morpheus sat with his chin propped on two pale fingers, looking as though he had been carved from bone and mild indigestion.

"The Court of the Unsleeping," boomed the bailiff, a seven-foot gargoyle built of basalt and misplaced confidence, "now calls Docket Four-Four-Nine: *Fist Loaf* versus *More-Uh*."

At the plaintiff’s table, First Love winced, his rosy cheeks deepening to the color of a bruised plum. He adjusted his dandelion-silk cravat and stood. 

"It’s *First Love*, Your Lordship," he said, his voice like a lute string plucked in an empty orchard. "And I am here regarding the recurring meadow of one Maximilian Miller, aged fourteen, of East Sussex."

Dream did not blink. Two points of cold starlight shifted in the dark hollows of his eyes. "**Proceed. Briefly.**"

"For six weeks, my Lord, I have tended the boy’s subconscious with the utmost delicacy," First Love said, gesturing to a floating parchment covered in pastel watercolor sketches. "A classic pastoral arrangement. Sweet clover, a gentle southerly breeze, and Clara from second-period geometry. Each night, they tumble into the grass. She laughs. She pins his wrists—playfully, my Lord, strictly PG-13—and leans in. Just before their lips meet, the alarm rings. He wakes with a fluttering heart and a pleasant, muddled ache." First Lovedabbed at his brow with a lace handkerchief. "It is artisanal work. Formative."

"It was a buffet left out in the sun," came a voice like gravel sliding over a coffin lid.

At the defense table, Mora didn't bother standing. She was draped across her chair in a tangle of oiled black hair, graveyard mist, and a remarkably well-fitted bodice. She was filing a three-inch iron claw against the mahogany edge of the desk. 

"The boy was lying flat on his back with his ribcage practically gift-wrapped," Mora said, blowing dust off her nail. "His heart rate was already up. His breathing was shallow. Do you have any idea how hard it is to find a clean thoracic cavity in East Sussex these days? Half the teenagers sleep on their stomachs with their phones under their chins. A girl’s gotta eat too, you know?"

"You dislocated the narrative!" First Love squeaked. "On Tuesday night, Clara straddled his waist, brushed a daisy from his cheek, and then *unhinged her jaw*, turned the color of a drowned turnip, and crushed his sternum until he couldn't move his toes!"

"I kept the straddling," Mora pointed out reasonably. "And I left the daisies. Actually, I think the daisies really made my eyes pop."

"**Silence,**" Dream said. The word was not loud, yet the ink in the court stenographer’s skull-cup froze solid. Dream’s long fingers drummed once against the obsidian armrest. He had spent the morning untangling a prophetic civil war in the Levant, and his afternoon was currently being held hostage by hormonal zoning laws. "**Call the corroborating witness.**"

The gargoyle bailiff stepped forward, squinting at his scroll. "The Court calls to the stand... *Clarissa of Second-Period Geese-Metry*!"

A shimmering figment of a fourteen-year-old girl in a pleated school skirt materialized in the witness box. She looked around the shadowy hall, mildlybored, chewing on a piece of dream-gum that tasted of nothing at all.

"State your function," First Love prompted gently.

"I’m the projection," the figment said. "I giggle, I smell like vanilla body spray, and my hair moves in slow motion even when there’s no wind. Except since Tuesday, around the third giggle, my spine elongates by four inches, my weight triples, and I start siphoning his life-breath through his teeth." She popped a bubble. "Honestly, the scheduling is a mess. Am I supposed to be giving him butterflies or mild hypoxia?"

"Hypoxia *is* a kind of butterfly," Mora muttered. "Just heavier."

"It is a violation of the Vernal Charter!" First Love cried, slamming his pastel sketches onto the table. "The boy is fourteen! If this continues, he won’t associate romance with sonnetry and longing—he’ll associate it with asphyxiation and women who smell of bog water!"

"Excuse me," Mora snapped, sitting up so fast her vertebrae clicked like castanets. "It is *peat moss* and *night-blooming jasmine*, and for your information, the kid hasn't tried to wake up early once since Thursday. Tuesday, yes, he panicked. Wednesday, he tried to pray. By Friday? He was fluffing his own pillow and waiting for the fog to roll in."

First Love gasped, clutching his pearls. "You lie!"

"Ask the projection," Mora said, gesturing with a claw.

Both entities turned to the witness box. The figment of Clara shrugged. "He did wear his nicer pajamas last night," she admitted. "And when I turned into a shrieking corpse-bride and pinned his lungs to the mattress, his pulse didn't read 'mortal terror' so much as 'terrified, yet weirdly intrigued.' It’s very confusing for my subroutines."

First Love looked as though someone had pissed in his birdbath. He turned desperately to the bench. "My Lord Morpheus, surely you see the danger here. If a nightmare squats upon a foundational romantic template, the mortal’s entire emotional architecture will be warped!"

Dream leaned back. A shadow passed across his face—first the familiar, bottomless weariness of an immortal bureaucrat, and then, at the very corner of his pale mouth, a fraction of a millimeter of upward curve. 

Both petitioners had been tedious. First Love was a sentimental pedant whose buttercup meadows cluttered the lower Dreaming like cheap greeting cards; Mora was a poacher who left half-chewed anxieties scattered across three counties. 

"**The Court has reached a verdict,**" Dream said. 

The bailiff banged his halberd on the floor. "All rise for the *Ver-Ducked*!"

"**Maximilian Miller’s subconscious is no longer a pristine pasture,**" Dream intoned, his voice rolling through the hall like distant thunder. "**To evict the Mare now would leave an absence the boy has already grown accustomed to. Yet to surrender the meadow entirely to the dark would starve the longing that draws him into sleep.**"

"So... I win?" Mora asked, squinting.

"**Neither of you wins,**" Dream said smoothly. "**The parcel is hereby converted into a joint tenancy. First Love, you will maintain the wildflowers, the golden hour light, and the initial approach. Mora, you will assume the projection at the moment of physical contact—specifically, three seconds prior to the kiss.**"

"Joint tenancy?!" First Love’s voice cracked. "My Lord, we have completely incompatible aesthetic philosophies!"

"I don't work with pastels," Mora protested, wrinkling her nose. "I’ll get pollen in my burial shroud."

"**You will collaborate,**" Dream said, and there was a distinct, cold gleam in the starlight of his eyes. "**Every night, between the hours of two and four, you will share the meadow, the projection, and the staging cues. You will file weekly harmony reports with Lucien. And if the boy wakes before the alarm due to a missed transition, I shall reassign you both to the recurring dental-examination dreams of retired tax inspectors.**"

First Love went pale. Mora’s jaw tightened. 

"As for young Maximilian," Dream murmured, resting his chin back upon his hand, "**he will grow up to write moderately successful gothic poetry, and have a very specific, very expensive taste in girlfriends. The Court is adjourned.**"

"All rise!" the bailiff roared. "Next on the docket: *The Boogeyman* versus *Sigmund Fraud*!"

prompt:
Sisyphus Gives Advice
Write a comedic scene in the style of Terry Pratchett featuring Sisyphus, who has started an advice column while continuing his eternal boulder-pushing. Rather than being bitter about his punishment, Sisyphus has developed a comfortably zen emotional intelligence and wisdom from his centuries of repetitive labor. Not in the cliche ways you might expect -- he's actually very grounded, warm & connected with the everyday human plight. He dictates responses to "Crow," his feathered familiar who serves as both scribe and mail carrier.
The piece should include Sisyphus thoughtfully answering several advice-seekers' letters about everyday problems (relationship troubles, work-life balance, dealing with difficult people, life purpose doubts) while periodically returning to his boulder-pushing duties. His advice should be surprisingly insightful and practical.
The humor should emerge naturally from the messages he receives, from mundane to risque. Sisyphus should genuinely enjoy helping others, finding meaning in this new pursuit while maintaining his boulder routine. The humour should be *understated and not forced*. Contrary to expectation, almost none of his advice involves boulder rolling metaphors (though he does sneak *one* subtle in there), nor a treatise on stoicism. We are also going against the obvious fish-out-of-water trope; in fact, he's surprisingly a natural at this.  In all of this , it's important to *show, don't tell*.
The format should be largely epistolary, with the occasional interjection for scene setting.
Crow insists on editorializing Sisyphus’s responses, adding snarky side notes. 1000 words.
response:
The mail sack on the third switchback of Tartarus always smelled faintly of damp wool, sealing wax, and the lingering desperation of people who bought their stationery in bulk. 

Sisyphus wedged a flat piece of shale under the granite’s southern curve, tested the hold with his hip, and wiped his palms on his tunic. 

"Right then," he said, his voice carrying the pleasant, gravelly warmth of a man who had spent three millennia breathing limestone dust. "Let’s do three before the ridge. Who’s on top?"

Crow, perched on a calcified root with a sharpened primary feather clamped in one claw and an inkhorn wedged between two stones, gave the parchment a disdainful peck. 

"Perfumed," Crow croaked. "Smells like crushed violets and poor judgment. Corinth postmark."

***

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
> 
> *My husband Hector and I have been married four years. Recently he suggested we introduce a bronze helmet and a very specific set of oiled leather greaves into the bedchamber. I don’t mind the greaves, truth be told, as the nights are draughty, but he insists on wearing the helmet with the horsehair crest during the—well, the marital act—and calling himself ‘The Siege Engine of Thebes.’ The horsehair tickles my nose terribly, and frankly, I cannot take a man seriously when I can only see his nostrils through a T-shaped slit. How do I tell him he is ruining the mood without crushing his spirit?*
> 
> *Yours in sneezing,*
> *Andromache-but-not-that-one*

***

Sisyphus leaned back against the sun-warmed granite, his eyes crinkling at the corners. "Ah. Bless him. He’s trying."

"He’s concussed," Crow muttered, dipping his quill. "Shall I write *Put a latch on the bedroom door and let him lay siege to the linen cupboard*?"

"You will not," Sisyphus said mildly. "Take this down."

***

> *Dear Andromache,*
> 
> *The thing about a bedroom is that it’s very small, and the outside world is very large, and sometimes a man who spends all day being a clerk or a turnip-weigher needs to feel like he could knock down a wall. There is no harm in the theatre of it.* 
> 
> *However, theatre requires a stage manager. Do not criticize the Siege Engine—men are terribly fragile when they are dressed as furniture or war machines. Instead, appeal to strategy. Tell him that a true commander must survey the field after the initial breach. Have him wear the helmet for the, ah, approach march, and then insist on unbuckling it yourself as the spoils of victory. People rarely mind having their props taken away if you make the undressing feel like part of the ceremony. Also, trim an inch off the horsehair with the kitchen shears when he’s at the baths. He won’t notice.*
> 
> *(Scribe’s Note: Or tell him Thebes had seven gates and none of them were interested in a man whose shin-guards squeak. —C.)*

***

"Did you add a note?" Sisyphus asked, his shoulder already dropping back into the worn hollow on the stone’s flank. 

"Fixed your spelling," Crow lied smoothly.

"I’m dictating."

"Fixed your tone, then. Push your pebble, old man. We’re losing the morning shade."

For forty minutes, the only sounds were the rhythmic *crunch-grind* of basalt against shale, Sisyphus’s steady, four-count breathing, and the occasional dry *scritch* of Crow preening his tail feathers on top of the boulder, riding it up like a minor dark emperor on a very slow parade float. 

At the false summit—where the wind came up from the Phlegethon smelling faintly of toasted sulfur—the stone did what the stone always did. It tipped, gathered a polite sort of momentum, and trundled back down to the ferns at the bottom, knocking the same three pebbles out of the same three ruts.

Sisyphus watched it go with the fond, critical eye of a bowler watching a decent delivery. "Drifted left at the gorse bush," he noted, strolling down the path with his hands in his pockets. "The frost’s heaving the chalk."

" thrilling," Crow said, fluttering down to the mail sack. "Next one’s on butcher’s paper. Heavy hand. Pressed so hard he nearly gutted the reed."

***

> *To the Man on the Hill,*
> 
> *I am an apprentice potter. Five days a week I throw eighty soup bowls a day. On the sixth day, the master looks at the kiln, says ‘Adequate,’ and sells them to a tavern where drunks drop them on the flagstones. By Tuesday they are shards in a ditch, and I am making eighty more. My cousin says I should run away to Athens and sculpt marble gods that last forever, so my life actually means something. Have I wasted my twenties on soup?*
> 
> *—Clay-Under- the-Nails*

***

Sisyphus reached the bottom, squatted beside his boulder, and gave its sun-heated side an affectionate pat. "Oh, I do hate the marble-god people," he murmured. "So drafty in the temples. Ready, Crow?"

***

> *Dear Clay,*
> 
> *Have you ever tried to eat lentil stew off a marble statue of Apollo? It runs right down his thighs and ruins the sandals.*
> 
> *Your cousin is confusing duration with usefulness. A marble god sits in a courtyard being stared at by tourists and shat upon by pigeons—*

***

"Oi," said Crow.

"Present company excepted," Sisyphus amended.

"Pigeons are flying bread-sacks. Put *majestic corvids*."

"I’m not putting *majestic corvids* in a letter about soup bowls."

***

> *—whereas a soup bowl holds hot broth for a cold carter at seven o’clock on a rainy Tuesday. The fact that the bowl breaks on Wednesday doesn’t mean the carter wasn't fed on Tuesday.* 
> 
> *Don't look at the ditch full of shards at the end of the week. Look at the thumb-groove you press into the rim so the tavern-girl doesn't burn her knuckles carrying four at once. Put a little swirl in the glaze on the bottom where only the person washing up will see it. Meaning isn’t something that happens when the work is finished; it’s just paying attention while your hands are wet. Besides, you’d be amazed how much comfort there is in a task where you already know where all the ruts in the road are.*
> 
> *(Scribe’s Note: He’s getting sentimental because the rock didn’t roll over his toe today. Ask your master for another half-obol a week; meaning doesn't buy turnips. —C.)*

***

Sisyphus set his calves, exhaled, and leaned in. The granite gave a companionable groan and rose half an inch out of the ferns. 

"One more while we’ve got the flat stretch?" Sisyphus asked, his shoulder blades bunching neatly under his linen tunic. 

Crow hopped along beside his left sandal, holding a scrap of vellum sideways. "Short one. From a woman in Argos."

***

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
> 
> *My mother-in-law lives with us. Every time I salt the stew, she sighs—just a tiny, whistling sigh through her teeth—and goes to sit in the corner staring at a portrait of her late husband. She never criticizes me aloud. If I ask what’s wrong, she says, ‘Nothing, dear, I’m sure your mother taught you the best she could.’ How do I keep from putting hemlock in her barley water?*
> 
> *—Simmering*

***

Sisyphus chuckled, a low, rumbling sound that vibrated right into the stone. *Step, plant, heave. Step, plant, heave.* "Oh, the whistling sigh. Hades tried that for the first four hundred years. Used to stand on the ridge with a clipboard looking disappointed."

"Until you asked him if he wanted a turn," Crow said.

"Until I asked him if he knew anything about lower-lumbar leverage," Sisyphus corrected. "Write to her before the incline gets steep."

***

> *Dear Simmering,*
> 
> *Never fight a martyr on the battlefield of suffering; they have brought their own cross and already know where the good light is.* 
> 
> *She sighs because she wants you to ask, so she can be brave at you. Next time you salt the pot, hand her the wooden spoon and say, ‘Give that three stirs to the left, Mother, you have the wrist for it.’ When she sighs, agree with her immediately and enthusiastically about something completely unrelated. ‘I know, the humidity is dreadful for the joints, isn’t it? Put your feet up.’ Deprive the sigh of its mysterious power by treating it like a sneeze. And salt the stew in the pantry before you bring the pot out.*
> 
> *(Scribe’s Note: Hemlock has an oily aftertaste and curdles goat’s milk. Purely botanical observation. —C.)*

***

"Seal them up," Sisyphus said, his breath coming a little deeper now as the path tilted toward the clouds. "Take them out on the noon thermal. And bring back some of those figs from the stall by the ferryman’s dock, will you? The purple ones."

Crow jammed the cork into the inkhorn and tucked the letters into his harness. "You still owe me two shiny buttons and a dead beetle for Tuesday’s run."

"Look under the flat shale by the third switchback," Sisyphus said, leaning his forehead against the cool, familiar grain of the rock as he took the next step up. "Found a bronze drachma from the Peloponnesian War this morning. Shiny enough to see your beak in."

Crow’s black eye gleamed. "I’ll be back by sundown. Try not to lose the rock while I’m gone."

"Oh," Sisyphus said cheerfully, "I generally know where to find it."

Not in the cliche ways you might expect -- he's actually very grounded, warm & connected with the everyday human plight.
