The format should be largely epistolary, with the occasional interjection for scene setting.
One of the advice letters is illegibly smudged, causing guesswork and hilarity. 1000 words.
response:
The granite was warm today, which made a nice change from Tuesday, when it had been merely damp. 

Sisyphus wedged his left heel into a familiar groove—he had named it *Clive* about four hundred years ago, largely because it looked like a Clive—and leaned his shoulder into the stone. 

On a flat outcrop three paces up the incline sat Crow. Crow was a bird of indeterminate age, ruffled plumage, and the general demeanor of a parish clerk who suspected everyone of stealing the communion wine. Held in his left claw was a stub of charcoal; pinned under his right was a sheaf of damp parchment rescued from the River Styx’s dead-letter eddy.

“Right then,” Sisyphus said, his voice only slightly compressed by the three tons of metamorphic rock resting against his collarbone. “Let’s have the first one. Mind the wings on the margin, you smudged the widow from Corinth last week and she thought I was advising her to burn her brother-in-law.”

Crow gave a dry, clicking rattle of his beak, cleared his throat—a sound like two pieces of slate being introduced at a party—and began to read.

***

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
> *My husband Hector has recently taken up amateur pottery. I wanted to be supportive, I really did, as the physician said he needed an outlet after the siege. However, we now have forty-seven amphorae in the vestibule, none of which hold water, and he has started referring to the dining table as ‘The Drying Kiln.’ Yesterday I found him whispering to a lump of wet clay in the pantry. When I asked when we might eat off plates that don’t taste of river silt, he said I was ‘stifling his terracotta period.’ Do I break the pots, or the husband?*
> *Yours in dust,*
> *Penelope of Thebes*

***

“Ah,” Sisyphus said. He took a short, measured breath, shifted his hips, and drove the boulder up two feet of shale. The stone grunted. Sisyphus grunted back, amicably. “Take this down, Crow.”

***

> *Dear Penelope,*
> *First of all, put down the mallet. A man in his terracotta period is a fragile creature, largely because he already knows the pots leak.*
> 
> *Nobody whispers to wet clay in a pantry because they think they are Phidias. They whisper to it because the clay doesn’t ask them what they’re going to do about the roof, or the taxes, or the strange clicking noise in the knees that starts around forty-five. Hector isn’t making amphorae, my love; he’s making small, round things he has complete control over, which is a rare luxury after a siege.*
> 
> *Do not mention the silt. Instead, clear out the small shed behind the olive press—yes, the one with the spiders—and put a latch on the outside and a very comfortable stool on the inside. Call it ‘The Studio.’ Men will voluntarily lock themselves in a cupboard for six hours a day if you call it a studio. Then, buy four nice glazed plates from the market, put them on the table, and ask him to make you a garden gnome. Nobody has ever had a nervous breakdown over a garden gnome. It lowers the stakes.*
> 
> *Warmly,*
> *Sisyphus*

***

“Did you spell ‘amphorae’ with the dipthong?” Sisyphus asked, pausing to wipe his brow with the back of a forearm that resembled braided oak. 

“Caw,” said Crow, which meant *I am an educated corvid, not a pigeon, thank you very much.*

“Good lad. Give us the next one while I get past the thorny bit.” 

He braced his calves. For the next forty seconds, the only sounds in that corner of Tartarus were the crunch of gravel, the steady, rhythmic bellows of Sisyphus’s lungs, and the distant, tinny wailing of the damned, which Sisyphus had long ago tuned out in much the same way one tunes out a neighbor’s wind chimes. They crested the mid-slope ridge. It was five yards from the summit. 

Sisyphus stepped back, dusting his hands. Together, man and bird watched the boulder teeter, sigh, and trundle briskly back down the hill, gathering a cheerful little cloud of dust before settling neatly at the bottom with a familiar *thump*.

“Good roll on that one,” Sisyphus noted, turning to stroll back down the path. It was a very pleasant walk down. People never talked about the walk down. You got the breeze right in your face, your hands were in your pockets, and you could really stretch the hamstrings. “Go on, then. Next letter.”

Crow squinted at a piece of vellum that looked as though it had traveled to the Underworld in someone’s boot.

***

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
> *I am an apprentice clerk in the temple of Hermes, and my supervisor, a man named Pheidippides, takes credit for all my ledgers. Whenever I balance the grain tallies, he presents them to the High Priest with a little flourish and says, ‘Another sleepless night for yours truly!’ Meanwhile, I am doing the work of three men and haven’t seen the sun since Tuesday. How do I show the High Priest the truth without looking like a sniveling rat?*
> *Sincerely,*
> *Tired in Tegea*

***

Sisyphus reached the bottom of the hill, gave the boulder an affectionate pat on its mossy flank, and settled his palms against the sweet spot. “Right. Ready?”

***

> *Dear Tired,*
> *You are making the classic mistake of assuming the High Priest is an idiot. High Priests rarely get to be High Priests without noticing who has ink on their elbows and who has pastry crumbs on their tunic.*
> 
> *Never accuse a superior of theft; it makes everyone in the room uncomfortable, and people will forgive wickedness long before they forgive embarrassment. What you need to do is become enthusiastically helpful. Next Tuesday, add a small, entirely invented column to the grain tally. Call it the ‘Adjusted Votive Tare.’ Make the numbers add up beautifully, and do not explain what it means.*
> 
> *When Pheidippides presents it with his little flourish, the High Priest will naturally ask what the Adjusted Votive Tare is. And Pheidippides, after a brief, silent prayer to the gods of middle management, will have to turn around and say, ‘Well, actually, my young apprentice here handles the Tare, let’s ask him.’*
> 
> *Once you are invited to speak, keep your voice level, explain that it’s a minor efficiency you’ve been testing to save the temple three drachmas a month, and then—this is the important bit—thank Pheidippides for ‘giving you the freedom to experiment.’ He won’t be able to contradict you without admitting he didn’t read the ledger, and he’ll be too terrified to steal your scroll next week in case you’ve hidden another trap in the arithmetic.*
> 
> *Pace yourself, too. There is always more grain tomorrow.*
> 
> *Best,*
> *Sisyphus*

***

“Hold on,” Sisyphus grunted, leaning his weight in as the gradient steepened near *Clive*. “Wait till I get my knee past this quartz vein. What’s the third one? Looks soggy.”

Crow held the third parchment at wing’s length, his head cocked at forty-five degrees. The ink had run in several directions, as if the writer had been weeping, or possibly sitting in a hip bath.

***

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
> *I am at my wits’ end. My lover, [smudged], insists that every time we [large water stain] we must first dress up as [illegible—looks like ‘ferrets’ or ‘Pharaohs’] and smear the [smudged] with two pounds of lukewarm [grease spot, smells faintly of tarragon]. I tried to be open-minded, especially after the incident with the [ink blot] at the harvest festival, but my knees simply cannot take the [smudged] anymore, and the neighbors are starting to ask why the [illegible] is always whistling.*
> *Please help,*
> *Chafed in Chalcis*

***

Sisyphus stopped pushing. Slowly, carefully, he wedged a convenient rock under the boulder’s base so he could stand upright and look at the parchment himself.

“Let me see that,” he said.

Crow hopped down onto the boulder and held it out. 

Sisyphus squinted. “That’s definitely ‘ferrets.’”

“Caw,” Crow disagreed, tapping a talon against the loop of the *P*.

“No, look at the tail on the second letter. Nobody puts a tail like that on an *h*. Although why you’d need tarragon for a ferret…” Sisyphus rubbed his chin, leaving a streak of granite dust across his beard. “Wait. Is that *ostrich*?”

Crow leaned in, sniffed the parchment, and sneezed.

“Well, whatever it is, we can’t leave them hanging. Clearly a matter of some urgency if something’s whistling.” Sisyphus removed the chock stone, took the weight back on his deltoids, and resumed his steady, rhythmic trudge upward. “Take a letter, Crow. Let’s keep it broad.”

***

> *Dear Chafed,*
> *Love is a banquet, certainly, though it sounds as if yours is currently being catered by a lunatic.*
> 
> *Now, I am the last man in the Underworld to judge what two consenting adults do with a pair of ferrets—or Pharaohs, your handwriting is a bit loose on the verticals—and a tub of herbed butter. If it brings a bit of warmth to the winter evenings, good for you. However, the golden rule of any shared enterprise, whether in the bedchamber or the assembly, is that both parties must be able to walk to the market the next morning without limping.*
> 
> *The trouble with ‘being open-minded’ is that if you don’t say anything the first time someone brings a poultry baster to bed, by the fourth time they naturally assume it’s your favorite part of the evening. You have accidentally trained your lover to think you enjoy having tarragon in your ears.*
> 
> *Tell them—over breakfast, when everyone is fully clothed and nobody is whistling—that your knees are retired from the festival circuit. Offer a compromise: keep the hats, lose the rodents, and save the tarragon for the roast chicken. Anyone worth keeping will prefer your company to a greased weasel.*
> 
> *Yours in solidarity,*
> *Sisyphus*

***

They were at the summit again. Sisyphus gave one last, companionable heave, and the boulder teetered on the lip of the peak. For a second, it hung there against the grey underworld sky, balanced on the knife-edge of gravity, before tipping over the far side and rumbling cheerfully back down toward the valley floor.

Sisyphus exhaled, rolling his shoulders until they gave a pleasant *pop*. 

“One more before lunch?” he asked.

Crow shuffled the stack, selected a small, neatly folded square of papyrus, and cleared his throat.

***

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
> *I am thirty-two years old. Every morning I wake up, I bake the bread, I sell the bread, I sweep the flour off the floor, and I go to sleep. The next morning, the floor is dusty again and the ovens are cold. Nothing I do stays done. What is the point of it all?*
> *Empty in Ephesus*

***

Sisyphus looked down the hill. At the bottom, his boulder had come to rest right beside a small patch of pale underworld dandelion that hadn’t been there yesterday. The walk down looked particularly nice from here.

“Read that back to me when we get to the bottom, Crow,” Sisyphus said, smiling faintly as he started down the path. “I want to get the wording just right.”

***

> *Dear Empty,*
> *You are looking at the flour on the floor, when you should be looking at the baker.*
> 
> *Of course nothing stays done. If bread stayed baked and people stayed fed, we’d all have nothing to do by Wednesday afternoon except sit in the square and pick fights with the Spartans. The universe is not a monument, my friend; it’s a kitchen. It’s meant to be used, dirtied, wiped down, and used again.*
> 
> *The mistake people make is thinking that the point of the day is to reach the end of it so they can cross it off a list. Do that, and you’re always pushing against the weight of tomorrow. Instead, pay attention to the heft of the dough. Notice the way the crust cracks when it hits the cool air. Talk to the woman who buys the crooked loaf on Thursdays. Get yourself a bird to argue with about spelling.*
> 
> *You don’t bake the bread so that the bread is baked forever. You bake the bread because you’re alive, and it’s morning, and someone is hungry. Put your shoulder into it. The walk back to the pantry is half the fun.*
> 
> *Warmly,*
> *Sisyphus*

prompt:
Sisyphus Gives Advice
Write a comedic scene in the style of Terry Pratchett featuring Sisyphus, who has started an advice column while continuing his eternal boulder-pushing. Rather than being bitter about his punishment, Sisyphus has developed a comfortably zen emotional intelligence and wisdom from his centuries of repetitive labor. Not in the cliche ways you might expect -- he's actually very grounded, warm & connected with the everyday human plight. He dictates responses to "Crow," his feathered familiar who serves as both scribe and mail carrier.
The piece should include Sisyphus thoughtfully answering several advice-seekers' letters about everyday problems (relationship troubles, work-life balance, dealing with difficult people, life purpose doubts) while periodically returning to his boulder-pushing duties. His advice should be surprisingly insightful and practical.
The humor should emerge naturally from the messages he receives, from mundane to risque. Sisyphus should genuinely enjoy helping others, finding meaning in this new pursuit while maintaining his boulder routine. The humour should be *understated and not forced*. Contrary to expectation, almost none of his advice involves boulder rolling metaphors (though he does sneak *one* subtle in there), nor a treatise on stoicism. We are also going against the obvious fish-out-of-water trope; in fact, he's surprisingly a natural at this.  In all of this , it's important to *show, don't tell*.
The format should be largely epistolary, with the occasional interjection for scene setting.
A minor deity stops by to offer pointless criticism of Sisyphus’s new hobby. 1000 words.
response:
The granite was particularly warm today, or perhaps Sisyphus had simply found the sweet spot between his shoulder blades. After three thousand years, you learn where the knots in the stone match the knots in your deltoids. 

Perched on a jagged outcropping of shale three yards up the incline was Crow. The bird was holding a trimmed goose quill in one claw and a small pot of squid ink in the other, looking like a very small, irritable magistrate.

"Next one," Sisyphus said, leaning his hip into the seven-ton curves of his punishment so he could wipe his brow. "Read it while we've got this nice bit of traction on the gravel."

Crow cleared his throat, which sounded like two roof tiles being rubbed together. 

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
> *My husband of twelve years has recently taken up amateur taxidermy. At first it was just the odd squirrel, which I could overlook, as a marriage requires compromise. However, last Tuesday he brought home an entire badger and suggested we incorporate it into our bedroom festivities. Not as a participant, you understand, just on the nightstand ‘for the atmosphere.’ I want to be a supportive partner, particularly as he has been very stressed at the tannery, but the glass eyes follow me, and frankly, they look judgmental. How do I tell him the badger is ruining the mood without crushing his creative spirit?*
> *Yours in trepidation,*
> *Hesitant in Thebes*

Sisyphus considered this, his heels digging into the scree as he took three measured steps upward. *Crunch. Crunch. Crunch.* 

"Right," Sisyphus said, breathing evenly through his nose. "Take this down, Crow. 

> *Dear Hesitant,*
> *The secret to any long-term endeavor is knowing where to put your feet, and right now, your husband has put his squarely in a badger. Let us be clear: it is wonderful that he has found a hobby to take his mind off the hides, and it is admirable that you wish to encourage him. However, the bedroom is a sanctuary of mutual enthusiasm, not a diorama.* 
> 
> *Do not make this about his craftsmanship. Compliment the sheen on the pelt. Praise the lifelike snarl, if there is one. Then, gently explain that while you love him very much, you cannot achieve a state of romantic vulnerability while being supervised by woodland fauna. Suggest the hallway table instead, where the badger may judge visitors, which is a much more traditional role for a badger.*
> *Warmly,*
> *Sisyphus*"

Crow’s quill scratched furiously against the parchment. "Are you sure you don't want to tell her to hit him with a shovel?" the bird asked. "It's shorter to write."

"People don't write to columns to be told to use shovels, Crow. They can think of shovels on their own. What have we got next?"

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
> *I am thirty-four years old and an Assistant Under-Clerk in the Municipal Grain Tallying Office. Every day I count sacks of barley. Every night I go home, eat barley soup, and sleep so I can return to count the barley again. My mother says I should be grateful for indoor work with no heavy lifting, and my supervisor says that in twelve years I may be promoted to Senior Under-Clerk, which involves lentils. I feel as though I am screaming inside a very small clay jar. Is this really all there is?*
> *Signed,*
> *Counting the Days*

Sisyphus paused. The crest of the hill was only ten paces away now—the treacherous bit where the grade steepened and the stone always tried to veer left into a patch of nettles. He adjusted his grip, finding the familiar thumb-holds worn smooth by millennia of sweat, and gave a mighty, practiced heave. 

The boulder crested the peak, balanced for one glorious, silent heartbeat against the grey underworld sky, and then—with the cheerful inevitability of a dog chasing a cart—thundered all the way back down to the bottom, kicking up a cloud of dust.

Sisyphus stretched his lower back, which gave a series of companionable pops, and began the walk down. It was always a lovely stroll down. Good for the knees.

"Ready?" Sisyphus asked as Crow glided down to land on his shoulder.

> *Dear Counting,*
> *First, stop listening to your supervisor about the lentils; men who dangle legumes twelve years in the future are rarely to be trusted.* 
> 
> *Second, your mother is right about the heavy lifting, though she misses the larger point. The trouble is not the barley. The trouble is that you are expecting the barley to love you back, or at least to tell you who you are. Barley is notoriously bad at this.* 
> 
> *Work is simply the thing you do to pay for the soup. When you expect the tally-sheet to provide the meaning of your existence, you are asking a very small piece of paper to carry a very large weight. Leave the barley at the office at five o'clock. Go learn the lute. Badly. Bake bread that is slightly too dense. Fall in love with someone who laughs at your jokes. The secret to a repetitive task is not finding joy in the task itself—though a good pair of boots helps—it is realizing that your mind remains entirely your own property while your hands are busy.*
> *Yours,*
> *Sisyphus*

"A bit philosophical," Crow muttered, dotting a period with unnecessary violence. "And here comes trouble."

The air at the base of the hill smelled abruptly of ozone and cheap laurel water. Phobetor, Under-Secretary for Minor Nightmares and Petty Anxieties (Third Class), materialized beside the boulder, holding a clipboard made of pressed bone.

"You're behind schedule," Phobetor said. He had the sort of voice that made people suddenly wonder if they had left the stove on. "Fourteen seconds slower on that last ascent. Is this because of the... the *correspondence*?" He pronounced the word as if it were a skin condition.

"Hello, Phobetor," Sisyphus said pleasantly, testing his grip on the stone again. "How's the sciatica?"

"Never mind the sciatica. It's irregular, Sisyphus. This is Tartarus. It's supposed to be a monument to the crushing futility of mortal ambition. You're supposed to be weeping and gnashing your teeth, not telling a baker's wife in Corinth how to set boundaries with her mother-in-law."

"She was coming over unannounced with her own sourdough starter," Sisyphus explained reasonably. "You have to nip that in the bud."

"It's not *bleak*!" Phobetor tapped his clipboard. "Lord Hades walked past yesterday and said you looked 'weirdly moisturized.' And your kerning on the scroll-work is dreadful. If you're going to distribute unauthorized psychological comfort from the Pit of Despair, at least use a ruler. Honestly, the whole tone is too breezy. Where is the existential dread? Where is the howling into the abyss?"

"I howled for the first four centuries," Sisyphus said, putting his shoulder to the rock and beginning the push. "Gave me terrible acid reflux. Besides, once you accept that the abyss isn't going to howl back, it's actually quite a peaceful place to get your thoughts in order. Tell you what—try rotating your hips outward when you stand with that clipboard. Takes the pressure right off the lumbar."

Phobetor opened his mouth to issue a formal reprimand, unconsciously shifted his stance, blinked in surprise as his lower back unkinked, and vanished in a sulky puff of sulfur.

"Every critic's the same," Crow sighed, hopping along beside Sisyphus's left foot. "One more before lunch?"

"Go on, then."

> *Dear Sisyphus,*
> *Every time I get close to finishing my treatise on the mating habits of the Aegean newt, I find a reason to abandon it. Last month I reorganized my spice rack alphabetically by point of origin. Yesterday I shaved the cat (he had mats, mostly). I am terrified that if I actually finish it, the Academy will read it and realize I know nothing about newts, or worse, that they won't read it at all. How do I make myself begin the final chapter?*
> *Sincerely,*
> *Stalled in Sparta*

Sisyphus smiled, his palms flat against the cool, rough granite as the incline began to bite into his calves.

> *Dear Stalled,*
> *Apologize to the cat immediately. They hold grudges.*
> 
> *As for the newts: you are trying to write a masterpiece, which is impossible, instead of trying to write three sentences before Tuesday, which is very easy. Forget the Academy. Half of them are asleep after lunch anyway. The trick to getting anything heavy moving is simply to stop looking at the top of the hill. Just lean your weight against the thing, find a foothold that doesn't slip, and get the momentum going. Once it's rolling, you'll be amazed how much of the work it does by itself.*
> 
> *Now go write one terrible paragraph about a newt. I'll be right here doing my bit.*
> *Best,*
> *Sisyphus*

prompt:
High Seas and Low Vices: British Naval Officer in the Opium Trade
Character: Lieutenant James Merrick, a high-ranking officer in the British Royal Navy stationed in Canton, China in the 1830s. Once promising and decorated, now struggling with a severe opium addiction he hides from his superiors.
Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. Told primarily in dialogue with the characters he interacts with. Focus on brief slices of his journey through the shadowy underworld of Canton: interactions with acquaintances, negotiations with local dealers, schemes and unsavoury jobs taken to fund his habit.
Writing Task: Use rich sensory details to describe a day in the life of James Merrick. Write for a real sense of time & place while avoiding cliche. First person, past tense. Merrick keeps a small jade figurine in his pocket that he anxiously rubs when withdrawal symptoms begin. 1000 words.
response:
The Pearl River smelled of fermented shrimp paste, pine tar, and the sour silt of low tide. On the quarterdeck of HMS *Vanguard*, the noon sun beat down on my woollen coat until the gold braid at my cuffs felt like heated wire. Beneath the heavy broadcloth, my shirt was sodden with a cold, greasy sweat that had nothing to do with the Canton heat.

"You have the look of a man who has swallowed a live eel, Mr. Merrick," Lieutenant Crofton said, resting his brass telescope against the taffrail. 

I forced my jaw to unclench, my right hand buried deep in my breeches pocket. My thumb found the familiar, cool contours of the jade *qilin*—a two-inch beast with a chipped horn I had won off a Portuguese supercargo in Macao. I rubbed the stone’s smooth belly until the skin of my thumb burned.

"A touch of the Whampoa ague, Crofton," I said, my voice scraping like dry hemp. "The damp gets into the marrow."

"Does it indeed?" Crofton didn't look at me; his eyes were fixed on the painted eyes of a passing salt junk. "And here I thought the ague was treated with Peruvian bark, not four-hour excursions into the Thirteen Factories."

"The purser’s manifests for the *Lintin* anchorage do not sign themselves."

"No," Crofton murmured, clicking his glass shut. "Though one wonders why a decorated first lieutenant of the Battle of Navarino now volunteers for clerk's work among the compradors. The Captain asked after your quadrant readings this morning. Your hand was shaking so badly yesterday the ink blotted the log."

"Tell Captain Vance I am seeing the East India Company’s surgeon at Creek Hong," I said, already turning toward the gangway. "I shall return before the dogwatch."

"Mind the sampan girls, James," Crofton called out, a thin edge of pity beneath his mockery. "They’ll have the buttons off your coat before you reach Jackass Point."

***

Hog Lane was a narrow gullet of slick granite flags, choked with the steam of boiling tripe and the sharp, medicinal tang of cassia bark. Sailor’s grog-shops lined the alley, their doorways hung with dried ducks glistening like varnished mahogany. I kept my cocked hat low, the cramp in my bowels tightening like agarrote. My thumb worked the jade *qilin* furiously, tracing the ridges of its carved scales to keep my teeth from chattering.

Inside the rear ledger-room of Old Kai’s chandlery, the air was cool and smelled of camphorwood and damp paper. Kai sat behind an abacus of black ironwood, his spectacles resting on the tip of a nose pitted by smallpox.

"You are early, Lieutenant," Kai said without looking up, his fingernails clicking against the beads. "The Patna chests have not yet cleared the receiving ships at Lintin."

"I am not here for raw ball-gum, Kai." I leaned both hands on his counter so he would not see my knees trembling. "I need two taels of prepared Malwa. The double-boiled tin."

Kai stopped clicking. He lifted his gaze to the tarnished gilt of my epaulettes. "Malwa is eight Spanish dollars the tael this week. The Viceroy’s river-cruisers seized two fast-crabs off Bocca Tigris on Tuesday. Everyone is dry."

"I have four dollars," I said, tossing the silver pillar-coins onto the ledger. They rang flat against the paper. "And the patrol schedule for the *Vanguard*’s longboats between the Second Bar and Danes Island through Sunday."

Kai’s thin lips parted, revealing teeth stained black with betel nut. He picked up the folded admiralty slip I slid across the wood, holding it toward the tallow lamp. 

"Only through Sunday?" he asked softly. "Last month you gave me a fortnight for sixtaels."

"Vance is changing the cipher on Monday," I lied, my stomach lurching as a hot flash prickled behind my eyes. My fingers dug into the jade stone in my pocket until the chipped horn bit my palm. "The moon is dark Friday night. Your smuggling boats can run the Back Reach with forty oars and never see a British lantern. Give me the tin, Kai. My bones are splitting."

"One tael and a half," Kai said, tucking the patrol schedule into his silk sleeve. "For a friend of the Crown."

"Two," I hissed, leaning over the counter until I could smell the sesame oil in his queue. "Or I take the cutter out myself on Friday and board the first crab-boat flying the house flag of Jardine’s broker."

Kai’s face remained as still as river mud. Without a word, he reached beneath the counter and produced a horn box no larger than a walnut.

***

The upper loft of the *Three Lanterns* floated on ironwood piles driven into the muck of the creek. Below the floorboards, the tide slapped against the timbers with a hollow, rhythmic *chug*. The room was dark, lit only by a dozen peanut-oil lamps scattered across bamboo sleeping platforms. Here, the smell was thick and unmistakable—burnt almonds, stale pond water, and the heavy, sweet rot of roasted poppy juice.

I shed my uniform coat, folding the brass buttons inward so they wouldn't catch the amber light, and stretched out on a greasy rattan mat beside a man in a frayed linen waistcoat. It was Pym, a dismissed third mate from an American tea clipper whose ankles were swollen with dropsy.

"Afternoon, Your Lordship," Pym wheezed, his eyes glassy and pinned to the size of mustard seeds. "Thought the Navy didn't drink from the bamboo before eight bells."

"Hold your tongue, Pym, and pass the needle."

"Touchy," he chuckled, a wet rattle in his chest. "The boy’s bringing the charcoal. What did you bring? Bengal?"

"Malwa."

Pym whistled low. "A gentleman’s tar. Did you sell another keg of the King’s gunpowder, or just your dead mother’s watch?"

"I sold nothing that concerns a Yankee beachcomber," I said. My left hand wasjerking now, a rhythmic twitch in the webbing between thumb and forefinger. I pulled the jade *qilin* from my pocket and set it on the lacquer tray beside the lamp. In the yellow glow, the stone looked the colour of mutton fat.

A bare-chested boy with a shaved forehead knelt between us. With an iron wire, he dipped into my horn box, drawing out a bead of dark paste. He twirled it over the lamp flame. It sizzled, bubbling like frying fat, expanding into a fragrant brown foam before he jammed it into the pinhole of the clay bowl.

"Your hand's like a tuning fork, Merrick," Pym observed, watching me take the heavy bamboo stem. "Best let the boy hold the bowl."

"I can hold my own pipe," I snapped, though my teeth clicked against the ivory mouthpiece.

"Aye," Pym murmured, rolling onto his back to stare at the soot-blackened rafters. "We all can, until the day we can't. Saw the *Samarang* drop anchor at Whampoa yesterday. Carrying dispatches from Portsmouth, they say. New commissions. You on the list for Commander yet, James?"

"Shut up, Pym."

"Just asking. A man with a gold medal from the King ought to have his own sloop by thirty."

I didn't answer. The boy held the clay bowl over the flame. I drew in—one long, deep pull that filled my chest with hot, velvety smoke. It tasted of焦burnt sugar and autumn leaves. 

Almost before I exhaled, the iron band around my skull snapped. The sour grease on my skin dried into a warm, prickling glow; the knives in my calves melted into warm tallow. Outside, the cries of the river hawkers and the creak of junk oars faded into a distant, pleasant hum, like bees in an English orchard. My fingers uncurled, brushing against the cold jade figurine on the tray, and for a few hours, I no longer needed to touch it.

prompt:
High Seas and Low Vices: British Naval Officer in the Opium Trade
Character: Lieutenant James Merrick, a high-ranking officer in the British Royal Navy stationed in Canton, China in the 1830s. Once promising and decorated, now struggling with a severe opium addiction he hides from his superiors.
Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. Told primarily in dialogue with the characters he interacts with. Focus on brief slices of his journey through the shadowy underworld of Canton: interactions with acquaintances, negotiations with local dealers, schemes and unsavoury jobs taken to fund his habit.
Writing Task: Use rich sensory details to describe a day in the life of James Merrick. Write for a real sense of time & place while avoiding cliche. First person, past tense. The scent of rotting mangoes permeates the alleyways leading to his regular den. 1000 words.
response:
The river below the stern gallery of HMS *Vindictive* looked as though it had been boiled in a tallow pot—yellow, greasy, and thick with cabbage stalks and bloated rats. My heavy wool coat was a woollen furnace in the Canton heat, the high collar chafing a neck already slick with the sour, cold sweat of an overdue pipe.

"You've the look of the Bogue fever about you, Merrick," Lieutenant-Commander Vance said, squinting through the haze toward the Lintin anchorage. He didn't look at me directly, which was a mercy. My left hand was jammed deep into my breeches pocket to keep the tremor in my fingers from rattling the brass buttons of my waistcoat. "Your skin's the colour of old sailcloth."

"Touch of the bilge-rot in my quarters, sir," I said. My tongue felt as though it had been dredged in salt. "And the Victualling Board’s manifest for the Macau stores is three hogsheads short of salt beef. If I don't go ashore and cane the comprador at the Creek Factory myself, the men will be chewing boiled leather by Tuesday."

"Send Midshipman Croft."

"Croft couldn't tell a picul of rice from a load of ballast, sir. The Chinese merchants would skin him before he cleared the landing steps."

Vance sighed, slapping at a sandfly on his jaw. "Take the jolly-boat, then. Be back before the evening gun. The Admiral's dining aboard tomorrow, and your division's brightwork is disgraceful."

"Aye, sir. Before the gun."

Twenty minutes later, I was off the sampan and swallowed by the din of Thirteen Factory Street. Here, the air was a suffocating soup of fried garlic, pig dung, and wet wool. I kept my bicorne pulled low, stepping over the open stone gutters where indigo dye ran like bruised blood toward the Pearl River. My ribs ached—that familiar, hollow cramp that meant I had an hour, perhaps less, before my stomach began to heave.

I ducked through the whitewashed archway of the Creek Factory and found Alistair Finch in a ground-floor counting house that smelled of damp tea-chests and sealing wax. He was a junior supercargo for Dent & Co., a boy with ink-stained cuffs and eyes too wide for the China trade.

"God's teeth, Merrick, shut the lattice," Finch hissed, wiping his nib on a rag. "If Jardine’s clerks see a King's officer in here at noon, they'll know the *Sylph* is unloading up-river."

"They won't know anything if you pay what was agreed," I said, unbuckling my sword belt only enough to fish a folded square of greased oilskin from my lining. I tossed it onto his ledger. "The patrol schedule for the Second Bar. *Vindictive* is careening her larboard side until Thursday, and the *Louisa* cutter has a sprung foremast. Your lorchas have forty-eight hours of blind water between Whampoa and the Bogue."

Finch unfolded the paper with trembling fingers. "Wait. This is in your own hand."

"Who else's would it be? The Chinese Imperial Commissioner's?"

"Yesterday you said thirty Spanish dollars," Finch said, his voice dropping as he unlocked a camphorwood strongbox. "I have twenty. Three of them are clipped."

"Thirty, Finch. My coxswain doesn't look the other way for copper cash."

"You don't pay your coxswain a farthing," Finch muttered, though he didn't dare look past my tarnished epaulettes into my eyes. "Everyone from here to Danes Island knows where your silver goes, Lieutenant. Look at your cuffs. There’s ash in the gold lace."

I leaned across the rosewood desk until my nose was six inches from his. "Give me the twenty, and the silver repeater in your waistcoat, or I'll have a boarding party on the *Sylph* before the tide turns and hang your Lascar crew from the yardarm for piracy."

He went white, unhooked the fat silver turnip watch from his chain, and dropped it into my palm alongside a roll of pillar dollars wrapped in coarse brown paper. 

I didn't walk; I half-trotted out the back passage into Hog Lane. The foreign factories gave way to a labyrinth of grey brick walls that leaned together until the sky was reduced to a dirty ribbon of white. As I turned into the narrow gut behind the Consoo House, the stench hit me—the heavy, fermented sweetness of rotting mangoes. Dozens of crates had been dumped behind the fruit-sellers' stalls, their bruised yellow skins split open in the heat, black with blowflies and oozing a syrupy liquor that stuck to the soles of my Wellington boots. That sickly, tropical decay was always the threshold. My mouth watered violently in response.

I shoved aside a curtain of greasy hemp sacking and stepped into the dark of Ah Fook’s back room.

The transition from the glare of the street left me blind for five seconds. Here, the mango-rot was braided with the thick, toasted-earth aroma of Bengal Patna—black gold boiled down from the poppy fields of the Ganges. The room was narrow as a coffin, lined with two tiers of bamboo bunks where coolies and disgraced lascars lay like timber.

"You late, Captain," a voice rasped from the corner. Ah Fook sat behind a low scale of bone and brass, his face illuminated only by the tiny, steady flame of a peanut-oil lamp. A crescent scar pulled his left eyelid down, giving him a look of perpetual, weeping sorrow.

"Lieutenant," I said, dropping onto the lowest bamboo pallet. My knees gave out before I could fold them properly. "And you know the tide waits for no man."

"Tide don't owe me twelve dollar from last Tuesday," Ah Fook said, not moving his long iron needle.

I threw Finch's silver watch onto the mat between us. The crystal was scratched, the case warm from my palm. "English movement. London make. Worth forty in Macau."

Ah Fook picked it up with two fingernails, held it to his ear, and spat into a porcelain spittoon. "Macau very far. Watch stolen, maybe. Mandarin soldier come, take watch, take my head. Give you four shell."

"Four?" A laugh tore out of my throat, ragged and wet. "That watch belonged to an East India Company gentleman ten minutes ago. Eight shells. Genuine Patna, Fook. None of that Malwa dross mixed with pig-fat you gave me Sunday. My lungs felt like they were coated in pitch."

"Six shell," he said, already dropping the watch into a drawer. "Four for the debt. Two for now."

"Three for now," I pleaded, the last shred of the Quarterdeck vanishing from my voice. My stomach knotted so hard I doubled over, pressing my forehead against the greasy bamboo. The smell of the rotting mangoes outside seemed to seep through the cracks in the masonry, mocking me. "Three, Fook. Have mercy. I've got to inspect the gun-deck at six bells."

Ah Fook looked at me for a long moment, his scarred eye glistening in the lamp-glow. Without a word, he dipped the long steel needle into a tiny horn pot of treacly brown paste. 

"You bring more paper from the big ship next time," he murmured, revolving the needle over the flame. "Watch too hard to sell."

"Whatever you want. Charts. Soundings. Gunpowder."

The paste bubbled, swelling into a pale,琥珀-coloured blister that hissed softly and gave off that first, divine breath of burnt poppies and autumn leaves. He pressed the sizzling bead into the clay bowl of the bamboo pipe and held it out.

My teeth clicked against the ivory mouthpiece. I drew deep, pulling the heavy, warm smoke down into the pit of my chest until the trembling in my thighs stopped, the mango-stench faded, and the King's Navy dissolved into grey ash.

High Seas and Low Vices: British Naval Officer in the Opium Trade
Character: Lieutenant James Merrick, a high-ranking officer in the British Royal Navy stationed in Canton, China in the 1830s. Once promising and decorated, now struggling with a severe opium addiction he hides from his superiors.
Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. Told primarily in dialogue with the characters he interacts with. Focus on brief slices of his journey through the shadowy underworld of Canton: interactions with acquaintances, negotiations with local dealers, schemes and unsavoury jobs taken to fund his habit.
Writing Task: Use rich sensory details to describe a day in the life of James Merrick. Write for a real sense of time & place while avoiding cliche. First person, past tense. A persistent cough that tastes of copper haunts him, which he attributes to the sea air when questioned. 1000 words.
response:
The Pearl River did not smell of water; by noon it smelled of boiled cabbage, bilge grease, and the sweet, fecal rot of the mudflats at low tide. I stood on the splintered planks of Jackass Point, the wool of my blue uniform coat sodden at the armpits and stiff with salt at the cuffs. Before me, the *HMS Volage* rode at anchor down toward Whampoa, mercifully out of sight behind a forest of junk masts and the fat hulls of East Indiamen. 

A spasm caught me beneath the breastbone. I doubled over the stone bollard, hacking into a cambric handkerchief until my ribs creaked. When I drew the linen back, the spittle was threaded with pink, and the back of my throat held the sharp, bright taste of a penny held on the tongue.

"You sound like a broken pump, Merrick." 

Lieutenant Arthur Vance stood three paces off, his boots immaculate despite the grey slush of the quay. He held a dispatch pouch under one arm and looked at me with the pinched distaste of a man who still wrote to his mother in Hampshire twice a month.

"It is the river damp, Arthur," I said, tucking the stained linen into my cuff before he could see it. I forced my shoulders back, though my collar felt two sizes too large for my neck. "The sea air off the Bocca Tigris does not agree with an English chest."

"The sea air did not keep you from the morning watch," Vance said, lowering his voice as two lascars trotted past under a yoke of salted hides. "Captain Elliot asked for the soundings from the Macao passage. Twice. Mr. Kippling had to tell him you were ashore seeing to the victualling receipts."

"And so I am." I tapped my breast pocket, which contained nothing but a pawn ticket from a Parsee broker in Hog Lane and three clipped Spanish dollars. "The compradors are thieves to a man. If one does not stand over their scales, they weigh the beef with the horn and hooves still attached."

Vance’s eyes dropped to my hands. I had forgotten to button my gloves; my fingernails were rimmed with a yellow-brown tarsal stain that no amount of pumice would shift. 

"You are thin, James," he said, the stiffness going out of him for a second. "And your eyes are like two burnt holes in a blanket. Come back to the ship. The surgeon has Peruvian bark—"

"Give Kippling my compliments," I interrupted, stepping around him toward the narrow brick throat of Old China Street. "Tell him I shall be aboard with the tide. A man cannot rush the Cantonese."

I did not look back to see if he watched me go. Within twenty yards, the open glare of the Factories gave way to the permanent twilight of the alleys, where bamboo awnings met overhead and the flagstones were slick with fish guts and slops. My shins ached—that hollow, marrow-deep cold that always preceded the cramps. Every cobble jarred my teeth.

I turned into the counting-house of Framjee Pestonjee behind the Danish Hong. The room smelled of camphorwood, dried cloves, and the sour mutton tallow they used to grease the iron strongboxes. Framjee did not rise from his stool; his white muslin turban gleamed in the gloom like a peeled egg.

"You are early, Lieutenant," he said, his abacus clicking—*clack-clack, clack*—beneath long, oiled fingers. "The *Sylph* has not yet cleared Lintin Island. I have no bills for you to sign."

"The *Sylph* anchored at three this morning off Nine Islands," I said, leaning both palms on his counter to stop the tremor in my knees. "Four hundred chests of Patna. You need the patrol boat at Second Bar to look toward the salt junks between midnight and two. Here."

I slid the Admiralty chart transcript—copied in my own hand by candle-end while the rest of the wardroom slept—across the rosewood. 

Framjee picked it up by the corner, holding it near a brass oil lamp. "Captain Elliot has doubled the guard boats since the Viceroy’s edict."

"And I have the roster for the week," I said. The cough took me again, dry as birch bark at first, then tearing loose at the bottom of my lungs. Copper flooded my gums, thick and warm. I swallowed it down. "A touch of the estuary ague. The sea air."

"Of course," Framjee murmured, not looking up from the paper. "The sea air in Canton is famously hard on the King’s officers. Especially those who sell their quadrant to pay for it."

"Thirty dollars, Framjee. In silver, not chop-coin."

"Fifteen," he said, his voice as flat as the ledger before him. "The Mandarin at the Hoppo’s office wants his grease too, and his palm is wider than yours. Ten in silver now, and a chit for Ah Choy’s house."

"Twenty, damn your eyes. If Elliot finds those soundings missing from the chart-chest—"

"Then you will hang from your own yardarm, Lieutenant, and you will not need the silver at all." He reached into a drawer without haste, dropped six scarred Carolus dollars onto the wood—they rang with a dull, leaden *chink*—and scratched three characters onto a strip of red tissue paper. "Take the side canal. The provost’s men were drinking at the *Three Cups* an hour ago."

I scooped the coins before they stopped spinning. My fingers were clumsy, numb at the tips.

Ah Choy’s was not the gilded barge of a mandarin’s poet; it was a cellar behind a cooper’s yard near the creek, where the hammers beat a deafening tattoo on iron hoops all day—*tonk-tonk, tonk-tonk*—drowning out whatever noises came from beneath the floorboards. 

A boy with a ringworm scar across his scalp lifted the matting for me. The air inside hit my face like a wet woollen blanket: the roasted-earth stench of Benares mud, stale sweat, and the rancid peanut oil of the little lamps. 

"Two pipes of the first boil," I told Ah Choy. She sat on a porcelain stool by the charcoal brazier, her teeth black from betel nut, scraping the dross from a bamboo stem with a long brass needle. 

"First boil gone to the supercargoes at the Creek Hong," she said in thebroken pidgin of the riverfront. She spat red juice into a sawdust box. "Have Malwa. Mixed with three-touch dross. Strong enough for sailor."

"I am not a foremast jack, you old crow," I rasped, though I was already climbing onto the greasy rattan bunk in the corner. I handed her the red tissue and four of Framjee’s dollars. "Give me the Patna. You keep a jar under the rice bin for the customs clerks."

She squinted at the silver, bit one coin with her back teeth, and grunted. "You cough like dead man, *Fan-kwei*. One day you die on my mats, make big trouble with the magistrate."

"It’s the salt wind," I muttered, letting my head fall back against the wooden neck-rest. My shirt was soaked through; the chill was in my kidneys now, twisting like a gimlet. "Bring the lamp."

When she laid the tray between us, the little flame reflected in my eyes like a harbor light after a gale. She worked the brown paste on the tip of the needle, turning it over the glass chimney until it bubbled and swelled, giving off that first faint, toasted-almond perfume that made the water rush into my mouth beneath the blood-taste. 

"Hold steady," she said, fitting the terracotta bowl to the bamboo. "Your hand shake like dog in rain."

I closed my lips around the ivory mouthpiece—worn down in a groove where a hundred other men had bitten it—and drew. One long pull, deep into the raw places behind my ribs. 

The cooper’s hammers outside seemed to fall into a slow, majestic measure. The copper in my throat turned to burnt sugar, then to nothing at all. The rot of the Pearl River retreated behind a warm, heavy curtain, and for three hours, the *Volage* could sink at her moorings for all I cared.

A neon jukebox in the bar keeps playing the same scratchy rock track on repeat. Length: 1000 words.
response:
The neon jukebox in the corner of *The Rusty Anchor* is dying a loud, electric death. Its cracked magenta tubing buzzes against the damp drywall, cycling through the exact same three-minute, scratchy garage-rock guitar riff for the fourth time in a row. When the track ends, the mechanical arm clunks, drops the needle right back into the worn groove, and the distorted bassline starts all over again.

Spike Spiegel rests his chin in his palm, a bent cigarette dangling from the corner of his mouth. His stomach growls—a hollow, familiar ache fueled by three days of bell peppers with no beef and a tab the bartender cut off twenty minutes ago. Before him sits a crumpled bounty flyer for a syndicate accountant named Mateo Vance, worth five million woolongs—or fifty thousand American dollars, depending on which corrupt port authority is paying out tonight.

Down at the other end of the sticky mahogany counter, a woman in frayed denim cutoffs and a black crop top slams a shot glass down hard enough to crack the wood.

"Hey, deaf bastard!" Revy barks at the bartender, her tribal tattoo coiling down her bare right arm as she points at the jukebox. "If that fucking record loops one more time, I’m putting two nine-millimeter holes through the speakers and one through your kneecap. Pour the Bacardi."

Spike exhales a thin ribbon of gray smoke, his mismatched eyes—one slightly lighter, forever seeing the world in two timelines—drifting over her. Dual shoulder holsters. Modified Beretta 92FS Inox pistols with ivory grips. She moves with the coiled, feral twitch of someone who doesn't just expect a firefight, but prays for one.

His kind of trouble.

He slides off his stool, long legs carrying him with a fluid, boneless slouch until he drops onto the seat beside her. He taps the ash of his cigarette into her overflowing tray.

"You’re gonna ruin a classic," Spike says, his voice a lazy, gravelly drawl. "I was just starting to appreciate the existential dread of the third chorus."

Revy turns her head slowly. A fresh cigarette hangs from her lips, unlit. She eyes the rumpled blue suit, the mop of dark green-black hair, and the easy, infuriating smirk on his face. Her eyes dip briefly to the bulge of the Jericho 941 holstered beneath his jacket, then back up to his face.

"Do I look like I want company, beanpole?" she snaps, flicking a Zippo open. The flame illuminates the sharp, dangerous curve of her jaw. "Walk away before you lose teeth."

Spike doesn't flinch. Instead, his long fingers dip down to the bar top, right where the corner of an identical bounty flyer pokes out from beneath her forearm.

"Mateo Vance," Spike murmurs, tilting his head. "Funny thing. I’ve been tracking that sweaty little numbers guy since Tuesday. Looks like we’re fishing in the same pond."

Revy’s eyes narrow into dark, lethal slits. She takes a slow drag of her smoke, blowing it directly into his face. "Wrong. *I'm* cashing in that fat bastard. You’re going to sit here, nurse your empty glass, and thank whatever god you pray to that I’m too thirsty to shoot you right now."

"See, I'd love to," Spike says, leaning an elbow on the bar and invading her space just enough to smell the cheap rum, gun oil, and sweat radiating off her skin. It’s an intoxicating mix. "Problem is, I’m broke. And hungry. Whatever happens, happens, sweetheart, but tonight it’s happening with Vance in my handcuffs."

Revy barks out a harsh, humorless laugh, though her gaze lingers a fraction of a second too long on his mouth. "You got balls, suit. Stupid ones, but they're there." She grabs the bottle of rum directly from the bartender's hand and shoves a second glass toward Spike, sloshing amber liquid over the rim. "Drink. Let’s see if you hold your liquor better than you hold your tongue."

Spike grins and knocks the shot back. It burns like industrial solvent. Revy matches him, slam for slam, three shots deep as the jukebox resets with a violent *clack-hiss* and the scratchy guitar riff begins its fifth loop. With every drink, the space between their stools seems to shrink. Her bare knee brushes against the fabric of his trousers; neither of them pulls away. They are two stray dogs circling the same bone, recognizing the exact same scent of gunpowder and fatalism in the other.

"I’m not a good person, not a bad person," Revy mutters against the rim of her fourth glass, her dark eyes locking onto his prosthetic one as if trying to read the ghost behind it. "I’m just here. And if you get between me and my money, I’ll put you in the dirt."

"Funny," Spike says softly, the lazy humor dropping from his voice for a heartbeat. "I’ve already died once. Didn't take."

The front door of the bar splinters inward.

Four local cartel hitters hired to guard Vance spill into the neon-lit gloom, submachine guns raised.

Neither Spike nor Revy blinks.

Revy moves first, kicking her barstool backward into the lead gunman’s shins while drawing both Sword Cutlasses in a flash of silver. Spike flows like water—dropping low, sweeping a second gunman’s legs out with a whip-fast Jeet Kune Do kick before drawing his Jericho from the hip.

The bar erupts into deafening thunder. Brass casings rain onto the linoleum like golden hail. Revy is a grinning demon in the strobe of muzzle flash, firing two-handed with terrifying symmetry, shredding bottles and bodies alike. Spike weaves through her line of fire with impossible grace, their backs brushing for a split second—heat and taut muscle—as his 9mm barks twice, dropping a shooter aiming for her head, while her left Beretta blows the gun out of the hand of a thug flanking his blind side.

One gunshot catches the neon jukebox. It explodes in a shower of purple sparks, the scratchy rock song dying in a warped, screeching groan.

Silence drops, heavy and thick with cordite.

Then, through the shattered front window, a shadow bolts down the rain-slicked alley toward the *Starlight Motel* across the street.

"Vance!" Revy snarls, vaulting over the bar.

Spike is right on her heels, vaulting the window frame. They hit the wet asphalt at a dead sprint, lungs burning with smoke and rum, shoulder to shoulder as they kick open the door to Room 104 on the ground floor.

The room is empty—save for an open bathroom window, curtains fluttering in the damp night breeze, and a briefcase handcuffed to the radiator, blown open and stripped clean. Vance—and the money—are already gone into the harbor fog.

"Mother*fucker*!" Revy kicks a cheap wooden chair, shattering it against the floral wallpaper. She spins around, chest heaving, crop top slick with rain, and levels both smoking Cutlasses squarely at Spike’s chest.

Spike’s Jericho is already up, the cold steel barrel aimed right between her eyes.

They stand three feet apart in the cramped, dingy motel room, red neon from the vacancy sign outside bleeding through the blinds and striping their skin in crimson and shadow.

"You slowed me down, asshole!" Revy hisses, her finger trembling on the triggers. Her breath comes hot and ragged, her eyes wide and wild.

"Me?" Spike steps forward. He doesn't lower his gun, letting the barrel of her right pistol press directly against his sternum, right over his steady heartbeat. "You stopped to shoot the jukebox."

"That song was pissing me off!"

Spike takes another half-step. Now his Jericho is tucked just beneath her chin, tipping her head up. They are close enough to share the same breath, the air between them vibrating with adrenaline, gunpowder, and an ache neither of them knows how to name without violence. Revy’s teeth clench; her free boot shifts between his feet, her thigh pressing hard against his hip. Her gaze drops to his lips, fierce and hungry and furious all at once.

"Pull it, Two Hands," Spike whispers, his thumb brushing the hammer of his gun as his eyes darken. "Or put 'em down and find something else to do with those fingers."

Revy’s breath hitches—just once. The twin barrels digging into his chest waver by a millimeter as the heat between them threatens to catch fire. Outside, sirens begin to wail in the distance. Inside Room 104, nobody lowers their weapon, and nobody pulls away.

A lazy ceiling fan barely stirs the smoky air inside the bar. Length: 1000 words.
response:
A lazy ceiling fan barely stirs the smoky air inside the bar. Neon light from a cracked window bleeds across the sticky mahogany counter, catching the rim of a half-empty bottle of Bacardi and the dull stainless steel of two modified Beretta 92FS pistols resting beside it.

Revy sits hunched on a crooked stool, a crumpled cigarette dangling from the corner of her mouth. Her black crop top clings to the sweat along her ribs, and the tribal dragon coiled around her right arm shifts as she pours another shot of rum. She is three drinks past patience. The bounty—a mid-level cartel accountant named Moretti with five million woolongs on his head—was supposed to walk through that door twenty minutes ago. 

Instead, the slatted wooden doors swing open to admit a tall, impossibly lanky man in a rumpled blue suit. His dark, fluffy hair looks like a bird’s nest, and a bent cigarette hangs from his lips at an angle that defies gravity. He stops just inside the threshold, hands buried deep in his pockets, his mismatched eyes scanning the dim booths with lazy, liquid detachment.

Revy’s eyes narrow. She knows a predator when she sees one, even when it dresses like a broke lounge singer. 

Spike Spiegel spots the empty stool two seats down from her and ambles over, his long legs moving with the loose, boneless grace of water. He drops onto the vinyl cushion with a quiet sigh, pulling a crumpled bounty flyer from his lapel and smoothing it against the bar top. Moretti’s sweating, mustachioed face stares up between them.

"Bartender," Spike says, his voice a smooth, baritone drawl. "Whatever’s cheap and burns. And if you’ve got anything with beef in it, I’m starving."

Revy’s boot slams against the brass footrail. "You’re in the wrong fucking bar, beanpole."

Spike turns his head slowly. His right eye—the fake one, slightly lighter than the left—catches the amber neon as he takes her in: the frayed denim shorts, the twin shoulder holsters, the twin Sword Cutlasses gleaming on the wood, and the murder simmering behind her dark eyes. A faint, crooked smirk tugs at his mouth.

"Funny," Spike murmurs, strike-lighting his Zippo and touching the flame to his cigarette. "The guy I’m looking for is supposed to be sitting in that back booth. Unless he got a very impressive makeover."

"Moretti’s mine," Revy snarls, resting her palm over the ivory grip of her right Beretta. The skull-and-crossbones inlay disappears beneath her fingers. "I tracked that greasy bastard across three districts. You want a cut, you can fish it out of the gutter after I’m done."

"Look, lady, I haven’t eaten anything but bell peppers with no meat for three days," Spike says, leaning an elbow on the bar. He blows a thin ribbon of smoke toward the ceiling fan. "Whatever happens, happens, sure—but my stomach’s making a pretty strong case for five million."

Revy lets out a sharp, humorless bark of a laugh. She grabs the bottle of rum and slides it across the scarred wood until it clunks against his wrist. "Drink, then. Because that’s all you’re getting tonight."

Spike doesn't flinch. He uncorks the bottle, tips his head back, and takes a long, unhurried pull. His throat works; when he sets the bottle down, his dark eyes hold hers. There is no fear in him—only a hollow, quiet amusement that makes the skin on the back of Revy’s neck prickle. Men either piss themselves when Two Hands looks at them, or they try to act tough before dying. This guy looks like he’s already dead and just sticking around to see how the joke ends.

It pisses her off. Worse, it makes her pulse kick higher.

Before she can curse him out, the back door of the bar splinters inward.

Three men in cheap kevlar burst out of the hallway, submachine guns raised, dragging a bleeding, zip-tied Moretti by his collar. One of the gunmen spots the pair at the bar and yells.

The room erupts.

Spike doesn't draw first; he kicks the barstool sideways, catching the bartender as he dives them both behind the heavy oak counter just as a hail of 9mm rounds shatters every mirror and liquor bottle on the wall. Glass rains down like sleet.

Revy doesn't bother with cover. She vaults backward off her stool with a feral grin, both 9mm Sword Cutlasses clearing leather in a silver blur. *Bang-bang-bang-bang.* The roar of her dual pistols is deafening in the cramped room, muzzle flash painting her grinning face in strobes of white and orange. Two gunmen drop before their brass hits the floorboards.

The third ducks behind an overturned table, spraying blind fire—until Spike rises from behind the bar like a phantom. His Jericho 941 barks once, twice. Both rounds punch through the center of the wooden table, and the gunman slumps silent.

Smoke hangs thick and acrid, stinging the throat. When the ringing clears, the back door is swinging on one hinge, and Moretti is gone—dragged out into the alley by a fourth man during the crossfire.

Revy spins, smoke curling from the long barrels of her Berettas, and levels one directly at Spike’s nose. Spike is already standing, his Jericho pointed casually at her sternum, his posture loose and balanced on the balls of his feet.

For three heartbeats, neither breathes. Revy’s chest heaves beneath her crop top, sweat glistening on her collarbone, gunpowder smudged across her cheek. Spike’s gaze drops briefly to her mouth, then back up to her eyes.

"Nice grouping," Spike says softly. "Little loud for my taste."

"Shut up," Revy rasps, though the heat in her stomach isn't just adrenaline anymore. "He went toward the Starlight Motel across the street. We split the bastard fifty-fifty, or I shoot your other eye out right now."

"Deal," Spike says, holstering the Jericho before she lowers hers.

***

Ten minutes later, rain hammers against the grimy window of Room 204 at the Starlight Motel.

Moretti is unconscious in the bathtub, bound with shower curtain rings and his own belt. Out in the main room, a single bedside lamp casts long, bruised shadows across peeling wallpaper and a sagging mattress. 

Revy sits on the edge of the bed, stripping a fresh magazine with practiced, violent clicks, a half-drunk bottle of stolen whiskey between her thighs. Spike leans against the dresser opposite her, his jacket off, white shirt unbuttoned at the collar, rolling a coin across his knuckles.

The silence between them is heavier than the gunsmoke still clinging to their skin.

"You move weird," Revy says suddenly, taking a swig of whiskey. She wipes her mouth with the back of her tattooed hand. "Like water. Who taught you that?"

"Nobody worth remembering," Spike says. He steps forward, plucking the bottle from between her knees. His fingers brush the bare skin of her inner thigh—warm, calloused, lingered just a fraction of a second too long. Revy doesn't pull back. Her jaw tightens. "What about you? Not many people can shoot two long-slides without breaking their wrists."

"I’m not a good person, not a bad person. I’m just here," Revy mutters, staring up at him through dark lashes. "And you don't stay here long without learning how to kill faster than the other guy."

Spike drinks, sets the bottle on the nightstand, and doesn't step away. He stands between her knees, towering over her, the scent of tobacco, rain, and cordite wrapping around them both. Revy tilts her chin up, defiance warring with a sharp, sudden hunger. Her hand slides slowly down to the grip of the Cutlass resting on the bedspread.

"You thinking about taking my half while I sleep, cowboy?" she whispers.

Spike leans down, bracing one hand on the mattress beside her hip. His face stops inches from hers, close enough that their breath mingles, warm and whiskey-sour. With his left hand, he lazily draws his Jericho and presses the warm muzzle lightly under her chin, tilting her face up just as the cold steel of her Beretta presses hard against his ribs, right over his heart.

Neither of them pulls the trigger. Revy’s free hand fists in the front of his shirt, yanking him another inch closer until his lips brush the corner of hers—rough, electric, and full of teeth.

"Like I said," Spike murmurs against her mouth, his thumb grazing the pulse hammering in her throat. "Whatever happens, happens."

The neon sign outside the Yellow Flag buzzes like a dying hornet, casting jaundiced stripes across the sticky mahogany bar. The air smells of stale beer, cheap tobacco, and the humid rot of Roanapur’s back alleys. 

Spike Spiegel sits on a wobbly stool, nursing a warm gin and tonic, his long legs folded awkwardly beneath the counter. His stomach growls—a hollow, familiar ache reminding him that the fridge back on the *Bebop* contains nothing but moldy bell peppers and zero beef. He fishes a bent cigarette from his crumpled pack, sticks it between his lips, and flips open his silver Zippo. A jagged ring of rust circles the base of the lighter, suggesting it’s been dropped in water more than once. He strikes the wheel. The flame catches, illuminating one dark brown eye that sees the present, and one lighter, prosthetic eye that never stops looking at the past.

"You're in my seat, Stretch," a voice rasps over the low murmur of the bar.

Spike doesn't turn his head, just shifts his gaze lazily to the left. The woman standing beside him is a walking arsenal wrapped in denim cutoffs and a black crop top. Twin custom Beretta 92FS pistols—polished stainless steel with ivory grips—hang from shoulder holsters like extensions of her ribs. A tribal dragon tattoo coils down her sun-bronzed right arm, flexing as she slams a crumpled bounty flyer onto the wet wood between them.

"Funny," Spike says, exhaling a thin plume of gray smoke. "Didn't see a name on it. Unless your name is 'Wet Floor.'"

Revy bares her teeth in something too sharp to be a smile. She takes the stool next to him anyway, signaling the bartender with two fingers. "Bacardi. Leave the bottle." She turns her amber eyes back to the lanky stranger in the rumpled blue suit. "You're looking for Mateo Vance. Fifty grand, alive. Thirty if he comes back in a bag."

Spike taps ash into a chipped saucer. "I prefer the fifty. Beef prices are up, and my partner has expensive tastes in losing money."

"Too bad," Revy says, ripping the cap off the rum bottle the bartender sets down and taking a long, burning pull straight from the glass neck. She wipes her mouth with the back of her thumb. "He’s mine. Dutch already spent half the advance on torpedo parts, and if you get in my way, I’ll ventilate that ugly blue suit."

Spike studies her. He knows killers—spent half his life as one for the Red Dragon Syndicate—and this girl reeks of cordite and bad history. She’s coiled tight, all ragged edges and hair-trigger rage, the exact opposite of water. Yet there’s a reckless rhythm to her that pulls at the suicidal streak buried beneath his ribs. 

"Tell you what," Spike says, sliding his empty glass toward her bottle. "Pour a starving man a drink, and we can flip a coin for him."

Revy snorts, a dark, genuine sound, and sloshes three fingers of rum into his glass. "You've got balls, fluff-head. Or a death wish."

"Already died once," Spike murmurs, knocking the drink back. The cheap rum burns a pleasant trail down to his empty gut. "Whatever happens, happens."

"Bullshit," Revy mutters, lighting her own cigarette from the tip of his before he can pull away. Her face is inches from his, close enough for him to smell gun oil and cheap lime soap on her skin. "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here. And while I'm here, I get paid."

Before Spike can answer, the front doors of the Yellow Flag splinter inward.

Mateo Vance doesn't wait to be hunted; he brings six cartel gunmen with him, submachine guns sweeping the room. Glass shatters as the first burst of automatic fire chews through the shelves of liquor behind the bar.

Spike moves like water—fluid, weightless, already dropping behind the overturned oak table before the brass casings hit the floor. Revy doesn't duck so much as explode. Her twin Sword Cutlasses clear leather with a metallic shriek, barking in a deafening, rhythmic cadence that paints the dim room in strobes of white-hot muzzle flash.

*Bang-bang-bang.* Two men drop by the jukebox, red mist blooming against the neon.

Spike pops up from cover, his Jericho 941 steady in a two-handed grip. Three crisp 9mm rounds punch through the smoke; two gunmen go down, and a third catches Spike's spinning heel kick square in the jaw when he rushes the flank. Bone cracks. Spike pivots, tracking Revy through the chaos. Watching her shoot is like watching a wildfire—brutal, hypnotic, and terrifyingly fast. When a stray cartel thug levels a shotgun at her exposed back, Spike fires across the room, dropping the man a split second before Revy spins, her smoking barrel passing an inch from Spike’s nose.

Their eyes lock through the drifting haze of gunpowder. Her chest heaves, sweat glistening on her collarbone, pupils blown wide with the high of the kill. Spike grins, slow and dangerous.

In the corner, Vance scrambles out the back window, clutching a bleeding shoulder.

***

Twenty minutes later, rain hammers against the cracked blinds of Room 104 at the Shangri-La Motel. 

Vance lies hogtied and unconscious in the bathtub, worth fifty thousand dollars to whoever walks out the door with him. In the center of the cramped, mildewed room, Spike and Revy stand three feet apart, soaked to the bone.

The click of hammers being cocked is louder than the thunder outside.

Revy’s right Cutlass is pressed directly beneath Spike’s chin, the hot barrel searing his skin. Spike’s Jericho is angled squarely between her breasts, resting against the damp cotton of her crop top, right over the frantic thudding of her heart.

Neither of them pulls the trigger.

"Your depth perception is shit with that fake eye, isn't it?" Revy whispers, though she doesn't move an inch. Rainwater drips from her dark ponytail onto her bare shoulders.

"At this range?" Spike’s voice is a low drawl, his thumb resting lightly on the hammer of his piece. "I don't need two eyes to hit what I'm looking at."

Revy steps forward instead of back, forcing the muzzle of his Jericho harder against her ribs. Her free hand comes up, fingers tangling roughly in his wet, yellow silk tie, yanking him down until their mouths are a breath apart. They are both bruised, smelling of wet wool, sulfur, and cheap rum, trapped in the electric gravity between a kiss and a double homicide.

"You're bad luck, Cowboy," she breathes against his lips, her finger tightening a fraction on the trigger.

"So I've been told," Spike says, his dark eyes dropping to her mouth as the rain beats on in the dark.

response:
A crimson harvest moon hangs bloated and low over the gabled roofs of the deserted Carinthian village, painting the cobblestones in the color of fresh arterial spray. The air is thick with the stench of copper and woodsmoke, until a sharper, altogether out-of-place scent cuts through the rot: lilac and gooseberries.

Yennefer of Vengerberg steps around the shattered wheel of an overturned haywain, her black velvet cloak trailing just above the mire. Around her, the mangled corpses of seven lesser bruxae and a pack of ghouls litter the square, torn apart not by silver blades or witcher signs, but by something wildly, gleefully excessive. Some are perforated by craters the size of fists; others look as though the shadows themselves have chewed them to ribbons and spat them out.

At the center of the carnage, seated atop the stone lip of the village well, is a man. Or something wearing the rough approximation of one.

He is draped in a tailored crimson coat and a wide-brimmed hat that belongs to no royal court Yennefer has ever visited. Twin circles of tinted orange glass sit perched on the bridge of his nose, catching the blood-red moonlight. In one gloved hand, he casually balances a massive, gleaming silver firearm—an absurdly intricate hand-cannon that reeks of blessed mercury and alchemical gunpowder.

"You're late, little witch," the stranger says. His voice is a rich, subterranean purr that vibrates in the marrow of her bones. "The appetizers have already gone cold."

Yennefer stops ten paces away. Her chin lifts, her raven curls framing a face sculpted by magic into cold, severe perfection. Beneath her lace choker, the obsidian star at her throat pulses once, drawing on the ambient ley lines intersecting beneath the square.

"If I had known a circus performer was handling the local pest problem, I wouldn't have ruined a good pair of boots," Yennefer replies, her tone dry enough to parch stone. Her violet eyes narrow as she reads his aura. She expects the cold, static void of a higher vampire—a Regis or a Dettlaff. Instead, she stares into a churning, bottomless abyss of screaming souls, ancient blood, and raw, sadistic malice. Her stomach turns in visceral revulsion, yet the scholar in her leans forward, transfixed. *What in the spheres is he?*

The man grins, an impossibly wide, jagged crescent of white teeth that stretches far past human anatomy. "A circus performer? Delightful. And here I thought chivalry was dead in these backwater centuries."

He rises from the well, unfolding to a towering height. Even before he moves, the shadow at his feet detaches from the cobblestones, sprouting dozens of glowing, blood-red eyes that blink up at her in hungry unison.

"You smell of springtime and deceit," Alucard murmurs, tilting his head so the brim of his hat obscures half his face. "And underneath that pretty skin... ah. Broken bone. Twisted spine. Costly magic, remaking clay from the inside out."

Yennefer's fingers twitch. The air between them snaps with ozone. "Keep sniffing, dog, and I'll turn your lungs to ash."

"Promise?" Alucard's laugh is a booming, unhinged bark of pure delight. In the blink of an eye, the massive silver pistol—the Jackal, though she has no name for it—is leveled at her forehead. "Show me, then. These pathetic night-crawlers couldn't even make me bleed. They called themselves vampires, yet they whimpered like cattle when the silver bit."

He doesn't pull the trigger—not yet. He wants to see what she does when the shadow of death falls across her throat.

Yennefer does not flinch, nor does she dive for cover. With a sharp flick of her wrist and a hissed Elder phrase, she twists the space directly in front of his barrel. When the deafening roar of the cannon shatters the village silence, the thirteen-millimeter exploding silver round vanishes into a shimmering tear in the air, reappearing three inches behind Alucard's left ear.

The bullet blows half his skull across the cobblestones in a spray of black gore and shattered bone.

His headless torso sways, coat fluttering, before a wet, gurgling chuckle bubbles up from his throat. Black tendrils of shadow and coagulated blood whip outward, snatching the scattered fragments out of the air. Within seconds, jawbone, eye socket, and pale flesh knit back together. He adjusts his crooked orange glasses with a white-gloved finger, grinning wider than before.

"Now *that*," Alucard purrs, "is a neat trick. No silver sword, no tedious prayers to a silent god. Just pure, arrogant willpower bending the world until it breaks."

Yennefer's pulse hammers against her ribs, though her expression remains a mask of glacial disdain. A direct hit from a consecrated projectile should have slowed even an Unseen Elder. He hadn't just regenerated; he had *enjoyed* it. He is an abomination—a gluttonous, self-loathing parasite wearing a nobleman's swagger—and yet the sheer, unapologetic magnitude of his power is intoxicating.

"You're sloppy," she says coldly, weaving chaos between her fingers until her palms glow with blinding violet fire. "You leave your guard open because you want to be hurt. That isn't strength. It's a tantrum."

For a fraction of a second, the manic amusement vanishes from Alucard's face, replaced by the ancient, hollow chill of a wallachian winter. The shadows erupt around him, towering twenty feet into the crimson sky, morphing into a writhing tapestry of Baskerville hounds and impaled soldiers.

"The bird of Hermes is my name," he whispers, stepping straight into her arcane light as the hounds lunge, "eating my wings to make me tame."

Yennefer doesn't retreat. She slams both hands outward, unleashing a forked torrent of incandescent lightning thatvaporizes the foremost shadow-hounds and blasts Alucard backward through the timber wall of the nearest tavern. Splinters and dust rain down. Before the debris settles, she is already weaving a binding sigil in the dirt, preparing to compress the building into a singularity of crushed stone.

Then, from directly behind her shoulder, cold leather brushes her cheek.

"I thought you were going to turn my lungs to ash, my lady," Alucard breathes into her ear, having phased through the shadow of the shattered haywain. His heavy silver pistol presses lightly against thesmall of her back, while her own arcane dagger—conjured in a heartbeat of pure instinct—rests flush against his jugular, buzzing with enough chaos magic to unmake his cells one by one.

Neither moves. The crimson moonlight bathes them both in red.

Alucard inhales deeply, drinking in the lilac and gooseberries, the static of her lightning, and the steel-trap refusal to yield in her violet eyes. "You are no monster," he notes softly, almost wistfully. "Just a woman who clawed her way to the top of the dirt pile and refuses to die."

"I'm not sweet, and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving—or lecturing—by a corpse in a tacky coat," Yennefer replies, pressing the glowing blade a fraction deeper until black blood wells against the magic. "Step back, or we find out how long it takes you to regrow from nothing."

Alucard stares down at her for a long, stretching moment. Slowly, the jagged, terrifying grin returns. He lowers his pistol, letting it vanish into the folds of his crimson coat, and tips his wide-brimmed hat in a mocking, theatrical bow.

"Another night, then, Yennefer of Vengerberg," he says, plucking her name from the surface of her thoughts as effortlessly as plucking a flower. "Keep that fire burning. Only a human can kill a monster... and I am always looking for a worthy executioner."

Before she can snap the portal shut around him, his body dissolves into a flock of red-eyed bats and liquid shadow, melting into the dark alleys beneath the blood moon, leaving only the smell of gunsmoke and the echo of his laughter behind.
