Above the corrugated tin roof of the lab, the salvaged solar array groaned against its rusted rebar mounts. Inside, the UV-sterilizer tube flickered with a dying violet buzz, casting spasmodic shadows across rows of cloudy mason jars.

Kael didn’t look up from the microscope. His right eye, swollen with an engineered tapetum lucidum spliced from a nocturnal stray, adjusted instantly to the sudden gloom. The world through the brass ocular lens remained sharp, glowing with a faint, sickly green bioluminescence. His left eye—still baseline human—watered andached, a constant migraine throb behind the temple where the viral vector had failed to cross the blood-brain barrier cleanly. 

"Hold the charge, you bastard," Kael muttered, his fingertips brushing the cooling fins of the thermal cycler. 

The PCR rig was a Frankensteinian monument to the Collapse. Its heating block was carved from an old engine manifold, wired to the heating element of a toaster oven and cooled by three high-RPM fans gutted from a pre-fall server rack. An ancient microprocessor, soldered onto a breadboard with stripped copper telephone wire, clicked rhythmically as it cycled temperatures: ninety-five degrees Celsius to denature, fifty-five to anneal, seventy-two to extend. 

Every time the solar rig outside hiccuped, the deep-cycle truck batteries beneath the workbench took the load with a sulfuric hiss. If the voltage dropped during the annealing phase, the primers would bind to the wrong sequences, and the last viable genetic material in Oakhaven would turn into useless biological soup.

In the center of the copper block sat four thin-walled plastic tubes. Inside them was the ghost of a tomato.

Before the boardrooms burned and the supply chains snapped, AgriCorp had perfected the art of the subscription seed. They called it *TeloLock*—a proprietary genetic switch woven into the telomeres of every drought-resistant, blight-proof crop on Earth. First-generation harvests were miracles of abundance. Second-generation seeds were sterile husks, programmed to trigger massive cellular apoptosis the moment they germinated. When AgriCorp’s orbital servers went dark during the Resource Wars, the annual license keys stopped broadcasting, and humanity’s food supply simply forgot how to reproduce.

Now, Kael was a grave robber of the genome, scraping degraded DNA out of desiccated decade-old husks and trying to patch the holes with wild weed sequences before the strands unraveled completely.

A heavy triple-knock rattled the airlock door—a salvaged walk-in freezer door sealed with inner-tube rubber. 

Kael reached under the bench, his knuckles brushing the grip of a pneumatic flechette pistol before he checked the periscope mirror. Standing in the swirling ochre dust outside was Vane. The fixer wore a filtration mask fashioned from a gas-station vapor canister and a trench coat stiff with dried mud and radiation-shielding lead tape.

Kael popped the latch. Vane slipped inside, bringing the smell of ozone and scorched alkali flatlands with him. He didn't wait for an invitation before pulling a vacuum-sealed thermos from his coat and setting it on the stainless-steel drainage table.

"The Foundry paid upfront," Vane said, his voice muffled and metallic through the respirator’s vox-grille. "Half a liter of pure *Taq* polymerase, cultured from a hot-spring vat up north, and four functioning solar cells. No micro-fractures."

Kael’s breath caught. Fresh enzyme. He had been purifying his own polymerase from scavenged bacteria in a pressure-cooker autoclave, losing half his batches to contamination. With pure *Taq*, he could run thirty cycles without the replication fidelity dropping into gibberish.

"And the catch?" Kael asked, wiping his hands on a rag stained with ethidium bromide. Beneath his fingernails, the skin was permanently blackened—necrotic tissue kept at bay only by a crude regeneration plasmid he’d injected two winters ago. The patch kept sepsis from killing him, even made his cuts seal in twenty minutes flat, though he had to pare away the excess keloid cartilage from his knuckles with a razor blade every Sunday.

Vane unscrewed the thermos lid. Liquid nitrogen vapor spilled over the lip, curling across the scratched metal table. With a pair of insulated tongs, the fixer lifted a glass ampoule containing three shriveled, obsidian-colored kernels.

"AgriCorp Series-9 Maize," Vane said. "Found in a sealed seed vault under an executive bunker in Nebraska."

Kael leaned in, his modified right eye dilating until the iris was swallowed by a reflective silver sheen. Even through the frost on the glass, he could see the telltale crystalline degradation along the seed coats. "They're ancient. The DNA inside those is going to look like confetti. Even if I amplify the fragments and splice out the TeloLock kill-switch using dandelion telomerase, the mutation rate will be astronomical."

"The Foundry doesn't want the kill-switch removed," Vane said quietly.

Kael froze, the hum of the server fans suddenly loud in the cramped room. "What?"

"Baron Krell wants the maize viable for planting this spring," Vane continued, leaning his gloved hands on the table. "High calorie, high yield. Enough to feed the Foundry’s labor camps and sell the surplus to the surrounding settlements—including yours. Next year, when Oakhaven's soil is exhausted and you come begging for seed stock, Krell wants the second generation to rot in the dirt. Just like the old days."

Kael stared at the ampoule. The copper taste of bile rose in his throat. Around them, Oakhaven was starving on a diet of bitter lichen and fibrous, half-mutated tubers that gave the children rickets. Kael’s own ribs pressed tight against his sweated shirt. He was thirty-two and looked fifty, his lymphatic system permanently inflamed from testing home-brewed viral therapies on himself to survive the winter plagues.

"He wants to play CEO," Kael whispered. "In the ashes."

"He has the diesel, Kael. He has the water purifiers. And right now, he has the only uncorrupted maize genome within five hundred miles." Vane tapped the thermos of enzyme. "Do the splice. Leave the termination sequence intact. Keep the *Taq* and the solar panels for your own garden projects. Everybody eats this autumn."

"And next autumn, Krell owns every throat in the valley."

"Next autumn is a luxury for people who survive this one," Vane replied. "I'll be back at sundown for the transfected embryos."

The freezer door thudded shut, sealing Kael back into the violet-tinged gloom. Outside, the wind died down, and the solar controller clicked as the voltage climbed back to fourteen volts. The UV lamp steadied into a harsh, unforgiving glare.

Kael looked at his toaster-manifold PCR rig. The cycle was finishing; the machine beeped twice—a tinny sound salvaged from a child’s toy—as the cooling fans spun up to full shriek. His settlement’s tomato batch was done, likely another failure of fragmented base pairs.

Slowly, he picked up the ampoule of Series-9 Maize. 

He had the restriction enzymes to leave the TeloLock switch intact, just as Krell ordered. It would be easy. Clean. Safe. 

Or, he could use a modified CRISPR-Cas9 cassette he’d been culturing in a jar of fermented beet juice. He could snip the AgriCorp termination sequence out of the maize, replace it with a dormant bacteriophage promoter, and key it to a specific chemical trigger—say, high-alkaline coal ash. The kind of ash that rained down daily around the Foundry’s smokestacks, while Oakhaven’s valley stayed clean upwind. 

Krell’s first harvest would grow tall and golden. And when the grain ripened in the Foundry's soot-choked air, the phage sequence would wake up and turn Krell’s monopoly into black slime on the stalk—while every seed planted in Oakhaven’s clean dirt would breed true for a thousand years.

Kael’s left temple throbbed, a sharp spike of pain reminding him of the price of sloppy genetics. He picked up a razor blade, shaved a ridge of overgrown cartilage off his thumb so he could grip the micropipette steady, and uncapped the ampoule.

response:
The bicycle wheel spun with a rhythmic, ticking click, its rusted spokes blurring in the greenish glow of the culture jars. 

Sora kept her foot on the pedal, maintaining a steady sixty revolutions per minute. Bolted to the wheel’s rim were twelve scavenged micro-tubes, their contents separating under the crude centrifugal force. When the timer—a gutted kitchen metronome—snapped its final beat, she let the wheel coast to a halt and reached for her micropipette. The instrument was a relic, its broken plunger replaced with the spring from a ballpoint pen and calibrated by the calloused pad of her thumb.

Around her, the lab hummed and wheezed like a dying lung. The thermocycler on the workbench was her masterpiece: a Peltier cooling plate ripped from a pre-Collapse wine fridge, married to the heating coil of a toaster oven and governed by an salvaged traffic-light logic board. Beside it sat a rack of empty *HelixCorp* cryo-canisters, their brushed-aluminum flanks still bearing the embossed, fading slogan: *TOMORROW’S HARVEST, TODAY.* 

Sora unscrewed the cap of a canister labeled *PROPRIETARY ADJUVANT – DO NOT REUSE* and drew up a measure of murky, home-brewed lysis buffer. 

Before the boardrooms went dark and the supply chains snapped, HelixCorp had perfected the ultimate subscription model. Every kernel of wheat, every soy pod, every blight-resistant tuber was coded with the *Chronos-Lock*—a synthetic telomere sequence coupled with a dormant endonuclease. The crops grew lush and nutrient-dense for a single season. But when the second-generation seeds germinated, the lock triggered, the enzymes woke, and the plant’s genome literally unzipped itself into sterile grey sludge. If you wanted to eat next year, you bought new seed. 

Then the grid died, the executives fled to orbital habitats or sealed bunkers, and the world was left with a billion tons of food that didn't know how to have children.

Sora coughed, a wet rattle that tasted of copper and sour yeast. She wiped her mouth with the back of her wrist, her eyes catching the faint, bioluminescent cyan tracing the veins beneath her translucent skin. 

Three winters ago, red-lung had swept through the settlement of New Cinder. With no antibiotics left in the ruins, Sora had spliced a bactericidal peptide template from bog-moss into an attenuated rhinovirus and inhaled it from a heated spoon. It had burned the infection out of her bronchi in forty-eight hours. It had also permanently rewired her tapetum lucidum and peripheral capillaries. Now, she could read the faded graduations on a pipette in pitch darkness without wasting battery power on a headlamp, though the trade-off was a constant, feverish metabolic itch and fingernails that grew thick and brittle as horn, requiring weekly filing with a metal rasp.

A triple knock sounded against the reinforced bulkhead door. Two fast, one slow.

Sora didn't reach for the cleaver under the bench; she didn't need to. The UV-reflective irises of her modified eyes could already see the thermal bloom of a single body standing outside in the drizzle. She slid the bolt back.

Vane stepped in, shaking acid rain from a tarp cloak. He was a runner for the Silt-Barons downriver, his left jaw distended by a calcified tumor caused by a bad batch of black-market bone-knitters. He didn't say hello. He just reached into his vest and set a lead-lined *HelixCorp* specimen tube onto the zinc table.

"Found it in an ag-inspector’s submerged lockbox near the old levee," Vane rasped, his voice permanently gravelled by scar tissue. "Cold-seal failed about a week ago. You got maybe four hours before the polymerase turns to vinegar and the template fragments beyond reading."

Sora picked up the tube. Through the frosted glass, she could see three shriveled, blackened kernels of *Amaranth-9*—high-protein, drought-proof, and nine years extinct in the wild. 

"That wasn't the deal, Vane," Sora said, holding the tube up to the glowing algae vats. "You promised me intact endosperm. This is already autolyzing. The Chronos-Lock has started chewing the base pairs."

"Which is why the Barons doubled the bounty," Vane said, leaning against the doorframe. "Fifty liters of refined diesel for the settlement's cistern pumps. Plus two sealed vials of porcine insulin for your old man. All you have to do is stitch a clean germline together, strip the suicide switch, and hand back half the viable callus cultures by sundown."

"And if the template is too degraded to amplify?"

Vane tapped the calcified lump on his jaw. "Then the Barons figure you’re taking up lab space somebody else could use. Tick-tock, splice-witch."

He slipped back out into the rain. 

Sora cursed softly and turned back to the bench. Fifty liters of diesel meant New Cinder wouldn't freeze come November. The insulin meant Marcus would keep his eyesight another year.

She cracked the seal on the specimen tube. The smell of rotting brassica and vinegar wafted out—the scent of cascading genetic apoptosis. Working fast, she crushed the best-looking kernel in a mortar cooled with liquid ammonia bled from an air-conditioner compressor. 

She didn't have a full sequence left; the DNA was shattered into ragged, overlapping fragments like a book put through a shredder. To rebuild the chromosome without the corporate kill-switch, she needed Overlap Extension PCR—tricking the fragments into priming each other until a whole, unbroken gene emerged from the wreckage.

She reached for another upcycled *HelixCorp* canister, this one housing her most precious commodity: *Taq* polymerase harvested from extremophile bacteria she cultured in a geothermal vent three miles outside the perimeter wall. She pipetted the enzyme, the crushed seed slurry, and custom flanking primers—painstakingly synthesized base-by-base over six months to bypass the *Chronos* promoter site—into a thin-walled reaction tube.

She slotted the tube into the toaster-oven thermocycler and flipped the toggle switch.

*Click. Hum.*

The heating coil glowed dull orange. Ninety-five degrees Celsius. Inside the plastic tube, the hydrogen bonds holding the dying corporate DNA together were snapping, the double helices unwinding into single strands. 

Sora leaned over the machine, her cyan-veined hands braced against the warm metal casing, watching the salvaged traffic-light board blink from red to amber. Fifty-five degrees. The primers were hunting in the dark, seeking out the ragged edges of the *Amaranth* code while ignoring the lethal corporate watermark. 

Her lungs rasped, the moss-gene in her chest flaring warm as her heart rate climbed. Around her, the settlement waited in the cold mud for a harvest that was never meant to exist, while inside a dead corporation's trash, thirty cycles of heat and cooling began to write the world back into life.

response:
Denaturation at ninety-five degrees Celsius. Annealing at fifty-eight. Extension at seventy-two. 

The rhythmic clicking of the automotive relays kept time with the throb behind Mara’s left temple. Before her on the stainless-steel mortuary table sat the heart of New Eden’s agricultural program: a polymerase chain reaction thermal cycler cobbled together from a cannibalized espresso machine boiler, two Peltier cooling plates pried out of a pre-collapse wine fridge, and the rusted heat-sink of an ancient server rack. 

Every ninety seconds, the rig hissed, venting a plume of sour steam that smelled of scorched copper and boiled agar. 

Beneath the table, pushing up through the hairline fractures in the linoleum tiles, clusters of *Mycena lux* pulsed with a sickly, bioluminescent viridian. They were remnants of Mara’s winter splicing tests—an attempt to cross subterranean cave fungi with fast-growing soy. The soy had rotted in the tray, its telomeres unspooling into useless chemical soup on day four, while the fungal spores had escaped into the grout. Now, they fed on the damp drywall and spilled nutrient broth, casting her subterranean laboratory in the watery, shadowless glow of an aquarium.

Mara leaned over the improvised transilluminator—a shoebox lined with tin foil and fitted with an ultraviolet bulb salvaged from a nail salon. She squinted through a shard of amber safety glass. Inside the agarose gel, cast in a shallow baking pan and buffered with boiled battery acid and baking soda, the ethidium bromide tags were finally separating.

Three glowing orange rungs on the ladder. The third band—the *Germination-Lock* sequence—was missing.

She exhaled, a rattle deep in her chest, and wiped her nose with the back of her wrist. A smear of dark, viscous blood came away on her sleeve, faintly iridescent under the UV light. The vector she’d injected into her own marrow three months ago to fight off the Red Rust spore-lung had saved her life, splicing extremophile tardigrade repair-proteins directly into her pulmonary epithelium. She could breathe air thick with mycotoxins that would liquefy a baseline human’s lungs in an hour. The trade-off was that her mucous membranes never stopped sloughing, her basal temperature ran a feverish thirty-nine degrees, and in complete darkness, the whites of her eyes shone like the mushrooms on the floor.

Self-medication in the wasteland was always a Faustian bargain written in base pairs.

A heavy triple-knock vibrated through the reinforced bulkhead door. Two seconds later, a single rap followed.

Mara snapped off the UV box, plunging the room into the fungal gloom. She drew a heavy pneumatic cattle-injector from her belt—loaded with forty milliliters of concentrated paralytic neurotoxin harvested from cone-snail cultures—and thumbed the brass latch on the peephole.

Vane stood in the concrete stairwell, rain sluicing off his waxed canvas duster. Behind him, two hired muscle from the Silt-Barons cradled sawed-off shotguns, their faces hidden behind Dual-Cartridge respirators. 

Mara unbolted the door. Vane stepped across the threshold, his heavy boots crushing a patch of glowing *Mycena* into luminescent green paste. He didn't apologize. Brokers never did.

"Smells like wet dog and vinegar in here, doc," Vane said, pulling down his damp bandana. His left eye was milky with a cataract; his right was unnaturally wide, the iris a jagged, spliced-in amber ring from some nocturnal predator. A cheap night-vision mod from the tenement clinics. It gave him constant migraines, Mara knew, because the optic nerve wasn't wired for the bandwidth.

"It's acetic acid and lysed *E. coli*," Mara replied, keeping the pneumatic pistol resting casually against her thigh. "And you're ten minutes early. The gel just finished running."

"And?" Vane stepped toward the mortuary table, his amber eye dilating as it adjusted to the gloom. "Tell me you broke the lock. The Barons have four hundred acres of black-earth silt cleared down by the riverbend, and the spring rains are starting. If we don't get seed in the mud by Friday, the whole sector starves by October."

"Monsanto-Bayer didn't spend forty billion dollars designing the Terminator-Nine cassette so a woman with an espresso machine could snip it out in an afternoon," Mara said sharply. 

She gestured to the cooling agarose tray. "Look at what they did to the genome before the boardrooms went dark. Every commercial crop on earth—wheat, maize, rice, soy—engineered with a generational suicide switch. The parent plant grows fat, resists drought, shrugs off locusts. Then, the moment the seed matures, an inducible Cre-recombinase enzyme triggers and shreds the embryonic DNA. One harvest. One season. You want next year's bread, you buy next year's license."

"Yeah, well, the sales reps are all skeletons in glass towers now," Vane grunted, reaching into his coat. "Did you excise the recombinase or not?"

"I couldn't excise it without collapsing the drought-resistance operon," Mara said, walking over to an old centrifuge made from a gutted blender motor taped to the concrete floor with duct tape. She pulled a micro-tube from the rotor. "The corporate coders braided the suicide switch right into the promoter region. Cut the lock, and the plant forgets how to drink water."

Vane’s hand froze inside his coat. Outside in the stairwell, one of the guards shifted his weight, the leather sling of his shotgun creaking. "You're telling me my advance bought nothing? Because if that's the play, Mara, the Barons will take the price out of your bone marrow. Literally. They know about your lungs."

"I didn't say I cut the lock," Mara said, holding the tiny plastic vial up to the green fungal light. Inside, suspended in clear buffer, floated a cloudy precipitate of plasmid rings. "I said I couldn't remove it. So I jammed it."

She set the vial on the steel table between them. 

"Where did you dig up that pre-collapse maize sample you brought me?" she asked.

"Sub-basement of an agritech vault outside Omaha," Vane said, his predator eye narrowing. "Cost me two scavengers to automated turrets. Why?"

"Because the vault's cooling failed twenty years ago," Mara said, a grim smile tugging at her cracked lips. "The sample was ninety percent degraded. Cytosine deamination everywhere—the DNA was rotting in the foil. Every other splicer in the valley would have thrown it in the incinerator. Worthless trash."

She tapped the side of the espresso-machine thermal cycler. 

"I used the rot. I ran forty cycles of error-prone PCR using a mutated *Taq* polymerase I cultured from the geothermal vents by the slag heaps. Instead of repairing the degraded maize DNA, I forced the enzyme to copy the mistakes across the Cre-recombinase site. I flooded the suicide switch with nonsense mutations until the protein folded inside-out, then I spliced in a telomerase promoter from these floor mushrooms to stabilize the chromosome ends."

Vane stared at the vial. "Speak trade-talk, doc."

"The maize will grow," Mara said softly. "It'll breed true. Second generation, third, tenth. The suicide gene is still in there, firing every autumn, but it's shooting blanks. And because of the fungal splice, the husks will glow faint green when the kernels are ripe enough to harvest."

Vane let out a long, whistling breath. Slowly, he withdrew his hand from his coat—not with a weapon, but with a heavy, lead-lined cylinder the size of a thermos. Frost clung to its brushed-steel seams as the humid lab air hit it.

"Twentythousand units of lyophilized *Thermus aquaticus* polymerase," Vane said, setting the cryo-canister on the steel table with a dull thud. "Lab-grade. Sealed in nitrogen before the fall. Plus three vials of restriction enzymes—*Eco*RI and *Bam*HI."

Mara’s breath caught. With pure, uncorrupted polymerase, she wouldn't have to brew half-blind enzymes in mason jars anymore. She could fix the blight-resistant potato strain for her own settlement on the roof. Heck, she might even synthesize an suppressor to stop her own nosebleeds.

She reached for the canister, her fingers trembling slightly from the low-grade splice-fever that never quite left her bones. 

Vane’s hand clamped over the top of the cylinder before she could lift it. His amber eye fixed on hers, gleaming in the dark.

"One condition from the Barons," Vane murmured. "You don't keep a mother-culture of this corn for your people topside. The riverbend holds the monopoly on viable grain. We find glow-in-the-dark husks growing in New Eden's planter boxes, we burn your greenhouse to the foundation."

Mara looked down at his hand, then over at the corner of the room, where a row of cracked mason jars sat next to the radiator, already cloudy with Dividing cells—the backup culture she had inoculated three hours before he knocked.

She met his mismatched gaze, letting the faint, eerie bioluminescence of her sclera catch the light. 

"Of course, Vane," she lied, her voice raspy and cool. "Bad for business if a crop lasts forever, right?"

He studied her for three heartbeats, then took the micro-tube, released the cryo-canister, and turned back toward the rain.

prompt:
Fok Horror: Útiseta

Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment.

First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words.

A distant church bell chimes once at exactly midnight, though no service is scheduled. Length: 1000 words.
response:
In October of 1995, the darkness in Norrbotten didn’t fall so much as it rose from the peat, thick and smelling of wet iron. Four months after my father’s transfer with the state forestry board had dragged us north from Stockholm, I still hadn't adjusted to the silence. In the city, night meant neon hums and distant traffic; in the village, it was a vast, suffocating emptiness pressing against my bedroom window. 

If it hadn’t been for Astrid, I would have gone mad before the first snow. 

I met her behind the school bike sheds in September, sharing a stolen Blend menthol while the other ninth-graders stared at my Doc Martens like I’d dropped from the moon. Astrid had pale, lashless eyes, a faded Europe patch safety-pinned to her denim jacket, and a grandmother who lived up toward the marshes and supposedly remembered the old ways—the ones the Lutheran priests had spent three centuries trying to scrub out of the valley.

At first, Astrid’s "midnight games" felt like harmless rural boredom, no different from the Ouija boards my friends and I had giggled over at sleepovers in Södermalm. We’d melted lead into cold water to see the initials of who’d ask Sara Lindqvist to the autumn dance, and buried a knotted birch twig under the football pitch right before Jesper Nilsson sprained his ankle. When Jesper actually limped into homeroom on crutches the next morning, a thrilled, uneasy shiver had gone through me. Astrid had only shrugged, popping her gum. *Told you,* she’d said. *You just have to know how to ask.*

Then came the last Friday of October, and she suggested *Útiseta*.

"Sitting out," she explained as we pushed our Crescents up the logging track where the gravel gave way to frost-stiffened heather. My Walkman was shoved deep into the pocket of my parka, the headphones tangled around a half-empty pack of Toy chewing gum. "Mormor says when the frost locks the ground, the dead get restless. If you sit on a *hög*—one of the old mounds—until the turn of the night, they’ll tell you things. Whatever you want to know."

"Like whether Marcus Eriksson actually broke up with Hanna?" I asked, my breath pluming white in the beam of her dynamo lamp.

"If that’s all you care about," Astrid said lightly. "Or who’s going to fail maths. Or who’s going to die before spring."

I laughed, waiting for her to join in, to admit we were just two fifteen-year-olds freezing our asses off for a cheap thrill. Instead, she leaned our bikes against a boundary stone and reached into her Fjällräven rucksack.

The mound rose out of the clearing ahead of us like the back of a sleeping beast, a swelling of turf and ancient river stones crowned by three stunted pines. The state heritage board had put up a little aluminum plaque at the base—*Iron Age Grave, c. 500 AD*—which somehow made it worse. A fairytale was one thing; bones under a government sign were another.

"Take the Walkman out," Astrid said, her voice dropping into that brisk, matter-of-fact register she used when quoting her grandmother. "No batteries. And take off your cross if you’re wearing one. If you carry church-iron or silver, they won’t come near, or else they’ll come angry."

My fingers hesitated at my collar, where the tiny silver chain from my confirmation lay warm against my throat. "Astrid, it’s minus four."

"Do it properly or go home, Stockholm," she said, not unkindly, as she unbuckled her plastic Casio watch and dropped it into her bag alongside my Walkman. From a greased paper parcel, she produced an iron pocketknife and two strips of dried pike that smelled rank and salty. "Put this under your tongue. Don't swallow it. When we sit on the crown, we sit back-to-back. No speaking. Look between the trees, not at the sky. And whatever you hear—even if it uses my voice, even if it calls you by your mother's name—don't answer until I pinch your wrist."

A gust of wind combed through the pines, a dry, hissing sound like tape unspooling. I slipped the silver chain over my head, tucked the foul, leathery fish into my cheek, and followed her up the slope.

The turf at the top of the mound felt strangely spongy beneath my jeans, as though the frost hadn't quite taken hold there. Astrid traced a wide circle around us in the hoarfrost with the point of her knife, then sat and pulled me down until our shoulder blades pressed together through our heavy coats.

For the first ten minutes, there was only the cold seeping into my tailbone and the ridiculousness of it all. My nose ran. The dried pike tasted of mud and old smoke. I stared at the black wall of spruce trees across the clearing, listening to the blood thrum in my ears, convinced that any second Astrid would burst out laughing and offer me a cigarette.

Then her spine went rigid against mine.

The wind had stopped. Not died down—stopped, as if a door had been shut. The woods around the clearing went utterly, impossibly still. My eyes watered in the dark, playing tricks with the birch trunks until they looked like pale, narrow figures standing just behind the treeline, heads tilted to watch us. 

Beneath us, the earth gave a faint, rhythmic thud, like a heel striking the underside of a floorboard. Once. Twice. 

*It’s your pulse,* I told myself, my heart hammering against my ribs. *It’s just the cold.*

A sound drifted across the heather from the south, three kilometers away down in the valley. 

*Dong.*

A single, heavy stroke of the parish church bell, cutting through the frozen air at exact midnight. 

My breath caught in my throat. There was no midnight service in the village—the vicar lived in the next town over and only drove up on alternate Sundays, and the belfry was locked from September to Advent. Yet the bronze vibration hung over the clearing, fading into a silence that felt suddenly crowded.

Right beside my left ear—not behind me, where Astrid sat, but *beside* me, close enough that I felt the stir of icy air against my cheek—something drew a long, rattling breath through wet teeth.

A voice, thin as dry reeds, whispered a name I hadn't told a soul in Norrbotten. Not even Astrid.

I didn't wait for the pinch on my wrist. I scrambled backward, breaking the circle with my heel, spitting the pike into the heather as I stumbled down the mound. Behind me, Astrid was already running, her boots crashing through the brush, neither of us daring to look back until the streetlights of the village finally bled through the trees.

Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words.

Thick mist clings to the edges of the burial mound, glowing under moonlight. Length: 1000 words.
response:
In the autumn of 1995, the silence of Västerbotten felt like a physical weight pressing against my eardrums. Six months earlier, my world had been the neon hum of Södermalm, the clatter of the Stockholm metro, and the comforting anonymity of concrete. When the state forestry board transferred my father north, we traded all of it for a red timber house at the edge of a logging village where the pine trees grew too close to the windows. I was sixteen, furious, and desperate for any distraction from the suffocating quiet.

That desperation was how I found Astrid—or how she found me. While the other kids at school stared at my second-hand Doc Martens with quiet suspicion, Astrid had simply slid into the seat beside me at lunch, smelling of woodsmoke and cheap vanilla perfume, and asked if I wanted to know who Marcus Lindqvist had been kissing behind the hockey rink.

She called them midnight games. Her *mormor*, she claimed, knew the old ways—the ones that predated the whitewashed Lutheran church in the valley by a thousand years. At first, it felt no different from the Ouija boards my friends and I had giggled over in city basements. We melted lead into cold water to read the shapes of our classmates’ secrets; we tied red wool around rowan twigs to make Karin Bergström trip during gym class. When Karin actually sprained her ankle two days later, we laughed until we couldn't breathe, high on the intoxicating blend of teenage malice and the illusion of power. We were bored girls turning ancient superstitions into a parlor game.

Until the night of the *útiseta*.

"It just means 'sitting out,'" Astrid said, her breath pluming white in the beam of my flashlight. We were walking along the tractor ruts behind the old parish boundary, the frost crunching beneath our boots. I had my Walkman clipped to my jeans, the headphones resting around my neck, still warm from the Smashing Pumpkins cassette I’d been playing to calm my nerves. "You sit on a *hög*—a burial mound—until the spirits come up through the soil to tell you what you want to know. Mormor says the dead hate being ignored, so if you wait long enough, they have to speak."

"And this is really going to tell us if Emil likes you?" I asked, pulling my oversized flannel jacket tighter. 

"It’ll tell us everything," she said, entirely matter-of-fact, as if she were explaining how to program a VCR.

The Bronze Age cairn rose out of the clearing ahead of us like the hump of a sleeping beast. Even now, decades later, I can close my eyes and see the geometry of that place. Thick mist clung to the edges of the burial mound, glowing under moonlight while the surrounding spruce forest remained swallowed in pitch black.

Astrid stopped at the border of the vapor. She reached into her canvas rucksack and pulled out a rusted iron sickle from her father’s toolshed, a carton of Blend cigarettes, and a ziplock bag filled with silver ten-krona coins and dried slaughterhouse blood she’d stolen from her uncle’s butcher shop.

"Take off the Walkman," she instructed, dropping to her knees in the wet heather. "No batteries. No plastic on the mound. And unbutton your coat—nothing can be knotted or bound, not even your shoelaces, or your mind gets tangled when they try to reach in."

"Astrid, it’s freezing," I said, though my fingers were already moving to my laces. There was an eerie precision to her rules that stripped away the rebellion of sneaking out after curfew. She wasn't smiling anymore. 

With the iron blade, she scratched a shallow furrow in the frost around the base of the mound, murmuring words in a dialect so thick and guttural it barely sounded like Swedish. She scattered the coins and the dark, flaking blood into the dirt, then lit two cigarettes at once, handing one to me. "Smoke it down to the filter, then throw it outside the line. Once we step over the iron mark, we sit back-to-back on the top. Whatever you hear, whatever you see, you do not speak, and you do not look behind you. If you speak before dawn, you trade places with whatever answered."

We finished the cigarettes in silence. My heart hammered against my ribs, a sudden, sharp vertigo washing over me as I realized how far we were from the highway, from my parents’ sleeping house, from anything rational. Yet the worst fear of sixteen is being called a coward. I tossed the glowing butt into the heather and followed her up the steep, grassy slope.

The ground at the summit was uneven, sunken in the center where the ancient timber chamber beneath had rotted and collapsed centuries ago. We sat down on the cold turf, our spines pressed together. Through two layers of wool and flannel, I could feel the rapid, shallow rise and fall of Astrid’s shoulder blades. 

For the first twenty minutes, there was only the numbing seep of frost through my jeans and the distant, lonely rush of wind in the canopy. My mind raced, trying to anchor itself in the mundane—my unfinished math homework, the hum of the refrigerator back home. 

Then, the wind stopped.

It didn't die down; it simply ceased, as if a heavy door had been shut. The silence that followed was absolute, thick and ringing. The glowing mist at the base of the mound began to curl upward, creeping over our unlaced boots like cold water. 

*Crack.*

A branch snapped at the edge of the clearing. Both of Astrid’s shoulders tensed against mine. 

It’s a moose, I told myself. Or a fox. My pulse throbbed so loudly in my ears that it began to sound like rhythmic footsteps—slow, dragging steps circling the iron line Astrid had cut into the earth. The air grew heavy with the copper tang of the butcher’s blood, mingling with something older: wet wool, peat moss, and the sweet, hollow rot of turned soil.

Then came the whispering.

At first, I thought it was Astrid. It was a dry, rasping sound, right beside my left ear, speaking in that same broken, archaic cadence she had used earlier. I shifted slightly, about to hiss at her to stop trying to scare me, when I felt her head tremble against the back of mine. She was biting her gloved knuckles to keep from crying out. It wasn't her.

The cold deepened, settling into my joints until my teeth ached. In the silver fog at the bottom of the slope, shadows began topool and lengthen, detaching themselves from the trunks of the pines. Was it the moonlight playing tricks on eyes strained by darkness and adrenaline? Hypothermia setting in? I wanted to believe it was psychological—a shared hysteria born of Astrid’s stories and my own isolation.

Except the ground beneath us gave a faint, unmistakable shudder, like a sleeper turning over in a narrow bed. Something brushed against the cuff of my jeans—something rough and freezing that felt horribly like knuckles grazing the fabric. And in my head, a voice that was not my own began to recite names, dates, and small, ugly truths I had no way of knowing, pouring into the dark like icy water into an open vessel, teaching me the terrible weight of getting an answer when you only meant to knock and run.

First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words.

Wind occasionally rustles the pine trees, sounding almost like faint whispers. Length: 1000 words.
response:
In the autumn of 1995, boredom in Norrland felt like a physical weight, pressing down from a sky the color of wet slate. My father’s transfer to the regional timber board had uprooted us from our third-floor apartment in Södermalm and dropped us into a village of forty houses, two closed shops, and a million spruce trees. Without Astrid, I think I would have simply dissolved into the damp moss.

She was the only other fifteen-year-old within five kilometers. While I wore oversized flannel and listened to bootleg Oasis cassettes, Astrid wore her dead grandmother’s hand-knitted woolens and smelled faintly of woodsmoke and crushed juniper. It was Astrid who invented what she called the midnight games. At first, they were harmless—melting lead into cold water to see which boys at the consolidated school in town liked us, or tying rowan twigs above a locker to make a mean girl trip on the stairs. When Maria Lindqvist actually sprained her ankle two days later, we giggled behind our hands in the cafeteria, drunk on the cheap, dizzying thrill of coincidence.

Then came the last Friday in October, and Astrid decided we were ready for *Útiseta*.

“Sitting out,” she explained as we pushed our bicycles up the logging road past the edge of the village. Her breath plumed white in the beam of my Dynamo flashlight. “Farmor said the old ones did it when they needed to know things nobody living could tell them. You sit on a *hög*—a burial mound—from midnight until the first cockcrow. If you don’t speak, and you don’t look back, the dead come up through the roots and whisper answers in your ear.”

“And what are we asking the ancient dead?” I asked, my sneakers slipping on gravel slick with frost. “Whether Jesper is going to break up with Sara before the winter dance?”

“Why not?” Astrid said, entirely serious. She adjusted the frayed strap of her Fjällräven backpack. “Secrets are secrets. The dead don’t care if it’s about a king’s war or who stole Sara’s silver ring from the gym changing room. They just want to be asked.”

We ditched our bikes in a ditch choked with dead bracken and climbed the ridge into the old forest. Up here, the commercial pine plantations gave way to twisted, ancient trees bearded with black lichen. At the crest stood Kungshögen—a broad, grassy dome rising unnaturally from the rocky soil, ringed by sunken stones. By day, it was just a lump where sheep sometimes grazed. At quarter to midnight, under a bruised, moonless sky, it looked like a sleeping chest waiting to draw breath.

Astrid unzipped her pack and laid out her supplies on a flat boulder with the brisk efficiency of someone setting up a picnic. First came a pack of Blend Menthols, stolen from her older brother. Then, a plastic zip-lock bag of coarse gray salt, two lengths of red wool yarn, and an iron nail as long as my middle finger, rusted to the color of dried blood.

“Take off your watch,” she ordered, tying a red thread around my left wrist. Her fingers were icy. “No ticking. No batteries. Leave your Walkman here, too. They hate new iron, and they hate noise.”

I unstrapped my plastic Casio and dropped it into my coat pocket, feeling a sudden, prickling reluctance. “Astrid, it’s freezing. We’re going to get hypothermia in twenty minutes.”

“We won’t stay till dawn,” she said, striking a match to light two cigarettes. In the brief flare of sulfur, her eyes looked huge, the pupils swallowing the pale blue. She handed me one, though she knew I only ever puffed without inhaling. “Just twenty minutes past twelve. Long enough to listen. Smoke this first—Farmor said you have to clear your mouth of house-air.”

The menthol tasted sharp and chemical against the rot-sweet smell of the forest floor. Above us, a gust of wind moved through the high crowns of the pines. The needles hissed together, rising and falling in a dry, rhythmic sibilance that sounded almost like faint whispers—like a room full of people talking just on the other side of a thick wall.

Astrid took the rusted nail and drove it into the turf at the base of the mound with the heel of her Dr. Martens boot. Then she poured a thin, crooked circle of salt around the crown of the hillock.

“Sit back-to-back,” she instructed, scrambling up into the ring. “Pull your coat over your head like a hood. Whatever happens, Linnea, do not say a word. If you speak to them without knowing the waking-rhymes, you give them your voice. And don’t look at me until I tap your shoulder three times.”

Feeling foolish, yet too proud to let a village girl think a kid from Stockholm was scared of the dark, I climbed into the circle and sat. The grass was stiff with rime, soaking through the seat of my jeans almost instantly. We pressed our shoulder blades together. Through two layers of wool and nylon, I could feel the rapid, shallow thud of Astrid’s heart.

I pulled my parka hood forward until the faux-fur trim blinded my peripheral vision, leaving only a narrow tunnel of dark trees ahead.

For the first five minutes, there was only the cold and the ringing silence of the north. My toes went numb. I tried to think of Jesper, or the math test on Monday, or the traffic noise back home on Hornsgatan—anything to anchor myself in 1995.

Then the wind returned.

It didn’t blow against my face. It seemed to drop straight down from the canopy, swirling around the base of Kungshögen. The pine needles rustled again, that dry, hurrying *shh-shh-shh*, except now my strained ears began to carve syllables out of the static. *Lin-ne-a.* No, just the branches scraping. *Kom.* Just birch leaves skittering over stone.

Behind me, Astrid went rigid. Every muscle in her back locked at once.

A sound came from the bottom of the mound, near the rusted nail. It wasn't the wind. It was the heavy, wet crunch of gravel shifting under weight—slow, deliberate, and far too heavy for a fox or a hare.

I held my breath until my lungs burned. The rational part of my brain, the part raised on television and asphalt, insisted it was a badger, or a stray dog, or my own blood pounding in my ears from the cold and nicotine. We were two fifteen-year-old girls playing a game in the dark. We had scared ourselves into a trance.

Then the smell hit me. The crisp scent of pine and frost vanished, replaced by the suffocating stench of bog-iron, wet sheep’s wool, and earth that had never seen the sun.

Something brushed the hem of my sneaker.

I squeezed my eyes shut. Against my spine, Astrid was trembling so violently her teeth clicked together, yet she didn't make a sound. The wind in the pines dropped dead, as if the forest itself had been told to hush, leaving only a low, rasping exhalation right beside my left ear—so close I felt the damp warmth of it stir the fur on my hood. It wasn't a voice, not quite, just the shape of a word formed by air passing over dry, hollow reeds.

*Three taps.*

Astrid’s fingers dug into my shoulder—one, two, three—and then she was scrambling down the mound, tearing through the salt circle without looking back. I didn't wait. I threw myself down the slope after her, my knees barking against the boundary stones, and we ran blindly down the logging road, abandoning the nail, the yarn, and the game to the dark.

We never tried to curse a classmate again, and though Astrid still sat next to me in school that winter, we never spoke of what we asked for on the mound—or the fact that by Monday morning, both of us knew exactly where Sara’s silver ring was buried.

prompt:
Young adult drama
Gone South
Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. A street musician's saxophone plays in the background as Taylor walks down a crowded street. 1000 words.
response:
### Gone South

The trucker who drove me down from Birmingham didn’t even slow to a complete stop on Canal Street. He just popped the passenger door, muttered something about not wanting to get mixed up in whatever kind of teenage sin I was running toward, and practically shoved me onto the asphalt. 

So here I am. Downtown New Orleans. Eight a.m., and the air already feels like breathing through a hot, wet washcloth wrapped around a bourbon bottle. 

Back in my dead-end Tennessee town, eight a.m. meant the shrill ring of first period and Mr. Henderson’s drone, or sitting in the guidance office listening to Mrs. Gable tell my mom on speakerphone about my *concerning behavioral patterns*. God, I hated that woman’s voice. Everything I ever did—bleaching my hair in the school bathroom, setting off a smoke bomb behind the bleachers, skipping pep rallies—was cataloged in her little manila folder as attention-seeking. And okay, maybe ninety percent of it was. When you’re trapped in a town consisting of three churches, a Dollar General, and a whole lot of aggressive nothing, you either rot from the inside out or you light a few fires just to watch the smoke.

Except two days ago, I hadn’t been lighting a fire for fun. Sitting at the kitchen table, staring at a chipped ceramic salt shaker while I told my parents who I actually am—that I wasn’t their daughter, that I hadn’t been for a long time, that my name was Taylor—that wasn’t a stunt. It was the truest thing I had ever let out of my mouth.

My dad’s silence had been worse than my mom’s crying. Then came the pastor’s phone number scribbled on a notepad. Then the talk about "programs." Forty-eight hours of suffocating panic later, I’d shoved three hoodies, two pairs of jeans, my binder, and eighty-six dollars of birthday cash into ajansport backpack and climbed out the bathroom window.

Now I’m walking down Royal Street, my shoulders aching from the straps of my pack, trying to look like I belong to the morning crowd of delivery guys, hungover tourists, and eccentric locals. Halfway down the block, an old guy in a sweat-stained fedora leans against a peeling wrought-iron lamppost, blowing into a tarnished tenor saxophone. The melody is slow, raspy, and aching—notes bending and dragging through the humid air like they’re too heavy to float. It follows me down the crowded sidewalk, threading through the clatter of café dishes and delivery trucks, making the lump in my throat swell until it hurts to swallow.

*You actually did it,* my brain whispers. One second I feel like a badass outlaw in an indie movie; the next, I’m sixteen, my stomach is cramping from hunger, and I realize nobody in the world knows where I am. Do my parents even care, or are they relieved the family embarrassment took out the trash themselves?

"You’re gonna get your pocket picked standing there like a deer in headlights, Tennessee."

I flinch, spinning around. 

Leaning against the brick wall of a closed tarot shop is a kid about my age—maybe seventeen. He’s got a buzzcut growing out in uneven bleached patches, a faded silver ring through his lower lip, and an oversized denim vest covered in frayed patches. A battered acoustic guitar case sits between his scuffed combat boots.

"How’d you know where I’m from?" I ask, instantly defensive, my hand dropping to my backpack zipper.

He nods toward my chest. I look down. Right. My faded *Chattanooga Lookouts* hoodie. Brilliant stealth work, Taylor.

"Dead giveaway," he says, flashing a crooked, gap-toothed grin that doesn’t quite reach his dark, restless eyes. "Plus, you’ve got that fresh-off-the-interstate stare. Like you’re waiting for the sky to fall on you. I’m Finch."

"Taylor," I say, keeping a solid five feet between us. "And I’m not waiting for anything."

"Sure you aren't. You got twenty bucks for breakfast, or are you broke-broke?"

"Why the hell would I buy you breakfast?"

"Because," Finch says, pushing off the bricks with a lazy stretch, "you clearly need to know where you can sit for three hours without the cops hassling you for loitering, and I know the spot. Consider a plate of beignets my consulting fee."

The saxophone down the street hits a low, gravelly run that vibrates right in my ribs. My stomach growls in answer. Look, I wasn’t born yesterday—Mom watched enough true crime to make anyone paranoid—but Finch weighs about a hundred and twenty pounds soaking wet, and it’s broad daylight. 

"Coffee and one order," I tell him. "And I hold my own wallet."

By noon, we’ve migrated from a corner bakery to the concrete steps leading down to the Mississippi River. The water is brown and wide and terrifyingly fast, churning past rust-streaked cargo ships. 

Finch eats like a stray dog who expects someone to snatch the plate away, tearing into the powdered-sugar dough while keeping one eye on the pedestrian path behind us. Every time a guy in uniform—even a security guard or a parking meter attendant—walks along the levee, Finch’s shoulders lock up and his thumb hooks into the strap of his guitar case.

"Who are you looking out for?" I ask, wiping powdered sugar off my chin.

Finch goes still for a half-second before forcing a shrug. "Nobody. Everybody. Quarter’s weird during the day. Night’s easier to blend in."

"You live down here?"

"Here and there. Crash at a squat over in the Marigny when the weather turns nasty." He pulls a loose thread on his denim vest, his gaze dropping to the muddy water. "Left Jacksonville four months ago."

"Bad home life?" I ask before I can stop myself.

A muscle jumps in his jaw. Reaching into his vest pocket, he pulls out a buzzing burner phone, stares at the cracked screen, and hits reject so hard his thumb goes white. "Let’s just say I owed some people favors I couldn't pay back, and my stepdad wasn’t exactly the forgiving type. Everybody down here is running from a ghost, Tennessee. What’s yours?"

I look down at my hands. Part of me wants to invent a story—tell him I stole a car or burned down a barn, the kind of delinquent legend that used to feel like armor back home. Instead, the truth slips out, quiet and raw.

"Told my parents they had the wrong kid," I say, my voice tight. "Told them my real name. They wanted to send me away to get fixed."

Finch stops picking at his vest. When he looks at me, the performing street-kid swagger drops away for a second. "Taylor suits you," he says simply. "Better than whatever they had on the birth certificate."

It’s such a small thing, said so casually, that my eyes sting. I have to blink hard at the river glare so he doesn’t see.

By late afternoon, the clouds roll in purple and heavy, and Finch takes me deeper into the Quarter to introduce me to "people who are good to know." That’s when the warm fuzzy feeling curdles right back into cold dread.

We stop in a narrow alley that smells like sour beer and frying oil, behind a T-shirt shop. A guy named Marcus—who has to be at least twenty-five, with a spiderweb tattoo on his elbow and eyes like flat black stones—is leaning against a dumpster. 

"Brought a new face?" Marcus asks, looking me up and down in a way that makes my skin crawl. Not the way guys back home looked at me when they thought I was a girl, just... sizing me up like a piece of scrap metal he might be able to sell by the pound.

"Just passing through," Finch says quickly, stepping half an inch in front of me. His voice is higher, tighter. "Taylor’s cool. Just needed to grab my stash from the locker."

"Storage ain't free, Finch. You're two days late on the cut from Decatur."

"I've got it," Finch lies—or maybe he doesn't, because he reaches into his pocket and pulls out a crumpled twenty. *My* twenty. The change from the bakery that I hadn't noticed him palming off the table when I went to grab napkins.

My heart slams against my ribs. I stare at the bill passing from Finch’s hand into Marcus’s palm. 

So that was it. I wasn’t a friend; I was a mark. Just a stupid, desperate hick from Tennessee who bought a sob story for the price of fried dough.

When we get back out to the street, the evening crowd is thickening, neon signs flickering to life in the humid dusk. Down at the corner, that same saxophone player—or another one playing the exact same mournful tune—is wailing into the twilight.

I stop dead on the sidewalk and yank my arm away when Finch reaches for my sleeve.

"You stole from me," I snap, my voice shaking with a toxic mix of rage and humiliation. "What was that back there? Who the hell is that guy?"

Finch looks around nervously, running a hand over his buzzed head. "Keep your voice down, okay? Look, I’m sorry about the twenty. If I didn't pay him today, he would’ve kept my bag, and my dead brother’s watch is in there."

"Oh, another great story!" I laugh, and it sounds jagged, almost hysterical. "Do you have a whole notebook of those for every idiot who gets off the highway?"

"I’m not lying!" Finch’s voice cracks, real fear flashing across his face. He digs into his vest and shoves a crumpled ten-dollar bill back into my chest. "Here. It’s half. It’s all I had left in my boot. And if I were trying to screw you over, Taylor, I would’ve left you in that alley. Marcus recruits kids who don’t have anywhere to sleep. They run packages for him, and when they get busted, he disappears. I stepped in front of you so he wouldn't ask your name."

I freeze, the crumpled ten-dollar bill crushed in my fist.

I look at Finch—at the dark circles under his eyes, the way his hands are trembling slightly, the burner phone buzzing again in his pocket that he refuses to answer. He’s a liar and a thief. He’s also seventeen, terrified, and the only person within five hundred miles who knows my real name.

Around us, tourists laugh with plastic hurricane glasses in their hands, oblivious. The saxophone music swells, brassy and sad and impossibly alive, wrapping around the wrought-iron balconies as the streetlights buzz on. 

Back in Tennessee, drama was a game I played because nothing ever happened. Here, the floor can drop out from under you in a heartbeat. I don’t trust Finch. I’d be an idiot to trust him. 

"You owe me ten bucks," I say, shoving his bill into my jeans pocket and adjusting the straps of my backpack. "And if you ever bring me near that guy again, I swear to God I’ll break your guitar over your head."

Finch lets out a breath that sounds half like a sigh, half like a laugh. "Deal, Tennessee. Come on. I know a porch in the Marigny where nobody checks locks."

I take a breath of the hot, strange air, and I follow him into the dark.

response:
The guy in the rusted-out Tacoma didn’t even pull all the way to the curb. He just leaned across the console, popped the passenger door over the roar of the I-10 overpass, and said, “End of the line, kid. Don’t leave trash in my cab.”

And just like that, I’m standing on Canal Street with forty-three dollars in crumpled singles, a JanSport backpack with a busted zipper, and the taste of stale gas-station coffee in my mouth. 

New Orleans hits you in the face like a wet, hot towel soaked in fryer grease, river mud, and old beer. Back in Pikeville, Tennessee, eight in the morning smells like pine needles and whatever cows died upwind. Here, the air feels chewed-up before it even gets to your lungs. I pull my phone out of my pocket. *12%.* No charger. In my thirty-minute hurricane of packing last night—shoving three hoodies, my binder, two pairs of jeans, and my birth certificate into my bag while my stepdad’s voice still rattled the drywall downstairs—I left the white cord plugged into the outlet beside my bed. Right next to the drywall dent where Pastor Rick’s Bible landed when I threw it.

Fourteen missed calls. Seven texts from Mom. The top notification banner just says: *Taylor please don’t do this you’re making a circus out of—*

I hit the side button before I can read the rest. *Making a circus.* That’s rich. When Mr. Henderson, the guidance counselor with the laminated tie and the halitosis, called home last month about my “concerning behavioral patterns”—specifically, setting off a smoke bomb behind the bleachers during the homecoming pep rally—that was me inventing drama because Pikeville is a sensory deprivation tank with a Dollar General. Coming out on Tuesday night wasn’t a stunt. I sat at the kitchen table with my palms sweating through my jeans and told them who I actually was, and Mom looked at me like I’d confessed to drowning the neighbor’s dog.

I switch the phone to Airplane Mode. Twelve percent has to last me until I figure out how not to die in Louisiana.

By noon, my boots are blistering my heels. I’ve wandered off the wide concrete stretch of Canal into the French Quarter, where the buildings look like wedding cakes left out in the rain—all peeling pastel paint and black iron balconies dripping with ferns. A brass band is blasting on the corner of Royal, the tuba player’s cheeks puffed out like a bullfrog’s. An old woman in a velvet turban tries to sell me a gris-gris bag from a folding table.

“You got a heavy shadow following you, baby,” she calls out, her voice like gravel in a blender. “Five dollars keeps the crossroads clean.”

“I’m broke,” I tell her, clutching my backpack straps tighter.

“Everybody broke ‘til the devil comes collecting,” she mutters, already looking past me at a couple in matching cruise-ship lanyards.

My stomach is doing this weird, hollow gymnastics routine. Half of me feels ten feet tall—like, holy shit, I actually did it, nobody here knows my deadname, nobody here went to Sunday school with my grandma. The other half is sixteen and terrified, waiting for a cop’s hand to clamp down on my shoulder, or worse, waiting to realize that nobody is actually coming to look for me at all.

That’s when I see the kid by the beignet stand on Decatur.

She’s about my age, maybe seventeen, wearing combat boots held together with silver duct tape and an oversized Metallica tee cropped with dull scissors. Her hair is buzzed on one side and dyed a faded, swampy green on the other. I’m watching her because she’s pulling off the cleanest sleight-of-hand I’ve ever seen: while a guy in khaki shorts takes a selfie with his powdered-sugar plate, she slides a twenty right out of the side pocket of his cargo shorts without breaking stride.

Then she looks up and catches me staring.

I freeze. Instead of bolting, she walks right over to the wrought-iron fence where I’m leaning, pulls a pack of crushed menthols from her waistband, and squints at me through the midday glare.

“You a narc, or do you always look like a deer in a bass pro shop?” she asks.

“Neither,” I say, trying to make my voice drop an octave so it doesn’t crack. “Nice fingers, though.”

She smirks, a flash of a chipped canine tooth. “I’m Jude. And you’re fresh off a Greyhound. Or a thumb, judging by the grease smudge on your elbow.”

“Taylor,” I say. “It was a Tacoma.”

“Where from?”

“Tennessee.”

Jude lets out a low whistle. “Long way to run. Come on, walk with me before Cargo Shorts checks his pockets. You look like you haven’t eaten since Mississippi.”

I know I shouldn’t follow a literal pickpocket down an alley that smells like boiled crawfish and bleach, especially when I don’t know the rules of this city. Back home, you know exactly who the bastards are—they wear varsity jackets or sit in the front pew. Here, everyone’s smiling and everyone’s hustling.

We end up sitting on the concrete steps by the riverfront, watching a massive rusted freighter push through the brown water of the Mississippi. Jude splits a paper bag of warm, stolen-money beignets with me. Powdered sugar gets all over my black hoodie, and I don’t even care.

“So what was it?” Jude asks, swinging her duct-taped boots over the edge. “Cops? Rehab? Parents find your stash?”

“Parents found out I’m not their daughter,” I say, staring at the muddy wake of the ship. Saying it out loud to a stranger makes my throat tighten up all over again.

Jude pauses with a piece of fried dough halfway to her mouth. For a second, the tough-kid posture drops off her shoulders. “Yeah. Okay. That’s a real one. Mine was my uncle in Baton Rouge. People think running away is some cinematic bullshit until you’re sleeping under a bridge by the parish line.”

As she reaches into her pocket for her lighter, the sleeve of her oversized shirt rides up. There’s a plastic hospital wristband still loops-tight around her left wrist, the printed barcode rubbed mostly gray, and a dark, yellowing bruise shaped like thumbprints just above her elbow. When she sees me looking, she yanks the袖 down fast, her jaw setting hard. 

A guy in a pristine white linen shirt and aviator sunglasses strolls past the boardwalk railing, slowing down just enough to give Jude a long, familiar look.

“Jude,” the guy says, his voice smooth and syrupy. “Thought you were checking in with Marcus at four.”

Jude’s whole body goes rigid beside me. “Tell Marcus I got the money. I’ll be on Esplanade tonight.”

The guy’s eyes flick over to me beneath the aviators, sizing up my JanSport, my boots, the fresh runaway panic probably radiating off my skin. “Who’s your friend? Looking for a place to crash?”

“Nobody,” Jude snaps, standing up so fast the paper bag flutters into the weeds. “Keep walking, Trey.”

Trey just smiles like he’s got all the time in the world and strolls off toward the jazz pavilion.

My heart is hammering against my ribs. “Who the hell is Marcus?”

Jude won’t look at me. Her hands are shaking as she stuffs the menthols back into her jeans. “Someone you stay away from if you’ve got half a brain cell, Tennessee.”

By the time the sun starts sinking behind the bridge, turning the sky the color of a fresh bruise, the temperature drops ten degrees. Neon signs flicker on down Bourbon Street, buzzing like angry hornets. I pull my phone out one last time, thumbing Airplane Mode off just for a second. *12%* blinks down to *11%.* One new voicemail from Mom. I don’t listen to it, just stare at the glowing rectangle until the screen times out.

“There’s an abandoned laundry mat off St. Claude,” Jude says quietly, adjusting her backpack. The streetlight catches the dark rings under her eyes, making her look about twelve and forty at the same time. “Roof doesn’t leak unless it’s a hurricane, and Marcus’s guys don’t know about it. You can crash there tonight. Or you can try the youth shelter on Magazine, if you don’t mind them calling your folks after seventy-two hours.”

I look down the street toward the Quarter, where drunken tourists are already screaming over a cover band, then back at Jude, who’s hiding hospital bracelets and owes stolen twenties to men in linen shirts. I don’t know if she’s saving my ass or leading me into a trap. I don’t know if I’m brave or just the dumbest kid to ever cross state lines.

“Lead the way,” I say, shoving my dead-weight phone deep into my pocket, and step off the curb into the dark.

response:
The semi-truck’s air brakes hiss like a pissed-off copperhead, and then the door is swinging open and I’m being told that *this is the end of the line, kid, I don't go past Elysian Fields.* 

My boots hit the cracked asphalt of New Orleans at 7:14 a.m. The air here doesn't just sit on you; it wraps around your throat like a wet flannel shirt. It smells like Chicory coffee, river mud, and three hundred years of bad decisions. 

I hike my backpack up. Five seconds later, the frayed nylon of the left strap loses its grip on my collarbone and slides right down to the crook of my elbow. Again. I’d packed the bag in thirty flat minutes last night—shoving in two hoodies, four pairs of underwear, my binder, a charger, and the crumpled $142 from my bottom sock drawer while my dad’s voice still vibrated through the floorboards downstairs. I hadn’t noticed the plastic buckle was cracked until I was already two miles down Highway 41 with my thumb out.

Now I’m standing on the edge of the French Quarter, and the adrenaline that carried me across the state lines of Alabama and Mississippi is curdling into something cold and sour in my stomach. 

*Concerning behavioral patterns.* That’s what Mr. Gable, the guidance counselor with the coffee-stained teeth, had called it last month when I set off the fire alarm during fourth-period algebra just to watch everyone stand in the rain. And okay, fair. In Pikeville, Tennessee, you either rot from the inside out or you strike a match just to see the dark blink. Mom had cried on the phone. Dad had taken my door off its hinges.

Only, two nights ago at the dinner table, over lukewarm meatloaf, I didn't strike a match for the hell of it. I told them the truth. I told them my name was Taylor—not the girl’s name on my birth certificate—and that I wasn’t going back into that box even if they nailed it shut. 

Mom didn't cry that time. She went stone-still and looked at me like I was a stranger who’d broken into her house and murdered her daughter. Dad reached for his belt, then his Bible, and I didn't wait to see which one won out. 

I shove the backpack strap back onto my shoulder. It slips immediately. *Goddammit.*

"You're gonna dislocate your arm doing that little chicken-wing dance, you know."

I spin around, my heart slamming against my ribs. A guy—maybe seventeen, maybe a rough fifteen—is sitting on an overturned milk crate beside a boarded-up jazz club. He’s wearing a faded Metallica tee with the sleeves ripped off, and a silver safety pin is shoved through the cartilage of his left ear. He’s peeling an orange with a pocketknife that looks about an inch past legal.

"I'm fine," I snap, yanking the strap up so hard the seam groans. "Just looking for a bathroom."

"Bathroom's for paying customers across the whole Quarter, Tennessee." He flicks a piece of orange rind into the gutter. 

I freeze. "How do you know where I'm from?"

He points the tip of the knife at my chest. For a second I think I’m being mugged before breakfast, and then I realize he’s pointing at my faded Dollywood hoodie. Right. Genius move, Taylor. Real incognito.

"I'm Rook," he says, popping an orange segment into his mouth. "And you got that Fresh Off the Greyhound look, except the Greyhound station's over on Poydras, which means you hitched. Give me the bag."

"Like hell I will." I step back, clutching the good strap. Every survival instinct I have is screaming. I don't know this kid. I don't know if he has three friends waiting down the alley to roll me for my hundred bucks. Back home, I knew every bastard within twenty miles and exactly what kind of mean they were. Here, the street signs are in French and the wrought-iron balconies hang over the sidewalks like cages.

Rook rolls his eyes, reaches into the cargo pocket of his shorts, and tosses something small and metallic at my feet. A heavy-duty safety pin, two inches long, the kind they use on laundry bags. 

"Pin the strap above the buckle," he says, leaning back against the brick wall. "Or keep doing thefunky chicken down Decatur. Doesn't matter to me."

I stare at the pin on the pavement, then at him. Slowly, keeping my eyes locked on his knife, I crouch down and pick it up. By noon, the heat is a physical weight, pressing down between my shoulder blades. The safety pin is holding—mostly—though every twenty minutes the fabric stretches and the bag sags sideways again, digging into my neck. I’m walking three paces behind Rook, even though I told him twice I didn't want company. 

He knows where the water fountains work near Jackson Square, and he knows which bakery on Chartres throws out the day-old croissants at eleven if you don't act like a creep about it. While we eat flaky, slightly squashed pastry on the levee watching a rust-bellied barge push up the Mississippi, the quiet between us gets loud.

"So what'd you do?" I ask, wiping crumbs off my chin. "Burn down a church?"

Rook’s jaw tightens. His eyes flick toward the river, then down to his knuckles, which are scarred over with old, pale crescents. For a second, the cocky street-rat act drops right off his face, and he looks terrified. Before I can look closer, a bruised-blue pickup truck rumbles past on the road behind us. Rook flinches so hard he drops his half-eaten croissant into the dirt, his body curling inward until the truck rounds the corner.

"Just didn't fit the family portrait," he mutters, his voice flat and sudden as a slammed door. He pulls his knees up, hiding the inside of his left wrist where a faded plastic hospital band—or maybe a juvenile detention band, the kind with the bar code—peeks out from under three braided leather bracelets. "People who say they want to help you out here? The ones with the vans and the free meal tickets near the bridge? Don't get in the van, Taylor. Especially not a guy named Marcus. He spots kids with heavy bags and nowhere to sleep."

A cold prickle runs down my spine, right under my damp shirt. "You know him?"

"I know enough," Rook says darkly, standing up and brushing off his jeans. "Sun's going down in four hours. This city changes teeth after dark."

By late afternoon, we’re cutting through an alley that smells of stale beer and fried oysters when an older guy in a linen shirt steps out from a service doorway. He’s got a warm, practiced smile that doesn't reach his eyes. 

"Hey, Rook," the guy says smoothly, his gaze sliding off Rook and landing squarely on me—on my overstuffed pack, my dusty boots, my raw, sunburned face. "Didn't think I'd see you around this block again. Who's your friend? You kids look like you could use a shower and some AC."

Rook goes rigid beside me. I can hear his breathing go shallow. 

*Marcus.*

I look at Marcus’s clean shirt and his easy smile, and then I look at Rook, who is one second away from bolting and leaving me here. Back home, I was the girl—the *boy*, the *person*, whatever I am—who threw rocks at hornets' nests just to feel my heart beat. And maybe I’m still crazy, because instead of backing down, all the rage from the last forty-eight hours—my dad’s red face, my mom’s dead eyes, the sheer terror of having nowhere to go—rises up into my throat like gasoline.

I step halfway in front of Rook and reach into my pocket, wrapping my fist around my phone charger so the bulk of the adapter pushes against the fabric like the butt of something heavy. 

"My uncle's a state trooper two blocks back at the precinct on Royal," I lie, my voice steady and loud enough to echo off the wet brick. "We're meeting him in three minutes. He's real particular about who talks to me."

Marcus’s smile thins out. He looks at my pocket, then at my eyes—which I know for a fact look half-feral right now—and raises his hands, palms out. "Easy, kid. Just being neighborly."

He ducks back into the traffic on Royal Street and disappears.

For ten seconds, neither of us moves. A streetcar clangs somewhere in the distance. The safety pin on my backpack finally gives up the ghost, popping open and jabbing me through my shirt as the left strap slithers down my arm again. 

"Your uncle's a trooper?" Rook breathes, staring at me like I’ve grown a second head.

"My uncle sells above-ground pools in Chattanooga," I say, my hands finally starting to shake as I try to refasten the bent pin with numb fingers. A laugh bubbles up in my chest—hysterical, ragged, and entirely too loud—right alongside the sudden, burning urge to cry. I am sixteen years old. My parents don't want me. I have a hundred and forty-two dollars and a broken bag in a city that wants to eat me alive. 

Rook watches me struggle with the strap. Slowly, he reaches out, takes the mangled safety pin from my trembling fingers, and threads it back through the heavy nylon twice, locking it shut. He doesn't ask why I left Tennessee, and I don't ask what he's running from in that blue pickup truck. 

"Come on, Dollywood," Rook says, nodding toward the glow of the neon signs flickering to life down the street. "I know a roof over on Chartres where the lock's busted. You can take first watch."

I hitch the bag up onto my shoulder. It holds—for now. I take a breath of the heavy, river-soaked air, and I follow him into the dark.

The Morska Conspiracy
